VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced January 19, 2021, would make numerous changes to voter registration and absentee voting law, create an elections crime hotline, and makes changes to ballot record preservation and chains of custody. Specifically, the bill would:

  • End automatic registration when people apply for their permanent fund dividend.
  • Require election officials to match a voter's signature on the absentee ballot envelope with their signature in their registration record. If the signature does not match, the ballot cannot be counted. Existing law requires that the voter's signature on the ballot envelope be notarized or, if a notary is not reasonably available, witnessed.
  • Prohibit voting by fax in state elections. Existing law allows this practice.
  • Criminalize as a misdemeanor possessing another's ballot unless the voter is the person's family member or caregiver, postal worker, or election worker performing official duties. Existing law does not have an explicit prohibition on third-party return of an absentee ballot.
  • Expand the felony of unlawful interference with an election by adding "intentionally opens or tampers with a sealed election ballot, certificate, or package of ballots without express authorization from the director" as a separate way of committing the offense.
  • Create a toll-free election offense hotline to receive telephone calls reporting election offenses. The toll-free hotline must be publicized and the public encouraged to provide information to the election division. The hotline must be continuously staffed while an absentee voting station is open, an early voting location is open, and for 24 hours after the polls open on election day. From then until all election results are certified, an election official must be continuously available to respond to calls. The hotline number must be on voting machines, ballot envelopes, and other election materials to provide maximum public notice of it.

  • Require the director to issue regulations creating a system to account for each used and unused ballot and paper record of an electronically generated ballot through a redundant, secure, and sealed system that tracks the location and entity that has custody of a ballot or record from the time the ballot is printed or paper record produced, until the applicable election is certified. The Division of Elections would be required to continually update the system adopted under this section to ensure that state election practices and procedures are consistent with the best practices and procedures.

Last Updated March 8, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 8, 2021, would allow people who are 16 or 17 years old to pre-register to vote. The Division of Elections would fully register them 90 days before their 18th birthday, but they would not be able to vote until they became 18.

Last Updated January 14, 2021

This omnibus bill, as amended by committee on May 15, 2022, would make voter registration continuous, including creating same day registration during early voting and on Election Day. In addition, the bill would eliminate the witness requirement to cast an absentee ballot, create a permanent absentee voter list, create a cure process for absentee ballots, provide prepaid postage on absentee ballots, and start processing absentee ballots earlier. The bill also requires the state to allow voters to choose to receive election materials in any language the state is required to offer them under federal law, and requires the Division of Elections to issue myriad regulations for list maintenance and election security. Finally, the bill makes other, smaller changes, and includes some provisions that the Voting Rights Lab does not track.

This bill would change laws relating to registering to vote by creating same day registration during early and election day voting, eliminating the registration deadline, allowing people to register when they electronically apply for an absentee ballot, and allow people to choose to receive election materials in a non-English language when they register to vote. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Allow voters to register on any day, including during early voting and on Election Day, and vote. People who register within 30 days of the election would be required to attest that they have been, or will have been, resident in the state and the house district in which they are voting for at least 30 days by the election, and show documentary proof of residency. In addition, people who register within 30 days of the election would be required to cast an in-person absentee ballot, or a special needs ballot, or a questioned ballot. The ballot envelope would constitute the voter registration application, and would allow a new registrant to affiliate with a political party, if they wished. Under existing law, voters may only vote in an election that occurs 30 or more days after they register, except that people may register and then immediately vote during a presidential election, for the offices of President and Vice President only.
  • Allow people to register to vote using an electronic absentee ballot application. Existing law allows paper absentee ballot applications to be used to register to vote, but not electronic ones. In addition, the paper absentee ballot application would be modified to allow a voter to affiliate with a party while registering, if they wish.

  • Allow people to indicate, as part of registering to vote, a non-English language for election materials, provided the language is one the state is required to offer under federal law. Existing voter registration forms do not offer this option.

    This bill would change laws relating to absentee voting (voting by mail) by allowing voters to sign their ballot certificates without a witness, verifying ballots by matching the voter's signature to one on file, creating a cure process to address signature issues, creating comprehensive ballot tracking, allowing voters to request non-English ballots, allowing voters to join a list to receive mail ballots automatically, and limiting absentee ballot application distribution. Specifically, the bill would:


  • Eliminate existing law's requirement that a voter's absentee ballot certificate signature be notarized or witnessed, and replace it with signature matching. Absentee ballots that are voted in-person with an elections official would not go through signature matching. The ID presented to the official to receive the ballot would be considered sufficient.
  • Require the Director of the Division to create a free, mobile-optimized mail ballot tracking system. The Division currently offers a limited ballot tracking service on its website. The bill would require the system to allow a voter to:
    • confirm the voter's ballot has been mailed by the Division.
    • track the date of the ballot's delivery to the voter.
    • confirm the Division's receipt of the voter's ballot.
    • determine whether their ballot's certificate has been reviewed.
    • determine whether their ballot has been counted.
    • determine why their ballot did not count, if it was rejected.
    • learn how to cure an issue with their ballot so that it will count, if possible.
  • Create a cure process. Existing law does not offer a cure process. The cure process would:
    • Require the Director of the Division of Elections to give a voter notice if the voter did not sign their ballot certificate, the voter's signature is determined not to match one in the voter's record, the voter's record does not include a signature, or if the voter provided insufficient identification. The notice would explain the issue and provide the voter a form to sign and return with a copy of ID sufficient to vote in person. The cure form would also be available on the Director's website.
    • Require the Director to give notice by phone, text and email, beginning within 24 hours of identifying the deficiency, if the voter's contact information is on file. The Director would give notice by first class mail within 48 hours of identifying the deficiency, but not more than five days after Election Day. Under existing law, if a ballot is postmarked on or before Election Day, it is timely if received by the 10th day after Election Day. Thus timely ballots with errors may not trigger notice by mail, and those voters may not have a phone number or email on file with the Director.
    • Require a voter who receives notice to return the form with a copy of ID sufficient to vote in person within 14 days after Election Day. If the voter returns the form and indicates they did not vote by mail, the ballot will not be counted, and the Director will refer the ballot signature and the voter's record signature to the attorney general for investigation.
    • Require the Division, after a voter cures a ballot envelope signature issue, to add the cure signature to the voter's record.
  • Require election officials to begin reviewing absentee ballot envelopes and voter certificates 10 days before election day, and allow election officials to begin sooner. Existing law requires absentee ballot processing to start seven days before ED. Earlier processing facilitates cure by identifying issues sooner.
  • Create a permanent absentee voter list available to all voters. Joining the list would become an option on the absentee ballot application form. A voter would remain on the list unless their ballot is returned as undeliverable or the voter fails to vote an absentee ballot for four years.
  • Allow a person to request an absentee ballot in any of the languages the state is required to offer by federal law, if they make the request when registering to vote or at least 45 days before election.
  • Require the government to pay the postage for returning an absentee ballot. Under existing law, postage is the voter's responsibility. Relatedly, the bill amends an existing crime so that paying the voter's postage does not commit the crime.
  • Allow an absentee ballot received by mail after Election Day that lacks a postmark to nonetheless count if the ballot envelope has a tracking bar code that documents the ballot was mailed on or before Election Day.
  • Prohibit the Division from mailing an absentee ballot application to a voter, unless the voter requests the application first. In addition, an application may not be distributed if it is partially filled out for a voter, the application must display who sent the application, and display on the outside of the envelope mailing it to the voter that is an application only, not a ballot.

  • Change the rules that allow the Division to conduct an election as a mail ballot election, sending all voters a ballot in the mail. Under the bill, the Division could conduct a mail ballot election if:

    • in an unincorporated community of 750 people or fewer, the Director determines that, because of an inability to hire election workers, facilitating organized in-person voting is unreasonable.
    • in an area affected by or threatened by a disaster when the Governor has issued a disaster declaration for certain reasons, including the outbreak of a disease or a credible threat of an imminent outbreak of disease.
    • it is held at a time other than when the general, primary, or municipal election is held. Of these three bases to hold a mail ballot election, existing law only includes this third basis. The other two would be new.

    This bill would change in-person voting by:


  • Requiring language assistance at voting locations for all languages required by federal law, and requiring related signage. Existing law has no comparable requirement.
  • Preventing early voting stations from being changed unless the location becomes unavailable, or is no longer appropriate to use, and the Director makes that determination public, in writing. Existing law has no comparable requirement.
  • Requiring the Director to appoint one or more registration officials to serve at each early voting location, whenever the location is open. Under existing law, registration is generally not available at voting locations.
  • Providing that, if a person appears at an early voting location but the election worker cannot verify their identity and residency, the voter would cast an in-person absentee ballot rather than vote early election-day style.
  • If possible, requiring voters be sent two written notices, instead of one required by existing law, when their election precinct or polling place changes.
  • Changing rules relating to photographing ballots. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Expanding an existing violation relating to conduct within 200 feet of the entrance of a polling place to prohibit physically displaying a photo, video, or other image of the person's or another person's marked ballot in an attempt to persuade a person to vote for or against a candidate, proposition, or question. The existing violation generally prohibits an attempt to persuade a person to vote for or against a candidate, proposition, or question.
    • Allowing voters to share ballot selfies or other images of their ballot in all other situations.
  • Requiring people voting a questioned ballot to sign a declaration attesting that the person is a qualified voter, is not disqualified, has not voted at the same election, and understands that a false statement on the declaration may subject the person to prosecution.
  • Setting minimum election worker pay. The election code does not currently specify a minimum wage.

  • Requiring poll watcher certificates be signed by the chairperson of the organization that appointed them. Existing law merely requires written proof of the appointment.

    This bill would create new election crimes and change alleged crime reporting by:


  • Creating a new way to commit the misdemeanor of unlawful interference with voting in the second degree, by prohibiting paying a person to collect and return someone else's ballot. The bill would create an exception to allow someone to provide a person who collects a voter's ballot with any of these:
    • materials having a nominal value bearing the name, likeness, or other identification of a candidate, political party, political group, party district committee, or organization, or stating a position on a ballot proposition or question.
    • food and refreshments provided incidental to an activity that is nonpartisan in nature and directed at encouraging persons to vote, or incidental to a gathering in support of or in opposition to a candidate, political party, political group, party district committee, organization, or ballot question or proposition.
    • care of the person's dependents in connection with the absence of the person from home for the purpose of collecting a ballot.
  • Creating new ways to commit the felony of unlawful interference in an election. Specifically, a person would commit the felony if they:
    • intentionally open or tamper with a signed ballot certificate, sealed ballot envelope, or package of ballots without express authorization from the Director of the Division, or
    • intentionally breach, hack, alter, or tamper with election machinery, including a tabulator, a program, a system, a server, or software used to verify identity, count or tabulate, or manage or control an election function.
  • Creating a new felony, called election fraud, that requires someone to commit unlawful interference in an election and change the outcome of the election.
  • Creating a new way to commit the crime of election official misconduct in the first degree, by knowingly disclosing, sharing, or reporting results, returns or any confidential election data with someone who is not an election official before the polls close on Election Day.

  • Requiring the Division to establish a toll-free election offense hotline to receive reports of election offenses under this chapter. The availability of the toll-free hotline would be publicized, and the public encouraged to report voter misconduct or other election offenses.

    This bill would change voter registration list maintenance by:


  • Requiring the Division of Elections to issue voter registration list maintenance regulations. These regulations would be required to:

    • Provide for review of the voter registration list for data breaches, the number of registered voters compared to eligible voters, and the names of deceased voters, persons convicted of a felony involving moral turpitude, persons not qualified to vote, and persons registered to vote in another state. The regulations would be required to specify records and databases for use in reviewing the master register.
    • Apply best practices to improve identity matching when comparing voter registration lists with the records and databases used to review the master register. The director would be required to develop a written maintenance schedule and guideline manual for the system and report on the system to the Senate Secretary and the Chief Clerk of the House of Representatives on or before the first day of the first regular session of each legislature.
    • Include a process to allow a voter to cancel their registration in person before an election official or electronically. The director of the Division would be required to prominently display related instructions at each polling place and on the Division's website.

    This bill includes provisions aimed at election and ballot security that the Voting Rights Lab does not track in detail. Specifically, the bill would:


  • Create risk-limiting audits.
  • Declare that it is Alaska's policy to reduce voting fraud using reasonable and affordable tools and technology.
  • Require the Division to issue ballot security regulations to:
    • Create a chain of custody that would account for the original of each used an unused ballot, absentee ballot certificate and envelope, and the paper record of an electronic ballot.
    • Void all unused ballots, spoiled ballots, and unopened packs of ballots without mutilating or destroying their "forensic integrity", following the closing of the polls.
    • Require ballots, including electronic ballots, to have a watermark or other security identifier.
    • Create a cybersecurity program.
  • Require certain security procedures relating to precinct ballot tabulators and for the state to use open-source software for electronic voting machines, if the software meets certain conditions and is available.
  • Require the Director of the Division of Elections to permit the inspection of election materials upon call by the Congress, the state legislature, or a court of competent jurisdiction. Existing law authorizes, but does not require, allowing such inspection.

  • Require the Division to give the Legislature a report by November 1, 2023 recommending how options for early voting may be expanded in rural communities and low income neighborhoods.

Last Updated November 14, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 18, 2021, would create a new civil enforcement structure for election laws other than campaign finance law. Individual citizens would be allowed to file complaints with the Division of Elections, which if substantiated would be referred to the attorney general for further action. The attorney general would also be authorized to initiate investigations. Regardless of how initiated, investigations could result in enforcement lawsuits or other civil enforcement actions by the attorney general to ensure election laws are followed.

Last Updated August 3, 2021

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 18, 2021, would change the information required on an absentee ballot application and ballot certificate, and would allow the state division of elections to choose to conduct a mail ballot election of any type in a jurisdiction with 750 or fewer people. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require voters applying for an absentee ballot to include two identifiers on the application, one of which must be their date of birth. Under existing law, voters applying for an absentee ballot are required to provide their date of birth and either their Social Security number or their driver's license/state ID number, unless they have neither. In that case, the voter may affirm not having either number. Although the bill does not address the existing application, it appears the intent is to eliminate a way to apply for an absentee ballot by affirming the lack of an identifier.
  • Require voters to include both identifiers on the absentee ballot voter's certificate when completing the ballot. Under existing law, when a person completes their ballot, their signature must be witnessed, and failing to properly complete the voter's certificate results in ballot rejection. This bill would both require voters to add their identifiers to their ballot certificates and require election officials to reject any ballots that lacked the identifiers on the certificates.

  • Allow the state division of elections to conduct any election in a community of 750 people or less by mail. Existing law only allows the division to conduct certain election types by mail, and does not basis the option on population.

Last Updated March 9, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 17, 2021, would:

  • Require all elections for state offices, state questions, and certain local offices or local question elections conducted by the state to be held as mail ballot elections. Under existing law, only certain local elections may be conducted by mail. The bill would create a mail ballot election process that:
    • requires ballots to be mailed to voters 29 days before the election unless they are UOCAVA voters, in which case federal deadlines would apply. Replacement ballots would be available to voters who need them.
    • allows voters to complete and return the ballot without involving a notary or witness. Existing law requires voters completing mail ballots to be witnessed. Instead, ballots would be verified by signature matching.
    • requires vote centers and drop boxes to be available for the 10 days before election day. Under existing law, the early voting period begins 15 days before Election Day, but voting is not required to be offered on each day. Drop boxes are allowed but not required, and the limited mail ballot elections currently allowed do not need to offer vote centers. However, in-person absentee voting must be offered.
    • allows third parties of the voter's choosing to return the voter's ballot, except that it would forbid using an intermediary who is paid by or who volunteers for a political party, political group, or business or organization to provide that service.
    • requires mail ballot processing and counting begin at least ten days before the election, at "ballot tabulation centers", which can be part of vote centers.
    • creates a cure process that requires notice to the voter within 48 hours of discovering the issue and not later than two days after the election, and gives the voter until 14 days after the election to cure.
  • Create ballot tracking that allows voters to know if their ballot has been mailed to them, if their returned ballot has been received and counted, and if not counted, why, and what steps the voter may take to have it counted, if any. The voter must also be able to request a replacement ballot using the system. The bill further requires that the system be optimized for mobile devices. Under existing law tracking is not required, but the Division of Elections voluntarily provides a tracking service. Nonetheless, that system is a more rudimentary tracking system than the bill would require.
  • Revise voter registration materials to allow voters to request ballots and other election materials in another available language when registering or re-registering to vote, and to provide an email, phone number, or both.

  • Add to the existing felony of unlawful interference with an election to punish a person who:

    • intentionally alters or destroys a ballot cast at an election or the returns of an election.
    • intentionally places a fraudulent ballot among official ballots.
    • falsely writes anything purporting to be written by an elections official in the performance of duties on the ballot.
    • takes a ballot, tampers with a ballot drop box, or otherwise intentionally attempts to hinder or delay the return of a vote-by-mail ballot to the division.
    • manufactures or knowingly uses a fraudulent return envelope.
    • sells, makes an offer with the intent to sell, purchases, or makes an offer with the intent to purchase, for money or other valuable consideration, an official ballot, replacement ballot, or return envelope.

Last Updated October 19, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on April 28, 2021, would make significant changes to voter registration, voter registration list maintenance, in-person and absentee voting, ballot verification, and other aspects of election law. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Change voter registration by:
    • allowing a person who is registering to vote in-person to show a Tribal ID, and removing the option to show a hunting or fishing license. Existing law itemizes acceptable ID types, and although Tribal ID is not an explicit option, any current and valid photo ID is.
    • making a parallel change to acceptable ID types for a person who is registering to vote by mail and who does not have a driver's license, state ID, or Social Security number.
    • requiring the director of the Division of Elections to issue regulations for voter registration. Those regulations much include provisions to use blockchain technology to protect election data and to develop a voter authentication system that assigns digital multi-factor authentication security identifiers to all registered voters, ensures a qualitative voter authentication method for voters voting at a location other than a polling place, and includes an alternative authentication process for voters unable to use digital multi-factor authentication. However, the bill does not define "digital multi-factor authentication" and does not make clear what steps a voter must take, or what information a voter must provide, to use the system. Similarly, the bill does not explain who is unable to use the system.
    • providing that when a person successfully registers to vote, the director or election supervisor must explain to a newly registered voter the process for obtaining the voter's digital multi-factor authentication security identifiers and the process for a voter unable to use digital multi-factor authentication.
    • providing that a voter's digital multi-factor authentication security identifiers are confidential, not part of the publicly available registration record.
    • requiring the director to develop a process to enable a voter to cancel their registration, and to prominently display instructions for a voter to cancel the voter's registration on every ballot envelope and at every polling location.
  • Revise the voter registration list maintenance processes by:
    • requiring the Division of Elections to use nationally recognized best practices and develop a system of protocols to review voter registration records and update the master register. The protocols must include reviews for deceased voters, people who have become disenfranchised, people who are ineligible, and persons registered to vote in another state. In addition, the protocols must address whether the number of registered voters on the master register exceeds the number of eligible voters in the state, and voter registration information data breaches.
    • mandating the review of available records and databases, which the bill says should include United States Postal Service forwarding databases, the Electronic Registration Information Center, the Interstate Voter Registration Crosscheck Program, motor vehicle records, Department of Corrections records, property and sales tax records, Social Security Administration databases, United States Department of Homeland Security records, jury duty records, Help America Vote Act records, and National Change of Address records.
    • performing an audit of the master registration list every two years, in consultation with an external, nationally recognized subject-matter expert, and report on the results by February 1 of each year of a general election. The bill would require the first audit to be completed and reported within 150 days after January 1, 2022, which is when most of the bill takes effect.
  • Change in-person voting by:
    • adding Tribal ID to the acceptable forms of in-person voting ID.
    • requiring in-person voters who lack a photo ID to supply one of the non-photo IDs existing law authorizes, and the voter's digital multi-factor authentication security identifiers, unless the voter is unable to use digital multi-factor authentication.
    • allowing people to challenge in-person voters who received an absentee ballot and force them to sign an affidavit before voting. False statements on such an affidavit would be punishable as a felony, rather than a misdemeanor as under existing law.
    • requiring people who complete in-person absentee early ballots to provide the voter's digital multi-factor authentication security identifiers on the ballot envelope unless they are unable to use such identifiers.
    • requiring people who complete questioned (provisional) ballots to provide the voter's digital multi-factor authentication security identifiers on the ballot envelope unless they are unable to use such identifiers.
    • requiring the software used for electronically generated ballots to be open source and created in the United States by American-owned companies using routers and servers in the United States and best-practice cyber security, and requiring the director to provide for digital multi-factor authentication to ensure sufficient chain-of-custody protections during electronic voting.
    • reducing the maximum number of ballots the board may issue to a voter who has spoiled their ballot, from a total of three ballots to two.
  • Change applying for an absentee ballot by:
    • restricting who may send voters absentee ballot applications. Under the bill, non-political third parties would be effectively prohibited from sending absentee ballot applications to voters. The Division of Elections, official candidates, recognized political parties, and ballot measure sponsors would be the only entities allowed to send them.
    • authorizing emailed applications
    • requiring voters to provide digital multi-factor security identifiers on their application, unless the voter is unable to use them.
    • changing the deadline to apply for an absentee ballot to 14 days before the election, instead of ten days before as existing law provides.
    • allowing a voter to request ballots for four years with a single application by checking a box on the application form. Under existing law, a voter may apply for all ballots in a calendar year.
  • Change completing and returning absentee ballots (including by electronic return) by:
    • requiring people who cannot reasonably access a notary or other official authorized to witness them complete the ballot to attest to that fact, and require their alternative witness to similarly attest as part of their witnessing the ballot.
    • requiring voters and their witnesses to legibly print their name, physical address, mailing address, and digital or telephone contact information on the space provided on the voter's certificate.
    • requiring voters to include their digital multi-factor authentication security identifiers, unless they are unable to use digital multi-factor authentication.
    • expanding a misdemeanor to criminalize third-party ballot return unless the voter expressly requested the assistance, the person did not solicit the ballot, and the person did not collect more than six ballots in a single election.
  • Change ballot verification by:
    • requiring that official ballots include a watermark, seal, or other identifier, and requiring the rejection of ballots lacking it. The director is authorized to promulgate a regulation to create an exception to this general rule.
    • rejecting ballots that are not signed by a notary or other authorized official unless the ballot includes a voter's certificate providing the attestation by the voter and witness that such officials were not reasonably available.
    • rejecting as untimely ballots mailed on or before Election Day but received later than the close of business on the seventh day after the election. Existing law allows ballots to be received as late as the tenth day after the election if the ballots were timely mailed.
    • rejecting ballots (including absentee and questioned (provisional) ballots) lacking digital multi-factor identifiers when the voter is able to use them.
    • creating a cure process for rejected absentee and questioned ballots. Immediately after rejecting an absentee ballot, the director would be required to make a reasonable effort to contact the voter and inform them how they may cure their ballot. The voter would have until 5 p.m. on the third day after Election Day to cure the ballot. Because of this deadline and the timeframe in which ballots may be timely, not all voters casting timely ballots will have an opportunity to cure them.
    • expanding the existing felony of unlawful interference in an election to punish intentionally opening or tampering with a sealed absentee ballot certificate, absentee ballot envelope, or package of ballots without express authorization from the director, or intentionally breaching, hacking, altering, or tampering with election machinery, including a tabulator machine, a program, a system, a server, or software used to verify identity, count, or tabulate, or manage or control any election function. In addition, the bill would create a new felony to punish someone who commits unlawful interference in an election and causes the outcome of the election to change.
  • Expand the felony of election official misconduct in the first degree to punish an official who knowingly discloses, shares, or reports, to a person who is not an election official, election results, returns, or any confidential election data before the polls close on Election Day.
  • Require the director to create a comprehensive ballot chain of custody regime meeting multiple specifications, and prevent the director and lieutenant governor from certifying the results of an election until each original ballot and paper record is accounted for, or, if an accounting irregularity cannot be reconciled, until the lieutenant governor refers the irregularity to the attorney general, informs affected candidates and sponsors, the president of the senate, and the speaker of the house of representatives, and provides public notice of the irregularities. Relatedly, the director would be required to issue regulations governing how precinct ballot counts are to be conducted.
  • Require the director to adopt regulations to maintain an accurate master register and create a best practices qualification system, as a separate section of law separate from the provisions relating to voter registration and voter registration list maintenance.
  • Expand the grounds for contesting election results to include (1) a breach of voter registration data that reveals voters' digital multi-factor authentication or other security identifiers sufficient to change the results of an election, or (2) ballot accounting irregularities sufficient to change the results of an election.
  • Expand the ability of the director to conduct mail ballot elections, but prohibit any mail ballot election until the director updates the master register and adopts a system protected by blockchain technology that provides for strict digital multi-factor authentication and ballot chain-of-custody protocols. Under the bill, the director could conduct a mail ballot election:
    • in an unorganized community with a population of 750 or less,
    • in a second class city with a population of 1,000 or less, upon the governing body's request,
    • in a second class borough with a population of 3,000 or less, upon the governing body's request,
    • in an area affected or threatened by a governor-declared disaster, if the Governor declares the emergency because of a natural disaster, a disease outbreak or a credible threat of an imminent outbreak of disease, or an enemy or terrorist attack or a credible threat of an imminent enemy or terrorist attack, or
    • if it is held at a time other than when the general, party primary, or municipal election is held.
  • Shift election authority to the legislature from the courts by forbidding the Division from obeying any judicial decision that would change election law unless the legislature provides express consent.
  • Prohibit electronic signatures unless they are notarized.
  • Require public disclosure of a security breach of a voter registration record or a voting machine.
  • Require police officers to receive at least four hours of instruction in detecting and investigating election fraud.

  • Require the permanent fund dividend application, which is used for automatic voter registration, to include space for the applicant to identify the house district in which they have been a resident for the past 30 days.

Last Updated March 23, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on May 14, 2021, would change when a voter's registration is made inactive, which is a step toward cancellation of the registration. Under the bill, a voter's registration will be made inactive if they do not vote for four years and fail to respond to a forwardable confirmation notice within 45 days after it is sent. In addition, a voter's registration will be made inactive if a nonforwardable initial address confirmation notice sent to the voter for reasons other than not voting is returned as undeliverable, and the voter fails to respond to a forwardable address confirmation message within 45 days after it was sent. Under existing law, before a voter may be sent a forwardable address confirmation notice and have their registration made inactive, the voter must both fail to vote for four years and have the nonforwardable confirmation notice returned as undeliverable.

Last Updated May 17, 2021

This bill currently has two versions, one as introduced on January 19, 2021, and one recommended as a substitute by the Committee on State Affairs on May 7, 2021.

As introduced on January 19, the bill would end automatic voter registration, end mail ballot elections at the local and state levels, criminalize most third-party ballot return, and make other changes to the election code.

The May 7 committee substitute is fundamentally different. That bill version would create a new voter identification regime using digital multifactor authentication that would apply to voting in person and by mail, would strengthen the notarization requirement for mail ballots, create new ways to invalidate mail ballots but also create a cure process, criminalize some third party mail ballot return, create a permanent absentee voter list, restrict sending mail ballot applications to voters, create other new election crimes, allow tribal ID for voter registration and voting, require a voter list maintenance procedures and audits, create new chain custody rules for ballots and other election materials, and would shift election authority to the Legislature. This bill version is very similar to AK H 196.

The committee substitute will not replace the original bill unless the Senate so votes when the bill reaches the floor, but it must clear another committee first. Both versions would make substantial changes to Alaska election law and are discussed below, but the bill tags relate to what is currently the official version, the bill as introduced in January.

Specifically, the bill as introduced on January 19 would:

  • End automatic voter registration for people applying for a permanent fund dividend, starting with permanent fund applications filed after December 31, 2021.
  • Repeal the state's ability to conduct certain types of elections by mail, and affirmatively prohibit localities from conducting such elections. Some Alaska communities, such as Anchorage, currently conduct all their elections by mail. The state regularly conducts certain education and other elections by mail.
  • Add to an existing misdemeanor possessing another's ballot unless the voter is a family member, household member, or caregiver, and the person possesses no more than one ballot other than their own. Election officials, postal workers, and couriers working in their official capacities would be exempt.
  • Criminalize as a felony intentionally opening or tampering with a sealed absentee ballot certificate and envelope or package of ballots without express authorization from the director of elections.
  • Create an election offense hotline that must be staffed throughout voting and publicized by the election division and on voting materials and in voting locations.
  • Prohibit absentee voting by fax in state elections.
  • Require counting absentee ballots as soon after they are verified as possible, however, the bill does not change the prohibition on counting absentee ballots before polls close, nor the need to review absentee ballots against in-person voter lists to ensure no one votes twice.
  • Respond to a court order suspending the requirement that a voter's mail ballot signature be witnessed due to a declared disaster emergency by requiring the division of elections to reimpose the requirement as soon as the emergency ends. For the November 2020 election, the state supreme court allowed the witness requirement to be suspended because of the Covid-19 pandemic.

  • Require the lieutenant governor to immediately notify the legislature of a security breach of a voter registration record or a voting machine.

    The bill version recommended by the committee on May 7, would instead:


  • Change voter registration by:
    • requiring the director of the division of elections to issue regulations creating a digital multi-factor authentication regime, and requiring all voters who can use it, to use it when applying for a mail ballot, completing a mail ballot, and appearing to vote in person. The director would also be required to create an alternative authentication method for voters who cannot use the digital multi-factor approach. These numbers would be a confidential part of a voter's record.
    • changing the acceptable forms of ID to include tribal ID but disallow the currently accepted hunting or fishing license.
    • increasing the penalty for knowingly making a false statement on a voter registration form to a felony, instead of the misdemeanor of exiting law.
    • including on the permanent fund dividend registration form space for the house district the voter has been a resident of for at least 30 days.
  • Change applying for a mail ballot by:
    • creating a permanent absentee voting list, by revising the absentee ballot application form to allow voters to join it. Voters would be removed if their ballot was returned as undeliverable, or if they failed to return an absentee ballot for four years.
    • shortening the time a voter has to apply, by requiring the application to be received by the division of elections 14 days before Election Day, rather than 10 days before as existing law provides.
    • allowing voters to apply for ballots by email.
    • requiring voters to include their digital multi-factor identifiers, unless they cannot.
    • prohibiting most non-election official third-parties from sending voters mail ballot applications, authorizing only the division of elections, official candidates, recognized political parties, and ballot initiative entities to send the applications, and the division only to voters who request them. The entity sending the application must be identified on the application.
  • Change completing and returning a mail ballot by:
    • strengthening the existing notarization and/or witness requirement. A voter would only be allowed to use a witness who is not a notary or an official authorized to administer oaths if the voter and the witness both attest in writing that such an official was not reasonably available. In addition, the voter would be explicitly required to show ID to the witnessing official before completing their ballot.
    • requiring voters who can use the digital multifactor identifiers to include the identifiers on their ballot certificate. This requirement applies to both voters who received the ballot in the mail and voters who are voting early using in-person absentee ballots.
    • requiring the voter and their witness to print name, physical address, mailing address, digital or phone contact info on ballot certificate
    • shortening the deadline to return a ballot to postmarked on or before Election Day and received within seven days of Election Day, instead of postmarked by Election Day and received within ten days.
    • expanding an existing misdemeanor to criminalize offering to return voters' completed ballots for them, or returning more than six even if the voters ask.
    • prohibiting electronic ballot signatures unless the ballot signature is also electronically notarized.
  • Change in-person voting by:
    • enabling an election official, poll watcher, or any voter, to challenge a voter on the grounds that the voter received an absentee ballot, with the consequence that the voter would complete a "questioned" (provisional) ballot. The voter would be required to use their multi-factor identifier with their questioned ballot if possible. In addition, the penalty for lying on a questioned ballot certificate would be increased from a misdemeanor to a felony.
    • adding tribal ID to the types of ID accepted at the polls, and removing hunting and fishing licenses.
    • requiring voters to use their multi-factor identifiers in addition to ID, if they can.
    • limiting the number of ballots a voter can spoil. An in-person voter would be allowed to spoil a ballot and receive another one, with a maximum of two. Existing law says three.
  • Change verifying and counting mail ballots to alter the timeline for reviewing and counting ballots, create new grounds for rejecting them, and create a cure process. Specifically, the committee substitute would change ballot verification and counting by:
    • requiring all mail ballots envelopes and certificates received at least seven days before the election to be reviewed by that date.
    • allowing ballot counting to begin as soon as envelopes and certificates are reviewed, but requiring results to remain confidential until the close of polls. Before a mail ballot is counted, the voter's eligibility must be confirmed and that they did not also vote in person.
    • rejecting ballots received by mail after Election Day, unless the ballot was either postmarked or encoded with a barcode documenting its timely mailing.
    • rejecting ballots lacking the multi-factor identifiers, if the voter was able to use them.
    • rejecting ballots signed by a witness instead of a notary or other officer able to administer oaths, unless the voter and the witness signed and included the attestation that no such officer was reasonably available.
    • rejecting ballots because the voters also cast an in-person ballot. In addition, the committee substituted provides that if a voter returned both a mail ballot and voted in person at the polls, and the election official determines the voter was not trying to have two ballots count, the in-person ballot would be counted.
    • rejecting ballots that lack a watermark, seal, or other identifier, unless the director issues a limited exception to the rule by regulation. Relatedly, the bill creates a requirement that ballots have such identifiers.
    • requiring the director of the Division of Elections to immediately make a reasonable effort to contact each absentee voter whose ballot has been rejected, explain why, and how it can be cured. The voter would have through 5 p.m. on the 3rd day after the election to cure their ballot, although ballots could be timely received through the seventh day after the election.
  • Require the director of the division of elections to create a comprehensive ballot chain of custody regime that would have impacts on election result certification and election contests, as well as impose certain requirements on election equipment. Specifically, the committee substitute would:
    • require the director to issue regulations creating a chain of custody system to account for the original of each used and unused ballot, absentee ballot certificate and envelope, and paper record of an electronically generated ballot.
    • prohibit certifying results until all the ballots are accounted for, or the director has publicly disclosed a detailed accounting of the discrepancy.
    • require the director to give notice to various elected officials, candidates and/or the sponsors or opponents of ballot measures, as well as the public, if a ballot is not accounted for, or there is a break in the chain of custody, lapse in system security, or the director anticipates such. Ballot collection and counting could not continue until the affected candidates or organizations have at least 24 hours' notice to appoint a watcher. Relatedly, the substitute would require the lieutenant governor to immediately notify the legislature and the public of a security breach of a voter registration record or a voting machine.
    • impose specific requirements for auditing and using ballot tabulators.
    • require the director to adopt regulations governing the precinct count for accuracy and speed, and to preserve the chain for custody.
    • add two grounds for contesting elections, namely a breach of voter registration data that reveals voters' digital multi-factor authentication or other security identifiers sufficient to change the results of an election, and ballot accounting irregularities sufficient to change the results of an election. The committee substitute would also clarify that failing to give notice of the opportunity to cure a ballot would not be grounds for contesting an election.
    • require software for voting by use of electronically generated ballots to be open source, developed entirely in the U.S. by a U.S. company using U.S. routers and servers and best practice cyber security.
  • Shift election authority to the legislature, taking it from the courts, by instructing the division of elections to disregard any judicial decision altering election statutes on the grounds that the decision is purely advisory unless the legislature provides express consent.
  • Change mail ballot elections by creating a new threshold before one may be conducted, and, once reached, expanding the ability of the division of elections to hold mail ballot elections. Specifically, the committee substitute would:
    • Provide that, before conducting an election by mail, the director must update the master voter registration list and adopt a system protected by the most functional application of distributed ledger technology, which may include blockchain, Hashgraph, DAG, Holochain, or Tempo, that provides for strict digital multi-factor authentication and ballot chain-of-custody protocols.
    • Allow the division to conduct a mail ballot election:
    • in an unorganized community with a population of 750 or less if the director determines that facilitating organized in-person voting in the community is unreasonable.
    • in a second class city with a population of 1,000 or less, upon the governing body's request
    • in a second class borough with a population of 3,000 or less, upon the governing body's request,
    • in an area affected or threatened by certain types of disasters as declared by the governor.
      or,
    • it is held at a time other than when the general, party primary, or municipal election is held. Only this last reason exists under existing law.
  • Create or expand election crimes. In addition to the expansion of an existing misdemeanor to reach certain people returning voters' completed, sealed ballots, the committee substitute would:
    • expand the felony of voter misconduct in the first degree to punish someone who votes in the name of an incapacitated person.
    • expand the felony of unlawful interference with an election to punish someone who:
    • intentionally opens or tampers with a sealed absentee ballot certificate, absentee ballot envelope, or package of ballots without express authorization from the director
    • intentionally breaches, hacks, alters, or tampers with election machinery, including a tabulator machine, a program, a system, a server, or software used to verify identity, count, or tabulate, or manage or control any election function.
    • create a new felony, named election fraud, to punish anyone who commits unlawful interference with an election sufficiently to change the outcome of the election.
    • expand the existing felony of election official misconduct in the first degree to punish someone who knowingly discloses, shares, or reports, to a person who is not an election official, election results, returns, or any confidential election data before the polls close on election day.
    • require police officers to receive at least four hours of instruction in detecting and investigating election fraud.
    • provide that if a voter's ballot is not counted because they did not meet the residency requirements, the director must tell the voter immediately by reasonably available means, must investigate, and if the director thinks the person knowingly violated the law, refer them to law enforcement.

  • Change voter list maintenance by:

    • requiring the division of elections to use nationally recognized best practices and develop a system of protocols to update the voter registration list to remove ineligible people.
    • requiring the division to consult with an external, nationally recognized subject-matter expert and audit the list every two years. The results of each audit must be reported by February 1 of each year to the Legislature, and the first audit would be done by May 30, 2022.
    • requiring the director to create a process for a voter to cancel their registration and prominently display instructions for the process on every ballot envelope and at every polling location.

This bill, as substituted by committee on April 28, 2021, would authorize civil enforcement of election laws, in addition to criminal enforcement authorized under existing law. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Allow any person to file a complaint with the Division of Elections alleging a violation of election laws. The complaint would have to be filed within 60 days of the certification of the election at issue or 30 days of the alleged violation, whichever is later. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill required complaints to be filed within 30 days of the election or the occurrence of the alleged violation. Complaints concerning campaigns for state offices, including campaign finance, would be referred to the Alaska Public Offices Commission. After deciding any other type of complaint potentially had merit, the Division could choose to refer it to the Attorney General. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Authorize the Attorney General to investigate the referred complaints, including the right to examine witnesses in writing under oath, and examine evidence. The Attorney General would report their findings to the Division. These provisions are modified. The previous version of the bill specifically authorized the Attorney General to conduct hearings.
  • Authorize the Division to make reasonable efforts to work with election officials to take corrective action where a violation has been found. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Authorize the Attorney General to bring a civil action for injunctive relief to prevent or stop violations of election laws. If the court finds that an individual has violated, or is about to violate, an election law, the bill would allow civil penalties of up to $25,000 for each violation and payment of investigation costs, and actual attorney's fees and costs. If suing a candidate or elected official, the Attorney General would have to file the cases within two years of the initial complaint. This is a modified provision. The previous version did not have the two year statute of limitations.
  • Allow complainants to sue over the alleged election law violation independent of any action of the Division or the Attorney General.

  • Authorize the Division and the Attorney General to issue regulations to implement these provisions. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.

Last Updated August 25, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 12, 2021, would change voter identification number requirements for absentee voting and allow for vote by mail elections in very small communities. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Add a new requirement to the absentee ballot application that applicants must provide their date of birth and one other "voter identifier," i.e., last four digits of a Social Security number, driver's license or state ID number, or voter identification number.

This bill, as introduced on May 19, 2021, addresses the actions the state would take if the federal government adopts any measure that requires the state to register voters or conduct elections for federal office in a manner that the Director of the Division of Elections determines is inconsistent state law. The bill acknowledges that the federal government could choose to conduct the federal elections in Alaska itself.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to voter fraud, prohibits a voter in this state from also voting in another state, provides further for criminal penalties, effects the requirement of a new or increased expenditure of local funds within the meaning of Amendment 621 of the Constitution of Alabama of 1901.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on May 17, 2021, modifies the criminal offenses related to voting multiple times in a single election. The bill:

  • Expands the multiple voting offense to include voting in the same, or equivalent, elections in both Alabama and another state. Under existing law, the provision only prohibited voting multiple times in the same election within the state. This provision was retained from a previous version of the bill.
  • Downgrades a first conviction for multiple or fraudulent voting from a Class C felony to a Class A misdemeanor. Subsequent offenses would remain Class C felonies. This provision was modified from a previous version of the bill, which would have made the change to Class A misdemeanor applicable for all multiple or fraudulent voting convictions.
  • Clarifies the intent requirement for attempted fraudulent voting to require that the voter have knowledge that they were not entitled to vote.   • Early voting would have to be available between 10 a.m. and 7 p.m. on each Saturday during the early voting period.
  • Counties would be required to establish at least one early voting center per 100,000 residents, although a county commission, by majority vote, could reduce the number of early voting centers when the commission determines that a lesser number of centers would be sufficient to meet the needs of early voters.
  • Early voting centers could be located in any branch of the county courthouse or courthouse annex, any government building generally accessible to the public, or any location that is used as an election day polling place.
  • Early voting would be conducted with the same processes as Election Day voting, including the rights of poll watchers.

Last Updated February 4, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to voter registration lists, revises the process used by the Secretary of State and boards of registrars to periodically update the statewide voter registration database, authorizes the Secretary of State to adopt rules, revises the publication reimbursement rate to counties relating to revising the statewide voter registration database.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on May 26, 2021, changes the process for removing voters from the registration list due to address changes. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires the use of NCOA data and targeted confirmation notices to determine whether voters have moved. Existing law had required the board of registrars to use quadrennial address confirmation mailings, sent to all registered voters, to confirm residence.
  • Requires boards of registrars to update the registrations of voters in the NCOA database who have changed addresses within their jurisdiction, and send these voters a return postage prepaid notice on which the voter may correct their updated address if necessary. Voters must submit address corrections by the registration deadline.
  • Requires the board of registrars to send notice to a voter's former address if NCOA flags a voter as having moved outside the board's jurisdiction. If the voter does not respond within 90 days or if the notice is returned as undeliverable, the voter is be placed on the inactive voter list.

Last updated on May 27, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on February 10, 2021, would:

  • Establish no-excuse absentee voting. Under existing law, voters must have a qualifying excuse to vote by absentee ballot.
  • Require mailed absentee ballot applications to be received ten days before Election Day. Under existing law, applications must be received five days before Election Day. This deadline would still apply for hand-delivered applications.

  • Require absentee election managers to begin verifying absentee ballots at 7 a.m. on Election Day. Under existing law, this process begins at 12 p.m.
  • Permit absentee election managers to appoint up to two assistants with the approval of the county commission.

VRLANALYSIS:

  • Confirmation mailings would only be sent to voters who have been flagged by the U.S. Postal Service as having changed addresses. Under existing law, all voters are sent a notice every four years.
  • Voters who are flagged as having moved outside their county of registration and sent a notice would have until the day after the second federal general election to vote or update their registration or they would be removed.

This bill, as amended on March 29, 2021, would propose state constitutional amendments and statutory changes to implement online voter registration in Arkansas. The bill would:

  • Require the Secretary of State to develop a secure online voter registration system that will allow a voter to provide an electronic signature or mark to complete and submit the application online. The applicant would need to provide a valid Arkansas driver's license number or the last four digits of their Social Security number. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require online registrants to verify their identity by showing photo ID the first time they vote following registration in the same manner required of individuals who register by mail. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require the Secretary of State to ensure the accuracy of the voter registration rolls by regularly identifying deceased voters using information from the Social Security Administration, verifying the address information provided by persons registering to vote or updating their registration, and cooperating with other states to develop systems to compare voter registration information to determine the eligibility of individuals to vote in Arkansas. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Prohibit the Secretary of State to promulgate emergency rules related to voter registration within 180 days of a federal elections without seeking the consent of the General Assembly. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.

A provision requiring the online voter registration system to be available in Spanish was removed from the bill on March 9, 2021.

NOTE: The proposed constitutional amendments contained in the bill would need to be approved by 2/3 of the members of both chambers of the state legislature to be enacted.

BILLSUMMARY: Amends election procedures, amends the requirements for election officials, amends the location of polling places, amends the law concerning the information contained in the voter registration list.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on April 30, 2021:

  • Requires the closure of any polling site for a preferential primary or general election to be approved by the State Board of Elections no later than 60 days before Election Day, except in the event of an emergency. Existing law required that poll closures be approved no later than 30 days before an election, which remains the rule for all elections other than primary or general elections. This provision was modified from the previous version of the bill. The previous version would have required approval 60 days before all elections, and would have specified that a qualifying emergency must be determined by unanimous vote of the State Board.
  • Establishes an appeals process for voters to contest the closure of a polling place for a primary or general election. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.

  • Requires electronic pollbooks to indicate whether voters have applied for an absentee ballot and requires election workers at early voting and Election Day polling locations to verify whether voters have done so. If records show that a voter has requested an absentee ballot, they must cast a provisional ballot. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

    Provisions that were amended out of the bill prior to enactment would have required a polling site to be located in any cities, municipalities, or towns that required one by ordinance, and would have required polling sites in cities of the second class and incorporated towns to have internet service and be ADA-compliant.

Last updated May 13, 2021.

This bill, as enacted on April 15, 2021:

  • Prohibits county clerks and other election officials to distribute unsolicited mail ballot applications or mail ballots to voters. The bill allows clerks to display a printable or downloadable ballot application on the internet, share links to application forms on social media, and make paper copies of application forms available for distribution or on request of a qualified voter. The previous version of the bill did not clarify the actions clerks were allowed to take to provide absentee voter applications.
  • Creates a presumption of intent to defraud of voter for purposes of felony prosecution when a person possesses more than four absentee ballots. Existing law created a presumption to intent to defraud when a person possesses more than 10 absentee ballots. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires the State Board of Election Commissioners to create a uniform statewide voter statement for absentee ballots. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires ballots that are made provisional due to non-matching information related to a designated bearer to be counted unless election officials determine the voter is otherwise ineligible. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.

  • Prohibits county clerks or their deputies to access absentee ballot materials returned by voters once the outer envelope of a returned ballot has been opened. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

    The bill also makes minor changes to aspects of election administration that Voting Rights Lab does not track.


Last Updated May 14, 2021

The address information of participants in the program will not be public record and will not be included on publicly-available lists of registered voters.

The previous version of the bill would have kept all registration information of program participants, including their names, off of publicly-available lists of registered voters.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2021, would enact changes to election procedures that would take effect when the Governor declares an emergency. The bill would, upon declaration of an emergency:

  • Allow any voter that fears their attendance at the polls would present a risk to their health or the health of others to cite the "unavoidably absent" excuse to vote by absentee ballot.
  • Waive the statutory deadline of seven days before Election Day for absentee ballot requests by mail and allow clerks to mail ballots to voters who request them within the seven day window.
  • Allow clerks to begin processing and canvassing the outer envelopes of absentee ballots fifteen days before Election Day. Existing law allows clerks to begin processing outer envelopes seven days before Election Day. Clerks would be required to provide daily notices of the locations and times for canvassing outer envelopes.
  • Waive the fifteen day notice requirement for local officials to change polling sites or vote centers and allow officials to move sites until three days before Election Day.

The provisions of the bill would remain in effect for 30 days following the Governor's declaration of emergency. The provisions may be extended beyond 30 days by a concurrent resolution of the General Assembly or a resolution of the Legislative Council if the General Assembly is not in session.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 19, 2021, would shift emergency authority over election administration from the Governor to the Secretary of State. The bill would:

  • Authorize the Secretary of State to modify statutory election requirements and adopt emergency rules as deemed necessary during a declared state of emergency. The bill would allow the Secretary to adopt emergency rules lasting up to 120 days with less than 30 days' notice when necessary.
  • Eliminate the authority of the Governor under existing law to suspend statutory requirements related to election conduct during a declared state of emergency.

Last updated July 19, 2021.

This bill, as amended on March 18, 2021, would:

  • Allow the voter to return their absentee ballot in person to the county clerk until 7:30 p.m. on Election Day. Existing law allows voters to return ballots until the close of regular business at the clerk's office on Election Day, but allows a voter's agent to return the ballot until 7:30 p.m. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Allow election officials to verify absentee ballots upon receipt. Officials would remain unable to tabulate ballots until the close of polls. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require election officials to notify voters by mail, email, or phone within 24 hours of determining a deficiency with the voter's absentee ballot. Ballots with deficiencies would be deemed provisional. Voters who fail to provide a copy of ID with their ballot would cure the deficiency in the manner required by the Arkansas constitution. Voters who fail to provide other information may supply the missing materials. Voters whose ballots were deemed provisional because the voter's name, address, date of birth or signature or the voter's agent's name or address were deemed non-matching would verify in writing under penalty of perjury that the voter was the person who submitted the ballot. Voters would be able to provide the necessary information in person, by phone, or electronically by the Monday after Election Day to have their ballot counted. If additional review by election officials determined that the voter's original ballot materials are sufficient and cure is no longer required, the voter would be notified by mail, email, or phone within 24 hours of the determination. The previous version of the bill would have given voters whose absentee ballots were deemed provisional until the close of certification of the election to cure the issue.
  • Allow all voters to use a single application to apply for absentee ballots for all elections for a calendar year. Existing law limits this option to voters who currently reside outside their county of registration. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires an election official who suspects fraud concerning absentee voting to file a complaint regarding the issue with the State Board of Election Commissioner s and the county prosecuting attorney within two weeks after certification of the election. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

A previous version of the bill would have required county clerks to accept ballots that are postmarked by Election Day and received by the county clerk within 10 days of Election Day. That provision was amended out of the text on February 3, 2021.

Last Updated March 19, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Concerns the investigation of violations of election law, establishes an election law violation hotline.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on April 27, 2021:

  • Prohibits individuals who have been convicted of election-related crimes from serving as election officials.
  • Creates a system of punishment for election officials found to have violated election laws, administered by the Joint Performance Review Committee. The bill authorizes sanctions including reprimands, decertification as an election official, transfer of election administration duties to the State Board of Elections, and the withholding of election funding.
  • Requires the Attorney General to establish a hotline for reports of violations of election law. The Attorney General must provide a toll-free telephone number and must also receive complaints by mail, email, or fax.
  • Creates a new Class A misdemeanor for submitting a false report of a violation of election law.
  • Allows local prosecuting attorneys who have a relevant conflict of interest to deputize the Attorney General to investigate and prosecute violations of election law.
  • Establishes procedures for the referral of allegations of election law violations by election officials to the State Board of Elections.

 

Last updated May 14, 2021.

This bill, as amended on April 21, 2021, would:

  • Require election workers to review all absentee ballots returned by voters contain all required materials in the outer and inner ballot envelopes and all submitted information, ID, and signatures belong to the voter and their agent, if one was used. Ballots with missing materials or information that election workers determine may not be that of the voter or agent will be considered provisional. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require election officials to contact voters with absentee ballots deemed provisional by mail, email, or phone within 48 hours of the determination. Voters may cure ballots with missing ID or voter statements by providing the missing information by noon on the Monday after Election Day. Voters may cure ballots with missing or mismatched voter or agent information by providing the missing information or verifying under penalty of perjury that the voter submitted the ballot in question by the Monday after Election Day. The previous version of the bill required voters to be notified of ballot issues within 24 hours of determination and gave voters until the close of business on the Monday after Election Day to cure.
  • Allow all eligible voters to apply for absentee ballots for a single election or for each election in a calendar year. Existing law allows only disabled voters or voters residing outside the county of registration to apply for ballots for all elections in a calendar year. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require all absentee ballots, other than UOCAVA ballots, to be counted by the close of business on the Thursday after Election Day. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require the State Board of Elections to develop rules and forms for the application, storage, labelling, and handling of absentee ballots. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

Last Updated April 22, 2021

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on March 18, 2021, requires the Secretary of State to use death records received from the state Department of Health to cancel matching voter registrations. The records, which existing law requires the Department of Health to send monthly and annually, include the decedent's name, date of birth, date of death, Social Security number, if available, usual legal residence at the time of death and, if available, the decedent's father's name or mother's maiden name. Existing law states that the Secretary "may" use this data to cancel registrations, and the bill would change that to "shall" cancel. While permissive with regard to the Secretary, existing law requires county election officials to cancel the records of deceased voters.

Last updated April 6, 2021.

This bill, as enacted on May 5, 2021, allows election officials to begin tabulating early ballots as soon as the ballot verification process is complete. Under previous law, tabulation could not start more than 14 days before Election Day. 

In Arizona, "early ballot" refers to both ballots that voters receive in the mail and to ballots that voted early in person. In both types of voting, the voter puts their completed ballot into a special envelope, signs the certificate on the envelope, and then returns the ballot. Both ballot types are processed the same way.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to election lawsuits, relates to settlements, relates to approvals.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on March 4, 2021, would shift some election litigation-related authority away from the Secretary of State and give it to county recorders or other officers in charge of elections.

Specifically, if a proposed settlement of an election-related civil action materially affects a county recorder or other officer in charge of elections, the Secretary of State would be prohibited from settling the case without consulting Arizona's county recorders or other officers in charge of elections. A county recorder or other officer of elections could object to the settlement based on the difficulty or impracticability of its requirements and provide evidence regarding that difficulty or impracticability. If the evidence is sufficient, the Secretary of State's settlement could not be approved without the consent of the county recorder or other officer of elections. In addition, a county recorder or other officer in charge of elections could join in any such civil action. These are modified provisions. As introduced, the bill would have applied to county recorders only. The amendment now includes other officers in charge of elections.

Last updated August 25, 2021.
