VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 15, 2021, would allow additional days of early voting, alter requirements relating to vote centers, and establish ballot drop off locations. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Allow county recorders, or other election officials authorized by the board of supervisors to administer early voting locations, to operate early voting polling places on the Saturday, Sunday, and Monday before the election, if they are able to do so and still update precinct registers before the polls open on Election Day. In addition, the bill clarifies that emergency voting is only available between 5 p.m. on the Friday before the election and 5 p.m. the Monday before the election if early voting has ended in the county. Under existing law, early voting ends at 5 p.m. on the Friday before the election, emergency voting is available on the three days before the election, and only county recorders, with the authorization of the board of supervisors, are allowed to operate early voting locations.
  • Potentially shift election authority away from county recorders by allowing county supervisors to authorize "other" election officials, in addition to the county recorder, to operate voting centers and ballot drop off locations. Existing law allows the board of supervisors to authorize only the county recorder to open voting centers, and does not address ballot drop off locations. This bill defines a ballot drop off location as a place where a voter may deliver a voted early ballot to a lawful custodian.
  • Clarify that voting centers may be used as early voting locations. Vote centers have been used as early voting locations under existing law.
  • Clarify that polling place requirements apply to voting centers, including the prohibition on firearms, the 75-foot limit on electioneering and other conduct, and voting. Existing law does not mention polling place requirements.
  • Require the board supervisors to appoint a "voting center election board" for each vote center location. Members would include at least one inspector, one marshal, and as many additional judges or clerks as necessary, and must include an equal number of Democrats and Republicans. The bill would authorize the election board to work in shifts so long as the required bipartisan balance is maintained, and would authorize people as young as 16 years old to staff the vote centers if certain requirements are met.

  • Allow voting centers to be used as ballot replacement locations during mail ballot elections, and allow a voter to receive a replacement ballot by affirming the original was not cast. In addition, the bill would allow a county to offer more than one ballot replacement location in mail ballot locations. Under existing law, a voter may only receive a replacement ballot by affirming that the original was lost, spoiled, destroyed, or not received.

Last Updated July 19, 2021

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced January 19, 2021, would increase the frequency of voter list maintenance using postal change of address information, and create a provision that would appear to require cancellation for a change of address without the address confirmation process required by the National Voter Registration Act. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require county recorders to use National Change of Address data every year, rather than every two years as existing law requires.

  • Require county recorders to cancel a voter's registration "when" they receive written information from the national change of address system that the voter has a change of address outside the county or the state. Existing law requires recorders to send a confirmation notice to anyone who appears to have moved, and cancelling their registration if they do not reply to the notice and do not vote in the succeeding two general elections. Such notice and delayed cancellation is required by the National Voter Registration Act.

    Last updated March 10, 2021.

The bill would have required the secretary of state and a committee of county recorders to operate and maintain the online voter registration system, beginning no later than December 31, 2023. If the secretary of state and committee of county recorders contracted with a third party for some or all of the operation and maintenance of the online voter registration system, the bill would have required that the website address for access to the system use the top-level domain .gov or .vote. The existing system was jointly developed by the Department of Transportation and the Secretary of State, and is currently maintained by both.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 26, 2021, would sharply curtail voting by mail by requiring an excuse to cast a mail ballot, significantly increase in-person early voting by extending the voting period and mandating vote centers, make the voter ID law more restrictive by limiting it to photo ID, allow a state or federal ID to validate voter registration while changing the rules for DMV to require proving citizenship to receive an Arizona driver's license or state ID, and increase the use of schools as polling places. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Sharply reduce voting by mail by eliminating no excuse mail voting. Existing law allows people to vote by mail without excuse, and statewide some 80% of voters cast ballots they receive in the mail. Under the bill, only people who are physically unable to cast a ballot during early voting, have a physical disability, are confined to a nursing home, are on military duty or are temporarily residing outside Arizona would be allowed to vote by mail.
  • Increase the availability of in-person voting by requiring counties to open vote centers for 30 days before the election. The number of required vote centers would vary by population. A county with less than 200,000 people could have no more than four, a county with between 200,000 and one million people could have no more than eight, and a county of one million or more could have no more than 15, as determined by their respective boards of supervisors. Existing law allows counties to offer vote centers but does not require them. The existing early voting period begins 27 days before Election Day.
  • Make the voter ID law more restrictive by making it photo ID only. Existing law allows voters to present two non-photo forms of ID.
  • Allow the proof of citizenship for voter registration to be verified with a state or federal ID. In tandem the bill would require proof of citizenship to obtain a state driver's license or ID card.

  • Require election precincts to be drawn to prioritize having a school in them, and change existing rules to make it easy for counties to site polling places in schools.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to voting rights, relates to felonies, relates to automatic restoration.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 26, 2021, would automatically restore all returning citizens' voting eligibility upon completion of probation or absolute discharge from imprisonment ("final discharge"). Under existing law, only people convicted of a single felony who have fully paid restitution are automatically restored to voting eligibility upon final discharge. People convicted of more than one felony or who have not paid restitution in full must wait two years and then apply to restore their voting eligibility. In addition, the bill would require the sentencing judge to inform the defendant when their voting eligibility would be restored.

Last updated January 27, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on January 27, 2021, would change the rules relating to observers of the ballot counting process and impose other counting transparency measures, would change how Arizona's electoral college votes are determined, and would make changes to the procedures for lawsuits challenging election results. 

With regard to observing the count and counting transparency, the bill would:

  • Allow at least 10 members of the public, drawn by lot from names submitted at least 17 days before the election, to join the other observers allowed by law and participate on equal terms.
  • Clarify that all observers be allowed to see each essential part of the proceedings at the counting center, and that only people authorized to actually process and count ballots and handle election supplies shall touch any ballot or ballot card or return.
  • Require the live video feed of the ballots in the tabulation room of the counting center to clearly display the ballots being counted and the electronic screens being used by the electronic vote adjudication board
  • Punish the members of the board of supervisors and the county recorder for any disruption in the video feed by barring them from reelection or any other public office for 10 years after they complete the term in which the video disruption occurred.
  • Require the images of all duplicated ballots to be posted to the county's website within twenty-four hours after duplication along with the determination by the board as to that voter's intent for each contest adjudicated. Ballots are duplicated because they are damaged or defective and cannot properly be counted by the automatic tabulating equipment.

With regard to Arizona's electoral college votes, the bill would shift power from local election officials and the Secretary of State to the Legislature, by empowering the Legislature to revoke a presidential elector's certificate of election by majority vote any time before the presidential inauguration, without regard to whether it is in regular or special session or has held hearings on the matter.

With regard to election contests, the bill would shift power away from the judiciary by preventing a timely filed case from being dismissed on the basis of laches, provide that people bringing an election contest are entitled to a jury trial, and clarify that presidential electors are among the officers whose election may be contested.

Last Updated September 30, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 27, 2021, would prohibit using vote centers, sharply limit the use of emergency voting sites, shift election authority from the Secretary of State to the Legislature, and narrow the misdemeanor prohibiting photographs or video within 75 feet of a polling place. Existing law allows emergency centers to be opened after early voting ends but before Election Day for voters who sign an affidavit certifying the emergency that necessitated their voting after early voting but before Election Day. Emergency voting centers are thus allowed to be open on a weekend.
  • Require the Secretary of State's Election Procedures Manual to provide for transparency and election security to the maximum extent allowed by law.
  • Require the Legislature to send personnel who are experts in electronic voting systems and procedures and in electronic voting system security to field check and review electronic voting systems and recommend needed statutory and procedural changes, in addition to the personnel existing law requires the Secretary of State to send for the same purpose.
  • Narrow the existing misdemeanor prohibiting taking photographs and video within 75 feet of a polling place by clarifying only photo or video of other voters and other voters' ballots are prohibited. The bill would explicitly exempt photos or video taken of election officials, and exempt photos or video taken by a voter of themselves or their own ballot.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 4, 2021, would expand automatic voting eligibility restoration, expand early voting, improve the cure process for missing ballot signatures, allow ballots cast after presenting ID to be excluded from signature matching, and make other changes to Arizona election law. Specifically, this bill would:

  • Automatically restore voting eligibility to all people convicted of felonies who paid their restitution and completed incarceration, parole and/or probation. Under existing law, only people convicted of a single felony are eligible for automatic restoration. People convicted of more than one felony, or people who have not paid their restitution, must apply for voting eligibility restoration.
  • Expand early voting by lengthening the early voting period through 5 p.m. on the Monday before the election. Under existing law, early voting ends at 5 p.m. on the Friday before the election. The bill does not mandate that early voting be offered on the Saturday or Sunday. As a conforming change, the bill would eliminate the existing emergency voting procedure that allows people to vote between 5 p.m. Friday before the election and 5 p.m. Monday before the election.
  • Expand the special election board available to ill or disabled voters by making it available to those in pretrial detention.
  • Potentially expand early voting by requiring county recorders to open early voting at their offices and as many other locations as required by the Election Procedures Manual. The current edition of the manual does not require additional locations.
  • Provide that early ballots cast in person after presenting the voter ID required to cast in-person ballots do not need to be additionally verified by signature comparison. Under existing law, the signatures of all early ballots are verified, although those cast in person after showing ID "should generally not be invalidated based solely on an allegedly inconsistent signature absent other evidence that the signatures were not made by the same person." Relatedly, the bill would end the ability of challengers to challenge the sufficiency of the envelope of an early ballot cast in-person after the voter presented ID.
  • Expand the existing cure process for mismatch signatures to missing signatures, which extends the deadline to cure a missing signature past the close of polls on Election Day to 5 p.m. on the fifth day after the election.
  • Facilitate recruitment of election workers by allowing people to be trained as one through August 1 of a general election year. Under existing law, training must be complete by January 1 of a general election year.
  • Require provisional ballot envelopes to require all the information needed to register to vote, and if the provisional ballot is rejected because the voter is not registered, the information must be used to register them.

  • Allow international election observers, impose security rules on electronic poll books, allow voting equipment to be tested 10 days before use in early balloting, rather than seven, and require unofficial return updates sent to the Secretary of State to include information about ballots remaining to be counted.

Last Updated March 10, 2021

If the voter returns the notice and ID, the voter's signature on the notice and the ID will be compared to the records on file, and if they do not match, the recorder must inform the voter. If the voter does not resolve the discrepancy, the recorder must not send the voter a ballot and must remove them from the list.

This bill, as introduced on February 4, 2021, would make adjustments to the process for removing deceased voters from the voter registration list and would broaden the definition of misdemeanor electioneering so that more speech and conduct are covered. Specifically, the bill would:

Although the new database would not be public, the bill would shift election authority to the Legislature by giving it the ability to access it to confirm deceased voters are being removed from the system.

The existing misdemeanor prohibits a person from knowingly, intentionally, by verbal expression and in order to induce or compel another person to vote in a particular manner or to refrain from voting, expressing support for or opposition to a candidate who appears on the ballot in that election, a ballot question that appears on the ballot in that election or a political party with one or more candidates who appear on the ballot in that election.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to elections, relates to legislative session, relates to procedures manual.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 4, 2021, would shift election authority to the Legislature in two ways.

First, the bill would require the Legislature to come into special session after every regular primary and regular general election. In the special session, the legislature may conduct hearings and receive evidence relating to any irregularities that occur during and after the election regarding voting, tallying the votes, and any other election procedures. The Legislature may vote to reject or confirm the preliminary results of the election. If the Legislature rejects the preliminary results, it would forward its findings to the office of the attorney general for possible civil or criminal action.

Second, the bill would eliminate the Governor's and Attorney General's ability to approve the Secretary of State's election procedures manual, instead allowing them to simply review it. After their review, the manual would be sent to the Legislature for its approval. The manual is reviewed and potentially revised every two years. Under existing law, the process ends December 31 of odd-numbered years. The bill would have the Legislature take part starting no later than the second Monday in January of the even-numbered year.

This bill, as introduced on February 8, 2021, would create automatic voter registration, create same-day registration, improve online registration, expand early voting, include Native Americans in voting location decisions, change the deadline to return an early (absentee) ballot to postmarked by Election Day, expand the existing early ballot cure process, and make multiple changes to campaign finance law. Specifically, this bill would:

  • Create automatic registration at DMV for people who provide proof of citizenship during their DMV transaction, and automatic registration updates at DMV for registered voters regardless of whether they provide citizenship documents as part of their transaction. The DMV information would be sent to the Secretary of State, who after screening the information for disenfranchised people and participants in the address confidentiality program, would send the information to county recorders. The recorders would then send an opt-out notice to potential registrants and potentially updated registrants, who would have 14 days from the date of mailing to return their responses. In addition, the Secretary of State would be charged with evaluating other agencies as source agencies for automatic registration. Source agencies would be required to accept Tribal ID numbers and non-traditional addresses. DMV and other source agencies would be required, upon receiving paper voter registration applications, to return them within five days to the appropriate county recorder. Finally, the Secretary would be required to compile and publicly distribute annual reports on the effectiveness of automatic voter registration.
  • Protect ineligible people who are automatically registered to vote from criminal prosecution unless the ineligible people acted intentionally to register while ineligible. Failing to return the opt-out card would not count as intentional action to register while ineligible. In addition, ineligible people automatically registered could not be prosecuted for voting unless they attempted to vote while knowing they were not eligible.
  • Create same-day registration during early voting and on Election Day. People would be required to prove residency as part of registration. Arizona's voter ID law would apply to the act of voting. If registration is confirmed real time, the voter would cast a regular ballot. If not, they would vote provisionally. Registration must be confirmed or rejected in time to allow the provisional ballots to count.
  • Require counties to involve Native American tribes in their jurisdiction to participate in drawing precincts, siting early voting locations, vote centers and polling places, and require counties to site at least one of each on Native land unless the tribe has no residents of the county.
  • Expand early voting by allowing early voting locations to remain open through 5 p.m. the day before the election. Under existing law, early voting ends at 5 p.m. on the Friday before the election.
  • Change the early (absentee) ballot return deadline to postmarked by Election Day and received within five business days afterward, instead of the close polls on Election Day.
  • Change the existing statutory cure process to include missing signatures as well as mismatched signatures, and for ballots received after Election Day but within the postmark-based deadline, set the cure process deadline from the date the ballot was received. Under existing regulation, missing signatures may be cured through the close of polls, and under existing statute mismatched signatures may be cured through the fifth business day after the election.
  • Prohibit ID requirements for returning an early ballot by personal delivery that do not apply to returning it by mail.
  • Change online registration to enable it to be completed without a driver's license or state ID, with a nontraditional address, and with any type of proof of citizenship accepted by the state.
  • Eliminate the 29-day-before-Election Day residency requirement, and require only that a registrant be a resident.
  • Revise the voter registration form to clarify that people who do not prove citizenship may be "federal only" voters.
  • Change the list maintenance program relating to address changes so that mailings based on change of address data no longer trigger inactive status. A voter would still be given inactive status if election mail is returned as undeliverable and the voter does not respond to a follow up notice.

Make numerous changes to campaign finance law.

This bill, as amended June 24, 2021, is primarily about appropriating moneys as part of the state budget. However, a few provisions address election law relating to voter list maintenance, voter registration, election crimes, and the allocation of election authority. Specifically, as amended the bill would:

  • Shift election authority relating to voter list maintenance away from the Secretary of State and give it to the Attorney General (A.G.) and the Legislature by:
    • Requiring the Secretary of State to provide access to the statewide voter registration database to a person designated by the Legislature, and to the election integrity unit of the A.G.'s office. These people would use their access to determine if the Secretary's list maintenance procedures for "federal only" voters comply with federal law. If their analysis determines that ineligible voters are on the list, the Secretary would be required notify the appropriate county recorder to remove them. The appointed people would report on their findings to the Legislature, Attorney General, and the Secretary.
  • Shift election authority to the Legislature and others by giving them oversight of the Secretary of State and county recorder voter registration and other processes, by:
    • Requiring each county recorder to report annually to the Legislature on their procedures regarding "federal only" voters, including the number of "federal only" voters in the county, the number that subsequently had their citizenship confirmed and became fully registered voters, and the number who were found ineligible and removed from the list. In addition, the recorders would be required to include a description of the obstacles to obtaining documentary proof of citizenship sufficient to convert federal-only voters to fully eligible voters.
    • Requiring the auditor general to review the law and processes used by Maricopa and Pima Counties for maintaining the county early voting lists, and the voter registration lists. The auditor general would also be required to review the law and processes related to the statewide voter registration list.
    • Requiring disclosures relating to certain voter registration activities. These are new provisions not in the previous version of the bill. Specifically, the bill would require the Secretary of State and each county recorder to (1) post on their public websites a list of each event at which they offer voter registration services within twenty-four hours after the event, and (2) report to the auditor general their total expenditures on voter registration programs and events, and describe the programs, noting whether they attended and whether they used any third-party data to conduct the programs. The auditor general would then report on this cumulative information to the Legislature and the Secretary of State.
  • Shift election authority by requiring the Attorney General and the county attorney to investigate and prosecute anyone who is ineligible and knowingly registers to vote.
  • Shift election authority related to lawsuits away from the Secretary of State and gives it to the Attorney General. These provisions are modified, but the substance is largely unchanged. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Declare that, as a general matter, the Attorney General represents the state with regard to defending state election laws, so that if the Attorney General and the Secretary of State disagree, the Attorney General represents the state.
    • Clarify that specifically, through January 2, 2023, the attorney general speaks for the state in all election litigation and may intervene on behalf of the state at any stage, regardless of whether any state agency, any political subdivision or any officer or employee of this state or any state agency or political subdivision is, or seeks to become, a party. In addition, among state officials, the Attorney General has the sole authority to direct the defense of the laws.

The bill would also:

  • Designate the Senate government committee to review the findings of the senate audit of the 2020 general election in Maricopa county and recommend legislation to the president of the senate based on the findings of the audit. This is a new provision not in the previous version of the bill.

The Department would return completed paper applications to the Secretary of State, who would then send them to the relevant county recorder.   • Require the Secretary to ask the U.S. Election Assistance Commission to include on the federal registration form Arizona's state-specific instructions to provide proof of citizenship. Create an election integrity fund to help county recorders pay for election security, cybersecurity and post-election hand tabulations. This is a new provision not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require ballots to be printed with certain anti-fraud measures. This is a new provision not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Create a task force to investigate campaign finance implications of certain social media company actions.

This bill, as enacted on July 9, 2021:

  • Prohibits election officials from delivering a mail ballot to a voter who has not requested one, except where a voter is on the active early voters list or an election is already authorized by law to occur by mail. Existing statutory law required voters to request a mail ballot, but did not include an express prohibition on officials issuing ballots without a voter's request. In 2020, an Arizona state court found an implied prohibition against doing so, when the state Attorney General challenged the Maricopa County recorder's intention to send mail ballots to voters without a request during the Covid-19 pandemic. The court issued a temporary restraining order, preventing the mailing of unrequested ballots.
  • Creates a new felony offense for an election official knowingly violating the prohibition on unauthorized delivery of mail ballots without a voter's request.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to elections, relates to state authority, relates to infringement, relates to opposition.
VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as adopted on April 7, 2021, declares that the Arizona Legislature opposes federal regulation of elections generally, and H.R. 1 in particular. Specifically, the resolution declares:

  • "That the Members of the Legislature oppose any attempt by the federal government to usurp, or otherwise interfere with, the state legislative sovereign authority over the management, control and administration of elections."

  • "That the Members of the Legislature oppose H.R. 1 and any subsequent enactment of the terms of this proposal and implore the Members of the United States House of Representatives and the United States Senate to oppose the same."

    Last updated April 9, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to recounts, relates to requests, relates to procedures, relates to audits.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on March 24, 2021, was not substantively changed. As amended on March 2, this bill shifts election authority by authorizing certain state officials and individuals to request recounts when an automatic recount is not triggered. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Authorize the Attorney General, Secretary of State, and Legislative Council, to request recounts of one or more precincts, vote centers, counties, other jurisdictions, or the entire election, if they make the request within five days of the completion of the canvass. Special district elections and other narrow election types are excluded. The state would be required to pay for the recount. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

Allow individuals to seek a similar recount, however, the individual would be required to post bond to pay for the recount. No criteria, such as being a registered voter or Arizona resident, limit which individuals would have this power. This is a new provision not in the previous version of the bill.

Last updated November 1, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to elections manual, relates to legislative council.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on February 24, 2021, would shift authority over elections away from the Secretary of State and the Governor, and give it to the Legislative Council by changing the approval process for the Elections Procedures Manual. Under existing law, the Secretary issues an Election Procedures Manual to "achieve and maintain the maximum degree of correctness, impartiality, uniformity and efficiency on the procedures for early voting and voting, and of producing, distributing, collecting, counting, tabulating and storing ballots." The Governor and Attorney General must approve the manual, which has the force of law.

This bill would change the approval process, eliminating the role of the Governor, and giving oversight duties to the legislative council, which is a committee of 13 legislators. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have eliminated the Attorney General's approval role as well and instead required the approval of a regulatory review committee normally focused on business regulations.

Last updated August 25, 2021.

This bill, as amended on February 16, 2021, was not substantively changed. As introduced on January 11, 2021, this bill would make it easier for county election officials to remove voters from the permanent early voter list, which is what Arizona calls the list of voters who receive a ballot in the mail for every election. Specifically, the county would be required to send a confirmation notice to voters on the list who do not cast their mail ballot in two consecutive primaries and general elections involving a federal, state or legislative office. If a voter does not respond to the notice within 30 days, the bill would require the county election official to remove them from the list.

Last Updated February 24, 2021

VRLANALYSIS:
On March 25, 2021, this bill was amended by striking the previous version and substituting a completely new bill. The new bill creates ways to remove voters from the permanent early (mail) voter list (PEVL), new ways to cancel voter registrations, and creates a new felony. Specifically, as amended, the new provisions of the bill would:

  • Remove people from the PEVL if:
    • The ballot is returned as undeliverable. Under existing law, the county clerk has an obligation to attempt to contact the voter at their new address to update their registration before making their registration inactive and removing them from the PEVL. The bill would eliminate the requirement that the clerk make this effort to update the voter's address.
    • Someone returns the unopened ballot and asserts the voter does not live at that address.
    • The county recorder confirms the voter has moved out of the county. The bill does not define what constitutes confirmation.
  • Cancel a voter's registration if the county recorder confirms the voter has registered to vote in another county. The bill does not define what constitutes confirmation.

Create a new felony for knowingly assisting another person who resides in another state in voting, including by forwarding a ballot addressed to that person.

The previous version of the bill, which was replaced by the above provisions, would have created a new felony offense for registering to vote without intending to remain in the state.

Last Updated April 1, 2021

This bill, as amended on June 21, 2021, would:

  • Require the county recorder to give the county attorney or the Attorney General, for the prosecutors' review and possible investigation, materials relating to the ballots that were rejected for mismatch signatures because the voter did not correct the signature by the cure deadline. This is a modified provision, in that which specific documents must be provided are slightly different, but the policy of investigating voters who didn't cure their ballots remains.
  • Require the county recorder, on or before February 1 of each year, to report on all the referrals to the Governor and the Speaker of the House, and provide a copy of the report to the Secretary of State. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Change the voter registration process at the DMV to facilitate cancelling a new state resident's registration in the new resident's prior state. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Create two new misdemeanors to punish election workers. One applies to violations of certain procedures relating to tabulation equipment operation and chain of custody of the equipment, and the other to proceedings at the central counting location. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require election officials to allow lawfully appointed observers to witness more aspects of the process, namely:
    • the connection and removal of any removable external device, removable data storage device or computer screen until the election data is officially recorded or the removable device is stored securely. The observers would have to be given a "reasonable view", which the bill defines as "a view from a distance that does not impede or interfere with the performance of the election worker's duties and that does not allow the disclosure of sensitive data or information." This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • all data storage devices used to account for original and duplicate ballots while the device is not securely locked and stored. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • all proceedings at the counting center generally, "to the fullest extent possible", again with a "reasonable view." This is a new provision.
  • Allow the officer in charge of the election to establish security procedures for the observation of each tabulating process, which may include limiting the number of observers in each room, and prohibiting observers from restricted areas and official county vehicles. This is a new provision.

Make changes to election law in areas that Voting Rights Lab does not track, such as:

  • requiring tabulation results be stored within the U.S. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • allowing Election Day voters who vote regular ballots to get a receipt for their ballot, either from the voting machine after submitting their ballot into it or from the elections official, that states whether the ballot will be tabulated on site or later, at the central counting location. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • specifying chain of custody rules relating to certain voting machine equipment. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • requiring workers involved in ballot processing and counting to sign an affidavit, and workers involved with ballot duplication to attest to the accuracy of their efforts. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 27, 2021, would facilitate the registration of eligible, incarcerated voters upon their release from confinement, provide on site early voting for people incarcerated in county jails, and provide mail ballot assistance for people incarcerated in county jails. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the state department of corrections or a county jail to give every person who is otherwise eligible to register to vote and who is in their custody the opportunity to register to vote on release from confinement. The entities would be required to give the eligible returning citizen a voter registration form, and transmit completed voter registration forms to the appropriate county recorder within five days after receipt.
  • Require counties with a population of more than 300,000, to establish a voting center at the county jail for persons who are temporarily in custody and awaiting trial. The voting center would enable any person who is otherwise eligible to vote in that county to receive the appropriate ballot for that person's residence and would operate as otherwise provided by law. The bill does not specify whether the voting center must open during early voting, on Election Day, or both.

  • Require county recorders to provide a request for an early ballot to each qualified, eligible voter who is in the custody of the county jail or the state department of corrections in their county.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 26, 2021, would automatically restore all returning citizens' voting eligibility upon completion of probation or absolute discharge from imprisonment ("final discharge"). Under existing law, only people convicted of a single felony who have fully paid restitution are automatically restored to voting eligibility upon final discharge. People convicted of more than one felony or who have not paid restitution in full must wait two years and then apply to restore their voting eligibility. In addition, the bill would require the sentencing judge to inform the defendant when their voting eligibility would be restored.

Last updated January 27, 2021.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 27, 2021, would give the Legislature new access to election data from county recorders and boards of supervisors. Specifically, the bill would allow the Senate President, the Speaker of the House, or if the legislature is in session, the majority of either house, to gain access to or copies of election data, including election results and other election records, and election equipment, systems, and facilities, after the tabulation of all ballots is completed and before issuance of the official canvass for the county.

Last updated November 1, 2021.

This bill, as enacted on May 11, 2021, removes voters from the permanent early voting list for failure to vote, and renames the list the "active early voting list." Specifically, the new law:

  • Qualifies a voter for removal from the permanent early voting list if the "voter fails to vote an early ballot in all elections for two consecutive election cycles." This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill provided for potential removal after not voting in "four consecutive elections," with elections defined as "any primary or general election for which there was a federal, statewide or legislative race on the ballot." Existing law expressly provided that failure to vote is not a ground from removal from the permanent early voting list.
  • Requires county recorders to issue removal notices by January 15 of each odd-numbered year to all voters who qualified for removal. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill required the notice to be sent by December 1 of each even-numbered year, to voters who failed to vote in "both the primary and general election for the two most recent general elections for federal office."
  • Gives voters 90 days to respond to the notice, or be removed from the list. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill gave voters 30 days to respond.

  • Changes all references to the "permanent early voting list" in the election code by deleting the word "permanent" and replacing it with "active." This a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have only removed the word "permanent".

Last Updated May 14, 2021

This bill, enacted on April 14, 2021, requires that during any of Arizona's mail ballot elections, replacement ballot centers must open at 6 a.m. Previous law required centers to be open until 7 p.m., but does not specify an opening time. In addition, the bill clarified that if there are insufficient people in a given precinct who are willing to serve as poll workers, anyone who is a registered Arizona voter may serve. Previous law simply noted that people from outside the precinct may serve if there are not enough workers from the precinct.

Other provisions of this bill make non-substantive and administrative changes to candidate petitions, uncontested elections, the timing of various local election processes, ballot name order, and similar issues.

Last Updated April 16, 2021

Ballots returned by mail would be rejected and could not be counted.

This bill, as enacted on May 5, 2021, requires ballot delivery envelopes to have an instruction to the effect of, "If the addressee does not reside at this address, mark the unopened envelope "return to sender" and deposit it in the United States mail." This provision was in the previous versions of the bill. Amendments prior to the bill's enactment made no substantive changes to its provisions.

This bill, as amended on February 22, 2021, was not substantively changed. As introduced on January 29, 2021, the bill would shorten early voting, create a new, more complex deadline for early (absentee) ballots returned by mail, and enable voters who surrender their early ballot at the polls to vote a regular ballot at the polls. Specifically, this bill would:

  • Direct county recorders to begin mailing requested early ballots to voters 22 days before the election, finishing up not later than 19 days before, instead of mailing ballots 27 through 24 days before the election as existing law provides. This change would not only give voters fewer days to complete and return their ballots, it would shorten the in-person early voting period because in-person early voting begins the day ballots are mailed. Thus this bill would require early voting to begin 22 days before the election rather than 27 days before the election.
  • Create a new, more complex ballot return deadline for voters who choose to return their early ballots by mail. The bill would require the ballot to be postmarked by the Thursday before Election Day, and received by close of polls on Election Day. Mailed ballots with later postmarks, even if received by the close of polls on Election Day would not count. Similarly, ballots postmarked by the Thursday before Election Day and received after the close of polls would not count. Existing law simply requires early ballots to be returned by the close of polls. Ballots returned by hand would continue to have the close-of-polls deadline.

  • Allow voters who surrender their early ballot at the polls to cast a regular, rather than a provisional, ballot. Existing law requires people who applied for early ballots to vote provisionally in person, even if they surrender their early ballot.

Last Updated March 8, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to elections, relates to hand count, relates to legislative auditor.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 29, 2021 would allow the Legislature to request a complete hand count of ballots in up to three contested races by an independent auditor of the Legislature's choosing at any time after completion of the unofficial returns and before the county canvass. 

The bill would require the Legislature to make its request in writing, and would require the county board of supervisors and the county recorder to cooperate with the independent auditor. The Legislature could exercise this power during regular primaries or regular general elections.

Last updated November 1, 2021.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 1, 2021, would

  • Require the hand count to be live streamed, and continue to allow official observers to also film the proceedings. The bill would repeal an existing rule expressly allowing election officials to stop the observers filming or remove the observers if their filming or conduct interferes or is disruptive.
  • Prohibit anything from occurring at the counting center unless observed by equal numbers of designated observers from each political party on the ballot, unless the county chair of the political party and each of that party's candidates waives that party's and candidate's presence.
  • Widen the margin for an automatic recount and for allowing a candidate-requested recount, and providing for the allocation of recount costs.

Provide the hand count be done by equal representatives of the political parties on the ballot unless the party waives participation or its candidate is not within the statutory recount margin in any race.

HISTORY: {"date":"02/03/2021","summary":"Additionally referred to SENATE Committee on RULES","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 1, 2021, would expand automatic voting eligibility restoration, expand early voting, improve the cure process for missing ballot signatures, allow ballots cast after presenting ID to be excluded from signature matching, and make other changes to Arizona election law. Specifically, this bill would:

  • Automatically restore voting eligibility to all people convicted of felonies who paid their restitution and completed incarceration, parole and/or probation. Under existing law, only people convicted of a single felony are eligible for automatic restoration. People convicted of more than one felony, or people who have not paid their restitution, must apply for voting eligibility restoration.
  • Expand early voting by lengthening the early voting period through 5 p.m. on the Monday before the election. Under existing law, early voting ends at 5 p.m. on the Friday before the election. The bill does not mandate that early voting be offered on the Saturday or Sunday. As a conforming change, the bill would eliminate the existing emergency voting procedure that allows people to vote between 5 p.m. Friday before the election and 5 p.m. Monday before the election.
  • Expand the special election board available to ill or disabled voters by making it available to those in pretrial detention.
  • Potentially expand early voting by requiring county recorders to open early voting at their offices and as many other locations as required by the Election Procedures Manual. The current edition of the manual does not require additional locations.
  • Provide that early ballots cast in person after presenting the voter ID required to cast in-person ballots do not need to be additionally verified by signature comparison. Under existing law, the signatures of all early ballots are verified, although those cast in person after showing ID "should generally not be invalidated based solely on an allegedly inconsistent signature absent other evidence that the signatures were not made by the same person." Relatedly, the bill would end the ability of challengers to challenge the sufficiency of the envelope of an early ballot cast in-person after the voter presented ID.
  • Expand the existing cure process for mismatch signatures to missing signatures, which extends the deadline to cure a missing signature past the close of polls on Election Day to 5 p.m. on the fifth day after the election.
  • Facilitate recruitment of election workers by allowing people to be trained as one through August 1 of a general election year. Under existing law, training must be complete by January 1 of a general election year.
  • Require provisional ballot envelopes to require all the information needed to register to vote, and if the provisional ballot is rejected because the voter is not registered, the information must be used to register them.

  • Allow international election observers, impose security rules on electronic poll books, allow voting equipment to be tested 10 days before use in early balloting, rather than seven, and require unofficial return updates sent to the Secretary of State to include information about ballots remaining to be counted.

Last Updated March 10, 2021

Anyone who registered within 28 days of Election Day, including as part of same day registration, must cast a provisional ballot. The bill would not allow a person to vote in a partisan primary held less than 29 days after they register. Under existing law, registration closes 29 days before Election Day.

  • Create automatic voter registration at DMV by providing that the information from an application or renewal of a driver's license, state ID, update of either be transmitted to the county recorder, who then sends the potential registrant an opt-out notice. If the voter does not opt out within 21 days of the notice being sent, the voter will be registered. Finally, the bill provides that an ineligible person registered through this method would not be guilty of false swearing or false registration.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to elections, relates to polling places, relates to standards.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 1, 2021, would require the Secretary of State, county recorders and other election officials to meet annually to consider and develop standards and procedures for the following:

  • Ensuring that a voter does not wait more than one hour to vote at a polling place or voting center.
  • Determining the appropriate number of polling places for an election and jurisdiction.
  • Ensuring that polling places and voting centers are established in locations that provide equal access for all persons, including ensuring access for persons who use public transportation or who have no transportation and for persons with disabilities.
  • Determining the appropriate level of staffing, the appropriate amount and type of equipment or systems used in each polling place or voting center and the number of ballots and other supplies and maintaining sufficient reserves of equipment, systems, ballots and personnel.
  • Providing timely and accurate information regarding polling place and voting center locations and hours of operation and ensuring the information is as broadly disseminated as possible.

  • Developing best practices for preventing and stopping intimidation or harassment of voters and potential voters.

    Last updated March 10, 2021.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on May 26, 2021, creates an ID number requirement to validate a mail ballot, sharply limits the types of ID that may be used, and adds supplying a missing or inconsistent ID number to the types of ballot defects that may be remedied using the existing cure process. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require voters to add their birthdate and add their driver's license number, their state nonoperating identification license number, or the last four digits of their Social Security number to their ballot certificate. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have allowed a voter to use their driver's license number or their voter registration number.
  • Enable a voter who failed to include an ID number, or who provided one that does not match their record, to address the deficiency using the existing cure process for mismatch signatures. This is a new provision not in the previous version of the bill.

  • Provide certain special districts with non-substantive exceptions relating to ballot envelope requirements. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

    When the bill was introduced, it would have required county recorders to send each voter a voter registration card every two years. That provision was amended out of the bill on March 4, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on February 1, 2021, would automatically restore voting eligibility to all people convicted of felonies after they complete incarceration, parole and probation. Everyone else must apply for eligibility restoration, and must wait two years before applying. BILLSUMMARY: Relates to elections, relates to Joint Legislative Audit Committee recount and audit authority.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 1, 2021, would allow a majority of the Joint Legislative Audit Committee to order an audit or a recount of a legislative or statewide election, including for presidential electors and congressional offices. 

If the Committee orders an audit, the custodian of the items requested in the audit must make them available to the Committee. The bill does not identify what would be audited or how it would be done. If the Committee orders a recount, it would be conducted according to normal recount procedures and the Secretary of State would be required to certify to the superior court the facts requiring the recount.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to voter registration databases, relates to death records, relates to conduct of elections, appropriates monies.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on March 29, 2021, would modify the voter registration list maintenance process for removing deceased voters, and would impose security measures for ballots, relating to the paper they are printed on and what precisely is printed. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the state department of health to send both the secretary of state and the county recorders monthly and annual lists of recently deceased people containing each decedent's name, date of birth, date of death, Social Security number (if available), usual legal residence, and, if available, father's name or mother's maiden name. Both the secretary and the recorders would be required to use the information to cancel voter registrations, although the bill does not specify which data points must match to confirm the match. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have required the secretary to use these death records to create a database county recorders could use to match records against their databases. Under existing law, only the secretary receives the specified list, and after identifying matches, cancels the registration in the statewide database and notifies the relevant county recorder to cancel the deceased voter's registration. Although existing statutes do not specify what data points must match, the December 2019 Election Procedures Manual, which has the force of law, requires cancellation if "if the first three letters of the first and last name, DOB, and SSN4 match in both records", and requires county recorders to investigate to confirm a "true match" "if the first three letters of the first and last name and DOB match in both records or there is a "hard match" against more than one existing registrant record."

  • Identify 10 ballot printing tactics to counter ballot fraud, and require the use of at least three of them to be considered "ballot fraud countermeasures". This is a new provision not in the previous version of the bill.

    Last updated March 30, 2021.

As a result of litigation, this law was deemed unconstitutional by the Arizona Supreme Court on state constitutional grounds relating to the subjects covered in the law, not about the merits of specific provisions. As a result, these election law provisions did not take effect.

This bill, as enacted June 30, 2021, primarily focuses on appropriations for the state budget. Among its non-budgetary provisions, the bill makes various changes to voter registration, voter list maintenance, prosecution of election crimes, and allocation of certain election authority.

In provisions slightly modified from the previous version, the bill:

  • Shifts election authority related to lawsuits away from the Secretary of State and gives it to the Attorney General, by:
    • Declaring that, as a general matter, the Attorney General has the authority to defend state election laws, and deeming the Attorney General's position "paramount" when there is disagreement with the Secretary of State or any other government official as to their defense.
    • Expressly providing that through January 2, 2023, the Attorney General "speaks for" the state in all election litigation and may intervene on behalf of the state at any stage, regardless of whether any state agency, any political subdivision, or any officer or employee of this state or any state agency or political subdivision is, or seeks to become, a party. In addition, among state officials, the bill provides that the Attorney General has the sole authority to direct the defense of the laws. Through January 1, 2023, the person elected Secretary of State is a Democrat, and the person elected Attorney General is a Republican. The people who will fill those roles after that date will be decided in November, 2022.
  • Shifts election authority relating to voter list maintenance away from the Secretary of State and give it to the Attorney General and the Legislature by:
    • Requiring the Secretary of State to provide access to the statewide voter registration database to an entity designated by the Legislature, and to the election integrity unit of the Attorney General's office, to determine whether the Secretary's list maintenance procedures for "federal only" voters comply with federal law. The appointed entity must report its findings to the Legislature, Attorney General, and the Secretary. If the analysis determines that ineligible voters are on the registration list, the Secretary must notify the appropriate county recorder, who must then remove them.
  • Shift election authority to the Legislature and others by giving them oversight of the Secretary of State and county recorder voter registration and other processes, by:
    • Requiring each county recorder to report annually to the Legislature on their procedures regarding "federal only" voters, including the number of "federal only" voters in the county, the number that subsequently had their citizenship confirmed and became fully registered voters, and the number who were found ineligible and removed from the list. In addition, the recorders would be required to include a description of the obstacles to obtaining documentary proof of citizenship sufficient to convert federal-only voters to fully eligible voters.
    • Requiring the Auditor General, who reports to the Legislature, to review the law and processes for maintaining the statewide voter registration database, the county early voting lists, and the voter registration lists for counties with a population of 1 million or more (i.e., Maricopa and Pima Counties).
    • Requiring disclosures relating to certain voter registration activities. These are new provisions not in the previous version of the bill. Specifically, the bill would require the Secretary of State and each county recorder to (1) post on their public websites a list of each event at which they offer voter registration services within twenty-four hours after the event, and (2) report to the Auditor General their total expenditures on voter registration programs and events, and describe the programs, noting whether they attended and whether they used any third-party data to conduct the programs. The Auditor General must report this cumulative information to the Legislature and the Secretary of State.
  • Requires the Attorney General and county attorneys to investigate and prosecute anyone who is ineligible and knowingly registers to vote.
  • Requires the Secretary to request the U.S. Election Assistance Commission to include on the federal registration form Arizona's state-specific instructions to provide proof of citizenship.
  • Requires the Arizona Game and Fish Department to offer voter registration services to applicants for a hunting, fishing, or trapping license, and to include a link to the online voter registration portal on its online application site. The Department must return completed paper applications to the Secretary of State, who must then send them to the relevant county recorder.
  • Designates "a special committee on the election audit," within the Senate government committee, to review the findings of the senate audit of the 2020 general election in Maricopa County and recommend legislation to the president of the Senate based on its findings.
  • Creates an "election integrity fund" to pay county recorder expenses for election security, cybersecurity, and post-election hand tabulations.
  • Requires paper ballots to include certain specific anti-fraud features. This is a new provision not in the previous version of the bill.

Creates a joint task force on unreported in-kind political contributions to investigate, among other things, campaign finance implications of certain social media company activities.

Note: One provision relating to litigation-related election authority was amended out of the bill before its enactment. It would have prohibited the Attorney General from giving the Secretary of State legal advice through June 30, 2023, and would have allowed the Secretary to hire an in-house attorney.

Last Updated December 9, 2021

This bill, as enacted on June 29, 2021:

  • Requires party-appointed challengers and party representatives to be Arizona residents and to be registered voters. Existing law did not impose limitations on who could be appointed.

This bill, as introduced on June 10, 2021, would criminalize as a felony mailing ballots to voters who did not apply for them. The bill would nonetheless explicitly allow ballots to be mailed pursuant to the already-allowed types of mail ballot elections, and to voters on the active early voters list. In effect, this provision would prevent additional types of elections from being held as mail ballot elections.

Before this bill was introduced, the Arizona Legislature passed a bill (HB 2792) with the identical substance, but it was vetoed by Governor Ducey along with many other bills. After this bill's introduction, the Legislature later passed, and Governor Ducey signed, HB 2905, which also has the same substance.

Although an application is required by existing law, during the 2020 presidential primary the Maricopa County recorder attempted to mail ballots to voters who did not apply for them to facilitate their avoiding exposure to Covid-19. The Attorney General sued and the recorder was prevented from sending the ballots.

Last Updated August 24, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to conduct of elections, relates to voters' rights.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 1, 2021 would create a ballot measure allowing voters to enact a voter's bill of rights. The voter's bill of rights would provide that: The voters in this state have the right to:

  • Register to vote without facing unnecessary barriers. (Voter reg-other)
  • Participate in fair elections in which elected officials are not choosing their own voters. (Redistricting-other)
  • Vote by mail or in person and know that their votes will count. (Absentee-Other)
  • Have equal access to the ballot no matter where in this state they live, what language they speak or what physical abilities they possess.
  • Propose and enact laws when elected officials fail to act.

  • Know that when they elect someone, the elected official will work for the voters, not donors or lobbyists.

    Last updated February 3, 2021.

HISTORY: {"date":"09/27/2021","summary":"Chaptered by Secretary of State.  Chapter No. 2021-312","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, enacted on September 27, 2021, makes permanent certain changes to California election law that were put in place for the November 2020 general election only, extends the receipt deadline for mailed ballots, and requires all counties to offer ballot drop boxes. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires counties to mail ballots to all active voters for each election, regardless of whether the county is otherwise conducting a traditional election with precinct polling places. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires election officials to permit all voters to use the certified remote accessible vote by mail system. Under existing law, only disabled, military, or overseas voters were permitted to use the remote voting system. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires the Secretary of State to maintain a comprehensive ballot tracking system and requires all counties to use the system or an equivalent. The Secretary's system must be accessible to voters with disabilities, and it must allow voters to receive tracking information by email or text. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires counties that do not hold mail ballot elections pursuant to the Voter's Choice Act to offer ballot drop boxes. Existing law permitted, but did not require, use of drop boxes. Counties must administer drop boxes as follows:
    • One ballot drop box per 30,000 voters or two drop boxes, whichever is greater.
    • Notwithstanding the general rule, at least one drop box for a jurisdiction with fewer than 30,000 registered voters. The county elections official must make a reasonable effort to provide a vote by mail ballot drop-off location in the jurisdiction where the election is held.
    • All boxes must be located as near as possible to established public transportation routes, and be open at least during regular business hours beginning not less than 28 days before Election Day. On Election Day, at least one vote by mail ballot drop-off location must be an exterior drop box that is available for a minimum of 12 hours per day.
      These provisions are modified from the previous version of the bill, which did not allow counties to set up only one drop box in jurisdictions with less than 30,000 voters.
  • Allows counties that have the necessary technology to begin processing mail ballots 29 days before the election. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law allows counties with the appropriate technology to process ballots beginning 15 business days before the election.

  • Changes the ballot receipt deadline by providing that ballots mailed on or before Election Day are timely if received by the seventh day after the election. If a ballot has no indication when it was mailed, but the voter's affidavit is dated on or before Election Day and it was timely received, it will count, as well. Existing law provided for timely receipt for only three days after Election Day. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

Last Updated December 29, 2021

HISTORY: {"date":"09/27/2021","summary":"Chaptered by Secretary of State.  Chapter No. 2021-314","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on September 27, 2021, establishes deadlines for the transmission of voter registration information from the Department of Motor Vehicles to the Secretary of State for the purpose of automatic voter registration and provides a program quality control regime. The bill:

  • Requires the Department of Motor Vehicles to transmit voter registration information to the Secretary of State within ten days after the Department accepts the completed driver's license or ID card application or renewals, or change of address form. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires the Department to transmit registration information on forms accepted within five days of the voter registration deadline for a state or federal election to be transmitted to the Secretary within five days of the Department's receipt. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

  • Creates a standard for determining when a registration form is complete for purposes of triggering these deadlines, namely, identifying that:

    • people do not need to pick a party, choose or reject becoming a permanent mail ballot voter, or indicate a language preference, for the application to be complete.
    • the Department must approve the registrant's identity documentation for the application to be complete.

    This standard and timeline are new provisions not in the previous version of the bill.


  • Creates a rule for the Department to submit completed registration forms when the documentation underlying the transaction with the Department is incomplete for the purpose of the Department transaction. Namely, the Department must transmit a completed registration if the reason the transaction paperwork is incomplete is unrelated to:

    • the Department's approval of the registrant's identity documentation, or
    • the ability of an elections official to prevent duplicate voter registrations or preregistrations, to assess the eligibility of the applicant, or to administer voter registration, preregistration, and other elections procedures.

    This rule is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill did not address identity documentation, only the election official's ability to appropriately process the application.


  • Delays implementation of the deadlines for transmission of voter registration applications and the requirement of transmitting complete applications when the underlying transaction documentation is incomplete until the "Digital eXperience Platform project" is completed or July 1, 2025, whichever is first. This is a new provision not in the previous version of the bill.
  • States that is the intent of the Legislature that the Department continue its best practice of sending notice to voters when there is a delay in processing completed voter registration applications, and that the notices continue to provide information about alternative options for submitting a voter registration application. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill specified particular notice and timeline rules for the Department when the Department is not able to transmit the information within the statutory deadlines.
  • Requires the Department to accept forms for the purpose of transmitting voter registration information even if the Department cannot otherwise accept the form due to an issue unrelated to the Department's ability to transmit voter registration information. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires the Department to designate an employee as the National Voter Registration Act coordinator, who has oversight and quality control duties. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

  • Creates a task force to review implementation of the program and issue recommendations for its improvement. The task force would meet at least quarterly and issue recommendations at least annually. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

Last Updated September 27, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Establishes the Citizens Redistricting Commission in the County of Riverside, which would be charged with adjusting the boundary lines of the districts of the Board of Supervisors of the County of Riverside. States the commission would consist of 14 members who meet specified qualifications. Requires the commission to adjust the boundaries of the supervisorial districts and adopt a redistricting plan, which would become effective 30 days following its submission to the county elections official.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 19, 2021, would create an independent redistricting commission for Riverside County to draw the county government districts and adopt them. In drawing the districts, the commission must consider set criteria, hold numerous public hearings both before and after creating a draft district plan, and upon adoption a plan, issue a report explaining the basis on which the commission made its decisions in achieving compliance with the criteria. The commission would have to create districts that are:

  • Reasonably equal in population with other districts, except where deviation is required to comply with the federal Voting Rights Act of 1965 or allowable by law.
  • Geographically contiguous.
  • Respectful of the geographic integrity of any city, local neighborhood, or local community of interest in a manner that minimizes its division to the extent possible without violating the population, contiguity, and compliance with the Voting Rights Act requirements. A community of interest is a contiguous population that shares common social and economic interests that should be included within a single district for purposes of its effective and fair representation. Communities of interest do not include relationships with political parties, incumbents, or political candidates.
  • Geographically compact to the extent practicable, where compactness would not conflict with other criteria. Geographically compact would mean that nearby areas of population are not bypassed for more distant areas of population.

  • Drawn without regard to the place of residence of any incumbent or political candidate. In addition, districts cannot be drawn to favor or disadvantage an incumbent, political candidate, or political party.

    Last updated February 24, 2021.
