HISTORY: {"date":"09/27/2021","summary":"Chaptered by Secretary of State.  Chapter No. 2021-318","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on September 27, 2021, revises myriad election crimes and creates a new felony relating to unofficial drop boxes.

Note: The bill was last amended on August 26, 2021 to add provisions relating to the disclosure of gubernatorial and Secretary of State candidates' tax returns, but was not altered with regard to the provisions Voting Rights Lab tracks. The last time tracked provisions were amended was July 15, 2021. The references below to changes in provisions from previous versions reflect the changes from the July 15 amendments.

This bill, as enacted on September 27:

  • Expands the definition of "electioneering" to prohibit obstructing access to ballot drop boxes. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill. Under existing law, electioneering included loitering near drop boxes, along with other traditional electioneering activity, but the offense did not expressly include obstruction of access.
  • Expands the area in which electioneering is prohibited to 100 feet from:
    • the entrance to a building that contains a polling place, an elections official's office, or a satellite location.
    • an outdoor site at which a voter may cast or drop off a ballot, including curbside voting areas.
      This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill expanded the radius of the prohibited zone from 100 feet to 200 feet, and added drop boxes. Existing law provided a radius of 100 feet from similar locations, but did not address outside sites or curbside voting, nor did it specify that the radius is from the building entrances.
  • Expands the existing electioneering misdemeanor for "prohibited acts within specified distance of a polling place" by:
    • Applying the prohibition to outdoor sites at which a voter may cast or drop off a ballot, and specifying that the 100 feet radius begins at the entrance to protected areas. Existing law set the protected area as 100 feet of the room where voters cast ballots, did not expressly prohibit activity near outdoor sites or curbside voting, and incorporated the previous, more narrow definition of electioneering.
    • Adding new prohibited conduct to the offense, to punish the following activity within the immediate vicinity of a voter in line: soliciting a vote, speaking to the voter about marking the ballot, or disseminating electioneering information.
      This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have expanded the zone of prohibition to 200 feet from these locations, and would have included a ballot drop box as a location from which the prohibited zone extended.
  • Expands the existing voter intimidation misdemeanor for "prohibited activities within 100 feet of a polling place," by:
    • Applying the prohibition to outdoor sites at which a voter may cast or drop off a ballot, and specifying that the 100 feet radius begins at the entrance to protected areas. Existing law did not specify where the 100 foot protected area began, and did not expressly prohibit activity near outdoor sites or curbside voting
    • Prohibiting individuals from obstructing ingress, egress, or parking in protected areas, with the intent to dissuade another person from voting. Under existing law, the offense only included soliciting a vote, speaking to the voter about their vote, certain activities related to addressing voter qualifications, and recording voters entering or existing the voting place.
    • Prohibiting individuals from doing the following within the immediate vicinity of a voter on line, with intent to dissuade a voter from voting: soliciting a vote, speaking to the voter about marking the ballot, or disseminating visible or audible electioneering information. Under existing law, this offense did not address conduct directed towards voters in line.

      This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill expanded the zone of prohibition from 100 feet to 200 feet from protected locations and a ballot drop box, and did not address ingress, egress, or parking.
  • Expands a corruption of voting offense to include displaying a container for the purpose of collecting ballots, with the intent to deceive a voter into casting a ballot in an unofficial ballot box, or to direct someone to place a ballot in such a box. The bill provides that evidence of intent to deceive may include using the word "official" on the container, or otherwise fashioning the container in a way that is likely to deceive a voter into believing that the container is an official collection box that has been approved by an election official. Existing law did not address unofficial drop boxes. This provision is slightly modified from the previous version of the bill, which used different language for the newly prohibited conduct.

  • Requires the secretary of state to issue regulations detailing how notice of prohibited electioneering and "activity related to the corruption of the voting process" should be given to the public. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. "Corruption of the voting process" is the chapter of the elections penal code that includes the crimes addressed by the bill.

    A provision in the previous version of the bill has been amended out of the enacted version. That provision declared the intent of the Legislature to enact legislation that increases the penalties for operating a polling place that falsely purports to be a location established by an election official.

    The enacted bill also contains provisions related to topics that Voting Rights Lab does not track, such as candidate filing requirements.

Last Updated December 29, 2021

HISTORY: {"date":"06/28/2021","summary":"Chaptered by Secretary of State.  Chapter No. 2021-034","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on June 28, 2021, creates special procedures for elections conducted in 2021, and makes changes to recall elections. The previous version of the bill did not address election law, or addressed it only relating to aspects of recall elections that Voting Rights Lab does not track. In provisions that are new to the enacted version of the bill, the bill:

  • Allows a county that has previously conducted a mail ballot election pursuant to the Voter's Choice Act to conduct 2021 elections largely pursuant to that law, except that the county may open fewer vote centers. Specifically, counties may choose to open one vote center per 30,000 registered voters on Election Day and each of the three days prior to it, and one per 60,000 registered voters on each of the seven days before that. If the county has fewer than 60,000 registered voters, the county must open at least one vote center. Under the Voter's Choice Act counties must open one vote center per 10,000 voters on Election Day and the three days before it, and one per 50,000 each day of the week before that.

  • Allows counties that have not conducted a mail ballot election pursuant to the Voter's Choice Act to consolidate precincts in a manner that parallels what counties were allowed to do for the November 2020 election, in conjunction with mailing all active voters ballots for that election. Under existing law, all counties were required to mail active voters ballots for elections in 2021, but no provision had been made to allow counties to consolidate polling places.

    Specifically, for counties that do not conduct Voter's Choice Act mail ballot elections, the bill:


  • Allows such counties to consolidate adjacent precincts so that as many as 10,000 voters are assigned to the same voting location. A similar provision was in place for the November general election in 2020.
  • Requires counties that choose to consolidate to open the consolidated polling locations from the Saturday before Election Day through the Monday before for at least eight hours each day at regular hours convenient for voters. On the day of the election, the consolidated polling location would be open for the normal hours of 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. A similar provision was in place for the November general election in 2020.
  • Requires such counties to site the consolidated locations within one of the consolidated precincts, in an accessible location as near as possible to established public transportation routes near public transportation, and to generally distribute the consolidated locations equitably throughout the county to offer voters maximum convenience. When considering locations, the county must consider proximity to communities with historically low mail ballot usage and the factors specified in the Voter's Choice Act, to the extent data are available.
  • Requires at least three accessible voting machines at each consolidated polling place, in addition to other accessibility requirements.
  • Requires a county choosing to use this procedure to provide at least two ballot drop boxes, or one per 15,000 voters, whichever is greater. One must be outside, and open for at least 12 hours a day. One drop box inside and one outside at the same location only count as one location. A similar provision was in place for the November general election in 2020.
  • Requires counties choosing to use this process to provide at least one location, open at least during regular business hours beginning not later than 28 days before Election Day, that must provide a full range of services. A similar provision was in place for the November general election in 2020. Specifically, election officials must enable a voter at this location to:
    • return, or vote and return, their mail ballot.
    • register to vote or update the voter's voter registration, and then vote.
    • receive and vote a provisional ballot.
    • receive a replacement ballot upon verification that the county has not already received a ballot from the voter. If the county elections official is unable to determine if the voter has already returned a ballot, the county elections official may issue a provisional ballot.
    • vote a regular, provisional, or replacement ballot using accessible voting equipment that provides for a private and independent voting experience.
  • Requires counties choosing to consolidate polling places to provide public notice of proposed consolidated polling place locations and ballot drop-off locations in all legally required languages, including on the elections official's internet website, and accept public comments on the final locations. If the election is called 70 or more days before Election Day, the elections official would accept public comment for at least five days after providing the notice. If the election is called less than 70 days before Election Day, the elections official would accept public comment for at least 48 hours. The elections official would be required to consider any comments and adjust locations to the extent the official deems appropriate. Notice of any such adjustments would be immediately posted on the county election official's internet website and social media platforms.

  • Requires consolidating counties to conduct a voter education and outreach campaign in all legally required languages, notifying voters about mail ballots, early voting opportunities, accessible voting options, and where and how to remedy any voting-related problem. A similar provision was in place for the November general election in 2020.

    The bill also makes changes applicable to all counties for elections conducted in 2021. Specifically, the bill:


  • Encourages all counties to provide drive-through ballot drop-off or voting locations. If a voter is waiting in a vehicle, the voter would be considered "in line" for the purposes of keeping the polls open a sufficient time to enable them to vote.
  • Allows any county to establish a vote center, polling place, or consolidated polling place in a location whose primary purpose is the sale and dispensation of alcoholic beverages.
  • Authorizes the Secretary of State to create a specified waiver process that counties may use to avoid requirements created by the bill.
  • Allows any county with the necessary computer capability to process mail ballots, not just mail ballot envelopes, beginning 29 days before Election Day. A similar provision was in place for the November general election in 2020. Existing law permitted ballot envelopes to be processed beginning 29 days before the election, but ballots could not be processed, even by counties with appropriate computer technology, until the 15th business day before the election.
  • Allows counties to omit a mail ballot application from the voter guide mailed to all voters, since all voters are being mailed ballots. A similar provision was in place for the November general election in 2020.
  • Deems mail ballots postmarked by Election Day timely if received within seven days. Under existing law, the receipt deadline was three days after Election Day. If a ballot is not postmarked, the bill would allow it to be timely if the voter dated their signature by Election Day and it was otherwise timely received by mail. For the November 2020 general election, ballots were timely if appropriately postmarked and received within 17 days of the election.
  • Requires counties to enable all voters to use the remote accessible system for mail ballots, not just military, overseas, and disabled voters. A similar provision was in place for the November general election in 2020.

  • Makes changes to recall elections in areas not tracked by Voting Rights Lab.

Last Updated September 4, 2021

HISTORY: {"date":"09/27/2021","summary":"Chaptered by Secretary of State.  Chapter No. 2021-319","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on September 27, 2021, improves California's signature matching process for validating mail ballots, improves the process for curing ballot errors, clarifies the deadline to cure ballot errors, limits ballot observers to watching signature comparison instead of signature and address comparison, and increases transparency about ballot rejection and cure.

The July 15 amendment required the Secretary of State to evaluate the cost and necessity of requiring election officials to attempt to contact voters whose ballots need curing more than once, using information in the voter's registration record or otherwise in their possession. Based on that review, the bill allows the Secretary to issue regulations imposing such requirements. Other than that change, the July 15 amendments did not change the substance of the bill.

Specifically, as enacted, the bill:

  • Establishes new procedures and criteria for signature comparison by:
    • Creating a presumption in favor of the signatures matching, including marks made by voters instead of signatures, when the marks were made according to election law. This provision of was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law did not provide a presumption of validity or invalidity.
    • Expressly providing that an exact signature match is not required to determine validity, and specifying that signatures sharing "similar characteristics" are valid. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law did not contain this rule, however it did provide that certain differences, such as nicknames and initials, do not justify determining the signatures do not compare.
    • Requiring election officials to consider all explanations for discrepancies between signatures that are specified in regulations promulgated by the Secretary of State. Such explanations must include a variation in signature style over time and the haste with which a signature is written. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law did not have a comparable provision.
    • Forbidding election officials from reviewing or considering a voter's party, race, or ethnicity when doing signature comparisons. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law did not have a comparable provision.
    • Creating a new process for determining signatures are sufficiently different to reject the ballot and begin the cure process. If the elections official determines that the signature "possesses multiple, significant, and obvious differing characteristics when compared to all the signatures in the voter's registration record," then two more election officials must review the ballot signature. Each of those officials must find "beyond a reasonable doubt that the signature differs in multiple, significant, and obvious respects when compared to all the signatures in the voter's registration record." In that case, the ballot would be set aside and the cure process initiated. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law simply provides that if a single election official determines the signatures do not compare, the ballot is set aside and the cure process initiated.
    • Providing that if an automated signature matching technology flags a signature as not matching, it would be subject to the same additional process as a ballot flagged by the initial election official as having a non-matching signature. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law required an election official to review and verify an alleged mismatch identified by automation.
    • Adding a catchall requirement that election officials doing signature comparisons must adhere to all applicable regulations promulgated by the Secretary of State. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Improves the notice provisions of the ballot cure process by:
    • Requiring the initial notice of either a mismatch or missing signature to be sent by first class mail. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill. Existing law simply required the official to "provide notice."
    • Requiring the initial notice of a mismatch or missing signature to be sent on or before the next business day after the mismatch is determined. If it is impracticable to send the notice on or before the next business day, including because of technological failure, notice must be sent as soon as practicable. In any case, notice must be sent not later than eight days prior to the certification of the election. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law required notice be provided a minimum of eight days before the certification of the election.
    • Requiring election officials include a return envelope with prepaid postage with the notice of a mismatch or missing signature for the voter to use when returning a cure statement. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill. Existing law did not have this requirement.
      *Authorizing but not requiring additional mailings and contact in person, by phone, email, or other method to give notice of either a mismatch or missing signature. In addition, the bill clarifies that the election official could use any information in the county election management system to try to contact the voter. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill. Existing law did not explicitly authorize or prohibit such additional notices or use of information.
    • Requiring the Secretary of State to evaluate the cost and necessity of requiring election officials to send additional written notices, using information in the voter's registration record or otherwise in their possession. Based on that review, the bill would allow the Secretary to issue regulations imposing such requirements. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
    • Requiring the signature on the voter's missing signature or mismatch cure statement be assessed using the same standards and process the bill would create for ballot signatures. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill. Existing law required the signatures on cure statements to be compared to signatures on file under existing standards and processes.
  • Clarifies the deadline to cure a ballot. Existing law required ballot cure by "5 p.m. two days prior to the certification of the election," but did not define what constitutes "certification of the election." The bill clarifies that certification occurs whenever the relevant election official sends a certified statement of the results of the election to the relevant governing body, an action that must be taken within 30 days of most elections (sooner for certain types of local elections). This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Gives the Secretary of State direction on issuing notice and cure regulations by:
    • Requiring the Secretary to "evaluate the necessity for procedures that will protect voters' personally identifying information" from election observers while election officials do signature comparison. The bill would authorize the Secretary to issue such a procedure by regulation. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill mandated that the Secretary evaluate the necessity for procedures to shield the voters' personally identifying information during the signature comparison process from both election officials doing the comparisons and from observers watching them do it.
    • Requiring the Secretary to consult with recognized election experts, voter access and advocacy stakeholders, and local election officials, when issuing or amending regulations about signature matching and ballot curing. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Limits ballot observers to observing and challenging ballot signatures during the signature comparison process. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law allowed observers to watch and challenge ballots based on the address verification process as well.

  • Requires election officials to report ballot rejection information to the Secretary of State using standardized statewide codes established by the Secretary within 31 days of the election. The Secretary must then publish a report with the information on the agency's website. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

    The bill also makes a minor technical change to provisions related to disclosure of voter records.

Last Updated December 30, 2021

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on March 31, 2022, changes how the state cancels the registrations of people imprisoned for felony convictions and informs those no longer imprisoned that their voting eligibility has been restored. In addition, the bill repeals certain sections of code relating to absentee ballot applications that were rendered obsolete by the recently enacted requirement to mail all active voters a ballot. Finally, the bill clarifies that UOCAVA voters and disabled voters may use the same-day registration process called "conditional registration" in the 14 days before Election Day, as all other voters can.

Specifically, as enacted, this bill changes voter registration list maintenance relating to felony convictions to:

  • End the requirement that clerks of courts send the Secretary of State and county election officials monthly reports of the names, addresses, and dates of birth of people convicted of felonies since the last report, and the related requirement that the Secretary or the county official use the data to cancel voter registrations. Instead, the bill creates a new requirement that the Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation send two lists to the Secretary of State every week, one of the people who have lost their voting eligibility in the previous week and one of the people whose eligibility has been restored in the previous week. Each list would include, for each person:
    • All known first names, last names, middle names, and name suffixes,
    • Date of birth,
    • Last known address,
    • Last four digits of their Social Security number, if available,
    • Driver's license/state ID number, if available, and
    • The date the person's imprisonment began, to the extent available, or the date a person's parole began, and, if applicable, ended, to the extent available.
  • Require the Secretary of State to identify voters who should be removed from the voter registry based on the list received from the Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation by matching each available data point on the list with the voter's information in the voter registry. The Secretary of State must also identify people whose voting rights have been restored by matching each available data point on the Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation list with the person's information in the voter registry. The Secretary must send the matches and underlying data points to the relevant county election official within three days of receiving them. Upon receipt of this information from the Secretary of State, county election officials must cancel the registrations of those who had lost their voting eligibility and notify people whose eligibility has been restored, along with information on how to register. The notification of restoration must be a form the Secretary must create. Existing law did not require election officials to give notice to people that their eligibility has been restored.
  • Protect people ineligible to vote from criminal prosecution for falsely voting or attempting to vote if they received and relied on the official notice that their voting eligibility had been restored and did not otherwise know they were, in fact, ineligible to vote. Existing law had no comparable provision.

  • Provide county election officials with immunity if they fail to act, or if they act, based on erroneous information received from the Secretary. Existing law had no comparable provision.

    The bill revises the voter registration form so that voters no longer have an option to join the obsolete permanent mail voting list, and repeals the requirement that election officials include a vote by mail ballot application in the voter's guide they mail to voters.

    The bill explicitly includes UOCAVA and disabled voters among those who may conditionally register (same-day register), and requires the Secretary of State to issue emergency regulations to enable them to use the process. Existing law provides that all eligible voters may use conditional registration for an election, but no provision is made to enable UOCAVA or disabled voters to conditionally register.

Last Updated June 17, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on June 14, 2021, would add an automatic voter registration process at DMV for people who prove citizenship while doing their DMV transaction while maintaining the existing automatic registration process for people who neither prove nor disprove citizenship status as part of their DMV transaction. In addition, the bill would enable the Secretary of State to designate new voter registration agencies and to convert them to automatic voter registration agencies using the same procedure as the one the bill would establish at DMV for people who prove citizenship. All of these provisions were in the previous version of the bill. The June 14 amendments were not substantive.

The new DMV process the bill would create would transmit the voter registration and registration update information for all people who prove citizenship as part of their transaction, and then send all such people a voter registration opt-out notice with a postage prepaid return envelope. The notice would enable a person to not only refuse registration, but to also choose a political party and to choose to join the permanent mail voting list. The existing automatic registration process at DMV requires people to opt out during the transaction, or affirm citizenship and other voter qualifications as part of the transaction.

These provisions were in the previous version of the bill. On April 28, amendments added language accessibility provisions, so that notices are sent with minority language translations as needed, and the initial notice sent to people upon being automatically registered enables people to select a language to receive ballots and other election materials going forward.

On May 20 the bill was amended to delay the new system's implementation and to add a clarification that the DMV and the Secretary of State would jointly create a process for DMV to verify information it receives against the voter registration database, and that the process could simply be the Secretary of State providing a copy of the statewide voter registration database to the Department of Motor Vehicles on a daily basis. The bill's new effective date would be the earlier of January 1, 2025 or five days after the date the Secretary of State certifies that the information technology infrastructure to substantially implement this act is functional.

As introduced on February 18, the bill would have required the Secretary of State to review the implementation of automatic voter registration at social service agencies in six other states and to file a report with the elections committee of each chamber of the state legislature on the projected cost and practicability of extending automatic voter registration to Medi-Cal beneficiaries. Those provisions were amended out of the bill on March 22.

This bill, as enacted on June 28, 2021, provides increased language accessibility for elections beginning in November 2022. Pursuant to the federal Voting Rights Act, existing law required five Colorado counties to provide election materials in Spanish or Ute. To further expand multilingual ballot access going forward, the bill:

  • Requires the Secretary of State to create a multilingual ballot hotline to provide translation services in each language that at least 2,000 Colorado residents aged 18 or older speak at home while speaking English less than very well, and any other languages the Secretary of State determines by rule are necessary. The hotline must begin operating when ballots are mailed to voters, and be available (1) anytime voter service centers are open, (2) Monday to Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., through the Friday before Election Day, and (3) on the Monday before Election Day and on Election Day from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. The Secretary must provide notice of the hotline on their website and by signage at polling locations and vote centers. This is a modified provision. As introduced, the bill would have identified the languages for translation using a narrower standard and would have required the translation services to be offered for more hours.
  • Requires a county to provide minority language sample ballots and in-person ballots if 2,000 citizens or 2.5% of the county's population speaks English less than very well and speaks a shared minority language at home. The Secretary must determine which counties must provide multilingual ballot access by referencing the most recent American Community Survey provided by the U.S. Census Bureau, and must provide these counties with the translations of statewide ballot questions or issues. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Allows counties to choose to create minority language sample ballots for each ballot style in the county or to create one master document containing translations of every candidate, question, and instruction that appears on any ballot in the county. Counties must make the translated sample ballots available to voters on the county's website and by signage at polling locations and vote centers, and provide notice of the availability of multilingual sample ballots with each mail ballot package. Counties must also ensure that sample ballot translations are performed by qualified translators. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires minority language in-person ballots to contain the same information as the English language ballot, and requires counties to provide notice with each mail ballot package that a voter may request a minority language ballot at any vote center or polling location in the county. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

  • Appropriates $82,800.00 to fund these services.

BILLSUMMARY: Concerns the drawing of voting districts by county governments.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on April 29, 2021, changes how Colorado counties that elect their commissioners by district draw those districts so that the process aligns with the changes the state made to other types of legislative districts in 2018. Many counties elect their commissioners without districts, but counties with more than 70,000 residents may choose to elect one or more commissioners by district. In that set of counties, the bill:

  • Requires counties to create independent commissions to draw the districts with myriad rules governing who may be a member to ensure the commission reflects the county. The county boards of commissioners may not make more than de minimis changes to the commission-drawn districts except through the public process procedure specified in the bill. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires commissions to hold at least three public hearings on redistricting with meaningful and substantial opportunities for public participation, soliciting community feedback after each, and publish all written comments on a related website. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Establishes various transparency and conflict of interest rules for commissions, and requires people lobbying them to be subject to lobbying rules. The prohibition on communications outside of the public hearing process includes communications about how plans will be drawn to satisfy statutory criteria, specific parameters related to the interpretation of those criteria, and requests for the drawing of additional plans. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

  • Requires commissions to draw districts that:

    • Are as nearly equal in population as possible but in no case deviate by more than five percent, using population statistics created by nonpartisan legislative staff to record prisoners at their last residential address rather than their address of incarceration. Under existing law, the districts did not have the five percent deviation limit, and prisoners were distributed in in a slightly different way. The language allocating prisoners in this bill tracks the method used in other types of districts.
    • Comply with the federal Voting Rights Act.
    • Preserve whole communities of interest and whole political subdivisions, such as cities and towns, as much as reasonably possible. Division of a city or town is permitted where, based on a preponderance of the evidence in the record, a community of interest's legislative issues are more essential to the fair and effective representation of residents of the district. When the commission divides a city or town, it shall minimize the number of divisions.
    • Are as compact as reasonably possible.
    • As a consideration after the others, are politically competitive. During the public hearings, the commission should solicit information about political competitiveness.
    • Do not protect incumbents. No district may be approved that is drawn to protect an incumbent.
    • Do not discriminate against racial or language minorities including by diluting their votes. These criteria provisions were in the previous version of the bill.

    The bill would also allow counties to create advisory committees to assist the independent commission, in addition to non-partisan staff. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.

    As introduced, the bill also included a provision that would have required judicial review and approval of maps drawn by the commission prior to their adoption by the county legislature. That provision was amended out of the bill prior to enactment.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 16, 2021, would create a proof of citizenship requirement to register to vote. People who are already registered to vote but who have not yet provided proof of citizenship must provide citizenship proof to have their votes counted. Colorado largely votes by mail, sending ballots to all registered voters. This bill would require election officials to send people who are registered but who have not provided proof of citizenship provisional ballots with provisional ballot envelopes. Voters would be required to return such provisional ballots in person, and such ballots would only count if the voter provides proof of citizenship. To vote in person, a person who had not yet provided proof of citizenship must provide it to receive a regular ballot. Otherwise, the person would cast a provisional ballot that would not count unless the voter provides proof of citizenship. The bill would allow these proofs of citizenship:

  • An unexpired U.S. passport or a legible certified photocopy of the pertinent pages of the passport, identifying the voter and showing the passport number,
  • A birth certificate or a legible certified photocopy of the birth certificate, along with a government-issued photo identification document, or

  • U.S. naturalization documentation, a legible certified photocopy of the naturalization documentation, or the number of the elector's certificate of naturalization. A voter who provides the number of the certificate of naturalization in lieu of the naturalization documentation shall not be registered until the county clerk and recorder verifies the number with U.S.C.I.S. in the Department of Homeland Security or its successor.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, introduced on February 16, 2021, would end Colorado's vote by mail system and shorten the early voting period from two weeks to one week before Election Day. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Abolish the existing vote by mail system by requiring voters who wish to vote by mail to affirmatively request receiving a mail ballot for all elections, rather than automatically receiving mail ballots.
  • Reduce the early voting period from 15 days before Election Day to six days before. The bill would require polling locations to be open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. during the six day early voting period, which would requiring early voting on both Saturday and Sunday. Under existing law, in-person early voting is generally available starting the fifteenth day before an election from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., and polling places must be open on Election Day from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.  Existing law requires early voting on the two Saturdays before Election Day, but Sunday voting is not required. 
  • Require all polling locations during early voting and on Election Day to be countywide vote centers. Under existing law, in-person voting is offered at countywide vote centers.
  • Reduce the number of required in-person voting locations by giving the county recorder discretion to decide how many locations to open, and where to site them. Existing law requires a minimum number of places based on population, and includes siting rules. 
  • Permit the counting of ballots during the seven-day voting period, and require that all ballots must be counted by the end of Election Day. Under existing law, ballot counting occurs throughout the 15-day voting period.

Note that this bill does not repeal existing provisions of the election statutes that establish vote by mail elections and a longer early voting period.

Last Updated February 19, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Concerns the procedures of the independent redistricting commissions.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on May 4, 2021, would make a one-time change the 2021 redistricting timeline to account for delays in census data and preserve the ability to participate in the process. The bill self-repeals July 1, 2023. The basic provisions were in the previous version of the bill, however, the May 4 amendments made two notable changes. First, the redistricting commission is prohibited from submitting a plan to the Colorado Supreme Court for final approval unless it has held a public hearing and enabled the public to comment on the plan. Second, the bill instructs the Colorado Supreme Court, in considering any litigation challenging redistricting relating to technical, rather than substantive, compliance with the redistricting rules embodied in the state's constitution and statutes to focus on whether the redistricting substantially complied with the rules.

Last updated May 5, 2021.

This bill, as enacted on June 23, 2021, changes several aspects of election law, including voter service and polling centers, drop boxes, jail voting, automatic voter registration, online voter registration, as well as myriad areas that Voting Rights Lab does not track, such as recall, initiative, recount, and internal political party procedures. Specifically, the bill:

  • Makes changes relating to siting voter service and polling centers (vote centers), and the services offered at them, by:
    • increasing the factors to be considered by the county clerk when siting vote centers. In addition to existing factors, the clerk must also consider, if the site was used in a past election, how many voters used it and what their wait times were. The number of voters and wait times at nearby locations may also be considered. In addition, clerks must consider the need to put vote centers in population centers that had lower turnout in previous elections.
    • providing that when determining whether a vote center must be sited on a state college campus, and for how long it must be open, enrollment data from fall 2020 must not be used because the Covid-19 pandemic impacted enrollment. Enrollment data from fall 2019 must be used instead.
    • requiring clerks to solicit public input on proposed vote center locations.
    • requiring vote centers to have cure affidavits on hand and enable voters to cure their already returned ballots.
    • requiring vote centers to have sufficient replacement ballots on hand, or the ability to print them on demand. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.
  • Changes the rules relating to drop boxes in two ways, by:
    • requiring drop boxes to be available until 7 p.m. on Election Day, and to remain open as necessary afterward to allow voters in line to use a drop box at the time polls close to remain in line and return their ballot. Existing law does not provide guidance for this situation. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • clarifying that new boxes may be placed at multipurpose buildings that include police facilities only if the facilities also include the county or municipal clerk's office. Existing boxes may remain where they are. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Addresses jail voting by:
    • requiring clerks to make efforts to coordinate with the county sheriff or the county sheriff's designee at each county jail or detention center to facilitate voting for all confined eligible voters. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • requiring the county clerk to include in the plan for the election that they submit to the Secretary of State how they will provide each county jail or detention center with voter information materials, and the process by which the county clerk and the sheriff will facilitate voter registration and the delivery and retrieval of mail ballots for confined eligible electors. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Changes the rules relating to challenging voters' right to vote at a polling location or in an election, by:
    • itemizing the allowed challenge grounds. Under the bill, a challenge can be made because the voter is not a citizen, did not live in Colorado for at least 22 days before the election, is not 18 by Election Day, or is neither a property owner nor the spouse of one, if that is a condition for participating in the election. Relatedly, the bill eliminates an election judge's ability to ask a challenged voter any questions "as may be necessary to test the person's qualifications" to vote, but preserves the question relating to each of the enumerated challenge grounds. Under existing law that was not affected by the bill, challenges to a voter's registration must be made at least 60 days before the election.
    • requiring the challenger to complete and sign a particular form to make their challenge. Existing law required the challenger to make the challenge in writing under oath, but did not require a form.
    • clarifying that, if the challenger is an election judge, a different election judge must ask the specified challenge questions. Existing law requires election judges to challenge voters they believe are not eligible to vote, and allows others to make challenges, but in all cases requires election judges to ask the challenge questions.
    • repealing the specified oath a challenged voter must swear before voting. All of these provisions related to challenging voters in person were in the previous version of the bill.
  • Changes challenges to mail ballots and provisional ballots by:
    • prohibiting challenging a mail ballot on the ground that the voter's signature does not match the reference signature. Signature matching must be addressed exclusively through the signature matching process and its related cure process. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • making clarifying changes to existing law's requirement that challenged ballots be counted unless the ballots were otherwise rejected for disqualifying reasons such as an incomplete ballot certificate. Under existing law not altered by the bill, ballots with incomplete ballot certificates or a deceased person's ballot with a forged signature are rejected without the need to challenge them, although incomplete ballot certificates may be cured and if so, the affected ballots counted. The bill preserves the requirement that if a ballot has been challenged and the challenge not withdrawn, the ballot and the challenge and the voter's response, if any, are given to the district attorney for investigation and resolution.
    • making a conforming change to existing law's requirement that most challenged ballots be counted to reflect the new prohibition on challenging ballots based on the voter's signature on the ballot certificate. Existing law exempted ballots challenged based on the voter's completion of the ballot certificate from the mandate that challenged ballots be counted. Now that ballots cannot be challenged on this basis, this exemption is no longer necessary. Ballots with certificate problems may be cured and then counted, but if the voter does not cure the issue, they are rejected without being challenged.
  • Changes automatic voter registration at the Department of Health Policy and Financing to facilitate updating voters' addresses and names. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Allows people to register to vote online using their Social Security number, and if that number doesn't enable the voter's electronic signature to be pulled from state records, creates processes for the voter to submit a signature. This provision is slightly modified from the previous version of the bill, but the substantive impact is the same. Under existing law, people could register to vote or update their registration online only if they had a driver's license or state ID number.
  • Requires state institutions of higher education to email voter registration information to all students, each semester. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Narrows the misdemeanor crime punishing voting twice or attempting to vote twice by adding an intent requirement and itemizing the prohibited acts more clearly. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Expands the misdemeanor offense of electioneering by broadening the definition to include "the distribution or display of campaign posters, signs, or other campaign materials or apparel, including materials or apparel promoting or opposing a candidate or displaying candidate's name, likeness, or campaign slogan." The bill creates an exception for individuals who are passing through the electioneering zone to access non-voting areas on the campus of a state institution of higher education. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Prohibits election judges from electioneering while serving as an election judge. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Tweaks the process for bringing ballots to residents of nursing homes by allowing ballots to be brought to the facilities as many as 45 days before Election Day. Existing law did not specify a start date. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Limits the information that in-person voters may be asked on a signature card to only their name and address, unless they are registering to vote or voting for the first time. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Changes the deadline for drawing precinct boundaries for partisan elections from 29 days before the precinct caucus day to 29 days before the first Tuesday in March. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires poll watchers appointed by unaffiliated candidates to be unaffiliated voters as reflected in the statewide voter registration system. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Makes changes to the process of conducting a recall election, by:
    • stating that what election officials must normally do 45 days before Election Day, they must do by the 35th day before a recall election. Under existing law, the adjustment for recall election procedures was to the 42nd day before the election.
    • giving the Secretary of State three business days, rather than 24 hours, to review and approve the county recorder's plan for conducting the recall election.
    • requiring the clerk's office to begin offering ballots or replacement ballots for pick up starting 22 days before the election, and to mail the ballots to voters between 22 and 18 days before the election. Existing law required clerks to mail recall election ballots no later than the 15th day before the election.
    • requiring voter service and polling centers to be open for eight hours a day, Monday through Friday, beginning eight days before Election Day, and for four hours on Saturdays. Sunday voting is neither required nor prohibited. On Election Day, the voter service and polling centers must open from 7 a.m. through 7 p.m.
    • clarifying that if a recall election is combined with a general election that has different rules for voter service and polling centers, the general election rules control. These provisions related to recall election procedures were in the previous version of the bill.

Makes numerous changes to areas of election law that Voting Rights Lab does not track. Several of these were amended prior to enactment.

Provisions from the previous version of the bill were amended out of the current text. They would have:

  • Prohibited a multipurpose building that includes a police station to be a vote center unless that facility also included the county or municipal clerk's office.

Expanded the categories of people eligible to request emergency replacement ballots and expanded the options for returning them.

Last Updated September 13, 2021

This bill, as amended on April 22, 2021, would make changes to voting and registration. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Regarding voter registration: 
    • Require automatic voter registration at voter registration agencies where the commissioner of motor vehicles obtains information from a customer confirming that they are qualified to register to vote unless the customer opts out.

    • Require that voter registration information be distributed at each high school in the state each fall.
  • Regarding voter eligibility:
    • Establish restoration of voting rights immediately following release from incarceration. Individuals in department of corrections custody who are being held in a community residence would retain their voting rights. Under existing law, rights are not restored until an individual has been discharged from parole and paid any fines imposed in conjunction with the conviction.
    • Eliminate the bar on voting by individuals who are "mentally incompetent," and permit legal representatives of voters with developmental disabilities to assist them with Election Day voting.
  • Regarding absentee voting:
    • Expand absentee voting eligibility by allowing voters to request absentee ballots on the basis of sickness or disability, broadly, and repeal language around COVID-19 and the 2020 election. Under existing law, absentee voting is only allowed due to the voter's own sickness or disability.
    • Allow absentee ballot applications by phone for voters with a signature on file with the secretary of state.
    • Codify online absentee ballot applications, with the secretary of state being required to transmit application information to the proper municipal registrar within two days of receipt of an application.
    • Make permanent the drop box procedures enacted for the 2020 election.
    • Make permanent the preprocessing of absentee ballots which was allowed for the first time for the 2020 election.
    • Expand eligibility for the permanent absentee list to include voters who are suffering from a long-term illness. Under existing law, only voters with a permanent physical disability are eligible.
    • Allow a police officer, registrar of voters, deputy registrar of voters or assistant registrar of voters in the municipality in which an applicant for an absentee ballot resides to serve as a designee of an emergency absentee voter in any circumstances. Under existing law, a police officer, registrar of voters, deputy registrar of voters or assistant registrar of voters may only serve as a designee for a voter when the voter has no caretaker or family member able and willing to act as their designee.
  • Regarding in-person voting on Election Day. The bill would:
    • Require that employers give employees paid time off in order to vote.
    • Permit a legal representative of a voter with a developmental disability to assist the voter in any task related to in-person voting so long as they present documentation of the legal relationship.
    • Bar possession of a firearm within a 200-foot radius of the entrance to a polling place.
  • Regarding other changes to Connecticut's election system:
    • End the practice of cancelling the registrations of voters who fail to respond to an address confirmation notice, so long as the notice is not returned as undeliverable.
    • Allow voters who returned an absentee ballot and prefer to vote on Election Day to withdraw their absentee ballot until 5 p.m. on the fourth day before Election Day. Under existing law, the deadline to withdraw an absentee ballot is 10 a.m. on Election Day.

A previous version of the bill contained provisions that were amended out of this version. Those provisions would have:

  • Required voters with developmental disabilities, or a caregiver, to certify that the voter met the requirements for registration as a voter as part of the registration process.

This omnibus bill, as enacted on June 23, 2021, addresses implementation of the state budget and various other topics , including provisions that expand voter registration, voter eligibility, and absentee and in-person voting options. Specifically, with regard to election law, the bill:

Facilitates voter registration by:

  • Requiring automatic voter registration, through an electronic system, for individuals who apply for services at designated voter registration agencies and are determined eligible to vote, unless the individual declines. Existing law made some provision for registration assistance at designated agencies, but did not require the use of an electronic system for transmitting registration applications.
  • Requiring voter registration agencies to obtain an affirmation of U.S. citizenship from individuals whose citizenship status cannot be determined, prior to electronic registration. Agencies are also expressly prohibited from registering individuals who are determined not to be U.S. citizens.
  • Allowing voters to keep their address confidential on the voter registration list if they submit a signed statement to the Secretary of State asserting that nondisclosure of their information is necessary for their safety or that of their family.
  • Prohibiting the publicly available voter registration list from including voters' unique identifiers, including driver's license and Social Security numbers, and requiring that the publicly available list only indicate a voter's birth month and year. Entities accessing the list for governmental purposes, including but not limited to jury administration, are authorized to view voters' full birthdates.

  • Requiring that voter registration information be distributed at each high school in the state each fall.

    Expands voter eligibility by:


  • Establishing automatic restoration of voting eligibility immediately following release from incarceration for a felony offense. Under existing law, voting eligibility was not restored until an individual had been discharged from custody, including any term of parole, and paid any fines imposed in conjunction with the conviction. The bill also eliminates disenfranchisement for individuals who are held in a community residence, rather than a correctional institution or facility, following a felony conviction, and requires Corrections officials to provide notification of voting eligibility under the new provisions to relevant individuals and the Secretary of State.

  • Eliminating the bar on mentally incompetent people registering to vote.

    Changes absentee voting procedures by:


  • Extending numerous provisions enacted for the 2020 election to apply to the November 2021 election, by resetting their effective dates to November 3, 2021. Among these extended provisions, the bill:
    • Effectively permits no-excuse absentee voting by adding a "sickness of Covid" qualifying excuse to vote absentee, which any voter may use (per guidance from the Secretary of State).
    • Requires voters who wish to withdraw their returned absentee ballot and vote in person on Election Day to make their request by 5 p.m. on the fourth day before the election. Existing law, which remains in effect after Nov. 3, 2021, permits voters to withdraw their absentee ballots up until 10 a.m. on Election Day.
    • Requires clerks to send absentee ballots to voters within 48 hours of receiving an application (or 72 hours, if the ballot is sent by an authorized third party vendor) rather than 24 hours.
    • Permits clerks to begin sorting received absentee ballots 14 days prior to Election Day, rather than seven days prior, and decreases the notice period for designating a central counting location from 20 days before the election to ten days before.
    • Requires review of absentee ballot envelopes, and rejection for missing signatures, to begin no earlier than 5 p.m. on the fourth day before the election, and requires counting to begin on Election Day. Existing law, which remains in effect after Nov. 3, 2021, authorizes the registrar of voters to determine the timeframe for ballot processing and counting.
    • Authorizes the Secretary of State to waive requirements for on-site absentee voting at state facilities, due to public health concerns.
  • Codifying the online absentee ballot application process by expressly requiring the Secretary of State to establish and maintain a system for receiving applications and electronic signatures, and requiring the Secretary to transmit applications to the proper municipal registrar within 24 hours of receipt.
  • Making permanent the use of drop boxes, originally enacted for the 2020 election. The bill expressly allows for drop box use in each election, primary, or referendum, and eliminates the existing requirement that clerks be escorted by a police officer when retrieving ballots from drop boxes located anywhere other than the clerk's office.
  • Expanding eligibility for the permanent absentee list to include voters who are suffering from a long-term illness. Under existing law, only voters with a permanent physical disability were eligible. The bill also gives voters on the list 60 days to respond to the annual residence confirmation notice, rather than 30 days as previously required.
  • Requiring the Secretary of State to provide electronic absentee ballots to voters who are unable to appear at the polling place due to visual impairment. The electronic ballots must be capable of being read by a computer-related device and printed, and must be counted if properly signed, returned, and otherwise in compliance with absentee voting requirements.
  • Eliminating supervised on-site absentee voting for locations where 20 or more absentee applications are received from the same address.
  • Authorizing the Secretary of State to suspend on-site supervised absentee voting at state care facilities, during declared states of emergency.
  • Establishing a bi-partisan task force to study the feasibility of using a single envelope for absentee ballot return, rather than two as currently required.

    Facilitates in-person voting on Election Day by:
  • Requiring employers to provide two hours of unpaid time off on election day to allow employees to vote, if the employee makes the leave request at least two days prior. The requirement is effective from passage of the bill through June 30, 2024.

  • Eliminating the ability of registrars to appoint challengers.

    In addition, the bill:


  • Requires the Secretary of State to create a system that allows individuals to submit an electronic signature for voting-related forms and applications, and grants the Secretary discretion to determine which documents may be electronically signed.
  • Requires town clerks to post election information on town websites within specific deadlines, in addition to newspaper notices as already required, and specifies that notice must include locations and times for election day registration.

  • Requires the Secretary of State to implement a pilot program for manual or electronic signature verification of absentee ballots for the 2022 election.

    Additional provisions in the bill relate to issues that Voting Rights Lab does not track, including administrative changes to election law and budgetary matters.

Last Updated September 3, 2021

This bill, as signed by the mayor on December 28, 2022, and enacted at the end of the Congressional review process on April 6, 2023, establishes a vote by mail election system in the District of Columbia, and makes other changes to election administration. Specifically, the bill:

  • Directs the board of elections to mail every eligible voter a ballot with return postage prepaid for every election. Under existing law, voters could vote by mail without an excuse but were required to apply for a ballot. The law was silent on payment of return postage.
  • Establishes a receipt deadline of 10 days after Election Day for mailed ballots, if the ballot is postmarked by Election Day. Under existing law, mailed ballots had to be postmarked by Election Day and received by the seventh day after.
  • Requires the board of elections to establish at least 100 ballot return drop boxes, each accessible for at least 10 hours a day. While existing law was silent on drop boxes, they were widely available for the 2020 and 2022 general elections.
  • Expressly permits a voter to vote at any Vote Center location, regardless of their address. Existing law had no express provision for universal access to vote centers, although board of elections practice permitted it.
  • Requires a ballot tracking system through which a voter can see when a ballot was mailed to them, when their ballot was received, and when and if their ballot was accepted or rejected. A ballot tracking system already existed but was required by law.
  • Directs the board of elections to promulgate rules for a signature verification process for mail ballots, including a notice and cure process for signature deficiencies. A notice and cure process already existed but is not required by law.

Additionally, the bill:

  • Converts the district's election precincts to vote centers where any registered voter may cast a ballot.
  • Makes Election Day a holiday for the D.C. public school system.
  • Establishes a process by which a "faithless" presidential elector can be removed and replaced.
  • Requires routine address confirmation of registered voters to occur by March 31 of odd-numbered years, rather than in January.
  • Changes the timing for ballot challenge hearings.

  • Requires the board of elections to establish a vote center at a Department of Corrections facility where eligible incarcerated individuals can vote.

    The bill also contains provisions related to aspects of election law that Voting Rights Lab does not track, such as public notice of election data, assistance to incarcerated individuals running for office, and other topics.

BILLSUMMARY: Creates new legislative districts following the U.S. Census was intended to ensure equal representation at all levels of government.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on June 8, 2021, would reform Delaware's redistricting process for state legislative districts following the 2020 census:

  • The majority and minority caucuses in each legislative chamber would select three members to serve on redistricting committees.
  • The redistricting committees would engage in a back-and-forth process wherein one caucus would have the ability to lock in districts proposed by the other caucus.
  • Maps drawn at each stage in the process would be required to be posted on a public website, and following agreement on a preliminary plan, there would be public hearings.
  • The entire legislature would then approve final maps.
  • If the legislature failed to adopt maps by September 30, or if the redistricting plan is found to be unconstitutional or in violation of federal law, legislative redistricting would then be done by by a judicial panel consisting of the Chancellor of the State of Delaware and three Superior Court judges, 1 from each county, as appointed by the President Judge of the Delaware Superior Court. One of the Superior Court judges would have to be of the same political party as the Chancellor of the State of Delaware, with the remaining two Superior Court judges being members of the opposing major political party.
  • The Delaware Supreme Court would have original jurisdiction over state court challenges to state legislative redistricting plans, and such challenges would have to be brough within 30 days of adoption of a plan.

Under existing law, the legislature is charged with drawing and adopting legislative maps based on prescribed criteria which would remain unchanged.

The bill would also change the deadline for reapportionment from June 30, 2021, to October 1, 2021.

Last updated September 1, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on March 2, 2021, makes major changes to the election code. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create same day registration both during early voting and on Election Day. The voter registration requirements for same day registration are the normal registration requirements, meaning no ID or proof of residency are required. To vote, however, a person must show photo ID.
  • Repeal the statutes that provide for a closing of the registration list before an election. Relatedly, the bill would eliminate a penalty for a third-party registration group turning in completed registration forms after the closing of the registration books.
  • Create a permanent absentee list by deeming a single request for a mail ballot to be sufficient to receive them indefinitely, rather than for two years as existing law provides.
  • Change the ballot return deadline from the close of polls to postmarked by Election Day and received within 10 days after Election Day.
  • Allow voters to complete the mail ballot return envelope using the last four digits of their Social Security number rather than their signature.
  • Allow voters "a reasonable time after the election" to cure deficiencies with their signature or Social Security number, rather than until 5 p.m. on the second day after the election, as existing law provides.
  • Shorten the deadline to apply for a ballot to be mailed to the voter by one day, requiring the request to be received by the 11th day before the election instead of the 10th day as existing law requires.
  • Require people, when registering, to affirmatively choose a political party or no affiliation. If they don't, the registration will be rejected. Existing law defaults people to no affiliation if they do not choose a political party when registering.
  • Allow a person whose registration was not verified and thus was required to cast a provisional ballot at the polls, "a reasonable amount of time after the election" to provide information sufficient to verify the registration, rather than by 5 p.m. on the second day after the election as required by current law.
  • Change the rules relating to provisional ballots to count them if the person was registered and eligible to vote in the county, as opposed to the precinct, at which the voter appeared and cast the ballot.
  • Allow people to pre-register to vote at DMV. People 16 or older may pre-register under existing law, but the DMV is not required to offer the service.
  • Prevent voters from being designated "inactive" because of a failure to return an address confirmation card unless they also have not voted in at least one of the two previous general elections.
  • Postpone the certification of general election results for state and federal offices from 14 days after the election to 21 days after the election, and give counties a related extension to report their results.
  • Shift election authority away from the Governor by changing the Secretary of State from an appointed to elected office. Under existing law, the Secretary of State is appointed by the Governor. The Secretary of State is in charge of the Division of Elections.
  • Require petitions to place an initiative on the ballot be submitted to the supervisor of elections grouped by petition circulator.
  • Designate Election Day a state holiday and require employers to pay normally a person who takes off for the time polls are open.
  • Require the state to maintain a strategic reserve of voting equipment that can be deployed to locations in the event of an emergency or equipment capacity issues due to unexpected voter turnout.
  • Require the state to determine if a secure method exists for receiving cast ballots electronically, and if so, to allow voters to return ballots electronically if they have good cause to do so.
  • Prohibit bullhorns and other sound amplification at polling places during voting hours and supervisor of elections' offices during a recount. Although the bill does not specify a penalty, violations of the election code without specified penalties are misdemeanors.
  • Allows voters to sue election administrators who do not comply with this code.

This bill, as introduced on March 2, 2021, would authorize counties to use county-wide "super voting sites" for early and Election Day voting, and would eliminate existing law's requirement to open a polling place in every precinct on Election Day. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Authorize counties to operate "super voting sites," and require them to be placed in locations that offer all voters in the county an equal opportunity to cast a ballot, insofar as is practicable, based upon demographics and the distribution of registered voters within the county. The sites must provide sufficient nonpermitted parking to accommodate the anticipated number of voters.
  • Require super voting centers to operate each day from 10 days before Election Day through Election Day, for at least 8 hours but not more than 12 hours each day, except on Election Day when the sites must open for the ordinary 12 hours. Counties could choose to open super voting sites as early as the 15th day before Election Day, or any day thereafter until the mandatory open date. In addition, the county could choose to offer additional super vote sites for just the day before Election Day and on Election Day. Existing law requires counties to offer early voting from the 10th day before the election through the third day before the election, but counties may choose to open early voting sites starting 15 days before the election through the second day before the election.
  • Eliminate the requirement that counties offer early voting at the office of the county supervisor, if they choose to operate super voting center locations.
  • Eliminate the requirement that counties provide a polling place for every precinct within the jurisdiction on Election Day, if they choose to operate super voting center locations.
  • Require voters at super voting sites to provide an affirmation, in addition to the existing ID requirement, confirming their address and acknowledging the criminal penalties for voter fraud. Existing law requires this affirmation only for early voting.
  • Allow counties to place a ballot drop boxes at a super voting site or any location that could qualify as a super voting site. Under existing law, counties must place ballot drop boxes at early voting sites and may place them anywhere that could qualify as an early voting site.
  • Require counties to submit their plan for super voting site locations and operating hours to the state election division 30 days before the election, and require the division to approve or deny the plan within five business days.
  • Require counties to upload into the county's election management system the results of all super voting site and vote-by-mail ballots that have been canvassed and tabulated after the polls close. Under existing law, tabulations of vote by mail and early votes must be uploaded the day before election day.
  • Make conforming changes throughout the election code relevant to optional super voting sites.
  • Expand the prohibited zone for offering assistance to voters from 100 feet to 150 feet, at all voting locations. It is a misdemeanor to solicit voters to offer assistance within the zone.
