This bill, as amended on April 19, 2021, requires ID to return a ballot to a drop box, limits third party return, regulates drop boxes, limits the ability to offer assistance to voters, expands the definition of prohibited solicitation of voters, makes it harder to settle election litigation, prohibits private election funding, makes changes to mail ballot applications and voter registration, and makes changes to areas of law the Voting Rights Lab does not track, such as audits, vacancies, and poll watcher badges. Specifically, the amended bill would:

  • Shift election authority by making it harder to settle lawsuits over election laws. The parties would be required to inform the Speaker of the House, the Senate President, and the Attorney General about settlement negotiations at key times, and state and county defendants would be prohibited from entering any settlement without sharing the information as required. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law has no comparable provision.
  • Change ballot verification and canvassing, by:
    • Requiring election supervisors to give political parties and candidates pre-canvass access to ballot certificates and reference signatures, which would facilitate ballot challenges. This is a new provision. Existing law does not explicitly require this access.
    • Requiring mail and provisional ballots to be verified by matching the ballot signature to signatures on file from the last eight years, and allows older signatures to be used if more recent ones are not on file. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have required election officials to use signatures from the past four years, and would have authorized older signatures only if necessary to find a signature done by the voter using pen and paper. Under existing law ballot signatures may be verified against more than one example of the voter's signature. Existing law does not explicitly limit which signatures canvassers may use.
    • Changing the technical rules relating to which ballots need duplicating and the duplication process, and give observers more capacity challenge duplicate ballots. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • Allowing mail ballot canvassing to begin after tabulating equipment is tested, which could be as early as 40 days before Election Day. Under existing law ballots may be canvassed no earlier than 22 days before Election Day. This change would mimic an executive order issued during the 2020 election cycle. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • Requiring supervisors of elections to post on their websites how many mail ballots had been received and how many remained to be counted, starting at the close of polls and continuing hourly during active canvassing. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • Requiring greater transparency about canvassing board membership. These provisions were modified to require the membership of the boards to be published on the completion of the logic and accuracy tests. The previous version of the bill required them to be posted before ballots were mailed to voters.
  • Restrict how a voter may return their mail ballot by requiring people returning ballots to staffed drop boxes to show their Florida driver's license or state ID:
    • If the voter is returning the ballot, and does not have such ID with them, the bill would require them to complete an affidavit that is then attached to the ballot before depositing it in the box.
    • If the voter's designee is returning the ballot, they must show their license or state ID to prove their name matches the designation form. If the designee does not have ID with them, they cannot deliver the ballot.
    • These are modified provisions. The previous version of the bill focused the ID requirement on proving the person's address because the previous version restricted designees based on whether they lived with the voter. Existing law does not require people using a drop box to show ID.
  • Restrict how a voter may return their mail ballot by regulating how a voter chooses someone to return their completed, sealed ballot:
    • To designate someone, the voter and designee would have to complete a form, and the form would have to be attached to the ballot. If a designee attempts to return a ballot to a drop box without the form, the ballot would not be accepted.
    • To enforce the rules, the bill would amend the existing misdemeanor punishing people for unlawfully possessing another's ballot so that it would track the new restrictions, and create a new felony to punish lying on a designation form.
    • The existing exception to the two-ballot limit for returning ballots that are neither the person's nor their immediate families', which allows for unlimited return by people who are not paid to gather ballots, would be eliminated.
    • These are modified provisions. The previous version of the bill would have allowed a voter to choose only their immediate family or housemate. This version allows voters to the same choices as existing law, but existing law does not require a formal designation form, much less that the form must be presented to use a drop box and be attached to the ballot.
  • Regulate drop boxes by:
    • Requiring drop boxes at early voting sites to be monitored by an election worker, and open only during early voting. This is a modified provision. The previous version would have allowed monitoring by an employee of the election supervisor. Existing law does not explicitly limit drop box hours at early voting sites to early voting hours, and allows monitoring of drop boxes by sworn law enforcement officers as well as employees of the election supervisor.
    • Requiring drop boxes at supervisors of elections' offices to be staffed by an election worker during office hours and under video surveillance at other times. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have allowed employees of the election supervisor to staff the drop box. Existing law does not require drop boxes at election supervisors' offices to be staffed, but if staffed, allows sworn law enforcement officers to do it as well as employees of the election supervisor.
    • Requiring drop boxes to be emptied daily at the end of early voting hours or more often as needed. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill mandated emptying only at the end of early voting hours. Existing law does not specify when drop boxes must be emptied.
    • Requiring election supervisors to announce drop box locations at least 30 days before an election, and prohibiting them from being moved. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law does not have similar requirements, and during the 2020 general election, mobile drop boxes were used.
    • Punishing election supervisors who operate drop boxes without following these rules with a $25,000 fine. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill imposed the penalty only for having a drop box at an early voting site open outside of early voting hours.
  • Restrict applying for an absentee ballot by:
    • Limiting each request to one general election cycle instead of two. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • Requiring a voter to provide their Florida driver's license number or state ID number or the last four digits of their Social Security number (SSN4), whichever may be verified by the election supervisor, to request a ballot. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law does not have a comparable provision.
  • Change interactions with voters during the in-person voting process by:
    • Expanding an existing misdemeanor by prohibiting people from offering to assist voters with casting their ballots within 150 feet of the entrance to a polling place or early voting site and applying the restriction to drop boxes. The existing misdemeanor prohibits such solicitation within 100 feet. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • Expanding a different prohibition on soliciting voters to prohibit "engaging in any activity with the intent to influence or effect of influencing voter". This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Prohibit the state, counties, and any other authority that conducts elections from accepting private funding or other support for election-related expenses or voter education or registration programs, except that in-kind donations of voting locations would be allowed. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill did not have an exemption in-kind donations of voting location. Existing law has no equivalent prohibition.
  • Change aspects of voter registration law by:
    • Changing rules relating to third party registration drives and requiring certain disclosures to voter registration applicants. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • Requiring closer cooperation between DMV and supervisors of elections to ensure that address changes at DMV are reflected in voters' registrations. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • Simplifying the attestation portion of the voter registration form relating to felony conviction and voting eligibility restoration to conform to changes in re-enfranchisement law. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • Requiring voters who wish to change their name or party affiliation to complete a new voter registration form rather than make the written request existing law authorizes. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have required voters to provide their Florida driver's license or state ID number, or SSN4 to update their party affiliation or name.
    • Requiring voters who wish to update their registration address by calling the election supervisor's office to provide to their Florida driver's license or state ID number, or SSN4. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Prohibit mailing ballots to voters who do not apply for them, effectively limiting the types of election that may be conducted by mail to the ones already authorized by law. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

Make other changes in areas Voting Rights Lab does not track, such as the length of certain county commissioners' terms, the process of nominating candidates for certain vacancies, the retention of election records, the approval timeline of voting machines, audits, and the content of election observer badges.

Three significant provisions relating to ballot verification have been amended out of this bill:

  • The April 19th amendments removed a requirement that election supervisors notify a voter's political party when that voter's ballot has been rejected for a missing or mismatch signature, after notifying the voter.

Earlier amendments removed:

  • a provision that would have required supervisors of elections to give candidates, political parties, and individual voters one or two days to review and challenge ballot signatures before ballots are opened and canvassed. The supervisors would have had to provide access to digital images of ballot certificates displaying voters' names, addresses, and signatures alongside images of the most recent signature on file. The ballot images would have been further required to be sorted or sortable by residential precinct. Relatedly, the previous version's requirement that voters' addresses be printed near the ballot signatures and a new crime for using a voter's signature from the election records have been amended out of this version.
  • a provision that would have required the voter to put their ballot in the secrecy envelope, potentially disqualifying "naked" ballots. This version of the bill would leave existing law in place.

This omnibus bill, which makes changes to mail voting, in-person voting, and several other aspects of election law, was enacted on May 6, 2021. As enacted, the bill:

  • Changes applying for a mail ballot by:
    • Requiring applicants for a mail ballot to include their Florida driver license number, identification card number, or the last four digits of their Social Security number on their application. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law did not require an ID number to request a mail ballot when making a phone or in-person request to have the ballot sent to the voter's registration address, or in the written request by the voter to send it to another address.
    • Reducing the number of elections each accepted application covers. After successfully applying for a mail ballot, voters will receive ballots for all elections through the end of the calendar year of the next ensuing general election. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Under existing law, voters who submitted a valid application received ballots through the end of the calendar year of the second ensuing general election.
    • Including grandchildren among the authorized "immediate family" members who may pick up a mail ballot on behalf of a voter.
  • Regulates drop boxes by:
    • Requiring drop boxes to be located so as to provide equal opportunity to cast a ballot, as far as is "practicable."
    • Limiting the availability of drop boxes at early voting sites to only those hours that early voting takes place. Drop boxes located at the office of the supervisor are not subject to the early voting hours limitation.
    • Requiring that all drop boxes be continuously staffed by an election supervisor's employee when in use. Existing law required boxes at early voting sites to be staffed by an election supervisor's employee or sworn law enforcement during early voting.
    • Requiring drop box locations be announced 30 days before an election and not changed except to correct a violation of drop box regulations, thereby eliminating mobile drop boxes.
    • Requiring drop boxes at early voting sites to be emptied daily at the end of early voting hours, and daily at supervisors' offices whenever the boxes are closed.
    • Creating a $25,000 fine to punish an election supervisor who operates a drop box in violation of statutory rules.
    • Including drop box locations among the voting sites where prohibitions against soliciting voters apply.
  • Expressly prohibits state officials from sending voters a mail ballot without the voter's request, except where specifically allowed elsewhere in the code.
  • Prohibits individuals from handling more than two additional mail ballots beyond their own and a ballot of an immediate family member. Existing law prohibited individuals from offering or accepting any financial benefit for handling more than two additional ballots, but otherwise imposed no limits on the number of ballots authorized third parties could handle on behalf of a voter. Violations of this rule are punishable as a misdemeanor, thus increasing the restriction expands the misdemeanor.
  • Requires election supervisors to give political parties and candidates pre-canvass access to ballot certificates and reference signatures, which would facilitate ballot challenges.
  • Changes the in-person voting experience, by:
    • Expanding the prohibition on general solicitation of voters to include "engaging in any activity with the intent to influence or the effect of influencing a voter" at voting sites, including drop boxes. The bill provides an exception for employees of, or volunteers with, the election supervisor's office to provide non-partisan assistance, including giving "items" to voters. Violation of the solicitation prohibition constitutes a misdemeanor offense.
    • Expanding the existing misdemeanor offense for soliciting voters to accept voting assistance by increasing the exclusion zone from 100 feet from the polls to 150 feet.
  • Shifts election authority by requiring the parties in certain election-related lawsuits to give notice to the Speaker of the House, the Senate President, and the Attorney General of both the fact of, and content of, settlement negotiations at key times. State and county defendants would be prohibited from entering any settlement resulting from a process that did not follow the notice requirements.
  • Prohibits the state, counties, and any other authority that conducts elections from accepting private funding or other support for election-related expenses or voter education or registration programs, except that in-kind donations of voting locations would be allowed.
  • Allows counties to begin canvassing mail ballots after testing tabulating equipment, which can occur not more than 25 days before Election Day. Under existing law, canvassing mail ballots could start not more than 22 days before Election Day.
  • Prohibits printing party affiliation or other partisan information on a ballot return envelope and requires that a code used by election supervisors, if any, be printed on it.
  • Revises the voter registration form to conform to changes in the law regarding restoration of voting rights following a criminal conviction.
  • Changes the rules applicable to third party voter registration organizations regarding deadlines to return completed applications and required notifications to applicants.
  • Requires the DMV to cooperate with the Secretary of State in new ways in updating voter registrations.
  • Requires people who update their registration address by means other than a voter registration form to include their driver's license, state ID, or partial Social Security number with their request. The bill also requires people who are making a change to their party affiliation or legal name to do so with a voter registration form, rather than by general written notice. Under existing law, these registration changes only required the voter to provide their date of birth or registration number.
  • Eliminates a public records exemption for voter registration information concerning voters' prior felony convictions and any restoration of voting rights they have been granted.
  • Requires load and security testing of the online registration system.
  • Makes numerous other changes to the election code in numerous other areas Voting Rights Lab does not track, including ballot duplication, canvassing board transparency, and audit reports. 

Provisions that amendments have removed from the bill at various times would have:

  • Eliminated drop boxes.
  • Heavily restricted third party ballot pick up and return.
  • Cancelled existing, approved mail ballot applications on file.
  • Specified which reference signatures must be used to verify mail ballots.
  • Required people to show ID to use a drop box or sign a special affidavit.
  • Required a person returning another voter's ballot to show written authorization from the voter, or sign an affidavit that they have the authorization.
  • Allowed people using the online voter registration system to use the voter's driver's license or state ID number or the last four digits of their Social Security number to complete the registration. Although existing law does not impose a specific requirement, the existing system requires both a driver's license or state ID number and the person's Social Security number to register online.

The sites must provide sufficient nonpermitted parking to accommodate the anticipated number of voters.
  • Require super voting centers to operate each day from 10 days before Election Day through Election Day, for at least 8 hours but not more than 12 hours each day, except on Election Day when the sites must open for the ordinary 12 hours. Existing law requires counties to offer early voting from the 10th day before the election through the third day before the election, but counties may choose to open early voting sites starting 15 days before the election through the second day before the election.

  • Require counties to upload into the county's election management system the results of all super voting site and vote-by-mail ballots that have been canvassed and tabulated after the polls close. BILLSUMMARY: Relates to voting rights restoration, revises conditions under which the voting disqualification for a persons conviction of a felony, other than murder or a felony sexual offense, terminates, requires certain entities to provide certain notification to the Department of State following a convicted felons release or discharge from state prison, county jail, parole supervision, release supervision, probation, or community control.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 2, 2021, would address the legal financial obligations (LFO) challenges returning citizens face in regaining their voting eligibility by ensuring they know what their LFO obligations are and how to resolve them, and providing for a full waiver of LFOs under certain circumstances. Specifically, this bill would:

  • Require the Department of State be notified whenever a returning citizen is given notice of the remaining terms of their sentence, including outstanding LFOs, as required by existing law.
  • Require the Department of State, within 30 business days of receiving such a notice, to send the returning citizen a notice that identifies the full amount of outstanding LFOs the person owes as a part of their sentence, how to pay the LFOs, how to establish a payment plan, and how to convert the financial obligation to community service. If the department does not timely send the notice, the full amount of outstanding LFOs would be waived.

  • Create a similar opportunity for people who did not receive notices of their remaining sentence obligations upon release. The existing law providing for those notices was enacted in 2019. The bill would allow people who were released without notice of their remaining LFOs to request an advisory opinion from the Department of State that would identify any remaining LFO amounts owed as part of the person's sentence and include instructions on how to pay them, establish a payment plan, and convert them to community service. If the Department does not respond to the request within 30 business days, the full amount of LFOs would be deemed waived.

    Last updated March 4, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on March 2, 2021, would make major changes throughout the election code. Specifically, this bill would:

  • Create same day voter registration during early voting or on Election Day. Only the ordinary registration requirements apply. To vote in Florida, the new registrant must show ID.
  • Repeal the ordinary voter registration deadline, so that voter registration is continuous. The bill would make conforming changes to other provisions.
  • Create a permanent absentee voter list open to all voters by making an application for a mail ballot an application for all elections until the voter cancels.
  • Change the ordinary mail ballot return deadline from the close of polls to the UOCAVA deadline of postmarked on or before Election Day and received no later than 10 days after Election Day.
  • Require counties to prepay the postage needed to return a mail ballot.
  • Allow people to verify their mail ballots either using their signature and its comparison to one on record, or by using the last four digits of their Social Security number.
  • Expand the existing cure process to allow people to correct the last four digits of their Social Security number, and change the deadline of the existing cure process to "a reasonable time after the election" rather than 5 p.m. on the second day after Election Day.
  • Shorten the window to apply to receive a ballot in the mail by one day, requiring applications to be received by the 11th day before the election rather than the 10th. In parallel, a designee becomes allowed to pick up mail ballots beginning 11 days before the election.
  • Require people to pick a political party or affirmatively choose not to affiliate with one when registering. Registration applications that don't indicate a choice will be rejected. Under existing law, people who do not make a choice are automatically registered as unaffiliated.
  • Allow people who are eligible for pre-registration under existing law to pre-register at DMV.
  • Change the timeline for removing a voter from the registration list who has allegedly moved. The bill would prevent a voter's status from being deemed inactive until they not only fail to respond to an address confirmation notice but also fail to vote in two general election cycles. Once assigned inactive status, a voter's registration may be cancelled if they do not appear to vote for two additional general election cycles. Under existing law, a person may be placed on inactive status when they fail to return the card.
  • Require counting of provisional ballots cast in the correct county rather than only those cast in the correct precinct.
  • Give a voter a "reasonable amount of time after the election" to verify their registration and enable their provisional ballot to count. Under existing law, this deadline is 5 p.m. two days after Election Day.
  • Require the state to maintain a strategic reserve of voting machines that can be distributed in emergencies or to deal with capacity issues created by unexpected turnout
  • Prohibit siting a polling place within a gated community unless all voters assigned to it live in that community.
  • Prohibit using bullhorns or other devices used to amplify sound in close proximity to a polling place during voting hours or an office of the supervisor during a recount. While a penalty for violations is not specified, unspecified violations of the election code are misdemeanors.
  • Allow private property owners who are hosting a polling place or early voting site to prohibit soliciting voters outside the no-solicitation zone. Existing law requires them to allow such solicitation.
  • Make the Secretary of State, who has authority over elections, an elected office rather than one appointed by the Governor.
  • Require petition signature pages to be submitted to the election supervisor grouped by the circulator who collected them, and allow certain electronic signatures.
  • Make general Election Days paid holidays.
  • Delay the general election certification of state and federal offices by one week, to 21 days after the election from 14.

  • Create a private right of action against election supervisors who violate the election code.

Last Updated July 19, 2021

  • Expand hours of early voting offered on weekdays from normal business hours to 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.
  • Establish mandatory hours for early voting on the second Sunday before Election Day.
  • Expand hours of early voting on the second Saturday before Election Day from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. to 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.
  • Bar jurisdictions from offering additional hours of early voting.
  • Require a minimum of one early voting location per 30,000 voters in a county, each with at least six ballot marking devices and three poll pads.

Last Updated June 11, 2021

This bill, as amended on March 23, 2021, would:

  • Change procedures for absentee voting. The bill would:
    • Require voters to provide an identification number from a Georgia-issued ID with their absentee ballot application or, if they do not have one, a photocopy of another type of ID. Existing law requires only that the application include sufficient information to identify the voter, address for ballot delivery, specific election for the request, and name and address of the requestor (if not the voter). This provision was retained from a previous version of the bill.
    • Prohibit all government officials from mailing unsolicited absentee ballot applications to voters, and prohibit anyone, other than a voter's relative, from providing an application pre-filled with the voter's information. This provision was retained from a previous version of the bill.
    • Require voters to provide a state-issued ID number, if they have one, or the last four digits of their social security number on the outer envelope containing their absentee ballots, in an area that is covered when the envelope is sealed. Voters who do not have either required ID number would be required to enclose a copy of alternative ID with their ballot. The bill would also make unsealing an absentee ballot without authorization a felony offense. Under existing law, voters are required to provide only a signed oath affirming their identity. This provision was retained from a previous version of the bill.
    • Permit drop boxes at registrars' offices or at early voting locations, only at times when early voting is being conducted at that location, and set out security protocols for handling ballots. This provision would result in drop boxes being unavailable once early voting ends, which is the Friday before Election Day. Existing law is silent as to drop boxes. This provision is modified from a previous version of the bill, which would have required counties to establish at least one drop box and limited the number of additional drop boxes counties could establish to the lesser of one per 100,000 registered voters or the number of early voting locations in the county.
    • Direct the secretary of state to develop the capacity to accept absentee ballot applications online, including images of required documents. This provision was retained from a previous version of the bill.
    • Eliminate signature comparison for the verification of absentee ballots and applications, and instead require comparison of identifying information provided. This provision was retained from a previous version of the bill.
    • Permit processing of absentee ballots to begin on the second Monday prior to Election Day, and require supervision of all absentee ballot processing by authorized security auditors. This provision is modified from a previous version of the bill, which would have allowed processing to begin on the third Monday prior to Election Day and did not require auditor supervision. Under existing law, ballot processing cannot begin until the opening of polls on Election Day.
    • Require that eligible voters held in detention facilities must be granted access to necessary personal effects for the purpose of applying for an absentee ballot. This is a new provision amended into this version of the bill.
    • Require that any organizations or individuals besides the secretary of state or county election officials that distribute absentee ballot applications include disclaimers identifying themselves and clarifying that the application did not come from the government. This provision, with slight modifications, was retained from a previous version of the bill.
    • Require county election officials to maintain a publicly available master list of absentee voters including names, date ballots were sent, whether the ballot has been returned, whether the ballot has been accepted, and the current status of the ballot. This is a new provision amended into this version of the bill. Under existing law, the publicly available master list only includes the names and addresses of voters who have been sent absentee ballots.
    • Authorize the secretary of state to audit information contained in absentee ballot applications and on absentee ballot envelopes for 24 months after an election. This is a new provision amended into this version of the bill.
  • Change the availability of early ("advanced") voting:
    • Require counties to offer early voting on the second and third Saturdays before Election Day, and on the second and/or third Sundays before Election Day. Required hours on early voting days would be from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., with discretion granted to extend the hours from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. This is a modified provision from a previous version of the bill, which would have required one additional early voting day "" either the third Saturday or Sunday before Election Day "" and limited county discretion for early voting days and times. Under existing law, counties must hold early voting during "normal business hours," with weekend voting required only on the second Saturday before Election Day from 9 a.m. "" 4 p.m., and they may offer additional early voting days and hours at their discretion.

  • Change Election Day voting:

    • Require that mobile polling places only be used when an existing polling place has been declared unfit for human occupation and the use has been approved by a superior court judge. Existing law imposes no limitations on local officials' discretion to use mobile voting facilities. This provision is modified from a previous version of the bill, which would have barred the use of buses or other mobile voting facilities except in cases of a state of emergency declared by the governor.
    • Permit counties to purchase their own voting equipment beyond what has been provided by the state, so long as that equipment has been certified for use by the secretary of state. This provision was newly amended into this version of the bill.
    • Require a paper component of the ballot, which could be produced on an electronic ballot marking devise. This provision was newly amended into this version of the bill.

    The bill also contains several other new provisions affecting elections that were amended into this version of the bill. These provisions would:


  • Require all ballots used in the state to include multiple security features, including some that can be validated at the polling place.
  • Require legislative approval, by joint resolution, before the state election board or secretary of state enter into any agreement or settlement that limits, alters, or interprets provisions of the election code.
  • Establish a process through which the state election board could recommend to a legislative delegation that a county superintendent within their jurisdiction be temporarily removed by a majority vote of the delegation.
  • Require the attorney general to establish a hotline where voters can lodge complaints and anonymous tips regarding voter intimidation, fraud, and illegal election activities.
  • Require the secretary of state to maintain a list of voters registered each week - including address, race, gender, and voter identification number - and make it available electronically for public inspection at no cost.
  • Require the secretary of state to obtain regular information from nongovernmental organizations of which it is a member regarding voters who may have moved to another state, died, or otherwise become ineligible to vote in the state.
  • Require county registrars to provide daily reports of absentee and early voting data during each voting period, to both the Secretary of the State and the public via county websites.
  • Prohibit the extension of polling place hours except by order of a county superior court judge, on good cause shown.
  • Bar counties from pausing the counting of ballots until the process is complete, once it has commenced at the close of polls. Existing law permits pausing the count once all contested races and questions are tallied, and resuming the count the following day.
  • Create a new felony offense for intentionally observing another voter casting a ballot except while providing assistance as authorized by law.
  • Delay reapportionment of municipal districts if census data is not published at least 120 days before the next municipal election.

  • Require that state election board emergency rules enacted in response to a public health emergency be submitted to the legislative judiciary committees at least 20 days before going into effect, and grant each committee the power to suspend adoption of an emergency rule within 10 days of submission. Existing law requires only that emergency rules be submitted as promptly as reasonably practicable, and does not provide for a committee override.

    A previous version of this bill contained several provisions that were amended out of this version of the bill. These provisions would have:


  • Replaced the secretary of state as chairperson of the state election commission with a nonpartisan chairperson selected by legislative leaders. The secretary of state would have served as a nonvoting ex officio member of the board.
  • Established a deadline for absentee ballot applications of 11 days before Election Day. Under existing law, there is no official deadline for absentee ballot applications although ballots cannot be issued the day before Election Day and are generally not issued on weekends.
  • Increased the period when a hospitalized voter may request an absentee ballot from five days before Election Day to ten days before.
  • Created a new felony offense for knowingly accepting an absentee ballot from a voter in order to return it, when unauthorized to do so.
  • Reduced the early voting period for general and primary runoff elections by changing the start date from the fourth Monday prior to Election Day, to no later than the second Monday before.
  • Required counties to make public notice of early voting dates, times, and locations, at least 14 days before voting begins.
  • Changed the earliest date for acceptance of an absentee ballot application from 180 days before Election Day to 78 days before Election Day.
  • Ended the practice of counting a person's vote if they cast a provisional ballot at the wrong precinct on Election Day.
  • Limited the ability of the state election board to issue emergency regulations to "circumstances of imminent peril to public health, safety, or welfare," and required notice of impending action to state officials. The bill would also have required the state board to certify that any emergency regulations are in "strict and exact" compliance with the election code, and provided that any such regulations will control where they conflict with statutory rules for administrative procedure.
  • Barred the distribution of "money or gifts," defined to include food and drinks, to voters at a polling place or standing in line to vote.
  • Granted superior court chief judges the power to appoint an acting election superintendent in counties without boards of elections and where there is a probate judge vacancy or the judge has been incapacitated.
  • Barred county election officials from accepting private grant funds.
  • Established a process for the selection of temporary election superintendents in counties without boards of election.
  • Required that when a precinct serves over 2000 voters and has wait times of over an hour (based on measurements taken three times on Election Day), the election superintendent must either reduce the size of the precinct no later than 60 days before the next general election or provide additional poll workers or voting machines at the precinct.
  • Permitted election superintendents, at their discretion, to establish fewer than the generally required one voting machine per 250 registered voters at a precinct for elections other than general elections.
  • Changed the period when absentee ballots may be sent to non-UOCAVA voters, from between 49-45 days before Election Day to 29-25 days before Election Day. Clerks would also have been required to respond to absentee ballot applications within three days during the early voting period.
  • Required voters casting absentee ballots to sign an attestation, under penalty of perjury, that they did not mark their ballot in the presence of anyone not authorized to assist them or allow an unauthorized person to return their ballot. The instructions to voters would also have included a number where voters could report any unauthorized third party who offered to deliver a ballot on their behalf or requested to observe the voter completing their ballot.
  • Required training for all poll watchers, using materials provided by the Secretary of State.

  • Permitted individuals to serve as poll officers in counties in which they neither live nor are employed by the county, if approved of by the election superintendents of both the county in which they live and the county in which they seek to serve as a poll officer.

Last Updated July 20, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 18, 2021, would:

  • Permit the state election board, following a hearing, to remove boards of registrars who do not perform list maintenance activities required under law.
  • Require that absentee ballots be printed on paper incorporating security features designed to prevent duplication.
  • Require voters to include photocopies of ID with their absentee ballot applications.
  • Bar the distribution of absentee ballot applications by anyone other than the secretary of state and county election officials.
  • Require voters to include photocopies of ID with their absentee ballots. The ballots of voters who failed to include photocopies would be considered provisional, and the voter would need to provide ID in order for the ballot to be counted.
  • Require election superintendents to record all ballot processing and counting proceedings and retain such records for two years following an election.

Last Updated July 19, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 1, 2021, would establish a process through which legislators could petition the state election board to suspend county or municipal election superintendents within their districts and appoint temporary replacements. The legislators would need to demonstrate that the superintendent in question demonstrated nonfeasance, malfeasance, or gross negligence in the administration of the elections for at least two elections in a two-year period.

Last updated July 20, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on March 5, 2021, would permit probate judges, who have the duties of the election superintendent in counties that do not have boards of elections, to declare in writing their desire to no longer serve as election superintendent and trigger a process to establish a board of elections.

Last updated August 2, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on March 22, 2021, would require counties in which over 5000 citizens of voting age are members of a single language minority and are limited-English proficient, or the illiteracy rate of the citizens in the language minority as a group is higher than the national illiteracy rate, the county must provide all election- and voting-related materials in that language.

Last Updated March 26, 2021

This resolution, as introduced on January 26, 2021, proposes an amendment to the state constitution to end disenfranchisement due to criminal convictions. Under existing law, those convicted of felonies of moral turpitude are disenfranchised until the completion of all the terms of their sentence, including financial obligations.

Last updated August 17, 2021.

This proposed constitutional amendment, as introduced on January 28, 2021, would establish a Citizens' Redistricting Commission:

  • Districts would have to be contiguous, of equal population, respectful of geographic boundaries, and in compliance with the U.S. Constitution, the Voting Rights Act, and any other applicable federal law.
  • Districts could not be drawn with the intent or result of abridging any individual's right to vote "on account of race, color, or language-minority status," including where its members have less opportunity than others to "elect representatives of their choice, whether as a single group or acting in concert with others."
  • Commission membership would be determined through a process involving the chief justice of the supreme court and legislative leaders in both parties meant to achieve membership representing both major political parties and unaffiliated voters.
  • The commission would be required to post proposed plans online, including underlying data, explanations of factors considered, to hold public meetings, and to consider public comment.
  • The state supreme court would be empowered to order a reapportionment plan if the commission failed to approve a valid plan.

Last updated on February 3, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on November 4, 2021, would establish state senate districts based on the results of the 2020 census.

This bill, as introduced on January 26, 2021, would establish ballot drop boxes:

  • Each county would be required to establish drop boxes at each early voting ("advance voting") location.
  • Drop boxes would be available beginning 49 days before a non-municipal primary or general election, for non-municipal runoff elections, drop boxes would on open the first day of early voting.
  • Counties would be required to establish video surveillance of drop boxes.
  • Counties would be required to empty drop boxes at least every 72 hours beginning, at the latest, on the second Monday before Election Day.

Last Updated January 28, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 27, 2021, would establish a photo ID requirement for absentee voters. Under this system:

  • Absentee voters would be required to include copies of an approved photo ID with their absentee ballot applications and ballot envelopes.
  • Ballots received without required ID would be treated as provisional and would only be counted if the voter verified their identity by producing photo ID.

Last Updated March 10, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 27, 2021, would expand poll worker eligibility to allow all Georgia residents to serve as poll workers at any location. Under existing law, poll workers must be residents of, or employed within, the county in which they serve, for municipal elections, poll workers must be residents of, or employed within, the municipality in which they serve.

Last updated on March 9, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on January 27, 2021, would establish a pilot program for providing grants to rural counties (those with populations under 50,000) to fund the establishment and operation of early ("advance") voting centers.

Last Updated February 1, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 27, 2021, would establish a permanent absentee voting list:

  • Voters could opt into receiving absentee ballots for all future elections via the general absentee ballot application.
  • Voters would be removed from the permanent absentee list if they are moved to inactive status, although their permanent absentee status will be restored if they respond to a confirmation notice updating or verifying their address.

Last Updated January 29, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 27, 2021, would remove drug crimes from the list of disenfranchising crimes.

Last updated on January 29, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on January 27, 2021, would allow increased preprocessing of absentee ballots beginning on the second Monday before Election Day. This would include opening the outer and inner envelopes and scanning the ballot. Under existing law, outer ballot envelopes may not be opened until polls open on Election Day, opening of inner envelopes and tabulation of ballots may not begin until 7 a.m. on Election Day.

Last Updated January 29, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to elections and primaries generally, so as to provide that the name and designation of the precinct appears on every ballot, provides for the use of holographic security devices on ballots, provides for the storage and retention of absentee ballots by precinct with chain of custody, provides for the manner of handling and processing ballots requiring duplication for processing, provides for the maintenance of certain lists of absentee voters, provides for related matters.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 1, 2021, would:

  • Require that after counting, absentee ballots be sorted and stored by precinct in sealed containers, with chain of custody logged until the ballots can be legally disposed of.
  • Require that ballot duplicates that must be created in the counting process be given unique serial numbers and kept with the original ballot at all times. The bill also contains provisions impacting policies areas that are not tracked by VRL.

Last updated on February 3, 2021.

This bill, as amended on February 18, 2021, would:

  • Require absentee voters to provide either (1) their date of birth and driver's license number or state identification number, or (2) a photocopy of a photo ID accepted for in-person voting when applying for an absentee ballot. Under existing law, voters are not required to provide an identifying number or document on an absentee ballot application submitted in person or by mail. This provision was retained from a previous version of the bill.
  • Require certain first-time voters who failed to provide ID while registering by mail to provide a copy of their photo ID with their absentee ballot application. Under existing law, these voters are required to do so only with their completed absentee ballot. This provision was retained from a previous version of the bill.
  • Authorize the Secretary of State to establish an online portal through which voters with state-issued driver's licenses or non-driver IDs could request an absentee ballot by submitting their identification numbers. Existing law does not contemplate an online application portal, however, the secretary of state has already established an online portal that requires an identifying number. This provision was retained from a previous version of the bill.
  • Eliminate signature matching for absentee ballot applications against signatures in the registration file. This is a new provision amended into this version of the bill.
  • Eliminate the provision that permits voters who are unable to complete the absentee application due to illiteracy or physical disability to make their mark on the application and have a third party complete the form and sign as a witness. This is a new provision amended into this version of the bill.

Last Updated February 22, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 1, 2021, would:

  • Prohibit the use of drop boxes. Existing statute does not contemplate drop boxes, however, they have been used in recent elections.
  • Expand the types of officials to which ballots may be personally delivered to include a registrar, deputy registrar, clerk of the board of registrars, or a clerk in the office of the absentee ballot clerk. Under existing law, voters may only personally deliver ballots to the board of registrars or to the absentee ballot clerk.

Last Updated February 3, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 1, 2021, would eliminate automatic voter registration at DMVs by requiring voters to "affirmatively and specifically" indicate their desire to register to vote. Under a memorandum between the DMV and secretary of state's office currently in effect, applicants for state IDs are automatically registered to vote unless they affirmatively opt out or fail to sign the appropriate signature blocks.

Last Updated February 3, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 1, 2021, would prohibit a person who votes in a federal general election in another state, then moves to Georgia, from voting in any federal runoff elections that may take place as a result of that election.

Last Updated February 3, 2021

This bill, as amended on March 1, 2021, would end no-excuse absentee voting by mail. Voters would be required to meet one of the following requirements to vote absentee by mail:

  • Be absent from their precinct during the time of the election.
  • Have official duties in connection with the election.
  • Be unable to vote in person due to a physical disability or needing to provide constant care for someone with a physical disability.
  • Be unable to vote in person due to personal observance of a religious holiday.
  • Be required to remain on duty in his or her place of employment for the protection of the health, life, or safety of the public during the entire time the polls are open.
  • Be 75 years of age or older.
    This provision was modified from a previous version of the bill, which would have required voters to be 65 years of age or older to qualify under the age excuse.

Last Updated March 2, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 1, 2021, would require county registrars to obtain, each month, identifying information about voters who have died from the county coroner, judge of the probate court, and all funeral homes in the county in order to facilitate list maintenance. Under existing law, the only mandated data source for this purpose are monthly reports from the county registrar of vital statistics.

Last updated on February 3, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on February 1, 2021, would prohibit any person other than the Secretary of State, an election superintendent, a board of registrars, or a candidate or campaign committee from distributing absentee ballot applications. Forms distributed by such a person or group would be required to have the name of the authorized entity printed on them.

Last Updated February 3, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 1, 2021, would grant poll watchers access to all areas in a tabulating center where ballots and election results are being received and processed. Election superintendents would only be permitted to restrict the movement and activities of poll watchers in as minimal way as possible to provide for the security of ballots and returns, and to prevent poll watchers from interfering in the tabulation. Under existing law, poll watchers are only permitted in designated locations within tabulating centers, including the check-in area, computer room, and duplication area.

Last Updated March 10, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 2, 2021, would:

  • Define "felonies of moral turpitude," as covering 37 specific felonies. Convictions for felonies of moral turpitude triggers disenfranchisement. Under existing law, this term has been interpreted to include all felony convictions and restoration of voting rights cannot take place until all requirements of the individual's sentence have been fulfilled, including financial obligations.
  • Establish disenfranchisement during incarceration for felonies that are not enumerated as being "of moral turpitude." For these convictions, restoration of voting rights would be automatic following incarceration. Under existing law, restoration for all felony convictions cannot take place until all requirements of the individual's sentence have been fulfilled, including financial obligations.

Last Updated February 4, 2021

This bill, as amended on April 4, 2022, would:

  • Clarify that members of county boards of elections can serve on performance review boards evaluating other counties. Under existing law, performance review boards are open to "local election officials."
  • Require secured storage and logged chain of custody for all ballots and ballot labels.
  • Direct the state election board to promulgate rules and regulations governing the securing and chain of custody of unused security paper.
  • Modify the requirement that employers give some employees time off on Election Day in order to vote by permitting employers to grant time off to vote during early voting.
  • Repeal the requirement that ballot returns be kept under seal.
  • Provide that all election returns be open to public inspection following certification of the election.
  • Direct the state bureau of investigations to identify and investigate violations of election law which, if established, would be sufficient to change or place in doubt the results.
  • Grant the state bureau of investigations the authority to issue, with the consent of the attorney general, subpoenas of election records.

These provisions were newly amended into this version of the bill. The previous version of the bill contained additional provisions that were amended out of this version. Those provisions would have:

  • Established the positions of chief elections assistance officer and election assistance coaches within the office of the secretary of state.   • Required the chief elections assistance officer to oversee on-site evaluations and training of low-performing county election officials.
  • Granted the state board of election the power to suspend low-performing superintendents if improvement was not made following evaluation and training.

This bill, as introduced on February 10, 2021, would establish same-day registration:

  • Same-day registrants would need to present proof of residency (Georgia driver's license, government issued photo identification card bearing the person's name and current address, current public or private college photo identification card with proof of residence on the campus of such institution, or current utility bill, bank statement, government check, payroll check, or other government document showing the person's name and current address) in addition to the standard photo ID required of all voters.

  • Such individuals would then be registered to vote and mailed information about how to cancel their registration.

  • Tribal ID

  • Have official duties in connection with the election.
  • Be unable to vote in person due to a physical disability or needing to provide constant care for someone with a physical disability.
  • Be unable to vote in person due to personal observance of a religious holiday.
  • Be required to remain on duty in his or her place of employment for the protection of the health, life, or safety of the public during the entire time the polls are open.

This bill, as enacted on March 25, 2021, addresses various aspects of absentee, early, and in-person voting, election crimes, and election administration. Specifically, the bill:

  • Modifies procedures for absentee voting. The bill:
    • Requires voters to provide an identification number from a Georgia-issued ID with their absentee ballot application or, if they do not have one, a photocopy of another type of ID. Existing law required only that the application include sufficient information to identify the voter, address for ballot delivery, specific election for the request, and name and address of the requestor (if not the voter).
    • Requires voters to provide a state-issued ID number, if they have one, or the last four digits of their social security number on the outer envelope containing their absentee ballots, in an area that is covered when the envelope is sealed. Voters who do not have either required ID number are required to enclose a copy of alternative ID with their ballot. Under existing law, voters were required to provide only a signed oath affirming their identity.
    • Requires at least one drop box per county for absentee ballot return, and allows for additional drop boxes depending on the number of county voters or early voting locations. Drop boxes are only permitted inside advance voting locations and may only be accessible while early voting is taking place, with "constant surveillance" required. The boxes also must be emptied daily. During a state of emergency declared by the governor, staffed drop boxes could be placed outside early voting locations. Existing law was silent as to drop boxes.
    • Requires the verification of absentee ballot applications and ballot envelopes by comparison of the voter's provided ID information, including date of birth, with their information on file, rather than by signature matching.
    • Creates a new felony for accepting an absentee ballot from a voter for delivery or return unless statutorily authorized to do so.
    • Prohibits the secretary of state and other government entities from sending absentee ballot applications to voters without a request.
    • Prohibits the distribution of absentee ballot applications with pre-filled fields, other than by an applicant's authorized assistant.
    • Creates a new misdemeanor for the handling of a completed absentee ballot application by anyone other than the voter, the voter's authorized relative, an authorized assistant, or various specified officials.
    • Requires a specific disclaimer on absentee applications mailed to voters by non-governmental organizations, which identifies the group and clearly states that the application did not come from the government.
    • Requires that absentee ballot applications include a wet ink signature from the voter. For the 2020 general election, the state established an online absentee ballot application system.
    • Bars third-party individuals and organizations who are not election officials from mailing absentee ballot applications to voters who have already requested or cast an absentee ballot, and requires third parties to consult voter lists to avoid doing so. Violations of this rule may lead to restitution payments of $100 per duplicate application processed by election officials, or the actual cost incurred in each affected county or municipality for the processing of duplicate absentee ballot applications. Third parties would not be liable for violating the provision if they relied on information that had been provided within five days of their mailing to voters. Note: This provision was retained from the previous version of the bill.
    • Requires that voters in jail be given access to necessary personal effects for the purpose of applying for and voting an absentee ballot.
    • Changes the earliest date for acceptance of an absentee ballot application from 180 days before Election Day to 78 days before Election Day, and requires applications for absentee-by-mail ballots to be received by the 11th day before an election. Existing law did not specify a cut-off date for requesting an absentee ballot to return by mail.
    • Changes the date that officials must begin issuing absentee ballots, from 49-45 days before Election Day to 29-25 days before Election Day. The bill also requires clerks to process absentee applications within three days of receipt during the early voting period.
    • Permits hospitalized voters to apply for an absentee ballot starting ten days before an election, rather than five days, and requires immediate processing of such requests.
    • Creates a new felony for an unauthorized individual knowingly unsealing a sealed absentee ballot envelope.
    • Permits preprocessing of absentee ballots starting on the third Monday before Election Day, rather than after the opening of polls, and allows party monitors to observe ballot processing.
    • Bars counties from pausing the counting of ballots until the process is complete, once it has commenced at the close of polls. Existing law permitted pausing the count once all contested races and questions were tallied, and resuming the count the following day.
    • Modifies the absentee voter oath to include affirmations that the voter was not observed while voting and will not give the ballot to anyone for unauthorized return, and requires ballots to list individuals who may return ballots on a voter's behalf.
    • Establishes ranked-choice voting for UOCAVA voters in general primary runoff elections.
    • Authorizes the secretary of state to audit information contained in absentee ballot applications and on absentee ballot envelopes for 24 months after an election.
  • Modifies early voting procedures. The bill:
    • Requires counties to offer weekend early voting on both the second and third Saturday before Election Day, with optional early voting on the second and/or third Sundays before. Required hours on early voting days are from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., with discretion granted to extend the hours from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. No additional early voting days, other than those specified in the provision, are allowed. Under existing law, counties were required to hold early voting during "normal business hours," with weekend voting required only on the second Saturday before Election Day from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., and could offer additional early voting days and hours at their discretion.
    • Eliminates the specific early voting period for runoffs for general primaries and general elections, which must begin on the fourth Monday before the election, and instead requires these runoffs to occur "as soon as possible," and no later than the second Monday before.
    • Requires that county boards of registrars publicly post early voting locations at least 14 days before voting begins.
  • Shifts authority for election administration. The bill:
    • Limits the ability of the state election board to issue emergency regulations to "circumstances of imminent peril to public health, safety, or welfare," and requires notice of impending action to state officials. The bill also requires the state board to certify that any emergency regulations are in "strict and exact" compliance with the election code, and provides that any such regulations will control where they conflict with statutory rules for administrative procedure.
    • Requires the state election board to submit proposed emergency rules to the house and senate judiciary committees at least 20 days prior to taking effect, and authorizes either legislative committee to suspend the rule by majority vote. Existing law required only that emergency rules be submitted as promptly as reasonably practicable, and did not provide for a committee override.
    • Replaces the secretary of state as chairperson of the state election board with a nonpartisan individual chosen by the legislature. The secretary of state is now a nonvoting ex officio member of the board.
    • Requires the Secretary of State and the State Elections Board to appoint an independent performance review board upon request from the governing authority of a county or from state lawmakers representing the county, or if there is evidence that calls into light the competence of a local election official.
    • Establishes a process through which up to four election superintendents at a time may be suspended by the state election board. County governing authorities now have the ability to petition the state election board, and the state election board would have the ability to initiate the process itself, based on an investigation by a performance review board. A majority of the board must find at least three violations of rules and regulations over the last two election cycles or demonstrated nonfeasance, malfeasance, or negligence in administering at least two elections within a two year period.
    • Requires five days' notice to the judiciary committees before the state election board or secretary of state enters into any agreement or settlement that limits, alters, or interprets provisions of the election code.
    • Grants superior court chief judges the power to appoint an acting election superintendent in counties without boards of elections and there is a probate judge vacancy or the judge has been incapacitated.
  • Changes procedures for in-person voting. The bill:
    • Creates a new misdemeanor for giving or offering a voter any "money or gifts," including food or drink, at a polling place.
    • Permits individuals to serve as poll officers in counties in which they neither live nor are employed by the county, with the approval of the election superintendents of both the county in which they live and the county in which they seek to serve as a poll officer.
    • Requires counties to divide precincts and/or add more poll workers and equipment for precincts that had over 2000 voters and wait times of more than one hour in the previous election.
    • Requires counties to post a notice of a polling place change at least seven days prior to an election, rather than on Election Day.
    • Bars the counting of provisional ballots cast out-of-precinct before 5 p.m. on Election Day. Provisional ballots cast out of precinct after 5 p.m. are counted if accompanied by a sworn statement that the voter cannot vote at their precinct before polls close. Under existing law, voters who appeared to vote at the wrong precinct in their county were permitted to cast a provisional ballot, which was counted as to all relevant elections following verification of their registration during the ballot counting process.
    • Prohibits mobile voting sites except in states of emergency declared by the governor. Existing law imposed no limitations on local officials' discretion to use mobile voting facilities.
    • Limits the applicability of existing, broadly applicable voting machine minimum requirements to statewide general elections.
    • Prohibits the extension of polling place hours except by order of a county superior court judge, on good cause shown.
  • Criminalizes additional aspects of the election system. The bill:
    • Creates a new felony for observing a person casting their ballot, with the exception of authorized assistants, individuals under 12 years old, or any minor child of the observed voter.
    • Creates a new misdemeanor for recording or photographing a voted ballot or the face of an electronic ballot marker while a vote is being cast or while a vote choice is being displayed.
    • Authorizes the attorney general to establish a hotline where voters can lodge complaints and anonymous tips regarding voter intimidation, fraud, and illegal election activities.
  • Alters the election code in several other ways. Additional provisions of the bill:
    • Bar election superintendents and boards of registrars from accepting private funding for election administration and directs the state election board to propose a method for accepting private funding at a state level and distributing the funds equitably around the state.
    • Require the secretary of state to regularly obtain information from the non-governmental voter information sharing organization it belongs to - i.e., ERIC - for the purpose of voter list maintenance.
    • Expressly provide that there is no limit on the number of voters that a single voter may challenge on eligibility to register or vote, and require registrars to hold hearings on challenges to voter registration eligibility within 10 days of filing. The bill also authorizes the state board to sanction registrars for failure to comply with challenge procedures.
    • Require counties to ensure designated locations for poll watchers allow them to fairly observe the procedures of voting and scanning.
    • Require training for poll watchers, to be provided by the organization they represent.
    • Require counties to report and post information about total number of ballots cast and rejected as soon as possible after the close of polls, and no later than 10 p.m., on Election Day.
    • Delay reapportionment of municipal districts in the event of delay of census data.

This proposed constitutional amendment, as introduced on January 26, 2021, would establish an independent, nonpartisan redistricting commission:

  • Districts would have to be contiguous, of equal population, respectful of geographic boundaries, and in compliance with the U.S. Constitution, the Voting Rights Act, and any other applicable federal law.
  • Districts could not be drawn with the intent or result of abridging any individual's right to vote "on account of race, color, or language-minority status," including where its members have less opportunity than others to "elect representatives of their choice, whether as a single group or acting in concert with others."
  • Apportionment plans could not be drawn with the intent to favor or disfavor a party or candidate.
  • Commission membership would be determined through a process involving the chief justice of the supreme court and legislative leaders in both parties meant to achieve membership representing both major political parties and unaffiliated voters.
  • The commission would be required to post proposed plans online, including underlying data, explanations of factors considered, to hold public meetings, and to consider public comment.
  • The state supreme court would be empowered to order a reapportionment plan if the commission failed to approve a valid plan.

If their documentation does not affirmatively demonstrate citizenship, the person would be required to sign an affirmation attesting to citizenship for their registration to be processed. VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 27, 2021, would make numerous changes relating to voter registration, voter list maintenance, ballot drop boxes, same-day registration, election crimes, and other areas of the election code. Some changes are purely technical or are conforming to reflect both changes proposed in this bill and to harmonize parts of the code with the state's shift to voting by mail last year. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Change voter registration deadlines by extending the deadline for regular voter registration in person and by mail from 30 days before an election to 15 days before, and counting mail applications postmarked by 15 days before. Online registration would no longer have a pre-election deadline. In-person same-day registration would continue to be available during early voting and on Election Day.
  • Change the voter registration list maintenance process in several ways:
    • To prevent cancellation for not voting unless the person has been identified as having an outdated or undeliverable address and has not voted in any election in the two preceding federal election cycles. The confirmation process to determine an address is outdated or undeliverable must be done according to federal law. Existing law allows voter registrations to be canceled for not voting after two federal election cycles without regard to an address change, and to be canceled for changes of address that are not verified according to the federal practice.
    • To allow the clerk to act on information about a voter's felony, citizenship, incompetence, or other status that would require a voter's cancellation if true without investigating the information. Existing law requires the clerk to make such investigation as may be necessary to prove or disprove the information, giving the person concerned, if available, notice and an opportunity to be heard.
  • Expand the availability of places of deposit (drop boxes). Under existing law, places of deposit may be available starting five business days before the election. This bill would allow them to be open eighteen days before, or whenever ballots are made available to voters.
  • Create a new misdemeanor prohibiting any person other than the postal service or the clerk, from sponsoring, establishing, or displaying a collection receptacle to receive voted mail ballots or ballot return envelopes in an election.
  • Make changes to the existing same-day registration process. Voters at the polls who are registered but do not appear on the list at the vote center could no longer use the process, voters using the process could no longer be challenged while doing so, voters whose registration cannot be verified on the spot can be required to cast provisional ballots, and the clerk would no longer mail such voters a registration card within 30 days after the election.
  • Extend the time that clerks are required to mail ballots to voters who registered or updated their registrations after the initial mailing. This bill would require ballots to be mailed to such people who had not yet voted through the seventh day before the election. Existing law requires ballots to be mailed only through 14 days before. Both the bill and existing law allow ballots to be mailed later if the clerk believes there is time for the voter to receive and return their ballot.
  • Allow voters to request replacement ballots without completing forms.
  • Clarify that the existing cure process applies to absentee ballots as well as mail ballots, and change the deadline for the voter to return cure documentation from five business days after Election Day to seven days. The clerk would be prohibited from validating ballots more than 10 days after the election.
  • Simplify an existing election misdemeanor to prohibit, among a list of actions, willfully destroying or defacing "election signage" while deleting from the same misdemeanor prohibiting willfully destroying or defacing" a list of voters, visual aids, or facsimile ballot."
  • Remove Election Day from the list of state holidays.

  • Make technical and conforming changes throughout.

Last Updated March 10, 2021

This bill, as enacted on June 28, 2021, creates automatic voter registration at state driver's licensing agencies.

Individuals applying for a new, renewed, or duplicate driver's license or state ID card are required to complete a special section of the application form to register to vote, update their registration, or decline to do either. The license or ID application will not be processed until applicants take one of these actions. Registration information will not be automatically transferred, regardless of whether the applicant opted out, if the applicant provides a document proving non-citizenship when applying for the license or ID. Under existing law, individuals applying for a driver's license or state ID were offered a separate voter registration form, but were not required to complete or affirmatively decline it to complete their license transaction. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill, but the language effectuating them was modified by the amendments.

A provision from the previous version of the bill was amended out of the current text. That provision would have required the DMV voter registration application to include information about the state's address confidentiality program.
