This omnibus bill, as enacted on July 6, 2021, makes numerous changes throughout the election code. Note that the March 24 version of the bill included the last substantive changes to provisions tracked by Voting Rights Lab. Subsequent versions contained only non-substantive changes. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires the department of public safety and the paroling authority to notify individuals on parole or probation of their eligibility to vote and provide them with information on how to register and vote. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill required only the department of public safety to provide voting information.
  • Revises the same day registration process by:
    • Allowing people to use the online voter registration system to register during early voting or on Election Day. Under existing law, individuals were only permitted to complete same day registration in person at voter service centers.
    • Prohibiting challenges to a voter's registration by deleting the provision that authorized them.
    • Removing a requirement that the clerk send a voter a notice within 30 days of registration.
    • Deleting language that allowed a person who is registered to vote but whose name does not appear on the county register to use the same day registration process.
    • Providing that if the clerk needs additional time to verify the voter's registration, the voter may cast a provisional ballot.
      These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.
  • Extends the regular voter registration deadline from 30 days before the election to 10 days before the election. Mailed registrations postmarked by the 10th day before the election must be accepted and processed for the election, as must registration applications completed at voter registration agencies by that date. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Because same day registration begins 10 business days before Election Day when voter service centers open, voter registration is now functionally continuous.
  • Changes the requirements for opening voter service centers. The bill requires each county to operate one voter service center, with no specified location, during business hours on the ten business days before the election and on Election Day until 7 p.m. Each county may open as many additional voter service centers, for varying days and times, as needed to meet the needs of their voters. Under existing law, counties were required to operate at least one voter service center at the clerk's office, and provide access to all their voter service centers for the full ten business day voting period at the same hours statewide. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have imposed specific voter service center siting requirements based on population.
  • Requires, as soon as practicable, the office of elections and the county clerks to make a determination of the optimal number and placement of voter service centers and places of deposit. In making the determination, they must consider:
    • Proximity to public transit,
    • Access to free parking,
    • Traffic patterns,
    • Proximity to communities with low rates of vehicle ownership,
    • Time and distance that a voter must travel to reach a voter service center or place of deposit,
    • Proximity to population centers,
    • Proximity to geographically isolated populations,
    • Proximity to official language minority communities,
    • Proximity to low-income communities,
    • Proximity to voters having disabilities,
    • The need for alternate voting methods for voters with disabilities,
    • Proximity to communities with historically low vote by mail usage, and
    • Proximity to communities of eligible voters who are not registered.
      This provision was in the previous version of the bill, however the April 13 amendments made small edits to the language of some of the factors to be considered, without adding or deleting a factor.
  • Requires county clerks, rather than the state office of elections, to make the official election proclamation for their county and to include the dates and hours voter service centers and places of deposit will be open.
  • Allows counties to open places of deposit when they mail out ballots. Existing law allowed their opening five business days before Election Day. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Allows ballot processing and tabulation to begin on the 18th day before the election. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Under existing law, ballot processing and tabulation were permitted to begin on the tenth day before the election.
  • Clarifies that both mail ballots and absentee mail ballots can be cured. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Updates list maintenance procedures. Specifically, the bill:
    • Requires the list maintenance process to identify voters with outdated or undeliverable addresses, to comply with federal law and its confirmation notice requirements. Only voters who were identified as having an outdated or undeliverable address using the new process and who failed to vote in any election in two federal election cycles will be removed. Existing law required clerks to remove voters who did not vote in two federal election cycles, without regard to the status of their address.
    • Eliminates the requirement that clerks must undertake an investigation to verify information received from other agencies before removing voters from the voter registration list due to death, felony conviction, incapacity, loss of citizenship or other disqualification, and instead deeming agency information as "prima facie evidence" for removal. The bill retains existing procedures for a voter to re-register or appeal a cancellation if they are removed under the new simplified removal process.

      These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires clerks to send the initial mailing of ballots so that voters will receive them at least 18 days before the election, rather than approximately 18 days before. In addition, clerks are required to mail ballots to voters who register by the tenth day before the election, or who update their registration by the seventh day before the election. Existing law required the clerk to mail ballots to voters who update their registration by the 14th day before the election. The bill retains existing language allowing clerks to continue mailing ballots if they believe there is sufficient time for the voter to receive and return the ballot. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Allows a voter to request a replacement ballot, as an alternative to the existing method of completing a replacement ballot application form. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Corrects the voter registration form to state the accurate maximum financial penalty of $10,000 for a class C felony, which is the category of offense for providing false information on a registration form. The existing form provision stated that the maximum financial penalty was $1,000. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Revises the voter registration form to allow the potential voter to indicate that they have a disability preventing them from reading standard print and allowing them to request to receive electronic ballots by email. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Expands the misdemeanor offense for prohibited campaigning at voter service centers and places of deposit, to include activities within a 200 feet perimeter of an area that is designated for voters waiting to vote. Under existing law, the 200 feet perimeter applied only to voting locations, adjacent parking lots, and nearby routes of access. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Creates a new misdemeanor offense for operating an unofficial place of deposit. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

  • Creates committees to advise the state and each county on serving special needs voters. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

    Provisions from the previous version of the bill were amended out of the current text. They would have:


  • Removed election days from the list of state holidays.
  • Allowed clerks to validate ballots up to 10 days after the election rather than existing law's seven days.

  • Changed the cure deadline to seven days after the election instead of existing law's five business days.

This bill, as introduced on January 22, 2021 would:

  • Make changes to the existing same day registration process. Specifically, voters who are registered but do not appear on the list at the vote center could no longer use the process, voters using the process could no longer be challenged while doing so, voters whose registration cannot be verified on the spot can be required to cast provisional ballots, the clerk would no longer mail such voters a registration card within 30 days after the election, and the voter affirmation would be updated to reflect the current penalty for a class C felony, which is the crime type covering lying on the registration form.
  • Change the ordinary voter registration deadline from 30 days before Election Day to 10 days before. Because same day registration begins 10 days before, this change would effectively make voter registration continuous.
  • Change the timeline for mailing ballots to voters so that the clerk continues mailing them to people who register by the tenth day before the election, and to voters who update their registrations by the 14th day before the election. Clerks could continue mailing ballots past these deadlines if they believed sufficient time remained for the voter to receive and return the ballot.
  • Change the replacement ballot rules to eliminate the need for an application.
  • Allow clerks to add voter service centers that are open for varying days and times to serve the needs of their voters. These would be in addition to vote centers apportioned to the county that must be open for the ten business days before the election during business hours. Existing law requires voter service centers to be open for the same days and hours statewide, and mandates the 10 business day, business hours voting period.
  • Allow county clerks to open places of deposit as soon as ballots are mailed, rather than starting five business days before Election Day, as existing law requires.
  • Change the deadline for a voter to cure their ballot from five business days after the election to seven days after, and clarify that the cure process applies to absentee ballots as well as mail ballots.
  • Change the deadline for clerks to stop trying to validate ballots from seven days after the election to ten days after.
  • Create a new misdemeanor to punish campaigning or electioneering within 200 feet of the last person in line at a voting location, including places of deposit. Existing law, which the bill would not amend, contains a misdemeanor for campaigning in a similar area.
  • Require the office of elections to publish a weekly report on its website of the number of ballots received, broken down by county and by ballots received by mail versus ballots cast in person. This report must be published on a daily basis during the last two weeks before the election.
  • Amend the voter registration form to remove the option to join the permanent absentee list. This is a non-substantive conforming change. Now that Hawaii conducts its elections by mail, the state's voter registration list is, in effect, a permanent absentee list.

  • Make numerous technical and conforming changes throughout the election code.

This bill, as enacted on March 8, 2021, makes changes to various areas of election law, including early voting, absentee voting, in-person voting, registration record maintenance, and others. Specifically, the bill:

  • Restricts early voting by:
    • Reducing the early voting period from 29 days before Election Day to 20 days before. This provision was modified from a previous version of the bill, which would have reduced the early voting period to 18 days before Election Day.
    • Removing the ability of a county election commissioner to establish satellite absentee voting locations at their discretion, leaving in place only a process by which commissioners can be petitioned to establish satellite locations. This provision was retained from a previous version of the bill.
  • Restricts absentee voting by:
    • Changing the absentee ballot receipt deadline to the close of polls on Election Day. Under existing law, absentee ballots were considered timely if they were received by Election Day, or if they had a postmark or barcode dated by the day before Election Day and were received by the Monday following the election. This provision was modified from the previous version of the bill, which would have eliminated postmarks as a dating method and retained barcodes alone.
    • Limiting third-party ballot return, including to a drop box, to immediate family members, household members, and caretakers. Under existing law, any third party could return a voter's ballot other than specific campaign-affiliated individuals. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • Reducing the absentee ballot application period from between 120-10 days before an election, to 70-15 days before. The bill also requires commissioners to notify voters who apply for an absentee ballot between 15 and 7 days before an election that their application cannot be processed, and provide instructions for other ways to vote, within 24 hours of receiving the request. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.
    • Reducing the absentee ballot voting period by moving the date when absentee ballots may be issued, from 29 days before Election Day to 20 days before Election Day. This provision was modified from a previous version of the bill, which would have changed the earliest issuing date to 18 days before Election Day.
    • Barring officials from pre-filling any fields on absentee ballot applications other than the date and type of election. This provision was retained from a previous version of the bill.
    • Barring election officials from sending voters unsolicited absentee ballot applications, while expressly permitting mailing of applications to voters that request them. This provision was modified from a previous version of the bill, which would have barred all mailing of applications to voters.
  • Authorizing the general assembly to direct the mailing of absentee ballot applications to all voters during a declared public health disaster, for primaries and general elections in even-numbered years. If the assembly is not in session, the legislative council may issue the direction by majority vote. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Modifies absentee voting in other ways, by:
    • Expressly allowing, but not requiring, the use of ballot drop boxes. The bill authorizes only one ballot drop box per county, which must be located at or near the county commissioner's office, and sets out requirements regarding security. Third parties who return a voter's ballot to a drop box must do so within 72 hours of retrieving the ballot or by the close of polls, whichever is earlier. Existing law was silent on drop boxes, although they were permitted in 2020 on county property without a number restriction. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • Expressly providing that a ballot affidavit is only "incomplete" if the voter's signature is missing, and permitting voters whose mail ballots are flagged as incomplete to cast a valid vote by either voting a provisional ballot, voting in person on Election Day, or providing their signature at the commissioner's office by the close of polls on Election Day. Existing law required voters to cure an incomplete affidavit in person by 5 p.m. on the day before the election. This provision was modified from a previous version of the bill, which would have also given voters whose ballots were received after the Saturday before Election Day until the Monday after Election Day to cure their ballots.
    • Requiring the state commissioner to issue daily reports during the absentee voting period with data concerning applications, ballots issued, and ballots returned. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • Allowing voters who are admitted to health care facilities outside their home county after the absentee ballot application deadline to request a ballot, and designate a third-party to return it, through Election Day. Existing law provided for this exception only when a voter is admitted to an out-of-county facility within three days of an election. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • Allowing counties to convene special election boards to begin counting absentee ballots on the day before Election Day for all elections. Existing law authorized this procedure for general elections only. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill. The bill also requires local officials to report absentee ballot data to the state commissioner following each primary and general election. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • In changing the voter registration and in-person voting processes, the bill also:
    • Moves the deadline for voter registration to 15 days before Election Day. Under existing law, the registration deadline was 10 days before general elections, and 11 days before all other elections. This was a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
    • Requires the state registrar carry out an annual verification of all voters in the registration file. The verification process must include cross-referencing data with records maintained by other states, and the registrar must issue an annual report to the legislature stating the number of registrations cancelled as a result of the maintenance process. The bill also specifies various sources for updating the voter file. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.
    • Makes participation in the National Change of Address Program mandatory for election officials, rather than optional, and requires officials to send notice to and mark as inactive any voter flagged by the NCOA system who did not vote in the most recent general election. Under existing law, voters who appear in the NCOA system were issued registration notices only after failing to vote in two or more consecutive general elections, and officials were authorized to issue annual confirmation notices rather than use the NCOA system. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • Requires local registration officials to submit an annual report to the state registrar, stating the number of registrations deemed inactive or cancelled. The bill also requires the state registrar to regularly audit voter registration maintenance procedures and refer violations to the county attorney or state attorney general. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.
    • Requires officials to notify voters when a polling place has changed by mail, at election offices, and on the local government website, at least seven days before an election. Under existing law, notice was required only by publication in a newspaper and could be issued up to four days before Election Day. This was a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
    • Requires polling places to close at 8 p.m. for all elections, and requires the state legislative service to post opening and closing times for polling places on its website, through July 1, 2025. Under existing law, polling places were required to close at 9 p.m. for most election types. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
    • Prohibits candidates from assisting voters or being present with the voter in the voting booth. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.
    • Creates a new misdemeanor for interference by a precinct election official or county commissioner with a person who is authorized to be at a polling place. This is a new provision amended into this version of the bill.
  • In changing other aspects of election administration, the bill:
    • Authorizes the state commissioner to oversee county election officials in the 60 days before and after an election, and report technical infractions of election rules. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • Creates new criminal offenses for election officials, including a new felony offense for failing to perform official duties and new aggravated misdemeanors for failing to perform required voter list maintenance and interfering with others' performing their proper roles at a polling place, including observers. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.
    • Increases penalties for various crimes existing that could be committed by election officials.
    • Authorizes law enforcement to take "all reasonable actions to prevent violations" of the law governing the canvass of votes. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • Permits the state election commissioner to issue guidance outside of the rulemaking process, to clarify election laws and rules. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • Requires the attorney general or county attorney to investigate allegations of election misconduct reported to the attorney general or county attorney and submit the results of the investigation to the state commissioner, explaining whether they will pursue charges.

This bill also contains provisions regarding aspects of election law that are not tracked by VRL and amendments to these provisions.

Last Updated November 16, 2022

This bill, as enacted on June 8, 2021, includes many provisions newly amended into the final version of the bill. These provisions:

  • Expand the definition of "immediate family" to include relatives to the fourth degree, expanding who can return absentee ballots on behalf of a voter. Under existing law, immediate family has its traditional meaning.
  • Eliminate the ability of caregivers to return absentee ballots, instead allowing disabled and blind voters to designate delivery agents via a form to be prescribed by the election commissioner. Delivery agents would be barred from delivering ballots for more than two voters and would be required to deliver ballots in person to the county election commissioner's office and present identification and sign an affidavit. Under existing law, caregivers are permitted to return ballots on behalf of a voter with no restrictions.
  • Bar county commissioners from sending address confirmation notices due to failure to vote when the registered voter was not yet 18 on the date of the last general election.
  • Permit voters to validate provisional ballots at the commissioner's office until the Monday following Election Day or by the time the results are canvassed, whichever is earlier.
  • Establish that a county commissioner who receives a petition for a satellite absentee voting site is not required to establish the site if the site is inaccessible to elderly and disabled voters, the site cannot meet needs for ballot security and secrecy, there is already a satellite location in that precinct, or the owner of the site demands payment for its use. Under existing law, commissioners are required to establish a satellite absentee voting site when prescribed petition requirements are met.

Other provisions retained from a previous version of the bill :

  • Require voters to present ID when making an attestation to confirm the identity of another voter who does not have a required form of ID.
  • Widen the sources that registrars may use to identify deceased voters, to include notice from the federal social security administration.

Require the state election commissioner to establish a website for tracking absentee ballots with the following information: whether the voter returned a ballot in person, by mail, or by voting in person at a satellite location, the date the absentee ballot request form was received by the county commissioner, the date the absentee ballot was mailed or given to the voter, the date the absentee ballot was received by the county commissioner, the date the county commissioner opened the outer envelope, whether there is a problem with the absentee ballot request form or absentee ballot that requires correction by the voter, along with instructions for the voter to contact the county commissioner as soon as possible to resolve the issue. Ballot tracking already existed in some form prior to the enactment of this bill but was not required by law and it is unclear based on publicly available information what data points were available to voters.

The bill also contains various provisions related to election topics that are not tracked by VRL.

Last Updated January 3, 2022

  • maintenance of incumbent-constituent relationships,

  • Incarcerated individuals would be counted at their last known address before going into custody.
  • Commission membership would be determined by leadership of both parties in both chambers of the legislature on an equal basis.
  • The commission would be required to hold public meetings, at least 35 public hearings, post proposed maps online, and provide an explanation of how their maps comply with relevant law.

This bill, as introduced on April 21, 2021, would create the Illinois Voting Protection Act, with provisions that would:

  • Prohibit voting qualifications or prerequisites that result in limiting the right to vote based on race, color, or membership in a language minority.
  • Guarantee either public notice and opportunity for public comment, or preclearance by the Attorney General, whenever any municipality proposes to enact any:
    • voting qualification,
    • prerequisite to voting,
    • new or expanded at-large electoral districts,
    • municipal border change that decreases the municipality's racial or language minority populations,
    • alterations to electoral district boundaries,
    • impediments to interpreters and language access, or
    • polling place consolidation.
  • Prohibit at-large elections that cause vote dilution on the basis of race, color, or language minority.
  • Ensure minority language access by requiring municipalities with populations of non-English speaking, single language minorities of more than 5% of the voting-age citizens or 10,000 voting-age citizens to ensure voting and election materials are available in those languages and mandating election officers are available to assist as interpreters.
  • Criminalize, at a felony level, bribery, intimidation, threats, or coercion that hinders, prevents, or attempts to hinder or prevent, election officers from holding an election.
  • Criminalize, at a misdemeanor level, knowingly communicating false information about an election date, time, place, or the voter's precinct, polling, place, or voter registration status, to a registered voter with the intent to impede the voter's exercise of the right to vote.
  • Criminalize, at a misdemeanor level, misrepresenting the contents of a ballot to a person who cannot understand the language of the ballot with the intent to deceive and induce a vote contrary to the voter's desire.
  • Create a civil penalty for any person acting under the color of law who stops a voter from voting or a ballot from being counted, except as permitted by official policies or procedures.
  • Create a cause of action in the Attorney General for any violation of this bill, permitting injunctive relief, civil penalties, attorney's fees and costs, compensatory damages, and punitive damage, without limitation.
  • Create an individual cause of action, including reasonable attorney's fees for prevailing plaintiffs, for:
    • a member of a language minority group to compel language access,
    • any voter impacted by municipal acts subject to public notice and comment,
    • any voter whose vote is diluted on the basis of race, color, or language minority,
    • any voter who is intimidated, threatened, or coerced in violation of existing criminal statutes, and
    • any voter who received false information criminalized by this bill.
  • Create a voter education and outreach fund to educate voters on their voting rights.

This resolution, as enacted on August 31, 2021, amends state legislative redistricting maps that became effective on June 4, 2021. The June state legislative maps were based upon data from the 2015-2019 American Community Survey, because the 2020 decennial Census data was not released to states timely in 2021, and the Illinois General Assembly was constitutionally required to redistrict its legislative districts by June 30, 2021. This resolution amends the June state legislative redistricting maps based upon the final 2020 Census data, taking into account the factors below, and redraws the June 2021 state legislative redistricting maps with the boundaries set forth in this resolution. The factors considered by the General Assembly in drawing these revisions to the state legislative redistricting maps are:

  • Substantial equality in population.
  • Consistency with the U.S. Constitution and the federal Voting Rights Act.
  • Compactness and contiguity.
  • Consistency with the Illinois Voting Rights Act.
  • The partisan composition of the district and overall plan.
  • Preservation of core or boundaries of the existing district.
  • Preservation of communities of interest.
  • Respect for political subdivisions.
  • Maintenance of incumbent-constituent relationships.
  • Public input and testimony.

  • Respect for geographic or natural boundaries.

This bill, as enacted on June 17, 2021, changes various provisions related to absentee and in-person voting, ballot accessibility, reapportionment, and voter education.

In provisions that were in the previous version of the bill, the bill:

Permits a sheriff in a county with a population of fewer than three million people to establish a temporary polling place in the county jail. Use of the polling place is limited to incarcerated individuals who are residents of the county and have not been convicted of the offense related to their detention. Existing law required counties with three million residents or more to provide polling places at local jails but did not require or authorize smaller jurisdictions to do so.

In provisions that are new to the enacted version of the bill, the bill:

  • Creates a permanent absentee voting list (called the "list of permanent vote by mail status" in Illinois), which enrolled voters will remain on until they request to be removed or change their registration, or the election authority receives confirmation that they are registered in a new county. The bill requires local election authorities to notify all qualified voters of this option in advance of primaries and general elections, and specifies the content of the enrollment form.
  • Requires the State Board of Elections to draft proposed legislation for a procedure to electronically transmit ballots to voters with disabilities and allow those voters to use assistive technology to vote an absentee ballot.
  • Requires election authorities to operate vote centers during polling place hours on Election Day, in the office of the election authority or the largest municipality in the jurisdiction. Any qualified voter may vote in such a vote center, regardless of their assigned precinct.
  • Creates a new state holiday on November 8, 2022, deemed "2022 General Election Day," with mandated closure of schools and all government offices not related to election administration.
  • Extends 2021 reapportionment deadlines and allows 2021 reapportionment to be based upon population data determined by any reasonable method, including the most recent American Community Survey 5-year data.
  • Mandates that every high school provide students with a voter registration explainer to be created by the State Board of Election and requires high schools to allow nonpartisan voter registration activities on their grounds, subject to reasonable regulations.
  • Alters deadlines for the 2022 primary elections, including nominating petition deadlines, absentee ballot application start dates and deadlines, and early voting periods.

Requires the State Board of Elections to issue written guidance to local elections authorities regarding ballot tracking and requirements for voting, curbside voting, early voting, and vote by mail.

The bill also contains numerous provisions that are not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, relating to election security, administrative cybersecurity, vacancy appointment procedures, primary candidate petitioning, and political committee expenditure limitations, as well as governmental operations provisions, gender-neutral language changes, and other technical changes unrelated to election law.

BILLSUMMARY: Sets forth redistricting principles, the hearing process, and summaries of Legislative Districts with respect to the 2021 General Assembly Redistricting Plan.
VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as adopted on August 31, 2021, amends the federal legislative district maps that became effective on June 4, 2021. The June 2021 federal legislative maps were based upon data from the 2015-2019 American Community Survey, because the Illinois General Assembly was constitutionally required to redistrict its federal legislative districts by June 30, 2021, and 2020 decennial Census data was not timely released to states. The resolution now establishes federal legislative district boundaries based upon the final 2020 Census data, taking the following factors into account:

  • Substantial equality in population.
  • Consistency with the U.S. Constitution and the federal Voting Rights Act.
  • Compactness and contiguity.
  • Consistency with the Illinois Voting Rights Act.
  • The partisan composition of the district and overall plan.
  • Preservation of core or boundaries of the existing district.
  • Preservation of communities of interest.
  • Respect for political subdivisions.
  • Maintenance of incumbent-constituent relationships.
  • Public input and testimony.

  • Respect for geographic or natural boundaries.

    The resolution describes the extent of changes to each district from the prior boundaries, which vary from no changes at all, to changes that leave districts substantially the same, renumbered, and/or significantly altered.

    Last updated November 30, 2021.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 5, 2021, would transition Indiana to vote-by-mail elections involving vote centers for all elections after January 1, 2024. Although the bill provides detailed provisions, it also creates a committee to study all related issues and recommend further amendments to state law to facilitate the switch to mail ballot elections. In addition to creating the interim study committee, this bill would require:

  • Counties that have not yet chosen to become vote center counties to go through the process to become vote center counties by July 1, 2023, or the Indiana election commission will make a vote center plan for them. In addition, counties that are already vote center counties may amend their plans but not rescind them. Under existing law, counties can, but need not, be vote center counties and may stop being vote center counties if they choose.
  • Mail voting and in-person voting options. Starting January 1, 2024, all voters could choose to cast ballots by mail, in person early in front of a voter board, or on Election Day at a vote center. Early in-person voting would be available at the circuit court clerk's office, a county board of elections and registration, and/or a satellite office starting 28 days before the election through noon on the day before Election Day. Voting must be offered weekdays and on the two Saturdays before Election Day. Voters can also have a traveling voter board bring their ballots to them, if the voters are confined due to illness or disability, or are providing care for such a person. This kind of voting may happen on Election Day. These options mirror what is currently available under existing law, except that on Election Day some counties offer traditional polling places instead of vote centers.
  • Special voting options to be given UOCAVA voters. Under existing law these voters have similar special options.
  • Replacement ballots to be available, and that voters be able to privately and independently cast and/or correct their ballots. Voters who need assistance could receive it, but assistants must sign a related affidavit. These provisions are substantially similar to existing law.
  • Ballots to be mailed to voters approximately six weeks before Election Day. Specifically, ballots must be printed and delivered to the clerk no more than 50 days before the election, and the clerk must mail them to voter within seven days of receiving them. Under existing law ballots are mailed to people who have a valid excuse to receive them and who properly apply for them. The timeline for mailing ballots under existing law is within five days of receiving ballots, or the day of receiving a proper application, whichever is later.
  • The county to include with the ballot an addressed, postage-paid return envelope. Existing law has a similar requirement.
  • No ID can be required to receive, cast or return a mail ballot. People who vote in person must show ID.
  • Multiple ballot return options. Voters could return their ballots by mail, to a drop box, or by delivering them to the election official's office. Existing law does not authorize or require drop boxes.
  • Limited third party return options. Voters could give their ballots to a member of their household or their properly designated attorney-in-fact to return for them. The third party must complete an affidavit on a form provided by the county election official and file it with them. Existing law is similar.
  • Ballots to be returned by 6 p.m. on Election Day. Under existing law, they must be returned by noon on Election Day.
  • Counties to provide ballot drop boxes at public locations, but does not require a specific number.

  • Voter ballot envelope signatures to be compared to reference signatures, and if the election board unanimously agrees the signatures don't match, the ballot must be rejected. If the board disagrees about the match, the ballot is labeled disputed. Voters whose ballots are rejected may vote in person if there is still time. Existing law also validates ballots based on signature matching.

Last Updated January 7, 2021

  • Allows a county registration office to cancel the registration of a deceased voter based on obituary information published on the website of a funeral home.   • Shifts the authority to authorize people to vote absentee due to an emergency from the state election commission to county election boards, and provides specific criteria for when the category applies. This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2021, would create virtually identical standards for drawing state and federal legislative districts, and for public participation. Specifically, when drawing initial maps for both kinds of districts, the Legislature must:

  • Make the population in each district as close to perfectly even as possible, although the population of state legislative districts may diverge by as much as 2% from the number that would be equal.
  • Make districts compact, to the extent possible consistent with the Voting Rights Act.
  • Make districts contiguous, while stating that touching at corners is not contiguous.
  • Keep precincts within a single district.
  • Keep political subdivisions within a single district to the extent possible, while being consistent with other criteria.
  • Minimize the division of geographical areas, such as neighborhoods of a city, public school corporation attendance districts, or regions of Indiana, where the residents have common cultural, ethnic, political, or socioeconomic interests that do not necessarily coincide with the boundaries of a political subdivision, while considering the effect that the plan has on language minority groups and racial minority groups as required by the federal Voting Rights Act.
  • As much as feasibly possible, create districts without unduly favoring any person or political party.

  • Not consider or identify the residential address of the incumbent. After drawing the initial maps, the Legislature may revise them and deviate from any of the criteria as long as the reasons for the deviations are explained and documented. In addition, the Legislature must ensure that the procedures are in place to provide the public with redistricting data and computer software for drawing maps, and create a process for the public to submit maps for the Legislature's consideration.

BILLSUMMARY: Establishes a Redistricting Commission to create, hold hearings on, take public comment about, and recommend plans to redraw general assembly districts and congressional districts, provides for the appointment of four commission members by the legislative leadership, establishes the redistricting commission nominating committee to receive applications from and evaluate applicants to fill the five remaining positions on the commission.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2021, would create an eight member independent redistricting commission to create and recommend plans to redraw General Assembly and Congressional districts after soliciting public input. Four of the eight members would chosen by legislative leaders of both the majority and minority parties, and four more would be chosen by the first four by pulling names randomly from three pools of applicants pre-screened by a special independent committee created by the bill according to a process specified in detail. One pool would be qualified Democrats, one would be qualified Republicans, and one would be qualified people of either no affiliation or third party affiliation. All eight commissioners must be independent of the legislature, meeting detailed requirements relating to their job histories and positions within political parties for the six years prior to appointment.

Once part of the commission, a person cannot communicate about redistricting with a legislator, member of Congress, other elected official, a candidate for any office, or numerous other people involved in politics unless that communication occurs during a public meeting of the commission. If any such communication occurs, the commissioners must make it part of the commission's public record.

The commission must establish an internet redistricting portal with appropriate software to allow the public to draw and submit maps. The commission must also use the legislative services agency to get census and other data, and have the agency draw maps and map descriptions based on the commission's instructions. Maps drawn at the commission's request and submitted by the public must be published by May 15 of a redistricting year. The commission must hold public hearings in every congressional district following detailed procedures. By August 1, the commission must submit a report to the legislature that includes plans and maps for congressional, state senate, and state representative districts, along with legislation to enact the plans. The legislature must convene to consider the plans before October 1, and must vote on them without amending them substantively. If the legislature rejects any plan, it must detail why, and the commission must submit a new plan within two weeks. If the legislature rejects that plan, the legislature can adopt any plan.

When creating the redistricting plans, the commission must follow these standards:

  • Districts must be established on the basis of population.
  • the population of a district of the house of representatives or the senate may not deviate from the ideal district population by more than two percent of the ideal district population unless, after the map's publication, the legislative services agency determines, by analyzing past voting patterns, that compliance with the Voting Rights Act necessitates changing a district's population. However, that change result in a district that deviates from the ideal population by more than 10%
  • Districts must be composed of contiguous territory. Areas that meet only at the point of adjoining corners are not contiguous.
  • Districts must be as compact as possible to the extent practicable while considering other provisions of this chapter and the federal Voting Rights Act.
  • Districts must not breach precinct boundaries.
  • To the extent possible consistent with the above criteria, district boundaries must seek to coincide with the boundaries of Indiana political subdivisions as follows:
    • The commission shall minimize the number of counties and cities divided among more than one district.
    • If there is a choice between political subdivisions to be divided, a more populous political subdivision shall be divided before a less populous political subdivision is divided, unless the division follows a county line.
  • A plan for senate districts may not include a senate district that includes the residence address of two or more senators, one or more of whose term expires at the second general election held after the redistricting year.

  • The commission shall consider the effect that a plan has on language minority groups and racial minority groups as required by the federal Voting Rights Act.

    Last updated January 15, 2021.

This bill, as enacted on April 23, 2021, changes various aspects of election law related to absentee voting procedures, ballot accessibility, requirements for voting sites, and funding for election administration. Unless otherwise noted, the provisions below are retained unchanged from the prior version of the bill. Specifically, the bill:

  • Changes processes for the request, return, verification, and cure of absentee ballots, and for voting in person after requesting an absentee ballot. The bill:
    • Changes the absentee ballot return deadline from noon on Election Day to 6:00 p.m. on Election Day. For certain counties that neither count absentee ballots in a central location nor use electronic poll books, absentee ballots received between noon and 6:00 p.m. will be processed separately from regular ballots.
    • Creates a cure process for ballot envelopes with disputed or missing signatures. If officials determine that there is a signature defect, the ballot is deemed provisional. The county election board must notify the voter of the signature defect by mail, and, if available, email and phone, within two business days. The voter has until noon on the eighth day after the election to cure by returning a signed affidavit by mail, fax, email, or in person. For mismatched signatures, if the affidavit signature matches that on the absentee ballot, the ballot is counted and the cure signature is used to update the voter's record. If there is a continuing mismatch, the ballot is rejected. For missing signatures, the affidavit signature is compared to the voter's signature in the registration record or on the ballot application and the ballot is only counted if they match. Note that these provisions track an existing process created by the Secretary of State in response to a 2020 court order. Under existing statutory law, mismatched or missing absentee ballot signatures were rejected outright, with no ability to cure.
    • Changes the signature verification process for absentee ballots, so that the ballot signature is compared upon receipt and no later than Election Day. If the county election board does not unanimously approve the signature, the ballot envelope is marked "signature disputed" and the ballot is to be treated as a curable provisional ballot. Under existing law, a signature that was not unanimously approved by the county election board caused the ballot to be rejected outright.
    • Expands who may return a voter's completed ballot for them by authorizing the voter to give the ballot to a family member, in addition to existing law's authorization of return by household members and attorneys-in-fact. The family member must complete the existing affidavit required of people returning others' ballots. The bill also amends the related criminal offense for returning a completed ballot for another person without authorization to conform to this change.
    • Expands a voter's options for hand-delivering their completed ballot by specifying that returning an absentee ballot to the county election board by hand includes delivery to early voting locations, namely the office of the circuit court clerk or the office of the board of elections and registration, a satellite office of the circuit court clerk, or a satellite office of a vote center.
    • Requires officials to reject absentee ballots returned to any drop box, container, or location that is not under the "physical control and supervision" of the county election board at the time they are deposited. If a ballot is rejected because it was returned to an improper drop-off location, the county election board must promptly notify the voter, if possible.
    • Expands the ability of voters to get replacement absentee ballots by allowing anyone who received a ballot by mail to turn it in to get another one, except that in a primary a voter may not replace the ballot for one party with the ballot of the other party unless the original ballot was erroneous. Under existing law, a replacement absentee ballot was only available if the ballot itself contained an error that required replacement.
    • Allows absentee voter boards to bring absentee ballot applications to confined registered voters and caregivers, and to approve qualifying applications on site and provide absentee ballots. Existing law only authorized bringing absentee ballots to these voters, not ballot applications.
    • Clarifies that Indiana National Guard members deployed or on assignment in Indiana may vote absentee.
  • Changes requirements related to accessibility for absentee and in-person voting. The bill:
    • Allows people with "print disabilities," i.e., visual or dexterity impairments, to request a voter registration form or an absentee ballot application by email, fax, or web portal.
    • Requires the secretary of state, with the approval of the election division, to develop a free access system that permits a voter with print disabilities to determine whether the voter's absentee ballot has been received by the appropriate county election board or board of elections and registration, regardless of the manner in which the absentee ballot was transmitted by the voter to the board.
    • Enables voters with print disabilities to receive and return an absentee ballot using the electronic absentee voting processes available to uniformed and overseas voters.
    • Defines what qualifies as an "accessible facility" for in-person absentee (early) voting. This provision has been modified from the previous version of the bill, which did not include some of the definitions and criteria for an "accessible facility" that were enacted.
    • Clarifies that accessible voting devices can include ones that mark optical scan ballots.
  • Prohibits a political subdivision that conducts or administers an election from receiving or expending funds received from a person for preparing, administering, or conducting elections, including registering voters other than the state or the federal government.
  • Requires local officials to post public notice of election information at least 21 days before an election, rather than 10 days before as previously required, and mandates that notice must include the dates, times, and locations for voting at the circuit court clerk's office, satellite offices, and regular polling places. This is a new provision that did not appear in the previous version of the bill.
  • Prohibits people who moved out of a school corporation district 30 days or less before a question presented election affecting that district from voting on that question.

  • Makes numerous other technical and conforming changes throughout the election code in areas the Voting Rights Lab does not track, or which are non-substantive.

Last Updated September 17, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 14, 2021, would make major changes to many aspects of Indiana election law. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Lengthen voting on Election Day by closing polls at 7 p.m. instead of 6 p.m., while keeping the 6 a.m. opening time.
  • Create same day registration on Election Day. To register on Election Day and then vote, the voter must:
    • prove their residence with documentation and another voter must sign a statement corroborating the voter's residence, while also proving their own residence
    • complete a voter registration form, and
    • sign a special affirmation that includes swearing the person has not already voted in the election.
    • if the voter does not use photo ID to prove their residence, they will be given a provisional ballot. Indiana requires photo ID to vote, and offers all registered voters who appear to vote without it a provisional ballot that counts if the ID is later provided.
  • Create no excuse absentee voting.
  • Create automatic voter registration at DMV with the applicant being given the option to opt out of registering to vote or updating their registration during the transaction.
  • Expand early voting by requiring county election officials to offer satellite locations in addition to their office. Countywide, one location must be offered for every 25,000 active voters in the county, and one for any remaining number. These must be placed in each municipality that has at least 25,000 active voters, for each 25,000 active voters in that municipality. Any remaining required locations may sited as the county chooses. A vote center county must site any required early voting locations in vote centers. Under existing law, satellite locations are allowed but not required.
  • Require absentee ballot tracking. Existing law allows it but does not require it.
  • Authorize counties to use ballot drop boxes, providing they are sited on public property, open for 28 days before the election, and certain rules relating security are followed.
  • Allow counties to scan absentee ballots before Election Day, so long as they are not tabulated before Election Day.
  • Change the process of sending an address confirmation to a voter who has newly registered or updated their registration to provide that if the confirmation is returned to the postal service due to an unknown or insufficient address, the voter's registration will be made inactive. Existing law requires the voter's registration to be cancelled.

  • Criminalize as a misdemeanor electioneering within 100 feet of a drop box.

BILLSUMMARY: Removes the authority of the Secretary of State to prosecute election crimes.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2021, changes who has authority to prosecute election crimes. Under the bill, prosecution authority would vest in the appropriate county or district attorney, who could request the attorney general to prosecute instead. The bill would eliminate the Secretary of State's existing ability to prosecute election crimes and the attorney general's existing authority to prosecute them without a request from the local prosecutor. The authority given the local prosecutor under the section of law amended by this bill would be expanded to include charges of conspiracy to commit election crimes, as well as the election crimes and attempts to commit election crimes.

Last updated August 19, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2021, would reduce the penalty for several election crimes, eliminate a safe harbor for the crime of election bribery, and redefine the crime of voting without being qualified to do so. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Reduce the penalty from a severity level 9, non-person felony to a class C misdemeanor for these election crimes:
    • knowingly marking or transmitting to the county election officer more than one advance (absentee) ballot
    • knowingly interfering with or delaying the transmission of any advance ballot application from a voter to the county election officer, or mailing, faxing, or otherwise causing the application to be sent to a place other than the county election office.
    • knowingly marking, signing, or transmitting to the county election officer the advance ballot or advance ballot envelope of another voter.
    • knowingly signing an application for an advance ballot for another person except as allowed by law.
    • knowingly intercepting, interfering with, or delaying the transmission of advance ballots from the county election officer to the voter.
    • knowingly and falsely affirming, declaring, or subscribing to any material fact in an affirmation form for an advance ballot.
    • Returning another's advance ballot except as allowed by law.
  • Reduce the penalty for voting without being qualified from a severity level 7, non-person felony to a class A misdemeanor, and would redefine this crime to include knowingly
    • voting or attempting to vote when not registered to vote.
    • voting or offering to vote more than once at the same election.
    • inducing or aiding any person to vote more than once at the same election.
      Existing law defines the crime merely as knowingly voting or attempting to vote while not being a citizen or otherwise not having the qualifications to vote.
  • Reduce the penalty for election tampering from a severity level 7 non-person felony to a severity level 8 felony.
  • Reduce the penalty for false impersonation of a voter from a severity level 8 non-person felony to a severity level 9 one.

  • Eliminate a safe harbor for election bribery by repealing a provision allowing gifts to voters that are worth $3 or less if given without regard to how the person voted on an issue or candidate.

    Last updated January 11, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2021, would allow Sedgwick County to convert its polling places into vote centers by allowing any county voter to vote at any polling place in the county starting with the 2021 primary. Nonetheless, as drafted the bill arguably would allow the county to do the conversion regardless of the new regulations.

BILLSUMMARY: Concerns census data, relates to data used in adopting senatorial and representative district boundaries, conforms law with certain amendments to the State constitution and repealing certain obsolete provisions, makes conforming revisions to certain references.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on April 9, 2021, amends state law relating to data used to apportion state legislative districts to conform with a state constitutional amendment adopted in 2019. Prior to the 2019 amendment, the state constitution required the state to adjust the census count to exclude nonresident military personnel and students, and to include resident military personnel and students at their permanent addresses, before apportioning state legislative districts. The amendment ended this adjustment. This law merely conforms statutes to match.

Last updated April 12, 2021.

This bill, as enacted on May 3, 2021, by legislative override of the governor's veto:

  • Changes the rules for returning a completed mail ballot ("advance voting ballot") on behalf of a voter. The bill requires both the voter and the person delivering the ballot to sign affidavits confirming that: the voter cast the ballot without undue influence on their voting decision, the voter authorized the other person to return their ballot, and the person returning the ballot has not delivered more than ten advance voting ballots for others during that election. In addition, candidates are prohibited from delivering a ballot on behalf of anyone other than an immediate family member. No person may return more than 10 advance ballots on behalf of other voters in a single election. Under previous law, if a voter wished someone else to return their ballot, the voter had to designate that person in writing, but the designee did not also have to sign a document, and there was no limit on the number of ballots a third party could return for others. This provision has been modified from the previous version of the bill, which would have permitted a total of five ballots to be returned on behalf of other voters.
  • Creates a new felony offense for knowingly returning a completed, sealed ballot for a voter in violation of the rules relating to such ballot return, and a new misdemeanor offense for returning more than ten ballots for others. This provision is modified from the previous version of the bill, which would have punished both violations as a felony. Note that the felony offense established here overlaps in part with the existing felony offense of "advance voting suppression," which punishes the failure to deliver a voter's ballot or unduly influencing an individual's vote.
  • Requires election officials to verify that the signature on the advance ballot envelope matches the signature on file in the county registration records, unless the voter has a disability that prevents them from signing the ballot or prevents them from signing consistently with their registration signature, and expressly authorizes verification "by electronic device or by human inspection." If the signatures do not match, the existing cure process would be followed. If the ballot is not cured, it would be rejected. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have required signature comparison for everyone who is able to sign the ballot. Existing law did not require signature verification, but the Secretary of State's Elections Standards urges counties to do signature verification. The existing cure process is created by statute.
  • Prohibits election officials from knowingly accepting or expending any funds from any person for election administration, other than funds provided for by law, and creates a new felony offense for doing so. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Creates a new felony offense for falsely representing oneself as an election official, including the Secretary of State, an employee of the Secretary, a county election commissioner or clerk, or employee of either, or an employee of the county election office. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Creates a new misdemeanor offense for a candidate for office assisting any voter in marking an advance voting ballot or signing the ballot form. Under existing law, there was no express prohibition on candidates providing assistance to voters. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Creates a new felony offense for knowingly backdating or otherwise altering a postmark of a mailed advance ballot to indicate it was mailed on a date other than the one the voter or voter's designee mailed the ballot, except as otherwise provided by federal law. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Expands the misdemeanor of electioneering to prohibit candidates from touching or handling a voter's ballot during the voting process, distributing or counting ballots, hindering or obstructing any voter from voting or from entering and leaving the polls, or hindering or obstructing any election board worker from performing election duties. The crime does not apply to a candidate returning their own or their family's ballots. This is a modified provision. The previous version did not exempt a candidate returning their family's ballots.
  • Shifts election authority away from the Secretary of State by eliminating the Secretary's discretion to extend the deadline for timely postmarked ballots to arrive. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

  • Requires the Secretary of State to publish on their website monthly, and 10 days before any election, the number of registered voters in each county and how many are registered with each political party. The monthly reports must also include how many registered voters in each county were identified as having undeliverable mail. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill required the pre-election report to be 20 days before the election.

    Provisions that were amended out of previous versions of the bill would have:

  • Declared that the governor does not have any authority to alter election laws or procedures by issuance of an executive order.
  • Declared that the executive branch of state government does not have any authority to alter the state election laws, except the Secretary of State may enter a consent decree or other agreement with any state or federal court regarding the enforcement of any election law or the alteration of any election procedure if the Legislative Council gives its specific approval.

  • Repealed a section of law that authorized the Secretary of State to designate temporary alternative methods for the distribution of ballots in cases of war, natural or man-made disasters, equipment failures or other emergency conditions or circumstances which make it impossible for voters in a voting area to obtain ballots as provided by law.

     

    Note: A Kansas federal court entered a permanent injunction in December 2024 against the provision of this bill that creates a felony offense for falsely representing oneself as an election official.

     

Last Updated December 16, 2024

This bill, as introduced on February 10, 2021, would shorten the deadline to return an advance (mail) ballot and eliminate existing discretion to alter it. The bill would require ballots to be postmarked by Election Day and be received by 5 p.m. the day after Election Day. In addition, the bill would take away the Secretary of State's existing authority to allow additional time, and would also prohibit an elected or appointed official or a court to change the deadline.

Under existing law, the ballot must be postmarked on or before Election Day and received by the last mail delivery of the third day after Election Day, unless more time is given by the Secretary of State. On May 3, 2021, the Legislature overrode the Governor's veto of this bill. On November 19, 2021, the U.S. District Court (D. Kan) blocked certain provisions from taking effect while litigation continued, and with orders on February 25, 2022 , May 4, 2023, and July 3, 2025, the District Court permanently enjoined those provisions. The affected provisions are noted below.

This bill, as enacted on May 3, 2021, regulates and restricts mailing advance (mail) ballot applications to voters, shifts election authority away from the executive and judicial branches, requires a true residence to register to vote, and expands the crime of election tampering. Specifically, the bill:

  • Regulates and restricts third-party mailings of advance ballot applications by:
    • Requiring specific disclosures to be printed on the exterior of the mailing and each page other than the application.
    • Requiring the enclosed advance mail ballot application to be the official form, and prohibiting any part of it from being pre-filled. In addition, a return envelope addressed to the appropriate county election office must be included. The court permanently enjoined election officials from enforcing the provision prohibiting pre-filling of parts of the form on May 4, 2023 and July 3, 2025.
    • Creating a new misdemeanor offense for sending applications without the required disclosure, sending unofficial forms, sending pre-filled forms, or directing that the form be sent anywhere other than the appropriate county elections office. Because the prohibition on pre-filling forms has been enjoined, presumably that crime has been as well.
    • Prohibiting any third party other than a state resident or someone otherwise domiciled in the state from sending ballot applications to voters. On February 25, 2022, this provision was permanently enjoined.
    • Creating a civil penalty for sending applications when not a state resident or otherwise domiciled in the state. Because the penalty relates to a provision that is enjoined, presumably this provision is blocked too.
    • Authorizing individuals to file written complaints with the state attorney general concerning violations of the in-state-only third-party mailing restrictions, and directing the attorney general to investigate and prosecute alleged violations. Because this provision relates to provisions that have been enjoined, presumably this provision is also blocked
  • Prohibits the governor from modifying election law or procedure by executive order.
  • Prohibits the executive branch generally from modifying state election laws, except that the bill would allow the secretary of state to enter a consent decree or other agreement with a state or federal court if the legislative coordinating council gives specific approval.
  • Recognizes that state courts have powers granted by article 3 of the state constitution, but otherwise prohibits state courts from having the authority to modify state election laws except by a consent decree or other agreement that the legislative coordinating council specifically approved.
  • Requires county election officers to record and maintain both a residential and a mailing address for each voter, if they are different. The residential address must be a physical location that can be occupied, with PO boxes and other non-residences expressly prohibited. A voter registration application that does not have such an address must be rejected.

Changes the felony offense of election tampering to include:

  • making or changing any election record unless the person is lawfully carrying out an election duty,
  • changing or attempting to change, alter, destroy or conceal any vote cast by paper ballot, election machine or computer
  • changing or attempting to change any vote by manipulating computer hardware, computer software, election machine, wireless or cellular transmission or vote tabulation methods, or
  • knowingly producing false vote totals. Previous law defined election tampering as making or changing any election record while being charged with no election duty.

Last Updated September 17, 2025

This bill, as introduced on February 10, 2021, would amend the Kansas constitution to address redistricting of federal, state legislative, and state education board of education districts. If the legislature, courts or governor by veto reject a map, the commission must send the legislature a replacement, and that process repeats until maps are enacted. In drawing maps, the commission may only consider what is required by the federal and state constitutions, and "preservation of political subdivisions and preservation of communities of interest. Except as expressly provided in this subsection, the commission shall not intentionally develop redistricting plans that favor or discriminate against any individual, political party or group."

BILLSUMMARY: Establishes the state reapportionment commission, proposes reapportionment plans for congressional, senate, representative and board of education districts, imposes requirements for enactment of such plans.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on April 7, 2021, would create a five member bipartisan, independent redistricting commission to create congressional and state legislative districts according to specified criteria for the legislature to consider and adopt. Under existing state law, which this bill would not change, each state board of education districts is an aggregation of four state senate districts. Thus this commission would also indirectly draw state board of education districts. Specifically:

  • The commission would appointed from a slate of 25 nominees chosen by the Kansas Supreme Court. Four members would be picked by the majority and minority leadership in both houses of the Legislature, one member each. The four would then choose a fifth from the list offered by the Court, and that fifth could not be a member of a political party already represented on the commission. That person would chair the commission.
  • When drawing the plans, the commission would create districts of equal population in a grid-like pattern across the state, and then adjust them to:
    • Comply with the constitution of the United States and the federal voting rights act of 1965,
    • Have equal population to the extent practicable,
    • Be geographically compact and contiguous to the extent practicable,
    • Respect communities of interest to the extent practicable,
    • Use visible geographic features, city and county boundaries and undivided census tracts to the extent practicable, and
    • Favor competitive districts if there is no significant detriment to the other goals, to the extent practicable.
  • Political party registration and voting history data would not be used to preparing redistricting plans, but could be used to test plans for compliance with the goals. The residence of incumbents or candidates would not be identified or considered in preparing reapportionment plans.

  • The commission would publish draft plans and receive public comments for at least 30 days. After the commission finalized its plans, reflecting any comments it chose to incorporate, it would submit them to the legislature. The legislative research department would then publish a report that includes illustrative maps, a summary of the standards the plan must meet, and the population in each district and its relative deviation from the ideal district population. Both houses of the legislature would have a week after that report is published to consider and vote on the plans. Substantive amendments would be prohibited. If a plan fails to pass a house, the house would have to adopt a resolution explaining to the commission why. Similarly, if a plan passes both houses but is vetoed by the governor, the governor would have to explain why in the veto message. The commission would then create and submit a new plan. This process would repeat until final plans are adopted for all offices.

    Last updated April 9, 2021.

This bill, as enacted on April 7, 2021:

  • Requires all applications for absentee ballots to be submitted through an online portal that would open 45 to 14 days before Election Day, with exceptions for UOCAVA voters and those requesting emergency absentee ballots. Voters who cannot access the portal would be able to make a request by phone or in person to a clerk, who would enter the request into the portal on their behalf. Under existing law, voters could apply for an absentee ballot by telephone, fax, mail, email, or in person, and applications were accepted until seven days before an election. This provision is modified from a previous version of the bill, which did not have specify the date the absentee application portal would open.

  • Establishes procedures for contesting election results. This is a new provision amended into this version of the bill.

    Several provisions were retained from the previous version of the bill. In these provisions, the bill:


  • Establishes early voting through no-excuse "in-person absentee voting," available during normal business hours on Thursday, Friday, and Saturday before Election Day. Under existing law, in-person absentee voting was only available to voters who have a valid excuse, and was required for at least 12 working days prior to an election.
  • Eliminates in-person, excuse-required absentee voting at clerks' offices during the period for absentee voting by mail.
  • Limits third-party return of ballots to voters' relatives, housemates, and caregivers.
  • Narrows the absentee excuse for aged, disabled, and ill voters by requiring that they be unable to appear at the polls during early voting, as well as on Election Day, to be eligible for an absentee ballot.
  • Permits consolidation of precincts and establishment of vote centers through a process wherein counties would petition the state board of elections and provides an explanation why the consolidation is desirable and how the consolidated location would serve as a "focal point to meet the needs of a diverse community."
  • Requires election officials to compare a voter's ballot signature with their "signature of record," which can include what appears on their voter ID or ballot application, and requires notice and opportunity to cure for voters whose signatures are flagged as mismatches. Cure must be completed by the close of polls on Election Day for the ballot to be accepted. Existing law required comparison between the signature on the voter's ballot and their voter registration card, and did not require notice of a mismatch or the opportunity to cure.
  • Requires election officials to report "irregularities" in mail-in ballots to the county attorney or Office of the Attorney General.
  • Permits ballot return via secure drop box and require that each county establish at least one drop box. Drop boxes must be immobile and under constant video surveillance.
  • Permits processing of absentee ballots to begin up to 14 days before Election Day. Under existing law, processing could not begin until 8 a.m. on Election Day.
  • Changes the deadline for challenges to mail-in ballots from before 8 a.m. on Election Day to before 8 a.m. on the day preceding an election.
  • Provides for automatic rejection of absentee ballots that have not been sent by the county clerk to a qualified voter, but have been returned to the county board of elections or central counting board.
  • Prohibits electioneering within 100 feet of a drop box.
  • Permits the use of ballot tracking technology.
  • Extends the period that clerks have to issue an absentee ballot, from within three days of ballots being made available or a voter's request, to within four days.
  • Bars the governor and secretary of state, while acting in concert during a declared state of emergency, from altering the manner in which an election is conducted, and specifying that no other official may suspend or revise any statutes related to elections. Under existing law, the governor and secretary of state were authorized to alter the time, place, and manner of elections in areas under a state of emergency.
  • Requires removal of a voter's name from the rolls within five days of receiving notice that they have registered in another jurisdiction.
  • Specifies how the residence of a person experiencing homelessness should be determined for voting purposes.

  • Specifies that voter registration forms and election education programs must be provided to high schools annually. Existing law required both, but did not specify how frequently they must be provided.

    The statute also contains provisions regarding voting machines and other changes to the election code.
