BILLSUMMARY: Relates to the annual canvass of persons registered to vote, provides for a supplemental annual canvass of persons registered to vote, provides relative to an inactive list of voters, provides for updating voter registration information, provides for an effective date, provides for related matters.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill was engrossed on May 18, 2021, with no substantive changes from the previous version. As introduced on March 17, the bill would:

  • Require each registrar of voters to conduct a supplemental canvass annually in order to identify voters who have moved and need to update their voter registrations to their current addresses.
  • Require registrars to place such registrants on the inactive list of voters until the registrant confirms that the address on the confirmation card is correct.
  • Directs registrars to transfer a voter's registration information to the parish of residence if the voter has permanently moved to a different parish and to cancel the voter's registration if the voter has permanently moved to a different state.
  • Provides that a voter's registration must be canceled after a period of two regularly scheduled federal general elections if the voter fails to respond to a confirmation card.
  • Require biannual publication of the list of inactive voters in a newspaper.

Last updated May 21, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Provides criteria for removing deceased persons from voter registration rolls.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on June 16, 2021:

  • Requires the Department of Health to include in its monthly report of deceased individuals to the Secretary of State a deceased's birthplace, mother's maiden name, and any aliases, in addition to information already mandated. Existing law required the report to contain the deceased's name, address, date of birth, sex, and social security number. This provision was retained from the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires the Department of State to remove deceased voters from the voter registration list within 30 days of receiving the Department of Health's monthly report of deceased individuals, when information exactly matches criteria determined by the Secretary of State. Existing law did not set out a deadline for removal following receipt of the monthly report, and authorized cancellation under existing criteria for removal due to duplicate or otherwise invalid registration. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires parish registrars to review the Secretary of State's list of voters who are reported deceased but not immediately removed from the registration file, within 30 days of receipt. Registrars must review the Department of Health's data on these individuals and determine whether their registration should be cancelled. Existing law did not include a deadline for reviewing the Secretary of State's list, and did not expressly require local registrars to review Health Department information. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires parish registrars to remove voters from the rolls within 30 days of receiving a certified copy of a deceased voter's death certificate. Existing law did not specify a deadline for removal. This provision was modified from the previous version of the bill, which would have required removal within three business days of receiving a death certificate.
  • Requires parish registrars to search obituaries for possible matches with registered voters and use the information to cancel a deceased voter's registration. Under existing law, registrars were permitted, but not required, to use obituary notices to remove deceased voters from the registration file. This provision was retained from the previous version of the bill.

Last updated July 26, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Provides for the period for the conduct of early voting in the presidential election.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on June 16, 2021, extends the early voting period for presidential elections by four days, by requiring early voting for these elections to be available from 18 to seven days before the election, rather than 14 to seven days before as generally required. This provision is modified from the introduced version of the bill, which would have changed the early voting start date for all elections.

Last updated July 26, 2021.

This bill, as enacted on June 10, 2021:

  • Ends the practice of suspending the registrations of voters who are convicted of a felony and sentenced to an "order of imprisonment," which is defined to include probation and parole, unless the voter is actually incarcerated as a result of the conviction. Under existing law, individuals with felony convictions are eligible to register and vote as long as they have not been incarcerated pursuant to the order within the last five years (unless convicted of certain election crimes). But prior to this bill's passage, existing law also required the registrar to suspend the registration of any voter under an "order of imprisonment," even if that person was never sentenced to a period of incarceration and therefore retained their voting eligibility.
  • Alters the reports sent by various law enforcement entities to election officials regarding individuals with felony convictions. The changes will enable election officials to ascertain whether the individual has been incarcerated within the last five years and is therefore ineligible to vote.
  • Removes the requirement that individuals who are newly registering to vote after being sentenced to an "order of imprisonment" provide documentation from a corrections official demonstrating that they have not been incarcerated pursuant to the order in the past five years. Note however, that R.S. 18:177 requires the same documentation of voters who are seeking to restore a suspended registration, and that provision remains unchanged.

  • Clarifies that "incarceration pursuant to an order of imprisonment" means confinement in a correctional facility, including time between conviction and sentencing that is credited as time served, and incarceration following revocation of probation or parole, but not incarceration for a violation of probation or parole that does not lead to revocation for the purposes of determining eligibility for restoration. Existing law did not define the term "incarcerated."

Last Updated September 8, 2021

This bill, as enacted on June 21, 2021:

  • Allows any parish, with written approval of the secretary of state, to conduct the preparation and verification of absentee by mail and in-person absentee ("early voting") ballots beginning three days before Election Day. Under existing law, verification could begin up to four days before Election Day during a state of emergency but otherwise could not start until the day before Election Day for parishes that had received over 1000 absentee ballots and on Election Day for other parishes. This provision is modified from a previous version of the bill, which would have allowed processing to begin a maximum of four days before Election Day, with permission from the secretary of state.
  • Repeals a provision that allowed parishes to process ballots beginning up to four days before Election Day, without secretary of state approval, when there was a declared state of emergency. This provision is retained from a previous version of the bill.

 

Last Updated July 27, 2021

This bill, as enacted on June 17, 2021:

  • Potentially expands early voting opportunities by allowing registrars to offer any number of branch offices for early voting. Existing law allows only one. In addition, the bill requires the registrar to post an official sample ballot at each early voting location, rather than a screenshot of a ballot.
  • Tweaks the additional early voting program run by the Secretary of State to require the registrar, with the approval of the Secretary, to determine the days of early voting at the site offered through the program 30 days before a primary and 21 days before a general election rather than the 25 days before required by existing law for both election types.
  • Creates a new misdemeanor, and for repeat offenses, a new felony, to punish the falsification of election information obtained from contacting a telephone number of the office of the secretary of state, clerk of court, or registrar of voters or impersonating the secretary of state, clerk of court, or registrar of voters in connection with any statutorily mandated election duty of election officials.
  • Amends the address confirmation process for general voter registration list maintenance to clarify that the registrar cannot mark a voter inactive until the voter failed to return the confirmation card within 30 days. Existing law does not specify how many days the registrar must wait to decide the voter has not returned the card. In addition the bill clarifies that the general rules relating to inactive status then apply.
  • Amends the timeline for conducting a recount of absentee and early ballots when the number of those ballots is sufficient to potentially change the outcome of the election. The bill begins the count on the fifth day after the election, or if that day is a weekend or holiday, the next working day, at "a time set by the secretary of state, in conjunction with the registrar of voters and the clerk of court" and clarifies that the deadline to request such a recount is the third calendar day after the election. Under existing law, the recount begins at 10 a.m. on the fifth day after the election, and the deadline to request it is the last working day before the recount.
  • Clarifies the procedure for updating or cancelling a voter's registration when the voter is challenged on the basis that the voter moved. The bill provides that, if a challenged voter completes an address confirmation card showing the voter has moved
    • within the parish, the registrar must update their registration.
    • to another parish, the registrar must transfer their registration accordingly.
    • out of state, the registrar must cancel their registration. Existing law merely states that the registrar should "change or cancel" the registration, without this specificity.
  • Changes the deadline for mailing notice to a voter that their absentee ballot has been successfully challenged from three business days after the challenge to four business days after the challenge.
  • Clarifies that a person may only return one other voter's ballot per election, unless they are returning the ballots of their immediate family, in which case the one ballot limit does not apply. Existing law does not include the "per election" language, which could be interpreted as limiting a person to returning only one other voter's ballot ever.

 

In addition, the bill makes a number of other technical changes to myriad sections of the election code not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, such as campaign finance reporting, testing of voting machines, and election dates. Some of these provisions were amended on April 26.

 

Last Updated October 26, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Provides relative to redistricting principles and criteria.
VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as adopted on June 10, 2021, establishes criteria for redistricting U.S. Congressional districts, state legislative districts, districts for members of the public service commission and board of elementary and secondary education, and state supreme court districts. The resolution:

  • Requires all districts to be drawn such that they are:
    • compliant with the U.S. Constitution, Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965, and other applicable federal and state laws,
    • contiguous,
    • comprised of whole election districts, and
    • based on population data provided by the federal census. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.

  • Requires all districts to be respectful of political subdivisions and natural geography, to the extent practicable, as a criterion "subordinate" to the preservation of communities of interest within the same district, to the extent practicable. This provision was modified from the previous version of the bill, which would have given the criterion equal weight to the other general requirements.

    In addition to these general criteria, the resolution:

  • Requires districts for Congress and state-level offices to be:
    • single member districts,
    • as near in population as possible for congressional districts, and substantially equal (not deviating more than 5% from the ideal size) for state districts, and
    • inclusive of the entire state.
      These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires districts for state-level offices only to also be consistent with traditional district alignments, to the extent practicable. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires state supreme court districts to meet the general requirements and include the entirety of the state. This provision is modified from the previous version of the bill, which would have applied all state-level office district requirements to supreme court district plans.

Last updated August 18, 2021.

This bill, as amended on June 1, 2021, would require that "hand delivery" of a completed absentee ballot be delivery directly to an employee of the registrar at the registrar's main office, a branch office, an early voting location, or a mobile registration unit. Under existing law, "hand delivery" is not further defined or clarified. This provision was modified from a previous version of the bill, which would not have included early voting sites.

BILLSUMMARY: Provides relative to acts prohibited during early voting or on election day.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on June 4, 2021, amends the criteria of prohibited activities for electioneering and voter intimidation, which are punishable by up to $500 and/or six months in prison. Specifically, the bill:

  • Clarifies that the bar on distribution and display of campaign or political materials at polling places applies to materials that "advocate for or against a candidate, proposition, or political party appearing on the ballot in the election."
  • Expands the bar on petition circulation at polling places to cover all petitions. Existing law only prohibited activity related to recall petitions.

 

A previous version of the bill included a provision that would have authorized individuals to remain within or outside a polling place even when directed to leave by an official, if they are present for a lawful reason. That provision was amended out of the bill prior to its enactment.

 

Last updated June 11, 2021.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on April 28, 2021, would:

  • Permit election officials in counties that have publicly owned utilities to use customer information from the utility to conduct list maintenance. This provision is retained from a previous version of the bill.
  • When the utility suggested the voter moved within the parish, the voter would be sent an address confirmation notice. This provision is modified from the previous version of the bill, which would have directed parish election officials to automatically change the registrations of voters the utility said moved within the parish.

A previous version of the bill would have made list maintenance using records from public utilities mandatory.

Last updated May 3, 2021.

This bill, as amended on June 7, 2021, would:

  • Require absentee voters to include a state-ID number and the last four digits of their social security number, with their absentee ballot applications and completed ballots. Voters who have not been issued either a state ID number or a Social Security number would be permitted to attest to that fact. This provision is modified from a previous version of the bill, which would only have required that voters provide their state-issued ID number, with an option to provide a social security number if they do not have a state-issued ID. The previous version of the bill also would not have accounted for voters without Social Security numbers.
  • Direct election officials to compare a voter's mother's maiden name and identifying number on their ballot envelope to the information on record. Under existing law, only the voter's name is compared against the record of approved absentee voters.
  • Permit challenges to absentee ballots based on information provided with the ballot not matching information in the voter's registration file.
  • Require early voters who do not have a photo ID to provide the last four digits of their social security number on the affidavit such voters must sign.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 29, 2021, would make several changes facilitating voting by people reentering from incarceration. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Designate correctional facilities as voter registration agencies that must provide absentee ballot applications, and either envelopes and stamps or transmission of the application, to eligible voters upon request.
  • Require correctional facilities to provide a reentering person with a voter registration form, declination form, an offer of assistance in completing the form, and either a stamp and envelope or transmission of the registration form.
  • Mandate that supervisors of correctional facilities:
    • Notify any reentering person whose right to vote was suspended while incarcerated that the person's right to vote is restored automatically upon discharge.
    • Transmit to the secretary of the commonwealth each month identifying information about newly convicted people whose right to vote is suspended and about reentering people who were disfranchised while incarcerated.
  • Mandate that the state secretary:
    • Update voter registration databases with information about disfranchised incarcerated people and reentering people,
    • Ensure that reentering people face no continued barriers to registration or voting.
    • Allow people who have not yet reentered to pre-register until they are discharged.
    • Develop a program to educate actors within the criminal justice system on the voting rights of people incarcerated for felonies, as amended by this bill. (Incarcerated Voting: Other)
    • Ensure that judges are informed of their obligation to notify defendants facing disfranchisement of the loss and restoration of their rights.
    • Ensure that correctional facilities are prepared to help eligible voters by providing necessary materials.
    • Ensure that the language on voter registration forms is clear that reentering people regain the right to vote automatically upon discharge.
    • Ensure that the department of correction is prepared to transmit the information to the state secretary required by this bill.
    • Ensure that probation and parole officers are informed of their responsibility to notify people that their voting rights are restored.
    • Create a publicly available, single publication detailing the voting rights of people charged with or convicted of crimes.

  • Prohibit courts from accepting guilty or nolo contendere pleas or admissions of sufficient facts from criminal defendants unless the court advises the defendant of the potential loss, and subsequent restoration, of voting rights during the plea colloquy. Failure to advise the defendant of the voting rights impacts can lead to mandatory vacatur upon motion and plea withdrawal. A defendant is presumed not to have received the advisement unless it is contemporaneously noted in the record. A previous advisement during another plea colloquy does not satisfy the requirements of the bill.

HISTORY: {"date":"09/12/2022","summary":"From JOINT Committee on ELECTION LAWS: Accompanied Study Order H5026","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 29, 2021, would expand absentee voting, expand early voting, create same day voter registration, strengthen automatic voter registration, and make other changes to the registration and the voting process. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Expand absentee voting (called "vote by mail" by Massachusetts) by:
    • Allowing any qualified voter to vote absentee in any primary or election, replacing existing excuse-only absentee voting.
    • Creating a permanent absentee voter list open to any qualified voter upon request.
    • Requiring the state secretary to mail applications for absentee ballots to all registered voters by July 15 of every even-numbered year, unless the voter already has an application for an absentee ballot on file. Ballots, however, could not be mailed unless a voter had an absentee ballot application on file.
    • Requiring registrars to include applications for absentee ballots with acknowledgement notices provided to people who register to vote or change their voter registration.
    • Providing postage paid returns for absentee ballot applications.
    • Making absentee ballot application forms available in multiple languages.
    • Providing absentee ballot applications on the websites of the state secretary and every municipal clerk or registrar.
    • Creating an internet portal, on or before June 30, 2022, for absentee ballot applications for any presidential or state primary or election.
    • Ending challenges to absentee ballots based on a lack of excuse.
    • For biennial state elections, allowing ballots postmarked on or before the day of the election received by 5:00 pm on the third day after the election to be accepted and counted.
    • Allowing pre-processing, including signature comparison and review of affidavit, of absentee ballots as soon as possible after receipt.
    • Allowing a voter whose absentee ballot is rejected to vote in person at an early voting site or at a polling place on election day. Any absentee ballot received after the voter votes in person will be rejected.
    • Allowing early counting of absentee ballots after pre-processing, provided that ballots will be secured and no results may be announced before the polls close on the day of the primary or election. All ballots that are not counted early shall be delivered to the precinct for counting in accordance with existing law.
    • Creating a deadline for absentee ballot applications that requests must be received on or before the 4th business day before the primary or election, except for people admitted to a health care facility.
    • Permitting absentee ballot return by mail, return to the clerk's office or an early voting site, or deposit in a secure drop box.
    • Clarifying that the absentee ballot of a person who dies before the primary of election will be counted if the person was alive when casting the ballot (defined as depositing the ballot in the mail or returning the ballot to the clerk's office, drop box, or early voting site).
    • Amending references in existing statutes to "absentee ballots" to "mail ballots," in accordance with the framework created in this bill.
  • Expand early voting by:
    • Expanding the early voting period for biennial state elections, and local elections held on the same day, to 4-17 days before the election, from the existing 1-11 days before the election.
    • Creating an early voting period for presidential or state primaries and state special elections, and local elections held on the same day, of 4-10 days before the primary or special election.
    • Creating an early voting period for any other local elections of the 10 days before the election, if timely approved by the local legislative body.
    • Requiring Saturday and Sunday early voting hours for state primaries, presidential primaries and biennial state elections, with more hours required of larger municipalities.
    • Mandating early voting at the clerk's office, through noon on the day before the primary or election, for people who will be absent from the municipality for the hours of voting on the day of a primary or election, regardless of whether early voting is otherwise required.
    • Eliminating early absentee voting by mail in favor of in-person early voting and no-excuse absentee voting, as set forth in this bill.
  • Enable same day registration at a voter's designated precinct or an early voting site.
    • Same day registration is allowed upon completing an affidavit of registration, attesting an oath, and presenting proof of residence including a photo ID or other document with the registrant's name and address.
    • If a person fails to present proof of residence, they may vote a provisional ballot which will be counted if they present proof of residence to the clerk within 2 days after a primary or 6 days after an election.
    • Allegations of illegal voter registration shall be investigated by the attorney general or district attorney.
    • Party affiliations cannot be changed during primaries under this provision.
  • Move the deadline for voter registration, including via registration sessions held by registrars of voters, to the tenth day before the election, from twenty days under existing law.
  • Mandate disability accommodations for absentee voting in presidential or state primary elections, including:
    • electronic accessible instructions,
    • blank electronic ballot with electronic filling, printing, and signing that does not collect or store personally identifying information,
    • return envelopes, and
    • hole-punched markers in place of wet signature for certification.
  • Clarify that automatic voter registration opt-out can only occur after receiving a notice from the registrar of the person's opportunity to decline to voter or adopt a party affiliation, except that this provision does not apply to the division of medical assistance or the commonwealth health insurance connector if necessary to comply with federal law.
  • Require the heads of correctional facilities to:
    • assist eligible incarcerated people with registering and applying for absentee ballots,
    • ensure the receipt, private voting, and return of absentee ballots by eligible incarcerated voters,
    • distribute written information about voting rights and procedures to all potentially eligible voters,
    • display posters of voting rights and procedures prepared by the state secretary.
  • Allow local clerks to appoint election officers, if there are not enough, without regard to political party, voter status, residence in the town, or inclusion on a political party's list.
  • Allow local clerks to appoint wardens, clerks, or inspectors, or their deputies, without regard to political party, voter status, residence in the town, or inclusion on a political party's list, if the position is vacant within the 3 weeks before a primary or election.
  • Grant local clerks discretion about whether to issue a second voting list to election workers at the ballot box. Under existing law, a second voting list is required.
  • Set a time limit and establish defenses for claims regarding the constitutionality of any provision of this bill providing for absentee voting.
  • Create a misdemeanor for early disclosure of absentee ballot results by an election official or worker.

  • This bill also has a provision which changes the ballot auditing process for Massachusetts.

Last Updated March 24, 2022

This bill, as introduced on March 29, 2021, would sharply reduce disenfranchisement for felony convictions by limiting disqualifying felonies to certain violent crimes. Specifically, the bill would disenfranchise only people who were convicted of:

  • A crime punishable by a life sentence in state prison.
  • Manslaughter.
  • Indecent assault and battery on a child under 14, with or without aggravating factors.
  • Attempt to murder by poisoning, drowning or strangling.

  • Assault with intent to commit rape.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 29, 2021, would enable eligible incarcerated voters to register, vote absentee, and vote in person on Election Day. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the administrator of a state or county correctional facility to facilitate and coordinate absentee voting by incarcerated eligible people by
    • providing information on eligibility,
    • distributing ballot applications,
    • assisting with mailing or returning ballot applications and completed ballots to municipal clerks,
    • working with the state secretary and municipal clerks to address issues,
    • ensuring eligible voters are notified of their eligibility upon detention and provided a voter registration form and information on their voting eligibility, residency options, and voting rights if released before an election or returning a ballot,
    • ensuring that eligible voters are provided, upon their release, with information on registering or updating their registration, upcoming elections, and their voting rights,
    • entering agreements with the state secretary and registration agencies of state, county, city, and town government,
    • conducting regular voter registration drives and assist with voter registration,
    • being authorized to conduct appropriate training of staff,
    • creating and providing all forms, material, and equipment necessary to carry out voter registration activities,
    • ensuring proper compliance with applicable provisions of federal and state law,
    • having the option to enter agreements with voting advocacy groups to encourage voter participation,
    • ensuring that voter education is part of regular educational programming at the state or county correctional facility,
    • creating a voter education guide for all eligible voters,
    • providing suggested deadlines to submit applications and ballots,
    • creating and disseminating election specific candidate guides,
    • designating secure and obvious pickup and drop-off spots for ballots and voter materials,
    • providing a secure ballot dropbox within the state or county correctional facility,
    • creating and maintaining a database with voting information, including registration status and eligibility, ballot access policies, practices, and programming, absentee ballot requests, and ballots cast. This information would be transmitted to the board of registrars or election commission of the city or town where the voter resides and to the state secretary. The database would not contain information on offenses or sentencing and would not be publicly accessible,
    • mailing a voter eligibility reminder to formerly incarcerated individuals at the address on file.
  • Require the state secretary to agree with the state or county correctional facility on the facility becoming an automatic voter registration agency, in the same way the secretary agrees with other such agencies, and

  • Require each city or town hosting a house of correction to open a polling place within it.

Last Updated April 16, 2021

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 29, 2021, would expand early voting and absentee voting (called early voting by mail in this bill) for primaries and biennial state elections, by:

  • Require Saturday and Sunday early voting hours, with more hours required for larger municipalities.
  • Mandating that the state secretary mail an absentee ballot application to all registered voters between 7 and 9 weeks before the primary or election, except to any voters with an absentee or early voting application already on file.
  • Direct local elections officials to include an absentee ballot application with all new voter registrations and voter registration changes from 2-9 weeks before the primary or election.
  • Require the state secretary and local elections officials to post absentee ballot applications on their websites.
  • Extend the deadline for applying for an absentee ballot from 4 days before the election to noon on the last day of early voting (the day before the primary or election under existing law).
  • Provide for postage prepaid returns of absentee ballot applications and absentee ballots.
  • Allow absentee ballot return by delivery to the clerk's office, deposit in a dropbox, or mail. Ballots received by the closing of the polls will be counted, as will ballots postmarked on or before the date of the biennial election that are received by 5:00 pm on the third business day after the biennial election.
  • Permit early tabulation of absentee and early voting ballots provided that the ballots are secured and no results may be announced before the polls close on the day of the primary or election.
  • Provide language accessibility in accordance with the federal Voting Rights Act and requirements governing the city of Boston.
  • Provide disability accommodations for absentee ballot applications, including accessible instructions, electronic filling of the application, return envelopes, and hole-punched markers in place of a wet signature.
  • A ballot is deemed cast when it is deposited into the mail or dropbox, hand-delivered to the appropriate election official, or completed in person at an early voting location. (Absentee Voting: Other)
  • Allow party designation changes to registrations for people voting early in primaries.
  • Accept electronic signatures that match the voter's handwritten signature.

Last Updated April 21, 2021

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on September 30, 2021, would create a five year pilot project in Suffolk County to improve the registration and voting access of eligible but incarcerated people, as well as help people released from incarceration and thus restored to eligibility to know their rights. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the state secretary to create and distribute certain educational materials, including:
    • distributing voter information signage and materials to Suffolk county correctional facilities 90 days before an election signage.
    • distributing to election officers of each city and town in Suffolk county materials detailing: the qualifications and rights of eligible incarcerated voters, the application process and how to process eligible incarcerated voters in the Voter Registration Information System, and current law pertaining to said rights and processes.
  • Require the officer in charge of each correctional facility in Suffolk County to publish policies and procedures that govern the facilitation of voting and voter registration for eligible voters in correctional facilities, including:
    • distributing voter education and election information.
    • assisting eligible incarcerated persons to register to vote and apply for absentee ballots in all primaries and elections, including distributing ballot request forms, voter registration forms, individual records that may serve as proof of residence for the purpose of voter registration, and voter information packets generated by the state secretary, community groups or other stakeholders.
    • providing for the timely receipt and return of mail-in ballots by eligible incarcerated persons.
    • establishing locations where eligible incarcerated persons may complete ballots and other paperwork in private.
    • tracking incarcerated persons' complaints related to voting or registration issues, the number of incarcerated persons who sought to vote and the outcome of said complaints and requests.
    • setting policies for collaborating with local elections officials, civic engagement community groups and other stakeholders.
  • Require the officer in charge of each correctional facility in Suffolk County to:
    • hang or distribute any informational posters or packets provided by the state secretary not later than July 15 of each even-numbered year, or, if received after that date, immediately upon receipt. In addition, they must continue distribution and informational announcements through the conclusion of any primary and general election.
    • appoint a subordinate officer at the facility to supervise the actions required by this section.
    • file a written report with the state secretary, not later than 14 days before every primary and general election, detailing the actions taken pursuant to this section. The report would be a public record.
  • Require the officer in charge of each Suffolk County correctional facility, on or before the fifteenth day of each month, to transmit to the state secretary lists containing information about persons:
    • convicted of a felony who, during the preceding period, have become ineligible to vote because of their incarceration,
    • convicted of a felony who, during the preceding period, have become eligible to vote because of their discharge from incarceration, and
    • detained pre-trial or convicted of a misdemeanor and incarcerated but eligible to vote.
  • Include in each list the following information for each person:
    • name
    • date of birth
    • status as incarcerated for a felony conviction, incarcerated but not disqualified or recently released
    • last 4 digits of social security number or driver's license number, if available
    • address on file
    • race or ethnicity
    • if held pretrial or serving a misdemeanor and eligible to vote, the name and address of the jail, prison or other facility where the person is detained.

  • Require the state secretary to report, not later than 6 months following each primary and general election:

    • the number of eligible incarcerated voters by municipality
    • the number of incarcerated voters who requested an absentee ballot and the outcome of that request by municipality, including the reasons for rejection if applicable
    • the number of incarcerated voters who requested to register to vote and the outcome of those requests by municipality, including the reason for rejection if applicable and
    • each municipality's policies and practices regarding outreach and enfranchisement of eligible incarcerated voters, if applicable.

  • Require the officer in charge of a correctional facility to notify, in writing, people who are soon to be released as follows:
    • people incarcerated for a felony conviction, that their voting rights will be restored upon discharge.
    • people whose right to vote was not suspended while incarcerated, that their voting rights shall be maintained upon discharge and that, if the individual requested or submitted a mail-in ballot application or ballot, the individual maintains the right to vote in-person so long as their mail-in ballot has not been processed.
  • Require, as part of the release process leading to the discharge of an individual whose right to vote was suspended while incarcerated, that the facility provide the individual with a voter registration form and offer the individual assistance in filling out the form. The correctional facility shall provide the individual with a postage guaranteed envelope or transmit the individual's completed voter registration form to the city or town where the individual claims residence. If the individual declines to register to vote, the facility shall provide the individual with a form indicating that the individual was provided with the voter registration form and declined to register and offer the individual assistance in filling out the form.

  • Require the state secretary to deliver a secured drop box for early voting to each correctional facility prior to the start of the early voting period for a primary or general election. An eligible incarcerated voter in receipt of an early voting ballot may complete and return the ballot by using the drop box prior to Election Day. To enhance security or voter access, ballot boxes shall be portable and may be rotated to each unit to enable incarcerated persons to place ballots in the boxes themselves. The state secretary shall deliver early voting ballots submitted by secured drop box to the appropriate city or town clerk before polls close on Election Day.

Last Updated November 4, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: (Constitutional Amendment) Establishes an independent redistricting commission.
VRLANALYSIS:
This proposed constitutional amendment, as introduced on February 22, 2021, would establish a redistricting advisory commission:

  • The commission would the sole authority to draw maps, which would then have to be approved by the legislature.
  • All districts would have to be contiguous, equal in population, and in compliance with federal constitutional and statutory requirements.
  • No district could be drawn for the purpose or with the effect of diluting the voting strength of any group based on race, ethnicity, or language minority status, or for the purpose of augmenting or diluting the voting strength of a political party or individual.
  • The commission could not consider residential address, party affiliation, or partisan voting history of any individual or groups of individuals, except to the extent necessary to avoid dilution of voting strength based on race, ethnicity or language minority status.
  • To the maximum extent possible, and in this order of priority, the maps would: (1) maintain the integrity of well-defined neighborhoods, (2) observe municipal boundaries, (3) establish senatorial districts that follow representative district boundaries, (4) establish councilor districts that follow representative district boundaries, and (5) promote geographic compactness of districts.
  • The commission also would be directed to consider communities of interest in determining which cities, towns, or neighborhoods to aggregate into a single district.
  • Commission membership would be selected through a process involving legislative leadership, the governor, the attorney general, and the secretary of the commonwealth.
  • All meetings of the commission and documents produced by the commission would be open to the public, the commission would be required to hold public hearings, and there would be a three-week comment public period on preliminary plans.
  • The supreme judicial court would have original jurisdiction over challenges to congressional districts.

Last updated February 25, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: (Constitutional Amendment) Specifies the method of apportioning the General Court.
VRLANALYSIS:
This proposed constitutional amendment, as introduced on February 21, 2021, would:

  • Require that legislative redistricting be done by county, establishing a system through which small counties would be considered part of other counties for redistricting purposes. Under the existing state constitution, subdivisions are to be kept intact to the extent possible, however, there are not specific instructions on how smaller counties are to be handled.
  • Allow the legislature, when considering larger counties and cities, to subdivide them, establish multi-member districts, or delegate to local government the decision on how to set up their representation.

Last updated September 7, 2021.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 29, 2021, would enable people to register to vote on Election Day and then cast a ballot. However, the potential voter may not be able to do the registration part of the process at the polling place, while casting the ballot would occur at the polling place. The bill leaves it to the registrars to decide where and during what hours to offer registration. After registering the potential voter, the registrar would immediately send the registration information to the voter's polling place so the voter could cast a ballot. Finally, if the new registrant provides sufficient identification when registering to allow validation of the registration, the voter would cast an ordinary ballot. If not, the voter would cast a provisional ballot and would have three days after the election to provide the ID needed to verify their registration and enable the ballot to count.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 29, 2021, would:

  • Expand and improve mail voting. The bill would:
    • Expand the availability of early voting by mail to all elections. Under existing law, early voting by mail is available only for biennial November general elections.
    • Direct the state secretary to establish and maintain an online portal through which voters could request early or absentee ballots.
    • Establish a ballot receipt deadline of 5 p.m. on the third day after Election Day, so long as the ballot was postmarked by Election Day. Under existing law, ballots must be received by election day.
    • Direct the state secretary to send mail ballot applications to all registered voters sixty days before a general election.
    • Require municipalities to establish at least one drop box per 15,000 registered voters, public locations accessible at least twelve hours a day, including business hours, prioritizing transit accessibility, availability of parking, equitable distribution, and access for persons with disabilities.     • Registrants would be required to provide proof of residence, defined to mean documentation with their registration address that is either a state-issued photo ID or another form of documentation such as a copy of a current utility bill, bank statement, government check, residential lease agreement, wireless telephone statement, paycheck, a government document or correspondence, or a current student fee statement or other document from a post-secondary educational institution that verifies the student's current address.
    • Voters who register on Election Day or at an early voting site and do not have the required documentation would be permitted to cast a provisional ballot that would be counted if they returned within two business days following a primary or six days after a general election to provide documentation to an appropriate local election official.
    • The attorney general or the proper district attorney would be required to investigate credible allegations of fraudulent same-day registration.
  • Modify the state's automatic registration system to require voters to opt out after being sent notice, rather than during the relevant transaction, except at certain health agencies as required by federal law.
  • Move forward the registration deadline, excluding same-day registration, from 8 p.m. to 5 p.m. on the 20th day before Election Day.
  • Expand the availability of in-person early voting. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Establish early voting in person and by mail for all state elections and give municipalities the ability to choose to conduct early voting for local elections. Under existing law, early voting is only available for biennial general elections.
    • Extend the period during which municipalities must offer early voting to be from the 17th to the 4th days before Election Day for general elections and from the 10th to 4th days before Election Day for primaries. Under existing law, early voting runs from the 11th to 4th days before Election Day.
    • Require weekend early voting on Saturdays and Sundays. Under existing law, local election officials have the option to offer early voting on weekends but are not required to do so.
  • Modify the process for early voting by mail. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require that applications for early voting by mail ballots be sent to all registered voters before any primary or general election. The applications would contain prepaid return postage.
    • Establish a postmark deadline of Election Day, with receipt by 5 p.m. on the third day after Election Day. Under existing law, ballots must be received by the close of polls at 8 p.m. on Election Day.
    • Move the application deadline to vote early by mail ballot from the fourth business day before an election to the seventh business day.
    • Permit family members to request early voting by mail ballots on behalf of a voter.
    • Require that prepaid return postage be included with early voting by mail ballots. Existing law is silent on postage.
    • Authorize ballot return via secured municipal drop boxes. Drop boxes were authorized for the 2020 election by temporary legislation.
    • Permit the opening and depositing into the tabulation machine of early voting by mail ballots as they are received. Under existing law, this cannot take place until Election Day.
    • Require the secretary of state to establish an online portal for the submission of early voting by mail ballot requests.
    • Establish that ballots cast by individuals who die before Election Day must be counted.
  • Facilitate voting by eligible individuals detained in a correctional facility, house of correction, or jail. It would do so by requiring:
    • The posting and distribution of voting information for eligible voters.
    • Assistance in registering to vote by eligible individuals.
    • Corrections officers to ensure that mail ballots are able to be received, cast privately, and returned by detained individuals.
    • Written reports from detention facilities before each election detailing actions taken in order to facilitate voting as required.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 13, 2021, would make several major changes to the election law. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require public participation, county approval and a judicial or attorney general finding of no discriminatory impact before moving or consolidating early or Election Day polling places in census tracts with at least 20% minority residents.
  • Change the mail ballot return deadline to postmarked by the day after Election Day.
  • Require boards of election to try to contact voters who failed to sign their mail ballots and give them until the end of the canvass to provide their signature.
  • Require local boards of election to contact voters who failed to sign their mail ballot applications to try to get their signatures so the application can be processed.
  • Prohibit people from videotaping people dropping off ballots at ballot drop boxes, unless they are part of an official board of elections security effort.

  • Requires major social media and other websites to report to the state board of elections the authors of certain kinds of false election information disseminated through the websites and information about the false claims' dissemination, and report certain electioneering by foreign principals and their agents. The State Board must then notify media and disseminate accurate information. If major social media and other covered websites fail to report this information to the State Board, the Board may penalize it up to $50,000 per occurrence.

Last Updated January 13, 2021

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 13, 2021, would create mail ballot elections for all elections. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require boards of election to send a mail ballot to every voter who is registered by the 21st day before the election. Ballots would be mailed to voters 18 to 14 days before the election, unless the voter does not get regular mail delivery, in which case ballots must be mailed 20-18 days before the election. Replacements may be mailed if there is time, sent electronically, or be made available for pick up.
  • Allow the voter to return the ballot by mail, by delivery to the board of elections, by delivery to an early voting site or Election Day polling place, and to any other place designated by the board of elections to receive ballots.

  • Create a signature matching requirement. Currently ballots are counted if they are signed, timely, and otherwise valid. The bill would require the board of election to match the signature on the ballot envelope to the signature in the registration record.

Last Updated January 4, 2021

This bill, as enacted on May 30, 2021, and crossfiled with MD S 283, facilitates registration and voting by college students and military personnel, and gives certain communities input into siting polling places. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires a local board of elections that is establishing precinct boundaries and designating the location of polling places to contact and obtain input from large residential institutional communities, including institutions of higher education, continuing care retirement communities, senior communities, and military installations. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires the State Board of Elections to create an electronic process for military voters to register and apply for absentee ballots using the federal postcard application and their military IDs, and specifies that a Common Access ID card may be used to verify a voter's identity and fulfill the signature requirement for postcard applications, but individuals may not register with the card alone. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires the State Board of Elections to maintain a page on its website that (1) explains in plain, easily understandable language the requirements for students enrolled in institutions of higher education to register to vote in the state, and (2) includes links to information regarding voter registration requirements and voting by absentee ballot in other states in which students enrolled in institutions of higher education may reside. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Expands the voter registration program required of public higher education institutions to also apply to private nonprofit higher education institutions that receive state operating or capital funding. These institutions are required to:
    • Provide a prominently placed link to the online voter registration system on the homepage of the online portal used by students to register for course work. If there are fewer than 15 clicks on the link in any calendar year, the school must relocate the link to a different, more conspicuous location and take any other appropriate steps to encourage students to use the link. Existing law required only public institutions to include the voter registration link on their course registration page, and had no specific requirements for adjusting its position based on student use.
    • File an annual report to either the state higher education commission or state higher education association by January 1 each year, indicating how many students used the link, and if fewer than 15, how the school will improve the link's use. Existing law required public institutions to report on use of the link, but did not set a threshold for improvement.

      This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires public institutions of higher education to create a program to register students to vote and report on its effectiveness. Specifically, each public institution of higher education would be required to designate a staff member as the student voting coordinator to develop and implement a student voting plan to increase student voter registration and voting. The student voting plan would cover the 2-year period immediately preceding each statewide general election, be updated after each statewide general election, include wide dissemination of key information such as voter registration process and deadlines, the process and deadlines for requesting and returning a ballot by mail, locations and dates for early voting and election day voting, including transportation options to the voting locations, information about same day registration, and a link from the institution's online student portal to the webpage concerning student voter registration and voting that is maintained by the state board or a webpage on the student portal that includes the same information. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    In addition, the plan must include:
    • the provision of voter registration materials at central locations and high-traffic areas. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • reasonable collaboration with the local board of elections regarding the placement of an early voting center or precinct polling place on campus, parking, campaign signs, voter access to campus without ID, polling place space requirements, a public education campaign, ballot drop box siting, and any other factors relating to the conduct of an election. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill only addressed placement of an early voting center or precinct polling place.
    • support of recognized student organizations engaged in increasing student voter registration and voting. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • any other related activities the institution determines are appropriate. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Specifies that student voting plans may not be used to disseminate information regarding how a student should vote or who they should vote for. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.

  • Requires student voting plans to be available to the public on each institution's website, and be given to the Maryland higher education commission and the State Board of Elections. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

    A provision from the previous version of the bill was amended out of the current text. It would have required the student voting plan to include a policy excusing students from class or school employment to vote on Election Day.

Last Updated September 5, 2021

This bill, as enacted on May 30, 2021, enables incarcerated people who are eligible to vote to register and vote, and facilitates the registration of people who were formerly incarcerated and had been ineligible during their incarceration. The April 12 amendments to the bill reversed changes that had been adopted on March 20, restoring the bill to the more limited scope it had when introduced. Specifically, the enacted bill:

  • Requires the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services to include voter registration forms and information about voting eligibility restoration with the discharge papers provided to formerly incarcerated people at their release. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires the Department to display signage about voting eligibility in parole and probation offices. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires the State Board of Elections to issue regulations creating a program to facilitate the registration and voting of eligible incarcerated people. The regulations must require the state or local boards to:
    • Disseminate information on voting eligibility and voter registration applications at least 30 days before the voter registration deadline. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have required at least two distributions of information within 60 days before the deadline to register to vote.
    • Disseminate information on absentee voting, absentee ballot applications, and absentee ballots in a timely way before each election. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • Provide frequent opportunities for people to register to vote and vote. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • Provide timely collection and return of voter registration applications, absentee ballot applications, and absentee ballots. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires the cooperation of correctional institutions. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires the Department of Corrections' website to prominently feature voting eligibility information. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

  • Requires the State Board of Elections to file an annual report on the program with the Legislature. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill required the report to include information relating to the ombudsman provisions that have been amended out of this bill.

    Provisions from the previous version of the bill were amended out of the current text. They would have:


  • Required correctional facilities to:
    • display signage about voting rights in high visibility spots in all areas where people are processed for intake or release.
    • provide a secure drop box that incarcerated individuals can use to easily submit voter registration forms, mail ballot applications, and mail ballots, while requiring the board of elections to pick up the election-related materials on a regular basis.
    • return to the local board of elections any ballot that was intended for an individual who has since been released.
    • designate an employee who would serve as the primary point of contact between the state board of elections and the facility.
  • Created a voting rights ombudsman for incarcerated individuals, appointed by the State Administrator. The ombudsman would have:
    • overseen implementation of the program,
    • made recommendations to the State Board, Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services, and correctional facilities on appropriate organizations and partnerships to assist facilitating voting by incarcerated people,
    • conducted scheduled visits to correctional facilities to facilitate implementation of the program, subject to necessary security procedures,
    • reported to the Legislature annually on the implementation of the program.
  • Required the State Board to provide a toll-free voter hotline for incarcerated individuals to receive information about voting, request voting materials, and report voting rights violations. The State Board would adopt regulations for this hotline in collaboration with the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services and correctional facilities.

  • Required the State Board to engage nonpartisan community organizations to facilitate voting by eligible voters.

Last Updated September 5, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to congressional districts standards, relates to Anti-Gerrymandering of Maryland's Congressional Districts.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 13, 2021 would amend the Maryland constitution to create redistricting standards for congressional districts. If adopted, each congressional district:

  • Must consist of adjoining territory, be compact, and substantially equal in population,
  • May not account for how individuals are registered to vote, how individuals voted in the past, or the political party to which individuals belong.

  • Must give "due regard" to natural boundaries and the boundaries of political subdivisions.

    Last updated January 15, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on January 13, 2021, would create a task force to study how various election policy changes impact voter participation and election security. Specifically, the study would consider the voter participation, election security, cost, and other major impacts of:

  • Expanding early voting and same-day voter registration during early voting to additional locations, days, and hours, especially the days immediately preceding Election Day,
  • Adopting a vote-by-mail system under which all registered voters receive a ballot by mail and may return the ballot by mail or by using a ballot drop box, and
  • Increasing the use of the State's current opt-in vote-by-mail system along with continued use of early voting centers and Election Day polling places for in-person voting, and
  • Any other policy changes that in the Task Force's estimation have the potential to increase voter participation.

The committee must make recommendations to the governor and legislature by December 31, 2022.

This bill, as enacted on April 9, 2021, increases the number of required early voting centers, sets standards for siting early voting centers, and clarifies the process for designating an additional vote center in addition to the required ones. Because Maryland offers early voting on one Saturday and one Sunday, these changes expand the availability of weekend voting as well as weekday voting. Specifically, the law:

  • Increases the number of early voting centers by requiring counties with:
    • fewer than 50,000 registered voters to have one early voting center.
    • at least 50,000 registered voters but fewer than 100,000 to have two early voting centers. Previous law required these counties to offer one.
    • at least 100,000 registered voters but fewer than 200,000 to have three early voting centers. Under previous law, counties with 125,000-300,000 registered voters had to offer three.
    • at least 200,000 registered voters but fewer than 300,000 to have five early voting centers. Previous law required these counties to have four.
    • at least 300,000 registered voters but fewer than 400,000 to have seven early voting centers. Previous law required with 300,000 to 450,000 registered voters to have seven early voting centers.
    • at least 400,000 registered voters but than 500,000 to have nine early voting centers. Previous law required counties with 450,000 registered voters or more to offer 11 early voting centers.
    • at least 500,000 registered voters but fewer than 600,000 to have 11 early voting centers.
    • at least 600,000 registered voters shall have 13 early voting centers.
  • Clarifies that to add an additional voting center, the county and local board of elections must agree to do so, and then the state board of elections must approve the decision.

Sets five criteria for siting early vote centers:

  • accessibility of the early voting center to historically disenfranchised communities, including cultural groups, ethnic groups, and minority groups,
  • proximity of the early voting center to dense concentrations of voters,
  • accessibility of the early voting center by public transportation,
  • ensuring equitable distribution of early voting centers throughout the county, and
  • maximizing voter participation, including through the use of community centers and public gathering places as locations for early voting centers.

Specifically, people who are disabled, pregnant, or authorized to make the request by the state board in the interest of public health and safety may request to vote curbside. This bill, as introduced on February 5, 2021, would define a drop box and prohibit an individual, an organization, an association, a political party, or any other person from collecting absentee ballots in a container that is styled as an official or unofficial drop box. Most of the bill, however, deals with the composition of the state board of elections. This bill, as amended on April 7, 2021, would create a cure process for mail ballot defects, allow mail ballot processing to begin 18 days before Election Day, create a new felony to punish tampering with a ballot drop box, and improve upon the regulation-created tracking for mail ballots by codifying a more specific system. All other provisions in the previous version of this bill have been amended out, including those relating to drop boxes, and those requiring the State Board of Elections to hire a usability consultant and issue two reports to the Legislature. Specifically, as amended, this bill would:

  • Require the State Board to issue regulations creating a cure process that would give a voter notice of a curable defect within three days after the defect is discovered, and an opportunity to cure the defect before the conclusion of the canvass. The process would allow a voter to:
    • supply a signature if the voter failed to sign the oath on the ballot envelope, and
    • choose among multiple methods of communicating with the local board to correct a problem with the voter's absentee ballot, including text message, an accessible online portal, a mailed form, and an in-person visit to the local board office.
      This is a modified provision. As the previous version did not specify that notice must be given within three days of discovering the defect.
  • Allow local boards of election to begin accepting, rejecting, opening and/or processing mail ballots 18 days before Election Day, provided they do not tabulate ballots before Election Day. Relatedly, the board would count the first ballot received from a voter, if more than one are received. This is a new provision not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Create a new felony to punish tampering with a drop box in myriad ways, and require the State Board to issue regulations for returning ballots to drop boxes. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill. Amended out of this bill were provisions relating to the number, siting, and security of drop boxes, as well as electioneering near them.
  • Change the instructions for mail ballots informing voters that a ballot placed in a mailbox after the last pick up on Election Day will not be postmarked on Election Day. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

Require the State Board of elections to create a ballot tracking system that updates within 72 hours of information changing and which available on its website, by toll-free phone call, and if the voter provides an email when applying for an absentee ballot, by email, through which a voter could learn:

  • when the local board received voter's absentee ballot application,
  • when the local board sent the voter their absentee ballot,
  • when the local board received the voter's completed absentee ballot, and
  • when the voter's absentee ballot is counted. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill. Existing Maryland regulations, but not statutes, require the State Board to offer similar tracking information mail ballot applications and ballots, but the methods of accessing the information, the accessibility of the tracking method, and the time frame for updating information are not specified in the regulations.
  • Required the State Board to analyze and report on the results of every statewide election, post the report on its website, and submit it to the Legislature.

Required the state board to hire a usability consultant to analyze communications about mail voting, and to report to the legislature on the consultant's recommendations and how the State Board will implement them.

Last Updated April 9, 2021

This bill, as enacted on May 30, 2021, creates a permanent absentee voter list available to all voters, authorizes and regulates drop box use, requires all local boards of elections to send all voters absentee ballot applications before the 2022 and 2024 primaries unless they are on the permanent absentee voting list, requires the State Board of Elections to have a usability analysis done on all its vote by mail communications, and requires the State Board of to give the legislature a report, by January 15, 2023, on the number of voters who voted in each precinct polling place during a primary or general election in 2018, 2020, and 2022. This bill is identical to its companion, S 683, which was also enacted. Specifically, the law:

  • Creates a permanent absentee voter list available to all voters. Voters can join the list at any time, and can choose to receive the ballots by mail, fax, or internet using the ordinary mail ballot application, or by submitting a written request. Voters can join the list by submitting a written request or by submitting an application online. In addition, they must choose a communication method for the State Board of Elections to reach them outside of ballot delivery. Before each election, the State Board will attempt to contact each permanent absentee voter by the voter's chosen method to confirm the voter's address, the voter's preferred method of receiving the ballot, the voter's desire to remain on the list, and to notify the voter that they must update the local board if any of these facts change. Ballots and notices, if sent by mail, will have a prominent statement on the envelope that it should be returned to the State Board if the voter no longer lives there. The voter will continue to receive a ballot for every election unless:
    • the voter requests to be removed from the list,
    • the voter's registration is lawfully cancelled,
    • the voter fails to return an absentee ballot for two consecutive statewide general elections, or
    • mail sent to the voter by the state or local board of elections is returned as undeliverable.
  • Requires local boards of elections to send all voters not on the permanent absentee ballot list an absentee ballot application before the primary in 2022 and 2024.
  • Authorizes and regulates drop box use by:
    • Defining a drop box and providing that it can be used to return mail ballot applications and voter registration applications as well as completed mail ballots.
    • Requiring approval by the state administrator for local boards' proposed location of drop boxes, according to the following criteria: (1) the accessibility of the ballot drop box to historically disenfranchised communities, including voters with disabilities, cultural groups, ethnic groups, and minority groups, (2) proximity of the ballot drop box to dense concentrations of voters, (3) accessibility of the ballot drop box by public transportation, (4) equitable distribution of ballot drop boxes throughout the county, and (5) maximizing voter participation, including through placement of ballot drop boxes at community centers and public gathering places.
    • Requiring local boards of election to provide security for drop boxes using 24/7 video monitoring and having personnel periodically visit them in person.
    • Requiring the State Board to establish chain of custody procedures and local boards to use them while emptying each drop box each day the drop box is open for use.
    • Create a new misdemeanor offense for canvassing, electioneering, or posting any campaign material in a manner that obstructs access to a ballot drop box, or placing any campaign material or any other unauthorized material on a ballot drop box.
  • Requires the State Board to report to the Legislature by January 15, 2023, how many voters voted in each precinct polling place in the primary and general elections of 2018, 2020, and 2022.

Requires the State Board to contract with a usability consultant by August 1, 2021, to review all the public informational materials and forms related to mail voting produced by the State Board, and require the consultant to make recommendations to the State Board by December 1, 2021, regarding ways the materials and forms could be made more usable, especially by socioeconomically diverse communities. By February 1, 2022, the State Board would have to report to the Legislature on the recommendations, and the actions it has or will take to implement them.

Last Updated September 10, 2025

This bill, as introduced on February 8, 2021, would impose signature matching requirements on mail ballot paper applications and on returned mail ballots. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Revise the mail ballot application to require the voter to choose to receive election communications by mail, email or text message.
  • Require election officials to verify a mail ballot application submitted on paper by comparing the signature on the application to the voter's registration record. If the official believes the signatures do not match, the official must contact the voter using the voter's chosen method and direct the voter to submit ID.
  • Require election officials to verify absentee ballots by comparing the voter's signature to their registration record. If the signature does not match, the official must contact the voter using the voter's preferred method and instruct them to provide additional ID or vote in person.
  • Require election officials to count a provisional ballot if a returned absentee ballot is rejected.
  • Allow a voter to use the following ID types to cure a mismatched signature on either an application or ballot envelope:
    • the individual's voter registration card,
    • the individual's Social Security card,
    • the individual's valid Maryland driver's license,
    • any identification card issued by a political subdivision of the State, the State, the federal government, or any unit of a political subdivision of the State, the State, or the federal government,
    • any employee identification card that contains a photograph of the individual, or
    • a copy of a current bill, bank statement, government check, paycheck, or other government document that shows the name and current address of the individual.

  • Require the state board of elections to provide local boards of elections with machines that can verify signatures

BILLSUMMARY: Requires each member of the State Board of Elections to have at least 5 years of experience in administering elections and have extensive knowledge of State election Laws, establishes the position of Racial Equity Coordinator within the State Board to ensure that all registered voters across the State receive the same treatment and access to resources, investigate racial disparities in ballot access and voter turnout, and make recommendations on ways to improve racial equity in the administration.

This bill, as introduced on February 12, 2021, would create a notice and cure process for absentee ballot defects and set requirements for absentee ballot design. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the State Board to adopt regulations that require local boards to provide notice of absentee ballot defects and the opportunity for the voter to cure. The rules must allow a voter to provide a missing signature, and allow for corrections of ballot defects by text, mail, online submissions, or in-person at the local board office. Existing law does not provide for a statewide notice and cure process.
  • Require the State Board of Elections to develop consistent designs for absentee ballot materials, including envelopes, forms, and instructions, for use by all local boards. Among the guidelines, the bill would require the certification of any individual assisting an absentee voter to be located on the ballot envelope. Designs would have to include options for envelopes where the voter's signature is visible outside and one where the signature is hidden, as well as a bi-lingual layout option.

This bill, as introduced on January 13, 2021, would create vote by mail elections for every election. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require boards of election to mail voters a ballot for each election.
  • Allow a voter to return the ballot by mail, by delivery to the board of elections, or by delivery to any other location authorized by the board.
  • Require the state board of elections to provide local boards with ballot drop boxes. The ballot drop boxes must be open for at least 13 hours on Election Day, until 8 p.m. Existing law does not require ballot drop boxes.
  • Require boards of election to open only as many polling places as they did for the November, 2020 election, and require all of those to be vote centers at which anyone in the county can vote. Existing law requires a polling place for every precinct.
  • Require the state board of elections to issue regulations allowing local boards to count absentee ballots before election day.
  • Allow the state board of elections, but does not require it, to issue regulations requiring boards to election to match the signature on the ballot envelope with the voter's signature in the registration record. Under existing law, ballots are counted if they are timely, signed and otherwise valid.
