This bill, as enacted on May 30, 2021, and crossfiled with MD H 156, facilitates registration and voting by college students and military personnel, and gives certain communities input into siting polling places. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires a local board of elections that is establishing precinct boundaries and designating the location of polling places to contact and obtain input from large residential institutional communities, including institutions of higher education, continuing care retirement communities, senior communities, and military installations. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires the State Board of Elections to create an electronic process for military voters to register and apply for absentee ballots using the federal postcard application and their military IDs, and specifies that a Common Access ID card may be used to verify a voter's identity and fulfill the signature requirement for postcard applications, but individuals may not register with the card alone. This provision was modified from the previous version of the bill, which did not include detail regarding use of the Common Access Card.
  • Requires the State Board of Elections to maintain a page on its website that (1) explains in plain, easily understandable language the requirements for students enrolled in institutions of higher education to register to vote in the state, and (2) includes links to information regarding voter registration requirements and voting by absentee ballot in other states in which students enrolled in institutions of higher education may reside. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Expands the voter registration program currently required of public higher education institutions to also apply to private nonprofit higher education institutions that receive state operating or capital funding. These institutions are required to:
    • Provide a prominently placed link to the online voter registration system on the homepage of the online portal used by students to register for course work. If there are fewer than 15 clicks on the link in any calendar year, the school must relocate the link to a different, more conspicuous location and take any other appropriate steps to encourage students to use the link. Existing law required only public institutions to include the voter registration link on their course registration page, and had no specific requirements for adjusting its position based on student use.
    • File an annual report to either the state higher education commission or state higher education association by January 1 each year, indicating how many students used the link, and if fewer than 15, how the school will improve the link's use. Existing law required public institutions to report on use of the link, but did not set a threshold for improvement.

      These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires public institutions of higher education to create a program to register students to vote and report on its effectiveness. Specifically, each public institution of higher education would be required to designate a staff member as the student voting coordinator to develop and implement a student voting plan to increase student voter registration and voting. The student voting plan would cover the 2-year period immediately preceding each statewide general election, be updated after each statewide general election, include wide dissemination of key information such as voter registration process and deadlines, the process and deadlines for requesting and returning a ballot by mail, locations and dates for early voting and election day voting, including transportation options to the voting locations, information about same day registration, and a link from the institution's online student portal to the webpage concerning student voter registration and voting that is maintained by the state board or a webpage on the student portal that includes the same information. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    In addition, the plan must include:
    • the provision of voter registration materials at central locations and high-traffic areas.
    • reasonable collaboration with the local board of elections regarding the placement of an early voting center or precinct polling place on campus, parking, campaign signs, voter access to campus without ID, polling place space requirements, a public education campaign, ballot drop box siting, and any other factors relating to the conduct of an election.
    • support of recognized student organizations engaged in increasing student voter registration and voting.
    • any other related activities the institution determines are appropriate.

      This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Specifies that student voting plans may not be used to disseminate information regarding how a student should vote or who they should vote for. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.

  • Requires student voting plans to be available to the public on each institution's website, and be given to the Maryland higher education commission and the State Board of Elections. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

    A provision from the previous version of the bill was amended out of the current text. It would have required the student voting plan to include a policy excusing students from class or school employment to vote on Election Day.

This bill, as enacted on May 30, 2021, provides eligible voters at the Baltimore City centralized booking facility with registration and mail ballot voting opportunities. Prior to enactment, the bill was amended on April 9 to expand its scope to apply to all correctional facilities with a capacity of 50 or more adults, and to require certain election signage in correctional facilities. Subsequent amendment on April 12 undid these changes.

As enacted, the bill:

  • Requires the State Board of Elections to provide a ballot drop box to the Baltimore City centralized booking facility, which must make the box available to eligible voters incarcerated therein. This is a modified provision. In the previous version of the bill, the drop box requirement applied to correctional facilities with a capacity of 50 or more adults ("covered correctional facilities").
  • Requires the Baltimore City centralized booking facility to cooperate with the state board in implementing the drop box usage and election material dissemination. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill required the cooperation of the covered correctional facilities and the display of Board signage.
  • Requires the Baltimore City centralized booking facility to distribute election materials and drop box instructions to eligible people, and to monitor the drop box. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill applied to all covered correctional facilities.
  • Enables people to register to vote, apply for absentee ballots, and return completed ballots by putting the materials in the drop box. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires the State Board, in collaboration with the Department of Public Safety, to issue related regulations. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill required the State Board to collaborate with both the Department of Public Safety and Corrections and covered correctional facilities.

  • Requires the local board of elections to provide staff to pick up the contents of the Baltimore City centralized booking facility drop box on an at least weekly basis, collect the box itself after an election-related deadline, return the collected materials to the State Board, and to report annually to the legislature on how many people registered and voted this way. BILLSUMMARY: Repeals certain provisions of law governing the inclusion and counting of incarcerated individuals in the population count used after each decennial census for the purpose of creating congressional and certain legislative districting plans, repeals certain provisions of law requiring the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services to submit certain information for certain incarcerated individuals to the Maryland Department of Planning and the Department of Legislative Services.

This bill, as introduced on January 29, 2021, would repeal the redistricting provisions that govern how people incarcerated in Maryland are counted for the purpose of state legislative, Congressional, and municipal districts, and the related requirement that the Department of Corrections provide the data necessary to effectuate the counting. Existing law requires people who were state residents prior to their incarceration in state or federal prison to be counted at their former state residence, and people incarcerated in Maryland who were not state residents prior their incarceration to be omitted from the redistricting count. This bill, enacted on April 10, 2021, creates a permanent absentee voter list available to all voters, authorizes and regulates drop box use, requires all local boards of elections to send all voters absentee ballot applications before the 2022 and 2024 primaries unless they are on the permanent absentee voting list, requires the State Board of Elections to have a usability analysis done on all its vote by mail communications, and requires the State Board of to give the legislature a report, by January 15, 2023, on the number of voters who voted in each precinct polling place during a primary or general election in 2018, 2020, and 2022. This bill is identical to its companion, H 1048, which was also enacted. Specifically, the law:

  • Creates a permanent absentee voter list available to all voters. Voters can join the list at any time, and can choose to receive the ballots by mail, fax, or internet using the ordinary mail ballot application, or by submitting a written request. In addition, they must choose a communication method for the State Board of Elections to reach them outside of ballot delivery. Before each election, the State Board will attempt to contact each permanent absentee voter by the voter's chosen method to confirm the voter's address, the voter's preferred method of receiving the ballot, the voter's desire to remain on the list, and to notify the voter that they must update the local board if any of these facts change. Ballots and notices, if sent by mail, will have a prominent statement on the envelope that it should be returned to the State Board if the voter no longer lives there. The voter will continue to receive a ballot for every election unless:
    • the voter requests to be removed from the list,
    • the voter's registration is lawfully cancelled,
    • the voter fails to return an absentee ballot for two consecutive statewide general elections, or
    • mail sent to the voter by the state or local board of elections is returned as undeliverable.
  • Requires local boards of elections to send all voters not on the permanent absentee ballot list an absentee ballot application before the primary in 2022 and 2024.
  • Authorizes and regulates drop box use by:
    • Defining a drop box and providing that it can be used to receive mail ballot applications and voter registration applications as well as completed mail ballots.
    • Requiring approval by the state administrator for local boards' proposed location of drop boxes, according to the following criteria: (1) the accessibility of the ballot drop box to historically disenfranchised communities, including voters with disabilities, cultural groups, ethnic groups, and minority groups, (2) proximity of the ballot drop box to dense concentrations of voters, (3) accessibility of the ballot drop box by public transportation, (4) equitable distribution of ballot drop boxes throughout the county, and (5) maximizing voter participation, including through placement of ballot drop boxes at community centers and public gathering places.
    • Requiring local boards of election to provide security for drop boxes using 24/7 video monitoring and having personnel periodically visit them in person.
    • Requiring the State Board to establish chain of custody procedures and local boards to use them while emptying each drop box each day the drop box is open for use.
    • Create a new misdemeanor offense for canvassing, electioneering, or posting any campaign material in a manner that obstructs access to a ballot drop box, or placing any campaign material or any other unauthorized material on a ballot drop box.
  • Requires the State Board to report to the Legislature by January 15, 2023, how many voters voted in each precinct polling place in the primary and general elections of 2018, 2020, and 2022.

Requires the State Board to contract with a usability consultant by August 1, 2021, to review all the public informational materials and forms related to mail voting produced by the State Board, and require the consultant to make recommendations to the State Board by December 1, 2021, regarding ways the materials and forms could be made more usable, especially by socioeconomically diverse communities. By February 1, 2022, the State Board would have to report to the Legislature on the recommendations, and the actions it has or will take to implement them.

This bill, as introduced on February 5, 2021, would shift election authority away from the governor and give it to county-level officials by changing who can appoint and remove members of a local board of elections. This bill, as introduced on February 9, 2021, would make applying for an absentee ballot more difficult but require notice to voters of an incomplete application, create a cure process for defective absentee ballots, expand early voting, create rules for ballot drop boxes and prohibit unofficial ones, allow pre-Election Day canvassing of mail ballots while creating a felony for premature release of vote totals, end distributing ballots by fax and limit who can receive them by email, make changes to absentee ballot packaging, and make numerous transparency-related changes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require voters using the official absentee ballot application to include their driver's license/state ID number and last four digits of their Social Security number. Under existing law, that information is needed only to use the online system, or to receive a ballot by fax or email.
  • Require local boards of election to contact voters if their absentee ballot applications are incomplete and enable them to complete them.
  • Create a cure process for ballot defects that requires local boards of election to send notice of the defect and cure process by mail and either email or phone within three days of the defect's discovery. The voter would have until the 10th day after the election to cure the ballot defect.
  • Shift the early voting period from the second Thursday before the election through the Thursday before to the second Monday before the election to the day before, expand the hours of voting in non-presidential elections from 10 a.m. through 8 p.m. to 7 a.m. through 8 p.m., require early voting centers to be located so that 80% of voters live within a five mile radius of one, and require each early voting center to have a ballot drop box.
  • Define a ballot drop box, require local boards of election to choose where they will be placed, prohibit unofficial drop boxes, and allow voters in line to use a ballot drop box at the time polls close to remain in line and use the drop box.
  • Allow local boards of election to begin canvassing ballots at 8 a.m. 15 days before Election Day. Existing law prohibits canvassing until the Wednesday after Election Day.
  • Create a new felony to punish the premature release of election results.
  • Eliminate the ability to receive a ballot by fax, and limit who may receive one by email to people who are subject to UOCAVA, are disabled, or would otherwise not be able to vote.
  • Require local boards that use two envelopes for absentee ballots to include a privacy sleeve for the ballot, and prohibit the return envelope for all counties' absentee ballots from disclosing voter's address, zip code, or party affiliation, and require the board to count otherwise sufficient mail ballots returned missing an envelope or privacy sleeve.
  • Require the board to notify a voter if the voter returned two legally sufficient ballots. Only the earlier ballot would count.
  • Allow unaffiliated voters to pick a political party at any time, including during same day registration, and

Make numerous transparency-related changes, including:

  • Requiring election results to be broken out by early, mail, and provisional vote.
  • Requiring the state board of elections to disclose, 48 hours before its next meeting, agendas, testimony, proposed minutes, and memoranda. In addition, minutes must be detailed and searchable. Existing law requires the disclosure of agendas and minutes. The bill would impose similar requirements on local boards of election, and in addition, require local boards to meet transparency standards the state board already must meet, such as live streaming meetings and posting unedited videos of meetings on their website.
  • Requiring candidates for Governor, U.S. Representative, and U.S. Senate to participate in at least one pre-primary debate, and at least one pre-general election debate. The bill also creates a debate commission to host and set standards for the debate.
  • Requiring ballot petitions to be written at a 6th grade reading level.

This bill, as introduced on February 9, 2021, would require a voter to show ID proving identity and address to receive a regular, instead of provisional, ballot when voting in person on Election Day or during early voting. If the voter does not show ID, or if the ID indicates a change of residence from the address of the voter's registration, the voter must cast a provisional ballot. Acceptable forms of ID would be a:

  • Current government""issued photo identification,
  • Utility bill, bank statement, government check, paycheck, or any other government document that shows the voter's name and address and is dated within 3 months before the election,
  • Voter notification card, or
  • The specimen ballot mailed to the voter by a local board.

  • Finally, the bill would expand an existing misdemeanor to criminalize willfully and knowingly voting or attempting to vote using a fake ID.

This bill, as enacted on June 17, 2021:

  • Establishes a notice and cure system The bill:
    • Clarifies that clerks are required to examine any witness certification on ballot envelopes upon receipt, in addition to reviewing the voter's envelope signature and affidavit.
    • Requires clerks to notify a voter within one business day of a determination that their ballot envelope has a defect, if the voter has provided a telephone number or email address on their ballot application. If the ballot is received on Election Day or within 24 hours of Election Day, clerks must make a good faith effort to notify the voter as quickly as possible.
    • If a voter has not provided a telephone number or email address, requires clerks to deem ballots with signature discrepancies as "accepted but challenged." If a voter has not provided contact information and their ballot envelope is missing a signature, or has an incomplete affidavit or witness certification, the clerk must reject the ballot and note the reason.
    • Allows voters to cure a signature discrepancy in person or by telephone by providing their name, date of birth, residence, and confirmation that they requested an absentee ballot. If cure is made by the deadline to return an absentee ballot, the ballot will be accepted. If the voter does not meet the deadline, the ballot will be deemed accepted but challenged.
    • Allows voters to cure a missing signature in person by signing the envelope in the clerk's office and having their ballot be accepted, or by confirming their identity over the phone and having their ballot be accepted but challenged. If the voter does not cure the missing signature by the deadline to return an absentee ballot, the clerk must reject the ballot.
    • Allows voters to cure defects related to aide or witness documentation by having that person make a correction in person at the clerk's office, which will deem the ballot accepted. The voter may also confirm their identity over the phone and provide information about the aide/witness, which will deem their ballot be accepted but challenged. If the defect is not cured by the deadline to return an absentee ballot, the clerk must reject the ballot.
    • Allows voters who receive notice of an envelope defect to request a second ballot, rather than taking steps to cure the ballot already submitted.
  • Regulates the use of drop boxes. The bill:
    • Authorizes municipalities to use drop boxes and requires any jurisdiction doing so to place one drop box outside the main municipal office building or the building where in-person absentee voting takes place. Local officials may operate additional boxes at other locations with approval from the Secretary of State.
    • Requires that drop boxes be labeled, secured in place, lockable, and periodically monitored by law enforcement, municipal staff, or a surveillance camera. The bill also specifies additional requirements for security and retrieval of ballots.
    • Under existing law, return of ballots to municipal drop boxes is permitted, and there are no regulations regarding their placement or other aspects of drop box use.

The bill also clarifies that the Bureau of Motor Vehicles may begin carrying out automatic registration activities starting January 1, 2022, but is not required to do so until June 1, 2022. These provisions are modified from the previous version of the bill, which did not include authorization for the earlier start date.
  • Changes information requirements for the early voting and absentee ballot application and voting processes. The bill:
    • Requires clerks to verify the identities of early ("in-person absentee") voters by confirming with the voter their residential address and date of birth and ensuring a match with the voter's registration record. Under existing law, voters casting absentee ballots in the presence of the clerk are not required to verify their identities.
    • Requires voters to provide their date of birth on written absentee ballot applications, in addition to the existing requirement of providing their name and residence. This is a new provision amended into this version of the bill.
    • Clarifies that voters who request an absentee ballot electronically must provide their name, date of birth, and residential address. Existing law did not expressly specify the information required in an electronic request, but did require that clerks "confirm" the applicant's address and birth date with registration records.
    • Requires clerks to request the telephone number and email address of all absentee ballot applicants.This provision is modified from the previous version of the bill, which permitted voters to provide contact information for notice of ballot defects but did not require clerks to request this information of all applicants.
    • Requires clerks to request the telephone number and email address of all absentee ballot applicants.This provision is modified from the previous version of the bill, which permitted voters to provide contact information for notice of ballot defects but did not require clerks to request this information of all applicants.

  • Requires that the secretary of state establish an online portal for absentee ballot tracking. Such a system launched in the fall of 2020 but was not then required by law. This is a new provision amended into this version of the bill.

This bill, as introduced on February 25, 2021, would enact numerous changes to absent voter ballot procedures in Michigan. The bill would:

  • Require election officials to mail each registered voter an absentee voter ballot application with a postage prepaid return envelope at least 75 days before each election.
  • Require election officials to accept absent voter ballots as timely if they are postmarked by Election Day and received within 48 hours of the close of polls on Election Day. Existing law requires ballots to be received by election officials by the close of polls to be considered timely.
  • Allow absent voter counting boards to begin verifying and tabulating, but not counting, ballots 22 days before Election Day. Existing law does not allow boards to meet until the morning of Election Day.
  • Require election officials to notify voters by mail, phone, or email if the voter's signature on an absent voter ballot or ballot application is missing or deemed mismatched. Voters with missing or mismatched signatures on applications may appear before the clerk in person and present acceptable voter ID before 8 p.m. on Election Day to receive an absentee ballot. Voters with missing signatures on ballots must be notified no later than 10 days before the certification deadline and may return an unsigned ballot statement to the clerk by 5 p.m. on the third day before certification. Voters with mismatched signatures on ballots may return a signature verification statement on the same timeline as that for unsigned ballot statements. Signatures on unsigned ballot statements and signature verification statements will be compared to voters' signatures on file, but the board must accept ballots from voters who return their statements in person and provide acceptable voter ID. Board of Elections guidance from 2020 provides for a notice and cure process, but there is no mandatory statewide process under existing statutory law.
  • Require election officials to provide prepaid return postage for absent voter ballots.
  • Exclude voters on the permanent absent voter application list from the numbered of registered voters counted for the purposes of drawing precincts, and expressly require that all cities and townships must have at least one election precinct.
  • Require election officials to provide five days' notice of the opening of absent voter counting boards. The notice must inform voters that they will not be able to cancel an absent voter ballot and have another issued after the board begins meeting to verify ballots.

This bill, as enacted on October 7, 2022, allows clerks of jurisdictions with at least 10,000 residents to begin processing absentee ballots (called "absent voter" ballots in Michigan) on the Sunday and Monday before Election Day, creates new rules relating to drop boxes, and revises certain voter registration list maintenance procedures. The preprocessing procedures build on and expand those that had been authorized for the November 2020 election only.

Specifically, with regard to preprocessing, the bill:

  • Authorizes city and township clerks in jurisdictions with at least 10,000 residents to preprocess absentee ballots on the Sunday and Monday before Election Day between 7 a.m. and 8 p.m., if the clerk gives the Secretary of State written notice at least 20 days before Election Day of the days, hours, and locations preprocessing will occur.
    • For the November 8, 2022 election, the Secretary must post such notices on their website not later than October 29, 2022, but in future years is required to post them within seven business days of receiving the notice.
    • Each city or township clerk must post the notice on their city or township's website as soon as possible but not later than seven business days before the election. If the location or hours change, the clerk must post a revised notice on the city or township's website not later than 24 hours before the ballot preprocessing begins.
  • Requires the board of election commissioners to appoint at least one election inspector from each major political party for the ballot preprocessing, and must appoint, as nearly as possible, an equal number from each major party. At least one person from each party must be present during the ballot preprocessing.
  • Allows political parties, incorporated organizations, and organized committees of interested citizens to appoint 1 challenger each for each six election inspectors serving at a preprocessing location. These challengers have the rights and obligations they are subject to at polling places.
  • Requires the policies and procedures adopted by the Secretary of State regarding handling the ballot return envelopes and the ballot secrecy envelopes to be followed.
  • Allows the standard processing steps up to and including verifying that the ballot number on the stub matches the one on the ballot return envelope label. Ballots could not be removed from secrecy envelopes as part of this process, and if a voter forgot to use one, the clerk must promptly put the ballot in a secrecy envelope.
  • Requires ballots in their secrecy envelopes to be stored in certain special containers and requires certain chain of custody procedures to be followed, including having one inspector of each major party who has been present during the preprocessing sign and date a poll book addendum, recording:
    • the number of ballot envelopes opened,
    • the number of ballot envelopes a voter did not sign and thus were returned to the city or township clerk
    • the number of ballot envelopes that were challenged, not opened, and set aside to be processed by election inspectors on Election Day.
  • Requires Election Day election inspectors to include in their process verifying the number of absentee ballot envelopes opened on Sunday and Monday and the number that were challenged each day.
  • Requires the Secretary of State to make a written report about the preprocessing conducted throughout the state and related information about the participating localities. The Secretary must submit the report to the legislative committees dealing with elections no later than March 1, 2023, and every two years thereafter.
  • Makes a conforming change by shortening the time a voter has to go to the clerk and spoil the absentee ballot they had returned to 5 p.m. on the Friday before Election Day instead of existing law's deadline of 10 a.m. on the day before Election Day.

Regarding drop boxes, the bill:

  • Creates new rules for drop boxes and clarifies existing ones. Specifically, the bill:

    • Clarifies that only ballot drop boxes ordered or installed after October 1, 2020, must be monitored by video. Existing law applied the requirement to all ballot drop boxes.
    • Clarifies that drop boxes must be in publicly accessible locations, rather than public locations.
    • Requires the city or township clerk, their deputy, or their employee to regularly inspect each drop box to confirm it meets all requirements. For 2022, these people must begin their inspections by October 20 and continue them through Election Day. In future years, the inspections must begin 75 days before Election Day. Existing law did not have a similar provision.
    • Requires the clerk, deputy, or their employee to pick up election materials from their drop boxes every business day during the 15 days before Election Day and on Election Day. The person picking up the materials must bring them immediately back to the clerk's office, although they could go to multiple boxes before heading to the clerk's office. In addition, the person must use specific containers to transport the ballots. Existing law did not have similar provisions.
    • Requires the city or township clerk, for all drop boxes not located on the grounds of a city or township clerk's office or in an official satellite clerk's office staffed by clerk employees, to document each time ballots are collected and maintain that documentation for 22 months following the election. The documentation must include the collection date, number of ballots collected, the location of the box, and the name of the person who collected the ballots. Existing law did not have a similar requirement.

    Regarding voter registration list maintenance relating to deceased voters, the bill:


  • Requires the Secretary of State to share, monthly, the cancellation of deceased voters' registrations with county clerks, in addition to sharing with cities and townships as existing law requires.
  • Creates two processes for the counties to use the deceased voter information, one through the end of 2022, and one thereafter. Until December 31, 2022, at least once a month the county clerk must forward a list of the last known address and birthdate of anyone 17 1/2 years of age or older who died in the county to all city and township clerks in the county. The city and township clerks will compare this information to their voter rolls and cancel the registrations of anyone they identify as deceased.
  • Beginning January 1, 2023:
    • Monthly on or before the second business day of the month, each county clerk must update the voter registration list to initiate the cancellation of deceased voters' registrations.
    • Starting on the Friday in July before an August election, and the first Friday in October before a November election, through the 16th day before the relevant election, each county clerk must update the registration list to initiate the cancellation of deceased voters' registrations by the close of business on Friday. During the 15 days before each August or November election, each county clerk must initiate such cancellations by the close of business each business day. Finally, each county clerk must notify relevant city or township clerks of any registrations that need to be canceled after 4 p.m. the day before the election.
    • Each time a county clerk updates the registration list, the Secretary of State would send an electronic message to the appropriate city or township clerk within 24 hours.
    • Each time the Secretary updates the voter registration list with deceased voter information using data it receives directly, the Secretary will send an electronic message to the appropriate city or township clerk within 24 hours. The Secretary must notify each appropriate city or township clerk of any registrations that need to be canceled after 4 p.m. on the day before an election so the registration could be canceled.
    • Whenever a city or township clerk receives a notice from the Secretary, they will compare the information to their registration records and complete the cancellation of the registration of the person identified as deceased.

  • Requires city and township clerks, upon learning that a voter who received an absentee ballot has died, to make their "best effort" to remove that voter's sealed return ballot envelope from processing and spoil the ballot.

    The bill requires city and township clerks to maintain a record that reconciles the number of absentee (absent voter) ballots the clerk receives with the number tabulated at polling places or absent voter counting board locations, for elections with a federal or state race on the ballot only

    • certain vendor employees who perform system maintenance and security functions on the qualified voter file, and
    • the director of elections and the staff of the bureau of elections.

  • Allowed designated voter registration agencies to:

    • Use an address different from the one in the agency's files, although the Secretary of State continues to be prohibited from doing so.
    • Add to, delete from, or change the qualified voter file in the week before the election, although county, city, and township clerks would have continued to be prohibited from doing so.
    • Place a person's name in the voter registration file when that person has not signed an application, although the Secretary of State and local clerks would have continued to be prohibited from doing so.

Last Updated July 13, 2022

This bill, as introduced on May 13, 2021, and as amended on June 22, 2021, would permit city or township clerks to provide an annual absentee ballot application with options to select a primary or special primary, an election or special election, a primary or special primary and the election immediately following such primary, or all primaries and elections in a calendar year. To the extent the form used by the local clerk has fewer options than a form promulgated by the secretary of state, the local clerk must honor the option selected by the voter on the secretary of state's form. Existing law only allows local clerks to create forms with absentee ballot application requests for a specific primary or election. The June 22 amendment would also clarify that the annual absentee ballot applications provided for in the bill could not be sent more than 75 days before the first election of the year.

Last Updated June 23, 2021

This bill, as introduced on May 18, 2021, would require the secretary of state to conduct signature verification training for local clerks before even-year primary elections, and would permit the secretary of state to conduct such trainings before other elections in the secretary's discretion. The trainings must include information on matching and verifying signatures. The secretary of state would be required to promulgate rules to implement these trainings.

Last Updated May 21, 2021

This bill, as amended on March 9, 2022, would change certain requirements and rules relating to poll workers. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require poll workers to be affiliated with a political party recognized by the Secretary of State. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Under existing law, poll workers must state their political affiliations, but their party of choice need not be recognized by the Secretary.
  • Require poll workers to attest, as part of their applications, to their party affiliations. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill required a separate affidavit. Existing law requires an application that asks for party affiliation, but the application does not require an attestation.
  • Require the clerk to provide to the chairperson of each precinct and absent voter counting board a list of the precinct election inspectors assigned to that location that certifies that those individuals have a complete precinct election inspector application on file, including the required political party affiliation. This is a new provision. Existing law does not have a similar requirement.
  • Require the clerk to make that list of workers available for public inspection. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have required the affidavits of party affiliation to be available for inspection by the public at the polling place where the poll worker is stationed. Existing law does not have a similar requirement.

  • Require the clerk to provide the county chairperson of each political party a certified list containing the political party affiliation for each precinct election inspector in the city or township. This is a new provision.

    Last updated March 11, 2022.

This bill, as amended on March 9, 2022, would allow political parties, incorporated organizations, and organized committees of interested citizens to each designate additional challengers and make other changes to rules relating to challengers. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Allow these groups to designate additional challengers per absentee voter counting board, if any area where the absent voter ballots are being processed cannot be properly viewed, including, but not limited to, any area where the adjudication machine or ballot tabulators are located. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill limited groups to appointing two additional challengers each.

  • Allow these groups to designate two challengers per clerk's office, including satellites, on Election Day, to observe and challenge same day registration and voting with the same powers as polling place challengers. These challengers must serve in an area designated by the clerk that must not interfere with the working operations of any other city or township clerk business. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill did not allow the clerk to designate an area for the challengers.

    Existing law provides that such groups may designate one challenger per counting board only, and on election day allows challengers in polling places only, not clerk's offices and satellite offices. This bill would make conforming changes to other parts of code addressing challengers, such as allowing a challenger to be appointed to multiple clerk's offices, satellite locations, and precincts, not simply precincts. Similarly, the prohibition on a challenger threatening or intimidating a voter would be expanded to clerk's offices and satellite locations. Finally, the bill would prohibit a person from serving as a challenger in any precinct in which that person is a candidate for office. Existing law prevents candidates from serving as challengers anywhere. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.

Last Updated March 11, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:
his bill, as introduced on June 1, 2021, would allow election challengers and poll watchers to videotape and photograph vote tabulations, would create a new crime prohibiting such people from photographing or videotaping voters, create a new election crime for interfering with such allowed recording or photography, and would mandate or permit additional opportunities for public observation of ballot verification and tabulation.

Specifically, the bill would:

  • Allow election inspectors, election challengers, and poll watchers to photograph or videotape the vote tabulations at a precinct, absent voter counting board, or other location,
  • Create a new misdemeanor to prohibit such inspectors, challengers, and poll watchers from photographing or recording voters entering, leaving, or voting at a precinct, or a voter's personal identification.
  • Create a new misdemeanor for a person who threatens, intimidates, impedes, or prevents an election inspector, election challenger, or poll watcher while photographing or recording vote tabulation,
  • Impose a penalty of up to 93 days imprisonment or a $1,000 fine for either misdemeanor.
  • Permit local clerks to provide live video coverage of ballot custody while ballots are in the tabulation room of a precinct, absent voter counting boards, or combined absent voter counting board for an election involving a statewide office, a legislative office, or a county office. If local clerks provide such live video coverage, it must be recorded and publicly available for 40 days after the election and must be date- and time-stamped. Disruptions in the feed do not affect the tabulation of ballots but the clerk must attempt to reinstate coverage as soon as practical.
  • Require that local clerks keep all locations at which signature verification occurs open at all times to election challengers and poll watchers.

  • Require the local clerk to post a public notice at least 14 days in advance of any counting to be done by an absent voter counting board.

Last Updated September 28, 2022

This bill, as introduced on June 3, 2021, changes the process for appointing poll workers (called election inspectors in Michigan). Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require poll workers to be selected in the following order of priority:
    • people on a list submitted by a major political party who have filed a completed application and are qualified,
    • people who are registered and qualified and who have filed a completed application.
      Within these priorities, individual poll workers shall be chosen by random selection, except that the board of election commissioners must ensure that the proportion of poll workers chosen from the two major political parties does not exceed 2:1. Under existing law, these priorities and ratios are not required.
  • Direct any local board of election commissioners that does not appoint an equal number of poll workers from each major political party to submit a report detailing its efforts to appoint an equal number.
  • Require local clerks to post notice on their websites about the process to be a poll worker, including the application and submission process. This must include an opportunity to apply electronically.

  • Direct local clerks to only accept applications for poll workers between 40-90 days before an election, except that applications can be submitted closer to the election if there are not enough poll workers at the deadline. Existing law does not specify any deadlines.

    Last updated June 4, 2021.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on June 3, 2021, would:

  • Require the secretary of state to establish an objective signature verification process and train clerks and precinct inspectors on it. This process may not include a presumption regarding the validity of a signature to be verified.
  • Require that poll workers (called election inspectors in Michigan) wear a badge with their first and last name during all times polls are open and when the poll worker is acting in an official capacity. Failure to comply with the requirement would be a misdemeanor punishable by a fine or up to 93 days imprisonment.
  • Establish additional rights and responsibilities for challengers, including that:
    • Challengers have the right to use an electronic device in a polling place but may not hinder or impede a voter's right to vote or right to a secret ballot.
    • Challengers have the right to stand or sit behind the processing table.
    • Challengers have the right to observe the processing of voters but may not impede voters.
    • Challengers have the right to obtain the vote results generated in the precinct after the polls close.
    • Challengers have the right to a written explanation from the chairperson of the board of election inspectors if expelled and to appoint their replacement upon expulsion.
    • Challengers must observe the election process from a reasonable distance that allows poll workers to perform duties while allowing challengers to clearly read and observe proceedings.
  • Specify that grounds for challengers to challenge the voting rights of a voter include that the voter is not present in the poll book, the voter is claiming the identity of another person who already voted, or that the voter's ID appears invalid or fraudulent.
  • Require that local clerks prohibit any poll worker or challenger who infringes on the rights of a challenger from overseeing or monitoring election activity for two years and mandate that the infringement be logged in the precinct log.

  • Require the secretary of state to include in mandatory election official and precinct inspector training:

    • signature matching,
    • the rights of election challengers,
    • that violation of the rights of election challengers is a felony,
    • badge requirements for poll workers, and
    • that violation of poll worker badge requirements is a misdemeanor.

Last Updated March 28, 2022

This bill, as introduced on June 3, 2021, would make several changes to the process of certifying county election results. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Permits a member of a board of county canvassers to rescind their vote on certification if the vote was made under duress, as long as the change is made before the board of state canvassers announces its determination of an election. If the county canvass board member's change in vote would reverse the certification of the county election results, then the results shall be rescinded.
  • Extends the time for county clerks to report the winner of an election or primary to the secretary of state from 14 days to 21 days.

  • Requires retention of ballots for 180 days after the final determination of the board of canvassers.

    Last updated June 4, 2021.

Governor Whitmer vetoed this bill on October 29, 2021.

This bill, as amended on October 7, 2021, would have changed the effective date for Michigan's address confidentiality program, given new ID prioritization to people seeking ID on Election Day, and effectively created free ID by eliminating the existing $10 fee when the Secretary of State does any of the following:

  • Issues an original or renewal state personal ID card,
  • Grants a late renewal of a state personal ID card,
  • Renews a corrected state personal ID card,
  • Changes the residential address on a state personal ID card, or
  • Corrects an error on a state personal ID card.

The bill was explicitly contingent upon the enactment of Michigan Senate Bill 303, which Governor Whitmer also vetoed.

Last Updated July 22, 2025

This bill, as introduced on June 22, 2021, would create a state election audit board to audit the results of the 2020 general election. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require an audit of the races of President/Vice President and Senator examining:
    • The ballots, poll books, and vote tallies of at least 10% of the precincts in each county.
    • The ballots, poll books, and vote tallies of at least 20% of the precincts in each city of more than 500,000 people (only Detroit qualifies).
    • The time poll books were generated and downloaded for use on election day, including supplements.
    • Whether an electronic poll book was connected to any network after being downloaded.
    • Whether changes were made to the poll book, and, if so, who made them.
    • The name of each voter who voted on election day without providing identification.
    • Information regarding the number of ballots voted, method of voting, method of return, time of receipt, and more.
    • Information regarding the electronic voting system software, testing, networking, and timestamps.
    • How unsolicited absentee ballot applications were sent. * Require an audit and log of all changes to the voter file made between January 1, 2020, and the start date of the audit, including the person who executed the change and their location.
  • Require audit staff to examine each ballot for "proper ink markings and depressions to confirm that the ballot was completed by an individual and not a machine" and "folded crease marks."
  • Require an audit of the 2,000 youngest voters who voted by absentee ballot and investigate:
    • Whether the voter actually voted.
    • Whether the voter voted by absentee ballot.
    • How the voter applied for their absentee ballot. Any such voter who cooperates with the investigation will not be subject to criminal or civil liability. This provision shifts election authority by vesting decisions about legal culpability with the legislature instead of the judiciary and prosecutors.
  • Require an audit of the 2,000 oldest first-time voters under the age of 80 and investigate:
    • Whether the voter actually voted.
    • Whether the voter voted by absentee ballot.
    • How the voter applied for their absentee ballot. Any such voter who cooperates with the investigation will not be subject to criminal or civil liability. This provision shifts election authority by vesting decisions about legal culpability with the legislature instead of the judiciary and prosecutors.
  • Create a 7 member board, consisting of:
    • one member appointed by the Senate majority leader,
    • one member appointed by the Senate minority leader,
    • one member appointed by the Speaker of the House,
    • one member appointed by the House minority leader,
    • the Auditor General or their designee,
    • one member who was a poll challenger for the 2020 general election, appointed by the Republican party,
    • one member who was a poll challenger for the 2020 general election, appointed by the Democratic party.
  • Require the board to contract with an impartial, nonpartisan third-party auditor, who must present an audit report to the state election audit board, the governor, the secretary of state, and the legislature within 90 days after the audit is commenced. Upon receipt of this report, the state election audit board has 14 days to submit its audit report with recommendations for corrective action by law enforcement, the judiciary, the secretary of state, and the legislature. Each member of the state election audit board may present their own audit report as well.
    *Specify audit procedures, including recording, equipment, and wardrobe.

  • Appropriate $2.5 million for the audit and allow the state election audit board to appropriate any private funds received for the audit.

    Last updated March 28, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on June 29, 2021, would prohibit election officials from accepting or expending any grant, gift, or funding from private individuals, corporations, organizations, or political parties for conducting an election, which includes:

  • voter registration,
  • voter eligibility review,
  • mailing election materials,
  • sharing voter information,
  • election advertising,
  • recruiting poll workers, or

  • purchasing or using tabulators, communications devices, signs, tents, voting facilities or locations, or drop boxes.

    Last updated July 21, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on July 1, 2021, would prohibit the state and any departments, agencies, or local elections authorities from accepting a gift, money or other consideration for election related activity or equipment from any individual or entity.

Last updated July 21, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on July 1, 2021, would eliminate the requirement that local clerks maintain a master file of voter registration cards. For local clerks that opt to maintain a master file, they must keep such file under their sole custody. Under existing law, local clerks must maintain a master file kept under their sole custody.

Last updated July 2, 2021.

This bill, as amended on March 9, 2022, would prohibit and restrict private funding of election administration. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Prohibit the state, or a department, agency, commission, or board of the state, from accepting money for an election-related activity, for election-related equipment, or for any election-related staff, from an individual or nongovernmental entity. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill prohibited the Secretary of State from accepting gifts of election-related equipment, including money to be used for obtaining such equipment, from "an individual or entity."

  • Prohibit a county, city, or township from accepting money for an election-related activity, for election-related equipment, or for any election-related staff, from an individual or nongovernmental entity, except that counties, cities, and townships could receive non-governmental assistance to site polling places and absent voter counting board locations. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have prevented a "county, city, village, or township clerk, or any other local election official" from accepting gifts of election-related equipment, including money to be used for obtaining such equipment, from "an individual or entity" and did not include the exceptions for siting voting and ballot counting locations.

    Last updated March 11, 2022.

This bill, as amended on March 9, 2022, would expand how a person may apply for an absentee ballot while also prohibiting any election officials from sending unsolicited absent voter ballot applications. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Allow voters to apply for an absentee ballot in person or in writing by mail, email, or facsimile. This is a new provision. Under existing, law voters may only apply in person or by mail.

  • Prohibit local clerks from sending an absentee voter ballot application unsolicited, unless the voter is on a permanent absentee voter application list. It would also prohibit the Secretary of State from sending any absentee ballot application to any voter at any time. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

Last Updated March 11, 2022

This bill, as introduced on August 18, 2021, would create a new misdemeanor punishing any individual who intimidates an election official or prevents an election official from performing their duties. Intimidation is defined as harassing conduct that would cause a reasonable person to feel terrorized, frightened, threatened, harassed, or molested, and that actually causes that effect upon the victim. A person found guilty is subject to a fine of up to $500, imprisonment of up to 90 days, or both.

Last updated January 26, 2022.

This bill, as amended on March 9, 2022, would change how voters may submit absentee ballot applications. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Authorize voters to submit absentee ballot applications by fax or email, in addition to applying in person and by mail as existing law allows. This is a new provision.

  • Require voters to physically sign absentee ballot applications, prohibiting the use of electronic or digital signatures, and prohibit the use of online absentee ballot applications that do not require a wet signature. Existing law is silent as to whether digital signatures are accepted.

Last Updated March 11, 2022

This bill, as amended on June 21, 2022, would require limited ID badges for challengers and documenting the resolution of challenges. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require clerks to provide all challengers with an ID badge identifying the person as a challenger, but forbid including the challenger's name, political party, or other identifying marks.
  • Require challengers to wear their ID badge at all times while acting as a challenger.
  • Require that challengers check in with election inspector chairpersons upon arrival and departure.

  • Mandate that election inspectors enter challengers' names, arrival and departure times, and any challenges and their resolutions into the poll book.

    Last updated June 22, 2022

Bill version 9/23/21: This bill, as introduced on September 23, 2021, would provide that all incarcerated people are eligible to vote. Under current Michigan law, people who are incarcerated after conviction are not eligible to vote.

Bill version 12/14/21: This bill, as introduced on December 14, 2021, would create several new crimes for people who threaten or harm election officials. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create a new misdemeanor for any person who communicates to any other person that he or she will physically harm an election official because that person is an election official. This offense is punishable by imprisonment up to one year and a fine of up to $1,000.

This bill, as amended on June 23, 2021, would have changed procedures for the removal of deceased voters from the qualified voter file. The bill would have:

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on April 13, 2021, would change numerous aspects of Minnesota election law.

Many of the bill's provisions remain unchanged from the previous version of the bill. They would:

  • Require Election Day-style early voting for federal, state, and county elections beginning 30 days before Election Day and ending at 5 p.m. on the day before Election Day. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require early voting be offered at county auditor and municipal clerk offices and may be offered at other locations approved by local election officials. Jurisdictions must offer one location for every 50,000 residents and must ensure that locations are geographically distributed to ensure a reasonable opportunity for all voters to vote early.
    • Require early voting hours to be available 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. weekdays (8 a.m. to 8 p.m. at least one weekday during the early voting period) and 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. on the final two Saturdays of the early voting period. Election officials must provide notice of early voting locations on their websites at least 14 days before the beginning of the early voting period.
    • Require early voters to sign the same polling place certificate as Election Day voters. The bill would also give city officials the option to provide Election Day-style early voting for city elections. Existing law provides a type of early voting through in-person, no-excuse absentee voting.
  • Restore the rights of persons convicted of felonies automatically following the completion of any term of incarceration for the felony. The bill would require officials at state and local correctional facilities to provide notice of restoration of voting eligibility and a voter registration form to each inmate upon release. The bill also requires the Secretary of State to prepare a publication detailing the voting rights of persons charged and convicted of crimes for distribution to various agencies involved in the criminal justice process.
  • Require election officials to accept absentee and mail ballot election ballots that are postmarked by Election Day and received by the election official no later than seven days after Election Day. The bill would also require election officials to accept ballots returned by hand delivery until 8 p.m. on Election Day. Existing law requires mailed ballots to be received by 8 p.m. on Election Day and hand-delivered ballots to be received by 3 p.m. on Election Day.
  • Require counties and localities to provide drop boxes for the return of absentee and mail ballot election ballots. The bill would require each jurisdiction to provide at least one drop box for every 20,000 registered voters. Boxes would be available 24 hours a day. Election officials would monitor boxes continuously through video surveillance or other means and would retrieve ballots from boxes at least once per day. Election officials would publish a preliminary list of drop box locations at least 35 days before the start of the absentee voting period and a final list of locations at least 15 days before the start of the absentee voting period. The bill would also apply existing prohibitions against electioneering to the area within 100 feet of a drop box.
  • Require automatic voter registration for persons completing transactions with the Department of Public Safety. Persons completing these transactions would receive a notice of registration that would provide instructions for opting out of automatic registration. The bill would authorize other state agencies to provide automatic voter registration if their application process collects sufficient data for voter registration purposes. The bill would also provide safe harbor against criminal prosecution for ineligible voters whose information is transmitted for voter registration purposes unless the person is aware of their ineligibility and takes voluntary action to apply for registration.
  • Create additional means for a person to prove residence for the purpose of Election Day registration. The bill would add a learner's permit, a receipt for any form of ID issued by the Department of Public Safety, and a notice of late registration containing the voter's current valid address to the list of documents sufficient to prove residence. An eligible voter who resides on a reservation but does not have a residential address recognized by the U. S. Postal Service could register to vote using the address of the tribal council headquarters as the voter's residential address. Additionally, eligible voters could prove residence by presenting one of:
    • 1) a driver's license, learner's permit, or state ID issued by Minnesota or any other state,
    • 2) a U.S. passport,
    • 3) a U.S. military or veteran photo ID card,
    • 4) a student photo ID card issued by a Minnesota postsecondary institution, or
    • 5) a tribal photo ID card issued by the tribal government of a tribe recognized by the Bureau of Indian Affairs that contains the individual's signature, with one of the following containing the voter's current address:
      • a) a utility bill, bank statement, credit card statement, or rent or mortgage statement,
      • b) a student fee statement, or
      • c) a residential lease. Student IDs would be permissible only if the postsecondary institution certifies them for use at least 60 days before Election Day.
  • Change the permanent absentee voter list to require election officials to automatically send absentee ballots to voters on the permanent absentee voter list prior to all elections. Existing law requires election officials to send ballot applications to all voters on the permanent absentee voter list prior to all elections.
  • Allow otherwise eligible individuals to pre-register to vote if they are at least 16 years old. Existing law allows individuals to pre-register only if they will be 18 by the time of the next general election.
  • Eliminate the limitation for one person to assist only three voters in any election.
  • Create new misdemeanor prohibitions against intimidation of voters, elections officials, and persons providing assistance to voters, deceptive practices to deter voting, and interference with registration or voting.
  • Require election officials to create voting instructions and sample ballots in the Spanish, Hmong, and Somali languages to be made available at polling places in print, electronic, and audio-visual formats.
  • Establish minimum requirements for language accessibility for polling places. If at least three percent of the voting age population of a precinct are members of a language minority, the precinct must be provided at least two copies of the voting materials translated to the primary language of the identified language minority. If at least 20 percent of the voting age population of a precinct, or if interested citizens otherwise provide election officials information that a need exists, the precinct must be provided at least four copies of the translated voter materials and at least one election judge certified to translate in the primary language of the identified language minority.
  • Require the Secretary of State to create a third party interface to allow voter registration groups to enter registration applications on the Secretary's registration website.
  • Require postsecondary institutions to file a list of students in campus housing or residing within 10 miles of campus with election officials.
  • Make the list of applicants for absentee ballots public record.

A provision from a previous version of the bill was amended out of the current text on February 4, 2021. It would have removed the requirement for a voter to have a witness sign an absentee or mail ballot election ballot.

Provisions related to redistricting, which VRL does not track, were amended out of the current text.

The April 13, 2021 amendments removed provisions to make changes to campaign finance laws.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 19, 2021, would:

  • Require election officials to create voting instructions and sample ballots in the Spanish, Hmong, and Somali languages to be made available at polling places in print, electronic, and audio-visual formats.
  • Establish minimum requirements for language accessibility for polling places. If at least three percent of the voting age population of a precinct are members of a language minority, the precinct must be provided at least two copies of the voting materials translated to the primary language of the identified language minority. If at least 20 percent of the voting age population of a precinct, or if interested citizens otherwise provide election officials information that a need exists, the precinct must be provided at least four copies of the translated voter materials and at least one election judge certified to translate in the primary language of the identified language minority.

Last updated January 20, 2021.

HISTORY: {"date":"01/21/2021","summary":"To HOUSE Committee on STATE GOVERNMENT FINANCE AND ELECTIONS","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 21, 2021, would create photo ID requirements for Election Day voting and same day registration. The bill would:

  • Require voters to present photo ID prior to voting in person. Acceptable forms of photo ID would include: 1) a driver's license, state ID, or voter ID card issued by the Minnesota Department of Public Safety that contains the voter's current address, 2) a tribal ID issued by a tribe recognized by the Bureau of Indian Affairs containing the voter's photo and current address, 3) an original receipt for a Minnesota driver's license, state ID, or voter ID accompanied by an expired driver's license or state ID issued by any state, 4) for residents of shelter facilities for battered women, a Minnesota driver's license or state ID containing the voter's former residential address accompanied by certification of residence in the facility, and 5) for students, a driver's license, state ID, or voter ID issued by any state accompanied by a copy of the student's fee statement containing the student's current address.
  • Require a person to show acceptable photo ID to prove identity and residency prior to registering on Election Day. Existing law only requires the registrant to proof residency in one of several ways, including vouching by another registered voter. Acceptable ID for Election Day registration would include: 1) a driver's license, state ID, or voter ID card issued by the Minnesota Department of Public Safety that contains the voter's current address, 2) a tribal ID issued by a tribe recognized by the Bureau of Indian Affairs containing the voter's photo and current address, 3) an original receipt for a Minnesota driver's license, state ID, or voter ID accompanied by an expired driver's license or state ID issued by any state, a U.S. passport, a local, state, or federal government photo ID card, a student photo ID from a postsecondary institution with a campus in Minnesota, or a tribal photo ID, 4) for residents of shelter facilities for battered women, a Minnesota driver's license or state ID containing the voter's former residential address accompanied by certification of residence in the facility, and 5) for students, a driver's license, state ID, or voter ID issued by any state accompanied by a copy of the student's fee statement containing the student's current address.
  • Create a free voter ID card that a voter may acquire through the Department of Public Safety. An applicant must present verification that the applicant is at least 18 years of age, is a citizen of the United States, and will have maintained residence in Minnesota for at least 20 days immediately preceding the next election.
  • Create provisional ballots that may be cast by voters who do not present valid photo ID when attempting to vote and voters whose eligibility to vote is challenged. The voter would complete a statement with identifying information and would have up to seven calendar days after Election Day to present photo ID sufficient under the bill for same day registration to the county auditor or municipal clerk to have the provisional ballot counted. Minnesota does not have provisional ballots under existing law and challenged voters are allowed to cast regular ballots after taking an oath administered by election workers and signing an eligibility certificate.

  • Require election officials to send a notice of registration to all new registrants that advises them of the photo ID requirements to vote in person.

Last Updated January 22, 2021

HISTORY: {"date":"01/25/2021","summary":"To HOUSE Committee on STATE GOVERNMENT FINANCE AND ELECTIONS","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 25, 2021, would:

  • Require voters to present photo ID prior to voting in person. Acceptable forms of photo ID would include:
    • 1) a driver's license, state ID, or voter ID card issued by the Minnesota Department of Public Safety,
    • 2) a valid U.S. military photo ID card containing the voter's current address,
    • 3) a tribal ID issued by a tribe recognized by the Bureau of Indian Affairs containing the voter's photo and current address,
    • 4) an original receipt for a Minnesota driver's license, state ID, or voter ID containing the voter's photo or, if without a photo, accompanied by an expired Minnesota driver's license, state ID, or voter ID, a U.S. passport, a state or federal government photo ID, a tribal photo ID, or a student photo ID from a college or university in Minnesota,
    • 5) a U.S. passport, tribal photo ID, or U.S. military photo ID not containing the voter's current address accompanied by one of 19 types of documents containing the voter's current address, including utility, financial, student, employment, and public benefit information,
    • 6) for students, a driver's license, state ID, or voter ID issued by any state accompanied by a copy of the student's fee statement containing the student's current address, or
    • 7) for voters in residential facilities, a Minnesota driver's license, state ID, or voter ID without their current address accompanied by certification of residence in the facility.
  • Require voters to show their photo ID to a witness prior to completing the certificate on an absentee ballot or mail ballot election ballot. The witness would note the type of ID presented on the ballot certificate. Ballots with incomplete ID certifications would be rejected. Witnesses would also need to provide a state ID number or the last four digits of their Social Security number on the absentee ballot certificate. Voters who attempted to procure valid ID but failed to do so may submit a sworn affidavit to that effect.
  • Require a person to show acceptable photo ID prior to registering on Election Day. Existing law only requires the registrant to proof residency in one of several ways, including vouching by another registered voter.
  • Create a free voter ID card that a voter may acquire through the Department of Public Safety. The voter ID application would require a voter to provide the last four digits of their Social Security number, proof of U.S. citizenship, and a photo ID document. Each voter ID would include a unique identifying number. The bill would also require the state to provide any vital record necessary for a voter to obtain a voter ID card free of charge. The voter ID card would need to be renewed by the voter every four years, except voters over age 65 would need to renew every eight years.
  • Create provisional ballots that may be cast by voters who do not present valid photo ID when attempting to vote. The voter would complete a statement with identifying information and would have up to seven calendar days after Election Day to present valid photo ID to the county auditor or municipal clerk to have the provisional ballot counted. Minnesota does not have provisional ballots under existing law.
  • Allow voters who attempted to procure valid ID but failed to do so to submit a sworn affidavit to that effect to verify absentee, mail, and provisional ballots.
  • Make conforming changes to voter registration forms, absentee ballot applications and certificates, and voter list maintenance activity to include the use of voter identification numbers in voter registration records.
  • Require the Secretary of State to conduct a public education campaign concerning the voter ID provisions enacted by the bill.
  • Move county and state canvassing and election certification deadlines to later dates to provide for the time to verify provisional ballots.

NOTE: The voter ID requirements of the bill would be effective June 1, 2023. The provisions relating to the availability of free voter ID would be effective June 1, 2022.

Last Updated July 22, 2025

This bill, as introduced on January 28, 2021, would:

  • Limit third party return of absentee ballots to certain relatives, a legal guardian, or household member of a voter and agents appointed by hospital patients and residents of health care facilities. Existing law allow a voter to appoint any person as an agent to return an absentee ballot.
  • Make return of an absentee ballot by a person other than those authorized by the bill a felony. The bill would also create a new felony offense for bribing, treating, or soliciting a voter to apply for, complete, or cast an absentee ballot.
  • Require a sentencing court to impose a nonwaivable $1000 assessment on individuals convicted of certain offenses related to voter fraud.
  • Require a county attorney to prosecute all reports of potential offenses related to voter registration and absentee voting for which probable cause exists. The bill would also require each county attorney who receives such reports to provide a report concerning the outcome of the investigation to the Secretary of State and the ranking members of the legislative committees responsible for elections procedures.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on March 4, 2021, would:

  • Create automatic voter registration related to driver's license transactions with the Department of Public Safety. The bill would also require the Department to transmit the information from all applications sufficient to establish eligibility to register to vote to the Secretary of State. The Secretary would then transmit the information for each registrant to the appropriate county auditor. The auditor would mail a notice to the registrant instructing them that they may decline to be registered within 20 days of completion of the triggering application. The previous version of the bill would have also created automatic voter registration for applications for medical assistance or MinnesotaCare with the Department of Human Services.
  • Allow other state agencies to implement procedures to participate in automatic voter registration. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

  • Prohibits the prosecution of an ineligible person whose registration information is transmitted pursuant to the procedures created by the bill unless the person knows of their ineligibility to vote and takes voluntary action to become registered. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 10, 2021, would:

  • Prohibit a third party from mailing an absentee ballot on behalf of another person. The bill would require all third party return to be in person and would require the third party to provide their name, address, and phone and sign a statement certifying compliance with the laws concerning third party return.
  • Require any person assisting a voter casting a ballot in person to provide their name, address, and phone number and sign a statement certifying compliance with the laws concerning voter assistance.
  • Prohibit an individual to be compensated on a per ballot basis for soliciting, collecting, or accepting absentee ballot applications. Individuals compensated for ballot solicitation, collection, or acceptance may not have pay withheld for failing to collect a minimum number of applications and may not receive bonus compensation for exceeding a certain number of applications.
  • Raise existing misdemeanor penalties related to undue influence or bribery related to voting to felonies. The bill would also create new felonies related to undue influence or bribery related to voter registration and absentee voting. The bill would also create felony penalties for violations of the bill's provisions related to third party ballot return and voter assistance.
