VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 15, 2021, would create new felony offenses for election crimes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Criminalize, as a felony, intimidation directed at a voter, election official, or other persons aiding the voting process.
  • Criminalize, as a felony, circulating information intending to impede or prevent a person from voting when the information is known to be materially false.
  • Criminalize, as a felony, acting under color of law to intentionally interfere with another person voting.
  • Criminalize, as a felony, intentionally aiding and abetting or conspiracy to commit any of the first three offenses.

  • Authorize the Attorney General to investigate and prosecute the offenses created by the bill.

    Last updated January 26, 2022.

This bill, as amended on February 25, 2021, would:

  • Authorize on-site provision of absentee voting at veterans homes and battered women's shelters. Existing law provides on-site absentee voting at health care facilities and hospitals. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Eliminate the three voter limit for persons providing assistance to voters completing their ballots. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Allow a town of any size to conduct elections by mail. Existing law allows only towns not located within a metropolitan county to conduct elections by mail. The bill would also allow a question-only election by mail to include an office election on the ballot if overlapping school and municipal jurisdictions contain at least one jurisdiction conducting a question-only election. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Allow registrants to opt to include either a Minnesota driver's license or state ID number or the last four digits of their Social Security number on the registration application. Existing law requires a registrant to list a Minnesota driver's license or state ID number if they have one. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Add residential treatment facilities and facilities administering adult foster care programs to the list of facilities for which an employee may vouch for residents for the purpose of Election Day voter registration. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Limit misdemeanor prohibitions against electioneering near polling locations to voting hours. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Designate lists of absentee ballot applicants and rejected absentee ballot applicants as public information lists that may be provided to certain persons on request. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Authorize the Secretary of State to prepare and send an absentee ballot to a participant in the Address Confidentiality Program. Existing law requires local election officials to prepare and send ballots to program participants. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Change procedures and timelines related to post-election sampling of Election Day registrations, canvassing, recounts, special elections, and post-election audits. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

A provision from the previous version of the bill was amended out of the current text. It would have allowed election officials to begin post-verification pre-processing of absentee and mail ballot election ballots beginning 14 days before Election Day.

Last Updated April 8, 2022

The bill would limit absentee voting to voters who are unable to attend their polling place on Election Day due to absence from their precinct, illness, disability, religious discipline or holiday, or service as an election judge in another precinct. The bill would effectively eliminate in-person, no-excuse early voting by requiring a voter to have an excuse to vote in person before Election Day.
  • Restore the rights of persons convicted of felonies automatically following the completion of any term of incarceration for the felony. Existing law requires an individual convicted of a felony to complete any term of probation or parole prior to restoration of their voting rights. The bill would require officials at state and local correctional facilities to provide notice of restoration of voting eligibility and a voter registration form to each inmate upon release. The bill also requires the Secretary of State to prepare a publication detailing the voting rights of persons charged and convicted of crimes for distribution to various agencies involved in the criminal justice process.

Existing law only requires the registrant to proof residency in one of several ways, including vouching by another registered voter. Election Day registrants who do not present acceptable photo ID may complete a voter registration application and cast a provisional ballot.
  • Create a free voter ID card that a voter may acquire through the Department of Public Safety. The voter ID application would require a voter to provide the last four digits of their Social Security number, proof of U.S. citizenship, and a photo ID document. Each voter ID would include a unique identifying number. The bill would also require the state to provide any vital record necessary for a voter to obtain a voter ID card free of charge.

The voter would complete a statement with identifying information and would have up to seven calendar days after Election Day to present valid photo ID to the county auditor or municipal clerk to have the provisional ballot counted. Minnesota does not have provisional ballots under existing law.
  • Prohibit candidates, parties, or campaign committees from mailing absentee ballot applications to voters.
  • Limit the existing permanent absentee voter list to allow persons to automatically receive an absentee ballot application before each election to voters with permanent illness or disability. The bill would also create a "ongoing absentee voter list" that would allow all other voters to sign up to receive an absentee ballot application before each election.
  • Make conforming changes to voter registration forms, absentee ballot applications and certificates, and voter list maintenance activity to include the use of voter identification numbers in voter registration records.
  • Require the Secretary of State to conduct a public education campaign concerning the voter ID provisions enacted by the bill.
  • Prohibit voting machines that connect to an outside network.

HISTORY: {"date":"02/25/2021","summary":"To HOUSE Committee on STATE GOVERNMENT FINANCE AND ELECTIONS","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 25, 2021, would:

  • Require Election Day-style early voting for federal, state, and county elections beginning 30 days before Election Day and ending at 5 p.m. on the third day before Election Day. Early voting must be offered at county auditor and municipal clerk offices and may be offered at other locations approved by local election officials. Voting hours must be available 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. weekdays (8 a.m. to 8 p.m. at least one weekday during the early voting period) and 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. on the final two Saturdays of the early voting period. Each polling location for early voting must offer at least one voting station and one ballot marking device for disabled voters. Election officials must provide notice of early voting locations on their websites at least 14 days before the beginning of the early voting period. Early voters must sign the same polling place certificate as Election Day voters. The bill would also give city officials the option to provide Election Day-style early voting for city elections. Existing law provides a type of early voting through in-person, no-excuse absentee voting.
  • Require election authorities conducting early voting pursuant to the new statutory provisions in the bill to be open from 8 a.m. to noon on the day before Election Day to allow voters to apply for and cast absentee ballots.
  • Create new felonies by applying existing prohibitions to certain third party conduct concerning absentee voting to early voting.
  • Repeal existing statutory provisions concerning the "alternative" procedure for in-person absentee voting that authorizes county auditors to place a ballot counter and ballot box in their offices during the seven days before Election Day.

Last Updated February 26, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 4, 2021, would allow county auditors to begin providing the "alternative procedure" for in-person absentee voting by placing a ballot box and ballot counter in the auditor's office 14 days before Election Day. The bill would also allow ballot boards to conduct certain post-verification pre-processing activities on absentee and mail ballots 14 days before Election Day. Existing law authorizes both activities to begin seven days before Election Day.

Last Updated March 13, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to redistricting, establishes redistricting principles for legislative and congressional districts.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 4, 2021, would establish redistricting criteria for federal congressional and state legislative districts. The bill would:

  • Require districts to be compact, contiguous, and as equal in population as practicable. State legislative districts may not deviate in population by more than one percent. Counties, cities, or towns should not be unduly divided unless necessary to achieve population equality. State representative districts must nest entirely in a senate district.
  • Prohibit districts to favor or disfavor any party or candidate. Districts must not dilute racial or ethnic voting strength and should seek to preserve communities of interest.

Last updated March 6, 2021.

HISTORY: {"date":"03/04/2021","summary":"To HOUSE Committee on STATE GOVERNMENT FINANCE AND ELECTIONS","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 4, 2021, would make numerous changes to Minnesota election law. The bill would:

  • Require Election Day-style early voting for federal, state, and county elections beginning 30 days before Election Day and ending at 5 p.m. on the day before Election Day. Early voting must be offered at county auditor and municipal clerk offices and may be offered at other locations approved by local election officials. Jurisdictions must offer one location for a number of residents to be specified by amendment and must ensure that locations are geographically distributed to ensure a reasonable opportunity for all voters to vote early.
  • Voting hours for early voting must be available 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. weekdays (8 a.m. to 8 p.m. at least one weekday during the early voting period) and 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. on the final two Saturdays of the early voting period. Election officials must provide notice of early voting locations on their websites at least 14 days before the beginning of the early voting period. Early voters must sign the same polling place certificate as Election Day voters. The bill would also give city officials the option to provide Election Day-style early voting for city elections. Existing law provides a type of early voting through in-person, no-excuse absentee voting.
  • Restore the rights of persons convicted of felonies automatically following the completion of any term of incarceration for the felony. The bill would require officials at state and local correctional facilities to provide notice of restoration of voting eligibility and a voter registration form to each inmate upon release. The bill also requires the Secretary of State to prepare a publication detailing the voting rights of persons charged and convicted of crimes for distribution to various agencies involved in the criminal justice process.
  • Require election officials to accept absentee and mail ballot election ballots that are postmarked by Election Day and received by the election official no later than seven days after Election Day. The bill would also require election officials to accept ballots returned by hand delivery until 8 p.m. on Election Day.     • Require each jurisdiction to provide at least one drop box for every 20,000 registered voters. Boxes would be available 24 hours a day. Election officials would monitor boxes continuously through video surveillance or other means and would retrieve ballots from boxes at least once per day.
    • Require election officials to publish a preliminary list of drop box locations at least 35 days before the start of the absentee voting period and a final list of locations at least 15 days before the start of the absentee voting period. The bill would also apply existing prohibitions against electioneering to the area within 100 feet of a drop box.
  • Remove the requirement for a voter to have a witness sign an absentee or mail ballot election ballot.
  • Create additional means for a person to prove residence for the purpose of Election Day registration. The bill would add a learner's permit, a receipt for any form of ID issued by the Department of Public Safety, and a notice of late registration containing the voter's current valid address to the list of documents sufficient to prove residence. An eligible voter who resides on a reservation but does not have a residential address recognized by the U. S. Postal Service could register to vote using the address of the tribal council headquarters as the voter's residential address. BILLSUMMARY: Relates to elections, provides principles and procedures related to the redistricting of congressional and legislative districts.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on April 15, 2021, would:

  • Establish a hierarchy of criteria for legislative consideration when drawing congressional and state legislative districts. The bill would require legislators to consider, in order: population equality, contiguity, nesting of state House districts within state Senate districts, minority representation and participation, communities of interest, existing political subdivisions including Native American reservations, lack of partisan bias, and natural geographic boundaries. Districts may not favor or disfavor any party or candidate. The bill would also require the legislature to create a Legislative Coordination Commission that would prepare reports regarding the consideration of the identified criteria.

The bill would require the legislature to conduct at least one public hearing in each existing congressional district to receive public testimony and input regarding the redistricting process. The legislature would publish proposed maps at least two weeks prior to legislative consideration and allow submission of public comment. The bill would also make legislative records of development, consideration, or adoption of redistricting plans public record.

This bill, as introduced on January 7, 2021, would require voters to present photo ID as proof of identity prior to voting. The bill would:

  • Require voters to present photo ID prior to voting in person. Acceptable forms of photo ID would include:
    • 1) a driver's license, state ID, or voter ID card issued by the Minnesota Department of Public Safety,
    • 2) a valid U.S. military photo ID card containing the voter's current address,
    • 3) a tribal ID issued by a tribe recognized by the Bureau of Indian Affairs containing the voter's photo and current address,
    • 4) an original receipt for a Minnesota driver's license, state ID, or voter ID containing the voter's photo or, if without a photo, accompanied by an expired Minnesota driver's license, state ID, or voter ID, a U.S. passport, a state or federal government photo ID, a tribal photo ID, or a student photo ID from a college or university in Minnesota,
    • 5) a U.S. passport, tribal photo ID, or U.S. military photo ID not containing the voter's current address accompanied by one of 19 types of documents containing the voter's current address, including utility, financial, student, employment, and public benefit information,
    • 6) for students, a driver's license, state ID, or voter ID issued by any state accompanied by a copy of the student's fee statement containing the student's current address, or
    • 7) for voters in residential facilities, a Minnesota driver's license, state ID, or voter ID without their current address accompanied by certification of residence in the facility.
  • Require voters to show their photo ID to a witness prior to completing the certificate on an absentee ballot or mail ballot election ballot. The witness would note the type of ID presented on the ballot certificate. Ballots with incomplete ID certifications would be rejected.
  • Require a person to show acceptable photo ID prior to registering on Election Day. Existing law only requires the registrant to prove residency in one of several ways, including vouching by another registered voter.
  • Create a free voter ID card that a voter may acquire through the Department of Public Safety. The voter ID application would require a voter to provide the last four digits of their Social Security number, proof of U.S. citizenship, and a photo ID document. Each voter ID would include a unique identifying number. The bill would also require the state to provide any vital record necessary for a voter to obtain a voter ID card free of charge. The voter ID card would need to be renewed by the voter every four years, except voters over age 65 would need to renew every eight years.
  • Create provisional ballots that may be cast by voters who do not present valid photo ID when attempting to vote. The voter would complete a statement with identifying information and would have up to seven calendar days after Election Day to present valid photo ID to the county auditor or municipal clerk to have the provisional ballot counted. Minnesota does not have provisional ballots under existing law.
  • Make conforming changes to voter registration forms, absentee ballot applications and certificates, and voter list maintenance activity to include the use of voter identification numbers in voter registration records.
  • Require the Secretary of State to conduct a public education campaign concerning the voter ID provisions enacted by the bill.
  • Move county and state canvassing and election certification deadlines to later dates to provide for the time to verify provisional ballots.

NOTE: The voter ID requirements of the bill would be effective June 1, 2023. The provisions relating to the availability of free voter ID would be effective June 1, 2022.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 19, 2021, would make numerous changes to Minnesota election law. The bill would:

  • Require voters to present photo ID prior to voting in person. Acceptable forms of photo ID would include:
    • 1) a driver's license, state ID, or voter ID card issued by the Minnesota Department of Public Safety,
    • 2) a valid U.S. military photo ID card containing the voter's current address,
    • 3) a tribal ID issued by a tribe recognized by the Bureau of Indian Affairs containing the voter's photo and current address,
    • 4) an original receipt for a Minnesota driver's license, state ID, or voter ID containing the voter's photo or, if without a photo, accompanied by an expired Minnesota driver's license, state ID, or voter ID, a U.S. passport, a state or federal government photo ID, a tribal photo ID, or a student photo ID from a college or university in Minnesota,
    • 5) a U.S. passport, tribal photo ID, or U.S. military photo ID not containing the voter's current address accompanied by one of 21 types of documents containing the voter's current address, including utility, financial, student, employment, and public benefit information,
    • 6) for students, a driver's license, state ID, or voter ID issued by any state accompanied by a copy of the student's fee statement containing the student's current address, or
    • 7) for voters in residential facilities, a Minnesota driver's license, state ID, or voter ID without their current address accompanied by certification of residence in the facility.
  • Require a voter to state a qualifying excuse to vote by absentee ballot. Existing law allows all registered voters to vote by absentee ballot without an excuse. The bill would limit absentee voting to voters who are unable to attend their polling place on Election Day due to absence from their precinct, illness, disability, religious discipline or holiday, or service as an election judge in another precinct. The bill would effectively eliminate in-person, no-excuse early voting by requiring a voter to have an excuse to vote in person before Election Day.
  • Restore the rights of persons convicted of felonies automatically following the completion of any term of incarceration for the felony. Existing law requires an individual convicted of a felony to complete any term of probation or parole prior to restoration of their voting rights. The bill would require officials at state and local correctional facilities to provide notice of restoration of voting eligibility and a voter registration form to each inmate upon release. The bill also requires the Secretary of State to prepare a publication detailing the voting rights of persons charged and convicted of crimes for distribution to various agencies involved in the criminal justice process.
  • Require voters to show their photo ID to a witness prior to completing the certificate on an absentee ballot or mail ballot election ballot. The witness would note the type of ID presented on the ballot certificate. Ballots with incomplete ID certifications would be rejected. Witnesses would also need to provide a state ID number or the last four digits of their Social Security number on the absentee ballot certificate.
  • Require a person to show acceptable photo ID prior to registering on Election Day. Existing law only requires the registrant to proof residency in one of several ways, including vouching by another registered voter. Election Day registrants who do not present acceptable photo ID may complete a voter registration application and cast a provisional ballot.
  • Create a free voter ID card that a voter may acquire through the Department of Public Safety. The voter ID application would require a voter to provide the last four digits of their Social Security number, proof of U.S. citizenship, and a photo ID document. Each voter ID would include a unique identifying number. The bill would also require the state to provide any vital record necessary for a voter to obtain a voter ID card free of charge.
  • Create provisional ballots that may be cast by voters who do not present valid photo ID when attempting to vote. The voter would complete a statement with identifying information and would have up to seven calendar days after Election Day to present valid photo ID to the county auditor or municipal clerk to have the provisional ballot counted. Minnesota does not have provisional ballots under existing law.
  • Prohibit candidates, parties, or campaign committees from mailing absentee ballot applications to voters.
  • Limit the existing permanent absentee voter list to allow persons to automatically receive an absentee ballot application before each election to voters with permanent illness or disability. The bill would also create a "ongoing absentee voter list" that would allow all other voters to sign up to receive an absentee ballot application before each election.
  • Make conforming changes to voter registration forms, absentee ballot applications and certificates, and voter list maintenance activity to include the use of voter identification numbers in voter registration records.
  • Require the Secretary of State to conduct a public education campaign concerning the voter ID provisions enacted by the bill.
  • Prohibit voting machines that connect to an outside network.

Last Updated July 22, 2025

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 24, 2021, would change procedures for voters whose registration status is challenged. The bill would:

  • Require an auditor or clerk to provide notice to a voter whose registration status is changed to challenged within seven days of the change. The notice must include the reason for the change and describe the process to contest the change.
  • Allow a challenged voter to file a petition with the appropriate election official contesting the change of their registration status. The voter may also request a review meeting. The election official must review the petition within seven days of receipt and must schedule the review meeting, if requested, within 14 days of receipt of the petition. A voter may appeal the election official's review decision to a district court.
  • Allow a voter to remove their challenged status by taking an oath and answering qualifying questions posed by an election judge at the polls.
  • Require election officials to provide a list of voters with challenged registrations for all polling locations. Election judges at polling locations must check the list for each voter to ensure they are not challenged. Challenged voters may remove their status by answering the qualifying questions. Challenged voters may participate in same-day registration to update their registration status, but must cast a challenged voter ballot.
  • Create challenged voter ballots that must be cast by voters whose registration status remains challenged but who wish to vote. The voter would complete a challenged ballot roster or certificate and a challenged voter ballot envelope, which would include the voter's name, address of residence, date of birth, voter identification number, and any other information prescribed by the Secretary of State. Election officials would compare the information on the challenged ballot envelope with information in the statewide voter registration system to determine the voter's eligibility to vote in the precinct. Voters would be notified of the decision to accept or reject their challenged ballot six to ten weeks after Election Day.
  • Require publicly available lists of registered voters to indicate challenged voters and when their status was changed. The list must also include removed or inactive registrations and the reason for the removal or inactivation of the registration.
  • Create new felony offenses for misrepresentation of a voter's identity when requesting a challenged ballot or requesting the ballot to be counted and challenging a voter's eligibility to vote knowing the challenge lacks merit or having reckless disregard for whether the challenge has merit.

Non-substantive technical amendments were made to the bill on March 4, 2021.

Last Updated July 22, 2025

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to redistricting, establishes redistricting principles for legislative and congressional districts.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on May 6, 2021 would establish redistricting criteria for federal congressional and state legislative districts. The bill would:

  • Require districts to be compact, contiguous, and as equal in population as practicable. State legislative districts may not deviate in population by more than two percent from the ideal population. Congressional districts must be as nearly equal in population as practicable. Counties, cities, or towns should not be unduly divided unless necessary to achieve population equality. State representative districts must nest entirely in a senate district. The previous version of the bill required state legislative districts to deviate in population by no more than one percent from the ideal population.
  • Prohibit districts to favor or disfavor incumbents. Districts must not dilute racial or ethnic voting strength and should seek to preserve communities of interest. The previous version of the bill also prohibited districts to favor or disfavor any party or candidate.

Last updated May 11, 2021.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on May 6, 2021, would create a hierarchy of criteria for consideration during legislative redistricting. The bill would:

  • Specify a list of criteria for the legislature to consider when drawing federal Congressional and state legislative districts. In order:
    • State senate districts should not divide a state house district.
    • Districts should not favor a party, candidate, or incumbent.
    • Population should be equal across districts. State legislative districts may not deviate in terms of population by more than one percent.
    • Districts should be composed of contiguous territory.
    • Native American reservations should not be divided between districts unless necessary to comply with constitutional requirements.
    • Districts should respects existing political subdivisions.
    • Districts should not concentrate or disperse African-American voters, Indigenous voters, voters of color, or voters belonging to language group minorities.
    • Districts should respect existing communities of interest.
    • Districts should be compact.
    • Districts should attempt to preserve the cores of existing districts.
  • Require the legislature to create a report detailing compliance with these criteria when establishing districts.

The previous version of the bill did not apply the criteria to federal Congressional districts and placed compactness higher in the hierarchy of criteria.

Last updated May 11, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2021, would require a voter to present an acceptable form of photo ID prior to voting in-person on Election Day or by casting an absentee ballot in person at the office of the election authority. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Limit acceptable forms of voter ID for in-person voting on Election Day or in-person absentee voting at the office of the election authority to three categories of photo IDs: 1) a nonexpired Missouri driver's license or nondriver's license, 2) a document issued by the United States or the State of Missouri containing the voter's name, photo, and an expiration date no earlier than the date of the last general election, or 3) unexpired photo ID issued by the Missouri National Guard, the U. S. Armed Forces, or the U. S. Department of Veteran Affairs to a member or former member of the Missouri National Guard or the U. S. Armed Forces. Existing law, as enforced, allows a voter to present several forms of non-photo ID and does not apply the voter ID requirement to persons voting absentee ballots in person. The bill would also eliminate the requirement that the Secretary of State provide public notice of voter ID requirements through various media and on online.
  • Require a voter attempting to vote in person who does not present an acceptable form of photo ID to vote provisionally. The voter would be required to complete a provisional ballot envelope that includes the voter's name, address, date of birth, and last four digits of their Social Security number. Under existing law, voters who do not have required ID at the polls may vote a regular ballot if they submit a sworn statement and provide a form of alternative ID. The bill would leave in place the existing provision that allows voters to verify a provisional ballot by returning to the polling location with a valid ID prior to the close of polls or by the election authority matching the voter's signature on the provisional ballot envelope to the signature.
  • Eliminate the requirement for a person seeking a nondriver's license for voting free of charge to complete a statement attesting that they do not possess any other form of acceptable voter ID.

This bill was substituted in committee on February 22, 2021, but not substantive changes were made.

This bill, as amended on March 24, 2021, would implement more rigorous voter ID requirements while also creating a three-week period of in-person, no excuse absentee voting before elections. The bill would:

  • Eliminate all of the acceptable forms of non-photo ID under existing law. The bill would require all voters voting in person on Election Day or voting an absentee ballot in person at the office of the election authority to present: 1) a valid Missouri driver's license or nondriver's license, 2) a document issued by the state of Missouri or the United States containing the voter's name and photo, or 3) photo ID of the voter which is issued by the Missouri National Guard, the United States Armed Forces, or the United States Department of Veteran Affairs to a member or former member of the Missouri National Guard or the U. S. Armed Forces. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Create in-person, no-excuse absentee voting beginning 21 days before Election Day. Any voter may cast an absentee ballot in person at a location designated by the local election authority. The voter would be required to present the same photo ID required in the bullet above and complete a statement of eligibility. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require voters who do not present an acceptable form of ID to complete an affidavit and vote a provisional ballot. Provisional ballots may be counted if the voter returns to the polling place with acceptable photo ID prior to the close of polls or the voter's signature on the provisional ballot affidavit matches the voter's signature in the voter registration records. Provisional ballots would be segregated from regularly cast ballots. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Narrow the qualifications for a voter or their caretaker to cast an absentee ballot by mail due to disability or illness. The bill would require a voter's qualifying disability or illness to be present on Election Day. The bill would also require the caretaker wishing to vote by absentee ballot to reside at the same address as their charge. Existing law does not contain the Election Day requirement for illness or disability or the caretaker's cohabitation requirement. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Provide that absentee ballots returned to authorized drop boxes or authorized locations other than the office of the election authority are deemed cast when received by the election authority. Existing law does not reference locations other than the office of the election authority where voters may return absentee ballots. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Authorize the Secretary of State to audit the registered voter list of any local election authority. The Secretary will verify, minimally, that the voter is alive, a resident within the jurisdiction of the election authority, and entitled to vote. The Secretary will direct the local authority to remove the names of voters found not to meet those criteria from the list. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Phase out electronic voting systems by January 1, 2022. Election officials must conduct all elections after that date with paper ballots. Local authorities may continue to provide electronic ballot marking equipment for voters with a disability while that equipment remains functional, but may not replace such equipment with new electronic ballot marking equipment. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Prohibit persons from collecting compensation for soliciting voter registration applications. Any person who solicits more than 10 applications would need to register with the Secretary of State for every election cycle that runs from one general election to the next. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Prohibit any amendment to the election code within six months of a presidential election. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Eliminate certain residency requirements for election commissioners, election judges, and challengers. The previous version of the bill removed residency requirements for election commissioners and judges, but not for challengers.
  • Eliminate the requirement for the state to conduct a presidential primary on the second Tuesday after the first Monday of a presidential election year. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Exclude voters' dates of birth from lists of registered voters made available to the public. The bill would also eliminate mandatory provision of voter lists to parties and candidates while also eliminating prohibitions on providing voter lists to the general public. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

Proof of citizenship could be a birth certificate, U.S. passport, naturalization documentation, another form of proof of citizenship established by the Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986, or a legible copy of an approved document. If a registered voter claimed to be a citizen but was unable to provide approved documentation, there would be a hearing wherein the voter could provide other proof of citizenship in person or in writing. If a registered voter failed to provide proof of citizenship within 30 days of receipt of the notice from the registrar, the registrar would purge the voter's registration from the statewide system.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on April 30, 2021, prohibits the Governor from suspending any statute prescribing election procedures or otherwise controlling the ingress or egress from a polling location during an emergency without the consent of the Legislature. The bill provides a method for the Governor to seek the Legislature's permission if the Legislature is not in session.

Last updated July 21, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Revises age requirements for election judges, relates to elections.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 16, 2021, would allow individuals who are at least 16 years old to serve as youth election judges in their county of residence. Existing law requires election judges to be registered voters, thus limiting the position to individuals who are at least 18 years old.

Last updated February 18, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on February 17, 2021, would eliminate the permanent absentee ballot list, end early voting, and make numerous anti-voter changes to absentee voting, voter list maintenance, and ballot return, verification and cure. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Repeal the permanent absentee voting list and make conforming changes to the election code.
  • End early voting by repealing the ability to vote an absentee ballot in person at the elections office.
  • Change absentee voting by:
    • requiring voters to apply for absentee ballots in person, use the official application form, and show photo ID. Despite showing ID, the voter's signature on the application would still be verified against their signature on file. Although in-person application would be required, the bill prohibits giving voters a ballot in person. Instead, ballots would be mailed to voters. Under existing law, absentee ballots may be applied for by mail using the official form or a written request that contains the necessary information, and the application is verified by signature matching. In addition, ballots can be picked up or voted at the election administrator's office.
    • eliminating the ability of provisionally registered voters to apply for and cast aberrant ballots, except that certain disabled provisionally registered voters may continue use a special electronic voting process. Those voters would face a new requirement to include a copy of a photo ID or other identifying document with their ballot. Under existing law, provisionally registered voters who vote absentee may include the ID with their ballot. If they do not, their ballot will be treated as a provisional ballot, and the voter will need to provide the ID for the ballot to count.
    • shortening the deadline to apply for absentee ballots to noon on the seventh day before Election Day. Under existing law, voters can apply through noon the day before the election.
    • shortening the deadline for voters to return their absentee ballots two hours before polls close, specifically, by 6 p.m. on Election Day instead of 8 p.m. Note, the bill appears to preserve the 8 p.m. deadline for disabled voters using a specific electronic voting process, although bill provisions contradict each other.
    • requiring absentee ballots to be mailed to voters at their registration address.
    • restricting the availability of replacement ballots. To get a replacement ballot, the voter would need to apply in person seven days before Election Day. Under existing law, voters can request replacement ballots in person, by mail, email, or fax, through the close of polls on Election Day.
    • ending the ability of UOCAVA voters to request a UOCAVA ballot through the close of polls on Election Day.
  • Change the existing cure process for missing or mismatch signatures by requiring them to be fixed by 6 p.m. on Election Day, instead of by 8 p.m., which is the close of polls and the deadline under existing law.

  • Change the voter list maintenance process by eliminating an exception to the address confirmation process aimed at people who did not vote in the preceding federal general election. The exception allows election administrators to exclude from the targeted mailing people who, in the same calendar year, applied for an absentee ballot for a federal general election or responded to an address confirmation notice sent to people on the permanent absentee ballot list.

Last Updated August 11, 2021

This bill, as enacted on May 14, 2021, clarifies that people who will be eligible to vote by the next election can register to vote before they are eligible, but may not receive a ballot until they are eligible, adds criteria to the congressional redistricting process, and repeals the ability of counties to experiment with voting equipment approved by the Secretary of State. Voting Rights Lab only tracks the first provision. On that issue, the bill expressly prohibits giving a ballot to someone who has legally registered to vote because they will be eligible by Election Day, but is not yet 18 or has not yet lived in Montana long enough to meet the residency requirement. Existing law, which the bill does not alter, prohibits people from voting until they are eligible, even if they are legally registered. 

Last Updated May 10, 2022

This bill, as enacted on May 14, 2021:

  • Would have prohibited giving or accepting any pecuniary benefit for the distribution, ordering, request, collection, or return of ballots, by requiring the Secretary of State to issue a rule to that effect by July 1, 2022. This provision is blocked by the injunction.
  • Requires the Secretary of State to adopt rules that define and govern "election security," by July 1, 2022, and issue an annual report on election security each year beginning with 2023. 

Last Updated October 3, 2022

This bill, as introduced on February 22, 2021, would make significant changes to Montana voter registration and ballot return law. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the DMV equivalent to determine if a person applying for a new or updated voter registration card is already registered to vote. If they are, but the information in the registration is different or incomplete, or if the voter's registration status is inactive, the DMV-equivalent would be required to send the voter's information to the secretary of state, who would use it to update the voter's registration, including restoring active status, and notify the county election official. The county would then send a notice to the voter along with a postage prepaid return card that the voter could use to make any corrections.
  • Require the DMV-equivalent to offer an applicant who is verified as not a registered voter the opportunity to register, and if they consent, to electronically transmit their relevant data to the secretary of state, who after updating the statewide database, would notify the relevant county official.
  • Create a new misdemeanor to punish providing or receiving a pecuniary or other benefit for distributing, ordering, requesting, collecting, delivering, or otherwise physically possessing more than two absentee ballots for each election in addition to the person's own ballot or a ballot belonging to an immediate family member. Immediate family member is defined as a spouse, parent, child, grandparent, or sibling. Existing law allows a person to return up to six voters' ballots, so long as they are a family member, household member, caregiver, or acquaintance. That law has been enjoined by state litigation.
  • Change the existing restrictions on who may return another voter's ballot. The bill would allow anyone to be designated by the voter to return their ballot, however, the person cannot be a candidate or a member of the candidate's paid staff unless that person is the immediate family or household member of the voter for whom they are returning the ballot. The person would be subject to the two ballot limit imposed by the new misdemeanor. Again, the existing restrictions have been enjoined by state litigation.
  • Prohibit people from knowingly collecting a person's unvoted ballot.

Repeal a requirement that someone returning another voter's ballot sign a registry and provide their identity and contact information when returning the ballot. Instead, the bill would change the ballot envelope to provide space for the name, signature and address of the person returning the ballot.

Last Updated February 24, 2021

This bill, as amended on March 29, 2021, would expand and protect early voting, Election Day voting, and same day registration for Native Americans, and expand the types of acceptable voter ID to include certain tribal IDs. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill. The March 29 amendments made two big picture additions to the bill. One clarifies that, to the extent existing litigation settlements provided stronger protections in the jurisdictions that they cover, the settlements would remain in force after the bill became law. The other new provision would require all negotiations entered into by a county and tribal government to implement the bill be conducted in good faith using a commitment to cooperation and collaboration, mutual understanding and respect, regular and early communication, a process of accountability for addressing issues, and preservation of the tribal-state relationship.

The specific provisions to expand and protect voting and registration opportunities for Native Americans, which were not modified from the March 19 version, would:

  • Require county election officials, for state and federal elections, to open at least one satellite voting office or alternative election office on Native land. The only difference between office types is that a satellite office is equipped with a sequential balloting machine, and an alternative office is not. The office is subject to certain rules:
    • The office must offer early voting, same day registration, replacement ballot pick up, any other service offered by the main election office, and must collect ballots from places of deposit on Native land, if any are established.
    • The office must open at least 30 days prior to Election Day, and the county and tribal government must agree in writing on the days and hours the office will be open in the 30 day period. Once an agreement as to location and its operation is reached, it remains in force for each election thereafter unless one side gives written notice by January 1 of a state or federal election year and the parties can agree on new terms. If new terms cannot be reached, the original agreement remains in force.
    • The office must comply with the Americans with Disabilities Act, have telephone coverage and a secure wired internet connection, be equipped with adequate, specified security features, and, if sited in a tribal government building, the tribe must indemnify the county for any injuries to suffered by an individual due to the premises' condition.
    • Counties and tribal governments may agree that because of specific geographic circumstances establishing a satellite or alternative election office is not warranted.
    • The existing State-tribal relations committee would be tasked with monitoring the implementation of these requirements, and reporting on it by September 15 of each year preceding the beginning of a regular legislative session if legislative changes are needed.

      Existing law has no equivalent provisions.
  • Require election officials to accept tribal photo ID as acceptable in-person voter ID even if the tribal ID does not include an address or an expiration date.
  • Require election officials to accept a copy of tribal photo ID as acceptable confirmation of a provisionally registered voter's registration when that voter is voting by mail, even if the tribal ID does not include an address or an expiration date.
  • Require, if a polling place on Native land is being relocated due to an emergency, the placement of the new location on Native land.
  • Require counties to publish the location of polling places on Native land when otherwise publishing polling place locations.
  • Require county election administrators to consult with tribal governing bodies each federal and state election to determine if additional places of deposit are necessary on Native land based on where voters live and the location of the election administrator's office or a satellite or alternative election office established pursuant to the bill. Under existing law, places of deposit are required in certain circumstances for mail ballot elections, but not necessarily on Native land.

  • Require the secretary of state to send tribal governments a copy of the enacted statute.

    The March 19 version amended out provisions in the previous version of the bill. As introduced, the bill would have allowed tribes to designate tribal buildings to serve as residential addresses for Native voters so long as the voters live in the same precinct as the building. Moreover, a voter would be allowed to use a nontraditional address as a current address as long as the nontraditional address contains enough detail to allow the voter to be assigned to the proper precinct.

Last Updated March 30, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 16, 2021, would allow disabled voters who receive their ballots electronically to return them electronically for federal primaries and federal general elections.

Last Updated March 18, 2021

This bill, as enacted March 16, 2021, primarily addresses accessibility measures for disabled voters. Specifically, the bill:

  • Defines disability for the purposes of the election code to include impairments to vision, hearing, mobility, or mental or physical functioning that creates difficulty for the process of voting. Existing law had not included impairments to mental or physical functioning within the definition.
  • Excludes "elderly" voters, defined as those 65 years old and above, from the category of individuals who must be served by accessibility-related accommodations. Such accommodations are now only required for voters who are disabled under the statutory definition.
  • Prohibits disabled voters from designating their employer, their employer's agent, or an officer or agent of their union, as their assistant for voting purposes.
  • Repeals the requirement that election officials ask disabled voters if they require assistance when they enter the polling place, and instead permits disabled voters to request assistance as needed.
  • Eliminates the requirement that voter interface devices for disabled voters must be located within a polling place, and exempts counties from the requirement to use them if there are fewer than 200 eligible voters in an election or the election is for an irrigation district.
  • Grants disabled voters more time to request reassignment to an accessible polling place by moving the request deadline from seven days before an election to two business days before Election Day.
  • Expressly provides that disabled voters may obtain assistance from their designated agents.
  • Expands the existing misdemeanor offense for deceiving a disabled elector by making the offense applicable to deception in the course of assisting a voter with making their signature or mark, and while assisting with the delivery and return of an emergency absentee ballot. Under existing law, the offense only applied to assistance provided to disabled voters at the polling place.
  • Requires county officials to publish the location of polling places at least two business days before an election. The deadline under existing law had been two days.

Last Updated April 24, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2021, shifts election authority away from appointed officials and gives it to elected officials. Specifically, the bill would require the election administrator in each county to be an elected official. Thus in any county that has an appointed election administrator, including an appointed county recorder, the bill requires the county's governing body to replace them by designating an elected official instead.

Last Updated July 19, 2021

This bill, as enacted on April 30, 2021, allows political parties to appoint at least one poll watcher to observe any ballot drop box used during a mail ballot election.

Last Updated May 17, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 13, 2021, would extend the regular voter registration deadline from 30 days before the election to 10 days before the election. Under existing law, voters may use the same day registration process after the close of the regular registration period.

Last Updated January 14, 2021

This bill, enacted on April 19, 2021, changes ID requirements for registering to vote, voting in person, and verifying a ballot cast provisionally because of a failure to show ID. The provision of this bill requiring individuals voting with a student ID to provide additional supporting documentation was struck down by the Montana Supreme Court in March 2024. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires a person who does not have a driver's license number, state ID number, or last four digits of their Social Security number to show photo ID to register to vote. The registrant may use a military identification card, a tribal photo identification card, a United States passport, or a Montana concealed carry permit (which may not have a photo). If the applicant cannot provide any of those forms of identification, they may register using any other photo identification showing their name and a current utility bill, bank statement, paycheck, government check, or another government document that shows the individual's name and current address. Previous law allowed a person who lacks a Montana driver's license and a Social Security number to register using only a current utility bill, bank statement, paycheck, government check, or another government document that shows the individual's name and current address.
  • Requires provisionally registered voters submitting a mail ballot to provide a form of documentation set out in the new ID requirements for voter registration, and permits any other mail voter to do so to ensure that their eligibility to vote will be recognized. Provisionally registered voters who do not provide the required documentation will have their mail ballots deemed provisional. Under existing law, the ID documentation requirements for provisionally registered voters, and permitted documentation for all others, tracked the previous voter registration requirements, i.e., submission of either a copy of any current and valid photo ID or specified non-photo ID.
  • Requires a voter who cast a provisional ballot because they failed to show the required ID at the polls to provide sufficient ID by 5 p.m. the day after the election to have their ballot counted. If the voter cannot provide a form of ID required for in-person voting, they may provide non-photo ID and sign an affidavit attesting which specific obstacle, of those listed on a form, they have to obtaining or presenting ID. Under existing law, provisional ballots were verified by matching the voter's signatures on their provisional ballot attestation and registration forms. The enacted bill retains the signature matching requirement, in addition to the new ID/attestation requirements.

Last Updated January 27, 2025

BILLSUMMARY: Revises laws related to polling place times, allows certain polling places to open later, requires notice to affected voters, requires certain consultations with governing bodies of Indian reservations.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on April 22, 2021:

  • Permits jurisdictions to change the opening time of polling places from 7 a.m. to as late as noon, for sites for that have fewer than 400 registered voters "who intend to vote at the voting place." The bill defines the number of voters who intend to vote at the polling place as the number of registered voters minus the number of people who applied for an absentee ballot. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law permitted later opening hours only for jurisdictions with fewer than 400 total registered voters.
  • Requires election administrators to notify voters by mail at least 30 days prior to an election if they decide to open a polling place later than 7 a.m. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law does not require notice to change the time polls open.

  • Prohibits reducing polling place hours for locations that lie partially or wholly within a Native reservation, until election officials have consulted that Native government about the potential reduction. This provision was amended into the bill on March 15.

    Last updated May 25, 2021.

The provisions of this law that VRL tracks were permanently enjoined as a result of litigation on February 3, 2022, and are not in effect. The law was blocked on a preliminary basis on the day the law was to take effect, and thus these provisions never had the force of law. 

This bill, as enacted on May 21, 2021, prohibits political committees from doing ordinary elections related activity on campus. Specifically, political committees cannot direct, coordinate, manage, or conduct any of the following in dorms, dining halls, or athletic facilities for a federal, state, local, or school election:

  • voter identification efforts,
  • voter registration drives,
  • signature collection efforts,
  • ballot collection efforts, or
  • voter turnout efforts. 

A political committee that engages in prohibited campus activity is subject to a penalty of $1,000 per violation, with each day of a continuing violation constituting a separate offense for the purpose of the fine.

These provisions are new to this version of the bill. The previous version addressed campaign finance regulations, which Voting Rights Lab does not track. Those additional provisions remain in the enacted bill.

 

Last Updated April 1, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on November 17, 2021, would establish a process for removing purported non-citizens from the voter rolls using data from jury summons responses. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require that superior court clerks, on a quarterly basis, transmit to the State Board of Elections a list of individuals who claim to be disqualified from jury duty because they are not a citizen of the United States. The list would include the person's name, address, date of birth, and other personal information from the master jury list, along with the reason for disqualification and date of disqualification. These reports would be public records.
  • The State Board of Elections would compare the jury information to voter registration records, identify matches, and pass the matches on to the proper county board of elections. The bill does not specify what would constitute a match sufficient to initiate a removal process.
  • County boards of elections would have to send notice within 30 days to the registered voter flagged as a potential non-citizen, and the registered voter would have 30 days to rebut the challenge to their registration with proof of citizenship.
  • If an individual believed to not be a citizen previously voted, the state board would pass that information to the district attorney for investigation for prosecution. Under existing law, there is no explicit process for removal of non-citizens from the voter rolls. These provisions were retained from a previous version of the bill.

The bill would also require that after each election, counties conduct audits under rules established by the state board of elections. The state board would then be required to select one-third of the counties in the state for an additional audit and provide a report to the legislature detailing its findings. This provision was newly amended into this version of the bill.

Last updated February 2, 2022.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 29, 2021, would propose a constitutional amendment to create an Independent Redistricting Commission to establish federal Congressional and state legislative districts. The bill would:

  • Create an Independent Redistricting Commission composed of 15 citizens to draw and approve federal Congressional and state legislative district maps following each decennial census. The amendment would explicitly eliminate any role in the redistricting process for the General Assembly.
  • Establish procedures for the selection of members of the Redistricting Commission. The Human Relations Commission would select 60 applicants from all applications submitted. The pool of 60 would be composed of 3 subpools of 20 applicants affiliated with each of the two major parties and 20 unaffiliated applicants. Eight applicants would be appointed as commissioners by state legislative leaders from both parties. The remaining seven would be selected randomly by the Human Relations Commission to yield a composition of five commissioners affiliated with each of the two major parties and five unaffiliated commissioners.
  • Establish qualifications for applicants to serve as commissioners. North Carolina registered voters who exceed political donation limits, serve or are relatives of persons who serve as elected or appointed officials, political parties, or employees of either, or are convicted of certain anti-government criminal offense or participate in certain anti-government activities would not be eligible to serve as commissioners.
  • Establish a hierarchy of criteria for the commission to apply when drawing districts. In order, the criteria are:
    • Population equality. The populations in state legislative districts must be within 5% of the ideal population for the districts. The populations in federal Congressional districts must be within .1% of the ideal population for the districts.
    • Districts must comply with federal and state constitutional and statutory requirements.
    • Districts should divide counties only when necessary.
    • Districts must be composed of contiguous territory.
    • Districts should divide municipalities only when necessary.
    • Districts should be compact.
    • Districts should not consider electoral results, political considerations, or incumbency.
    • Districts should divide communities of interest only when necessary.
  • Establish procedures for commission operations. Nine votes, including three votes from commissioners selected from each of the three subpools, would be necessary to approve maps. The Commission must conduct open meetings and make its records public. The Commission would maintain a public website with Commission records and notices available in English and Spanish. The Commission must provide at least 14 days notice prior to any meeting at which the Commission will vote.
  • Establish a timeline for completion of the Commission's duties, as follows:
    • The Commission must hold 10 public hearings within 30 days of the receipt of census data.
    • The Commission must propose preliminary redistricting plans within 50 days of the receipt of census data.
    • The Commission must hold 10 additional public hearings within 70 days of the receipt of census data.
    • The Commission must publish proposed and alternative final plans within 90 days of the receipt of census data.
    • The Commission must vote to adopt final plans within 110 days of the receipt of census data.
    • The Commission must appoint a special master to assist drawing maps if they were unable to approve final maps within 130 days of the receipt of census data.
    • The special master must propose final maps to the Commission within 150 days of receipt of census data.
    • The Commission must voter to adopt the plan submitted by the special master within 160 days of the receipt of census data.
    • The amendment would set a hard deadline for the creation of new maps of October 1 of each year ending in 1.
  • Allow the General Assembly to assign local redistricting duties to the Redistricting Commission.
  • Apply existing remedial provisions for district maps deemed unenforceable by a court to the Redistricting Commission.

NOTE: The amendments require approval of 60% of the members of each chamber of the General Assembly prior to submission to the voters, who must approve the amendments by a simple majority.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 30, 2021, would propose a constitutional amendment to create an Independent Redistricting Commission to establish federal Congressional and state legislative districts. The bill would:

  • Create an Independent Redistricting Commission composed of 15 citizens to draw and approve federal Congressional and state legislative district maps following each decennial census. The amendment would explicitly eliminate any role in the redistricting process for the General Assembly.
  • Establish procedures for the selection of members of the Redistricting Commission. The Human Relations Commission would select 60 applicants from all applications submitted. The pool of 60 would be composed of 3 subpools of 20 applicants affiliated with each of the two major parties and 20 unaffiliated applicants. Eight applicants would be appointed as commissioners by state legislative leaders from both parties. The remaining seven would be selected randomly by the Human Relations Commission to yield a composition of five commissioners affiliated with each of the two major parties and five unaffiliated commissioners.
  • Establish qualifications for applicants to serve as commissioners. North Carolina registered voters who exceed political donation limits, serve or are relatives of persons who serve as elected or appointed officials, political parties, or employees of either, or are convicted of certain anti-government criminal offense or participate in certain anti-government activities would not be eligible to serve as commissioners.
  • Establish a hierarchy of criteria for the commission to apply when drawing districts. In order, the criteria are:
    • Population equality. The populations in state legislative districts must be within 5% of the ideal population for the districts. The populations in federal Congressional districts must be within .1% of the ideal population for the districts.
    • Districts must comply with federal and state constitutional and statutory requirements.
    • Districts should divide counties only when necessary.
    • Districts must be composed of contiguous territory.
    • Districts should divide municipalities only when necessary.
    • Districts should be compact.
    • Districts should not consider electoral results, political considerations, or incumbency.
    • Districts should divide communities of interest only when necessary.
  • Establish procedures for commission operations. Nine votes, including three votes from commissioners selected from each of the three subpools, would be necessary to approve maps. The Commission must conduct open meetings and make its records public. The Commission would maintain a public website with Commission records and notices available in English and Spanish. The Commission must provide at least 14 days notice prior to any meeting at which the Commission will vote.
  • Establish a timeline for completion of the Commission's duties, as follows:
    • The Commission must hold 10 public hearings within 30 days of the receipt of census data.
    • The Commission must propose preliminary redistricting plans within 50 days of the receipt of census data.
    • The Commission must hold 10 additional public hearings within 70 days of the receipt of census data.
    • The Commission must publish proposed and alternative final plans within 90 days of the receipt of census data.
    • The Commission must vote to adopt final plans within 110 days of the receipt of census data.
    • The Commission must appoint a special master to assist drawing maps if they were unable to approve final maps within 130 days of the receipt of census data.
    • The special master must propose final maps to the Commission within 150 days of receipt of census data.
    • The Commission must voter to adopt the plan submitted by the special master within 160 days of the receipt of census data.
    • The amendment would set a hard deadline for the creation of new maps of October 1 of each year ending in 1.
  • Allow the General Assembly to assign local redistricting duties to the Redistricting Commission.
  • Apply existing remedial provisions for district maps deemed unenforceable by a court to the Redistricting Commission.

NOTE: The amendments require approval of 60% of the members of each chamber of the General Assembly prior to submission to the voters, who must approve the amendments by a simple majority.

Last updated April 1, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on March 31, 2021, would make numerous changes to North Carolina election law. The bill would:

  • Require voters to have only one witness sign their absentee ballot return envelope. Existing law requires the voter to have two witnesses sign the ballot or to have it notarized.
  • Require election officials to mail a return postage prepaid absentee ballot request form to all registered voters 90 days before each primary or general election.
  • Require election officials to provide return postage for absentee ballots.
  • Require counties to provide a secure drop box outside the office of the county board of elections beginning 15 days before Election Day. The bill would authorize counties to provide additional drop boxes at their discretion.
  • Require counties to notify voters with missing or mismatched absentee ballot signatures to allow the voters to cure the issue. The bill would require officials to notify voters no later than eight days before the county canvass. Voters would have until two days before the county canvass to correct the issue. Voters who are notified in time would have the option to vote in person on Election Day.
  • Create a presumption that a voter's signature on an absentee ballot is valid. Election officials could reject a ballot for mismatched signatures only if multiple, significant, and obvious differences existed between the ballot signature and the comparison sample.
  • Allow voters to request an absentee ballot request form by phone. The bill would also allow voters to deliver requests to the county board of elections in person or by mail, email, or fax.
  • Allow counties to provide flexible early voting hours at alternate early voting sites. Existing law requires all alternate one-stop (early) voting locations to offer the same hours statewide.
  • Require election officials to accept all absentee ballots returned by mail, postmarked or not, that are received no later than three days after Election Day.
  • Require driver's license offices to offer automatic voter registration beginning January 1, 2022. Individuals conducting transactions with these offices would be given the opportunity to decline registration and to affiliate with a political party. The Department of Transportation would transmit data sufficient for voter registration to the Board of Elections.
  • Require offices providing applications for public assistance, programs for individuals with disabilities, and employment benefits to offer automatic voter registration beginning January 1, 2023. Individuals conducting transactions with these offices would be given the opportunity to decline registration and to affiliate with a political party. The relevant agencies would transmit data sufficient for voter registration to the Board of Elections.
  • Create a presumption that automatic registrations are officially authorized and would make an ineligible individual automatically registered liable for criminal prosecution only if the individual willfully, knowingly, and with fraudulent intent provide false information while registering.
  • Require re-entering citizens to be advised of the availability of automatic voter registration at the designated offices.
  • Require the State Board of Elections to develop an online voter registration system. The system would require an applicant to have a North Carolina driver's license or nonoperators ID card to complete registration online.
    • NOTE: The N.C. Department of Transportation currently offers an online voter registration system, but it is not required by statute.
  • Provide the Executive Director of the State Board of Elections with emergency authority during a pandemic or national health crisis declared by the President or the Governor.
  • Make the date of the November general election in even-numbered years a state holiday.
  • Remove requirements for a majority of the three election judges in a voting precinct to be residents of the precinct. The bill would also establish that, when possible, all precinct officials should not be affiliated with the same political party.

Last Updated July 19, 2021

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on April 12, 2021, would establish redistricting criteria for federal Congressional and state legislative districts to be drawn following the 2020 census. The bill would:

  • Establish a hierarchy of redistricting criteria to apply to drawing federal Congressional and state legislative districts. The criteria would be, in order of priority:
    • Districts must be equal in population. Congressional districts may not deviate by more than one person, if possible. State legislative districts may not deviate by more than 5% in either direction, for a total allowable deviation of 10%.
    • Districts must be composed of contiguous territory.
    • Districts should not split counties or existing political subdivisions unless necessary and in compliance with existing judicial decisions.
    • Districts should not divide communities of interest unless necessary to achieve one of the criteria above.
    • Districts should be compact.
  • Prohibit districts to be drawn to favor any candidate or party.
  • Require the General Assembly to employ a third-party consultant to apply election data from the previous 10 years to each of 20,000 alternative district plans to determine the extent that the plans may favor a party or candidate and the extent to which districts may be gerrymandered due to "cracking" or "packing" of various interest groups.

Last updated May 6, 2021.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on November 18, 2021:

  • Repeals existing language allowing the State Board of Elections to enter into a consent agreement in election litigation with the consent of the Attorney General when the General Assembly is not in session.
  • Requires the joint approval of the Speaker of the House and the President Pro Tempore of the Senate for a consent agreement in litigation in which the legislative leaders are parties or in which they have intervened. The requirement applies to non-election litigation as well as election litigation. Under existing law, other parties had authority to settle litigation without legislative approval. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Limits the length of a state of emergency declaration by the Governor, and therefore the effective period of any executive orders issued pursuant to such an order, to 30 days unless the Governor receives the consent of the Council of State and 60 days unless the Governor receives the consent of the General Assembly. A similar provision had previously been amended out of the bill before being re-added to the enacted version.
  • Appropriates $2.8 million in unspent HAVA funds for "enhanc[ing] technology and continu[ing] improvements in elections cybersecurity". This provision was newly amended into this version of the bill.

Previous versions of the bill contained provisions that were amended out of this version. Those provisions would have:

  • Transferred investigative authority for election fraud and crimes from the State Board of Elections to the State Bureau of Investigation.
  • Limited the ability of the Attorney General to intervene in certain elections-related lawsuits without the consent of the Council of State.

Note: This bill is a general appropriations bill and contains many additional provisions unrelated to election law that are not tracked by the Voting Rights Lab.

Last updated November 29, 2021.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on April 7, 2021, would establish redistricting criteria for federal Congressional and state legislative districts to be drawn following the 2020 census. The bill would:

  • Establish a hierarchy of redistricting criteria to apply to drawing federal Congressional and state legislative districts. The criteria would be, in order of priority:
    • Districts must be equal in population. Congressional districts may not deviate by more than one person, if possible. State legislative districts may not deviate by more than 5% in either direction, for a total allowable deviation of 10%.
    • Districts must be composed of contiguous territory.
    • Districts should not split counties or existing political subdivisions unless necessary and in compliance with existing judicial decisions.
    • Districts should not divide communities of interest unless necessary to achieve one of the criteria above.
    • Districts should be compact.
  • Prohibit districts to be drawn to favor any candidate or party.
  • Require the General Assembly to employ a third-party consultant to apply election data from the previous 10 years to each of 20,000 alternative district plans to determine the extent that the plans may favor a party or candidate and the extent to which districts may be gerrymandered due to "cracking" or "packing" of various interest groups.

Last updated April 13, 2021.
