  • Require voters to have only one witness sign their absentee ballot return envelope. Existing law requires the voter to have two witnesses sign the ballot or to have it notarized.
  • Require driver's license offices to offer automatic voter registration beginning January 1, 2022. Individuals conducting transactions with these offices would be given the opportunity to decline registration and to affiliate with a political party. The Department of Transportation would transmit data sufficient for voter registration to the Board of Elections.
  • Require offices providing applications for public assistance, programs for individuals with disabilities, and employment benefits to offer automatic voter registration beginning January 1, 2023. Individuals conducting transactions with these offices would be given the opportunity to decline registration and to affiliate with a political party. The relevant agencies would transmit data sufficient for voter registration to the Board of Elections.
  • Create a presumption that automatic registrations are officially authorized and would make an ineligible individual automatically registered liable for criminal prosecution only if the individual willfully, knowingly, and with fraudulent intent provide false information while registering.
  • Require re-entering citizens to be advised of the availability of automatic voter registration at the designated offices.
  • Require the State Board of Elections to develop an online voter registration system. The system would require an applicant to have a North Carolina driver's license or nonoperators ID card to complete registration online.
    • NOTE: The N.C. Department of Transportation currently offers an online voter registration system, but it is not required by statute.
  • Allow voters to deliver absentee ballot requests to the county board of elections in person or by mail, email, or fax.
  • Encourage election officials to provide polling locations on the campuses of colleges with enrollments of at least 4500.
  • Repeal existing code provisions requiring the cancellation of a voter's registration if they fail to respond to an address confirmation notice or attempt to vote for two general elections after the sending of the notice. The bill would allow the cancellation of a voter's registration following the sending of an address confirmation notice only if the notice is returned as undeliverable.
  • Enact provisions creating non-partisan appellate judge elections, procedures to livestream legislative proceedings, rules to regulate the content of political ads, and campaign finance disclosure rules.
  • This bill also contains provisions relating to redistricting which are not tracked by Voting Rights Lab.

NOTE: The constitutional amendments require approval of 60% of the members of each chamber of the General Assembly prior to submission to the voters, who must approve the amendments by a simple majority.

This bill, as enacted on April 30, 2021, makes changes to various aspects of absentee voting, canvassing, and voter-related record keeping. Specifically, the bill:

  • Creates a statutory process for notice of potential mismatched signatures on absentee ballots and cure. Election officials must first attempt to contact voters with potential mismatched signatures by phone, and if unable to speak with the voter, by mail. The voter will receive notice of the issue with instructions for how to cure the issue within six days after Election Day. The voter may cure the issue in writing or in person and will need to provide a copy of or present the ID used when applying for the ballot. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Prohibits election officials to mail an absentee ballot to a voter without the voter applying for the ballot in jurisdictions that do not conduct elections primarily by mail ballot. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Prohibits the use of non-public funds for election administration, with exceptions for the use of privately-owned facilities as polling locations, provision of food to poll workers, and non-monetary donations of supplies to process ballots or votes. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Creates a new Class A misdemeanor for violating the prohibition on use of private funds for election administration. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Limits the mailing of absentee ballot applications in jurisdictions conducting elections primarily by mail ballot to active voters and persons eligible to vote for the first time. Existing law allowed applications to be mailed to all voters in the central voter file. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Permits all voters to receive their absentee ballot by electronic delivery, if they provide a fax number or email address. Existing law limited electronic delivery of ballots to UOCAVA voters only. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires absentee ballot applications and return envelopes to include an advisement to voters that the signatures on applications will be compared to the signatures on return envelopes for verification. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Eliminates the requirement that the Secretary of State notify county auditors after removing voters from the central voter file due to death or after receiving notice of a voter's name change due to marital status, or after designating a voter as inactive. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Allows visually impaired voters to request an absentee ballot they may mark and return electronically. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires each county to create an absentee ballot precinct to count all absentee ballots cast in the county. Existing law authorized, but did not require, the creation of absentee ballot precincts. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Creates a new Class C felony offense for the destruction, at any time, of ballots, ballot boxes, voter lists, or voting supplies. Under existing law, this offense was a felony only if the destruction occurred during an election or the canvassing period, and was otherwise a misdemeanor. The bill also creates a new felony for negatively impacting the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of a voting system, and raises the severity of tampering with a voting system or preventing its use from a Class A misdemeanor to a Class C felony. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.
  • Moves the date of the county canvassing meeting from six days after Election Day to 13 days after Election Day, and makes a corresponding change to the deadline for voters to provide ID if their ballot was cast aside due to failure to present required documentation, up to the new start date. These are new provisions that were not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Relaxes rules about the use of places where alcohol is sold as polling locations by prohibiting the use of such locations only if alcohol is being sold during voting hours or while election officials are working. Under existing law, elections could not be held in any room where alcohol was "commonly" sold. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires local election officials to add the names of individuals who voted in an election that were not already in the central voting file to the file before the county canvass meeting. Existing law gave local officials up to 45 days after Election Day to add the names. The bill also requires the Secretary of State to query the list of names in the central voter file to determine if any individual voted more than once prior to the meeting of the state canvassing board. Existing law gave the Secretary up to 85 days after Election Day to query the list. This provision has been modified from the previous version of the bill, which required local officials to add names to the central voting file within 12 business days after Election Day.
  • Makes numerous other changes to election issues that VRL does not track, including time limits on in-person ballot marking, canvassing and certification procedures, paper ballots, initiative procedures, nominating petitions, recount procedures, and ballot format and retention. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.

Last Updated August 24, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 7, 2021, would establish procedures for the Redistricting Committee of the Legislature when creating districts for the state's congressional representatives, the state legislature, judges of the state Supreme Court, the Board of Regents of the University of Nebraska, the Public Service Commission, and the State Board of Education. The bill would:

  • Require contiguous districts to be drawn based on politically-neutral criteria and equality of population, subject to a deviation of one percent or less.
  • Require the use of federal census data only when drawing districts. Districts should be drawn with deference to county and municipal boundaries when possible, and without consideration of the party affiliation or previous voting behavior of residents or registered voters.
  • Require the Redistricting Committee to hold at least one public hearing in each congressional district to hear public comment on the proposed districts. The map-drawing bills would not be eligible for legislative consideration until at least fourteen days after the last public hearing.
  • Require the Governor to call a special session within thirty days of adjournment if the Legislature fails to enact bills to create districts within the scheduled legislative session. The Redistricting Committee must begin the special session with a new initial version of the map.

Last updated January 8, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Adopts the proposed guidelines to be used by the Legislature during the 2021 redistricting process.
VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as adopted on May 26, 2021, sets for the criteria to guide the legislature in the 2021 redistricting process. Specifically, the resolution provides that:

  • 2020 Census data will be used for redistricting.

  • District boundaries shall:

    • Follow county lines,
    • Be compact and contiguous,
    • Create districts that are easily identifiable and understandable,
    • Preserve communities of interest,
    • Allow for the preservation of cores of prior districts,
    • Where feasible, coincide with existing political subdivisions,
    • Not be intended to favor a political party or demographic factors, except as required by the U.S. laws and Constitution,

    • Create districts that are substantially equal in population, with U.S. House districts having no more than 1% overall deviation, and state legislative districts, Supreme Court districts, board of regents districts, public service commission districts, and state board of education districts having no more than 10% overall deviation.

BILLSUMMARY: Modifies the procedures for ongoing verification of the information contained in voter checklists, and provides that where there is not a full match of name, date of birth, and residence, the Secretary of State shall provide information of partial matches for further review and confirmation by the town or city.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on July 23, 2021, facilitates voter list maintenance. The bill:

  • Requires the secretary of state to provide information on possible matches between death records and voter registrations to town clerks for investigation where there is not a full match.
  • Requires the division of motor vehicles to transmit address changes on vehicle registrations to municipal clerks in both the origin and destination locations.
  • Restricts the passing from clerks to checklist supervisors of information received from death notices to those that are full matches to voter registrations. Where there is only a possible match, municipal clerks are required to investigate further.
  • Requires the secretary of state to verify that all registrations of voters sharing a place and date of birth and a substantially similar name are in fact unique voters. The secretary must forward any apparently duplicative registrations to municipal clerks, who will then investigate and inform the secretary of the outcome of the investigation. Should the investigation show that an individual voted more than once in any election, such information must be forwarded to the attorney general for further investigation or prosecution.
  • Requires the secretary of state to use NCOA annually and provide relevant records to municipal clerks.

  • Requires municipalities to forward to checklist supervisors buyer and seller names from property transactions should they receive an inquiry.

    These provisions were in the previous version of the bill, which was amended on May 13 and May 20 with no substantive changes.

    Last updated September 9, 2021.

This bill, as amended on May 27, 2021, would require the state attorney general to analyze requests for absentee ballots for state general elections and presidential primary elections for evidence of misuse. The analysis would be required to include the number of absentee ballots mailed to a common address and significant differences in the number of ballots that were requested from a city or town. The results of the analysis and any additional actions identified would have to be reported to the house and senate committees with jurisdiction over elections within 120 days of a covered election.

These provisions are modified from a previous version of the bill, which would have required the secretary of state to prepared a report on the use of mail ballots generally after each election and required clerks to make absentee voter lists available for public inspection 60 days after Election Day.

Last Updated February 11, 2022

  • Voters could show the clerk a valid photo ID before Election Day.
  • Voters could have their absentee ballot application notarized.

Note: New Hampshire does not engage in signature matching following a 2018 court order regarding a slightly different statutory scheme.

Last Updated February 25, 2022

Existing law did not specify how the list must be provided to candidates or the cost. This provision is modified from the previous version of the bill. The previous version would have made electronic transmission of the list optional rather than mandatory, and did not include the requirement that the list be provided for free.

This bill, as introduced on January 12, 2021, would:

  • Remove the requirement that a voter carry out verifiable acts carrying out an intent establish and maintain a domicile.
  • Remove the requirement that applicants for registration provide documentary evidence of their qualifications or attest that none exists by completing a qualified voter affidavit.
  • Defines domicile as "that place, more than any other, where [the voter] sleep[s] most nights of the year, or to which [they] intend to return after a temporary absence."
  • Remove the requirement that an applicant for registration in the final 30 days before an election use a special form, retaining that form only for registration on Election Day.
  • Establish a Domicile Affidavit for same-day registrations.
  • Allow same-day registrants who do not have an approved photo ID to establish their identity via "any reasonable means," including other forms of photo ID or verification by another registered voter.
  • Remove the requirement that the secretary of state mail letters to all new registrants within 30 days of an election informing them that new New Hampshire residents must get a New Hampshire driver's license without 60 days of becoming a resident of the state.
  • Direct the secretary of state to cease participating in Crosscheck and to prepare a report for legislators regarding potentially joining ERIC.

BILLSUMMARY: Establishes an independent advisory commission on redistricting.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2021, would establish an independent advisory commission for redistricting:

  • Criteria for consideration would be contiguity, compactness, and the integrity of communities of interest (including economic, social, cultural, geographic, racial, ethnic, or historic identities, but not common relationships with political parties or candidates).
  • The commission would be required to draw districts in compliance with state and federal law.
  • Maps could not unduly favor or disfavor any racial or language group, political party, incumbent officeholder, or political candidate.
  • Ultimately, the legislature would retain the power to approve suggested maps.
  • Maps and underlying data would have to be released seven days before consideration.
  • The commission would be chosen by legislative leaders, with those ten members then choosing another five who are not affiliated with either major party.

A previous version of this bill contained provisions that were amended out of the current text, which would have permitted preprocessing of absentee ballots and a notice and cure process for defective ballot envelopes. In these deleted provisions, the bill would have:

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on 8/24/20, would create same day new voter registration for Election Day and early voting. The bill would also move the deadline for voter registration and updating existing registrations closer to Election Day. The bill would:

  • Allow voters to register and vote at their polling place on Election Day or at any location providing in-person vote-by-mail ballot voting beginning 45 days before Election Day.
  • Require same day registrants to provide an approved form of ID (photo not required), a voter registration form, and an affidavit attesting that they are not registered elsewhere, have lived in the county for 30 days, and have not voted previously in the current election.
  • Move the general deadline for new registration and address/name change updates from 21 days before Election Day to eight days before Election Day.
  • Allow county clerks to accept voter change of residence notices. Under current law, only municipal clerks and county commissioners of registration.
  • Require officials to notify applicants within two business days of the reasons for rejection of a voter registration application.
  • Moves the deadline for moving from one county to another and being eligible to vote in the new county from 21 days before Election Day to 30 days before Election Day.
  • Makes registering more than once, registering under a false name, attempting to vote more than once, and registering in an election district other than one in which a person resides crimes of the fourth degree.
  • Changes voter registration forms and instructions to voter registration agencies to reflect the deadline changes contained within the bill.

Last Updated December 16, 2020

BILLSUMMARY: Requires an early voting period for in person voting for the 2020 general election, makes an appropriation.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on 8/25/20, would create "Election Day"-style early voting in New Jersey for the November 2020 general election only. The bill would:

  • Create an early voting period for voters to cast ballots in person on voting machines beginning the 14th day before Election Day and ending the day before Election Day. Early voting must be offered every day, including weekends, during the early voting period, from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m.
  • Require early voting to be offered at every municipal clerk's office. Additionally, counties with populations of at least 150,000 but less than 300,000 must designate five additional early voting locations. Counties with populations of 300,000 or more must designate seven additional early voting locations.
  • Require additional early voting locations to be placed based on geography and population density. Additional locations must be at public facilities, but may not be located at public schools.
  • Require the Secretary of State and county boards to publicize the availability and rules concerning early voting.
  • Prohibit voters who participate in early voting to vote by mail-in ballot or on Election Day. Early voters must sign a certificate which provides a warning of the penalties for fraudulent voting.

Last updated on March 9, 2021.

HISTORY: {"date":"08/25/2020","summary":"To ASSEMBLY Committee on STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on 8/25/20, would create "Election Day"-style early voting in New Jersey for the November 2020 general election and would raise poll worker pay. The bill would:

  • Create an early voting period for voters to cast ballots in person on voting machines beginning the 14th day before Election Day and ending the day before Election Day. Early voting must be offered every day, including weekends, during the early voting period, from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m.
  • Require early voting to be offered in at least one location at a public facility in each municipality.
  • Require the Secretary of State and county boards to publicize the availability and rules concerning early voting.
  • Prohibit voters who participate in early voting to vote by mail-in ballot or on Election Day. Early voters must sign a certificate which provides a warning of the penalties for fraudulent voting.
  • Allow counties to begin canvassing early votes at the opening of polls on Election Day.
  • Create a penalty of ten days of incarceration, in addition to other penalties required by law, for intimidating, threatening, or coercing, or attempting to intimidate, threaten, or coerce, a voter during the 2020 general election period and releasing a voter's ballot information after the ballot has been voted, sealed, and delivered to the appropriate election officials during the 2020 general election period.
  • Raise poll worker pay to $400/day
  • Require counties to consider appointing members of the district board of elections that are under the age of 35, including high school and college students, and state employees who have been furloughed because of the pandemic.

Last Updated March 9, 2021

This bill, as enacted on January 18, 2022:

  • Prohibits law enforcement officers from being stationed at polling places for general maintenance of peace and order, except officers may be assigned specifically for the transportation of election materials to and from a polling place. The bill also provides an exception for when a law enforcement officer is called by the election officials to assist in a specific emergency at a polling place or at a senior residential center. This provision was modified from the previous version of the bill, which did not address senior residential centers.
  • Prohibits law enforcement officers from serving as members of a district election board unless they are off duty. The bill also prohibits law enforcement officers from serving as authorized challengers located within their jurisdiction of law enforcement service with the exception that officers who are candidates on the ballot may serve as challengers if otherwise authorized by law. A law enforcement officer may not remain within 100 feet of a polling location except for the act of voting, unless the officer's personal residence is within 100 feet of a polling place. This provision was modified from the previous version of the bill to condition the limitation on service as a challenger to the officer's jurisdiction.
  • Prohibits ballot drop boxes from being placed within 100 feet of the entrance or exit of a law enforcement agency. Existing drop boxes in certain locations are exempt from this prohibition. The previous version of the bill did not include the exemption for existing drop boxes.
  • Prohibits electioneering activity within 100 feet of a drop box. A person who violates this provision may be charged with a disorderly persons offense. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Allows a county to open only the drop box nearest to the office of the municipal clerk and the drop box at the county board of elections office during a municipal, school board, or special election. Existing law does not address drop box availability during municipal-only elections. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

Last Updated March 29, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:

This bill, as amended on February 24, 2021, would create "Election Day-style" early voting for New Jersey general, primary, and municipal elections. The bill would:

  • Require all counties to offer early voting beginning 4 days before each non-presidential primary, 6 days before any presidential primary and 10 days before any general election. Early voting would end 2 days before any election for which it is conducted. Municipalities conducting municipal elections in May will have the option to provide early voting beginning 4 days before the election and ending two days before the election. The previous version of the bill required counties to provide early voting beginning 15 days before any general election, and did not require early voting before primary elections.
  • For general and primary elections, counties must provide between three and five locations for early voting. Counties with more than 150,000 registered voters and fewer than 300,000 registered voters must provide between five and seven locations, and counties with 300,000 or more registered voters must provide between seven and ten locations. Counties should consider geography and population density when selecting locations. All locations must be in public buildings, but may not be located in schools. Voters may vote early at any location in the county, regardless of their registered address. Counties may provide more early voting locations that those required by the bill at their own expense. The previous version of the bill only required counties to provide the lower number of locations in the ranges listed in the current version of the bill.
  • For municipal elections, municipalities must offer between one and three early voting locations if they opt to provide early voting. Rules regarding locations are the same as those for general elections. The previous version of the bill only required municipalities to provide one early voting location.
  • Require counties and municipalities providing early voting to maintain voting hours at all locations Monday-Saturday 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. and Sunday 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require early voting locations to use electronic poll books that can update registration information in real time. The bill would also require early voting locations to use a system to print ballots on demand. The bill would require voters to cast provisional ballots if the electronic poll books do not function. The previous version of the bill required early voters to complete and sign an early voting certificate prior to voting.
  • Repeal existing law limiting a candidate, party, or public question to a single challenger at a polling location absent express permission by a district board of elections. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Provide that no more than two challengers for any candidate, group of candidates, party, or public question may serve at an early voting location. The previous version of the bill provided that challengers at early voting locations would be subject to the same requirements and limitations as those at Election Day polling locations.
  • Prohibit localities from canvassing early voting ballots until the close of polls on Election Day. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require newspaper notices of elections and sample ballots mailed to voters to include information about the days, hours, and locations for early voting. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Allow county clerks to electronically display sample ballots at early voting locations. Clerks who choose to do so would be required to post sample ballots in multiple languages. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.

Last Updated February 25, 2021

If such a voter failed to vote in the following two consecutive federal general elections, the commissioner would delete the voter's registration. The voter would receive notice within five days of: 1) placement into the inactive file, 2) the commissioner's decision to begin the registration deletion process, and 3) removal from the statewide registration system.

BILLSUMMARY: Transfers Division of Elections from Department of State to Department of Law and Public Safety, designates Attorney General as chief election official and requires two bipartisan co-directors.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 12, 2021, would:

  • Make the Attorney General the state's chief election officer. Existing law makes the Secretary of State the chief election officer.
  • Transfer the Division of Elections from the Department of State to the Department of Law and Public Safety.
  • Create two co-directors to administer the Division of Elections. Each co-director would be appointed by the Governor with the advice and consent of the state Senate. One co-director would be selected from the Governor's political party and one would be selected from the party that received the second-most votes in the most recent election for Governor.

Last updated February 2, 2022.

HISTORY: {"date":"01/27/2021","summary":"To ASSEMBLY Committee on STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 27, 2021, would:

  • Create a process for voters who return a vote by mail ballot without a Certification of Mail-In Voter or a detached Certificate to cure the issue by completing a cure form and a replacement Certificate. The voter would be subject to the general cure deadline of 48 hours prior to certification.
  • Allow persons who receive vote by mail ballots that are addressed to voters who no longer reside at the location due to a change of address or death to return the ballot to the county clerk with a notation indicating why the ballot is being returned. The bill would also require ballot mailing envelopes to be clearly marked as nonforwardable. Returned ballots indicating the the voter has died must be forwarded to the registration commissioner within 30 days, and the commissioner must investigate to determine whether they have taken action on the voter's registration prior to that time.
  • Require registration commissioners to cancel the registrations of voters who are confirmed to be deceased within 30 days of the determination. Existing law requires cancellation "as soon as practicable."

Last Updated January 29, 2021

Existing law limit individuals without a clear intent to return to the U.S. to voting in federal elections only.

The provision permitting overseas voters to vote in local elections was amended out of the June 21 version of the bill before being restored in this version.

Last Updated November 22, 2021

This bill, as enacted on April 9, 2021:

  • Requires a drop box to be placed in any municipality with an average or per capita income at or below 250% of the federal poverty guideline whenever possible. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Removes the requirement for a drop box to be placed at certain municipal clerks' offices and the campuses of community colleges. This provision was added back to the bill after having been removed from an earlier version.
  • Adds to the factors that officials must considering when locating drop boxes, by including travel time, proximity to other voting locations, and commuter traffic patterns.
  • Requires counties to post the location of drop boxes within the county on the county website, at least45 days before an election, and to provide a list of locations with the vote by mail ballot materials sent to voters. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

HISTORY: {"date":"06/02/2021","summary":"To ASSEMBLY Committee on STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT","meta":["[]"],"order":0}

  • Expand the list of curable defects with vote-by-mail ballots to include a missing Certificate of Mail-in Voter, missing inner envelope, missing mail-in ballot, incomplete or incorrect information of the person who provided assistance to the voter, or incorrect outer envelope.
  • Require cure letters and documentation a voter must return to complete the cure process to include prepaid return postage. The bill would also require cure forms to notify the voter that they may receive assistance completing cure forms as long as the assistant completes an assistor portion of the cure form.
  • Create a presumption that the signature on a vote-by-mail ballot is that of the voter. The bill would require election officials to liberally construe rules regarding ballot verification in favor of the voter and possible cure of any defect.
  • Require each county board to update the online ballot tracking system to indicate that a voter's ballot is received from the voter within 24 hours of receipt. The bill would require each county board to maintain a list of voters with ballots eligible for cure beginning 30 days before each Election Day that must be updated every 24 hours.
  • Require county boards of election to meet at least weekly beginning 45 days before Election Day to verify vote-by-mail ballots. Existing law requires county boards to meet weekly beginning three weeks before Election Day.

BILLSUMMARY: Revises certain requirements for district board members and polling places for June 2021 primary election, provides reimbursement for National Guard assistance with 2020 primary and general elections, makes appropriation.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on June 3, 2021, enacts temporary provisions for the June 8, 2021 primary election responding to the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic. For the June 8, 2021 primary, the bill:

BILLSUMMARY: Proposes constitutional amendment to change Legislative Apportionment Commission Membership, establishes new requirements on commission for process and legislative district composition.
VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as introduced on January 14, 2020, would propose a constitutional amendment concerning redistricting. The amendment would:

  • Establish guidelines for the selection of members of the Apportionment Commission. 12 members will be appointed by party and legislative leaders, equally divided between the two major parties. The 13th member would be selected by the Chief Justice of the state supreme court. All persons appointing members to the Commission must consider ethnic, gender, and racial diversity. Existing law requires 10 members on the Commission and for the Chief Justice to appoint an 11th member to the Commission only if the original 10 are unable to agree on final maps.
  • Require the Commission to enact maps with an equal number of state legislative districts favoring each major political party. 25% of the districts must favor either party by no more than 5%. If the Commission is considering multiple maps, it should favor the map that best preserves communities of interest in the same district.
  • Move the deadline for completion of maps from one month after receipt of census information to two months after receipt.
  • Require the Commission to conduct at least three public hearings in different parts of the state prior to voting on final maps. The amendment would also require the Commission to host a website with public information concerning the redistricting process.

NOTE: If 3/5 of the members of both chambers of the legislature pass this resolution, it will be submitted to the voters at the next general election conducted at least three months after passage. If a majority, but fewer than 3/5, of the members of both chambers pass the resolution, it would require passage by a majority of both chambers of the next iteration of the state legislature ('22-'23) prior to submission to the voters.

VRLANALYSIS:
As introduced on January 14, 2020, this bill, entitled "The Democracy Act", would:

  • Require "Election Day-style" early voting to be offered for general elections beginning 15 days before Election Day until the day before Election Day.
  • Require a minimum number of early voting locations in public facilities in each county, depending on population.
  • Require early voting to be offered each day of the early voting period, including Saturdays and Sundays, during set hours each day.
  • Require voters casting a ballot during early voting to sign a certificate prior to voting.
  • Require counties providing early voting to provide notification of times and locations to voters.
  • Permit municipalities holding elections in May to offer early voting under similar rules if they choose.
  • Change the automatic voter registration process through the Motor Vehicle Commission to one where a person is automatically registered when conducting a transaction involving a driver's license or a non-driver's ID card and may opt out later after receiving notification of the registration.
  • Require the Secretary of State to establish an online voter registration system for which an applicant must provide a driver's license/state ID number and the last four digits of the social security number and which will allow a voter to sign up to receive mail-in ballots for future elections. Since this bill was introduced, legislation enacted an online registration system that required a driver's license/state ID or the last four digits of the voter's Social Security number.
  • Require the Secretary of State to provide online tracking of mail-in ballots. Since this bill was introduced, other legislation created ballot tracking.
  • Allow a voter to sign up to automatically receive mail-in ballots for all future elections or merely all future general elections. Existing law allows a registering voter to sign up to receive all future ballots by mail. A voter that is signed up to receive ballots for all future elections who fails to return a ballot in four consecutive elections will be moved to the list of voters receiving ballots for general elections only.
  • Require county clerks to provide return postage for military-overseas ballots, mail-in ballots, and elections conducted entirely by mail.
  • Allow military-overseas voters to use the federal write-in absentee ballot and transmit it to the clerk by air mail or electronic means.
  • Allow persons who are at least 17 years old and will be 18 years old by the first election in which they expect to vote to preregister to vote.
  • Allow voters that have received a mail-in ballot to return the ballot to the polling place on Election Day and vote a regular ballot. Such voters will vote a provisional ballot if they do not return the unvoted ballot to the polling place. This provision allows some people to vote a regular ballot who cannot under existing law. Existing law requires people who have been sent a mail ballot to vote by provisional ballot if they choose to vote in person.
  • Create felony punishment for deceptive voting practices related to providing false information to voters or other actions designed to intimidate or deter voting.
  • Provide new rules relating to providing voter information in languages other than English and filling Congressional vacancies.

NOTE: New Jersey currently offers early voting by in-person voting of mail-in ballots beginning 45 days before Election Day and ending the day before Election Day.

Last Updated December 17, 2020

This bill, as amended on 8/25/2020, would make temporary changes for the conduct of the November 2020 general election and permanent changes effective February 1, 2021.

The temporary changes for the November 2020 general election are identical to ones made by Governor Murphy's Executive Order No. 177. All of the temporary provisions are new provisions that were not in the previous version of the bill. This portion of the bill would:

  • Conduct the 2020 general election primarily by vote-by-mail ballot. All active registered voters would be mailed ballots on the 29th day before Election Day.
  • Require clerks to mail ballots to voters requesting ballots between the 13th day before Election Day and the 29th day before Election Day within three business days of approval of the application.
  • Provide prepaid return postage for mail ballots
  • Require each municipality to have at least one polling location open on Election Day. Each county must open at least 50% of its normal polling locations, if possible. If a county cannot reach the 50% threshold, the county must provide large voting centers to accommodate multiple districts. All schools will be closed and made available to serve as polling places.
  • Allow voters to return their completed mail ballots to their polling place on Election Day. Voters who do not return their ballot to the polling place will be allowed to vote by provisional ballot.
  • Require poll workers and challengers to adhere to CDC guidelines regarding face coverings. Voters will be encouraged, but not required, to adhere to CDC guidelines regarding face coverings. Polling locations will adopt procedures to allow for social distancing and proper sanitation.
  • Require each county to provide at least 10 drop box locations. The county must place the boxes according to geography and population density to best serve the needs of voters. The Secretary of State must establish guidelines concerning the placement and security of drop boxes and schedule for ballot pick-up. Each polling location will post a list of the county's drop box locations.
  • Require county boards to accept mail ballots that are postmarked by Election Day and received no later than 8 p.m. on November 10. County boards must also accept ballots delivered by the postal service that lack a postmark and are received by the board no later than 48 hours after the close of polls on Election Day.
  • Require county boards to meet at least four days a week beginning October 13 to verify vote-by-mail ballots. Boards may begin canvassing inner envelopes beginning 10 days before Election Day.
  • Move the date of the county canvass meeting to November 20. General law requires the meeting to occur the Wednesday following Election Day.
  • Waive the requirement for poll workers to be residents of the county in which they would serve.
  • Make early disclosure of the contents of a mail-in ballot a crime of the third degree (felony).

The permanent changes would take effect on February 1, 2021. The permanent changes would:

  • Require counties to provide ballot return drop boxes no later than 45 days before all elections. All drop boxes must be accessible to the public 24 hours a day and monitored by security cameras. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Provide that if a voter timely returns a vote-by-mail ballot to a drop box in a county in which the voter does not reside, the county board of that county will deliver the ballot to the correct county board, who must accept and process the ballot. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require counties to place at least one drop box at every government building containing the office of the county clerk or a municipal clerk of a municipality with a population greater than 5,000. Counties must also place at least one drop box on the main campus of every county community college, state college and university, and independent college and university with enrollment greater than 5,000. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require each county to provide at least 10 drop boxes, placed at county or municipal government buildings. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require the secretary of state to establish guidelines for county boards concerning placement and number of drop boxes. The guidelines must consider population, geography, voter convenience, public transportation, and security. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

NOTE: This bill was substituted by the identical bill NJ A 4475, which was enacted in August 2020.

This bill, as amended on 8/25/2020, would create a process to cure problems with vote by mail ballots. The bill would:

  • Require clerks to notify a voter whose vote-by-mail ballot has been rejected within 24 hours of the decision by sending the voter a cure letter by mail or email that explains the reason for the decision and a pre-printed cure form with instructions for the voter to cure the deficiency that led to the rejection decision. The voter will also receive a return envelope with pre-paid postage for the cure form. The clerk must also attempt to contact the voter by phone. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill did not provide for email or phone contact with the voter.
  • Provide voters up to 48 hours before the final certification of election results (generally, a date 15-18 days after Election Day) to cure problems with vote by mail ballots. If the reason for rejection is mismatched signatures, the voter may cure by completing the cure form and providing an identification number or a copy of one of various forms of ID (photo not required). This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill gave voters up to 14 days after Election Day to cure problems with mail ballots.
  • Require clerks to compare the signature on vote by mail ballots with the voter's signature on the ballot application and in the statewide registration system. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill required signature comparison with the statewide registration system and the Motor Vehicle Commission database, but not the ballot application.
  • Require the secretary of state to develop guidance on signature comparison, and notice and cure procedures for distribution to county boards of election. The secretary must publish signature comparison guidelines for distribution to county boards of election. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Create a presumption that a signature on a vote-by-mail ballot is that of the identified voter, unless their is a clear discrepancy that cannot be reasonably explained. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require the vote by mail ballot tracking system to be prominently displayed on the Department of Elections' website under a "Track My Ballot" portal. The ballot tracking system will coordinate information with the statewide voter registration system regarding the acceptance, rejection, and acceptance post-cure of mail ballots. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would also have included information about when and how clerks notified voters of mail ballot issues in the public tracking website.
  • Require the notice of rights posted at in-person polling locations to include advisement about notice and cure procedures for vote by mail ballots. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require the Secretary of State to conduct a voter education campaign concerning signature matching and ballot curing provisions at least 30 days before each election. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require county boards of election to reject a vote-by-mail ballot if the inner ballot envelope is unsealed. Current law requires rejection if both the outer and inner envelopes are unsealed. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Refer disputes about a voter's qualifications or the validity of a vote-by-mail ballot after the cure process created by the bill to the Superior Court. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Change mail ballot application and provisional ballot forms to allow the voter to provide email and telephone information to facilitate contact from the clerk regarding ballot issues. This provision would not take effect until February 1, 2021. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.

NOTE: This bill was substituted by the identical bill NJ A 4276, which was enacted in August 2020.

Last Updated December 17, 2020

This bill, as amended on 8/25/2020, would:

This provision was in the previous version of the bill, but would have been effective immediately.

This bill, as enacted on March 30, 2021, creates "Election Day-style" early voting for New Jersey general, primary, and municipal elections. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires all counties to offer early voting beginning four days before each non-presidential primary, six days before any presidential primary, and 10 days before any general election. Early voting for all elections must end two days before Election Day. Municipalities are permitted, but not required, to offer early voting for regular municipal elections starting the fourth day before an election and ending the second day before. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Sets out requirements for early voting locations and operating hours:
    • Counties must provide between three and five locations for early voting for general and primary elections, unless they reach certain voter population thresholds. In counties with more than 150,000 registered voters and fewer than 300,000 registered voters, officials must provide between five and seven locations, and counties with 300,000 or more registered voters must provide between seven and ten locations. Counties may provide additional early voting locations beyond the designated requirements, but operating costs will only be reimbursed by the state within the statutory ranges. This provision was modified from the previous version of the bill, which required counties to only provide the lower number of locations in the ranges now enacted.
    • Counties must, as possible, consider geography and population density when selecting early voting locations. All locations must be in public buildings, but may not be located in schools, and must meet federal accessibility requirements. Voters may vote early at any location in the county, regardless of their registered address.
    • Municipalities that opt to provide early voting must offer between one and three early voting locations (additional sites are permitted, but will not be funded by the state). The previous version of the bill required municipalities to provide only one early voting location.
    • Requires counties and municipalities to operate all early voting locations Monday-Saturday 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. and Sunday 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Provides that no more than two challengers for any candidate, group of candidates, party, or public question may serve at an early voting location. The previous version of the bill provided that challengers at early voting locations would be subject to the same requirements and limitations as those at Election Day polling locations.
  • Requires early voting locations to use electronic poll books that can update registration information in real time. The bill also requires early voting locations to use a system to print ballots on demand, and requires voters to cast provisional ballots if the electronic poll books do not function. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Prohibits localities from canvassing early voting ballots until the close of polls on Election Day. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires newspaper notices of elections and sample ballots mailed to voters to include information about the days, hours, and locations for early voting. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Allows county clerks to electronically display sample ballots at early voting locations. Clerks who choose to do so are required to post sample ballots in multiple languages. The previous version of the bill required electronic sample ballots in the five most commonly spoken languages in the state according to the most recent census data.
  • Makes various changes to existing provisions throughout the election code to include reference to early voting.

A provision from a previous version of the bill was amended out of the text on February 11, 2021. It would have required early voters to complete and sign an early voting certificate prior to voting.

  • The voter does not use a mail-in ballot for any election in a two-year period, or

Prior to removing a voter from the permanent list, a county clerk would be required to notify the voter in writing, indicating the reasons for removal and instructing the voter on the necessary steps to continue to vote by mail. If the voter did not respond to the notice within 30 days of mailing, the county clerk would remove that voter from the list and send that voter a notice of removal. The county clerk would also be required to include an application to re-apply to vote by mail with the notice of removal.

Under existing law, clerks can only remove voters from the list at the voter's request or if the voter is moved to the inactive list.

BILLSUMMARY: Proposes constitutional amendment to modify legislative redistricting schedule if receipt by Governor of decennial census of United States is delayed.
VRLANALYSIS:

The amendment would maintain existing legislative districts for the state legislative elections conducted in the year ending in 1 and certify the new legislative districts following the November general election held in that year. The new legislative districts would then apply to elections conducted beginning in the year ending in 3.

NOTE: If 3/5 of the members of both chamber of the state legislature pass this bill, the amendment would be submitted to voters at the next general election three months or later after the passage of the bill. If a majority, but fewer than 3/5, of the members pass the bill, it would be carried over to the next iteration of the legislature ('22-'23) and, if passed by a majority of that legislature, would then be submitted to the voters.

HISTORY: {"date":["08/20/2020","08/20/2020"],"summary":["INTRODUCED","To SENATE Committee on STATE GOVERNMENT, WAGERING, TOURISM AND HISTORIC PRESERVATION"],"meta":["[]","[]"],"order":[1,0]}
BILLSUMMARY: Proposes constitutional amendments to establish redistricting standards for Apportionment Commission, requires Chief Justice of Supreme Court to select 11th member from pool of general public applicants, requires commission to hold public hearings.
VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as introduced on August 20, 2020, would propose a constitutional amendment related to redistricting. The amendment would:

  • Change the apportionment of legislative districts to require each legislative district to be represented by one Senator and two Assembly members.
  • Establish criteria for drawing state legislative districts.
    • Districts must be contiguous, compact, and as equal as practicable in population.
    • Districts may not be drawn to favor a political party or incumbent.
    • Districts may not be drawn to dilute the voting strength of any language or racial minority.
    • Districts may not be drawn in consideration of incumbent addresses, the political affiliation of registered voters, or previous election results.
  • Move the deadline for completion of maps from one month after receipt of census information to two months after receipt.
  • Establish guidelines for the selection of members of the Apportionment Commission. 10 members will be appointed by party and legislative leaders, equally divided between the two major parties. The 11th member would be selected by the Chief Justice of the state supreme court. The 11th member must be an unaffiliated registered voter and would serve as the chair of the Commission. All persons appointing members to the Commission must consider ethnic, gender, and racial diversity. Existing law requires the Chief Justice to appoint an 11th member to the Commission if the original 10 are unable to agree on final maps.
  • Require the Commission to conduct at least three public hearings (one each in the northern, central, and southern parts of the state). The amendment would also require the Commission to host a website with public information concerning the redistricting process.

NOTE: If 3/5 of the members of both chambers of the legislature pass this resolution, it will be submitted to the voters at the next general election conducted at least three months after passage. If a majority, but fewer than 3/5, of the members of both chambers pass the resolution, it would require passage by a majority of both chambers of the next iteration of the state legislature ('22-'23) prior to submission to the voters.

Last updated August 20, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on January 28, 2021, would create a redistricting process for state representatives, state senators, state educational commission members, and congressional representatives that uses an independent commission to draw the maps based on set criteria and substantial public participation, and requires the legislature to adopt one of the proposed maps without amendment. In addition, it would enable any public participant to appeal one of the commission's proposed maps to the state supreme court according to a streamlined process. When deciding the appeal, the court could affirm the map or reject and vacate it, but the court could not amend it. Under existing law, the legislature draws and enacts maps as ordinary legislation, which the governor may veto. In the 2010 redistricting cycle, after the governor vetoed the legislature's adopted plans, a trial court drew maps that were rejected by the state Supreme Court. Following the state Supreme Court's instructions, the trial court drew new maps which were upheld.

The commission created by this bill must hold at least six public meetings either virtually or in various regions of the state before proposing the district plans. Thereafter the commission must propose 3 to 5 maps for each set of offices, outlining why the maps meet the required criteria, and then hold no fewer than six public rule hearings, either virtually or in various regions of the state, for the purpose of adopting district plans. As part of adopting the district plans, the commission must provide written evaluations of each that address how each satisfies the required criteria, the ability of racial and language minorities to elect candidates of their choice, a measure of partisan fairness and the preservation of communities of interest, and indicate which district plan in each set best meets the all the requirements. After the commission adopts the plans, a public participant may appeal one or more of them to the state supreme court, which will either affirm or reject the plan. If the court rejects it, the commission must amend it.

Once the plans are adopted by the commission, they are sent to the Legislature for consideration. For each office the legislature may any of the plans proposed to it, but if it cannot choose a plan, the legislature must adopt the plan the commission has designated as best meeting all of the requirements. The legislature may not amend any of the plans. The bill acknowledges that the governor may veto whatever the legislature adopts, but it does not specify a separate post-veto process.

In addition to the public participation requirements, when drawing the maps, the newly created commission:

  • Must create district plans composed of single-member districts. Existing law provides for single-member districts.
  • Must create district plans composed of contiguous territory, provided that districts that meet only at the points of adjoining corners are not contiguous. Existing law requires districts to be contiguous, but does not define the term.
  • Must comply with all applicable federal laws.
  • Must ensure that congressional districts are as equal in population as practicable.
  • Must create state office districts that are as close to equal in population as possible. Any deviation must not exceed plus or minus five percent and must be based on:
    • compliance with applicable federal law,
    • consideration of tribal government,
    • the avoidance of diluting the representation of communities of interest,
    • the avoidance of fragmenting governmental subdivisions, or
    • the preservation of the core of existing districts, provided that the district plan meets all other requirements provided by this section.
  • May use, rely upon or reference precincts and units of population that are smaller than precincts, and may rely upon or reference the most recent federal decennial census data provided by the United States census bureau and other reliable sources of demographic data. Existing law does not have a comparable provision.

  • Must not:

    • propose or adopt district plans to favor a political party or incumbent.
    • use, rely upon or reference partisan data, such as voting history or party registration data, except that voting history in elections may be considered to comply with applicable federal law.
    • create district plans to intentionally dilute the representation of communities of interest.
    • create district plans to intentionally preserve the cores of existing districts unless the district plan meets all other requirements.

    When a district plan satisfies all of these requirements, the commission shall adopt those district plans that are most compact, as determined by a measure of length-width compactness or perimeter compactness.

    Last updated February 1, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to Native American polling place protection.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on April 6, 2021, creates rules for polling places on Native lands during declared emergencies, and would amend rules relating to them during ordinary times. Specifically, during a declared emergency, the bill:

  • Prohibits the elimination or consolidation of a polling place on Native land, or change to the days or times voting is offered at such place, without the written agreement of the relevant Native government.
  • Requires the county clerk to provide a mobile or alternate voting location on Native land upon written request, if the election is a statewide election, the Native government had not previously requested one, and the current request is at least 98 days before the election or at least 49 days if the request is backed by a court order.
  • Requires the county clerk to open an Election Day polling place on Native land upon written request, if the election is a statewide election, no Election Day polling place exists on the Native land, voters registered within the Native land are unable to leave the Native land during the time voting is occurring, and the written request is at least 84 days before the election or 35 days before if backed by a court order.
  • Suspends the requirement that all voters in the county be able to use the polling place on Native land if the land is inaccessible or its borders closed.

  • Requires the Secretary of State to reimburse the county clerk for all necessary and reasonable expenses for complying with this law.

    During non-emergency times, the bill:

  • Prohibits the elimination or consolidation of a polling place on Native land without the written agreement of the Native nation, tribe or pueblo on which the polling place is located.

    Note: A previous version of the bill included a provision that would have given Native peoples less time to request a mobile or alternate early voting site on their lands each election cycle during non-emergency times. This provision was amended out of the bill.

Last updated September 28, 2021.

This bill, as amended on March 12, 2021, was substantially revised. As amended, the bill would create a temporary "voter education and elections task force" with a specified, bipartisan composition and a broad mission to "study and provide recommendations on best practices to educate the voters of New Mexico on electoral procedures, voter registration and election safeguards[, and to] evaluate opportunities for improvements to the electoral process to maximize voter accessibility and accurate voter rolls while continuing to maintain efficient and secure elections." As introduced, the bill would have created a "voter roll cleanup task force" with a much narrower mission, to "study and provide recommendations on best practices to assure the voters of New Mexico of the validity and reliability of New Mexico voter rolls." In both forms, the task force was scheduled to report its recommendations to the legislature by December 31, 2021, and cease to exist.

As amended, the task force would be composed of:

  • Six legislators, three from each major party. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Four members of the public, two from each of the major parties, all of whom who have expertise in elections, campaigns and private sector organizational structure and operations and who reflect New Mexico's ethnic, cultural and geographic diversity. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill did not reference the political party of the public members.
  • Four county clerks, two from each of the major parties. This is a modified provision. As introduced, three clerks were to be appointed, without reference to their political parties.
  • The secretary of state or their appointee. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • The secretary of taxation and revenue, or a designee of the secretary who has oversight or knowledge of data collection and system operations within the taxation and revenue department. This is a modified provision. As introduced, the bill called for the inclusion of the director of the motor vehicle division of the taxation and revenue department, or a designee of the director who has oversight or knowledge of the motor vehicle division's databases and information technology operations.
  • Advisory members, including one representative each from the state registrar, the state assessor and the administrative office of the courts, and an appointee of the United States postal service in New Mexico if the postal service so chooses. This is a modified provision. As introduced, such people were full members of the committee.

  • Two people who would have been appointed under the bill as introduced would not be included in the current version are the secretary of information technology, or a designee of the secretary who has oversight or knowledge of databases, cybersecurity and information technology operations, and a representative of the census program at the state data center, appointed by the secretary of economic development.

    Reflecting change in the mission of the task force, the amended bill requires the task force to consider a correspondingly broader range of topics and policies than the original bill did.

Last Updated March 15, 2021

This bill, as introduced on December 8, 2021, would impose guidelines for redistricting state and federal legislative districts, requiring that legislative committees engaged in redistricting must:

  • Create districts as equal in population as possible. State districts may only have a deviation of a maximum of 5%.
  • Keep precincts in the same district, unless splitting the precinct is required by federal law.
  • Create plans that comply with the Voting Rights Act of 1965. In doing so, race may be considered but cannot be the predominant consideration, nor can race be a dominant consideration over race-neutral districting considerations.
  • Create single-member districts only.
  • Create districts that are contiguous, compact, preserve communities of interest, and respect political and geographic boundaries. Redistricting can also seek to preserve the core of existing districts and incumbency.

  • Use decennial census data.

    Last updated December 10, 2021.

This bill, as amended on February 17, 2021, would change the redistricting process timeline by requiring certain map adjustments to be made by 90 days after receipt of the census data, rather than by June 30th of the year the adjustments were required. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. In addition, the bill would require the base maps created for the purpose of redistricting to show, in addition to the other boundaries and features already required, Indian nation, tribe and pueblo boundaries. This is a new provision not in the previous version of the bill. The bill would also change the timing of municipal redistricting. Local governments subject to districting and whose members are not elected at the regular local election must create or redraw districts in the year the census data is received, and each local public body subject to districting whose governing body members are elected at the regular local election must create or redraw districts in the calendar year following the receipt of the census data. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Under existing law, all local bodies redistrict the calendar year after receiving the census data. Finally, the bill would adjust the criteria for local redistricting by adding specific population requirements. Local districts must be nearly equal in population as practical, but within five percent of the mean, and cannot result from splitting a precinct into two or more districts for any elected office unless necessary to comply with federal law or to preserve communities of interest. Existing law does not have the five percent of the mean requirement. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

Last updated February 24, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 1, 2021, would:

  • Limit opt-in voter registration for new registrants to people who provided proof of citizenship during the relevant in-person transaction. People who do not provide such proof but are already registered voters will have their registrations automatically updated if needed. Existing law authorizes all individuals qualified to vote to opt in to being simultaneously registered to vote when applying for (or renewing) a driver's license or state ID.
  • Provide a detailed process for electronic records of people who proved citizenship and appear to be eligible to vote to be sent from the DMV to the secretary of state. After determining whether or not the person is already registered, the secretary then sends the records of new registrants to the relevant county clerk. The clerk then sends notice to the person that they have been registered to vote, including a postage prepaid and pre-addressed return card by which the person may decline to be registered to vote, affiliate with a political party, and request a mail ballot for the next election.
  • Provide protections against criminal prosecution if ineligible people are registered through this method, even if they try to vote after being registered this way. To be prosecuted, the registered ineligible person would have had to knowingly and willfully taken voluntary action to register to vote with knowledge that the person is an unqualified voter or ineligible to register or knowingly and willfully voted with knowledge that the person is an unqualified voter or ineligible to vote.
  • Authorize the secretary of state to designate other agencies for opt-in voter registration if they collect sufficient information.
  • Require the secretary to issue an annual report detailing the numbers of new, updated and declined registrations through this program.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to redistricting, enacts the redistricting act, creates the citizen redistricting committee, directs the committee to develop district plans for approval by the legislature and governor, provides duties, establishes requirements for creating district plans and public participation in the process, declares an emergency.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on March 13, 2021, would create, as of June 2021, a citizen redistricting committee composed of seven embers, one appointed by the Speaker of the House, one appointed by the House minority leader, one appointed by the Senate President Pro Tempore, one appointed by the Senate minority leader, two people, not members of either of the two largest political parties in the state, appointed by the state ethics commission, and one member appointed by the state ethics commission who is a retired justice or judge. The previous version of the bill created this committee as of April 2021. The substantive responsibilities of the committee are substantially unchanged from the previous version of the bill, except where noted below, and would include the responsibilities to:

  • Adopt redistricting plans for the state congressional districts, state legislative districts, and other state offices required to be redistricted.
  • Hold at least 6 public meetings, with virtual participation options and at least one meeting on tribal lands, before publishing redistricting plans. The virtual participation and tribal land meeting requirements were added in the most recent amendment.
  • Base redistricting on:
    • creating population equality in districts,
    • maintaining existing precincts,
    • complying with the federal Voting Rights Act of 1965,
    • creating single-member districts only,
    • using traditional districting principles,
    • contiguity,
    • preserving communities of interest,
    • considering political and geographical boundaries,
    • preserving the core of existing districts.
  • Report its adopted district plans to the legislature by October 30, 2021.

  • Comprise members who are New Mexico voters, who are not New Mexico public officials, candidates, lobbyists, state political party office holders, relatives of legislators or the public education commission, or employee of the legislature or other office subject to redistricting, and who have not been any of the foregoing in the preceding two years.

    A previous version of this bill would have created a different redistricting committee composed of members of the legislature and would not have set forth criteria to consider in redistricting. Those provisions were previously amended out of the bill.

    The March 13, 2021 amendment is available at https://www.nmlegis.gov/Sessions/21%20Regular/bills/senate/SB0015JC1.pdf.

    The March 9, 2021 amendment is available at https://www.nmlegis.gov/Sessions/21%20Regular/bills/senate/SB0015FS1.pdf.

    Last updated September 10, 2021.
