This bill, as amended on March 11, 2021, would make substantial changes throughout the election code, many of which were made by the prior version. In short, the amended bill would require vote centers, change same day registration, change mail ballot application, completion, return, verification, cure, and counting, change certain aspects of voter registration, and make changes to campaign finance, recounts, and other aspects of election law not tracked here. Specifically, the amended bill would:

  • Change the rules relating to consolidation of polling places by:
    • Requiring, rather than allowing, the board of county commissioners to consolidate precincts into voter convenience centers. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • Requiring the board of supervisors expressly determine that the location of each voter convenience center will make voting convenient and accessible to voters of the county and will not result in delays for voters in the voting process. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have repealed an existing statutory provision that required the board of supervisors to make similar findings before choosing to consolidate polling places. Instead of repealing that section, the amended bill changes the requirement to make it applicable to the required vote centers.
    • Eliminating the requirement that the voter convenience center have ballots available for voters from all precincts authorized to vote there. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • Requiring clerks to send voters in mail ballot election precincts notice of their ability to vote in-person at any vote center in the county. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Change same day registration in key ways. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Expand same day registration by offering it at any alternate voting location (early voting), mobile alternate voting location (early voting), or Election Day voting location. In addition, the bill would allow same day registration at clerk's offices on the day before Election Day. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill. Existing law offers same day registration during early voting only at alternate voting locations only if the county clerk has assigned a registration officer to that location, and at clerk's offices only through the Saturday before Election Day.
    • Restrict the types of ID that can be used to register to vote or update a registration during the same day registration process. Under the bill, the voter must provide photo ID issued by a government, including a federally recognized Indian nation, tribe or pueblo, or an educational institution that shows the name of the voter, resembles the voter, and either contains an address that matches the registration address or is supported by a utility bill, bank statement, government check, paycheck, or other government document that contains an address matching the registration address and is dated within 90 days of the registration. This is a modified provision. The previous version listed a student ID as among the ID types that could verify an address when coupled with a listed photo ID type, and it did not require the address document to be issued within 90 days of its use. Existing law allows any photo ID plus any document that contains an address in the county.
    • Provide that a provisional ballot cast by a same day registrant because the voting location could not synchronize with the county voter database would count once the clerk determines the voter did not cast another ballot in the same election and if no challenge is successfully made. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • Change the start date and the codification location of a statutory requirement that the secretary of state and the DMV-equivalent develop a procedure to import the list of eligible but unregistered people with a driver's license or state ID into the voter registration electronic management system prior to an election to facilitate processing a new same day voter registration. The new start date for this process would be July 1, 2023. Existing law would require it to begin June 1, 2021, and would also require the approval of the voting system certification committee. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Change the rules for returning a mail ballot and drop boxes, by:
    • Expanding who may return a voter's completed ballot for them. Existing law only allows the voter's caregiver or immediate family member, defined as the voter's spouse, children, parents, and siblings, to return a voter's ballot. The bill would also allow a domestic partner, grandchildren, grandparents, or a person with whom the voter has a continuing personal relationship to return the voter's ballot.
    • Expanding an existing felony punishing the unlawful possession of a mail ballot to include establishing, designating, or operating a receptacle to receive voted ballots unless the person is the county clerk.
    • Expanding an existing felony punishing the unlawful possession of keys to include possessing ballot drop box keys without clerk authorization.
    • Clarifying that ballot drop boxes may be unsupervised provided the security provisions of existing law are followed.
    • Allowing the clerk to appoint messengers to collect ballots from drop boxes.
      These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.
  • Change the process for completing a mail ballot in several ways. The bill would:
    • Require the voter to include the last four digits of their Social Security number (SSN4) along with their signature on the affirmation. A similar provision applied to the November 2020 general election pursuant to a temporary law.
    • Change the ballot envelope so that it contains notice of third-party return restrictions, the voter's name is preprinted on the envelope, and the form no longer requires the voter to fill out their name, address, and year of birth.
    • Edit the language of the certificate to clarify the statement is being made under penalty of perjury and modify the attestation.
      These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.
  • Change mail ballot verification and create a cure process. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require the clerk to verify the ballot within one business day of receiving it.
    • Require the clerk to immediately send the voter notice if the ballot is missing a signature or the SSN4, or if the SSN4 does not match the voter's record.
    • Give the voter until end of the provisional ballot appeal process to cure the ballot. This deadline is after the county canvass report has been approved. In addition, the bill amends the provisional ballot law to make clear that the reason a ballot was provisional can be cured by the voter through the end of the appeal process.
    • Clarify that the clerk's verification of a ballot may be challenged by or before the absentee voter board.
    • Clarify that when a person who registered to vote by mail must include identification with their ballot, the clerk may open the inner ballot envelope to see if the information was included with the ballot, if the information is not otherwise provided. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.
  • Change the ballot counting timeline and process by:
    • Allowing verified mail ballots to be counted, not just processed, by 7 a.m. on Election Day. Existing law prohibits counting until after the close of polls.
    • Specifying that absentee ballots be counted on Election Day until 11 p.m., unless finished earlier, and that counting continue from 9 a.m. to 8:30 p.m. each succeeding day until finished. In addition, if the election board does not finish by 11 p.m. on election night, the clerk would be required to notify the county sheriff and/or the state police to arrange ballot security for the night. If the sheriff/state police are unavailable, the clerk or the chief deputy must stay to guard the ballots, and election observers are allowed to stay as well. (BRVC-other) This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill addressed the timing of the count but not the security guard procedure.
    • Requiring the county canvass to include a report of the final vote counts for all contests by mail ballots, in-person early votes, and Election Day in-person votes, and include separate reports on federal qualified electors and provisional ballots. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.
  • Change the processes relating to applying for a mail ballot in several ways. The bill would:
    • Change the deadline for applying to receive a ballot by mail from the Thursday immediately before the election to fourteen days before Election Day. In addition, the bill would clarify that replacement ballots are not subject to this new deadline.
    • Change the rules relating to UOCAVA voters so that the application is timely if it is received no later than seven days before the election, unless the UOCAVA voter fails to provide information allowing electronic delivery of the ballot. In that case, the deadline would be two weeks before election day. In addition, the UOCAVA voter may apply once and receive ballots for all subsequent elections through the conclusion of the election cycle.
    • Modify the notice a clerk must give a voter if the clerk rejects the voter's application for a mail ballot to include information about how the voter may address the reason for the rejection, and, if the reason is that the application is too late include a list of early and Election Day polling locations. (Absentee-other)
    • Allow the application for a mail ballot to request a voter's political party even if the election the ballot is for is not a partisan primary.
    • Provide that an application for a mail ballot must be made through the official Secretary of State website, or on the official paper form sent to the voter by the county clerk.
    • Clarify that the prohibition on accepting electronic applications for mail ballots from third parties applies to electronic transmission of paper forms.
    • Notify first time voters who registered to vote by mail but did not supply sufficient ID with their registration application, that when returning a mail ballot they must include the missing ID or waive the right to secrecy in that mail ballot.
    • Create a replacement ballot process for participants in the address confidentiality program that requires them to appear in person at the office of the county clerk and complete a certain affidavit.
      These provisions were all in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require the Secretary of State to send every voter a notice for each statewide election 50 days prior to the election. The notice would include the date and purpose of the election, a web address to request a mail ballot, a phone number to request a mail ballot application, early and Election Day in-person voting opportunities, and mail ballot return opportunities. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Change electronic voter registration process at the DMV-equivalent by:
    • Preventing transmission of a potential voter's registration information if it does not include the potential voter's full Social Security number. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • Requiring all signatures the DMV has for a particular person be transmitted with the registration information, not simply the one with the most current transaction. This is a new provision not in the previous version of the bill.
    • Changing the back-end process for automatically updating a voter's registration address during a DMV transaction. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Change maintenance of the voter registration list by:
    • Requiring the secretary of state to develop a general, uniform, nondiscriminatory program for county clerks to investigate and reconcile information received from the secretary, and to identify voters who may be eligible for cancelation from the statewide voter registration list, including safeguards to ensure eligible voters are not removed in error. In particular, the secretary would have to provide a procedure to cancel registrations for voters who are confirmed to have voted in another state or to have died as reflected on the Social Security master death index file, and to identify voters who, by getting a driver's license or state ID in another state, appear to have moved to that state. These apparent out-of-state movers would be sent the ordinary address confirmation mailings. This is a new provision not in the previous version of the bill.
    • Requiring county clerks to cancel the registrations of people who voted in another state or who obtained a driver's license or state ID in another state. This is a new provision not in the previous version of the bill.
    • Requiring the county clerks to process registrations and cancellations received after the close of registration but not as part of same day registration by the first business day after the county approves the canvass instead of 35 days after the election. In addition, clerks would be allowed to process such records starting the Monday after the election. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Clarify that the requirement for a Social Security number to complete a voter's registration is a requirement for a full Social Security number, and that a voter must vote a provisional ballot if they have not provided a full Social Security number. These edits to existing law do not appear substantive. In addition, the bill would clarify that a voter who cast a provisional ballot for failure to provide their full Social Security number would have until the end of the period of counting provisional ballots, including any appeals, to provide it. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require the secretary of state to issue and/or approve all forms required by the election code. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require the secretary of state to maintain an election security program within the bureau of elections and specifies the requirements of the program. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Redefine an "election-related organization" to exclude organizations involved in election monitoring or voter turnout who did not register with the Secretary of State at least 90 days before a regular statewide election or at least 63 days before a special election or an election to fill a vacancy in the U.S House. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

Make changes to campaign finance, recount, and other areas of election law not tracked here.

 

Provisions from prior versions have been amended out of this bill. Specifically, this bill would no longer:

  • Change the voter registration form so it no longer requests the voter's gender. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • End same day registration on Election Day. This provision was in the original bill version only.
  • Repeal rules applying to third-party registration drives. This provision was in the original bill version only.

 

Last Updated May 10, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 1, 2021, would create a redistricting process for state representatives, state senators, state educational commission members, and congressional representatives that uses an independent commission to draw the maps based on set criteria and substantial public participation, and requires the legislature to adopt one of the proposed maps without amendment. In addition, it would enable any public participant to appeal one of the commission's proposed maps to the state supreme court according to a streamlined process. When deciding the appeal, the court could affirm the map or reject and vacate it, but the court could not amend it. Under existing law, the legislature draws and enacts maps as ordinary legislation, which the governor may veto. In the 2010 redistricting cycle, after the governor vetoed the legislature's adopted plans, a trial court drew maps that were rejected by the state Supreme Court. Following the state Supreme Court's instructions, the trial court drew new maps which were upheld.

The commission created by this bill must hold at least six public meetings either virtually or in various regions of the state before proposing the district plans. Thereafter the commission must propose 3 to 5 maps for each set of offices, outlining why the maps meet the required criteria, and then hold no fewer than six public rule hearings, either virtually or in various regions of the state, for the purpose of adopting district plans. As part of adopting the district plans, the commission must provide written evaluations of each that address how each satisfies the required criteria, the ability of racial and language minorities to elect candidates of their choice, a measure of partisan fairness and the preservation of communities of interest, and indicate which district plan in each set best meets the all the requirements. After the commission adopts the plans, a public participant may appeal one or more of them to the state supreme court, which will either affirm or reject the plan. If the court rejects it, the commission must amend it.

Once the plans are adopted by the commission, they are sent to the Legislature for consideration. For each office the legislature may any of the plans proposed to it, but if it cannot choose a plan, the legislature must adopt the plan the commission has designated as best meeting all of the requirements. The legislature may not amend any of the plans. The bill acknowledges that the governor may veto whatever the legislature adopts, but it does not specify a separate post-veto process.

In addition to the public participation requirements, when drawing the maps, the newly created commission:

  • Must create district plans composed of single-member districts. Existing law provides for single-member districts.
  • Must create district plans composed of contiguous territory, provided that districts that meet only at the points of adjoining corners are not contiguous. Existing law requires districts to be contiguous, but does not define the term.
  • Must comply with all applicable federal laws.
  • Must ensure that congressional districts are as equal in population as practicable.
  • Must create state office districts that are as close to equal in population as possible. Any deviation must not exceed plus or minus five percent and must be based on:
    • compliance with applicable federal law,
    • consideration of tribal government,
    • the avoidance of diluting the representation of communities of interest,
    • the avoidance of fragmenting governmental subdivisions, or
    • the preservation of the core of existing districts, provided that the district plan meets all other requirements provided by this section.
  • May use, rely upon or reference precincts and units of population that are smaller than precincts, and may rely upon or reference the most recent federal decennial census data provided by the United States census bureau and other reliable sources of demographic data. Existing law does not have a comparable provision.

  • Must not:

    • propose or adopt district plans to favor a political party or incumbent.
    • use, rely upon or reference partisan data, such as voting history or party registration data, except that voting history in elections may be considered to comply with applicable federal law.
    • create district plans to intentionally dilute the representation of communities of interest.
    • create district plans to intentionally preserve the cores of existing districts unless the district plan meets all other requirements.

    When a district plan satisfies all of these requirements, the commission shall adopt those district plans that are most compact, as determined by a measure of length-width compactness or perimeter compactness.

    Last updated February 3, 2021.

The rules committee amended and passed this bill on March 9, 2021, without substantively changing its core provisions. As introduced on February 1, 2021, this bill would create a permanent absentee voter list available to all voters. Once on the list, a voter could be removed only if:

  • the voter fails to return a mailed ballot in two consecutive elections, including at least one general election,
  • the county clerk has sent a mailed ballot or other piece of election mail to the voter's mailing address that was subsequently returned as undeliverable,
  • the voter's certificate of registration is lawfully canceled,
  • the voter updates the certificate of registration indicating an address that is outside of the county for which the voter is listed on the permanent absentee list, or

  • the voter submits a written request to the county clerk requesting to be removed from the permanent absentee list.

Last Updated March 10, 2021

As enacted on April 5, 2021, this bill creates special rules for the 2021 election to fill U.S. Representative Deb Haaland's seat after her confirmation as President Biden's Secretary of the Interior. The rules created by this law self-repeal on December 31, 2021. For this election, the bill:

  • Requires election day polling places open in 2019 or thereafter to operate as county-wide vote centers. This provision was modified from a previous version of the bill, which allowed counties to opt out of operating voter centers.
  • Prohibits the closure or consolidation of a polling place located on Indian nation, tribal or pueblo land, or the modification of voting days or times, without the written agreement of the Indian nation, tribe or pueblo. If, as a result of public health concerns, voters registered within the Indian nation, tribe or pueblo are unable to leave the Indian nation, tribe or pueblo during voting, there shall be at least one polling location within the Indian nation, tribe or pueblo. Similar rules were used for elections in 2020.
  • Requires the Secretary of State to send election information to certain voters fifty days before the election, which must include notice of the date of the election, a website where a voter may request a mailed ballot, a phone number where a voter may request a paper mailed ballot application, and in-person voting information.
  • Requires each mailed ballot sent to a voter in the election to contain a notice regarding return options, and guidance that a ballot returned by mail should be sent no later than seven days before the election.
  • Moves the general deadline to apply for a ballot by mail from five days before the election to 14 days before the election. If an untimely request is received, the clerk must send the voter notice of the rejection with information about early and Election Day in-person voting options.
  • Requires clerks to send notice about a requested ballot to the voter's registration address, when the voter requests that their ballot be mailed to another address.
  • Requires voters to provide the last four digits of their Social Security number on the return envelope of a mail ballot, under the privacy flap. Existing law requires voters to provide a Social Security number for voter registration, but does not have a general requirement to provide the number on mail ballots.
  • Requires clerks to reject a ballot that is missing either the voter's signature or their Social Security number, and notify the voter within one day of the rejection. The voter has until the day before the election to cure, in addition to any post-election process. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Current regulations, issued in part because of special, 2020-only election law, already provide this cure process. Notably, the bill amends this section with language that requires that, when the clerk rejects an absentee ballot application, the clerk must send notice to both the mailing address in the registration record, and if different, to the address the voter requested the ballot be sent to.
  • Requires counties to have a law enforcement officer guard the room where ballots are stored overnight if the absentee ballot canvass is not completed by 11 p.m. on election night.
  • Permits challengers to observe clerks' determinations concerning whether to accept or reject a ballot, and take notes. Challenges may not be made to the clerk directly, but must be made before the absent voter board as required under existing law.
  • Allows clerks to process registrations, updates, and cancellations that must be handled after the election pursuant to existing law beginning on the first Monday following the election, and requires that such processing must begin the first business day following approval of the report of the county canvass.
  • Requires the Secretary of State to procure and distribute sufficient PPE for all voting locations.

  • Preserves rules applicable to UOCAVA voters, other than special deadlines expressly provided in the bill.

Last Updated May 13, 2021

This bill, as enacted on May 25, 2021, would make changes to public voter information available regarding voters with confidential or fictitious addresses. Specifically, this bill would prohibit disclosure of such a person's phone number or email address, in addition to their actual or fictitious address which are already protected under current law. The bill would also extend the obligation to keep this information confidential to the Secretary of State and city clerks. Existing law only imposes confidentiality obligations on county clerks.

This bill contains other provisions regarding fictitious address confidentiality not relevant to voting rights.

Last Updated June 7, 2021

These are new provisions that were not in the previous version of the bill.

This bill, as enacted on June 2, 2021, creates universal mail ballot voting, slightly shortens the period for mail ballot return, requires access to drop boxes, and slightly shortens the period for mail ballot cure and specifies ballot verification and cure procedures, among other changes.

 

Specifically, the bill:

  • Creates a universal mail ballot voting system, with mail ballots automatically sent to all eligible voters for each election. Voters may opt out of receiving a mail ballot by submitting written notice to the appropriate clerk. Under prior law, any eligible voter could request a mail ballot, and election officials were permitted to send all voters mail ballots (without having received a request) in certain elections only. 
  • Slightly shortens the period for mail ballot receipt, requires access to drop boxes, and creates a felony offense for unauthorized operation of a drop box. The bill:
    • Moves the receipt deadline earlier for mail ballots postmarked by Election Day, to four days after Election Day. If a ballot postmark cannot be determined, the ballot is timely if received by the third day after the election. Under prior law, the receipt deadline was seven days after. 
    • Requires counties to establish a drop box at every polling place in the county, and authorizes operation of additional drop boxes. Prior law was silent as to drop boxes.
    • Creates a new class E felony offense for unauthorized operation of a drop box.
  • Slightly shortens the period for curing a mail ballot, specifies cure procedures, and creates new signature verification training requirements. The bill:
    • Moves the deadline for curing a mail ballot defect earlier by one day, to six days after Election Day. Under prior law, the deadline was 5 p.m. on the seventh day after Election Day. 
    • Allow voters to cure signature mismatches by answering questions about their personal data, including date of birth, or by providing proof of identification, for signature mismatches at the polling place and on mailed ballots. Prior law required officials to "ask the voter to confirm whether the signature used for the absent ballot belongs to the voter," but did not specify whether or how voters should confirm their identity. 
    • Permits use of electronic signature matching technologies, in addition to manual verification, and requires accuracy testing. 
    • Requires annual training on forensic signature verification, approved by the secretary of state, for officials who conduct signature matching.
  • Moves the deadline for online voter registration later, to the day of the election or primary. Under prior law, the online registration deadline was the Thursday preceding the election.
  • Requires a minimum number of polling places (which may include vote centers) for early voting and Election Day voting, based on county population. 
  • Moves the deadline later for Indian tribes to request polling locations within a reservation or colony, and expressly permits request of a drop box, instead of or in addition to a polling place.
  • Requires the secretary of state to access data from the Department of Vital Statistics at least once a month, to 'match' information with the voter list. Specific matching criteria are not detailed.
  • Permits certain election officials to use an alternate address on their driver's license.
  • Makes numerous conforming changes related to the new universal mail ballot system and other new provisions.

 

The bill also contains additional provisions concerning topics that are not tracked by Voting Rights Lab. 

 

Last Updated October 23, 2024

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to elections, authorizes a funeral director to notify the county clerk of the death of a person, requires a county clerk to cancel the preregistration or registration to vote of a person when notified by a funeral director that the person has died, provides other matters properly relating thereto.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 17, 2021, would expand the bases for canceling a voter's registration or preregistration due to voter death to include circumstances where a funeral director has provided the county clerk with notice of the death of a residence. Upon the receipt of such a notice, on a form prescribed by the Secretary of State and containing the funeral director's signature and a notarization or two witness signatures, the county clerk must cancel the voter's registration or preregistration. Under existing law, a county clerk can only cancel a voter's registration or preregistration for voter death upon the county clerk's personal knowledge or receipt of an authenticated death certificate.

This bill, as enacted on June 11, 2021:

  • Requires the Secretary of State to develop a pilot program to carry out a risk-limiting audit for the 2022 general election results. The bill also extends the effective date for an existing provision that requires counties to perform a risk-limiting audit of elections prior to certification, from January 1, 2022, to January 1, 2024. These are new provisions that were not in the previous version of the bill.

This bill, as enacted on June 11, 2021:

  • Expands automatic voter registration agencies from the only existing voter registration agency (the DMV) to include:
    • the Department of Health and Human Services,
    • any agency that accepts applications for Medicaid,
    • the state Health Insurance Exchange, and
    • any other state or tribal agency designated by the governor.
  • Requires automatic registration of customers at automatic voter registration agencies when the customer, in the course of their transaction, provides information demonstrating they are qualified to vote, including:
    • proof of identity,
    • proof of citizenship,
    • residence, and
    • date of birth.
  • Prohibits county clerks from rejecting automatic voter registrations or updates solely on the basis that the registration does not contain the person's electronic signature. In such cases, the clerk must obtain a signature by one of the following:
    • return of mailed notice,
    • requesting the on-file signature from the DMV or other method approved by the Secretary of State, or
    • requesting a signature from the voter the first time they vote in person and comparing that signature to an approved form of voter ID.
  • Requires county clerks to send a notice (by mail or email) to a person whose information is transmitted by an automatic voter registration agency with information regarding the person's party affiliation, affirmation, and an opportunity to opt out of registration. This notice replaces the opportunity to decline registration at a voter registration agency that is the process in existing law. A voter's failure to return the notice is not a declination to register and a voter will be registered if they do not affirmatively opt out.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to legislative affairs, creates the Reapportionment and Redistricting Advisory Commission, prescribes the membership of the Commission, sets forth the duties of the Commission, provides other matters properly relating thereto.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on May 29, 2021, would create the Reapportionment and Redistricting Advisory Commission, which would:

  • Comprise one member appointed by the Speaker of the Assembly, one member appointed by the Senate majority leader, one member appointed by the Assembly minority leader, one member appointed by the Senate minority leader, and three members appointed by the foregoing members. Membership is restricted to people who have not been registered lobbyists, candidates, elected officials, party officials, political consultants, state employees, or relatives of any of of those categories in the preceding four years.
  • Develop a reapportionment plan that:
    • Complies with federal and state law.
    • Has districts with approximately equal populations.
    • Creates contiguous districts.
    • Do not dilute racial or language minority participation.
    • Do not unduly advantage or disadvantage a political party.
    • Reflect political subdivisions.
    • Do not divide communities of interest.
    • Are reasonable compact.
    • Are politically competitive.
  • Plans are approved on the vote of at least 5 members, which must include the vote of at least one member of the largest political party, one member of the next-largest political party, and one member who is not a registered member of either of the two largest political parties.

  • The plan must be submitted to the legislature within 180 days after each decennial census.

BILLSUMMARY: Proposes to amend the Nevada Constitution to remove the constitutional provisions governing the Legislature's authority to apportion Senators and members of the Assembly among counties or legislative districts of the State and create an Independent Redistricting Commission vested with the power to apportion Senators and members of the Assembly in the Legislature and members of the United States House of Representatives among districts established by the Commission.
VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as introduced on March 17, 2021, proposes a constitutional amendment establishing an independent redistricting commission:

  • Criteria to be considered, in priority order, would be:
    • Contiguity
    • Not being drawn with the intent or result of denying or abridging the equal of racial or language minorities to participate in the political process or elect representatives of their choice
    • Not unduly advantaging or disadvantaging any political party, when considered on a statewide basis
    • Protecting the integrity of communities of interest, defined to include, without limitation, racial, ethnic, social, cultural, geographic, or historical identities, but not including communities based on political affiliation.
    • Compactness
    • Competitiveness to the extent practicable without impairing compliance with other goals.
  • The commission would have final approval over maps. Under existing law, the legislature draws and approves maps.
  • Commission membership would be chosen by the party leaders in both chambers of the legislature, with their selections choosing another three nonpartisan members.

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2021, would create rudimentary ballot tracking and would require election officials to give voters notice of absentee ballot defects and an opportunity to cure them. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires election officials to give notice online or in writing that they have received a cast absentee ballot, and whether or not they have accepted it. Existing law does not offer this tracking service.

  • Requires election officials, if they reject a ballot, to provide the voter with written documentation or online confirmation that such ballot was not accepted. The notice must provide an explanation detailing the reason why the absentee ballot was not accepted and how the ballot may be corrected. Existing law, enacted in 2020, offers a more comprehensive cure process. As this bill amends a different section of election law, if enacted, both cure provisions would exist, and it is unclear how they would interact. If election officials apply the comparatively vague language of this bill to provide less notice and opportunity to cure than required under existing provisions, the bill could potentially decrease existing voter protections. If the bill would merely reinforce the specific existing requirements that election officials must provide notice and an opportunity to cure, it would make no substantive changes.

Last Updated January 12, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Amends the municipal home rule law, in relation to the division of a county into districts for the apportionment of members of its local legislative body.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on October 27, 2021, creates new rules for the redistricting of counties outside of counties wholly within a city (i.e., outside of New York City) and municipalities. Specifically, for county and municipal redistricting, the bill requires the relevant legislature to:

  • Draw single member districts with as equal population as practicable, and multi-member districts with population proportionate to their numbers in the relevant legislature.

  • Draw all districts so that they comply with federal and state constitutional requirements, and:

    • Do not have the intent or result of denying or abridging the equal opportunity of racial or language minority groups to participate in the political process or to diminish their ability to elect representatives of their choice.
    • Consist of contiguous territory.
    • Are as compact in form as practicable.
    • Do not have the purpose of discouraging competition or favoring or disfavoring incumbents or other particular candidates or political parties. The maintenance of cores of existing districts, of pre-existing political subdivisions including cities, villages, and towns, and of communities of interest shall also be considered. To the extent practicable, no villages, cities or towns except those having more than forty percent of a full ratio for each district shall be divided.
    • Promote the orderly and efficient administration of elections. The relevant legislature must consider these criteria in the priority order listed.

    All of these provisions were in the prior version of the bill. However, one criterion in the previous version of the bill was amended out of this version. It would have required the relevant legislature to draw distracts that to the extent practicable, "unite communities defined by actual shared interests, taking account of geographic, social, economic, and other factors that indicate commonality of interest."

    Last updated December 30, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2021, would mail all registered voters a ballot for each election in which they are qualified to vote, by amending the absentee ballot section of the election code. As a result, the bill would make most elections mail ballot elections, although certain specialty elections, like school board elections, would not be affected.

In addition, the bill would restrict who a voter could choose to return their completed, sealed ballot by forbidding people from returning more than one ballot other than their own. Thus a voter could choose anyone to return their ballot, provided that person had not returned anyone else's. Existing law does not restrict a voter's choices in any way.

Note: the New York Constitution requires a voter who wishes to vote by mail to have an excuse to be absent from the polls. In November, 2021, voters may ratify a proposed amendment to eliminate the excuse requirement.

Upon receipt of the sworn statement, the board of elections would protect the confidentiality of the voter's record for four years, although the victim could renew the protection. This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2021, would change the absentee ballot processing and canvassing timeline, and make a conforming change to the in-person voting process. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require each local board of elections to establish a process to canvass absentee ballots as they are received, rather than after Election Day as current law requires.
  • Require the canvassers, after rejecting a ballot, to notify voters that they must cure their ballot to have it counted or that it has been rejected and cannot be cured. If the ballot envelope cannot be cured and the voter learns of the issue before Election Day, the voter has the opportunity to get another mail ballot or vote in person. Because ballots may be processed before Election Day, but boards of election can choose to wait until after Election Day, the bill would increase voters' opportunity to successfully cast a ballot. Nonetheless, because the existing cure deadline is tied to when a voter is given notice, rather than to Election Day, earlier notice does not increase the time a voter has to cure the mail ballot with a defect. The earlier notice simply facilitates voting a new ballot if the first one is not successfully cured.

  • Require voters who appear to vote in person but who are marked on the voter list as having cast a mail ballot to vote an affidavit (provisional) ballot.

This bill, as amended on May 6, 2022, would increase the number of eligible votes counted in every election. Specifically, the bill would require county boards of election to count all the votes on provisional ballots (called affidavit ballots in NY) that a person who voted at the wrong polling place was eligible to cast, provided that the voter was in the correct county and Assembly district. Existing law requires counties to reject these ballots entirely, although counties are required to count the ballots of voters who cast their ballots in the correct polling place for their election district, even if they voted in the wrong district.

Previous versions of this bill had achieved this result by eliminating the ability to challenge a ballot on the basis that the voter appeared at the wrong polling place, instead allowing the challenge only if the voter did not vote in the correct county. However the underlying law changed, and no longer granted third parties the ability to challenge an affidavit ballot on that basis. On January 11, 2022 this bill was amended to reflect that change and ceased addressing challenge grounds.

BILLSUMMARY: Establishes an apportionment commission to create apportionment plans for congressional and state legislative districts based on decennial federal census, which shall be considered by and voted upon by the state legislature, eliminates the legislative task force on demographic research and reapportionment.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2021, would create an 11 member independent redistricting commission to create a redistricting plan for federal and state offices using certain criteria. The commission would then submit the plan to the legislature, which would be required to vote on implementing legislation without amendment. If the legislature rejected the bill, or the governor vetoed it, the commission would be required to submit another plan, and the approval process would repeat. If the second plan was rejected, the legislature could amend the implementing legislation until it passed, although the same map-drawing criteria would apply.

The New York Constitution has several provisions relating to redistricting that conflict with provisions in this bill, and others which are consistent with it but differ in specificity. As a result, if this bill were enacted, to the extent the provisions conflicted with the state constitution, the provisions would be void. To the extent the state constitution was consistent with the bill but more highly specified, the constitution-specified details would control. To the extent the bill was more specified and could be viewed as implementing the constitutional requirement, the provision could take effect. Although New York voters will have the opportunity to adopt an amendment to the state constitution in November 2021 that would alter the constitution's redistricting provisions, the amendment would not resolve this issue. The same conflicts and differences in specificity would remain.

For example, the constitution requires a 10 member independent redistricting commission, not an 11 member one as the bill creates. Although 8 of the members of both commissions would be appointed the same way, the constitution requires a process for its remaining two that is different than the bill's process for the bill's remaining three. The amendment on the ballot would not solve this conflict. Similarly, the constitution requires the commission to have co-chairs, and the bill provides for a single chair. The number of members required for a quorum and for certain votes to be effective also differ between the bill and the constitution. In addition, while the basic mechanics of the legislature's consideration and adoption of the plan are the same, details relating to deadlines and other matters conflict.

The commission created by the bill would be required to obey the following rules when creating a plan:

  • Congressional districts must be as nearly equal in population as is practicable.
  • Both legislative and congressional districts must be contiguous, including that no district consist of parts entirely separated by the territory of another district of the same body.
  • A populated census block could not be divided by a district boundary, unless the populated part of such block is within a single district.
  • Districts cannot be intended to or result in a denial or abridgement of minority voting rights, including the opportunity of minority voters to participate in the political process, and to elect the candidates of their choice.
  • Districts cannot be drawn with an intent to favor or oppose any political party, any incumbent federal or state legislator, or any previous or presumed candidate for office.

  • So long as the other criteria are met, these additional criteria must be considered, in this order of priority:

    • The most and least populous senate districts must be within one percent of the mean population of all senate districts, and the most and least populous assembly districts must be within one percent of the mean population of all assembly districts. The commission would be prohibited from advantaging any region of the state by creating multiple districts in a region that differ from the mean population by more than one percent.
    • Counties must not be divided in the formation of districts, except to create districts wholly within a county. Where division of counties is unavoidable, more populous counties shall be divided in preference to the division of less populous counties.
    • County subdivisions must not be divided in the formation of districts, except to create districts wholly within a county subdivision. County subdivisions with larger populations shall be divided in preference to the division of those with smaller populations.
    • Incorporated villages must not be divided in the formation of districts.
    • Districts must be as compact in form as possible.
    • Districts must unite communities defined by actual shared interests, taking account of geographic, social, economic, and other factors that indicate commonality of interest, and
    • Districts must be formed so as to promote the orderly and efficient administration of elections.

    The state constitution requires its redistricting commission to consider, subject to the requirements of the federal constitution and statutes and in compliance with state constitutional requirements, the following principles when creating state senate, assembly, and congressional districts:

  • When drawing district lines, the commission must consider whether such lines would result in the denial or abridgement of racial or language minority voting rights, and districts must not be drawn to have the purpose of, nor result in, the denial or abridgement of such rights. Districts must be drawn so that, based on the totality of the circumstances, racial or minority language groups do not have less opportunity to participate in the political process than other members of the electorate and to elect representatives of their choice. This provision differs from the bill by requiring the consideration of language groups, and is generally more detailed and specific.
  • To the extent practicable, districts must contain as nearly as may be an equal number of inhabitants. For each district that deviates from this requirement, the commission shall provide a specific public explanation as to why such deviation exists. The bill would provide more restrictive population requirements, but perhaps could be viewed as implementing this provision. The bill does not specifically mandate deviations to be publicly explained.
  • Each district must consist of contiguous territory. The bill would provide a specific approach to "contiguous" that could be viewed as implementing this provision.
  • Each district must be as compact in form as practicable. The bill would de-prioritize compactness, which may or may not be viewed as implementing this provision if it were to become law.
  • Districts must not be drawn to discourage competition or for the purpose of favoring or disfavoring incumbents or other particular candidates or political parties. Within that constraint, the commission must consider maintaining the cores of existing districts, of pre-existing political subdivisions, including counties, cities, and towns, and of communities of interest. The bill has a somewhat different provision regarding district competitiveness, does not address cores of existing districts, and has highly specified provisions relating to the treatment of counties, cities, towns and communities of interest.
  • In drawing senate districts, towns or blocks which, from their location may be included in either of two districts, must be placed most equalize the population within the districts. The bill does not have an equivalent provision, but does specify a measure of population parity.

  • The existing requirements that senate districts not divide counties or towns, as well as the 'block-on-border' and 'town-on-border' rules, remain in effect. The bill does not have specifically equivalent language, but does have detailed specifications about counties, towns, and census blocks.

    Both the bill and the state constitution require their redistricting commissions to hold several hearings, but they require different hearing locations. The bill would require hearings in:

  • The cities of Albany, Buffalo, Syracuse, Rochester, Glen Cove, and White Plains, and
  • The counties of Bronx, Kings, New York, Queens and Richmond. (Each of those counties contains a borough of New York City.) The constitution would require hearings in:
  • The cities of Albany, Buffalo, Syracuse, Rochester, and White Plains, and

  • The counties of Bronx, Kings, New York, Queens, Richmond, Nassau, and Suffolk. (These counties would comprise New York City and the rest of Long Island.)

    Note: The above discussion is not an exhaustive list of the differences between the constitution and the bill, nor does it address the differences between the bill and the potential amendment to the relevant parts of the constitution on the ballot in November.

    Last updated August 17, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Proposes a constitutional amendment, relates to the number of state senators and inclusion of incarcerated persons in the federal census for population determination for redistricting purposes and to the functioning of the independent redistricting commission in the determination of district lines for congressional and state legislative offices.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2021, would amend New York's constitution to change redistricting procedures and cap the number of state senators at the existing 63. New York's redistricting process begins with an independent commission substantially appointed by the Legislature, and the commission submits maps and enabling legislation to the Legislature for its approval. The proposed constitutional amendment would change the existing process by:

  • Changing the timeline for the commission to submit plans to the legislature to reflect New York's change to state primaries in June, rather than in September.
  • Ensuring that total population is the basis by ensuring that non-citizens and Natives are counted.
  • Counting incarcerated people in the community of their last residence, rather than their place of incarceration.
  • Changing the rules relating approving plans proposed by the commission. New York's constitution currently requires different vote thresholds if one party controls both houses of the legislature, versus if different parties control each house. The amendment would eliminate all voting distinctions based on party control, making it easier for a single party to control redistricting.
  • Providing that if the commission fails to vote on a plan by the deadline, it must give the legislature all plans in its possession, both completed and in draft form, and the data upon which such plans are based.

If this bill is passed, the next step in the constitutional amendment process is for voters to approve it.

Last updated January 13, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to mandatory training curriculum for election commissioners and key staff of boards of elections and to model poll worker training programs, requires the State Board of Elections to develop and provide to each county materials for a model poll worker training program which the counties may use to train individuals to serve as poll workers in state and county elections.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 1, 2021, would require the state board of elections to develop a mandatory curriculum for election worker instructors, who, once certified, could then teach election workers. The statewide, standardized program would ensure the election workers learned and could teach:

  • The ability to serve a diverse electorate with complete confidence and respect,
  • Professionalizing the delivery of all election day services,
  • Providing assistance to voters with disabilities and those with limited English language proficiency, ensuring the dignity and privacy of such individuals, and to individuals who are members of racial or ethnic minorities, complete familiarity and comfort with all voting systems in use in poll sites, including ballot marking devices or other systems/services available to voters with disabilities, and

  • The ability to recognize and resolve a variety of issues which may arise in poll sites.

    The bill would further provide that the state board's trainers and all certified poll worker instructors utilize industry-proven training techniques aimed at adult learners including role-based training and hands-on training opportunities using official election day forms and poll site voting systems, and may further include a web-based component and companion video.

    Last updated March 22, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on February 1, 2021, would create a strict photo ID requirement to vote in person or vote by mail, and a process by which people without ID could obtain one for free. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require a voter to show a current and valid government issued photo ID to vote in person.
  • Require a voter to enclose a copy of a current and valid government issued photo ID to apply for an absentee ballot.
  • Define "current and valid government issued photo ID" to include current and valid government issued photo identification shall include:
    • a New York state driver's license or non-driver ID,
    • a United States Passport,
    • an identification card issued by a United States educational institution,
    • a United States military identification card,
    • a government issued medical card or any identification card issued by the United States or the state of New York.

  • Create a process for people who lack ID to obtain one for free. To obtain a free ID, people who have sufficient documentation to receive a non-driver's ID would present that to the DMV along with an affidavit in which the voter attests that they lack a necessary ID to vote and that the election is at least seven days away. If the voter does not have the documentation to obtain a non-driver's ID but was born in New York, the bill would allow them to use the affidavit to get a free birth certificate. The birth certificate and affidavit would be sufficient to receive a free ID. Finally, the bill also provides that the DMV can issue the free ID if the voter presents the affidavit, "and a certificate of birth or any other form of documentation accepted by the [DMV] to prove the person's identity." Presumably that is how a voter born outside New York could obtain such an ID. The free IDs would be good for four years.

Last Updated August 16, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 1, 2021, would alter the part of the election code that allows an election to be continued past Election Day as a result of a disaster or emergency. This bill would change the standard for allowing an election to be continued from one based on turn out to one focused on the impossibility of voting due to the disaster or emergency. In addition, the bill would require publicity by press release to media, rather than publication of notice in newspapers, and would qualify the requirement to mail notice to voters by stating it must be "to the extent practicable." Finally, the bill would allow internal political party candidate nominating processes to be postponed up to a week because of a disaster or emergency.

Last updated February 4, 2021.

This bill would make major changes to New York's election code. Specifically the bill would:

  • Create same day registration both during early voting and on Election Day. Other than authorizing registration at voting locations, the bill does not prescribe any particular process.
  • Require the state board of elections or any local board of elections to submit proposed changes in administration, regulations, policies, practices and procedures affecting certain counties to the civil rights bureau of the attorney general's office for approval. The counties that must comply with the pre-approval process are those with at least ten percent African American, Hispanic, Asian and/or Native American registered voters who average fifty percent or less voter turnout over the past five general elections and/or have any minority voter complaints or government enforcement actions within the past ten years. This process shall not apply to any changes made pursuant to law.
  • Create a new section of code to provide for automatic voter registration at DMV, all of the existing voter registration agencies, and at certain points in time, such as when people register for classes at a state school or are restored to voting eligibility after having committed a felony. New York enacted a more limited automatic voter registration bill in December, 2020, that provided for automatic registration at DMV and several other agencies. This bill does not address that new law, and it is unclear how the duplicative provisions would interact if this bill were to become law. The provisions of the existing statute take effect January 1, 2023. This law would apply to elections in 2024 and beyond. In addition, this bill would require voter registration agencies to send updates of voter registration information to the state board of elections within 24 hours, and require state or county election officials to review the information, make any changes needed, and send notice to a voter whose registration has been updated.
  • Require boards of election to offer online registration by placing links on their websites to enable people to apply for voter registration or update their registrations, receive online assistance with applying to register to vote, enable online completion and submission of the mail voter registration application form, including assistance with providing a signature in electronic form, and enable online receipt of completed voter registration applications. Under existing law it is possible to electronically submit an application to register to vote on the DMV website, however, that process is not integrated into the statewide voter registration database as a fully electronic registration system is. In addition, a law enacted in 2019 requires the state board of elections to offer an online voter registration system that is integrated with the state voter registration list. That system has not yet launched.
  • Require local boards of election to offer by telephone services parallel to those the bill would require to be offered online.
  • Require the state board of elections to report annually on statewide voter registration changes and status, by method of registration and, to the extent possible, race of applicant.
  • Require the state board of elections to publish voter registration list maintenance standards that identify what criteria will be used to match information about an address change, conviction, ruling of incompetency or death to a voter's registration, that identify duplicate registrations, and that determine which data sources are most reliable for resolving conflicts among data sources. In addition, the bill would require the state board of elections to establish numerous specified privacy and security policies relating to 3rd party access to the voter registration list and protection of data privacy.
  • Create a new misdemeanor to punish knowingly misusing or knowingly allowing misuse of information in the voter registration database or the information supplied to maintain it.
  • Prohibit challenges to a voter's registration and require election officials to allow a registered person to vote, if the challenge is based on a vote caging document, unverified match list, or error or omission on the voter's registration form so long as the error or omission is not related to eligibility. The bill defines a vote caging document as a nonforwardable document a third party sends to a registered voter at the registration address that is returned to as undelivered or undeliverable, or any document sent to a registered voter instructing the voter to return the document, but the document is not so returned, unless at least two election cycles have passed since the date of the attempted delivery. The bill defines an unverified match list as a list produced by matching the information of registered voters or applicants for voter registration to a list of individuals who are ineligible to vote in the registrar's jurisdiction, by virtue of death, conviction, change of address, or otherwise, unless one of the pieces of information matched includes a signature, photograph, or unique identifying number ensuring that the information refers to the same individual.
  • Create a new misdemeanor to punish third parties who allow make challenges to a voter based on vote caging documents, unverified match lists, or errors and omissions on registration applications unrelated to eligibility.
  • Revise the voter registration form to allow the applicant to provide an email address and choose to receive election notices by email. The bill would also require the relevant board of elections to send election related notices to a voter's email address if the voter provided an email address for that purpose.
  • Require local boards of election to make accessible absentee ballot applications available to disabled voters and get state board of elections approval for their approach.
  • Create a new misdemeanor to punish people who knowingly and willfully deprive, defraud, or attempt to deprive or defraud any other person of their free and fair exercise of the right to vote by the communication of election-related information that the person knows is materially false, fictitious, or fraudulent. "Election-related information" means any oral or written communication regarding the time or place of an election, criminal penalties associated with voting, an individual's voter registration status or eligibility to vote, or the explicit endorsement of any person or organization of a candidate.
  • Expand the permanent absentee voter list to make UOCAVA voters eligible.
  • Impose reporting requirements on state and local boards of elections to ensure compliances with UOCAVA procedures.
  • Authorize state employees to work as election workers for up to six days without loss of pay or other leave.
  • Require the state board of elections to create a model poll worker training program.
  • Add a new provision in the absentee voting portion of the election code to require signature matching to verify retuned absentee ballots. The canvassing portion of the election code already requires such matching.
  • Require the state board of elections to expand and improve its voter information hotline so that it provides immediate assistance to questions and complaints from individuals voting or seeking to vote, or registering to vote or seeking to register to vote. The hotline must be usable by people with limited English skills or who are disabled. The existing hotline provides only information relating to a voter's existing registration.
  • Require the voter to mark a paper ballot, either directly or using a ballot marking device that produces a non-tabulated paper ballot that the voter can review, and require the paper ballots be tabulated by hand or by a tabulation machine.
  • Provide grants to fund required studies of ensuring fully accessible paper ballot marking.
  • Create a ballot audit process for elections that are contested and the winner received less than 80% of the vote.
  • Prohibit members of the state board of elections from taking an active role in any campaign unless it involves a member of their immediate family.

The New York constitution requires people to register at least 10 days before an election. The legislature has completed its part of the process to amend this requirement out of the constitution, however, to be effective voters must ratify the amendment in November, 2021.

The previous version of the bill would have raised the pay only for people working in New York City. Under existing law, no minimum is set outside of New York City, and in New York City the minimum is $130.
  • In New York City, a certain type of election worker called an election coordinator would receive at least $350/day. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have paid these workers $400/day. Under existing law, these workers earn at least $200/day.

  • People would be paid at least $50 to attend training sessions. This is a new provision. Under existing law, people must be paid at least $25 to attend a training session.

This bill, as amended on February 19, 2021, would make several changes relating to restoring voting eligibility after a felony conviction. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Restore voting eligibility to people convicted of felonies and sentenced to incarceration when their incarceration ends. Under existing law, people must complete parole as well. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • End the ability to challenge voters at the polls based on a felony conviction. This is a new provision not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require judges, prior to accepting a defendant's plea of guilty to a felony offense, to advise the defendant on the record that conviction will result in loss of the right to vote while the defendant is serving a felony sentence in a correctional facility and that the right to vote will be restored upon the defendant's release. This is a modified provision. In the previous version of the bill, a judge would have been required to give the same notice when sentencing a defendant after conviction.
  • Require inmates being released on parole be given notice that their voting rights are restored when released. This is a new provision not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require the presiding officer at a revocation hearing to give the alleged violator notice that if returned to prison for a violation they will lose voting eligibility during their incarceration. This is a new provision not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require the department of corrections or the chief administrator of a local corrections facility, as appropriate:
    • to give notice to returning citizens, verbally and in writing that their voting rights will be restored upon release
    • to provide returning citizens with a voter registration application and a declination form and offer assistance in filling out the appropriate form. If the potential voter chooses, the department shall transmit the completed application upon such person's release to the state board or local board where such person resides.
    • to provide them written information distributed by the board of elections on the importance and the mechanics of voting. This is a slightly modified provision. The previous version used different language to effectuate the same result.
  • Require the department of corrections to notify each person serving a period of community supervision of their right to vote and provide them with voter registration application and a declination form, offer such person assistance in filling out the appropriate form, and provide such person written information distributed by the board of elections on the importance and the mechanics of voting. If the person so chooses, the department shall transmit the completed application to the state board or local board where such person resides. This is a slightly modified provision. The previous version used different language to effectuate the same result.

  • Require the state board of elections to develop and implement a program to educate attorneys, judges, election officials, corrections officials, including parole and probation officers, and members of the public regarding these requirements. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

This bill, as introduced on February 4, 2021, would create automatic voter registration, same day voter registration, and online voter registration. Note, New York enacted an automatic voter registration law in December, 2020. However, the system this bill would enact differs in significant ways from the enacted system. Notably, this bill does not amend the existing automatic registration system. Instead, this bill creates new sections of code. As introduced, this bill would:

  • Create automatic voter registration at DMV, all existing voter registration agencies, and as parts of certain events, such as signing up for classes at a city or state university or regaining eligibility after a felony conviction. The DMV and voter registration agencies are already part of the enacted automatic voter registration system. Because this bill does not reference the enacted legislation it is unclear how locations covered by both this bill and enacted law would function.
  • Create same day registration on both Election Day and during early voting. Note, the bill does not specify any particular process to be followed.
  • Create online voter registration with these features:
    • an online application for voter registration
    • online assistance with applying to register to vote
    • online completion and submission by applicants of the mail voter registration application including assistance with providing a signature in electronic form
    • online receipt of completed voter registration applications.
  • Require boards of election to offer those same registration services by automated telephone process. (Voter registration-other)

  • Require voter registration applications to enable voters to provide an email address and receive future voting information by email.

    Note: New York's constitution requires people to register at least 10 days before an election. However, the legislature has completed its part of the process of amending this requirement out of the constitution. Voters will have the opportunity to ratify the change November 2, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on February 4, 2021, would require the state board of elections or a local board of elections to get written approval from the state attorney general before implementing any changes to voting qualification, prerequisites to voting, administration, regulations, policies, practices or procedures with respect to voting, if those changes would apply to a county with a population of at least ten percent of members of a protected class, a county which has been subject to a court order or government enforcement action based voting discrimination, or a county that was previously subject to pre-clearance under Section 5 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 and has not been granted an exemption from such pre-clearance requirements. This bill, as introduced on February 4, 2021, would allow voters to apply for absentee ballots by sending email or using an online portal if offered. In addition, it would eliminate the requirement that any voter who requested an absentee ballot by any method other than submitting a formal application with an original signature submit a completed paper application with their original signature with their completed ballot, or at least before the ballot is canvassed. The bill also changes the ballot return deadline for military, overseas and federal write-in ballots from postmarked the day before Election Day to Election Day, a change that makes the deadlines consistent with that for all other ballots.

Portable early voting sites need not be open for the full duration of the early voting period. Instead, they must be open for at least three consecutive days. In addition, the locations must be selected to provide the maximum number of voters in a county with adequate access to early voting, taking into consideration population density, travel time to the polling place, proximity to other early voting poll sites, public transportation routes, commuter traffic patterns and such other factors the board of elections deems appropriate. Locations must be chosen at least 14 days before the election.

This bill, as introduced on February 4, 2021, would create a new misdemeanor for the crime of "interfering in the election process by electronic means". The bill would define the crime as being committed by a person who, with intent to interfere with an election, places or causes to be placed, multiple calls by telephone or other electronic means, or sends or causes to be sent, multiple messages by text, email, fax, computer application, tablet application, telephone application or other electronic means, or any combination thereof, to obstruct, prevent or interfere with:

  • the reporting of poll results by any polling place
  • the receipt of poll results by a local or state board of elections
  • the ability of a political or party organization to place calls or send messages used for the purpose of encouraging people to vote, or

  • the ability of a political or party organization to place calls or send messages used for the purpose of arranging transportation for people to or from their polling place.

This bill, as introduced on February 4, 2021, would provide some special procedures for elections in 2021, primarily relating to absentee ballots, but also expanding early voting opportunities. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require boards of election to send all eligible voters to receive an absentee ballot application for all 2021 elections they are eligible to vote in, with a prepaid postage return envelope.
  • Allow all voters to vote absentee in any 2021 election using Covid-19 as an illness excuse.
  • Require boards of election to accept electronic and phoned absentee ballot applications without requiring the voter to complete a paper application later.
  • Require prepaid return postage to be provided for all absentee ballots.
  • Forbid boards of election from bringing absentee ballots into nursing homes and similar facilities, instead requiring them to provide the ballots by mail.
  • Require boards of election, village clerks, or other parties conducting village elections to develop a plan to allow registered voters to drop off completed absentee ballots at the office of the board of elections or village clerk before or on election day, without requiring the voter to wait in line with in-person voters.
  • Require boards of election to process ballots but not count absentee ballots before Election Day. Under existing law, pre-Election Day processing is allowed but not required.
  • Require the state board of elections to create a standard absentee ballot return envelope for use statewide. The state board created such an envelope for the 2020 general election.
  • Increase the number of required early voting sites. The bill would require one per 50,000 eligible voters or fraction thereof in every town or city and would require one for every 50,000 eligible voters in the county. Under existing law, counties are required to offer one per 50,000 registered voters up to a cap of 10, and are not required to site one in every town or city. In addition, the bill would require early voting sites to remain open until 9 p.m. on every day they are open.
  • Require local boards of election to send their voters an information package regarding absentee and in-person voting.
  • Require local boards of election to file reports with the state identifying their staffing plans and needs for the election and canvassing period.

  • Modify numerous procedures related to nominating candidates.

This bill, as introduced on February 5, 2021, would require funeral directors to file death certificates with the state department of health or the New York City department of health, which in turn will provide them to the state board of elections at least monthly.
