This bill, as introduced on February 9, 2021, would define ballot harvesting, place restrictions on third-party absentee ballot application assistance, and criminalize ballot harvesting or violating the restrictions. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Define ballot harvesting as:
    • the making or submission of an application for an absentee ballot on behalf of another voter, unless done in accordance with the bill's rules, and
    • the collection, distribution or submission to a board of elections, of voted or unvoted absentee ballots, unless done in accordance with the bill's rules.

    • the third party is a family member of the voter within three degrees of consanguinity, or

  • Allow a third party to collect, distribute or submit to a board of elections, a voted or unvoted absentee ballot, if the third party is:
    • a family member of the voter within three degrees of consanguinity,
    • a caregiver of the voter, if such voter has filed with the board of elections, a notarized statement executed by the voter, that the third party is in fact a caregiver of the voter, with permission to collect, distribute and/or submit such voter's absentee ballot, or
    • an election official employed by the board of elections exclusively engaged in and performing their official duties, or
    • a United States postal service employee exclusively engaged in and performing their official duties, or

This bill, as amended on May 28, 2022, would create a comprehensive legal regime to prevent discriminatory election laws, rules, and practices. Titled "The John R. Lewis Voting Rights Act" (NYVRA), the bill would create preclearance requirements to prevent discriminatory voting practices from being adopted, private rights of action to facilitate injunctive and other relief against discriminatory practices, and require boards of election to provide all key voting materials in minority languages.

The bill would create a preclearance regime by requiring "covered entities" to seek permission to implement a "covered policy." The bill would create two preclearance procedures that a covered entity could use: asking the Attorney General, or petitioning a court. When granting preclearance, regardless of the method, the decision-maker must decide that the covered policy will not diminish the ability of protected class members to participate in the political process and elect their preferred candidates. If a covered entity enacted or implemented a covered policy without seeking preclearance, or in defiance of a decision denying preclearance, the Attorney General or anyone else with standing could sue to enforce preclearance. Finally, the bill authorizes the Attorney General to issue necessary rules. Specifically, under the bill, a covered entity could seek preclearance by:

  • Asking the Civil Rights Bureau of the Attorney General (Bureau), and if the covered entity is a county or city board of elections, giving simultaneous notice to the State Board of Elections. A public comment process would follow.
    • The Bureau would publish the policy on its website and invite public comment. The bill specifies timelines for public comment depending on what type of policy is being reviewed, and provides that the Bureau's review would be ongoing during the public comment, but prevent the Bureau from deciding on preclearance until public comment ended.
    • The Bureau would preclear or reject the recommendation in writing, and, if it grants preclearance, could do it temporarily, denying preclearance thereafter, so long as the decision to deny preclearance comes within 60 days of the policy's submission. If the Bureau failed to decide within the specified timelines, preclearance would be granted, although the Bureau could get one 20 day extension for good cause. In addition, the bill authorizes the Bureau to issue rules for an expedited process for a covered policy in certain emergencies.
    • A covered entity could appeal of a denial of preclearance in the Supreme Court of New York for Albany County or New York County on an expedited basis. Further appeals would follow ordinary practice, except for expedited timing.
  • Asking a designated court, but also giving a copy to the Bureau. New York has four judicial departments statewide, and the bill designates a particular county's supreme court for covered entities in each department. The covered entity would submit the covered policy to the appropriate court, and give a copy to the Bureau. The court would grant or deny preclearance within 60 days. If the court does not rule within 60 days, the covered policy would be denied. Appeals would be done in the normal way but would be given calendar preference and expedited pretrial and trial proceedings.
  • These would be "covered entities":
    • any political subdivision which, within the previous twenty-five years, has become subject to a court order or government enforcement action based on voting-related discriminatory practices under specified state laws, federal laws, or the Fourteenth or Fifteenth Amendments of the U.S. Constitution.
    • any political subdivision which, within the previous twenty-five years, has become subject to at least three court orders or government enforcement actions for any violations of state or federal civil rights law or the Fourteenth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution concerning discrimination against members of a protected class.
    • any county in which the arrest rate of a protected class of at least ten thousand voting-age citizens or whose members comprise at least ten percent of the county's voting-age citizens exceeds that of the citizen voting-age population of the county by at least twenty percent at any point within the previous ten years, or
    • any political subdivision in which, based on data made available by the United States census, the "dissimilarity index" of any protected class consisting of at least twenty-five thousand citizens of voting age or whose members comprise at least ten percent of the citizen voting-age population of the political subdivision, is more than fifty concerning non-Hispanic white citizens of voting age within the political subdivision at any point within the previous ten years, and
    • any board of elections that is contained within a covered entity, or which itself contains a covered entity.

  • These would be covered policies:

    • Method of election, meaning at-large versus district-based,
    • Form of government, which is not defined,
    • Annexation of a political subdivision,
    • Incorporation of a political subdivision,
    • Consolidation or division of political subdivisions,
    • Removal of voters from enrollment lists or other list maintenance activities,
    • Number, location, or hours of any election day or early voting poll site,
    • Dates of elections and the election calendar, except for special elections,
    • Registration of voters,
    • Assignment of election districts to election day or early voting poll sites,
    • Assistance offered to members of a language-minority group, and
    • Any other topic properly designated by the Bureau.

    The bill would create prohibitions on voter disenfranchisement that the Attorney General, individuals, and organizations could enforce. These prohibitions and the methods of enforcing them are highly specified by the bill, including defining key terms, creating a pre-litigation process, and awarding attorneys' fees upon certain outcomes. Specifically, the bill would:


  • Prohibit voter suppression. The bill prohibits laws, rules, policies, or procedures that result in a denial or abridgment of the right of a protected class member to vote. A violation would be established upon a showing that, based on the totality of the circumstances, the protected class has less opportunity than the rest of the electorate to elect candidates of their choice or influence the outcome of elections.
  • Prohibit vote dilution. The bill prohibits a political subdivision or a board of elections from using a method of election that has the effect of impairing the ability of members of a protected class to elect candidates of their choice or influence the outcome of elections as a result of vote dilution.
    • A violation would be established in a political subdivision using an at-large method of election and, either: voting patterns of protected class members in that subdivision are racially polarized, or under the totality of the circumstances, protected class members' ability to elect candidates of their choice or influence election outcomes is impaired.
    • A violation would be established in a political subdivision using a district-based or alternative method of election, if it is shown that candidates or electoral choices preferred by members of the protected class would usually be defeated, and either: the voting patterns of the protected class members within the political subdivision are racially polarized, or under the totality of the circumstances, protected class members' ability to elect candidates of their choice or influence election outcomes is impaired.
  • Grant standing to a broad range of plaintiffs. Any of these parties could file voter suppression or vote dilution claims:
    • the Attorney General,
    • any aggrieved person,
    • an organization whose membership includes or is likely to include aggrieved persons,
    • an organization whose mission would be frustrated by a violation of this section,
    • an organization that would expend resources to fulfill its mission as a result of a violation of this section, or
    • coalitions of different protected classes, provided their combined voting preferences are polarized against the rest of the electorate.
  • Create a pre-litigation process. Plaintiffs would be required to notify using a "NYVRA notification letter" potential defendants before filing suit, and the bill would enable jurisdictions to fix the alleged problem without litigation by getting a "NYVRA proposal" approved by the Bureau. The bill facilitates addressing problems by awarding attorneys fees to plaintiffs whose actions change the defendants' behavior.

  • Upon a finding of a violation, the court would be required to order a tailored remedy, including ones that are inconsistent with any other provision of law if the inconsistent provision of law would prevent the court from ordering an otherwise appropriate remedy. Finally, the court would be required to consider remedies submitted by the parties, but could not defer to or prioritize a remedy simply because the political subdivision proposes it. Remedies could include, but not be limited to:

    • a district-based method of election,
    • an alternative method of election,
    • new or revised districting or redistricting plans,
    • elimination of staggered elections so that all members of the governing body are elected on the same date,
    • reasonably increasing the size of the governing body,
    • under certain conditions, moving the dates of elections to be concurrent with the primary or general election dates for state, county, or city office,
    • transferring authority for conducting the political subdivision's elections to the board of elections for the county in which the political subdivision is located,
    • additional voting hours or days,
    • additional polling locations,
    • additional means of voting such as voting by mail,
    • ordering of special elections,
    • requiring expanded opportunities for voter registration,
    • requiring additional voter education,
    • modifying the election calendar,
    • the restoration or addition of persons to registration lists, or
    • retaining jurisdiction for such period on a given matter as the court may deem appropriate, during which no redistricting plan shall be enforced unless and until the court finds that such plan does not have the purpose of diluting the right to vote based on protected class membership, or in contravention of the voting guarantees provided by New York, except that the court's finding shall not bar a subsequent action to enjoin enforcement of such redistricting plan.

    The bill creates a special process for political subdivisions when they convert from an at-large method of electing their government to one that involves districts or some other method of election, or for whenever a political subdivision that is already using district-based elections changes those districts.

    Finally, the bill requires boards of elections to provide certain kinds of language assistance to minority language groups.


  • If a board of elections or a political subdivision that administers elections meets any of these criteria it must provide language assistance:
    • more than two percent of the voting-age citizens of a political subdivision (but not less than 300 people) are members of a single language-minority group and have limited English proficiency,
    • more than four thousand of the citizens of voting age of such political subdivision are members of a single language-minority group and have limited English proficiency, or
    • if a political subdivision contains all or any part of a Native American reservation, more than two percent of the Native American citizens of voting age within the Native American reservation are members of a single language-minority group and have limited English proficiency.
  • The language assistance must include voting materials in the covered language of an equal quality to the corresponding English language materials, including registration or voting notices, forms, instructions, assistance, or other materials or information relating to the electoral process, including ballots. Nonetheless, if the language of the applicable minority group is oral or unwritten, the board of elections or political subdivision is only required to furnish oral instructions, assistance, or other information relating to registration and voting.
  • A board of elections may ask a court to provide English-only materials, and a court will grant the request if the determination that language assistance was required was unreasonable or an abuse of discretion.
  • The bill creates a private right of action to enforce the language assistance requirement.

  • These language accessibility provisions would not apply to certain special district elections. The exempt districts are county and town improvement districts that are subject to special fees for the real estate the districts manage.

    One section was amended out of this bill on May 4, 2022. Those provisions would have created a state depository of election information that can be used to identify discrimination, among other purposes. This bill, as introduced on June 1, 2021, would overhaul the timing and mechanics of the mail and affidavit (provisional) ballot canvassing process to require ballot processing and canvassing to start earlier, prescribe the ballot envelope cure process in more detail, and change how partisan observers respond to election officials' decisions regarding counting ballots. In addition, the bill would require people who received a mail ballot but go to the polls to vote in person to cast affidavit ballots, require the State Board of Elections to issue myriad rules to effectuate the purposes of the bill, and make conforming changes and technical corrections to other sections of election law. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require a voter who was sent a mail ballot but who goes to an early voting site or Election Day polling place to cast an affidavit ballot. Existing law allows such voters to cast regular ballots, because mail ballots are not canvassed until after the close of polls on Election Day.
  • Require the local board of elections to establish bipartisan teams of canvassers to begin reviewing ballot envelopes within four days of receiving a returned ballot, except that ballots must be reviewed within one day of receipt on or after Election Day, and:
    • If the board determines the ballot is returned by a voter on the registration list, is timely, and the envelope is sealed, signed, and the signature matches a reference signature, the envelope would be opened and the ballot saved for tabulating.
    • If the board determines the ballot envelope has a curable defect, the board must begin the cure process within one day of determining the defect exists. Ballot envelopes that are timely cured are opened and the ballot saved for tabulating.
    • If the board receives two envelopes from the same voter, the one returned first will be set aside, unless by the time the later ballot envelope is received the first has been opened and canvassed. If two are received and it is not possible to determine which the voter returned first, both will be set aside.
    • If the bipartisan team of reviewers disagrees on whether the ballot envelope should be opened, require the ballot envelope to be opened and the ballot saved for tabulating. This rule also applies if the team disagrees about whether a cure affirmation resolves a ballot envelope defect.
    • If, upon opening the envelope, the canvassers find a ballot missing, they must make a record of what is missing. If the canvassers find more than one ballot for the same races, all such ballots must be rejected.
    • If the ballot envelope is completely unsealed and it has been received before Election Day, the board must notify the voter by mail within three business days, and by either email or telephone, if such information is available in the voter's registration information. The notice must include other options for voting, and, if time permits, a new ballot.
    • If the board determines the ballot was returned by a person who is not on a registration list, there is no name on the ballot envelope, the ballot was returned late, such ballot envelope shall be set aside unopened for further review.
    • If the board determines a ballot envelope has a defect that cannot be cured, the ballot envelope will be set aside, and the board must mail the voter notice within three business days, and by either electronic mail or telephone, if the board has such contact information in the voter's registration information. The notice must include other options for voting, if any, and, if time permits, provide the voter with a new ballot.
    • The day before the first day of early voting, all ballots ready for tabulation would be scanned into a tabulation machine, but not tabulated. Ballots that the tabulation machine cannot process would be secured, unexamined, until after the close of polls on Election Day.
    • After the close of polls on the last day of early voting, all valid ballots not previously scanned on the day before the first day of early voting would be scanned into tabulation machines in the same manner.
    • Tabulation of scanned ballots may begin one hour before the close of polls on Election Day, however results may not be released until after the close of polls.

      Under existing law, ballots are not canvassed until after Election Day, although ballot envelopes may be reviewed upon receipt to identify curable defects. Later received, timely absentee ballots are counted and earlier received ones set aside. When ballot envelopes are going to be opened, political parties and candidates receive notice so that they are able to observe the process and object to ballot envelopes being opened. If an objection to opening a ballot is made and the canvassing board splits on whether to reject the ballot, it is set aside for three days to enable the objector to get a court order mandating the ballot be set aside. Absent a court order, the ballot envelope will be opened after three days. The bill would eliminate this ability of these partisan actors to challenge a ballot envelope that the bipartisan canvassing board has either determined should be opened, or that they have split on whether it should be opened. Similarly, existing law provides that if the canvassing team splits on whether to open a ballot envelope, the ballot envelope is set aside for three days to allow an interested party to get a court order. Absent a court order to the contrary, after three days these ballot envelopes are opened.
  • Identify which ballot envelope defects are curable, and which do not need to be cured for the ballot to be counted. Specifically:
    • Any of these mistakes can be cured:
    • the voter failed to sign the ballot envelope.
    • the voter's signature on the ballot envelope signature does not correspond to their registration signature.
    • the voter used a mark instead of a signature, but the voter's witness did not sign the ballot envelope.
    • the voter returned the ballot without a ballot affirmation envelope in the return envelope.
    • the person that has provided assistance to the voter signed the ballot envelope, but the voter did not.
    • the envelope was signed by someone other than the voter, but not the voter.
    • Any of these ballot envelope "defects" do not need to be cured:
    • the ballot envelope is undated or has the wrong date, provided it is postmarked on or prior to Election Day or is otherwise timely received.
    • the voter signed or marked the ballot affirmation envelope at a place on the envelope other than the designated signature line.
    • the voter used a combination of ink (of any color) or pencil to complete the ballot envelope.
    • papers found in the ballot envelope with the ballot are materials from the board of elections, such as instructions or an absentee ballot application sent by the board of elections.
    • an extrinsic mark or tear on the ballot envelope appears to be there as a result of the ordinary course of mailing or transmittal.
    • the ballot envelope is partially unsealed but there is no ability to access the ballot.
      These provisions are similar to those used to settle litigation between the League of Women Voters and the State Board of Elections for the November 2020 election, and are similar to temporary emergency regulations issued by the State Board of Elections that applied to elections in early 2021 but have since expired.
  • Specify the process to cure a ballot:
    • Within one day of rejecting a ballot for a curable defect, the board must send to the voter's registration address and, if different, the mailing address indicated on the ballot application, a notice explaining the reason for such rejection and the procedure to cure the rejection. The board must also send the notice by either email or telephone, if such information is available to the board in the voter's registration record.
    • The voter may cure the defect by filing a duly signed affirmation attesting to the same information required by the ballot affirmation envelope and attesting that the signer of the affirmation is the same person who submitted the ballot envelope. The board shall include the State Board of Elections affirmation form with the notice.
    • The voter must return the cure affirmation to the board no later than seven business days after the board's mailing of the notice or the day before the election, whichever is later.
    • If the board determines that such affirmation addresses the curable defect, or if the bipartisan canvassing team splits on whether it addresses the curable defect, the rejected ballot envelope would be opened and the ballot canvassed.
    • This process would also apply to affidavit (provisional) ballots.

      The process under existing law is similar, however the cure deadline is always seven business days after the notice has been sent to the voter, the notice sent when a ballot has been rejected for a non-curable defect does not have to include information about other options to vote or a new ballot, and the identified curable defects are missing signatures and mismatch signatures.
  • Create new rules for canvassing affidavit (provisional) ballots. Within four business days of the election, the board of elections would review all affidavit ballots cast at voting locations, and:
    • If a timely, valid absentee ballot is received from a voter who cast an affidavit ballot in person, the absentee ballot will be canvassed and the provisional ballot set aside. If an eligible voter who was sent an absentee ballot votes an affidavit ballot in person and the absentee ballot is not timely received, the affidavit ballot will be canvassed.
    • Affidavit ballots would be canvassed if cast at the correct polling place by eligible voters:
    • who moved within the state after registering. These voters' ballots will be canvassed even if they did not include their prior registration address, if the provided information is sufficient to identify the voter.
    • who are in inactive status.
    • whose registration was incorrectly transferred to another address even though they did not move.
    • whose registration poll records were missing on the day of such election.
    • who had not had their identity previously verified.
    • whose registration poll records did not show them to be enrolled in the party in which they are enrolled and the election is a primary. In addition, a primary affidavit ballot would be canvassed if the voter was automatically registered or pre-registered to vote for the first time at least twenty-five days before the primary, appeared at such primary election, and indicated on the affidavit ballot envelope the intent to enroll in such party.
    • who had been incorrectly identified as having already voted.
    • a ministerial error by the board of elections or any of its employees caused the ballot envelope not to be valid on its face.
    • the voter was not on the voter registration list but the canvassing team finds the voter submitted a voter registration application through the electronic voter registration transmittal system.
    • the affidavit ballot envelope contains enough information for the canvassing team to determine the voter's eligibility based on the statement of the affiant or records of the board, even if the envelope is not completed perfectly.
    • If an affidavit ballot is invalid due to a missing signature on the affidavit ballot envelope, or because the signature on the affidavit ballot envelope does not correspond to the registration signature, the voter will be given notice of the cure process.
  • Create a new, post-Election Day process for political parties and candidates to review ballot envelopes that have been disqualified and seek to have the ballots counted. Specifically:
    • Within four business days after Election Day, the local board of elections will have bipartisan canvassing teams re-review ballot envelopes that have been rejected, including those which were not timely cured.
    • Political parties, candidates, and independent bodies entitled to appoint watchers would be given at least five days notice of this review, and may provide as many watchers as they were allowed to appoint to an election district on Election Day.
    • The watchers would be able to object to the board's determination that a ballot envelope is invalid, but the ballot envelope would not be opened absent a court order.

  • Change the litigation rules relating to challenging ballot canvassing. Specifically:

    • Suits could be filed to challenge the rejection of ballots, instead of the acceptance and/or rejection of ballots.
    • The court could order a rejected ballot to be counted if the court is convinced of its validity for any reason, including that the rejection was caused by a ministerial error on the part of the board of elections. Existing law appears to limit the court to reinstating only those ballots cast by eligible voters which were rejected because of such ministerial error.
    • Create a new cause of action, based on procedural irregularities or other facts arising during the election that suggest a change or altering of the canvass schedule may be warranted, to enable a candidate to seek an order for temporary or preliminary injunctive relief or an impound order. To obtain such relief, the petitioner must show by clear and convincing evidence, that, because of procedural irregularities or other facts arising during the election, the petitioner will be irreparably harmed.

Last Updated June 11, 2021

VRLANALYSIS:
On June 9, the Assembly passed the Senate version of this bill, S7150, sending it to the Governor, who signed it into law on November 24, 2021. As a result, this bill is moot.

This bill, as introduced on June 2, 2021, would provide that, if the redistricting commission has not voted on a Congressional redistricting plan or plans by January 15, 2022, then the commission must give the legislature all the plans, draft plans, and data that the commission has produced and the legislature will create its own plans. Existing law does not address what happens if the redistricting commission fails to timely submit plans.

Last updated November 30, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on August 25, 2021, would require people to provide their full Social Security Numbers (SSN) when registering to vote, provide a copy of a current and valid Social Security Card when applying for an absentee ballot, and require some voters to show ID when voting in person or returning their absentee ballot. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require a person to include a full SSN on their voter registration application. Under existing law, a person may use their driver's license number, state ID number, last four digits of their SSN, or affirm that they have none of those numbers and use documentation like a recent utility bill to verify their ID when they vote for the first time.
  • Require a voter to provide a copy of their current and valid Social Security Card when applying for an absentee ballot. Existing law does not require an ID number to request an absentee ballot.
  • Create a new ID requirement to vote in person or when returning a mail ballot, and exempt a significant number of voters from the new requirement. Voters subject to the new ID requirement to show when voting in person, or include with their mail ballot when returning it:
    • a current and valid Social Security Card
    • a current utility bill, bank statement, government check, paycheck, or other government document that shows the name and address of the voter.

  • Exempt from the new voter ID rule UOCAVA voters, voters who are otherwise allowed by federal law to vote other than in person, and voters who, when registering, provided:

    • a copy of their current and valid Social Security Card,
    • at least the last four digits of their SSN, and the local board of elections matched it with an existing state identification record bearing the number, name and date of birth of the voter, or
    • a copy a current utility bill, bank statement, government check, paycheck, or government document that shows the name and address of the voter.

    Notably, people who registered to vote using their driver's license or state ID number would be subject to the new voter ID requirement.

    Existing law does not require a voter to show ID when voting in person or by mail unless it is the first time the voter has attempted to vote, and when they registered to vote they did not provide an ID number or other identifying documentation.

Last Updated September 13, 2021

This bill, as introduced on October 20, 2021, would shift election authority by allowing the state board of elections to remove a local board of elections commissioner for any willful violation or neglect of duty, or willfully disobeying any law, decision, order, settlement, rule or regulation of the state board of elections. Under existing law, only the Governor may remove a local commissioner for cause, using the same process as removing a sheriff for cause. The bill also changes the term of election commissioners from two to four years and makes small changes to their appointment process, issues Voting Rights Lab does not track.

Last updated October 21, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on October 20, 2021, would require notice to voters when an early voting location is changed before voting starts. If the location change is far enough in advance, notice must be given no later than five days before voting starts. If it changes later than that, notice must be given as soon as practicable. Finally, the bill prohibits moving the location of early voting within 48 hours of the early voting period beginning. Existing early voting law does not have comparable provisions, however, similar notice provisions apply to changes to Election Day polling places. The ban on changing the polling place within 48 hours of voting beginning does not exist for Election Day polling places.

Last updated March 2, 2022

Note: On January 19, 2022, this bill was substituted by its Senate companion, SB 7565. As a result, this bill will no longer move. The Senate bill was passed by the Assembly and sent to the Governor.

This bill, as amended on January 12, 2022, would enable voters to choose to vote by mail in village elections because of the risks posed by Covid through December 31, 2022.

While this substance was in the previous version of the bill, that version had extended the excuse to February 1, 2024, and had taken a different drafting approach. This version expressly reinstates the covid-excuse related language that had self-repealed from existing law on January 1, 2022, rather than amend the effective period of the law that had temporarily created that excuse, which was its previous drafting approach.

This bill follows in the wake of voters' rejection of a constitutional amendment that would have allowed the Legislature to enact no excuse absentee voting.

Last Updated January 27, 2022

This bill, as introduced on December 13, 2021, would prohibit localities from expanding the electorate to include anyone not eligible to vote in state elections, which would include noncitizens. In addition, the bill would protect eligible persons by prohibiting the abridgment of their rights to register to vote and vote by the action of a county, city, town or village, including by the enactment of local law.

Existing law has no comparable provisions, however, the bill was introduced soon after New York City granted non-citizens the ability to vote in local elections.

Last Updated December 15, 2021

Last Updated January 25, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2021, would create a new misdemeanor for the crime of "interfering in the election process by electronic means." The bill defines the crime as a person who, with intent to interfere with an election, places or causes to be placed, multiple calls by telephone or other electronic means, or sends or causes to be sent, multiple messages by text, email, fax, computer application, tablet application, telephone application or other electronic means, or any combination thereof, to obstruct, prevent or interfere with:

  • the reporting of poll results by any polling place
  • the receipt of poll results by a local or state board of elections
  • the ability of a political or party organization to place calls or send messages used for the purpose of encouraging people to vote, or

  • the ability of a political or party organization to place calls or send messages used for the purpose of arranging transportation for people to or from their polling place.

    Last updated January 6, 2021.

This bill was substituted by its identical Assembly companion, NY A 4158, on May 23, 2022, which the Senate then passed. NY A 4158 was then sent to the Governor for signature on August 5, 2022. As a result, this bill will not advance further.

As introduced on January 6, 2022, this bill would prohibit the private funding of permissive or required referendums or other ballot questions.

Last updated August 15, 2022.

This bill, as amended on April 20, 2022, would require boards of election to provide translators at polling places whenever at least 15 percent of the voting-age citizens in an election district speak the same non-English language at home, based on the most recent Census data.

Last updated April 27, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2021, would require boards of election to count ballots cast by eligible voters who voted in the correct county but the wrong polling place or wrong election district.

Last Updated January 6, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2021, would require the state board of elections or a local board of elections to get written approval from the state attorney general before implementing any changes to voting qualification, prerequisites to voting, administration, regulations, policies, practices or procedures with respect to voting, if those changes would apply to a county with a population of at least ten percent of members of a protected class, a county which has been subject to a court order or government enforcement action based voting discrimination, or a county that was previously subject to pre-clearance under Section 5 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 and has not been granted an exemption from such pre-clearance requirements. Preclearance is not required for "any changes made pursuant to law."

Last updated January 11, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2021, would enable the New York City Board of Elections (NYC BOE) to launch and temporarily operate an online voter registration system that is integrated with the state voter registration database. NYC BOE could operate the system until the State Board of Elections (SBOE) launches the online voter registration system existing law requires it to create. At that point, the NYC BOE system would be subsumed into the SBOE system.

Currently, New York voters may complete a voter registration application form using an online portal offered by the Department of Motor Vehicles. However, the DMV system is not integrated with the voter registration database and as a result, the DMV manually gives boards of elections new and updated registrations, a system that has led to registrations not being processed. In 2019 a law was enacted to require the SBOE to launch a fully electronic online voter registration system, but that system has not yet launched.

Last Updated August 24, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2021, would allow voters to request absentee ballots by phone. In addition, voters requesting ballots by phone would not be required to submit a written application at a later date. Existing law does not authorize phone requests for absentee ballots, and does require all voters who request a ballot using any writing other than an official application to submit a written application with or before casting an absentee ballot.

Last Updated January 6, 2021

This bill, as enacted on June 24, 2022, prohibits boards of election from rejecting absentee ballots because they include stray marks or writing, if the voter's "express intent" is "unambiguous." Under existing law, the existence of stray marks on an absentee ballot was grounds for disqualifying an otherwise valid vote, even if the voter's intent was otherwise clear.

Last Updated July 20, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2021, would change the timing of the address confirmation registration list maintenance process from annually in February to annually in January.

Last updated January 6, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2021, would change the voter registration form to include space for a voter's email address, and would require the boards of election to notify voters of polling place changes by email as well as by mail.

Last Updated January 6, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2021, would allow the state and/or local jurisdictions to place signs on highways reminding voters of an upcoming election and/or an upcoming registration deadline. Signs reminding motorists of an upcoming election can be posted beginning three days before Election Day through Election Day, and signs giving notice of a voter registration deadline may be placed five days before the deadline.

Last Updated January 6, 2021

This bill, as enacted on July 16, 2021, changes the application period for requesting a mailed absentee ballot. Specifically, the bill:

  • Eliminates the requirement that applications for absentee ballots must be made no more than 30 days before the election, thereby allowing voters more time to apply.

  • Changes the deadline for requesting a mailed ballot by requiring all applications to be received by the Board of Elections at least 15 days before an election. Existing law required that applications be mailed to the Board at least seven days before an election. The bill retains the existing deadline for requesting in-person delivery of an absentee ballot, which is the day before Election Day.

Last Updated August 29, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2021, would change the language of absentee ballot affirmations so that it clearly tracks existing law on when voting eligibility lost to a felony conviction has been restored. Specifically, the new language would clarify that voting eligibility has been restored when a person has been discharged from parole or has completed the maximum term of their sentence.

Last updated on January 12, 2020.

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2021, would allow New York voters who are overseas to apply for absentee ballots by fax or email or an online portal, and would allow them to return cast ballots electronically.

Last Updated January 12, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2021, would revise the process of challenging voters at the polling place in two ways. First, before making the challenge, the challenger must take an oath in front of the election worker that the challenge is being made in good faith, and the challenger must sign a related document. Second, the oaths to be taken by a challenged voter may be taken by the voter signing a form, unless the voter is illiterate or has difficulty with the written document, or requests that the oaths be administered orally. Under existing law the challenger need not take an oath and the challenged voter is orally given the needed oaths.

Last updated January 12, 2021.

This bill, as enacted on December 6, 2022, requires county boards of election to count provisional ballots ("affidavit ballots") of eligible voters who cast a ballot at the wrong polling place, provided that the voter was in the correct county and Assembly district. Under previous law, provisional ballots were counted only if a voter appeared at the correct polling place (including when the voter appeared in the incorrect election district).

Last updated February 28, 2023.

This bill, as introduced on January 13, 2021, would allow the New York City Board of Elections to consolidate election districts so that each one serves no more than 4,000 active registered voters. Under existing law, statewide no election district may serve more than 1,150 active registrants.

Last updated January 13, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2021, would broaden the methods of requesting an absentee ballot to include any written instrument signed by the voter, and would change the deadline to request a ballot to be mailed to the voter. Under the bill, the voter could request a ballot to be mailed to them on the day before Election Day. It is not clear that such a deadline would enable a voter to receive and return the ballot in time. Under existing law, the request must be mailed seven days before Election Day, although a ballot can be picked up in person the day before Election Day.

Last Updated August 24, 2021

This bill, as introduced January 6, 2021, would sharply raise election worker pay in New York City. Minimum election inspector pay would rise from $130/day to $300/day, and minimum election coordinators pay from $200/day to $400/day. Outside of NYC, county legislatures would set the pay for their counties' elections.

Last updated January 7, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2021, would make a voter's email address and telephone number as provided on their voter registration form confidential.

Last Updated January 13, 2021

This bill, as amended on April 20, 2022, would declare that absentee ballots returned in envelopes sealed with tape or another method other than the envelope adhesive, but which showed no signs of tampering, are valid and must be counted without requiring the voter to take further action. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have required boards of election to make a good faith effort to contact the voter, and would have allowed the ballot to count if the voter confirmed in writing that they cast the ballot returned it in the envelope in the observed condition. Existing law does not specifically address such ballots.

Last Updated April 21, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2021, would shift election authority by enabling individual commissioners of a board of elections to order a voting machine audits when certain criteria exist, instead of requiring the entire board to order the audit.

Last updated July 19, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Proposes a constitutional amendment, relates to the number of state senators and inclusion of incarcerated persons in the federal census for population determination for redistricting purposes and to the functioning of the independent redistricting commission in the determination of district lines for congressional and state legislative offices.
VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as adopted on February 11, 2021, proposes an amendment to the New York Constitution to change redistricting procedures and cap the number of state senators at the existing 63. For the constitutional amendment to become adopted, the proposal must be approved by a majority of voters in the November 2021 election. New York's existing redistricting process begins with an independent commission substantially appointed by the Legislature. The commission submits maps and enabling legislation to the Legislature for its review and adoption. The proposed constitutional amendment would change the existing process by:

  • Changing the timeline for the commission to submit plans to the legislature to reflect New York's change to state primaries in June, rather than in September.
  • Requiring state authorities to prepare a tabulation of inhabitants if the federal census fails to count the "total" population of the state. The current constitution only requires a state tabulation if federal census figures do not include "aliens or Indians not taxed."
  • Requiring state authorities to enumerate incarcerated people in the community of their last residence, if the federal census does not include these individuals at their last residence.
  • Changing the rules relating to approving plans proposed by the commission. New York's constitution currently requires different vote thresholds if one party controls both houses of the legislature, versus if different parties control each house. The amendment would eliminate all voting distinctions based on party control, making it easier for a single party to control redistricting.
  • Providing that if the commission fails to vote on a plan by the deadline, it must give the legislature all plans in its possession, both completed and in draft form, and the data upon which such plans are based.

  • Making various changes to specific districting criteria.

    Last updated September 9, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2021, would require boards of election to mail ballots to people who properly applied for them according to schedule based on when the boards received the applications. Specifically, if the board received the application:

  • 60 or more days before the election, the board must mail the ballot by the 46th day before the election, or deliver it by then at its office.
  • Between 59 and 46 days before the election, the board must mail the ballot by the 42nd day before the election, or deliver it by then at its office.
  • Between 45 and 30 days before the election, the board must mail the ballot with four days of receiving the application, or deliver it by then at its office.
  • Between 29 and 15 days before the election, the board must mail the ballot within three days of receiving the application, or deliver it by then at its office.
  • Between 14 and seven days before the election, the board must mail the ballot within two days of receiving the application, or deliver it by then at its office.

  • If an application was postmarked as having been timely mailed by the seventh day before the election and received after that day, or if an application is delivered to the board at its office after that day, the board shall make every reasonable effort to mail or deliver the ballot on the same day.

    Under existing law, the Board begins mailing and delivering ballots 30 days before the election, and for applications received after that date must simply send or deliver ballots as soon as practicable after confirming the validity of the application.

Last Updated January 7, 2021

This bill, as enacted on May 4, 2021, shortens the period of time that people convicted of felonies and incarcerated are disenfranchised, requires notice to people at several key times relating to their voting eligibility, requires the state to give returning citizens voter registration forms, and if desired, registration assistance, and requires a related education program. Specifically, the bill:

  • Automatically restores voting eligibility for people who have been disenfranchised due to imprisonment for a felony conviction, immediately upon their release from incarceration. Under existing law, eligibility was automatically restored following incarceration and any period of parole. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires judges to inform defendants on the record, prior to accepting a guilty plea, that being incarcerated will cause disenfranchisement during the period of incarceration. This is a modified provision. As introduced, the bill would have required a judge to provide notice to the defendant upon sentencing after trial as well.
  • Requires the department of corrections to give verbal and written notice of restored voting eligibility whenever a person is being released to parole or released from incarceration. The returning citizen must be given registration forms and, if desired, assistance completing and returning them. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires notice of loss of voting eligibility whenever a person violates parole such that their parole will be revoked. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires the department of corrections to give notice to each person serving a period of community supervision verbally and in writing of their right to vote and provide them with an application for voter registration and a declination form, offer them assistance in filling out the form, and provide them written information distributed by the board of elections on the importance and the mechanics of voting. If the returning citizen chooses, the department must return the registration to the appropriate board of elections. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires the state board of elections to develop and implement a program to educate attorneys, judges, election officials, corrections officials, including parole and probation officers, and members of the public regarding these changes to voting eligibility restoration. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

  • Eliminates the ability to challenge a voter at a polling place as ineligible due to a felony conviction. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.

BILLSUMMARY: Provides that any plan of apportionment relating to the division of a county, except a county wholly contained within a city, into districts for the purpose of apportionment or reapportionment of members of its local legislative body shall be subject to federal and state constitutional requirements, further provides for standards to be followed for such plan.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2021, addresses redistricting for county legislatures. The bill would require counties to follow federal and state standards, and in addition imposes additional rules. Specifically, the bill would also require the redistricting plan to provide substantially equal weight for all of the residents of that county in the allocation of representation in the local legislative body. In meeting that goal, no town except a town having more than one hundred ten percent of a full ratio for each representative, shall be divided in the formation or representation areas. Adjacent representation areas in the same town or city shall not contain a greater excess in population than five percent of a full ratio for each representative. In addition, the plan must provide substantially fair and effective representation for the people of the county as organized in political parties. Finally, representation areas must be of convenient and contiguous territory in as compact form as practicable.

Last updated January 11, 2021.

This bill, as enacted on December 22, 2021, overhauls the timing and mechanics of the mail and affidavit (provisional) ballot canvassing process to start them earlier, prescribes the ballot envelope cure process in more detail, and changes how partisan observers respond to election officials' decisions regarding counting ballots. In addition, the bill requires a voter who wish to vote in person after receiving a mail ballot to cast an affidavit ballot, requires the State Board of Elections to issue myriad rules to effectuate the purposes of the bill, and makes conforming changes and technical corrections to other sections of election law.

Regarding voting in person after having been sent a mail ballot, the bill:

  • Requires such a voter to cast an affidavit ballot, whether they are attempting to vote during early voting or on Election Day. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have allowed in-person early voters to complete a regular ballot, and in-person Election Day voters to complete a regular ballot if they surrendered the mail ballot. Under existing law, all eligible, registered voters on the list at the voting location vote a regular ballot without regard to whether they were mailed a ballot.

    Regarding mail ballot processing, canvassing, and the cure process, the bill:


  • Requires bipartisan canvassing teams to begin reviewing mail ballot envelopes within four days of receiving a returned ballot, except that ballots must be reviewed within one day of receipt on or after Election Day. This provision was modified from the previous version of the bill, which would have required ballot envelope review to begin 40 days before the election. Under existing law, mail ballot canvassing begins after the close of polls, and must start no more than 14 days after a general or special election, and eight days after a primary.
  • Changes mail ballot rejection criteria and process:
    • If the board determines the ballot was returned by a person who is not on a registration list, there is no name on the ballot envelope, or the ballot was returned late, the ballot envelope must be set aside unopened for further review after the election, at which time third parties may object to the rejection. Under existing law, ballots were rejected unopened when the voter had already voted in person in the election, the name and address on the envelope did not match the voter's registration records, the envelope had no name at all, or the ballot was unsealed. Such ballots were not reviewed further, except for unsealed ballots, which required notice to the voter and the opportunity to cure.
    • If a voter was issued a second mail ballot, and the first ballot is returned before the second ballot, the board must set aside the first ballot to allow the voter time to return a later vote. If a second ballot is received after a voter's first ballot has been reviewed and opened, the second ballot must be set aside. Existing law provided that when two ballots are received, the later-executed ballot must be counted, but did not specify that boards must hold a ballot unopened when a second ballot has been issued but not yet returned. Under existing law, if the board could not identify which ballot was later, it would have rejected both ballots.
    • If the bipartisan team of reviewers disagrees on whether the ballot envelope should be opened, the envelope must be opened and the ballot saved for tabulating. Under existing law, if the team disagreed, or if a challenge was made to the ballot and the team could not agree on the challenge, the ballot would have been set aside unopened for three days and then opened unless a court order directed otherwise. The three day delay existed to allow parties to seek a court order.
    • If the board determines a ballot envelope has a defect that cannot be cured, the board must mail the voter notice within three business days, and give notice by either email or telephone, if the board has such contact information in the voter's registration information. The notice must include other options for voting, if any, and, if time permits, provide the voter with a new ballot. Under existing law, the board was required to notify the voter within three business days that their ballot had been rejected, but the content of the notice was not specified, and there was no duty to try electronic notice methods if the contact information existed or to send another ballot if sufficient time remained.
    • If the ballot envelope is completely unsealed and it has been received before Election Day, the board must notify the voter by mail within three business days, and by either email or telephone, if such information is available in the voter's registration information. The notice must include other options for voting, and, if time permits, a new ballot. Existing law required notification to the voter "forthwith," but did not specify a timeframe or particular methods of contact. signed by someone other than the voter.

  • Identifies which ballot envelope defects must be cured for a ballot to count, and which do not need to be cured. Most, but not all of the curable defects were addressed by existing law, and existing law did not itemize defects that did not need cure. Specifically, the bill provides that the following defects must be cured:

    • the voter failed to sign the ballot envelope. This defect was curable under existing law.
    • the voter's signature on the ballot envelope signature does not correspond to their registration signature. This defect was curable under existing law.
    • the voter used a mark instead of a signature, but the voter's witness did not sign the ballot envelope. This defect was curable under existing law.
    • the voter returned the ballot without a ballot affirmation envelope in the return envelope. This defect was curable under existing law.
    • the person that has provided assistance to the voter signed the ballot envelope, but the voter did not. Existing law did not provide an opportunity to cure this defect.
    • the envelope is signed by someone other than the voter and not the voter. Existing law did not provide an opportunity to cure this defect.

      The bill provides that ballots with the following ballot envelope "defects" do not require cure, and will count as is:
    • the ballot envelope is undated or has the wrong date, provided it is postmarked on or prior to Election Day or is otherwise timely received.
    • the voter signed or marked the ballot affirmation envelope at a place on the envelope other than the designated signature line.
    • the voter used a combination of ink (of any color) or pencil to complete the ballot envelope.
    • papers found in the ballot envelope with the ballot are materials from the board of elections, such as instructions or an absentee ballot application sent by the board of elections.
    • an extrinsic mark or tear on the ballot envelope appears to be there as a result of the ordinary course of mailing or transmittal.
    • the ballot envelope is partially unsealed but there is no ability to access the ballot.

    The provisions detailing curable defects and defects not needing cure were not in the previous version of the bill. Nonetheless, the provisions are similar to those in the settlement agreement between the League of Women Voters and the State Board of Elections for the November 2020 election, and are similar to temporary emergency regulations that were issued by the State Board of Elections for elections in early 2021, expired, and were re-adopted on an emergency basis.


  • Maintains the basic notice and cure process that existing law provided, but amended it to give some voters more time to cure their ballot envelope defects. Specifically, under the bill, the voter must return the cure affirmation to the board no later than seven business days after the board's mailing of the notice, or the day before the election, whichever is later. Under existing law, the deadline to cure was seen business days after notice was sent for all ballots.
  • Provides that if the board decides the voter's affirmation cures the defect, or if the bipartisan canvassing team splits on whether it cures the defect, the rejected ballot envelope would be opened and the ballot canvassed. Under existing law, if the board split, the potentially cured ballot would be set aside for three days and then opened unless a court order directed otherwise.
  • Changes the canvassing of affidavit (provisional) ballots. Within four business days of the election, the board of elections must begin canvassing the affidavit ballots cast at voting locations. Under existing law, affidavit ballots were canvassed along with absentee ballots, but the earlier processing of absentee ballots results in a separate process. Most of the affidavit ballot canvassing provisions are the same as under existing law, however, the bill codifies the rules in a different place. In addition, under the bill:
    • If a timely, valid absentee ballot is received from a voter who cast an affidavit ballot in person, the absentee ballot will be canvassed and the affidavit ballot set aside. If an eligible voter who was sent an absentee ballot votes an affidavit ballot in person and the absentee ballot is not timely received, the affidavit ballot will be canvassed. Existing law had no comparable provision because people who were mailed absentee ballots cast regular ballots at the polls, not affidavit ballots.
    • The board must enter information into the ballot tracking system to enable a voter who cast an affidavit ballot to determine if it was counted.
  • Changes requirements for tabulation of mail ballots:
    • The day before the first day of early voting, all ballots ready for tabulation must be scanned into a tabulation machine, but not tabulated. Ballots that the tabulation machine cannot process must be secured, unexamined, until after the close of polls on Election Day. Existing law did not require any processing or tabulation prior to Election Day.
    • After the close of polls on the last day of early voting, all valid ballots not previously scanned on the day before the first day of early voting must be scanned into tabulation machines in the same manner.
    • Tabulation of scanned ballots may begin one hour before the close of polls on Election Day, however results may not be released until after the close of polls.
  • Creates a new, post-Election Day process for political parties and candidates to review ballot envelopes that have been disqualified and seek to have the ballots counted. These are new provisions that were not in the previous version of the bill. Specifically:
    • Within four business days after Election Day, the local board of elections will have bipartisan canvassing teams re-review ballot envelopes that have been rejected, including those which were not timely cured.
    • Political parties, candidates, and independent bodies entitled to appoint watchers will be given at least five days notice of this review, and may provide as many watchers as they were allowed to appoint to an election district on Election Day.
    • The watchers are permitted to object to the board's determination that a ballot envelope is invalid, but the ballot envelope will not be opened absent a court order.

  • Changes the litigation rules relating to challenging ballot canvassing. Specifically:

    • In the ordinary course, suits may be only filed to challenge the rejection of ballots, instead existing law's allowing suits to challenge the acceptance and/or rejection of ballots. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
    • The court may order a rejected ballot to be counted if the court is convinced of its validity for any reason, including that the rejection was caused by a ministerial error on the part of the board of elections. This is a new provision. Existing law appears to limit the court to reinstating only those ballots cast by eligible voters which were rejected because of such ministerial error.
    • The bill creates a new cause of action, based on procedural irregularities or other facts arising during the election that suggest a change or altering of the canvass schedule may be warranted, to enable a candidate to seek an order for temporary or preliminary injunctive relief or an impound order. To obtain such relief, the petitioner must show by clear and convincing evidence, that, because of procedural irregularities or other facts arising during the election, the petitioner will be irreparably harmed. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill provided for similar substance but added two different sections of law.

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2021, would define and criminalize communicating deceptive information that prevents or deters someone from voting, and would separately define and criminalize voter suppression. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create a new misdemeanor for spreading false information regarding:
    • the time, place, or manner of any election,
    • the qualifications for on voter eligibility, including any penalties associated with voting by ineligible voters,
    • information regarding a voter's registration status or eligibility, or
    • the political party affiliation of any candidate.
  • Allow anyone impacted by the dissemination of the deceptive information to seek a court order for preventative relief, or may apply for a permanent or temporary injunction, restraining order, declaratory judgment, or other order.
  • Create a misdemeanor for voter suppression. Under the bill, to "suppress" means to use force, authority or an abuse of power to prevent, restrain, inhibit or compel another from acting in his or her own interests or intentions, or into not acting at all.

  • Provide that if someone is convicted of either new misdemeanor, and then is convicted of another one, they will then be guilty of a felony.
