This bill, "The John R. Lewis Voting Rights Act," as enacted on June 20, 2022, creates a comprehensive legal regime to prevent discriminatory election laws, rules, and practices using preclearance requirements and private rights of action to facilitate injunctive and other relief against discriminatory practices, and requires boards of election to provide all key voting materials in minority languages. The bill's protections extend to protected class members, namely a class of eligible voters who are members of a race, color, or language-minority group. The bill defines "language-minority group" as individuals who are American Indian, Asian American, Alaskan Native, or of Spanish heritage.

The bill creates a preclearance regime by requiring "covered entities" to seek permission to implement a "covered policy" using either of two preclearance procedures: asking the Attorney General or petitioning a court. When granting preclearance, regardless of the method, the decision-maker must decide that the covered policy will not diminish the ability of protected class members to participate in the political process and elect their preferred candidates. If a covered entity enacts or implements a covered policy without seeking preclearance, or in defiance of a decision denying preclearance, the Attorney General or anyone else with standing may sue to enforce preclearance. Finally, the bill authorizes the Civil Rights Bureau to issue necessary rules related to the new requirements. Specifically, under the bill, a covered entity may seek preclearance by:

  • Submitting the policy to the Civil Rights Bureau of the Attorney General (Bureau), and if the covered entity is a county or city board of elections, giving simultaneous notice to the State Board of Elections. A public comment process must then follow.
    • The Bureau must publish the policy on its website and invite public comment. The bill specifies timelines for public comment depending on what type of policy is being reviewed. The Bureau may continue its review during the public comment, but may not decide on preclearance until public comment has ended.
    • The Bureau must preclear or reject the recommendation in writing, and, if it grants preclearance, may do so temporarily, denying preclearance thereafter, so long as the decision to deny preclearance comes within 60 days of the policy's submission. If the Bureau fails to decide within the specified timelines, preclearance must be granted, although the Bureau is granted one 20-day extension for good cause. In addition, the bill authorizes the Bureau to issue rules for an expedited process for a covered policy in certain emergencies.
    • A covered entity may appeal a denial of preclearance in the Supreme Court of New York for Albany County or New York County on an expedited basis. Further appeals must follow the ordinary practice, subject to expedited timing.
  • Submitting the policy to a designated court, as specified by the bill, with supplemental provision to the Bureau. The court must grant or deny preclearance within 60 days. If the court denies preclearance or fails to rule within 60 days, the covered policy must not be implemented. Appeals must follow ordinary practice, subject to expedited timing.
  • "Covered entities" include:
    • any political subdivision which, within the previous 25 years, has become subject to a court order or government enforcement action based on voting-related discriminatory practices under specified state laws, federal laws, or the Fourteenth or Fifteenth Amendments of the U.S. Constitution.
    • any political subdivision which, within the previous 25 years, has become subject to at least three court orders or government enforcement actions for any violations of state or federal civil rights law or the Fourteenth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution concerning discrimination against members of a protected class.
    • any county in which the arrest rate of a protected class of at least 10,000 voting-age citizens or whose members comprise at least 10 percent of the county's voting-age citizens exceeds that of the citizen voting-age population of the county by at least 20 percent at any point within the previous ten years, or
    • any political subdivision in which, based on data made available by the United States census, the "dissimilarity index" of any protected class consisting of at least 25,000 citizens of voting age or whose members comprise at least 10 percent of the citizen voting-age population of the political subdivision, is more than 50 concerning non-Hispanic white citizens of voting age within the political subdivision at any point within the previous 10 years, and
    • any board of elections that is contained within a covered entity, or which itself contains a covered entity.
  • "Covered policies" include:
  • The bill also creates prohibitions on voter disenfranchisement that the Attorney General, individuals, and organizations may enforce, including definitions of key terms, creation of a pre-litigation process, and the award of attorneys' fees upon certain outcomes. Specifically, the bill:
    • method of election, meaning at-large versus district-based,
    • form of government, which is not defined,
    • annexation of a political subdivision,
    • incorporation of a political subdivision,
    • consolidation or division of political subdivisions,
    • removal of voters from enrollment lists or other list maintenance activities,
    • number, location, or hours of any election day or early voting poll site,
    • dates of elections and the election calendar, except for special elections,
    • registration of voters,
    • assignment of election districts to election day or early voting poll sites,
    • assistance offered to members of a language-minority group, and
    • any other topic properly designated by the Bureau.
  • Prohibits voter suppression. The bill prohibits laws, rules, policies, or procedures that result in a denial or abridgment of the right of a protected class member to vote. A violation would be established upon a showing that, based on the totality of the circumstances, the protected class has less opportunity than the rest of the electorate to elect candidates of their choice or influence the outcome of elections.
  • Prohibits vote dilution. The bill prohibits a political subdivision or a board of elections from using a method of election that has the effect of impairing the ability of members of a protected class to elect candidates of their choice or influence the outcome of elections as a result of vote dilution.
    • A violation would be established in a political subdivision using an at-large method of election and, either: voting patterns of protected class members in that subdivision are racially polarized, or under the totality of the circumstances, protected class members' ability to elect candidates of their choice or influence election outcomes is impaired.
    • A violation would be established in a political subdivision using a district-based or alternative method of election if it is shown that candidates or electoral choices preferred by members of the protected class would usually be defeated, and either: the voting patterns of the protected class members within the political subdivision are racially polarized, or under the totality of the circumstances, protected class members' ability to elect candidates of their choice or influence election outcomes is impaired.
  • Grants standing to a broad range of plaintiffs. Voter suppression or vote dilution claims may be filed by:
    • the Attorney General,
    • any aggrieved person,
    • an organization whose membership includes or is likely to include aggrieved persons,
    • an organization whose mission would be frustrated by a violation of this section,
    • an organization that would expend resources to fulfill its mission as a result of a violation of this section, or
    • coalitions of different protected classes, provided their combined voting preferences are polarized against the rest of the electorate.
  • Creates a pre-litigation process. Plaintiffs are required to notify potential defendants, using an "NYVRA notification letter," before filing suit, and jurisdictions are authorized to remedy alleged problems without litigation by implementing an "NYVRA proposal" approved by the Civil Rights Bureau. If a jurisdiction implements an approved proposal, prospective plaintiffs may request reimbursement for the costs associated with the NYVRA letter, up to a capped amount.
  • Upon a finding of a violation, the court is required to order a tailored remedy, including ones that are inconsistent with any other provision of law if the inconsistent provision of law would prevent the court from ordering an otherwise appropriate remedy. Finally, the court is required to consider remedies submitted by the parties, but may not defer to or prioritize a remedy simply because the political subdivision proposes it. Remedies may include, but are not be limited to:
  • The bill prohibits voter intimidation, deception, or obstruction that causes or reasonably will have the effect of causing a voter to vote or not vote, or register, in some way. Standing is conferred on individuals in a protected class, organizations with protected members, organizations with a mission to ensure voting access, and the attorney general. On finding a violation, courts may issue remedies including, but not limited to, additional time to cast a ballot, and successful plaintiffs are entitled to attorneys' fees.
  • The bill creates a special process for political subdivisions when they convert from an at-large method of electing their government to one that involves districts or some other method of election, or whenever a political subdivision that is already using district-based elections changes those districts.
  • Finally, the bill requires boards of elections to provide certain kinds of language assistance to minority language groups.
    • a district-based method of election,
    • an alternative method of election,
    • new or revised districting or redistricting plans,
    • elimination of staggered elections so that all members of the governing body are elected on the same date,
    • reasonably increasing the size of the governing body,
    • under certain conditions, moving the dates of elections to be concurrent with the primary or general election dates for state, county, or city office,
    • transferring authority for conducting the political subdivision's elections to the board of elections for the county in which the political subdivision is located,
    • additional voting hours or days,
    • additional polling locations,
    • additional means of voting such as voting by mail,
    • ordering of special elections,
    • requiring expanded opportunities for voter registration,
    • requiring additional voter education,
    • modifying the election calendar,
    • the restoration or addition of persons to registration lists, or
    • retaining jurisdiction for such period on a given matter as the court may deem appropriate, during which no redistricting plan shall be enforced unless and until the court finds that such plan does not have the purpose of diluting the right to vote based on protected class membership, or in contravention of the voting guarantees provided by New York, except that the court's finding shall not bar a subsequent action to enjoin enforcement of such redistricting plan.
  • If a board of elections or a political subdivision that administers elections meets any of these criteria it must provide language assistance:
    • more than two percent of the voting-age citizens of a political subdivision (but not less than 300 people) are members of a single language-minority group and have limited English proficiency,
    • more than 4,000 of the citizens of voting age of such political subdivision are members of a single language-minority group and have limited English proficiency, or
    • if a political subdivision contains all or any part of a Native American reservation, more than two percent of the Native American citizens of voting age within the Native American reservation are members of a single language-minority group and have limited English proficiency.
  • The language assistance must include voting materials in the covered language of an equal quality to the corresponding English language materials, including registration or voting notices, forms, instructions, assistance, or other materials or information relating to the electoral process, including ballots. Nonetheless, if the language of the applicable minority group is oral or unwritten, the board of elections or political subdivision is only required to furnish oral instructions, assistance, or other information relating to registration and voting.
  • A board of elections may ask a court for permission to provide English-only materials, and a court will grant the request if the determination that language assistance was required was unreasonable or an abuse of discretion.
  • Standing to enforce the language assistance requirements is granted to any aggrieved individuals, organizations whose membership includes aggrieved persons or members of a protected class, organizations whose mission, in whole or in part, is to ensure voting access and such mission would be hindered by a violation of this section, and the attorney general.
  • These language accessibility provisions would not apply to certain special district elections related to real estate fees.
  • The bill also includes provisions concerning procedures for implementation of redistricting plans, which Voting Rights Lab does not track.
  • One section was amended out of this bill on May 4, 2022. Those provisions would have created a state depository of election information that could be used to identify discrimination, among other purposes. Separate legislation that would create such a database has since been introduced. On May 28, 2022, provisions creating a "preclearance commission" and a third preclearance procedure were also amended out of the bill.

Last Updated January 31, 2025

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2021, would increase the number of early voting sites boards of election are required to offer. Under current law, counties must offer one for every 50,000 registered voters, up to a total of 10. The bill would remove the cap. Counties with fewer than 50,000 registered voters would still be required to offer one. In addition, the bill would reduce the reasons a county could choose to assign voters to a particular early voting site rather than let them use any site in the county and make a change to voting machine testing to further facilitate county-wide vote centers for early voting.

Last Updated March 8, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2021, would designate public libraries, public housing authorities, and high schools, as voter registration agencies. Public libraries would be required to provide the voter registration assistance whenever someone 18 or older applied for a library card. Housing authorities would be required to provide the assistance as part of the initial application for assistance or for recertification. Public high schools would be required to offer the service to seniors upon their graduation.

Last Updated January 8, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 8, 2021, would create a new misdemeanor criminalizing voter intimidation or harassment, and would disenfranchise anyone convicted of it. The bill defines voter intimidation or harassment as, while acting with the intent to influence how a person votes, either placing such person in reasonable fear of physical injury, or threatening retaliation against them for voting for a certain candidate, proposition or ballot measure. Retaliation would include, but is not limited to, changes to employment status, including changes to job titles, hours, or wages.

Note: After this bill's introduction, the New York changed its law relating to restoring voting eligibility after a conviction. The bill text reflects the old law.

Last updated August 25, 2021.

This bill, as enacted on March 9, 2021, designates the county seat of Washington County as the location for the jurisdiction's one required early voting site, rather than the county's most populous municipality as otherwise required throughout the state. Note that under existing law, boards of election are authorized to operate additional early voting sites, beyond the minimum required.

Last Updated April 26, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2021, would ensure that polling places in a cities with a population of one million or more have the capacity to serve voters by requiring at least one voting machine for each 1,400 registered voters in such cities.

Last updated March 8, 2021.

This bill, as amended on January 11, 2022, was not substantively changed. As introduced on January 12, 2021, this bill would increase the number of early voting locations required in cities or towns with a population of more than 100,000 but less than 1 million based on the most recent decennial census. The relevant board of elections would be required to open one per every 50,000 people in such city or town, up to a total of 11 early voting locations, and to site them on public transportation routes to the extent practicable. Existing law requires county boards of election and the NYC board of elections to open one site per 50,000 registered voters in their jurisdiction, up to ten total, unless another provision of law requires them to open more. In addition, existing law requires one early voting site to be located in the most populous city or town.

Last Updated January 18, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 12, 2021, would create an exception to the existing law's automatic restoration of voting eligibility after a disenfranchised person completes their parole or maximum term of incarceration. People convicted of sex offenses who committed to civil imprisonment in a hospital or institution remain disenfranchised during the time of his or her confinement to such hospital or institution.

Last updated January 15, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on January 13, 2021, would increase the early voting period from eight days to 15 days by having the early voting period by starting early voting 17 days before the election instead of ten days before the election as existing law provides. The end of the early voting period would remain the second day before the election.

Last updated January 14, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on January 13, 2021, would create same day registration at every early voting and election day polling place. The process would be called "conditional registration", and conditional registrants must cast affidavit (provisional) ballots. These ballots will count if the voter registration information is verified through matching at the DMV, the Social Security Administration, or otherwise, either before or during the canvass.

Note: The New York Constitution Art. II, Section 5 requires that people register at least ten days before Election Day. However, the Legislature completed its part of the process to amend this provision out of the New York Constitution, and voters will have the opportunity to ratify it November 2, 2021. This bill acknowledges the constitutional provision.

Last updated October 26, 2021.

This bill, as enacted on October 28, 2021, eases the requirements for a victim of domestic violence to keep their voter registration record, and thus their address, confidential. The bill replaces the prior requirement under existing law for victims to obtain a court order granting confidentiality, and instead allows victims to submit an affidavit to the relevant board of elections establishing their grounds for confidentiality. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. The bill also provides that records will be made confidential for four years, and that victims may reapply for confidential status at the end of the four year period. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.

Last Updated November 27, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 14, 2021, would allow school district elections to be held in any building owned or leased by the district so long as it met the accessibility requirements for polling places. Existing law requires elections to be held in a school unless the district does not have one.

Last updated January 15, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on January 14, 2021, would define "illness" within the absentee excuses available for municipal elections to enable anyone to vote absentee during the Covid-19 pandemic. New York added an identical provision for absentee voting in state and federal elections before the November 2020 election. Both provisions will expire January 1, 2022.

Last Updated January 15, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Amends the Election Law, relates to absentee voting by residents of nursing homes and other long-term care facilities, provides that inspectors of the board of elections shall not physically deliver ballots to residents of such facilities.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on July 16, 2021, would temporarily prevent boards of election from providing the normal in-person absentee voting assistance at nursing homes and similar residential facilities to minimize Covid-19 related risks. The prohibition would expire on December 31, 2021.

Last updated July 20, 2021.

HISTORY: {"date":"01/05/2022","summary":"To SENATE Committee on BUDGET AND REVENUES","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 14, 2021, would require income tax, property tax, and real estate transfer tax forms to include a voter registration option. If the person who is paying the income or property tax or purchasing the real estate wishes to register, they check a box on the form. After receiving a return with the box checked, the tax authority gives the potential registrant's information to the state board of elections, which forwards it to the relevant local board of elections. At that point, the local board of elections sends the potential voter a notice that allows the voter to opt out of registration, correct errors, and/or choose a political party. The notice also tells the voter to submit proof of citizenship and New York residence as otherwise required by law and the penalties for false registration. Under existing law, people do not provide documentation of citizenship to register, and the bill does not create a requirement to submit any.

Last Updated January 15, 2021

HISTORY: {"date":"01/05/2022","summary":"To SENATE Committee on CRIME VICTIMS, CRIME AND CORRECTION","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 15, 2021, would require the chief administrative officer of a correctional facility to notify a person who is being discharged who is 18 years or older of his or her right to vote, and provide such person with a form of application for voter registration together with written information distributed by the board of elections on the importance and the mechanics of voting.

Note: New York disenfranchises people convicted of felonies who are incarcerated only while they are incarcerated.

Last Updated June 15, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 15, 2021, would criminalize "ballot harvesting" as both a felony and a misdemeanor, depending on whether the ballot harvesting was willful. Ballot harvesting is defined as:

  • Submitting an absentee ballot application signed by the voter if the person submitting it is not a family member of the voter or does not have a notarized authorization to submit the application. Even with a notarized authorization, a person can only assist one voter per election.

  • Collecting, distributing, or submitting to the board of elections a voter's ballot unless the person submitting the ballot is the voter's family member or a caregiver who has a notarized authorization certifying the person as a caregiver of the voter, or an election official, postal worker, or courier, in each case acting within their official duties.

Last Updated January 20, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 19, 2021, would require people to submit proof of citizenship when registering to vote or when voting for the first time after having registered by mail, if such proof was not included with the mail registration. The bill considers any of the following proof of citizenship:

  • An original or certified copy of a birth certificate establishing United States citizenship,
  • A valid United States passport,
  • A certificate of naturalization or citizenship, or

  • Anything else the board of elections determines establishes United States citizenship.

Last Updated January 25, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 19, 2021, would require the absentee ballot affirmation envelope contain a notice that the voter must sign the envelope.

Last Updated January 25, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 19, 2021, would change New York's automatic voter registration law, enacted December 22, 2020, in ways consistent with a press release issued by Governor Cuomo when he signed the law. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Expand the state entities required to automatically register voters to include the State University of New York.
  • Set staggered deadlines for various agencies to begin automatically registering people ranging from January 1, 2023 to January 1, 2025. Existing law takes effect on January 1, 2023.

  • Change the notice to voters that failure to join a political party excludes them from voting in a primary and remove the requirement that counties prepay postage on the return card that allows automatically registered unaffiliated voters to pick a party. Under existing law, counties must send the prepaid postage return card to such voters within 21 days of their automatic registration.

Last Updated January 25, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 20, 2021, would expand early voting by requiring counties that are otherwise required to open more than one early voting location to open one on at least one state university or community college campus that has at least 2,500 students. If the county is only required to open one early voting location, the bill would require the board of elections to give that county additional discretionary funding for early voting if that county designates any state university or community college campus located in that county as an additional polling place for early voting for at least three consecutive weekdays during the early voting period. Under existing law, early voting locations are open for the entire early voting period and there are no siting requirements specific to state university or community colleges.

Last Updated January 25, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 20, 2021, would prohibit boards of election from using school properties that have instructional space as early voting sites, and would allow school superintendents to refuse to allow boards of election to use non-instructional school buildings as early voting sites.

Last Updated March 9, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 20, 2021, would require residents to provide their Social Security number when registering to vote. New York generally requires residents to provide their DMV number or Social Security number to vote. Those without either form of ID can use a valid photo ID, a current utility bill, bank statement, paycheck, government check or some other government document that shows name and address. Individuals registering online must provide a DMV-issued driver's license, permit, or non-driver ID and the last four digits of their Social Security number.

Last Updated July 22, 2025

This bill, as introduced on January 22, 2021, would change how level 2 and level 3 sex offenders vote by criminalizing their voting in person at a polling place located in a school, but facilitating their voting by mail by adding an excuse tailored to them and placing them on the permanent absentee voter list. The absentee ballot application would be edited to reflect conforming changes. If such a sex offender votes at a polling place sited in a school, they can be convicted of either a new felony or a new misdemeanor, depending on the details. Sex offenders whose polling place is not in a school would still be able to vote in person.

Last Updated August 12, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 22, 2021, would prohibit using any public or private elementary school, secondary school or preschool as a polling place.

Last updated January 25, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on January 22, 2021, would create election crimes relating to impersonating candidates or elected officials and regulate social media. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Add to the existing felony of criminal impersonation, impersonating an elected official or candidate for an elected office with intent to obtain a benefit or injure or defraud another by communication by internet website or electronic means.
  • Repeal an existing misdemeanor relating to fraud in a primary, caucus or convention.
  • Create a new felony, criminalizing fraud in connection with a primary election, caucus or convention. In addition to the felony, violators shall also be subject to a civil penalty for each violation.
  • Requires social media companies to close a social media account within 24 hours of receiving notice alleging that the account is committing criminal impersonation in the first degree or fraud in connection with any primary election, caucus or convention.

  • Empowers the state board of elections to take enforcement actions against a social media company that failed to address a complaint by any elected official or candidate for elected office alleging criminal impersonation or fraud in connection with any primary election, caucus, or convention.

    Last updated January 25, 2021.

This bill, as enacted on December 23, 2022, changes the voter registration deadline to 10 days before any election. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires registration forms returned by mail to be postmarked by the 15th day prior to an election, and received by the 10th day before. Previous law required an application to be postmarked by the 25th day prior to an election and received by the 20th day before.

  • Permits in-person return of a registration form up to 10 days before any election. Under previous law, the general deadline for application return was the 25th day before an election, and in-person return was permitted up to the 10th day before for special elections only.

    Note: The state constitution requires registration to close at least 10 days before an election. While early voting begins 10 days before Election Day, existing law prevents election officials from registering someone to vote at the board of elections on a voting day, and does not provide for registration at a voting location. As a result, the new registration deadline does not create same-day registration on the first day of early voting.

Last Updated March 1, 2023

This bill, as introduced on January 26, 2021, changes the rules relating to challenging voters in three ways. First, it would require people sending mailers to voters for the purpose of later challenging their right to vote to file copies of the mailer, the list of recipients and identifying information relating to the sender with the State Board of Elections within two days of the mailing. Failure to file creates a presumption against using the mailing to challenge a voter. Second, it would require challengers to complete a challenge affidavit for each voter they challenge. Finally, the bill would specify what questions are to be asked of a challenged voter to verify their eligibility.

Last updated January 28, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on January 27, 2021, changes the definition of an election misdemeanor to allow a voter to take a picture of their ballot and share it on social media so long as the photo does not include any other voter or any other voter's ballot. In addition, the bill criminalizes forcing a voter to photograph their ballot or to share such a photograph on social media. This new crime would be a misdemeanor.

Last updated January 28, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on January 27, 2021, would:

  • Expressly include within the felony offense of "misconduct of election officers," the wrongful cancellation of a voter's registration or refusal to allow a voter to cast a ballot due to their inactive status. Under existing law, this offense includes the violation of "any right" under the provisions of the Election chapter.
  • Eliminate a ground for cancelling a voter's registration by deleting the provision that requires cancellation when a voter has not voted in two general elections after being placed in inactive status and the board of elections has not received any information that they reside in the same city or county where they were last registered. The bill would also expressly require that the board of elections verify any of the listed grounds for cancellation before removing a voter.
  • Create an "inactive poll ledger" containing all inactive voters, and require that the board of elections distribute the list to all county election districts. Existing law requires the board to maintain an inactive voter list organized by election district, but does not require distribution of the list.

  • Restore inactive voters to active voter status if they cast a valid affidavit ballot, and require that a valid ballot be counted.

    Last updated August 25, 2021.

This bill would add clarifying language to the New York constitution to provide that every citizen, including those incarcerated in correctional facilities, is eligible to vote. Relatedly, the bill would repeal the portion of the constitution that requires the Legislature to disenfranchise people convicted of bribery or infamous crime.

Last updated February 1, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on January 27, 2021, would create same day registration during early voting and on Election Day. To register, the person would need to provide the proof of identity and residency that is required under federal law for voter registration, which includes numerous non-photo ID options. In addition to that ordinary voter registration requirement, the potential registrant would need to sign an affidavit attesting to their eligibility, their length of residence, and that they had not already voted in the election. If the voter complies with these requirements they may cast a regular ballot. If they cannot provide the ordinary proof of identity and residency to register, they will be allowed to cast an affidavit (provisional) ballot. The affidavit ballot will count if the voter provides the proof of identity and residency needed to register. Under existing law, similar provisions apply to voters who registered by mail but did not provide such documentation as part of their mail application. Note: The New York State Constitution requires people to register 10 days before an election to be eligible to vote in that election, however, the Legislature has undertaken the process to amend the constitution to eliminate that requirement. The process is not complete, but could be by January 1, 2022, the proposed effective date of this bill.

Last updated January 29, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on January 27, 2021, would require the State Board of Elections to study mail ballot elections, voting by phone, and voting by internet, and report back to the Legislature within 24 months of the effective date of the bill. As part of its study, the State Board is authorized to conduct a mail ballot election pilot project.

Last Updated January 29, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 29, 2021, would allow people who are 17 years old to vote in a primary, including a presidential primary, if they will be 18 by the related general election.

Last Updated February 1, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Directs the Queens County Board of Elections to provide language assistance in Bengali, Punjabi and Hindi.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 29, 2021 would require the Queens county board of elections to provide written language assistance in the Bengali, Punjabi and Hindi languages including, but not be limited to, ballots, signs, voter mailings, employee and volunteer training materials and information on such board's website.   • instructions in Bengali, Punjabi and Hindi regarding the criteria and application process for obtaining an absentee ballot, and

    Last updated February 1, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on January 30, 2021, would allow voters to apply for absentee ballots by fax, email, and through an online portal. Voters who apply this way would not be required to submit a paper application with their ballot. Existing law allows for requests by fax, but not by email or internet portal.

Last Updated February 2, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 30, 2021, would designate every court and law enforcement agency, when such entities are issuing licenses to carry, possess, repair or dispose of firearms, as voter registration agencies. In addition, the bill would expand when all voter registration agencies must offer services. Specifically, the agencies would be required to provide voter registration upon "participation in activities or use of facilities of the agency", in addition to existing law's requirement that they offer voter registration upon initial application for services, renewal or recertification for services, and change of address relating to such services.

Last Updated January 9, 2023

This bill, as introduced on January 30, 2021, would create a strict photo ID requirement to vote in person or by mail. Specificially, the bill would require:

  • An in-person voter who did not present ID to complete an affidavit (provisional) ballot. For the ballot to be counted, the voter would have to present acceptable photo ID to the local board of elections within three days.
  • A mail voter to enclose a copy of photo ID with their ballot. If the mail voter lacked current and valid photo ID, the board of elections could count the ballot if they confirmed the validity of the ballot.

  • The Department of Motor Vehicles to issue the basic identification the voter qualifies for free if the voter is eligible for Medicaid.

    The bill defines acceptable photo IDs as:


  • a New York state driver's license or non-driver ID
  • a United States passport
  • an identification card issued by a United States educational institution
  • a United States military identification card
  • a government issued medical card or

  • any identification card issued by the United States or the state of New York.

    The bill would create a limited exception for certain voters not appearing in person. Specifically, if a voter:


  • registered to vote by mail, and when so doing, enclosed a copy of acceptable photo ID, or their driver's license number, state ID number, or last four digits of their Social Security number,
  • is entitled to vote by mail because they are a UOCAVA voter,
  • is entitled to vote other than in person section 3(b)(2)(B)(ii) of the Voting Accessibility for the Elderly and Handicapped Act, or

  • is entitled to vote otherwise than in person under any other federal law,

    Then they are exempt from the ID requirements.

Last Updated August 16, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Proposes a constitutional amendment, relates to the number of senators and the apportionment of Senator districts, provides that each Senator district shall be comprised of one county in its entirety.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 30, 2021, would change how state senate districts are drawn by requiring one senate district with one senator per county, contiguous with the county's borders. Under existing law state senate districts are drawn using census data and the ordinary redistricting process.

Last updated March 5, 2021

This bill, as introduced January 31, 2021, would create no excuse absentee voting and a permanent absentee voter list open to all voters. In addition, voters who apply for absentee ballots would be prohibited from voting in person. Under existing law, an excuse is required to vote, although until January 1, 2022 "illness" in an existing excuse is defined in a way that allows any voter to invoke it during the pandemic. Also under existing law, voting in person takes primacy over voting absentee so that people who return absentee ballots are allowed to cast regular ballots in person. The absentee ballot is simply rejected after Election Day.

Note: New York's constitution requires voters to have an excuse to vote absentee. The Legislature has started the process of amending the constitution to remove this requirement.

Last Updated February 2, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 1, 2021, would provide that, during states of emergency, all voters are eligible to vote absentee and all voters would be automatically sent absentee ballots. Note: The New York constitution Art. II Section 2 requires an excuse related to physical absence, illness or disability. The Legislature has completed its part of the process to amend that provision out of the constitution. To finish amending the constitution, voters must ratify the amendment in November, 2021.

Last Updated August 25, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 1, 2021, would allow the board of elections, upon request, to appoint watchers of a referendum election held at the town or village level. Appointed watchers must be equitably distributed from the pro and anti sides of the referendum.

Last updated February 3, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to increasing the amount of compensation for chairmen, election inspectors and ballot clerks for fire districts elections.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 2, 2021, would increase election worker pay for fire district elections.

Last updated February 3, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on February 2, 2021, would enable voters to cure problems with their affidavit (provisional) ballots. The board of elections must send the voter notice within one day, and if the voter cures the defect within seven days of the notice being sent, the ballot will count.

Last updated February 5, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on February 2, 2021, would make Braille or large print absentee ballots available for any visually impaired voter who requests them at least 30 days before an election. The bill would require related rule making in consultation with experts to ensure the ballots are well designed and to govern the distribution, casting and canvassing of such ballots.

Last Updated February 3, 2021

This bill, as enacted on December 22, 2021, expands the availability of early voting by increasing the number of required early voting locations and expanding weekend early voting hours. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires local boards of elections in counties with at least 500,000 registered voters to open at least one early voting location for each increment of 40,000 voters. In all other counties, the local board of elections must open one early voting site for each increment of 30,000 registered voters, up to a total of 10, unless a different provision of law requires more, and must have at least one. These are modified provisions. The previous version of the bill treated all counties the same and required one early voting site for each increment of 35,000 registered voters. Existing law required one site per 50,000 registered voters up to ten, unless a different provision of law requires more.
  • Expands weekend early voting hours by requiring at least eight hours between 9 a.m. and 8 p.m. on each Saturday, Sunday, and legal holiday in the early voting period. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have expanded voting hours on both weekday evenings and weekends. The weekday expansion would have required voting until 9 p.m. on a third evening at one or more locations and the weekend expansion would have been at least 10 hours between 9 a.m. and 9 p.m. each weekend day. Existing law required two weekday evenings until 9 p.m. at one or more locations, and at least five hours of early voting between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m.

  • Clarifies siting requirements to ensure that the largest city in the county has at least one early voting location, and if the county has no cities, the largest municipality. This is a new provision. Existing law required only the largest municipality to have at least one site.

Last Updated January 4, 2022

This bill, as amended on November 19, 2021, would continue to change the process of registering to vote at DMV by requiring anyone applying to register to vote at DMV to include a Social Security number as part of their application. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Under existing law, Social Security numbers are not required as part of any voter registration process. In addition the bill would alters the drivers' license type that may be obtained by people who do not document their legal right to be in the United States. The amendment related to those provisions.

Last Updated November 22, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 8, 2021, would require locating both an early voting site and an election day polling place on any college or university campus that has three hundred or more voters with active status registered at an address on a contiguous property owed by the college or university.

Last Updated March 8, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 8, 2021, would criminalize as a misdemeanor knowingly distributing voter registration forms with the party affiliation pre-filled.

Last updated February 9, 2021.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 10, 2021, would facilitate poll worker recruitment by allowing full time college students to serve as election workers in the county they go to school even if they are registered to vote in a different county. To be an election worker, the student must:

  • be registered to vote in New York
  • not hold elective office
  • not be a candidate for any public office to be voted for by the voters of the district they would serve, and not be the spouse, parent or child of such a candidate, and

  • be able to speak and read the English language and write it legibly.

    Last updated August 23, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on February 10, 2021, would require boards of election to mail an absentee ballot application to everyone who applied to vote absentee in the previous election, and to create a list of people boards of election must mail an absentee ballot application for each election. Any voter could apply to join that permanent absentee ballot application list.

Last Updated February 12, 2021

This bill, as introduced on Feb. 10, 2021, would permit nonpartisan poll monitors at polling places, in addition to the politically-affiliated "watchers" authorized under existing law. The bill would set out regulations for these nonpartisan poll monitors including the definition of qualified civic organizations and ballot issue committees, a limit of two monitors from each entity, verification and credential requirements, and restrictions on participation by candidates and their family members.

Last updated February 15, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on February 10, 2021, would create a new felony to punish any person or entity, other than the board of elections, who erects, displays or maintains an absentee ballot drop-off box or receptacle.

Last Updated February 12, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 10, 2021, would require voters entering a polling place and voting to wear a mask during the state disaster emergency declared pursuant to Executive Order No. 202 of 2020, which relates to Covid-19. On June 24, 2021, Governor Cuomo issued Executive Order No. 210, which repealed No. 202, rendering this bill moot.

Last updated November 5, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on February 12, 2021, would create same day voter registration, require automatic provision of absentee ballots to all voters, and establish a new centralized voter registration information system. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Establish same day registration, allowing residents to register to vote at their polling place on Election Day. Under existing law, voter registration applications must be delivered in person or postmarked by the 25th day before an election.
  • Establish no-excuse absentee voting, and repeal the existing provisions that require excuses to vote an absentee ballot. Those existing provisions limit absentee voting to voters who expect to be absent from their residence, are ill or admitted to the hospital, or are incarcerated.
  • Require local boards of election to mail an absentee ballot to all registered voters prior to all elections, and to keep records related to issued ballots and voter information. Under existing law, voters must request an absentee ballot.
  • Repeal the existing provision concerning application for a regular absentee ballot, and replace it with provisions that detail the process for requesting that automatic absentee ballot be sent to an address other than the voter's address on file.
  • Make conforming changes to various absentee voting provisions to reflect the elimination of the excuse and application requirements.
  • Require the state board of elections to implement, in a uniform and nondiscriminatory manner, a single, uniform, official, centralized, interactive, computerized statewide voter registration database system. The system would be defined, maintained, and administered at the state level, contain the voter registration lists maintained by each county board of elections, and assign a unique identifier to each legally registered voter. Although counties would be allowed to maintain lists in a parallel system, they would need to facilitate the state's maintenance of the state system.
  • Create a legal presumption that, absent affirmative proof of fraud, special absentee ballots cast by board of election employees are valid.

  • Make minor changes to the requirements for the affidavit required when a voter's information is missing or incorrect on the registration record at the polling place.

    Note: New York's constitution requires voters register a minimum of 10 days before an election and have an excuse to vote absentee. The legislature has completed its part of the process to amend both provisions out of New York's constitution. Voters may ratify or reject the changes November 2, 2021.

Last Updated November 5, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 16, 2021, would allow school officials to request the cancellation of a polling place designation at a school if its use would unreasonably interfere with usual activities for the location. Under existing law, schools are the sole exception to the cancellation request process that applies to all other designated polling sites.

Last updated February 18, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on February 18, 2021, would require the county seat of Seneca County to have at least one location for early voting instead of the most populous municipality in the county. Existing law requires the municipality in each county with the highest population to have at least one location for early voting.

Last Updated April 26, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 22, 2021, would require poll workers to allow attorneys residing in New York and licensed to practice law therein to enter polling places. The bill is amending the section related to poll watchers, and according to the sponsor's memo, is intended to allow attorneys to serve as poll watchers anywhere in the state instead of merely the county in which they are registered. However, the bill does not require attorneys to be appointed poll watchers to enter polling places.

Last updated February 18, 2022.

BILLSUMMARY: Amends the municipal home rule law in relation to the division of a county into districts for the apportionment of members of its local legislative body.
VRLANALYSIS:
On June 9, The Senate passed the Assembly's version of this bill, A 229, sending it to the Governor. As a result, this bill is moot.

This bill, as amended on May 25, 2021, would create new rules for the redistricting of counties outside of counties wholly within a city, namely, outside of New York City, and municipalities.

For county and municipal redistricting, the bill would require the relevant legislature to:

  • Draw single member districts be drawn with as equal population as practicable, and multi-member districts with population proportionate to their numbers in the relevant legislature.

  • Draw all districts so that they comply with federal and state constitutional requirements, and:

    • Do not have the intent or result of denying or abridging the equal opportunity of racial or language minority groups to participate in the political process or to diminish their ability to elect representatives of their choice.
    • Consist of contiguous territory.
    • Are as compact in form as practicable.
    • Do not have the purpose of discouraging competition or favoring or disfavoring incumbents or other particular candidates or political parties. The maintenance of cores of existing districts, of pre-existing political subdivisions including cities, villages, and towns, and of communities of interest shall also be considered. To the extent practicable, no villages, cities or towns except those having more than forty percent of a full ratio for each district shall be divided.
    • Promote the orderly and efficient administration of elections.
      The relevant legislature must consider these criteria in the priority order listed.

    All of these provisions were in the prior version of the bill. However, one criteria in the previous version of the bill was amended out of this version. It would have required the relevant legislature to draw distracts that to the extent practicable, "unite communities defined by actual shared interests, taking account of geographic, social, economic, and other factors that indicate commonality of interest".

    Last updated June 14, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on February 25, 2021, would require boards of election serving counties that have a million or more residents, excluding New York City, to open at least one early voting site in each town or city in the county. As written, the bill would apply to Suffolk and Nassau counties. Opening an early voting site in each town or city in Suffolk County would require ten locations, which is the current minimum required by law, but would require different placement of them than the county used in 2020. Meeting the requirement in Nassau County would not require more than the current statutory minimum. In both counties, the most common political subdivision is a village.

Last Updated March 1, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 26, 2021, would repeal the portions of New York election law that disenfranchise people for being convicted and incarcerated for a felony.

Note: New York's constitution, at Art. II, Section 3, provides that "The Legislature shall enact laws excluding from the right of suffrage all persons convicted of bribery or of any infamous crime." Other bills propose to eliminate this language from the state constitution.

Last updated March 1, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on March 1, 2021, would require the board of elections serving a city with a population of one million or more to provide all the information it provides in English in Haitian Creole, including registration or voting notices, forms, instructions, voting systems, ballot marking devices and ballots in Haitian Creole. Such board of elections would also be required to disseminate citywide a booklet that includes: a voter registration form in English with instructions in Haitian Creole, instructions in Haitian Creole regarding the criteria and application process for absentee voting, and a section with general voter information in Haitian Creole. Finally, such a board of elections must provide one or more Haitian Creole-speaking interpreters at each polling location in election districts in any county that has a population comprised of five percent or more of people who identify as being Haitian according to the most recent United States census.

Last Updated March 3, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 1, 2021, would require a board of elections in a city with a population of over one million to provide the same information in Haitian Creole that it provides in languages other than English on its website. In addition, it would be required to disseminate citywide a booklet that includes: a voter registration form in English with instructions in Haitian Creole, instructions in Haitian Creole regarding the criteria and application process for obtaining an absentee ballot, and a section with general voter information in Haitian Creole including frequently asked questions.

Last Updated March 3, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 3, 2021, would amend the New York constitution to enshrine voting protections. If enacted, no citizen could be denied the right to vote because of his or her failure to comply with any prerequisite for voting or registration for voting requiring him or her to show photo ID or prove citizenship, among other things. In addition, the state and its subdivisions would be prohibited from restricting third-party organizations or individuals from registering voters in good faith.

Last Updated March 5, 2021

This bill, as amended on March 5, 2021, would require the St. Lawrence County board of elections to open an early voting location in the county seat instead of in the most populous municipality in the county. This provision was in the previous version of the bill, the May 19 amendment was not substantive. Existing law authorizes boards of election to open as many early voting sites as they wish, above a statutory floor. The number of required sites is one per 50,000 registered voters, up to a total of 10.

Last Updated May 20, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 8, 2021, would require an early voting location in the county seat of Allegany County instead of in its most populous municipality, as existing law requires. Nonetheless, the local board of elections has the discretion to open an early voting site in the most populous municipality.

Last Updated April 26, 2021

This bill, as enacted on April 26, 2021, allows all voters to vote absentee in a school board election using the illness excuse, by temporarily redefining to include the risks created by the pandemic. The law would self-repeal as of January 1, 2022.

Last Updated June 11, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 11, 2021, would prohibit public school buildings from being used as early voting locations.

Last Updated August 16, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 15, 2021, would create numerous voter protections, including a preclearance procedure, crimes against voter intimidation and suppression, protection against vote dilution, and publicizing a voter's bill of rights. In addition, the bill would require the state board of elections to issue a uniform polling place procedures manual by regulation. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the state and any political subdivision or municipal corporation to seek an attorney general opinion or a declaratory judgment from the state supreme court (New York's trial court) before any voting qualification or prerequisite to voting, or standard, practice, or procedure with respect to voting different from that in force or effect on January 1, 2021, can be enforced. For the change to be enforced, either the court must rule that the change to election law, standard, practice, or procedure neither has the purpose nor will have the effect of denying or abridging the right to vote on account of race or color, religion, gender, gender identity, sexual orientation or disability, or violates the constitution of the state of New York, or the attorney general must decide not to take action to block its enforcement on such grounds.
  • Define and criminalize as a felony voter suppression and voter intimidation, and conspiring to do either.
  • Provide that the willful violation of any of the voter protections is a misdemeanor.
  • Define and prohibit vote dilution.
  • Require the posting in polling places and distribution to voters of a Voter's Bill of Rights, that would inform people they have the right to:
    • Inspect a sample ballot before voting.
    • Cast a ballot if he or she is in line when the polls are closing.
    • Ask for and receive assistance in voting, including assistance in languages other than English where required by federal or state law.
    • Receive a replacement ballot if he or she makes a mistake prior to the ballot being cast.
    • Cast a provisional ballot if his or her eligibility to vote is in question.
    • Vote free from coercion or intimidation by election officers or any other person.
    • Cast a ballot using voting equipment that accurately counts all votes.

  • Require the state board of elections to adopt by regulation a statewide polling place procedures manual that would cover:

    • regulations governing solicitation by individuals and groups at the polling place,
    • procedures to be followed with respect to voters whose names are not on the precinct register,
    • proper operation of the voting system,
    • ballot handling procedures,
    • procedures governing spoiled ballots,
    • procedures to be followed after the polls close,
    • rights of voters at the polls,
    • procedures for handling emergency situations,
    • procedures for handling and processing provisional ballots, and
    • security procedures.

    Last updated March 16, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on March 16, 2021, would allow the governor to suspend or delay an election in a jurisdiction subject to a state or federal disaster emergency. If the election is delayed or suspended, it must be rescheduled as soon as practicable. In addition, in an election in a jurisdiction affected by an emergency within 14 days of the election, voters may vote absentee without further excuse. Finally if a voter appears at the wrong polling place in the right county because of the emergency, they may cast an affidavit (provisional) ballot and have their ballot count for any races they are qualified to vote in.

Last Updated March 18, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 18, 2021, would end felony disenfranchisement in New York and would require the department of corrections, in collaboration with the state and county boards of election, to facilitate inmate voter registration and voting. The incarcerated voting program must include access and assistance with voter registration forms and a mechanism for voting, including, but not limited to, absentee ballots. In addition, upon a person's discharge from a correctional facility or community supervision, the department shall notify them of their right to vote and provide them with a voter registration application and written information distributed by the board of elections on the importance and the mechanics of voting.

Note: New York's constitution Art. 2, Section 3 says "The Legislature shall enact laws excluding from the right of suffrage all persons convicted of bribery or of any infamous crime."

Last Updated March 22, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 18, 2021, would require the board of elections serving any city of one million or more residents to provide Russian interpreters in an election precinct that serves a population at least 5% of whom speak Russian as their first language.

Last updated March 22, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to mandatory training curriculum for election commissioners and key staff of boards of elections and to model poll worker training programs, requires the state board of elections to develop and provide to each county materials for a model poll worker training program which the counties may use to train individuals to serve as poll workers in state and county elections.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 18, 2021, would require the state board of elections to develop a mandatory curriculum for election worker instructors, who, once certified, could then teach election workers. The statewide, standardized program would ensure the election workers learned and could teach:

  • The ability to serve a diverse electorate with complete confidence and respect,
  • Professionalizing the delivery of all election day services,
  • Providing assistance to voters with disabilities and those with limited English language proficiency, ensuring the dignity and privacy of such individuals, and to individuals who are members of racial or ethnic minorities, complete familiarity and comfort with all voting systems in use in poll sites, including ballot marking devices or other systems/services available to voters with disabilities, and

  • The ability to recognize and resolve a variety of issues which may arise in poll sites.

    The bill would further provide that the state board's trainers and all certified poll worker instructors utilize industry-proven training techniques aimed at adult learners including role-based training and hands-on training opportunities using official election day forms and poll site voting systems, and may further include a web-based component and companion video.

    Last updated March 22, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on March 18, 2021, would alter the part of the election code that allows an election to be continued past Election Day as a result of a disaster or emergency. This bill would change the standard for allowing an election to be continued from one based on turn out to one focused on the impossibility of voting due to the disaster or emergency. In addition, the bill would require publicity by press release to media, rather than publication of notice in newspapers, and would qualify the requirement to mail notice to voters by stating it must be "to the extent practicable." Finally, the bill would allow internal political party candidate nominating processes to be postponed up to a week because of a disaster or emergency.

Last updated August 16, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on March 19, 2021, would buttress the existing program for bringing absentee ballots to voters in residential facilities by requiring the board of election to give the voting deputies extra ballots and enabling them to help voters apply for ballots when the deputies don't have enough ballots for all eligible voters who wish to have one.

Last Updated March 23, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 22, 2021, purports to create automatic voter registration at many state and local agencies, create online voter registration, and create same day registration. In 2020 and 2021, New York enacted a substantial automatic registration scheme that covers many of the agencies this bill would involve, enacted an online voter registration law, and began the process of amending the state constitution to enable same day voter registration. Thus many of the provisions of this bill are moot, or cannot yet take effect were the bill to become law. To the extent the provisions are not moot, the bill would:

  • Create automatic voter registration at all public housing authorities listed in article thirteen of the public housing law, the department of corrections and community supervision, the division of military and naval affairs and any agency designated by the state board of elections not otherwise covered. The other agencies the bill identifies are already part of the existing automatic registration law. The existing automatic voter registration law will take effect at various agencies in stages, beginning in 2023 and continuing through 2025.
  • Require online registration to include the ability to receive assistance online, to request future communications by email, and to make updating registration including address and email easy. The existing online registration statute would not prohibit such features, but would not require them. The existing statute gives the State Board of Elections discretion in designing the system. This system is to take effect April 12, 2021, or whenever the State Board says the technology is ready.

  • Create same day registration during early voting and on Election Day.

Last Updated March 23, 2021

This bill, as introduced March 29, 2021, would require the Delaware County board of elections to open the early voting location current law requires to be located in the municipality with the largest population in the county seat instead. Existing law requires one early voting location per 50,000 registered voters, including one in the most populous municipality, but allows county boards of election to site as many early voting locations as they wish.

Last Updated April 26, 2021

This bill, as introduced on April 12, 2021, would authorize all voters to vote absentee without excuse, and would establish a right to cancel one's absentee ballot by voting in person. Under existing law and the New York Constitution, an excuse is required to vote absentee. The Legislature has begun the process of amending the state constitution to remove the excuse requirement. In addition, under existing law, if a person casts an absentee ballot, they are allowed to vote a regular ballot in person and have their absentee ballot set aside.

Last Updated April 13, 2021

This bill, as introduced on April 15, 2021, would allow a person to register to vote at any residence to which the voter maintains a continuous connection with an intent to return, including a second or vacation home.

Last Updated April 16, 2021

This bill was substituted by its Assembly companion, A 6478, on May 12. As a result, this bill is functionally moot, and will no longer advance. A 6478 was passed by the Senate, sending it to the Governor.

This bill, as introduced on April 15, 2021, would require a board of elections to locate an early voting site for a special, primary, or run-off primary election in the municipality with the highest population within the county within which the voters are eligible to vote. Existing law requires an early voting site to be located in the municipality with the highest population. As the bill notes, however, in certain elections it is possible that no voter in such a municipality is eligible to vote.

Last Updated May 14, 2021

On May 19, 2021, this bill was substituted by its Assembly companion, which has identical language. As a result, this bill is functionally moot and will no longer advance.

This bill, as introduced on April 15, 2021, would add a new requirement for educating voters about the relocation of an election day polling place. Specifically, the bill would require local boards of election to post a yellow sign on the door of the old polling place announcing the relocation and the new polling place address. The sign must be posted on or before the opening of the polls on Election Day or the first day of early voting.

Last Updated May 20, 2021

This bill, as introduced on April 15, 2021, would both narrow and expand the exception to the misdemeanor election crime punishing giving voters meat, drink, tobacco, refreshment or provision. The bill would allow gifts of drink, refreshment, or provision worth up to five dollars, provided the gift does not identify the person or entity supplying such provisions. The existing exemption allows gifts of meat, drink, tobacco, refreshment or provision worth up to one dollar, provided the gift does not identify the person or entity supplying such provisions.

Last updated August 16, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on April 19, 2021, would make the Department of Environmental Conservation a voter registration agency for its work issuing hunting and fishing licenses. The bill requires the Department to create integrated forms, requires registration only if a person affirmatively checks a box, requires the Department to retain the record of the potential voter's decision not to register, and requires the Department to submit the forms to the boards of elections in a timely manner consistent with other voter registration agencies.

Last Updated April 21, 2021

This bill, as introduced on April 19, 2021, would require the State Board of Elections to review death data from the Social Security Administration and use it to cancel the registrations of deceased voters. If a voter appears at the polls and asserts they were improperly removed, they may cast a provisional ballot which will count if the error is confirmed.

Last updated October 25, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on April 21, 2021, would require a registrar who is otherwise filing a death certificate to also file it with the board of elections of the county in which the registrar is appointed.

Last updated December 6, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on April 23, 2021, would require the Wayne County board of elections to site an early voting location in the county seat. Under existing law, the Wayne County board of elections may open as many sites as it would like, but must site one early voting location in the municipality with the highest population, not in the county seat.

Last Updated April 26, 2021

On June 9, the Senate replaced this bill with its Assembly companion, A 6046, and then passed A 6046, sending it to the Governor. As a result, this bill is effectively moot.

This bill, as introduced on April 26, 2021, would allow voters to apply for absentee ballots by email, or if offered by the state or local boards of election, through an internet portal, and would not require absentee ballot requests to be signed. The bill would self-repeal at the end of 2021.

Last Updated June 10, 2021

The Senate passed the Assembly version of this bill, A 4186B, sending it to the Governor. As a result, this bill is effectively moot.

This bill, as amended on May 12, 2021, would enable voters to track all aspects of their absentee ballot applications and ballots. The May 12 amendment simply clarified that the tracking system could be integrated with the U.S. Postal Service system, and that local Boards of Elections could launch a non-compliant system before the effective date of the bill, provided that compliant services would be offered when the State Board of Elections launches the system the bill creates. As amended, the bill would:

  • Require the State Board of Elections and local boards of election to create integrated absentee ballot tracking databases so that voters could use either the state site or their local boards' sites, and provide that these systems may also be integrated with the U.S. Postal Service's tracking system. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill did not explicitly authorize the systems to be integrated with the U.S. Postal Service's tracking system.
  • Provide that voters can use the system without creating an account to access it. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Enable voters to learn if their local board of elections:
    • received the voter's request for an absentee ballot, approved or rejected the request, and, if rejected, why. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • mailed or delivered an absentee ballot to such voter for the upcoming election, the date of such mailing or delivery, and if mailed, the date the ballot is expected to be received by the voter. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • received the voter's ballot because it was returned as undeliverable. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • received the voter's completed absentee ballot. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • determined the ballot envelope needs to be cured. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • counted or rejected such voter's completed absentee ballot and, if rejected, why. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

  • Allow local Boards of Elections to launch tracking systems prior to the January 1, 2022 effective date of this bill that do not comply with the provisions of this bill. However, the local systems would be required to provide the services mandated by this bill when the State Board of Elections launches its system, and could meet that requirement by giving the State Board the necessary information. This is a new provision.

Last Updated June 10, 2021

This bill, as introduced on April 28, 2021, would conform mail ballot return deadlines for special ballot types, such as federal write-in ballots, to the deadline for ordinary mail ballots. The existing deadline for ordinary ballots is postmarked by Election Day and received within seven days after. The existing deadline for special ballots is postmarked by the day before Election Day and received within seven days after. This bill would require all ballots to be postmarked by Election Day and received within seven days after.

In addition, the bill would make a temporary change to absentee ballot law to remove the requirement that people who request a ballot using a method other than a paper application must submit a paper application with their returned ballot in order to have their ballot count. The requirement would again be imposed after the provision self-repeals on December 31, 2021.

Last Updated June 10, 2021

This bill, as introduced on April 29, 2021, would require all voters to show ID or enclose it with their mail ballot when they vote in their first federal or state election. All of the types of ID that would meet this requirement prove citizenship. Specifically, first time voters would have to show, or include with their mail ballot, one of these:

  • current and valid United States passport,
  • New York state issued REAL ID,
  • New York state Enhanced ID,
  • social security card,
  • birth certificate, or

  • nationalization papers.

    If a voter failed to include one of these with their mail ballot, or did not bring one to vote in person, the voter could complete an affidavit (provisional) ballot that would count if it were otherwise valid and the voter was an eligible voter.

Last Updated May 3, 2021

On June 9, 2021, the Senate passed the Assembly version of this bill, A6970A, sending it to the Governor. This bill is now moot.

This bill, as amended on May 21, 2021, would create an online portal through which qualified voters could apply for an absentee ballot, and would change the deadline to receive an absentee ballot in the mail, as opposed to picking it up in person. The May 21 amendment did not substantively change the bill from its May 19th version. As amended on May 19, the bill would:

  • Change the deadline to apply to receive a ballot in the mail to received by the board of elections by the fifteenth day before the election, instead of existing law's deadline of mailed to the board of elections by the seventh day before the election. The deadline to pick up a ballot in person, including through an agent, would remain the day before the election. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

  • Create an absentee ballot application portal with certain features. It would:

    • enable a person to upload their signature, and if none is uploaded, would enable the system to pull the voter's signature from DMV or other records, if it is there.
