This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • provide reasonable accommodations to improve accessibility for persons with disabilities and shall be compatible for use with standard online accessibility assistance tools for persons with visual, physical or perceptive disabilities. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • provide the personal online absentee ballot application in any language required by the federal Voting Rights Act of 1965 in any county in the state. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • be integrated with the state board of elections, such that a voter can apply through the state board of elections' website or the local board of elections' website. This is a new provision.

Last Updated June 10, 2021

This bill, as introduced on May 4, 2021, would require the Steuben County board of elections to open an early voting site in the county seat. Boards of elections can open as many more as they choose.

Last Updated May 10, 2021

This bill, as introduced on May 19, 2021, would increase the maximum number of voters per election district from 1,150 to 2,000.

Note, on June 2 the Senate voted to approve this bill's Assembly companion, A 7478, thereby rendering this bill moot. It will not advance further.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to redistricting of congressional, senate and assembly districts, relates to the submission of a plan for redistricting of congressional, senate and assembly districts.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on November 24, 2021, provides that, if the redistricting commission has not voted on a Congressional redistricting plan or plans by January 15, 2022, then the commission must give the legislature all the plans, draft plans, and data that the commission has produced and the legislature will create its own plans. Existing law did not address what happens if the redistricting commission fails to timely submit plans.

Last updated December 30, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on August 20, 2021, would shift election authority by allowing the state board of elections to remove a local board of elections commissioner for any willful violation or neglect of duty, or willfully disobeying any law, decision, order, settlement, rule or regulation of the state board of elections. Under existing law, only the Governor may remove a local commissioner for cause, using the same process as removing a sheriff for cause. The bill also changes the term of election commissioners from two to four years and makes small changes to their appointment process, issues Voting Rights Lab does not track.

Last updated October 21, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on September 8, 2021 would require voters to return absentee ballots earlier and would require in-person voters who are eligible to complete affidavit (provisional) ballots to show ID before receiving an affidavit (provisional) ballot. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require absentee ballots to be postmarked by the first day of early voting, and ballots returned by mail that lack a postmark to be received by Election Day. Existing law deems ballots postmarked by Election Day and received within seven days thereafter timely, and allows ballots returned by mail without a postmark to be received by the day after Election Day.
  • Require in-person voters who did not provide identification when registering to vote to show one of the types of identification needed to complete registration before receiving an affidavit ballot. Under existing law, voters who show such ID vote a regular ballot, and the bill would not resolve this conflict.

  • Require all other voters who are eligible to complete affidavit (provisional) ballots to show an ID sufficient to register to vote before receiving the affidavit ballot. Under existing law, voters do not need to show such ID before receiving the ballot.

    The bill does not change what ID types are acceptable, except that it requires certain types to be printed and dated within 120 days of the election. Acceptable ID includes:


  • a driver's license or department of motor vehicles non-driver photo ID card or other current and valid photo identification, or

  • if printed and dated within 120 days of the election, a copy of a current utility bill, bank statement, government check, paycheck or other government document that shows the name and address of the voter.

Last Updated September 9, 2021

This bill, as amended on February 1, 2022, would narrow and expand an existing misdemeanor aimed at preventing someone from bribing voters to allow unbranded gifts of water, soft drinks, snacks, or other refreshments of nominal value to people in polling places or in line to vote without regard to a specific dollar amount. Under existing law, people cannot give refreshments to anyone in a polling place unless they are worth $1 or less. The existing misdemeanor does not address voters in line outside of a polling place.

Last updated February 3, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on October 20, 2021, would allow people living overseas in a U.S. territory or possession who were domiciled in New York before moving overseas to vote in federal elections as a New York resident, even if they are also registered to vote in the U.S. territory or possession in which they reside.

Last Updated October 21, 2021

This bill, as introduced on October 27, 2021, would require the board of elections to create a website and mobile application that allows voters to track their mail ballots. The website and application would not require a voter to create an account to use it, and would allow the voter to learn that the board of elections:

  • received the voter's request for an absentee ballot,
  • approved or rejected such request, if and, if rejected, why,
  • mailed or delivered an absentee ballot to the voter, including the ability to see the status of the mailed absentee ballot by United States postal service intelligent mail barcode or successor technology,
  • received the voter's completed absentee ballot, and

  • determined that the voter's completed absentee ballot was invalid, and, if so, why.

    The bill would require the information in the website and app to be updated daily.

Last Updated October 28, 2021

This bill, as enacted on January 21, 2022, permits voters to vote by absentee ballot due to risks posed by COVID-19 through December 31, 2022. The COVID-19 excuse in effect in 2020 and 2021 under existing law automatically repealed on January 1, 2022. The bill also enables voters in village elections to invoke the Covid-19 risk excuse through the end of 2022.

Note: This bill follows in the wake of voters' rejection of a constitutional amendment that would have allowed the Legislature to enact no-excuse absentee voting.

Last Updated August 29, 2022

This bill, as introduced on December 15, 2021, would prohibit localities from expanding the electorate to include anyone not eligible to vote in state elections, which would include noncitizens. In addition, the bill would protect eligible persons by prohibiting the abridgment of their rights to register to vote or vote by the action of a county, city, town or village, including by the enactment of local law.

Existing law has no comparable provisions, however, the bill was introduced soon after New York City granted non-citizens the ability to vote in local elections.

Last Updated December 16, 2021

This bill, as enacted on March 26, 2022, extends the temporary excuse for absentee voting in school district elections due to the risk of COVID-19, through January 1, 2023. The existing provision for this temporary absentee excuse expired on January 1, 2022.

Last Updated July 20, 2022

This bill, as introduced on December 27, 2021, would require the Warren County Board of Elections to open an early voting site in the county seat. Under existing law, the Board must open an early voting site in the municipality with the greatest population instead. Under both the bill and existing law, the Board could choose to open more than the required number of locations.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on September 29, 2021, addresses public participation in congressional redistricting, along with numerous other provisions that are unrelated to election law. Regarding redistricting, the bill:

  • Requires the existing Ohio redistricting commission to set up a website that allows the public to:
    • Submit a proposed congressional district plan.
    • Access the federal decennial census data necessary to create a proposed congressional district plan.
    • View proposed congressional district plans submitted by members of the public.

  • Requires a plan submitted by a member of the public to contain visual representations of the proposed congressional districts.

  • Requires the co-chairpersons of the Ohio redistricting commission to notify the members of the Ohio redistricting commission whenever a proposed plan is submitted by a member of the public, and to post it on the commission's web site for the public to view. These are new provisions that were not in the previous version of the bill.

This bill, as enacted on June 30, 2021, is the general appropriations bill. In elections-related provisions, the bill:

  • Prohibits a public official to settle a lawsuit in any way that nullifies, suspends, enjoins, alters, or contradicts any provision of the Ohio Code.

 

A provision that was line-item vetoed by the Governor would have also allowed state legislative leaders to intervene in cases challenging the constitutionality of a state law or claiming that federal law preempts a state law, and in cases challenging state legislative and congressional district maps.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended December 12, 2022, would make various changes to early voting and the mail ballot voting process. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Change the early voting period and ID verification process. The bill would:
    • Shorten the early voting period by one day, by ending early voting on the Sunday before Election Day rather than Monday, as offered under existing state policy. The six hours that in-person absentee ballot voting had previously been available on that Monday would be redistributed through the rest of the period. The bill would also codify specific days and hours of early voting for various types of elections, generally following existing availability under Secretary of State policy directives (existing statutory law requires early voting at each local board office, but does not specify days/times of availability).
  • Specify that for voters who provide their driver's license or last four digits of their social security number to prove their identity when early voting, election officials must verify that the information matches the voter's registration file. Existing law permits early voters to use these ID numbers, but does not have an express requirement that the number be verified at the time of voting.
  • Change the process for requesting a mail ballot ("absent voter ballot"). The bill would:
    • Move the general deadline for domestic and UOCAVA voters to apply for a mail ballot by any method to the close of business on the seventh day before Election Day. Under existing law, applications must be received by noon on the third day before an election, or if delivered in person, by 6 p.m. on the last Friday before.
    • Create an online application process for mail ballots. A voter applying online would be required to provide two forms of identification: a driver's license number or state ID number, and the last four digits of their social security number. The bill would leave in place the requirement that written applications require only a single form of identification.
    • Require individuals who request a mail ballot in writing to use an official application form promulgated by the secretary of state. Under existing law, any written application is accepted if all required information is included.
    • Require voters applying for mail ballots with a paper application to provide an Ohio DL/ID number if they have one. Voters without a state ID would provide the last four digits of their Social Security number. Voters without either number would provide a copy of acceptable voter ID. Existing law allows voters to choose which form of ID they will provide with a mail ballot application.
    • Prohibit any public official or employee from paying for the return postage of a mail ballot application form. Existing law prohibits local boards of election only from providing return postage for a mail ballot application.
  • Change aspects of returning and processing mail ballots. The bill would:
    • Limit the board of elections in each county to providing a single location for the in-person return of mail ballots, which must be located at the office of the board. If the board has multiple locations in a county, only one of the offices may be designated.The board may place a single drop box outside of the office, which must be under constant video surveillance and available at all times from the day after the close of registration through 7:30 p.m. on Election Day. Existing law has been interpreted by an Ohio appeals court to permit the board of elections to establish multiple such locations for personal return. The bill additionally clarifies that existing prohibitions on anyone other than a relative of the voter or an employee of the post office possessing another person's mail ballot apply to a person personally delivering a mail ballot to the board of elections.
    • Change the receipt deadline for properly postmarked mail ballots to the seventh day after an election. Under existing law, ballots that are postmarked by the day before Election Day are counted if they are received by the tenth day after Election Day. The bill would also move the date the board of elections begins counting late-arriving and cured absentee ballots, from the eleventh day after Election Day to the eighth day. The timing for completing the count would be moved earlier accordingly.
    • Prohibit any public official or employee from paying for the return postage of a mail ballot. Existing law prohibits local boards of election only from providing return postage for mail ballots.
    • Require the board of elections in each county to begin processing and verifying mail ballots before the close of polls on Election Day, though the ballots still could not actually be counted until the polls close. Existing law permits, but does not require, processing before the end of the voting period.
    • Repeal a provision of law under which an overseas or military voter's absentee ballot that is placed inside the return envelope but not inside the identification envelope may be placed inside the identification envelope by an election official to ensure the ballot is counted. It is unclear whether the ballot of any person voting an absentee ballot who incorrectly places their ballot inside the return envelope in this manner would be counted under the bill.
  • Create a new felony offense for unauthorized third-party return of a mail ballot.

  • Remove the requirement that high school student precinct officers must be enrolled in their senior year of school to serve. The bill leaves in place the requirements that they be 17 years old, U.S. citizens, and a resident of the county.

    The bill also contains additional provisions related to aspects of election law that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

    The previous version of the bill contained provisions that were amended out of the current version. These provisions would have:


  • Changed various aspects of voter registration. Specifically, provisions would have:
    • Expanded options for initiating and renewing voter registration by creating opt-in "automated voter registration" related to transactions with the registrar of motor vehicles, and creating new procedures for voters to make address changes on their registration at various state agencies, online, and polling places (with effective date after the current election). Provisions would have also established that for voters who submit multiple registration forms, the most recent form will be the effective one.
    • Required election officials to treat a new registration form indicating that a voter has moved to a new county as authorization to cancel the old registration. Existing law requires a voter to complete a separate form to authorize cancellation of the old registration.
  • Changed rules related to return and verification of mail ballots. Specifically, provisions would have:
    • Allowed county boards of elections to provide no more than three drop boxes on the premises of the county board's office during the 10 days immediately before Election Day only.
    • Required election officials to reject absentee ballots that are returned without the inner identification envelope.
    • Required election officials to count provisional ballots cast by voters if the voter's address or signature in the voter registration system does not match the information on the provisional ballot affidavit if the voter's registration was updated through the automated voter registration system and the voter's information prior to the update matches the information provided by the voter with the provisional ballot. Similarly, the previous version of the bill would have required election officials to remake ballots of voters who voted in the wrong precinct due to an error of the automated system to allow their votes for offices for which they were eligible to vote to count.
  • Changed rules related to voting sites and accessibility. Provisions would have:
    • Established curbside voting for early voting and Election Day voting locations for voters with disabilities that prevent them from entering a polling location without endangering their health. The bill would also have expanded curbside voting eligibility to all voters when the governor declares a state of emergency.
    • Increased accessibility for individuals with disabilities at county boards of elections and polling locations.
  • Changed procedures related to address confirmation. Provisions would have required election officials to review National Change of Address (NCOA) information in the first quarter of each year and to send an address confirmation notice to individuals identified as having changed address. The previous version of the bill would also have changed the requirements for a voter to avoid cancellation of registration after receiving an address confirmation notice.
  • Made changes to voter ID procedures. Provisions would have allowed voters to use an electronic copy of a bank statement or utility bill as voter ID. The previous version of the bill also made numerous amendments to allow a person to use a state ID card number for the same identification purposes they can currently use a driver's license number (voter registration, absentee ballot applications, etc.).

Last Updated January 19, 2023

This bill, as introduced on May 11, 2021, would make numerous changes to Ohio election law. The bill would:

  • Require county election officials to send mail ballots to all active registered voters between 14-20 days before Election Day for all elections. Voters who have requested their ballot to be sent to an address outside Ohio will have their ballot sent 14-29 days before Election Day.
  • Eliminate the requirement for voters to provide an ID number or copy of ID when returning a mail ballot. Election officials will continue to verify mail ballots through signature comparison.
  • Requires election officials to provide prepaid return postage for mail ballots.
  • Requires all mail ballots to be returned by the close of polls on Election Day. Existing law allows election officials to accept ballots postmarked by the day before Election Day if they are received no later than 10 days after Election Day.
  • Require all mail ballot to have a pre-printed tracking number. The voter can use the tracking number on a website provided by election officials to track when the ballot is received by the board of elections, whether the ballot has an issue and, if so, if the cure addendum has been filed, whether the board has accepted or rejected the ballot, and when the ballot is counted.
  • Change the process for curing problems with mail ballots. The voter would be notified of an issue with their mail ballot within two days of discovery of the issue. Notification can occur by mail, email, or text. The voter may cure by providing a cure addendum that includes the voter's driver's license or state ID number, last four digits of their Social Security number, or a copy of valid voter ID no later than 10 days after Election Day. Existing law sets the deadline for cure at seven days after Election Day.
  • Allow election officials to use computer software for signature verification of mail ballots. Ballots with signatures flagged as non-matching will be reviewed by election officials.
  • Repeal existing law requiring voters who are issued mail ballots to cast a provisional ballot if voting in person. A mail ballot cast by a voter would be rejected if the voter's record shows that the voter cast a ballot in person.
  • Allow eligible voters who are unable to travel to a voting location due to a disability, confinement in jail, or a hospitalized child to apply for assistance with mail voting no later than noon on the third day before Election Day. For such applications, election officials will send a bipartisan team of election workers to the voter to administer mail voting.
  • Require counties to provide "voter service polling centers" at which voters who reside in the county may vote in person, obtain mail ballots, and return mail ballots.
  • Establish requirements for the minimum number of voter service polling centers (VSPC) a county must provide:
    • For a county with at least 250,000 active registered voters, the county must provide one VSPC for every 75,000 active registered voters between the 15th and fifth days before Election Day, one VSPC for every 20,000 active registered voters between the fourth and second day before Election Day, and one VSPC for every 12,000 active registered voters on the day before Election Day and Election Day.
    • For a county with at least 37,500 but fewer than 250,000 active registered voters, the county must provide one VSPC for every 75,000 active registered voters between the 15th and fifth days before Election Day, one VSPC for every 20,000 active registered voters between the fourth day and the last day before Election Day, and one VSPC for every 12,000 active registered voters on Election Day.
    • For a county with at least 10,000 but fewer than 37,500 active registered voters, the county must provide at least one VSPC during the 15 days before Election Day and at least three VSPCs on Election Day.
    • For a county with fewer than 10,000 active registered voters, the county must provide at least one VSPC beginning 15 days before Election Day through Election Day.
  • Allow counties to discontinue the provision of precinct-based polling locations no later than 90 days before an election.
  • Require all counties to discontinue the provision of precinct-based polling locations after the first statewide general election in an even-numbered year at which less than 50% of all votes are cast at precinct-based polling locations.
  • Require polling locations to post notices including a sample ballot, dates/times/locations of in-person voting opportunities, and rules concerning provisional voting.
  • Require counties to provide drop boxes for the return of mail ballots that are available 24 hours a day beginning on the 15th day before Election Day. The bill establishes a minimum number of drop boxes for counties:
    • Counties with at least 250,000 active registered voters must provide one drop box for every 12,500 active registered voters.
    • Counties with at least 37,500 but fewer than 250,000 active registered voters must provide one drop box for every 15,000 active registered voters.
    • Counties with at least 15,000 but fewer than 37,500 active registered voters must provide at least two drop boxes.
    • Counties with fewer than 10,000 active registered voters must provide at least one drop box.
  • Change procedures concerning provisional ballots. All provisional ballots would have a tracking number the voter may use to track the status of the ballot. Voters will be notified if the provisional ballot affirmation is incomplete. The voter may cure the issue with the provisional ballot affirmation by submitting an addendum with the missing information that includes the voter's driver's license or state ID number, last four digits of the voter's Social Security number, or a copy of valid voter ID no later than 10 days after Election Day. Election officials may use computer software to compare the voter's signature on the provisional ballot affirmation with the voter's signature in registration records to verify provisional ballots.
  • Require election officials to notify voters if mail ballot applications are incomplete to allow them an opportunity to correct the application.
  • Require election officials to compare information obtained from the National Change of Address (NCOA) program with the statewide voter registration list on a monthly basis. If information obtained through NCOA suggests the voter has moved to another county in Ohio, the voter's registration would be automatically updated and the voter would be sent an acknowledgment notice with instructions for declining the registration update. If information obtained through NCOA suggests the voter has moved to another state, the voter would be sent an address confirmation notice.
  • Allow voters whose registration addresses were updated automatically due to information obtained from NCOA to cast a provisional ballot in the correct voting location for their residential address and to correct the erroneous registration with the information on the provisional ballot affirmation. The bill would also create a safe harbor to prevent individuals whose addresses are updated automatically but incorrectly from prosecution for fraudulent registration unless the voter knowingly takes action to register in the wrong location.
  • Allow individuals to register to vote and update their voter registration or party affiliation by:
    • Submitting a registration form in person at a voter registration agency, probate court, or court of common pleas
    • Submitting a registration form by mail
    • Registering through the online voter registration portal
    • Completing a form at a voting location.
  • Require election officials to send an acknowledgment notice to newly registered voters or voters who update their registration or party affiliation. The acknowledgment notice will inform the voter if the registration form is incomplete and provide instructions to resolve the issue.
  • Repeal existing provisions that require county officials to cancel the registration of voters that move to another county in Ohio.
  • Require voters to select a political party affiliation, or choose to be unaffiliated, when registering to vote. Currently registered voters would be affiliated automatically with the party of the primary in which they have voted in the previous two years.
  • Allow a voter to vote in a party primary only if the voter is registered as affiliated with the party. Voters may change party affiliation at the polling location. Party candidates must also be registered as affiliated with the party with which they wish to affiliate on the ballot.
  • Provide a space on voter registration applications for an applicant to provide a phone number and email address.
  • Make a voter's party affiliation and active status publicly available information.
  • Allow participants in the address confidentiality program to change their party affiliation with the program application. The bill would also prohibit poll observers to observe the verification of ballots of program participants.
  • Require polling place officials to maintain mail ballots returned to polling locations separately. At the end of each voting day, two poll workers, one affiliated with each major political party, will transport the returned mail ballots to the office of the county board.
  • Create a pilot program for UOCAVA voters to submit mail ballots electronically.
  • Require high school election workers to state a political party affiliation. The bill would also limit the number of election workers in special question elections or single party primaries.
  • Add affiliation with a political party whose principles a voter does not support to the list of conduct that can constitute election falsification under Section 3599.11. The bill would add bribery to induce someone to affiliate or refrain from affiliating with a political party to election-related bribery prohibited under the Code. The bill would also add tampering with a drop box to the conduct prohibited by Section 3599.24.
  • Create a fifth degree felony for reckless disclosure of a vote count before 7:30 p.m. on Election Day.
  • Elevate the severity of numerous election-related offenses from a fifth degree felony to a fourth degree felony. The bill also elevates the severity of a second or subsequent election-related offense from a fourth degree felony to a third degree felony.
  • Change deadline for the appointment of certain observers.
  • Change the questions election officials are required to ask voters who are challenged due to their citizenship status.
  • Change procedures concerning voting equipment, interpreters, counting and certification, electioneering, preservation of election materials, and filling candidate and office vacancies.

BILLSUMMARY: Delineates the public records, public meetings, and other requirements with which the Ohio Redistricting Commission, the General Assembly, and the Legislative Task Force on Redistricting, Reapportionment, and Demographic Research must comply during the redistricting process, makes an appropriation, declares an emergency.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on May 18, 2021, would provide a framework for public participation in the congressional and state legislative redistricting process. The bill would:

  • Require the redistricting commission to hold at least one hearing per week and to issue a weekly progress report of the drawing of state legislative maps. The commission would begin holding hearings at least three weeks before any vote to approve final maps. The commission would create a website that includes the same population and redistricting data used by the commission to allow members of the public to create and submit legislative maps and to provide written comment. The records of the commission would be public records. The commission would provide at least 72 hours notice before any public hearing. Hearings must be held in public locations that are ADA compliant and accessible by public transportation. Hearings must also allow for virtual testimony.
  • Require state legislative leaders for both parties to hold at least one hearing per week and to issue a weekly progress report of the drawing of congressional maps. The joint legislative committee on redistricting would begin holding hearings at least three weeks before any vote to approve final maps. The committee would be composed of an equal number of majority party and minority party members. The records of the committee would be public records. The committee must allow for virtual testimony at hearings and must develop a system to accept proposed congressional maps from the public.
  • Require the legislative redistricting task force to provide at least 72 hours notice before any meeting or hearing. All task force meetings would be open to the public. The records of the task force would be public records.

Last updated May 19, 2021.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on July 27, 2021, would repeal recently enacted provisions recently that limit authority to settle litigation and administer elections. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Repeal statutes that prohibit a public official to accept private donations for election administration.
  • Repeal provisions that prohibit a public official to settle a lawsuit in any way that alters, suspends, enjoins, or contradicts any provision of the Ohio Code.

Last updated March 3, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on August 12, 2021, would make extensive changes to Ohio elections law.

The bill would restrict types of ID a voter may provide to be able to vote in person and would require a voter to provide a copy of such ID with a voter registration application or an application to vote by mail. The bill would:

  • Define "photo identification" as: 1) an unexpired Ohio driver's license, commercial driver's license, or state ID card showing the current or former address of the voter, or 2) an expired Ohio driver's license, commercial driver's license, or state ID card accompanied by an unexpired military ID card.
  • Requires registration applicants to provide all of: an Ohio driver's license or state ID number, the last four digits of their Social Security number, and a copy of the front and back of a form of photo identification as defined above. Online registration applicants will need to upload the copy of photo ID.
  • Require voters casting a ballot in person to show photo identification or an unexpired U.S. passport. Voters with a religious objection to being photographed may sign an affidavit to that effect and may cast a ballot without showing photo ID.
  • Require mail ballot voters to provide their Ohio driver's license or state ID number, the last four digits of their Social Security number, and a copy of the front and back of a form of photo identification on mail ballot applications and on mail ballot identification envelopes.
  • Require third parties returning voter registration applications and mail ballots to show photo identification.

The bill would limit voting by mail to voters with a qualifying excuse and limit methods of mail ballot return. The bill would:

  • Require voters to have one of these qualifying excuses to be eligible to vote by mail:
    • Disability, infirmity, or illness that prevents the voter from safely traveling to the polls
    • Absence from the county during the period for in-person absentee voting or on Election Day
    • Confinement following a misdemeanor conviction or while awaiting a trial for a felony or misdemeanor
    • Confidential voter record
  • Prohibit the use of drop boxes for mail ballot return. Ballots returned to a drop box would not be counted.
  • Require voters or third parties returning mail ballots to show photo ID. Third parties may return no more than three ballots. Existing law limits third party return to certain family members of a voter, but places no limits on the number of ballots a third party may return.
  • Prohibit local or state election officials from sending unsolicited mail ballot applications to voters. Existing law allows the Secretary of State to send mail ballot applications to all voters for general elections.
  • Prohibit election officials, political parties, non-governmental entities, or individuals from sending unsolicited mail ballots to voters.
  • Prohibit state and local election officials from pre-filling any information on mail ballot applications.
  • Require election officials to provide mail ballots to voters by mail and not in person except for limited circumstances.
  • Require mail ballot applicants to use the form developed by the Secretary of State.
  • Require voters who applied for or cast a mail ballot who wish to vote in person to cast a provisional ballot.

The bill would decrease the number of days in the early voting (in-person absentee) period in phases over time. The bill would:

  • Allow voters to cast in-person absentee ballots at the office of the county board of elections during the 14 days before Election Day for elections conducted prior to January 1, 2023. Existing law allows voters to begin casting in-person absentee ballots 28 days before Election Day.
  • Allow voters to cast in-person absentee ballots at the office of the county board of elections during the seven days before Election Day for elections conducted after January 1, 2023.
  • Prohibit election officials from tabulating in-person absentee ballots before the close of polls on Election Day.

The bill would establish new guidelines for voting equipment and ballot tabulation. The bill would:

  • Require the hardware and software for all voting and tabulation equipment to be manufactured in the USA. Equipment manufactured by foreign-owned companies would be prohibited from use in Ohio elections.
  • Require the source and object code for all voting and tabulation equipment to be available for public inspection. Beginning January 1, 2023, all equipment must implement blockchain technology to create an unalterable record of the equipment's activity.
  • Require logic and accuracy testing for each piece of voting and tabulation equipment. The testing must be uniform for all ballot types and the results must be reported to the Secretary of State.
  • Require auto-tabulation equipment to date and time stamp each ballot scanned.
  • Require all formatting and coding of election equipment to be conducted by bipartisan teams.
  • Prohibit the connection of voting or tabulation equipment to the internet. The bill would make the act of connecting such equipment to the internet a fourth degree felony.
  • Require the Secretary of State to develop guidance for the identification and interpretation of recurring errant marks on optical scan ballots.

The bill would also:

  • Allow a voter who moves to a new address within the same precinct but fails to update their registration records prior to the deadline to cast an absentee ballot in person at the office of the county board of elections.
  • Allow a voter who moves to a new address in a different precinct in the same county or in a different county but fails to update their registration records prior to the deadline to cast a provisional ballot at the office of the county board of elections during the time period that in-person absentee voting is available.
  • Require voters casting a ballot in person on Election Day to sign the precinct poll book. Existing law requires the voter to write their name and address in the poll book.
  • Allow counties to appoint registered voters and high school students from adjoining counties as precinct election officials. The bill would also limit precinct election officials to seven hours of work in a day.
  • Require motor vehicle registrars to provide free state IDs to any applicant. Existing law requires registrars to provide free state IDs to unemployed applicants and veterans with service-connected disabilities rated at 100 percent.

  • Require drivers' licenses and state ID cards to display the citizenship status of the holder.

Last Updated January 27, 2022

This bill, as enacted on January 6, 2023, tightens voter ID requirements for most in-person and mail voters, restricts mail voting, limits ballot drop-off locations, and shortens the early voting period, among other changes. Specifically, the bill:

  • Restricts acceptable forms of voter ID for in-person and mail voters by:
    • Limiting the types of accepted voter ID to only an unexpired (1) Ohio driver's license or state ID card, including probationary or provisional licenses, (2) US passport, or (3) US military ID, Ohio National Guard ID, or US Dept. of Veterans Affairs card. Under previous law, acceptable voter ID was defined as any unexpired ID issued by the state or federal government that included the voter's name, photo, and current address.
    • Prohibiting the use of alternative voter ID through a utility bill, bank statement, government check, paycheck, or other government document containing the person's name and address. Previous law permitted this alternative form of ID for voter registration, in-person voting, provisional ballot voting, mail ballot applications, and mail ballot voting.
    • Requiring in-person voters who lack an accepted form of voter ID and must vote a provisional ballot, to provide required ID at the office of the board of elections no later than the fourth day after Election Day for the ballot to be counted. Previous law permitted these voters to validate their provisional ballot by providing their driver's license or state ID number, or the last four digits of their Social Security number on the ballot, or providing an accepted form of photo or non-photo ID within seven days of the election. The change in deadline applies to challenged voters, as well. Voters who lack required ID due to sincere religious objection to being photographed are permitted to submit an affidavit to have their provisional ballot counted.
    • Requiring that a voter applying for or voting a mail ballot (known as an "absent voter's ballot" in Ohio) provide their driver's license number, a copy of a photo ID, or the last four digits of their social security number. Under previous law, these voters were able to provide other forms of non-photo identification such as a utility bill, bank statement, government check, paycheck, or other government document containing their name and address, and state ID numbers were not expressly accepted.
  • Waives the fee for the initial issuance or renewal of a state ID card issued by the Bureau of Motor Vehicles for persons 17 years of age or older and clarifies that in any circumstance under which a voter can use an Ohio driver license number for purposes of identification, a state ID card identification number could also be used. Under previous law, only disabled veterans were eligible for free ID cards.
  • Restricts the mail voting period and application process by:
    • Moving the deadline to apply for a mail ballot ("absent voter ballot") to the close of business on the seventh day before Election Day. Under existing law, the general application deadline was noon on the third day before an election, and the extended deadline for applications made in person was 6 p.m. on the Friday before an election.
    • Expressly prohibiting any public office, official, or employee from providing an unsolicited mail ballot application, other than specified authority for the Secretary of State, and prohibiting these entities from prepaying return postage for a mail ballot application or completed ballot. Previous law prohibited only an election board from prepaying postage for mail ballots and applications.
    • Requiring the Secretary of State to keep extensive statistics about the issue of unsolicited mail ballot applications, for distributions made under existing requirements for a specific legislative budget allocation. Previous law required the budget allocation for these mailings, but did not require data collection.
    • Requiring an applicant for a mail ballot to use an official application form promulgated by the Secretary of State, and making conforming changes for rejection and notice to a voter for applications that are not made on the form. Under previous law, applications were accepted in any form, as long as all the required information was included.
  • Makes changes to the return and verification of mail ballots by:
    • Requiring a mail ballot to arrive at the office of the board of elections by the fourth day after Election Day in order to be counted. Under previous law, as long as the ballot was postmarked by the day before Election Day, it could arrive at the office as late as the tenth day after Election Day.
    • Requiring voters to cure a deficiency of their mail ballot envelope by the fourth day after Election Day. Previous law permitted corrections through the seventh day after Election Day.
    • Limiting the board of elections in each county to providing a single location for the personal return of absentee ballots, which must be located at the office of the board. If the board has multiple locations in a county, only one of the offices may be designated. The board may place a single drop box outside of the office, which may only be open to receive ballots during hours the board's office is open and must be under constant video surveillance, with video available to the public. The bill also prohibits the opening of a drop box or handling of its contents by anyone other than a bipartisan team of election officials, and requires reports to the Secretary of State about the number of returned ballots, which must then be posted on the agency's website. Previous law was interpreted by an Ohio appeals court to permit the board of elections to establish multiple such locations for personal delivery. The bill additionally clarifies that previous prohibitions on anyone other than a relative of the voter or an employee of the post office possessing another person's absentee ballot apply to a person personally delivering an absentee ballot to the board of elections.
    • Requiring the board of elections in each county to begin processing and verifying absentee ballots before the close of polls on Election Day. Under previous laws, this process is permitted, but not required. Ballots still may not actually be counted until the polls close.
    • Repealing a provision of law under which an overseas or military voter's absentee ballot that is placed inside the return envelope but not inside the identification envelope may be placed inside the identification envelope by an election official to ensure the ballot is counted. It is unclear whether the ballot of other voters who incorrectly place their ballot inside the return envelope in this manner will be counted going forward.
  • Creates a new felony offense for unlawful return of another individual's mail ballot.
  • Makes changes to the in-person early voting process by:
    • Shortening the early voting period by one day, eliminating the Monday before Election Day. The six hours that in-person mail ballot voting had previously been available on that Monday will be redistributed through the rest of the period.
    • Expressly permitting the use of voting machines or tabulators for ballots cast during in-person early voting.
  • Permits a voter who is physically unable to enter a polling place to vote a ballot from the voter's vehicle at all polling places. Previous law permitted this practice only at a polling place location that had received an exemption from accessibility requirements after a good faith effort to comply with those requirements. The bill also expressly prohibits voting curbside or at the door of a polling place under any other circumstances.

  • Repeals the requirement that high school student poll workers must be seniors.

    The bill also contains additional provisions related to issues that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

    Note: In July 2024, a federal district court permanently enjoined Ohio from implementing or enforcing the felony penalty for unlawful return of a mail ballot created under this law against disabled voters and those who assist them. The court ruled that limiting who a disabled person may select to assist them in returning their mail ballot violates the Voting Rights Act of 1965. 
     

Last Updated July 24, 2024

  • Requires county election boards to cancel the registration of deceased voters within 30 days of receiving the state Department of Health monthly list of resident deaths. This bill, as introduced on February 1, 2021, would require the Secretary of the State Election Board to cancel the registration of deceased voters within 30 days of receiving information from the state department of health. Existing law does not set a deadline, and instead provides for the information to be given to the Secretary who cancels the registrations "thereafter". This bill, as introduced February 1, 2021, would change the information witnesses and agents must put on absentee ballot return envelopes. Specifically, the bill would require witnesses to print their name as well as sign as required by existing law, and clarify that the address the witness must write is their residential address. BILLSUMMARY: Directs the Secretary of State to refer to the people for their approval or rejection of proposed new sections to Article V of the Constitution of the State of Oklahoma, provides for House and Senate districts, specifies power of redistricting, defines terms, creates the Citizens' Independent Redistricting Commission, provides for composition and qualification of the Commission, provides for application and selection of Commissioners, provides for funding of the Commission.
VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as introduced on November 15, 2021, proposes a state constitutional amendment that would take redistricting power away from the Legislature and give it to a Citizens' Independent Redistricting Commission for state legislative and congressional districts. This resolution would specify how the Commission is chosen, how it operates, and how final maps are adopted. If adopted, this process would be in place for the 2030 Census.

In addition, the resolution would provide that Oklahoma have 48 state senators and 101 state representatives, which are the current numbers in the Legislature. However, the state constitution's existing provisions result in 101 state representatives using a population based formula that this resolution would repeal. The existing number of state senate seats is also required by the existing state constitution, and their geographic basis is determined by a formula not replicated by this resolution. Nonetheless this resolution would not repeal that Constitutional provision and it is unclear how the state's existing constitutional requirements relating to districts for state senators would interact with the rules proposed by this amendment, to the extent they conflict.

With regard to the Citizens' Independent Redistricting Commission, this resolution would:

  • Create a nine member Commission, with three Commissioners from each of the two largest political parties and three not affiliated with either party. Each of these Commissioners must meet certain standards to avoid conflicts of interest.
  • Create a selection process to choose the nine Commissioners. People would apply to be Commissioners, in a process overseen by a special master appointed by the current Chief Justice of the Oklahoma Supreme Court. The Chief Justice would also appoint a panel of three retired Oklahoma state appellate judges, which would review the applications and create three pools of 20 applicants, one for each of the three political affiliations to be represented on the Commission. To be placed in the pool, an applicant would have to be approved by all three panelists, and would have to possess relevant experience and skills identified by the resolution. In addition to the nine, the panel would choose one alternate from each pool. The resolution also provides mechanisms for for-cause removal and replacement of Commissioners.
  • Require transparency by requiring all Commission votes be taken by roll call and published on the Commission's website, along with meeting transcripts, minutes, and redistricting plan details. Relatedly, the Commission would provide the public at least forty-eight (48) hours' notice for all public meetings and hearings, and all meetings and hearings except for executive session would be livestreamed and transcripts made publicly available via electronic archive. With narrow exceptions, Commissioners would be prohibited from discussing redistricting matters with members of the public outside of an open meeting of the Commission.
  • Provide for public participation in part by having the Commission develop and maintain a website that creates a public Plan drawing system and allows members of the public to:
    • monitor and comment on the Commission's work,
    • access the data sets and utilize the tools necessary to draw plans,
    • view prior district maps for comparison,
    • submit proposed plans and maps indicating communities of interest.
  • Require the Commission to count incarcerated people in their home communities, whether they are incarcerated in state or federal prisons.

  • Require the Commission to create districting plans using criteria.

    Specifically, the Commission would have to create plans that:

  • Comply with the United States Constitution and all applicable federal law, including the requirement that it equalize total population.
  • Are contiguous.
  • Maximize compliance with these criteria in the following order of priority:
    • Preserving communities of interest to the extent practicable. A community of interest would be defined as an area with recognized similarities of interests, including but not limited to, racial, ethnic, economic, social, cultural, geographic, tribal, linguistic, or historic identities. Communities of interest would not include common relationships with political parties, officeholders, or political candidates.
    • Upholding racial and ethnic fairness. No redistricting plan would be drawn to have the effect of denying or abridging the equal opportunity of racial or ethnic minority groups to participate in the political process or to diminish their ability to elect representatives of their choice, whether alone or in coalition with others.
    • Upholding political fairness. No plan would, when considered on a statewide basis, unduly favor or disfavor a political party. Undue favor to a political party shall be determined using the proposed map, data from the last ten (10) years of statewide elections, and the best available statistical methods on identifying inequality of opportunity to elect.
    • Respecting the geographic integrity of political subdivision boundaries to the extent preceding criteria have been satisfied.
    • Achieving compactness. A draft plan would be compact to the extent preceding criteria have been satisfied.

  • Do not consider any of the following factors, except to the extent necessary to comply with the other criteria and to enable the plan to be measured against the external metrics required by the resolution:

    • the residence of any member or candidate of the Oklahoma House of Representatives, Oklahoma State Senate, or U.S. Congress, and
    • the political party affiliation or voting history of the population of a district.

    The resolution specifies process for the Commission to adopt plans. Specifically, the resolution would:

  • Require the Commission to develop and publish publicly no more than two (2) preliminary Plans for the redistricting of the Oklahoma House of Representatives, Oklahoma State Senate and Federal Congressional Districts, and release all proposed maps for comment in formats that are easily accessible and readable by members of the public. To develop these plans, the Commission would hold at least one public hearing in each Congressional District at which members of the public may provide input relevant to redistricting, and more generally develop and publish a preliminary plan publicly, including digitally downloadable maps and Census block equivalency assignments of each district, accepting public comment for at least 14 days.
  • Require the Commission approve final Plans for State House of Representatives and Senatorial and Federal Congressional redistricting, by an affirmative vote of at least six of the nine Commissioners, including at least one Commissioner affiliated with each of the two largest political parties in the state and one Commissioner who is unaffiliated with either of the two largest political parties in the state. To hold a vote, the Commission would convene a voting meeting, open to the public, at which the Commission may vote. If the Commissioners vote to approve a preliminary plan, it would become law.
  • Require the Commission to issue, with all preliminary and final plans, written evaluations that measure the maps against external metrics covering all the required criteria.
  • Require the the Commission to complete the process by adopting final plans within 120 days after the release of the federal Census data. If the Commission does not approve one or more needed plans on time, a fallback procedure is specified for any uncompleted plans.

  • Create a fallback procedure in which the special master would create a report for the Oklahoma Supreme Court that advises the Court of the available Plans and provides enough information for the Court to approve a plan. The Court would then have 30 days to approve a plan. The Court-approved plan would have to be consistent with the required criteria.

    The resolution would also create a special litigation process for any challenges to an adopted final plan. Specifically, the resolution would:

  • Give the Oklahoma Supreme Court original and exclusive state-court jurisdiction to hear and decide all challenges to the Commission's actions and final plans, limited to remedy only the specific violation alleged on the specific plan challenged.
  • Create a 30-day window after plan approval in which any aggrieved resident may petition the Oklahoma Supreme Court to invalidate that plan. All petitions challenging a plan would be consolidated and given precedence over other civil proceedings.

  • Provide that if the Oklahoma Supreme Court concludes that a plan approved by the Commission is invalid, the special master would use the fallback procedure to enable the Court to pick a plan. If the Court finds a violation in a plan produced under the Fallback Mechanism, then the Court's remedy would be constrained by the required criteria.

    Last updated November 16, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on November 15, 2021, would require a "forensic" audit of the 2020 election in every precinct in nine counties conducted by an "independent third party" appointed by the Governor, the President Pro Tempore of the Senate, and the Speaker of the House of Representatives. These elected officials are all Republicans, and the bill does not identify any particular qualifications for the independent third party. Moreover, the term "forensic" is not defined, nor are any processes to be followed by the "independent third party" specified.

The nine counties to be reviewed would be the three largest by population, the three smallest by population, and three more randomly picked by the "independent third party". For the purpose of picking the counties, population would be defined by 2020 Census data. BILLSUMMARY: Proposes amendment to Oregon Constitution establishing Citizens Redistricting Commission to adopt redistricting maps for Senate, House of Representatives and United States Congress.
VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as introduced on January 19, 2021, would propose a constitutional amendment to be presented to the voters to create a Citizens Redistricting Committee responsible for defining federal Congressional and state legislative districts. The bill would:

  • Create a Citizens Redistricting Committee composed of 12 citizen commissioners responsible for defining federal Congressional and state legislative districts. Commissioners must be registered Oregon voters, hold the same political affiliation for the three years preceding appointment to the Commission, and either vote in two of the three preceding general elections or reside in Oregon. The bill would also establish prohibitions for prospective commissioners that include election, appointment, employment, or relationships with elected officials, political parties, campaigns, lobbyists, legislative employees, campaign contractors, and political donors.
  • Establish a review panel of three administrative law judges to review applications for commissioners and to select a pool of 150 prospective commissioners consisting of 50 applicants affiliated with each of the two largest political parties in the state and 50 applicants unaffiliated with either party. The Secretary of State would randomly draw 2 names from each of the three subpools to determine the first six commissioners. The selected commissioners would then select the remaining six commissioners by selecting two individuals from each subpool while considering the racial, ethnic, geographic, and gender diversity of the state. The Governor would have authority to remove commissioners in certain circumstances. The Commission would select a chair and vice chair, who may not be affiliated with the same political party. The Commission would require seven votes to approve maps, with at least one vote from a commissioner from each of the three selection subpools.
  • Require the Commission to conduct an open and transparent process for drawing district boundaries. The Commission would conduct at least 10 public hearings prior to proposing a final map and at least five public hearings after proposing a final map. The Commission would hold at least one hearing in each Congressional district and each of six identified geographical regions in Oregon. The Commission would provide at least 14 days' notice prior to each hearing. Hearings would allow for remote public testimony via video technology. Commission records would be public records.
  • Establish criteria for the Commission to consider when defining districts. The Commission must consider equality of population, contiguity, existing political subdivisions and communities of interest, and competitiveness when drawing districts. The Commission may not consider incumbency, favor any party or candidate, or dilute any language or ethnic identity group.
  • Require the Commission to approve final maps and submit a report outlining the procedures used to draw the maps by August 15 of each year ending in 1. If the members of the Commission cannot agree on a map by August 15, four members of the Commission may submit a map to the Supreme Court of Oregon for review by August 29. Additionally, any registered Oregon voter may challenge a proposed final map from the Commission by petition to the Supreme Court of Oregon filed by September 1 of the year ending in 1. The Supreme Court may approve the map submitted by the Commission or remand the map to the Commission to be redrawn and resubmitted to the Supreme Court.
  • Prohibit commissioners to hold or run for public office, serve in a politically appointed position, be employed to consult or advise an office holder, or participate in lobbying activities during their terms as commissioners and for three years following the end of their terms.

NOTE: The amendment would require approval by a simple majority vote of both chambers of the Legislative Assembly prior to submission to the voters, who would also need to approve the amendment by a simple majority.

Last updated January 19, 2021.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 26, 2021, would create procedures for state legislative and federal congressional redistricting. The bill would:

  • Require the legislative redistricting committee to conduct four public hearings in different parts of the state prior to the adoption of a preliminary plan for state legislative or federal congressional districts. The bill would also require the records of the hearings and consideration by the legislative redistricting committee to be public record.
  • Allow a member of the public to file an exception to a state legislative redistricting plan within 15 days of the plan's adoption. The commission would hold two public hearings, to include testimony, following the filing of an exception.
  • Require state legislative districts and federal congressional districts to be drawn so as not to dilute the voting power of racial and language minorities or to divide precincts. Districts should be drawn in consideration of communities of interest, responsiveness, and existing natural boundaries. Districts may not favor or disfavor any incumbent, candidate, or party. Additionally, federal congressional districts must be compact, contiguous, and minimally disruptive of existing political subdivisions.
  • Prohibit the chair of the legislative redistricting commission to be a current or recent officeholder, lobbyist, candidate, or employee of any officeholder, candidate, or party or the spouse of a person with one of those statuses.

Last updated February 27, 2021.
