This bill, as amended on June 21, 2021, was an omnibus bill that would have made many changes to the Pennsylvania Election Code. The bill would have:

  • Changed the deadline for absentee and mail-in ballot applications to the third Monday before the election or primary. This change would have made the deadline 15 days prior to the election, instead of the existing seven days.
  • Eliminated a provision that appeared to prohibit people who were incarcerated in the last five years from registering to vote, contrary to other provisions of the bill which explicitly removed that restriction.
  • Changed early voting vote center locations and times, specifically to:
    • Require that each county must have at least one early voting vote center, with an additional location for each 100,000 residents. Counties would have only been required to provide up to five vote centers, but could provide up to ten.
    • Mandate early voting vote center hours of 7:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. daily.
    • Add locations where early voting vote centers can be established to include public and private schools, colleges, and universities, and eliminating the possibility of siting early voting vote centers at a city hall.
  • Changed ballot return location requirements to:
    • Clarify that the county board of election office may serve as a ballot return location.
    • Prohibit a county from operating a ballot return location any time that representatives of two parties are unable to monitor that ballot return location.
    • Exclude expenses for operating a ballot return location from state reimbursement.
  • Created a new election crime prohibiting duress and intimidation of elections officials. This crime would have been a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $10,000 and up to four years' imprisonment.
  • Allowed disabled voters to use any experimental electronic voting system provided for UOCAVA voters, and direct the Secretary of the Commonwealth to investigate the viability of using blockchain technology to verify such electronic voting systems.
  • Changed pre-canvassing timelines for absentee and mail-in ballots to allow pre-canvassing to be done only between the hours of 7:00 a.m to 11:00 p.m. during the five days prior to the election, and while polls are open on Election Day. Under existing law, pre-canvass cannot begin until 7:00 a.m. on Election Day.
  • Changed canvassing timelines for absentee and mail-in ballots to require canvassing to begin immediately upon the close of the polls on Election Day. Under existing law, canvassing must be started by the third day after the election.
  • Allowed county boards of elections to use paper district register cards for one year after the effective date of this bill, before requiring the electronic poll books mandated by this bill.
  • Changed the audit provisions of the previous version of the bill to:
    • Require that absentee and mail-in ballots be subjected to a ballot comparison audit with a risk limit of 1% and ballots cast in person on voting machines be subjected to a ballot-polling audit with a risk limit of 1%.
    • Create an exception to mandatory results-confirming audits for uncontested elections.
  • Provided that the Pennsylvania House of Representatives may intervene in a lawsuit challenging the constitutionality of this Act upon a majority vote of that chamber.
  • Clarified that the voter fraud hotline created by the bill will also take reports of any known or suspected intimidation or duress of poll workers, judges of elections, election officials, or elections observers.
  • Changed the requirement that poll workers be registered voters in the district in which they are appointed to instead require only that they be registered voters in the county in which the polling place is located.
  • Limited date of birth confidentiality to voters who have an active protection from abuse order, only for the duration that such order is in effect.
  • Mandated the Secretary of the Commonwealth to develop and offer the training, free of charge, prescribed by the Election Law Advisory Board under this bill.
  • Prohibited the Secretary of the Commonwealth from decertifying voting machines purchased by a county prior to 2024 for failure to comply with the standards set forth.
  • Eliminated provisions regarding methods of computing and announcing returns by the counties.
  • Mandated signature verification, requiring that the county board of elections verify that a ballot signature matches the voter's signature on file.
  • Created a mandatory cure process. For failure to provide ID or a matching signature, a county board of elections would have been required to notify the voter by mail, email, phone call, or text message and provide the voter an opportunity to cure by the close of the polls. Cure could have included providing proof of ID and an affirmation that the voter is the same person who returned the absentee or mail-in ballot or providing an affirmation that the voter is the same person who returned the absentee or mail-in ballot and that the voter is indigent and cannot obtain proof of identification. Certain errors would have been incurable, such as failure to include a secrecy envelope or lack of identity information on the secrecy envelope. For such incurable errors, a county board of elections would have been required to notify the voter and direct the voter to vote on Election Day with a provisional ballot or apply for an emergency absentee ballot.
  • Prohibited counties and the Department of State from maintaining a permanent mail-in voting list and instead require voters to request a mail-in ballot for each election, even when elections are held within the same calendar year.
  • Changed voter ID requirements to accept a voter registration card of the type created by this bill or an affidavit with the voter's signature and the last four digits of the voter's Social Security number. Under existing law, photo ID is required for voters unless they have a religious objection to being photographed, but the enforcement of voter ID requirements has been enjoined since a 2014 court decision. While on paper this bill would add two non-photo ID options, it restricts the voter ID options practically available to Pennsylvania voters under current law and jurisprudence.
  • Created new voter registration requirements, which track existing requirements except that this bill would have:
    • Required voters to provide new information, including the last four digits of the voter's Social Security number and the voter's driver's license or ID number. If the voter does not have a Social Security number, the voter's identity can be confirmed through alternate means. A voter's failure to provide a license or ID number could not have formed the basis for rejection of their voter registration. Clerks and registrars would have been required to verify these data upon receipt of a voter registration application.
    • Codified a requirement that the Department of State provides online voter registration, which is already available in Pennsylvania.
    • Required elections officials to reject a voter registration 25 days before an election, instead of the existing 10 days before an election.
    • Created a method of birthdate privacy for a voter who has made a claim under abuse protection statutes.
    • Codified a court decision that eliminates the statutory bar to registration for people who have been incarcerated in the past five years for a felony.
  • Required county boards of elections to establish in-person early voting at vote centers by the 2025 primary. Early voting would begin the second Friday prior to an election and end the first Wednesday prior to an election. This bill would also have authorized county boards of elections to establish satellite election offices, which could only be located in early voting locations after the initiation of early voting. Before in-person early voting would have been required under this bill, though, voters would have lacked an early in-person voting option because other provisions of this bill limited the ability to vote an absentee or mail-in ballot in person. Under this bill, voter centers would have had to:
    • Meet the requirements for a polling place.
    • Be announced at least 30 days before the establishment of an early voting center.
    • Be located in a permanent public library, courthouse, public or private school, college, or university, or government-owned building.
    • Be distributed throughout the county.
    • Be ADA accessible and meet the criteria for polling places.
    • Use the same type of voting machines that the county uses on election day.
    • Have continual staff and video monitoring for all hours of early voting, including overnight.
    • The Department of State would have been required to reimburse counties half the costs of operating early vote centers.
    • Moved the voter registration deadline to 30 days before an election, from the current 15-day deadline.
  • Limited absentee and mail-in ballot return options to only the following specified methods:
    • By mail, while eliminating existing prepaid postage.
    • In person to a county board of elections office during its hours of operation.
    • By drop box, provided that a drop box:
      • may only be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. during the seven days before an election,
      • must be staffed by at least one paid inspector of elections from each of the two political parties with the highest number of voters in the state,
      • must be video monitored during all hours of operation (with recordings retained for 2 years),
      • must have ballots collected daily after 8:00 p.m.,
      • before the adoption of early voting, must be in a location that complies with all requirements for polling places. After the adoption of early voting, must be in an early voting location,
      • must be in a fixed location announced 30 days in advance, and
      • must have the inspectors of election verify the identity of each person returning a ballot, must review each ballot for envelope completion, and must date-, time-, and location-stamp each returned ballot.
    • Counties would have been required to provide at least one drop box location and may have an additional location for every 100,000 residents.
    • Ballot return by another registered voter in the voter's household would have been permitted, but any voter returning more than one ballot must be informed by the inspectors of the penalties for unlawful collection of ballots.
  • Changed absentee and mail-in ballot application procedures to:
    • Require applications to have at least two of the following, or be rejected: last four digits of Social Security number, driver's license number, and voter registration number.
    • Prevent election officials from mailing absentee or mail-in ballots earlier than 29 days before the election.
    • Prohibit voters from applying for an absentee or mail-in ballot in person.
    • Mandate that the Secretary of the Commonwealth provide electronic applications for absentee and mail-in ballots. Under existing law, the Secretary is authorized, but not required, to create such a system.
    • Require the county board of elections to investigate any absentee or mail-in ballot returned as undeliverable and mail a notice to the voter's registered address if a voter requests an absentee or mail-in ballot be mailed to any other address.
  • Changed canvassing and pre-canvassing methods. Specifically, the bill would allow party representatives to view and observe pre-canvass and canvass activities, which must also be recorded. It would also require machine sorting and extracting to assist in processing of absentee and mail-in ballots. Machines used must have signature verification capabilities used by the county.
  • Created a voter's bill of rights, a senior voter's bill of rights, and a disabled voter's bill of rights. All voters would have the right to:
    • vote,
    • have their vote accurately counted,
    • vote if they are in line when polls close,
    • ask for and receive assistance in voting,
    • receive up to 2 replacement ballots,
    • an explanation if their registration or identity is in question,
    • cast a provisional ballot,
    • written instructions, and oral instructions upon request,
    • vote free from coercion or intimidation, and
    • vote on a working, accurate voting system.

    • In addition, senior and disabled voters would have had the right to:
    • receive any assistance necessary to cast a ballot and
    • move to the front of the line at a polling place.
    • Seniors would have had the right to receive assistance through supervised voting, while disabled voters would have had the additional rights to:
    • bring a qualified service animal into a polling place or elections office,
    • vote using an accessible voting machine,
    • a polling place that complies with ADA accessibility requirements, and
    • request a ballot be brought outside the polling place, provided the vote is cast within 150 of the entrance to the polling place, the voter marks their ballot secretly in the presence of two election officers (one from each party), who must deposit the ballot in a voting machine immediately. The electronic poll book must be brought to the voter and the use of this method must be recorded.
  • Increased the fines and imprisonment time for each election crime, in all cases doubling the fines and the imprisonment term or range. Despite the different imprisonment terms, none of the misdemeanor election crimes would be increased to felonies. In addition, the bill would have created new crimes for:
    • Disclosing results of a pre-canvassing meeting. Doing so would have been classified as a third-degree misdemeanor (despite the felony-level long potential term of imprisonment) punishable by a $5,000 fine and/or imprisonment up to 4 years, except that if a chief clerk or member of a county board of elections, return board, or board of registration commissioners does so, it would have been a third-degree felony punishable by a $30,000 fine and/or imprisonment up to 14 years.
    • Willfully collecting or returning absentee or mail-in ballots in violation of state law. This would have been a third-degree felony punishable by a $30,000 fine and/or imprisonment up to 14 years.
  • Established a bureau of election audits within the Auditor General, shifting all audit authority from county boards of elections and the Department of State, and requiring that the new bureau conduct result-confirming audits of each election (except those in which a full manual recount occurred), including:
    • a risk-limiting audit after every election that is contested,
    • an audit of election machine logs,
    • an audit of returned absentee and mail-in ballots, including examination of outer and secrecy envelopes,
    • an audit comparing retained paper ballots with number of recorded votes, and
    • an audit of pre-election equipment testing,
    • conduct performance audits at least once every 5 years, and
    • publicly post methodology and results publicly.
  • Altered the powers and duties of the Secretary of the Commonwealth. Some specific changes would have included:
    • A new requirement to provide a free photo ID to any registered elector upon request.
    • A new limitation that the Secretary must distribute, after approval by the Election Law Advisory Board, all private election grant funds and public funds for voter education equally across the state based upon the most recent census.
    • A new requirement to make all communications between the Secretary and at least three county election directors publicly available.
    • A new requirement to publish a list of registered voters at least 5 days before an election.
    • A new requirement to obtain a list of deceased people and compare it to the voter database monthly.
    • Creating and maintaining a tracking system for absentee and mail-in ballots.
    • Reimbursing counties for the cost of annual training the Pennsylvania Election Law Advisory Board must require under this bill.
    • Limiting the Secretary's powers to only those authorized in the Pennsylvania Statutes or Pennsylvania Consolidated Statutes.
  • Altered the powers and duties of county boards of elections. Some specific changes would have included:
    • A new requirement that the board capture and store voter signatures.
    • Requiring that the board provide each voter with a "durable" voter registration card that includes the voter's signature.
    • Removing the authority of boards to make rules, regulations, and instructions.
    • Requiring boards to use electronic poll books, with reimbursement from the Department of State.
    • Requiring boards to decline any private grant money unless received from the Secretary of the Commonwealth.
    • Requiring board to seek a record of deaths and compare to the registered voter list at least monthly. Under existing law, boards do not have to proactively seek out information about deceased voters periodically.
  • Mandated that the Department of State report certain information to the legislature after each election, including incidents of absentee and mail-in ballots being sent to the wrong person, absentee and mail-in ballots being voted by a person other than the voter, and absentee and mail-in ballots returned by means not permitted by law.
  • Expanded the authority of the Election Law Advisory Board, requiring it to:
    • Make official instructions and procedures manual by December 31 of each odd-numbered year.
    • Establish training standards for poll workers, election officials, and election observers.
    • Receive reports from county boards of elections regarding voter education.
  • Created new powers and duties for the Attorney General relating to elections, specifically requiring the Attorney General to appoint an independent prosecutor to review election complaints, who would have been required to publish a report after each election detailing:
    • the total number of complaints filed and to whom,
    • a summary of how complaints were investigated, and
    • recommendations for reducing the number of future complaints.
  • Required that every ballot cast be open to public inspection, under certain conditions, after an election, and for the entire time ballots are required to be retained.
  • Created new procedures for county boards of elections when announcing returns and locating discrepancies in return numbers, including granting such board subpoena power. A board would be empowered to correct returns in accordance with recount results or to exclude the poll or the district, as to any, some, or all offices, candidates, questions, and parties, if the ballot box contains more ballots than there are electors, or more ballots from one party than there are electors of that party, or more ballots than voters who voted.
  • Imposed new technical requirements for voting machines, which must be publicly tested before voting machines can be approved. All specifications are not set forth in this commentary, but notable requirements include manufacturing within the U.S., allowing for direct comparison of machine interpretation and human interpretation of the same ballot, and utilizing open-source software. Voting system vendors would have had ongoing requirements to report known defects and the Department of State would have reporting requirements regarding voting system performance and defects.
  • Specified that the constitution vests authority for prescribing election law in the Legislature.
  • Established supervised voting in assisted living facilities and nursing home facilities at the request of an administrator.

This bill, as introduced on October 13, 2021, is an omnibus bill that makes many changes to the Pennsylvania Election Code. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require county boards of elections to establish in-person early voting at vote centers by the 2025 primary. Early voting would begin the second Friday before an election and end the first Wednesday before an election. Counties would be required to provide at least one early voting vote center. Under this bill, voter centers would have to:
    • Meet the requirements for a polling place.
    • Be open for the hours of 7:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. daily.
    • Be announced before the establishment of an early voting center.
    • Use electronic poll books capable of printing the appropriate ballot for the voter, which would be voted using the same type of voting machines that the county uses on election day.
    • Have continual staff and video monitoring for all hours of early voting, including overnight.

      The Department of State would be required to reimburse counties half the costs of operating early vote centers.
  • Create a mandatory cure process. For failure to sign or date the declaration on the ballot envelope, a county board of elections must notify the voter by mail, email, phone call, or text message and provide the voter an opportunity to cure by the close of the polls. "Naked" ballots which lack secrecy envelopes or ballots with secrecy envelopes that contain identifying marks can be cured by elections officials by placing the ballot in a new secrecy envelope and segregating the erroneous secrecy envelope for tabulation.
  • Create a true permanent mail-in ballot list by treating a voter's application for a mail-in ballot as a request to receive mail-in ballots for all subsequent elections indefinitely, until the voter requests of the permanent mail-in ballot list. Under existing law, voters who apply for a mail-in ballot may request mail-in ballots for the rest of the calendar year. and Prohibit counties and the Department of State from maintaining a permanent mail-in voting list and instead require voters to request a mail-in ballot for each election, even when elections are held within the same calendar year.
  • Change the deadline for absentee and mail-in ballot applications to fourteen days before the election or primary. Existing law sets the deadline seven days before the election or primary.
  • Change absentee and mail-in ballot application procedures to:
    • Require applications to have at least two of the following, or be rejected: last four digits of social security number, driver's license number, and voter registration number.
    • Prevent election officials from mailing absentee or mail-in ballots earlier than 29 days before the election.
    • Prohibit voters from applying for an absentee or mail-in ballot in person.
    • Mandate that the Secretary of the Commonwealth provide electronic applications for absentee and mail-in ballots. Under existing law, the Secretary is authorized, but not required, to create such a system.
    • Require the county board of elections to investigate any absentee or mail-in ballot returned as undeliverable and mail a notice to the voter's registered address if a voter requests an absentee or mail-in ballot be mailed to any other address.
  • Limit absentee and mail-in ballot return options to only the following specified methods:
    • By mail, while eliminating explicit authorization for counties to provide prepaid postage.
    • In person to a county board of elections office during its hours of operation.
    • By dropbox, provided that a dropbox:
    • may only be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. during the seven days before an election,
    • must be video monitored during all hours of operation (with recordings retained for 60 days),
    • must have ballots collected at least every 24 hours on weekdays, and
    • must be in a location announced in advance.
  • Require that counties provide at least one drop box location.
  • Retain existing authorization for registered voters to return the ballot of another registered voter in the voter's household and also add authorization for voters to return the ballot of a person for whom the deliverer has a power of attorney.
  • Change canvassing and pre-canvassing methods and timelines. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Allow party representatives to view and observe pre-canvass and canvass activities, which must also be recorded.
    • Require machine sorting and extracting to assist in processing absentee and mail-in ballots. Machines used must have signature verification capabilities used by the county.
    • Provide that pre-canvassing of absentee and mail-in ballots may begin up to seven days before Election Day. Under existing law, pre-canvassing cannot begin until 7:00 a.m. on election day.
    • Require canvassing of absentee and mail-in ballots to begin by 8:00 a.m. on the day after Election Day. Under existing law, canvassing must be started by the third day after the election.
  • Change certain Election Day procedures, specifically naming materials required for election day, delivery and pick up procedures, changing the prevailing time for poll opening and closing to local time, rather than Eastern Standard time.
  • Create a voter's bill of rights, a senior voter's bill of rights, and a disabled voter's bill of rights. All voters would have the right to:
    • vote,
    • have their vote accurately counted,
    • vote if they are in line when polls close,
    • ask for and receive assistance in voting,
    • receive up to 2 replacement ballots,
    • an explanation if their registration or identity is in question,
    • cast a provisional ballot,
    • written instructions, and oral instructions upon request,
    • vote free from coercion or intimidation, and
    • vote on a working, accurate voting system.

      In addition, senior and disabled voters have the right to:
    • receive any assistance necessary to cast a ballot and
    • move to the front of the line at a polling place.
      Seniors have the right to receive assistance through supervised voting, while disabled voters have the additional rights to:
    • bring a qualified service animal into a polling place or elections office,
    • vote using an accessible voting machine,
    • a polling place that complies with ADA accessibility requirements, and
    • request a ballot be brought outside the polling place, provided the vote is cast within 150 of the entrance to the polling place, the voter marks their ballot secretly in the presence of one election official, who must deposit the ballot in a voting machine immediately. The electronic poll book must be brought to the voter and the use of this method must be recorded.
  • Increase the fines and imprisonment time for each election crime, in all cases doubling the fines and the imprisonment term or range. Despite the different imprisonment terms, none of the misdemeanor election crimes would be increased to felonies. In addition, the bill would create new crimes for:
    • Disclosing results of a pre-canvassing meeting. Doing so would be a third-degree misdemeanor (despite the felony-level long potential term of imprisonment) punishable by a $5,000 fine and/or imprisonment up to 4 years, except that if a chief clerk or member of a county board of elections, return board, or board of registration commissioners does so, it would a third-degree felony punishable by a $30,000 fine and/or imprisonment up to 14 years.
    • Willfully collecting or returning absentee or mail-in ballots in violation of state law. This would be a third-degree felony punishable by a $30,000 fine and/or imprisonment up to 14 years.
  • Prohibiting duress and intimidation of elections officials. This would be a misdemeanor (despite the felony-level long potential term of imprisonment) punishable by a fine of up to $10,000 and up to four years' imprisonment.
  • Require a risk-limiting audit to be conducted after each election by the county board of elections and the Department of State before certification, which would be conducted under the following process:
    • Election officials would conduct the audit by manually tallying results and comparing the tally results to the results from the vote tabulating system using a statistical model. During the audit, votes are manually tallied until the statistical model shows strong statistical evidence that the outcome produced by the tabulating system will match the outcome from the manual tally.
    • Races and audit units would be selected at random.
    • Audits would be conducted in public view with published results.
  • Alter the powers and duties of the Secretary of the Commonwealth. Some specific changes include:
    • A new requirement to make all elections administration communications publicly available.
    • A new requirement to publish a list of registered voters at least 5 days before an election.
    • A new requirement to obtain a list of deceased people and compare it to the voter database monthly.
    • Creating and maintaining a tracking system for absentee and mail-in ballots.
  • Alter the powers and duties of county boards of elections. Some specific changes include:
    • Requiring boards to use electronic poll books, with 100% reimbursement from the State Treasurer.
    • Requiring boards to publish the voter bill of rights, senior voter bill of rights, and disabled voter bill of rights at each polling place.
  • Change the responsibilities and compensation of local election officials and poll workers. Specifically, this bill would:
    • Increase the compensation of poll workers from a range of $75-200 to a new range of $175-300, with 50% of the cost of paying poll workers to come from the Department.
    • Increase the mileage reimbursement rate for poll worker to match the IRS standard mileage rate, with 50% of the cost of mileage reimbursement to come from the Department.
  • Mandate that the Department of State report certain information to the legislature after each election, including incidents of absentee and mail-in ballots being sent to the wrong person, absentee and mail-in ballots being voted by a person other than the voter, and absentee and mail-in ballots returned by means not permitted by law.
  • Require the Secretary of the Commonwealth to create a voter fraud hotline created to take reports of any known or suspected voter fraud, intimidation or duress.
  • Impose new technical requirements for voting machines, which must be publicly tested before voting machines can be approved. All specifications are not set forth in this commentary, but notable requirements include manufacture within the U.S., allow for direct comparison of machine interpretation and human interpretation of the same ballot, and utilize open-source software. Voting system vendors would have ongoing requirements to report known defects and the Department of State would have reporting requirements regarding voting system performance and defects. This bill would also require the State Treasurer to reimburse counties for the full cost of replacing voting machines or ballot processing machines.
  • Establish supervised voting in assisted living facilities and nursing home facilities at the request of an administrator.

  • Require that ballots be watermarked with the county name.

This bill, as introduced on December 14, 2021, would make a number of changes to voting in Pennsylvania, including to same-day registration, absentee and mail-in ballot applications, return, and processing, voter registration, electronic pollbooks, and more. Specifically, the bill would.

  • Create same-day registration, whereby a person who appears in person on Election Day in their own district may vote a provisional ballot if they provide one of the enumerated types of voter ID, which include 14 categories of photo and nonphoto ID. The person's application to register must be approved or denied within seven days after Election Day, and the provisional ballot cannot be counted until the person's application to register is approved. If the county board of elections approves the voter's application while the voter is at the polling place, the voter may vote a regular ballot.
  • Create a uniform statewide period of Election-Day style early in-person voting, with voting booths and electronic voting systems. Under existing law, early voting is in the style of in-person absentee voting, with mail-in ballots available to any voter at the county board of elections. More specifically, the bill's early voting provisions would:
    • Provide that any voter may vote in any early voting location in the voter's county.
    • Begin the early voting period on the 17th day before Election Day and end the early voting period at 5:00 p.m. the Saturday before Election Day. Generally, each early voting location must be open from 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., except that the second weekend before Election Day, the early voting location must be open from 8:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. A county may, but need not, establish longer hours for early voting. Under existing law, absentee in-person voting ends at 5:00 p.m. the Tuesday before Election Day and is typically only available during business hours on weekdays.
    • Require that counties track every voter who votes during early voting.
    • Require at least one early voting location in every county, and require an additional early voting location for every 100,000 residents of the county. Counties may establish additional early voting locations but are not required to do so.
    • Require that any early voting location must be in a location eligible to be selected as a polling place and must be accessible to disabled people. Counties must also consider locations' proximity to public transportation, the availability of parking, travel times, commuter traffic patterns, geographic features affecting access and convenience, equitable distribution across the county, population density, existing locations that serve a large number of electors, use of public buildings, cost savings from public buildings, and security considerations. Locations must be published in a newspaper and online at least a week before the early voting period begins. A list of all locations must also be provided to the secretary of the commonwealth.
    • Permit temporary early voting locations which are permitted to have different days and hours of operation than those required for permanent early voting locations. The schedules and locations of a temporary voting location must be posted on the county board's website.
    • Allow candidates and parties to appoint an election watcher for the early voting location, provided the watcher is a qualified voter of the county the watcher is serving.
    • Ensure the security of ballot boxes, scanners, and tabulators at all early voting locations.
  • Alter deadlines for applying for absentee and mail-in ballots by:
    • Extending the deadline for applying in-person for absentee and mail-in ballots from 5:00 p.m. the Tuesday before Election Day to 5:00 p.m. the day before Election Day.
    • Making the deadline for mailed absentee and mail-in ballot applications eight days earlier. Under existing law, the deadline is 5:00 p.m. the Tuesday before Election Day. This bill would make the new deadline 5:00 p.m. the fifteenth day before Election Day.
  • Change absentee and mail-in voting by:
    • Providing postage prepaid on the outer envelope that is returned by a voter. Under existing law, counties can opt to provide prepaid postage on absentee and mail-in ballots.
    • Requiring an Intelligent Mail barcode allowing for mail tracking of the ballot when it is sent to the voter and the ballot when it is returned by the voter.
    • Requiring the secretary of the commonwealth to develop a system by which voters can track their ballots. Existing law does not require such a system, although ballot tracking exists in practice.
  • Alter rules about drop boxes by:
    • Requiring all counties to provide the greater of (1) two drop boxes or (2) one ballot drop box for every 50,000 residents of the county. The drop boxes must be arrayed throughout the county, subject to the campus requirement below. Counties may, but are not required to, provide additional drop boxes. Existing law is silent on drop boxes, although many jurisdictions have, in practice, used drop boxes in previous elections.
    • Requiring all counties to provide at least one drop box within one mile of each public university or community college. It is unclear whether these campus drop boxes are in addition to the ones required by population, or if this is a siting requirement.
    • Requiring that all drop boxes be sited in accessible locations.
    • Requiring that drop boxes be in use beginning 40 days before an election.
    • Requiring that drop box return be ended at 8:00 p.m. on Election Day, to coincide with the close of the polls.
    • Clarifying that voters may return the ballots of any members of their household who are registered at the same address.
    • Requiring that ballots be removed from drop boxes at least once every 24 hours, except Saturday and Sunday, by at least 2 people displaying proper ID. Once removed, the ballots must follow a chain of custody procedure to be developed by each county board of election and utilize a ballot drop box collection form containing certain information delineated in the bill.
    • Specifying that a person who interferes with removal of ballots from a drop box or interferes with the deposit of a ballot into a drop box commits a criminal offense.
    • Requiring that a county board of elections select and fix ballot drop box locations at least 65 days before the election, and announce those locations to the public at least 55 days before an election. Locations may be changed at any time, provided that the county must immediately update its website with the new locations.
    • Requiring that drop boxes have clear labeling, signage, and warning about prohibited tampering and disallowed return processes.
  • Change absentee and mail-in ballot preprocessing and processing by:
    • Requiring election workers, upon receipt of an absentee or mail-in ballot, to record the date of receipt in the voter's record and examine the voter's declaration to verify completion. If received absentee or mail-in ballots have completed declarations, the ballots shall be set aside until pre-canvassing. If they do not, the election worker shall note it into the voter's record and the bother shall be notified by letter, by email, and by phone of the error and shall be provided with a cure form.
    • Allowing county boards to begin pre-canvassing ballots at 9:00 a.m. on the 21st day before Election Day, and requiring that county boards must begin pre-canvassing ballots by 7:00 a.m. on Election Day at the latest. Under existing law, pre-canvassing cannot begin before 7:00 a.m. on Election Day. Pre-canvassing may only continue until 8:00 p.m. on Election Day. Under existing law, there is no specified end time for pre-canvassing.
    • Allowing a county board of elections to duplicate an absentee or mail-in ballot that is so damaged that it cannot be read by automatic tabulating equipment. Such ballots must be labeled "duplicate" and bear a serial number matching that of the damaged ballot.
  • Create mandatory statewide cure for incomplete declarations on absentee and mail-in ballots. The cure form requires the voter to provide an ID number or a copy of a a photo ID, government-issued document, utility bill, phone bill, bank statement, government check, paycheck, or tax or rent receipt which lists the voter's name and address. If the form is returned by noon on the sixth day after Election Day, the ballot shall be counted. Under existing law, voter can cure defects in the same time frame, but there is no mechanism to notify voters of curable defects. This provision would clarify that a missing or inaccurate date on a voter's envelope declaration is not a fatal defect that must be cured. It would also clarify that a ballot not being sealed into an inner envelope is not a fatal defect, and instead would allow election workers to place the ballot into an inner envelope in a manner that maintains the secrecy of the ballot for further pre-canvassing and/or canvassing.
  • Change voter registration processes by:
  • Allowing voters to pre-register to vote at age 16. Such pre-registrants will automatically become registered upon their 18th birthdays. This bill would also allow preregistered 17-year-olds who will be 18 at the time of the general election to vote in the primary associated with the general election.
    • Adding each institution within the state system of higher education as a voter registration agency.
    • Requiring the department of transportation to send completed voter registration applications electronically within one day of a voter's completion of the forms. Under existing law, the department has five days to transmit applications. This provision also eliminates certain procedures for processing voter change of address applications received from the department of transportation.
    • Allowing county election officials to take no action if they receive a voter registration application that is an exact duplicate of a person already in the SURE system (Pennsylvania's statewide voter roll).
  • Change voter list maintenance processes by allowing removal of voters from the rolls based upon information received from ERIC by the department of state.

  • Requires that county boards of election use electronic pollbooks that allow real-time tracking of voters by December 31, 2024, at which time they will replace paper poll books and shall be used for voter certificates, voting check lists, numbered lists of voters, district registered, and management of voter rolls during elections. The Secretary of State would be responsible for creating specifications for electronic poll books. The bill appropriates $7 million to the department of state for counties' procurement of electronic poll books.

    The bill also creates funding for electronic poll books and election infrastructure through bonds in provisions not tracked by Voting Rights Lab.

The agencies would transmit the voter's name, age, address, and electronic signature to the Secretary of State, would would then provide the information to the appropriate registration commission. The commission would send the registrant a notice with instructions for how to decline registration within 21 days and how to adopt a political party affiliation.

Last Updated January 29, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 10, 2021, would:

  • Create same day voter registration at Election Day polling locations. The registrant would prove residency by displaying a driver's license or other document approved by the Department of State or a written statement by a voter registered in the election district stating that they know the registrant as a resident of the election district. Same day registrants would vote regular ballots, which could not be processed until the close of polls.
  • Create a new misdemeanor offense for registering, altering the registration, or assisting in wrongful registration of someone during same day registration.

  • Require a county board to send a mail registration verification notice to a random sampling of 25% of Election Day registrants and investigate any notice returned as undeliverable.

    Last updated March 23, 2022.

BILLSUMMARY: Provides for congressional reapportionment and reapportionment criteria, provides definitions, provides committee responsibilities.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on June 22, 2021, is a strike-all amendment that eliminates all previous provisions regarding state legislative and federal congressional redistricting in favor of new redistricting provisions for federal congressional districts set forth in this amendment. These new provisions would:

  • Vest redistricting responsibility in the state government committee of the Senate and the state government committee of the House and require those committees to:
    • Determine the ideal population for each congressional district.
    • Develop a public comment process and the opportunity for citizen congressional reapportionment plans.
    • Conduct at least four public hearings.

  • Set the criteria for redistricting in order of priority:

    • Population cannot deviate more than 0% from the ideal population set by the legislative committees, unless necessary to prevent the division of any political subdivision.
    • Keeping political subdivisions intact, including a prohibition on dividing voting precincts.
    • Keeping school district boundaries intact, unless doing so would divide a political subdivision.
    • Contiguity.
    • Compactness.
    • Compliance with the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

    The previous version of the bill would have created a legislative redistricting committee with creating districts and holding public hearings. The chair of that committee could not have been a current or recent officeholder, lobbyist, candidate, nor could the chair have been an employee or spouse of any officeholder, candidate, or party. Criteria for redistricting under that version, that have now been amended out of the bill, would have included:

  • Non-dilution of the voting power of racial and language minorities.
  • A prohibition on dividing precincts.
  • Consideration of communities of interest, responsiveness, and existing natural boundaries.
  • Neutrality as to incumbency, candidate, or party.
  • Compactness.
  • Contiguity.

  • Preservation of existing political subdivisions.

    Last updated June 24, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on March 10, 2021, would:

  • Create a process to notify voters with signatures deemed mismatching on absentee and mail-in ballots and provide them with an opportunity to cure the issue. The bill would require election officials to notify the voter by mail, phone, text, or email and inform the voter that the voter must provide, either in person or by sending a copy, of proof of identification and an executed affirmation stating that the voter is the individual who voted the ballot in question. Indigent voters who are unable to obtain proof of identification would be able to swear to that on the affirmation.
  • Require poll watchers observing mail ballot canvassing activity to have a clear line of sight and stand no farther than six feet away from away from where canvassing is occurring.
  • Require election officials to deliver all returned absentee and mail ballots to the county board for canvassing by 2 a.m. on the day after Election Day.

NOTE: This bill would create a cure process for mismatched signatures on mail ballots. Pennsylvania law does not require signature matching to verify mail ballots.

Last Updated March 16, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 3, 2021, would require the Department of Transportation to maintain a record of individuals who were ineligible to register to vote when applying for a driver's license due to their age and to notify them when they turn 18 that they are eligible to vote.

Last Updated March 5, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 10, 2021, would allow a voter who is unaffiliated with a political party to select a party's ballot at a primary without needing to permanently enroll with that party to vote in that particular primary.

Last Updated March 15, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 11, 2021, would repeal existing code provisions that create mail-in ballots that allow a voter to cast a ballot remotely without an excuse. The bill would also eliminate early voting in the form of in-person mail-in ballot voting.

Last Updated March 15, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 11, 2021, would create a Voter's Bill of Rights in Pennsylvania. The bill would:

  • Specify rights belonging to all voters. Among the specified rights, a voter must be allowed to return a mail ballot and vote in person on Election Day and a voter who is unable to read or write must be allowed to apply for a special needs ballot no later than 10 days before Election Day. Voters must be able to cast their ballots free from intimidation or coercion.
  • Allow any voter who feels any of their enumerated rights are being denied to call local law enforcement.
  • Require the Voter's Bill of Rights to be posted at all polling locations.

Last Updated March 15, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 15, 2021, would create a voter ID requirement for in-person voting in Pennsylvania. The bill would:

  • Require a voter to present ID prior to voting in person. The voter could satisfy the requirement by presenting a valid form one of the following types of photo ID: 1) a Pennsylvania driver's license or ID card, 2) a photo ID card issued by an agency of Pennsylvania or the United States, 3) a U.S. passport, 4) a student photo ID card, 5) an employee photo ID card, or 6) a U.S. armed forces photo ID card.
  • Allow voters who do not have one of the forms of photo ID to present two forms of the following types of ID: 1) nonphoto ID issued by an agency of Pennsylvania or the United States, 2) a firearm permit, 3) a current utility bill or bank statement, or 4) a government check or paycheck.
  • Require voters who are unable to satisfy the ID requirement to cast a provisional ballot. The provisional ballot would be verified by comparing the voter's signature on the provisional ballot envelope with the voter's signature in the registration records.

NOTE: Pennsylvania has existing statutory voter ID provisions, but they were declared unconstitutional by a state appellate court in 2012.

Last Updated March 16, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Provides for qualifications of chairperson of the Legislative Reapportionment Commission.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 17, 2021, would establish qualifications for the chairperson of the Legislative Reapportionment Commission. An eligible individual must: 1) have voted in at least two of the last three general elections, 2) not registered, or have a spouse have registered, as a lobbyist in the five years preceding the appointment, 3) not have been nominated, or have a spouse who has been nominated, for elective office in the five years preceding the appointment, and 4) have not served, or have a spouse who has served, as a staff member for a party, political committee, political action committee, or elected official in the five years preceding the appointment.

The technical amendments on March 23, 2021, made no substantive changes to the bill.

Last updated March 24, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on April 9, 2021, would allow otherwise eligible individuals to preregister to vote when they reach age 16. Existing law allows individuals to register only if they will be 18 by the time of the next general election.

Last Updated April 10, 2021

This bill, as introduced on April 1, 2021, would eliminate the permanent mail-in voting list that allows voters to sign up to receive a mail-in ballot application automatically before each election under existing law. The bill would also prohibit anyone other than the Department of State or a county board of elections to send a mail-in ballot application to a voter.

Last Updated April 2, 2021

This bill, as introduced on April 14, 2021, would task the Auditor General of Pennsylvania with coordinating and managing an audit of the 2020 general election. The Auditor General is required to investigate, including through use of witness and document subpoenas, and report the following, by county and for Pennsylvania overall:

  • The number of incidents, and actions taken in response to such incidents, where:
    • an absentee ballot (in Pennsylvania, this includes excuse-only "absentee" ballots and no-excuse "mail-in" ballots) was sent to the wrong person or address,

    • an absentee ballot was returned in an unauthorized manner, notwithstanding any court order.
  • Issues encountered with an approved electronic voting system and recommendations of verifications of tabulated votes as compared to reported votes.
  • A review of inconsistent treatment of:
    • mail-in ballots received after 8:00 p.m. on Election Day,
    • deficient ballots processed by counties,
    • poll watcher and authorized representative access, including inconsistencies due to political affiliation, and
    • standards used to determine the eligibility of absentee, in-person, and provisional ballots.
  • Incidents regarding the use, usage, and monitoring of drop boxes.
  • The number of absentee ballot applications received.
  • The number of approved absentee ballot applications.
  • The number of absentee ballots canvassed.
  • The number of qualified voters who voted a provisional ballot.
  • The number of provisional ballots canvassed.
  • The number of absentee ballot applications received from a person who was not a registered voter but who timely submitted a voter registration application after the absentee ballot application was received.
  • The number of voter registration applications received fewer than 30 days and fewer than 15 days before the general election.
  • The date and time absentee ballot pre-canvassing began.

  • The date and time absentee ballot canvassing began.

    Last updated August 27, 2021.
