VRLANALYSIS:
Governor Wolfe vetoed this bill on July 8, 2022.

This bill, as amended on June 6, 2022, would have expanded candidates' and political parties' ability to appoint watchers, specified access that watchers must be given, and increased the penalties for three existing election crimes. Specifically, the bill would have:

  • Allowed each candidate to appoint three poll watchers per precinct in primary, general, special, and municipal elections. Existing law limits candidates to two poll watchers per precinct.
  • Allowed political parties to appoint three watchers per precinct in which they have a candidate, in any primary, general, special, and municipal election. Existing law does not give parties the right to appoint watchers for a primary but otherwise allows these appointments.
  • Allowed registered voters to serve as poll watchers anywhere in the Commonwealth. Existing law requires a person to be a registered voter of the county in which they wish to serve as a poll watcher. Governor Wolfe's veto message highlighted this provision.
  • Allowed poll watchers inside the enclosed space where ballots are counted after polls close, but required them not to interfere with the counting of ballots. Existing law requires poll watchers to remain outside the enclosed space.
  • Required the county board of canvassers to give a person allowed to watch the pre-canvassing or the canvassing of mail ballots a clear line of sight to view and hear the proceedings at a distance of six feet or less, without impeding the canvassing. Existing law does not address the specific access that must be given.
  • Increased the penalty for the crime of denying lawful watchers the access they are entitled to. Specifically, the crime becomes a misdemeanor of the second degree, rather than an unspecified misdemeanor, and an election official accused of committing the crime would face possible penalties of two years in prison, instead of one, and/or a $5,000 fine, up from $1,000. In addition, a person convicted would forfeit the pay earned during the election, and if it had been paid, would be required to refund the county.
  • Increased the penalty for voter intimidation from a second-degree misdemeanor to a first-degree misdemeanor and provided that any person accused of it would face possible penalties of three years in prison, up from two, and/or a $10,000 fine, up from $5,000.

  • Increased the penalty for the crime of hindering or delaying the performance of a duty under the election code to a second-degree misdemeanor, rather than an unspecified misdemeanor. A person accused of this crime would have faced a possible two-year prison term and/or a fine of $2,500, up from $500.

Last Updated July 11, 2022

BILLSUMMARY: (Joint Resolution) Proposes an amendment to the Constitution of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, provides for the Legislative Reapportionment Commission.
VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as introduced on April 20, 2021, would propose a state constitutional amendment to create an Independent Reapportionment and Redistricting Commission. The amendment would:

  • Create an Independent Reapportionment and Redistricting Commission to draw federal Congressional and state legislative districts. The Commission would be composed of 11 members. The Governor would appoint three applicants who are not affiliated with either major party. The majority and minority leader of each chamber of the General Assembly would each appoint two applicants affiliated with the same party as the leader. Individuals who have worked as lobbyists, held elective, appointed, or judicial office, or held a public position in support of a public official in the previous five years would not be eligible to serve on the Commission.
  • Establish criteria for the Commission to use when drawing district maps. State legislative districts must be drawn with the fewest divisions on existing political subdivisions while maintaining allowable deviations in population. Congressional districts must be composed of compact and contiguous territory and must not divide existing political subdivisions unless absolutely necessary while maintaining allowable deviations in population. The Commission may not consider the address of any individual, political affiliation of registered voters, or previous election results unless required to do so by federal law.
  • Require the votes of seven commissioners (2 each from both major party and 2 unaffiliated commissioners) to approve maps. The Commission would be required to conduct at least six public hearings prior to the proposal of final maps.
  • Make the General Assembly the back up to the Commission. If the Commission is unable to approve final maps by October 1 of the year ending in 1, the Commission will submit two to three alternative maps to the General Assembly, who must approve maps by a 2/3 vote by December 31 of the year ending in 1. If the General Assembly fails to approve maps, it will submit the same maps to the state supreme court for approval.
  • Require the state supreme court to appoint a special master to assist with appeals of approved final maps and consideration of maps submitted by the General Assembly.

NOTE: The amendment must be approved by a simple majority of both chambers in consecutive sessions prior to submission to the voters, who must also approve the amendment by a simple majority.

Last updated April 21, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: (Joint Resolution) Proposes an amendment to the Constitution of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, provides for the Legislative Reapportionment Commission for the purpose of reapportioning and redistricting the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.
VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as introduced on April 20, 2021, would propose a state constitutional amendment to create an independent Legislative and Congressional Redistricting Commission. The amendment would:

  • Create a Legislative and Congressional Redistricting Commission to propose and approve district maps for federal Congressional and state legislative districts. The Commission would be composed of 11 members (four affiliated with each major party and three unaffiliated with either party). The Secretary of the Commonwealth would create three subpools of applicants: one for each of the major parties and one for unaffiliated applicants. The Secretary would randomly draw 40 names. The majority and minority leader of each chamber of the General Assembly could strike two names from each subpool. The Secretary would then randomly draw from the remaining applicants in each subpool to select the commissioners.
  • Establish qualification on applicants and prohibitions on commissioners after service.
    • Applicants must not have changed political affiliation in the three years prior to their application and must have voted in at least two of the last three general elections.
    • Applicants must not have held or have an immediate family member hold public or judicial office in the previous five years.
    • Applicants and their spouses must not have served as paid staff members to members of Congress, state legislators, or the Governor in the previous five years.
    • Applicants and their spouses must not have registered as lobbyists in the previous five years.
    • Applicants and their spouses must not served as staff members for a political party or candidate and must not have been nominated for party office in the previous five years.
    • Commissioners may not serve as legislative or party staff or register as a lobbyist for three years after their term.
    • Commissioners and their spouses may not be nominated for or hold public office or party office for five years after the commissioner's term.
  • Require the votes of seven commissioners to approve maps. Votes to approve must include at least two votes from commissioners affiliated with each major party and two votes from commissioners unaffiliated with either party.
  • Prohibit the commission to consider any person's address, the political affiliation of any registered voter, or previous election results when drawing districts.
  • Establish a process and timeline for the Commission to approve maps:
    • The Commission must hold four public hearings in geographically diverse areas no later than 30 days before the deadline for submission of preliminary plans on July 1 of each year ending in 1.
    • The Commission must hold four public hearings in geographically diverse areas no later than 30 days before the deadline for submission of final plans on August 15 of each year ending in 1.
    • If the Commission is unable to approve final maps by August 15, the Commission must develop a second preliminary plan and hold four public hearings in geographically diverse areas. The Commission must then approve a final plan by October 15.
    • If the Commission is then unable to approve a final plan, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court would appoint a special master to develop a redistricting plan to be approved by the court.
  • Allow any registered voter to file a petition challenging an adopted final map in the Pennsylvania Supreme Court within 30 days of the certification of the final map. The Commission would have sole authority to defend a petition.

NOTE: The amendment must be approved by a simple majority of both chambers in consecutive sessions prior to submission to the voters, who must also approve the amendment by a simple majority.

Last updated April 21, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on April 27, 2021, would allow county boards of election to begin pre-canvassing absentee and mail-in ballots 21 days before Election Day. Under existing law, pre-canvassing may begin at 7 a.m. on Election Day. Pre-canvassing includes inspecting and opening envelopes, and counting and tallying votes.

Last Updated May 21, 2021

This bill, as introduced on May 6, 2021, would require the Auditor General to create a telephone hotline and web form to accept allegations of election fraud from identified, non-anonymous registered Pennsylvania voters. The hotline and form would be required for all general, municipal, special and primary elections and would be available for a 30 day period beginning on the date of each election. In addition, within 30 days of the effective date of this bill, the Auditor General would be required to establish a hotline and form to receive reports of fraud for the November 3, 2020 election and all elections from that date until the effective date of the bill. The Auditor General must prepare a report detailing reported fraud within 120 days after an election and submit it to certain legislative leaders and staff.

Last updated January 27, 2022.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to qualifications of electors, provides for qualifications of electors at primaries, relates to party organization, provides for only enrolled electors to vote at primaries or hold party offices, relates to nomination of candidates, provides for candidates to be nominated and party officers to be elected at primaries and providing for procedure for unenrolled electors to cast primary ballots.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced May 28, 2021, would allow voters without a party affiliation to vote in primary elections. The bill would apply to elections for president, U.S. Senator, U.S. Representative, and all other state elective offices. Voters could choose which party's primary the voter wishes to vote in, and the voter is deemed a member of that party for that election only.

Last updated June 1, 2021.

This resolution, as amended on June 23, 2021, proposes a constitutional amendment that would require voter ID from qualified voters. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require that a voter provide proof of valid ID when not voting in person. Under the previous version of the bill, a voter not voting in person would have been required to provide a copy of their valid ID.
  • Require a voter to show valid ID before receiving a ballot when voting in person. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

  • Define valid ID as a valid government-issued ID, unless otherwise provided by law. Under the previous version of the bill, valid ID would have included, but not been limited to, valid government-issued ID.

Last Updated June 29, 2021

This bill, as introduced on June 21, 2021, would change the timing for absentee ballot (which includes "absentee ballots" and "mail-in ballots" in Pennsylvania) applications, delivery of precinct absentee ballots to the county board of elections, and pre-canvassing. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Move the deadline for applying for absentee and mail-in ballots earlier, requiring that they be received no later than 5:00 p.m. on the fifteenth day before the election or primary. Under existing law, applications received by 5:00 p.m. on the first Tuesday before the primary or election must be processed.
  • Mandate that the county board of elections pre-canvass absentee ballots at least once before election day at the county courthouse or the county board of elections offices. When pre-canvassing is completed, the county board of elections may begin opening unchallenged ballots, rejecting ballots that reveal the identity of the voter, and counting votes at 8:00 on the Tuesday before the election. Under existing law, this process may not begin until 7:00 a.m. on the morning of the election.

  • Require that poll workers deliver all absentee ballots to the county board of elections by 2:00 a.m. on the day after the election.

Last Updated June 23, 2021

This bill, as introduced on August 11, 2021, would amend the Pennsylvania Election Code and vest election administration and campaign finance oversight power in a to-be-established Election Commission and strip the Secretary of the Commonwealth and the Department of State from all such powers that they currently hold. Specifically, the bill would divest the following powers from the Secretary of the Commonwealth and reallocate them to the Election Commission:

  • Establishing and administering websites or portals that allow voters to:
    • Apply for an absentee or mail-in ballot.
    • Apply for permanent absentee voter status.
    • Determine the status of their provisional ballot.
  • Promulgating election administration regulations.
  • Tabulating vote counts for statewide offices based on certified returns received from county boards of elections.
  • Certifying votes for national convention delegates, members of the state committee, and members of the Pennsylvania General Assembly.
  • Ordering recounts and recanvasses when unofficial returns meet statutory standards for recounts.
  • Approving alterations to election districts received from a county board of elections.
  • Approving voting machines and electronic voting systems (including experimental UOCAVA electronic voting systems) and procuring such machines and systems for counties that fail to do so within statutory timeframes. This power includes the power to decertify voting machines and to apply for bonds for reimbursements to counties that must procure new voting machines due to decertification.
  • Forming an advisory board for the statewide voter registration system known as SURE.
  • Creating a procedure for reviewing complaints under HAVA.
  • Prescribing forms for:
    • absentee and mail-in ballot applications,
    • absentee ballot inner and outer envelopes,
    • voter assistance forms,
    • nominating candidates for office,
    • candidate finance report disclosures, instructions, and the penalties for non-filing,
    • ballots, ballot boxes, ballot envelopes, ballot labels, certificates, returns, and other voting supplies,
    • HAVA complaint forms,
    • return sheets, and
    • political committee registration, receipt/expenditure, and annual forms.
  • Prescribing procedures for:
    • minimum capacity standards at election districts,
    • ballot secrecy measures for in-person voting,
  • Being a member of the Pennsylvania Election Law Advisory Board.
  • Receiving certified primary and election results and reports of election activities from county boards of elections.
  • Reimbursing county boards of elections for costs incurred in special elections and in mailing and handling absentee ballots.
  • Handling many aspects of candidate nominations, including:
    • Designating to the county boards of elections the offices for which candidates will be nominated.
    • Accepting nominations for candidates, verifying candidates, and accepting any subsequent withdrawals or revocations for candidates in national and state offices to be filled in a November general election, candidates for judges of courts of records, and candidates in all special elections for federal, state, and local offices and verifying such candidates. The list of candidates for these offices must be provided to the county boards of elections.
    • Determining the ballot order of candidates for offices whose nominating forms are filed with the Election Commission.
    • Accepting filing fees from candidates whose nominating forms are filed with the Election Commission.
  • Certifying statewide and county-wide political parties and accepting rules instituted by the state committee for each political party, including delegate rules.
  • Determining the wording for constitutional amendments and other ballot questions.

  • Campaign finance oversight, including publishing campaign contribution information and contracting for audit services and working with such auditor on random audits of campaign expenditures.

    Last updated January 27, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on August 11, 2021, would create an Election Day state holiday on the Tuesday following the first Monday in November in each even numbered year. On the holiday, the commonwealth and its political subdivisions must provide two hours of paid leave to its employees. Private employers are specifically exempted from having to provide paid leave on the Election Day holiday.

Note: the bill proposes legislative findings, including that "voting is a right and a privilege that is a civil duty and responsibility of residents within a free society."

Last updated August 18, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on August 11, 2021, would create an Election Commission to administer and oversee elections and campaign finance in lieu of the Secretary of the Commonwealth and the Department of State. The Election Commission would have the powers set forth in accompanying bill PA S 819. This bill would:

  • Create the Election Commission, comprising three commissioners, with one appointed by the Governor, one appointed by the President pro tempore of the Senate, and one appointed by the Speaker of the House. If those three are all members of the same party, the minority leader of the Senate will appoint a member instead of the President pro tempore of the Senate. The Governor's appointee serves as the chair of the Election Commission. Commissioners cannot:
    • be a member of political party's committee,
    • be an officer in a partisan political organization,
    • be a public official or candidate for public office,
    • be the spouse, parent, grandparent, sibling, child, or grandchild of an elected office holder or candidate in Pennsylvania, or
    • be a state or local governmental lobbyist.
  • Create four-year terms for members of the Election Commission, with a maximum of two terms possible for each commissioner.
  • Specify that any constitutionally-mandated function of the Secretary of the Commonwealth will not be performed by the Election Commission.
  • Set forth additional duties for the Election Commission in addition to those set forth in PA S 819, including:
    • Promulgating and distributing standardized voter registration, absentee ballot application, and voter death notice forms.
    • Developing, establishing, implementing, and administering the statewide voter registry (known as "SURE" in Pennsylvania).
    • Implementing and enforcing the driver's license voter registration system and voter registration at all public agencies that provide public assistance.
    • Overseeing UOCAVA voting.
    • Submitting an annual report to the General Assembly on election administration and recommendations for improvements.
    • Developing an annual budget request.
    • Holding hearings.
    • Retaining records.
    • Auditing local elections records and seek remedies for local noncompliance with election procedures.
  • Provide for the Election Commission to hire a full-time executive director and provide that the current staff of the Bureau of Commissions, Elections and Legislation at the Department of State remains employees of the Department of State but reports to the Election Commission.

  • Relocate existing entities or boards relating to elections or campaign finance that are currently located within the Department of State to be located in the Elections Commission.

    Last updated February 14, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on September 17, 2021, would change existing law on absentee voting (which, in Pennsylvania, includes both "absentee voting" and "mail-in voting") and the powers and duties of the Secretary of the Commonwealth. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Change existing law governing absentee voting applications, ballot return, pre-canvassing, and canvassing, by:
    • Eliminating the existing permanent mail-in ballot list, which currently allows voters to automatically receive a mail-in ballot application every year and which also allows a voter to apply to receive a mail-in ballot for all election in the year following application. This bill would also prohibit election officials from establishing permanent mail-in voting lists in the future.
    • Moving the deadline for absentee ballot applications from the existing deadline of 5:00 p.m. the Tuesday before the primary or election to 14 days before the primary or election, except that a voter who hand-delivers their own absentee ballot application has until 5:00 p.m. the Tuesday before the primary or election to do so.
    • Defining acceptable methods of absentee ballot return to mailing the ballot via USPS, in-person delivery by the voter to the county board of elections during office hours, and in-person delivery by the voter to a drop box established by the county board of elections. Under existing law, return of absentee ballots to a drop box is not addressed statutorily.
    • Regulating drop boxes by requiring that drop boxes, if established by a county board of elections, be monitored during all hours of operation, with recordings available to the public after vote counting. Ballots would be collected immediately after closing every night, or at 8:00, whichever is earlier. Drop boxes must be in fixed locations that meet accessibility requirements applicable to polling places, with locations announced at least 30 days prior to their establishment.

  • Change the Secretary of the Commonwealth's powers and duties by:

    • Requiring the Secretary to conduct monthly list maintenance for statewide deaths by seeking additional sources for deaths, including Department of Health records, newspaper obituaries, letters testamentary, and letters of administration issued by the office of register of wills. This maintenance must be conducted daily in the two weeks before every election and primary.
    • Repealing the Secretary's power to develop voluntary professional certification and training and replacing this power with a requirement that the Secretary provide assistance and reimbursement to county election officials for mandatory annual poll worker and election observer trainings, which must include training on voter rights and responsibilities, sample ballots, and election observer rights and responsibilities.
    • Directing the Secretary to provide official instructions and procedures manuals on voting and ballot procedures, including department directives and troubleshooting documents.
    • Requiring the Secretary to make rules regarding tramitting ballots and election materials to and from polling places.
    • Mandating that the Secretary create a tracking system for absentee ballots. Under existing law, tracking exists but is not statutorily required.
    • Requiring the Secretary to participate in ERIC and ensure that statewide voter registration data is updated with data obtained from ERIC and NCOA.
    • Directing the Secretary to provide uniform standards for drop box implementation and to publish a list of drop box locations in each county and throughout the state.

Last Updated September 19, 2021

This resolution, as introduced on September 28, 2021, would propose three "separate and distinct" amendments to the state constitution.

  • The first proposed constitutional amendment would end mail-in voting by requiring only in-person voting except as permitted by the constitution. Under existing constitutional language, absentee voting is permitted only for narrow reasons. This amendment would also mandate that all ballots cast other than in-person (except those received from military or overseas voters) be received by 5:00 p.m. the Friday before an election. Under existing law, absentee and mail-in ballots must be received by 8:00 p.m. on Election Day.
  • The second proposed constitutional amendment would require that any ballot cast other than in-person be subject to signature verification. Under existing law, signature verification is not expressly required and its use has been judicially enjoined.
  • The third proposed constitutional amendment would prohibit the creation, existence, or maintenance of a permanent absentee voter list. Under existing law, voters may be placed on a list to permanently receive absentee or mail-in ballot applications. There are specific provisions under existing law providing access to this permanent list to disabled voters.

In Pennsylvania, constitutional amendments have to be passed by a majority in two consecutive legislative sessions then submitted to voters as a ballot question.

Last Updated October 20, 2025

This bill, as introduced on October 19, 2021, would place a moratorium on no-excuse absentee (called "voting by mail-in ballot" in Pennsylvania) until the earlier of the 2023 primary election and enactment of legislation that "addresses any problem associated with voting by an official mail-in ballot."

Last Updated October 20, 2021

This bill, as enacted on July 11, 2022, prohibits private funding of elections and enforces the prohibition with a new misdemeanor offense, creates an election administration grant program for counties with specific conditions regarding election conduct, and requires counties to do a one-time self-audit and to make a specified report. Specifically, the bill:

  • Prohibits any governmental units from accepting gifts, donations, grants, or funding from private and non-governmental entities to register voters, or to prepare for, administer, or conduct an election. Governmental units are limited to accepting appropriations from federal, state, and local governments from taxes, fees, and other sources of public revenue. The bill exempts from this blanket prohibition on private funding donations of voting locations, volunteer services, and goods with a nominal value.
  • Creates a new second degree misdemeanor offense for accepting prohibited private funding for election-related expenses, punishable by up to two years in prison and/or a fine of up to $5,000.
  • Creates a grant program under which counties can receive a share of state election appropriations, based on the percentage of the state's registered voters that are registered in their county. The grants could be used for specified election processes. Counties must report on how the funds are spent, and as a condition of receiving a grant, a county must agree to:
    • Begin pre-canvassing at 7 a.m. on Election Day and continue without interruption until all ballots received by that point have been pre-canvassed.
    • Begin canvassing mail-in and absentee ballots at 8 pm on Election Day and continue without interruption until all such ballots have been canvassed.
    • Announce and post on its website, no later than 12:01 am on the day after Election Day, an unofficial total of mail-in and absentee ballots received for the election
    • Certify that they have done certain voter registration list maintenance activities within the preceding 12 months.
    • Submit any required post-election audit with the certification of results, which will be posted on the Department of State's website.
  • Requires the county boards of elections to prepare and submit to the Secretary of the Commonwealth, not later than five days prior to each election, a statement of the total number of registered voters in each election district by political party or other designation. The Secretary must submit that information to the legislative data processing center and publicly report on the total number of registered voters by party in each county before Election Day

  • Requires county boards of election, no later than 75 days after the bill's effective date, to do an internal review of practices and certify to the Department of State that the county is in compliance with:

    • Voter registration approval rules
    • Canceling deceased voters' registrations
    • Confirming voters' addresses
    • Complying with ballot custody rules
    • Enforcing voter ID rules
    • Pre-canvassing and canvassing of mail-in and absentee ballots

  • Hold at least 4 public hearings on proposed districts.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 26, 2021, would make numerous changes to Rhode Island election law. The bill would:

  • Create "Election Day-style" early voting for all elections. The bill would require local boards of canvassers to offer early voting for all voters beginning 20 days before Election Day until 4 p.m. on the day before Election Day. Each local board would select the locations for early voting, and each town and city would have at least one location.
  • Require early voting locations to be open for voting during normal business hours on weekdays during the early voting period. The bill would also require locations to be open from noon to 4 p.m. on Saturday and Sunday for the two weekends prior to a general election and for one weekend prior to all other elections. Local boards would be able to provide additional hours at their discretion.
  • Require local boards to publicize early voting locations and hours by publication in newspapers of general circulation, at the boards' offices, and on a city or town's website.
  • Eliminate the statutory requirement for a voter to be unable to vote in person to be eligible to apply for a mail ballot. Rhode Island will generally accept any reason for a voter's inability to vote in person, but this bill would remove the requirement to have a reason altogether.
  • Eliminate the requirement for a voter to have a notary or two witnesses sign their mail ballot.
  • Allow any registered voter to sign up for the permanent mail ballot list to automatically receive a mail ballot prior to each election. Existing law allows voters who are indefinitely confined due to illness or infirmity or who are disabled to sign up to automatically receive mail ballot applications before each election.
  • Require the Board of Elections to develop procedures to notify voters of issues with mail ballots by mail, text, phone, or email within one business day of discovery of the issue. The notice would describe the nature of the issue and instruct the voter how to cure the issue. The voter would have until 5 p.m. seven days after Election Day to complete the necessary steps to cure the issue and have the mail ballot counted. Existing law requires election officials to notify voters by mail or email and sets the cure deadline for primary elections at three days after Election Day.
  • Require the Secretary of State to create an online portal to allow voters to request mail ballots. The online portal would be offered with the online voter registration system and both would be offered in multiple languages.
  • Require state election officials to develop an online ballot tracking system that uses unique identifiers assigned to each mail ballot to allow voters to track their mail ballots. Rhode Island currently offers ballot tracking, but it is not required by statute.
  • Require election officials to accept as timely mail ballots returned by mail if they are postmarked by Election Day and received by election authorities no later than seven days after a general election and three days after a primary election. Ballots returned by mail and delivered without a postmark must be received by the day after Election Day. Existing law requires mail ballots to be received by election officials by the close of polls on Election Day to be considered timely.
  • Require local officials to provide secure drop boxes for mail ballot return beginning 30 days before each election. Each city or town must have at least one drop box, and must offer at least one drop box for every 20,000 registered voters. Election officials must also provide a drop box on the campus of any college or university with an enrollment of at least 500 students. Cities or towns providing multiple drop boxes should place them for maximum voter convenience and make them accessible for voters with disabilities.
  • Require all drop boxes to be clearly labelled with notices concerning tampering, voter hotlines, and postage. Boxes should be subject to video surveillance when possible. Outdoor boxes must be available to voters 24 hours per day, seven days a week, while indoor boxes must be available during the business hours of the building in which they are located. All boxes must be available to voters on Election Day when polls are open. Any voter in line at a drop box at the close of polls must be allowed to deposit their ballot.
  • Allow voters to return mail ballots to any early voting or Election Day polling location.
  • Require local officials to publicize the location of drop boxes on their website beginning 33 days before each election.
  • Allow election officials to begin verifying mail ballots 20 days before Election Day. Existing law allows verification to begin 14 days before Election Day.
  • Require election officials to compare the voter's signature on a mail ballot return envelope with the voter's signature in the statewide voter registration system for verification. Existing law requires officials to compare the voter's return ballot envelope signature with the voter's signature on the mail ballot application.
  • Allow initial signature comparison for ballot verification to be conducted by an election official or signature verification device. If a signature is deemed non-matching by initial review, it will be reviewed by two election officials from different parties. If both officials deem the signature non-matching, the ballot would be subject to the notice and cure provisions of this bill.
  • Allow a voter who has applied for a mail ballot to cast a regular ballot at an early voting location or Election Day polling place if they surrender their mail ballot. If the voter is unable to surrender their mail ballot, they may cast a provisional ballot.
  • Allow voters to apply for a mail ballot in person with the local board beginning 20 days before Election Day until 4 p.m. on the day before Election Day. Existing law sets the mail ballot application deadline at 21 days before Election Day.
  • Require mail ballot return envelopes to be designed so the voter's signature and identifying information is concealed by the envelope's flap. The bill would also require election officials to provide voters a secrecy sleeve for mail ballot return. Ballots would not be rejected for a voter's failure to return a secrecy sleeve.
  • Allow election officials to begin sending mail ballots to voters 30 days before Election Day.
  • Require the Secretary of State to use information obtained from the Social Security Administration's master death list to identify deceased voters subject to cancellation of registration. The bill would also require the Secretary to develop rules for updating voter registration lists at least four times a year based on information from the National Change of Address program of the U.S. Postal Service.
  • Allow visually impaired voters to apply for tactile or Braille mail ballots on the online ballot application portal or when applying to be placed on the permanent mail ballot voter list.
  • Require the Secretary of State to make available a toll free voter hotline with information about the voting process, registration, and polling locations. The hotline should offer information in multiple languages.
  • Create a voter access study commission to review the implementation and make recommendations concerning in-person early voting, mail voting, voter registration, voter access for individuals with disabilities, language minorities, victims of domestic violence, and individuals experiencing homelessness or housing insecurity.

Last Updated February 27, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Creates a redistricting commission to adopt a redistricting plan for all general assembly and congressional districts, provides for a possible right of appeal of the plan, to the state supreme court.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 26, 2021, would create a state redistricting commission to create and propose district maps for Rhode Island's federal congressional and state legislative districts. The bill would:

  • Create a state redistricting commission composed of seven members appointed by state legislative leaders and the state ethics commission. To be eligible to serve on the redistricting commission, a person may not have, within the two years prior to their appointment, held public office or have been a candidate for public office, lobbyist, state party officer, a relative within the first degree of consanguinity of a member of congress or the state legislature, or an employee of congress or the state legislature.
  • Require the redistricting commission to hold at least six public hearings prior to the creation of proposed plans and at least six public hearings after publication of proposed plans. The commission must provide the public with 30 days notice prior to a public meeting.
  • Require the commission to draw districts that are contiguous and comply with federal law. Congressional districts must be as equal in population as possible, while state legislative districts may not vary in population by more than 5%. Districts may not favor any incumbent or party, be drawn using partisan data, dilute communities of interest, or intentionally preserve the cores of existing districts. State legislative districts should minimally disrupt existing political subdivisions. Of the proposed plans that meet the above criteria, the commission should approve the districts that are most compact.
  • Require the commission to approve 3-5 district maps each for federal congressional and state legislative districts. The commission would submit the approved maps to the state legislature for approval and submission to the Governor for final approval or veto.
  • Allow any person who presented testimony or comment at a public hearing to appeal a district map to the state supreme court. The court may affirm the map or annul a map and refer it back to the commission, but may not alter a map in any way.

Last updated February 27, 2021.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on July 6, 2021:

  • Requires redistricting to be conducted in accordance with the Voting Rights Act, in addition to the US and Rhode Island constitutions. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill did not expressly require compliance with the Voting Rights Act.

    In provisions that were in the previous version of the bill, the bill:

  • Creates an 18-member commission, whose members are appointed by state legislative leaders of the majority and minority parties, to draft and present redistricting plans for state legislative and federal congressional districts to the General Assembly.
  • Requires districts to adhere to certain criteria:
    • Districts should be roughly equal in population, meaning that congressional districts may not deviate in population by more than 1% and state legislative districts may not deviate in population by more than 5%.
    • Districts should be compact.
    • Districts should respect existing political subdivisions and geographic features.
    • Districts should maintain the representation of communities of interest.
    • Districts should be composed of contiguous territory.
    • State senate districts should divide state representative districts as little as possible, and federal congressional districts should divide state senate districts as little as possible.
    • The commission should avoid the creation of voting districts composed of fewer than 100 potential voters.
  • Requires the commission to conduct open meetings before drafting redistricting plans, the records of which must be made public.

  • Requires the commission to submit its final plan by January 15, 2022.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 4, 2021, would make numerous changes to Rhode Island election law. The bill would:

  • Create "Election Day-style" early voting for all elections. The bill would require local boards of canvassers to offer early voting for all voters beginning 20 days before Election Day until 4 p.m. on the day before Election Day. Each local board would select the locations for early voting, and each town and city would have at least one location.
  • Require early voting locations to be open for voting during normal business hours on weekdays during the early voting period. The bill would also require locations to be open from noon to 4 p.m. on Saturday and Sunday for the two weekends prior to a general election and for one weekend prior to all other elections. Local boards would be able to provide additional hours at their discretion.
  • Require local boards to publicize early voting locations and hours by publication in newspapers of general circulation, at the boards' offices, and on a city or town's website.
  • Eliminate the statutory requirement for a voter to be unable to vote in person to be eligible to apply for a mail ballot. Rhode Island will generally accept any reason for a voter's inability to vote in person, but this bill would remove the requirement to have a reason altogether.
  • Eliminate the requirement for a voter to have a notary or two witnesses sign their mail ballot.
  • Allow any registered voter to sign up for the permanent mail ballot list to automatically receive a mail ballot prior to each election. Existing law allows voters who are indefinitely confined due to illness or infirmity or who are disabled to sign up to automatically receive mail ballot applications before each election.
  • Require the Board of Elections to develop procedures to notify voters of issues with mail ballots by mail, text, phone, or email within one business day of discovery of the issue. The notice would describe the nature of the issue and instruct the voter how to cure the issue. The voter would have until 5 p.m. seven days after Election Day to complete the necessary steps to cure the issue and have the mail ballot counted. Existing law requires election officials to notify voters by mail or email and sets the cure deadline for primary elections at three days after Election Day.
  • Require the Secretary of State to create an online portal to allow voters to request mail ballots. The online portal would be offered with the online voter registration system and both would be offered in multiple languages.
  • Require state election officials to develop an online ballot tracking system that uses unique identifiers assigned to each mail ballot to allow voters to track their mail ballots. Rhode Island currently offers ballot tracking, but it is not required by statute.
  • Require election officials to accept as timely mail ballots returned by mail if they are postmarked by Election Day and received by election authorities no later than seven days after a general election and three days after a primary election. Ballots returned by mail and delivered without a postmark must be received by the day after Election Day. Existing law requires mail ballots to be received by election officials by the close of polls on Election Day to be considered timely.
  • Require local officials to provide secure drop boxes for mail ballot return beginning 30 days before each election. Each city or town must have at least one drop box, and must offer at least one drop box for every 20,000 registered voters. Election officials must also provide a drop box on the campus of any college or university with an enrollment of at least 500 students. Cities or towns providing multiple drop boxes should place them for maximum voter convenience and make them accessible for voters with disabilities.
  • Require all drop boxes to be clearly labelled with notices concerning tampering, voter hotlines, and postage. Boxes should be subject to video surveillance when possible. Outdoor boxes must be available to voters 24 hours per day, seven days a week, while indoor boxes must be available during the business hours of the building in which they are located. All boxes must be available to voters on Election Day when polls are open. Any voter in line at a drop box at the close of polls must be allowed to deposit their ballot.
  • Allow voters to return mail ballots to any early voting or Election Day polling location.
  • Require local officials to publicize the location of drop boxes on their website beginning 33 days before each election.
  • Allow election officials to begin verifying mail ballots 20 days before Election Day. Existing law allows verification to begin 14 days before Election Day.
  • Require election officials to compare the voter's signature on a mail ballot return envelope with the voter's signature in the statewide voter registration system for verification. Existing law requires officials to compare the voter's return ballot envelope signature with the voter's signature on the mail ballot application.
  • Allow initial signature comparison for ballot verification to be conducted by an election official or signature verification device. If a signature is deemed non-matching by initial review, it will be reviewed by two election officials from different parties. If both officials deem the signature non-matching, the ballot would be subject to the notice and cure provisions of this bill.
  • Allow a voter who has applied for a mail ballot to cast a regular ballot at an early voting location or Election Day polling place if they surrender their mail ballot. If the voter is unable to surrender their mail ballot, they may cast a provisional ballot.
  • Allow voters to apply for a mail ballot in person with the local board beginning 20 days before Election Day until 4 p.m. on the day before Election Day. Existing law sets the mail ballot application deadline at 21 days before Election Day.
  • Require mail ballot return envelopes to be designed so the voter's signature and identifying information is concealed by the envelope's flap. The bill would also require election officials to provide voters a secrecy sleeve for mail ballot return. Ballots would not be rejected for a voter's failure to return a secrecy sleeve.
  • Allow election officials to begin sending mail ballots to voters 30 days before Election Day.
  • Require the Secretary of State to use information obtained from the Social Security Administration's master death list to identify deceased voters subject to cancellation of registration. The bill would also require the Secretary to develop rules for updating voter registration lists at least four times a year based on information from the National Change of Address program of the U.S. Postal Service.
  • Allow visually impaired voters to apply for tactile or Braille mail ballots on the online ballot application portal or when applying to be placed on the permanent mail ballot voter list.
  • Require the Secretary of State to make available a toll free voter hotline with information about the voting process, registration, and polling locations. The hotline should offer information in multiple languages.
  • Create a voter access study commission to review the implementation and make recommendations concerning in-person early voting, mail voting, voter registration, voter access for individuals with disabilities, language minorities, victims of domestic violence, and individuals experiencing homelessness or housing insecurity.

Districts should not diminish the voting power or representation of racial and language minorities or communities of interest. Districts should be compact and composed of contiguous territory that minimally disrupts natural and political subdivisions. Districts should not favor or disfavor any political party.
  • Require the commission to create a website to provide public access to information about the map-drawing process. Meetings of the commission should be open to the public and its records should be available for public inspection. The commission must hold at least four public hearings prior to proposing any maps. The commission must provide at least seven days for public comment on any map it proposes and must hold at least four public hearings after proposing maps.
  • Require the commission to propose final maps for adoption by the General Assembly by January 15, 2022, unless the late release of census data makes that deadline untenable, at which point the deadline would move to March 15, 2022.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on April 8, 2021, would alter the state's existing automatic voter registration system by requiring different procedures depending on whether the documents the person submits with their DMV transaction demonstrate U.S. citizenship or not. Under existing law, all qualified individuals are automatically registered to vote during DMV transactions, unless they choose to opt out during the transaction, if they provide proof of identity and residence and certify through documentation or a declaration that they are citizens. This bill would:

  • Limit automatic voter registration at the DMV to only those applicants who present documentation of citizenship, and change the opt-out process. For individuals who provide citizenship documentation, voter registration information would be automatically transmitted to election officials, who would subsequently send a notice of registration to the applicant. The bill would also allow the DMV to look at its records to determine if the individual had previously submitted documentation demonstrating U.S. citizenship even if they did not during the current transaction. If the DMV found such documentation, the DMV would also send the person's information to election officials, triggering the same notice. If the applicant failed to decline registration within 14 days of receipt of that notice, the applicant would be registered to vote. Under existing law, automatic voter registration requires only certification of citizenship, not documentation, and the DMV must provide the opportunity to opt out during the transaction itself.
  • End automatic voter registration for individuals who do not present affirmative documentary proof of citizenship at the DMV, and instead provide an opt-in streamlined registration process for these applicants. Individuals whose documentation neither proves nor disproves citizenship would be given the option to affirmatively choose to register by certifying their citizenship status, which may be done by declaration.
  • Provide that if the DMV has access to information to determine whether someone is already registered to vote and determines that an applicant is already registered, then the DMV would treat the transaction as a registration update and would send the person's information to election officials without regard to whether the person provided citizenship documentation in their DMV application.
  • Exempt from automatic registration people who are doing a DMV transaction using their business address rather than their residential address. Such people would be offered the opt-in streamlined registration process.
  • Prohibit automatic voter registration or streamlined voter registration at the DMV for any individual who fails to certify, by documentation or declaration, that they are a U.S. citizen, and expressly prohibit the agency from offering the opportunity to register to individuals who have documented their non-citizenship. Existing law requires certification of citizenship for registration at the DMV, but does not include an express prohibition on offering registration when documentation of non-citizenship has been provided. Nonetheless, existing law expressly contemplates registration of eligible individuals only.
  • Expand which additional agencies beyond the DMV may offer automatic voter registration, by permitting agencies to do so if they either collect documentary proof of citizenship or can verify citizenship by database matching or other means deemed reliable by the Secretary of State. Existing law limits automatic voter registration to only those non-DMV agencies that verify citizenship through documentation. The bill would also require non-DMV agencies that process transactions for multiple individuals eligible for registration to register each individual according to the procedures applicable to the DMV process.
  • Permit agencies that are not authorized to offer full automatic voter registration to make automatic updates to voter registration address information, if the Secretary verifies that the agency collects sufficient information to do so.


Last Updated October 14, 2025

  • Requires redistricting to be conducted in accordance with the Voting Rights Act, in addition to the US and Rhode Island constitutions. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill did not expressly require compliance with the Voting Rights Act.

    In provisions that were in the previous version of the bill, the bill:

  • Creates an 18-member commission, whose members are appointed by state legislative leaders of the majority and minority parties, to draft and present redistricting plans for state legislative and federal congressional districts to the General Assembly.
  • Requires districts to adhere to certain criteria:

  • Requires the commission to conduct open meetings before drafting redistricting plans, the records of which must be made public.

  • Requires the commission to submit its final plan by January 15, 2022.

BILLSUMMARY: (Joint Resolution) Adopts a specific constitutional procedure, including an independent redistricting commission, for redistricting.
VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as introduced on April 30, 2021, would create an independent redistricting commission for redistricting beginning in 2022 and every ten years thereafter.

  • Redistricting would be based upon the following criteria, in order of priority:
    • Compliance with the constitution through population equality based on the most recent decennial census.
    • Provide racial and language minorities equal opportunity to participate in the political process without dilution.
    • Geographic contiguity.
    • Partisan fairness.
    • Geographic integrity of political subdivisions or communities of interest.
    • To the extent that it does not conflict with previous criteria, compactness.
    • The commission cannot consider incumbency (whether favoring or disfavoring) and cannot act with the purpose or effect of diluting the voting strength of any language or ethnic identity group.
  • The commission must hold at least 5 public hearings before proposing a redistricting plan and at least 5 hearings after proposing a redistricting plan, in locations throughout the state. These meetings must have at least 7 days' notice. Any changes to proposed plans must be available to the public for three days, with an opportunity for public comment.
  • The commission's membership would:
    • Be 15 people, with 5 members from the majority party by registration, 5 members from the minority party by registration, and 5 members who are not members of either the majority or minority party, to be chosen from a pool of applicants, who are screened by the Secretary of State for qualifications. 6 people (2 from each party affiliation category) are chosen from this pool at random, and those 6 people then select the remaining 9 members (3 from each party affiliation category) based on qualifications, by a vote of at least 4 of the original 6 members, including at least one affirmative vote from each party affiliation category.
    • Be disqualified if they hold elective office at the federal, state, or local level, serve as staff or paid consultants to any legislature or political party, or have not been registered federal, state, or local lobbyists in Rhode Island in the past 5 years.
    • Be ineligible from holding federal, state, or local elective or appointive office in Rhode Island for 5 years after the termination of their appointments.
    • Be ineligible, along with their immediate family and household members, from being paid staff or consultants for Rhode Island legislators at any level or registered federal, state, or local lobbyists in Rhode Island for 3 years after the termination of their appointments.
  • The commission must approve 3 final maps by January 1, 2023, to certify to the secretary of state, with an explanation of the maps' compliance with the listed criteria. The commission may only approve final redistricting maps only upon the affirmative vote of at least 8 commission members, including at least one affirmative vote from each party affiliation category. If no maps are approved with the requisite votes, the secretary of the state shall petition the state Supreme Court to appoint a special master to draw a map following the listed criteria.
  • The general assembly must fund the redistricting commission at the level necessary to fulfill the commission's work, in an amount at least equal to the amount appropriated in the most recent redistricting cycle.

  • The Rhode Island Supreme Court has original and exclusive jurisdiction to any proceeding to challenge a certified final map. The commission has the sole legal standing to defend a certified final map, and the general assembly must fund any actions by the commission to defend such a map. Any registered voter may petition for mandamus within 45 days after the commission certifies a final map to prevent implementation of the map.

    Last updated May 4, 2021.

  • Required the department of corrections to provide individuals with information about when they will become eligible to vote and how to register upon release from DOC custody.
  • Required disenfranchised individuals to have paid all restitution owed before becoming eligible for restoration of voting rights. Under existing law, rights are restored upon discharge from probation and parole regardless of outstanding financial obligations.

BILLSUMMARY: (Joint Resolution) Proposes an amendment to the state Constitution, provides for an Independent Reapportionment Commission, provides for the membership of the commission and the manner in which members of the commission are chosen, provides for the duties of the commission, provides for the approval of proposed apportionment plans, provides for apportionment in the event that a proposed apportionment plan is not approved by referendum.
VRLANALYSIS:
This proposed constitutional amendment, as introduced on February 17, 2021, would establish an independent redistricting commission:

  • Plans would be submitted to voters for approval.
  • If the referendum failed, the supreme court would appoint a three-member tribunal to draw final maps, which would become law.
  • Maps would be drawn to create districts that are contiguous and, to the greatest extent possible, compact, while maintaining and respecting the integrity of political subdivisions, neighborhoods, and communities of interest, not considering relationships with political parties, incumbents, or political candidates, the place of residence of any incumbent or candidate.
  • Districts could not be apportioned for the purpose of favoring or discriminating against an incumbent, political candidate, or political party.
  • All deliberations of the commission would be public.
  • Commission membership would be selected by a three-member panel chosen by the inspector general.

Last updated February 18, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Establishes the State Fairness, Accountability, and Integrity in Redistricting Act to establish the criteria and process for apportionment plans created by the General Assembly.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on April 14, 2021, would establish requirements for the legislature in drawing congressional and legislative maps:

  • Maps would have to:
    • Comply with the U.S. Constitution, federal law, and the South Carolina Constitution.
    • Be as nearly equal in population as possible
    • Be contiguous to the extent practicable.
    • Be as compact as possible.
    • Reflect natural, historical, geographical, and municipal and other political lines, as well as the right of all South Carolinians to fair representation and equal access to the political process.
    • Give consideration to communities of interest, including, but not limited to, geographical areas where residents share cultural and historical characteristics, economic interests, or have common political interests that do not necessarily coincide with the boundaries of a political subdivision. Communities of interest do not include relationships with political parties, incumbents, or political candidates.
    • Make a reasonable effort to ensure that incumbent legislators remain in their current districts and are not placed into districts where they will be compelled to run against other incumbent members.
    • Preserve the cores of existing districts, to the extent possible.
    • Give consideration to political subdivisions.
  • Incarcerated individuals who were residents of the state before their incarceration would be counted in the population where they lived prior to incarceration. Incarcerated individuals who were not residents of South Carolina before they were incarcerated would not be counted for redistricting purposes.
  • Public hearings and a comment period would be required.

Last updated April 21, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on December 6, 2021, would change certain aspects of applying for and voting absentee ballots. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require voters to provide an ID number on their absentee ballot application, defined as either the voter's voter registration notification number, driver's license number, or state issued identification card number. This bill would require that the envelope be designed so as to obscure the voter's ID number from view. If an applicant fails to include their ID number, their ballot will be treated as a provisional ballot.
  • Change the dates on which a person may request an absentee ballot application, with requests for applications only being allowed from 78 days before an election to 11 days before an election. Under current law, absentee ballot applications can be requested at any time during the calendar year of the election in which the voter wishes to vote absentee.
  • Require that the address in the voter's absentee ballot application be the same address as is on file in the state election commission's voter registration system. Under current law, the applicant need only include their current address. If a voter wishes their ballot be mailed to an address other than their on-file address, the request must be made in writing, signed by the voter, and include the voter's ID number.
  • Prohibit a person from serving as a witness on more than five absentee ballot applications.
  • Require that return envelopes included with all absentee ballots be marked "return to sender" to prevent forwarding. Existing law is silent about forwarding return envelopes for absentee ballots.
  • Prohibit a person from requesting "absentee applications for more than qualified electors in addition to himself."

Last Updated December 24, 2021

This bill, as introduced December 6, 2021, would:

  • Require the executive director of the state election commission to establish rules and regulations for voter registration by private entities.
  • Require that publicly conducted audits be conducted immediately following an election, with the audit completed and results publicly available no later than seven days after certification. Existing law requires the executive director of the state election commission to conduct reviews, audits, or other post-election analysis of county board of elections and voter registration, but does not specify a timeline or require that results of such activities are made public.
  • Require that registrations be deleted within seven days of confirmation that a voter has deceased, is no longer qualified to vote in the precinct in which they are registered, have been convicted of a disenfranchising crime, requirests in writing that their registration be removed, or who is otherwise no longer qualified to vote. Under existing law, no timeline is specified.
  • Require the executive director of the state election commission to conduct a general list maintenance program annually. Under existing law, the executive director is required to maintain a statewide voter registration database but a timeline or frequency for list maintenance activities is not specified.
  • Allow the state election commission, at the discretion of the executive director, to use the United State Postal Service's change of address data to conduct list maintenance.
  • Require that notice be sent to a registered voter within seven days of receipt by a county board of elections of information identifying a discrepancy between the registration database and information collected by another state agency. Under existing law, the county board is required to "contact" such voters in an unspecified way, and no timeline is prescribed.
  • Require that voters who do not respond to address confirmation notices sent as a result of a new registration through a voter registration agency within 30 days be placed on the inactive list for eventual removal. Under existing law, only registrants whose confirmation mailing is returned as undeliverable are removed.

Last Updated December 24, 2021

This bill, as introduced on December 6, 2021, would amend the definition of domicile for voting purposes to make clear that a person who enters another state, county, or municipality and votes in such other location has changed their domicile for voting purposes. For general purposes, registering to vote in a new location is considered an act indicating a change in domicile. The bill would also remove certain factors from consideration in deciding whether a person has changed their domicile for voting purposes, including:

  • the voter's address on legal and financial documents,
  • the voter's address for club or organizational membership, and
  • a voter's temporary relocation due to medical care.

BILLSUMMARY: Requires each county election commission that establishes convenient voting centers to provide a report to the coordinator of elections within 90 days after each general election evaluating and analyzing the use of convenient voting centers.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on May 12, 2021, makes several changes to the requirements for establishing Election Day vote centers (called convenient voting centers in Tennessee). The original version of the bill contained a single provision that required counties that used vote centers to issue a report on their operation within 90 days of an election. That provision was amended out of the enacted version of the bill. In new provisions, the enacted bill:

  • Prohibits the state coordinator of elections from approving a county's vote center pilot project unless the county used at least one early satellite voting location throughout the early voting period for the most recent regular November election.
  • Amends the narrow population ranges that define which counties may participate in a vote center pilot project.
  • Extends the availability of vote center pilot programs to all federal, state, and local elections in 2022. Existing law applied only to local elections in 2019 and to federal, state, and local elections in 2020.
  • Allows any county that has previously piloted the use of vote centers and reported favorably on their use to establish permanent vote centers, regardless of the population limits set forth in this version of the bill. Existing law tied eligibility for permanent vote centers to participation in a pilot project during 2018.
  • Establishes the bill's effective date as January 1, 2022. This provision is modified from the previous version of the bill, which would have set the effective date as the date of enactment.

Last updated May 17, 2021.
