BILLSUMMARY: Relates to the composition of districts for the election of members of the State House of Representatives.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on October 25, 2021, draws the districts for seats in the Texas House of Representatives by reference to specific state counties and 2020 federal census data. These provisions are new to the enacted version of the bill. The previous version of the bill established district boundaries by general reference to a map file in the redistricting computer system operated by the Texas Legislative Council.

Last updated November 17, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on July 8, 2021, would make extensive changes to Texas elections procedures.

The bill would create a new requirement for mail ballot voters to include "exact match" ID numbers on ballot applications and return envelopes. The bill would also create a procedure to notify voters of certain issues with their mail ballots and give them an opportunity to go to the clerk's office to correct the issue or cancel their mail ballot and vote in person. The bill would:

  • Require a mail ballot voter to provide a Texas driver's license or state ID number, if they have one, when applying for and when returning a mail ballot. If the applicant lacks a Texas driver's license or state ID number, they must provide the last four digits of their Social Security number. If the applicant lacks either number, they must attest that they lack the numbers on the application or ballot carrier envelope.
    • If the ID number provided on the mail ballot application or ballot carrier envelope does not exactly match the ID number provided on the voter's registration application the ballot application or ballot will be rejected.
    • If the ID number provided on the ballot carrier envelope matches the ID number provided on the voter's registration application, the signature provided by the voter on the carrier envelope will be rebuttably presumed to match the voter's signature in their registration records.
    • Voters may use the numbers from expired IDs for mail ballot applications if the license or ID is "otherwise valid."
  • Require early voting ballot boards and signature verification committees that determine an mail ballot has a missing or mismatched voter signature, missing statement of residence, or missing witness information to: 1) return the carrier envelope by mail if the committee or board determines there is enough time to allow the voter to supply the missing information and return the ballot before the close of polls on Election Day, or 2) notify the voter of the defect by phone or email and inform the voter that they may come to the early voting clerk's office in person no later than the sixth day after Election Day to cure the defect or cancel their vote by mail application to allow them to vote in person. Election officials must take one of the two actions described above within two business days after discovering a defect.
  • Allow a voter to cancel their mail ballot application after the close of early voting and vote in person on Election Day if they receive a notice of mail ballot defect from the early voting clerk.
  • Require all mail ballot applications to be in writing with a wet (ink on paper) signature. Electronic and photocopied signatures would not be accepted.
  • Require mail ballots returned in person to be received by an election official at the time of delivery. The receiving official must record the voter's name, signature, and type of ID.
  • Allow election officials to use any known signature of the voter for mail ballot signature comparison.
  • Require the early voting clerk to report determinations of any voter's Election Code violation made by the early voting ballot board or signature verification committee to the Attorney General for criminal investigation.
  • Require ballots voted by mail to be tabulated and stored separately from ballots voted by personal appearance and separately reported on returns. The bill would also require ballots counted at central counting stations, precinct polling places, and ballots voted by mail to be tabulated and reported separately.
  • Require electronic records of mail ballot material to record both sides of any application, envelope, or ballot recorded.

The bill would prohibit outdoor and drive-through polling locations, even in cases of emergency or state proclamations of disaster. The bill would also define the daily time period in which early voting may occur. The bill would:

  • Prohibit a voter from voting from inside a vehicle unless the voter qualifies for curbside voting under current provisions of the Election Code.
  • Require early voting locations to be located indoors.
  • Require early voting locations in most counties to offer early voting for at least nine hours per day on weekdays during the early voting period. Voting hours are limited to between 6 a.m. and 10 p.m. Counties with fewer than 1,000 registered voters must offer early voting for only four hours per day on weekdays.
  • Lower the population threshold for mandatory extended early voting hours during the last five days of early voting from counties with a population of at least 100,000 to counties with a population of at least 55,000. Those counties must provide early voting for at least 12 hours per day on the last five days of early voting. Voting hours are limited to between 6 a.m. and 10 p.m.
  • Lower the population threshold for mandatory weekend early voting hours during the last five days of early voting from counties with a population of at least 100,000 to counties with a population of at least 55,000. Those counties must provide early voting for at least 12 hours on Saturday and six hours on Sunday. Voting hours are limited to between 6 a.m. and 10 p.m. on Saturday and between 9 a.m. and 10 p.m. on Sunday.
  • Require counties participating in the countywide polling place program to use the same methodology for the placement of temporary branch early voting locations that they use for placement of countywide polling places.

The bill creates new documentation requirements for individuals providing assistance to voters with mail ballots and at polling locations. The bill also creates new criminal offenses aimed at individuals providing assistance. The bill would:

  • Create a new standard form and oath for third parties assisting voters to complete. The form must be completed when assisting a person voting in person or by mail. The form would be incorporated into the standard form on a mail ballot carrier envelope.
    • The form requires the assistant to provide their name and address, relationship to the voter, and whether the assistant accepted any form of compensation from a candidate, campaign, or PAC.
    • The new oath requires the assistant to affirm that:
    • the voter represented that they are eligible to receive assistance,
    • the assistant will confine their assistance to reading or directing the voter to read the ballot and marking or directing the voter to mark the ballot,
    • the assistant did not pressure, encourage, or coerce the voter into choosing the assistant, and
    • the assistant will not communicate information about how the voter voted to another person.
  • Make failure to complete the oath or form when assisting a voter voting by mail a state jail felony unless the assistant is related to the voter within the second degree by affinity or the third degree by consanguinity or a previously known attendant or caregiver assisting a voter with a disability.
  • Make providing "vote harvesting services" for compensation and providing compensation for "vote harvesting services" third degree felonies. The bill defines "vote harvesting services" as "in-person interaction with one or more voters, in the presence of the ballot or during the voting process, intended to deliver votes for a particular candidate or measure."
  • Make knowingly collecting or possessing a ballot in connection with "vote harvesting services" a third degree felony.
  • Make exceptions to the vote harvesting provisions for:
    • An activity not performed in exchange for compensation or benefit,
    • Interactions that do not directly involve an official ballot, ballot by mail, or an application for ballot by mail,
    • Interactions that are not conducted in-person with a voter, or
    • Activity that is not designed to deliver votes for or against a specific candidate or measure.

The bill gives partisan poll watchers greater authority in polling locations and threaten election officials with criminal charges if they remove or obstruct poll watchers that the official perceives to be disruptive or intimidating to voters. The bill would:

  • Make an election officer's failure to accept a poll watcher authorized by a political party or candidate a Class B misdemeanor.
  • Make obstructing the view of a watcher or distancing a watcher to make observation not reasonably effective a Class A misdemeanor.
  • Allow poll watchers to sit or stand close enough to see and hear election officers conduct observed activity, except as otherwise prohibited by law. Watchers may not be denied free movement where election activity is occurring.
  • Allow poll watchers to observe all election activities related to polling place closure, including the sealing and transfer of a data storage device. A watcher may follow the transfer of election materials from the polling place to a regional tabulating center or central counting location.
  • Allow a poll watcher's appointing authority to obtain injunctive relief, a writ of mandamus, or any other remedy available at law if the authority believes the watcher has been obstructed. The Secretary of State may obtain injunctive relief, a writ of mandamus, or any other remedy available at law if the Secretary believes a state inspector has been obstructed.

The bill would prohibit election officials from enacting procedures based on local need to increase voter access and would enforce those prohibitions with criminal penalties. The bill would:

  • Prohibit a public official from creating, altering, modifying, waiving, or suspending any election standard, practice, or procedure mandated by law or rule.
  • Make the issuance by an election judge of a provisional ballot affidavit containing information the judge knows to be false to a voter a state jail felony.
  • Make it a state jail felony to solicit, receive, or accept compensation for assisting voters or collecting ballots. The bill would also prohibit an individual from compensating or offering to compensate anyone for the same activities. The bill makes an exception for attendants and caregivers previously known to the voter.
  • Create a state jail felony offense for perjury in connection with election procedures.
  • Prohibit an early voting clerk, subject to punishment as a state jail felony, from:
    • Soliciting the submission of an application by a person who did not request one,
    • Distributing an application to a person who did not request one unless otherwise authorized by law,
    • Authorizing the expenditure of public funds to facilitate third party distribution of an application to a person who did not request one, or
    • Completing any portion of an application to vote by mail and distribute the application with intent that the applicant will return the application to the early voting clerk.
    • The bill would create exceptions to allow officials to provide access to an application to vote by mail from a publicly accessible Internet website, to lawfully sign an application for a voter, and to provide a person or the public general information about voting by mail, the voting by mail process, and deadlines.
  • Prohibit an early voting clerk or other election official from distributing mail ballots or balloting materials to anyone who did not first apply for them. A violation of the prohibition would be a class A misdemeanor.
  • Make voting in an election in Texas after voting in an election in another state in which a federal office appears on the ballot and the Election Day for both states is the same day punishable as "illegal voting".
  • Establish that a person may not be convicted of illegal voting solely because they signed a provisional ballot affidavit unless corroborated by other evidence that they knowingly committed the offense. This provision would apply to conduct that occurred prior to the enactment of the bill, but would not overturn existing convictions.
  • Add "altering the ballot of another or otherwise causing a ballot to not reflect the intent of the voter", "preventing a voter from casting a legal ballot in an election they are eligible to vote in", and "giving a voter false information to prevent them from voting in an election they are eligible to vote in" to the list of conduct that can constitute election fraud. The bill would also raise the severity of the offense of election fraud from a class A misdemeanor to a state jail felony if committed by an election officer in their official capacity.

The bill would also:

  • Require information in a voter registration form to be provided by the voter.
  • Allow digital correction of voter registration information for all voters. Existing law limits this to voters who remain in the same county.
    • If the voter notifies the county in which they are currently registered that they have moved to a new county, that information and the voter's original application will be forwarded to the new county. The two counties will coordinate cancellation of the old registration and creation of a new registration in the new county of residence.
  • Require a registrar who determines an ineligible voter registered or attempted to vote in an election, they will deliver an affidavit to the attorney general, Secretary of State, and county prosecuting attorney.
  • Require sentencing courts to advise individuals convicted of felonies of the effect of the conviction on their right to vote. The court must make an affirmative finding of guilt and enter the affirmative finding in the judgment of the case.
  • Require state trial and appellate courts with jurisdiction over election-related cases seeking injunctive relief to prioritize hearings in such cases beginning 70 days before a general or special election.
    • Any person who communicates with an appellate court with the intention to influence the composition of a three-judge panel can be charged with a state jail felony.
    • Any person who communicates with a trial court with the intention to influence the court or judge assigned to a case can be charged with a class A misdemeanor. The offense rises to a state jail felony if it is committed by a person acting in their official capacity as an election official.

Last Updated July 19, 2021

    • Completing any portion of an application to vote by mail and distribute the application with intent that the applicant will return the application to the early voting clerk.
    • The bill would create exceptions to allow officials to provide access to an application to vote by mail from a publicly accessible Internet website, to lawfully sign an application for a voter, and to provide a person or the public general information about voting by mail, the voting by mail process, and deadlines.
  • Prohibit an early voting clerk or other election official from distributing mail ballots or balloting materials to anyone who did not first apply for them. A violation of the prohibition would be a class A misdemeanor.
  • Make voting in an election in Texas after voting in an election in another state in which a federal office appears on the ballot and the Election Day for both states is the same day punishable as "illegal voting".
  • Establish that a person may not be convicted of illegal voting solely because they signed a provisional ballot affidavit unless corroborated by other evidence that they knowingly committed the offense. This provision would apply to conduct that occurred prior to the enactment of the bill, but would not overturn existing convictions.
  • Add "altering the ballot of another or otherwise causing a ballot to not reflect the intent of the voter", "preventing a voter from casting a legal ballot in an election they are eligible to vote in", and "giving a voter false information to prevent them from voting in an election they are eligible to vote in" to the list of conduct that can constitute election fraud. The bill would also raise the severity of the offense of election fraud from a class A misdemeanor to a state jail felony if committed by an election officer in their official capacity.

The bill would also:

  • Require information in a voter registration form to be provided by the voter.
  • Allow digital correction of voter registration information for all voters. Existing law limits this to voters who remain in the same county.
    • If the voter notifies the county in which they are currently registered that they have moved to a new county, that information and the voter's original application will be forwarded to the new county. The two counties will coordinate cancellation of the old registration and creation of a new registration in the new county of residence.
  • Require a registrar who determines an ineligible voter registered or attempted to vote in an election, they will deliver an affidavit to the attorney general, Secretary of State, and county prosecuting attorney.
  • Require sentencing courts to advise individuals convicted of felonies of the effect of the conviction on their right to vote. The court must make an affirmative finding of guilt and enter the affirmative finding in the judgment of the case.
  • Require state trial and appellate courts with jurisdiction over election-related cases seeking injunctive relief to prioritize hearings in such cases beginning 70 days before a general or special election.
    • Any person who communicates with an appellate court with the intention to influence the composition of a three-judge panel can be charged with a state jail felony.
    • Any person who communicates with a trial court with the intention to influence the court or judge assigned to a case can be charged with a class A misdemeanor. The offense rises to a state jail felony if it is committed by a person acting in their official capacity as an election official.

This bill, as amended on April 8, 2021, would use stiff criminal penalties to enforce new prohibitions on election-related activity by third parties providing voter assistance, election officers, local election administrators, and voters. The bill would:

  • Create a new standard form and oath for third parties assisting voters to complete. The form requires the assisting individual to provide their name, address, the manner of assistance provided, the reason assistance was provided, and their relationship to the voter. The form must be completed when assisting a person voting in person or by mail. The form would be incorporated into the standard form on a mail ballot carrier envelope. A previous version of the bill would have required assistants to provide a form of ID acceptable for voting when completing the form.
  • Change the standard oath for voter assistants to include language for the assistant to affirm they have not pressured, encouraged, coerced, or intimidated the voter to make any particular choices when voting. The previous version of the bill did not include "encouraged" or "coerced" in the new oath language.
  • Make failure by an assistant to complete the oath or form when assisting a voter voting by mail a state jail felony unless the assistant is related to the voter within the second degree by affinity or the third degree by consanguinity. The offense would rise to a felony of the third degree if the third party fails to complete the form while also offering unlawful assistance to the voter. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Make a false statement in connection with the voter assistance oath a class A misdemeanor. If the prosecution can prove the individual made a false statement in connection with assisting three or more voters in a four year period, the offense is punishable as a state jail felony. The previous version of the bill would have limited the application of the felony punishment to assistance of three or more voters in a single election.
  • Create state jail felonies for individuals to solicit, receive, or accept compensation for assisting voters or collecting ballots. The bill would also prohibit an individual to compensate or offer to compensate anyone for the same activities. An officer, director, or agent of an entity committing the prohibited acts would also be guilty of the offense. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Make providing "vote harvesting services" for compensation and providing compensation for "vote harvesting services" felonies of the third degree. The bill would define "vote harvesting services" as "direct interaction with one or more voters in connection with an official ballot, ballot by mail, or an application for ballot by mail that are performed with the intention that ballot be cast for a specific candidate or measure." This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Make knowingly collecting or possessing a ballot in connection with "vote harvesting services" a felony of the third degree. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Make an election officer's failure to accept an authorized poll watcher a Class B misdemeanor. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Make the removal of a poll watcher for any reason other than an offense related to the conduct of an election a class A misdemeanor. A previous version of the bill would have limited authorized removal to the watcher's commission of an offense constituting election fraud.
  • Make the issuance by an election judge of a provisional ballot affidavit containing false information entered by the election judge to a voter a state jail felony. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Add "counting invalid votes", "failing to count valid votes", and "altering the ballot of another or otherwise causing a ballot to not reflect the intent of the voter" to the list of conduct that can constitute election fraud. The bill would also raise the severity of the offense of election fraud from a class A misdemeanor to a state jail felony. A previous version of the bill did not include the prohibition against altering ballots and would have made election fraud a felony of the second degree.
  • Create a state jail felony offense for perjury in connection with election procedures. This is a new provision that was not in the original version of the bill.
  • Allow poll watchers to observe the sealing and transfer of any memory storage device from voting equipment. The bill would also allow poll watchers to observe the in person return of mail ballots by voters on Election Day. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Define specific lists of persons who may be present during election activity at a polling location, early voting ballot board, or central counting station. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Prohibit a public official, subject to punishment as a state jail felony, to:
    • Solicit the submission of an application by a person who did not request one,
    • Distribute an application to a person who did not request one unless otherwise authorized by law,
    • Authorize the expenditure of public funds to facilitate third party distribution of an application to a person who did not request one, or
    • Complete any portion of an application to vote by mail and distribute the application with intent that the applicant will return the application to the early voting clerk.
    • The bill creates an exception to allow election officials to post a link to a mail ballot application on a website. The previous version of the bill did not contain this exception.
  • Prohibit an early voting clerk or other election official to distribute mail ballots or balloting materials to anyone who did not first apply for them. A violation of the prohibition would be a state jail felony. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Prohibit a public official to alter or suspend an election procedure mandated by law or rule. A previous version of the bill would have made a violation a state jail felony and would have allowed alteration of rules if approved by the Secretary of State.
  • Establish that voting in a Texas election and another state's election conducted on the same day constitutes the offense of illegal voting, a state jail felony. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Give priority to docketing and hearing cases seeking injunctive relief for election-related conduct in district courts, courts of appeals, and the Texas Supreme Court within 60 days of elections. The bill would require hearings within 24 hours of a request by a party or the submission of a final brief in a case. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require courts to assign judges for hearings in elections-related cases on a random basis. The bill would make it a state jail felony for a person to speak to a clerk in any way to influence a judicial assignment for an elections-related case. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require local registrars of deaths and county clerks to provide abstracts of death certificates and probate applications within seven days of their preparation. Existing law allows these items to be sent within 10 days of preparation. A previous version of the bill would have required transmission of the materials within one day of their preparation.
  • Require election officers to maintain a log of all paper ballots issued and spoiled at polling locations using electronic voting systems that use paper ballots to record votes cast. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

A provision from a previous version of the bill was amended out of the text on April 1, 2021. It would have allowed state attorneys to apply to the Court of Criminal Appeals to appoint a special prosecutor for the investigation and prosecution of election-related offenses within 60 days of an election if the state attorneys determined they do not have adequate time or resources to conduct and conclude the investigation to quickly deter unlawful conduct.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to processes to address election irregularities, provides a civil penalty.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on September 20, 2021, would authorize retroactive and future reviews of election practices and results in Texas elections at the whims of losing candidates, party chairs, and election judges. The bill would:

  • Allow a candidate or party chair in a state or county election to make a written request for an explanation and documentation to a county clerk related to an action taken by an election official that appears to violate a provision of the Election Code, irregularities in precinct results, or inadequacy or irregularity of documentation preservation required by the Election Code.
    • The clerk must respond to the request within 20 days with a written explanation and documentation.
    • If the requesting party is not satisfied with the clerk's response, the requesting party may demand a further explanation from the clerk. The clerk must respond to this request within 10 days.
    • If the requesting party is still not satisfied with the clerk's response, the requesting party may request the Secretary of State to audit the issue. The requesting party will provide all of the documentation related to the request and the clerk's responses to the Secretary.
    • If the Secretary determines that the clerk's responses were insufficient to address the issue, the Secretary will perform an audit of the issue. The Secretary will issue a notice of the findings of the audit.
    • If the Secretary determines that a violation of the Election Code has occurred, the Secretary will issue a special notice that requires the clerk to remedy the issue within 30 days or face continuing civil penalties until the situation is rectified. The Secretary will also publish a list of clerks against whom civil penalties have been assessed.
  • Allow state or county chairs to request a review of the results of the 2020 general election by submitting a request to the county clerk. The county clerk must appoint an "election review advisory committee" composed of an equal number of members from each of the two major parties. The review would include all mail ballots and Election Day ballots from selected precincts and at least three randomly selected early voting locations (unless the county has fewer than three early voting locations, in which case all early voting ballots would be included).
    • The review can consist of no more than five contested races. If the request for review contains more than five races, five of the identified races must be randomly chosen for review. One of the races must be for presidential electors, federal office, statewide office, or state legislative office.
    • The committee must determine an acceptable margin of error for the county prior to beginning the review. If the review of any contested race falls outside the agreed margin of error, the committee will conduct another review after randomly selecting different precincts.
    • If any of the second reviews of contested races fall outside the agreed margin of error, the committee will conduct a final review. The final review will cover the entire county or the entire portion of the county containing the state legislative race at issue.
    • The committee will provide a report of the review to various county and state officials. The Secretary of State will provide notice of the results of the review to the Governor, Lieutenant Governor and each member of the legislature. The notice will include whether the review confirmed election results, differed by an amount within the accepted margin of error, or differed by an amount greater than the margin of error. If the review differed by an amount greater than the margin of error, the Secretary will attach a report to the notice detailing likely causes of the discrepancy and recommended measures to avoid similar discrepancies in the future.

Last updated September 20, 2021.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on August 7, 2021, would would eliminate the requirement for a voter to present photo ID prior to voting in person. The bill would:

  • Make a voter's registration certificate an acceptable form of identification and the first form to be requested by a poll worker prior to the voter being accepted to vote at a polling location. Existing law requires a voter to present an accepted form of photo ID prior to voting.
  • Allow voters who fail to present a voter registration certificate to present an alternative form of ID. Acceptable forms of ID would include all forms of photo ID sufficient for voting under existing law (except a Texas handgun license) or a copy of a utility bill, bank statement, government check, government document, or official mail from a government entity that includes the voter's name and current address.
  • Allow voters with a registration certificate indicating they are registered in a different precinct and who are not on the precinct's list of registered voters to vote a regular ballot if they complete an affidavit attesting to their residence in the precinct in which they are offering to vote and that they are not attempting to vote more than once in the election.
  • Require voters who do not present a registration certificate and are not on a precinct's list of registered voters to vote provisionally unless the poll worker can determine the voter is registered and the voter presents an acceptable alternative form of ID.
  • Reduce the severity of illegal voting from a second degree felony to a third degree felony. The bill would also reduce the severity of attempted illegal voting from a state jail felony to a Class A misdemeanor.

Last Updated August 10, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to establishing principles to govern redistricting plans enacted by the legislature.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on September 20, 2021, would establish principles for redistricting Texas state legislative seats, the state board of education, and congressional representatives. Specifically, the bill would require the legislature to ensure that the plan, including any modifications to it:

  • Would not unnecessarily divide counties and municipalities, and would draw district boundaries coterminous with the boundaries of counties and municipalities to the extent practicable.
  • Would keep intact communities of interest defined by social, economic, racial, ethnic, cultural, industrial, commercial, and geographic commonalities, to the extent practicable.
  • Would protect minority voting rights in accordance with applicable state and federal constitutional and statutory requirements, including the federal Voting Rights Act of 1965.

  • Would create districts as nearly equal in population as practicable in accordance with the other principles.

    Existing redistricting requirements are specified by the Texas constitution, the federal constitution, and federal law. Generally, districts must be approximately equal in population, and may not be drawn for the purpose or have the effect of denying or abridging the right to vote on the basis basis of race, color, or language group. In addition to these general requirements, state senate districts must be contiguous. State house districts must be apportioned based on population and respect county boundaries according to certain rules. State board of education districts do not have specific standards beyond the general ones.

    Last updated September 20, 2021.

The voter must provide a DPS number or the last four digits of their Social Security number to verify their identity on the attestation form. Voters may submit the necessary form in person, or by fax, mail, or email. Voters have until nine days after Election Day to submit the form.
  • Create pre-processing requirements for mail ballots. The bill would allows all jurisdictions to begin delivering mail ballots to the early voting ballot board 13 days before ED. The bill requires early voting ballot boards to begin delivering ballots seven days before Election Day and requires delivery to occur daily through Election Day. All ballots received by seven days before Election Day must be verified no later than four days before Election Day.
  • Allow voters who receive a notice of ballot defect from the clerk to cancel their mail ballot application after the close of the early voting period and vote in person on Election Day.

Last Updated July 9, 2021

Under existing law, electors are not allowed to be faithless in any circumstances.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to improvements to election integrity, including through a partial count of auditable voting system ballots, creates a criminal offense.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on August 7, 2021, would:

  • Require a partial count audit of voted ballots following the initial tabulation. Generally, counties would hand recount the ballots in 10% of the ballot boxes used in an election. County party chairs would meet and select the precincts and ballot boxes subject to the partial recount. If a partial recount reveals a disparity of more than 20 votes between the initial reported outcome of an election at a polling place and the results determined by the partial count, the county must conduct a countywide recount. The bill would allow poll watchers to observe every stage of the partial recount.
  • Allow county party chairs to purchase and install video surveillance equipment at polling locations and central counting locations. The Secretary of State must adopt rules to prevent tampering with ballot boxes, keep ballot boxes in surveilled areas, allow poll watcher to observe the transportation of ballot boxes, require surveillance equipment not to record voters' faces, and prevent interference with the surveillance equipment. The bill would make interference with the surveillance equipment or prevention of poll watcher observation related to the surveillance equipment a third degree felony.

Last updated November 1, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to establishing principles to govern redistricting plans enacted by the legislature.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on October 6, 2021, would establish criteria for redistricting plans for congressional and state legislative seats. Specifically, the bill would require a redistricting plan to:

  • Respect the integrity of the state's basic geographic regions to the extent practicable.
  • Avoid unnecessarily dividing counties and municipalities, creating district boundaries coterminous with the boundaries of counties and municipalities, to the extent practicable. If division of a county or municipality is unavoidable, district lines would follow boundaries such as rivers, mountains, state highways, or residential subdivisions to the extent practicable.
  • Keep intact communities of interest defined by social, economic, racial, ethnic, cultural, industrial, commercial, and geographic commonalities, to the extent practicable.
  • Be geographically compact and composed of convenient contiguous territory.
  • Not be drawn with consideration to partisan political effect or with intent to favor or disfavor any specific person, political party, or other organization.
  • Comply with applicable state and federal constitutional and statutory requirements, including the federal Voting Rights Act of 1965.
  • Be equal in population as nearly as practicable in accordance with the other principles described by this subsection.

  • Be drawn in a manner that does not discriminate on the basis of race, color, or membership in a language minority group by ensuring the voting strength of racial, ethnic, and language minorities in the districts is not intentionally or inadvertently diluted in a manner that deprives minority voters of an equal opportunity to elect a candidate of their choice. This requirement would be in addition to that imposed by federal law.

    Last updated October 8, 2021.

  • Require the redistricting committee in each chamber of the Legislature to conduct at least 10 public hearings. The committee must conduct at least five hearings after census data is published. BILLSUMMARY: Relates to processes to address election irregularities, provides a civil penalty.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on September 1, 2021, would authorize retroactive and future reviews of election practices and results in Texas elections at the whims of losing candidates, party chairs, and election judges. The bill would:

  • Allow a candidate or party chair in a state or county election to make a written request for an explanation and documentation to a county clerk related to an action taken by an election official that appears to violate a provision of the Election Code, irregularities in precinct results, or inadequacy or irregularity of documentation preservation required by the Election Code.
    • The clerk must respond to the request within 20 days with a written explanation and documentation.
    • If the requesting party is not satisfied with the clerk's response, the requesting party may demand a further explanation from the clerk. The clerk must respond to this request within 10 days.
    • If the requesting party is still not satisfied with the clerk's response, the requesting party may request the Secretary of State to audit the issue. The requesting party will provide all of the documentation related to the request and the clerk's responses to the Secretary.
    • If the Secretary determines that the clerk's responses were insufficient to address the issue, the Secretary will perform an audit of the issue. The Secretary will issue a notice of the findings of the audit.
    • If the Secretary determines that a violation of the Election Code has occurred, the Secretary will issue a special notice that requires the clerk to remedy the issue within 30 days or face continuing civil penalties until the situation is rectified. The Secretary will also publish a list of clerks against whom civil penalties have been assessed.
  • Allow state or county chairs to request a review of the results of the 2020 general election by submitting a request to the county clerk. The county clerk must appoint an "election review advisory committee" composed of an equal number of members from each of the two major parties. The review would include all mail ballots and Election Day ballots from selected precincts and three randomly selected early voting locations (unless the county has fewer than three early voting locations, in which case all early voting ballots would be included).
    • The review can consist of no more than five contested races. If the request for review contains more than five races, five of the identified races must be randomly chosen for review. One of the races must be for presidential electors, federal office, statewide office, or state legislative office.
    • The committee must determine an acceptable margin of error for the county prior to beginning the review. If the review of any contested race falls outside the agreed margin of error, the committee will conduct another review after randomly selecting different precincts.
    • If any of the second reviews of contested races fall outside the agreed margin of error, the committee will conduct a final review. The final review will cover the entire county or the entire portion of the county containing the state legislative race at issue.
    • The committee will provide a report of the review to various county and state officials. The Secretary of State will provide notice of the results of the review to the Governor, Lieutenant Governor and each member of the legislature. The notice will include whether the review confirmed election results, differed by an amount within the accepted margin of error, or differed by an amount greater than the margin of error. If the review differed by an amount greater than the margin of error, the Secretary will attach a report to the notice detailing likely causes of the discrepancy and recommended measures to avoid similar discrepancies in the future.

Last updated September 2, 2021.

Attempts would be punished as third degree felonies.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to the Independent Citizen Redistricting Commission.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 12, 2021, would establish an Independent Citizen Redistricting Committee and define its procedures for drawing of federal congressional districts. The bill would:

  • Establish the Independent Citizens Redistricting Committee that will be responsible for drawing congressional districts. The Committee would be composed of 14 members: five majority party members, five minority party members, and four independent members. Nine members would be required to constitute a quorum, and nine votes would be required to approve any Commission action.
  • Provide that the State Auditor would select a citizen applicant review panel to review the applications for selection to the Committee. The review panel will be composed of three members: one from the majority party, one from the minority party, and one independent. The review panel would select a subpool of 20 applicants each from the majority party, minority party, and independent applicants. The majority and minority party leaders of each chamber of the state legislature would exercise two strikes from each of the three subpools, leaving 12 applicants in each of the three subpools. The review panel would then randomly draw eight names from those remaining in the subpools to become the first eight members of the Commission: three each from the majority and minority party and two independents. The first eight members of the Commission would then appoint the remaining six members from the remaining name in the subpools: two from each party and two independents.
  • Provide that the Commission would select a chair and vice chair by a 2/3 vote. The two officers may not be affiliated with the same party.
  • Establish rules for the Commission to draw congressional districts. The districts must comply with the federal and state constitutions, be equal in population, comply with the Voting Rights Act, be contiguous, and respect borders of existing political subdivisions and communities of interest. The Commission must try to draw compact districts while maintaining the other required criteria. The Commission may not consider incumbency when drawing districts.
  • Require the Commission to hold open meetings and provide public information regarding the redistricting process. The Commission would hold at least one hearing in every proposed congressional district and conduct public outreach for input and testimony. The Commission would make a preliminary map publicly available and allow at least 14 days for public comment.
  • Require the Commission to complete the final map by September 15 of each year ending in 1. If the Commission would fail to meet its deadline, the Secretary of State would petition the Texas Supreme Court to appoint special masters to draw the final map.
  • Provide that any registered voter may sue for a writ of mandamus or prohibition within 45 days of the certification of the final map to the Secretary of State. The Commission would have exclusive standing to defend the final map in such a proceeding.

Last updated January 12, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to improvements to election integrity, including through a partial count of auditable voting system ballots, creates a criminal offense.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on July 15, 2021, would:

  • Require a partial count audit of voted ballots following the initial tabulation. Generally, counties would hand recount the ballots in 10% of the ballot boxes used in an election. County party chairs would meet and select the precincts and ballot boxes subject to the partial recount. If a partial recount reveals a disparity of more than 20 votes between the initial reported outcome of an election at a polling place and the results determined by the partial count, the county must conduct a countywide recount. The bill would allow poll watchers to observe every stage of the partial recount.
  • Allow county party chairs to purchase and install video surveillance equipment at polling locations and central counting locations. The Secretary of State must adopt rules to prevent tampering with ballot boxes, keep ballot boxes in surveilled areas, allow poll watcher to observe the transportation of ballot boxes, require surveillance equipment not to record voters' faces, and prevent interference with the surveillance equipment. The bill would make interference with the surveillance equipment or prevention of poll watcher observation related to the surveillance equipment a third degree felony.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to the reapportionment of state legislative, congressional, and judicial districts and the creation, function, and duties of the State Redistricting Commission.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 12, 2021, would define procedures for the Texas Redistricting Commission that would be created by the adoption of the proposed constitutional amendment in TX HJR 59. The bill would:

  • Prohibit the Commission to consider incumbency, the residence of any candidate, past political party performance, or prior voting history when drawing districts, except when necessary to comply with federal law.
  • Require the Commission to conduct at least four public hearings concerning proposed plans in geographically diverse locations. The Commission would provide at least 14 days notice prior to any public hearing.
  • Require the Commission to publish a publicly-available report for each plan or modification that includes the population of each district, the criteria used for creation of the plan, and maps of each district. The Commission would also publish all data related to hearings, meetings, and plan consideration on the internet.
  • Require the Commission to submit adopted plans to the Governor, Secretary of State, and the presiding officers of both chambers of the state legislature.
  • Allow any person aggrieved by a redistricting plan to challenge the plan by petition to the Supreme Court of Texas.
  • Prohibit a member of the Commission to participate in their own political campaign or that of another candidate, serve on the state legislature within three years of the adoption of a redistricting plan, or participate in lobbying activities.
  • Establish the Commission as the backup to the Judicial Districts Board if the Board is unable to complete its duties.

Last updated January 14, 2021.

The bill would also make numerous changes to existing language to conform with the transfer of voter registration duties/authority from local registrars to the Secretary.
  • Require the Secretary of State to verify the citizenship of every applicant for registration through the Department of Public Safety or require the applicant to provide proof of citizenship in the form of a U.S. passport, birth certificate, or citizenship papers (the last two must be accompanied by photo ID). If requested from the applicant, proof must be presented in person, except an applicant may mail a copy of their birth certificate or citizenship papers with a copy of photo ID.
  • Require the Department of Public Safety to require proof of citizenship (same as above) with all registration applications completed during licensing transactions.
  • Repeal existing code provisions authorizing the appointment of deputy volunteer registrars and high school deputy registrars to conduct to facilitate third party voter registration drives.
  • Require the Secretary of State to conduct an audit of the entire state's voter registration list as of September 1, 2021. The Secretary would use data related to the death, conviction, or disqualification due to adjudication of mental incapacity of voters. The bill also reference a requirement to use data from the "Interstate Crosscheck" program for voters registered in other states.

NOTE: The Crosscheck program was suspended by litigation settlement in 2019, but Texas did join the Electronic Registration Information Center (ERIC) in 2020.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to the time for making required reports of deceased residents of this state to a voter registrar and to the secretary of state.

The previous version of the bill would have required the transmission of the monthly date within one day of its preparation.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to the reading and marking of a ballot by a person occupying a voting station or by the person's child.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on May 4, 2021, would allow a child under 18 years of age to accompany their parent into a voting station. A child under 14 would be allowed to help the parent read and mark their ballot. The bill would not make such minor children subject to other statutory requirements for assisting voters. The bill would require the Secretary of State to develop education materials regarding the procedures to allow a child under 14 to read and mark a ballot that will be posted on the websites of the Secretary and county election officials.

The previous version of the bill did not require the development of educational materials.

Last updated May 6, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on January 26, 2021, would eliminate the requirement for a voter to present photo ID prior to voting in person. The bill would:

  • Make a voter's registration certificate an acceptable form of identification and the first form to be requested by a poll worker prior to the voter being accepted to vote at a polling location. Existing law requires a voter to present an accepted form of photo ID prior to voting.
  • Allow voters who fail to present a voter registration certificate to present an alternative form of ID. Acceptable forms of ID would include all forms of photo ID sufficient for voting under existing law (except a Texas handgun license) or a copy of a utility bill, bank statement, government check, government document, or official mail from a government entity that includes the voter's name and current address.
  • Allow voters with a registration certificate indicating they are registered in a different precinct and who are not on the precinct's list of registered voters to vote a regular ballot if they complete an affidavit attesting to their residence in the precinct in which they are offering to vote and that they are not attempting to vote more than once in the election.
  • Require voters who do not present a registration certificate and are not on a precinct's list of registered voters to vote provisionally unless the poll worker can determine the voter is registered and the voter presents an acceptable alternative form of ID.
  • Reduce the severity of illegal voting from a second degree felony to a third degree felony. The bill would also reduce the severity of attempted illegal voting from a state jail felony to a Class A misdemeanor.

Last Updated January 28, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to election fraud, increases a penalty.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 26, 2021, would raise the severity of the crime of election fraud from a Class A misdemeanor to a state jail felony.

Last updated March 9, 2021.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on June 7, 2021, requires the Secretary of State to develop and maintain an online tracking system to allow a voter to track the status of their early voting by mail application and ballot. Voters using the system must provide: 1) their registration address and the last four digits of their Social Security number, and 2) a driver's license or personal identification number issued by the Department of Public Safety. The system must assign each mail ballot carrier envelope a unique barcode or tracking number, and must provide updates when:

  • the voter's early voting by mail ballot application is received by the early voting clerk
  • the application is accepted or rejected
  • the clerk mails the ballot materials to the voter
  • the clerk receives the completed ballot from the voter, and

  • the early voting ballot board accepts or rejects the voter's ballot.

    Note: The previous version of the bill did not include the requirement for carrier envelopes to include a barcode or tracking number.


Last Updated June 9, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 26, 2021, would prohibit political subdivisions, homeowners' and property owners' associations, and property managers from enforcing a rule that prevents an individual from interacting with occupants of residential units for the purposes of assisting them with voter registration or expressing support or opposition to a political party, candidate, or ballot measure. The relevant authorities would be able to enforce reasonable restrictions on the time, place, and manner of the authorized activities.

Last Updated January 28, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 26, 2021, would authorize early voting clerks to designate any number of alternative drop-off locations for early voting by mail ballots.

Last Updated January 28, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to the elements of the offense of illegal voting.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 27, 2021, would clarify the intent requirements for the crime of illegal voting. The bill would require the voter to know of particular circumstances that make the individual ineligible to vote and to know that those circumstances make the voter ineligible to convict the individual of the offense. Existing law merely requires the individual to know they are not eligible to vote to be convicted.

Last updated March 9, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on January 27, 2021, would automatically treat an application for an early voter ballot by mail for a main election as a ballot application for any resulting runoff election. Existing law gives the voter an option to apply for ballots for both elections.

Last Updated January 28, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to the inclusion of an incarcerated person in the population data used for redistricting according to the person's last residence before incarceration.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 28, 2021, would require federal, state, and local officials who operate a facility for the confinement of commitment of individuals to determine the last known residence of each individual prior to their incarceration or commitment. The State Comptroller will adjust census data to reallocate identified individuals to their last known residential address.

Last updated August 13, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on January 29, 2021, would expand the existing excuse related to childbirth to allow any voter giving birth or expecting to give birth within nine months of Election Day to cast an early voting by mail ballot. Existing law limits the childbirth excuse to voters with expected or likely confinement due to childbirth on Election Day.

Last Updated February 1, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 29, 2021, would:

  • Allow signature verification committees and early voting ballot boards that determine an early voting by mail ballots has a missing or mismatched voter signature, missing statement of residence, or missing witness information to: 1) return the carrier envelope by mail if the committee or board determines there is enough time to allow the voter to supply the missing information and return the ballot before the close of polls on Election Day, or 2) notify the voter of the defect by phone or email and inform the voter that they may come to the early voting clerk's office in person to correct the defect or cancel their vote by mail application to allow them to vote in person. The bill would require the board or committee that applies the optional notice and cure process to do so for all early voting by mail ballots.
  • Allow voters to cancel their application for an early voting by mail ballot after the close of the period for early voting by personal appearance if the voter receives a notice of ballot defect from a signature verification committee or early voting ballot board.
  • Require the early voting by mail ballot application to include a space for the voter to indicate a change of address within the same county. The bill would require the early voting clerk to notify the registrar of the change of address, which the registrar would use to update the voter's registration record. The bill would also eliminate the need to send such a voter a statement of residence form to accompany their early voting by mail ballot.

Last Updated February 1, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 29, 2021, would require the Secretary of State to create a unique application for an early voting by mail ballot for permanent caretakers of persons with a disability whose presence is necessary to protect the life or safety of the person with the disability such that it will prevent the caretaker from appearing at the polling place on Election Day. Following acceptance of the caretaker's application, the ballot would be delivered, marked, and processed in the same manner as other early voting by mail ballots.

Last Updated February 1, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 29, 2021, would require a signature verification committee or early voting ballot board to notify a voter if the committee or board determines that an early voting by mail ballot could be rejected due to a missing or mismatched voter signature or missing witness information to provide the voter an opportunity to correct the issue by the close of polls on Election Day. The bill would allow the committee or board to appoint two members from different political parties to take the defective ballot to the voter to allow the voter to correct the issue. The bill would not require the committee or board to notify the voter if it determines that there is not enough time for the voter to cure prior to Election Day.

Last Updated February 1, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 3, 2021, would require each county registrar to develop procedures to allow a person to complete a voter registration application over the Internet by September 1, 2021.

Last Updated February 4, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to the use of a movable structure as a polling place in a county participating in the countywide polling place program.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 4, 2021, would allow counties participating in the countywide polling place program to use moveable structures as Election Day polling places.

Last updated February 5, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on February 4, 2021, would make changes to the State Board of Education districts in Texas.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to reporting of Early voting totals.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on May 19, 2021, allows any registered voter in a county to file a complaint with the Secretary of State to report early voting clerks who fail to post the required daily roster of voters who have cast early voting ballots in person or by mail. The Secretary must establish a system for receiving and recording complaints, and must maintain a list of which clerks failed to comply with the reporting requirements.

Last updated July 19, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on February 5, 2021, would:

  • Create automatic voter registration during transactions in person, by mail, or online with the Department of Public Safety, including initial applications and renewals for driver's licenses and ID cards and changes of address. The Department of Public Safety will automatically transmit the information of any person completing a transaction who is eligible to vote to the Secretary of State unless the person indicates while completing the transaction that they do not wish to have their information transmitted for registration purposes.
  • Require the Secretary of State to implement a program to allow a person with an unexpired Texas driver's license or ID card to submit a voter registration application on the state's official website. The websites of the Secretary of State and the Department of Public Safety must provide a link to the online voter registration site. A digital copy of the signature of any person who registers online will be transmitted from the Department of Public Safety to the Secretary of State.

Last Updated February 6, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 9, 2021, would allow county officials to designate alternative locations for in-person return of early voting by mail ballots. The bill would also allow voters to return their early voting by mail ballots in person during the early voting period. Existing law limits ballot return to office of the early voting clerk on Election Day.

Last Updated February 9, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 9, 2021, would require election officials to allow poll watchers to stand close enough to election-related activities at polling locations, early voting ballot boards, or central counting locations to allow them to see and hear the activity. The bill would also make preventing a poll watcher from seeing and hearing election-related activities a class B misdemeanor.

The bill failed in committee after a committee substitute was offered on April 15, 2021.

Last Updated April 27, 2021

This bill, as amended on April 15, 2021, would prohibit the return of mail ballots to unattended receptacles other than a mailbox or common carrier receptacle.

The previous version of the bill would have prohibited all in person return of mail ballots.

Last Updated April 23, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to the registration of voters at a polling place and related procedures.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 9, 2021, would allow an eligible voter to register to vote at an early voting location or Election Day voting location by completing a voter registration application, presenting proof of ID, and executing an affidavit affirming that they are eligible to vote in the election and are only voting once. Acceptable forms of ID for same day registration would include: 1) a Texas driver's license, permit, or ID card containing the voter's current address, or 2) a utility bill dated within the last 30 days addressed to the voter, combined with i) a Texas driver's license, permit, or ID card, regardless of whether it contains the voter's current address, ii) a U.S. passport, or iii) a U.S. military photo ID. Voters accepted for same day registration will cast a regular ballot.

Last updated February 11, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on February 10, 2021, would:

  • Require early voting ballot boards to appoint an alternate presiding judge from the opposite major political party of that of the presiding judge. The bill would also allow early voting ballot boards to appoint members from any political party if a political party appearing on the ballot fails to submit list of names of persons eligible to serve.
  • Require a signature verification committee to appoint a vice chair from the opposite major political party of that of the chair. The bill would also establish that a tie vote of the committee regarding the acceptance of the signature on a ballot or application would result in the acceptance of the signatures. Existing law requires a majority vote of the committee to accept signatures.

Last Updated February 11, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 10, 2021, would require an early voting ballot application to include a space for a voter to provide an e-mail address. The bill would also require the early voting clerk to attempt to contact the voter via email to correct issues that could lead to the rejection of the early voting ballot application.

Last Updated February 11, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 10, 2021, would require the Secretary of State to establish a secure website to allow an individual with an unexpired Texas driver's license or ID card to submit an initial application to register to vote or to update their existing voter registration record.

Last Updated February 11, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 10, 2021, would lower the minimum age to preregister to vote to 17 years and 6 months. Existing law requires an individual to be 17 years and 10 months old to preregister.

Last Updated February 11, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 8, 2021, would authorize presidential electors to be "faithless" and vote for a candidate other than the one voters chose in one circumstance. 

Specifically, prior to the electors voting to choose a President, the presidential and vice presidential candidates who received the most votes in the state would have to certify their fitness to serve. If a majority of the electors rejected that certification, deciding that the candidates were not fit to serve, they would be able to vote for the other candidate. Under existing law, electors are not allowed to be faithless in any circumstances. 

Last Updated February 8, 2022

This bill, as introduced on February 10, 2021, would:

  • Allow a voter to return their early voting by mail ballot in person during the early voting period to an early voting polling location or the early voting clerk's office.
  • Require signature verification committees and early voting ballot boards to notify voters who fail to sign the ballot carrier envelope or for whom the carrier envelope signature cannot be verified to provide them an opportunity to cure the issue. Voters would have until five days after Election Day to cure the issue by appearing at the early voting clerk's office to sign the carrier envelope or affirm that they signed the envelope. If the committee or board determines that it would be possible to mail an unsigned carrier envelope to the voter to have the voter sign it and return it by mail by five days after Election Day, then the voter may cure an unsigned carrier envelope by mail.
  • Require the Secretary of State to provide an online ballot tracking portal on the Secretary's website that will allow a voter to track when the clerk receives the voter's ballot application, when the clerk mails the ballot to the voter, when the clerk receives the completed ballot from the voter, and whether the ballot is accepted or rejected.

Last Updated February 18, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 11, 2021, would allow voters to apply for absentee ballots for two calendar years (beginning in an odd-numbered year) on a single application.

Last Updated February 12, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to the date of the general primary election to be held in 2022.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 11, 2021, would authorize the Governor, Lieutenant Governor, and Speaker of the House to postpone the 2022 general primary by written agreement if the legislature does not complete a redistricting plan by September 1, 2021.

Last updated August 2, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on February 11, 2021, would authorize counties to provide early voting up to the day before Election Day. Existing law requires counties to end early voting on the fourth day before Election Day. The bill would require counties to provide early voting for at least 12 hours on a weekday or Saturday during the extended early voting period, and at least five hours on a Sunday.

Last Updated February 12, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 12, 2021, would allow only carrier envelopes for early voting by mail ballots for primary elections to include any notation of the voter's political party.

Last Updated March 9, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 12, 2021, would require election officials to provide electronic versions of election forms, election proclamations, registration notices, lists of appointed election judges and training times, and precinct boundary change notices on their official websites. The bill would also permit officials to provide an electronic form of a list of registered voters on request if the list is maintained in electronic form.

Last Updated February 16, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 12, 2021, would require county clerks to provide voters who qualify to vote early by absentee ballot for November elections held in even-numbered years with a preprinted ballot application that would apply to all elections held before December 31 of the next even-numbered year. The bill would allow voters to return the application in the carrier envelope with their ballot.

Last Updated February 15, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to the cancellation of a person's voter registration on notice that the person has acknowledged that the person is not a citizen.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 12, 2021, would require local registrars to cancel the registration of any person whose name appears on a list of persons excused or disqualified from jury service due to their citizenship status.

Last updated February 15, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to qualifications and registration of certain voters on parole or mandatory supervision.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 16, 2021, would restore the voting eligibility of individuals convicted of felonies released from incarceration on parole or mandatory supervision. Voters who are incarcerated for a felony sentence or on probation or community supervision for a felony would remain ineligible to vote.

Last updated February 17, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on February 16, 2021, would require the Secretary of State to develop a voter education pamphlet for residents of long-term health care facilities. The bill would require an employee of each facility to advise the residents of the facility audibly of their voting rights based on the information contained in the pamphlet at least 30 days before Election Day. The bill would also require facilities to make copies of the pamphlet available to residents in common areas.

Last Updated February 18, 2021

This bill, as introduced on February 22, 2021, would require an early voting clerk to include a unique code readable by electronic device with each early voting by mail ballot. Upon return of the ballot by the voter, the code on the ballot would be compared with the code recorded by the early voting clerk on provision of the ballot. If the codes do not match, the ballot would be rejected.

Last Updated February 23, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to voting system equipment, creates a criminal offense.

The county must consider population density in selecting the location of each polling place, so that each polling place serves approximately the same number of voters.

Last updated February 24, 2021.

VRLANALYSIS:

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to the composition of districts for the election of members of the United States House of Representatives from the state.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 23, 2021, would make changes to the federal Congressional districts in Texas.

  • Allow local jurisdictions with populations less than 100,000 to provide varying days and hours at temporary branch early voting locations. BILLSUMMARY: Relates to the statement of residence required to vote.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to the State Redistricting Commission.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 8, 2021, would establish the process to appoint members of the Texas Redistricting Commission that would create district maps for federal Congressional, state legislative, and State Board of Education districts and establish procedures for its work. The bill would:

  • Prohibit individuals from serving on the commission if, within the 10 years preceding their potential selection, they: 1) held certain political offices, 2) were employees of certain office holders, political parties, or campaign committees, 3) participated in lobbying activities, 4) contributed a defined minimum amount of money to any legislative candidate, or 5) have an immediate family member who would be disqualified for any of the first four reasons.
  • Require the state auditor to create 3 subpools of the 20 most qualified applicants from each of the majority party, minority party, and unaffiliated pools of applicants. The majority and minority caucuses of each chamber of the state legislature may then strike up to two names from each subpool, for a total of eight possible strikes from each subpool. The auditor would then randomly draw three names from the remaining majority and minority party subpools and two names from the remaining unaffiliated subpool. Those names would constitute the first eight members of the commission. Those eight members would then select the remaining six members of the commission by selecting two more names from each of the three subpools. The first eight commissioners must consider the diversity of Texas, including racial, ethnic, geographical, and gender diversity, when selecting the remaining six commissioners. The fully constituted commission would select a chair and vice chair, who may not be affiliated with the same party.
  • Require the commission to conduct an open and transparent process for creating district maps. The commission would maintain a public website to provide information about the ongoing map-drawing process. The commission would provide at least 14 days' notice prior to any meeting of the commission prior to September of the year ending in 1, at which time only three days' notice would be required. The commission would display preliminary maps for at least 14 days to allow public comment.
  • Authorize the governor to remove a commission member for substantial neglect of duty, gross misconduct in office, or inability to discharge the duties of office with the concurrence of 2/3 of the state senate.

NOTE: This bill is contingent on the enactment of the state constitutional amendment proposed in TX HJR 127 that would create the Texas Redistricting Commission.
