VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on June 15, 2021, makes numerous substantive and technical changes to Texas election law.

In new provisions that were amended into the May 26, 2021 version, the bill:

  • Allows counties with populations under 100,000 greater flexibility in the operation of temporary early voting locations. The counties may provide early voting at any day or time during the early voting period, and temporary locations may vary in the days and hours of operation. Each temporary location must offer voting on at least two consecutive days for at least eight hours per day.
  • Requires the statement of residence form to include a space for the voter to provide their county of residence.

In provisions that were in the previous version of the bill, the bill:

  • Moves the deadline for in-person return of mail ballot applications from 18 days before Election Day to 11 days before Election Day. The new in-person deadline matches the existing deadline for return by other authorized means.
  • Expands authorization for the use of countywide polling places to include use in any election conducted by a county, any joint election, or any election held under a contract for election services. Under existing law, elections that were eligible for countywide polling places were more narrowly drawn.
  • Requires mandatory training for election judges to include training related to service on an early voting ballot board and central counting station.
  • Specifies that applicants who return their voter registration application by fax must subsequently submit "a copy of the original" application with an original signature and permits doing so by personal delivery. Existing law required submission of a "copy" of the application by mail, and did not expressly specify that the form must include an original signature.
  • Expressly authorizes the secretary of state to order corrective action when election officials delay or cancel an election without specific statutory or judicial authority. Existing law authorizes the secretary to order corrective action only when an official's action "impedes" the free exercise of voting rights.
  • Requires voter registration cards to include only the voter's year of birth, rather than full birthdate as formerly provided by existing law.
  • Allows registrars to cancel the oldest registration of a voter in cases where there is a strong match for duplicate registrations in more than one county.
  • Allows election judges at polling locations to contact the registrar to determine if a voter's name has been accidentally left off of the precinct voter list. Voters accidentally left off the list may vote a regular ballot, while other voters not on the list must cast a provisional ballot. The bill also requires election officials to maintain a registration omissions list at each polling place to document the name, address, and voter registration number of each voter who was not on the precinct voter list but was allowed to cast a ballot, and the reason they were allowed to vote.
  • Makes individuals who are civilly committed as a sexually violent predator and ordered to reside in a Texas Civil Commitment Office facility eligible to vote by mail. The bill allows the individual to have their ballot delivered to the facility or a relative.
  • Allows election officials ten days to complete the verification and counting of provisional ballots. Existing law required verification and counting to be completed seven days after Election Day. The bill also prohibits making provisional ballot records available for public inspection until the business day after the completion of verification and counting.
  • Authorizes watchers to observe signature verification committee meetings during the performance of their duties. Existing law authorized watchers at early voting board meetings, but did not specifically permit observers at signature verification meetings.
  • Makes various changes to UOCAVA voting. The bill makes UOCAVA voting procedures available to members of the Texas National Guard or another state's National Guard and their spouse and dependents if the guard member is serving active duty on the order of the President or Governor. It also allows UOCAVA voters to return the federal postcard application in person or by common carrier, in addition to the current authorization for return by mail or electronic means, and allows UOCAVA voters to apply for a ballot for an election held in January or February within 60 days of the election, even if the application is returned in the previous calendar year. The bill also moves the deadline for requesting delivery of a ballot by email from seven days before an election to 11 days before.
  • Authorizes the early voting clerk, rather than the commissioners court, to select early voting locations in counties with populations between 100,000 and 120,000.
  • Requires registrars to remove a voter's name from the registration suspense list on receipt of a new voter registration application or updated information from the voter.
  • Makes technical changes to various provisions, including election notices, the countywide polling place program, and recount and petition procedures. The bill also includes various provisions that address topics Voting Rights Lab does not track.

Provisions from a previous version of the bill were amended out of the text on April 14, 2021. They would have:

  • Allowed voters to personally deliver their mail ballots to the county's main early voting polling location during the early voting period or on Election Day. Existing law allows the voter to personally deliver the ballot to the early voting clerk on Election Day only.
  • Moved the deadline for election officials to provide the record of voters in an election from 30 days after Election Day to five days after completion of the county canvass.

Last Updated August 2, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to procedures for public involvement in redistricting of state legislative districts and congressional districts.

The website would allow members of the public to comment on the redistricting process.
  • Require the redistricting committee in each chamber of the Legislature to conduct at least 10 public hearings. The committee must conduct at least five hearings after census data is published. Each hearing must be in a different congressional district. A hearing must be held in the district with the greatest population change from the previous census. The committees must provide seven days' notice prior to a hearing.
  • Require the committees to publish proposed plans to the website at least 72 hours prior to reporting the plan favorably out of committee. Each chamber must conduct at least two additional hearings after the committee reports a plan to the full chamber.
  • Require each chamber of the Legislature to post information concerning a final redistricting plan on the website and, if practicable, newspapers of general circulation, within seven days after passage by the full chamber.

The bill would also prohibit any alteration of voting standards, practices, or procedures unless the Governor declares a disaster.

Last updated March 10, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on March 9, 2021, would:

  • Allow only voters who return their unvoted mail ballot to vote a regular ballot at a polling location. The bill would require voters who applied for mail ballots but vote in person for other reasons to vote a provisional ballot. Existing law allows a voter who lost or did not receive their mail ballot to sign an affidavit and vote a regular ballot.
  • Require election officials to maintain a log of each ballot returned. The log would include the voter's name, a unique identifying number assigned to the voter, the voter's signature, and the date and time of the ballot's return.

Last Updated March 10, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 9, 2021, would require voters who submit a fax or email application for a mail ballot to submit a copy of the same application by mail no later than the seventh business day before Election Day. Existing law requires such voters to submit a copy of the application by mail no later than the fourth business day after the fax/email transmission.

Last Updated August 14, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 9, 2021, would:

  • Create a misdemeanor for a member of an early voting ballot board to handle balloting materials outside the presence of a member of the board from a different political party. The bill would also require all members of an early voting ballot board to complete an oath in which they affirm knowledge of this criminal penalty.
  • Require the early voting clerk to create a report of all early voting ballots received by the deadline that have not been accepted or rejected as of the close of polls on Election Day. The bill would prohibit the subsequent acceptance of any early voting ballot not contained with the report.
  • Create various anti-nepotism provisions to prohibit relatives of a certain degree of affinity or consanguinity to serve together as election judges, election clerks, or members of early voting ballot boards or signature verification committees.

Last Updated March 10, 2021

This bill, as amended on April 27, 2021, would:

  • Require ballots returned by mail to be postmarked by the fourth day before Election Day and received by 5 p.m. the day before Election Day to be considered timely. The previous version of the bill would have required mail ballots to be received by 5 p.m. on the fourth day before Election Day to be considered timely.
  • Move the deadline to apply for a mail ballot from 11 days before Election Day to 15 days before Election Day. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Allow counties of any population to begin verification of mail ballots 24 days before Election Day. Existing law allows counties with populations of at least 100,000 to begin verification 13 days before Election Day and other counties to begin verification four days before Election Day. The previous version of the bill would have allowed counties to begin verifying mail ballots 20 days before Election Day.
  • Require counties to provide 24 hours' notice before any meeting of the early voting ballot board at which ballots will be verified or counted. The bill would also require counties to provide 72 hours' notice before the beginning of operations of a central counting station. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Prohibit counties to generate a tally of mail ballots until Election Day. The time a county may generate a tally would depend on whether the county counts mail ballots by hand or machine and the size of the county. The previous version of the bill would have required counties to complete all counting of mail ballots between 3 p.m. and 7 p.m. on Election Day.

Last Updated May 5, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to eligibility to serve as an interpreter in an election.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 9, 2021, would expand the availability of interpreters to assist individuals voting in person. The bill would:

  • Allow a person assisting a voter with interpretation to assist the voter in both reading and marking the ballot. Existing law limits the interpreter to reading the ballot to the voter. The interpreter would take the same oath required of other individuals providing assistance.
  • Allow an election officer to appoint an interpreter for a voter. Existing law requires the voter to select the interpreter. The election officer may appoint an interpreter who is a registered voter in the county or an adjacent county.
  • Allow a voter to appoint any person they want to serve as an interpreter except for their employer, an agent of their employer, or an officer or agent of a labor union to which the voter belongs. Existing law requires the voter to appoint a registered voter from the voter's county of residence and does not contain prohibitions related to employers or labor unions.

Last updated March 10, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to conduct constituting the criminal offense of election fraud, increases a criminal penalty.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on April 21, 2021, would:

  • Add prohibited acts that can constitute the offense of election fraud, including altering another voter's ballot, causing a ballot to be voted by a deceased or otherwise ineligible voter, voting more than once in an election, making a false statement on a voter registration application, discarding or destroying another person's ballot without their consent, and, as an election officer, counting an invalid ballot or not counting a valid ballot. The bill would raise the penalty for a violation of the election fraud statute from a class A misdemeanor to a state jail felony if committed by an election official and make an attempt to commit one of the prohibited acts a class B misdemeanor. The previous version of the bill would have raised the severity of all violations of election fraud to a second degree felony.
  • Add coercion of an individual to make a false statement on a voter registration application to the list of prohibited conduct under the statute. The previous version of the bill would have raised the punishment for making a false statement on a voter registration application from a class B misdemeanor to a felony of the second degree and did not contain the attempt offense.
  • Create the offenses of perjury in connection with certain election procedures to prohibit an individual from knowingly making a false statement on a voter registration application or other declaration or affidavit under the Election Code. A violation would be a state jail felony. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Add voting in federal elections in two states on the same day to the list of conduct that constitutes the offense of illegal voting. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Allow voters who are prosecuted for making a false statement on a voter registration application or illegal voting to be prosecuted for additional offenses if the same conduct would constitute additional offenses. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

Last updated April 30, 2021.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 9, 2021, would prohibit any state or local election official to create, alter or suspend any voting standard, practice, or procedure in a manner not expressly authorized by the Election Code.

Last updated July 19, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on March 9, 2021, would establish a pilot program for the video recording of ballot counting.

Last Updated March 10, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to prohibiting the secretary of state from waiving or suspending the application of certain election law provisions.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 10, 2021, would prohibit the Secretary of State to waive or suspend the application of an election statute or regulation.

Last updated July 19, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on March 10, 2021, would require a voter to include an ID number with a mail ballot application and a mail ballot return envelope. Acceptable ID numbers for both purposes would include: 1) the number from an election ID certificate or an unexpired driver's license or personal ID issued by the Department of Public Safety, 2) a voter registration number, 3) the number of an unexpired U.S. passport, or 4) a Social Security number. The bill would also change the format of the mail ballot application and mail ballot return envelope to allow the voter to provide the ID numbers.

Last Updated March 15, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 10, 2021, would require the Secretary of State to provide every person who has regained their eligibility to vote following disenfranchisement due to a felony conviction with a notice of the restoration of their eligibility and a voter registration application.

Last Updated March 11, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to the elements of the offense of illegal voting.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 10, 2021, would specify the level of knowledge required to commit the offense of illegal voting. To commit the offense, the voter would have to be aware of: 1) the particular circumstances that make the person ineligible to vote and 2) that those circumstances make the person ineligible to vote.

Last updated March 11, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on March 10, 2021, would:

  • Require the Secretary of State to develop an electronic system to allow voters to track the status of their mail ballots. The system would require the voter to provide their name, registration address, and a driver's license or state ID number or their date of birth. The system would inform the voter when their ballot is received by the early voting clerk and whether the ballot is accepted or rejected.
  • Require early voting ballot boards and signature verification committees to immediately notify voters of potential issues with their ballots prior to rejecting the ballots. The notice would include instructions for how the voter may correct the issue to have their ballot counted. Voters would have until four days after Election Day to correct issues.
  • Add spaces for voters to provide an email address and to indicate if they wish to receive text messages on mail ballot applications. The early voting clerk would contact voters with clerical errors on an application to allow them to fix errors via email, phone, or text. Voters would not be able to change the address or county of residence included on the original application.
  • Require early voting ballot boards to generate a daily report of the voters who have cast ballots by mail during the in-person early voting period. The report would include identifying information of the voter and whether the ballot was accepted or rejected.

Last Updated March 11, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 10, 2021, would require all voter registration agencies to allow voters who apply for services or update their information on the internet to complete a voter registration application online.

Last Updated March 11, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 10, 2021, would provide that an indication of gender on a photo ID used by a voter that does not align with the gender expression or identity of the person seeking to vote does not invalidate the form of ID for the purpose of accepting a voter for voting. The bill would also require election judges to receive training for the acceptance of photo ID that may not align with a person's presenting gender expression or identity.

Last Updated March 11, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 10, 2021, would require training for volunteer deputy voter registrars to be conducted in person.

Last Updated March 11, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 10, 2021, would allow caretakers and family members who are accompanying voters physically unable to enter the polling place without personal assistance or likelihood of injuring the their health to participate in curbside voting. The bill would not allow drivers for transportation network companies (Uber, Lyft, etc.) who are conveying eligible voters to use curbside voting.

Last Updated March 11, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 10, 2021, would make voting in two elections with the same election date in which federal offices appear on the ballot punishable as the felony offense of illegal voting.

Last Updated March 11, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 10, 2021, would:

  • Allow a voter to cancel a mail ballot they've requested and vote a regular (non-provisional) ballot in person at an early voting location or Election Day voting location if the voting location uses technology that allows the election judge to confirm the voter has not returned the mail ballot to inform the early voting clerk to not count a mail ballot from the voter.
  • Change the provisional ballot process to allow the voter to update registration information on the provisional ballot affidavit. The bill would allow polling locations to collect provisional ballot affidavits electronically. The bill would also require the provisional ballot envelope to include a space for the voter to write the reason for voting provisionally from a standardized list of reasons.
  • Allow voters required to complete a statement of residence to do so electronically.

Last Updated March 11, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to the elements of the offense of illegal voting and to procedures for a person voting a provisional ballot.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 11, 2021, would:

  • Clarify the intent requirements for the crime of illegal voting. The bill would require the voter to know of particular circumstances that make the individual ineligible to vote and to know that those circumstances make the voter ineligible to convict the individual of the offense. Existing law merely requires the individual to know they are not eligible to vote to be convicted.
  • Require election officials to advise a person of the requirements to be eligible to register to vote before the person votes a provisional ballot. The bill would create an exception to the crime of illegal voting for a person to vote provisional ballot without first receiving the required advisement.

Last updated March 12, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to the composition of districts for the election of members of the State Board of Education.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 11, 2021, would make changes to the State Board of Education districts in Texas.

Last updated September 28, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to voter qualification and registration.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 11, 2021, would clarify the data compared by the Secretary of State to Department of Public Safety records during the quarterly review of the statewide voter registration list. The bill would require the Secretary to compare, at a minimum, each voter's full legal name, former name (if applicable), date of birth, residence address, driver's license or state ID number, signature, Social Security number, documentation of lawful presence, and citizenship status. The Secretary may cancel the registrations of suspected ineligible voters for whom a strong data match exists. The Secretary would inform local registrars of weak data matches of suspected ineligible voters to allow the registrar to conduct additional investigation.

Last updated March 16, 2021.

This bill, as reported by committee on May 21, 2021, would authorize presidential electors to be "faithless" and vote for a candidate other than the one voters chose in one circumstance. 

Specifically, prior to the electors voting to choose a President, the presidential and vice presidential candidates who received the most votes in the state would have to certify their fitness to serve. If a majority of the electors rejected that certification, deciding that the candidates were not fit to serve, they would be able to vote for the other candidate. Under existing law, electors are not allowed to be faithless in any circumstances.

Last Updated February 8, 2022

This bill, as introduced on March 11, 2021, would allow individuals who are voting by mail due to a disability and members, spouses, and dependents of members of the U.S. Armed Forces to use an accessible mail ballot marking system to mark their ballot. The voter would return the ballot in the same manner required of other mail ballot voters.

Last Updated March 11, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 11, 2021, would provide a procedure for e-mail transmission of mail ballot materials to voters with disabilities. After completing the ballot, the voter would return the ballot in the same manner as that required of other mail ballot voters.

Last Updated March 12, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 11, 2021, would explicitly narrow the disability excuse to vote by mail to exclude lack of transportation, an illness that does not otherwise prevent the voter from leaving their residence, and a requirement to go to work as reasons sufficient to establish a disability to allow an individual to vote by mail.

Last Updated March 12, 2021

This bill, as enacted on June 15, 2021, clarifies the nature of a disability that qualifies a voter to cast a mail ballot. The bill:

  • Expressly excludes the following from constituting a "sickness or physical condition" that qualifies a voter to vote by mail: lack of transportation, sickness that does not otherwise prevent a voter from appearing at the polling place on election day without a likelihood of needing personal assistance or of injuring the voter 's health, or a requirement to go to work on Election Day. This provision was modified from the previous version of the bill, which would have excluded illnesses that did not otherwise prevent a voter from leaving their home.
  • Modifies the childbirth qualification for absentee voting to specify that it applies to voters expecting to give birth within three weeks before or after Election Day. Existing law permitted voting by mail due to "expected or likely confinement for childbirth on election day." This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires voters to affirm a disability that meets the statutory requirement on the mail ballot application. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

Last Updated June 21, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 11, 2021, would require voters to register their affiliation with a political party to be able to vote in primary elections, sign petitions, and run for office. The bill would:

  • Require local registrars to send a notice to all currently registered voters by October 1, 2021, informing the voters that they must register their affiliation with a political party by December 31, 2021, if they wish to participate in that party's primary elections in 2022.
  • Require new registration applicants to note any political party affiliation on the application.
  • Require currently registered voters who switch party affiliation to wait one year before voting in the primary of the new party of affiliation.
  • Create a felony offense for voting or attempting to vote in the primary of a party with which the voter is not affiliated.

Last Updated March 13, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 11, 2021, and amended on April 27, 2021, would:

  • Change the standard of proof for signature verification on mail ballots. The bill would require election officials to determine that the signature on the ballot and the ballot application belong to the voter. The bill's language creates an implicit presumption that signatures do not match. Existing law requires officials to determine that signatures are non-matching, creating the implicit presumption that signatures do match.
  • Allow poll watchers to observe the process of mail ballot verification and central counting location procedures.
  • Change procedures regarding retention of verified mail ballots, ballot duplication, and determining voter intent.

Last Updated May 5, 2021

Existing law allows polling places at personal residences as long as the residence does not belong to a candidate or relative of a candidate.

  • Make providing "vote harvesting services" for compensation and providing compensation for "vote harvesting services" felonies of the third degree. The bill defines "vote harvesting services" as "direct interaction with one or more voters in connection with an official ballot, ballot by mail, or an application for ballot by mail that are performed with the intention that ballot be cast for a specific candidate or measure."
  • Make knowingly collecting or possessing a ballot in connection with "vote harvesting services" a felony of the third degree.

  • Apply rules related to the conduct of poll watchers at early voting ballot boards to watchers at signature verification committees.

Last Updated May 1, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 12, 2021, would allow county and state party chairs to appoint poll watchers for a ballot measure election. The bill would also allow the appointing authority for a poll watcher to complete the certificate of appointment electronically.

Last Updated March 16, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 12, 2021, would require a wet signature (ink on paper) for all mail ballot applications and for the signatures of voters and any person assisting the voter on mail ballot carrier envelopes. Neither the Texas Constitution nor Texas law currently imposes such a requirement.

BILLSUMMARY: Proposes a constitutional amendment establishing the State Redistricting Commission to redistrict the State Legislature and State congressional districts and revising procedures for redistricting.
VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as introduced on September 27, 2021, proposes an amendment to the Texas Constitution to create the Texas Redistricting Commission to draw and adopt congressional and state legislative districts. The proposed amendment defines how the board would be composed and conduct business, and what criteria it must consider when drawing maps. Specifically, the resolution would:

  • Create a seven member commission composed of:
    • four members appointed by senior legislators of both parties,
    • a fifth appointed by three of the first four, and
    • two appointed by that fifth member who are retired federal judges who had been appointed to the bench by presidents of different parties.
  • Require the members of the Commission to meet myriad qualifications designed to ensure competence and political independence.
  • Require an affirmative vote of at least five of the seven commissioners to adopt a redistricting plan or modify it.
  • Set criteria that any redistricting plan must meet. The resolution requires that districts and redistricting plans:
    • Comply with federal and state constitutions and law.
    • Not discriminate on the basis of race, color, or membership in a language minority group by ensuring the voting strength of racial, ethnic, and language minorities in the districts is not diluted in a manner that deprives minority voters of an equal opportunity to elect a candidate of their choice.
    • Be composed of contiguous territory, and territory that touches only at a point is not considered contiguous.
    • Not divide a community of interest other than a community based on a relationship with a political party or candidate for public office, to the extent reasonable.
    • Coincide with the boundaries of political subdivisions of the state and divide the smallest number of counties, municipalities, and school districts possible, to the extent reasonable.
    • Contain a population as nearly equal as possible to the population of any other district in the plan for congressional districts. In a redistricting plan for the Texas Senate or Texas House of Representatives the overall range of population deviation from the district with the largest population to the smallest may not exceed 2.5 percent.
    • Give preference to dividing a more populous political subdivision before a less populous one, if one must be divided, unless drawn along a county line that divides a municipality.
    • Not purposely favor or discriminate against a political party or any other group.
  • Require the Commission create the opportunity for public comment on proposed plans and consider the comments before adopting a plan or modification. Relatedly, the Commission must make detailed data supporting the plans public.
  • Requires the Legislature to enact implementing laws and to fund the Commission's work.

  • Replaces the existing Legislative Redistricting Board with the Commission to serve as a back up for drawing judicial districts if the Judicial Districts Board fails to do so in a timely way.

    Last updated September 28, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Proposes a constitutional amendment establishing the State Redistricting Commission to redistrict the State Legislature and State congressional districts and revising procedures for redistricting.
VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as introduced on January 12, 2021, would propose a constitutional amendment to submit to the voters that would create the Texas Redistricting Commission that would assume authority for defining federal Congressional districts and state legislative districts from the state legislature. The bill would:

  • Create the Texas Redistricting Commission that would be responsible for defining federal Congressional districts and state legislative districts. The Commission would be composed of seven citizen members. Four members would be selected by the majority and minority party leaders of each chamber of the legislature. The four members selected by legislative leaders would then appoint a fifth member who will serve as the Commission's presiding officer. The presiding officer will then appoint the final two members, who must be retired federal judges who were appointed by Presidents of different political parties.
  • Prohibit any person to serve on the Commission who 1) holds elective or appointed office (other than retired federal judge), 2) holds an office in a political party, 3) is employed by an elected or appointed official, a candidate, or an entity whose primary purpose is to support or oppose a candidate, 4) has held any of the three previously described positions within the three years prior to their appointment to the Commission, 5) conducts lobbying activities, or 6) is related within the second degree by consanguinity to any elected or appointed official.
  • Establish criteria for the Commission to consider when defining districts. Districts must be contiguous, equal in population within a deviation of 2.5%, minimally divisive of existing political subdivisions, and compliant with federal law. Plans may not favor any party or group. If division of existing political subdivisions is necessary, the Commission would favor dividing more populous subdivisions over less populous ones. The amendment would require the affirmative votes of five members of the Commission to adopt a plan.
  • Set the terms of Commission members at 10 years. The amendment would also prohibit Commission members from being candidates for state legislative office within three years of the adoption of a plan created by a Commission on which the member served.
  • Require the Commission to reconvene to draw a new plan if one previously adopted becomes unenforceable due to court order or action of another appropriate authority.
  • Establish the Commission as the backup to the Judicial District Board. The Commission will define judicial districts if the Board is unable to do so.

NOTE: The amendment requires the approval of 2/3 of each chamber of the state legislature prior to submission to the voters, who would then need to approve the amendment by a simple majority.

Last updated January 14, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Proposes a constitutional amendment establishing the State Redistricting Commission to redistrict the State Legislature and State congressional districts and revising procedures for redistricting.
VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as introduced on March 4, 2021, would propose a constitutional amendment to establish the Texas Redistricting Commission to define the boundaries of federal Congressional districts and state legislative districts in Texas. The amendment would:

  • Create a seven-member commission composed of four members appointed by state legislative leaders from each party, a fifth members selected by the original four members, and two other members, who must be retired federal judges appointed by presidents from different parties, appointed by the fifth member. Commissioners may not currently hold public or party office, be an employee of a public officer, a candidate for Congress, or a lobbyist, or be related to a public official within the second degree of consanguinity. Commissioners may not be candidates for state legislative office for three years after the adoption of a redistricting plan.
  • Create a priority order of criteria for the Commission to consider when drawing districts. Districts must, in order: 1) not discriminate based on race, color, or language minority groups, 2) be contiguous, 3) respect communities of interest, 4) not divide existing political subdivisions unless necessary, 5) maintain equivalence of population between districts (state legislative districts may not deviate more than 2.5 percent in population), 6) not favor or discriminate against any party or group.
  • Require the Commission to undergo training regarding its duties provided by a legislative agency that has provided redistricting services to the legislature.
  • Require the Commission to conduct an open and public process, including submitting a preliminary report to the public and allowing for comment on proposed maps.

NOTE: The amendment requires the approval of 2/3 of each chamber of the state legislature prior to submission to the voters, who would then need to approve the amendment by a simple majority.

Last updated March 10, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Proposes a constitutional amendment establishing the State Redistricting Commission to redistrict the State Legislature, State congressional districts, and State Board of Education districts and revising procedures for redistricting.
VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as introduced on March 8, 2021, would propose a constitutional amendment to establish the Texas Redistricting Commission to define the boundaries of federal Congressional districts, state legislative districts, and State Board of Education districts in Texas. The amendment would:

  • Create a 14-member citizen commission composed of five members affiliated with the majority party, five members affiliated with the minority party, and four members unaffiliated with either party. The state legislature would establish the initial procedures for selection of commission members by legislation, but would need a 2/3 majority of each chamber to enact any amendment to the selection procedures once they are initially enacted. Nine members would constitute a quorum of the commission, and approval of any commission action (including final maps) would require the affirmative vote of at least nine commissioners (at least three of each of the majority party, minority party, and unaffiliated members).
  • Require the commission to establish districts in consideration of relative population equality, contiguity, existing political subdivisions, communities of interest, and compactness. The amendment would prohibit the commission to favor any incumbent, political party, or candidate when drawing districts. The commission must conduct an open and transparent process for consideration of district boundaries.
  • Prohibit commission members from holding elected federal, state, county, or municipal office for 10 years from the date of their appointment. The amendment would also prohibit commission members to hold appointed office, be employed by an elected official, or conduct lobbying activities for five years from the date of their appointment.
  • Require the commission to approve final maps and reports by September 15 of each year ending in 1. The amendment would designate the Texas Supreme Court, with the assistance of special masters, as the backup if the commission is unable to approve final maps by the deadline.
  • Designate the commission as the sole party with authority to defend the approved maps. The amendment would allow any registered voter to file a petition in the Texas Supreme Court within 45 days of approval of the final maps.
  • Designate the commission as the secondary backup to the state legislature and the Judicial Districts Board for the creation of state judicial districts.

NOTE: The amendment requires the approval of 2/3 of each chamber of the state legislature prior to submission to the voters, who would then need to approve the amendment by a simple majority.

Last updated March 9, 2021.
