VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on September 7, 2021, makes extensive changes to election procedures in Texas. These changes apply to voting by mail, voting in person, election crimes, voter registration, and election security.

The enacted version was drafted by the conference committee, which made one change. The conference committee report removed a provision from the previous version of the bill that would have clarified the intent necessary to commit the offense of illegal voting to avoid convictions for voters who mistakenly attempt to vote when they are not eligible. All of the other provisions were in the previous version of the bill.

The bill creates new requirements for applying for mail ballots, returning mail ballots, and verifying mail ballots, including procedures to allow voters to be notified of certain issues preventing their ballot from being counted, and gives notified voters an opportunity to correct the issues or cancel their mail ballot and vote in person.
Specifically, the bill:

  • Changes applying for a mail ballot by:
    • Requiring voters to include a Texas driver's license, state identification, or election identification certificate number, if they have one, when applying for a mail ballot. Voters may use the numbers from expired IDs if the license or ID is "otherwise valid." If the applicant lacks a Texas driver's license, election identification certificate, or state identification number, they must provide the last four digits of their Social Security number. If the applicant lacks either number, they must attest that they lack the numbers on the application. Existing law did not require an ID number to apply for a ballot.
    • Requiring the early voting clerk to reject the mail ballot application if the ID number does not identify the same voter identified on the voter's registration application.
    • Requiring the early voting clerk to notify a voter within two business days of the rejection of a mail ballot application. The notice must include information regarding the ability of the voter to correct a missing or non-matching ID number using the online tracking tool created by legislation that passed in the regular session. If the voter corrects an ID number using the online tool, the clerk will issue a ballot.
    • Requiring all mail ballot applications to be in writing with a wet (ink on paper) signature. Electronic and photocopied signatures would not be accepted. Explicitly requiring a wet ink signature did not change existing law, which already required an application submitted by fax or email to be followed by a hard copy application with a wet ink signature.
    • Prohibiting any public official from sending a mail ballot application to a voter who does not first request one. The bill would make an exception for the public officials who are candidates.
  • Creates new crimes for election officials related to mail ballot applications. Early voting clerks, subject to punishment as a state jail felony, are prohibited from:
    • Soliciting the submission of an application by a person who did not request one,
    • Distributing an application to a person who did not request one unless otherwise authorized by law,
    • Authorizing the expenditure of public funds to facilitate third party distribution of an application to a person who did not request one, or
    • Completing any portion of an application to vote by mail and distribute the application with intent that the applicant will return the application to the early voting clerk.
    • The bill would create exceptions to allow officials to enable voters to download an application to vote by mail from a publicly accessible Internet website, to lawfully sign an application for a voter, and to provide a person or the public general information about voting by mail, the voting by mail process, and deadlines.
  • Changes completing and returning a mail ballot by:
    • Requiring voters to include a Texas driver's license, state identification, or election identification certificate number, if they have one, on the ballot carrier envelope. Voters may use the numbers from expired IDs if the license or ID is "otherwise valid." If the applicant lacks a Texas driver's license, election identification certificate, or state identification number, they must provide the last four digits of their Social Security number. If the applicant lacks either number, they must attest that they lack the numbers on the application. Existing law did not require an ID number to return a ballot.
    • Requiring voters who choose to return their ballots by hand on election day to give them to an election official, who, at the time of delivery, must record the voter's name, signature, and type of ID. Existing law did not require this information to be recorded by an election official at the time of delivery.
  • Changes voting in person after applying for a mail ballot. The bill requires a voter attempting to vote in person although records indicate they applied for a mail ballot to cast a provisional ballot unless the voter returns the unvoted ballot. Existing law allows voters to sign a statement and vote a regular ballot if the ballot was never delivered or the voter did not apply for a mail ballot.
  • Changes verifying mail ballots. Specifically:
    • If the ID number provided on the ballot carrier envelope does not identify the same voter identified on the voter's registration application, the ballot will be tossed out if the voter does not correct the error. This is a new ground for rejection, as ballot envelopes did not include voters' ID numbers under existing law.
    • If the ID number provided on the ballot carrier envelope identifies the same voter identified on the voter's registration application, the signature provided by the voter on the carrier envelope is rebuttably presumed to match the voter's signature in their registration records. Nonetheless, every signature is still subject to a comparison process. Ballots with matching ID numbers can still be tossed out if signatures are determined not to match.
  • If a majority of the signature verification committee decides the ballot signature does not match the signature on the ballot application, the committee may choose to use any signature of the voter on file to attempt to find a match, however, the committee need not compare any additional signatures. Existing law had limited the committee's choices to any two or more signatures made within the previous six years.
  • Members of early voting ballot boards and signature verification committees are explicitly allowed to take notes necessary to perform their duties. Notes must not contain personal identification information and must be delivered to the presiding judge for delivery to and retention by the custodian of records. Existing law had no comparable provision.
  • If the early voting ballot board or signature verification committee determines a voter violated the Election Code, the early voting clerk must report the determination to the Attorney General for criminal investigation.
  • Creates cure processes. Specifically:
    • Election officials must provide notice and an opportunity to cure a missing or mismatched voter signature, missing or mismatched ID number, missing statement of residence, or missing witness information to notify voters if the committee determines there is enough time to return the voter's ballot by mail and for the voter to correct the issue and return the ballot to election officials. Existing law provided no opportunity to correct errors.
    • Election officials may choose to notify voters whose mail ballots have defects that they may cancel their mail ballot application and vote in person or go to the early voting clerk's office to correct mail ballot defects no later than the sixth day after Election Day. If the early voting ballot board or signature verification committee takes either of the authorized actions related to notice and cure with respect to any ballot in an election, it must do so for all ballots in an election. Existing law provided no opportunity to correct errors.
    • In addition to the other cure methods, voters may correct ID number errors using the online ballot tracking system passed during the regular session.
    • In addition to the other cure methods, voters who receive a notice of a mail ballot defect from the early voting clerk may cancel their mail ballot application after the close of early voting and vote in person on Election Day.
    • To enable these processes to work, election officials must provide members of an early voting ballot board or a signature verification committee with sufficient information to perform their duties. The Secretary of State will adopt rules to prevent board and committee members from retaining or sharing personally identifiable information in the statewide voter registration database.

The bill changes in-person voting by prohibiting outdoor and drive-through polling locations, even in cases of emergency or state proclamations of disaster, as well as changing rules relating to the procedure allowing disabled people to vote in their cars. The bill:

  • Requires Election Day and early voting locations to be located indoors.
  • Prohibits a voter from voting from inside a vehicle unless the voter is disabled and qualifies for curbside voting under current provisions of the Election Code.
  • Allows poll watchers to observe curbside voting, including entering the vehicle while the voter completes their ballot.

Requires any person transporting seven or more curbside voters to complete a form attesting to whether the person is merely providing transportation or is providing assistance with voting. The form is not required if the driver is related to each voter within the second degree by affinity or the third degree by consanguinity.

The bill changes in-person voting by defining the daily time period in which early voting may occur, and imposing siting rules. Specifically, the bill:

  • Limits the hours that early voting will be available. The bill requires early voting locations in most counties to offer early voting for at least nine hours per day on weekdays during the early voting period. Voting hours are limited to between 6 a.m. and 10 p.m. Counties with fewer than 1,000 registered voters must offer early voting for only four hours per day on weekdays.
  • Lowers the population threshold for mandatory extended early voting hours during the last five days of early voting. The bill lowers the threshold from counties with a population of at least 100,000 to counties with a population of at least 55,000. Those counties must provide early voting for at least 12 hours per day on the last five days of early voting. Voting hours are limited to between 6 a.m. and 10 p.m.
  • Lowers the population threshold for mandatory weekend early voting hours. The bill lowers the threshold from counties with a population of at least 100,000 to counties with a population of at least 55,000.
    • Those counties must provide early voting on Saturday for at least 12 hours. Voting hours are limited to between 6 a.m. and 10 p.m.
    • Those counties must provide early voting on Sunday for at least six hours. Voting hours are limited to between 9 a.m. and 10 p.m.
  • Requires counties participating in the countywide polling place program to use the same methodology for the placement of temporary branch early voting locations that they use for placement of countywide polling places.

The bill creates new documentation requirements for individuals providing assistance to voters with mail ballots and at polling locations. It also creates new criminal offenses aimed at individuals providing assistance. The bill:

  • Creates a new standard form and oath for third parties assisting voters to complete. The form must be completed when assisting a person voting in person or by mail. The form will be incorporated into the standard form on a mail ballot carrier envelope.
    • The form requires the assistant to provide their name and address, relationship to the voter, and whether the assistant accepted any form of compensation from a candidate, campaign, or PAC.
    • The new oath requires the assistant to affirm that:
    • the voter represented that they are eligible to receive assistance,
    • the assistant did not pressure or coerce the voter into choosing the assistant, and
    • the assistant will not communicate information about how the voter voted to another person.
  • Makes failure to complete the oath or form when assisting a voter voting by mail a state jail felony unless the assistant is related to the voter within the second degree by affinity or the third degree by consanguinity.
  • Makes providing "vote harvesting services" for compensation and providing compensation for "vote harvesting services" third degree felonies. The bill defines "vote harvesting services" as "direct interaction with one or more voters in the physical presence of an official ballot, ballot by mail, or an application for ballot by mail that are performed with the intention that ballot be cast for a specific candidate or measure."
  • Makes knowingly collecting or possessing a ballot in connection with "vote harvesting services" a third degree felony.
  • Makes exceptions to the vote harvesting provisions for:
    • An activity not performed in exchange for compensation or benefit,
    • Interactions that do not directly involve an official ballot or ballot by mail,
    • Interactions that are not conducted in-person with a voter, or
    • Activity that is not designed to deliver votes for or against a specific candidate or measure.
  • Makes it a state jail felony to solicit, receive, or accept compensation for assisting voters or collecting ballots. The bill also prohibits an individual from compensating or offering to compensate anyone for the same activities. The bill makes an exception for attendants and caregivers previously known to the voter.

The bill gives partisan poll watchers greater authority in polling locations and threatens election officials with criminal charges if they remove or obstruct poll watchers that the official perceives to be disruptive or intimidating to voters. The bill:

  • Makes an election officer's failure to accept a poll watcher authorized by a political party or candidate a Class A misdemeanor.
  • Makes obstructing the view of a watcher or distancing a watcher to make observation not reasonably effective a Class A misdemeanor.
  • Allows poll watchers to sit or stand close enough to see and hear election officers conduct observed activity, except as otherwise prohibited by law. Watchers may not be denied free movement where election activity is occurring.
  • Allows poll watchers to observe all election activities related to polling place closure, including the sealing and transfer of a data storage device. A watcher may follow the transfer of election materials from the polling place to a regional tabulating center or central counting location.
  • Prohibits a presiding election judge from removing a watcher for a violation of law unless the violation is observed by an election judge or clerk after the watcher has been previously warned that their conduct violated the law.
  • Allows a presiding election judge to call a law enforcement officer to have a watcher removed for a breach of the peace.
  • Allows a poll watcher's appointing authority to obtain injunctive relief, a writ of mandamus, or any other remedy available at law if the authority believes the watcher has been obstructed. The Secretary of State may obtain injunctive relief, a writ of mandamus, or any other remedy available at law if the Secretary believes a state inspector has been obstructed.
  • Requires individuals wishing to serve as poll watchers to complete an online training course developed by the Secretary of State. The course will provide the watcher with a certificate of completion. The watcher must present a certificate of completion and a certificate of appointment prior to serving at a polling location.

The bill prohibits election officials from enacting procedures based on local need to increase voter access. The bill enforces those prohibitions with criminal offenses. Existing law has no comparable provisions. The bill:

  • Prohibits a public official from creating, altering, modifying, waiving, or suspending any election standard, practice, or procedure mandated by law or rule.
  • Prohibits an early voting clerk or other election official from distributing mail ballots or balloting materials to anyone who did not first apply for them. A violation of the prohibition would be a class A misdemeanor.
  • Makes an election official liable for a civil penalty for a violation of the Election Code. The civil penalty can include termination of employment and loss of employment benefits.
  • Prohibits any person from serving as an election official if they have been convicted of an offense under the Election Code.

The bill changes voter registration update procedures. The bill:

  • Requires voters, not people conducting voter registration drives or county registrars, to complete the eligibility and identification portions of a registration form.
  • Allows digital correction of voter registration information for all voters. Existing law limits this to voters who remain in the same county.
    • Provides that if a voter notifies the county in which they are currently registered that they have moved to a new county, that information and the voter's original application will be forwarded to the new county. The two counties will coordinate cancellation of the old registration and creation of a new registration in the new county of residence.
  • Requires a registrar who determines an ineligible voter registered or attempted to vote in an election to deliver an affidavit to the attorney general, Secretary of State, and county prosecuting attorney.

The bill establishes new procedures for judicial proceedings related to elections. Existing law had no comparable provisions. The bill:

  • Requires sentencing courts to advise individuals convicted of felonies of the effect of the conviction on their right to vote.
  • Requires trial courts with jurisdiction over election-related cases seeking injunctive relief to prioritize hearings in such cases beginning 70 days before a general or special election.
  • Requires election-related cases for which more than one district court has jurisdiction to be randomly assigned to a district court. Any person who communicates with the court with the intention to influence the court or judge assigned to a case can be charged with a class A misdemeanor. The offense rises to a state jail felony if it is committed by a person acting in their official capacity as an election official.
  • Requires state appellate courts with jurisdiction over election-related cases seeking injunctive relief to prioritize hearings in such cases beginning 70 days before a general or special election. Three-judge panels would be selected randomly. Any person who communicates with the court with the intention to influence the composition of a three-judge panel can be charged with a state jail felony.
  • Creates a civil cause of action for petitions alleging a violation of various sections of the Election Code related to voter registration, voter assistance, mail voting, or election fraud. Parties must file an action within 45 days of certification of the election. The contestant must prove their allegations by a preponderance of the evidence. Losing parties will be liable for $1000 damages for each violation. Prevailing parties may be awarded attorneys fees.
  • Allows suits against election officials alleging violations of the Election Code while acting in their official capacity to be brought against officials only in their official capacity.

The bill contains several provisions requiring election officials to purge the registration records of certain voters and refer them for possible criminal investigation. Existing law had no comparable provisions. The bill:

  • Requires a registrar to send a notice requiring confirmation of U.S. citizenship to any registered voter who indicates a non-citizenship status in relation to a motor vehicle record. The bill requires the Secretary of State to establish a procedure to compare information with Department of Public Safety data to verify the citizenship status of voter registrations on a monthly basis. The bill allows the Secretary to compare information related to a DPS transaction that occurs only after the voter's registration becomes effective.
  • Requires the Secretary of State to review quarterly information received about persons excused from jury duty because they are not residents of the county in which they are registered to vote. The Secretary of State will refer information to local prosecuting attorneys or the Attorney General for investigation of whether the voter committed an election offense.
  • Requires the Secretary of State to monitor each registrar's compliance with list maintenance requirements for individuals excused from jury service due to an indication they are not U.S. citizens. If a registrar fails to correct a violation of list maintenance requirements within 30 days after notification, the Secretary will correct the violation and notify the Attorney General that the registrar failed to make the correction. The county served by the registrar is liable for a $1000 civil penalty for each violation corrected by the Secretary.

The bill contains numerous criminal provisions concerning election conduct. The bill:

  • Creates a state jail felony offense for knowingly committing perjury by making a false statement on a voter registration application or while completing an oath, declaration, or affidavit required by the Election Code.
  • Expands and narrows the existing crime of "illegal voting" while reducing its penalty from a second degree felony to a class A misdemeanor.
    • Expands the crime of illegal voting by including voting in an election in Texas after voting in an election in another state in which a federal office appears on the ballot and the Election Day for both states is the same day.
    • Narrows the crime of illegal voting by providing that a person may not be convicted of it solely because they signed a provisional ballot affidavit, unless corroborated by other evidence that they knowingly committed the offense.
  • Creates a state jail felony for offering, soliciting, receiving, or accepting compensation to coerce or induce another person to make a false statement on a registration application.
  • Expands the existing crime of election fraud to include:
    • intentionally causing a false statement to be provided to an election official or on a mail ballot application or return envelope or an election-related form,
    • "altering the ballot of another or otherwise causing a ballot to not reflect the intent of the voter",
    • "preventing a voter from casting a legal ballot in an election they are eligible to vote in",
    • "giving a voter false information to prevent them from voting in an election they are eligible to vote in",
    • "causing the ballot to not reflect the intent of the voter",
    • "causing or enabling a vote to be cast more than once in the same election", and
    • "discarding or destroying a completed ballot without the voter's consent".
    • The bill also raises the severity of the offense of election fraud from a class A misdemeanor to a state jail felony if committed by an election officer in their official capacity.
  • Makes the issuance by an election judge of a provisional ballot affidavit containing information the judge knows to be false to a voter a state jail felony.

The bill contains several provisions concerning voting equipment and ballot security. Existing law had no comparable provisions. The bill:

  • Makes all communications between a public official and a voting systems vendor public information.
  • Requires custodians of election records to post a licensed peace officer at central counting stations near ballot boxes containing voted ballots.
  • Requires central counting stations in counties with populations of 250,000 or more to develop a protocol to ensure that electronic devices inside a central counting station necessary to count votes are equipped with software that tracks all input and activity on the devices.
  • Requires presiding judges of polling locations to run zero tapes to confirm the public count on voting machines before opening polling places. The bill also requires presiding judges to run results tapes immediately after closing polling places.
  • Requires all counties with a population over 100,000 to implement a video surveillance system that retains a record of all areas containing voted ballots. The video must be publicly available via livestream. Video must be retained until the later of the end of the calendar year in which the election is held or until an election contest has been resolved.
  • Prohibits counties operating a central counting system for optically-scanned ballots from using a system with a data storage disc that allows information to be modified once it is written on the disc beginning in 2026.
  • Requires the presiding judge of a central counting station to provide a written reconciliation of votes and voters at the close of tabulation for Election Day and again after the station meets for the last time to process late-arriving ballots by mail and provisional ballots.
  • Requires ballots voted by mail to be tabulated and stored separately from ballots voted by personal appearance and separately reported on returns. The bills would also require ballots counted at central counting stations, precinct polling places, and ballots voted by mail to be tabulated and reported separately.
  • Requires electronic records of mail ballot material to record both sides of any application, envelope, or ballot recorded.
  • Expands the type of voting systems a county participating in the countywide polling place program may use.

The bill also:

  • Requires the Secretary of State to conduct a study regarding the implementation of educational programs to help voters with disabilities understand how to use voting systems.
  • Protects voters with disabilities from any prohibition or limitation on their ability to request a reasonable accommodation or modification of election procedure to which they are entitled under federal or state law.
  • Requires four randomly chosen counties to conduct audits every two years of all of their elections in the past two years. Two counties must have total populations below 300,000. Two counties must have total populations of 300,000 or more. A county may not be selected for audit in consecutive audit cycles. In 2020, 18 of Texas' 253 counties had a population of 300,000 or more. The bill does not define the scope of these audits, but requires the Secretary of State to issue related rules as needed.
  • Increases the post-election filing periods for election contests.
  • Repeals Election Code sec. 127.201(f), which allows the Secretary of State to waive and reinstate certain audit requirements for electronic voting equipment.

Last Updated November 22, 2021

This bill, as amended on July 13, 2021, would make extensive changes to Texas elections procedures.

The bill would create a new requirement for mail ballot voters to include ID numbers on ballot applications and return envelopes. The bill would also create a procedure to notify voters of certain issues with their mail ballots and give them an opportunity to go to the clerk's office to correct the issue or cancel their mail ballot and vote in person. Unless otherwise noted, all of these provisions were in the previous version of the bill. The bill would:

  • Require a mail ballot voter to provide a Texas driver's license, state ID, or election ID certificate number, if they have one, when applying for and when returning a mail ballot. If the applicant lacks a Texas driver's license, state ID, or election ID certificate number, they must provide the last four digits of their Social Security number. If the applicant lacks either number, they must attest that they lack the numbers on the application or ballot carrier envelope. The previous version of the bill did not include election ID certificates in the list of acceptable ID for mail ballot applications and carrier envelopes.
    • If the ID number provided on the mail ballot application does not match the ID number provided by the voter on their registration application, the application with be rejected. If the ID number provided by the voter on their ballot carrier envelope does not identify the same voter identified on the voter's registration application the ballot will be rejected. The previous version of the bill required the number provided on the carrier envelope to match the number provided by the voter on their registration application.
    • If the ID number provided on the ballot carrier envelope identifies the same voter identified on the voter's registration application, the signature provided by the voter on the carrier envelope will be rebuttably presumed to match the voter's signature in their registration records. The previous version of the bill required the number provided on the application or carrier envelope to match the number provided by the voter on their registration application.
    • Voters may use the numbers from expired IDs for mail ballot applications if the license or ID is "otherwise valid."
  • Allow early voting ballot boards and signature verification committees that determine an mail ballot has a missing or mismatched voter signature, missing statement of residence, or missing witness information to: 1) return the carrier envelope by mail if the committee or board determines there is enough time to allow the voter to supply the missing information and return the ballot before the close of polls on Election Day, or 2) notify the voter of the defect by phone or email and inform the voter that they may come to the early voting clerk's office in person by the close of polls on Election Day to cure the defect or cancel their vote by mail application to allow them to vote in person. If election officials opt to provide a notice and cure opportunity for any mail ballot, they must do so for all eligible ballots. Election officials must take one of the two actions described above within two business days after discovering a defect.
  • Allow a voter to cancel their mail ballot application after the close of early voting and vote in person on Election Day if they receive a notice of mail ballot defect from the early voting clerk.
  • Require all mail ballot applications to be in writing with a wet (ink on paper) signature. Electronic and photocopied signatures would not be accepted.
  • Require mail ballots returned in person to be received by an election official at the time of delivery. The receiving official must record the voter's name, signature, and type of ID.
  • Allow election officials to use any known signature of the voter for mail ballot signature comparison.
  • Require the early voting clerk to report determinations of any voter's Election Code violation made by the early voting ballot board or signature verification committee to the Attorney General for criminal investigation.
  • Require ballots voted by mail to be tabulated and stored separately from ballots voted by personal appearance and separately reported on returns. The bill would also require ballots counted at central counting stations, precinct polling places, and ballots voted by mail to be tabulated and reported separately.
  • Require electronic records of mail ballot materials to record both sides of any application, envelope, or ballot recorded.

The bill would restrict outdoor and drive-through polling locations. The bill would also define the daily time period in which early voting may occur. Unless otherwise noted, all of these provisions were in the previous version of the bill. The bill would:

  • Prohibit a voter from voting from inside a vehicle unless the voter qualifies for curbside voting under current provisions of the Election Code.
  • Require early voting and Election Day polling locations to be located indoors. The bill would make an exception for polling places damaged and rendered unusable in a disaster. In that case, the county commissioners court may authorize the use of a tent or similar temporary movable structure for a single election. The previous version of the bill did not contain the exception.
  • Require early voting locations in most counties to offer early voting for at least nine hours per day on weekdays during the early voting period. Voting hours are limited to between 6 a.m. and 9 p.m. Counties with fewer than 1,000 registered voters must offer early voting for only four hours per day on weekdays.
  • Lower the population threshold for mandatory extended early voting hours during the last five days of early voting from counties with a population of at least 100,000 to counties with a population of at least 30,000. Those counties must provide early voting for at least 12 hours per day on the last five days of early voting. Voting hours are limited to between 6 a.m. and 9 p.m.
  • Lower the population threshold for mandatory weekend early voting hours during the last five days of early voting from counties with a population of at least 100,000 to counties with a population of at least 30,000. Those counties must provide early voting for at least 12 hours on Saturday and six hours on Sunday. Voting hours are limited to between 6 a.m. and 9 p.m.
  • Require counties participating in the countywide polling place program to use the same methodology for the placement of temporary branch early voting locations that they use for placement of countywide polling places.

The bill creates new documentation requirements for individuals providing assistance to voters with mail ballots and at polling locations. The bill also creates new criminal offenses aimed at individuals providing assistance. Unless otherwise noted, all of these provisions were in the previous version of the bill. The bill would:

  • Create a new standard form and oath for third parties assisting voters to complete. The form must be completed when assisting a person voting in person or by mail. The form would be incorporated into the standard form on a mail ballot carrier envelope.
    • The form requires the assistant to provide their name and address, relationship to the voter, and whether the assistant accepted any form of compensation from a candidate, campaign, or PAC.
    • The new oath requires the assistant to affirm that:
    • the voter represented that they are eligible to receive assistance,
    • the assistant did not pressure, encourage, or coerce the voter into choosing the assistant, and
    • the assistant will not communicate information about how the voter voted to another person.
    • The previous version of the bill also required the assistant to swear that the assistant will confine their assistance to reading or directing the voter to read the ballot and marking or directing the voter to mark the ballot.
  • Make failure to complete the oath or form when assisting a voter voting by mail a state jail felony unless the assistant is related to the voter within the second degree by affinity or the third degree by consanguinity.
  • Make providing "vote harvesting services" for compensation and providing compensation for "vote harvesting services" third degree felonies. The bill defines "vote harvesting services" as "direct interaction with one or more voters in the physical presence of an official ballot, ballot by mail, or an application for ballot by mail that are performed with the intention that ballot be cast for a specific candidate or measure." The previous version of the bill defined vote harvesting services slightly differently.
  • Make knowingly collecting or possessing a ballot in connection with "vote harvesting services" a third degree felony.
  • Make exceptions to the vote harvesting provisions for:
    • An activity not performed in exchange for compensation or benefit,
    • Interactions that do not directly involve an official ballot, ballot by mail, or an application for ballot by mail,
    • Interactions that are not conducted in-person with a voter, or
    • Activity that is not designed to deliver votes for or against a specific candidate or measure.

The bill contains restrictions on curbside voting. All of these provisions were in the previous version of the bill. The bill would:

  • Require any person transporting three or more curbside voters to complete a form attesting to whether the person is merely providing transportation or is providing assistance with voting. The form is not required if the driver is related to each voter within the second degree by affinity or the third degree by consanguinity.
  • Allow poll watchers to observe curbside voting, including entering the vehicle while the voter completes their ballot.

A provision from the previous version of the bill was removed from the current text. It would have prohibited a person other than a curbside voter to be in the vehicle while the voter votes unless that person would be entitled to accompany the voter to the voting station under the law.

The bill gives partisan poll watchers greater authority in polling locations and threaten election officials with criminal charges if they remove or obstruct poll watchers that the official perceives to be disruptive or intimidating to voters. Unless otherwise noted, all of these provisions were in the previous version of the bill. The bill would:

  • Make an election officer's failure to accept a poll watcher authorized by a political party or candidate a Class A misdemeanor. The previous version of the bill made this offense a Class B misdemeanor.
  • Make obstructing the view of a watcher or distancing a watcher to make observation not reasonably effective a Class A misdemeanor.
  • Allow poll watchers to sit or stand close enough to see and hear election officers conduct observed activity, except as otherwise prohibited by law. Watchers may not be denied free movement where election activity is occurring.
  • Allow poll watchers to observe all election activities related to polling place closure, including the sealing and transfer of a data storage device. A watcher may follow the transfer of election materials from the polling place to a regional tabulating center or central counting location.
  • Allow a poll watcher or their appointing authority to obtain injunctive relief, a writ of mandamus, or any other remedy available at law if the authority believes the watcher has been obstructed. The Secretary of State may obtain injunctive relief, a writ of mandamus, or any other remedy available at law if the Secretary believes a state inspector has been obstructed.
  • Require the Secretary of State to develop a training manual for poll watcher that must be given to each watcher prior to service. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.

The bill would prohibit election officials from enacting procedures based on local need to increase voter access. All of these provisions were in the previous version of the bill. The bill would:

  • Prohibit a public official from creating, altering, modifying, waiving, or suspending any election standard, practice, or procedure mandated by law or rule.
  • Prohibit public officials from sending mail ballot applications to voters who do not first request them. The bill would make an exception for public officials who are candidates in the election.
  • Make the issuance by an election judge of a provisional ballot affidavit containing information the judge knows to be false to a voter a state jail felony.

The bill contains several provisions requiring election officials to purge the registration records of certain voters and refer them for possible criminal investigation. All of these provisions were in the previous version of the bill. The bill would:

  • Require a registrar to send a notice requiring confirmation of U.S. citizenship to any registered voter who indicates a non-citizenship status in relation to a motor vehicle record. The bill would require the Secretary of State to establish a procedure to compare information with Department of Public Safety data to verify the citizenship status of voter registrations on a monthly basis. The bill allows the Secretary to compare information related to a DPS transaction that occurs only after the voter's registration becomes effective.
  • Require the Secretary of State to review quarterly information received about persons excused from jury duty because they are not residents of the county in which they are registered to vote. The Secretary of State would refer information to local prosecuting attorneys or the Attorney General for investigation of whether the voter committed an election offense.
  • Require the Secretary of State to refer individuals for investigation by the Attorney General if the Secretary suspects "reasonable cause" exists to believe the individual has committed a criminal offense related to voting.

The bill also contains several provisions concerning voting equipment and ballot security. All of these provisions were in the previous version of the bill. The bill would:

  • Require any tabulating equipment used by election officials to lack wireless connectivity beginning in 2024.
  • Require presiding judges and election clerks to maintain a log of chain of custody of election records and supplies.
  • Require custodians of election records to post a licensed peace officer near ballot boxes containing voted ballots.
  • Require counties with populations of at least 100,000 to implement a video surveillance system that retains a record of all areas containing voted ballots. Counties with populations under 100,000 may implement such a system.
    • Counties with populations of at least 100,000 must livestream the video from the surveillance system. Counties with populations under 100,000 may livestream such video.
    • Video must be retained until the later of the end of the calendar year in which the election is held or until an election contest has been resolved.
  • Makes all communications between a public official and a voting systems vendor, other than communication related to the bidding process, public information.
  • Require central counting stations in counties with populations of 250,000 or more to develop a protocol to ensure that electronic devices inside a central counting station necessary to count votes are equipped with software that tracks all input and activity on the devices.
  • Require presiding judges of polling locations to run zero tapes to confirm the public count on voting machines before opening polling places. The bill would also require presiding judges to run results tapes immediately after closing polling places.
  • Prohibit counties operating a central counting system for optically-scanned ballots from using a system with a data storage disc that allows information to be modified once it is written on the disc beginning in 2024.
  • Require the presiding judge of a central counting station to provide a written reconciliation of votes and voters at the close of tabulation for Election Day and again after the station meets for the last time to process late-arriving ballots by mail and provisional ballots.

The bill would also:

  • Require information concerning an applicant's eligibility and the applicant's ID number in a voter registration form to be provided by the voter. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Allow digital correction of voter registration information for all voters. Existing law limits this to voters who remain in the same county. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • If the voter notifies the county in which they are currently registered that they have moved to a new county, that information and the voter's original application will be forwarded to the new county. The two counties will coordinate cancellation of the old registration and creation of a new registration in the new county of residence. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require a registrar who determines an ineligible voter registered or attempted to vote in an election, to deliver an affidavit to the attorney general, Secretary of State, and county prosecuting attorney. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require the Secretary of State to monitor each registrar's compliance with list maintenance requirements for individuals excused from jury service due to an indication they are not U.S. citizens. If a registrar fails to correct a violation of list maintenance requirements within 30 days after notification, the Secretary will correct the violation and notify the Attorney General that the registrar failed to make the correction. The county served by the registrar is liable for a $1000 civil penalty for each violation corrected by the Secretary. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require voters for whom records indicate they applied for a mail ballot to cast a provisional ballot in person unless the voter returns the unvoted ballot. Existing law allows voters to sign a statement and vote a regular ballot if the ballot was never delivered or the voter did not apply for a mail ballot. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Allow poll watchers to observe activities related to the notice and cure process. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require sentencing courts to advise individuals convicted of felonies of the effect of the conviction on their right to vote. The court must make an affirmative finding of guilt and enter the affirmative finding in the judgment of the case. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require state trial and appellate courts with jurisdiction over election-related cases seeking injunctive relief to prioritize hearings in such cases beginning 120 days before a general or special election. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Create a civil cause of action for candidates or parties harmed by voter harvesting services. Successful litigants may recover damages in the amount of all compensation paid in exchange for vote harvesting services, the fair market value of any benefit given for vote harvesting services, a $35,000 penalty, and attorney fees, costs, and fees. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Create a new category of election contests for petitions alleging a violation of various sections of the Election Code related to voter registration, voter assistance, mail voting, or election fraud. The contestant must prove their allegations by a preponderance of the evidence. Losing parties will be liable for $1000 damages for each violation. Prevailing parties may be awarded attorneys fees. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Impose civil penalties on election officials who violate any provision of the Election Code, including possible job and employment benefits loss.

This bill, as amended by the conference committee report on May 29, 2021, would enact numerous changes to Texas election laws and add several new elections-related crimes. The bill would:

  • Limit early voting on weekdays to between 6 a.m. and 9 p.m. at main and permanent branch early voting locations. Weekday early voting must be provided for at least nine hours per day, except territories with fewer than 1,000 registered voters must provide early voting for four hours each weekday. Existing law requires such territories to provide early voting for three hours each weekday. This provision was in the version of the bill passed by the Senate.
  • Lower the population threshold from 100,000 to 30,000 for counties to provide at least 12 hours of early voting on each weekday during the last week of early voting for primary and general elections and on the last two weekdays of early voting for a special election. Voting in this period is also limited to 6 a.m. to 9 p.m. This provision was in the version of the bill passed by the Senate.
  • Require counties with populations of at least 30,000 to provide early voting for at least 12 hours on the last Saturday of the early voting period at main and permanent branch early voting locations. Voting is limited to 6 a.m. to 9 p.m. on this Saturday. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require counties with populations of at least 30,000 to provide early voting for at least six hours on the last Sunday of the early voting period. Voting is limited to between 1 p.m. and 9 p.m. on this Sunday. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Specify that voters in line when an early voting location closes will be allowed to vote. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require permanent and temporary branch early voting locations to conduct voting inside the branch office or in another room in the building containing the branch office. Permanent or temporary branch polling locations may not be in a tent, movable structure, parking garage, parking lot, or other facility designed primarily for vehicles. This provision is similar to a provision in the version of the bill passed by the Senate.
  • Require counties participating in the countywide polling place program to apply the same methodology it uses for placement of countywide polling locations to determine the location of temporary branch polling locations. Existing law concerning countywide polling locations requires each county commissioners precinct to contain at least one countywide polling location and for the total number of polling locations in any county commissioner's precinct to not exceed more than twice the number of polling locations in any other county commissioner's precinct. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Change the definition of a disability that qualifies a voter to vote by mail to one that renders the voter not capable of appearing at the polling place on Election Day without needing personal assistance or injuring the voter's health due to the voter's illness, injury, medical confinement ordered by a health care professional, or mental or physical disability. The bill excludes the following from the definition of disability that qualifies a voter to vote by mail:
    • Lack of transportation to the polling location
    • Illness, injury, or disability that does not prevent the voter from appearing at the polling place on Election Day without a likelihood of needing personal assistance or of injuring the voter 's health, or
    • Requirement to appear at the voter 's place of employment on election day. The disability definition provisions are similar to provisions in the version of the bill passed by the Senate.
  • Require applicants for mail ballots on the grounds of disability to specifically select the grounds on which they are eligible when completing the ballot application. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require a mail ballot applicant to provide a DPS number on the application if they have one. If the applicant lacks a DPS number, they must provide the last four digits of their Social Security number. If the applicant lacks either number, they must attest that they lack the numbers on the application. Voters may use the numbers from expired IDs for mail ballot applications if the license or ID is otherwise valid. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require a mail ballot voter to provide a DPS number on the ballot carrier envelope if they have one. If the voter lacks a DPS number, they must provide the last four digits of their Social Security number. If the voter lacks either number, they must attest that they lack the numbers on the application. Voters may use the numbers from expired IDs for mail ballots if the license or ID is otherwise valid. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require election officials to reject mail ballot applications and ballots if the ID number provided by the applicant or voter does not match the identification information in the voter's registration records. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Establish that the signatures on mail ballot carrier envelopes with ID numbers that match the ID numbers in the voter's registration records will be rebuttably presumed to be those of the voter. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Allow comparison of the voter's signature on the ballot carrier envelope with any known signature of the voter. Existing law specifies certain samples that may be used. This provision was in the version of the bill passed by the Senate.
  • Require voters for whom records indicate they applied for a mail ballot to cast a provisional ballot in person unless the voter returns the unvoted ballot. Existing law allows voters to sign a statement and vote a regular ballot if the ballot was never delivered or the voter did not apply for a mail ballot. This provision was in the version of the bill passed by the Senate.
  • Require mail ballots returned in person to be received by an election official at the time of delivery. The receiving official must record the voter's name, signature, and type of ID provided. This provision implicitly prohibits drop boxes. This provision was in the version of the bill passed by the Senate.
  • Require a person assisting a voter to vote in person or by mail to complete a form stating the name and address of the assistant, the relationship of the assistant to the voter, and whether the assistant is receiving any form of compensation from a candidate, campaign, or political committee. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Add language to the voter assistant oath in several places for the assistant to swear under penalty of perjury:
    • The voter represented to the assistant that they are eligible to receive assistance.
    • The assistant will confine their assistance to reading or marking the voter's ballot or directing the voter to do the same.
    • The assistant did not encourage, pressure, or coerce the voter into choosing them to assist.
    • The assistant will not communicate how the voter voted to another person, and
    • The assistant understands that if they provided assistance to a voter not eligible for assistance, the vote may not be counted.
    • The previous version of the bill modified the oath less extensively than this version.
  • Make failure by an assistant to complete the oath or form when assisting a voter voting by mail a state jail felony unless the assistant is related to the voter within the second degree by affinity or the third degree by consanguinity or a household member of the voter. The previous version of the bill exempted known caregivers of voters with disabilities.
  • Prohibit the provision, solicitation, and acceptance of compensation for assisting voters with mail ballots. An offense is a state jail felony. Existing law prohibits compensation based on a quota or number of voters assisted. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Prohibit a person other than a curbside voter to be in the vehicle while the voter votes unless that person would be entitled to accompany the voter to the voting station under the law. This provision was in the version of the bill passed by the Senate.
  • Allows poll watchers to observe curbside voting, including being inside the vehicle while the voter completes the ballot. This provision was in the version of the bill passed by the Senate.
  • Require any person transporting three or more curbside voters at a time to complete a form attesting to whether the person is merely providing transportation or is providing assistance with voting. The form is not required if the driver is related to each voter within the second degree by affinity or the third degree by consanguinity. This provision was in the version of the bill passed by the Senate.
  • Allow an eligible individual to receive assistance reading or marking a ballot. Existing law only allows assistance with marking a ballot. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Create voter registration portability by requiring a registrar who receives information that a voter has moved to another county to forward the information along with the voter's original voter registration application to the registrar in the new county. The registrars must coordinate the cancellation of the registration in the old county and creation of a new registration in the new county. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Allow digital correction of voter registration information for all voters. Existing law limits this to voters who remain in the same county. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require the Secretary of State to monitor each county's compliance with voter list maintenance provisions. If the Secretary determines that a county has a number of registered voters equal to or greater than the number of people eligible to register in the county, the Secretary will notify the registrar in writing.
    • Within 30 days of receiving notice, the registrar must refute the allegation of registered voters exceeding the number of eligible voters or develop a remediation plan.
    • If a registrar fails to respond to a notice, refutes the allegation, or fails to comply with the remediation plan, the Secretary shall require the registrar to attend a training course, publish notice that the county is undergoing an audit, audit the voter registration list for the county, and identify voter list maintenance provisions with which the registrar is not complying.
    • If a registrar fails to comply with voter list maintenance provisions after identification of the provisions by the Secretary, the Secretary shall withhold funds for financing VR from the registrar and inform the attorney general that the registrar may be subject to civil penalties of $1000/day.
    • This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require the Secretary of State to monitor each registrar's compliance with list maintenance requirements for individuals excused from jury service due to an indication they are not U.S. citizens. If a registrar fails to correct a violation of list maintenance requirements within 30 days after notification, the Secretary will correct the violation and notify the Attorney General that the registrar failed to make the correction. The county served by the registrar is liable for a $1000 civil penalty for each violation corrected by the Secretary. This provision was in the version of the bill passed by the Senate.
  • Prohibit Election Day polling places in tents, other movable structures, or facilities primarily designed for motor vehicles. Voters may not vote from inside a vehicle unless they meet the requirements for curbside voting.
  • Provide that poll watchers may observe and report on irregularities in the conduct of an election, but may not interfere with the conduct of an election or obstruct the electoral process. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Allow poll watchers to stand or sit close enough to see and hear election officers conduct election activity. Watchers may not be denied free movement where election activity is occurring. This provision was in the version of the bill passed by the Senate.
  • Allow poll watchers to observe all activities related to closing a polling location, including the sealing and transfer of data storage devices used by the voting system equipment. Watchers may follow the transfer of election materials from the polling location to a regional tabulating center or central counting station. Regional tabulating centers and central counting stations must accept the same number of poll watchers as polling locations. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Clarify the definition of unlawfully obstructing the view of a watcher or distancing the watcher from an election procedure in a manner that would make observation not reasonably effective. An offense is a Class A misdemeanor. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Create a class B misdemeanor for an election officer to refuse to accept a watcher for service when required to do so by the Election Code. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Create an oath for poll watchers. This provision was in the version of the bill passed by the Senate.
  • Entitle watchers who believe they were unlawfully prevented or obstructed from the performance of their duties to seek an injunction or writ of mandamus. This provision was in the version of the bill passed by the Senate.
  • Require all voting systems to provide an auditable paper record beginning September 1, 2026. Counties may be reimbursed for the costs of retrofitting or replacing equipment if federal or state funding is available. This provision was in the version of the bill passed by the Senate.
  • Make providing "vote harvesting services" for compensation and providing compensation for "vote harvesting services" third degree felonies. The bill would define "vote harvesting services" as "direct interaction with one or more voters in connection with an official ballot, ballot by mail, or an application for ballot by mail that are performed with the intention that ballot be cast for a specific candidate or measure." The previous version of the bill made this offense a class A misdemeanor.
  • Make knowingly collecting or possessing a ballot in connection with "vote harvesting services" a third degree felony. The previous version of the bill made this offense a class A misdemeanor.
  • Make exceptions to the vote harvesting criminal provisions for:
    • An activity not performed in exchange for compensation or benefit.
    • Interactions that do not directly involve an official ballot, ballot by mail, or an application for ballot by mail.
    • Interactions that are not conducted in-person with a voter, or
    • Activity that is not designed to deliver votes for or against a specific candidate or measure.
    • This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Create a civil cause of action for candidates or parties harmed by voter harvesting services. Successful litigants may recover damages in the amount of all compensation paid in exchange for vote harvesting services, the fair market value of any benefit given for vote harvesting services, a $35,000 penalty, and attorney fees, costs, and fees. Parties to vote harvesting civil actions have the ability to compel a voter to reveal their vote in the same manner than parties to election contests. This provision was in the version of the bill passed by the Senate.
  • Make the issuance by an election judge of a provisional ballot affidavit containing information the judge knows to be false to a voter a state jail felony. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Establish that voting in a Texas election for federal office and another state's election conducted on the same day constitutes the offense of illegal voting, a state jail felony. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Provide that a person may not be convicted of illegal voting solely because they signed a provisional ballot affidavit, unless corroborated by other evidence that the person knowingly committed the offense. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Adds "counting invalid votes", "failing to count valid votes", "altering the ballot of another or otherwise causing a ballot to not reflect the intent of the voter", "preventing a voter from casting a legal ballot in an election they are eligible to vote in", and " giving a voter false information to prevent them from voting in an election they are eligible to vote in" to the list of conduct that can constitute election fraud. The bill would also raise the severity of the offense of election fraud from a class A misdemeanor to a state jail felony if the person commits the offense while acting in their official capacity as an election officer. The bill does not define what constitutes a "valid" or "invalid" vote for the purposes of criminal enforcement. The previous version of the bill did not contain the elevated punishment for election officials.
  • Prohibit a public official, subject to punishment as a state jail felony, to:
    • Solicit the submission of an application by a person who did not request one.
    • Distribute an application to a person who did not request one unless otherwise authorized by law.
    • Authorize the expenditure of public funds to facilitate third party distribution of an application to a person who did not request one, or
    • Complete any portion of an application to vote by mail and distribute the application with intent that the applicant will return the application to the early voting clerk.
    • The bill would create exceptions to allow officials to provide access to an application to vote by mail from a publicly accessible Internet website and to provide a person or the public general information about voting by mail, the voting by mail process, and deadlines.
    • This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Prohibit an early voting clerk or other election official to distribute mail ballots or balloting materials to anyone who did not first apply for them. A violation of the prohibition would be a class A misdemeanor. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Create a state jail felony offense for perjury in connection with election procedures. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Prohibit a public official to create, alter, modify, waive, or suspend any election standard, practice, or procedure mandated by law or rule. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Adds preventing an employee from early voting to the conduct that can constitute the Class C misdemeanor of unlawfully prohibiting an employee from voting. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Create a new category of election contests for petitions alleging a violation of various sections of the Election Code related to voter registration, voter assistance, mail voting, or election fraud. The contestant must prove their allegations by a preponderance of the evidence. If the number of votes illegally cast is equal to or greater than the margin of victory, the court may declare the election void without seeking to determine how individual voters voted. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require appellate courts with jurisdiction over election-related cases seeking injunctive relief to prioritize hearings in such cases beginning 120 days before a general or special election. Three-judge panels should be selected randomly. Any person who communicates with the court with the intention to influence the composition of a three-judge panel can be charged with a state jail felony. The previous version of the bill required priority status for such cases beginning 70 days before Election Day.
  • Require trial courts with jurisdiction over election-related cases seeking injunctive relief to prioritize hearings in such cases beginning 120 days before a general or special election. Election-related cases for which more than one district court has jurisdiction to be randomly assigned to a district court. Any person who communicates with the court with the intention to influence the composition of a three-judge panel can be charged with a class A misdemeanor. The offense rises to a state jail felony if it is committed by a person acting in their official capacity as an election official. The previous version of the bill required priority status for such cases beginning 70 days before Election Day.
  • Require a sentencing judge to inform a person convicted of a felony how the conviction will affect their right to vote. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require counties with populations of at least 100,000 must implement a video surveillance system that retains a record of all areas containing voted ballots. Counties with populations under 100,000 may implement such a system. Counties with populations of at least 100,000 must livestream the video from the surveillance system. Counties with populations under 100,000 may livestream such video. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Defines the list of persons who may be lawfully present at polling locations, meetings of an early voting ballot board, or central counting station.
  • Require mail ballot signatures to be signed by the voter with ink on paper. The bill would prohibit electronic or photocopied signatures for mail ballot applications. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Prohibit ballots to be arranged to allow a person to vote for all candidates from a single party in a single motion or gesture. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Amend existing provisions concerning ballot security and retention, unopposed candidates, election equipment procurement and testing, results reporting, venue and authority of courts in certain elections-related cases, and public education and information concerning elections.
  • Make the provisions of the bill severable. If one section of the bill is declared unenforceable, the remaining provisions would maintain the effect of law. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

Several provisions from versions of the bill passed by either chamber prior to referral to the conference committee were excluded from the conference committee report. They would:

  • Require the Secretary of State to develop and maintain an online tracking system to allow a voter to track the status of their early voting by mail application and ballot. The voter would be required to provide: 1) their registration number or address, and 2) a driver's license or personal identification number issued by the Department of Public Safety or their social security number. The system would provide updates when the voter's early voting by mail ballot application is received by the early voting clerk, when the application is accepted or rejected, when the clerk mails the ballot materials to the voter, when the clerk receives the completed ballot from the voter, and when the early voting ballot board accepts or rejects the voter's ballot.
  • Create a process to notify voters of issues with their mail ballots and allow them an opportunity to correct the ballot to have it counted. Voters would be notified of errors within one business day of discovery of the error by the EVBB. Missing and mismatched signatures may be cured by a cure attestation form. The voter must provide a DPS number or the last four digits of their Social Security number to verify their identity on the attestation form. Voters may submit the necessary form in person, or by fax, mail, or email. Voters have until nine days after Election Day to submit the form.
  • Create pre-processing requirements for mail ballots. The bill would allows all jurisdictions to begin delivering mail ballots to the EVBB 13 days before ED. The bill requires EVBBs to begin delivering ballots seven days before Election Day and requires delivery to occur daily through Election Day. All ballots received by seven days before Election Day must be verified no later than four days before Election Day.
  • Eliminate the prohibition for poll watchers to have devices to record sound and images. Watchers may record any activity in the polling location except for the voter completing their ballot in the polling station. The bill would allow the recording of a voter in the voting station if the watcher reasonably believes the voter is receiving unlawful assistance. The bill would prohibit the poll watcher to distribute or share images or audio from the polling location with anyone other than the Secretary of State.
  • Establish a formula for the distribution of countywide polling place locations in counties with populations over 1 million based on dividing the number of voters in each district in the previous election by the number of voters in the county in the previous election to determine a percentage of polling locations to place in each district. The bill would require poll workers and equipment to be divided roughly evenly between all countywide polling locations, with no more than 5% deviation between polling locations.
  • Require local registrars of deaths and county clerks to provide abstracts of death certificates and probate applications within seven days of their preparation. Existing law allows these items to be sent within 10 days of preparation.
  • Provide voter registration forms to public high schools twice a year.
  • Require the Secretary of State to approve any private donation to assist a local election authority with election administration in excess of $1,000. The bill would require the Secretary to seek the unanimous consent of the Governor, Lieutenant Governor, and Speaker of the House to approve any such donation.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to the establishment of the State Redistricting Commission.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on July 8, 2021, would:

  • Establish procedures for the selection of members of the Texas Redistricting Commission that will conduct redistricting for federal congressional and state legislative districts. Texas voters who are 25 or older would be eligible to serve as commissioners. Persons who hold public office, are candidates for public office, have held public office the last four years, work for an elected official or a campaign for state or federal office, or are a registered lobbyist may serve as a commissioner. Persons selected as commissioners would be prohibited from similar activities during their term as commissioners.
  • Provide that commissioners would serve 3-year terms. Eight commissioners would be appointed by majority and minority party leaders in each chamber of the state legislature each appointing two commissioners. The eight commissioners would then select the ninth member from the pool of independent applicants. The ninth member will be the presiding, non-voting member who would only vote to break ties. Five votes would be required to adopt any redistricting plan.
