BILLSUMMARY: Relates to processes to address election irregularities, provides a civil penalty.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on October 5, 2021, would authorize retroactive and future reviews of election practices and results in Texas elections at the whims of losing candidates, party chairs, and election judges. The bill would require the review of 2020 results to be conducted by hand, and would create an oversight committee of 10 legislators to receive and consider the results of the reviews. All ten would be appointed by the Republican Lieutenant Governor or the Republican Speaker of the House.

With regard to future elections, the bill would:

  • Allow a candidate, county or state party chair, presiding judge or alternate presiding judge, or head of a specific-purpose political committee that supports or opposes a ballot measure to initiate a review process. The eligible person would start the process by making a written request for an explanation and documentation to a county clerk or other authority conducting an election related to:
    • an action taken by an election official that appears to violate a provision of the Election Code,
    • irregularities in results in a precinct or at a polling place or early voting polling place, or
    • inadequacy or irregularity of documentation preservation required by the Election Code.
  • Establish timelines and next steps:
    • The clerk or other authority must respond to the request within 20 days with a written explanation and documentation.
    • If the requesting party is not satisfied with the clerk or other authority's response, the requesting party may demand a further explanation. The clerk or other authority must respond to this request within 10 days.
    • If the requesting party is still not satisfied with the response, the requesting party may request the Secretary of State to audit the issue. The requesting party must provide all of the documentation related to the request and the clerk or authority's responses to the Secretary.
    • Within 30 days of that request, the Secretary may make a determination that a violation has occurred solely on the basis of the evidence submitted, or the Secretary may decide that the responses were insufficient and choose to audit the identified irregularity at the expense of the county or other authority conducting the election. The Secretary will issue a notice of the findings of the audit to the requesting party and the county clerk or other authority conducting the election.
    • If the Secretary determines that a violation of the Election Code has occurred, the Secretary will issue a special notice that requires the clerk to remedy the issue within 30 days or face continuing civil penalties until the situation is rectified. The Secretary will also publish a list of clerks against whom civil penalties have been assessed. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.
  • Allow state or county chairs to request a review of the results of the 2020 general election by submitting a request to the county clerk. The county clerk must appoint an "election review advisory committee" composed of an equal number of members from each of the two major parties. The review would be conducted manually, and include, for each reviewed race:
    • all ballots voted by any method in a precinct or polling place in which the number of ballots cast exceeded the total number of voters accepted for voting in the precinct or at the polling place
    • a random selection of ballots voted by mail, totaling 20 percent of all ballots voted by mail in the election and including both the original ballot and any duplicate made of the ballot, and an equivalent number of carrier envelopes and the associated application for a ballot to be voted by mail,
    • a random selection of ballots voted by mail that were rejected, totaling 20 percent of all ballots voted by mail in the election that were rejected,
    • ballots voted on election day from three randomly selected polling places in the county, or 20 percent of election day polling places in the county, whichever is greater, and
    • the greater of 1,000 early ballots or 10 percent of all early ballots, randomly selected from each of three early voting polling places or 20 percent of early voting polling places, whichever is greater, or if the county has fewer than three early voting polling places, all early voting polling places in the county.
  • Limit the number of races reviewed. The review could consist of not less than three nor more than five contested races or ballot measures. If the request for review contains more than five races, five of the identified races must be randomly chosen for review. The selected races must include ones for federal office, statewide office, and state legislative office.
  • Set out how the review would proceed:
    • All random selections by the county clerk would be done under the observation of the committee.
    • The Secretary of State would determine an acceptable margin of error for the county prior to beginning the review.
    • The committee would begin with the review within 20 days for the request. If the review of any contested race falls outside the agreed margin of error, the committee will conduct another review after randomly selecting different precincts.
    • If any of the second reviews of contested races fall outside the agreed margin of error, the committee would conduct a final review. The final review would cover the entire county or the entire portion of the county containing the state legislative race at issue.
    • The committee would provide a full report of the review to various county and state officials. The Secretary of State would provide notice of the results of the review to the Governor, Lieutenant Governor and each member of the legislature. The notice will include whether the review confirmed election results, differed by an amount within the accepted margin of error, or differed by an amount greater than the margin of error. If the review differed by an amount greater than the margin of error, the Secretary will attach a report to the notice detailing likely causes of the discrepancy and recommended measures to avoid similar discrepancies in the future. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill, with the exception that the review be done manually.
    • Create a ten member joint committee of five senators appointed by the lieutenant governor and five representatives appointed by the speaker of the house.
    • Task the committee with overseeing compliance with the two review processes created by this bill.
    • Require the Secretary of State to give the joint committee quarterly reports about any actions the Secretary takes regarding reviews of elections held after the 2020 election.
    • Require an election review advisory committee reviewing the 2020 election to give the joint committee quarterly reports.
  • Require the joint committee to, as necessary, produce a report detailing:
    • all actions reported to the committee,
    • any findings made by the committee, and
    • recommendations for legislative action. All of these provisions relating to the joint committee are new. The previous version of the bill did not create the joint committee.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to processes to address election irregularities, provides a civil penalty.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on September 2, 2021, would authorize retroactive and future reviews of election practices and results in Texas elections at the whims of losing candidates, party chairs, and election judges. All of the provisions listed were in the previous version of the bill. The bill would:

  • Allow a candidate or party chair in a state or county election to make a written request for an explanation and documentation to a county clerk related to an action taken by an election official that appears to violate a provision of the Election Code, irregularities in precinct results, or inadequacy or irregularity of documentation preservation required by the Election Code.
    • The clerk must respond to the request within 20 days with a written explanation and documentation.
    • If the requesting party is not satisfied with the clerk's response, the requesting party may demand a further explanation from the clerk. The clerk must respond to this request within 10 days.
    • If the requesting party is still not satisfied with the clerk's response, the requesting party may request the Secretary of State to audit the issue. The requesting party will provide all of the documentation related to the request and the clerk's responses to the Secretary.
    • If the Secretary determines that the clerk's responses were insufficient to address the issue, the Secretary will perform an audit of the issue. The Secretary will issue a notice of the findings of the audit.
    • If the Secretary determines that a violation of the Election Code has occurred, the Secretary will issue a special notice that requires the clerk to remedy the issue within 30 days or face continuing civil penalties until the situation is rectified. The Secretary will also publish a list of clerks against whom civil penalties have been assessed.
  • Allow state or county chairs to request a review of the results of the 2020 general election by submitting a request to the county clerk. The county clerk must appoint an "election review advisory committee" composed of an equal number of members from each of the two major parties. The review would include all mail ballots and Election Day ballots from selected precincts and three randomly selected early voting locations (unless the county has fewer than three early voting locations, in which case all early voting ballots would be included).
    • The review can consist of no more than five contested races. If the request for review contains more than five races, five of the identified races must be randomly chosen for review. One of the races must be for presidential electors, federal office, statewide office, or state legislative office.
    • The committee must determine an acceptable margin of error for the county prior to beginning the review. If the review of any contested race falls outside the agreed margin of error, the committee will conduct another review after randomly selecting different precincts.
    • If any of the second reviews of contested races fall outside the agreed margin of error, the committee will conduct a final review. The final review will cover the entire county or the entire portion of the county containing the state legislative race at issue.
    • The committee will provide a report of the review to various county and state officials. The Secretary of State will provide notice of the results of the review to the Governor, Lieutenant Governor, and each member of the legislature. The notice will include whether the review confirmed election results, differed by an amount within the accepted margin of error, or differed by an amount greater than the margin of error. If the review differed by an amount greater than the margin of error, the Secretary will attach a report to the notice detailing likely causes of the discrepancy and recommended measures to avoid similar discrepancies in the future.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to the State Redistricting Commission.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 25, 2021, would establish the process to appoint members of the Texas Redistricting Commission that would create district maps for federal Congressional and state legislative districts and establish procedures for its work. The bill would:

  • Prohibit individuals from serving on the commission if, within the 10 years preceding their potential selection, they: 1) held certain political offices, 2) were employees of certain office holders, political parties, or campaign committees, 3) participated in lobbying activities, 4) contributed a defined minimum amount of money to any legislative candidate, or 5) have an immediate family member who would be disqualified for any of the first four reasons.
  • Require the state auditor to create 3 subpools of the 20 most qualified applicants from each of the majority party, minority party, and unaffiliated pools of applicants. The auditor would then randomly draw three names from the majority and minority party subpools and two names from the unaffiliated subpool. Those names would constitute the first eight members of the commission. Those eight members would then select the remaining six members of the commission by selecting two more names from each of the three subpools. The first eight commissioners must consider the diversity of Texas, including racial, ethnic, geographical, and gender diversity, when selecting the remaining six commissioners. The fully constituted commission would select a chair and vice chair, who may not be affiliated with the same party.
  • Require the commission to conduct an open and transparent process for creating district maps. The commission would maintain a public website to provide information about the ongoing map-drawing process. The commission would provide at least 14 days' notice prior to any meeting of the commission prior to August of the year ending in 1, at which time only three days' notice would be required. The commission would hold at least one public hearing in each state senate district with live audio and video transmission. The commission would display preliminary maps by July 1 of the year ending in 1 for at least 14 days to allow public comment. The commission would display subsequent preliminary maps for at least 7 days and final maps for at least three days to allow public comment.
  • Authorize the governor to remove a commission member for substantial neglect of duty, gross misconduct in office, or inability to discharge the duties of office with the concurrence of 2/3 of the state senate.

NOTE: This bill is contingent on the enactment of the state constitutional amendment proposed in TX SJR 28 that would create the Texas Redistricting Commission.

The bill would also require a registrar to conduct an annual investigation of real estate sales to determine if any voter who fails to vote in any election, submit an application to vote early by mail, or submit a change in voter registration for two years after a general election has moved to a location outside the county. If the registrar develops information through either means indicating that a voter has changed residence outside the county, the registrar will send an address confirmation notice to the voter, which could lead to the suspension of the voter's registration if the voter fails to respond within 30 days.

Last updated February 4, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to the establishment of the State Redistricting Commission.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 4, 2021, would:

  • Establish procedures for the selection of members of the Texas Redistricting Commission that will conduct redistricting for federal congressional and state legislative districts. Texas voters who are 25 or older would be eligible to serve as commissioners. Persons who hold public office, are candidates for public office, have held public office the last four years, work for an elected official or a campaign for state or federal office, or are a registered lobbyist may serve as a commissioner. Persons selected as commissioners would be prohibited from similar activities during their term as commissioners.
  • Provide that commissioners would serve 3-year terms. Eight commissioners would be appointed by majority and minority party leaders in each chamber of the state legislature each appointing two commissioners. The eight commissioners would then select the ninth member from the pool of independent applicants. The ninth member will be the presiding, non-voting member who would only vote to break ties. Five votes would be required to adopt any redistricting plan.
  • Require the Commission to establish districts that are contiguous, compact, and nearly equal in population. The Commission would establish districts that are separated by natural geographic barriers, artificial barriers, or existing political subdivisions.
  • Require the Commission to complete redistricting by November 15 of each year ending in 1. If the Commission fails to do so for any map, the Texas Supreme Court would complete redistricting by December 30.
  • Allow any aggrieved person to file a petition challenging any map. If a court declares a map unenforceable, the Commission would reconvene to draw new maps.
  • Require the Commission to file reports with the Secretary of State at the conclusion of their work that includes final maps, populations of each district, and the criteria used to create the districts.

NOTE: This bill would be contingent on the passage of the constitutional amendment proposed in TX SJR 34.

Last updated February 5, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to the residence address of a voter for purposes of a response to a confirmation notice sent by the voter registrar.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on June 16, 2021:

  • Eliminates the requirement that residence for voter registration be determined by Texas common law (except as otherwise defined by statute), and specifies that individuals may not establish residence for the purpose of influencing the outcome of an election, or at a previous residence, or at any place they have not inhabited. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Authorizes clerks to issue address confirmation notices to individuals when they have reason to believe an individual is registered with a commercial post office box or other non-residence address. This is a new provision, amended into the bill after its introduction. Existing law authorized confirmation notices only when a registrar had reason to believe the voter's current residence was "different" than the address on their registration record.
  • Requires all voters who receive an address confirmation notice to provide a sworn affirmation of their address, in addition to the existing requirement of providing a signed, written response that includes all the information required for registration. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires voters who are registered with a commercial post office box or other non-residential address to also provide documentation of their residence, in addition to the general address confirmation information and sworn affirmation. Accepted documentation is limited to a copy of a driver's license or state ID, a handgun license, an appraisal district document, a utility bill, or a tax document. The documentation requirement does not apply to voters who are members of the armed forces and their spouses, full-time students living on campus at a higher education institution, voters whose addresses are confidential, and certain police officers, judges, and judges' spouses. Individuals whose residence has no address may provide an affidavit detailing the location of their residence. This provision is modified from the previous version of the bill, which would have required all voters receiving an address confirmation notice to provide documentation, not just those with non-residential addresses.

Last updated July 9, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on March 5, 2021, would standardize hours for early voting in all jurisdictions. The bill would:

  • Apply existing requirements for counties with populations greater than 100,000 to have extended early voting hours in the final five days of early voting to all counties. The bill would requires all counties to conduct early voting for 12 hours per day on the last five days of early voting. The bill would also prohibit counties to offer more than 12 hours of early voting on any day.
  • Set standard times for early voting in all counties. During the weekdays of the first week of early voting, voting would be offered from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. On Saturdays, voting would be offered 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. On Sundays, voting would be offered 1 p.m. to 6 p.m. On the last five days of early voting, voting would be offered from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.

Last Updated March 6, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 9, 2021, would:

  • Prohibit Election Day and early voting polling locations from being located in a tent, movable structure, or facility designed primarily for motor vehicles. The bill would prohibit a voter from voting inside a motor vehicle unless they qualify for curbside voting under existing law.
  • Prohibit a curbside voter's driver from remaining in the vehicle while the curbside voter completes their ballot unless the driver would be eligible to accompany the voter into the voting booth inside the polling location.
  • Allow a poll watcher to observe the process of curbside voting.
  • Make providing "vote harvesting services" for compensation and providing compensation for "vote harvesting services" third degree felonies. The bill would define "vote harvesting services" as "direct interaction with one or more voters in connection with an official ballot, ballot by mail, or an application for ballot by mail that are performed with the intention that ballot be cast for a specific candidate or measure." The bill would also make knowingly collecting or possessing a ballot in connection with "vote harvesting services" a third degree felony.
  • Create a civil cause of action for candidates or parties harmed by vote harvesting services. Successful litigants may recover damages in the amount of all compensation paid in exchange for vote harvesting services, the fair market value of any benefit given for vote harvesting services, a $25,000 penalty, and attorney fees, costs, and fees.
  • Create a state elections tribunal to hear and decide election administration disputes. The tribunal would consist of a former Texas Supreme Court justice and two election law experts who are members of different political parties. The tribunal would have concurrent jurisdiction with district court to enjoin violations of the Election Code.
  • Make the knowing refusal to accept an eligible poll watcher by an election official a Class A misdemeanor.
  • Establish that a poll watcher may not be denied free movement throughout the location in which the watcher is serving. The bill would allow the watcher or their appointing authority the ability to seek injunctive relief to enforce Election Code provisions.
  • Prohibit a county commissioners court to accept a monetary donation over $1000 for use in administering elections without the written consent of the Secretary of State.
  • Require the Secretary of State to develop model election procedures. The model procedures may differ between jurisdictions based on population. Deviations from the model procedures will be presumed to be invalid and subject to injunctive relief unless the local official gets written permission from the state elections tribunal prior to implementation.
  • Add new requirements for voting equipment, ballot security, and the appointment and training of officials at polling places, early voting ballot boards, and central count locations.

Last Updated August 20, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to verification of the accuracy of voter registration applications and voter registration lists.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 9, 2021, would clarify the data compared by the Secretary of State to Department of Public Safety records during the quarterly review of the statewide voter registration list. The bill would require the Secretary to compare, at a minimum, each voter's full legal name, former name (if applicable), date of birth, residence address, driver's license or state ID number, signature, Social Security number, documentation of lawful presence, and citizenship status. The Secretary may cancel the registrations of suspected ineligible voters for whom a strong data match exists. The Secretary would inform local registrars of weak data matches of suspected ineligible voters to allow the registrar to conduct additional investigation.

Last updated March 10, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on March 9, 2021, would prohibit any government agency or public official to waive or suspend any section of the Election Code. The bill would also prohibit the suspension of any part of the Election Code during a state of emergency.

This bill, as amended on April 13, 2021, would would make numerous changes to the voter list maintenance process in Texas. The bill would:

  • Require the Secretary of State to develop rules determining what matching criteria constitutes a strong match and weak match of information to identify voter registrations for cancellation due to lack of U.S. citizenship based on information received from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security or the Texas Department of Public Safety. A voter for whom a strong match exists could have their registration cancelled by the Secretary. A voter for whom a weak match exists would have their information referred to the county of residence for additional investigation. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill

Many of the bill's provisions are unchanged from the previous version. These provisions would:

  • Make the Secretary of State, rather than local registrars, primarily responsible for voter registration list maintenance. The Secretary would conduct most day-to-day list maintenance activities and would conduct all hearings on challenge of registration applications and appeals of cancellations of registration.
  • Make the effective date of voter registration applications 30 days after approval by the registrar rather than 30 days after submission of the application.
  • Require the Secretary of State to verify the citizenship of every initial application for or change of voter registration through the Department of Public Safety or require the applicant to provide proof of citizenship in the form of a U.S. passport, birth certificate, or citizenship papers (the last two must be accompanied by photo ID). If requested from the applicant, proof must be presented in person, except an applicant may mail a copy of their birth certificate or citizenship papers with a copy of photo ID.
  • Require the Secretary of State to implement a program to allow a person with an unexpired Texas driver's license or ID card to complete a voter registration application on the state's official website. The websites of the Secretary of State and the Department of Public Safety would provide a link to the online registration portal. Each online applicant must consent to the use of the signature on file with the Department of Public Safety for voter registration purposes and provide the audit number and date of issuance of the applicant's Texas driver's license or personal identification card. Online applicants would also need to provide election officials an original application with the applicant's original signature to make the online registration effective.
  • Require all voter registration applications other than those submitted thorough the Department of Public Safety to be forwarded to the Secretary of State to verify the applicants eligibility to vote and citizenship status.
  • Require a sentencing judge to inform a person who is convicted of a felony of the conviction's effect on the person's voting eligibility at the time of sentencing. The bill would require officials to maintain a list of all persons for whom they receive an abstract of felony conviction. The bill would also require election officials to maintain a record of each person who has lost voting eligibility due to a felony conviction that includes the expected date the person will regain eligibility. Officials would remove the individual from the list of persons for whom an abstract of felony conviction has been received on the expected date of restoration of eligibility or when the officials receive other confirmation the person's eligibility has been restored.
  • Require the Secretary of State, as frequently as possible, to use information received from the National Change of Address program and any interstate voter registration program to identify voters who may have changed address. The Secretary would send identified voters an address confirmation notice. The bill would also require the Secretary to send an address confirmation notice to any voter who does not vote, apply for a mail ballot, or update their registration for two years following a general election. The Secretary would make a note on the voter's registration records that an address confirmation notice has been sent.
  • Clarify procedures for the identification of deceased voters for cancellation of their voter registration.
  • Require the Secretary of State to determine the criteria for a strong match and weak match for list maintenance purposes and to apply the criteria to all reasons for cancellation of voter registration. Existing law only requires the use of strong match/weak match procedures to deceased voters.
  • Require local registrars to forward information about unlawful registrations to the Secretary of State. The Secretary would forward information regarding registration by ineligible persons to the Attorney General.
  • Add failure to comply with statutory requirements for the removal of non-citizens and deceased voters to the list of reasons that can expose local registrars to have state funding withheld.
  • Require any authority possessing election records to turn them over to investigating peace officers or prosecutors on written request.
  • Eliminate the prohibition on challenging voter registration application more than two days after a determination that the voter is eligible. The bill would also eliminate the ability of a challenged applicant to orally request a hearing.

Last Updated July 19, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 10, 2021, would:

  • Expand eligibility for curbside voting by changing the definition of "physically unable to enter the polling place" to include a voter who cannot enter a polling place without likelihood of injuring another voter's health, including by infecting them with a disease with which the voter was diagnosed that is capable of person-to-person transmission.
  • Allow any voter accompanying a voter eligible for curbside voting, except for a paid driver, to also vote their ballot curbside.
  • Require early voting and Election Day polling locations to post clear signage describing the availability of curbside voting. The signs must provide instructions in English, Spanish, and any other language required by the Voting Rights Act.

Last Updated March 13, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to an exception to the application of the offense of illegal voting.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 11, 2021, would create an exception to the crime of illegal voting for a person to cast or attempt to cast a provisional ballot while not knowing of the particular circumstance that made them ineligible to vote or that the particular circumstance made them ineligible.

Last updated March 13, 2021.

This bill, as amended on April 22, 2021, and May 7, 2021, would require a voter to provide their Texas driver's license or state ID number when applying for and returning a mail ballot. Voters without a Texas driver's license or state ID must provide the last four digits of their Social Security number.

A previous version of the bill would have required the voter to provide a photocopy of acceptable voter ID when applying for a mail ballot and would have made false statements related to ID on mail ballot applications punishable as perjury.

Last Updated August 20, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to the prevention of fraud in the conduct of an election.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 11, 2021, would add counting invalid votes or altering a report to include invalid votes and failing to count valid votes or altering a report to exclude valid votes to the list of conduct that can constitute the offense of election fraud. The bill would also raise the severity of the offense of election fraud from a Class B misdemeanor to a felony of the second degree.

Last updated March 13, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on March 11, 2021, would make numerous changes to the conduct of mail ballot voting. The bill would:

  • Require election officials to notify voter of issues with their mail ballot applications or ballots that could lead to rejection. Applications with errors other than missing or mismatched voter signatures may be corrected or replaced with a new application. Applications with signature issues may be corrected by the voter appearing in person with acceptable voter ID to sign the application or by mailing a copy of acceptable photo ID with a new application. Ballot defects may be cured by, time allowing, sending the ballot back to the voter to correct the defect prior to the close of polls on Election Day or having the voter appear in person with acceptable voter ID prior to the close of polls to correct the defect. The voter with a defective ballot may also cancel the ballot application by appearing in person at the early voting clerk's office.
  • Define a disability sufficient to qualify a voter to vote by mail ballot as illness, injury, medical confinement, or mental or physical impairment that prevents the voter from appearing at a polling place during the early voting period and on Election Day. The bill would also require any voter applying for a mail ballot due to disability to provide certification of the disability from a licensed physician or chiropractor or accredited Christian Science practitioner.
  • Require election officials to conduct voter signature verification of a mail ballot application prior to issuing a mail ballot to the voter.
  • Raise the penalty for unlawful voter assistance from a class A misdemeanor to a state jail felony.
  • Create a Class B misdemeanor for a person to assist more than one mail ballot applicant, in the presence of the applicant, to complete a mail ballot application, unless the assistant is a defined relative of the voter or an early voting clerk. The bill would also invalidate any application completed in violation of the prohibition against assistance of multiple applicants.
  • Make unlawful assistance of or unlawfully receiving compensation to assist a mail ballot voter with a disability or over the age of 65 punishable as the felony of exploitation of a disabled or elderly individual.
  • Prohibit early voting clerks to send a mail ballot application form to a voter unless the voter requests the form or the clerk verifies that the voter is eligible to vote by mail due to age.
  • Require persons providing assistance to mail ballot voters to attest to the manner of assistance and their relationship to the voter on the ballot carrier envelope.
  • Allow poll watchers to challenge mail ballots for irregularities or violations of law. The challenge would be resolved by a vote of the early voting ballot board.
  • Require a wet signature (ink on paper) on all mail ballot applications. The bill would also invalidate any ballot applications on which the reason for voting by mail has been pre-marked by someone other than the voter.
  • Allow poll watchers to observe voting activity at countywide polling places and signature verification committees. The bill would also provide an exception to the prohibition of video recording of voting activities to allow poll watcher to record the counting of ballots.
  • Require early voting ballot boards and signature verification committees to be composed of an equal number of members from each of the two major parties when possible. The bill would also provide that tie votes of an early voting ballot board or signature verification committee would be broken by the chair.
  • Make UOCAVA voting procedures available to members of the Texas State Guard, Texas National Guard, another state's National Guard, or a reserve component of the U.S. armed forces and their spouses and dependents if the guard member is serving active duty on the order of the President or Governor.
  • Require early voting clerks to maintain logs of actions taken on mail ballot applications and mail ballot verification.
  • Require mail ballots to be tabulated and reported separately from ballots voted in other manners.
  • Require clear labelling for ballots that must be duplicated for tabulation purposes. The bill would also require members of both parties to be present during duplication and would allow poll watchers to observe the duplication process.

Last Updated March 13, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 11, 2021, and amended on April 22, 2021, would:

  • Create a system of state election marshals to investigate allegations of violations of elections laws and to file criminal charges when appropriate. The bill would also give election marshals the authority to impound election records or equipment during an investigation.
  • Disqualify a district or county court judge in any proceeding seeking injunctive relief against an election official serving a geographic area within the judge's jurisdiction. The bill would require the appointment of a substitute judge from a jurisdiction outside that of the election official.
  • Require the presiding judge of each administrative judicial region to appoint enough visiting judges to hear emergency reviews of elections cases beginning 60 days before an election. The bill would require cases to be heard within three hours of the request for hearing in the period beginning 45 days before Election Day and ending on the Friday before Election Day and within one hour of the request for hearing in the period between the Saturday before Election Day and the final canvass.

Last Updated July 19, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 11, 2021, would:

  • Prohibit an early voting clerk to provide more than one location for in-person return of mail ballots.
  • Allow poll watchers to have image and sound recording devices in a polling location to record voters when they reasonably believe the voter is receiving unlawful voting assistance.
  • Allow poll watchers to be present at signature verification committees. The bill would allow watchers to sit close enough to verify the voters' signatures during signature verification by a committee or early voting ballot board. The bill would also allow a watcher to record the name and contact information of any voter for whom the watcher believes their voting process involved a violation of law.
  • Raise the severity of the offense of unlawfully obstructing a poll watcher from a Class A misdemeanor to a state jail felony. The bill would include distancing watchers to make observation ineffective in the offense's list of prohibited conduct. The bill would also give the Attorney General concurrent jurisdiction to prosecute alleged commission of the offense.
  • Establish that a polling location in which voting activity occurs in multiple rooms as two polling locations for the purpose of determining the authorized number of poll watchers.
  • Allow poll watchers to observe the in-person return of mail ballots on Election Day.

Last Updated March 16, 2021

This bill, as introduced on March 11, 2021, would make numerous changes to Texas election law. The bill would:

  • Eliminate the eligibility for voters age 65+ and otherwise eligible voters confined in jail to vote by mail ballot.
  • Require the Secretary of State to verify the citizenship of every applicant for registration through the Department of Public Safety or require the applicant to provide proof of citizenship in the form of a U.S. passport, birth certificate, or citizenship papers (the last two must be accompanied by photo ID). Applicants may present proof in person or mail a copy of their birth certificate or citizenship papers with a copy of photo ID.

BILLSUMMARY: Proposes a constitutional amendment establishing an independent redistricting commission to establish districts for the election of the members of the United States House of Representatives elected from this state, the State Senate, and the State House of Representatives.
VRLANALYSIS:
Bill version 9/20/21: This resolution, as introduced on September 20, 2021, proposes an amendment to the Texas Constitution to create an independent redistricting commission to draw U.S. Congressional and state legislative districts, and give it power to draw judicial districts if the Judicial Districts Board fails to do so timely.

The commission's membership would be bipartisan, each member of which would have to meet multiple criteria designed to ensure independence, diversity, and competence. The membership would selected by the "select committee" from a nomination list by a nonpartisan agency according to a specified process that included public comment. The select committee would consist of four state legislators appointed by the majority and minority leadership of each house. The commission would employ technical experts, legal counsel, consultants, and other staff the commission considers appropriate. Under existing law, the Legislature draws the state and federal maps.

The resolution would establish criteria for redistricting, requiring that plans:

  • Comply with the United States Constitution, including the requirement that districts equalize total population.
  • Comply with the Voting Rights Act of 1965 and all applicable federal laws.
  • For state legislative districts, comply with all applicable laws of Texas.
  • Provide racial, ethnic, and language minorities with an equal opportunity to participate in the political process and to elect candidates of choice and may not dilute or diminish their ability to elect candidates of choice whether alone or in coalition with others.
  • Respect communities of interest, neighborhoods, and political subdivisions to the extent practicable and after compliance with the other requirements.
  • Define "community of interest" as an area with recognized similarities of interests, including ethnic, racial, economic, tribal, social, cultural, geographic or historic identities. The term may, in certain circumstances, include political subdivisions such as counties, municipalities, tribal lands and reservations, or school districts. The term would not include common relationships with political parties or political candidates.
  • Not consider the residence of any member of the United States House of Representatives, the Texas Senate, or the Texas House of Representatives or a candidate for one of those offices.

  • Except as necessary to comply with the other criteria, not consider the political party affiliation or voting history of the population of a district.

    In addition, the resolution would require that. at the statewide level, the redistricting plan not unfairly favor or disfavor a particular political party. The determination of whether a redistricting plan has the effect of unfairly favoring or disfavoring a political party would be based on the totality of circumstances, including whether the plan results in durable partisan bias as determined by scientifically accepted measures of partisan fairness and whether alternative complaint plans would have resulted in less durable levels of partisan bias.

    The commission would be required to solicit public input before and after publishing draft plans, both online and through hearings across the state. After the commission develops final plans, the commission adopts them by majority vote including support from at least one a member affiliated with each major party and one affiliated with neither.

The resolution does not contemplate a process if the commission fails to adopt a plan.

The proposed amendment would create a 14-member independent Texas Redistricting Commission to draw and adopt congressional and state legislative districts, while giving the Commission back up authority to draw judicial districts, replacing the Legislative Redistricting Board. If the Commission is unable to adopt maps, the proposed amendment would create a process for the Texas Supreme Court to appoint special masters to adjust the boundary lines of the proposed maps until the maps are approved.

Specifically, the proposed amendment would:

  • Create a redistricting commission of five Republicans, five Democrats, and four people of neither party, each of whom must have a specific history of voting in primaries and general elections that demonstrates both their authenticity as party (or non-party) members and their active engagement in voting.
  • Require approval of at least three members from each of the three categories to adopt a final redistricting map.
  • Requires the Commission to "conduct an open and transparent process enabling full public consideration of, and comment on, the drawing of district lines", without specifying what that means.
  • Require the Commission to draw districts that:
    • Comply with the U.S. Constitution.
    • For Congressional districts, include an equal number of people, as nearly as practicable.
    • For state legislative districts, include reasonably equal numbers of people as the other districts for that office unless deviation is necessary to comply with the Voting Rights Act or is allowable by law.
    • Comply with the Voting Rights Act.
    • Are geographically contiguous.
    • Respect the geographic integrity of each municipality county, local neighborhood, and local community of interest, in a manner that minimizes its division to the extent possible without violating any of the previously listed requirements.
    • Are geographically compact, so that nearby areas are not bypassed for more distant population, to the extent practicable and to the extent it does not preclude compliance with any of the other criteria.
    • Do not consider the place of residence of an incumbent or a candidate, and must not have the purpose of favoring or discriminating against an incumbent, political candidate, or political party.
  • Defines community of interest, for the purpose of redistricting, as a contiguous population that shares common social and economic interests that should be included in a single district for purposes of that population's effective and fair representation. Explicitly excluded from the definition are communities based on relationships with political parties, incumbents, or political candidates.
  • Requires the Commission to issue a report with each of the final three maps that explains how the maps comply with the criteria.
  • Creates a back up role for the Texas Supreme Court. If the Commission fails to adopt a particular map, the Secretary of State must petition the Texas Supreme Court to appoint special masters to adjust the boundary lines of the districts in that map using the same criteria.
  • Creates rules for litigation relating to redistricting maps. The proposed amendment would:
    • give the Texas Supreme Court original and exclusive jurisdiction in all cases in which a certified map is challenged
    • give the Commission sole standing to defend a final map.
    • give any registered voter standing to seek an order prohibiting the state from implementing the map on the grounds that it violates state or federal constitutions or law.
  • Assign the Commission the back up role for drawing judicial districts currently held by the Legislative Redistricting Board and abolish the board.

  • Require the legislature to adopt statutes providing for selecting the commission members and other necessary implementing steps, and provide that any subsequent changes be approved by supermajorities following special rules.

    Last updated September 30, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Proposes a constitutional amendment establishing the State Redistricting Commission to redistrict the State Legislature and State congressional districts and revising procedures for redistricting.
VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as introduced on January 25, 2021, would propose a constitutional amendment to establish the Texas Redistricting Commission to define the boundaries of federal Congressional districts and state legislative districts in Texas. The amendment would:

  • Create a 14-member citizen commission composed of five members affiliated with the majority party, five members affiliated with the minority party, and four members unaffiliated with either party. The state legislature would establish the initial procedures for selection of commission members by legislation, but would need a 2/3 majority of each chamber to enact any amendment to the selection procedures once they are initially enacted. Nine members would constitute a quorum of the commission, and approval of any commission action (including final maps) would require the affirmative vote of at least nine commissioners (at least three of each of the majority party, minority party, and unaffiliated members).
  • Require the commission to establish districts in consideration of relative population equality, contiguity, existing political subdivisions, communities of interest, and compactness. The amendment would prohibit the commission to favor any incumbent, political party, or candidate when drawing districts. The commission must conduct an open and transparent process for consideration of district boundaries.
  • Prohibit commission members from holding elected federal, state, county, or municipal office for 10 years from the date of their appointment. The amendment would also prohibit commission members to hold appointed office, be employed by an elected official, or conduct lobbying activities for five years from the date of their appointment.
  • Require the commission to approve final maps and reports by August 15 of each year ending in 1. The amendment would designate the Texas Supreme Court, with the assistance of special masters, as the backup if the commission is unable to approve final maps by the deadline.
  • Designate the commission as the sole party with authority to defend the approved maps. The amendment would allow any registered voter to file a petition in the Texas Supreme Court within 45 days of approval of the final maps.
  • Designate the commission as the secondary backup to the state legislature and the Judicial Districts Board for the creation of state judicial districts.

NOTE: The amendment requires the approval of 2/3 of each chamber of the state legislature prior to submission to the voters, who would then need to approve the amendment by a simple majority.

Last updated January 26, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Proposes a constitutional amendment establishing the State Redistricting Commission to redistrict the United States House of Representatives and the State Legislature.
VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as introduced on February 4, 2021, would propose a constitutional amendment to replace the Legislative Redistricting Board with the Texas Redistricting Commission. The state legislature would enact the general law for the composition and procedures of the Commission, which would adopt redistricting plans for federal congressional and state legislative districts beginning in 2030. The Commission would also serve as the secondary backup for creation of judicial districts.

NOTE: The amendment requires the approval of 2/3 of each chamber of the state legislature prior to submission to the voters, who would then need to approve the amendment by a simple majority.

Last updated February 5, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Proposes a constitutional amendment establishing the State Redistricting Commission and providing redistricting procedures for state legislative, state judicial, and congressional districts.
VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as introduced on March 3, 2021, would propose a constitutional amendment to change procedures for drawing federal congressional and state legislative districts. The bill would:

  • Create the Texas Redistricting Commission, composed of elected and appointed officials representing both major parties. The bill would require the affirmative vote of at least two commissioners representing each major party to approve maps.
  • Invest primary authority for creating and approving state legislative district maps in the Texas Redistricting Commission. The Commission would be required to finalize state legislative maps six months after the publication of decennial census data. The Commission would conduct at least three public meetings, which would be broadcast electronically, after the introduction of proposed maps.
  • Make the state legislature the backup authority for approving state legislative maps if the Commission is unable to approve maps by the deadline. If the legislature approves new maps by a bipartisan supermajority, those maps would remain effective until the next census. If the legislature only approves maps by a simple majority, those maps must be composed of compact districts that do not unduly interfere with existing political subdivisions or favor any party or incumbent. State legislative maps approved by a simple majority of the legislature would remain effective for two general elections, after which the Commission would reconvene to draw new districts.
  • Invest primary authority for creating and approving federal congressional maps in the state legislature. Congressional districts must be compact, contiguous, considerate of communities of interest, and only split municipalities in defined circumstances. The legislature would conduct at least two public hearings, which would be broadcast electronically, after the introduction of proposed maps. The state legislature would be required to approve final maps by a bipartisan supermajority vote of at least 3/5 of the members of each chamber by May 1 of the year following the census.
  • Make the Commission the backup authority for approving federal congressional maps if the state legislature is unable to approve maps by the deadline. The bill would require the affirmative vote of at least two commissioners representing each major party to approve maps. If the Commission is unable to approve federal congressional maps six months after the release of decennial census data, authority would shift back to the state legislature, who could approve a map under the same 3/5 vote requirement or a temporary one with additional conditions by a simple majority.
  • Reconvene the Commission to draw new maps if a state legislative map is determined to be unenforceable by a court of competent jurisdiction. The bill would also reconvene the state legislature is a federal congressional map is determined to be unenforceable by a court of competent jurisdiction.
  • Make the Commission the secondary backup to the legislature for creating state judicial districts. Existing law makes the Judicial District Board the primary backup for creating state judicial districts.

NOTE: The amendment requires the approval of 2/3 of each chamber of the state legislature prior to submission to the voters, who would then need to approve the amendment by a simple majority.

Last updated March 4, 2021.

This resolution, as introduced on March 9, 2021, would propose a constitutional amendment to prohibit state and local election officials to send a mail ballot application to a voter unless the voters first requests one.

BILLSUMMARY: Proposes a constitutional amendment establishing an independent redistricting commission to establish districts for the election of the members of the United States House of Representatives elected from this state, the State Senate, and the State House of Representatives.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 10, 2021, would create the Independent Redistricting Commission to draw district maps for state legislative and federal congressional districts. The bill would:

  • Create an Independent Redistricting Commission composed of fifteen members appointed by a non-partisan legislative agency to draw and approve district maps for state legislative districts and federal congressional districts. The members of the Commission would be selected from three subpools (majority party, minority party, independent) of 12 applicants approved by a select legislative committee. The nonpartisan committee would select two members from each of the three subpools. The six selected Commission members would then select the remaining nine members by selection three members from each of the subpools. When selecting the remaining nine members, the first six members must consider the demographic diversity of the state and ensure that racial, ethnic, and language minorities have representation.
  • Require the Commission to draw districts in consideration of the following criteria, in order: 1) districts must comply with the U.S. Constitution, the National Voting Rights Act, and state law, 2) districts must provide racial, ethnic, and language minorities with an equal opportunity to participate in the political process, and 3) districts must respect communities of interest, neighborhoods, and political subdivisions to the extent practicable. District may not favor or disfavor a political party. Districts may not consider the residence of officeholders or candidates and may not consider previous partisan voting behavior.
  • Require the Commission to provide public access throughout the redistricting process. Meetings and hearings must be open to the public and provide support for multiple languages. The Commission must maintain a website to provide information about the map drawing process and allow individuals and organizations to provide comment.
  • Require the Commission to conduct at least three hearings at geographically diverse locations before proposing a preliminary redistricting plan. The Commission must give at least 14 days' notice before each hearing. The Commission must publish the preliminary plan in multiple media and allow at least 30 days post-publication for public comment. The Commission must conduct at least three hearings at geographically diverse locations after proposing the preliminary redistricting plan. The Commission would then schedule a final public hearing to vote on adoption of the plan. Adoption of the plan would require a majority vote of the Commission, with at least one vote from a commissioner selected from each of the three subpools.
  • Prohibit registered voters to serve as commissioners if, within the 10 years before or after the date of appointment: 1) the individual or an immediate family member holds or is a candidate for public office, 2) the individual or an immediate family member is an officer or employee of a political arty, campaign committee, or political action committee, 3) the individual or an immediate family member registers as a lobbyist, 4) the individual or an immediate family member is an employee of a public official, a state contractor, or a political donor in an amount exceeding $1,000, 5) the individual has committed a criminal or civil violation of the Federal Election Campaign Act, or 6) the individual or an immediate family member is an agent of a foreign principal.
  • Make the Commission the secondary backup, after the state legislature and the Judicial Districts Board, for the redistricting of state judicial districts.

NOTE: The amendment requires the approval of 2/3 of each chamber of the state legislature prior to submission to the voters, who would then need to approve the amendment by a simple majority.

Last updated March 11, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Provides for removal of a voter's name from the official register of voters upon the voter's death.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on February 15, 2021, sets out specific requirements for the removal of deceased voters from the official register. Specifically, it:

  • Requires county clerks to cancel a voter's registration within ten business days of receipt of information indicating the voter is deceased. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires the Lieutenant Governor to review the state register of voters 90 days before a regular primary or regular general election to ensure that all deceased voters have been removed from the register. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires the state registrar, within five business days of registering a death certificate for a Utah resident, to provide the Lieutenant Governor with the decedent's name, last known residential address, date of birth, and date of death, and any other information requested by the Lieutenant Governor to assist the county clerk in identifying the decedent. The Lieutenant Governor must transmit the information to the appropriate county clerk within one business day of receipt. The previous version of the bill would have required the state registrar to transmit the identifying information of the deceased individual within five calendar days of registering the death certificate.
  • Requires the Lieutenant Governor to make U.S. Social Security Administration data regarding deceased individuals available to county clerks. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

Last updated April 28, 2021.

This bill, as enacted on March 16, 2021, expands mail ballot tracking in Utah. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires the Lieutenant Governor to create a ballot tracking system that will provide a voter a text message or an email notification when their ballot is mailed to the voter, when the ballot is received by the county clerk, and when the ballot is counted. The voter must opt in to the notification system to participate. A previous version of the bill would have automatically sent text and email notifications unless the voter opted out.
  • Requires the Lieutenant Governor to provide a website to allow a voter to track their ballot by entering identifying information. The Lieutenant Governor currently maintains a tracking website, but it is not required under existing law. The tracking system also requires an offline tracking procedure, such as a toll-free telephone number, for a voter to use to track their ballot. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires the ballot tracking and notification system to be active by May 1, 2022. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Permits voters to provide their email address and telephone number for ballot tracking purposes by adding new fields, as needed, on voter registration forms, alternate address forms for mail ballots, and change of address notices sent by county clerks for list maintenance purposes. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

  • Requires notice, on various forms, that a voter's telephone number is among the types of registration information available only to government entities.

Last Updated April 20, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to elections, relates to preclearance of certain covered practices required, requires the governing body of a covered jurisdiction, prior to enacting or seeking to administer any voting qualification or prerequisite to voting, or any standard, practice, or procedure with respect to voting, to either institute an action in the Circuit Court of the City of Richmond for a declaratory judgment that the covered practice neither has the purpose or effect of denying or abridging the right to vote.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 13, 2021, would require cities and counties with voting age populations that contain two or more racial or ethnic groups that each constitute 20 percent of the voting age population to obtain preclearance for certain election-related changes from the Attorney General or the Circuit Court for the City of Richmond. The activities that would require preclearance include: 1) adding at-large seats or converting single district seat to at-large seats for any local governing body or school board, 2) changes to boundaries of the city or county that reduces by more than five percentage points the proportion of the jurisdiction's voting age population that is composed of a single racial or language minority group, 3) changes to the boundaries of wards or election districts, 4) restrictions on the ability of any person to provide interpreter services to voters in any language other than English and on the creation or distribution of voting materials in any language other than English, and 5) reduction in the number of polling places or consolidation or relocation of polling places.

Last updated January 17, 2021.

This bill, as enacted on March 31, 2021:

  • Requires local election officials to provide an absentee ballot drop-off location at the office of the general registrar, each voter satellite office (early voting location), and each Election Day polling place. The bill also authorizes local election officials to designate other drop-off locations that must be located on public property. Ballots must be collected at least once daily. The bill requires officials to post the drop-off locations on the county's website at least 55 days before Election Day and to include a list of drop-off locations with the instructions for absentee ballots. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires election officials to verify absentee ballots upon receipt. Existing law authorized election officials to take certain pre-processing actions, but did not require them. The bill also requires election officials to begin scanning absentee ballots into an optical scan device seven days before Election Day, but no tabulation may occur until the close of polls on Election Day. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires election officials to contact any absentee voter who returns their ballot by the Friday before Election Day with an issue that could lead to the ballot's rejection. Within three days of receipt of the ballot and discovery of the issue, the officials must provide the voter with instructions for how to cure the deficiency, and the voter has until noon on the Friday after Election Day to cure the issue. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires election officials to provide prepaid return postage for absentee ballots. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Changes the options for in-person voting for voters who have requested and/or received an absentee ballot:
    • Voters who have received an absentee ballot may return the ballot unopened or unmarked to the office of general registrar, and may then vote in person at the office or on Election Day at their polling place or a central absentee voter precinct. Existing law did not expressly allow for voting at the registrar's office after returning an unused ballot.
    • Voters who requested but did not receive an absentee ballot may sign a statement to that effect on a day before Election Day and vote a regular ballot. Under existing law, voters who did not receive their absentee ballot were required a vote a provisional ballot in person.
    • Voters who have received their absentee ballot and choose not to return it, for any reason, may vote a provisional ballot in person. Existing law provided the option of provisional in-person voting only if a voter had not received their absentee ballot or had lost it.
      These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.
  • Prohibits election officials from rejecting an absentee ballot due to an unsealed outer envelope (if the inner envelope is sealed), lack of full name or middle name or initial on the voter certificate (if the first and last name are provided), or missing date of signature on the voter certificate. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Moves all voters on the existing special annual absentee voter list to the permanent absentee voter list scheduled to take effect on July 1, 2021. The voters will have the opportunity to opt out of the permanent absentee voter list. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires election officials to provide a tool to all voters with a visual impairment or print disability to allow them to remotely receive and mark absentee ballots using screen reader assistive technology. The bill requires outer envelopes provided to voters using the remote marking tool to contain a tactile marking indicating that it is the outer envelope. The bill also prohibits election officials from rejecting a ballot returned by someone using the remote marking tool because the ballot is printed on regular paper or the voter's signature or address are in the wrong position on the ballot return envelope. The previous version of this bill would have required the provision of the remote marking tool, but did not include the requirement for a tactile marking on outer envelopes or the prohibitions against ballot rejection for the specified reasons.
  • Eliminates the requirement for voters who register by mail to vote in person the first time they vote in the city or county of registration. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Allows a person to apply for and cast an emergency absentee ballot with the assistance of a designated representative if the voter is prevented from voting on Election Day due to their hospitalization or illness, the hospitalization, illness, or death of a spouse, child, or parent, or other emergency found to justify receipt of an emergency absentee ballot that occurred after the deadline for applying for an absentee ballot. Existing law allowed emergency absentee voting only when the emergency prevented the voter from applying for a ballot before the deadline. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires election authorities that process absentee ballots by hand to begin doing so by noon on Election Day. Existing law permitted authorities to begin hand processing ballots starting at 3 p.m. on Election Day. A previous version of the bill would have made the 3 p.m. start time mandatory rather than permissive.
  • Requires cities and counties to establish at least one central absentee voter precinct within the jurisdiction, and makes various procedures at the precincts mandatory rather than optional. Existing law permitted, but not require, the operation of central absentee voter precincts.

Last Updated June 14, 2021

This bill, as enacted on April 7, 2021, creates requirements and procedures to prohibit the state and localities from changing voting laws and practices in any way that discriminates against voters based on race, color, or membership in a language minority group. Specifically, the bill:

  • Prohibits any jurisdiction from imposing or applying any voting-related practice or procedure that results in the denial or abridgement of the right to vote based on race, color, or membership in a language minority group. Violations of the provision are established by a totality of circumstances determination that political processes are "not equally open to participation" by protected classes. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill also included individuals of Hispanic or Latino origin as members of the protected class.
  • Requires any locality seeking to change any "covered practice" (e.g., eliminating or consolidating polling places, redistricting, implementing at-large districts for governing bodies, changes to language accessibility) to seek preclearance through a public notice, comment, and hearing process or through the Attorney General's office. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Authorizes the Attorney General to commence actions in civil court to obtain injunctive relief and impose civil penalties for actions taken that are contrary to the bill's stated purpose of preventing race and language-based voting discrimination. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Creates new civil actions for any individual engaging in voter intimidation, threat, coercion, or communication of false information to voters. Prevailing parties would be entitled to attorney fees. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Creates a new civil action for any individual acting under color of law who refuses to permit a qualified voter to vote, or who fails to tabulate, count, or report a qualified vote. This provision has been modified from the previous version of the bill, which would have made the prohibited conduct a Class 1 misdemeanor offense.
  • Requires any implementation of at-large elections for a governing body to not impair the ability of minority groups to elect members of their choice or influence the outcome of an election. The bill also gives any member of an affected minority group the right to commence a civil action in circuit court to prevent the implementation at-large districts that are discriminatory. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires localities meeting certain thresholds of voting age population membership in language minority groups (including Native American groups) to provide election materials in the language of the applicable minority group. These localities must also provide interpretation services in the applicable languages at polling places. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Adds voter satellite offices (early voting locations) as locations for existing criminal prohibitions against voter intimidation (Class 5 felony) and provision of false information regarding the time, place, and manner of an election (Class A misdemeanor). This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Creates the Voter Outreach and Education Fund to educate voters on the rights ensured by federal and state constitutional and statutory law and potential remedies for violations. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

Last Updated June 3, 2021

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to polling places, relates to prohibited activities, relates to unlawful possession of a firearm, relates to penalty, prohibits any person from knowingly possessing a firearm within 40 feet of any building, or part thereof, used as a polling place, including one hour before and one hour after its use as a polling place, except for a qualified law-enforcement officer or retired law-enforcement officer, any person occupying his own private property that falls within 40 feet of the polling place.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on March 31, 2021:

  • Prohibits knowingly possessing a firearm within 40 feet of any entrance of a polling place during the time polls are open or within one hour of opening or after closing, except for police officers, individuals on their own private property, or on-duty security guards. A violation of this prohibition is a Class 1 misdemeanor.
  • Prohibits knowingly possessing a firearm within 40 feet of a building used as a meeting place for the local election board meeting to ascertain the results of an election, or the location of a recount, except for police officers, individuals on their own private property, or on-duty security guards.
  • Expands the period of time when individuals may not loiter, electioneer, interfere with a voter, or possess a firearm within 40 of a polling place, to include the hour before and after the polling place is open. Under existing law, prohibitions on polling place activity only applied when polling places were open and ballots were being counted.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to redistricting, relates to Virginia Redistricting Commission, relates to transparency in redistricting process, relates to reallocation of prison population, requires meetings and hearings of the Virginia Redistricting Commission to be livestreamed, whether held virtually or in person, and to allow for public comment, meetings and hearings that are held in person are required to be conducted in different regions of the Commonwealth, including the Northern Virginia region.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on February 4, 2021, would:

  • Require all meetings and hearings of the Redistricting Commission to be open to the public, held at times and locations convenient to the public, and conducted in multiple languages. Meetings and hearings may be held virtually or in person. In person meetings and hearings should be conducted in geographically diverse locations. All hearings must be livestreamed and allow for public comment. Video and transcripts of all meetings and hearings must be archived and available on a website maintained by the Commission. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require the Commission to publish any plan for federal Congressional or state legislative districts on its website and subsequently conduct at least three hearings with public comment. If the Commission must propose a new plan after the General Assembly fails to adopt a plan approved by the Commission, it must publish the new plan and subsequently conduct at least one hearing with public comment. The previous version of the bill would have required the Commission to hold at least one public hearing following any adjustment to a plan following public comment.
  • Require all meetings and hearings of the Virginia Supreme Court that become necessary to create redistricting plans if the Commission fails to submit any plan that gains the approval of the General Assembly to be open to the public. The two special masters tasked with creating the plan for the Court must agree to the submission of the plan to the Court for approval. The Court must hold at least one public hearing after the submission of any plan to the Court by the special masters. The previous version of the bill would have required the Court to appoint a third special master if the first two can not agree on a map and would have made all of the meetings and deliberations of the Court and the special masters concerning the creation of any redistricting plan public record subject to FOIA.

A provision from the previous version of the text was amended out of the current text. It would have allocated Virginia non-residents in state and federal correctional facilities to a state unit not tied to a specific geographic location for population counting purposes. Existing law allocates Virginia non-resident inmates to the location of the correctional facility.

Last updated February 7, 2021.
