BILLSUMMARY: Proposes a constitutional amendment (first resolution), relates to apportionment, relates to criteria for legislative and congressional districts, relates to Virginia Citizens Redistricting Commission, provides for the establishment of the Virginia Citizens Redistricting Commission (the Commission), a 10-member commission responsible for establishing legislative and congressional districts following a decennial census.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on 1/16/2020, would propose a constitutional amendment to add requirements for legislative districts and establish a citizen commission for the creation of legislative districts. The amendment would:

  • Create a Virginia Citizens Redistricting Commission that would be responsible for drawing congressional and state legislative districts beginning in 2031.
  • Require a panel of five retired circuit court judges to select 22 eligible citizens among applicants to serve on the Commission. The pool of 22 must consist of five citizens affiliated with each of the two major parties and 12 citizens unaffiliated with either party. The pool of 22 would be submitted to state legislative leaders, who would exercise strikes to reduce the final makeup of the Commission to three members affiliated with each major party and four unaffiliated members.
  • Require the Commission to draw congressional and legislative districts by July 1 of each year ending in 1. The final map must be approved by at least seven of the members of the Commission, including at least one member affiliated with each of the two major parties.
  • Require districts to comply with considerations of equal protection respecting race, color, and language minority groups. Districts should, as much as practicable, adhere to existing political boundaries and should not separate communities of shared interest.
  • Require resulting maps to be tested in a hypothetical election using an open-source algorithm to determine partisan shift by precinct. The proposed districts must result in a partisan deviation of no greater than one from a tie, or the proposed districts must be redrawn.

NOTE: In the November 2020 general election, Virginia voters approved an amendment to the state constitution to establish a 16-member redistricting commission composed of legislators and citizens.

Last updated 12/16/2020.

VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as enacted on February 27, 2021, proposes a constitutional amendment that would suspend the "fundamental right to vote" of otherwise eligible voters during incarceration for a felony conviction, and would automatically restore the right to vote upon release. The proposed amendment would also modify the criteria for ineligibility due to mental incapacity, to disenfranchise individuals only upon a specific finding that they are unable "to understand the act of voting." The previous version of the proposed amendment did not expressly provide for automatic restoration of voting rights upon release from incarceration. BILLSUMMARY: Relates to standards and criteria for congressional and state legislative districts, provides criteria by which congressional and state legislative districts are to be drawn, including equal population, racial and ethnic fairness, protection of racial and language minorities to participate and elect a preferred candidate, contiguity, and compactness.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 8, 2020, would establish the following criteria for drawing state legislative and federal Congressional districts:

  • Districts should be as equal in population as practicable.
  • Districts should be drawn in accordance with federal and state laws addressing racial and ethnic fairness.
  • Districts may not be drawn with the purpose or effect of denying or abridging the right to vote on account of race, ethnicity, or color. Districts may not be drawn to deny racial or language minorities participation in the political process.
  • Districts must be composed of contiguous territory.
  • Districts must be compact.

This bill, as enacted on April 7, 2021, changes various aspects of absentee voting, including new requirements for drop boxes, accessibility, and ballots processing. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires local election officials to provide an absentee ballot drop-off location at the office of the general registrar, each voter satellite office (early voting location), and each Election Day polling place. The bill also authorizes local election officials to designate other drop-off locations that must be located on public property, and requires ballot collection at least once daily. Local officials must post drop-off locations on county websites at least 55 days before Election Day and must include a list of drop-off locations with the instructions for absentee ballots. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires election officials to verify absentee ballots upon receipt. Existing law authorized election officials to take certain pre-processing actions, but did not require them. The bill also allows election officials to begin scanning absentee ballots into an optical scan device before Election Day, without initiating ballot totals, and requires them to do so beginning seven days before Election Day. This provision has been modified from the previous version of the bill, which did not contain the requirement to begin scanning seven days before Election Day.
  • Requires election officials to contact any absentee voter who returns their ballot by the Friday before Election Day with an issue that could lead to the ballot's rejection. Within three days of receipt of the ballot and discovery of the issue, the officials must provide the voter with instructions for how to cure the deficiency, and the voters have until noon on the Friday after Election Day to cure the issue. Existing law had no general requirement for notice and cure of ballot defects. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Prohibits election officials from rejecting an absentee ballot due to an unsealed outer envelope (if the inner envelope is sealed), lack of full name or middle name or initial on the voter certificate (if the first and last name are provided), or missing date of signature on the voter certificate. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires election officials to provide a tool to all voters with a visual impairment or print disability to allow them to remotely receive and mark absentee ballots using screen reader assistive technology, and requires outer envelopes provided to voters using the remote marking tool to contain a tactile marking indicating that it is the outer envelope. The bill also prohibits election officials from rejecting a ballot returned by someone using the remote marking tool because the ballot is printed on regular paper or the voter's signature or address are in the wrong position on the ballot return envelope. The bill exempts voters using the remote ballot marking tool from the requirement to have a witness sign their return envelope. These are new provisions that were not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires each city or county to conduct absentee ballot verification at a central absentee precinct. The bill also establishes that failure of election officials to comply with the bill's pre-processing requirements may not constitute grounds for an election contest and will not invalidate the absentee ballots. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires the Department of Elections to convene a work group to evaluate methods for sorting absentee ballots by the precinct of the voter and reporting absentee ballot totals by precinct. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.

Last Updated June 3, 2021

This bill, as enacted on April 7, 2021, creates requirements and procedures to prohibit the state and localities from changing voting laws and practices in any way that discriminates against voters based on race, color, or membership in a language minority group. Specifically, the bill:

  • Prohibits any jurisdiction from imposing or applying any voting-related practice or procedure that results in the denial or abridgement of the right to vote based on race, color, or membership in a language minority group. Violations of the provision are established by a totality of circumstances determination that political processes are "not equally open to participation" by protected classes. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. NB: As introduced, the bill would have included individuals "of Spanish heritage" among the protected class, but that language was amended out in the Jan. 26 version.
  • Requires any locality seeking to change any "covered practice" (e.g., eliminating or consolidating polling places, redistricting, implementing at-large districts for governing bodies, changes to language accessibility) to seek preclearance through a public notice, comment, and hearing process or through the Attorney General's office. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Authorizes the Attorney General to commence actions in civil court to obtain injunctive relief and impose civil penalties for actions taken that are contrary to the bill's stated purpose of preventing race and language-based voting discrimination. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Creates new civil actions for any individual engaging in voter intimidation, threat, coercion, or communication of false information to voters. Prevailing parties would be entitled to attorney fees. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Creates a new civil action for any individual acting under color of law who refuses to permit a qualified voter to vote, or who fails to tabulate, count, or report a qualified vote. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires any implementation of at-large elections for a governing body to not impair the ability of minority groups to elect members of their choice or influence the outcome of an election. The bill also gives any member of an affected minority group the right to commence a civil action in circuit court to prevent the implementation at-large districts that are discriminatory. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requires localities meeting certain thresholds of voting age population membership in language minority groups (including Native American groups) to provide election materials in the language of the applicable minority group. These localities must also provide interpretation services in the applicable languages at polling places. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Adds voter satellite offices (early voting locations) as locations for existing criminal prohibitions against voter intimidation (Class 5 felony) and provision of false information regarding the time, place, and manner of an election (Class A misdemeanor). This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Creates the Voter Outreach and Education Fund to educate voters on the rights ensured by federal and state constitutional and statutory law and potential remedies for violations. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

Last Updated June 7, 2021

This bill, as enacted on June 7, 2021, establishes a vote by mail system for state general elections, and addresses various aspects of absentee voting and early voting. Specifically, the bill:

  • Establishes a vote by mail system for all state general elections. Ballots must be sent to all active registered voters beginning not later than 43 days before Election Day and by October 1, and must include prepaid return postage. The bill also sets out rules for in-person voting on Election Day, depending on whether a voter turns in their mailed ballot or not, and for issuing absentee ballots to voters whose registration changes after the Secretary has issued the universal ballot mailing. These are new provisions amended into this version of the bill.
  • Expressly authorizes the use of drop boxes for ballot return and establishes a process for state funding of drop box acquisition by municipalities. Boxes must be located on municipal property, secured in place, available 24/7, and be under 24-hour video surveillance or within sight of the municipal building. The boxes must be available from at least 43 days before an election, through the close of business on the day before Election Day. While drop boxes were used in some jurisdictions in the November 2020 election, existing law was silent as to their use. This is a new provision amended into this version of the bill.
  • Requires verification of absentee ballots to begin 30 days before Election Day. Under existing law, clerks were authorized, but not required, to initiate ballot verification starting 30 days before an election. This is a new provision amended into this version of the bill.
  • Creates a notice and cure process whereby clerks must mail a postcard to the voter by the next business day following rejection of a ballot, informing them of any defect and the right to correct the error. If a ballot is rejected within five days of Election Day, clerks are required to contact the voter as soon as possible using whatever contact information is available rather than mailing notice. Voters may correct a defect on their ballot, or submit a new ballot, in person at the clerk's office or at the voter's polling place on Election Day, or may request receiving a new ballot by mail. A voter may only correct a defective ballot twice in a single election. This provision is modified from a previous version of the bill, which would have required election officials to make every reasonable effort during normal business hours to contact a voter whose ballot was deemed defective in order to allow the voter to correct the defect.
  • Permits the establishment of outdoor polling places and drive-up voting if an indoor alternative exists at or near the location that can be used in the event of inclement weather. This is a new provision amended into this version of the bill.
  • Requires clerks to provide instructions on absentee ballots in a form prescribed by the Secretary of State. Existing law set out general instruction requirements that clerks were required to "substantially" follow. This a new provision amended in to this version of the bill.
  • Requires officials to count the ballot that is received first in the event that a voter returns both their originally mailed ballot and a replacement ballot. Existing law required officials to count the ballot with the earliest postmark.
  • Bars candidates and paid campaign staff from delivering to the clerk's office or to a drop box the ballots of voters other than their immediate family. The bill also prohibits any individual, other than a justice of the peace, from returning more than 25 ballots to a town clerk or drop box. Under existing law, there was no limit on the number of ballots an individual could return on behalf of others. This is a new provision amended into this version of the bill.
  • Permits municipal legislative bodies and school boards using the Australian ballot system to mail ballots to all registered voters for their elections. This is a new provision amended into this version of the bill.
  • Requires the Secretary of State to consult with municipalities and stakeholders on improving voter access for non-English speakers and provide recommendations to the relevant legislative committees. This is a new provision amended into this version of the bill.
  • Requires the Secretary of State to issue a report by Jan. 30, 2023, addressing the implementation of universal vote by mail for municipal and primary elections and the implementation of a voter verification system.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 12, 2021, would overhaul how elections are conducted in Washington by ending the state's mail ballot election system, providing for voting at polling places on Election Day and at vote centers during a sharply shortened early voting period that must include weekend days, requiring an application to vote by mail, requiring a photo ID to apply for a mail ballot or to vote in person, creating a free photo ID for voters who need it, eliminating same day registration, and shortening the deadline to return a mail ballot.

Specifically, the bill would:

  • End mail ballot elections and create precinct-based polling place voting on Election Day by:
    • Requiring an accessible polling place in every election precinct, and if one is not available, requiring one to be sited within a reasonable distance of the precinct. Polling places would be required to be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. on Election Day. Existing law does not provide for per-precinct polling places, only countywide vote centers. Vote centers must remain open until 8 p.m. on Election Day, but a start time is on Election Day is not prescribed.
    • Requiring anyone who wishes to vote in person to show a valid photo identification, such as a driver's license or state identification card, student identification card, or tribal identification card, or a voter identification card issued by a county election officer. The requirement would appear to apply to both early and Election Day voting. Existing law has ambiguous language about showing ID when voting in person at vote center, which also applies to early and Election Day voting. In practice, some counties require ID to receive a new ballot and vote it in person at a vote center. The bill does not amend or repeal this language, its ID requirement would be in a separate section.
    • Providing for a free voter ID program through which registered voters who lack ID could obtain a photo Voter ID from their county auditor.
    • Allowing political parties to appoint observers to watch in-person voting at polling places and to review the registration lists to determine who has and hasn't voted.
    • Expanding an existing misdemeanor relating to voting at a vote center to punish interfering with a person attempting to vote at a polling place or at a voting center.
    • Requiring anyone who applied for an absentee ballot, but who wishes to vote in person, to complete a provisional ballot.
  • Restrict early voting by shortening the early voting period, but facilitate it by requiring weekend hours. The bill would require vote centers to be open from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. on the two Saturdays and the Sunday before Election Day. No other early voting would be offered, and on Election Day vote centers would be open from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., one hour less than polling places. Under existing law, early voting at vote centers begins 18 days before Election Day, and must be offered during business hours. Although weekend voting is not required, counties may choose to offer it, and some do.
  • Change mail voting by:
    • Eliminating mail ballot elections and requiring people to apply for a mail ballot. Applications would have to be made between 90 days before Election Day and the day before, and voters would be required to provide a copy of photo ID with their application. Voters could apply for a mail ballot for a single election, or, if applying for a primary or special election ballot, may also apply for any associated general election, or for any immediately subsequent primary and general election pair.
    • Shortening the deadline to return a mail ballot by changing it from postmarked by Election Day to received by 8 p.m. on Election Day.
    • Restricting who a voter may choose to return their completed ballot for them, by making it a felony for anyone to collect a voter's blank or completed ballot except the voter, the voter's family, household member, or caregiver, or an election worker or postal worker doing their jobs. Existing law does not limit who a voter may chose to return their completed ballot.
    • Requiring county auditors to give, upon request, the list of voters who applied for mail ballots. The list must be kept current, updating within one day of receiving a request.
    • Allowing challenges to people requesting absentee ballots before their ballots have been received back.
  • Eliminate same day registration by requiring people to register, or update their registrations, 14 business days before Election Day. The early voting period created by the bill would begin between seven and six business days before Election Day (because it begins on a Saturday.)
  • Make Election Day a state holiday.

  • Change dates on which certain local elections may be held so that they are held on Election Day in November or on the day a state primary could be held.

Under the bill, the clerk would ask if an applicant wishes to register or update their registration, and then the clerk would give the applicant a signature pad that asks five questions relating to voter qualification. The bill does not include any matching criteria or other rules about how such database would be used to cancel or update voter registrations.

This bill, as enacted on March 30, 2022, would attempt to protect election officials by enabling them to keep their residential address confidential and criminalizing certain types of harassment of them. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Allow any election official who is targeted with threats or harassment, and any family members residing with them, to apply to the Secretary of State to have an address designated by the Secretary serve as their address. The application would include an affidavit that the election official is a target of criminal threats and harassment, a designation of the Secretary as agent for service of process and receipt of mail, their residential address and any phone number where the applicant can be contacted by the Secretary, their signature, and the date of their signature. Upon filing the application, the Secretary would certify the applicant as a program participant and the election official would remain in the program for four years, unless they withdrew earlier, and could renew the protection if needed. The program would enable the election official to put the Secretary-designated address on key documents such as their driver's license and vehicle registration. Submitting false information to join the program is a felony.  Existing law allows "criminal justice participants" to use the program.
  • Redefine cyberstalking into cyber harassment, and make committing cyber harassment punishable as a felony instead of a misdemeanor if certain people are victims, including an election official who is performing the participant's official duties or election official's official duties at the time of the cyber harassment or because the election official took an action taken or decision during the performance of their official duties.
  • Define cyber harassment as a person, who with intent to harass or intimidate any other person under circumstances not constituting telephone harassment, makes an electronic communication to that person or a third party and the communication:
    • Uses any lewd, lascivious, indecent, or obscene words, images, or language, or suggests the commission of any lewd or lascivious act 
    • Is made anonymously or repeatedly
    • Contains a threat to inflict bodily injury immediately or in the future on the person threatened or to any other person, or
    • Contains a threat to damage, immediately or in the future, the property of the person threatened or of any other person, and
    • With respect to the threats, they would cause a reasonable person, with knowledge of the sender's history, to suffer emotional distress or to fear for the safety of the person threatened, or the threats reasonably caused the threatened person to suffer emotional distress or fear for the threatened person's safety.

This bill, as amended on May 11, 2021, would have regulated private grants for election administration, prohibited certain people from being election officials, and prohibited certain people from assisting with ballot tabulation. Specifically, the bill would have:

The Commission would be required to distribute grants throughout the state on a per capita basis to offset the municipality's election administration expenses, unless a municipality would receive less than $25. If any municipality would receive that little, the Commission may retain the grant funds and expend them consistent with decisions of its joint finance committee. The amendment clarified that funds distributed to municipalities would be for offsetting election administration costs.
  • Prohibited the Commission from accepting donations or private grants if the donor requires the Commission to use the money for specific purposes or to repay the money for any reason. This is a new provision not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Prohibited counties and municipalities from entering certain contracts relating to election administration. This is a new provision. The prohibited contracts are those that include:
    • Any requirement governing election administration.
    • Any requirement for the repayment of private resources for election administration.
    • The transfer of any power relating to election administration to anyone state law does not already give that power.

Violations of these prohibitions would have been felonies.

  • Prohibited certain people from working as election officials. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Specifically, people would be prohibited from being election officials if are also employees of:
    • a candidate committee, legislative campaign committee, political action committee, independent expenditure committee, political party, recall committee, and referendum committee.
    • a political organization required to register with the federal elections commission.
    • an issue advocacy group.

Created a felony to punish anyone who assists in counting or tabulating votes at an election unless the person is a resident of this state, is a tabulator or election official who is trained to the extent provided by law, and has signed the official oath and returned it to the municipal clerk with respect to that election. The bill would correspondingly require facilities to admit outside special deputies in all other circumstances.
    • Require employees who are appointed special deputies to be a qualified voter of the municipality where the home is located, take a two hour online training course created by the Wisconsin Election Commission, take and submit a certain oath regarding their duties as special voting assistants, work in pairs, and if possible, be of different political parties. These are new provisions and do not have a parallel in existing law.
    • Prohibit any other current employees from assisting an occupant in requesting, completing, or returning the occupant's absentee ballot. This is a new provision, and would effectively prevent employees from providing any voting assistance in ordinary times. Existing law has no parallel.

This bill, as introduced on March 23, 2021, would make significant changes to absentee voting by "indefinitely confined" people. Indefinitely confined people do not need to submit a copy of their ID when applying for an absentee ballot, and they can apply once and then continue to receive absentee ballots until they are no longer indefinitely confined. The bill does not change these consequences of having indefinitely confined status, however, it does significantly change how people get and maintain indefinitely confined status. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the Wisconsin Election Commission to facilitate the removal of people on the indefinitely confined voters list who joined the list between March 12, 2020, and November 3, 2020. Anyone removed this way could reapply for indefinitely confined status. This provision is related to a controversy over how Covid risk relates to indefinitely confined status.
  • Require voters claiming indefinitely confined status to attest to their status, and if they are under 65 years old, the statement of their indefinitely confined status must be signed by an attending health care professional.
  • Create a felony to punish making a false statement to qualify as indefinitely confined.
  • Require clerks to remove voters from the list who fail to confirm their indefinitely confined status within 30 days of notice sent by the clerks. The bill would further require clerks to send voters on the indefinitely confined list such a notice every two years. Under existing law, people are removed from the list at their request, upon receipt of reliable information that the voter is no longer indefinitely confined, or because the voter fails to respond to notice sent because they failed to complete and return the ballot that was mailed to them. Those reasons would continue under the bill.

  • Clarify that the existence of an outbreak or epidemic of a communicable disease in a voter's community does not qualify the voter as indefinitely confined for purposes of receiving absentee ballots automatically under this subsection.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 23, 2021, would make it harder for voters to return their completed, sealed mail ballots. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Restrict who a voter could choose to return the voter's completed, sealed mail ballot to immediate family members and legal guardians. The bill defines "immediate family" as parent, child, spouse, and sibling. Only if a voter does not have an immediate family member or legal guardian in the state, and the voter cannot return their ballot themselves, would the bill would allow the voter to designate another voter, in writing, to return their ballot for them. A person can only be designated to return one ballot for a voter that is not their immediate family member per election. Under existing law, no restrictions are imposed on who may return a voter's mail ballot for them.
  • Create a new felony to punish anyone who returns a voter's completed, sealed mail ballot, other than an immediate family member, legal guardian, or person designated in writing as the bill would allow.
  • Prohibit the use of secure drop boxes, by creating an exclusive list of ways mail ballots may be returned that does not include drop boxes. Drop boxes, which were used at a small scale in Wisconsin for years but which became widespread in 2020, were specifically authorized by the Wisconsin Election Commission's interpretation of existing law.
  • Authorize clerks to hold mail ballot "collection events" under certain limited circumstances that parallel the rules under which clerks may conduct early voting. Specifically, starting 14 days before the election and ending on the Sunday before the election, a clerk would be allowed to open a ballot collection site that is as near to their office as practicable and fully accessible for people with disabilities. The clerk staff the ballot collection site themselves with the executive director of the board of election commissioners, or employees of the clerk or the board of election commissioner. All of these rules apply to early voting sites. However, unlike early voting sites, at ballot collection sites voters would be able only to return sealed, completed ballots. A voter would not be allowed to apply for and receive a ballot. Existing law does not address ballot collection sites. However, in the fall of 2020, the city of Madison relied upon existing Wisconsin Election Commission guidance to hold "Democracy in the Park" events at which voters could return their mail ballots for the November 2020 election. Those events would be illegal under this bill.

  • Authorize one new way a voter may apply for a mail ballot. Under the bill, a voter to use a "for-profit commercial delivery service moving parcels nationally and internationally" to send their ballot application to the clerk. Such services are not currently on the list of ways a voter may apply for a mail ballot.

VRLANALYSIS:
On June 22, 2021, the Assembly passed the Senate version of this bill, S 212, sending it to the Governor. As a result, this bill is moot and will no longer advance.

On June 16, 2021, the committee recommended this bill, which defines what information must be included on a ballot certificate to be complete, and addresses how clerks should act when a voter returns a completed absentee ballot with a defect in the ballot certificate, with amendments that would make it match its Senate companion. Specifically, as recommended by the committee, the bill would:

  • Require clerks to reject ballots for having an incomplete certificate if any of the following are missing or either the voter or the witness:

    • printed first name
    • printed last name
    • house or apartment number
    • street name
    • municipality
    • signature.

    Thus a voter or a witness who included a zip code but not the municipality would cause the ballot to be rejected. This provision is new.


  • Create a new misdemeanor to punish anyone who corrects a defect in a voter's certificate unless they are the voter or the voter's witness. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill simply forbade clerks from correcting defects, and created other crimes, retained in this version, that appear to criminalize correcting ballot defects for a voter. Existing law, as interpreted by the Wisconsin Election Commission, allows clerks to fill in missing components of witness addresses in certain circumstances.
  • Require the clerk to put a notice of the defect in the voter's voter information page in the online voter registration website, and allow the clerk to choose to contact the voter directly. The bill does not make clear if the voter will know the notice has been put in their voter information page unless they happen to check the page. Although existing law does not require notice of defects, the Wisconsin Election Commission guidance encourages clerks to contact the voter directly. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill did not specifically authorize the clerk to contact the voter directly.

  • Create new felonies to punish clerks for actions that appear to include helping a voter cure their ballot. Specifically, the bill would create new felonies in the list of election frauds to punish election officials if they:

    • intentionally assist or cause the casting or counting of a vote or the receipt of a registration that is invalid for any reason.
    • intentionally assist or cause the rejection of or failure to otherwise count a valid vote or the rejection of a valid registration.
    • intentionally fail to promptly report an election official election fraud violation to the commission and to the district attorney for the county in which the violation occurred, unless the violation is intentionally disclosing the name or address of a voter whose registration is confidential, in which case the election official commits a misdemeanor.

    A provision in the previous version of the bill has been amended out of this version. It would have required the clerk to mail a defective ballot back to the voter when the clerk discovers the defect. Existing law allows the clerk to mail the ballot back if there is time for the voter to correct the defect.

Last Updated July 20, 2022

HISTORY: {"date":"03/15/2022","summary":"Failed to pass pursuant to Senate Joint Resolution 1","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
The Assembly passed the Senate version of this bill, S204, sending it to the Governor on June 22, 2021. As a result, this bill is moot and will no longer advance.

As recommended by committee with amendments on June 16, 2021, would substantially change how voters apply for absentee ballots, including in-person absentee ballots (early voting), and tweak the process for registering to vote online.

In short, the major provisions of the bill would require most voters to submit photo ID when applying for an absentee ballot by eliminating one exemption and limiting another, require an application for every primary and general election pair instead of once per year, require sick and disabled voters to apply for ballots more often and through a more difficult process, remove certain people from the list of sick and disabled voters, prohibit clerks from mailing absentee ballot applications to people who have not requested them, require a specific form be used to apply for the ballot, and require a voter's signature for both electronic absentee ballot applications and electronic voter registration applications.

Specifically, the bill would:

  • Eliminate a major exception to the requirement that a voter submit a copy of their photo ID to apply for an absentee ballot, and limit another one:
    • Voters who submitted a copy of their ID when previously applying for an absentee ballot, have not moved, and have not changed their name, would have to submit a copy of their ID with each application. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Under existing law, once the ID has been submitted, a voter need not do it again unless they moved or changed their name.
    • Indefinitely confined voters would be required to submit a copy of their ID with their application, unless they apply online using their driver's license or state ID number, or unless they do not have ID. In the latter case, they may submit a sworn written statement from a U.S. citizen who is 18 years of age or older affirming their identity under penalty of perjury. Although this would be the new rule, the bill appears to preserve the existing ability of an indefinitely confined voter to avoid submitting ID with their application if their ballot witness attests on the ballot to the voter's identity and address. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have required these voters to submit a copy of their ID without exception. Existing law does not require these voters to submit an ID with their application. Instead, they may obey the general ID rule or have their ballot witness affirm their identity.
    • The existing exemption for overseas voters would be maintained. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have eliminated this exemption.
  • Require ordinary voters to apply for absentee ballots for every primary and general election pair. If the voter does not return the primary ballot, they will not be sent the general election ballot without another application, and will not be given notice that they will not. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have required an application for every election. Under existing law, voters may apply once and then receive ballots for each election in the calendar year so long as they keep returning completed ballots and remain eligible to vote. If they do not return a completed ballot, the clerk will give them five days' notice that they will cease receiving ballots unless they renew the application, if possible.
  • Overhaul the rules relating to indefinitely confined voters by making them engage in a two-step application process and, for each application for ballots, limiting the number of elections for which they can receive ballots, and creating new felonies to punish lying in connection with obtaining this status or ballots. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require a voter to apply for indefinitely confined status by filing a statement with the municipal clerk affirming that the elector is indefinitely confined because of age, physical illness, infirmity, or disability. The statement would contain the voter's name, address, date of signature, and signature. The Wisconsin Election Commission would be required to make a form for this statement, and the form would warn voters that attempting to use the sworn statement to avoid the ID requirement when the voter possesses ID is a felony. This application would need to be renewed every four years. This is a new provision. The previous version of the bill would have preserved the existing process for obtaining indefinitely confined status. Under existing law, indefinitely confined voters attest to their status under penalty of perjury by checking a box on the ordinary absentee ballot application form.
    • Clarify that the existence of a public health emergency, a disaster, or an epidemic of a communicable disease would not qualify a voter for indefinitely confined status. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. The relationship of Governor Evers' safer at home order during the Covid-19 pandemic and indefinitely confined status was litigated in 2020.
    • Remove certain voters from the existing list of indefinitely confined voters. Specifically, the Wisconsin Election Commission would be required to facilitate the removal of voters who joined the list between March 12, 2020 and November 3, 2020. Governor Evers declared a public health emergency due to Covid-19 on March 12, 2020. This provision is new.
    • Require an indefinitely confined voter to apply for absentee ballots using ID as above, and receive ballots for every election in the calendar year, unless removed from the list earlier. A voter would be removed from the list if they fail to return a ballot, cease to be indefinitely confined because of age, illness, infirmity or disability, ask to be removed from the list, or fail to renew their indefinitely confined status. Voters would have a duty to immediately inform the clerk if they are no longer indefinitely confined, although the clerk can learn the voter is no longer confined from anyone. If not from the voter, the clerk must verify the information. This is a new provision. Under existing law indefinitely confined voters receive ballots for every election that occurs during their confinement unless they are removed from the list because they are no longer indefinitely confined, they fail to return a ballot, or ask to be removed from the list. If they fail to return a ballot, existing law requires the clerk to mail the voter notice that if the voter does not respond within 30 days, the voter will be removed from the list. If the clerk is removing the voter from the list because someone other than the voter reported them as no longer indefinitely confined, the clerk is to give the voter five days notice if possible. These notice provisions would be eliminated by the bill.
  • Create new felonies to punish someone for:
    • Falsely making any statement for the purpose of qualifying as indefinitely confined.
    • Intentionally providing false information on, using, or attempting to use the sworn statement to avoid providing proof of ID when the voter possesses valid proof.
    • Falsely affirming another person's identity on the sworn statement used for voters who do not have ID.
  • Prohibit clerks from mailing absentee ballot applications to people who did not request the application, and prohibit political committees from giving voters applications with a return mailing address that is different from the address of the appropriate clerk. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill. However, the previous version of this bill also created a felony to punish clerks who mailed absentee ballot applications to people who did not request them. That provision has been amended out of this bill.

  • Require people applying for an absentee ballot to complete an absentee ballot application using a form designed by the Wisconsin Election Commission that includes various questions specified by the bill. The standardized form required by the bill would ask each voter, applying by mail or in person as part of early voting:

    • their municipality and county of residence,
    • their name, date of birth, and contact information, including their telephone number, fax number, and electronic mail address,
    • the street address of their legal voting residence,
    • for which election they want the absentee ballot,
    • whether they are a military or overseas elector,
    • their confidential identification serial number if they have a confidential registration,
    • which method they want to receive the absentee ballot, and
    • whether the voter is in the hospital.

    This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Under existing law, voters may make a written request for an absentee ballot, but they need not use a standardized form, and when voting in-person absentee (early voting), they generally complete a single form on the ballot envelope that serves both as the application for the ballot and the voter's certificate.


  • Create a new felony to punish a clerk who issued an absentee ballot to someone who did not complete the standardized form, or who did not properly apply online or, if disabled or hospitalized, did not properly apply pursuant to the provisions applicable to them. This provision effectively prevents mail ballot elections. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require clerks to write their initials on absentee ballots rather than have their initials pre-printed or stamped on the ballots. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Change the rule for applying for an absentee ballot electronically to require the voter to include their written signature as part of the process, although the language may allow the clerk to use the voter's electronic signature in pdf form. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law does not require a written signature as part of the application, but does require an application with an original signature to be returned with the ballot.
  • Change the rule for electronic voter registrations so that the Commission maintains a copy of the registration form that has the voter's electronic signature. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill required the signature to be a pdf file and made available to the municipal clerk or the board of election commissioners. Existing law does not require such a copy to be maintained.

  • Require clerks to post updates at their office and on the internet about the number of absentee ballots distributed to voters, received back from voters, and the number counted, beginning at 9 p.m. on Election Day and every hour thereafter until the ballots have all been canvassed.

    A provision in the previous version of the bill has been amended out of this one. That version would have enabled voters to join a list to receive an absentee ballot application every election, but not a ballot.

Last Updated June 24, 2021

This bill, as introduced on May 4, 2021, would allow absentee ballot canvassing to start the day before Election Day, allow municipalities to combine certain polling places, change the timeline for mailing absentee ballots to voters, create new felonies to punish election officials for their actions when counting absentee ballots or for releasing information about absentee votes early, and change nominating rules for independent candidates. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Allow municipalities that count absentee ballots at a central location, rather than the polls, to begin canvassing absentee ballots as early as 7 a.m. the day before Election Day. If a municipality begins canvassing the day before Election Day, they must stop by 10 p.m. and begin again no earlier than 7 a.m. Election Day. Overnight, the ballots must be secured according to specific procedures. Each day ballots are being canvassed, the clerk must post at the clerk's office and on the internet a statement of how many ballots were canvassed and how many remain to be canvassed. Canvassed ballots could not be tabulated until the canvass is complete or the close of polls, whichever is later. Under existing law, these municipalities may begin canvassing on Election Day, anytime after polls open but before 10 p.m.
  • Create a new felony to punish anyone who intentionally acts to know or provide information about accumulating or final results before the canvass is complete or the polls close, whichever is later.
  • Create a new felony to punish a member of the board of absentee ballot canvassers or other election official who willfully neglects or refuses to perform any of the duties required by the central count rules.
  • Change the timeline of mailing absentee ballots so that they are sent to regular voters no later than the 21st day before the election, and to military and overseas voters no later than the 45th day before the election. Existing law mails ballots to all electors no later than 47 days before the election.
  • Allow cities, villages or towns with fewer than 35,000 residents to combine a polling place with an adjacent city, village or town with fewer than 35,000 residents.

  • Change the rules relating to independent nominating petitions, which VRL does not track, and clarify that the only voters to whom presidential-only ballots may be given are new state residents and former state residents otherwise qualified to receive them.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to legislative and congressional redistricting.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on June 11, 2021, would create a comprehensive redistricting regime for Congressional and State Legislative districts. It would also provide for automatic deadline shifting when the Census delivers its data late. The new redistricting process would require the Legislative Research Bureau to propose and analyze districting plans based on criteria set by the bill, under the supervision of a Redistricting Advisory Commission. The Legislature would consider and vote on the plans according to certain rules set out in the bill. Specifically, the new redistricting process proposed by the bill would:

  • Require 33 State Senate districts, each to be composed of three Assembly districts. This is the same number and structure of state legislative districts as Wisconsin currently has. However, the bill would allow the Bureau to propose a different number of districts, so long as there are at least 54 assembly districts and no more than 100, the number of senate districts is at least 1/4 of the number of assembly districts and is not more than 1/3 of them, and each senate district is comprised of only whole assembly districts.
  • Require the Legislative Research Bureau to use the new census data to publish an analysis of the population of current legislative and congressional districts, reporting the extent to which the existing districts violate population standards created by the bill.
  • Create a Redistricting Advisory Commission. The Advisory Commission would:
    • Consist of five people, four of which are appointed by the state legislative leaders of both parties, and which would choose a fifth. These people must be eligible to vote in Wisconsin, cannot be office holders, relatives or employees of a member of the legislature or a member of Congress, or be directly employed by the Legislature or Congress.
    • Advise the Bureau in relation to any decision the Bureau must make in preparing a redistricting plan if if the bill is not clear, and if the Bureau requests the advice.
    • Oversee the work of the Bureau employees doing the redistricting work.
    • Enter contracts for hiring experts to assist the Bureau, if at least 3/4 of the members agree, and terminate a contract employee, again, if 3/4 of the members agree.
    • Educate the public and hold public hearings on the redistricting plans the Bureau submits to the Legislature for enactment, and submit a report on the hearings to the Legislature. Specifically, the Advisory Commission would:
    • make available to the public copies of the bill, maps illustrating the plan, a summary of the criteria for the plan's development, and a statement of the population in each district and its relative deviation from the ideal district population.
    • hold hearings in different geographic regions fo the state, including at least one in each Congressional district. However, only one hearing may be held in the city of Madison. Whenever practicable, the Advisory Commission must hold the hearings on weekends.
    • report to the legislature summarizing the information and testimony. The report can include any comments and conclusions that the Commission members deem appropriate concerning information and testimony the Commission received at the hearings or was otherwise presented to it.
  • Require the Bureau to prepare redistricting plans for legislative and Congressional districts using multiple criteria. Specifically, the new districts must:
    • Satisfy population requirements imposed by the Wisconsin Constitution and the U.S. Constitution.
    • Satisfy the requirements of Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act.
    • Satisfy a population based formula to minimize the deviation in population across districts. The ideal district population is the population of the state divided by the number of districts.
    • Under the formula for state legislative districts, the average deviation from the ideal population, across all districts, cannot be more than one percent. In addition, the difference in population between any two districts, including the largest district and the smallest, cannot be more than 10 percent of the smallest district. The only exception is for deviations needed to meet the requirements of the Voting Rights Act.
    • Under the formula for Congressional districts, each district must be as close to the ideal population as practicable and cannot deviate from the population ideal by more than one percent, unless necessary to comply with the Voting Rights Act.
    • Minimize the division of political subdivisions. District boundaries would follow the boundaries of the smallest political unit, the ward, and to the extent compatible with the state and federal constitutions, follow the boundaries of political subdivisions as well. The number of divided political divisions would have to be as small as possible, and if a choice exists between dividing two political subdivisions, the more populous one must be divided. If a municipality straddles a county line, the boundary can be drawn following the county line without violating a rule.
    • Be convient, contiguous territory.
    • Be compact. The bill lays out two detailed approaches to calculating how compact a district is.
    • Not be drawn with the intent or result of denying or abridging the equal opportunity of racial or language minorities to participate in the political process or elect representatives of their choice.
    • Not be drawn to favor a political party, incumbent legislator or member of Congress, or any other person or group, except as needed under the state and federal constitution and the Voting Rights Act in relation to racial and language minorities.
    • Not use these data, except to test the "efficiency gap" and the competitiveness of each district as the bill also requires:
    • political affiliations of registered voters.
    • previous election results
    • demographic information, except to meet the requirements of the state and federal constitutions and the Voting Rights Act
    • Not use the home addresses of incumbent legislators or members of Congress
  • Require the Bureau, when preparing its plans, to test the efficiency gap and competitiveness of each district and make the results public, including on the internet, not later than 72 hours before the first public hearing on a plan.
  • Mandate a specific process for adopting districts. Specifically:
    • The Legislative Research Bureau would submit identical bills embodying the redistricting plan to both chambers of the Legislature. The Advisory Commission would begin public hearings.
    • Expeditiously, but not less than seven days after the Commission gives the Legislature its report, each chamber would consider the bill. No amendments would be allowed. If either chamber rejects the plan, it would be sent back to the Bureau for revision, along with information that the chamber may direct regarding why the plan was rejected.
    • The bureau would create a new plan, and again submit bills reflecting it to both chambers within 21 days of the vote rejecting the first plan. The new plan would have to be expeditiously introduced and voted on not less than seven days after its introduction. If the bills again are rejected, again reasons would be given to the Bureau, and again the Bureau would submit new plans within 21 days. This third plan can be amended, but any amendment must be approved by a three-fourths vote in each house, and the bill itself must be approved by a three-fourths majority.

  • Create standards for litigation based on population inequality. If a suit is filed challenging state legislative districts based on population inequality, the Legislature has the burden of justifying any variance between a district's population and the ideal district population greater than 10 percent. If a suit challenges Congressional districts, the Legislature has the burden of justifying any variance between the ideal district population and the actual district population greater than one percent.

    Last updated June 14, 2021.

This bill, as introduced on June 14, 2021, would require investigations of potential double voting and related criminal referrals after every general election. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the Wisconsin Election Commission, no later than 30 days after each general election, to request, obtain, and investigate information from the Electronic Registration Information Center, Inc. relating to whether any registered Wisconsin voter may have voted in both Wisconsin and another state, or whether any Wisconsin voter who was no longer eligible to vote because of a felony conviction or mental incapacity nonetheless voted. If, based on the investigation, the Commission decides there is probable cause that one or more voters voted illegally, the Commission would have to refer those cases to the appropriate district attorney and the Attorney General. In addition, the Commission would have to report to the Legislature the individual's identity and the municipality, county, and state where the individual is alleged to have voted in the election.
  • Strengthen an existing requirement that, after completing a required post-election audit, the municipal clerk must send the Commission and the relevant district attorney copies of communications between the clerk and voters relating to any voter the municipal clerk believes, based on the audit, to have voted twice in the election. The bill would strengthen this existing requirement by requiring the Commission to investigate these referrals and to ensure that the district attorney also received the letter and any follow up information.
  • Require the Commission, if it finds probable cause after investigating the reports from clerks, to refer the cases to the appropriate district attorney and the Attorney General. In addition, in a report the Commission is already required to file with the Legislature relating to these clerk reports, the bill would require the Commission to include information relating to the number of letters the commission received after an election and the number of referrals made, a detailed description of each referral, and the outcome of the referral. The reporting on the criminal referrals would include whether the referral resulted in a criminal prosecution, an explanation of the disposition of that prosecution, and, if the referral did not result in a criminal prosecution, the reasons for not prosecuting.

  • Allow the Commission to initiate these investigations without a sworn complaint being filed first. Normally the Commission cannot initiate an investigation without a sworn complaint.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on December 7, 2021, would change how allegedly deceased voters are removed from voter registration database, and create a felony to punish a member of the Wisconsin Election Commission (WEC) or their staff who fail to follow the new process. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the WEC to seek and obtain the most recent records of all deaths of residents of this state on an at least monthly basis. Under existing law, municipal clerks or the commission are required to check vital statistics records to identify deceased voters and mark their registrations "ineligible", but the frequency is not specified. In practice, the state Department of Health Services generates a list of deceased residents and sends it to the WEC, which uses it to flag registrations for municipal clerks. The municipal clerks review the information and change the status of the registrations accordingly. Neither the statute nor the Elections Administration Manual published by the WEC indicates how frequently this is done. The state registrar of vital statistics must publish an annual report of vital statistics, but nothing prohibits more frequent data sharing with clerks or the WEC, and regulations generally require registrars to make vital statistics data available.
  • Require the WEC to remove a voter from the registration list if their name, address, and date of birth match a deceased person's record. Under existing law and practice, municipal clerks, not the WEC, change the status of a voter's record from "eligible" to "ineligible" if the record is matched to a deceased person's. Under existing law, "ineligible" voters' records are maintained in the registration list, but they are not included in the lists of voters used in each election. Existing law also does not identify which datapoints must match for a clerk or the WEC to decide that registration record and a death record refer to the same person.

  • Create a new felony to punish any member of the WEC or their staff who "willfully neglects or refuses to perform" these death-based registration list maintenance practices. Under existing law, no parallel crime exists. Instead, the willful neglect or refusal of an election official to perform a required duty is punishable by disqualification to act as an election official for five years.

    Last updated January 17, 2022.

  • Retain as much as possible the core of existing districts, thus maintaining existing communities of interest, and promoting the equal opportunity to vote by minimizing disenfranchisement due to staggered Senate terms
  • Be compact

  • Promote continuity of representation by avoiding incumbent pairing unless necessary to further another principle stated above and

  • Follow natural boundaries where practicable and consistent other principles, including geographic features such as rivers and lakes, manufactured boundaries such as major highways, and political boundaries such as county lines.
