Governor Evers vetoed this bill on August 10, 2021. This bill would have made it harder for voters to return their completed, sealed mail ballots by sharply restricting a voter's choices. The June 22 amendments clarified that a ballot could be returned by commercial mail carrier, not just the U.S.P.S., restricted "ballot collection events" to a single site, and did not otherwise alter the basic policies of the bill. Specifically, the final version of the bill would have:

  • Restricted who a voter could choose to return their completed, sealed mail ballot. Under the bill, the voter could have choosen immediate family members, legal guardians, or any registered voter, provided that the registered voter did not return more than two ballots that did not belong to them or their immediate family. Thus a church pastor could have returned only two congregants' ballots, or a caregiver could have returned only two clients' ballots. The bill defined "immediate family" as parent, child, spouse, sibling, grandparent or grandchild. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill. Under existing law, voters are free to choose anyone to return their completed, sealed mail ballot for them.
  • Created a new felony to punish anyone who returned a voter's completed, sealed mail ballot, other than an immediate family member, legal guardian, or person designated in writing as the bill would have allowed. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Severely restricted the use of secure drop boxes. Under the bill, at most a drop box could have been used at the clerk's office, an early voting site, a ballot collection event, or a polling place. The bill did not mention drop boxes, but limited ballot return to these locations. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law also does not address drop boxes, but standalone drop boxes sited for voter convenience were used at a small scale in Wisconsin for years and became widespread in 2020, with clerks relying on the Wisconsin Election Commission's interpretation of existing statutes.
  • Authorized clerks to hold mail ballot "collection events" under certain limited circumstances that parallel the rules under which clerks may conduct early voting. Specifically, starting 14 days before the election and ending on the Sunday before the election, a clerk would have been allowed to open a single ballot collection site that was both as near to their office as practicable and fully accessible for people with disabilities. The event would have been required to be staffed by the clerk, the executive director of the board of election commissioners, or employees of the clerk or the board of election commissioners. All of these rules also apply to early voting sites. However, unlike early voting sites, at ballot collection sites voters would have been able to return sealed, completed ballots only. A voter would not have been allowed to apply for and receive a ballot. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill did not limit these events to a single site. Existing law does not address ballot collection sites. However, in the fall of 2020, the city of Madison relied upon Wisconsin Election Commission guidance to hold "Democracy in the Park" events at which voters could return their mail ballots for the November 2020 election. Those events would have been illegal under this bill.

  • Authorized one new way a voter could have applied for and returned a mail ballot. Under the bill, a voter could have used a "for-profit commercial delivery service moving parcels nationally and internationally" to send their ballot application to the clerk, or return their ballot. Such services are not currently on the list of ways a voter may apply for or return a mail ballot. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill only authorized applying for ballots using such services, not returning them.

Last Updated October 22, 2021

Governor Evers vetoed this bill on August 10, 2021. This bill, as amended June 9, 2021, would have substantially changed how voters apply for absentee ballots, including in-person absentee ballots (early voting), and tweaked the process for registering to vote online.

In short, the major provisions of the bill would have required most voters to submit photo ID when applying for an absentee ballot by eliminating one exemption and limiting another, required an application for every primary and general election pair instead of once per year, required sick and disabled voters to apply for ballots more often and through a more difficult process, removed certain people from the list of sick and disabled voters, prohibited clerks from mailing absentee ballot applications to people who have not requested them, required a specific form be used to apply for the ballot, and required a voter's signature for both electronic absentee ballot applications and electronic voter registration applications.

Specifically, the bill would have:

  • Eliminated a major exception to the requirement that a voter submit a copy of their photo ID to apply for an absentee ballot, and limited another one:
    • Voters who apply to receive a ballot by mail, who are not "indefinitely confined" nor uniformed nor overseas, would have had to submit a copy of their ID when applying for an absentee ballot, every time they apply. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Under existing law, once a voter submitted their ID with an application, they need not do it again unless they moved or changed their name.
    • Indefinitely confined voters would have been required to submit a copy of their ID with their application, unless they applied online using their driver's license or state ID number, or unless they did not have ID. In the latter case, they would have been able to submit a sworn written statement from a U.S. citizen who is 18 years of age or older affirming their identity under penalty of perjury. Although this would have been the new rule, the bill had appeared to preserve the existing ability of an indefinitely confined voter to avoid submitting ID with their application if their ballot witness attests on the ballot to the voter's identity and address. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have required these voters to submit a copy of their ID without exception. Existing law does not require these voters to submit an ID with their application. Instead, they may obey the general ID rule or have their ballot witness affirm their identity.
    • The existing exemption for overseas voters would have been maintained. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have eliminated this exemption.
  • Required ordinary voters to apply for absentee ballots for every primary and general election pair. If the voter did not return the primary ballot, they would not have been sent the general election ballot without another application, and would not have been given notice that they will not. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have required an application for every election. Under existing law, voters may apply once and then receive ballots for each election in the calendar year so long as they keep returning completed ballots and remain eligible to vote. If they do not return a completed ballot, the clerk will give them five days' notice that they will cease receiving ballots unless they renew the application, if possible.
  • Overhauled the rules relating to indefinitely confined voters by making them engage in a two-step application process and, for each application for ballots, limiting the number of elections for which they can receive ballots, and creating new felonies to punish lying in connection with obtaining this status or ballots. Specifically, the bill would have:
    • Required a voter to apply for indefinitely confined status by filing a statement with the municipal clerk affirming that the elector is indefinitely confined because of age, physical illness, infirmity, or disability. The statement would have contained the voter's name, address, date of signature, and signature. The Wisconsin Election Commission would have been required to make a form for this statement, and the form would have warned voters that attempting to use the sworn statement to avoid the ID requirement when the voter possesses ID is a felony. This application would have needed to be renewed every four years. This is a new provision. The previous version of the bill would have preserved the existing process for obtaining indefinitely confined status. Under existing law, indefinitely confined voters attest to their status under penalty of perjury by checking a box on the ordinary absentee ballot application form.
    • Clarified that the existence of a public health emergency, a disaster, or an epidemic of a communicable disease would not qualify a voter for indefinitely confined status. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. The relationship of Governor Evers' safer at home order during the Covid-19 pandemic and indefinitely confined status was litigated in 2020.
    • Removed certain voters from the existing list of indefinitely confined voters. Specifically, the Wisconsin Election Commission would have been required to facilitate the removal of voters who joined the list between March 12, 2020 and November 3, 2020. Governor Evers declared a public health emergency due to Covid-19 on March 12, 2020. This provision is new.
    • Required an indefinitely confined voter to apply for absentee ballots using ID as above, and receive ballots for every election in the calendar year, unless removed from the list earlier. A voter would have been removed from the list if they failed to return a ballot, ceased to be indefinitely confined because of age, illness, infirmity or disability, asked to be removed from the list, or failed to renew their indefinitely confined status. Voters would have a duty to immediately inform the clerk if they are no longer indefinitely confined, although the clerk could learn the voter was no longer confined from anyone. If not from the voter, the clerk would have had to verify the information. This is a new provision. Under existing law, indefinitely confined voters receive ballots for every election that occurs during their confinement unless they are removed from the list because they are no longer indefinitely confined, they fail to return a ballot, or ask to be removed from the list. If they fail to return a ballot, existing law requires the clerk to mail the voter notice that if the voter does not respond within 30 days, the voter will be removed from the list. If the clerk is removing the voter from the list because someone other than the voter reported them as no longer indefinitely confined, the clerk is to give the voter five days notice if possible. These notice provisions would have been eliminated by the bill.
  • Created new felonies to punish someone for:
    • Falsely making any statement for the purpose of qualifying as indefinitely confined.
    • Intentionally providing false information on, using, or attempting to use the sworn statement to avoid providing proof of ID when the voter possesses valid proof.
    • Falsely affirming another person's identity on the sworn statement used for voters who do not have ID.
  • Prohibited clerks from mailing absentee ballot applications to people who did not request the application, and prohibit political committees from giving voters applications with a return mailing address that is different from the address of the appropriate clerk. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill. However, the previous version of this bill also created a felony to punish clerks who mailed absentee ballot applications to people who did not request them. That provision has been amended out of this bill.

  • Required people applying for an absentee ballot to complete an absentee ballot application using a form designed by the Wisconsin Election Commission that includes various questions specified by the bill. The standardized form required by the bill would ask each voter, applying by mail or in person as part of early voting:

    • their municipality and county of residence,
    • their name, date of birth, and contact information, including their telephone number, fax number, and electronic mail address,
    • the street address of their legal voting residence,
    • for which election they want the absentee ballot,
    • whether they are a military or overseas elector,
    • their confidential identification serial number if they have a confidential registration,
    • which method they want to receive the absentee ballot, and
    • whether the voter is in the hospital.

    This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Under existing law, voters may make a written request for an absentee ballot, but they need not use a standardized form, and when voting in-person absentee (early voting), they generally complete a single form on the ballot envelope that serves both as the application for the ballot and the voter's certificate.


  • Created a new felony to punish a clerk who issued an absentee ballot to someone who did not complete the standardized form, or who did not properly apply online or, if disabled or hospitalized, did not properly apply pursuant to the provisions applicable to them. This provision effectively prevents mail ballot elections. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Required clerks to write their initials on absentee ballots rather than have their initials pre-printed or stamped on the ballots. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Changed the rule for applying for an absentee ballot electronically to require the voter to include their written signature as part of the process, although the language may allow the clerk to use the voter's electronic signature in pdf form. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law does not require a written signature as part of the application, but does require an application with an original signature to be returned with the ballot.
  • Changed the rule for electronic voter registrations so that the Commission maintains a copy of the registration form that has the voter's electronic signature. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill required the signature to be a pdf file and made available to the municipal clerk or the board of election commissioners. Existing law does not require such a copy to be maintained.

  • Required clerks to post updates at their office and on the internet about the number of absentee ballots distributed to voters, received back from voters, and the number counted, beginning at 9 p.m. on Election Day and every hour thereafter until the ballots have all been canvassed.

    A provision in the previous version of the bill has been amended out of this one. That version would have enabled voters to join a list to receive an absentee ballot application every election, but not a ballot.

Last Updated August 11, 2021

Governor Evers vetoed this bill on August 10, 2021. This bill, as amended on June 9, 2021, would have changed the rules relating to the process by which special voting deputies bring absentee ballots to qualifying retirement homes and residential care facilities. Specifically, the bill would have:

  • Created a felony to punish employees of the facilities who coerce an occupant of the home or facility to apply or not apply for an absentee ballot, or to cast or refrain from casting a ballot, or to cast a ballot for or against a candidate or ballot question. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have created a felony to punish an employee if they "influence" an occupant of the home or facility, rather than "coerce" them.
  • Required the administrator of the facility to provide notice to each relative of an occupant for whom the home or facility has contact information, if the occupant intends to vote by absentee ballot with the special voting deputies, and allow the relative to be in the room in which voting is being conducted. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Under existing law, relatives can request to be told.
  • Changed the rules relating to whether current or former employees of residential care facilities may be appointed as special voting deputies to assist residents with applying for, completing or returning a ballot. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Allowed former employees of residential care facilities to be appointed special voting deputies. This is a new provision. Under existing law a person must not have been employed or retained by such a facility for at least two years prior to appointment.
    • Allowed current employees to be appointed if the facility denies access to outside special voting deputies because the governor has declared a public health emergency within 60 days preceding the election for which the deputies are appointed or guidance issued by the department of health services or the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services recommends that the family members of the occupants be denied entry. The bill would correspondingly require facilities to admit outside special deputies in all other circumstances. The bill would have required these employees to:
    • be a qualified voter of the municipality where the home is located.
    • take a two hour online training course. The Wisconsin Election Commission would be required to create the course.
    • take and submit a certain oath regarding their duties as special voting assistants.
    • work in pairs, and if possible, be of different political parties.
      These are new provisions and do not have a parallel in existing law.
    • Prohibited any other current employees from assisting an occupant in requesting, completing, or returning the occupant's absentee ballot. This is a new provision, and would effectively prevent employees from providing any voting assistance in ordinary times. Existing law has no parallel.
  • Changed the window of time within which this voting procedure may be offered in facilities. Under the bill, the deputies could assist residents with their ballots on any day between the fourth Monday before the election and 5 p.m. on the sixth working day before the election. The date the deputies would visit the facility, or the employees would offer the service, could be set anytime prior to the 11th working day before the election. This is a new provision. Existing law allows the service to be offered between the fourth Monday before the election and 5 p.m. the Monday before the election, with the date finalized no later than the sixth working day before the election.

  • Clarified that, although all relatives who are notified that an occupant has chosen to vote using this method "may" be present in the room in which voting is being conducted, only one relative or the legal guardian per occupant "may accompany the deputies to observe the absentee voting." This is a new provision and has no parallel in existing law.

Last Updated August 11, 2021

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 16, 2021, would make significant changes to absentee voting by "indefinitely confined" people. Indefinitely confined people do not need to submit a copy of their ID when applying for an absentee ballot, and they can apply once and then continue to receive absentee ballots until they are no longer indefinitely confined. The bill does not change these consequences of having indefinitely confined status, however, it does significantly change how people get and maintain indefinitely confined status. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the Wisconsin Election Commission to facilitate the removal of people on the indefinitely confined voters list who joined the list between March 12, 2020 and November 3, 2020. Anyone removed this way could reapply for indefinitely confined status. This provision is related to a controversy over how Covid risk relates to indefinitely confined status.
  • Require voters claiming indefinitely confined status to attest to their status, and if they are under 65 years old, the statement of their indefinitely confined status must be signed by an attending health care professional.
  • Create a felony to punish making a false statement to qualify as indefinitely confined.
  • Require clerks to remove voters from the list who fail to confirm their indefinitely confined status within 30 days of notice sent by the clerks. The bill would further require clerks to send voters on the indefinitely confined list such a notice every two years. Under existing law, people are removed from the list at their request, upon receipt of reliable information that the voter is no longer indefinitely confined, or because the voter fails to respond to notice sent because they failed to complete and return the ballot that was mailed to them. Those reasons would continue under the bill.

  • Clarify that the existence of an outbreak or epidemic of a communicable disease in an voter's community does not qualify the voter as indefinitely confined for purposes of receiving absentee ballots automatically under this subsection.

Last Updated June 15, 2021

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on April 14, 2021, would prohibit private grants for election administration, prohibit certain people from being election officials, and prohibit certain people from assisting with ballot tabulation. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Prohibit state agencies, municipalities or counties from receiving private grants for election administration, except as expressly allowed by the election code. A violation of this prohibition would be a felony. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill did not prohibit state agencies from receiving private grants.
  • Prohibit state agencies, municipalities or counties from entering into an election administration contract that contains any requirement governing election administration or the transfer of an election duty or power to a person not having that duty or power under state law. This is a new provision.
  • Prohibit certain people from working as election officials, namely, people who are also employees of:
    • a candidate committee, legislative campaign committee, political action committee, independent expenditure committee, political party, recall committee, and referendum committee.
    • a political organization required to register with the federal elections commission.
    • an issue advocacy group. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.

  • Create a felony to punish anyone who assists in counting or tabulating votes at an election unless the person is a resident of this state, is a tabulator or election official who is trained to the extent provided by law, and has signed the official oath and returned it to the municipal clerk with respect to that election. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

    Last updated July 12, 2022.

VRLANALYSIS:
The Senate amended this bill on June 9, 2021 by adopting an amendment recommended by the committee on May 19. As amended on June 9, this bill would limit a voter's options for returning their completed, sealed mail ballot by requiring the ballot to be delivered to the permanent office of the municipal clerk, to the voter's polling place on Election Day, or to a drop box as authorized by the bill. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill did not authorize returning the ballot to a voter's Election Day polling place. Under existing law as interpreted by the Wisconsin Election Commission, voters may return their completed, sealed ballot to the clerk as the clerk decides in their discretion, including to a secure drop box, an early voting location, and Election Day polling places. Drop boxes were broadly used in the 2020 election cycle.

In addition, the bill would limit drop boxes as follows:

  • Municipalities may have only one drop box each, sited at the permanent clerk's office, unless the municipality has 70,000 or more residents. Such a municipality could have three additional drop boxes, so long as none of them are sited in a public park. Any such boxes would have to be under video surveillance 24/7, and the video recordings retained for 22 months. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill limited all municipalities to one drop box.
  • The drop box sited on the property of the clerk's permanent office must be permanently located and accessible for drive-up delivery. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill required the drop box to be attached to the outside of the clerk's permanent office.
  • Drop boxes must be secured with a lock, include a tamper-proof seal with a serial number on the access door, be moisture-resistant, include a slot that is only large enough to allow for the insertion of a return envelope, and satisfy the accessibility requirements under the federal Americans with Disabilities Act. This a modified provision. The previous version of the bill did not specify a lock and tamper-proof seal with a serial number.
  • The clerk would have to publicly empty the drop box once a day, at a time posted at the box and on the clerk's website. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill required the box to be emptied once each day at 9 a.m.
  • Voters would have to return their ballots to the drop box by 5 p.m. on Election Day to be considered timely. This is a new provision. Polls close at 8 p.m. on Election Day.

  • The clerk must post the locations of the drop boxes on the state's voter information website. This is a new provision.

Last Updated June 11, 2021

Governor Evers vetoed this bill on August 10, 2021. This bill, as amended on April 14, 2021, would have made changes to election observing rules. Specifically, the bill would have:

  • Expanded what activity election observers may observe. The bill would require election officials to grant observers "uniform and nondiscriminatory access to all stages of the election process, including the certification of election technologies, absentee voting in person, canvassing, elector appeals, vote tabulation, and recounts." Under existing law, observers can witness early voting, Election Day voting, absentee ballot canvassing, and recounts. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Regulated the appearance and conduct of election observers. Specifically, an observer
    • would have been required to wear a badge with the first initial and last name of the individual. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill required the badge to show the observer's full name and the name of the organization, if any, the individual is representing.
    • would have been prohibited from wearing any campaign material advocating voting for or against a candidate or for or against any position on a ballot question, and if they did, could have been expelled by the municipal clerk, chief inspector, or board of canvassers. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • would have been prohibited from interfering with any elector in the preparation or casting of the elector's ballot or hindering or preventing the performance of the duties of any election official. If an election observer does interfere, they can be fined up to $500. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Required the board of canvassers, during a recount, to create observation areas that are no more than three feet from a table where ballots and other election-related materials are being examined and processed. This is a new provision not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Expanded misdemeanor election frauds that election officials can commit to punish intentionally obstructing an election observer's access to observe election procedures. This is a new provision not in the previous version of the bill.

Provisions in the previous version of the bill that have been amended out of this version would have:

  • Required election officials to give observers of in-person voting access that is no more than three feet away from the table at which voters check-in and/or register to vote. Existing law allows election officials to position observers between three and eight feet away.
  • Created a misdemeanor to punish any election observer who violates the partisan clothing rules more than once.

Last Updated February 11, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on May 19, 2021, would require the Wisconsin Election Commission to create a standard absentee ballot application and an internet absentee ballot application portal.

The absentee ballot application portal would through the state's voter public access Internet site, and would require the voter to provide their or their agent's original signature or an electronic pdf of their signature. This is a new provision not in the previous version of the bill.

The standard absentee ballot application must contain certain questions specified by the bill, and must be completed by all absentee voters, including in-person absentee (early) voters. The only people exempt from the new application would be those being served by special voting deputies at certain retirement or residential care homes. The standard application must ask:

  • the voter's municipality and county of residence.
  • the voter's name, date of birth, and contact information, including as applicable their telephone number, fax number, and electronic mail address.
  • the street address of the voter's legal voting residence.
  • the election at which the voter intends to vote absentee.
  • whether the voter is a military or overseas elector.
  • the voter's confidential identification serial number if the elector has obtained a confidential registration.
  • the lawful method by which the voter prefers to receive the absentee ballot.

  • whether the elector is hospitalized.
    These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.

Last Updated July 22, 2021

Governor Evers vetoed this bill on August 10, 2021. This bill, as amended May 11, 2021, would have defined what information must be included on a ballot certificate for the certificate to be complete, and would have addressed how clerks should act when a voter returns a completed absentee ballot with a defect in the ballot certificate. Specifically, as amended the bill would have:

  • Required clerks to reject ballots for having an incomplete certificate if any of the following are missing or either the voter or the witness:

    • printed first name
    • printed last name
    • house or apartment number
    • street name
    • municipality
    • signature.

    Thus a voter or a witness who included a zip code but not the municipality would have caused the ballot to be rejected. This provision is new, added by the May 11 amendment.


  • Created a new misdemeanor to punish anyone who corrects a defect in a voter's certificate unless they are the voter or the voter's witness. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill simply forbade clerks from correcting defects, and created other crimes, retained in this version, that appear to criminalize correcting ballot defects for a voter. Existing law, as interpreted by the Wisconsin Election Commission, allows clerks to fill in missing components of a witness's address in certain circumstances.
  • Required the clerk to put a notice of the defect in the voter's voter information page in the online voter registration website, and allowed the clerk to choose to contact the voter directly. The bill does not make clear if the voter will know the notice has been put in their voter information page unless they happen to check the page. Although existing law does not require notice of defects, Wisconsin Election Commission guidance encourages clerks to contact the voter directly. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill did not specifically authorize the clerk to contact the voter directly.

  • Created new felonies to punish clerks for actions that appear to include helping a voter cure their ballot. Specifically, the bill would have created new felonies in the list of election frauds to punish election officials if they:

    • intentionally assisted or caused the casting or counting of a vote or the receipt of a registration that is invalid for any reason.
    • intentionally assisted or caused the rejection of or failure to otherwise count a valid vote or the rejection of a valid registration.
    • intentionally failed to promptly report an election official election fraud violation to the commission and to the district attorney for the county in which the violation occurred, unless the violation is intentionally disclosing the name or address of a voter whose registration is confidential, in which case the election official would have committed a misdemeanor.

    A provision in the previous version of the bill has been amended out of this version. It would have required the clerk to mail a defective ballot back to the voter when the clerk discovers the defect. Existing law allows the clerk to mail the ballot back if there is time for the voter to correct the defect.

Last Updated August 11, 2021

VRLANALYSIS:
On May 17, 2022, the Legislature failed to override Governor Evers' veto.

Governor Evers vetoed this bill on April 15, 2022. As amended on February 24, 2022, this bill would have shifted election authority away from the Wisconsin Election Commission (WEC) by enabling people to skip a WEC administrative process and go straight to court to test the validity of any decision, action or failure to act on the part of any election official with respect to most aspects of election law.

In addition, the bill would have changed where such suits could be filed. Initially, for any violation other than one relating to election notices, campaign finance, ethics, lobbying, or certain related chapters and subchapter of Wisconsin statutes, suit could have been filed where the violation allegedly occurred. After 60 days, if no such action had been filed, suit could have been brought in any county contiguous with that county.

For suits relating to election notices, campaign finance, ethics, lobbying, or certain related chapters and subchapter of Wisconsin statutes, the bill would have required suit to be brought in the county within which the defendant resides, although the defendant could have chosen to move the suit to where the allegedly illegal conduct happened.

Under existing law, if, after completing the existing administrative process, a person sues over the alleged violation of any part of the election code, they must file suit where the defendant lives, although the defendant can choose to move the suit to where the allegedly illegal conduct happened.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on February 22, 2022, would allow absentee ballot canvassing to start the day before Election Day, create new election crimes, change the timeline for mailing absentee ballots to voters, change nominating rules for independent candidates, and change certain ballot security measures. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Allow clerks in municipalities that do not use the central count process, and require municipalities that do, to begin canvassing absentee ballots at 7 a.m. the day before Election Day. If canvassing begins the day before Election Day, the canvass must recess once all of the ballots are canvassed, or 10 p.m., whichever comes first. Canvassing would begin again on Election Day at 7 a.m., and continue until all ballots received by close of polls (8 p.m.) have been processed. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill did not give municipal clerks using election inspectors the discretion to begin canvassing early, and would have allowed but not required central count municipalities to begin canvassing the day before. If canvassing began before Election Day at the central count location, the previous version also required that it adjourn at 10 p.m. and begin again at 7 a.m. on Election Day. Under existing law, all municipalities may begin canvassing on Election Day, anytime after polls open but before 10 p.m. To facilitate municipal clerks' discretion, this version of the bill would clarify that absentee ballots must be delivered to election inspectors of the proper ward or election district, not the polling place, by 8 p.m. (close of polls) on Election Day.
  • The public would be allowed to observe the canvassing by the municipal clerks using election inspectors, however, the election inspectors would be able to order the removal of anyone who disrupts the process. This is a new provision. Existing law gives the same power to inspectors at central count locations.
  • At the end of the first day of canvassing, every four hours of canvassing on Election Day before polls close, and every hour after polls close, the clerk must post at the clerk's office and on the internet a statement of how many ballots were canvassed and how many remain to be canvassed. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill simply required daily disclosures.
  • Canvassed ballots could not be tabulated until the canvass is complete or the close of polls, whichever is later. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Create a new felony to punish anyone who intentionally acts to know or provide information about accumulating or final results before the canvass is complete or the polls close, whichever is later. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • If canvassing recesses, ballots and tabulators would need to be secured according to certain procedures. Before beginning again, the clerk would have to inspect for signs of tampering, and if any were found, the clerk would notify the Wisconsin Elections Commission and then conduct a recount according to existing procedures. The amended bill applies these rules to both municipalities that do central count, and to the municipal clerks gaining the discretion to begin processing before Election Day. The previous version only applied the rules to the central count locations because it only addressed them.
  • Create a new felony to punish a member of the board of absentee ballot canvassers or other election official who willfully neglects or refuses to perform any of the duties for absentee ballot canvassing. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Under existing law, willfully neglecting or refusing to perform duties is punishable by being disqualified from working as an election official for five years.
  • Change the timeline of mailing absentee ballots so that they are sent to regular voters no later than the 21st day before the election, and to military and overseas voters no later than the 45th day before the election. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law mails ballots to all electors no later than 47 days before the election.

    Require municipal clerks to post notice of the testing of electronic voting machines on their websites. This is a new provision.

  • Change the rules relating to independent nominating petitions, which VRL does not track, and clarify that the only voters to whom presidential-only ballots may be given are new state residents and former state residents otherwise qualified to receive them.

    A provision in the previous version of the bill has been amended out of this one. The previous version would have allowed cities, villages, or towns with fewer than 35,000 residents to combine a polling place with an adjacent city, village, or town with fewer than 35,000 residents.

This bill, as introduced on June 4, 2021, would shift the timeline for the local redistricting process based on the 2020 Census to account for the delays in the delivery of the Census data. The bill would not make any substantive changes to the redistricting process.

Last updated June 7, 2021.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on June 10, 2021, would create a comprehensive redistricting regime for Congressional and State Legislative districts. It would also provide for automatic deadline shifting when the Census delivers its data late. The new redistricting process would require the Legislative Research Bureau to propose and analyze districting plans based on criteria set by the bill, under the supervision of a Redistricting Advisory Commission. The Legislature would consider and vote on the plans according to certain rules set out in the bill. Specifically, the new redistricting process proposed by the bill would:

  • Require 33 State Senate districts, each to be composed of three Assembly districts. This is the same number and structure of state legislative districts as Wisconsin currently has. However, the bill would allow the Bureau to propose a different number of districts, so long as there are at least 54 assembly districts and no more than 100, the number of senate districts is at least 1/4 of the number of assembly districts and is not more than 1/3 of them, and each senate district is comprised of only whole assembly districts.
  • Require the Legislative Research Bureau to use the new census data to publish an analysis of the population of current legislative and congressional districts, reporting the extent to which the existing districts violate population standards created by the bill.
  • Create a Redistricting Advisory Commission. The Advisory Commission would:
    • Consist of five people, four of which are appointed by the state legislative leaders of both parties, and which would choose a fifth. These people must be eligible to vote in Wisconsin, cannot be office holders, relatives or employees of a member of the legislature or a member of Congress, or be directly employed by the Legislature or Congress.
    • Advise the Bureau in relation to any decision the Bureau must make in preparing a redistricting plan if if the bill is not clear, and if the Bureau requests the advice.
    • Oversee the work of the Bureau employees doing the redistricting work.
    • Enter contracts for hiring experts to assist the Bureau, if at least 3/4 of the members agree, and terminate a contract employee, again, if 3/4 of the members agree.
    • Educate the public and hold public hearings on the redistricting plans the Bureau submits to the Legislature for enactment, and submit a report on the hearings to the Legislature. Specifically, the Advisory Commission would:
    • make available to the public copies of the bill, maps illustrating the plan, a summary of the criteria for the plan's development, and a statement of the population in each district and its relative deviation from the ideal district population.
    • hold hearings in different geographic regions fo the state, including at least one in each Congressional district. However, only one hearing may be held in the city of Madison. Whenever practicable, the Advisory Commission must hold the hearings on weekends.
    • report to the legislature summarizing the information and testimony. The report can include any comments and conclusions that the Commission members deem appropriate concerning information and testimony the Commission received at the hearings or was otherwise presented to it.
  • Require the Bureau to prepare redistricting plans for legislative and Congressional districts using multiple criteria. Specifically, the new districts must:
    • Satisfy population requirements imposed by the Wisconsin Constitution and the U.S. Constitution.
    • Satisfy the requirements of Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act.
    • Satisfy a population based formula to minimize the deviation in population across districts. The ideal district population is the population of the state divided by the number of districts.
    • Under the formula for state legislative districts, the average deviation from the ideal population, across all districts, cannot be more than one percent. In addition, the difference in population between any two districts, including the largest district and the smallest, cannot be more than 10 percent of the smallest district. The only exception is for deviations needed to meet the requirements of the Voting Rights Act.
    • Under the formula for Congressional districts, each district must be as close to the ideal population as practicable and cannot deviate from the population ideal by more than one percent, unless necessary to comply with the Voting Rights Act.
    • Minimize the division of political subdivisions. District boundaries would follow the boundaries of the smallest political unit, the ward, and to the extent compatible with the state and federal constitutions, follow the boundaries of political subdivisions as well. The number of divided political divisions would have to be as small as possible, and if a choice exists between dividing two political subdivisions, the more populous one must be divided. If a municipality straddles a county line, the boundary can be drawn following the county line without violating a rule.
    • Be convient, contiguous territory.
    • Be compact. The bill lays out two detailed approaches to calculating how compact a district is.
    • Not be drawn with the intent or result of denying or abridging the equal opportunity of racial or language minorities to participate in the political process or elect representatives of their choice.
    • Not be drawn to favor a political party, incumbent legislator or member of Congress, or any other person or group, except as needed under the state and federal constitution and the Voting Rights Act in relation to racial and language minorities.
    • Not use these data, except to test the "efficiency gap" and the competitiveness of each district as the bill also requires:
    • political affiliations of registered voters.
    • previous election results
    • demographic information, except to meet the requirements of the state and federal constitutions and the Voting Rights Act
    • Not use the home addresses of incumbent legislators or members of Congress
  • Require the Bureau, when preparing its plans, to test the efficiency gap and competitiveness of each district and make the results public, including on the internet, not later than 72 hours before the first public hearing on a plan.
  • Mandate a specific process for adopting districts. Specifically:
    • The Legislative Research Bureau would submit identical bills embodying the redistricting plan to both chambers of the Legislature. The Advisory Commission would begin public hearings.
    • Expeditiously, but not less than seven days after the Commission gives the Legislature its report, each chamber would consider the bill. No amendments would be allowed. If either chamber rejects the plan, it would be sent back to the Bureau for revision, along with information that the chamber may direct regarding why the plan was rejected.
    • The bureau would create a new plan, and again submit bills reflecting it to both chambers within 21 days of the vote rejecting the first plan. The new plan would have to be expeditiously introduced and voted on not less than seven days after its introduction. If the bills again are rejected, again reasons would be given to the Bureau, and again the Bureau would submit new plans within 21 days. This third plan can be amended, but any amendment must be approved by a three-fourths vote in each house, and the bill itself must be approved by a three-fourths majority.

  • Create standards for litigation based on population inequality. If a suit is filed challenging state legislative districts based on population inequality, the Legislature has the burden of justifying any variance between a district's population and the ideal district population greater than 10 percent. If a suit challenges Congressional districts, the Legislature has the burden of justifying any variance between the ideal district population and the actual district population greater than one percent.

    Last updated June 14, 2021.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on June 10, 2021, would require investigations of potential double voting and related criminal referrals after every general election. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the Wisconsin Election Commission, no later than 30 days after each general election, to request, obtain, and investigate information from the Electronic Registration Information Center, Inc. relating to whether any registered Wisconsin voter may have voted in both Wisconsin and another state, or whether any Wisconsin voter who was no longer eligible to vote because of a felony conviction or mental incapacity nonetheless voted. If, based on the investigation, the Commission decides there is probable cause that one or more voters voted illegally, the Commission would have to refer those cases to the appropriate district attorney and the Attorney General. In addition, the Commission would have to report to the Legislature the individual's identity and the municipality, county, and state where the individual is alleged to have voted in the election.
  • Strengthen an existing requirement that, after completing a required post-election audit, the municipal clerk must send the Commission and the relevant district attorney copies of communications between the clerk and voters relating to any voter the municipal clerk believes, based on the audit, to have voted twice in the election. The bill would strengthen this existing requirement by requiring the Commission to investigate these referrals and to ensure that the district attorney also received the letter and any follow up information.
  • Require the Commission, if it finds probable cause after investigating the reports from clerks, to refer the cases to the appropriate district attorney and the Attorney General. In addition, in a report the Commission is already required to file with the Legislature relating to these clerk reports, the bill would require the Commission to include information relating to the number of letters the commission received after an election and the number of referrals made, a detailed description of each referral, and the outcome of the referral. The reporting on the criminal referrals would include whether the referral resulted in a criminal prosecution, an explanation of the disposition of that prosecution, and, if the referral did not result in a criminal prosecution, the reasons for not prosecuting.

  • Allow the Commission to initiate these investigations without a sworn complaint being filed first. Normally the Commission cannot initiate an investigation without a sworn complaint.

    Last updated August 31, 2021.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on June 24, 2021, would eliminate drop boxes except inside the office of the municipal clerk, would prohibit ballot collection anywhere other than the clerk's office or a location offering in-person absentee early voting, which itself must be set up as near as practicable to the clerk's office, and would require someone returning another voter's ballot to track their activity in a registry in the clerk's office.

Existing law does not directly address drop boxes, but the Wisconsin Elections Commission has interpreted it to authorize drop box use. While used for years in the state in limited ways, drop box use became widespread during the 2020 election. Similarly, existing law does not directly address whether clerks can choose to receive ballots outside their offices in person, as opposed to through drop boxes, but relying on Commission guidance, in 2020 the City of Madison held "Democracy in the Park" events to collect completed, sealed ballots. This bill would prohibit such events.

Finally, existing law does not restrict who may return a voter's ballot for them, or impose other restrictions on the process. This bill would require anyone returning another voter's ballot to bring it in person to the office of the municipal clerk and make entries in a log book maintained by the clerk. Specifically, the person would print their name, residential street address, their relationship to the voter, and the voter's name in the log book. In addition, the person would sign and date their log entry.

Last Updated July 6, 2021

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on November 30, 2021, would change how allegedly deceased voters are removed from voter registration database, and create a felony to punish a member of the Wisconsin Election Commission (WEC) or their staff who fail to follow the new process. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the WEC to seek and obtain the most recent records of all deaths of residents of this state on an at least monthly basis. Under existing law, municipal clerks or the commission are required to check vital statistics records to identify deceased voters and mark their registrations "ineligible", but the frequency is not specified. In practice, the state Department of Health Services generates a list of deceased residents and sends it to the WEC, which uses it to flag registrations for municipal clerks. The municipal clerks review the information and change the status of the registrations accordingly. Neither the statute nor the Elections Administration Manual published by the WEC indicates how frequently this is done. The state registrar of vital statistics must publish an annual report of vital statistics, but nothing prohibits more frequent data sharing with clerks or the WEC, and regulations generally require registrars to make vital statistics data available.
  • Require the WEC to remove a voter from the registration list if their name, address, and date of birth match a deceased person's record. Under existing law and practice, municipal clerks, not the WEC, change the status of a voter's record from "eligible" to "ineligible" if the record is matched to a deceased person's. Under existing law, "ineligible" voters' records are maintained in the registration list, but they are not included in the lists of voters used in each election. Existing law also does not identify which datapoints must match for a clerk or the WEC to decide that registration record and a death record refer to the same person.

  • Create a new felony to punish any member of the WEC or their staff who "willfully neglects or refuses to perform" these death-based registration list maintenance practices. Under existing law, no parallel crime exists. Instead, the willful neglect or refusal of an election official to perform a required duty is punishable by disqualification to act as an election official for five years.

    Last updated January 17, 2022.

BILLSUMMARY: Concerns public policy regarding plans that establish state legislative districts.
VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as adopted on September 28, 2021, declares certain criteria as public policy for state legislative redistricting. Specifically, the resolution announces that state legislative districts should:

  • Comply with the federal and state law
  • Give effect to the principle that every citizen's vote should count the same by creating districts with nearly equal population, having population deviations that are well below that which is required by the U.S. Constitution
  • Retain as much as possible the core of existing districts, thus maintaining existing communities of interest, and promoting the equal opportunity to vote by minimizing disenfranchisement due to staggered Senate terms
  • Be compact
  • Be legally contiguous
  • Respect and maintain whole communities of interest where practicable
  • Avoid municipal splits unless unavoidable or necessary to further another principle stated above, and when splitting municipalities, respect current municipal ward boundaries
  • Promote continuity of representation by avoiding incumbent pairing unless necessary to further another principle stated above and

  • Follow natural boundaries where practicable and consistent other principles, including geographic features such as rivers and lakes, manufactured boundaries such as major highways, and political boundaries such as county lines.

    Last updated September 29, 2021.

BILLSUMMARY: Creates the Independent Redistricting Commission of the Joint Committee on Government and Finance.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 16, 2021, would create an independent redistricting commission to draw district maps for congressional and state legislative seats. The commission must hold public hearings in each congressional district, publish draft plans and receive public comment on the draft plans for at least 30 days after they have been published. When finalized, the commission's plans would be submitted to the legislature for its approval without amendment. If the legislature rejects the commission's maps, the commission would revise and submit a new set of maps. Again the legislature would have to vote on the maps without amendment. If the legislature rejects the second set, the commission shall prepare and submit a third set, but the legislature may amend the maps before approving them.
In creating its maps, the commission must strive to create districts of equal population in a grid-like pattern across the state, adjusted as necessary to comply with the Federal and State Constitutions, the federal Voting Rights Act, and to the extent practicable, to:

  • Make the districts equal in population.
  • Keep the districts compact and contiguous. Compactness means not including more distant population while bypassing nearer population. Odd shapes should be avoided.
  • Not favor an incumbent, candidate, or political party, and not to augment or dilute the voting strength of a language or racial minority group.
  • Use as district boundaries visible geographic features, city, town, and county boundaries, and undivided census tracts.
  • Favor competitive districts, but not to the significant detriment of other goals.

  • Respect the geographic integrity of any city, county, and local neighborhood, or local community of interest in a manner that minimizes their division without violating other requirements. Districts should be within a single county if possible, and if not must include contiguous counties. When a legislative district contains more than one county or a portion of a county, the counties or portion of a county in the district must be directly connected by roads and highways which are designated as part of the interstate highway system, the United States highway system, or the state highway system. When creating the maps, the commission may not use any of the following data: Address of incumbent Legislators or members of Congress, Political affiliations of registered voters, Previous election results, and Demographic information, other than population head counts, except as required by the Constitution and laws of the United States. When the Redistricting Commission determines, by an affirmative vote of at least five of its six members recorded in its minutes, that it cannot complete its duties for a legislative district by fully complying with the criteria, the criteria shall not apply to the Redistricting Commission or legislative redistricting plan it shall adopt.

    Last updated February 22, 2021.

This bill, as introduced March 2, 2021, would make major changes to the election code, including creating no-excuse absentee voting, expanding early voting, eliminating signature matching as a ballot and in-person verification requirement, creating a cure process, allowing pre-Election Day ballot processing, and more. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Make major changes to mail voting, including to applications, completing and returning the ballot, verifying mail ballots and counting them. Specifically, the bill would:
    • create no excuse absentee voting. Existing law requires a voter to have an excuse to vote by mail.

This bill, as introduced on March 9, 2021, would create an independent redistricting commission to propose a redistricting plan with maps for congressional and state legislative districts, which the legislature would then consider for adoption.   • Create an iterative map drawing and approval process. The commission sends one set of plans to the legislature, which must adopt or reject the plan without amendment. If it is adopted, it goes to the governor for approval of veto. If it is rejected by the legislature or governor, the commission must offer a new plan, and again, the legislature must vote on it without amendment and, if approved, the governor must also approve it. If the second plan is rejected, the commission must offer a third plan. The legislature is allowed to amend this plan as part of its consideration. If the legislature and governor fail to enact the third plan, all three plans as originally created by the commission are presented to the state's highest court, which then picks one. Each time the commission draws maps, it must consider the same criteria and follow the same public comment rules.
  • Identify what the commission must consider in drawing the maps. Specifically, when drawing the congressional and state maps, the commission must start with districts of equal population in a grid-like pattern across the state, that are adjusted as necessary to
    • comply with the U.S. Constitution and the Voting Rights Act.
    • make districts as equal in population as practicable.
    • be geographically compact and contiguous to the extent practicable.
    • use visible geographic features, city, town and county boundaries, and undivided census tracts, to the extent practicable.
    • favor competitive districts to the extent possible, without creating a significant detriment to the previous goals.
  • Identify what the commission cannot consider when drawing maps. Specifically, when drawing maps, the commission:
    • cannot consider party registration and voting history data, although it can be used to test the maps' compliance with the required criteria.
    • cannot consider the place of residence of candidates or incumbents.

  • Require the commission to solicit public input after creating draft maps for at least 30 days, including by holding three public hearings in geographically distinct areas of the state to present the plan and hear public comments.

This bill, as introduced on January 18, 2022, would create a cure process to empower voters to ensure their ballots are counted, rather than rejected for errors completing the ballot envelope. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Enable voters to remedy these errors:
    • The voter forgot to sign the certificate on the envelope. Voters' signatures must be notarized or witnessed, and the bill does not address a ballot that is signed but lacks notarization or a witness signature.
    • The voter forgot to date the ballot envelope certificate or provided an improper date on the certificate, if the ballot is timely received, namely received or postmarked on or before the day of the election.
    • The voter registered to vote by mail, failed to provide sufficient identification at that time to complete their registration, and failed to provide it with their ballot.
  • Give the voter notice and opportunity to cure the errors by:
    • Requiring the director of the division of elections to immediately update the existing free access system voters may use to discover whether their ballot was counted, and if not, why. Under existing law, this information may be updated as late as 60 days after the certification of a general election.
    • Mailing the voter notice of the ballot rejection and the process to cure it within three days of rejecting it, but no later than 10 days after Election Day.
    • In addition, if the information is available and the election official chooses, contacting the voter by phone, text message or email.
  • Enable the voter to cure the error by providing proof of identification on or before the 10th day after Election Day:
    • In person at a polling location or other location designated by the division of elections, or
    • Along with signing a form affidavit created by the division of elections. The bill does not address how the voter would obtain the affidavit or how they would return it.

  • Change applying for, and returning, mail ballots by:
    • Allowing one application to request ballots for every election in four years, and allowing voters to reapply to continue receiving ballots. Under existing law, a single application can request ballots for every election in the calendar year.
    • Providing prepaid return postage for mail ballots. Under existing law, the state does not provide postage.

The Division of Elections currently enables a voter to track if their absentee ballot application was accepted or if a correction is needed, if the ballot was mailed, or if the ballot was received.
    • Restricting a voter's choices for someone to return their mail ballot for them to a family member, caregiver, or postal worker, and expanding an existing misdemeanor to enforce the restriction. Existing law is silent on who a voter may choose to return their ballot.
  • Change mail ballot processing and verification by:
    • Requiring election officials to start reviewing ballot certificates no later than ten days before Election Day. Under existing law, ballot certificate review must begin no later than seven days before Election Day.
    • Requiring signature match verification, on top of the existing witness/notary requirement, for mail ballots. The bill would require the division of elections to issue regulations creating a process using signature matching equipment, require signature match training, prohibit disqualifying a signature because the voter used an initial or a common nickname. If a signature was found not to match one on file, the ballot would be rejected, even if that signature was notarized. Under existing law, the signature needs to be notarized, or if a notary is not reasonably available, witnessed.
    • Creating a cure process to enable voters to address a missing signature or a mismatched signature. Presumably, the missing signature could be a missing notary or witness signature, as well as the voter's signature. The election official would, within 48 hours but no later than two days after Election Day, send notice of the issue to the voter by mail, and if the contact information is provided, by email, phone, or text message. The voter would have until 14 days after Election Day to return the required form and a copy of their driver's license, state identification card, other current and valid photo identification, birth certificate, passport, or hunting or fishing license.

      Under existing law, a ballot that is postmarked on or before Election Day is timely even if it is received 10 days after Election Day. As structured, voters whose ballots arrive three or more days after Election Day would not be given notice or an opportunity to cure.     • Requiring the Director of the Division of Elections to send copies of the signature on the voter's return envelope and the signature stored in voter registration records to the Attorney General for investigation if the voter fails to cure their ballot within 14 days.     • Setting up a toll-free election fraud hotline and requiring the Division of Elections to publicize it. Because the hotline does not require verified complaints, it could be subject to malicious, false reporting.     • Requires the Division to issue regulations creating a process for using databases to check for voters who died, moved, were convicted of a disqualifying felony, or are otherwise unqualified, such as on the grounds of citizenship. being underage, and revise the statewide voter registration list accordingly. This bill, as introduced on February 22, 2022, would ban myriad funding sources for election administration, require an undefined "forensic audit" after each state election, and make multiple other changes to the election code primarily relating to video surveillance, ballot accounting, and hand counts. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the Division to adopt a poll watcher handbook that includes methods for documenting misconduct by election officials and require it be posted on the Division's website.

  • Require the Division to record video while ballots are being cast or votes are being counted.

  • Require watermarked or other special paper for ballots, change ballot preservation and accounting procedures, require videotaping of ballot duplication, require transparent ballot boxes kept under video surveillance, require a chain of custody, and "dual control" protocols.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 22, 2022, would require mail ballots to be verified by signature matching as well as by a notary or witness, create a cure process for missing and non-conforming signatures, create comprehensive mail ballot tracking, restrict whom a voter may choose to return their ballot, enforcing the restriction with a crime, create a permanent absentee ballot list, and require the state to pay the postage to return a mail ballot. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Add signature matching to the existing notary or witness requirement for verifying mail ballots, require the use of automated signature matching, require the Director of the Division of Elections to issue related regulations including for training of election officials.
  • Create a cure process for uncounted ballots if the issue is a missing signature, a non-conforming signature, or the lack of a signature in the voter's registration record. If a mail ballot has any of those issues:
    • the Director would give notice within 48 hours, but no later than two days after Election Day, by mail to the voter's registration address, and if provided, their email address or by telephone call or text. The notice would include a form. No cure process exists under existing law. However, under existing law unchanged by the bill, mail ballots are timely if they are postmarked by Election Day and received by the 10th day after the election.
    • the voter would confirm they returned a ballot, provide identification sufficient to register to vote, and provide a signature for verification by the 14th day after the election.
    • the Director would refer ballots and voters for criminal investigation by the Attorney General if the voter returns the cure affidavit indicating that they did not return a ballot or the voter simply does not attempt to cure their ballot by timely returning their form.
    • the Division would update a voter's record to include the signature submitted as part of the cure process if the cure is successful.
  • Create a comprehensive ballot tracking system. Existing law does not require ballot tracking, but the Division offers a system that provides less information that the bill would require. The system created by the bill would enable a voter to:
    • confirm that the voter's ballot has been sent by the Division,
    • track the date of the ballot's delivery to the voter,
    • confirm the Division's receipt of the voter's ballot,
    • determine whether the voter's certificate has been reviewed,
    • determine if the signature on the voter's ballot is missing or is determined not to match the signature in the voter's registration record,
    • learn the process by which the voter may cure the lack of signature or verify the voter's identity,
    • determine whether the voter's ballot has been counted, and
    • if the voter's ballot was not counted, the reason the ballot was not counted.
  • Restrict third-party ballot return. Existing law is silent on third-party ballot return. Specifically, the bill would expand an existing misdemeanor to criminalize knowingly possessing another person's ballot, unless the person is:
    • a family member of the voter
    • a caregiver of the voter
    • a postal worker or election officials doing their official duties
    • a person collecting a ballot on behalf of an Alaskan 501(c)(3) charitable or educational organization who is also a registered voter or an employee of the organization.
  • Allow voters to apply once and receive mail ballots indefinitely unless they fail to vote a mail ballot for four straight years or a previous ballot was returned as undeliverable.

  • Require the state to pay return postage for mail ballots.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 15, 2022, would:

  • Shift the voter ID requirement for absentee voters from the application stage to the ballot return stage.
  • Require county absentee ballot managers to submit to the secretary of state and attorney general a list of all voters who requested absentee ballots sent outside their county of registration and who requested a ballot sent to an address where more than four ballots were requested.
  • Bar county officials from extending regular business hours in order to facilitate in-person absentee voting. Existing law is silent on county election office hours.
  • Require additional record-keeping about absentee ballots by county officials, including the use of tracking numbers.
  • Allow absentee ballots received between noon on Election Day and six days after Election Day to be counted as provisional ballots. Under existing law, ballots received by mail after noon on Election Day are not counted.
  • Increase the number of poll watchers permitted to be present during the counting of absentee ballots from one per authorized entity to one per every 10,000 absentee ballots.

Last Updated February 21, 2022

This bill, as introduced on February 16, 2022, would:

  • Direct election officials to provide voters with a registration update form on Election Day if their address has changed within the same precinct.
  • Direct election officials to inform voters of the proper precinct if a voter appears at the incorrect precinct in their county of registration. Such voters would be given paperwork to minimize their wait time when they appear at their proper precinct.
  • A voter who was directed to a different precinct but believed that they were entitled to vote at the precinct where they appeared would be given a provisional ballot. An inspector could file a challenge statement laying out the reasons why they believe the voter was not qualified to vote at that precinct.

Existing law does not prescribe a procedure for when a voter appears at the incorrect precinct or has changed addresses within a precinct.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 8, 2022, would:

  • Establish automatic voting rights restoration for individuals with most disenfranchising criminal convictions. Individuals convicted of certain violent or sex crimes would not be eligiible for automatic restoration. Under existing law, all individuals must apply to the board of pardons and paroles for a certificate of eligibility before they can register to vote.
  • Establish eligibility for restoration upon completion of supervision and payment of all restitution and fines, and either payment of all court fees or a year of compliance with a payment schedule or community service plan. Under existing law, all financial obligations must be paid before an individual is eligible for restoration.
  • Require the board of pardons and paroles to conduct a review of individuals' eligibility to register to vote upon release from incarceration, discharge from supervision, or pardon, and to notify the individual of their findings and whether their rights were restored. Under existing law, no notice to voters regarding restoration of rights is required other than in response to an application by the voter.
  • Require transmission to the secretary of state of the names and addresses of individuals whose voting rights have been restored. Those who were registered prior to disenfranchisement would be automatically re-registered to vote.
  • Direct the board of pardons and paroles to develop a community service program in which individuals demonstrating economic hardship could voluntarily participate in in order to offset court fees and costs.

Last updated March 15, 2022.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on March 29, 2022, would:

  • Establish automatic restoration of voting rights for most individuals convicted of disenfranchising felonies upon the payment of all ordered victim restitution or a year of compliance with a payment plan or alternate community service program for indigent individuals and the earlier of (1) release from incarceration or (2) release from probation or parole. Under existing law, individuals must fulfill all requirements of their sentence, including incarceration, probation, parole, and all financial obligations, in order to be eligible to apply for restoration.
  • Require the board of pardons and paroles to transmit to the secretary of state the names of individuals whose rights were restored, the secretary of state would then transmit this information to the proper county election officials. Individuals who were registered to vote prior to being disenfranchised would not need to re-register. Existing law does not result in individuals whose rights are restored being re-registered.

The above provisions were all retained from the previous version of the bill. The bill also contains several provisions that were newly amended into this version of the bill. These provisions would:

  • Clarify that restoration requirements must be completed for each disenfranchising conviction before rights are restored.
  • Establish a priority order for financial obligations arising out of a disenfranchising conviction.
  • Expand the list of sex crimes for which a conviction is permanently disenfranchising.
  • Remove impeachment from the list of crimes that are permanently disenfranchising.

Last updated April 6, 2022.

Boards of registrars would be directed to refuse registration to any individual who applies using a prefilled application and provide the would-be registrant with notice and an explanation within 10 days. Violations of this prohibition would be a Class C felony.
  • Prohibit any individual or entity, other than the secretary of state or a county absentee election manager from providing any registered voter with an absentee ballot application on which any field, other than the return address, has been prefilled without the voter's consent. Violation of this prohibition would be a Class C felony.

Officials acting in good faith to execute their duties would not be criminally or civilly liable for any failure to do so. Under existing law, "willfully and knowingly" failing to perform duties required is a Class C misdemeanor.
