This bill, as enacted on April 29, 2022, provides returning citizens notice when their voting eligibility has been automatically restored, or when they have become eligible to apply to have their eligibility restored, as the case may be, and changes how people who committed their crimes out of state, or committed federal crimes, have their eligibility restored. The bill also eliminates the waiting period for people who must apply and streamlines the process. Although the bill speaks of "civil rights", that term includes the right to vote. Only the right to a firearm is treated differently.

Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires the sentencing judge to inform the defendant on the record of how and when their voting rights will or could be restored, and include that information in the court's order and judgment of guilt. Existing law required judges to inform defendants of the future restoration of their rights as part of sentencing but did not require the information to be conveyed on the record or made part of the court's order and judgment.
  • Requires the probation department, at the time the person completes probation, to give the person a copy of the court's order and judgment of guilt. Existing law had no comparable provision.
  • Requires the state department of corrections to provide the court's order and judgment of guilt when the person is absolutely discharged from imprisonment unless they are being discharged to a term of probation. Existing law had no comparable provision.
  • Requires the clerk of the court to notify the department of public safety that a person's civil rights have been automatically restored, including whether that includes the right to a firearm. Existing law required the clerk generally to give such notice when the court restores civil rights but did not address notice if rights have been automatically restored.
  • Narrows who is eligible for fully automatic restoration to people who committed their first felony by committing a state law crime in Arizona. People who committed their first felony by committing a federal crime or a crime in another state are required to apply to have their eligibility restored. Nonetheless, the judge is required to grant the application without holding a hearing or receiving a response from the state. Under existing law, only people with a prior felony conviction or who have not fully paid all restitution were required to apply for restoration, and that application was not automatically granted.
  • Allows a person who was discharged from incarceration or probation and is not eligible for automatic restoration to apply for discretionary restoration immediately upon discharge. Under existing law, such a person had to wait two years before applying.
  • Streamlines the application process for a person discharged from incarceration by eliminating the requirement that the application includes a certificate of discharge from the director of the state department of corrections or the equivalent person in the federal or other state's corrections system.

  • Makes changes to the restoration of the right to a firearm.

Last Updated June 27, 2022

    • it is not practicable for election staff to be present, in which case the county would provide 24 hour video surveillance of the drop box, retaining the video for four years.

This bill, as introduced on January 12, 2022, would prohibit election officials from using countywide vote centers and instead require all in person voters be assigned to a particular precinct to vote. This bill, as introduced on January 12, 2022, would require people to show ID to return a completed, sealed ballot to a polling place, vote center, or emergency voting center, and if the person is returning someone else's ballot, they also would have to sign a document attesting that they are one of the people allowed to return a voter's ballot for them. The ID must show the voter's name or the agent's name, as applicable, but need not include a photo. Anyone who knowingly returns a ballot in violation of those provisions would commit a new felony. Under existing law, only a family member, household member, or caregiver may return a voter's ballot for them, and no one is required to present ID or sign an affidavit to return a ballot. People who violate the existing restrictions on returning a voter's ballot for them are already subject to felony prosecution, but no felony yet exists for a voter returning their own ballot.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 12, 2022, would create a new, affirmative duty for county recorders and the Secretary of State to verify that the name, address, date of birth and driver's license number of a voter registration applicant are valid and accurate, and create a new felony to punish election officials if they willfully fail to do so.

In Arizona, people may apply for voter registration without providing a driver's license number. The bill does not clarify what "valid and accurate" means in terms of an address or name, such as whether the applicant must include a middle initial or name, if they have one, for their name to be accurate, or how the provision would intersect with laws allowing people to apply using nontraditional addresses, such as Native people living on reservations or homeless people.

Last Updated January 21, 2022

This bill, as enacted on July 6, 2022, codifies several new provisions relating to voter registration list maintenance that are substantially similar to ones Governor Ducey vetoed earlier in the year. These provisions focus on identifying and canceling registrations due to non-citizenship, change in address, and death.

 

Note: The provision of this bill that requires recorders to investigate the citizenship of voters who "the county recorder has reason to believe are not citizens," by using the systematic alien verification for entitlements program was enjoined by a federal court on February 29, 2024 and again by the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals on February 25, 2025. However, recorders can investigate the citizenship of voters who have not provided documentary proof of citizenship using this system.

 

In provisions related to searching for non-citizens registered to vote, the bill creates new requirements for coordination of state and federal data to identify non-citizens for cancellation. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires recorders, monthly, to investigate the citizenship of voters who "the county recorder has reason to believe are not citizens," by using the systematic alien verification for entitlements program, to the extent practicable. Neither the bill, existing law, nor the current Election Procedures Manual (EPM) specify matching criteria to ensure a person in the database is the same person that is registered to vote. Existing law had no comparable provision.
  • Requires recorders to compare the list of "Federal only" voters to "the electronic verification of vital events system maintained by a national association for public health statistics and information systems," if accessible, to identify non-citizens. Existing law had no comparable provision, and this process is not addressed in the EPM.
  • Requires the Secretary of State to compare, monthly, the state voter registration list to the driver's license database maintained by the Department of Transportation (DOT), and notify county recorders of any individuals who are registered to vote and are not citizens. The bill does not specify what constitutes a match between entries on the DOT database and the voter roll, and does not include any provisions to address potentially stale DOT data from being used to cancel the registration of voters who naturalized before registering. Existing law had no comparable provision for routine comparison of DOT and voter data.
  • Requires the jury commissioner or jury manager to send the Secretary of State and the county recorder a summary report derived from jury questionnaire data that indicates a person is not a U.S. citizen. The report must only include the "information that is necessary to accurately identify the person in the voter registration database." While existing law did not impose this jury reporting requirement, the existing Elections Procedures Manual addresses receipt of jury information and provides guidance on confirming matches to prevent the improper cancellation of citizens' registrations.
  • Requires cancellation of a voter's registration when the county recorder receives and confirms information that a voter is not a citizen. Before the voter's registration may be canceled on this basis, the recorder must notify the voter by forwardable mail that, if they do not respond within 35 days with documentary proof of citizenship, their registration will be canceled. A postage prepaid return envelope must be included with the notice. Existing law did not require notice prior to canceling registration due to confirmed non-citizenship. The EPM, however, does require notice to a voter before canceling registration based on citizenship information from jury questionnaires.
  • Requires county recorders to refer a voter whose registration was canceled for non-citizenship to the county attorney and Attorney General for criminal investigation. Existing law had no comparable provision.
  • In provisions related to searching for voters who have moved, the bill adds new requirements for coordination of residency data from state officials. Specifically, the bill:
  • Requires the Department of Transportation to send to the Secretary, monthly, a list of people who the Department has been notified were issued a driver's license or other state-issued identification in another state. Within 10 days of receiving that information, the Secretary must send the list to county recorders. The bill does not specify which official must determine matches between the DOT list and statewide voter registration list, requiring only that recorders must "promptly" send notice by forwardable mail to the identified voters, along with a postage prepaid return form for the voter to confirm they still reside in Arizona and are not registered to vote elsewhere, or that they have moved. The notice must further explain that if the voter does not respond within 90 days, their registration will be made inactive. Existing law had no comparable provision.
  • Requires the Secretary to compare the voter registration list to the DOT database every month to identify voters who have moved, and notify the relevant county recorders. While the bill does not explicitly state what action the recorders must then take, existing law provides for standard procedures when a recorder has information that a voter may have moved.
  • Requires the jury commissioner or jury manager to send the Secretary of State and the county recorder a summary report derived from jury questionnaire data that indicates a person does not live in the county for which they were called for jury duty, and requires a streamlined cancellation process for identified voters. The jury report must include only the "information that is necessary to accurately identify the person in the voter registration database." After receiving the report, recorders must send listed individuals notice by forwardable mail, with a postage prepaid return form, requesting confirmation of the voter's residence in the county and that the person is not registered to vote elsewhere. If the individual does not respond within thirty-five days, their registration will be canceled. The bill also specifies that registration must be canceled when a recorder receives written notice of an address change by way of a form from the voter directly. Existing law required recorders to cancel registration if they received "written information from the person registered" that their address had changed, without identifying specific sources, and required following the process for inactive status prior to cancellation. The bill does not alter requirements for registration procedures related to change of address information received from the postal service.
  • In provisions related to searching for voters who have died, the bill:
  • Requires recorders, monthly, to compare the county's voter registration database to the Social Security Administration database to the extent practicable. The bill does not identify the ineligibility criteria the recorder would be investigating, but presumably, it is death. Existing law has no comparable provision. The EPM does not address using the Social Security Administration database, although it does direct recorders to be reasonably certain of a "true match" when using death data from a reliable source other than the Secretary, who gets it from the Arizona Department of Health Services.
  • Clarifies that a recorder must cancel a deceased voter's registration when they are informed and confirm that the registered person is dead. Under existing law, registration was canceled when the recorder "knows of the death of the person registered."
  • Requires the recorder, after canceling the registration, to send notice by forwardable mail informing the voter that their registration was canceled and why along with instructions on how to register if the person is qualified.
  • The bill also:
  • Requires the Secretary of State to report to the Legislature, every quarter, the following:
    • The number of deaths reported to the Secretary by the Department of Health Services, the number of notices the Secretary sent to recorders based on that data, and the number of registrations canceled as a result.
    • The number of people reported to the Secretary as having received out-of-state licenses or IDs, to recorders based on that data, and the number of registrations made inactive and the number canceled as a result.
    • The number of people who stated on a jury questionnaire that they are not citizens, the number of notices sent based on that data, and the number of registrations canceled as a result.
    • The number of people who stated on a jury questionnaire that they do not live in the county, the number of notices sent based on that data, and the number of registrations canceled as a result.
    • The number of inactive registrations canceled under the standard process.
  • Revises the state voter registration form to include a statement that if the registrant permanently moves to another state, the registrant's voter registration will be canceled.

Last Updated February 28, 2025

This bill, as introduced on January 12, 2022, would require the Auditor General to "conduct systems and procedures audits of offices conducting the general election." The bill does not describe the requirement further but would appropriate $800,000 for the activity.

Under existing law, the Auditor General's activities have a financial focus, and it already has the authority to "Perform procedural reviews for all state agencies at times determined by the auditor general. In addition, existing law requires the Auditor General to "prepare an audit plan for approval by the [Joint Legislative Audit] committee and report to the committee the results of each audit and investigation and other reviews conducted by the auditor general." Thus the Joint Legislative Audit Committee would have the power to shape the design of the review.

This bill, as introduced on January 12, 2022, would sharply limit the availability of early voting by allowing it only for primaries and general elections, and only on the weekend and Monday immediately before Election Day. Under existing law, early voting is available for all elections, and begins 27 days before Election Day. Weekend availability is optional, except that early voting is not available on the weekend or Monday before Election Day except at an "emergency" vote center, which voters must attest to having an emergency to use.

Last Updated January 16, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 13, 2022, would sharply expand the automatic restoration of voting rights of people who had been disenfranchised for a felony conviction. Specifically, the bill would automatically restore all returning citizens' voting rights when they complete probation or are finally discharged from incarceration. The bill would also require the judge, at sentencing, to inform defendants of the timing of automatic restoration.

Under existing law, only people who have no prior felonies and who have paid restitution in full, in addition to completing probation or being finally discharged from incarceration are entitled to automatic restoration. Everyone else must apply, and the restoration is a discretionary decision of a judge. In addition, people who are not eligible for automatic restoration and who have been finally discharged from incarceration must wait two years before applying. People who are not eligible for automatic restoration but complete probation do not need to wait to apply. Finally, existing law already requires the sentencing judge to inform the defendant of their right to the restoration of civil rights, however the requirement is imposed in a different section of law than the bill amends.

Last updated January 16, 2022.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 13. 2022, would make it easier for election officials to site polling places in schools and fire stations by eliminating reasons schools can refuse to host them, while requiring election officials to prioritize using public schools and any other school that receives state or local funding as a polling place and requiring school and fire district boards to work with election officials to choose polling place locations.

Under existing law, schools are not similarly prioritized, the boards do not have an affirmative duty to coordinate with election officials, and schools may refuse to host polling places by stating they do not have space or because hosting would jeopardize the safety or welfare of their children.

Last updated January 14, 2022.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 13, 2022, would end emergency voting between 5 p.m. on the Friday before the election and 5 p.m. on the Monday before the election. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Repeal counties' ability to designate emergency vote centers in that time frame. Current law allows counties to offer these vote centers, and allows people to cast ballots at them, if the voter attests to having an emergency before receiving a ballot.

  • Repeal the ability of a person who becomes ill, hospitalized, or disabled after 5 p.m. on the Friday before the election to request a ballot be brought to them. Current law allows such requests and requires county recorders to honor them when possible.

Last Updated January 16, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill was amended on March 21, 2022, to replace all of its provisions with new ones. As amended, it would completely overhaul how elections are conducted in Arizona. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Eliminate in-person early voting. Under existing law, voters may begin to vote early in person when ballots are mailed to mail voters.
  • Require voters to have an excuse to vote by mail. Under existing law, any voter may choose to vote by mail. The bill would authorize mail voting if:
    • the voter expects to be outside this state at the time of the election
    • the voter is physically unable to go to the polls because the voter is hospitalized or in a nursing home.
    • the voter has a visual impairment.
    • the voter is an absent uniformed services voter or overseas voter or their spouse or household member. Separately, the bill would restrict absentee voting during presidential primaries to these UOCAVA voters.
  • Eliminate the Active Early Voting List. Under existing law, voters may join this list and be mailed a ballot for every election.
  • Shift election authority:
    • away from county recorders and give it to the county board of supervisors. Under the bill, the recorder would only be responsible only for providing an adequate number and type of ballots, pens, tables, and other equipment as necessary for the various polling places located in precincts as determined by the number of registered voters in the precincts. Existing law gives recorders substantially more authority, including over early voting.
    • away from the Secretary of State, Governor, and Attorney General, and give it to the Legislature by repealing the Elections Procedures Manual. Under existing law, the Secretary of State issues the manual with the approval of the Governor and Attorney General to ensure uniform practices statewide.
  • Make several changes relating to polling places. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Prohibit the board of supervisors, county recorder, and officer in charge of elections from requiring that a voter, a board worker, or any other person wear a facial mask at a polling place or other voting or tabulating location or be vaccinated against or tested for a virus as a condition of entering a polling place or other voting or tabulating location.
    • Limit the number of voters who may be assigned to an election precinct when it is established to 1,500 registered voters, and require an adequate number of polling places in each precinct. Under existing law, no cap is imposed on precincts, and an adequate number of polling places overall must be established, although not necessarily in each precinct.
    • Prohibit the board of supervisors from changing a polling place unless voters are given notice by mail at least two years in advance. Existing law does not require similar notice
    • Require public schools to make space available for polling places upon the counties' request and require counties to prioritize using public schools and government offices for polling places. Under existing law, schools may refuse to open polling places because they lack space or their students would be endangered.
    • Prohibit using emergency polling places, which allow electioneering to be restricted, unless an Act of God renders it necessary. Under existing law, places can be designated emergency polling places for other reasons.
    • Repeal a provision allowing polling place consolidation if the number of people who are on the active early voting list indicates that fewer polling places are needed. Since the bill repeals that list, that consolidation provision is also repealed.
    • Allow representatives from political parties in polling places and the 75-foot no-electioneering zone even if the party has no candidates on the ballot.
  • Prohibit the use of countywide vote centers in addition to or instead of polling places. Under existing law, the board of supervisors may choose to authorize them.
  • Eliminate emergency vote centers. Under existing law, counties may open these centers to serve voters who, because of a reason that arose after the end of early voting and before 5 p.m. on the day before the election, cannot vote on Election Day.
  • Make changes related to election equipment and ballot counting. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Restrict electronic voting machine use to disabled voters who need them.
    • Prohibit using ballot tabulators for all ballots except absentee ballots, instead requiring all other ballots to be counted by hand. Notwithstanding this provision, other parts of the bill appear to require all ballots to be counted by hand.
    • Require ballots to be sorted by precinct before and after counting.
    • Repeal the existing hand count audit.
    • Repeal a recently enacted requirement that ballot paper has at least three of a list of anti-fraud measures and replacement with a general requirement that ballot paper for primaries and general elections include a hologram, an identifiable sequence marking, or another similar system for preventing fraud, and that allows a voter to receive a uniquely marked or numbered ballot.

  • Increase the severity of the felony that currently prohibits giving voters a mail ballot unless they applied for it while editing the crime so that it would read "A voter who requests a onetime absentee ballot pursuant to this section or for an election conducted pursuant to section 16-409 or article 8.1 of this chapter, a county recorder, city or town clerk or other election officer may not deliver or mail an absentee ballot to a person who has not requested an absentee ballot for that election."

    In addition to these changes, the bill would mandate certain principles for all primary and general elections, directing the legislative council staff to propose conforming legislation. Those principles would be:


  • A voter may not receive or vote a ballot unless the voter has presented valid state-issued identification.
  • Except for absentee ballots, all voting shall occur on Election Day, in person, by the voter at the voter's election precinct polling place.

  • All ballots shall be counted by hand and canvassed and the returns made within twenty-four hours after the polls are closed.

    All of these provisions are new, having replaced the previous version of the bill entirely. The previous version of the bill would have changed certain rules relating to poll watchers, although it would not change their powers, duties, or who appoints them. Specifically, the bill would have:


  • Required the county chairman of each party to appoint a person for each precinct who would act as a challenger for that party. Under existing law, the county chairman may, but not must, appoint challengers for each precinct.
  • Limited the number of challengers per party to one per polling place. Existing law allows the parties to agree to appoint more.
  • Required the challengers to remain in the polling place until completion of the tabulation of votes in the polling place and transmittal or delivery of those results to the county recorder. Existing law does not have a parallel requirement.

  • Allowed election processes to continue even if a required challenger is absent.

Last Updated March 23, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 13, 2022, would narrow an existing election crime by allowing voters to take selfies with their ballots, and allowing anyone within the 75-foot zone in which electioneering is prohibited to photograph election workers. Although the crime continues to prohibit photographing other voters, that prohibition will be hard to enforce in light of the ability to photograph election workers, as photographs of election workers could easily include voters in the background. In addition, allowing partisan poll watchers to photograph election workers could be intimidating.

This bill, as amended May 23, 2022, would give county recorders a limited veto of election litigation settlements by the Secretary of State, and would enable county recorders to such litigation as a party. The bill does not address litigation settlements by the Attorney General. Existing law has no equivalent provisions. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Prohibit the Secretary of State from settling election litigation that materially affects county recorders without consulting them, and if a recorder demonstrates or otherwise provides evidence that the settlement would be impractical or difficult, the settlement cannot be approved without the consent of three-fourths of the county recorders.   • Allow country recorders to join election litigation with the characteristics that would enable them to veto settlement. The bill does not address how this provision would change or expand counties' ability to join in election litigation more generally.

This bill, as amended on April 18, 2022, would give the legislature a role in an election process currently overseen by the Secretary of State. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Allow the legislature to send experts in electronic voting systems and procedures and electronic voting system security to field check and review electronic voting systems and recommend needed statutory and procedural changes. These people would be in addition to those that existing law requires the Secretary of State to use. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have required the legislature to send a second set of electronic voting system experts.
  • Provide that these experts can recommend changes to the Elections Procedures Manual as well as "statutory and procedural changes". This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require the Elections Procedures Manual to provide for transparency and election security to the maximum extent allowed by law, and emphasize that a conflict between statutes and the Elections and Procedures Manual is resolved in favor of the statutes. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.

  • Require the Secretary of State to report to the Speaker of the House of Representatives and President of the Senate on any recommended statutory and procedural changes to electronic voting systems and procedures and electronic voting system security.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 13, 2022, would give the Auditor General $500,000 to review the voter registration and mail voting related processes at the state and local level, and would impose new reporting requirements on the Secretary of State and county recorders relating to voter registration events. Specifically, in addition to making the appropriation, the bill would:

  • Require the Auditor General to review the processes and compliance with statutory requirements for maintaining the statewide voter registration database, county early voting lists and the county voter registration databases, including the cancellation of registrations. Under existing law, the Auditor General focuses on finances, not election law. In addition, existing law gives the Legislative Audit Committee authority to shape the Auditor General's audits.
  • Require the Secretary of State and county recorders to notify the auditor general of their total expenditures for voter registration programs and events, and shall provide a description of those programs and events, including any political party affiliation.
  • Require the Secretary of State and the county recorders to specify their attendance at these programs, events and outreach activities and whether they used any third-party data in conducting these programs, events and activities.

  • Require the Auditor General to submit a report on its findings to the President of the Senate and the Speaker of the House of Representatives, and give a copy to the Secretary of State.

Last Updated January 16, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 13, 2022, would create both same day registration and automatic voter registration. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create same day registration by:
    • Allowing people to register to vote during the 28 days before an election and on Election Day. People who register during that window would be required to have lived in the county and precinct in which they are registering for at least 29 days. Under existing law, registration ends 29 days before an election, and a person must have resided in the state for at least 29 days prior to registration.
    • Allowing a person registered within the 28 days before an election to vote a provisional ballot, whether during early voting or on Election Day, except that no one who registers in that window may vote in a partisan primary. The new registrant would not be entitled to vote a regular ballot until an election that occurs at least 29 days after the election for which they registered.
    • Expressly providing that on Election Day, registration can happen at the polling place. A person registering then would be required to prove residency. The bill does not state that registration may happen at an early voting site. However, early voting must be available somewhere beginning 27 days before the election, whether at the recorder's office or elsewhere, and if at the recorder's office, registration services would be simultaneously available.
  • Create automatic voter registration at the DMV by:
    • Providing that a person who completes an application for a driver's license, a non-operator's license, or is renewing or updating either, and is otherwise qualified to vote, will have an application for voter registration automatically transmitted to the county recorder.
    • Requiring the county recorder, upon receipt of the applicant's information, to send the person a notice explaining how to opt out of voter registration. If the person does not opt out within 21 days, they would be registered to vote.
    • Requiring the director of the department of transportation and the Secretary of State, in consultation with the county recorders, to issue rules to effectuate automatic voter registration.
    • Providing that an ineligible voter who is unknowingly registered through this process has not committed false registration or false swearing.

Last Updated September 4, 2025

This bill, as introduced on January 13, 2022, would allow voters who received a mail ballot to bring their completed, sealed ballot to their Election Day voting location, show the ID necessary to vote in person, and then remove their ballot from the envelope and feed it into the tabulator. Doing this would prevent their ballot from being disqualified on the basis that their signature on the ballot envelope was missing or did not match their signature on record.

Last Updated January 14, 2021

This bill, as introduced on January 13, 2022, would give the Legislature a role in choosing the President by changing how Arizona chooses presidential electors. Specifically, the bill would provide that each Congressional district would choose one elector based on the popular vote in that district, and the Legislature, voting as a whole, would choose two more. If the Legislature's vote was a tie, each competing candidate would get one elector.

Last updated January 14, 2022.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 13, 2022, is only partially drafted. As written, it creates a felony to punish election officials who verify signatures on mail ballot envelopes without following "a _____ factor signature verification process as prescribed by the secretary of state's instructions and procedures manual". The current version of the Secretary of State's Elections Procedures Manual does not prescribe a specific signature verification process. Instead it directs election officials to compare the ballot envelope signature to the various signatures the voter has on file, and then instructs elections officials on the actions they should take if they are, or are not, satisfied that the ballot envelope signature matches.

Last Updated January 16, 2022

This bill, as enacted on March 30, 2022, makes registering to vote substantially more onerous by requiring applicants to provide proof of their location of residence and by expanding Arizona's proof of citizenship requirements. The bill also limits access for "federal-only" voters who have not provided documentation of citizenship proof of citizenship by prohibiting voting in presidential elections and voting by mail for other federal races. In addition, the bill requires the Attorney General and county recorders to investigate certain applicants' citizenship status, requires prosecution of non-citizen registered voters, and imposes criminal liability on recorders who fail to carry out required investigations.

 

Note: The provision of this bill requiring applicants to list their birthplace as a prerequisite to registering to vote was enjoined by a federal court on February 29, 2024 and struck down by the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals on February 25, 2025. Additionally, the provision of this bill that requires voters who use a federal form to provide proof of citizenship when voting for president or by mail was struck down by the U.S. Supreme Court on August 22, 2024 and by the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals on February 25, 2025.

 

Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires individuals applying to register to vote to prove their "location of residence." Documentation may include, but is not expressly limited to, a valid Arizona driver's license or state ID number, or any form of photo ID accepted to vote in person. Existing law had no documentation requirement for residency. Note that the bill leaves in place provisions that permit voter registration for qualified individuals who do not reside at a "fixed, permanent, or private structure," but does not clearly address how such applicants can meet the new proof of residency requirement.
  • Creates a new felony offense for election officials knowingly failing to reject any registration application, other than one made by the federal form, that lacks documentary proof of citizenship.
  • Requires county recorders to reject registration applications, other than those made by the federal U.S. Election Assistance Commission form, if they are not accompanied by documentary proof of citizenship, and to notify applicants of rejection on this ground. Under existing law (as modified following litigation in 2013), applicants who did not provide citizenship documentation with their state application form, but were otherwise qualified, were designated to receive a federal-only ballot for congressional and presidential races. Existing law also required notice of missing or incomplete applications only with regard to the voter's name, date of birth, residence, or signature.
  • Requires recorders who receive a registration application on the federal form that is not accompanied by documentary proof of citizenship to investigate the applicant's citizenship status. If the recorder confirms U.S. citizenship and the applicant is otherwise eligible, the recorder registers the person as a full ballot voter. If the recorder confirms the applicant is not a U.S. citizen, the recorder must reject the application, notify the applicant, and forward the application to the county attorney and attorney general for investigation. If the recorder is unable to confirm the applicant's citizenship status, they must notify the applicant that they will not be allowed to vote by mail in any election, or for president by any voting method until they provide such documentary proof. Existing law had no provisions regarding verification of citizenship for applicants using the federal registration form. As noted above, applicants who did not provide documentation were designated for federal-only ballots, which included both presidential and congressional races.
  • Requires recorders to use "all available resources" to investigate applicants' citizenship including certain state and federal databases, provided the county has access to them. The named databases are:
    • the Department of Transportation database of Arizona driver licenses and IDs
    • the Social Security Administration databases
    • the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services systematic alien verification for entitlements program, if practicable
    • a national association for public health statistics and information systems' electronic verification of vital events system
    • any other state, city, town, county, or federal database and any other database relating to voter registration to which the county recorder or officer in charge of elections has access, including an Electronic Registration Information Center database
  • Requires recorders to document their efforts to investigate citizenship.
  • Creates a new felony offense for a recorder failing to attempt verification of citizenship for federal form applicants and knowingly registering an applicant who is later determined to be a non-citizen.
  • Restricts voting access for federal-only voters by prohibiting individuals, other than UOCAVA voters, who have registered without providing documentary proof of citizenship from voting in presidential elections and voting by mail. Under existing law, federal-only voters were permitted to vote in presidential elections and vote by mail in federal elections.
  • Requires the Attorney General to investigate the citizenship of all currently registered voters who did not provide documentary proof of their citizenship, prosecute any non-citizens discovered, and report to the Legislature. Specifically:
    • The Secretary of State and county recorders must give the Attorney General a list of federal-only voters and copies of their registration forms by October 31, 2022.
    • The Attorney General must then use "all available resources" to investigate citizenship, at a minimum using the same databases identified for county recorder use. The Secretary of State is required to give the Attorney General access to the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements Program.
    • Once identified, the Attorney General must prosecute any non-citizen registrants.
    • By March 31, 2023, the Attorney General must report to the Secretary of State, the Senate President, and the Speaker of the House on all findings relating to the citizenship status of federal-only voters.
  • Requires voter registration applicants to state their place of birth, in addition to the date. Note: The bill does not amend provisions concerning the voter registration form to require this information.
  • Makes conforming changes to other parts of the election code.

Previous versions of the bill included a provision that was amended out on February 24, 2022, that would have required recorders to reject all applications that did not include documentary proof of citizenship. This provision would have effectively prevented any further registration of federal-only voters, capping the list to those currently on it.

 

NOTE: This law takes effect on December 31, 2022, per separately enacted legislation, SB 1638, which was signed into law on April 22, 2022.

 

Last Updated February 28, 2025

This bill, as amended on February 22, 2022, would require the Secretary of State and each county recorder to post on their respective public websites a list of each event they attend and provide voter registration services. Each event would be posted on the public website within twenty-four hours after their or their staff's attendance. The event listing would include, at a minimum, the location, title of the event, and all organizations affiliated with the event. A similar provision was enacted last year but invalidated by the Arizona Supreme Court because of how it was enacted, not the merits of the provision.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 13, 2022, would eliminate in-person early voting, repeal the active early voter list, require an excuse to vote by mail, require all ballots to be counted by hand. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Eliminate in-person early voting. Under existing law, in-person early voting is available beginning 27 days before Election Day.
  • Repeal the active early voting list. This is a list of people who have requested to vote by mail in every election, keep their address up to date and vote at least once every four years.
  • Make related changes, specifically:
    • Facilitating polling place consolidation by eliminating a requirement that the county board of supervisors make a specific finding that the number of voters on the active early voting list is substantially likely to reduce the number of voters using one or more specific polling places for that election before consolidating polling places for that election.
    • Requiring a sample ballot be sent to all voters. Under existing law, people on the list to receive a mail ballot are not sent sample ballots.
  • Require an excuse to vote by mail. Specifically, the voter must expect to be away from their precinct on Election Day, be unable to attend the polls because of a tenet of their religion, or be a UOCAVA voter. Under existing law, anyone can vote by mail, and most do.
  • Allow mail ballots to be challenged on the grounds that the voter fraudulently claimed eligibility
  • Repeal provisions of code expressly authorizing political committees and other organizations to distribute mail ballot applications.
  • Require all ballots be counted by hand, prohibiting the use of electronic tabulators except by disabled voters who need them. Ballots would be organized and segregated by precinct, both before and after counting.
  • Repeal all of the code provisions relating to hand count audits.
  • Repeal the code provisions providing for ballot duplication so that ballots may be read by tabulators.

  • Eliminate the requirement that an electronic voting machine allow the voter to vote on ballot propositions.

Last Updated January 26, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 13, 2022, would eliminate the active early voting list, require voters who wish to vote by mail to request a ballot for each election, create a new form of ID and require it to vote in person, require documentary proof of citizenship to obtain that ID, and prohibit the use of unmonitored drop boxes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • State that notwithstanding any other provision of law, voters who wish to vote by mail must apply for a ballot every election. Under existing law, voters may request to be on the active early voting list, which entitles them to a mail ballot for every election. Although the bill does not repeal the section of code creating the active early voter list or references to it throughout the code, this provision would render it ineffective.
  • Require voters to return their own mail ballots, except in special district mail ballot elections, by making it a felony for anyone else to return it. Under existing law, a voter may give their ballot to a family member, a household member, or a caregiver to return.
  • Prohibit unmonitored drop boxes.
  • Create a new form of ID, called a voter identification card. The county recorder would be required to issue this card to all registered voters who prove citizenship and provide two documents that validate their Arizona residency. To prove citizenship, the voter could use a U.S. birth certificate, a current U.S. passport, or U.S. naturalization papers.
  • Require in-person voters to show their voter identification card and verify they are the person named on it with any two of:
    • their signature
    • their fingerprint
    • an unique security code that issued to them. Existing law requires voters to show either a photo ID or two other forms of identification. The bill does not provide for voting locations to have a way to validate fingerprints, nor does the bill provide a process for issuing voters an unique security code. Nonetheless the bill does have a provision requiring the legislative council staff to prepare conforming legislation for consideration in the next legislative session.

Last Updated October 3, 2025

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 21, 2022, would radically overhaul Arizona's election laws, give the Legislature the right to invalidate the results of any election, and give the Legislature the authority to audit any election. Beyond the provisions relating to increasing the Legislature's power, the bill would eliminate early voting, end no-excuse mail voting, shift election authority from the County Recorder to the county Board of Supervisors, eliminate vote centers and make other election day voting site changes, prohibits a mask, vaccine, or testing mandate for voters, election workers, or other election participants at voting and tabulating locations, require all ballots be counted by hand and all results be completed within 24 hours of the polls closing. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the Legislature to review the results of each regular primary and general election, and decide to accept or reject the election results. if the legislature accepts the election results, the election canvass and related certifications and proclamations may proceed as otherwise provided by law. If the Legislature rejects the election results, any qualified voter could sue for a new election.
  • Allow the Legislature to audit election results for any regular primary or general election. The bill does not provide any information about how it would audit an election.
  • Eliminate early voting. Under existing law, in-person early voting begins 27 days before Election Day, which is also the day ballots begin to be mailed to those who have requested them.
  • Eliminate counties' ability to open vote centers for emergency voting in on the weekend and day immediately before Election Day. Under existing law, counties may open such centers between Friday 5 p.m. and Monday 5 p.m., and to use them, voters must sign a document attesting they have a reason that they must vote in the window.
  • Require a voter have an excuse to vote by mail and eliminate a voter's ability to choose to receive a mail ballot for every election, instead requiring the voter to apply for a mail ballot for each election. Under existing law, voters may request a mail ballot for one, or for all, elections going forward, and voters need not have an excuse to choose to vote by mail. Under the bill, the allowable excuses would be:
    • The voter expects to be out of state on Election Day.
    • The voter is hospitalized or in a nursing home.
    • The voter has a visual impairment.
    • The voter is an absent uniformed services voter or overseas voter as defined in federal law, or the spouse or household member of such a person.
  • Increase the criminal penalty for mailing a ballot to a voter who has not applied for one from a class 5 felony to a class 2 felony.
  • Shift election authority from the County Recorder to the county Board of Supervisors, so that the Recorder would supply ballots and other equipment, and the Board would "perform or supervise all other election related duties." Under existing law, the Recorder has broad authority to administer elections, and the Board has a significant role as well.
  • Shift election authority away from the Secretary of State by eliminating the Elections Procedures Manual, which is a biennial regulatory document that is drafted by the Secretary of State and reviewed and approved by the Governor and the Attorney General. After such approval, the manual has the force of law. The bill does not repeal the Secretary's general rule making authority.
  • Change the availability of in person voting on Election Day by:
    • Eliminating counties' ability to offer vote centers, either in addition to or instead of precincts.
    • Limiting precincts to no more than 1,500 voters, as of the day the precinct is drawn, and requiring an adequate number of polling places in each precinct.
    • Prohibiting the Board of Supervisors from changing a polling place "unless the voters in that precinct are notified by mail at least two years in advance."
    • Prioritizing using schools and government offices as polling places. As part of prioritizing schools, the bill eliminates a principal's ability to refuse to make school space available for a polling place on the grounds that space is not available or the safety or welfare of the children would be jeopardized.
    • Allowing emergency voting locations only if an act of God forces the change from an existing polling place.
    • Limiting the use of electronic voting machines and tabulators to people with disabilities.
    • Requiring paper ballots for all other voters, and requiring hand tabulation of ballots.
    • Prohibiting the Board or the Recorder or any other officer in charge of elections from requiring that a voter, election board worker or any other person wear a face mask, be vaccinated against, or be tested for a virus as a condition of of entering a polling place or other voting or tabulating location.

  • Change ballot counting by requiring all ballots be sorted by precinct, before and after counting, and by counting all ballots by hand. In conjunction with the mandatory all-balot hand count, the bill repeals the hand count audit.

This bill, as amended on May 23, 2022, would change the conditions under which an emergency voting site may be designated, and under which electioneering can be restricted at an early voting site or an election day polling place.

The bill would allow a county to open and site an emergency vote center only if needed to respond to war, civil unrest, or a natural disaster that makes it likely that large numbers of voters will be substantially impaired in their ability to vote on Election Day. Under existing law, emergency vote centers can be opened to serve voters who attest that, due to a change in their situation that arose after 5 p.m. on the Friday before Election Day and before 5 p.m. on the Monday before Election Day, they cannot vote on Election Day and must use the emergency vote center.

The bill would also limit counties' ability to restrict electioneering at voting locations, allowing restrictions in the area that electioneering is normally allowed only if the county recorder has exhausted all other options to site the voting location and the only available, appropriate location requires a ban on electioneering.

One provision was amended out of this version of the bill. It would have repealed counties' existing authority to use countywide vote centers in addition to, or instead of, precinct polling places.

Last updated May 24, 2022.

Governor Doug Ducey vetoed this bill on May 27, 2022. The bill would have required the Secretary of State and county recorders to use new databases and do new, substantial, open-ended investigations to identify and remove ineligible voters from the registration list. The bill focused on identifying non-citizens, deceased people, and people who had moved out of state.

Importantly, the bill did not include matching criteria or a process to confirm that a person who is identified as a non-citizen, deceased, or moved is the same person as the registered voter. The current Elections Procedures Manual, which has the force of law and went into effect in 2019, specifies such criteria and processes for certain data sets, but not every situation the bill addressed.

Specifically, the bill would have changed the list maintenance data sources and processes by:

  • Requiring recorders, monthly, to compare voters in their counties that "the county recorder has reason to believe are not United States citizens" with the systematic alien verification for entitlements program to verify their citizenship status, to the extent practicable. The bill did not indicate what constitutes a "reason to believe" a voter is not a citizen. Nor did the bill, existing law, or the Election Procedures Manual specify how data from this system should be used to ensure a person in the database is the same person that is registered to vote. Existing law has no comparable provision.
  • Requiring recorders to compare voters who have not provided documentary proof of citizenship, who are known as "Federal only" voters, to "the electronic verification of vital events system maintained by a national association for public health statistics and information systems", if accessible. This process has no comparable provision in existing law and is not addressed in the Manual.
  • Requiring the jury commissioner or jury manager to send the Secretary of State and the county recorder a summary report derived from jury questionnaire data that indicates a person is not a U.S. citizen or a county resident. The report would include only the "information that is necessary to accurately identify the person in the voter registration database. Existing law does not impose this requirement. Nonetheless, recorders do receive this jury information, and the Elections Procedures Manual addresses how they should confirm a match between the person and the voter to prevent the cancellation of citizens' registrations.
  • Requiring recorders to "regularly review relevant city, town, county, state, and federal databases" to which the recorder has access to ensure that registered voters are eligible to vote. This blanket open-ended duty does not provide guidance that enables recorders to determine if they are in compliance with it. Existing law has no comparable provision and nothing similar is addressed in the Manual. Under existing law, an election official who knowingly fails or refuses to perform a duty in the manner prescribed by law commits a misdemeanor.
  • Requiring the Secretary of State to compare, monthly, the state voter registration list to the driver's license database maintained by the Department of Transportation (DOT), searching for voters who have moved or have been identified as non-citizens. The Secretary would have then notified the appropriate recorder of such voters in their counties. Existing law does not require a similar process for the Secretary. Instead, the Secretary transmits data about voters who have potentially moved, but investigating matches is left to the recorders, who follow an address confirmation process specified by federal and state law.
  • Requiring the Department of Transportation to send to the Secretary, monthly, a list of people issued a driver's license or other state-issued identification in another state, to the extent the Department has been informed of them. Within 10 days of receiving that information, the Secretary would have sent the county recorders a list of voters in their counties who moved out of state. Presumably the duty to match the list of people who moved to the statewide voter registration list would have been imposed on the Secretary. Existing law has no comparable provision.

  • Requiring recorders, monthly, to compare the county's voter registration database to the Social Security Administration database to the extent practicable. The bill did not identify the ineligibility criteria the recorder would be investigating, but presumably, it is death. Existing law has no comparable provision. The Manual does not address using the Social Security Administration database, although it does direct recorders to be reasonably certain of a "true match" when using death data from a reliable source other than the Secretary, who gets it from the Arizona Department of Health Services.

    The bill would have expanded the list of reasons a voter's registration must be canceled and provided a pre-cancelation notice to voters. Specifically, the bill would have:

  • Provided for cancellation when the county recorder receives and confirms information that a voter is not a citizen. Under existing law, registrations are canceled for all grounds of ineligibility, including non-citizenship, but the statutes do not specifically name non-citizenship as a basis for cancellation.
  • Referred a voter whose registration was canceled for non-citizenship to the county attorney and Attorney General for criminal investigation. Existing law has no comparable provision.
  • Provided for cancellation when the recorder receives and confirms information that the voter has been issued a driver's license or state ID by another state. Existing law allows cancellation when a voter has been confirmed as moving out of state but does not specifically address a person being issued an out-of-state ID.
  • Provided for cancellation on any otherwise unspecified grounds of ineligibility. Existing law does not have a similar catchall provision, however, no one is allowed to be registered to vote if they are not eligible.
  • Clarified that cancelation for death occurs when the recorder "is informed and confirms that the person registered is dead." Under existing law, the recorder cancels the registration when the recorder "knows of the death of the person registered."
  • Required recorders to send pre-cancellation notice to voters whose registrations had been identified for cancellation based on their alleged non-citizenship, and given the voters 90 days to respond with documentary proof of their citizenship. The Election Procedures Manual requires pre-cancellation notice when a recorder believes a non-citizen is registered based on juror questionnaires.
  • Required recorders to send pre-cancellation notice to a person who has been identified as having moved out of state, to both their registration address and the out-of-state address the person is believed to have moved to. The person would have had 90 days to respond and prevent cancellation. Under existing law, when a county recorder believes someone has moved from their registration address, they begin an address confirmation process that involves forwardable mail.
  • Required recorders to send pre-cancellation notice to a person whose registration the recorder intends to cancel under the catchall ineligible provision. The person would have had 90 days to respond and prevent cancellation. Existing law has no comparable provision.

  • Require the Secretary to report to the Legislature, on a quarterly basis, the number of deaths reported to the Secretary by the Department of Health Services and the number of resulting registration cancellation notices sent by the Secretary to county recorders. Existing law does not have a similar requirement.

    Last updated May 31, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on February 3, 2022, would create same day registration during early voting and on Election Day, provided the person is qualified, eligible, has resided in their precinct at least 29 days before Election Day, completes the voter registration form, and the election is not a partisan primary. Such voters would complete provisional ballots.

On Election Day, this service would be available at polling places. On Election Day, registering voters would be required to prove residence as well as meet the other criteria. Proof of residency is not defined, however, voters in Arizona must show ID to vote, and it is possible that some or all of those ID types would suffice. The bill also does not specify whether registration services would be available at all early voting locations, however, people would be allowed to register during the 28 days preceding Election Day and be eligible to vote in the election.

Last updated February 6, 2022.

This bill, as enacted on May 27, 2022, no longer addresses areas of election law that Voting Rights Lab tracks. A previous version of the bill would have created a new type of audit, called an "election integrity audit" that would review myriad election processes, in addition to vote totals. The Auditor General would have been required to conduct one each election cycle in four counties, with the cooperation of state and local officials, and the bill would have created new criminal offenses to enforce their cooperation. The previous version of the bill would have also created reporting and compliance procedures based on the results of the "election integrity audits."

Last Updated June 27, 2022

This bill, as amended on June 23, 2022, would expand the use and public sharing of voter data derived from voter registration records, change the rules for being removed from the list of voters who get a ballot mailed to them automatically, improve the transparency and administration of the existing hand count audit and other ballot processes, and expand the locations challengers are allowed.

The bill would change the availability and use of voter registration record information by:

  • Allowing precinct registers and other lists or information derived from voter registration forms to be used for any noncommercial use. Under existing law, such information may be used only for purposes relating to a political or political party activity, a political campaign or an election, for revising election district boundaries, or for any other purpose specifically authorized by law.

  • Requiring the county recorder, Secretary of State, and other officers in charge of elections to provide for electronic access to voter registration information. The person requesting the information would be required to establish an electronic profile with the information provider and attest to the noncommercial use. Existing law does not require electronic access to voter registration information.

    The bill would allow a voter to be removed from the active early voters list by making a verbal request and sufficiently identifying themselves. Under existing law, a voter must make the request in writing.

    The bill would make changes to the existing ballot review, hand count audit procedure, and central counting location procedures that would improve transparency and integrity, and facilitate the ability of the parties to ensure the audit happens. Specifically, the bill would:


  • Require a voter's political party to be redacted during the signature match process to validate early ballots.
  • Improve transparency by:
    • Requiring the officer in charge of the elections to publish procedures for the existing hand count audit, including times and locations, on their website no later than the Tuesday before Election Day.
    • Requiring counties to make the results of the hand count audit available on the county's website, as well as the Secretary of State's website. Under existing law, only the Secretary is required to publicly post the results.
    • Requiring live video recording of the hand count audit on the same terms existing law requires of central count procedures.
    • Allowing appointed observers to witness electronic vote adjudication activities.
  • Change the hand count audit by:
    • Making it more likely to occur by increasing the likelihood that political parties will appoint sufficient people. The bill would allow a tiering of appointment power so that if the party's county chair failed to appoint a sufficient number, the state party chair could appoint people, and if needed, then the legislative district party chair could appoint people. If still not enough people had been appointed by 9 a.m. on the Thursday before the election, the election official would give the county chairs a list of eligible people offered by any party in the state by 5 p.m. on the Friday before the election. Under existing law, the hand count can occur if there are at least two people appointed by each political party for each precinct to be audited, and these people must be appointed by the county party chair.
  • Reducing bipartisanship by requiring counties to ensure when practicable that not more than 75% of the people conducting the hand audit are members of the same political party, except if a recognized party failed to provide sufficient participants by 9 am the day after the election, the count could proceed without regard to the affiliation of the participants. The count would not proceed unless a sufficient number of appointed people arrive and they were appointed by 5 pm on the Thursday after the election. Under existing law, the hand count cannot proceed if more than 75% of participants belong to one party.

  • Improving the integrity of the audit by requiring all proceedings to be under the direction of the board of supervisors or other officer in charge of the elections, and by explicitly allowing the same observers as are allowed at the counting center.

    The bill would expand what election activity lawfully appointed challengers may witness, and who within a political party may appoint them. Specifically:


  • In addition to being allowed in polling places, challengers would be allowed in voting centers and locations at which electronic processing of ballots occurs. If the county chairperson of a political party did not appoint challengers, the state party chair could, and if they did not, the legislative district chairperson could.

  • Finally, the county chairman of each party, by written appointment addressed to the county officer in charge of elections, would be allowed to appoint someone to observe the proceedings at a third-party vendor that processes returned affidavit envelopes on behalf of a county. The county would forward that information to the vendor. If more than one county contracts with the same vendor, or if the county party chairman does not appoint a party representative, the state party chairman would be allowed to make the designation.

    A provision was amended out of the bill on March 21, 2022. It would have allowed the public to access and post information from voter records that existing law keeps confidential, namely a voter's month and day of birth, father's name and/or mother's maiden name, state or country of birth, signature, and email address.

    The June 23, 2022 amendments removed provisions that would have allowed people to post voter registration records on the internet and which would have correspondingly narrowed a felony related to exposing voter registration information.

Last Updated July 11, 2022

This bill, as introduced on February 7, 2022, would make substantial changes throughout the election code. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Eliminate early voting. Under existing law, in person early voting begins 27 days before Election Day, the same day early ballots are mailed to voters.
  • Require a voter have an excuse to choose to vote by mail. Under existing law, voters do not need to justify their choice to vote by mail. The bill would require a voter attest to having one of these excuses:
    • the voter expects to be outside this state at the time of the election.
    • the voter is physically unable to go to the polls because the voter is hospitalized or in a nursing home.
    • the voter has a visual impairment.
    • the voter is an absent uniformed services voter or overseas voter as defined in federal law, or their spouse or household member.
  • Eliminate the active early voting list. Under existing law a voter can join the list when they apply for a mail ballot, and then continue to receive mail ballots without further application so long as they keep their address current and vote at least once every four years.
  • Eliminate counties' ability to use vote centers, including emergency voting centers, requiring all in-precinct voting be done at precinct polling places. Existing law allows vote centers in addition to, or instead of, polling places, and allows counties to offer vote centers for people who cannot vote on Election Day for a reason that arises after the end of early voting. 
  • Impose new limits on precincts and polling places. Specifically:
    • precincts would be capped at 1,500 voters. Existing law has no similar cap.
    • every precinct would be required to have one or more polling places. Existing law allows vote centers.
    • polling places could not be relocated unless voters assigned to the precinct were notified by mail at least two years in advance, unless an act of God renders a previously set polling place as unusable. Existing law allows greater flexibility.
    • schools could not refuse a county's request to hold a polling place even on the grounds of student safety or a lack of space. Counties would be directed to use schools as polling places. Existing law allows schools to refuse.
  • Limit ID types for voting to "valid state issued identification". Under existing law, voters have many more options.
  • Shift election authority from the County Recorder to the County Board of Supervisors. The bill would make the Recorder responsible only for providing ballots, pens, tables and other equipment as necessary for the precinct polling places. The county board of supervisors would perform or supervise all other election related duties. Under existing law, the Recorder sites early voting locations and conducts voter registration and registration list maintenance.
  • Shift election authority away from the Secretary of State by repealing the Elections Procedures Manual, a regulatory document the Secretary proposes every two years, which takes on the force of law after its review and approval by the Attorney General and Governor. Under existing law, many details of election procedures not specified in statute are set forth in the manual, assuring uniform practice across the state.
  • Prohibit mask or vaccine mandates for a voter, a board worker or any other person at a polling place or other voting or tabulating location.
  • Require all votes be on special paper ballots unless a disabled voter needs other equipment. Each voter's paper ballots would be uniquely marked or numbers.
  • Forbid the use of ballot tabulators. Ballots cast at polling places would be counted at them. Only absentee ballots would be counted at a central location. Ballots would be separated by precinct both before and after tabulation. Relatedly, the existing hand count audit would be repealed. Under existing law, early in-person votes and mail ballots are generally counted at a central location, and votes cast at vote centers do not need to be separated by precinct for tabulation.

Repeal counties' authority to offer a place of deposit for voters to return ballots in mail ballot elections.

Last Updated February 8, 2022

This bill, as introduced on February 7, 2022, would make extensive changes throughout the election code and related amendments to the state constitution. These changes include creating automatic voter registration, same day registration, expanding early voting, and other improvements to voter access. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Allow eligible residents to register to vote without regard to their length of residency. Under existing law, people must be residents of their precinct for 29 days before they may register.
  • Create automatic voter registration at the department of transportation for people who prove citizenship while applying for, renewing, updating or correcting a driver's license or state ID. People who do not provide proof of citizenship during the transaction but who are already registered could have their registration updated automatically as needed. The DOT would send the information to the Secretary of State, who would send it on to the appropriated county recorders. The recorders would mail the voters notice, with a postage prepaid return envelope, enabling the voters to opt-out of the registration or registration update, to choose a political party, and to choose to join the active early voting list. The voter would have 14 days to opt out. Failing to opt out would not count as committing the crime of falsely registering. If a voter's application is incomplete, they would have until the close of polls to complete it and retain their eligibility to vote in that election. The bill would require the Secretary of State and Director of the Department of Transportation to issue related rules after consulting with the county recorders. The bill would also require the Secretary of State to report on the program's effectiveness each year and evaluate other state agencies as possible automatic voter registration agencies.
  • Create same day registration during early voting and on Election Day at all voting locations, and allow a voter to prove residency for the purpose of registration with any of the ID they need to show to vote. If the person's registration can be verified when they register, they will be given a regular ballot. If not, they will be given a ballot that will be counted if, by the time for processing provisional ballots ends, the voter's eligibility was not disproved. In addition, a voter who is not affiliated with a political party would be allowed to use this process to participate in a partisan presidential primary.
  • Require online voter registration systems to enable a person who lacks a driver's license or state ID to use the system, and require the system to accept any proof of citizenship that is valid under Arizona law. The system must accept nontraditional addresses. Existing law does not provide the same specifications for the existing system.
  • Require boards of supervisors or the officer in charge of elections to provide notice to Native tribes within the county and work with the tribe to open at least one polling place, early voting location or voting center on Native land unless the tribe certifies no members live within the county. The bill would create a cause of action to enable tribes to enforce these provisions.
  • Extend early voting through 5 p.m. on the day before Election Day, provided the county can update precinct records and other election materials for Election Day voting. Early voting ends at 5 p.m. the Friday before Election Day under current law.
  • Change the early ballot return deadline to postmarked on or before Election Day and received within five business days of Election Day, while preserving existing law's deadline the close of polls (7 p.m.) on Election Day for ballots returned by hand.
  • Extend the deadline for a voter to cure a missing signature on their early ballot envelope so that it conforms to the deadline to cure an inconsistent signature, namely, five business days after Election Day if the election includes a federal race, and three for other elections. Under existing law, missing signatures can be addressed only through the close of polls.
  • Prohibit imposing additional requirements on returning an early ballot by hand that are not imposed on returning one by mail.
  • Revise the voter registration form to clarify that a person who does not provide documentary proof of citizenship may vote for federal offices only. The existing form says that the applicant's registration will be rejected without such proof. Nonetheless under existing law people who register without providing such proof are able to vote for federal offices.
  • Provide that, if a voter moves within the county but fails to respond to a notice sent by the recorder, the voter's registration remains active. Under existing law, the voter's registration is marked inactive and the voter may be required to attest to their address when voting. Under existing law, the voter's registration is marked inactive and the voter may be required to attest to their address when voting. Marking a voter's registration inactive is the first step in a process to cancel the voter's registration.
  • Provide that an official notification from any government agency in Arizona that the agency has received documentary proof of citizenship for a person would enable the voter's registration to be updated accordingly.
  • Guaranty voters the right to a secret ballot.
  • Require the Secretary of State and other officers in charge of elections to consider risk limiting audits according to certain specifications.

  • Make changes to campaign finance, an area of law Voting Rights Lab does not track.
