VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on June 23, 2022, would require the Auditor General to do "Election Integrity Audits" through the end of December, 2029, and would require the Secretary of State to publish on the internet lists of voters registered to vote, people who voted, and ballot images. The bill also has provisions relating to other duties of the Auditor General that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

The bill would define Election Integrity Audits as "an audit of limited scope for the purpose of ensuring the accuracy and reliability of specific elections processes, including review of preelection and post election activities", and require the Auditor General to conduct them. The Auditor General's normal duties relating to financial analyses. The bill would provide for the conduct of these limited audits by:

  • Requiring the Auditor General to have a dedicated team audit at least one randomly chosen county each election cycle. The audit team would examine at least one area within:
    • Voter registration, voter registration list maintenance, active early voting list maintenance,
    • Early ballot processing and signature verification, including separating early ballots into batches, drop box security, and early ballot election processing boards,
    • Ballot tabulation, including ballot adjudication and duplication, security while tabulating, and logic and accuracy testing.
    • The administration of polling places, vote centers, or central counting centers, and the chain of custody of ballots, equipment, and removable storage devices.
  • Authorizing the Auditor General to make recommendations to the counties, Secretary, and Legislature to address audit findings.
  • Allowing a county to respond to an audit in writing to:
    • Agree with or dispute the audit findings, and
    • State whether and how the county board of supervisors, the county recorder, or both will act on the recommendations.
  • Requiring a county to submit to the Auditor General, upon request, written status reports on implementing the Auditor's recommendations during the two years following the audit. If at the end of two years, the recommendations are not fully implemented, the Auditor would retain the ability to monitor implementation. The county would also be required to post the audit report and implementation progress on its website for 24 months, and participate in any Joint Legislative Audit Committee hearing related to the audit.
  • Requiring the Auditor General to report Election Integrity Audit findings, recommendations, and implementation status to the Legislature, Governor, Secretary of State, and Attorney General.
  • Requiring county recorders, county elections departments, the Department of Transportation, and the Secretary of State to give the Auditor General access to requested people and records. During Arizona's discredited review of the 2020 election, the state senate sued election officials for such access. Under the bill, the election and other officials would be required to give access to:
    • Any personnel or data the Auditor General wishes, including access to electronic data or any data or property from a third party that the Auditor General deems necessary.
    • Polling places, vote centers, and central counting centers.
  • Requiring all officers of any state agency, broadly defined, or political subdivision, to provide the Auditor General with needed facilities and the records requested in the form and time prescribed.

  • Creating felonies to require cooperation that would be enforced by the Attorney General. Specifically, it would be a felony if any officer of person who:

    • knowingly fails or refuse to allow the required access, or
    • otherwise knowingly obstructs or misleads the auditor general.

    Concerning the Secretary of State publishing lists of voters and voting records, the bill has two sets of provisions, one of which creates an ongoing process, and one which creates a pilot program. The provisions creating an ongoing process would:


  • Require the county officer in charge of elections to give to the Secretary of State, 10 days before each primary and general election, a list of all registered voters, both active and inactive. The Secretary would immediately make the list public on the internet. The list would include the voters' names, addresses, years of birth, and precinct numbers, but other personal identifying information would be redacted. Voters with confidential registrations would be redacted, but the total number of them would be included. Existing law allows the public to view voter registration information in the county recorder's office, and requires the redaction of additional personal information.
  • Not later than 48 hours after the delivery of the official county canvass, require the county official in charge of the election to submit to the Secretary of State for publishing on the Secretary's website certain information. Existing law has no comparable provision. The information to be published would be:
    • a list of all persons who voted and their method of voting. This list would include voters' names, addresses, years of birth, and precinct number, but all other personal identifying information would be redacted before submitting it to the Secretary.
    • all ballot images. Although people could view, download, or print these images, a person would be prohibited from altering the contents of an image from the database, and the prohibition would be enforced with a misdemeanor.
    • the cast vote record in a sortable format. The "cast vote record" would be electron records of voters' selections as captured by a tabulation device from a ballot or ballot image, and which cannot be linked to specific voters. A person would be prohibited from altering the contents of the cast vote record from the database, and the prohibition would be enforced with a misdemeanor.
  • Limit distribution of the information by:
    • Requiring a person who wishes to access the data to provide their name, email, telephone number, and street address to the Secretary of State.
    • Forbidding anyone who gets such access from providing the lists or information derived from them to anyone who did not provide such information to the Secretary,
    • Requiring each person accessing the data to confirm they will not share the information in the prohibited manner, and
    • Creating a misdemeanor to enforce the prohibition.
  • Prohibit the published information from being used for commercial purposes.

  • Require the officer in charge of the election to ensure that paper ballots are sorted and stored in a manner that allows for convenient retrieval. Existing law does not have a comparable provision.

    The provisions creating a pilot program would be limited to the 2022 general election, and would:


  • Require the county officer in charge of elections to give the Secretary of State images of ballots cast in the November 2022 general election not later than forty-eight hours after the official county canvass. The Secretary would immediately make the images available to the public by way of an online database or web portal in a convenient downloadable format. This database would remain available for the two years after the election.
  • Require the Secretary to require a person seeking to access the ballot image database to provide the person's name, email address, telephone number and street address.
  • Require any person who receives access to the database not provide information derived from it to anyone who has not received access from the Secretary. An accessing person must confirm that they would not share the information with an unauthorized person. Anyone who improperly shares the information would be subject to a misdemeanor.
  • Require the officer in charge of elections to provide for an identifying indicator to be linked to ballots or ballot images, or both, that when combined with access to the cast vote records, would allow a person a reasonable basis to independently confirm tabulation results. The bill would prohibit the identifying indicator from being linked to a voter.
  • Require the county officer in charge of elections to ensure that paper ballots are stored in a manner that allows for convenient retrieval.
  • Absolve the secretary of state, county recorder or other county officer in charge of elections of liability for any personal identifying information, handwritten statements or other notations made or provided by the voter that are included in the ballot images.

One provision of the bill was amended out on February 28, 2022. It would have required early and provisional ballots to be sorted by precinct before and after tabulation, and early, provisional, and Election Day ballots would have been stored by precinct.

Last Updated July 12, 2022

This bill, as introduced on February 7, 2022, would expand the Attorney General's authority to enforce the election code. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Expand the Attorney General (AG)'s jurisdiction to races for members Congress and presidential elector. Under existing law, the AG has authority over state races.
  • Authorize the AG, in doing enforcement, to:
    • issue written investigative demands to any person.
    • examine under oath any person.
    • examine by means of inspecting, studying or copying any account, book, computer, document, minutes, paper, recording or record.
    • issue all forms of subpoenas to any person, whether or not the person is located within this state.

  • Define, for these purpose, "Person" broadly to include government entities and officers.

    Last updated February 8, 2022.

This bill, as amended on June 22 and engrossed on June 24, 2022, would heavily restrict ballot drop boxes, sharply limit voting from cars, and limit who could distribute forms to request mail ballots. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Prohibit Maricopa and Pima Counties, and any other county that eventually becomes home to more than one million people, from using ballot drop boxes. Currently, the third-largest county is Pinal County, which has about 450,000 residents. Existing law has no similar restriction.
  • Prohibit all other counties from using unmonitored ballot drop boxes, except that these counties may use a drop box located:
    • Inside a voting location in which election staff are present and monitoring the drop box.
    • Inside an office or other facility used by the officer in charge of elections and in which election staff are present and monitoring the drop box.
    • If it is not practicable to staff the location, the drop box must be under 24/7 video surveillance and the video recordings must be maintained for four years.
  • Prohibit people from receiving and casting a ballot from a vehicle or other conveyance unless the service is necessary to comply with the Americans with Disabilities Act.
  • Limit who could distribute early (mail) ballot request forms to political parties and election officials. Existing law does not limit who may distribute such forms but does impose rules for returning them if the forms are distributed by candidates, political committees, or other organizations.
  • Limit who could distribute forms requesting to join the active early voting list to political parties and election officials. This restriction would not apply to certain elections conducted by special taxing districts. Existing law does not limit who may distribute such forms but does impose rules for returning them if the forms are distributed by candidates, political committees, or other organizations.

  • Prohibit county recorders from using certain voter signatures as the only signature for signature comparison purposes. Specifically, the recorder could not use the signature of a voter on a preprinted request for an early (mail) ballot or to update their registration as the sole comparison signature unless that form is an official one printed by the officer in charge of elections. Existing law does not have a comparable provision.

Last Updated July 11, 2022

This bill, as introduced on February 7, 2022, would increase the frequency of voter list maintenance based on the death of voters. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the department of health services to send death data to the Secretary of State every week. Under existing law, the department sends this data every month.

  • Require the Secretary of State to obtain the full file of death data from the Social Security Administration for list maintenance 90 days before each primary and general election and weekly thereafter until Election Day. The Secretary would be required to promptly cancel the registration of any deceased voter and notify the relevant county recorder. Existing law does not have a similar requirement.

    The bill does not identify how the Secretary should ensure the deceased person and the registered voter are the same, however, the Elections Procedures Manual does.

    Last updated February 8, 2022.

This bill, as amended on February 24, 2022, would create a ballot proposition to change what information a voter must provide to cast an early ballot (including by mail) and what information must be verified for the ballot to be valid. Relatedly the bill would expand the existing cure process. In addition, the bill would change the voter ID rules for in-person voting, and create a cause of action for any voter to sue an election official to require them to follow the rules in this bill, or to seek a declaratory judgment to interpret the bill. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require voters who are choosing to vote by mail to include an ID number on their ballot certificate. For their ballot to count, the ID number would have to match one on file. The ID numbers a voter could choose to use would be their driver's license number, state ID number, last four digits of their Social Security number, or their voter registration number. These are modified provisions. The previous version of the bill required the voter to include a copy of their photo ID with their ballot. Existing law does not require an ID number to complete a mail ballot.
  • Require voters who are choosing to vote by mail to put their date of birth on the ballot certificate. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law does not require the voter's date of birth to complete a mail ballot.
  • Require election officials to verify the ID number and date of birth, along with the voter's signature, before accepting the ballot for counting. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill required election officials to verify the ID document and the voter's date of birth. Under existing law, ballots are verified through signature matching.
  • Expand the existing cure process to enable a voter to correct a missing or non-matching ID number by the 5th business day after the election, if a federal office is on the ballot, or three business days after for all other elections. This is a modified provision. The previous version extended the opportunity to cure to provide a copy of ID or correct a date of birth mismatch. Under existing law, missing and mismatched signatures can be cured.
  • Require a person assisting a voter with their mail ballot to put their phone number and relationship to the voter on the ballot certificate, along with their name and address. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Under existing law, the assistant must put their name and address only.
  • Revise in-person voter ID rules to require everyone to show valid, unexpired photo ID to receive a ballot, and if the address on their photo ID does not match their registration address, or if the photo ID does not show an address, the voter would have to provide a second document that does show their correct address, like a utility bill. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

  • Require the Department of Transportation to issue a state ID at no charge if the person applying for it attests they need it for voter ID, whether to register or to vote. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

Last Updated February 25, 2022

The amendment would provide that any law or regulation that burdens a citizen's fundamental right to vote must be narrowly tailored to further a compelling governmental interest. In addition, the amendment would state that it provides robust protection for the right to vote beyond the guarantees of the equal protection clause of the fourteenth amendment to the united states constitution.

This bill, as introduced on January 10, 2022, would require a review of the state's voter registration database and associated registration procedures for "federal-only" voters, namely those that did not provide documentary proof of citizenship when registering to vote. In addition, the bill would impose new reporting duties on county recorders and eliminates state and local law enforcement discretion. Existing law does not have similar provisions, however, the 2021 budget law blocked by the Arizona Supreme Court as unconstitutional did contain similar provisions. Notably, the ruling of unconstitutionality related to the combination of topics in the law generally, not any of the specific provisions. Specifically, this bill:

  • Requires the Secretary of State to give access to the state voter registration system to a person or entity appointed by the Legislature, and to the Election Integrity Unit of the Attorney General's office, so that those parties can verify whether the list maintenance procedures with regard to those voters comply with federal law. The bill would require the Legislature to appoint someone "qualified" in two or more states to "analyze a state's voter registration rolls for compliance with federal law regarding voter registration list maintenance procedures." "Qualified" is not defined, and the bill does not require the person to have approvals or certifications of any kind. Nor does the bill indicate any processes that the person must follow, a timeline for completion, a funding source, or a budget.
  • Require the person reviewing the database to give a report on their findings to the Legislature, the Attorney General, and the Secretary of State. If "the analysis determines" that ineligible people are registered to vote, the Secretary must notify the relevant county official, who must then cancel those voters' registrations.
  • Require each county recorder to file a new, annual report with the Legislature regarding federal-only voter registration procedures. Specifically, the report must cover:
    • a description of the procedures
    • how many federal-only voters are registered in the county.
    • how many federal-only voters later updated their registrations with citizenship information and became fully registered.
    • a comprehensive description of the obstacles faced by federal-only voters in getting the documentation that would enable them to be fully registered.
    • the number of voters who were removed from the list as ineligible after having been registered as a federal-only voter.

  • Require the Arizona Attorney General and the county attorneys to investigate and prosecute, as appropriate, anyone who knowingly registers to vote despite being ineligible.

    Last updated January 26, 2022.

Note: A similar provision was among those struck down in the 2021 budget bill by the Arizona Supreme Court, on the grounds that the subject matter was unrelated to the bill's title and therefore violated constitutional requirements for legislative transparency.

This bill, as introduced on January 10, 2022, would create the "Election Bureau", a new executive branch agency. The Election Bureau would gain the authority to investigate allegations of election fraud, which the bill authorizes any eligible voter to make. To facilitate its investigations, the Bureau would be given subpoena power and the power to conduct hearings.

Although one part of the bill adds the new Bureau to the list of entities able to enforce the election code, including through "civil and criminal actions," another section of the bill suggests it would not gain prosecutorial power. That part of the bill says that if the Bureau "determines that there is a substantial likelihood of fraudulent action," it would "make any appropriate referral to a prosecutorial agency". In addition, the bureau would publicly report any findings and conclusions. The bill budgets $5 million to create the Bureau. Existing law has no comparable provisions, but the Attorney General has an "Election Integrity Unit."

Under existing law, the valid ballots, if discovered in time, would be counted. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require election officials to reject any valid ballot that had not been included in the chain of custody documentation. This is a modified provision. As introduced, the bill required valid ballots to be rejected if they were misplaced and not included in the initial tally.
  • Create a misdemeanor to criminalize knowingly placing a ballot into the collection, verification, or tabulation process outside of the official chain of custody. This is a modified provision. As introduced, the misdemeanor criminalized misplacing a ballot if the misplaced ballot was excluded from the initial tally.

  • Create a cause of action to enable early and provisional voters who are disenfranchised this way to sue the state for compensation. People who vote at a polling place do not have contact information associated with their ballot and thus cannot be given the equivalent opportunity.

This bill, as amended on June 23, 2022, would give the Legislative Council and any Arizona resident a limited right to request a recount in any general election for which an automatic recount is not triggered.

Specifically, the amended bill would allow the Legislative Council to request a recount of the total number of votes cast in the election or the total number of votes cast at any precinct, voting center or district or other jurisdiction or any combination of those portions of an election, on these terms:

  • If requested by a state resident, the individual must post bond with a superior court in a form and amount that the court deems sufficient to cover the recount. If requested by the Legislative Council, the state must pay for the recount. This provision was in the previous version of the bill, except that it was not limited to state residents.
  • The request must be made within five days of the completion of the canvass.
  • The recount must be conducted pursuant to the procedures in place for an automatic recount.

  • The requested recount would be in parallel to the ongoing election process. A county recorder or other applicable election officer who is conducting a requested recount may continue with election preparation, comply with statutory deadlines and perform other duties required by law without regard to the recount.

    The new recount request power would not apply to certain specialty general elections, namely those for precinct committeemen, school district governing boards, community college district governing boards, fire district boards or fire district chiefs or secretary-treasurers and boards of other special districts, or to ballot measure or question elections held by those jurisdictions.

    In addition to shifting election authority in this manner, this bill would also make changes to the hand count audit, an area of law Voting Rights Lab does not track.

    Amendments made on June 23, 2022 narrowed the ability to request a recount to the Legislative Council. The previous version would have allowed the Secretary of State or the Attorney General to request these recounts as well.

    Last updated June 27, 2022.

This bill, as enacted on June 6, 2022:

  • Requires a county recorder to contact the recorder in another jurisdiction if they receive credible information that a voter in their county has registered to vote there. Upon confirming that the voter has re-registered in the other county, the recorder must cancel the voter's previous registration and remove them from the active early voting list, if applicable. The bill does not indicate what criteria must match for a recorder to confirm that the voter moved. Existing law had no comparable provision.
  • Requires a person who receives an early ballot addressed to someone who no longer lives at the residence to mark the ballot "not at this address" and place it in the mail for return. Existing law had no comparable provision.
  • Requires a recorder who receives an early ballot returned because the voter is no longer at the address to attempt confirming the voter's new address according to existing procedures. Existing law had no comparable provision.

  • Creates a new felony offense for knowingly providing a "mechanism" for voting to an individual who is registered in another state, including by forwarding an early ballot addressed to another person.

Last Updated June 30, 2022

Under existing law, the Attorney General and the Governor must approve it.

Under existing law, ballots returned to voting locations were simply transported to early election boards for processing and counting.

This bill, as introduced on January 24, 2022, would eliminate early voting, require voters to have an excuse to choose to vote by mail, repeal the active early voting list, repeal counties' ability to choose to use vote centers in addition to, or instead of, polling places, and repeal counties' ability to open emergency vote centers to serve voters who, for a reason occurring after 5 p.m. on the Friday before the election and before 5 p.m. on the Monday before cannot vote on Election Day.

Specifically, the bill would:

  • End early voting. Under existing law, early voting begins 27 days before Election Day, which is when mail ballots are sent out.
  • Require voters to have an excuse to choose to vote by mail. Under existing law, voters may choose to vote by mail without justifying their decision. Under the bill, the allowed excuses would be:
    • The voter is physically unable to go to the polls due to illness, hospitalization or other confinement.
    • The voter is an absent uniformed services voter or overseas voter as defined in federal law, or a spouse or household member of the absent uniformed services voter or overseas voter.
  • Repeal the active early voting list. Under existing law, voters can choose to join a list to receive a mail ballot for every election going forward. As long as they vote the mail ballot with sufficient frequency, they stay on the list.
    • As part of adjusting the election code to the elimination of the active early voting list, the bill would require sample ballots be sent to all voters. Under existing law, sample ballots are only sent to the voters who are not on that list, as those voters will be mailed an actual ballot.

  • Eliminate counties' existing discretion to choose to use vote centers in addition to, or instead of, precinct based polling places. Under existing law counties have, and routinely use, this discretion.

Last Updated January 26, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 24, 2022 would eliminate counties' existing discretion to offer vote centers and would require all ballots be completed on paper and counted by hand, with a limited exception for equipment needed for disabled voters.

Specifically, the bill would:

  • Eliminate counties' existing ability to offer countywide vote centers in addition to, or instead of, precinct-based polling places.
  • Eliminate counties' existing ability to offer emergency vote centers to serve the needs of voters who, for a reason that arises after 5 p.m. on the Friday before Election Day and before 5 p.m. on the Monday before, can no longer go to the polls on Election Day. Under existing law, such voters must attest to their emergency, and then may vote at an emergency vote center. The bill would preserve an existing alternative procedure that allows disabled or confined voters to request a ballot be brought to them, including voters who became confined or disabled in those few days before Election Day. Voters who no longer can vote on Election Day but are not confined or disabled would no longer have an emergency option.
  • Prohibit using electronic voting machines or tabulators, except to meet the needs of disabled voters, requiring everyone else to vote a paper ballot. Existing law has no parallel requirement.
  • Require all paper ballots be counted by hand, and repeal the hand count audit. Under existing law, electronic tabulators are used, and a hand count audit, along with logic and accuracy checks, verify the accuracy of the tabulators.
  • Require all ballots to be organized by precinct, before and after counting. Under existing law, ballots cast at countywide vote centers are not sorted by precinct when tabulated.

Last updated January 27, 2022.

This bill, as amended on March 10, 2022, would create new, blanket authorizations for election observers that create a risk of voter and election worker intimidation. The bill would provide, notwithstanding any other law, that:

  • All election observers must be allowed uniform access to all stages of the election process, beginning with ballot design through tabulation of the final vote. The bill does not explain how this access is to be provided for activities such as ballot design. The bill does prohibit observers from entering county or other vehicles while they are transporting election equipment or supplies. This is a modified provision. The previous version did not bar observers from entering vehicles.
  • Election observers must be allowed to document their observations, ask questions of election officials and receive timely answers. The bill prohibits the observer from disrupting the process being observed with their questions, and requires the questions to be directed to a person in a supervisory role or designated respondent. This is a modified provision. As introduced the bill did not prohibit the observer from disrupting the process or identify who the observer should ask their questions.
  • All election observers must be allowed to be in proximity to the process closely enough to observe whether the process is being conducted correctly. The bill does not clarify how close this provision would allow the observer to come to a person who is voting, or to the voter check in station, or to voters more generally. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Election observers may only be ejected from voting locations for significant concerns on the approval of the inspector and the marshal, or troubleshooter, if available. The bill further provides that the election observer may notify the political party chairman who may appeal the ejection to the officer in charge of elections, whose decision is final. The bill does not define "significant concerns". This is a modified provision. As introduced, the bill did not limit the provision to voting locations or include troubleshooters. In addition, the previous version referred to the county recorder rather than the officer in charge of elections.

  • Elections observers must receive standardized, uniform training from their political party before observing any aspect of the election process. The training would be based on the Elections Procedures Manual. This is a new provision, not in the previous version of the bill.

    Last updated March 11, 2022.

This bill, as enacted on June 6, 2022:

  • Authorizes a new "on-site tabulation" process for "early ballots" (mail ballots), in which voters may personally insert their early ballot into a tabulating machine at their polling place or voting center. On-site tabulation must take place in a separate area, and ballots cast through the process must be tallied separately.

  • Specifies voter ID requirements for returning an early ballot at on-site tabulation locations. Under existing law, all early ballots, whether received by the voter in the mail or obtained by the voter at a voting location after showing ID, have their envelope affidavit signature verified against the voter's signature on file before the ballot is counted. The bill provides for the following alternative procedures at on-site tabulation locations:

    • If a voter shows a form of voter ID required for in-person voting, election officials must confirm that the name and address on the ballot affidavit matches registration records and must give voters an opportunity to complete any missing information on the affidavit if necessary. Once confirmed, voters may submit their early ballot to the tabulating machine.
    • If a voter does not have required voter ID, they may either deposit their completed early ballot and affidavit envelope in an official drop box, or they may surrender the early ballot to election officials and vote a provisional ballot.

Last Updated June 30, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 25, 2022, would require the county recorder to use national change of address data to initiate an address confirmation process every month. Under existing law, it is done every year.

Last updated January 26, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on January 25, 2022, would end early voting, require an excuse to vote by mail, repeal the list that allows any voter to receive a mail ballot every election, and make related changes throughout the code. Specifically, the bill would:

  • End early voting. Under existing law, early voting begins 27 days before Election Day, when mail ballots are sent to those who have requested them.
  • Repeal counties' discretion to offer emergency vote centers to serve voters who, for a reason that arises after 5 p.m. on the Friday before an election and before the 5 p.m. on the Monday before an election, cannot vote on Election Day.
  • Require voters have an excuse to choose to vote by mail. Under existing law, any voter may choose to vote by mail, and most do. Specifically, the bill would require the voter to attest to one of the following excuses in order to choose to vote by mail:
    • The voter expects to be absent from their precinct at the time of the election.
    • The voter is physically unable to go to the polls.
    • The voter is sixty-five years of age or older.
    • The voter's place of residence is more than fifteen road miles from their polling place.
    • The voter cannot attend the polls on the day of the election because of the tenets of their religion.
    • The voter has a visual impairment.
    • The voter is an absent uniformed services voter or overseas voter as defined in federal law, or a spouse or household member of the absent uniformed services voter or overseas voter.
  • Repeal the active early voting list. Under existing law, any voter may request to receive a ballot by mail for all elections going forward, and may remain on the list of those who have requested mail ballots as long as they vote sufficiently frequently. As part of this repeal, the bill would also:
    • Facilitate polling place consolidation for an election by eliminating the requirement that the county board of supervisors make a specific finding that the number of people on the list to receive mail ballots is likely to substantially reduce the number of voters appearing at one or more specific polling places for that election. Under the bill, consolidation could happen if the board simply makes a "a specific finding" without regard to what the finding must be about.
    • Require all voters be sent sample ballots for primaries and general elections. Under existing law, sample ballots are sent to all voters not on the active early voting list. Voters on the list receive ballots, not sample ballots.
  • Limit the ability to request a mail ballot before the normal window to request them opens, and to have one request provide ballots through the next federal general election, to uniformed services or overseas voters. Under existing law, people on the address confidentiality list, namely people whose life or safety could be jeopardized if their address were known, such as domestic violence victims or law enforcers, are also allowed to request mail ballots early and through the next federal general election without joining the active early voting list.

  • Repeal explicit authorization for candidates, political committees, or other organizations to distribute mail ballot request forms to voters, and repeal related rules for their return. The bill does not replace the repeal with an explicit ban on application distribution.

Last Updated January 30, 2022

This bill, as enacted on July 6, 2022, requires all counties that use early (mail) ballots to offer a ballot tracking system available on their websites that enables voters to learn whether their ballot has been received by the officer in charge of the election and whether the early ballot has been verified and tabulated. This requirement will take effect December 31, 2023. Existing law did not require ballot tracking, but the Secretary of State has offered tracking on their website, as has Maricopa County.

The bill appropriates $250,000 to the Secretary of State to fund improvements to the Arizona voter information database to enable counties to offer the required tracking.

Last Updated July 12, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 25, 2022, would create a new felony aimed at enterprises prohibiting them from knowingly communicating to a registered voter, by any means, false information that is intended to impede the voter in exercising the voter's right to vote and that relates to:

  • the date, time, or place of the election.
  • the voter's precinct, polling place, or voter registration status.
  • the voter's eligibility to register or vote.
  • the voter's status on the active early voting list.
  • information regarding early or mail-in ballots.
  • information on how to obtain a ballot.

  • information on how to vote or the location of an early voting location, voting center, or emergency voting center, including the office of the county recorder or other officer in charge of elections.

    The bill would apply to:

  • any corporation, partnership, association, labor union, or other legal entity.
  • any group organized under section 527 of the internal revenue code.

  • any group of persons who are associated in fact although not a legal entity.

    The bill has multiple provisions relating to the enforcement of the new felony. The bill would provide:

  • That a prosecution may be initiated in either the jurisdiction where the communication was made or the one in which it was received. Prosecutions could be brought by the Attorney General or county attorneys, either on their initiative or because they have received a written complaint. The bill would grant both types of prosecutor subpoena and other investigatory powers. If the corporation or organization fails to cooperate with the authorized investigatory demands, a court may make certain findings and then order compliance. If the corporation or organization continues to fail to cooperate, the bill would authorize the court to:
    • hold the relevant person in contempt.
    • grant the requested injunctive relief.
    • dissolve the corporation.
    • grant any other relief the court deems proper.
  • That the Attorney General may dissolve a corporation by establishing in court that the corporation committed this felony.

  • That a registered voter who receives such false information may file a civil suit in superior court for injunctive or similar relief, in either the county where the communication was made or the one in which it was received. The court would be allowed to award a prevailing plaintiff attorneys' fees.

    Last updated January 30, 2022.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 26, 2022, would create same day registration during both early voting and on Election Day, and create automatic voter registration at the DMV with an option to decline registration after the transaction. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Allow people to register to vote during the 28 days before Election Day and be eligible to vote a provisional ballot in any election other than a partisan primary, if they have resided in their precinct for at least 29 days and complete a voter registration application. Under existing law, registration closes on the 29th day before Election Day, and early voting begins 27 days before the election. Thus same day registration would be available throughout early voting. Although the bill does not expressly provide for voters to both register and receive an early ballot as part of the same transaction, both services are available at county recorder offices, and the bill does not impose any restriction on completing both steps at the same time. However, the bill does not expressly provide for both services to be available at early voting locations.
  • Allow people to register to vote and complete a provisional ballot at their polling place on Election Day if they complete a registration form and prove their residence. The bill does not indicate what constitutes proof of residence.

  • Create automatic voter registration at the DMV by:

    • Providing that a person will be registered to vote when applying for a driver's license or renewal, a state ID or renewal, or is making changes to their license or ID, if they are qualified to vote.
    • Requiring notice be sent to the automatically registered person to enable them to decline to register, and providing that if they do not decline to register within 21 days of the notice being sent to them, their registration will be effective.
    • Requiring the Department of Transportation and the Secretary of State, to consult with all the county recorders and then issue rules implementing the automatic registration system.
    • Providing that a person who is not qualified to register and who nonetheless unknowingly registers through the automatic process is not guilty of false registration or false swearing.

Last Updated January 30, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 26, 2022, would expand voting opportunities for college students. Specifically the bill would:

  • Require counties to place a polling place or vote center on the main campus of each state university in the county.

  • Require counties to place at least one ballot drop box at each state university satellite location, each community college campus, and community college satellite location in their county.

Last Updated January 30, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 26, 2022, would expand the early voting period and change who has authority to authorize multiple early voting locations. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the county board of supervisors to authorize siting early voting locations other than the county recorder's office, but allow the county recorder to make changes to where those locations ae sited by notifying the board and the public. Under existing law, the county recorder has the authority to open additional early voting locations without the permission of the county board of supervisors.

  • Allow county recorders to offer early voting through the day before Election Day, except that early voting must end as needed to ensure that precinct registers and other election materials can be revised to indicate who has voted, who has requested mail ballots, and which voters are on the inactive list. To the extent early voting is offered after 5 p.m. on the Friday before Election Day, a voter would not need to attest to having an emergency to cast a ballot. Such attestation would still be required to vote between the close of early voting and 5 p.m. on the Monday before Election Day.

    Last updated January 30, 2022.

This bill, as amended on March 10, 2022, would prohibit using internet-connected voting or tabulation equipment, and create new misdemeanors to enforce those prohibitions. In addition, the bill would require counting center activities to be on non-stop video posted on the county website. All of these are new provisions. As introduced, the bill regulated what kind of voting equipment the Secretary of State could approve, an area of election law voting rights lab does not track. Those provisions remain in the bill.

This bill, as amended on February 22, 2022, would prohibit counting early ballots, whether returned by mail or in person, prior to Election Day. The bill would not change the timeline for verifying, and thus curing ballots. Under existing law, early ballots may be counted after they are verified. Note, prior to the February 22 amendment, this bill did not address election law.

Last Updated March 1, 2022

This bill, as enacted on June 7, 2022, makes it easier for people who receive "early ballots" (mail ballots) to cast regular ballots in person rather than provisional ballots and adjusts certain rules relating to the address confidentiality program for registered voters, along with various technical changes throughout the election code. Specifically, concerning the two substantive issues above, the bill:

  • Allows a person who was sent an early ballot to complete a regular ballot at a voting location if certain conditions apply. Existing law required all such voters to vote a provisional ballot. Under the bill, a voter who was sent an early ballot may now cast a regular ballot in person by showing the ID required of all voters, if:
    • the voter surrenders the early ballot, unless there is some reason other than having been sent a mail ballot that requires them to complete a provisional ballot, or,
    • the election is being conducted using electronic poll books or other equipment that enables continuous updates of voting activity regarding who was sent an early ballot, the system indicates the voter's ballot was not returned or was not accepted, and there is no reason other than having been sent an early ballot that requires them to complete a provisional ballot.

  • Changes the address confidentiality program by requiring the Secretary of State to update the statewide voter registration system to secure the existing registration of a new program participant before notifying the county recorder of the participant's status, current residence, and substitute address for the county recorder to update in their system. Existing law simply requires the Secretary to check the participant's status in the state system before notifying the recorder to make the voter's registration confidential and does not specify what information the Secretary must send to the recorder.

    The bill also contains additional provisions related to election law that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

Last Updated June 27, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 26, 2022, would end early voting and make the state primary and general election days holidays for government employees and require private employers to allow employees who give them notice before Election Day to leave work to vote without penalty.

Last updated January 30, 2022.

This bill, as amended on March 3, 2022, would expand the Attorney General's authority to enforce election law, both civilly and criminally, and grant both the Attorney General and county attorneys broad investigative powers to use in enforcing election law. Specifically, as amended the bill would:

  • Extend the Attorney General's authority to enforce the election code, civilly and criminally, to elections for Congress and President. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Under existing law, the Attorney General only has authority relating to state elections, including for state offices, legislative offices, justices, initiatives, and referenda.

  • Grant both the Attorney General and county attorneys broad investigative powers to use when enforcing election law. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill granted the new powers to the Attorney General only.

    On February 10, all of the provisions in the bill when it was introduced were stripped from the bill and replaced with new provisions. The provisions stripped from the bill would have:


  • Created a new class 2 felony to punish knowingly and falsely claiming U.S. citizenship while registering to vote.
  • Created a new class 2 felony to punish a person who knowingly and falsely claims a potential registrant may register as a "federal only" voter.

  • Revised the voter registration form so that it informs potential voters that falsely claiming to be a U.S. citizen is a class 2 felony.

Last Updated March 14, 2022

This bill, as enacted on May 23, 2022, requires the clerks of superior courts to send the Secretary of State a free, monthly list of individuals convicted of felonies in that county, which includes the person's name, date of birth, Social Security number, if available, usual legal residence, and if available, father's name or mother's maiden name. The Secretary of State may only use the lists to cancel voters from the statewide voter registration database and notify the appropriate county recorder to cancel their registration.

Under existing law as stated in the Elections Procedures Manual, the Secretary periodically received felony conviction information from the superior courts that included each convicted person's name, address, and the last four digits of their Social Security number, and after processing the information in the statewide database would then notify county recorders of "hard" and "soft" matches. County recorders cancelled hard matches and undertook further investigation of soft matches, only cancelling them if they were "true" matches. The bill does not address this process.

Last updated June 30, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on January 26, 2022, would limit the number of voters who could be assigned to a precinct, eliminate counties' ability to offer vote centers in addition to or instead of precincts, both during early voting and on Election Day. Under the bill, each precinct would be limited to 1,250 registered voters of a single political party and 2,000 registered voters overall, at the time the precinct is formed. If a precinct exceeds these limits after it is drawn, it must be split the next time precincts are drawn, namely, on or before October 1 of the year before a general election. Counties would be prohibited from combining precincts for an election if the resulting precinct would exceed these limits.

This bill, as introduced on January 27, 2022, would facilitate the registration and voting of eligible incarcerated people. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require recorders in counties with 300,000 or more residents to open a vote center at the county jail for people who are temporarily in custody awaiting trial. Currently Maricopa, Pima, and Pinal counties have populations that large. Existing law has no comparable provision.
  • Require all county recorders to give a request for an early (mail) ballot to each qualified, eligible voter in the custody of the county jail or the state department of corrections in their county, and, upon receipt of completed request, a ballot. Existing law has no comparable provision.

  • Require the state department of corrections and every county jail to give every person released from their confinement who is eligible to register a mail voter registration form, and transmit completed forms to the appropriate county recorder with five days. Existing law has no comparable provision.

This bill, as introduced on January 27, 2022, would automatically restore the voting rights of a person convicted of a felony when they complete probation or are absolutely discharged from imprisonment. Under existing law, only people convicted of a single felony who have also paid all ordered restitution have their voting rights automatically restored. Everyone else must apply for restoration, and those who were absolutely discharged from imprisonment and who are not eligible for automatic restoration must wait two years before applying. The bill would also require notice of automatic restoration at the time of sentencing. Notice is already required under existing law, but in a different section of the code.

This bill, as amended on March 8, 2022, would:

  • Require voting and tabulating equipment to have certain features, such as an inability to connect to the internet or to have those features able to be blocked or disabled during voting and tabulation. Electronic poll books would be exempted from this internet connectivity prohibition. These are modified provisions. The previous version of the bill did not exempt electronic poll books from the internet ban.
  • Create chain of custody protocols and provide for election observers to witness certain aspects of handling the equipment if they are present. However, the bill allows election procedures to go forward if no observers are present, and explicitly prohibits observers from entering county vehicles. These are modified provisions. The previous version of the bill stated that observers "shall" be present and did clarify that the election processes could go forward if they were not, nor did it ban observers from county vehicles.
  • Enforce these provisions by creating two misdemeanors. The amendment modified the definition of the crime by providing that a person "knowingly" take the prohibited actions.

  • Videotape users of the drop boxes in a way that links them to the ballots they deposit.
  • Prohibit more than one ballot being deposited at a time.
  • Prohibit one person from depositing more than seven ballots per visit.

"Early" ballots include those mailed to voters and those cast by voters in person before Election Day.

Specifically, the officer in charge of the election would need to post on their website:

  • Ten days before the election, the list of active and inactive voters who are eligible to vote, redacting birthdates and ID numbers.

  • After the election but five days before the county canvass, images of all the tabulated ballots, and the cast vote record, in sortable formats. Tabulators must, as they tabulate, mark the ballots with numbers so the electronic images and the physical ballots can be linked.

This bill, as introduced on January 28, 2022, would require election officials to maintain detailed records of "voting irregularities" and require the officials to give the records to the President of the Senate, the Speaker of the House, and the Secretary of State. The bill would create a misdemeanor to enforce this requirement, but the bill does not define "voting irregularities".

Separately, the bill would make the chain of custody records for election equipment and ballots subject to legislative subpoena, and create a misdemeanor to punish election officials who do not maintain the records.

This bill, as amended on March 10, 2022, would require the officer in charge of the election to record certain information about ballots that needed duplication or adjudication, post that information on their website, and report it to the Legislature. Knowingly failing to do so would be a misdemeanor. This is a modified provision. As introduced, the crime of failing to record, post, and record the information did not need to be "knowingly" committed.

The information to be recorded and reported would be the number of ballots with each type of defect or damage, further separated by ballot type. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

This bill, as introduced on January 31, 2022, would give the Auditor General authority to audit various election processes either on their initiative or at the request of one of the chambers of the Legislature. The Auditor General's ordinary duties relate to finances and financial practices, and they report to the Legislature's Joint Legislative Audit Committee, which has the authority to shape their work.

Specifically, the bill would give the Auditor General the power to conduct one or more broad audits of county elections for state and federal offices, looking beyond the tabulation of votes. The audits could include reviews of voter rolls, election systems, voting equipment, ballot tabulation equipment, and compliance with state law and the Elections Procedures Manual.

Last updated February 10, 2022.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 31, 2022, would require counties with 500,000 or more residents to do a special, duplicative ballot counting process. Currently only Maricopa and Pima Counties are large enough to qualify. Specifically, the bill would require these counties to:

  • Count all ballots at the polling place.
  • Have the vote total verified by two persons of different political parties. The bill does not identify whether these people need to be election officials.
  • Recount the ballots at the central counting location, and have the totals verified by two different people of different political parties.
  • If the totals are different, hand count the ballots and have the totals verified by two different people of different political parties.

Note, the bill does not address ballots cast at vote centers or returned by mail.

Last updated February 2, 2022.

HISTORY: {"date":"03/14/2022","summary":"In SENATE.  Read third time.  Failed to pass SENATE","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on March 10, 2022, addresses lawsuits challenging election outcomes, and creates new consequences of a judicial ruling that the wrong outcome was declared. The bill would:

  • Provide that if the court determines the declared winner of a general election did not in fact receive the highest number of votes, or in the case of a ballot measure decided at a general election, sufficient votes, the court must order that portion of the election to be repeated within 90 days of the court's order. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill did not limit the provision to general elections. Under existing law, if an election contest results in a ruling that the declared outcome was incorrect, the judge orders the correct outcome be recognized instead. The bill does not address the section of law providing for that outcome, and thus it is unclear what would happen if this bill became law and such an election contest occurred.

  • Provide that any person determined by the court to be criminally responsible for misconduct, fraud or illegal votes that resulted in the wrong outcome being declared is liable for the costs of the court-ordered second election. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill declared that anyone responsible for the misconduct, fraud, or illegal votes, rather than criminally responsible, would be guilty of a misdemeanor as well as liable for the cost of the new election. Existing law has no comparable provisions.

    Last updated March 14, 2022.

This bill, as amended on March 8, 2022, would make changes throughout the election code. The bill would regulate voter registration activity, increase the frequency of voter registration list maintenance aimed at identifying people who have moved, require signature match training for workers who validate early (mail and in-person early) ballots, expand who could participate in the optional hand count audits existing law allows, create a new duty to post ballot images online and a crime to enforce it, and create a new, comprehensive, prospective audit process for major aspects of election administration to be conducted under the auspices of the Auditor General. The Auditor General reports to the Joint Legislative Audit Committee, which has authority to review and approve its audit plans, and typically audits financial compliance.

Many of these provisions were in the previous version of the bill. One major set of provisions has been amended out of this version. The removed provisions would have codified existing dropbox regulations.

Concerning voter registration activity, the bill would:

  • Require people doing voter registration drives to return or mail completed registrations to the appropriate county recorder or the Secretary of State within five days, or to the appropriate county recorder before the deadline to register to vote for the next election, whichever is earlier. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law does not impose similar requirements on such registration volunteers.
  • Require certain people doing voter registration drives to register with the Secretary of State before registering people. Specifically, a volunteer who registers at least 25 people, or anyone paid to register people, must register. Once registered, the person would be assigned a number that they must put on all completed registration forms they solicit, assist with, or collect. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require the Secretary of State to create related rules in the Elections Procedures Manual, application form, and post on the Secretary's website the necessary information and form. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. The application to register voters would be signed before a notary and include:
    • the person's full name, residence address, telephone number, and email address.
    • the name, address, and telephone number of any entity or organization for which the person is volunteering or by whom the person is paid.
    • a statement that the person consents to the jurisdiction of the courts of this state in resolving any disputes concerning assisting in, soliciting, or collecting voter registrations.

With respect to address-related voter list maintenance, the bill would:

  • Change the frequency of voter registration list maintenance activity recorders do to identify voters who have moved to require recorders to do it every month on the first day of the month, except for a month in which the recorder is conducting an election. This is provision was in the previous version of the bill. Under existing law recorders do the process at least once a year on or before May 1.
  • Change the consequence of a voter not responding to the address confirmation mailing. If a voter does not return the notice sent as part of that process, they will be required to provide affirmation or confirmation of their address when they vote. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law allows an election official to require such affirmation or confirmation but does not require it.

  • Require county recorders, upon learning a voter has a forwarding address, to send a notice to the forwarding address explaining voting materials cannot be forwarded that differs depending on whether the forwarding address is permanent or temporary. The notice to a voter with a permanent change would instruct them to re-register. The notice to a temporary address would instruct the voter to apply to receive a ballot at that address if they wished to be mailed one. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law requires recorders to send notices to forwarding addresses after non-forwardable mail to the voter has been returned, but does not specify the notice include this information.

    Concerning signature match training, facilitating the hand count, and posting ballot images, the bill would:


  • Require training in signature matching for all election workers who verify early ballots. The signature matching training would be a standalone class based on FBI training and include a test on the course material. The Election Procedures Manual only addresses training for signature matching in a section relating to petition signatures, not early ballots, but requires the recorder to ensure that workers doing the signature matching are properly trained. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Make conducting the statutory, optional hand count audit easier by expanding those authorized to participate in it to include unaffiliated people. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require the officer in charge of the election to post a searchable database of ballot images online for any election that includes a federal office, within 48 hours of the delivery of the official county canvass. Certain special district elections would be exempt from this requirement. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill. Existing law has no comparable requirement.
  • Prohibit the Secretary of State, county recorder, or other officer in charge of elections from being held liable for any personally identifying information, handwritten statements, or other notations that a voter put on their ballot. The substance of this provision was in the previous version, however, the text has been redrafted.

  • Create a new felony to enforce the requirement to post the ballot images. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

    Finally, the bill would create a new audit process called an "election integrity audit" to be conducted by the Auditor General, who reports to the Joint Legislative Audit Committee, or the Auditor General's authorized representatives. The Joint Legislative Audit Committee has the authority to review and approve the Auditor General's audit plans. The Auditor General would be required to create a specific team to do these audits. Each federal election cycle the Auditor would audit every county with at least one million residents and two randomly selected smaller counties. Based on current population statistics, Maricopa and Pima counties have more than one million residents, and the other 13 counties do not. Indeed, the third-largest county currently has less than a half-million residents. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.

    The audits would include one of the below processes on a rotating basis. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill provided that the audits of Maricopa and Pima counties would focus on a single process, but the audits of the small counties would include all of them each time. Specifically:


  • Voter registration, maintenance of voter registration rolls, and maintenance of the active early voting list.
  • Early ballot processing and signature verification processing, including the separation of early ballots into batches or other groupings, ballot dropbox security, and early ballot election processing boards.
  • Tabulation of ballots, including ballot adjudication and duplication, security issues while tabulating, and logic and accuracy testing and administration.

  • Polling place administration, voting center administration, central counting center administration, and chain of custody of ballots, equipment, and removable storage devices.

    The bill would require the person conducting the "election integrity audit" to be given access to certain personnel, data, and locations. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill. Specifically, access would be granted to:


  • Any personnel and data from the county recorder's office and any county elections department, the Department of Transportation, and the Secretary of State, that the auditor general deems necessary to perform the new type of audit, including data and property from a third party.

  • Polling places, voting centers, and central counting centers.

    To enforce these provisions, the bill would:


  • Expand an existing crime relating to denying access to the Auditor General to cover knowingly obstructing or misleading the Auditor General and raise the penalty for that crime from a class 2 misdemeanor to a class 6 felony. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require the Attorney General to supervise the prosecution of people who allegedly commit that crime. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Create a recommendation and reporting process involving the Auditor General and the audited counties that allows counties to disagree with and respond to the Auditor's recommendations. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Reports would be given to the President of the Senate, Speaker of the House, Joint Legislative Audit Committee, Governor, Secretary of State, and Attorney General. In addition, certain reports would be required to be posted on the audited counties' websites and maintained on the sites for 24 months. This provision was modified to mandate the 24 month period.

  • Appropriate $3,938,865 to fund the audits. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have appropriated $4,622,000.

    The February 16 amendments removed provisions relating to drop boxes. Those provisions would essentially have codified rules relating to drop boxes in the Elections Procedures Manual. Specifically, the bill would have required:


  • Dropboxes to be marked, securely designed, placed in a secure location approved by the county board of supervisors, and their locations must be posted on the county's website. Ballot removal and transport would have been subject to specific chain of custody and bipartisanship rules.

  • Drop boxes not open to the public before the 27th day before an election, be inspected before use to ensure they are empty and undamaged, and be locked and made unavailable after the last person in line at the close of polls on Election Day has delivered their ballot.

    • Dropboxes to either be permanent fixtures or locked, sealed, and continuously monitored by an election worker. Permanently affixed, unmonitored boxes would have been subject to differing security rules depending on whether they are indoor or outdoor.

Last Updated March 9, 2022

People with prior felony convictions, or people who did not pay ordered restitution must wait two years before applying.

In addition, the bill would require notice to people about automatic restoration by:

  • Requiring probationers who request voting information to be given information from the Secretary of State.

  • Requiring the Secretary of State to maintain a website, linked to the main site, with information about the voting rights of people with a criminal history.

HISTORY: {"date":"02/28/2022","summary":"In HOUSE.  Read third time.  Passed HOUSE","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
Voters rejected the voter ID document and ID number proposition created by this bill at the November, 2022 general election.

As adopted on February 28, 2022, this resolution created a ballot proposition that, if it had been ratified by voters, would have changed what information a voter must provide to cast an early ballot (including by mail) and what information must be verified for the ballot to be valid. Relatedly the proposition would have expanded the existing cure process to address these new requirements. Finally, the proposition would have changed the voter ID rules for in-person voting, and created a cause of action for any voter to sue an election official to require them to follow the rules in this bill or to seek a declaratory judgment to interpret the bill.

Specifically, the resolution created a ballot proposition that, if voters had ratified it, would have:

  • Required voters who vote an early ballot by mail to include an ID number on their ballot affidavit and their date of birth. For the ballot to be counted, the ID number and date of birth would have had to be confirmed, in addition to existing requirements for signature matching. Accepted ID numbers would have included a driver's license number, state ID number, last four digits of the voter's Social Security number, or the voter's registration number. Under existing law, the only verification element on the early ballot affidavit is the voter's signature.
  • Expanded the existing cure process in light of the new affidavit requirements, to permit voters to correct a missing or non-matching ID number, or a date of birth that was not confirmed. Existing law allows for cure of missing or unmatching voter signatures, which is the only current verification element of the affidavit.
  • Required an individual assisting a voter with casting an early ballot to provide their phone number and relationship to the voter on the ballot affidavit, in addition to the current requirement of providing their name and address.
  • Required all in-person voters to present an accepted form of photo ID to vote a regular ballot, by eliminating the existing option of providing two forms of non-photo ID as an alternative. The proposition would have also changed the criteria for accepted single forms of photo ID by eliminating ID issued by state or local governments other than Arizona driver's licenses or Arizona state IDs and expressly requiring the ID be unexpired. Under existing law, ID cards are only deemed invalid if they are expired "on their face." Note that while the proportion created by the bill would have eliminated the non-photo ID option entirely, it would have preserved the other existing alternative to single ID, which permits a voter to provide a form of valid, unexpired photo ID that lacks the voter's registration address, or a passport or military ID, plus a second document that includes the registration address. Existing law further provides that voters who do not have accepted forms of voter ID but provide some form of tribal identification may vote a regular provisional ballot that is verified by signature matching. All other voters who lack accepted voter ID at the voting place must vote a conditional provisional ballot that is only counted if they provide required ID within the statutory deadline.

Required the Department of Transportation to issue a state ID at no charge if the person applying for it attests they need it for voter registration or voting.

Last Updated May 15, 2023

HISTORY: {"date":"02/01/2022","summary":"Additionally referred to SENATE Committee on RULES","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 31, 2022, would amend the state constitution to limit the types of ID a voter may use to vote in person, while creating one new one. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Eliminate non-photo ID choices. Under existing law, voters can show a single photo ID or two non-photo IDs, which could include tribal IDs without photos, utility bills, bank statements, vehicle registration, vehicle insurance cards, a government ID, or any official election mail.
  • Newly specify that acceptable photo ID types include certain types, all of which would fit in the category of "United States federal, state or local government issued identification." That category is part of the acceptable IDs under existing law, and would remain a category under the bill.
  • Newly specify that acceptable photo ID would include a student or employee identification card for a private or public college, including a community college, a university or a postgraduate or technical school that is located in this state. While existing law does not address student ID in particular, it provides that any valid form of ID with the voter's photograph, name, and address, and the name and address must be reasonably the same as in the precinct register. Given that those requirements would continue to apply to the specified student IDs, the bill's inclusion of them also does not change existing law.
  • Create a new form of ID, called an "Arizona Voter Photo Identification card." The bill would require the Secretary of State to issue this voter photo ID for free, upon a sworn application by a voter that includes the applicant's:
    • full legal name. This data point would need to be supported by documentation.
    • residence address as listed in the applicant's voter registration file. This data point would need to be supported by documentation.
    • date of birth. This data point would need to be supported by documentation.
    • height, weight and gender.
    • the date on which the Secretary issued it, and
    • a unique identifying number.

  • Provide that the ID is only available to people who lack any of the other acceptable ID forms, is valid only for voting, and is available only as long as the voter resides at the address. If they move, they may surrender it and apply for a new one at the same address.

Last Updated February 3, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on January 26, 2023, would repeal California's mail voting system (both the Voters Choice Act and the requirement that all counties mail their active voters a ballot) and replace it with a system that requires people to apply for a mail ballot each election, join a list to receive mail ballots for each election, or vote in person either early or on Election Day. Prior to the Voters Choice Act and the requirement that all voters be mailed a ballot statewide, California similarly allowed anyone to apply for a mail ballot or join a list to receive a ballot automatically. As part of making this wholesale change to California election law, the bill would:

  • Require applicants to apply for their ballot at least seven days before Election Day, and provide that election officials begin processing applications 29 days before Election Day. Under existing law, all active voters are mailed a ballot 29 days before Election Day without an application.
  • Eliminate vote centers and repeal minimum drop box requirements. Only counties conducting elections under the Voters Choice Act use vote centers, but every county is required to offer minimum numbers of drop boxes based on population and other requirements.
  • Restrict who can return a voter's completed ballot for them to family and household members. Under existing law, voters may choose anyone to return their ballot for them.
  • Shorten the ballot return deadline from postmarked on or before Election Day and received by the seventh day after the election to postmarked similarly but received by the third day after the election.
  • Repeal a provision that allows any registered voter to electronically receive a mail ballot.
  • Streamline the process for uniformed voters to get a mail ballot when they submit a federal postcard application by deeming the postcard to be both a registration application and a mail ballot application.
  • Make Election Day a state holiday.

  • Make numerous conforming changes throughout the code.

    The previous version of this bill would have further limited mail voting by requiring voters to justify their decision to vote by mail with one of the authorized excuses, but that requirement was amended out of this version.

Last Updated December 27, 2022
