This bill, although amended on April 7, 2022, was not substantively changed. As amended on March 29, 2022, this bill would provide funding, guidance, and regulations to improve counties' voter registration efforts. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill. The amendments appropriated $15,000,000 for the effort and made nonsubstantive or made minor changes to details, as indicated below. Specifically, the amended bill would:

  • Create civic education and voter outreach programs aimed at students supported by a $15,000,000 fund overseen by the Secretary of State. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill lacked a specific appropriation. Under existing law, the Comptroller distributes some of the funding the Secretary would be overseeing.

  • Repeal a requirement that the Secretary of State issue regulations requiring counties to identify and register eligible voters and replace that requirement with a new one. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill. The bill would require that the Secretary:

    • Adopt guidance for counties to use in identifying, registering, and preregistering qualified electors who are not registered to vote.
    • Adopt guidance for a participating county to design and implement a program of civic engagement intended to support the State Seal of Civic Engagement for high school students. This State Seal is one component of the civic education programs created by the bill.
    • Adopt regulations prescribing minimum requirements for these programs.
    • Adopt regulations for applying for grants from the Civic Learning, Outreach, and Engagement Fund. This Fund would be created by this bill, and grants could be awarded to counties that are eligible in terms of voter registration. Eligible counties would be those with less than 80 percent of potential voters registered during the most recent presidential election. This is a slightly modified provision. The amendment renamed such counties "eligible" instead of "underperforming" and changed the reference document to the Secretary of State's Statement of Vote for the General Election instead of the Secretary's "Report or Registration."
    • Periodically update the regulations the Secretary of State promulgates under this section. The bill also provides that if a county does not pursue programs that comply with the guidance and regulations, the Secretary can adopt a program for it. Existing law requires the Secretary to step in if a county does not, rather than simply authorize the Secretary to act.

HISTORY: {"date":"09/29/2022","summary":"Chaptered by Secretary of State.  Chapter No. 2022-807","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on September 29, 2022, requires notice to voters before canceling their registrations for imprisonment, mental incapacity, death, or being in inactive status for four years. In addition, it overhauls the process for identifying and removing voters based on mental incapacity and requires notice to people who regained their voting rights as part of mental incapacity proceedings. All of these changes take effect beginning January 1, 2024.

Specifically, starting January 1, 2024, the bill:

  • Requires county elections officials to send a forwardable notice by first-class mail to a voter between 15 and 30 days before canceling the voter's registration because of mental incapacity, imprisonment for a felony conviction, death, or because their registration is inactive and they have not voted in two federal election cycles. The notice must be in the voter's preferred language if the Voting Rights Act requires the county to provide materials in that language. The bill specifies the content of the notice, including that the voter may respond using the enclosed, postage prepaid return card or by phone. Finally, the official is explicitly allowed to provide additional notices and to contact the voter by other methods. Existing law did not require a pre-cancellation notice.
  • Changes how election officials learn about people who have lost or gained voting rights based on mental incapacity to specify the details of the process. Under existing law, the court clerk forwards relevant court orders to the Secretary and the appropriate county elections official, but what information must be forwarded is not specified. The bill requires each county's superior court clerk to notify the Secretary of State monthly of all findings made by the court regarding any person's competency to vote and the total number of court proceedings since the clerk's last report. The Judicial Council, consulting with the Secretary, must adopt related rules and create related forms. The forms must enable the clerks to report:
    • All known first names, middle names, last names, and name suffixes of the voter.
    • The voter's last known address.
    • The voter's date of birth.
    • The last four digits of the voter's Social Security number and their driver's license number or state ID number, if available.
    • The court case number, the date of the order affecting the person's voting rights, which section of the election code the order is made under, and whether the order disqualifies or restores the person's ability to vote.
    • A certification, if applicable, that the individual has been disqualified from voting due to the court's finding by clear and convincing evidence that the individual is incapable, with or without reasonable accommodations, to communicate a desire to participate in the voting process.
  • Changes how the Secretary uses information about mental incapacity by specifying what information must match for a voter's registration to be flagged for possible cancellation or restoration and imposing a timetable. Under the bill, the Secretary identifies a match only if a registered voter in the statewide list matches a person in the clerk's report with regard to every datapoint provided. The Secretary must complete the matching process and notify the relevant county elections official within three days of receiving the information from the court clerk. The county elections official then sends the pre-cancelation notice to the voter or a notice of restoration, as applicable, and takes further steps according to the result of the notice. Existing law did not identify what information must match nor did it set the timetable for notice to the county election official.

  • Creates a new responsibility to give people notice that their voting rights have been restored. Specifically, if a county elections official receives notice from the Secretary that someone in the county has had their voting rights restored, the official must notify the individual and provide information on how to register. If the address in the notice from the Secretary is different from the voter's address in county records, the election official must send notice to both addresses.

    Relatedly, the bill would create two safe harbors. Specifically:

  • A county or county elections official is not liable for canceling a registration or sending a notice of restoration, or failing to do either, when the county or county elections official received erroneous information from the Secretary of State.

  • A person who is ineligible to vote but is officially notified by the process that they are eligible, who subsequently registers or preregisters to vote, and then votes or attempts to vote, is presumed to have acted with official authorization and has not committed a crime, unless they know they are not eligible and attempt to vote anyway.

    Finally, the bill requires the Secretary of State to create a report and develop an annual training for court and county election officials. The report must indicate the number of voting rights disqualifications and the number of voting rights restorations for felony and mental incapacity reasons since the last report and would be available on the Secretary's website. The training, developed in consultation with the Judicial Council, will educate court and county election officials about the legal standards for voting rights disqualification, the duties of court investigators, and the reporting requirements for courts related to voting rights disqualification and restoration.

    Last updated September 30, 2022

HISTORY: {"date":"09/26/2022","summary":"Chaptered by Secretary of State.  Chapter No. 2022-554","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on September 26, 2022, attempts to protect election workers by creating three ways election workers of various types can keep their personal information confidential. First, certain election workers can keep their address, phone, and email as included in their voter registration record confidential on the same terms that police officers can. Second, precinct board members whose names were publicly posted under existing law will no longer have their names so posted. Last, the bill expands an existing robust confidentiality program to include people who face threats of violence or harassment from the public because of their work for a public entity, explicitly including election workers.

The first program allows "qualified election workers" to keep their residence address, phone, and email in their registration record confidential for two years at a time, renewable upon application. To participate in this address confidentiality program, the election worker, election officer, or their immediate relative, must attest in their application that they are a qualified election worker and that a life-threatening circumstance applies to them or their family. Precinct board members are not "qualified" for this purpose, but anyone working for the Secretary of State or a local election office who performs election-related work and interacts with the public or is observed by the public doing election-related work is, even if they have non-election duties as well. The Secretary of State must report on the number of applications, the number of participants in each county, and any allegations of misuse. Under existing law, police officers have a similar opportunity.

The second program requires the lists of precinct workers posted for each election to contain the workers' party preference but not their names. Existing law required posting their names as well as party preference. The bill does not alter existing law's other requirements for how the list is updated, posted, and archived.

The third program is an expansion of a program that protects reproductive health care workers to offer the program's protections to anyone who, because of their work for a public entity, faces threats or violence. That program enables a participant to use a Secretary of State address as their official legal address, and designate the Secretary as their agent for service of process. Participants in the program can have their voter registration information made confidential upon showing their program certification. A person is generally in the program for four years and may reapply, but a minor in the program must renew upon turning 18. The Secretary of State must report to the Legislature annually on the number of applications, the number of participants in each county, and any allegations of misuse.

To participate in this address confidentiality program, a person must apply in person and receive counseling. The application must include:

  • Documentation that the person or their immediate relative is about to begin employment or contract work at, or is already employed at or works as a contractor at, a public entity in an occupation where workers have faced threats of violence or harassment from the public because of that work.
  • One of three types of certified statements:
    • a certified statement by a person affiliated with the applicant's place of work stating that the office or any of its employees is or was the target of threats or acts of violence or harassment within one year of the date of the application,
    • a certified statement signed by the worker that they have been targeted within one year of the date of the application because of their election work, or
    • a workplace violence restraining order that was based on threats or violence connected to the applicant's work. The bill criminalizes falsely attesting to any of these forms as a misdemeanor.
  • A sworn statement that the applicant fears for their safety or the safety of their family because of their election work affiliation. The bill criminalizes falsely attesting as a misdemeanor.
  • A designation of the Secretary of State as agent for purposes of service of process and receipt of mail.
  • The mailing address and phone number where the applicant can be contacted by the Secretary of State.

  • The address or addresses that the applicant requests not be disclosed.

Last Updated September 29, 2022

This bill, as amended on April 6, 2022, improves voting access for people with certain disabilities. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Allow the Secretary of State to certify a voting method that enabled certain disabled people to complete and return a ballot remotely, privately, independently, and electronically. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require county election officials to offer the certified system to qualifying voters. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

  • Allow the covered disabled voters, if no such system is available in their county, to return their ballot by fax. To be counted, the ballot must be received by the elections official by the close of polls on Election Day and be accompanied by a signed voter's certificate. This is a new provision.

This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 7, 2022, would completely overhaul how Colorado conducts elections, eliminating in-person early voting and ending the current mail ballot election system. The bill would require ballots to be cast in person on Election Day generally, and create an excuse-based mail ballot system for those who could not vote in person on Election Day. In addition, the bill would require all ballots to be counted by hand and would withdraw the state from the Electronic Registration Information Center. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require voters to show state-issued ID to receive a ballot and generally require them to vote in person, on Election Day, at the polling place assigned to their precinct. Despite this requirement, the bill would have counties send all registered voters ballots 22 days before Election Day. The voter would not be allowed to cast the ballot, however, without appearing at their polling place and showing ID. Under existing law, all registered voters are mailed ballots without applying for them, may complete and return the ballots by mail or by dropping them off at drop boxes or voter service and polling centers. In addition, they may choose to vote in-person at voter service and polling centers that open 15 days before Election Day. If they vote in person, they must show ID to receive a ballot, but ID types beyond state-issued ID are allowed.
  • Impose several requirements relating to in-person voting locations, specifically:
    • Prohibiting vote centers, allowing precinct-based polling places only. Under existing law, counties offer voter service and polling centers, at which any voter in the county may vote if they prefer to vote in person.
    • Requiring a polling place within every precinct, except that if none are available the polling place can be sited in an adjacent precinct. Public schools would be required to provide space for a polling place if asked.
    • Prohibiting changing a polling place unless the voters in the relevant precinct are notified by mail at least two years in advance. Nonetheless, the bill appears to also allow for changing polling places for necessity, and for emergency polling places if an "act of God" renders a polling place unusable.
    • Requiring voters to be assigned to election precincts, and limiting the number of voters per election precinct to 1,500 when initially assigned. The bill would allow clerks to later combine or split precincts.
    • Requiring voters generally to use paper ballots, limiting electronic voting machines to people who need them to be able to vote independently.
    • Restricting who may be within 100 feet of a polling place, prohibiting certain behavior within the boundary, and creating a misdemeanor to enforce the rules.
    • Prohibiting election officials from requiring that a voter, election worker, election judge, or any other person wear a facial mask at a polling place or other voting or tabulation location or be vaccinated or tested for a virus as a condition of entering a polling place or other voting or tabulating location.
  • Limit voting by mail to people with any one of a list of excuses that explain their inability to vote in person at their precinct polling place on Election Day. Allowed excuses would be:
    • the voter expects to be outside this state at the time of the election.
    • the voter is unable to go to the polls because they are hospitalized or in a nursing home.
    • the voter has a visual impairment.
    • the voter is covered by the uniformed and overseas citizens absentee voter act.
  • Require applications for absentee ballots to be received by 5 p.m. on the 11th day before the election. If the application is not complete, the clerk would be required to attempt to notify the voter. However, if a voter experiences an emergency between 5 p.m on the Friday before the election and 5 p.m. on the Monday before that prevents them from voting at their precinct polling place on Election Day, they would be allowed to show ID, attest to the emergency, and then vote using a procedure chosen by the clerk. Under existing law, voters do not apply for ballots. If they will be away, they inform the clerk where to send their ballot.
  • Create a misdemeanor to prohibit voters from giving their completed absentee ballot to anyone to return for them. Specifically, it would be a misdemeanor to receive a ballot from anyone other than an election official. Under existing law, voters may choose anyone to return their ballot for them, provided no one returns more than 10 ballots.
  • Create a misdemeanor to prohibit clerks from sending absentee ballots to voters who do not apply for them according to the rules. Existing law has no parallel as ballots are mailed to voters without voters applying for them.
  • Require absentee ballots to be returned by the close of polls on Election Day and require the voter to sign the certificate on the ballot envelope. These provisions parallel existing law for mail ballots.
  • Limit absentee voters' ability to get a replacement ballot to a ballot replacement center that is open from 6 a.m. to 7 p.m. on the day of the election. To receive the replacement ballot, the voter would attest that the original was lost, spoiled, destroyed, or not received. Under existing law, voters may obtain replacement ballots before Election Day and may obtain them at multiple locations.
  • Withdraw the state from the Electronic Registration Information Center (ERIC), a multi-state partnership to improve the accuracy of voter rolls. Colorado has been a member of ERIC since its founding in 2012.
  • Repeal a prohibition on trying to get a voter to reveal how they voted, and a related prohibition on election officials, watchers, or anyone else revealing how someone voted. The bill would create a new misdemeanor to criminalize knowingly soliciting a voter to show the voter's ballot, or receiving from a voter a ballot prepared for voting unless the person is an election official or otherwise authorized by law. The bill would create another new misdemeanor to criminalize showing another voter's ballot to any person after it is prepared for voting, revealing the votes, except to an authorized person lawfully assisting the voter.
  • Create two felonies. One forbids a person from knowingly forging or counterfeiting the returns of an election, and the other forbids knowingly substituting, forging, counterfeiting, or tampering with election results by electronic means.
  • Creates misdemeanors to punish:
    • a voter who makes a false statement as to the voter's inability to mark a ballot.
    • a voter who interferes with another voter within the 100 foot limit of a polling place or within 100 feet of the main outside entrance to a voting location.
    • anyone who tries, within the 100-foot limit, to induce a voter to vote for or against a candidate or issue.
    • a voter who, before the close of an election, defaces or destroys a sample ballot posted by election officers or defaces, tears down, removes, or destroys a card of instructions posted for voters.
    • a voter who removes or destroys supplies or conveniences furnished to enable a voter to prepare the voter's ballot.
    • a voter who hinders the voting of others.
    • a voter who votes in a county in which the voter no longer resides.
    • a voter who fails to return their ballot to the election official before leaving the polling place or on-site voting location.
    • anyone who intentionally disables or removes from the polling place, on-site voting location, or custody of an election official a voting machine or a voting record.
  • Require ballots to be counted by hand by precinct and the returns made within 24 hours of the polls closing.
  • Require election judges to compare the number of paper ballots cast with the number of votes cast as noted in the statewide voter registration database.
  • Require special anti-fraud ballot paper and create new rules for authorizing, testing, and using electronic voting machines.

  • Set forth rules for observing proceedings at the counting center, and require live video recording of the custody of the ballots while they are in a tabulation room.

Last Updated March 2, 2022

This bill, as enacted on June 2, 2022, creates new criminal offenses related to misconduct against election officials, and permits officials to keep their personal information private. Specifically, the bill:

  • Creates a new misdemeanor offense for threatening, coercing, or intimidating an election official, in writing or verbally, or attempting such conduct, with the intent to:

    • impede or interfere with the official while the official is performing their duties, or
    • retaliate against the official for their performance of their duties.

    The offense does not apply to enforcement actions taken by the Secretary of State or by a designated election official against an election judge for a violation of a statute, rule promulgated by the Secretary, or of the election judge's oath.

  • Allows an election official or election worker (with the exception of temporary employees of local jurisdictions or the secretary of state) to request removal of their personal information, and that of their immediate family, from state or local records that are available on the internet. The request must be in writing and include an affirmation that the election official has reason to believe dissemination of the information poses "imminent and serious threat" to their safety. Protected personal information includes the official's home address, home and mobile phone numbers, pager number, personal email, photograph, directions to their home, and photographs or descriptions of their home, vehicle, or vehicle license plates. State or local officials who receive such a request are prohibited from knowingly making the information available, subject to certain exceptions for insurance and settlement entities.

  • Creates a new misdemeanor offense for an individual to knowingly make available on the internet personal information about an election official or election worker, or their immediate family, if the dissemination of personal information poses an imminent and serious threat to the safety of the election official or the election official's immediate family, and the person making the information available knows or reasonably should know of the imminent and serious threat.

    A previous version of the bill contained a provision that was amended out prior to enactment. That provision would have created a presumption that disclosing the information to a non-exempt party posed an imminent and serious threat to the safety of the election official or their immediate family, if a federal, state, or local law enforcement agency has issued a safety advisory or warning for election officials that is in effect and applies to the election official.

This bill, as enacted on June 2, 2022, expands state oversight of local election officials, increases the qualifications and training of local election officials, mandates new election equipment security procedures, and creates new crimes to enforce the new security procedures. Note: In the wake of the 2020 election, security issues and conflict arose between the Mesa County Clerk and the Secretary of State over election equipment access the clerk gave to an unauthorized person. That clerk and other employees of that office currently face criminal charges. Similar issues are being raised in other localities.

Specifically, the bill:

  • Creates an expedited process to enable the Secretary of State, through litigation brought by the Attorney General, to enforce the election code by seeking injunctions. Under existing law, these suits followed ordinary civil procedure.
  • Changes requirements relating to the "certification program" administered by the Secretary of State, which educates election officials on election procedures and compliance with federal law. Specifically, the bill:
    • Expands who must be certified to conduct elections, by requiring certification for a designated election official for a county, a coordinated election official for a county, and, at the Secretary's discretion, employees in the election division of the Department of State. The bill also "strongly encourage[s]" the Secretary to obtain certification. Existing law required certification for only the county clerk and recorder, their employees who are directly responsible for overseeing elections, and other employees at the discretion of clerks and recorders.
    • Requires certifications to be completed sooner than previously required under existing law. Under the bill, certification must be completed within one year of undertaking responsibilities that trigger the requirement, except that county or deputy clerks must complete the certification before serving as a designated election official or coordinated election official, or within six months of taking office, whichever is sooner. Existing law required certification within two years of coming within the requirement.
    • Prohibits individuals from serving as a designated election official or coordinated election official unless they have completed and maintained their certification. The Secretary may waive this requirement for individuals appointed to the elections official role three months or less before an election.
    • Expands the certification curriculum to include voter registration and list maintenance, accessibility, coordinated elections, mail ballot and in-person voting processes, voting systems testing, risk-limiting audits, and the canvass. Under existing law, the curriculum addressed only general election law, the federal Help America Vote Act of 2002, and professional development.
  • Prohibits individuals from serving as the designated election official for a county or as the coordinated election official for a county if they have been convicted of an election offense under any state's law, or if they have been convicted of any offense or conspiracy to commit sedition, insurrection, treason, conspiracy to overthrow the government by use of force or violence, or any similar federal offense.
  • Expands the existing misdemeanor offense for willful interference with, or willful refusal to comply with, rules from the Secretary of State or their agent, to also include non-compliance with orders or acceptable use policy for the statewide voter registration system.
  • Creates a new misdemeanor offense for willfully interfering with, obstructing, or retaliating against any person who is notifying the Department of State that they reasonably believe a potential violation relating to the rules, orders, or acceptable use policy for the statewide voter registration has occurred or will occur.
  • Creates new felonies relating to tampering with voting equipment. Specifically, the bill:
    • Creates a new felony offense for tampering with, accessing without authorization, or granting unauthorized access to, electronic or electromechanical voting equipment or an election-night reporting system. This new felony offense replaces an existing misdemeanor offense that prohibited tampering with electronic voting equipment with the intent to change vote tabulation to reflect inaccurate results.
    • Creates a new felony offense for knowingly publishing or causing to be published passwords or other confidential information relating to a voting system. The bill also automatically revokes authorized access for engaging in the prohibited conduct.
  • Creates a process that would allow the Secretary to review and certify results for a county when a majority of a canvassing board in a county is unable to or does not certify the abstract of votes for any reason by the deadline. The bill would allow the Secretary to delegate this authority to a registered Colorado voter, after consulting with the relevant board of county commissioners.
  • Creates new security rules for election equipment storage involving key card access and video surveillance.
  • Forbids a county from creating or allowing any person to create an image of any voting system component's hard drive without the express written permission of the Department of State.
  • Generally requires the use of ballot tabulators and clarifies when ballots may be counted by hand instead of using tabulation equipment.

  • Appropriates $1,117,000 to the Department of State to implement the provisions of the bill, $1 million of which is allocated for compliance with new security measures.

This bill, as enacted on April 8, 2022, expands the statutory excuses required to vote absentee. Specifically, the bill:

  • Expands the general requirements for voting absentee by requiring that a qualified voter must be unable to appear for in-person voting on the day of an election. Existing law required a voter to be unable to appear "during all the hours of voting."
  • Expands the existing illness excuse by eliminating the requirement that a voter personally be ill and instead permitting absentee voting on the broad ground of "sickness." Under current interpretation of state law, sickness includes caregiving for another ill person and exposure to disease, such as Covid-19.
  • Expands the existing disability excuse by eliminating the requirement that a voter personally be disabled and instead permitting absentee voting on the broad ground of "disability." Current interpretation of disability in the voting context includes caregiving for another disabled individual, and frailty due to old age or a medical condition.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as reissued on April 13, 2022, would create a state voting rights act with certain explicit protections for historically disenfranchised groups. The bill, as amended, retains many provisions of the bill as introduced, but modifies others as described below. Specifically, the bill, as amended, would:

  • Require preclearance by the judiciary or the Secretary of State before certain covered jurisdictions are permitted to make certain electoral changes. A covered jurisdiction is one that:
    • has, in the past 25 years, been subject to any court order or governmental enforcement action based on a violation of the right to vote or protected class discrimination set forth of this bill, the federal Voting Rights Act, state or federal civil rights laws, the 14th or 15th Amendments to the U.S. Consistution,
    • has failed to provide data to the statewide database established by this bill in the previous five years,
    • has disproportionate arrest rates of protected class members based on metrics set forth in this bill in the previous ten years, or
    • has an inadequate dissimilarity index (which measures racial segregation) based on metrics set forth in this bill in the previous ten years.

      A covered jurisdiction must seek judicial review before it enacts changes to its laws or policies regarding:
    • redistricting,
    • method of election,
    • form of government,
    • annexation, incorporation, dissolution, consolidation, or division of the municipality.
    • removal of individuals from voter lists or other activities concerning the voter list,
    • admission of electors,
    • number, location, or hours of a polling place,
    • assignment of districts to polling place locations,
    • assistance offered to voters in a protected class, or
    • any other matter identified for preclearance by the Secretary of State following formal rulemaking.
      When considering a preclearance request, the decider must provide notice of the proceedings, provide an opportunity for comment by interested parties (if the Secretary of State is the decider), and must decide within enumerated time frames. Preclearance may only be granted if the policy will not diminish the ability of voters in a protected class to participate in the electoral process or elect their preferred candidates.
  • Explicitly prohibit any voting laws or practices that result in the denial or abridgment of the right to vote for a person in a protected class. This includes laws and practices that impair the ability of voters in a protected class to elect candidates of their choice or to influence the outcome of elections. The bill would also prohibit methods of election that impair the ability of voters in a protected class to elect candidates of their choice or to influence the outcome of elections. Laws and practices that violate this provision include, but are not limited to:
    • At-large elections in municipalities with racially polarized voting or when this method of voting, based on the totality of circumstances, impairs the ability of voters in a protected class to elect candidates of their choice or to influence the outcome of elections.
    • District-based elections or alternative methods of elections in which the candidates of choice for voters in a protected class would usually be defeated if the municipality has racially polarized voting or when this method of voting, based on the totality of circumstances, impairs the ability of voters in a protected class to elect candidates of their choice or to influence the outcome of elections.
  • Prohibit the use of race, color, language, or any characteristic as a proxy for race, color, or language minority group for redistricting, except when those characteristics were used only to the extent necessary to comply with the federal Voting Rights Act, the federal or state Constitutions, or this bill.
  • Require municipalities to provide language assistance to language minority groups. Language assistance required by this bill includes voting materials in the minority language and oral supports for any unwritten minority language. A municipality contains a language minority group if:
    • more than 2% of citizens of voting age in the municipality "are members of a single language minority group and speak English 'less than very well,'"
    • more than 4,000 citizens of voting age in the municipality "are members of a single language minority group and speak English 'less than very well,'" or
    • the municipality contains any portion of a Native American reservation and more than 2% of the Native American citizens of voting age on the reservation "are members of a single language minority group and speak English 'less than very well.'"
      The amended version of the bill contains a new provision not in the previous version of the bill which would create a cause of action in any member of a language minority to enforce the language minority requirements.
  • Peg the definition of a protected class to 52 U.S.C. 10301. In the previous version of the bill, protected class was broadly defined as a group consisting of members of a race, color or language minority group.
  • Create a cause of action, along with procedures to institute, advance, and/or settle that cause of action, for violation of the terms of this bill in:
    • a voter in a protected class,
    • an organization whose membership includes voters in a protected class,
    • an organization whose mission would be frustrated by a violation of this bill,
    • an organization that would expend resources to fulfill its mission if this bill were violate, or
    • the State Elections Enforcement Commission. Under the previous version of the bill, the office of the Secretary of the State was the agency that had a cause of action to enforce the provisions of this bill.
  • Grant courts broad power to fashion remedies for violations of this bill, such as:
    • changing the municipality's method of election,
    • revising districting or redistricting plans,
    • changing the timing of the municipality's elections or the hours for elections,
    • increasing the size of the legislative body,
    • requiring additional polling locations,
    • ordering special elections, and
    • restoring or adding people to voter rolls.

      Courts may also award fees and costs to prevailing parties other than the state or a municipality.
  • Create a new civil offense for any person to engage in intimidation, deception, or obstruction that affects the rights of voters to exercise their right to vote. Any aggrieved person, affected organizations, or the State Elections Enforcement Commission may file an action in court on the basis of such a violation, and the court may order appropriate remedies tailored to address the violation. Violators shall also be liable for damages including nominal damages and compensatory or punitive damages for willful violations. This is a modified provision - the previous version of the bill granted the Secretary of the State, not the State Elections Enforcement Commission, the cause of action for voter intimidation, deception, and obstruction.
  • Require that all municipalities that are changing their voting method or redistricting must hold at least two public meetings before drawing new boundaries, must make draft plans available to the public, and hold at least two public hearings after drawing new boundaries.

  • Create a statewide database of information regarding population, demographics, election results, registry lists, maps, polling place locations, redistricting plans, and additional information to assist municipalities with creating and implementing legal elections practices. This database will be housed within the Office of the Secretary of State and managed by an employee of that office who must meet certain qualifications. The amended version of the bill slightly eases the qualifications required of the database manager. The amended version of the bill also clarifies that ultimate responsibility rests with the Secretary of the State and not with the administrator of the database. Finally, the amended version of the bill adds to the Secretary of the State's reporting requirements for the statewide database, to require reporting the legislative committees of cognizance upon launch, in addition to the requirement, retained from the previous version of the bill, that the Secretary of the State publish online a report of municipalities required to offer language assistance, and the languages required.

This bill, as signed by the mayor on December 28, 2022, and enacted at the end of the Congressional review process on March 10, 2023, expands the existing automatic voter registration system by providing for automatic "preapproval" of registration through transactions at various city agencies, creates new rules regarding activation of preapproved registration, and makes various minor changes to the existing automatic registration process.

Specifically, the bill:

  • Establishes a new procedure for automatically preapproving eligible individuals for registration through certain city agency transactions, if they are not automatically registered during the transaction itself. Previous law had no procedure for preapproved registration - only automatic full registration through the DMV, Dept. of Corrections, and other designated agencies. The bill:
    • Requires the DMV, Dept. of Health Care Finance, and other designated agencies to provide information to the Board of Elections for any individual who meets voter eligibility criteria but is not automatically registered, and unless determined to be ineligible to vote, requires the Board to designate these individuals automatically preapproved for registration. Note that existing law requires the DMV to provide the opportunity to decline automatic voter registration during a transaction. The bill does not make an express exception to automatic preapproved registration for individuals who were not enrolled due to opting out.
    • Requires the Board to issue notice of preapproval to the individual, including instructions on how to be removed from the list, how to "activate" their registration, and how to request that their information on the preapproval list be kept confidential.
    • Permits preapproved registrants to activate their registration online, by mail return of the notification form, in person at the Board's office, in person at a vote center, or by returning a mail ballot.
    • For mail ballot activation, requires preapproved registrants with no signature on file to provide the last four digits of their social security number on the ballot, in addition to the required signature, and deems this signature the signature on file going forward.
    • For in-person activation at a vote center, expressly provides that preapproved registrants are not required to show proof of residence and may select a party affiliation prior to voting. Previous law required any individual registering for the first time at a polling place to provide proof of residence, and required party affiliation 21 days before an election. Individuals who activate their preapproved registration at the polling place and have no signature on file must provide either their DMV-issued ID number or last four digits of their social security number.
    • Deems preapproved registrants ineligible to sign nominating petitions for a candidate, or petitions for an initiative, referendum, or recall, and provides that signing such petitions does not activate a preapproved registration.
    • Requires the Board to implement procedures to regularly update the preapproved list with information from various sources.
  • Requires election officials to automatically send preapproved registrants a mail-in ballot for general elections in the four years after they are added to the list.
  • Changes the limitations on registration within 21 days of an election, for preapproved individuals who are activating their registration during this period. Under previous law, during the 21 days before an election, individuals could not change their party affiliation and new registration applications could only be made in person. The bill permits preapproved voters to activate their registration during this 21 day window by mail, online, or in person, and choose a party affiliation.
  • Revises various provisions related to procedures for new registrations to also include activation of preapproved registration.
  • Eliminates the option for individuals to decline updating their existing voter registration when updating relevant information at the DMV, and requires various city agencies (and federal agencies by agreement) to convey change of name and address information to the Board of Elections for automatic updates. The Board is required to issue the voter notice of the update, and "immediately" make any corrections provided by the voter.
  • Directs the Board of Elections and DMV to develop a procedure for determining whether an applicant at the DMV is pre-registered or registered to vote at the address provided to the agency. Previous law required automatic registration through DMV transactions, but did not expressly specify agency coordination to determine an applicant's registration status.
  • Requires the Board of Elections to use information from the Dept. of Health Care Finance and other agencies, in addition to existing sources, to identify voters who have updated their name or address, as part of routine voter list maintenance.

  • Expressly prohibits automatic voter registration agencies from registering individuals who indicate they are non-U.S. citizens and/or provide documentation of non-citizenship. Previous law required the automatic registration process to gather information regarding an applicant's citizenship, but did not include these express provisions.

This bill, as enacted on April 1, 2022, draws new state legislative maps based on the results of the 2020 census.

Last updated April 4, 2022.

Note: This legislation was blocked from going into effect by the Delaware Supreme Court on October 7, 2022.

 

This bill, as enacted on July 22, 2022, establishes no-excuse absentee voting ("voting by mail") for general elections, non-presidential primary elections, and certain special elections. These provisions largely reenact the temporary provisions put in place for 2020 elections. Specifically, the bill:

  • Permits any qualified, duly registered voter to request and cast a mail ballot. Under existing law, voting by mail was available only to absentee voters with a qualifying excuse. The bill leaves the excuse-required absentee system in place, alongside no-excuse mail voting.
  • Requires voters to provide on both their mail ballot applications and on their ballot envelopes either the last four digits of their Social Security number or their state-issued driver's license or non-driver ID number. Existing law for excuse-required absentee ballots, which remains unchanged by the bill, does not require voters to provide an identification number for requesting or returning an absentee ballot.
  • Requires applicants to complete a handwritten or electronic application form, sign and date the form, and return the application to the Department of Elections by the deadline set by the agency to submit their request (currently, seven days before an election). Existing law for excuse-required absentee ballots requires application by 12 p.m. the day before an election. Note: While the bill does not require, or expressly permit, officials to offer electronic applications, the Department of Elections permits application for mail ballots, as well as absentee ballots, through its online portal.
  • Directs county officials to send ballots to applicants between 30 and seven days before an election, and requires sending ballots within three days of the receipt of an application during this period, if required materials are available. The bill specifies that officials are not prohibited from sending ballot materials to voters who apply less than seven days before an election. Under existing law applicable to excuse-required absentee ballots, officials are required to issue ballots between 60 and four days prior to an election.
  • Requires the Department of Elections to provide pre-paid postage mail ballot return envelopes in the ballot package, as required for absentee ballots under existing law.
  • Directs county election officials to begin verifying and opening mail ballot envelopes 30 days before Election day. Under existing law for excuse-required absentee ballots, which the bill does not change, officials may not begin verifying absentee ballot envelopes until the Friday before an election.
  • Establishes the same requirements for mail ballots as currently apply under existing law to excuse-required absentee ballots for:
    • rejection of mail ballots
    • tabulation of ballots cast for the wrong district
    • maintenance of ballot records "for the prevention of fraud"
    • "politically balanced" election judges
    • standards for tabulation equipment
    • online ballot tracking
  • Expressly authorizes the use of drop boxes for the return of mail ballots. Existing law was silent as to drop boxes for absentee ballots, although their use was temporarily authorized in 2020.

The bill also contains provisions regarding election equipment and the handling of ballots that are not tracked by Voting Rights Lab.

Last Updated October 19, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2022, would require a "forensic audit" by an "independent third party" of the 2020 general election in every county with a population of 250,000 or more. This threshold would make the bill applicable to 24 of Florida's 67 counties.

The bill does not specify any qualifications for the third party, nor does it identify any standards or processes for the review of the 2020 election. The bill requires the review to begin by April 15, 2022 and be completed within 60 days. Thirty days after the completion of the review, the third party would be required to submit a report to the Governor, the President of the Senate, the Speaker of the House of Representatives, the Secretary of State, the Division of Elections, and each supervisor of elections detailing any anomalies or discrepancies in voter data, ballot data, or tabulation.

Last updated January 17, 2022..

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2022, would require high schools to teach their students how to use the online voter registration system to register or preregister to vote. As part of the lesson, schools would be required to include the opportunity to register using the system.

Last Updated January 11, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2022, would make a voter's email, phone number, party affiliation, and day of birth confidential. The voter's month and year of birth would not be protected. Only certain people or entities could request the newly confidential information, and then only for specified purposes. To obtain the information, those people would be required to sign an affidavit taking responsibility for ensuring that the information is only used as authorized. The people and entities allowed to request the newly confidential information would be:

  • The voter.
  • A canvassing board or an election official acting in his or her official capacity, for official purposes only.
  • A political party or official thereof, a candidate who has filed qualification papers, an elected official, or a political committee, for political purposes only.

  • A person who receives permission to access the information from the office of the Secretary of State, for any purpose authorized by such office.

Last Updated January 11, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2022, would make applying for a mail ballot easier by allowing people to apply as part of their voter registration application and on the return envelope of their mail ballot, and make changes to the timing and process of calling special elections. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the department of state to update the uniform statewide voter registration application to include a checkbox for an applicant to request a vote by mail ballot.
  • Require the online voter registration system to allow an applicant to check a box to request a mail ballot.
  • Require the return envelope for a mail ballot to have a preprinted statement and check box a voter could use to request additional mail ballots through the end of the next general election.

  • Make changes to the process and timeline of calling special elections to fill vacancies, an area Voting Rights Lab does not track.

Last Updated January 11, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2022, would make substantial changes throughout the election code, including creating same day registration, automatic voter registration, a permanent absentee voter list, and much more. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create same day registration during early voting or on election day, without specifying any new registration requirements, or whether a same day registrant would vote a regular ballot or a provisional ballot.
  • Create automatic voter registration and pre-registration at the DMV. The applicant would have an opportunity to opt out of registration during the transaction.
  • Create a permanent absentee ballot list by allowing a voter to request to receive mail ballots until they cancel their request or first class mail sent to the voter by the supervisor of elections is returned as undeliverable.
  • Change applying for a mail ballot more generally by:
    • making the deadline to apply for a mail ballot from 5 p.m. on the 10th day before Election Day to 5 p.m. on the 11th day before Election Day.
    • allowing a voter's designee to pick up as many ballots as voters have designated them to pick up, repeal paperwork requirements, and extend the time period in which a designee may act to match the new deadline. Under existing law a designee may only pick up two ballots per election other than their own or for members of their immediate family, the designee must submit a written authorization from the voter and a photo ID, must complete an affidavit themselves, and may pick up the ballot for a voter anytime between Election Day and nine days before an election.
    • providing that if the deadline falls on a day the office of the supervisor is usually closed, the deadline is extended until the next business day.
  • Require the county to prepay the return postage for mail ballots.
  • Allow voters to choose to validate their mail ballots by signing the oath with either their signature or the last four digits of their Social Security number (SSN4).
  • Revise the required instructions for mail ballots to include the option to sign using an SSN4.
  • Revise ballot canvassing and cure provisions to enable a ballot to be counted if it is signed using an SSN4 instead of the voter's signature. Specifically, ballots may be counted if signed with an SSN4 that matches the voter's SSN4 on file, and if the number on the ballot does not match, the voter must be notified and given an opportunity to correct it using the existing process.
  • Repeal the ability of any voter or candidate to present at the canvassing of ballots to challenge ballots on the basis of the voter's certificate or cure affidavit.
  • Count provisional ballots completed by eligible voters if they completed a provisional ballot for the correct county, even if the appeared to vote at the wrong precinct in the county.
  • Prohibit siting a polling place in a gated community unless all voters assigned to it live within the gated community.
  • Explicitly allow people to give voters food, water, or other items, so long as the voters are standing in line to vote and are outside the no-solicitation zone.
  • Prohibit bullhorns and other sound amplification devices in close proximity to a polling place during voting hours and an office of the supervisor of elections during a recount.
  • Require the Division of Elections to maintain a strategic elections equipment reserve, including tabulation machines, printers, and other equipment, that can be deloped in case of emergency or because of capacity issues created by unexpected voter turnout.
  • Change voter registration by requiring a voter to select a political party or affirmatively select no party affiliation. Supervisors of elections would be prohibited from registering a voter who does not make an affirmative choice, and require the supervisor to notify the voter that they must complete a new application and make the affirmative choice. Under existing law, registrants who do not pick a party are automatically registered unaffiliated.
  • Change voter registration drives by:
    • Repealing a requirement that organizations doing voter registration drives make specific statements to applicants during the registration process. Existing law requires groups to state that they might not return the form on time and advise the applicant that the applicant can return the form. In addition, existing law requires the organization to explain how register online, and how to determine if their voter registration application has been delivered.
    • Repealing a fine that could be levied against an organization doing a voter registration drive if they do not submit the forms to the division of elections or the supervisor of elections in the county in which the voter lives.
  • Give voters more time before their names are removed from the voter registration list by providing that a voter's registration cannot be marked inactive unless they have not participated two consecutive general elections, in addition to failing to return the address confirmation final notice card or the final notice is returned undeliverable. Under existing law a voter's registration may be marked inactive based on the final notice regardless of a voter's voting history. Once a voter's registration is marked "inactive", they may reactivate it, but if they do not reactivate it by the second general election after the registration was marked inactive, their registration is canceled.
  • Interferes with local election administration by creating a new cause of action that allows any voter or any candidate to sue the relevant supervisor of elections for noncompliance with election law. Plaintiffs would be entitled to an immediate hearing, and any filing fees or costs would be waived, and attorneys fees awarded to the prevailing party.
  • Shift election authority by making the Secretary of State, the highest election authority in Florida, elected rather than appointed by the Governor.
  • Make General Election Day a paid holiday.
  • Broaden the applicability of the special provisions of law that are currently applicable to UOCAVA voters only. The bill would repeal the words "uniformed services voter or an overseas" throughout the section, making the section apply to "absent voters". "Absent voter" is not a defined term in the bill. Under the bill, an absent voter's mail ballot for a presidential primary or a general election is timely if it is postmarked on or before Election Day and is returned within 10 days of Election Day. Under existing law, all mail ballots other than those from UOCAVA voters must be received by 7 p.m. on Election Day. The bill does not amend the provisions of law setting the general mail ballot return deadline.

  • Make changes to areas of election law Voting Rights Lab does not track, such as candidate filings, rules for filling vacancies, ballot initiative signature gathering, ballot design, and certification deadlines.

Last Updated August 2, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2022, would increase the transparency of the redistricting process by eliminating a public records exception for draft redistricting plans or amendments to plans and requests for drafts or amendments. In addition to allowing disclosure of those documents, the bill would make available any supporting documents associated with such plan or amendment. Under existing law, the supporting documents become available only after the plan or amendment is filed.

Last updated January 11, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2022 would effectively repeal substantial parts of the 2021 election law known as "SB 90". Specifically, the bill would:

  • Repeal the requirement that notice of litigation settlement negotiations, at various points in time, must be given to the President of the Senate, the Speaker of the House of Representatives, and the Attorney General. This provision would shift election-related authority away from those officers. The requirement that these officers be given a role in election-related litigation they had not chosen to intervene in was added to Florida law by SB 90.
  • Repeal the prohibition on using private funds for election related expenses. This provision was added to Florida law by SB 90.
  • Repeal a requirement that individuals and groups conducting registration drives notify applicants about the online voter registration system and make other disclosures. In addition the bill would maintain the requirement that registrations be delivered to the supervisor of elections within 14 days of collecting them, but repeal the prohibition on returning them after the deadline to register for the upcoming election. These disclosure requirements and delivery prohibition were added to Florida law by SB 90.
  • Repeal a requirement that a voter who wishes to update their address, name, or party affiliation give the supervisor of elections the last four digits of their Social Security number, their driver's license number, or their state ID number, whichever one the supervisor has on file. The requirement was added to Florida law by SB 90.
  • Repeal a prohibition on offering to help voters with their ballots within 150 feet of a drop box. The prohibition was added to Florida law by SB 90.
  • Repeal a requirement that voters applying for mail ballots must provide a driver's license number, state ID number, or the last four digits of their Social Security number, whichever may be verified in the supervisor of election's records. The requirement was added to Florida law by SB 90.
  • Repeal a prohibition on mailing mail ballots to voters who had not applied for them. This prohibition was added to Florida law by SB 90.
  • Repeal a requirement that the return mailing envelope for a mail ballot bear the voter's name, any encoded mark used by the supervisor's office, and not include the political party of the voter on the envelope. These provisions were added to Florida law by SB 90.
  • Repeal multiple provisions relating to drop boxes that were added to Florida law by SB 90. Specifically, the bill would:
    • repeal the time constraints for ballot drop box use for drop boxes other than at the office of the supervisor of elections.
    • repeal the requirement that drop boxes, wherever sited, be monitored by employees of the supervisor's office.
    • repeal the requirement that drop box locations be submitted to the division of elections at least 30 days before an election, and could not be changed later unless the division approves the move to correct a violation of drop box siting rules.
    • repeal rules about the timing of emptying drop boxes and chain of custody provisions.
    • repeal a $25,000 civil penalty for supervisors who operate a drop box out of compliance with drop box rules.
  • Repeal changes to the prohibition on soliciting voters that were made by SB 90. Specifically, the bill would:
    • repeal the application of the solicitation ban to within 150 of a drop box.
    • repeal the expansion of the definition of prohibited solicitation to include "engaging in any activity with the intent to influence or effect of influencing a voter.'
    • repeal language that allowed private property owners to prohibit anyone other than a candidate or candidate's designee from soliciting voters on their property, outside the no-solicitation zone, while their property is being used a voting location.

  • Eliminate restrictions on returning voters' ballots for them. Prior to SB 90, Florida law prohibited people from being compensated for returning more than two ballots other than their own or an immediate family member's. SB 90 tightened the restriction by prohibiting returning more than two such ballots regardless of compensation.

Last Updated August 2, 2022

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to restoration of voting rights, revises definition of term completion of all terms of sentence to remove provisions requiring full payment of certain fines and fees and providing payment is not deemed completed upon conversion of financial obligation to civil lien, respectively.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2022, would automatically restore the voting rights of more people who had been disenfranchised by a felony conviction by sharply reducing the barrier posed by legal financial obligations. Specifically, a person could regain their voting rights by completing incarceration, probation, and/or parole, and satisfying any outstanding restitution. They would no longer be required to satisfy any other legal financial obligation to regain their voting rights. A person could satisfy restitution by:

  • Paying in full,
  • Completing any community service ordered in lieu of financial payment, and

  • Having the obligation waived by the court, which is only possible with the victim's consent.

    The bill would also repeal a sentence in the code prohibiting restitution from being deemed satisfied upon its conversion to civil debt, which implies such conversion would also satisfy the debt and allow restoration.

    Under existing law, a person must satisfy all legal financial obligations--restitution, fines, and fees--in one of the three ways specified above before their voting rights are automatically restored. Also under existing law, none of the legal financial obligations may be deemed satisfied upon its conversion to civil debt.

    Last updated January 11, 2021.

This bill, as amended on February 28, 2022, changes several aspects of state election law. The bill, as amended, retains a number of the provisions from the previous version of the bill, alters some of the provisions from the previous version of the bill, and deletes other provisions from the previous version of the bill. Unless specifically noted, the provisions described below are unchanged from the previous version of the bill. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Increase the frequency of required voter list maintenance and expand the types of list maintenance local election officials must conduct beginning January 1, 2023. Under existing law, supervisors of election must conduct list maintenance every two years in odd-numbered years, using any of the three processes enumerated in statute. The first of these existing processes targets voters who may have moved through U.S. Postal Service national change of address data. The second existing process allows election officials to mail address confirmation to all registered voters and then target voters whose mailings are returned as undeliverable. The third existing process allows election officials to send mailings to voters who have not voted in the previous two years and to target voters whose mailings are returned as undeliverable. The previous version of the bill would have mandated both of the first two processes, conducted in alternating years, and would have retained the third process as an additional, optional list maintenance process. This bill, as amended, would:
    • Require that list maintenance be conducted either by using national change of address data or by sending address confirmation mailings to all registered voters and targeting, for removal, voters whose mailings are returned as undeliverable.
    • Require annual list maintenance activities using one of the two list maintenance processes authorized by the bill, as amended, as chosen by the supervisor of elections.
    • Require election officials who do not send address confirmation mailings to all voters for list maintenance to send mailings to voters who have not voted in the previous two general elections and to target voters whose mailings are returned as undeliverable for potential removal. This process would be conducted in odd-numbered years. Under existing law, this is one of the optional voter list maintenance processes election officials may choose. Under existing law, inactivity is based on not voting in the previous two years, rather than the two election-cycle period specified by the bill as amended. The previous version of the bill would have tracked existing law more closely by keeping this process optional and retaining the two-year inactivity benchmark from existing law.
    • Require that list maintenance mailings be sent to the voter's residential address, except for certain temporarily registered voters. If the initial mailing is returned as undeliverable, other notifications must be sent to the voter's mailing address. Existing law does not specify which address list maintenance mailings must be sent to. The previous version of the bill required some, but not all, initial address confirmation mailings to be sent to residential addresses.
    • Require the voters who have been placed on the inactive list to confirm their residential address before being restored to the active list. This confirmation is not required by existing law and did not appear in the previous version of the bill.
    • Require that election officials send an address confirmation final notice to all of a voter's addresses on file if an earlier address confirmation notice is returned as undeliverable or if the supervisor receives no response within 30 days of the notice.
    • Require that address confirmation requests include instructions for voters to update their registration online and instructions that the voter should return the confirmation request within 30 days.
    • Require address confirmation final notices to include an advisement that the voter may have to confirm their address of legal residence before voting if they fail to respond to the final notice.
  • Require interagency data sharing of information related to voter list maintenance by:
    • Requiring circuit court clerks to send election officials information about the terms of each felony sentence, including legal financial obligations, for any person in the clerk's records who resides in the state and has been convicted of a felony in the last month. Under existing law, circuit court clerks are not required to send this information to election officials, although it is relevant to people's ability to restore their voting eligibility. The previous version of the bill would have required circuit court clerks to provide this information for all people in their system, not just newly-convicted people.
    • Requiring the department of state to consider information received from the department of highway safety and motor vehicles when identifying deceased registered voters. Under existing law, the department of highway safety and motor vehicles is not a data source regarding deceased voters for the department of state.
    • Requiring the department of highway safety and motor vehicles to send election officials the name, address, date of birth, social security number, and driver's license number or state ID number of any person who transacts with the department of highway safety and motor vehicles and attests that they are a non-citizen. This information would be reported monthly.
  • Create an office of election crimes and security within the department of state, headed by a director appointed by the secretary of state and staffed with investigators who are not sworn law enforcement personnel. This office would have the responsibility to:
    • Oversee the voter fraud hotline, including investigating complaints.
    • Initiate and conduct investigations into voter fraud based on information from other sources.
    • Refer appropriate matters to prosecutors.
    • Report to the Governor, President of the Senate, and the Speaker detailing information on the investigations conducted by the Office.
  • Increase investigation of purported election crimes by requiring the governor, in consultation with the department of law enforcement, to appoint at least one sworn special officer to conduct election-related investigations in each region, in addition to having the authority to conduct other, non-election-related, duties. The bill, as amended, specifies that election-related investigations take precedence, a provision that did not appear in the previous version of the bill. Under existing law, the Governor currently has the discretion to appoint special law enforcement officers, but is not required to. These special officers would be subject to existing rules concerning law enforcement officers in polling locations.
  • Increase criminal and civil penalties for election offenses by:
    • Punishing, as a felony, collecting more than 2 mail ballots other than the person's own or that belonging to an immediate family member. This is a misdemeanor under existing law.
    • Punishing, as a felony, signing a fictitious name to a petition for a candidate, minor political party, or issue. This is a misdemeanor under existing law.
    • Punishing, as a felony, paying an initiative petition signature collector on a per signature basis. This is a misdemeanor under existing law.
    • Raising the cap on fines for certain violations by third-party registration organizations to $50,000. Under existing law, the cap is $1,000.
    • Creating a new $1,000 fine for any person who is convicted of the existing offense of collecting voter registration applications on behalf of a third-party organization who alters the voter registration application of any applicant without the applicant's consent. This fine is assessed for each application altered. This provision did not appear in the previous version of the bill.
  • Require the department of state to conduct a feasibility study on requiring ID numbers on mail ballots, including consideration of interagency data sharing, protection of voters' privacy, modifications to canvassing procedures, costs, and voter education. The department would be required to report the results of the study to legislative leaders by January 1, 2023. This study was required under the previous version of the bill, but details of the study were amended.
  • Modify the canvass observation process slightly by requiring observers at canvassing locations to sign an affidavit affirming their knowledge that disclosing election results observed while the election is ongoing is a felony.
  • Expand the existing prohibition on private funds for election-related expenses to further prohibit private funding of any election administration expense, including the costs of "any litigation related to election administration."
  • Prohibit ranked-choice voting for local, state, or federal elective office.
  • Repeal the existing law prohibiting election workers from asking voters for more information about their address if their voter ID address matches the address on file. This provision did not appear in the previous version of the bill.

  • Move the deadline for requesting supervised voting in an assisted living facility or nursing home earlier, from 21 days under existing law to 28 days under the amended version of the bill. This provision did not appear in the previous version of the bill.

    This bill also contains provisions not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, including provisions that would change petition signature verification processes and timing of county commissioner races after redistricting.

    The previous version of the bill contained provisions that would have changed mail ballot verification by requiring an additional envelope for returned mail ballots and requiring voters to include an ID number on their returned mail ballots. These provisions have been deleted in their entirety from the bill as amended. These provisions would have:

    • Imposed an additional layer of mail ballot verification on top of the existing signature match process. The bill would have required a voter to provide the last four digits of their state driver's license or state ID on a newly-created "certificate envelope" when returning their ballots. Voters who lacked these forms of ID would have been required to provide the last four digits of their Social Security number. If one of these numbers was not on the certificate envelope, it would have been rejected, even if voters wrote an ID number on the secrecy envelope for their mail ballot. The ID number requirement would have had at least two hidden consequences. First, voters who have at least one of these types of ID but do not have the number(s) on file would not have been able to successfully vote by mail at all. The bill attempted to mitigate this risk by requiring election officials to send mailings seeking this information every two years and also would require the department of state to report a plan to obtain these ID numbers for all registered voters to legislative leadership by January 1, 2023. A second hidden consequence would have been that voters who do not have any of these ID numbers can register to vote under existing law but would have been unable to successfully vote by mail in future elections.
    • Rejected any ballot that did not have a correct ID number on the certificate envelope, any ballot with an unsigned certificate envelope, and any ballot with a signature mismatch or missing signature on the certificate envelope. Under existing law, missing and mismatched signatures on the secrecy envelope lead to ballot rejection. The new ID match requirement would have had a hidden consequence: voters whose records contain only one ID number but who use an ID number from a different type of ID when returning the ballot would have had their ballot rejected.
    • Allowed voters to remedy ID number issues using the existing cure process for missing and mismatched signatures.
    • Required election officials to send an ID number solicitation to all voters who do not have a state driver's license number, a state ID number, or the last four digits of their social security number on file. This process would have been conducted every two years, in odd-numbered years. These mailings would have been sent to the voter's mailing address and would have been required to include a notice that willfully submitting false registration information is a third-degree felony.

Last Updated March 25, 2022

In addition, the bill would give people more time to register to vote by changing the deadline from 29 days before Election Day to 14 days before.
