This bill, as enacted on April 25, 2022, changes several aspects of state election law, primarily relating to voter registration list maintenance, election law enforcement, and drop boxes.

Regarding voter registration list maintenance, the bill:

  • Increases the frequency of mandatory voter list maintenance related to voter addresses and alters requirements for data sources. Specifically, beginning January 1, 2023, the bill:
    • Requires officials to perform address-based list maintenance annually, rather than biennially as was required by existing law.
    • Requires officials to carry out their address-based list maintenance process using either (1) Postal Service change-of-address data, and/or (2) data from returned, non-forwardable mailings sent to all voters in the jurisdiction. If an official does not use address data from returned general mailings, they must supplement the annual Postal Service data process with additional biennial maintenance using data from returned, non-forwardable address confirmation requests sent to voters who have not voted in the past two general elections (or intervening elections) and have not updated their registration during that time. Under existing law, officials were permitted to base their biennial address-based maintenance on one or more data sets from the Postal Service, returned non-forwardable general mailings, and/or returned non-forwardable address confirmations sent to voters who had not voted or updated their registration in the last two years.
    • Requires officials to send initial address confirmation requests to the voter's address of legal residence. If the request is returned undeliverable, another request must be sent to the voter's mailing address on file, if different. Existing law did not specify to which address the confirmation notice must be sent.
    • Requires officials to send an "address confirmation final notice" to all of a voter's addresses on file if initial confirmation requests sent per Postal Service data have been returned as undeliverable, with no indication of an address change, or there was no response from the voter within 30 days. Final notice must also be sent to all of a voter's addresses on file if any other non-forwardable mail is sent to the voter and returned with no indication of an address change.
    • Alters the process for reactivating registration after a voter has failed to make the required response to an address confirmation final notice and has been placed in "inactive" status. In addition to taking one of the actions required by existing law - to update their registration, request a vote-by-mail ballot, or appear to vote - the bill requires voters to also confirm their address of legal residence to restore their active status.

Requires new interagency data sharing of information related to voter list maintenance. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires circuit court clerks to include in their monthly report to the Department of State information about the terms of each felony sentence, including legal financial obligations, for any person in the clerk's records who resides in the state and has been convicted of a felony in the last month. Under existing law, the monthly report was limited to data on mentally incapacitated individuals, and individuals who indicated a change of address on jury service forms. Note: While existing law requires election officials to consult data from court clerks (among other sources) to remove voters due to convictions and restore eligibility, there was no comparable provision in existing law requiring monthly reports of convictions.
  • Requires the Department of State to consider information received from the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles when identifying deceased registered voters, in addition to the existing mandatory sources of Department of Health and federal Social Security data.
  • Requires the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles to include in its monthly report to the Department of State the name, address, date of birth, Social Security number, and driver's license number or state ID number of any person who presents evidence that they are a non-citizen as part of being issued a new or renewed driver's license or state ID.
  • Creates an Office of Election Crimes and Security within the Department of State, headed by a director appointed by the Secretary of State and staffed with investigators who are not sworn law enforcement personnel. This office has the responsibility to:
    • Oversee the voter fraud hotline, including investigating complaints.
    • Initiate and conduct investigations into voter fraud based on information from other sources.
    • Refer appropriate matters to prosecutors.
    • Report annually to the Governor, President of the Senate, and the Speaker of the House detailing information on the investigations conducted by the Office.
  • Increases investigation of purported election crimes by requiring the Governor, in consultation with the Department of Law Enforcement, to appoint at least one sworn special officer to conduct election-related investigations in each region. These special officers are subject to existing rules concerning law enforcement officers in polling locations, and may only conduct other investigations if doing so does not hinder or interfere with their election-related duties. Under existing law, the Governor was permitted, but not required, to appoint special law enforcement officers to investigate election-related crimes.

Increases criminal and civil penalties for various election offenses. The bill:

  • Raises the misdemeanor offense of collecting more than two mail ballots other than the person's own or one belonging to an immediate family member to a felony offense.
  • Raises the misdemeanor offense of signing a fictitious name to a petition for a candidate, minor political party, or issue to a felony offense.
  • Raises the misdemeanor offense of paying an initiative petition signature collector on a per signature basis to a felony offense.
  • Raises the cap on total fines for third-party registration organizations failing to properly deliver voter registration applications, from $1,000 for violations in a calendar year to $50,000.
  • Creates a new $1,000 fine for any third-party registration organization whose agent is convicted of the existing offense of altering an application without the applicant's consent. The fine will be imposed for each instance of alteration.
  • Expands the existing felony offense for releasing election results before the close of polls. Under existing law, election officials and employees are prohibited from releasing election results prior to the close of polls. The bill widens the prohibition by applying the offense to any person authorized to observe, review, or inspect ballot materials or observe canvassing, and expands the prohibited conduct to also include releasing any information about votes cast.

Regarding drop boxes, the bill:

  • Renames drop boxes as "secure ballot intake stations," and limits drop box locations to only those permanent branch offices of election supervisors that meet the criteria for offices used for early voting and are open at least 40 hours a week using normal business hours. Existing law permitted drop boxes at any permanent branch office.

Regarding other areas of election law, the bill:

  • Alters the uniform statewide voter registration application to include a statement informing the applicant that third-party voter registration organizations might not deliver the application to election officials for up to 14 days after completion and that the registrant may instead return their own application or register online. The bill also repeals the existing provision that required third-party voter registration organizations to notify applicants of this information.
  • Requires the Department of State to conduct a feasibility study on requiring ID numbers on mail ballots, including consideration of interagency data sharing, protection of voters' privacy, modifications to canvassing procedures, costs, and voter education. The department is required to report the results of the study to legislative leaders by February 1, 2023.
  • Modifies the canvass observation process by requiring observers at canvassing locations to sign an affidavit affirming their knowledge that disclosing election results observed while the election is ongoing is a felony.
  • Expands the existing prohibition on the use of private funds for election-related expenses by prohibiting private funding "for any type of expenses related to election administration," and expressly including costs of "any litigation related to election administration" within the prohibition. Under existing law, the prohibition on private funds was limited to use for "election-related expenses or voter education, voter outreach, or registration programs."
  • Prohibits ranked-choice voting for local, state, or federal elective office.
  • Repeals the existing provision that prohibited election workers from asking voters for more information about their address if their voter ID address matched their address on file, and the provision that prohibited using the address on a voter's ID to confirm their legal residence. The bill leaves in place the prohibition on using a voter ID address to challenge a voter's legal residence.
  • Requires officials to send out ballots in mail ballot elections according to the existing timeframe required for issuing mail ballots to UOCAVA voters. The bill also alters the timeframe for canvassing in mail ballot elections, by requiring the process to match existing procedures for the canvass of mail ballots in regular elections.
  • Moves the deadline for requesting supervised voting in an assisted living facility or nursing home, from 21 days before the election to 28 days before.
  • Removes the existing restriction that oval vote targets are the only permissible type of vote target on ballots.

This bill also contains provisions not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, including provisions that change petition signature verification processes and the timing of county commissioner races after redistricting.

A previous version of the bill contained provisions that would have changed mail ballot verification by requiring an additional envelope for returned mail ballots and requiring voters to include an ID number on their returned mail ballots. These provisions have been deleted in their entirety from the bill as enacted. These provisions would have:

  • Imposed an additional layer of mail ballot verification on top of the existing signature match process. The bill would have required a voter to provide the last four digits of their state driver's license or state ID on a newly-created "certificate envelope" when returning their ballots. Voters who lacked these forms of ID would have been required to provide the last four digits of their Social Security number. If one of these numbers was not on the certificate envelope, it would have been rejected, even if voters wrote an ID number on the secrecy envelope for their mail ballot. The ID number requirement would have had at least two hidden consequences. First, voters who have at least one of these types of ID but do not have the number(s) on file would not have been able to successfully vote by mail at all. The bill attempted to mitigate this risk by requiring election officials to send mailings seeking this information every two years and also would require the department of state to report a plan to obtain these ID numbers for all registered voters to legislative leadership by January 1, 2023. A second hidden consequence would have been that voters who do not have any of these ID numbers can register to vote under existing law but would have been unable to successfully vote by mail in future elections.
  • Rejected any ballot that did not have a correct ID number on the certificate envelope, any ballot with an unsigned certificate envelope, and any ballot with a signature mismatch or missing signature on the certificate envelope. Under existing law, missing and mismatched signatures on the secrecy envelope lead to ballot rejection. The new ID match requirement would have had a hidden consequence: voters whose records contained only one ID number but who use an ID number from a different type of ID when returning the ballot would have had their ballot rejected.
  • Allowed voters to remedy ID number issues using the existing cure process for missing and mismatched signatures.
  • Required election officials to send an ID number solicitation to all voters who do not have a state driver's license number, a state ID number, or the last four digits of their social security number on file. This process would have been conducted every two years, in odd-numbered years. These mailings would have been sent to the voter's mailing address and would have been required to include a notice that willfully submitting false registration information is a third-degree felony.

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2022, would increase the transparency of the redistricting process by eliminating a public records exception for draft redistricting plans or amendments to plans and requests for drafts or amendments. In addition to allowing disclosure of those documents, the bill would make available any supporting documents associated with such plan or amendment. Under existing law, the supporting documents become available only after the plan or amendment is filed.

This bill, as introduced January 11, 2022, would require counties to give each voter who requests a mail ballot a postage prepaid envelope to return the ballot in. Under existing law counties are not required to pay the postage, but some voluntarily do.

This bill, as introduced January 11, 2022, would require high schools to teach their students how to use the online voter registration system to register or preregister to vote. As part of the lesson, schools would be required to include the opportunity to register using the system.

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2022, would make applying for a mail ballot easier by allowing people to apply as part of their voter registration application and on the return envelope of their mail ballot, and make changes to the timing and process of calling special elections. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the department of state to update the uniform statewide voter registration application to include a checkbox for an applicant to request a vote by mail ballot.
  • Require the online voter registration system to allow an applicant to check a box to request a mail ballot.
  • Require the return envelope for a mail ballot to have a preprinted statement and check box a voter could use to request additional mail ballots through the end of the next general election.

Last Updated January 11, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2022 would effectively repeal substantial parts of the 2021 election law known as "SB 90". Specifically, the bill would:

  • Repeal the requirement that notice of litigation settlement negotiations, at various points in time, must be given to the President of the Senate, the Speaker of the House of Representatives, and the Attorney General. This provision would shift election-related authority away from those officers. The requirement that these officers be given a role in election-related litigation they had not chosen to intervene in was added to Florida law by SB 90.
  • Repeal the prohibition on using private funds for election related expenses. This provision was added to Florida law by SB 90.
  • Repeal a requirement that individuals and groups conducting registration drives notify applicants about the online voter registration system and make other disclosures. In addition the bill would maintain the requirement that registrations be delivered to the supervisor of elections within 14 days of collecting them, but repeal the prohibition on returning them after the deadline to register for the upcoming election. These disclosure requirements and delivery prohibition were added to Florida law by SB 90.
  • Repeal a requirement that a voter who wishes to update their address, name, or party affiliation give the supervisor of elections the last four digits of their Social Security number, their driver's license number, or their state ID number, whichever one the supervisor has on file. The requirement was added to Florida law by SB 90.
  • Repeal a prohibition on offering to help voters with their ballots within 150 feet of a drop box. The prohibition was added to Florida law by SB 90.
  • Repeal a requirement that voters applying for mail ballots must provide a driver's license number, state ID number, or the last four digits of their Social Security number, whichever may be verified in the supervisor of election's records. The requirement was added to Florida law by SB 90.
  • Repeal a prohibition on mailing mail ballots to voters who had not applied for them. This prohibition was added to Florida law by SB 90.
  • Repeal a requirement that the return mailing envelope for a mail ballot bear the voter's name and any encoded mark used by the supervisor's office, as well as a prohibition on putting the political party of the voter on the envelope. These provisions were added to Florida law by SB 90.
  • Repeal multiple provisions relating to drop boxes that were added to Florida law by SB 90. Specifically, the bill would:
    • repeal the time constraints for ballot drop box use for drop boxes other than at the office of the supervisor of elections.
    • repeal the requirement that drop boxes, wherever sited, be monitored by employees of the supervisor's office.
    • repeal the requirement that drop box locations be submitted to the division of elections at least 30 days before an election, and could not be changed later unless the division approves the move to correct a violation of drop box siting rules.
    • repeal rules about the timing of emptying drop boxes and chain of custody provisions.
    • repeal a $25,000 civil penalty for supervisors who operate a drop box out of compliance with drop box rules.
  • Repeal changes to the prohibition on soliciting voters that were made by SB 90. Specifically, the bill would:
    • repeal the application of the solicitation ban to within 150 of a drop box.
    • repeal the expansion of the definition of prohibited solicitation to include "engaging in any activity with the intent to influence or effect of influencing a voter.'
    • repeal language that allowed private property owners to prohibit anyone other than a candidate or candidate's designee from soliciting voters on their property, outside the no-solicitation zone, while their property is being used a voting location.

  • Eliminate restrictions on returning voters' ballots for them. Prior to SB 90, Florida law prohibited people from being compensated for returning more than two ballots other than their own or an immediate family member's. SB 90 tightened the restriction by prohibiting returning more than two such ballots regardless of compensation.

Last Updated March 3, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2022, would make substantial changes throughout the election code, including creating same-day registration, automatic voter registration, a permanent absentee voter list, and much more. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create same-day registration during early voting or on election day, without specifying any new registration requirements, or whether a same-day registrant must vote a regular ballot or a provisional ballot.
  • Create automatic voter registration and pre-registration at the DMV. The applicant would have an opportunity to opt-out of registration during the transaction.
  • Create a permanent absentee ballot list by allowing a voter to request to receive mail ballots until they cancel their request or first class mail sent to the voter by the supervisor of elections is returned as undeliverable.
  • Change deadlines for applying for a mail ballot more generally by:
    • making the deadline to apply for a mail ballot from 5 p.m. on the 10th day before Election Day to 5 p.m. on the 11th day before Election Day.
    • allowing a voter's designee to pick up their ballot between Election Day and 11 days before the election. Under existing law, a designee may pick up the ballot for a voter anytime between Election Day and 9 days before an election.
    • providing that if the deadline falls on a day the office of the supervisor is usually closed, the deadline is extended until the next business day.
  • Require the county to prepay the return postage for mail ballots.
  • Allow voters to choose to validate their mail ballots by signing the oath with either their signature or the last four digits of their Social Security number (SSN4).
  • Revise the required instructions for mail ballots to include the option to sign using an SSN4 and to include information about returning the ballot to drop boxes or the supervisor's office.
  • Revise ballot canvassing and cure provisions to enable a ballot to be counted if it is signed using an SSN4 instead of the voter's signature. Specifically, ballots may be counted if signed with an SSN4 that matches the voter's SSN4 on file, and if the number on the ballot does not match, the voter must be notified and given an opportunity to correct it using the existing process.
  • Count provisional ballots completed by eligible voters if they completed a provisional ballot for the correct county, even if they appeared to vote at the wrong precinct in the county.
  • Prohibit siting a polling place in a gated community unless all voters assigned to it live within the gated community.
  • Explicitly allow people to give voters food, water, or other items, so long as the voters are standing in line to vote and are outside the no-solicitation zone.
  • Prohibit bullhorns and other sound amplification devices in close proximity to a polling place during voting hours and an office of the supervisor of elections during a recount.
  • Require the Division of Elections to maintain a strategic elections equipment reserve, including tabulation machines, printers, and other equipment, that can be deployed in case of emergency or because of capacity issues created by unexpected voter turnout.
  • Change voter registration by requiring a voter to select a political party or affirmatively select no party affiliation. Supervisors of elections would be prohibited from registering a voter who does not make an affirmative choice and require the supervisor to notify the voter that they must complete a new application and make the affirmative choice. Under existing law, registrants who do not pick a party are automatically registered unaffiliated.
  • Change voter registration drives by:
    • Repealing a requirement that organizations doing voter registration drives make specific statements to applicants during the registration process. Existing law requires groups to state that they might not return the form on time and advise the applicant that the applicant can return the form. In addition, existing law requires the organization to explain how to register online, and how to determine if their voter registration application has been delivered.
    • Repealing a fine that could be levied against an organization doing a voter registration drive if they do not submit the forms to the division of elections or the supervisor of elections in the county in which the voter lives.
  • Give voters more time before their names are removed from the voter registration list by providing that a voter's registration cannot be marked inactive unless they have not participated in two consecutive general elections, in addition to failing to return the address confirmation final notice card or the final notice is returned undeliverable. Under existing law, a voter's registration may be marked inactive based on the final notice regardless of a voter's voting history. Once a voter's registration is marked "inactive", they may reactivate it, but if they do not reactivate it by the second general election after the registration was marked inactive, their registration is canceled.
  • Create a new cause of action that allows any voter or any candidate to sue the relevant supervisor of elections for noncompliance with election law. Plaintiffs would be entitled to an immediate hearing, and any filing fees or costs would be waived, and attorneys fees awarded to the prevailing party.
  • Shift election authority by making the Secretary of State, the highest election authority in Florida, elected rather than appointed by the Governor.
  • Make General Election Day a paid holiday.
  • Broaden the applicability of the special provisions of law that are currently applicable to UOCAVA voters only. The bill would repeal the words "uniformed services voter or an overseas" throughout the section, making the section apply to "absent voters". "Absent voter" is not a defined term in the bill. Under the bill, an absent voter's mail ballot for a presidential primary or a general election is timely if it is postmarked on or before Election Day and is returned within 10 days of Election Day. Under existing law, all mail ballots other than those from UOCAVA voters must be received by 7 p.m. on Election Day. The bill does not amend the provisions of law setting the general mail ballot return deadline.

Make changes to areas of election law Voting Rights Lab does not track, such as candidate filings, ballot initiative signature gathering, ballot design, and certification deadlines.

This bill, as introduced on January 24, 2022, would repeal 2021 Senate Bill 202 in its entirety and return the state's election law to where it stood prior to March 25, 2021. The bill would:

  • Modify procedures for absentee voting. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Eliminate the requirement that voters provide an identification number from a Georgia-issued ID with their absentee ballot application or, if they do not have one, a photocopy of another type of ID. Prior law required only that the application include sufficient information to identify the voter, address for ballot delivery, specific election for the request, and name and address of the requestor (if not the voter).
    • Eliminate the requirement that voters provide a state-issued ID number, if they have one, or the last four digits of their social security number on the outer envelope containing their absentee ballots, in an area that is covered when the envelope is sealed. Voters who do not have either required ID number are required to enclose a copy of alternative ID with their ballot. Under prior law, voters were required to provide only a signed oath affirming their identity.
    • Eliminate all references to drop boxes in the code. Existing law requires at least one drop box per county for absentee ballot return, and allows for additional drop boxes depending on the number of county voters or early voting locations. Drop boxes are only permitted inside advance voting locations and may only be accessible while early voting is taking place, with "constant surveillance" required. The boxes also must be emptied daily. During a state of emergency declared by the governor, staffed drop boxes could be placed outside early voting locations.
  • Eliminate the requirement that absentee ballot applications and ballot envelopes be verified by comparison of the voter's provided ID information with their information on file, and reinstate signature matching.
    • Eliminate the felony of accepting an absentee ballot from a voter for delivery or return without statutory authorization to do so.
    • Eliminate the prohibition on the secretary of state and other government entities sending absentee ballot applications to voters without a request.
    • Eliminate the prohibition on the distribution of absentee ballot applications with pre-filled fields.
    • Eliminate the misdemeanor of handling of an absentee ballot application by anyone other than the voter, the voter's authorized relative, an authorized assistant, or various specified officials.
    • Eliminate the requirement that a disclaimer be included on absentee applications mailed to voters by non-governmental organizations identifying the group.
    • Eliminate the requirement that absentee ballot applications include a wet ink signature from the voter.
    • Eliminate the bar against third-party individuals and organizations mailing absentee ballot applications to voters who have already requested or cast an absentee ballot and the corresponding fine scheme.
    • Eliminate the requirement that voters in jail be given access to necessary personal effects for the purpose of applying for and voting an absentee ballot.
    • Change the earliest date for acceptance of an absentee ballot application from 78 days before Election Day to 180 days before Election Day, and eliminate the requirement that applications for absentee-by-mail ballots be received by the 11th day before an election.
    • Change the date that officials must begin issuing absentee ballots, from 29-25 days before Election Day to 49-45 days before Election Day, and eliminate the requirement that clerks process absentee applications within three days of receipt during the early voting period.
    • Change the date after which hospitalized voters may apply for an emergency absentee ballot from ten days before an election to five days before an election, and eliminate the requirement that such applications be processed immediately.
    • Eliminate the felony for an unauthorized individual knowingly unsealing a sealed absentee ballot envelope.
    • Bar preprocessing of absentee ballots before the opening of polls. Under existing law, ballots may be preprocessed starting the third Monday before Election Day.
    • Repeal provisions allowing party monitors to observe absentee ballot processing.
    • Permit pausing the counting once all contested races and questions were tallied, and resuming the count the following day. Under existing law, counties may not pause the counting of ballots until the process is complete.
    • Remove from the absentee voter oath the affirmations stating that the voter was not observed while voting and will not give the ballot to anyone for unauthorized return.
    • Eliminate ranked-choice voting for UOCAVA voters in general and primary runoff elections.
    • Remove the secretary of state's authority to audit information contained in absentee ballot applications and on absentee ballot envelopes for 24 months after an election.
  • Modify early voting procedures. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Eliminate the requirement that counties offer early voting on the second Saturday before Election Day, and allow additional early voting hours at county discretion. Under S.B. 202, counties are not allowed to offer early voting beyond what is prescribed in the code.
    • Restore the early voting period for runoffs for general primaries and general elections, requiring that such period begin on the fourth Monday before the runoff election. Under S.B. 202, runoff early voting begins "as soon as possible," and no later than the second Monday before Election Day.
  • Shift authority for election administration. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Restore the ability of the state election board to issue emergency regulations outside of "circumstances of imminent peril to public health, safety, or welfare," and requires notice of impending action to state officials.
    • Eliminate the requirement that the state board certify that any emergency regulations are in "strict and exact" compliance with the election code.
    • Eliminate the requirement that the state election board submit proposed emergency rules to the house and senate judiciary committees at least 20 days prior to taking effect.
    • Eliminate the power of either legislative judiciary committee to suspend emergency rules by majority vote..
    • Restore the secretary of state as chairperson of the state election board.Under S.B. 202, the chair is a nonpartisan individual chosen by the legislature. The secretary of state is currently a non-voting ex officio member of the board.
    • Eliminate the ability of the Secretary of State and the State Elections Board to appoint an independent performance review board upon request from the governing authority of a county or from state lawmakers representing the county, or if there is evidence that calls into light the competence of a local election official.
    • Eliminate the process through which up to four election superintendents at a time may be suspended by the state election board.
    • Eliminate the requirement that five days' notice be given to the legislative judiciary committees before the state election board or secretary of state enters into any agreement or settlement that limits, alters, or interprets provisions of the election code.
    • Eliminate superior court chief judges' power to appoint an acting election superintendent in counties without boards of elections and there is a probate judge vacancy or the judge has been incapacitated.
  • Change procedures for in-person voting. The bill would:
    • Eliminate the misdemeanor of giving or offering a voter any "money or gifts," including food or drink, at a polling place.
    • Bar individuals from serving as poll officers in counties in which they neither live nor are employed by the county with the approval of the election superintendents of both the county in which they live and the county in which they seek to serve as a poll officer. This was permitted under S.B. 202.
    • Eliminate the requirement that counties divide precincts and/or add more poll workers and equipment for precincts that had over 2000 voters and wait times of more than one hour in the previous election.
    • Eliminate the requirement that counties post a notice of a polling place change at least seven days prior to an election.
    • Permit the counting of provisional ballots cast out-of-precinct before 5 p.m. on Election Day.
    • Grant local officials discretion over the use of mobile voting facilities. Under S.B. 202, mobile voting sites may only be used in states of emergency declared by the governor.
    • Repeal a prohibition on the extension of polling place hours without an order from a county superior court judge, on good cause shown.
  • Modify the criminalization of various aspects of the election system. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Eliminate the felony for observing a person casting their ballot, with the exception of authorized assistants, individuals under 12 years old, or any minor child of the observed voter. Eliminate the misdemeanor for recording or photographing a voted ballot or the face of an electronic ballot marker while a vote is being cast or while a vote choice is being displayed.
    • Repeal the authorization of the attorney general to establish a hotline where voters can lodge complaints and anonymous tips regarding voter intimidation, fraud, and illegal election activities.
  • Alter the election code in several other ways. Additional provisions of the bill would:
    • Eliminate the bar on election superintendents and boards of registrars accepting private funding for election administration.
    • Eliminate the requirement that the secretary of state regularly obtain information from the non-governmental voter information sharing organization it belongs to - i.e., ERIC - for the purpose of voter list maintenance.
    • Repeal the express provision that there is no limit on the number of voters that a single voter may challenge on eligibility to register or vote, and require registrars to hold hearings on challenges to voter registration eligibility within 10 days of filing.
    • Repeal the state board of elections' ability to sanction registrars for failure to comply with challenge procedures.
    • Eliminate the requirement that counties designate locations for poll watchers to allow them to fairly observe the procedures of voting and scanning.
    • Eliminate the requirement that organizations provide poll watcher training to the watchers representing them.
    • Eliminate the requirement that counties report and post information about the total number of ballots cast and rejected as soon as possible after the close of polls, and no later than 10 p.m. on Election Day.
    • Repeal the delay of the reapportionment of municipal districts in the event of delay of census data that was enacted in 2021.

This bill, as introduced January 27, 2022, would authorize the use of ballot-return drop boxes in the event that 2021 S.B. 2022 is repealed. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Permit county registrars to establish drop boxes on county or municipal government property that is accessible to the public.
  • Allow drop boxes to be open from 49 days before an election to the close of polls at 7 p.m. on Election Day.
  • Require that drop box locations have adequate lighting and that a video recording device be used to monitor each location. Video recordings would be available to the public, upon request, either free or at a reasonable charge.
  • Establish procedures for collecting ballots from drop boxes.

Under existing law, drop boxes are permitted at early voting locations and may only be accessible while voting is taking place. This bill is intended as a follow-on to House Bill 941, which would repeal 2021 Senate Bill 202 in its entirety, including the language authorizing drop boxes.

A previous version of the bill contained several provisions that were amended out of this version. These provisions would have:

  • Prohibited all county government bodies from accepting private funds for election administration. The state board of elections would have been empowered to accept such funds and would have sole discretion over their distribution. Under existing law, county boards of elections are prohibited from accepting private funds for election administration, but other county government bodies are not.
  • Clarified that members of a county board of elections may serve on a performance review board evaluating a different county's board of elections. Existing law states that "local election officials" may serve on review boards.
  • Lowered the minimum number of voting booths or enclosures that a county must provide at each polling location, to one booth per 250 registered voters who have not cast a ballot. Under existing law, counties are required to prove one booth per 250 registered voters, regardless of how many voters cast a ballot before Election Day.
  • Modified the disclaimer required to be included with absentee ballot applications sent to voters by third parties to include the mailing organization's name. Under existing law, disclosures must only state that the application was not sent by the government. The bill would also clarify that the code does not prohibit making blank absentee ballots available to voters or directing voters to the website where absentee ballot applications can be obtained.
  • Established more strict chain of custody documentation requirements for unvoted and voted ballots, absentee ballots collected from drop boxes, and provisional ballots, including secured cases for transportation, logged custody, and numbered, tamper-proof seals. Existing law does not prescribe specific procedures for the handling of voted ballots.
  • Eliminated the right of "political bodies" without a candidate on the ballot for a given election to designate poll watchers. Under existing law there is no such limitation.
  • Modified the standard of access poll watchers must be granted from guaranteeing them the ability to "fairly" observe the process to "meaningfully" observe the process.
  • Made explicit that, subject to reasonable regulations to prevent overcrowding and interference with official duties, poll watchers are entitled to meaningful access to polling places, early ("advance") voting locations, tabulation centers, and locations where absentee ballots are verified, processed, adjudicated, and scanned. Existing law only explicitly contemplates poll watcher presence at polling places.
  • Permitted the registrar, election superintendent, or a designee of the poll manager, registrar, or superintendent, to make reasonable regulations about poll watcher conduct to prevent interference with the conduct of the election. Under existing law, only poll managers may make such regulations.

  • Expanded the scope of an existing felony to cover willfully preventing any election official from performing their duties. Under existing law, only willfully preventing a poll officer from doing their duties is a felony.
  • Established a felony for using or threatening force or violence in a manner that would prevent a reasonable poll officer or election official from executing their duties, materially interrupting or improperly interfering with the execution of a poll officer's or election official's duties, or acting in any other manner to intimidate any poll officer or election official from faithfully performing his or her duties.

This bill, as introduced on February 28, 2022, would substantially change voter registration to require proof of citizenship and change other requirements, impacting same day registration, registration by mail, and online registration. The bill would also make voter ID rules more restrictive, while also enabling certain voters to get a free ID. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Change the general voter registration requirements by:
    • Requiring acceptable proof of citizenship. Existing law requires an applicant to state whether the voter is a U.S. citizen but does not require documentation.
    • Clarifying that a voter's full name for the purposes of completing an application for registration includes the voter's full legal name, including the voter's full first, full middle and full last name. Existing law requires a voter's full name, but does not clarify that the name should include the voter's first, middle and last name.

  • Create a new felony offense for giving, promising to give, or receiving money or other valuable consideration for viewing or disseminating a photograph of a partially or fully complete ballot.

    Last updated on August 3, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on November 22, 2022, would create new crimes prohibiting false and misleading statements in an election, and new civil actions for related injunctive relief. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create a Class A misdemeanor prohibiting a person from knowingly or recklessly making, publishing, broadcasting, or circulating, any false or misleading designed to affect the vote on any public question on the ballot or relating to any candidate for election to public office, or causing any such statement to be made, published, broadcast, or circulated.
  • Allow a candidate or certain people who had a role in putting the question on the ballot to sue for an injunction to enforce the prohibition on false or misleading statements. To win the injunction, the violation would need to be proved by clear and convincing evidence.
  • Create a Class A misdemeanor prohibiting a person from knowingly and with intent to affect the outcome of a campaign for political office from:
    • working for a candidate or having someone work for a candidate for the purpose of impeding the candidate's campaign for nomination or election or for the purpose of reporting information about the candidate without the knowledge of the candidate or the candidate's organization, or
    • promising, offering, or giving any valuable thing or valuable benefit to any person working for a candidate or campaign to influence them to improperly discharge their campaign duties or obtain information about the candidate or the candidate's campaign organization.
  • Create a Class A misdemeanor prohibiting a person from knowingly and with intent to affect the outcome of a campaign for political office from taking any of these actions:
    • making a false or misleading statement concerning the education completed or attempted by a candidate, their professional licenses or job history, their criminal record, confinement for mental illness, military service, or voting record.
    • falsely identifying the source of a statement, issuing statements under the name of another person without authorization, or falsely stating the endorsement of or opposition to a candidate by a person or publication.
    • disseminating a false or misleading statement concerning a candidate designed to promote the election, nomination, or defeat of the candidate, if the statement is designed for that purpose.
  • Create a Class A misdemeanor to prohibit knowingly or recklessly making a false or misleading statement about a candidate's stance on an issue to affect the outcome of a campaign.
  • Allow a candidate who suffers a false or misleading statement prohibited by either crime to bring a civil action against the speaker. A violation would be required to be proven by clear and convincing evidence.
  • Create a Class A misdemeanor to prohibit a person, with an intent to mislead a voter in connection with their campaign or another's campaign for nomination or election, from falsely communicating that they are an incumbent when they are not.
  • Allow a candidate affected by the prohibited statement of incumbency to bring a civil action against the speaker. A violation would be required to be proven by clear and convincing evidence.
  • Create a Class A misdemeanor to prohibit any person, with actual malice, from publishing or sponsoring the publication of libel per se or defamation per se in any political or electioneering communication. Libel and defamation per se would be broadly defined as a written or verbal statement that tends to expose a living person to hatred, contempt, ridicule, or obloquy, to deprive them of the benefit of public confidence or social intercourse, or to injure them in that person's business or occupation. People could make or sponsor such statements about themselves without violating the prohibition.
  • Allow a candidate affected by the prohibited statement to sue for an injunction. A violation would be required to be proved by clear and convincing evidence.

  • Make adherence to the existing code of fair campaign practices mandatory instead of voluntary, and enforceable through criminal and civil sanctions.

    Last updated December 9, 2022

This bill, as enacted on May 13, 2022, changes the processes for absentee voting - called "vote by mail" in Illinois - for voters with "print disabilities" (physical or cognitive disabilities that prevent them from effectively reading or using printed material), and permits greater use of duplicate ballots when ballots are unreadable. Specifically, the bill:

  • Creates a new certified remote accessible absentee voting system for voters with print disabilities for use during general elections, which allows such voters to receive a ballot electronically and mark and verify the ballot using assistive technology. Voters must print the completed ballot and return it per existing return rules for absentee ballots.
  • Requires the State Board of Elections to establish procedures by which voters may access the remote accessible absentee system, and issue certification standards.
  • Requires election officials to electronically send an absentee ballot to voters with print disabilities within two business days after the receiving the voter's application to use the remote accessible vote by mail system, if the jurisdiction has already begun sending ballots by mail. Under existing law, all absentee ballots were required to be sent to voters within three days of receiving a valid application.
  • Requires the application for one-time or permanent electronic absentee ballot delivery for voters with print disabilities to be substantively similar to that for conventional ballots.

  • Allows judges of election to determine that a ballot may be duplicated if that ballot cannot be counted by the automatic tabulating equipment for reasons other than damage or defectiveness. Under existing law, only defective or damaged ballots were allowed to be duplicated for automatic tabulation.

Last Updated May 31, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 5, 2022, would require photo ID to vote. Under existing law, voters are not required to show ID of any type to vote at the polls. Specifically, this bill would:

  • Require any voter to show a photo ID to vote in person, which must be a valid, current government-issued ID card including the voter's name, photo, and address, including:
    • Illinois driver's licenses,
    • state ID cards,
    • Illinois disabled person ID cards,
    • senior citizen ID cards,
    • FOID cards, and
    • U.S. passports.
  • Mandates that any voter failing to show photo ID must cast a provisional ballot, which can only be counted if the voter provides photo ID at the county clerk or board of election commissioner's office within 10 days after voting.
  • Requires the secretary of state to provide, free of charge, each registered voter lacking another photo ID with a voter ID card including the voter's name, signature, photograph, and current residential address.

  • Creates an exemption for voters who have a religious objection to be photographed and allows such voters to vote a provisional ballot and sign an affidavit claiming this exemption.

Last Updated January 6, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 5, 2022, would mandate ballot tracking for absentee ballot packages mailed by election officials and completed ballots returned by voters, beginning July 1, 2022. This bill would mandate that the tracking is updated when a ballot is sent to a voter, received back by the election official, and when the ballot is counted. It would also allow a voter to opt in to email or text notifications when tracking status updates. Existing law does not mandate ballot tracking, although it is, in practice, currently offered in many jurisdictions in Illinois.

Last Updated January 6, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 5, 2022, would change voter list maintenance practices. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the county coroner or other person responsible for death certificates to transmit a certified record of death to the county clerk within seven days after a person's death.
  • Require the county clerk to monthly request permanent change of address forms submitted to the USPS and update the registration of any person whose address appears to have changed.
  • Require the coroner and county clerk to report quarterly to the county board on their compliance with the practices required by the bill. This report would be publicly available on request, and a requester is authorized to file suit if the report is not timely produced. People are also authorized, under this bill, to enforce the list maintenance provisions of the bill in court.

  • Authorize a court to impose penalties of between $2,500 and $5,000 for each instance of failure to comply with the list maintenance or public reporting requirements of the bill, with additional penalties for continued violations permitted.

    Last updated January 13, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on January 5, 2022, would require the State Board of Elections to develop procedures to audit signatures on ballot applications, requiring each election authority to select a random 1% of the absentee ballot applications submitted to the jurisdiction for auditing.

Last updated January 26, 2022.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 18, 2022, would change the automatic voter registration process at state agencies. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Add the Department of Healthcare and Family Services as an automatic voter registration agency.
  • Allow documents that demonstrate a person's citizenship and voting age to be used to support a dual-purpose application (one that serves as either an application to register to vote or an application to change the voter's registered residential address or name). Under existing law, only identification documents meeting REAL ID standards may serve as the basis for a dual-purpose application. This bill would also allow documents that are silent as to citizenship to serve as the basis for a dual-purpose application. The bill makes clear that an identity document that affirmatively shows a person's noncitizen status cannot be the basis for a voter registration application.
  • Eliminate all provisions suggesting that an applicant may opt out of automatic voter registration at the time of the transaction, and instead reinforce that the only mechanism for opting out is after the transaction, in response to a notice sent by election officials.

  • Eliminate requirements that the registration agency inform an applicant of qualifications to vote, the penalties for false application, how automatic registration works, and that declining to register is confidential and does not affect the services a person is otherwise seeking to receive.

Last Updated January 19, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 19, 2022, would allow people to preregister to vote on their 16th birthday. Under existing law, only 17-year-olds who will be 19 by the general election can register to vote. This bill would also provide that online voter registration will be done through a portal rather than a website. This bill would also allow 16-year-olds to circulate petitions.

Last Updated January 31, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 21, 2022, would create an independent redistricting commission to create new district boundaries following the 2020 federal decennial census for state legislative districts and federal congressional districts. The plans would be approved by the legislature. The bill is specifically limited to the 2020 redistricting cycle. Under existing law, the legislature both draws and approves maps. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Draw new boundaries that meet the following criteria, listed in order of priority:
    • Compliance with the U.S. Constitution and federal law.
    • Substantially equal population.
    • Provide racial and language minorities equal opportunity to participate in the political process and elect candidates of their choice.
    • Provide racial and language minorities who are not a minority in a given district with an opportunity to substantially influence the outcome of an election.
    • Contiguity.
    • Compactness.
    • Respect political boundaries.
    • Respect communities of common interest.
    • Non-discriminatory towards a political party or individual.
  • Require the commission to hold at least ten public hearings throughout the state before adopting a plan. There must be a meaningful opportunity for racial and language minorities to participate in the public hearings, including targeted notices.
  • Require the chief justice and the next most senior justice of a different political party to appoint 16 commissioners, with seven each from the two major political parties and two not affiliated with those parties. Commissioners must meet certain independence criteria. At least ten commissioners are required for every action of the commission.

  • Provide a backup process where the chief justice and the next most senior justice of a different political party appoint an additional member of the commission, who may not be affiliated with either major political party, who will submit a redistricting plan to the legislature.

    Last updated January 24, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on January 21, 2022, would make permanent a requirement currently in place for 2022 only that every election authority provide at least one vote center where, on Election Day, any voter may vote regardless of which precinct they are assigned to. The location must be set at least 40 days before Election Day.

Last updated January 24, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on January 21, 2022, would exempt local election officials from sending notice of the availability of permanent vote by mail status to voters already on the permanent vote by mail list and voters who have explicitly requested off the permanent vote by mail list. Under existing law, local election officials must send such notice to all voters, including those exempted by this bill.

Last Updated January 24, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 21, 2022, would allow certain jurisdictions -- counties organized as a township -- to appoint only three judges of election to each precinct, rather than five.

Last updated January 25, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on January 21, 2022, would authorize election authorities to elect to provide absentee voting (called "vote by mail" in Illinois) options or on-premises voting options to physically incapacitated voters. Under existing law, election authorities must provide on-premises voting at veteran's homes, hospitals, nursing homes, and other facilities to physically incapacitated voters.

Last Updated January 24, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 21, 2022, would require local election officials to create a system for electronically sending an absentee ballot (called a "vote by mail" ballot in Illinois) to voters with disabilities, which would allow the voter to mark the ballot with assistive technology, either through the to-be-created electronic system or on paper. Voters using this system would be required to use a specific application, on which they would have to verify that they have a disability and without the electronic system, the voter would be denied the opportunity to vote privately and independently. The bill would also add unreadable ballots to the types of ballots that will be processed differently, like damaged or defective ballots.

Last Updated January 24, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 21, 2022, would change the information required on the voter registration application, by no longer requiring the county or state of birth or parents' first names. The bill would also change the availability of voter registration records and would specifically:

  • Prohibit personal, private, or commercial use of voter registration data.
  • Provide the records, at cost plus 15%, to a person upon an affidavit that they will be used for election, scholarly, or journalistic purposes. If the entity requesting the information is a 501(c)(3), the records will be furnished without charge or at a reduced charge.
  • Prohibit placing voter registration information on the Internet.
  • Prohibit disclosing driver's license numbers, state ID card numbers, social security numbers, or other unique identifiers.
  • Prohibit providing registration records to any person living outside of the U.S.
  • Make violation of these provisions a felony when knowingly committed. Under existing law, any unlawful disclosure is a felony.

  • Limit civil liability for government employees' unauthorized disclosure to only instances of gross negligence or willfulness.

Last Updated January 24, 2022

This bill, as introduced on November 14, 2022, would require each election authority, 90 to 45 days before each general election, to notify all qualified voters who neither had joined the list of voters to receive a mail ballot for each election nor had opted out of joining such a list of their option to do either by completing and returning the application form enclosed with the notice. This provision would narrow an existing requirement that provides such notice be sent to all qualified voters regardless of their prior joining of the list or their prior opting out from joining it prior to each general or consolidated election. Relatedly, the bill would revise the application to join the list to include an explicit opt-out option.

Last Updated December 9, 2022

This resolution, as introduced on January 14, 2022, proposes a state constitutional amendment that would change redistricting processes for federal congressional and state legislative districts. Specifically, the resolution would:

  • Require redistricting to consider the following criteria, in order of priority:
    • Comply with federal laws including the Voting Rights Act,
    • Be substantially equal in population,
    • Provide racial and language minorities with equal opportunity to participate and elect candidates of their choice,
    • Provide racial and language minorities who do not have a majority of a district with an opportunity to influence the outcome of an election through the creation of crossover districts, coalition districts, or influence districts, all as defined in the bill,
    • Be contiguous,
    • Be compact,
    • Respect the integrity of units of local government,
    • Respect communities of common social or economic interest,
    • Not discriminate for or against any political party or person.
  • Direct the supreme court chief justice and most senior justice of a different political party from the chief justice to select 17 people to form an independent redistricting commission, which shall redraw districts in 2023 for 2024 and thereafter in years ending in one, following a federal decennial census. Characteristics for commission members are outlined in the bill and include political party, residence, past elected or appointed positions, candidacies, lobbyists, and more.
  • Require the commission to hold at least 20 public hearings throughout the state before adopting a redistricting plan. As part of public access, the commission must give opportunities for participation by language and racial minorities, including translation, virtual participation, and terminals for members of the public to access maps and data.
  • Require that the commission publish a report explaining the plan's compliance with state and federal law.

  • Create original, exclusive jurisdiction in the state supreme court for actions regarding redistricting.

    Under existing law, redistricting was done by a legislative redistricting commission and considered fewer criteria (only compactness, contiguity, and population).

    Last updated January 18, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on January 5, 2022, would create automatic voter registration for people obtaining or renewing a driver's license, permit, or ID card at the DMV. Indiana does not provide automatic voter registration under existing law, although a person may register to vote at the DMV. Specifically, this bill would:

  • Require the DMV to collect information about the applicant's eligibility to vote, including citizenship.
  • Allow a person to opt out of voter registration at the time of the DMV transaction. No choice defaults to applying to register to vote.

  • Specify that a signature on the DMV transaction is an attestation that the applicant meets eligibility requirements unless the applicant has opted out of registering, and is made under penalty of perjury.

Last Updated January 6, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on January 18, 2022, adds additional provisions that deal with early voting and absentee voting. It leaves the other provisions of the bill, as introduced, unchanged, except as noted below. Specifically, the amendment would:

  • Change all the absentee voting excuses dealing with absence on Election Day to not only require that the voter be absent on that day, as is required under existing law, but to also require that the voter be absent for the entire period when a voter may vote absentee in person. This bill also changes references to the in-person absentee voting period, which is accessible by any voter and does not require a statutorily authorized excuse, so that it would be known as "early voting."

  • Require that voters who electronically submit an absentee ballot application provide either their Indiana driver's license number or the last four digits of their social security number.

    The provisions from the bill, as introduced, that are retained in the amendment would:


  • Eliminate the requirement that voters who cast provisional ballots receive a notice from the circuit court clerk within 3 days after Election Day informing them why their ballot is provisional and describing what actions the voter must take to have their ballot counted and the deadlines for such actions.
  • Rename audits currently called "risk-limiting audits" to "post-election audits" and make such audits permanent and mandatory statewide. Under existing law, risk-limiting audits were only required in certain pilot counties. The mechanics of these audits, however, are not changed by this bill.

  • Extend the sunset date from 2023 to 2028 for a requirement that counties must engage cybersecurity experts to ensure that county services, including voting, are not at risk. The amendment would only require these activities to the extent appropriations are available.

    The bill, as introduced, eliminated statutory authorization to use fax to interact with election authorities. The amendment, however, removes these sections and would continue to allow fax communications with election authorities.

Last Updated January 22, 2022
