VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 5, 2022, would change aspects of absentee voting eligibility and applying for absentee ballots. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Change one of the absentee voting excuses (called "voting by mail" in Indiana) for people who will be absent from the county. Under existing law, a voter may vote by mail if they have a specific, reasonable expectation of being absent from the county on Election Day. Under this bill, the voter would have to have a specific, reasonable expectation of being absent from the county during the entire early voting period and on Election Day.
  • Prohibit any election official from sending an absentee ballot application to a voter who has not requested an application.
  • Require that a voter provide, on their absentee ballot application, the last four digits of the voter's social security number and a full ID number for either an Indiana driver's license number, an Indiana nondriver's identification card, or voter registration identifying number. The bill would require that the application be rejected if election officials cannot match at least one of the numbers with the voter's registration record. Under existing law, a voter applying for an absentee ballot must provide the last four digits of their social security number or state that the voter does not have a social security number.

  • Require that any person or group that sends an absentee ballot application to a voter must include, on the envelope, a statement identifying the sender, that the application is unsolicited, and that the application was not sent by an elections official.

Last Updated January 18, 2022

This bill, as enacted on March 18, 2022, changes the process for redrawing the boundaries of local and school board districts following a federal decennial census. Provisions in the enacted bill were all in the previous version of the bill, with the exception noted below. Specifically, the bill:

  • Establishes the deadline for redistricting such districts.
  • Exempts officials from redrawing boundaries if existing districts satisfy all applicable laws.
  • Provides that, in the event of a conflict between a map and a legal description of the district, the legal description controls.

  • Changes the makeup of the board that redraws the district. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.

    Last updated March 24, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2022, would change absentee ballot applications, limit the authority of the state election commission and the governor, and require mandatory statewide risk-limiting audits. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require that a voter include on their absentee ballot application either their Indiana driver's license number or their Indiana state ID number, along with a copy of the same document as the document number the voter used. Failure to include the number or a copy of the voter's ID would result in a mandatory denial of the absentee ballot application. The existing absentee ballot application requests the voter to provide the last four digits of their social security numbers or state they do not have a social security number, but absentee ballots are not rejected for failure to complete these fields.
  • Explicitly prohibit the Indiana election commission from increasing vote by mail or absentee vote by mail or changing the time, place, or manner of holding an election. Existing law is silent as to the commission's authority to do these things.
  • Prohibit the governor from altering the time, place, or manner of holding elections, including expanding vote by mail or absentee voting, based upon an executive order issued during a declared emergency. Existing emergency authority is silent as to voting- and election-related executive orders.

  • Eliminate the existing risk-limiting audits conducted in certain pilot counties and replace them with mandatory risk-limiting audits to be conducted by each county election board before certifying election results.

Last Updated January 18, 2022

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to poll hours, provides that the polls close at 8 p.m., permits a voter to register at the polls by completing a voter registration form and an affirmation that the person has not voted elsewhere in the election and by providing proof of residence.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2022, would create same-day voter registration for every election statewide. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require same-day registrants to meet all voter eligibility requirements and provide all of the following:
    • A voter registration form witnessed by two poll workers from different political parties (or one poll worker and the precinct inspector if there are not two poll workers from different parties).
    • Proof of residence, in the form of a current photo ID, a current utility bill, bank statement, government check, paycheck, or other government documents that shows the name and address of the applicant, or a statement by any other voter in the precinct corroborating the voter's residency, who must provide an approved ID and must sign the statement in the presence of two poll workers from different political parties (or one poll worker and the precinct inspector if there are not two poll workers from different parties).
    • An affirmation signed by the voter including a statement that the voter has not already voted in the election.
  • Require a same-day registrant who cannot provide proof of residence to vote a provisional ballot, which will be counted if the voter files a copy of the required documentation in the county registration office or the precinct election board.

  • Require the counter voter registration office to add the name of same-day registrants to the registration record of the county. If a notice mailed to a same-day registrant in the course of adding that person to the county records is returned as undeliverable, the county voter registration office shall follow the existing steps to remove the person from the registration rolls.

    Last updated January 12, 2022.

BILLSUMMARY: Relates to Redistricting Commission, requires the General Assembly to establish a commission to draw congressional and legislative districts not later than July 1, 2027, acknowledges that this proposed amendment has not been previously agreed to by a General Assembly.
VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as introduced on January 11, 2022, would amend the state constitution and ultimately require a ballot question submitted to the state's voters, and would require the legislature to create a commission to draw congressional and legislative districts by July 1, 2027, based upon the number of inhabitants in each district and other criteria established by law.

Last updated January 12, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on January 4, 2022, would create a permanent absentee voter status for elderly or disabled voters. A voter seeking permanent absentee voter status would apply for permanent absentee voter status in the same manner that voters currently apply for absentee ballots. Once granted permanent absentee voter status, the clerk will place the voter on a permanent absentee voter list and send the voter an absentee ballot each time there is an election in the voter's precinct. Ballots cast by a voter with permanent absentee voter status are treated the same as other absentee ballots. Voters will be removed from the permanent absentee voter list if the voter fails to return an absentee ballot in three consecutive statewide general elections, although the voter may apply for reinstatement at any time after removal.

Last Updated January 5, 2022

This bill, as enacted on March 11, 2022, expands the existing ban on local governments accepting funds for conducting elections, by specifically prohibiting the acceptance of private monetary donations for employing temporary election workers. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. The bill also creates a new requirement that state agencies must report every state employee whose salary is funded, in whole or in part, from donated money, and establishes specific reporting requirements for donations made to the Secretary of State. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill specified that the report must be limited to the identity of the employee and the portion of their salary funded by donated money. The enacted bill does not include this limitation.

Last updated March 16, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2022, would repeal the excuse-based absentee voting process currently used in Indiana and replace it with no-excuse absentee voting. All other facets of the existing absentee voting process remain unchanged by this bill.

Last Updated January 7, 2022

This bill, as enacted on March 15, 2022:

  • Creates a new felony offense for casting more than one ballot in the same election, except when voters are casting a replacement ballot under law.
  • Allows the Indiana election division to convene all local election officials at times it deems necessary. Under existing law, such meetings were only permitted to be held in a year in which a general or municipal election was not held.
  • Clarifies that nothing in the existing statutes regarding handling ballots and elections materials and equipment after ballots are counted prohibits a local election official from performing a post-election audit.

  • Clarifies that the absentee ballot application deadline for voters with print disabilities who intend to vote by email or fax, regardless of the method the voter uses to return the application, is the ordinary 11:59 p.m. 12 days before Election Day. This clarification addressed potential ambiguity created when provisions relating to these voters were added to the code last year.

    A previous version of the bill contained provisions that were deleted prior to enactment. Those deleted provisions would have:


  • Changed absentee voting processes by:
    • Requiring that all absentee ballots must be printed on security paper featuring authentication markers.
    • Extending the deadline for a voter who receives an absentee ballot to provide additional documentation from noon on Election Day to 6:00 p.m. on Election Day.
    • Requiring counties to provide notice to voters if an absentee ballot signature mismatch has occurred, via mail, email if available, and phone call, if available, within two days after the signature mismatch determination. This would have been a conforming change, as notice of signature mismatch is already required under existing law.
    • Altering the ability of a county election board to scan a vote absentee ballot. Under existing law, such ballots may be scanned beginning seven days before Election Day with no exceptions. This bill would only allow such scanning to begin in the optical scan ballot system permits the retraction of a previously scanned ballot for a voter who is later found disqualified.
    • Requiring that the county election board unanimously agree an absentee ballot envelope signature is genuine before accepting the absentee ballot for counting. Under existing law, the county election board's unanimity is not explicitly required.
    • Allowing election officials to use ballot secrecy waiver forms as an additional source of signature for signature verification.
    • Allowing counties to begin counting absentee ballots at 6:00 a.m. on Election Day in a central counting location. Under existing law, counting may only begin after electronic pollbooks are updated to include absentee ballots received, which may be done as late as noon on Election Day.
  • Changed voter registration processes by:
    • Requiring the Bureau of Motor Vehicles to forward the information of any people who decline to register to vote to the Indiana election division. Under existing law, only registrations are forwarded.
    • Requiring that the statewide voter registration system be altered to add a feature that flags potential non-residential addresses submitted on voter registration applications.
  • Changed the last day for voter list maintenance activities from 90 days before Election Day to 70 days before Election Day.
  • Eliminated the requirement that a circuit court provide a voter who voted a provisional ballot with notice of what is required before the provisional ballot can be counted.
  • Changed references to risk-limiting audits to instead refer to such audits as post-election audits, and to no longer refer to the counties subject to them as pilot counties. Provisions would also have set a deadline for post-election audits to be completed by the final Friday in June, for primary elections, and December 20 for general elections, and would have clarified that post-election audits are not prohibited by other sections of the election code.
  • Eliminated a voter's ability to officially communicate or make requests or returns to elections officials via fax.

  • Provisions regarding the candidate nomination process, candidate reporting requirements, and municipal administration that are not tracked by Voting Rights Lab were also previously deleted from the bill.

Last Updated June 21, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 10, 2022, would change absentee ballot applications, limit the authority of the secretary of state and governor regarding elections, and require a certain kind of audit pilot. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require that a voter include on their absentee ballot application either their Indiana driver's license number or their Indiana state ID number, and provide a copy of the same document as the document number the voter used. Failure to include either the number or a copy of the voter's ID would result in a mandatory denial of the absentee ballot application. The existing absentee ballot application requests the voter to provide the last four digits of their Social Security number or state they do not have one, but absentee ballot applications are not rejected for failure to complete these fields.
  • Prohibit anyone from providing a voter with an absentee ballot application with the voter's driver's license number, state ID number, voter registration record number, or partial social security number prefilled. Existing law already prohibited anyone from pre-filling a voter's voter ID number.
  • Explicitly prohibit the Indiana Election Commission from increasing vote by mail or absentee vote by mail or changing the time, place, or manner of holding an election. Existing law is silent as to the commission's authority to do these things.
  • Prohibit the Governor from altering the time, place, or manner of holding elections, including expanding vote by mail or absentee voting, based upon an executive order issued during a declared emergency.
  • Require the Secretary of State to enter into contracts to retrospectively audit all of the computer equipment to be used in the 2022 general election in 10 counties identified as pilot counties. These counties are a mix of urbanicity and population sizes. The contractors engaged for the audit must be certified by the federal Election Assistance Commission and cannot be vendors of election equipment used in Indiana. Information obtained from the audit would be submitted by these contractors to the Secretary of State, Attorney General, and Chair of each Senate and House committee with jurisdiction over election matters in a report by December 31, 2022.

  • Require the Secretary of State to enter contracts to audit all the computer equipment used in randomly selected counties in each general election beginning January 1, 2023. This bill, as amended on March 23, 2022, would reduce the time people have to register to vote before an election, shorten the deadline to return advance (mail) ballots, limit the use of ballot drop boxes, and expand in-person early voting. As introduced, the bill did not address election law, however, after it passed the first chamber, a committee recommended replacing the text with a bill limiting drop boxes. That March 7, 2022 proposed committee substitute became, with further amendment, the version of the bill. References to the previous version are to that proposed substitute.

As amended, the bill would:

  • End voter registration 23 days before an election generally, and process registration applications received at voter registration agencies by the 24th day before the election or were postmarked by the 24th day before the election. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Under existing law, registration ends 20 days before an election, and applications must be received by voter registration agencies or be postmarked by the 21st day before the election.
  • Shorten the deadline to require voters to return their advance (mail) ballots to the close of polls on Election Day. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Under existing law, advance ballots may be postmarked by Election Day so long as they are received by the third day after Election Day.
  • Restrict and regulate drop box use by:
    • Explicitly authorizing voters to return their advance ballots to dropboxes. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Although existing law is silent on drop boxes, the Secretary of State and Governor authorized their use in 2020 and funded counties' acquisition of drop boxes.
    • Limiting drop box use to one per 30,000 registered voters. This provision was in the previous version. Existing law does not limit the number of drop boxes.
    • Requiring drop boxes to be staffed by an employee of the county election office, located inside a state or municipal building where employees of the state or municipality are physically present, or located inside any other building and staffed by two authorized poll agents registered with different political parties. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill allowed video surveillance instead of staffing and did not address placing drop boxes inside buildings. Existing law does not require surveillance or staffing of dropboxes.
    • Requiring drop boxes to be closed when the county election office is closed, except that on Election Day they must be open until 7 p.m., the close of polls. People in line at 7 p.m. would be allowed to deposit their ballots, but no one new would be allowed to join the line. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law requires advance (mail) ballots to be returned by close of polls or postmarked by Election Day.
    • Requiring dropbox signage explaining the limitations and crimes relating to returning other voters' ballots. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law does not have a comparable provision.
    • Requiring the Secretary of State to issue implementing regulations that must include a requirement to keep ballots returned to dropboxes separate from other ballots. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Expand in-person advance (early) voting so that it begins 10 days before the election and ends at noon the day before. Counties could choose to offer more days, but early voting could not begin more than 23 days before the election.. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Under existing law, it begins the Tuesday before the election, ends at noon the day before, and counties may choose to offer more days, but early voting cannot begin more than 20 days before the election.

  • Change certain other aspects of mail voting, specifically:

    • Allowing advance (mail) ballot applications to be processed beginning 93 days before a November general election, and received still earlier. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Under existing law, applications for advance ballots cannot be received earlier than 90 days before.
    • Requiring advance (mail) ballots to be sent to voters 23 days before the election to everyone who had applied by then, and within two business days of receiving an application thereafter. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Under existing law, ballot mailing begins 20 days before the election.
    • Requiring voters who return their advance ballots by mail to use the U.S. Postal Service or any other delivery service that provides the voter with a receipt indicating the ballot was mailed and allowing the voter to verify the ballot was delivered. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law has no comparable provision, and the Secretary of State offers ballot tracking on the Secretary's website.

This bill, as enacted on May 10, 2022, creates a new biennial election review using an unspecified process that targets certain jurisdictions for more frequent review, begins an address confirmation process if a person doesn't vote for four years, gives poll watchers new access to confirm voting machines are not connected to the internet, and creates a new felony relating to a new ballot chain of custody process. Specifically, the bill:

Creates a new election audit process carried out by the Secretary of State, according the following requirements:

  • Audits must occur in the calendar year immediately after an even-numbered year general election.
  • The Secretary must audit four counties. While the bill provides the counties be selected "at random" from the state's 105 total, selection criteria ensure some counties will be audited much more frequently than other counties. Each cycle must include:
    • one county with a voting-age population of more than 90,000 people. Based on the 2020 Census, five counties have more than 90,000 total residents, so the number of counties that have more than 90,000 people aged 18 or older may be fewer than five.
    • one county with a voting-age population of more than 20,000 people and less than 90,000. Based on the 2020 Census, 22 counties have a total population in this range, so the number with that many people aged 18 or older may be less.
    • two counties with a voting age population of fewer than 20,000 people. Based on the 2020 Census, 78 counties have a total population in this range.

  • The scope of review is unbounded, with the bill requiring only that they cover "procedures used for election administration and election records for the elections held during the previous two calendar years." The Secretary of State is granted discretion to issue rules and regulations to enumerate the specific records and procedures to be examined.

    The bill also broadens the scope of the existing post-election audit process, by requiring audits in even-numbered election years for any federal, statewide, or state legislative race that is within 1% of the total number of votes tallied on election night, as determined by the Secretary of State. Note, this tally would not be complete, as ballots returned by mail on or before Election Day are timely if they are received by the third day after Election Day. Nonetheless, in this situation, the bill:


  • Requires the existing routine audit process to be followed, but applied to 10% of all county precincts, rather than 1% as normally required, with a minimum of one precinct in the county audited. These precincts would be in addition to the 1% of precincts required for certain races under the existing process.

  • Requires, when this audit is announced, counties to make available to authorized poll agents the signed and certified official abstracts from all precincts, not only those precincts subject to the audit. The abstracts would be available for review until the commencement of the original canvass.

    The new law also impacts other areas of election administration. Specifically, the law:


  • Requires election officials to send address confirmation notices to registered voters who have not voted or engaged in other election-related activity for four years. If the notice is returned as undeliverable, the voter's registration must be marked inactive and will be canceled if the voter does not take an election-related action for another two general election cycles. Existing law did not include failure to engage in election activity as a trigger for registration confirmation or cancellation.
  • Requires that electronic voting systems have no connectivity to the internet any other network, and requires election judges to make all electronic voting systems and tabulating equipment available for review by any candidate or authorized poll agent so they can ensure non-connectivity. This access must be granted before, during, and after the operation of the polling place. Existing law had no comparable provision.
  • Requires the Secretary of State, in consultation with county election officers, to develop a ballot chain of custody affidavit process.
  • Creates a new felony offense for altering or falsifying information in a ballot custody affidavit, with the intent to hinder, prevent, or defeat a fair election.
  • Expands an existing felony prohibiting frauds relating to electronic voting machines to reach the same conduct directed at electronic poll books.

  • Clarifies existing exceptions to existing election crimes to allow certain candidates to engage in the otherwise prohibited activity.

    The bill also includes provisions relating to electronic poll books, electronic voting machines and tabulators, ballot paper, and notices of testing election equipment that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

Last Updated September 20, 2022

This bill, as introduced February 1, 2022, would:

  • Establish no-excuse absentee voting. A desire to vote by absentee ballot would be added to the qualifying reasons for requesting an absentee ballot.

Under existing law, in-person, no-excuse absentee voting is available the Thursday, Friday, and Saturday before an election.
  • Establish same-day registration on Election Day. Voters would be permitted to register to vote at their precinct on Election Day and cast a regular ballot. Election Day registrants would be required to sign the affidavit signed by voters who are challenged.

This bill, as enacted on April 7, 2022:

  • Establishes specific requirements for the hours of early voting (carried out through the "no-excuse in-person absentee" process), by mandating that voting be available for at least eight hours between 6 a.m. and 8 p.m. on the Thursday, Friday, and Saturday before an election. Under existing law, counties were required to offer early voting during "normal business hours" on these days.
  • Expands access to in-person voting for excused absentee voters, during the six days preceding the early voting period for no-excuse absentee voting. While existing law had no comparable provision, existing State Board of Elections regulations required counties to offer in-person excuse-required absentee voting at clerks' offices during this same period (i.e., at least 12 days business days before an election). In addition to the existing general absentee excuses for UOCAVA voters, students temporarily residing out-of-state, other temporary residency out-of-state (while otherwise maintaining voting eligibility), and inability to appear during early voting or on Election Day due to age, disability, or illness, the bill establishes additional qualifying excuses specific to in-person absentee voting. The in-person process is now newly available to:
    • Voters who will be absent from their county during early voting and on Election Day
    • Voters who have surgery, or whose spouses have surgery, scheduled and will be hospitalized during the early voting period and on Election Day
    • Voters in uniformed service who will be confined to a military base during early voting and on Election Day
    • Voters in the last trimester of pregnancy
    • Voters who are scheduled to work during all the days and hours, including their commute time, of early voting and Election Day
    • Voters who are serving in election administration during the current election cycle
  • Sets out general requirements for early voting and in-person excused absentee voting sites, including:
    • Establishing rules for confidentiality of ballot tallies and voting equipment security
    • Requiring any official who is recording or witnessing the ballot tally to report irregularities to the county attorney or state attorney general
  • Expands eligibility for absentee voting by mail to include all individuals who will be absent from their county during all hours and on all days of early voting and on Election Day, without specifying a particular reason. Existing law limited this excuse to absence from the county due to employment. Note that those voters who will be present in their counties but working and/or commuting during all early voting hours and on Election Day, are only eligible for in-person excused absentee voting.
  • Permits disabled voters to receive a mail-in ballot through the state's online portal, in addition to requesting a ballot.
  • Modifies the requirements for canceling a mail-in ballot when a voter learns they will not be absent from their county. Under existing law, voters were required to cancel an absentee ballot if they know at least seven days before an election that they will be present in their county on Election Day. The bill also requires cancellation if the voter will be present during the early voting period.
  • Expressly includes U.S. citizenship among the qualifications to vote in Kentucky elections.
  • Prohibits the connection of voting tabulation equipment to any network, including the internet, or communication with any external devices.
  • Creates a new Class D felony for an election official knowingly and intentionally connecting or attempting to connect a voting machine, voting equipment, or voting system that tabulates or aggregates votes to a public network, including the internet.

  • Requires that audit regulations promulgated by the state board of elections establish the protocol by which ballots are checked, compared, and verified with the results produced by vote tallying equipment to ensure accuracy. The bill also requires the state's audit pilot program to include individuals representing the State Board of Elections, the Office of the Secretary of State, and no fewer than 5% of Kentucky's counties, and requires that findings be made public.

  • Expand the early voting (in-person absentee voting) period to begin 12 working days before Election Day and include the two Saturdays before Election Day. In practice, all voters would likely be able to request and cast absentee ballots in person at the beginning of absentee voting roughly 50 days before Election Day. Under existing law, in-person, no-excuse absentee voting is available the Thursday, Friday, and Saturday before an election.
  • Establish same-day registration on Election Day. Voters would be permitted to register to vote at their precinct on Election Day and cast a regular ballot. Election Day registrants would be required to sign the affidavit signed by voters who are challenged.

This bill, as enacted on April 13, 2022:

  • Modifies the minimum number of counties whose election results must be inspected for irregularities by the attorney general after each election, from 5% of counties to 12 counties.
  • Establishes the secretary of state as the tie-breaking vote on the state board of elections. Under existing law, the secretary of state was a non-voting member.
  • Eliminates the power of the executive director of the state board of elections to cast a tie-breaking vote regarding the selection of a chair of the board.
  • Repeals provisions establishing that the chair of the state board of elections is to be chosen by a majority of the voting members of the board. The bill does not specify how the board's chair is to be chosen.
  • Requires that voting equipment and ballot boxes be kept under video surveillance for 30 days following any election, in addition to the existing requirement that they remain locked during this period.

  • Modifies requirements for election equipment, including a prohibition on equipment used in tabulating or aggregation votes from connecting to the internet.

A previous version of this bill would have removed a credit or debit card bearing the voter's name from the list of qualifying forms of secondary ID that may be used at the polls by voters who lack photo ID and have a reasonable impediment preventing them from obtaining one. This bill, as introduced on March 3, 2022, would establish the Kentucky Committee on Legislative Redistricting. The committee would be composed of a faculty member from each public university in the state. The committee would be changed with drawing state legislative and U.S. congressional districts that:

  • Deviated minimally in population
  • Varied minimally from existing district lines
  • Were as compact in size as feasible
  • Were comprised of whole counties and communities insofar as was feasible
  • Recognized patterns of geography, social interaction, trade, political ties, and common interest among communities
  • Complied with other traditional redistricting principles

The legislature would then separately consider the plans proposed by the committee. If the legislature rejected a plan from the committee, the committee would have five days to propose a new plan in response to the reasons for rejection articulated by the legislature. The legislature would then enact the maps presented to it without opportunity to amend them.

Under existing law, the legislature draws and approves state and federal legislative district maps.

This bill, as vetoed by the governor on June 17, 2022, would require the Department of State to do a new, annual list maintenance practice triggered by a person not voting or otherwise taking voting or registration-related actions in the previous 10 years. Under existing law, not voting does not trigger a registration confirmation process. Specifically, the Department would:

  • Identify these voters.
  • Mark these voters' registrations "inactive" and send them a "supplemental address confirmation card" that the Department would develop. The confirmation card would be a postage prepaid and pre-addressed return card sent by forwardable mail.

  • Take certain actions depending on whether or how the voter responds. Specifically, if the voter:

    • responds that they have not moved or have moved within the parish, the registrar will restore the registration to "active" status, and if necessary, revise the voter's address.
    • responds that they have moved outside the parish but within the state, the registrar will transfer the registration appropriately and mark it "active".
    • responds that they have moved out of state, the registrar will cancel their registration.
    • does not respond, their registration would remain "inactive" and be subject to cancellation if the voter does not vote in the following two federal election cycles.

    Last updated July 19, 2022.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 14, 2022, would allow the state central committee of a recognized political party with at least 25% of the state's registered voters affiliated with it to appoint Election Day poll watchers and super watchers on the same terms that candidates may under existing law, and would allow them to appoint early voting watchers. Candidates' appointment powers would not change. Specifically, under the bill these political parties could:

  • Appoint one watcher at every precinct on Election Day in which the party has an affiliated candidate on the ballot.
  • Appoint super watchers in each parish who would have access to any Election Day precinct within their assigned parish provided the party they are serving has an affiliated candidate on the ballot in that precinct, and no other super watcher is present in that precinct. The number of super watchers who could be appointed to a parish would depend on the size of the parish. Specifically,
    • In a parish with fewer than fifty thousand registered voters, the party may designate one.
    • In a parish with fifty thousand or more but fewer than one hundred thousand registered voters, the party may designate two.
    • In a parish with one hundred thousand or more but fewer than one hundred-fifty thousand registered voters, the party may designate three.
    • In a parish with one hundred-fifty thousand or more but fewer than two hundred thousand registered voters, the party may designate four.
    • In a parish with two hundred thousand or more registered voters, the party may designate five.

  • Appoint watchers during early voting. Existing law does not address watchers during early voting. Specifically, under the bill:

    • Covered political parties could appoint one early voting watcher at each early voting location where the party has a candidate on the ballot, as space permits.
    • Any qualified Louisiana voter who is not a candidate could serve as an early voting watcher. Under existing law, watchers must be voters of the state who are not candidates and are not entitled to assistance while voting.
    • Early voting watchers would have the same powers and restrictions as Election Day watchers. Under existing law, watchers are subject to the authority of the registrar or deputy registrar and may report infractions of the law, may take notes, and may observe activity in the voting location. Watchers may not participate in specified voting processes, may not electioneer or otherwise engage with voters, may not interfere with the registrar or deputy registrar's performance of their duties.

    Last updated March 16, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on March 14, 2022, would establish a system for notifying voters about defective ballots and creating an opportunity to cure. Specifically the bill would:

  • Require the parish registrar to mail written notice to a voter when a ballot has been rejected, including a description of the defect and instructions on how to cure. Registrars would have the option of additionally contacting a voter by phone or email if such information was contained in the voter's registration record.
  • Require voters seeking to cure a defective ballot to appear at the registrar's office in person. If the ballot was rejected for missing a required witness signature, an employee of the registrar would serve as witness.
  • Require a majority of the parish board of election supervisors to reach a determination regarding the validity of a cured ballot.
  • Direct the secretary of state to establish an online method for voters to check the status of a ballot.

 

The bill would also clarify that ballots that do not have the voter's signature, a required witness signature, or are accompanied by an affidavit that was otherwise incomplete would be rejected.

This bill, as introduced on March 14, 2022, would amend the state constitution to establish a 15-member redistricting commission for congressional and state legislative districts:

  • Four commission members would be selected by each legislative chamber, no more than two of whom could be from the same political party. Commission members would be required to receive a supportive vote from two-thirds of the nominating chamber. Each chamber would be required to "give due consideration to the demographics of the population of the state, including but not limited to geography, gender, ethnicity, race, and political party affiliation," and, to the extent practicable, select commissioners that reflect the diversity of the state.
  • Three commission members would be chosen by the governor, and three by the state supreme court, giving due consideration to the diversity of the state and with no more than two of each chamber's selections being from the same political party. A final commissioner would be selected by the other 14 commissioners, requiring a vote of more than two-thirds of the 14.
  • Commissioners could not be elected or appointed public or political officeholders, an immediate family member of an official who holds an office subject to redistricting, a public employee, an employee of a public official or of a legal entity in which a public official holds an interest, a registered lobbyist, a member or employee of a political party committee, a manager or consultant for a political party, candidate, committee, or campaign, a registered voter in another state, or someone who had changed party affiliation in the prior three years. Commissioners also could not seek public office nor register as a lobbyist for a period of three years following service on the commission.
  • The commission would be required to hold at least one public meeting within each congressional district in the state.
  • The commission would be directed to submit to the legislature three alternative plans for each legislative chamber and the U.S. Congress, with a two-thirds affirmative vote required to submit a plan.
  • The legislature would be required to adopt one of the three plans without amendment.
  • If the legislature failed to submit three plans as required, the state supreme court would take over redistricting.
    Under existing law, the legislature draws and approves redistricting maps, and the governor has the ability to veto.

Last updated March 22, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on April 5, 2022, would:

  • Require prospective voters to provide documentary proof of U.S. citizenship as part of the registration application. Acceptable forms of proof would include photocopies of the following:
    • Birth certificate
    • U.S. Passport
    • Naturalization papers
    • Other forms of documentation established pursuant to the federal Immigration and Control Act of 1986.
  • Explicitly provide that neither a drivers license, including a REAL ID, nor proof of having been registered to vote in another state qualifies as proof of U.S. citizenship.
  • Clarify that only a citizen of the United States may register to vote in Louisiana.

Last Updated April 6, 2022

This bill, as enacted on June 18, 2022, requires that primary election polling place information be posted on the website of the secretary of state and clarifies that parish election officials may post polling place information on their websites. Under existing law, notice was required only in the official journal of the parish. The bill also requires parish officials to report all polling place changes to the secretary of state, in addition to the existing requirements to notify candidates and voters by various means. The Secretary must post the information on the agency website, and local officials are permitted, but not required, to post on their websites, as well. All websites offering information about polling location changes must also provide voters with the option to subscribe to electronic notifications for changes.

Last updated July 25, 2022.

This bill, as enacted on June 18, 2022, directs the secretary of state to promulgate and adopt rules for the uniform and standardized review and cure or rejection of deficient absentee by mail ballots by parish boards of election supervisors. While the state had existing regulations establishing a notice and cure process, there was no existing statutory provision requiring a uniform process.

Last Updated July 25, 2022

This bill, as enacted on June 16, 2022:

  • Grants the secretary of state the authority to take unilateral action to ensure the successful execution of an election during a declared state of emergency within 45 days of an election with regard to relocation or consolidation of polling places within a parish, potential shortages of commissioners, or shortages of voting machines. The secretary of state is required to provide notice to the governor and relevant legislative committees of problems identified and proposed solutions and to submit a report following the election. Under existing law, the governor and relevant legislative committees were required to agree that emergency action was necessary before the secretary of state could issue or implement an emergency plan.
  • Requires the secretary of state to post on their website any polling locations that change due to a declared emergency.

Last updated June 30, 2022.

This bill, as enacted on June 6, 2022:

  • Permits emergency election plans to include responses to "other impairments that affect participation in or the integrity of the electoral process." Under existing law, emergency plans only covered the relocation or consolidation of polling places within a parish, potential shortages of commissioners and absentee commissioners, and shortages of voting machines.
  • During an emergency, permits the secretary of state to conduct early voting at times and locations accessible to any affected voters when necessary and feasible. Under existing law, the secretary of state could conduct early voting for displaced voters only and only at parish registrar offices.
  • Expands emergency election procedures to be applicable in an emergency "or disaster."
  • Requires a joint meeting of the Senate Committee on Senate and Governmental Affairs and the House Committee on House and Governmental Affairs within 10 days of an emergency or disaster certification by the secretary of state. Although they function as a joint committee, a majority of members from each chamber is required in order to act.
  • Directs the secretary of the senate and clerk of the house of representatives to utilize "any method necessary" to allow legislators to vote on proposed emergency election plans. Existing law did not provide for voting by legislators outside the standard legislating process in the capital.
  • Permits the secretary of state to submit alternative emergency plans to the Joint Committee for consideration and to modify plans based on input from the Joint Committee. Under existing law, the secretary could only submit a single plan at a time for affirmative or negative votes.
  • Requires that an approved emergency election plan would then be presented to each full legislative chamber and the governor for approval or disapproval, and the governor would have five days to act. Both legislative chambers could also override a gubernatorial objection by two-thirds vote. Under existing law, there was no time requirement for gubernatorial action, and it was not clear that negative action by the governor could be overridden by the legislature.

Last updated June 13, 2022.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 26, 2022, would:

  • Regarding the registration process:
    • Move the voter registration deadline later, from noon on the 20th day before an election to noon on the tenth day before.
  • Regarding automatic voter registration:
    • Move the final day to complete a transaction at an automatic voter registration agency and vote in the following election from 21 days before the election to 10 days before the election.
    • Change the opt-out timing for automatic voter registration from during the relevant agency transaction to after the voter receives a mailer presenting them with the opportunity to decline to register, with an exception at the state health insurance exchange, if necessary to comply with federal law.
  • Regarding early voting:
    • Expand early voting to all state and federal general elections and primaries, with a municipal option for municipal elections. Under existing law, early voting is only available for biennial November general elections. For primary elections and special elections, early voting would be available during clerks' normal hours, and clerks would have the option to add additional hours.
    • Extend the early voting period for biennial general elections from starting the 11th business day before the election to starting the third Saturday before the election.
    • Require minimum weekend early voting hours based on municipality size, with municipalities with 75,000 or more registered voters required to offer at least eight hours each day. Under existing law, weekend hours are not required but may be offered at the discretion of the municipal clerk.
    • Direct the state secretary to conduct a public awareness campaign regarding early voting.
  • Regarding requesting mail ballots:
    • Require early voting by mail ("absentee") applications to be mailed to each voter at least 45 days before a presidential or state primary or biennial state election. Applications would be mailed in any required language. Under existing law, there is no requirement to mail applications to voters who do not request them.
    • Allow Boston residents to request mail ballots printed in a variety of different languages.
    • Direct the state secretary to establish a system for requesting mail ballots online that does not require a voter's signature.
    • Permit electronic signatures for early mail ballot requests. Existing law is silent on electronic signatures.
    • Require prepaid postage on mail ballot return envelopes.
    • Explicitly allow ballot return by drop box, to a clerk's office, by mail, or electronic return for individuals with disabilities.
  • Regarding the return, verification, or cure of mail ballots:
    • Direct the opening of early voting ballot outer envelopes upon receipt.
    • Require signature matching between early voting applications and ballot envelopes.
    • Establish a notice and cure process for ballots with defective signatures or affidavits. Clerks would notify the voter and send the voter a replacement ballot automatically upon rejection of their original ballot.
    • Clarify that a ballot cast by a voter who dies between casting the ballot and Election Day should be counted.
  • Regarding voter list maintenance:
    • Direct the state secretary to join ERIC.

Last Updated September 5, 2025

Last Updated September 5, 2025

This bill, as introduced on January 31, 2022, would:

  • Move the voter registration deadline later, from noon on the 20th day before an election to noon on the tenth day before.
  • Move the final day to complete a transaction at an automatic voter registration agency and vote in the following election from 21 days before the election to 10 days before the election.
  • Change the opt-out timing for automatic voter registration from during the relevant agency transaction to after the voter receives a mailer presenting them with the opportunity to decline to register, with an exception at the state health insurance exchange, if necessary to comply with federal law.
  • Establish same-day registration at the polling place on Election Day. Voters would have to provide proof of residence and sign an affidavit, then cast a regular ballot. Voters without proof of residence could cast a provisional ballot then produce proof of residence to the clerk by six days after a general election or two business days after a primary.
  • Direct the attorney general or proper district attorney to investigate and prosecute upon receiving "credible information or allegation of illegal voter registration, or credible information or allegation of illegal multiple voting."
  • Expand early voting to all state and federal general elections and primaries, with a municipal option for municipal elections. Under existing law, early voting is only available for biennial November general elections. For primary elections and special elections, early voting would be available during clerks' normal hours, and clerks would have the option to add additional hours.
  • Extend the early voting period for biennial general elections from starting the 11th business day before the election to starting the third Saturday before the election.
  • Require minimum weekend early voting hours based on municipality size, with municipalities with 75,000 or more registered voters required to offer at least eight hours each day. Under existing law, weekend hours are not required but may be offered at the discretion of the municipal clerk.
  • Require absentee ("early voting by mail") applications to be mailed to each voter at least 45 days before a presidential or state primary or biennial state election. Applications would be mailed in any required language. Under existing law, there is no requirement to mail applications to voters who do not request them.
  • Direct the state secretary to establish a system for requesting early or absentee ballots online that does not require a voter's signature.
  • Permit electronic signatures for absentee ("early by mail") ballot requests. Existing law is silent on electronic signatures.
  • Require prepaid postage on mail ballot return envelopes.
  • Explicitly allow ballot return by drop box, to a clerk's office, by mail, or electronic return for individuals with disabilities.
  • Direct the opening of early voting ballot outer envelopes upon receipt.
  • Require signature matching between early voting applications and ballot envelopes.
  • Establish a notice and cure process for ballots with defective signatures or affidavits. Clerks would notify the voter and send the voter a replacement ballot automatically upon rejection of their original ballot.
  • Require the state secretary to collect data on the voter eligibility status and changes to voter eligibility status from criminal justice agencies as part of their intake and release processes.
  • Require, as part of the release from incarceration of an individual who is eligible to vote, that the correctional facility provide information about voting rights, a voter registration form, assistance completing the form, and, unless the voter declines, a postage prepaid envelope and returning the form on the voter's behalf.
  • Require correction facility administrators to report to the state secretary a monthly list including (i) individuals convicted of a felony who, during the preceding period, have become ineligible to vote because of their incarceration, (ii) individuals convicted of a felony who, during the preceding period, have become eligible to vote because of their discharge from incarceration, and (iii) individuals detained pre-trial or convicted of a misdemeanor who are eligible to vote. The list would include (i) name, (ii) date of birth, (iii) the last 4 digits of social security number, or driver's license number, if available, (iv) address on file, (v) whether the person is held pre-trial or serving a misdemeanor and eligible to vote, (vi) the name and address of the jail, prison, or other facility where they are detained, and (vii) race and ethnicity.
  • Clarify that eligible voters who are incarcerated may use their place of incarceration as their voting address if they do not have a permanent address.
  • Require correctional facility staff to develop and publish policies to facilitate voter registration, distribute voting information, provide vote by mail applications, facilitate proof of residence, ensure timely delivery of election mail, including ballots.
  • Require that correctional facilities report to the secretary of state and the public any measures taken to facilitate voting by eligible incarcerated individuals, the number of applications received from incarcerated voters, the number of applications rejected from incarcerated voters, and the number of ballots received from incarcerated voters.
  • Require that online registration be available in English, Spanish, Portuguese, and Chinese (Mandarin and Cantonese), and any additional languages the state secretary deems necessary. Currently, online registration is available in English, Spanish, Mandarin, and Khmer.
  • Allow Boston residents to request absentee ballots printed in a variety of different languages.
  • Clarify that a ballot cast by a voter who dies between casting the ballot and Election Day should be counted.
  • Direct the state secretary to join ERIC.
  • Direct the state secretary to conduct a public awareness campaign regarding early voting.

Last Updated March 21, 2022

This bill, as enacted on June 22, 2022:

  • Expands in-person early voting availability. Specifically, the bill:
    • Requires early voting for presidential or state primaries, vacancy primaries and elections, and any city/town elections occurring on the same days, in addition to existing availability for biennial state elections. The bill also permits in-person early voting for city or town elections, and specifies procedures for adopting and administering early voting in these elections.
    • Changes the in-person early voting period for biennial state elections to the 17th through the 4th day before Election Day, inclusive. Prior law provide in-person early voting for these elections from the 11th day before an election through the 2nd business day before. The bill also requires in-person voting for presidential and state primaries, and vacancy primaries and elections, from the 10th through the 4th day before an election, inclusive.
    • Requires weekend early voting, with various requirements for voting hours and days depending on municipality size. Municipalities with over 25,000 registered voters are required to have both Saturday and Sunday early voting, with varying hours requirements. Under prior law, municipalities were permitted, but not required, to offer early voting on the weekend.
  • Permits municipalities with up to 40,000 registered voters to offer in-person early voting for only a portion of the town clerk's business hours. Under prior law, early voting was available during all town clerk business hours in all municipalities.
  • Requires local election officials to publicly post the location of early voting sites at least five days before the voting period begins. Prior law required public notice at least seven days prior.
  • Applies existing requirements related to mandatory notices and prohibited electioneering at Election Day polling places to in-person early voting locations. The bill also requires jurisdictions to provide police officers at all polling places, without exception. Under existing law, jurisdictions were permitted to exercise their discretion as to whether to provide police officers at early voting locations.
  • Expands mail ballot early voting availability and modifies application and voting procedures. Specifically, the bill:
    • Requires early voting by mail in any municipal preliminary or election, presidential or state primary or election (including special elections), and vacancy primary or election. Municipalities may vote to not provide early voting by mail for local elections, unless they fall on the same day as a mandatory early voting election. Prior law permitted early voting, in-person or by mail, for biennial state elections only.
    • Directs the secretary of state to mail early voting ballot applications, with prepaid return postage, to all voters registered within 60 days of an election. The applications must be mailed to voters at least 45 days before an election, and must be in any language required for compliance with federal law. The bill also requires local officials to include an early voting ballot application with all acknowledgment notices following new or updated voter registration. Prior law had no comparable provisions.
    • Moves the application deadline for early voting mail ballots from the fourth business day before an election to the fifth business day before Election Day.
    • Requires the secretary of state to establish an online application portal for early voting by mail ballots and excuse-required absentee ballots. Applications must also be available on the secretary of state website and all city and town websites. Prior law had no comparable provisions.

    • Requires local officials to notify a voter if they determine that the applicant is not a registered voter or their family member, and to preserve the application for a specified period. Prior law had no comparable provision related to the rejection of an application.
    • Requires officials to provide early voting mail ballots in another language, if required for compliance with federal law. Prior law had no comparable express provision.
    • Requires officials to provide accessible mail ballots to voters with disabilities, including accessible means for ballot return. Prior law had no express provisions related to ballot accessibility for early mail voting.
    • Requires early mail voters who request a substitute ballot to return their spoiled ballot by 5 p.m. on the fifth day before the election to receive a replacement. Prior law had no express provisions concerning replacement early mail ballots.

    • Moves the application deadline for excuse-required absentee ballots from the fourth day before an election, to the fifth day before.

Prior law required this verification process for absentee ballots, but had no comparable provision for mailed early voting ballots.

    • Changes the registration deadline from 8 p.m. on the 20th day before an election to 5 p.m. on the 10th day before an election.

The bill also permits individuals to vote if they are registered through the automatic registration process at least 10 days before an election. The deadline under existing law was at least 21 days prior to an election.
    • Requires registrars to make registration continuously available on the last day of the registration period from 9 a.m. - 5 p.m., rather than 9 a.m. - 8 p.m. as previously required. This bill, as introduced January 12, 2022, would add a new data source regarding deceased Maryland residents to be used in removing deceased voters from the voter roll.

Specifically, the bill would require the State Administrator of the State Board of Elections to arrange to receive the names and addresses of deceased Maryland residents who are at least 16 years old and who died within the past 30 days from Maryland crematories, morticians, and funeral directors. Once a voter has been identified as potentially deceased, the local election director sends the voter a notice to confirm that they are deceased. This bill, as introduced on January 13, 2022, would change the mail ballot application and ballot verification process, most significantly by requiring both paper-based applications and ballot envelopes to be verified by signature matching, and creating a notice and cure process for voters to resolve any determinations that their signature on the application or ballot did not match the one on file. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Change applying for a mail ballot by:
    • Requiring the voter to indicate whether they would like to be communicated with by mail, email, or text message, paralleling the requirement for voters who choose to join the permanent absentee ballot list.
    • Requiring the local board of elections to verify the voter's signature on a paper application or written request by matching it to a signature in the voter's record. An online application, which does not involve a signature but does require ID numbers, would not be subject to this requirement.
    • Requiring the local board to notify the voter using the voter's preferred method of communication, if the board cannot match the voter's signature using the signatures on file. The board would direct the voter to provide any of the forms of identification that existing law allows a voter to use to defeat a challenge to their identity at a polling place.
  • Change verifying a mail ballot by:
    • Requiring the local board of elections to verify the signature on the ballot envelope by matching it to a signature in the voter's record.
    • Requiring the local board of elections to notify the voter using their preferred method of communication, if the board cannot match the voter's ballot envelope signature to one on file. That notice would direct the voter to explain why their signature does not match, and to vote in person or enable the counting of their mail ballot by providing one of the forms of identification that existing law allows a voter to use to defeat a challenge to their identity at a polling place.
    • Requiring the local board, if a mail ballot is ultimately rejected but the voter appeared at their polling place and voted a provisional ballot, to count the provisional ballot. Under existing law, all voters who are issued absentee ballots must vote a provisional ballot if they appear to vote in person, and if they have returned both ballots, both are rejected as illegal double voting.
  • Require the State Board of Elections to provide each local board machines to electronically verify signatures.

  • Require the State Board of Elections to issue regulations providing for signature verification on ballot applications and ballots. Because the bill does not address key aspects of the notice and cure process, such as deadlines, presumably they would be specified in the regulations. Although the bill does not explicitly address missing signatures, a missing signature cannot match a signature on file. Thus it is possible these regulations could require boards of election to do the notice and cure process for missing signatures as well.

    • the individual's voter registration card,
    • the individual's Social Security card,
    • the individual's valid Maryland driver's license,
    • any identification card issued to the individual by a political subdivision of the State, the State, the federal government, or any unit of a political subdivision of the State, the State, or the federal government,
    • any employee identification card of the individual that contains a photograph of the individual and is issued by the employer of the individual in the ordinary course of the employer's business, or
    • a copy of a current bill, bank statement, government check, paycheck, or other government document that shows the name and current address of the individual.

    Under existing law, signatures on ballot applications and ballot envelopes do not go through a verification process. Ballots are counted if the envelopes are signed, sealed, and returned on time.

Governor Larry Hogan vetoed this bill on May 27, 2022. The bill would have created a fully specified cure process to enable mail voters to have their ballots counted instead of rejected, and to facilitate cure, would have allowed boards of election to begin verifying mail ballots earlier than under current law. Finally, the bill would have created new rules for canvassing absentee and provisional ballots when a voter has returned more than one absentee ballot or has returned an absentee ballot and cast a provisional ballot in person. Specifically, the bill would have:

  • Required boards of election, when they receive a mail ballot, to review the envelope to see if the voter signed the oath. Existing law requires the board to verify the ballot has been signed as part of the post-election absentee ballot canvass process.
  • Allowed boards of election to begin processing mail ballots beyond verifying that the oath has been signed at 8 a.m. eight business days before early voting. Under existing law, mail ballot envelopes cannot be opened before 8 a.m. on the Wednesday after Election Day. If counties choose to use a "three envelope" approach to mail ballots, the voter's signature--or the fact that it is missing--cannot be seen until someone opens the outer envelope.
  • Created a cure process for voters who failed to sign the oath on their ballot envelopes by requiring the State Board of Elections to issue regulations, and specifying parameters for them. On December 31, 2021, the State Board did issue regulations to require local boards to enable voters to cure a missing signature, however, those regulations lack the details included in this bill. Specifically, the regulations required by this bill would have had to:
    • require the local board to give the voter notice of the issue as soon as practicable, but no later than three business days after discovering it. The existing regulation requires "prompt" notice.
    • give the voter until 10 a.m. on the 10th day after Election Day to address the issue. The existing regulation does not set a deadline.
    • give the voter multiple methods of communicating with the local board to correct the failure to sign the oath on the ballot envelope, including by mail, email, and in-person, and beginning June 1, 2023, by text message and an accessible online portal as well. The existing regulation requires notice to be sent to the voter using the method the voter chose when applying for the ballot, and if that method does not succeed, by another method. However, the existing regulation does not address how the voter can communicate with the board.
    • allow the voter to supply the missing signature to the local board through a digital picture message sent by email, and beginning June 1, 2023, by mobile telephone text message. The existing regulation does not specify how a voter may address their missing signature.
  • Required local boards of elections to count a voter's earliest returned legally sufficient ballot, if a voter returns more than one ballot in separate envelopes, regardless if the ballots are absentee or provisional. Existing law provides that if a voter returns more than one absentee ballot, the latest-returned ballot counts, and if a voter returns both an absentee ballot and a provisional ballot, both are rejected.
  • Prohibited the tabulation of absentee ballots before the close of polls on Election Day generally, but specifically allow pre-Election Day tabulation for the 2022 statewide primary only, while providing that the tabulated results could not be released before the close of polls on Election Day. Under existing law, absentee ballots are not canvassed, and therefore cannot be tabulated, until after Election Day.
  • Required local boards to prepare and release tabulation returns at the end of each day of canvassing, beginning after the polls close on Election Day. Under existing law, boards must release a single, final statement of results. The results must be by precinct, except that absentee ballots must not be reported by precinct.

  • Required canvassing totals by local boards of election to present early, absentee, and provisional voting separately, and the totals prepared by the State Board to be presented in each of those categories by precinct. Under existing law, neither the State nor the local boards of election are required to report their results by vote type.

Last Updated May 31, 2022

This bill, as introduced on February 10, 2022, would require mail ballots to be verified by matching the signature on the ballot certificate with the voter's signature on file. The bill would also create a cure process for voters whose ballots are rejected for non-matching signatures and missing signatures. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the State Board of Elections to issue regulations detailing a signature matching process, and require local boards of elections to use it to verify ballots. Under existing law, mail ballots are counted if they are signed by the voter, properly sealed, and timely returned.
  • Authorize using machines to do signature matching and require the State Board to give such a machine to a local board that requests it.

  • Create a cure process for missing and non-matching signatures. Specifically:

    • The local board would notify the voter of the discrepancy no later than the second Sunday after the election.
    • Allow the voter to cure within two days of receiving the notice. The voter could cure by signing a signature verification statement. If the signature on the verification statement is verified, the voter's ballot would count. If the statement signature is also rejected, the ballot would not count.
    • Allow a voter to cure a missing signature by submitting an unsigned ballot statement by the second Sunday after Election Day. Regulations adopted on December 31, 2021, provide for a notice and cure process for ballots missing a signature, however, a cure deadline is not specified in the regulations.

This bill, as introduced on February 17, 2022, would offer curbside voting, defined as privately and independently completing and casting a secret ballot at an outside location, during both early and Election Day voting. Specifically:

  • Outdoor voting would be available to:
    • voters physically unable to enter the polling place,
    • voters likely to have their health harmed by entering the polling place,
    • voters who are pregnant,
    • voters authorized to make the request by the state board of elections in the interest of public health and safety, or
    • voters with disabilities recognized by the federal Americans with disabilities act.
  • Outdoor voting would be available whenever polls are open for early and Election Day voting.
  • Outdoor voting would be available:
    • within 150 feet of each early voting center during early voting,
    • within 150 feet of the office of the local board of elections, or if that location is not practicable, at each polling place chosen by the State Board of Elections in collaboration with the local board.
    • within the plain view of the observing election judges, who will maintain a record of each use of curbside voting.
  • Each outdoor voting location would include:
    • signage about the process
    • an area at which a voter can obtain information from candidates and other campaigners
    • a method that a voter can use to request curbside voting that does not require a cell phone or for the voter to call ahead.

  • The State Board would be required to issue any needed regulations.

This bill, as introduced on January 26, 2022, would give voters a remedy when a municipal or county government has adopted a method of electing its government that impairs the ability of a protected class to elect candidates of their choice, or their ability to influence the outcome of an election, as a result of the dilution or abridgment of their rights. Specifically, counties and municipalities would be prohibited from adopting such an electoral system, and the Attorney General would be given the power to sue to enforce the prohibition, seeking an injunction, damages, or other relief. To bring an enforcement action, the Attorney General would need to show a protected class engages in polarized voting, as defined by federal case law interpreting the Voting Rights Act of 1965, and that the electoral system has the dilutive or abridging effect. Proof of intent would not be required.

To prove a protected class engages in polarized voting, the bill would direct a court to consider:

  • The methodologies for estimating group voting behavior, as approved in federal case law, to enforce the federal Voting Rights Act of 1965.
  • The elections of the governing body of the county or municipality.
  • Ballot question elections.
  • Elections where at least one candidate is a member of a protected class.

  • Other electoral choices that affect the rights and privileges of members of a protected class.

    To prove the prohibited dilutive or abridging effect, the bill would establish each of these factors as probative, but not necessary:

  • The history of discrimination.
  • The use of electoral devices or other voting practices or procedures that may enhance the dilutive effects of a method of election, including at large elections.
  • The denial of access to the processes determining which groups of candidates will receive financial or other support in a given election.
  • The extent to which members of a protected class bear the effects of past discrimination in areas such as education, employment, and health that hinders the ability to participate effectively in the political process, and

  • The use of overt or subtle racial appeals in political campaigns.

    When weighing these factors, the bill would instruct judges that:

  • Elections conducted before the filing of an enforcement action would be more probative to establish the existence of polarized voting than elections conducted after the filing of an action.
  • The election of candidates who are members of a protected class and who were elected before an enforcement action may not preclude a finding of polarized voting that results in an unequal opportunity for a protected class to elect candidates of its choice.

  • The fact that members of a protected class are not geographically compact or concentrated may not preclude a finding of polarized voting or a violation, but it may be considered.

    • Requiring a clerk, after rejecting an application because the signature does not match the one on file or is missing, to contact the voter by phone or email within three business days and not later than 8 pm on Election Day, whichever is earlier. If the voter's email is not available, the clerk must contact the voter by phone and first-class mail. Under existing law, the clerk must, as soon as practicable but no later than 48 hours after the determining the issue or by the close of polls, whichever comes first, notify the voter by mail, telephone, or email.

The verification form may be submitted by mail, fax or email.

    • Allowing clerks to contact voters if their ballot certificate signature is missing or does not match the one on file before rejecting the ballot. The notice would be given not more than 48 hours after the close of polls by phone or email. If they cannot reach the voter or cannot resolve the signature issue, the clerk would reject the ballot. Existing law does not have a comparable provision.
    • Requiring clerks to contact voters if the clerk rejects a voter's ballot because the certificate is not signed or the signature does not match the one on file. The clerk must give the notice by telephone and email as soon as practicable, but not more than 48 hours after the close of the polls on Election Day. If an elector's email address is not available, the clerk must notify the elector by telephone and first-class mail. The voter would be able cure the issue by delivering to the clerk a signature verification statement or an unsigned ballot statement, by mail, by facsimile, or by email. The voter would have until 72 hours after the close of the polls on Election Day to deliver the statement. The voter's signature on these statements would be compared to the ones on file, and if they match, the ballots would count. If the voter appears in person and shows voter ID, the ballot would count even if the signatures do not match. Under existing law, voters are given notice by mail, phone, or email only if the signature issue is determined before 8 p.m. on the day before Election Day. Voters who receive notice under existing law appear in person to provide a signature, or if there is sufficient time left, spoil their ballot and receive a new absentee ballot.
    • Requiring the clerk to post the forms of the signature verification statement and unsigned ballot statement on the city or township website. The forms must include the city or township clerk's mailing address, email address, and fax number. The bill specifies the language for each form.
