VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 23, 2022, would establish robust signature matching standards, change the processes for notifying voters of a signature issue on an absentee ballot application or ballot, and expand the ways a voter may cure the issue. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Change the rules for giving voters notice of a missing or mismatched signature on a ballot application or a ballot. If the clerk discovers the issue six or more days before the election, the clerk would be required to notify the voter within one business day of discovering the issue. If the clerk discovers the issue five or fewer days before the election but before 8 p.m. on the day before the election, the clerk would be required to notify the voter on the same day as discovering the issue. Notice would be given by telephone and email. If a voter's email address is not available, the clerk would give notice by telephone and first-class mail. Under existing law, if the issue with an application or ballot is discovered by 8 p.m. on the day before Election Day, the clerk must give the voter notice as soon as practicable, within 48 hours and before the close of polls, by mail, telephone, or email. Notice is not otherwise required.
  • Enable voters to resolve signature issues in additional ways. Under existing law, cure methods are not specified for applications. To solve ballot issues, voters may appear in person to sign the ballot or may spoil the ballot and receive another, if there is time. The bill would allow voters to:
    • Sign the application or ballot with the missing signature, or provide the clerk a new, matching signature.
    • Complete and submit to the clerk a signature cure form as prescribed by the secretary of state.
    • Follow another form or method as specified by the clerk on the city or township website or as provided in the city or township clerk's office.
  • Enable clerks to assist voters by collecting the signature cure form, or by bringing the application or ballot with the missing signature to the voter. Existing law has no comparable provision.
  • Maintain the existing deadline to cure of close of polls on Election Day.
  • Provide that a signature could be rejected as not sufficiently matching only if it "differs in significant and obvious respects from the signature on file." Slight similarities would be resolved in favor of the voter. An exact match would not be required, and specified standards would need to be followed. Before deciding a signature did not match, the clerk would be allowed to contact the voter about the issue. Such contact would not count as notice if the signature is determined to not match and the ballot rejected.
  • Require election officials doing signature matching to consider whether there are any "redeeming qualities" present, and require the bureau of elections to provide examples of questionable signatures and redeeming qualities. The bill gives as examples of redeeming qualities:
    • Similar distinctive flourishes.
    • More matching features than nonmatching features.
    • It appears the mismatch was caused by the voter's hand trembling or shaking.
    • Only part of the signature matches the signature on file, such as if only the first letters of the first and last name match.
    • The signature is partially printed but partially matches the signature on file.
    • The signature is a recognized diminutive of the voter's full legal name.
    • The signature omits a middle name, replaces a middle name with an initial, or replaces a middle initial with a name.
    • The signature style has changed slightly from the signature on file.
  • Require election officials doing signature matching to consider all of the following explanations for any discrepancies in a signature:
    • Evidence of trembling or shaking in a signature could be health-related or the result of aging.
    • The voter may have used a diminutive of his or her full legal name,
    • The voter's signature style may have changed slightly over time.
    • The signature may have been written in haste.
    • The surface of the location where the signature was made may have been rough, soft, uneven, or unstable.
    • The age of the voter.
    • The age of the signature or signatures contained on the master card or in the qualified voter file.
    • The possibility that the voter has become disabled.
    • The voter's primary language.
    • The quality of the digitized signature contained in the qualified voter file.
    • Any other plausible reason for the discrepancy.

  • Create rules for determining precisely when a clerk has received ballots and applications to trigger the notice rules. One of these rules would require clerks who choose to use drop boxes to receive absentee ballot applications or ballots to retrieve any applications or ballots before the close of their business hours on every day they open for business.

This bill, as amended on June 21, 2022, would require all challengers and poll workers to be trained for each election with a curriculum created by the Secretary of State. Specifically, the bill would:

This training would be for each county clerk, each political party, incorporated organization, or organized committee of interested citizens that seeks to designate election challengers.

  • Require the Secretary to maintain a list of the political parties and groups that completed the training, post it online, and keep county clerks informed.
  • Require political parties and groups who have been trained to train the people the party or group intends to appoint as challengers. The parties and groups must hold separate training for the people who wish to be challengers at an absent voter counting board. The party or group would give each person who completed the training a certificate of completion and impose a civil fine of up to $2,500 for each time a party or group issues such a certificate to someone who did not do the training.
  • Require each potential challenger to take the training within 90 days of the election at which they intend to serve as a challenger and forbid them from serving as a challenger unless they have a signed certificate for completing the training. However, if a person trained for a primary election, they could work the associated general election without being trained again provided the law did not change in between.

Under existing law, the county clerks do this list maintenance monthly, sending local clerks a list of deceased registrants.
    • Requiring the Secretary of State to send an electronic notification to the appropriate city or township clerk each time the county clerk updated the statewide registration list this way, and whenever the Secretary updates the list for deceased registrants. Each time a local clerk received an electronic notification, the clerk would compare it to the local voter roll and complete the cancellation of each deceased voter's registration. Existing law does not require such electronic notifications, but does requires clerks to cancel registrations using the list sent by county clerks once a month.
    • Requiring the county clerk and the Secretary to inform city and township clerks of voter registrations that need to be canceled after 4 p.m. on the day before an election. Existing law does not have a similar provision.
  • Include county clerks in the list of clerks with whom the Secretary of State shares canceled voter registration information.

  • Require the Secretary to post on the Department of State website at least once a month the total number of registrations canceled broken down by month, year, county, city, and township.

    Last updated March 18, 2022

This bill, as introduced on March 23, 2022, would establish robust signature matching standards, change the processes for notifying voters of a signature issue on an absentee ballot application or ballot, and expand the ways a voter may cure the issue. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Change the rules for giving voters notice of a missing or mismatched signature on a ballot application or a ballot. If the clerk discovers the issue six or more days before the election, the clerk would be required to notify the voter within one business day of discovering the issue. If the clerk discovers the issue five or fewer days before the election but before 8 p.m. on the day before the election, the clerk would be required to notify the voter on the same day as discovering the issue. Notice would be given by telephone and email. If a voter's email address is not available, the clerk would give notice by telephone and first-class mail. Under existing law, if the issue with an application or ballot is discovered by 8 p.m. on the day before Election Day, the clerk must give the voter notice as soon as practicable, within 48 hours and before the close of polls, by mail, telephone, or email. Notice is not otherwise required.
  • Enable voters to resolve signature issues in additional ways. Under existing law, cure methods are not specified for applications. To solve ballot issues, voters may appear in person to sign the ballot or may spoil the ballot and receive another, if there is time. The bill would allow voters to:
    • Sign the application or ballot with the missing signature, or provide the clerk a new, matching signature.
    • Complete and submit to the clerk a signature cure form as prescribed by the secretary of state.
    • Follow another form or method as specified by the clerk on the city or township website or as provided in the city or township clerk's office.
  • Enable clerks to assist voters by collecting the signature cure form, or by bringing the application or ballot with the missing signature to the voter. Existing law has no comparable provision.
  • Maintain the existing deadline to cure of close of polls on Election Day.
  • Provide that a signature could be rejected as not sufficiently matching only if it "differs in significant and obvious respects from the signature on file." Slight similarities would be resolved in favor of the voter. An exact match would not be required, and specified standards would need to be followed. Before deciding a signature did not match, the clerk would be allowed to contact the voter about the issue. Such contact would not count as notice if the signature is determined to not match and the ballot rejected.
  • Require election officials doing signature matching to consider whether there are any "redeeming qualities" present, and require the bureau of elections to provide examples of questionable signatures and redeeming qualities. The bill gives as examples of redeeming qualities:
    • Similar distinctive flourishes.
    • More matching features than nonmatching features.
    • It appears the mismatch was caused by the voter's hand trembling or shaking.
    • Only part of the signature matches the signature on file, such as if only the first letters of the first and last name match.
    • The signature is partially printed but partially matches the signature on file.
    • The signature is a recognized diminutive of the voter's full legal name.
    • The signature omits a middle name, replaces a middle name with an initial, or replaces a middle initial with a name.
    • The signature style has changed slightly from the signature on file.
  • Require election officials doing signature matching to consider all of the following explanations for any discrepancies in a signature:
    • Evidence of trembling or shaking in a signature could be health-related or the result of aging.
    • The voter may have used a diminutive of his or her full legal name,
    • The voter's signature style may have changed slightly over time.
    • The signature may have been written in haste.
    • The surface of the location where the signature was made may have been rough, soft, uneven, or unstable.
    • The age of the voter.
    • The age of the signature or signatures contained on the master card or in the qualified voter file.
    • The possibility that the voter has become disabled.
    • The voter's primary language.
    • The quality of the digitized signature contained in the qualified voter file.
    • Any other plausible reason for the discrepancy.

  • Create rules for determining precisely when a clerk has received ballots and applications to trigger the notice rules. One of these rules would require clerks who choose to use drop boxes to receive absentee ballot applications or ballots to retrieve any applications or ballots before the close of their business hours on every day they open for business.

Last Updated March 25, 2022

This bill, as introduced on March 23, 2022, would require the Secretary of State to maintain an online absentee ballot application portal that meets certain requirements. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require a voter to provide their name, complete driver's license or state ID number, full date of birth, last four digits of their Social Security number, and eye color to apply for a ballot using the system. If the voter has a digital signature on file with the Secretary, digitally stored by the DMV, that signature will be used for the application. If the voter does not, the system would allow the voter to provide a manual digital signature by uploading a photograph of their signature. Existing law does not require the Secretary to offer an online application portal, but the Secretary has chosen to offer one on the Secretary's website. The current system only requires a driver's license or state ID number, and does not allow for a voter to upload a signature if they have a license or state ID but their signature is not electronically stored at DMV.
  • Require the online form to otherwise be substantially the same as the paper form.

  • Require the Secretary to forward applications submitted through the system to the appropriate city or township clerk.

Last Updated March 25, 2022

This bill, as introduced on June 9, 2022, would make it a felony to give money to local governments or election officials for anything related to turning out voters, including mailing absent voter applications to all voters.

Specifically, the felony prohibits: "either directly or indirectly, giv[ing], lend[ing], or promis[ing] any money or other consideration to the secretary of state, a county, city, township, or village, or any election official in this state to influence, either directly or indirectly, the electors to vote in person or by absent voter ballot."

Last updated June 13, 2022

This bill, as introduced on September 7, 2022, would expand the reasons an eligible, registered voter could get an "emergency" absentee ballot (called "absent ballot" in Michigan). Emergency absentee ballots are available for voters with a listed justification after the ordinary absentee ballot application deadline of 4 p.m. on the day before Election Day but before 4 p.m. on Election Day. Prior to the deadline for ordinary absentee ballots, voters do not need a justification to vote by mail.

Under the bill, if the registered voter was or is detained in jail in a way that made it impossible for the voter to apply by the regular absentee ballot deadline, the voter could apply for an "emergency" absentee ballot. Under existing law, only people who become physically disabled or absent from their city or township because of sickness or death in their family occurred at a time that made applying before the deadline impossible.

Last Updated September 8, 2022

This resolution, as introduced on June 9, 2022, proposes an amendment to the state constitution to recognize that people are eligible to vote at 18 years old, and to allow people who are 17 at the time of the primary but will be 18 by the associated general election to vote in the primary.

Last Updated June 13, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 31, 2022, would require voter ID to vote in person and by absentee ballot and would restrict voting access in several other ways. Specifically, this bill would:

  • Require voters to provide documentary proof of identity and residence when voting in person. Voter who lack proof of identity and residence cannot receive a regular ballot, but will instead be given a provisional ballot. Under existing law, a voter must confirm their name, address, and date of birth before voting, but need not provide documentary proof of that information. Under this bill, proof of identity and residence includes:
    • A driver's license, state ID, or voter ID with the voter's photo and current address.
    • A valid military ID with the voter's photo and current address.
    • A tribal ID card that contains the voter's photo and current address.
    • A receipt for a driver's license, state ID card, or voter ID card that includes the voter's photo and current address. If it does not include a photo, the voter must also provide an expired license or state ID, a passport, a governmental ID card, a student ID card, or a tribal ID card.
    • A document that includes a photo (passport, government ID, tribal ID, or military ID) along with a document that includes the voter's address (utility bill, government check, high school ID and transcript, college ID and transcript, employment pay stub, unemployment statement, assisted living statement, insurance policy, income tax return or statement, property tax statement, certificate of vehicle title, property deed, social security statement, mortgage documents, residential lease, professional license, draft card, or military orders).
  • Require that voters who use same-day voter registration on Election Day or when submitting an absentee ballot ballot application must present proof of identity and residence. Under existing law, only proof of residence is required.
  • Allow voters to use their voter ID number as an acceptable ID number type for absentee ballot applications. Under existing law, voters must provide their driver's license number, state ID card number, or the last four digits of their social security number, or they can state that they do not have any of these numbers. This bill would also require that local election officials verify the ID number listed on a voter's absentee ballot application and reject any applications where the number is not valid or is not assigned to the voter requesting the absentee ballot.
  • Change absentee ballot and vote-by-mail ballot return requirements by:
    • Allowing voters to use their voter ID number as an acceptable ID number type for absentee ballot envelopes. Under existing law, voters must provide their driver's license number, state ID card number, or the last four digits of their social security number, or they can state that they do not have any of these numbers.
    • Requiring voters show proof of identity and residence to the witness signing their ballot. Voters who attempted to procure proof of identity and residence cut were unable to may sign a sworn affidavit as to their identity, eligibility, and inability to secure proof of identity and residence with an explanation of the reason why they could not obtain it.
    • Requiring that witnesses to voter's absentee ballots must swear that the voter showed the witness proof of identity and residence and note the documentation the voter provided. The witness must provide their own ID number or a statement that the witness does not have a driver's license number, state ID card number, voter ID card number, or the last four digits of their social security number. If a witness fails to provide the information or lists documents that are not authorized by law, the absentee ballot will be rejected.
    • Prohibiting third party return of a voter's absentee ballot. Under existing law, a voter may designate an agent to return their absentee ballot.
  • Require the state registrar or local election officials to issue a free voter photo ID card to any applicant who does not have a current Minnesota driver's license or state ID card. To obtain a free voter ID card, the applicant must provide:
    • their name,
    • their date of birth,
    • their address,
    • the last four digits of the applicant's social or a certification that the applicant does not have a social security number,
    • a physical description of the voter,
    • proof of citizenship,
    • the length the applicant has lived at their current resident, and
    • a photo ID or a sworn statement that the voter has a religious objection to being photographed.
  • Change provisional ballot procedures to require that a person who votes a provisional ballot due to lack of documentary proof of identity and residence must sign a sworn statement on the provisional ballot envelope as to their identity, eligibility, and that they have not previously voted in the election. The provisional ballot will only be counted if the voter appears in person before the county auditor or municipal clerk within seven days after Election Day and presents proof of identity and residence or executes an affidavit swearing that the voter attempted to procure proof of identity and residence but was unable to do so. If a voter fails to appear in person, their provisional ballot will not be counted under any circumstances.
  • Require the secretary of state to conduct a public education campaign to inform voters of the ID requirements created by this bill.
  • Make new requirements for early voting locations to require that all early voting locations must be at a precinct polling place and must be open during the entire early voting period for the same hours and days as the county auditor's office.
  • Require that anyone assisting a voter must provide their name, address, phone number, and signature to the election judge.
  • Prohibit local election officials from accepting private grant funds for conducting elections.
  • Prohibit compensating people from being paid per application for soliciting, collecting, or accepting absentee ballot applications.
  • Alter elections crimes by:
    • Creating a new felony for assisting a voter in a manner not authorized by law.
    • Expanding the existing misdemeanor of undue influence on voters to include influence in registering to voter or applying for an absentee ballot. The existing misdemeanor is also increased in severity to a felony.
    • Expanding the existing felony of bribing a voter to include providing things of monetary valuable or offering other consideration to induce a voter to register to voter or apply for an absentee ballot.

  • Move the start date for canvassing primaries and elections later after Election Day.

    This bill also contains provisions relating to appropriations and other topics not tracked by Voting Rights Lab.

Last Updated July 13, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 31, 2022, would change the criteria that the legislature must consider when redistricting federal congressional districts and state legislative districts in 2022. The bill would allow the legislature to consider geographic areas and populations counts used by the GIS office of the legislative coordinating commission. This bill would require the legislature to consider, in the following order of priority:

  • Neutrality of impact on political parties, candidates, and incumbents.
  • Nesting, in that a senate district must consist of two whole representative districts.
  • Population equality.
  • Minority representation, as measured by the ability of racial, ethnic, and language minorities to:
    • participate in the political process and elect candidates of their choice and
    • provide racial and language minorities who are not the majority in a district with the opportunity to substantially influence the outcome in an election.
  • Preservation of communities of interest.
  • Respecting the geographic boundaries of tribal reservations, which may only be divided if:
    • a portion of the reservation is not contiguous with another portion of the reservation or
    • even with a division, the known population of the reservation is wholly within a single district.
  • Compactness and contiguity.

  • Preservation of political subdivisions.

    Last updated February 1, 2022.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on February 17, 2022, makes no substantive changes to the previous version of the bill, although it does add an appropriation to implement the provisions of the bill. Otherwise, the bill, as amended, is unchanged, and would:

  • Create a specific early voting period beginning 30 days before Election Day and ending the day before Election Day for all federal, state, and county elections, and for city elections if the city meets technical standards and chooses to offer it. Under existing law, voters may vote an absentee ballot in person before Election Day at the county auditor or town clerk's office. Early voting during this period would be conducted similar to Election Day in-person voting and would have these features:
    • Early voting would be conducted from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. every weekday, except that early voting remains open until 5:00 p.m. the day before Election, is open from 10:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. the two Saturdays before Election Day, and must be open from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. on at least one weekday during the period.
    • Early voting would be available at the county auditor's office, at municipal clerk's offices (if they meet certain criteria), and at other city- or county-owned buildings designated by local election officials. If there are insufficient governmental buildings, local election officials may use other suitable locations meeting existing standards for polling places.
    • There must be at least one polling place for every 50,000 people in the county in geographically distributed locations.
    • Each early voting polling place must have at least one voting station and one ballot marking device for disabled voters.
    • Each polling place must have an electronic ballot counter.
    • Local election officials may establish additional polling places which may be open for fewer than 46 days. If these are in use, their location and hours must be available on the websites for both local election officials and the secretary of state.
    • Notice of days, times, and locations for early voting must be provided to voters at least 14 days before the early voting period starts.
    • A voter's participation in early voting must be recorded immediately. Any voter who has participated in early voting must not be permitted to vote at any other time in that election.
    • Ballots cast during the early voting period must be processed and counted by a ballot board.
    • These provisions do not take effect until the statewide voter registration system has been shown to allow for the conduct of early voting and until voting equipment that can tabulate all the ballot styles in the county is certified for use in the state.
  • Convert the existing list which allows a voter to automatically receive an absentee ballot application before each election into one that allows a voter to automatically receive an absentee ballot before each election. Voters in vote-by-mail jurisdictions within the state are not eligible for this status. This bill also creates deadlines for sending these ballots: 46 days before Election Day for all elections except for town general elections held in March. For those elections, the ballots must be sent 30 days before Election Day.

  • Extend the time to process early and absentee ballots. Under existing law, such ballots can be processed beginning seven days before Election Day. This bill would permit them to be processed on the day before the beginning of early voting, or 31 days before Election Day.

Last Updated February 22, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 3, 2022, would eliminate the requirement that voters provide proof of residency when registering to vote. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Eliminate the requirement that applicants to register to vote by mail must include their driver's license number, state ID number, or the last four digits of their social security number.
  • Change same-day voter registration processes by:
    • Eliminating the requirements that a same-day voter registration applicant must make an oath and provide proof of residency. However, such voters would only be provided with a provisional ballot. Under existing law, voters who register to vote on Election Day are entitled to vote a regular ballot. A provisional ballot would be counted under this bill if the person's voter registration is accepted. A voter would be notified after the election if their provisional ballot was rejected.
    • Allowing a tribal ID card that lacks an address to be used for same-day voter registration. Under existing law, only tribal ID cards containing the voter's address may be used for same-day registration to provide residency.
    • Requiring that any same-day registrants be entered into the voter registration system within three days after Election Day. Under existing law, they must be entered within 42 days after Election Day.
    • Requiring the secretary of state to conduct a public awareness campaign to encourage people to register to vote before Election Day.
  • Change processes for voters who simultaneously return an absentee ballot and apply to vote by:
    • Eliminating the requirement that voters who are simultaneously registering to vote and returning an absentee ballot present proof of residence to the witness for the absentee ballot.
    • Requiring election officials to open ballot envelopes to determine if there is a voter registration application in the envelope. If so, then the application must be removed and the envelope resealed. The auditor would then promptly process the application. Under existing law, the voter registration application is processed by the absentee ballot board during absentee ballot processing.
  • Change requirements for challengers by allowing challengers to prove their residency by presenting a student ID or a student fee statement in addition to the other forms of ID already named in statute.

  • Change the time for canvassing primary and general elections, in provisions not tracked by Voting Rights Lab.

HISTORY: {"date":["03/17/2022","03/17/2022"],"summary":["From HOUSE Committee on JUDICIARY FINANCE AND CIVIL LAW DIVISION:  Do pass","Rereferred to HOUSE Committee on WAYS AND MEANS"],"meta":["[]","[]"],"order":[1,0]}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on March 10, 2022, would make minor changes to the previous version of the bill, which would prohibit certain actions that election officials or that interfere with the administration of elections, and would provide for civil and criminal penalties for violations. Unless noted below, the provisions described were retained from the previous version of the bill. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Define election officials to include local election officials and workers. The previous version of the bill also included members of the state canvassing board in the definition of election workers, but they are no longer included in the definition in this version of the bill.
  • Prohibit anyone from directly or indirectly threatening violence, harm, or loss, including economic loss, against another with the intent to influence an election official in the performance of their official duties. The bill would allow election officials to bring a civil action for violations, in which the movant need not show that the perpetrator intended to cause intimidation.
  • Prohibit anyone from intentionally hindering, interfering with, or preventing election officials from performing their official election duties.
  • Prohibit anyone from knowingly disseminating personal information about election officials without their consent if the dissemination poses an imminent and serious threat to the election official or their family's safety and the person disseminating the information should know of any imminent and serious threat. The bill defines personal information as the election official's address, directions to their house, or photos of their house. The definition of personal information is a new provision that did not appear in the previous version of the bill.
  • Prohibit anyone from knowingly making false allegations against an election official about the official's performance of official duties with the intent to influence the official's performance of their duties.
  • Prohibit anyone from intentionally physically obstructing an election official's access to or egress from a polling place, canvassing board meeting, or other places where the election official performs elections duties.
  • Create a new misdemeanor for any person who commits one of the prohibited acts described in the bill.
  • Create a civil action for an election official injured by one of the prohibited acts described in this bill. The election official could recover damages, costs of investigation, and reasonable attorney fees.
  • Create a civil action in the attorney general for actions prohibited by this bill, in which the attorney general can recover damages, costs, of investigation, reasonable attorney fees, and civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation.

  • Create vicarious liability for any of the prohibited actions for a person who intentionally conspires with, aids, incites, coerces, or assists in other ways a person who violates the provisions of this bill.

    Last updated March 24, 2022.

HISTORY: {"date":"02/21/2022","summary":"To HOUSE Committee on STATE GOVERNMENT FINANCE AND ELECTIONS","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 21, 2022, would change the state's voter ID requirements, absentee voting procedures, election crimes, and other aspects of election law. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require documentary proof of identity, in the form of voter ID, in many situations where it is not currently required, by:
    • Requiring photo ID and proof of residence to vote in person. Under existing law, voters affirm their identity and residence under penalty of perjury but are not required to provide documentation.
  • Requiring that anyone lacking proof of ID or proof of residence when voting in person would be required to cast a provisional ballot. Provisional ballots would only be counted if a voter presents photo ID and documents proving their residence within seven days after Election Day unless the voter attempts to procure these documents but is unable to and attests to that fact.
  • Requiring photo ID for anyone registering to vote on Election Day. Under existing law, photo ID is typically required but can be waived if a registered voter or residential facility employee signs an oath affirming the voter's identity, based on the affiant's personal knowledge.
    • Requiring photo ID for any person applying to vote at the time they return an absentee ballot or a mail ballot. This provision would require that the witness signing the voter's absentee ballot show photo ID to demonstrate their identity. Under existing law, the voter needed to only show the witness proof of residence. This provision would also require the witness to provide their own driver's license number, state ID number, voter ID number, the last four digits of their social security number, or a statement that they do not have any of these numbers. Ballots lacking this information would be rejected.
    • Expanding the types of ID numbers required on absentee ballot applications, absentee ballot envelopes, and mail ballot envelopes to include voter ID numbers. Under existing law, applicants must provide their driver's license number, state ID number, the last four digits of their social security number, or a statement that they do not have any of these ID numbers. This bill would require that the voter's ID number be verified and reject any application with an invalid ID number.
    • Providing free voter IDs to any person who lacks a driver's license or state ID card. Applicants must provide a social security number (or a certification that they do not have one), proof of citizenship, and a photo ID (unless they have a religious objection) before obtaining a free voter ID. Voter IDs would have a unique ID number, the person's name, date of birth, address, signature, and description. This bill would also provide that people who need a certified vital record can obtain the record for free if the person attests that it is to obtain a voter ID card.
    • Requiring the secretary of state to conduct a public education campaign regarding the new ID requirements of this bill and the availability of free voter ID.
  • Change absentee voting processes by:
    • Prohibiting anyone from being paid for soliciting or collecting absentee ballot applications from voters on a per-voter basis.
    • Eliminating voters' ability to designate an agent to return their absentee ballots to election officials. Instead, voters would be required to mail or deliver their ballots personally.
    • Authorize only those polling places which are open for the entire absentee voting period to the same extent as the office of the county auditor. This would prohibit mobile or pop-up polling places as well as polling places that operated during extended hours.

This bill, as introduced on February 24, 2022, would move the deadline for combining polling places in off-cycle years earlier, except in emergencies. The bill also alters candidate filing dates, local election dates, primary dates, and redistricting dates in provisions not tracked by Voting Rights Lab.

Last updated May 17, 2022.

This bill, as amended on May 2, 2022, would change early voting, election funding, absentee voting and ballot processing, and more. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require any designated additional early voting locations, other than the county auditor's office, to be a designated Election Day precinct polling place. When the county auditor administers absentee voting, the polling place must be open for in-person absentee voting for the entire absentee period, during the same days and hours as the county auditor's office. When the municipal clerk administers absentee voting, the polling place must be open for in-person absentee voting for the entire absentee period during the clerk office's regular business hours. Existing law provides only that auditors may offer early voting at an "additional polling place," in addition to the auditor's office, and does not specify required polling place times.
  • Prohibit a county, city, or school district from accepting contributions "in any form" from businesses or nonprofit organizations to pay for election administration. Existing law does not contain a similar requirement.
  • Change requirements for the absentee ballot application process and absentee ballot package design. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require any person or entity mailing absentee ballot applications or sample ballots to voters to include a statement stating that the mailing is not an official government election communication, that the mailing was not at the request of a government official, and that if a sample ballot is sent, the sample ballot is not an official ballot and must not be cast.
    • Prohibit the mailing of a pre-filled absentee application. Existing law is silent as to providing voters with pre-filled application forms.
    • Require the absentee ballot package to include a "signature envelope," and rename the "ballot envelope" as a "secrecy envelope." The bill would require the new signature envelope to enclose the secrecy envelope, and require that a return envelope may either be the signature envelope itself, if it includes a flap to conceal identifying information, or a third enclosure that will fit the signature envelope inside. Existing law requires the use of only a return envelope and ballot envelope.
    • Require the certificate of eligibility to vote absentee to be printed on the back of the signature envelope, instead of on the return envelope as required by existing law.
    • Require absentee ballots to include a "security marking," such as a watermark or ultra-violet mark, that enables the ballot to be authenticated.
  • Change requirements for ballot return and processing, including increased drop box security measures. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Permit an absentee ballot to be "personally delivered" to the office of the county auditor or municipal clerk, as an alternative to return by mail or drop box. Existing law permits an absentee ballot to be "left with the county auditor or municipal clerk."
    • Expressly prohibit a voter's designated agent from returning a ballot to a drop box. Existing law permits a third party to return a voter's ballot in person or by mail, but does not include an express prohibition on return to a drop box.
    • Require each ballot drop box to be continually livestreamed (i.e., live footage made available on the public website of the Department of Information Technology Services) during the absentee voting period and on Election Day. Existing law requires drop boxes to be continually recorded, with no real time public access to footage, during only the absentee voting period.
    • Require that all drop boxes must be located within 100 feet of a door to the building where a county auditor or municipal clerk's office is located, must be available during the entire absentee voting period, and must be assigned a unique ID number. Existing law has no comparable provisions regarding placement, availability, or identification numbers. The bill would also require existing signage for drop boxes to include a statement notifying voters that they may only return their own ballot to the box, and display of the box identification number.
    • Require election officials to maintain a log for each drop box, which must include the box's unique ID number, the date and time of ballot collection, the name of the collector, and the number of ballots collected. The bill would also require election officials to total the number of ballots collected from each box during each day of the absentee voting period and submit the totals to the local ballot board and the Secretary of State, prior to the meeting of the canvassing board. The Secretary would then be required to submit the totals by county to the state canvassing board and ranking minority members of the legislative election committees. Existing law does not contain similar requirements.
    • Prohibit the Secretary of State from adopting or implementing rules regarding the use of drop boxes. Existing law has no express prohibition on the Secretary's discretionary authority over drop boxes.
    • Increase the frequency of drop box collection from once every business day to once every day.
  • Change absentee ballot board procedures. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require absentee ballot board members to verify the presence of security markings on accepted absentee ballots, and reject ballots that do not contain such a mark. Under existing law, board members may reject absentee ballots upon opening them only if more than one ballot is contained in a return envelope.
    • Authorize the presence of observers appointed by major and minor parties, or by candidates in nonpartisan races, at absentee ballot board meetings. Observers must be appointed at least 30 days before the start of the absentee voting period and election officials must be notified of the observer's appointment and identifying information. The bill would prohibit certain individuals from acting as observers, and require all appointees to complete election judge training. The observer would be allowed to be within four feet of the ballots or envelopes, and be permitted to observe the process of examining, accepting or rejecting envelopes, opening envelopes and duplicating ballots, depositing absentee ballots into a ballot box, and counting and tabulating ballots. The bill would prohibit observers from handling ballots, preparing lists of individuals who have or have not voted, or interfering with the board's conduct, and would authorize the board to remove a disruptive observer. The bill would also require election officials to provide written notice to observers at least seven days before any board activity that they are authorized to observe.
    • Require ballot board activity to be livestreamed during the absentee voting period, on Election Day, and on the day after the election if absentee ballots are being processed. The livestream recording must, at minimum, record the process of examining, accepting, or rejecting envelopes, the opening envelopes and duplicating ballots, the deposit of absentee ballots into a ballot box, and the counting and tabulating of ballots. The bill would require livestream cameras to be positioned to capture board members conducting required activities, all ballots in the room where such activities take place, and all doors to the room where the activities take place. To the extent possible, cameras must be positioned to avoid recording private data on absentee ballots or other documents.
    • Require the ballot board to stop all activity if the livestream is interrupted and appointed observers are not present. Activity would be resumed only when the livestream was restarted, the observers arrived, or local officials arranged for the activities to be recorded through other means that substantially comply with the livestream requirements.
    • Prohibit an absentee ballot board from including deputy county auditors or deputy city clerks, unless the auditor or clerk has been appointed as an election judge. Existing law permits the appointment of a deputy county auditor or deputy city clerk to an absentee ballot board as long as they have had training in processing and county of absentee ballots.
  • Establish the classification of information entered into the electronic voter registration system and make changes to regulations regarding the submission and transmission of registration information. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Classify all information in the state electronic voter registration system as public information, except the following "private data": identifying information related to a minor, or a voter's date of birth, driver's license number, ID number, military ID number, passport number or any part of the voter's social security number. The bill would also expressly prohibit the publicly available voter list from including anything deemed private data. Existing law does not expressly classify public and private data on the voter registration list. Provisions require only that officials make publicly available a voter's name, address, year of birth, and voting history.
    • Require anyone requesting public voter list information to confirm in writing that the information will not be used for purposes unrelated to elections, political activities or law enforcement. While existing law prohibits using the list for these purposes, it does not require a written affirmation to comply.
    • Reduce the amount of time the county auditor has to enter voter registration application information submitted on Election Day into the statewide voter registration system, from 42 days after an election to before the canvassing of the election. The bill would also eliminate the option for the Secretary of State to post a county's application upload deadline on their website, and would instead require the Secretary to post each county's actual compliance date.

    • Reduce the amount of time the county auditor has to post the voting history of every voter from six weeks after an election to prior to the canvass of an election.
  • Specify requirements for newly mandated livestreaming of election activities. Livestreams must be publicly available on the Department of Information Technology Services (DITS) website, and all footage must be recorded and preserved by the department for at least 22 months. The Secretary of State and local election officials would be required to provide information on their websites about how to access video data through the DITS, and the department would be prohibited from charging any fee for the footage. The bill would deem the recordings public data, and authorize DITS to obscure any visible private data concerning individuals.
  • Change the public notice requirements for testing for mandatory testing of election equipment.
  • Prohibit vaccine requirements for election judges or members of a ballot board. Existing law does not contain a similar requirement.
  • The bill also contains numerous provisions related to the state budget and areas of election law that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

A number of provisions that Voting Rights Lab does track were amended out of the current version of the bill. In those provisions, the previous version would have:

  • Changed the ID numbers that would be acceptable for voter registration by:
    • Allowing any voter to register using the last four digits of their social security number. Under existing law, only voters who lack a state driver's license or state ID can register with the last four digits of their social security number.
    • Providing that a voter who lacks a driver's license number, state ID number, and social security to register with their name and date of birth only if either the voter's information can be verified in another government database or if the voter registration application was accepted before January 1, 2004.     • Intimidating or interfering with election officials in the performance of their official duties,
    • Disseminating the personal information of an election official or their family if such dissemination poses a threat,

This bill, as introduced on March 17, 2022, would change numerous provisions of existing voting law, and specifically would:

  • Allow any town of any size in any county to provide exclusively vote-by-mail elections, with no in-person voting locations other than the offices of local elections officials. Under existing law, only towns located in non-metropolitan counties may utilize vote-by-mail elections.
  • Expand UOCAVA voting rights to emergency responders and utility workers deployed during the absentee voting period during a declared state of emergency.
  • Provide that a voter registration may be processed if a voter does not list a state driver's license number, state ID number, or the last four digits of the voter's social security number if the voter lacks all those ID numbers, as long as either the voter's information can be verified in another government database or the voter registered to vote before January 1, 2004. Existing law does not require local election officials to verify the voter's information in a government database if the voter lacks the specified types of ID numbers.
  • Change the process for providing absentee ballots to an address confidentiality program participant, so so that the secretary of state can either request a ballot from local election officials and mail it to the participant, or can use the statewide voter registration system to prepare the participant's ballot personally. Under existing law, only the first option is available to the secretary of state. The bill also specifies that a participant in the address confidentiality program must be permitted to cast a ballot at the presidential nomination primary. Existing law is silent as to that point.
  • Allow local election officials to deliver ballots to veterans' homes and battered women's shelters in the same manner as they are delivered to health care facilities and hospitals under existing law.
  • Change the timing for siting polling place locations to:
    • Require that changes to Election Day polling place locations must be changed by ordinance or resolution by December 31 of the previous year, without exception. Existing law provides several exemptions to this deadline.
    • Require that in-person absentee voting locations be designated at least 14 weeks before Election Day. Under existing law, this provision only explicitly applies to March elections.
  • Expand the definition of residential facilities whose employees are permitted to vouch for same-day registrants' identities to include assisted living facilities, residential treatment programs, and adult foster care programs.
  • Require that all in-person absentee voting locations have at least one electronic ballot marker for voters with disabilities. Under existing law, electronic ballot markers are only required in polling places that have implemented an accessible voting system.
  • Eliminate the existing restriction that a person who assists the voter in a voting booth may assist no more than three voters per election in such a manner.
  • Clarify that electioneering boundaries are only applicable during voting hours. Existing law is silent as to that point.
  • Require the State Canvassing Board to declare candidates who received the highest number of votes for each office after completion of the canvass to be duly elected.

  • Change all references to "residing" within existing statute to "maintaining residence."

    This bill also changes rules relating to special elections in provisions not tracked by Voting Rights Lab.

This bill, as introduced on March 21, 2022, would change a number of provisions of existing election law including, but not limited to, absentee ballot return, drop boxes, and same-day voter registration. Specifically, this bill would:

  • Prohibit a voter's designated agent from depositing the voter's absentee ballot into a drop box. Under existing law, such agents may return an absentee ballot on behalf of the voters they represent, and the method of return is not restricted.
  • Change standards for drop boxes by:
    • Requiring that drop boxes be livestreamed continually, in a publicly-accessible manner, and that the recording be retained.
    • Requiring each drop box to be located within 100 feet of a door to an election official's office. Under existing law, drop boxes need not be located in specific locations tied to election official office locations.
    • Requiring that each drop box be available for the entire absentee voting period. This would be a new requirement on top of existing requirements.
    • Requiring that each drop box be assigned a unique identification number. This would be a new requirement on top of existing requirements.
    • Requiring each drop box to include signage about the prohibition on returning the absentee ballot of another person to a drop box and about the drop box's unique identification number.
    • Requiring that only the county auditor or municipal clerk may collect ballots from drop boxes and must do so daily. Under existing law, other election officials may collect ballots, and they need only be collected once every business day.
    • Requiring that the person collecting ballots from drop boxes must maintain a log of collections including time, collecting individual, and number of ballots collected, along with the unique identifier of each drop box. This information must be submitted to the secretary of state daily. Before the state canvassing board meets, the secretary of state must compile the totals and submit them to the legislative committees of cognizance.
  • Prohibit the secretary of state from making rules to implement or supplement the provisions of the bill dealing with reporting on absentee ballots collected from drop boxes.
  • Require that all ballot board activity, including examining, accepting, and rejecting envelopes, opening envelopes, sorting absentee ballots, and counting and tabulating absentee ballots, be recorded and retained, as well as livestreamed in a manner available to the public.
  • Require local election officials to enter same-day registrants into the statewide voter registration system within two days after Election Day. Under existing law, local election officials must enter same-day registrants within 42 days after Election Day.
  • Mandate that the secretary of state electronically transmits voter registration information to local election officials. Under existing law, the secretary of state may mail or electronically transmit applications.
  • Tweak existing law regarding the premature disclosure of vote counts. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Define a premature disclosure as one made before all ballots, including absentee ballots, have been counted and totaled. Existing law is silent as to whether absentee ballots must be counted before vote counts can be released.
    • Prohibit the disclosure of absentee vote counts to the same extent as Election Day vote counts. Under existing law, disclosure of absentee vote counts was prohibited, but not in the same manner or using the same language as applied to Election Day vote counts.

  • Impose reporting requirements on the secretary of state regarding drop box security and integrity and video recording of election activities. This report must be issued to the legislative committees of cognizance and must include accounting for grants and their expenditure.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on April 7, 2022, prohibits a county canvassing board from certifying election results until it has completed two tasks: a ballot reconciliation certification already required by law and a post-election review already required by law. The existing reconciliation requires poll workers to determine if the number of ballots to be counted matches the number of ballots in the ballot, describes how to quality control to achieve correct numbers, and the process to take if the numbers cannot be made to match. The existing post-election review is a manual count of ballots to ensure proper performance by tabulation machines and must be completed in the period between 11 and 18 days after Election Day. Under existing law, the state canvassing board meets on the third Tuesday following Election Day, meaning that the additional pre-certification tasks required of county canvassing boards will generally not impact the certification of statewide elections.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on April 8, 2022, would change the state's voter ID requirements, absentee voting procedures, election crimes, and other aspects of election law. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require documentary proof of identity, in the form of voter ID, in many situations where it is not currently required, by:
    • Requiring photo ID and proof of residence to vote in person. Under existing law, voters affirm their identity and residence under penalty of perjury but are not required to provide documentation.
    • Requiring that anyone lacking proof of ID or proof of residence when voting in person would be required to cast a provisional ballot. Provisional ballots would only be counted if a voter presents photo ID and documents proving their residence within seven days after Election Day, unless the voter attempts to procure these documents but is unable to and attests to that fact.
  • Requiring photo ID for anyone registering to vote on Election Day. Under existing law, photo ID is typically required but can be waived if a registered voter or residential facility employee signs an oath affirming the voter's identity, based on the affiant's personal knowledge.
    • Requiring photo ID for any person applying to vote at the time they return an absentee ballot or a mail ballot. This provision would require that the witness signing the voter's absentee ballot show photo ID to demonstrate their identity. Under existing law, the voter needed to only show the witness proof of residence. This provision would also require the witness to provide their own driver's license number, state ID number, voter ID number, the last four digits of their social security number, or a statement that they do not have any of these numbers. Ballots lacking this information would be rejected.
    • Expanding the types of ID numbers required on absentee ballot applications, absentee ballot envelopes, and mail ballot envelopes to include voter ID numbers. Under existing law, applicants must provide their driver's license number, state ID number, the last four digits of their social security number, or a statement that they do not have any of these ID numbers. This bill would require that the voter's ID number be verified and reject any application with an invalid ID number.
    • Providing free voter IDs to any person who lacks a driver's license or state ID card. Applicants must provide a social security number (or a certification that they do not have one), proof of citizenship, and a photo ID (unless they have a religious objection) before obtaining a free voter ID. Voter IDs would have a unique ID number, the person's name, date of birth, address, signature, and description. This bill would also provide that people who need a certified vital record can obtain the record for free if the person attests that it is to obtain a voter ID card.
    • Requiring the secretary of state to conduct a public education campaign regarding the new ID requirements of this bill and the availability of free voter ID.
  • Change absentee voting processes by:
    • Prohibiting anyone from being paid for soliciting or collecting absentee ballot applications from voters on a per-voter basis or from being deprived of pay for failure to collect a minimum number of absentee ballot applications.
    • Eliminating voters' ability to designate an agent to return their absentee ballots to election officials. Instead, voters would be required to mail or deliver their ballots personally.
    • Authorizing only those polling places which are open for the entire absentee voting period to the same extent as the office of the county auditor. This would prohibit mobile or pop-up polling places as well as polling places that operated during extended hours.
    • Requiring that any third party assisting a voter provide their name, address, and phone number, along with a statement certifying compliance with legal obligations for third party assistance.
  • Create and expand elections crimes by:
    • Expanding the existing election crime prohibiting undue influence on voters to include coercing a person to register to vote or to apply for an absentee ballot. This would also change the existing misdemeanor to a felony.
    • Expanding the existing election felony prohibiting bribing voters to include bribing voters to register to vote or to apply for an absentee ballot.
    • Creating a new felony for a person assisting a voter in marking their ballot in a manner not authorized by law.
  • Require the secretary of state to annually report to legislative leadership their proposed legislation, which, according to this bill, should only be legislation that would codify matters that would otherwise be adopted through administrative rulemaking.
  • Extend the timeframe for canvassing ballots after primaries and elections.

  • Make additional conforming changes to other sections of the election code.

    This bill contains a provision unrelated to election law and thus untracked by Voting Rights Lab.

Last Updated April 11, 2022

This bill, as introduced on February 21, 2022, would create early voting and make other changes to the Election Code. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create a specific early voting period beginning 30 days before Election Day and ending the day before Election Day for all federal, state, and county elections, and for city elections if the city meets technical standards and chooses to offer it. Under existing law, voters may vote an absentee ballot in person before Election Day at the county auditor or town clerk's office. Early voting during this period would be conducted similar to Election Day in-person voting and would have these features:
    • Early voting would be conducted from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. every weekday, except that early voting remains open until 5:00 p.m. the day before Election, is open from 10:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. the two Saturdays before Election Day, and must be open from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. on at least one weekday during the period.
    • Early voting would be available at the county auditor's office, at municipal clerk's offices (if they meet certain criteria), and at other city- or county-owned buildings designated by local election officials. If there are insufficient governmental buildings, local election officials may use other suitable locations meeting existing standards for polling places.
    • There must be at least one polling place for every 50,000 people in the county in geographically distributed locations.
    • Each early voting polling place must have at least one voting station and one ballot marking device for disabled voters.
    • Each polling place must have an electronic ballot counter.
    • Local election officials may establish additional polling places which may be open for fewer than 46 days. If these are in use, their location and hours must be available on the websites for both local election officials and the secretary of state.
    • Notice of days, times, and locations for early voting must be provided to voters at least 14 days before the early voting period starts.
    • A voter's participation in early voting must be recorded immediately. Any voter who has participated in early voting must not be permitted to vote at any other time in that election.
    • Ballots cast during the early voting period must be processed and counted by a ballot board.
    • These provisions do not take effect until the statewide voter registration system has been shown to allow for the conduct of early voting and until voting equipment that can tabulate all the ballot styles in the county is certified for use in the state.

Voters in vote-by-mail jurisdictions within the state are not eligible for this status. This bill also creates deadlines for sending these ballots: 46 days before Election Day for all elections except for town general elections held in March. For those elections, the ballots must be sent 30 days before Election Day.

This provision would require that the witness signing the voter's absentee ballot show photo ID to demonstrate their identity. Under existing law, the voter needed to only show the witness proof of residence. This provision would also require the witness to provide their own driver's license number, state ID number, voter ID number, the last four digits of their social security number, or a statement that they do not have any of these numbers. Ballots lacking this information would be rejected.

Under existing law, applicants must provide their driver's license number, state ID number, the last four digits of their social security number, or a statement that they do not have any of these ID numbers. Applicants must provide a social security number (or a certification that they do not have one), proof of citizenship, and a photo ID (unless they have a religious objection) before obtaining a free voter ID. Voter IDs would have a unique ID number, the person's name, date of birth, address, signature, and description. This bill would also provide that people who need a certified vital record can obtain the record for free if the person attests that it is to obtain a voter ID card.

    • Prohibiting anyone from being paid for soliciting or collecting absentee ballot applications from voters on a per-voter basis.
    • Eliminating voters' ability to designate an agent to return their absentee ballots to election officials. Instead, voters would be required to mail or deliver their ballots personally.
    • Authorize only those polling places which are open for the entire absentee voting period to the same extent as the office of the county auditor. This would prohibit mobile or pop-up polling places as well as polling places that operated during extended hours.

  • Make additional conforming changes to other sections of the election code.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on March 30, 2022, is essentially unchanged from the version of the bill. This bill, as amended, would change a number of provisions of existing election law including, but not limited to, absentee ballot return, drop boxes, and same-day voter registration. Specifically, this bill would:

  • Prohibit a voter's designated agent from depositing the voter's absentee ballot into a drop box. Under existing law, such agents may return an absentee ballot on behalf of the voters they represent, and the method of return is not restricted.
  • Change standards for drop boxes by:
    • Requiring that drop boxes be livestreamed continually, in a publicly-accessible manner, and that the recording be retained. The recording must be retained and made available on the county's website pursuant to specifications set forth in the bill. The previous version of the bill did not include specifics of record retention.
    • Requiring each drop box to be located within 100 feet of a door to an election official's office. Under existing law, drop boxes need not be located in specific locations tied to election official office locations.
    • Requiring that each drop box be available for the entire absentee voting period. This would be a new requirement on top of existing requirements.
    • Requiring that each drop box be assigned a unique identification number. This would be a new requirement on top of existing requirements.
    • Requiring each drop box to include signage about the prohibition on returning the absentee ballot of another person to a drop box and about the drop box's unique identification number.
    • Requiring that absentee ballots must be collected from the drop box by election officials every calendar day. Under existing law, ballots must only be collected from drop boxes once every business day.
    • Requiring that the person collecting ballots from drop boxes must maintain a log of collections including time, collecting individual, and number of ballots collected, along with the unique identifier of each drop box. This information must be submitted to the secretary of state and the county canvassing board daily. Before the state canvassing board meets, the secretary of state must compile the totals and submit them to the legislative committees of cognizance and the state canvassing board.
  • Prohibit the secretary of state from making rules to implement or supplement the provisions of the bill dealing with reporting on absentee ballots collected from drop boxes.
  • Require that all ballot board activity, including examining, accepting, and rejecting envelopes, opening envelopes, sorting absentee ballots, and counting and tabulating absentee ballots, is recorded and livestreamed, as well as subject to observation by a person appointed by a candidate or party. The observer would be permitted to question or present challenges to the head election official and could record any activities described. Disruptive observers could be removed at the direction of the ballot board.
  • Require local election officials to enter same-day registrants into the statewide voter registration system before that election's canvass. Under existing law, local election officials must enter same-day registrants within 42 days after Election Day.
  • Mandate that the secretary of state electronically transmits voter registration information to local election officials. Under existing law, the secretary of state may mail or electronically transmit applications.
  • Tweak existing law regarding the premature disclosure of vote counts. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Define a premature disclosure as one made before all ballots, including absentee ballots counted by 8:00 on Election Day, have been counted and totaled. Existing law is silent as to whether absentee ballots must be counted before vote counts can be released.
    • Prohibit the disclosure of absentee vote counts to the same extent as Election Day vote counts. Under existing law, disclosure of absentee vote counts is prohibited, but not in the same manner or using the same language as applied to Election Day vote counts.
  • Impose new reporting requirements on the secretary of state regarding drop box security and integrity and video recording of election activities. This report must be issued to the legislative committees of cognizance and must include accounting for grants and their expenditure.

  • Require local election officials to give public notice of the time and place of testing of election equipment.
