VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 25, 2022, would change several aspects of election law in the state, and would specifically:

  • Change same-day registration procedures by requiring that anyone using same-day registration must use a regular voter registration application and may only vote a provisional ballot. Under existing law, voters using same-day registration must present one of the enumerated forms of proof of residency (a requirement eliminated in this bill), but after doing so, voters are be permitted to vote a regular ballot. The bill would also strike existing law related to the process for verifying same-day registrants' registrations and replace them with a requirement that all registrations must be entered no later than three days after Election Day.
  • Change the process for registering to vote simultaneously with submitting an absentee ballot. Under existing law, a voter registering to vote as part of their absentee ballot must provide proof of residence to the witness who signs their ballot. This bill would strike this requirement and only require that a voter complete the voter registration application, which requests an ID number from people who have one, but does not specifically require proof of residency. When local election officials receive absentee ballots, they must immediately open them and remove and immediately process any voter registration applications.
  • Change the measures for determining when a voter registration submitted by mail is incomplete. Under existing law, the registration of a new voter who registers by mail is incomplete if election officials cannot verify the voter's driver's license number, state ID number, or the last four digits of the voter's social security number. Under this bill, a voter's registration is incomplete if the election official cannot verify if the voter is eligible to vote, without reference to any specific data points. If a mailed registration is incomplete, the bill would provide that a voter could complete their registration by submitting a completed voter registration application at least 20 days before Election Day, using same-day registration on Election Day, or using absentee voting and following existing same-day registration procedures for absentee voters. Existing law provides these options to voters, but also allows voters to prove proof of residence in the same manner as authorized for same-day registration, an option that would be eliminated under this bill since this bill eliminates the proof of residency requirements for same-day registrants.
  • Limit the existing "alternative procedure" for early voting that is available in some locations in the seven days prior to Election Day. This "alternative procedure" is more akin to Election Day-style early voting than the standard early voting process in Minnesota, which is an in-person absentee process. Under existing law, the "alternative procedure" is available to any voter, but under this bill, it would not be available to same-day registrants. Same-day registrants would still be permitted to use the standard, in-person absentee process for early voting.
  • Require that election workers verify that a voter's status is not challenged before allowing the voter to vote in person. If the voter is challenged, the voter must cast an "administrative-challenged ballot" if the challenge is based on the voter's reported death, name change, adjudication of mental incapacity, felony conviction, or citizenship, or a "verification-challenged ballot" if the challenge is for any other reason. Under existing law, such verification is not required and there are no similar categories of challenged ballots. Both of the new challenge processes proposed by the bill would require the voter to sign a specific roster or certificate, complete a challenged ballot envelope, and require the voter to list their name, residential address, date of birth, voter ID number, and to swear to their eligibility and that they have not previously voted int he same election. Administrative-challenged ballots would only be counted if a bipartisan group of election workers review the voter's information in the statewide voter registration system and determine that the voter was not challenged or should not have been challenged. Otherwise, the ballot will be rejected. Verification-challenged ballots would only be counted if the voter personally appears at the office of a local election official within seven days of Election Day with proof of eligibility to vote in the precinct where the voter cast their ballot. Voters whose ballots are rejected under these provisions would receive notice six to ten weeks after Election Day.
  • Require that election officials must publish a list of voters who cast provisional ballots, whose provisional ballots were rejected, who cast challenged ballots and the type, and whose challenged ballots were rejected. Existing law does not provide for publication of this type of information.
  • Change list maintenance procedures for voters whose status has been changed in the statewide voter registration system based on reported death, name change, conviction, adjudication of mental incapacity, or discovery of noncitizenship. Under existing law, voters' statuses are automatically changed based on this information, with no notice necessarily being given to a voter. This bill would instead require that election officials mail a notice to such voters that includes information on the change in status, the information underlying the change in status, and a description of the process to contest the change. This process would require the voter to:
    • File a contest petition with the entity providing the information underlying the removal.
    • Allow the voter to request a review meeting which must be scheduled within 14 days of the agency receiving the petition.
    • After reviewing the petition and holding the meeting, if requested, the agency must determine if the data is accurate. If the agency determines that no change to the data is required, the agency must notify the voter. If a change is required, the agency must notify the voter and the secretary of state, who must remove the challenged status.
    • Create a process for the voter to appeal to the district court.
  • Make public, as part of the already publicly available voter list, information on whether the voter's status was challenged in the statewide voter registration system at the time the list was prepared, including the date of the change. The list would also have to include previously-registered voters who were removed or made inactive, and the reason for the removal or inactivation.
  • Add reporting requirements, mandating that local election officials report information about voters whose name, date of birth, or ID numbers cannot be verified daily for the six days after Election Day. This information was already required to be reported but the frequency and timing was not previously specified.
  • Change the dates by which primary and general election canvasses must occur.

  • Require the secretary of state to conduct a public awareness campaign to encourage people to register to vote before Election Day.

Last Updated March 1, 2022

This bill, as amended on April 7, 2022, makes significant changes to provisions of the previous version of the bill that do not deal with voting rights and are untracked by Voting Rights Lab. The provisions of the previous version of the bill dealing with elections are unchanged in the April 7 amendment. These provisions would:

  • Add requirements for absentee ballot drop boxes, including requiring that drop boxes must:
    • be continually livestreamed, rather than recorded as required under existing law,
    • be located within 100 feet of the door of the building housing the office of a local election official,
    • be available during the entire absentee voting period,
    • be assigned an unique identification number,
    • display signage including more language than previously required, including warnings against depositing the ballot of another into the drop box and displaying the box's unique identification number,
    • have ballots removed at least once daily, whereas under existing law ballots are collected every business day. In addition, those collections must be logged with certain pieces of information and reported to the secretary of state.

      The bill also restricts the secretary of state's rulemaking authority to adopt rules relating to drop boxes.
  • Prohibit third parties from returning the absentee ballot of someone for whom they are acting as an agent to a drop box.
  • Add requirements for additional early voting locations, other than the office of local election officials, requiring that additional polling places must:
    • be at a precinct polling place,
    • be open for the entire absentee voting period, and
    • be open during the same days and hours as the local election official office.
  • Require that third parties who mail absentee ballot applications or sample ballots to voters must include a statement informing the voter that the mailing is not sent by or at the request of election officials, and that the sample ballot is not an official ballot. The bill also prohibits third parties from prefilling absentee ballot applications.
  • Authorize political parties to appoint absentee ballot board observers in all elections with a partisan race, with the power to observe opening envelopes, duplicating ballots, accepting ballots, rejecting ballots, depositing absentee ballots into a ballot box, and counting and tabulating ballots. Appointments must be made at least 30 days before the start of the absentee voting period. Observers would be required to complete election judge training. The bill would prohibit people related to candidates and members of the absentee ballot board from being appointed as observers. The bill would require that observers be allowed within four feet of ballots and envelopes, but would prohibit observers from handling ballots, preparing a list of voters of any type, and interfering in the conduct of the absentee ballot board.
  • Require that absentee ballot boards be livestreamed during the absentee voting period, on Election Day, and on the day after Election Day if ballots are being processed. The bill specifies which activities must be livestreamed, including accepting ballots, rejecting ballots, duplicating ballots, and counting and tabulating ballots.
  • Prohibit any unit of local government from accepting private funding from a for-profit business or non-profit organization for the purpose of paying election expenses.
  • Require that voters using same-day voter registration must be entered into the statewide voter registration system before the canvass for that election begins, with no extensions possible. Under existing law, this information must be entered within 42 days after the election and the secretary of state may extend that deadline.
  • Make certain information in the statewide voter registration confidential, including:
    • identifying information related to a minor,
    • a voter's date of birth (though year of birth may be public),
    • a voter's ID number, including, but not limited to, any portion of the voter's social security number,
    • information about the voter's presidential primary political party, except that this information is available to political parties, and
    • information about a voter who has requested to withhold the voter's name for the safety of the voter or their family.
  • Alter the existing prohibition on early release of election count results. Under existing law, no one may disclose counts from a given precinct until all count results from that precinct are available. This bill would specify that count results are not completed until all absentee ballots received by 8:00 p.m. on Election Day have also been counted.
  • Clarify and standardize existing statutory language regarding the envelopes sent as part of the absentee ballot package. Under existing law, all voters receive a secrecy envelope to enclose their ballot. Some jurisdictions send two additional envelopes: an inner signature envelope with the voter's signed certification of eligibility, ID number, and witness or notary signature, and an outer mailing envelope that does not contain the voter's personal information. Other jurisdictions combine these, providing an outer envelope that contains the voter's signature, ID number, and witness or notary signature, with this information covered by an additional flap. This bill clarifies these options and standardizes the language used to refer to each envelope type. Note, though, that the bill appears to require all three types of envelopes, although the remaining provisions of the bill appear to allow the signature and return envelopes to be merged into a single envelope.
  • Require the secretary of state to report to relevant legislative committees by January 15, 2024, detailing the administration of grants for drop box security, including who received the grants, the amount of the grant, and the purpose of the grant. The secretary of state must also submit another report to relevant legislative committees by January 15, 2024, detailing the administration of grants for staffing, livestreaming, and paper ballot security, including who received the grants, the amount of the grants, and the purpose of the grant.
  • Prohibit local election officials from serving on absentee ballot boards unless they are also appointed as an election judge. Under existing law, such election officials are explicitly permitted to serve on absentee ballot boards.
  • Require the secretary of state to electronically transmit voter registration information to local election officials. Under existing law, that information can be transmitted by mail or electronically.
  • Require certain markings, ostensibly for security, on paper ballots.
  • Mandate public notice requirements for the existing public testing of voting systems.

  • Make appropriations for the mandates imposed by the bill.

    This bill contains provisions dealing with campaign finance requirements that are not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, although many campaign finance provisions that appeared in previous versions of the bill were deleted by the April 7 amendment.

    This bill also contains numerous provisions that do not deal with election law that are not tracked by Voting Rights Lab. These provisions were extensively amended, and quite a few new provisions were added, by the April 7 amendment.

Last Updated July 13, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 18, 2022, would change numerous provisions of existing voting law, and specifically would:

  • Allow any town of any size in any county to provide exclusively vote-by-mail elections, with no in-person voting locations other than the offices of local elections officials. Under existing law, only towns located in non-metropolitan counties may utilize vote-by-mail elections.
  • Expand UOCAVA voting rights to emergency responders and utility workers deployed during the absentee voting period during a declared state of emergency.
  • Provide that a voter registration may be processed if a voter does not list a state driver's license number, state ID number, or the last four digits of the voter's social security number if the voter lacks all those ID numbers, as long as either the voter's information can be verified in another government database or the voter registered to vote before January 1, 2004. Existing law does not require local election officials to verify the voter's information in a government database if the voter lacks the specified types of ID numbers.
  • Change the process for providing absentee ballots to an address confidentiality program participant, so that the secretary of state can either request a ballot from local election officials and mail it to the participant, or can use the statewide voter registration system to prepare the participant's ballot personally. Under existing law, only the first option is available to the secretary of state. The bill also specifies that a participant in the address confidentiality program must be permitted to cast a ballot at the presidential nomination primary. Existing law is silent as to that point.
  • Allow local election officials to deliver ballots to veterans' homes and battered women's shelters in the same manner as they are delivered to health care facilities and hospitals under existing law.
  • Change the timing for siting polling place locations to:
    • Require that changes to Election Day polling place locations must be changed by ordinance or resolution by December 31 of the previous year, without exception. Existing law provides several exemptions to this deadline.
    • Require that in-person absentee voting locations be designated at least 14 weeks before Election Day. Under existing law, this provision only explicitly applies to March elections.
  • Expand the definition of residential facilities whose employees are permitted to vouch for same-day registrants' identities to include assisted living facilities, residential treatment programs, and adult foster care programs.
  • Require that all in-person absentee voting locations have at least one electronic ballot marker for voters with disabilities. Under existing law, electronic ballot markers are only required in polling places that have implemented an accessible voting system.
  • Eliminate the existing restriction that a person who assists the voter in a voting booth may assist no more than three voters per election in such a manner.
  • Clarify that electioneering boundaries are only applicable during voting hours. Existing law is silent as to that point.
  • Require the State Canvassing Board to declare candidates who received the highest number of votes for each office after completion of the canvass to be duly elected.
  • Change all references to "residing" within existing statute to "maintaining residence."
  • This bill also changes rules relating to special elections in provisions not tracked by Voting Rights Lab.

Last Updated July 22, 2025

This bill, as introduced on March 23, 2022, would prohibit threats, violence, interference with, or doxing of election officials. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create new election offenses, at a gross misdemeanor level, for any person who:
    • Intimidates any person, including by actual or threatened force, violence, restraint, loss of employment, economic reprisal, and other harm with the intent to influence an election official in the performance of their election administration duties.
    • Intentionally interferes with an election official's performance of their election administration duties.
    • Knowingly and without consent distributes the personal information of an election official or their family member if the dissemination poses an imminent and serious threat to the safety of the election official or their family member and that threat is known or should be known to the person disseminating the information.
    • Knowingly makes false allegations against election officials about the election official's performance of their election duties, with the intent to influence or tamper with the election official's performance of their duties.
    • Intentionally, physically obstructs election official's access to a polling place or election administration location.
    • Aids others in the commission of any of the foregoing offenses. Such person would have vicarious or conspiracy liability for the primary offense.
  • Define an election official as a member of the State Canvassing Board, a county canvassing board, a county auditor, a municipal clerk, a member of an absentee ballot board, an election judge, an election judge trainee, or any other individual assigned by a local or state governmental unit to perform official duties related to elections.
  • Create a private right of action for any election official injured by an act prohibited by the bill. The election official could recover damages, costs, and fees, as well as equitable relief.

  • Involve the attorney general in violations of this bill by:

    • Authorizing the attorney general to bring a civil action for damages, costs, fees, and civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation of this bill.
    • Authorizing the attorney general to seek an injunction if there is a reasonable basis to believe that a person is committing or intends to commit one of the acts of election worker intimidation prohibited in this bill.
    • Directing the attorney general to investigate violations of, and assist in the enforcement of, election official intimidation and interference prohibited by this bill.

    Last updated March 24, 2022.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 21, 2022, would change many aspects of Missouri's election laws related to photo ID, voter registration, absentee ballot applications, election audits, and more. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require photo ID to vote in person. Under existing law, a voter may use non-photo ID in certain circumstances. This bill would require anyone lacking photo ID to vote a provisional ballot, which can only be verified if the voter shows photo ID at their polling place on Election Day and the voter's signature on their provisional ballot affidavit matches the voter's signature on file. Under existing law, showing ID and signature matching are each independently sufficient methods of validating a provisional ballot. This bill would also provide free nondriver's licenses for anyone for voting purposes. Under existing law, a voter can only receive a free nondriver's license if they aver that they lack other forms of voter ID.
  • Change voter registration processes by:
    • Requiring the DMV to transmit voter registration forms within three days of completion. Under existing law, the DMV has five days to transmit such forms.
    • Directing the director of revenue to use electronic voter registration application forms and electronic transmission of voter registration data.
    • Requiring electronic transmission of an image of a voter's signature.
    • Allowing an election authority to remove names from a voter registration list at any time if the authority identifies an individual not entitled to vote under the laws of the state.
  • Eliminate the excuse for absentee voting that allowed voters particularly susceptible to COVID-19 to utilize absentee voting in 2020 elections.
  • Prohibit any person from distributing unsolicited absentee ballot applications.
  • Prohibit any executive or administrative order from authorizing or expanding the use of mail-in ballots.
  • Prohibit the state or any political subdivision from receiving or expending private money for preparing, administering, or conducting an election, including registering voters.
  • Establish a joint committee on elections, comprising seven members from the house (four from the majority party, three from the minority party) and seven members from the senate (four from the majority party, three from the minority party). The committee would appoint an election integrity committee, which would:
    • Implement a random auditing system to audit the election results of two precincts. One precinct shall be chosen by random draw from a subset of the five largest precincts and the other precinct shall be chosen by random draw from a subset of the one hundred smallest precincts. The audit shall look for discrepancies in vote counts. If any discrepancy likely affect the outcome of any election is shown by clear and convincing evidence, a second audit shall be conducted by two independent teams. If the second audit confirms discrepancies, a statewide election investigation will be ordered by the joint committee on elections, the election integrity committee, or the secretary of state, including a recount.
    • Conduct risk assessments of each election authority in the state to identify security risks.
    • Begin meeting on October 1, 2022 and be reappointed following every general election thereafter.
    • Comprise 20 members, representing one majority party member and one minority party member from each congressional district, two majority party at-large members, and two minority party at-large members.
  • Authorize the secretary of state to audit the list of registered voters for any election authority for accuracy and direct the election authority to remove the names of unauthorized voters uncovered by the audit.
  • Authorize the secretary of state, exclusively, to promulgate rules pertaining to election equipment, election security, testing of election equipment, and election equipment contracting. The bill also mandates that all tabulation equipment be air-gapped and not connected to a network and proscribes the use of touchscreen, direct-recording, or electronic vote-counting machines after January 1, 2023. Instead, election authorities will be required to use hand-marked paper ballots, except that disabled voters may use paper ballot marking devices for accessibility.
  • Change the process for appointing election judges to allow the major political parties to provide election authorities with lists of candidates. Under existing law, the election authority must choose election judges to ensure equal representation to the major political parties, but the parties do not have a role in selecting election judges. This bill would also require four election judges, two from each party, at each polling place, compared with the two total election judges required under existing law.
  • Permit county political parties to appoint challengers for each location where ballots are counted and verified. Under existing law, challengers are only permitted at absentee ballot counting locations. The bill would also allow candidates to select their own watchers.
  • Require that each election authority count all ballots cast, unused ballots, spoiled ballots, and provisional ballots after each election to ensure that the number of ballots sent by the election authority to precincts is the same as the number of ballots returned to the election authority after the close of the polls.
  • Require that ballots be retained for at least one year after certification, and create a class one election offense for intentionally destroying or tampering with archival ballots.

  • Create a new misdemeanor for distributing unsolicited absentee ballot applications.

Last Updated January 27, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 5, 2022, would expand the secretary of state's powers of local elections officials and change the qualifications to be election workers. Specifically, the bill would:

Last Updated January 14, 2022

This bill, as enacted on June 29, 2022, creates early voting, makes changes to voter ID requirements, absentee voting, voter registration, and voter list maintenance, and establishes new rules for election-related litigation. Specifically, the bill:

  • Creates early voting by allowing all eligible voters to use the in-person absentee voting process, beginning the second Tuesday before an election, at a location designated by the election authority. Voters are required to present the same types of ID as are required to vote on Election Day. Under existing law, there was no generally available early voting. All absentee voting, both in-person and by mail, was instead limited to individuals with a qualifying excuse, and with limited exceptions these voters were required to have their absentee ballots notarized (with no additional voter ID required). The bill retains this excuse-based process alongside the early voting option.
  • Makes changes to voter ID requirements. Specifically, the bill:
    • Eliminates the option for voters who lack required photo ID at the polling place to provide an affidavit and alternative form of identification vote a regular ballot. The bill instead requires these voters to cast a provisional ballot. The ballot will be counted, per existing rules, if the voter returned to the polling place before the close of polls with required photo ID or if signature matching between the affidavit and voter file confirmed their identity. Note: While existing statutory law requires voters to submit an affidavit along with alternative forms of ID for a regular ballot, a 2020 judicial decision struck down the affidavit requirement. Voters had been permitted to provide alternative ID alone to meet the voter ID requirement for a regular ballot.
    • Repeals the requirement that an applicant for a free nondriver's license for the purposes of voting must swear under penalty of perjury that they do not have any other form of accepted voter ID.
    • Repeals the requirement that the Secretary of State must provide public notice of the personal photo identification voting requirement through various forms of media such as advertisements, public services announcements, radio, and television, and on the Governor's website. The bill retains only the requirement that notice must be provided on the Secretary's website.
  • Makes changes to absentee voting. Specifically, the bill:
    • Prohibits the use of drop boxes to return absentee ballots. Under existing law, ballots could be returned by mail, in person to the local election authority office, or to "additional sites" authorized by election officials.
    • Expands absentee voting excuses to include employment as a first responder, healthcare worker, or member of law enforcement.
    • Restricts the illness or physical disability excuse for absentee voting to those voters who are incapacitated or confined on Election Day specifically. Existing law did not specify that the impairment must exist on Election Day itself. The bill also requires caregivers to live at the same address as an incapacitated or confined individual in their care to qualify for an absentee ballot under the provision. Existing law had no such residency requirement.
    • Repeals provisions allowing voters who move within the state to vote absentee at elections for presidential and vice presidential electors, United States senators, Congressional representatives, state elected officials and statewide questions, and propositions and amendments from their new residential jurisdiction, after registering to vote in that jurisdiction. Note that new provisions elsewhere in the bill permit some intrastate movers to update the address for their voter registration at any time through Election Day, and subsequently vote a regular ballot.
    • Prohibits any individual, group, or party from soliciting a voter to obtain an absentee ballot application, and prohibits pre-filling information on applications. The bill also expressly permits state and local election authorities to assist voters. Existing law was silent as to soliciting voters to obtain absentee applications and pre-filling forms and did not expressly permit election authorities to assist voters.
    • Establishes that absentee ballots are considered "cast" when received in person before Election Day or received by mail before the close of polls on Election Day. The election authority is also required to hand mark or stamp each absentee ballot envelope as it is received, indicating the date and time the absentee ballot was received. Existing law did not provide a deadline for when absentee ballots must be received to be considered "cast," however, under existing law, all ballots received by the closing of the polls on Election Day had to be counted.
    • Allows voters who are hospitalized, confined during illness or injury, or confined to a care facility on Election Day to have their absentee ballot application and absentee ballot delivered, witnessed, and returned by a team appointed by the election authority. Existing law did not specify that a voter must have been confined to a facility on Election Day for the absentee application or ballot to be delivered, witnessed, and returned by an appointed team.
    • Requires an election authority to appoint a team to deliver, witness, and return the absentee ballots of voters at the same address, if the authority receives ten or more absentee ballot applications from that address, as long as the address is not an apartment building. Existing law permitted, but did not require, ballot delivery in these circumstances and limited the authority to only those counties with a charter government, cities not located within a county, and in cities with a population of more than 300 people that are situated in more than one county.
    • Adds voters who are members of the United States Space Force to those covered under UOCAVA.
  • Makes changes related to voter registration requirements, registration procedures at the DMV, and registration drives. Specifically, the bill:
    • Requires voters to be registered in the state of Missouri by the registration deadline prior to an election, rather than being registered in their specific jurisdiction.
    • Permits a voter who has changed residence within the state and has not been removed from the voter registration list to complete a change of address form in person at the office of the election authority on any day after the registration deadline through Election Day, and requires the voter to present a form of ID acceptable for voting to do so. Under existing law, voters who moved within the state before the registration deadline and failed to update their registration were prohibited from voting, and those who did so after the registration deadline could only vote an absentee ballot for state and federal elections.
    • Requires the DMV to use electronic voter registration forms and securely transfer electronic voter registration information to election authorities. Existing law permitted electronic voter registration but did not require it.
    • Reduces the amount of time the DMV has to send voter registration information to local election officials, from within five business days to within three business days after the applicant completes a driver's license application.
    • Specifies that individuals who present documentation of non-citizenship when transacting with the DMV must not be offered the opportunity to register to vote. Existing law required registration applicants at the DMV to provide proof of citizenship, a valid Missouri driver's license, or other form of personal ID, but did not expressly prohibit registration access for individuals with documented non-citizenship status.
    • Prohibits compensation for soliciting voter registration applications, except by the government or by a person compensated by the government, and repeals the requirement to report compensation and payor information to the Secretary of State. Existing law allowed compensation for soliciting voter registration applications as long as the solicitor was registered with the secretary of state.
    • Requires any "voter registration solicitor" who solicits more than ten voter registration applications to register with the Secretary of State for each relevant election cycle. Existing law required registration of only those voter application solicitors who were paid to solicit more than ten applications.
    • Changes registration processes related to party affiliation. Registration applications may be amended to allow for selection of party affiliation, and local election officials are required to inform voters of the new affiliation option in all mailed materials until 2025. Voters are also be permitted to declare a party affiliation during the check-in process at any election.
  • Makes changes to the maintenance and use of the voter registration list. The bill:
    • Requires election authorities to include a voter's party affiliation and year of birth, instead of date of birth, among data provided on public electronic media or print outs containing voter information, and prohibits such data from being used for commercial purposes. Existing law prohibited the commercial use of any information contained in any state or local voter registration system, but did not explicitly prohibit commercial use of such information when released in through public electronic media or when printed out.
    • Requires election officials to send voter history data to the state voter registration system within three months after the election, instead of within six months.
  • Expressly prohibits vote-by-mail elections and the use of mail-in ballots, including by executive or administrative order, and requires direct repeal of the provision to authorize any expansion of the use of mail-in ballots in the future. The bill also formally repeals expired mail-in ballot provisions that were specifically applicable to the 2020 election.
  • Prohibits public officials from entering into any settlement or compromise related to civil litigation that would nullify, suspend, enjoin, alter, or conflict with any provisions related to election administration. The bill also requires parties in such litigation to provide pleadings to the legislature within 14 days of filing a claim, and authorizes the house and senate leadership to intervene in the proceedings.
  • Authorizes the Secretary of State to audit the list of registered voters "to ensure accuracy," and requires that any audit determine, at a minimum, whether election officials have performed certain specific list maintenance measures. Local election officials must be required to make updates as directed by the Secretary within 90 days of notification, and if they fail to do so, the Secretary is authorized to withhold state funding. The bill also prohibits any modification of the voter list audit process within 26 weeks of a presidential election. Existing law did not contain a similar provision.
  • Prohibits the state or any political subdivision from receiving or spending private election donations, with the exception of in-kind donations from entities that are not a candidate, candidate committee, or campaign committee. Existing law was silent as to private funding for election administration.
  • Requires the official ballot to be a paper ballot hand marked by the voter or any other means permitted by law, beginning on January 1, 2024. Existing law did not require exclusive use of paper ballots.
  • Removes the requirement that a board of election commissioners employee be a resident and a registered voter of the commissioner's appointed jurisdiction for at least a year before appointment. This bill, as introduced on January 5, 2022, would change a number of provisions of elections law relating to photo ID, absentee voting, voter list audits, election equipment and cybersecurity, voter registration, and poll worker requirements. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require photo ID for all people voting in person, whether on Election Day or during in-person absentee voting. Under existing law, other forms of non-photo ID are accepted. This bill provides that any person lacking photo ID must vote a provisional ballot, which can only be counted if the voter returns to the polling place before the close of the polls with photo ID and the voter's signature on the provisional ballot is matched to the voter's signature on file. Under existing law, the voter may validate their provisional ballot by providing acceptable photo or non-photo ID, or by having their signature matched. This bill also provides that any person may receive a nondriver's license for voting purposes free of charge. Under existing law, free nondriver's licenses are only available to voters who aver that they lack any other acceptable ID.
  • Create statewide early voting for all voters by changing the existing excuse-required in-person absentee voting to no-excuse in-person absentee voting. The early voting period would be from the third Tuesday before the election through the day before the election. The bill specifically ties in-person absentee to photo ID requirements for no-excuse in-person absentee voting and provides that if photo ID is invalidated or held unconstitutional, no-excuse in-person absentee voting shall be null and void.
  • Change absentee voting by:
    • Altering one absentee voting excuse to require that a voter claiming incapacity or confinement due to illness or physical disability must actually be confined for those reasons on election day. Under existing law, the incapacity or confinement need not specifically occur on election day.
    • Prohibiting any executive or administrative order from authorizing the use of mail-in ballots without legislative action.
  • Authorize the secretary of state to audit any election authority's list of registered voters to ensure accuracy, verifying that the voter is alive, residing in the election authority's jurisdiction, and entitled to vote. If any voters are on the list who do not satisfy those criteria, the secretary of state shall direct the election authority to remove that voter and can conduct follow-up audits to ensure such voters are removed. The secretary of state may withhold funds from any election authority that does not cooperate.
  • Change the requirements for election equipment to require that all tabulating equipment is not connected to a network and is air-gapped. This bill would also require that all touchscreen, direct-recording, or electronic vote-counting machines are removed from circulation as they wear out by January 1, 2022. By January 1, 2023, all elections must exclusively use hand-marked paper ballots (or paper ballot marking devices for disabled voters).
  • Change the requirements and process for appointing elections staff and poll workers to:
    • Permit local election authorities to use staff and volunteers who reside outside of the election authority's jurisdiction. Under existing law, poll workers must reside within the jurisdiction unless the election authority obtains the express permission of the election authority for the jurisdiction where the poll worker lives. Existing law is silent as to residency requirements for other elections staff and for poll watchers and challengers.
    • Require election authorities to choose judges of election from a list provided from each major political party within the jurisdiction. Under existing law, the party affiliation of judges of election is considered but such workers are not selected from party-supplied lists.
    • Permit candidates to select poll watchers paid for at the candidate's expense.
  • Change the process for registering to vote at voter registration agencies to:
    • Require the DMV to transmit completed voter registration applications to the relevant election authority within three days of completion. Under existing law, the DMV has five days to transmit such applications.
    • Require voter registration agencies to use electronic voter registration forms and transfer them electronically.
    • Require voter registration agencies to transmit electronic signature images to election authorities.
  • Change the information and uses permitted for the voter roll to:
    • Remove the requirement that election authorities provide voter lists to all candidates and parties automatically. Now, such information will only be available upon request.
    • Eliminate voters' dates of birth from being listed in electronic or hard copy printouts of the voter roll.
    • Prohibit voter information from being used for commercial purposes.
    • Eliminate the ability of candidates, party committees, or campaign committees to obtain a list of absentee voters.
  • Prohibit paying anyone to solicit voter registration applications and require that volunteers who solicit more than ten applications register every election cycle with the secretary of state. Under existing law, such people can be paid, and only paid workers must register while volunteers are exempt.
  • Require election authorities to join the Center for Internet Security and allow the secretary of state to review their cybersecurity through testing. The secretary of state may withhold funds from election authorities who do not comply with such reviews or who are in violation of cyber security requirements.

  • Require election authorities to count all ballots cast, unused, spoiled, and voted provisionally to ensure that that number matches the number of ballots sent to each precinct. Discrepancies must be reported to the secretary of state.

    This bill also contains provisions regarding the initiative petition process which are not tracked by Voting Rights Lab.

The bill would also allow election authorities to record the vote tabulation process if such records are available to the public as public records. Existing law is silent as to the authority to record vote tabulation.
  • Allow an election authority to remove a person from a voter registration list at any time if a review identifies that the person is not entitled to vote. The bill does not provide matching criteria or safeguards against mistaken removals. Existing law provides processes for removing voters on the basis of changes of residency, death, disenfranchising convictions, and adjudication of incompetency.

    • Requiring election authorities to be members of the Center for Internet Security and allow cyber security reviews of their offices and equipment. The secretary of state may withhold funds from any election authority who fails to cooperate.
    • Requiring election authorities to retain ballots for at least a year after certification of the results of the election.
    • Requiring elections authorities to count all ballots cast, unused, spoiled, and provisional ballots to ensure that the number of ballots sent to each precinct matches the number of ballots returned by each precinct. Discrepancies must be reported to the secretary of state.
    • Providing the number of absentee ballots cast and the number of in-person ballots cast.

This bill, as introduced on January 5, 2022, would change the rights of and requirements for poll workers, challengers, and watchers. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create a new misdemeanor for election officials who obstruct the rights of a challenger or watcher.
  • Require election officials to provide access to all stages of the election process.   • Prohibit challengers and watchers from wearing or displaying campaign material regarding candidates or ballot measures. Existing law is silent as to the use or display of such materials.
  • Allow challengers and watchers to bring in voter lists to observe. Existing law is silent as to the use of such lists.

This bill, as introduced on January 5, 2022, would change a number of existing laws regarding voter ID, absentee voting, voter registration, and more. Specifically, the bill would:

The provisional ballot will only be counted if the voter appears at the polling place by 7:00 p.m. on the day of voting with a valid photo ID and the election authority verifies the voter's identity by signature comparison.   • Change voter registration processes by:

    • Requiring that voter registration agencies utilize electronic voter registration applications and submit the forms electronically to election authorities. Under existing law, paper forms are still permitted.
    • Require that any person who registers more than ten voters must register with the state of Missouri every election cycle. Under existing law, only people paid to register voters were required to register.
  • Change the qualifications of election workers and challengers by:

    • Providing that election judges shall be selected from lists provided by the major political parties in the jurisdiction. Under existing law, election judges must be selected to ensure at least one judge from each major political party, but the party does not provide lists to the election authority.

    • Eliminating the option that a candidate or party may obtain a list of absentee voters.

If this audit results in a determination that maintenance is required, the local election authority shall have 30 days to make the updates. If the local election authority does not timely make those updates, the secretary of state's office may withhold funding from the local election authority. This is a new authority conferred upon the secretary of state.

    • Prohibiting the use of touchscreen, direct-recording, or electronic vote-counting machines after January 1, 2024, except that machines currently in use may continue to be used during their useful life for disabled voters. Beginning January 1, 2024, all voters must use hand-marked paper ballots, except that disabled voters may use paper ballot marking devices.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on April 13, 2022, would make changes to voter ID requirements, early voting, absentee voting, voter registration, and voter list maintenance, and would restrict federal authority over state and local elections. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Make changes to voter ID requirements. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Eliminate the option for voters who lack required photo ID at the polling place to provide an affidavit and alternative form of identification, and be permitted to vote a regular ballot. The bill would instead require these voters to cast a provisional ballot. The ballot would be counted, per existing rules, if the voter returned to the polling place before the close of polls with required photo ID or if signature matching between the affidavit and voter file confirmed their identity. Note: While existing statutory law requires voters to submit an affidavit along with alternative forms of ID for a regular ballot, a 2020 judicial decision struck down the affidavit requirement. Voters are currently permitted to provide alternative ID alone to meet the voter ID requirement for a regular ballot.
    • Repeal the requirement that the Secretary of State provide public notice of the photo voter ID requirement.
    • Repeal the requirement that an applicant for a free nondriver's license for the purposes of voting must swear under penalty of perjury that they do not have any other form of accepted voter ID.
    • Authorize the Secretary of State to audit the list of registered voters "to ensure accuracy," and require that any audit determine, at a minimum, whether election officials have performed certain specific list maintenance measures. Local election officials would be required to make updates as directed by the Secretary within 30 days of notification, and if they failed to do so, the Secretary would be authorized to withhold state funding. The bill would also prohibit any modification of the voter list audit process within 26 weeks of a presidential election. Existing law does not contain a similar provision.
  • Create an early voting process. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Create early voting by establishing a no-excuse in-person absentee voting process. This process would require the voter to cast a ballot at either the office of the election authority or at another location designated by the election authority, and would require voters to provide the same types of voter ID required to vote on Election Day. Under existing law, there is no generally available early voting. All absentee voting, both in-person and by mail, is instead limited to individuals with a qualifying excuse, and, with limited exceptions, these voters must have their absentee ballots notarized (with no voter ID required). The bill would retain this existing excuse-based process alongside the new early voting option. Note: The bill does not set out a specific early voting period, however existing law requires that absentee ballots be available to voters by the sixth Tuesday before Election Day.
  • Make changes to absentee voting. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Restrict the illness or physical disability excuse for absentee voting to those voters who are incapacitated or confined on Election Day specifically. Existing law does not specify that the impairment must exist on Election Day itself. The bill would also require caregivers to live at the same address as an incapacitated or confined individual in their care to qualify for an absentee ballot under the provision. Existing law has no such residency requirement.
    • Repeal provisions permitting individuals who have contracted or are at high-risk of contracting Covd-19 to vote absentee.
    • Repeal provisions allowing voters who move within the state to vote absentee at elections for presidential and vice presidential electors, United States senators, Congressional representatives, state elected officials and statewide questions, and propositions and amendments from the voters new residential jurisdiction, after registering to vote in that jurisdiction. Note that new provisions elsewhere in the bill would permit intrastate voters to update the address for their voter registration at any time through Election Day.
    • Prohibit any individual, group, or party from soliciting a voter to obtain an absentee ballot application, and prohibit pre-filling information on applications. Existing law is silent as to soliciting voters to obtain absentee applications and pre-filling forms.
    • Establish that absentee ballots are considered "cast" when received in person before Election Day or received by mail before the close of polls on Election Day. Existing law does not provide a deadline for when absentee ballots must be received to be considered "cast," however, under existing law, all ballots received by the closing of the polls on election day must be counted.
    • Allow voters who are hospitalized, confined during illness or injury, or confined to a care facility on election day to have their absentee ballot application and absentee ballot delivered, witnessed and returned by a team appointed by the election authority. Existing law does not specify that a voter must have been confined to a facility on Election Day for the absentee application or ballot to be delivered, witnessed, and returned by an appointed team.
    • Require an election authority to appoint a team to deliver, witness and return the absentee ballots of voters at the same address, if the authority receives ten or more absentee ballot applications from that address, as long as the address is not an apartment building. Existing law permits, but does not require, ballot delivery in these circumstances and limits the authority to only those counties with a charter government, cities not located within a county, and cities with a population of more than 300 people that are situated in more than one county.
    • Add voters who are members of the United States Space Force to those covered under UOCAVA.
  • Make changes related to voter registration requirements, registration procedures at the DMV, and registration drives. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require voters to be registered in the state of Missouri by the registration deadline prior to an election, rather than being registered in their specific jurisdiction.
    • Permit a voter who has changed residence within the state and has not been removed from the voter registration list to complete a change of address form in person at the office of the election authority on any day after the registration deadline through Election Day, and require the voter to present a form ID acceptable for voting to do so. Under existing law, voters who move within the state before the registration deadline and fail to update their registration are prohibited from voting, and those who do so after the registration deadline may only vote an absentee ballot for state and federal elections.
    • Require the DMV to use electronic voter registration forms and securely transfer electronic voter registration information to election authorities. Existing law permits electronic voter registration but does not require it.
    • Reduce the amount of time the DMV has to send voter registration information to local election officials from within five business days to within three business days after the applicant completes a driver's license application.
    • Specify that individuals who present documentation of non-citizenship when transacting with the DMV must not be offered the opportunity to register to vote. Existing law requires registration applicants at the DMV to provide proof of citizenship, a valid Missouri driver's license, or other form of personal ID, but does not expressly prohibit registration access for individuals with documented non-citizenship status.
    • Require the Secretary of State the DMV to develop a process in which the DMV may check an individual's name and address against the state voter registration list to determine whether the individual is already registered to vote and if so, whether the registration name and address are correct. Existing law does not contain a similar provision.
    • Prohibit compensation for soliciting voter registration applications, except by the government or by a person compensated by the government, and repeal the requirement to report compensation and payor information to the Secretary of State. Existing law allows compensation for soliciting voter registration applications as long as the solicitor is registered with the secretary of state.
    • Require any "voter registration solicitor" who solicits more than ten voter registration applications to register with the Secretary of State for each relevant election cycle. Existing law requires registration of only those voter application solicitors who are paid to solicit more than ten applications.
    • Require election officials to send voter history data to the state voter registration system within three months after the election, instead of within six months.
  • Make changes to the maintenance and use of the voter registration list. The bill would:
    • Permit election authorities to include a voter's year of birth, instead of date of birth, on public electronic media or print outs containing voter information, and prohibit such information from being used for commercial purposes. Existing law prohibits the commercial use of any information contained in any state or local voter registration system, but does not explicitly prohibit commercial use of such information when released in through public electronic media or when printed out.
    • Repeal the requirement that the Secretary of State provide candidates or parties with a list of absentee ballot applicants upon request.
    • Repeal the requirement election authorities provide candidates and parties with full voter registration lists upon request.
  • Create the Missouri Elections Sovereignty Act. These provisions would impose significant new procedures for election administration that do not exist under existing law. The provisions would:
    • Assert the State's authority to regulate state and local elections.
    • Bifurcate state and federal elections when there are differences in regulations for time, place and manner of holding elections.
    • Exempt state and local elections from federal regulation to the extent permitted by the U.S. Constitution.
    • Require any state agency or agent who receives communication regarding election laws from the Department of Justice or other federal agency to notify the governor and General Assembly within five days. This section would expire on Feb. 1, 2025.
    • Require any entity involved in state election administration that intends to implement any federal election guidance on state elections to notify the General Assembly at least 30 days before implementation. All implementation of federal guidance would require approval by the Assembly, which could comprise abstaining from a legislative vote within 30 days of the notification. The Act would impose a fine of $5,000 for violations of these provisions, to be accrued every 30 days until the implementation was withdrawn. This section would expire on Feb. 1, 2025.
    • Require any official election administrator who intends to accept or disburse federal election funds to notify the General Assembly of this intent at least 30 days before accepting the funds, or, if the funds have already been accepted, 30 days before the funds are disbursed. Acceptance of funds would be subject to legislative approval, which could comprise abstaining from a vote within 30 days of notification. The Act would impose a fine of the amount of the federal funds plus $1,000 for violation of the provisions. This section would expire on Feb. 1, 2025.
    • Permit the speaker of the house and president pro tempore of the senate to intervene to defend the house or the senate, respectively, or to jointly defend the general assembly against an action in a state or federal court challenging the validity of a statute.
  • Require the official ballot to be a paper ballot hand marked by the voter or by a marking device designed to assist voters requesting such assistance, beginning on January 1, 2024. Existing law does not require exclusive use of paper ballots.
  • Create a new Class D felony offense for tampering with an election official, which is defined as disseminating an election official's family's personal information through any means, including on the internet, for the purpose of harassment, intimidation, or influence. Election officials would include election judges, challengers, watchers, and other volunteers or employees for the election authority. Tampering that results in death or bodily injury of an election official or their family member would be a Class B felony offense.
  • Remove the requirement that a board of elections commissioners employee be a resident and a registered voter of the commissioner's appointed jurisdiction for at least a year before appointment. The bill would also exempt county clerk employees from residency and voter registration requirements, except as expressly directed by the board.
  • Impose limits on touchscreen voting machines and grant the Secretary of State authority to oversee cybersecurity measures for voting systems.
  • Require automatic tabulating equipment to be unconnected from any network or internet access.
  • The bill also contains additional provisions related to election administration and other topics that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

This bill, as introduced on January 5, 2022, would create automatic voter registration during transactions at many voter registration agencies. Missouri does not currently have automatic voter registration at any agency. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create automatic voter registration during certain transactions at a variety of state agencies, which include:
    • the department of revenue,
    • the department of social services,
    • local housing authorities,
    • the University of Missouri system,
    • the department of corrections,
    • the department of labor,
    • the department of health and senior services,
    • the bureau of vital records,
    • local health departments,
    • recorders of deeds, and
    • any other agency designated by the secretary of state.
  • Requiring the agencies performing automatic voter registration to provide a name, address, date of birth, proof of citizenship or attestation, ID number (driver's license number, state ID number, or last four digits of social security number), and the applicant's signature to the secretary of state for each applicant at least monthly. If the agency does not have the applicant's signature, the secretary of state will create a process to ensure that the person's signature is captured during the voting process.
  • Requiring the secretary of state to develop forms and processes for agencies, including a script to notify voters that registration is optional but a voter must expressly opt out to avoid being registered to vote.

  • Require the secretary of state to send a notice to all eligible applicants permitting the applicant to opt out of voter registration and explaining that a failure to respond within 45 days will result in the applicant being registered to vote. This notice would also be required to inform applicants that they must opt out if they do not meet voting eligibility requirements. The postage for the return form will be paid by the secretary of state.

Last Updated January 6, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 18, 2022, would create no-excuse absentee voting, same-day voter registration, automatic voter registration, and make absentee voting more accessible. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create same-day voter registration by eliminating the current deadline of the fourth Wednesday before Election Day. Same-day registration would be available through online voter registration, any voter registration location established by the secretary of state, any election authority statewide, and any polling place.
  • Create automatic voter registration using driver's license information, state ID information, tax records, school enrollment records, and other records. The bill tasks the secretary of state with creating a program where the secretary of state creates lists of recommended individuals to add to the voter rolls that would be passed along to local election officials who shall verify the voters and register any eligible voters. Eligible voters would be sent a notice of automatic registration. People who returned the enclosed card declining to register would not be registered, while all others would be added to voter registration lists.

  • Facilitate absentee voting by:

    • Allowing online absentee ballot applications.
    • Eliminating the notary requirement for absentee ballots.
    • Extending the absentee ballot return deadline from the close of the polls on Election Day to seven days after Election Day, if the ballot is postmarked by Election Day.
    • Creating online ballot tracking to indicate when a voter's ballot has been received and counted, and, if not counted, the reason why. The online tracking system would also provide cure information to voters.
    • Permitting relatives and guardians to submit absentee ballot applications on behalf of a voter.
    • Eliminate the requirement that new residents submit absentee ballot applications in person.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 24, 2022, would require photo ID, increase barriers to obtaining absentee ballots, involve the legislature in details of election administration, and make changes to election equipment. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require photo ID for voting in person. Under existing law, voters can provide photo or nonphoto ID, and voters lacking ID can still receive a regular ballot upon executing an affidavit as to their identity. A person lacking photo ID would only be permitted to vote a provisional ballot, which would only be counted if the voter returns to the polling place before the close of the polls with photo ID or if the voter's signature is verified by the election authority. Under existing law, photo and nonphoto ID are both acceptable to validate a provisional ballot. The bill would also expand the availability of free photo IDs to anyone. Under existing law, only people who lack any ID may obtain a free photo ID.
  • Require that any federal funds received for elections be put into an election fund, with the legislature in charge of appropriating the funds in that fund.
  • Require that the legislature review any federal laws regarding elections administration before any elections official implements them.
  • Require all state agencies to notify the governor and legislative leadership of communications received from the federal government relating to elections.
  • Require voters to include their voter ID number on their application for absentee ballot. Under existing law, absentee ballot applications already request the last four digits of the voter's social security number.
  • Explicitly prohibits the use of absentee ballots except as authorized by the legislature, including by executive or administrative order.

  • Phase out all electronic election equipment by 2023 and replace it with paper ballots for everyone except disabled voters, who may continue to use currently in-use electronic equipment or paper ballot marking devices.

Last Updated February 7, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 26, 2022, would change a number of provisions of election law and would require photo ID, create early voting, ban ballot curing, narrow absentee voting eligibility and access, and more. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require photo ID for in-person voting. Under existing law, photo and nonphoto IDs are accepted. A person lacking photo ID would be required to vote a provisional ballot, which would only be counted if the voter returned to the polling place on Election Day with a photo ID or the voter's signature is verified against the voter's signature on file. Under existing law, a provisional ballot will be counted if a voter presents photo or nonphoto ID. To facilitate this requirement, this bill expands the availability of free photo ID.
  • Create early voting. Under existing law, only voters with an absentee voting excuse may return a ballot before Election Day, but under this bill, any voter could use in-person absentee voting to vote early, regardless of whether they have a qualifying excuse.
  • Prohibit election officials from ballot curing, which the bill defines as altering or modifying a ballot, ballot application, or ballot envelope, or inviting a voter who has already cast a ballot to modify their ballot, ballot application, or ballot envelope to correct violations.
  • Narrow eligibility for and access to absentee voting by:
    • Requiring that any voter who wishes to vote absentee due to incapacity or confinement due to illness or physical disability must actually be incapacitated or confined on Election Day. The need for Election Day confinement is not present in existing law.
    • Prohibiting anyone from soliciting a voter to apply for an absentee ballot.
    • Prohibiting pre-filled absentee ballot applications.
  • Change voter registration processes by:
    • Permitting a voter who has moved within the state to update their address on Election Day at the office of the local election authority. Under existing law, such voters were subject to the current voter registration deadline of 27 days before Election Day.
    • Requiring voter registration agencies to collect and transmit registration information electronically.
    • Requiring the division of motor vehicle and drivers licensing to transmit voter registration applications within 3, rather than 5, days of completion by the applicant.
    • Prohibiting paying people who register voters and requiring all such people to register with the secretary of state. Under existing law, paying voter registration solicitors is not prohibited, and only paid solicitors must register.
    • Limiting access to the voter list to preclude its use for commercial purposes.
    • Ending candidates' and parties' ability to access a list of voters who have applied for an absentee ballot.
  • Change the requirements for election workers, poll watchers, and challengers, by:
    • Requiring local election officials to provide a designated area where challengers and watchers, on a nondiscriminatory basis, can observe all stages of the election process.
    • Eliminating any requirements or ability to require election workers, watchers, and challengers to reside in the jurisdiction they serve.
    • Change the process of appointing election workers to grant more of a role to political parties.
    • Allow watchers to be present at all ballot counting locations. Under existing law, they may only be at absentee ballot locations.
    • Allow candidates to select their own watchers at their own expense.
    • Require candidates and watchers to wear name badges and prohibit them from wearing campaign materials.
  • Permit the secretary of state to audit the voter list for any local election official for accuracy and to assess the local election official's compliance with list maintenance requirements. The secretary of state will notify local election officials of updates required and can withhold funds from local election officials who do not comply within thirty days.
  • Make changes to election equipment requirements, including requiring paper ballots except for disabled voters, offlining electronic voting equipment except for disabled voters, requiring tabulators to be non-networked, and
  • Prohibit state and local election officials from receiving or expending private grant funds for election administration or voter registration.
  • Prohibit election officials and the governor from permitting the use of absentee ballots to a greater extent than allowed by statute. This provision appears to preclude the governor from issuing an executive order expanding absentee voting during emergencies.

  • Create new election offenses for:

    • Election officials who engage in ballot curing, as defined in the bill. This offense would be a misdemeanor.
    • Tampering with data collected or transmitted by voter registration agencies, which would be a felony.

Last Updated February 7, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on March 30, 2022, proposes significant changes to the Missouri constitution regarding the electoral process. Specifically, the bill proposes constitutional amendments that would:

  • Change voter eligibility from applying to "all citizens" who meet certain criteria, to "only citizens" who do so. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Limit voters to a single vote per office or issue, effectively prohibiting ranked-choice voting and some other alternative electoral systems. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law does not contain a similar limitation.
  • Require that a party can only have one candidate in a general election, who must be the top vote-getter at the primary. This provision would effectively prohibit top-two type primaries and other alternative primary models. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law does not contain a similar requirement.
  • Require all elections to be conducted by paper ballot or by any mechanical method allowed by law. This a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill. Existing law requires voting by ballot or mechanical means, with no specific requirement for paper ballots.
  • Require every voting machine used to conduct an election to be tested and certified before every election in which the machine will be used, and require testing and certification to meet federal standards. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill. Existing law did not contain a similar requirement
  • Require every voting machine to produce a permanent paper record for each vote cast, which must be available for the voter to inspect and verify at the time their vote is cast, and be kept for use in any election audit. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill. Existing law does not contain a similar requirement.

Last updated April 10, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on January 5, 2022, would change a number of existing laws regarding voter ID, absentee voting, and more. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require photo ID for voting in person, whether on Election Day or via absentee in-person voting. Under existing law, some forms of non-photo ID are accepted for in-person voters. This bill would allow a person who lacks photo ID to vote a ballot that will only be counted if the voter's signature is verified by two judges, one from each major political party. The voter can track whether the ballot is verified and counted and appeal a decision not to verify the signature by providing photo ID. These ballots will only be counted once all such ballots are determined either eligible or ineligible.
  • Create no-excuse absentee in-person voting. Under existing law, an excuse is required to vote absentee in-person. This bill would permit absentee in-person voting at the election authority's offices, beginning on the sixth Tuesday prior to the election. Beginning the third Tuesday before the election, absentee in-person voting could be held at up to one additional site in the jurisdiction. Absentee in-person voting must end by 5:00 p.m. on the day before Election Day.
  • Changes the acceptable excuses for absentee voting by:
    • Eliminating the excuse for absentee voting established in 2020, which would allow a person particularly susceptible to COVID-19 to vote absentee in the year 2020.
    • Requiring that any person using the excuse of incapacity or confinement due to illness or disability be actually confined or incapacitated on Election Day. Under existing law, there is no specific requirement that the voter experience confinement or incapacity on Election Day.
  • Clarify that absentee in-person ballots are deemed cast when received prior to Election Day, while mailed absentee ballots, or those returned to an authorized dropbox, are deemed cast when received, as long as they are received prior to the closing of the polls on Election Day. Ballots voted on Election Day are deemed cast when successfully submitted into the ballot box.
  • Require that election equipment:
    • Only use paper ballots hand marked by the voter, beginning January 1, 2023, except that disabled voters may use paper ballot marking devices for accessibility. (115.013, 115.237)
    • Be air-gapped and not connected to a network, if the equipment is involved in tabulation.

  • Include members of the Space Force within the definition of a UOCAVA voter.
