Bill Version 3/28/22: This bill, as amended on March 28, 2022, would create early voting, and make changes to voter ID requirements, absentee voting, voter registration, voter list maintenance, and other aspects of election law. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create early voting by allowing all eligible voters to use the in-person absentee voting process. Voters would be required to present the same types of ID required to vote on Election Day. Under existing law, there is no generally available early voting. All absentee voting, both in-person and by mail, is instead limited to individuals with a qualifying excuse, and with limited exceptions these voters must have their absentee ballots notarized (with no additional voter ID required). The bill would retain this excuse-based process alongside the early voting option.
  • Make changes to voter ID requirements. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Eliminate the option for voters who lack required photo ID at the polling place to provide an affidavit and alternative form of identification, and be permitted to vote a regular ballot. The bill would instead require these voters to cast a provisional ballot. The ballot would be counted, per existing rules, if the voter returned to the polling place before the close of polls with required photo ID or if signature matching between the affidavit and voter file confirmed their identity. Note: While existing statutory law requires voters to submit an affidavit along with alternative forms of ID for a regular ballot, a 2020 judicial decision struck down the affidavit requirement. Voters are currently permitted to provide alternative ID alone to meet the voter ID requirement for a regular ballot.
    • Repeal the requirement that an applicant for a free nondriver's license for the purposes of voting must swear under penalty of perjury that they do not have any other form of accepted voter ID.
    • Repeal the requirement that the Secretary of State provide public notice of voter ID requirements through, at a minimum, advertisements and public services announcements in print, and on broadcast and cable television, radio, and official state websites.
  • Make changes to absentee voting. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Expand absentee voting excuses to include employment as a first responder, healthcare worker, or member of law enforcement.
    • Restrict the illness or physical disability excuse for absentee voting to those voters who are incapacitated or confined on Election Day specifically. Existing law does not specify that the impairment must exist on Election Day itself. Existing law has no such residency requirement.
    • Repeal provisions allowing voters who move within the state to vote absentee at elections for presidential and vice presidential electors, United States senators, Congressional representatives, state elected officials and statewide questions, and propositions and amendments from the voters new residential jurisdiction, after registering to vote in that jurisdiction. Note that new provisions elsewhere in the bill would permit some intrastate voters to update the address for their voter registration at any time through Election Day, and subsequently vote a regular ballot.
    • Prohibit any individual, group, or party from soliciting a voter to obtain an absentee ballot application, and prohibit pre-filling information on applications. The bill would also expressly permit state and local election authorities to assist voters. Existing law is silent as to soliciting voters to obtain absentee applications and pre-filling forms and does not expressly permit election authorities to assist voters.
    • Establish that absentee ballots are considered "cast" when received in person before Election Day or received by mail before the close of polls on Election Day. The election authority would also be required to hand mark or stamp each absentee ballot envelope as it is received, indicating the date and time the absentee ballot was received. Existing law does not provide a deadline for when absentee ballots must be received to be considered "cast," however, under existing law, all ballots received by the closing of the polls on Election Day must be counted.
    • Allow voters who are hospitalized, confined during illness or injury, or confined to a care facility on Election Day to have their absentee ballot application and absentee ballot delivered, witnessed and returned by a team appointed by the election authority. Existing law does not specify that a voter must have been confined to a facility on Election Day for the absentee application or ballot to be delivered, witnessed, and returned by an appointed team.
    • Require an election authority to appoint a team to deliver, witness and return the absentee ballots of voters at the same address, if the authority receives ten or more absentee ballot applications from that address, as long as the address is not an apartment building. Existing law permits, but does not require, ballot delivery in these circumstances and limits the authority to only those counties with a charter government, cities not located within a county, and in cities with a population of more than 300 people that are situated in more than one county.

    • Require voters to be registered in the state of Missouri by the registration deadline prior to an election, rather than being registered in their specific jurisdiction.

    • Reduce the amount of time the DMV has to send voter registration information to local election officials, from within five business days to within three business days after the applicant completes a driver's license application.

Existing law requires registration applicants at the DMV to provide proof of citizenship, a valid Missouri driver's license, or other form of personal ID, but does not expressly prohibit registration access for individuals with documented non-citizenship status.

Existing law allows compensation for soliciting voter registration applications as long as the solicitor is registered with the secretary of state.

    • Require election authorities to include a voter's year of birth, instead of date of birth, on public electronic media or print outs containing voter information, and prohibit such data from being used for commercial purposes. Existing law prohibits the commercial use of any information contained in any state or local voter registration system, but does not explicitly prohibit commercial use of such information when released in through public electronic media or when printed out.
    • Repeal the requirement that the Secretary of State provide candidates or parties with a list of absentee ballot applicants upon request.
    • Repeal the requirement election authorities provide candidates and parties with full voter registration lists upon request.
    • Require election officials to send voter history data to the state voter registration system within three months after the election, instead of within six months.
  • Expressly prohibit vote-by-mail elections and the use of mail-in ballots, including by executive or administrative order, and require direct repeal of the provision to authorize any expansion of the use of mail-in ballots in the future. The bill would also formally repeal expired mail-in ballot provisions that were specifically applicable to the 2020 election. *
    Authorize the Secretary of State to audit the list of registered voters "to ensure accuracy," and require that any audit determine, at a minimum, whether election officials have performed certain specific list maintenance measures. This bill, as introduced on January 5, 2022, would alter a number of provisions relating to voter access, including requiring photo ID, imposing additional absentee ballot application requirements, increasing the power of poll watchers, changing voter list maintenance practices, allowing voters to call for election result audits, restricting certain types of election funding, and changing standards for election equipment and ballots. This bill would require that anyone lacking photo ID must vote a provisional ballot, which will only be counted if the voter returns to the polling place before 7:00 p.m. on the day of voting with a photo ID or the voter's signature on the provisional ballot is matched to the voter's signature of record. Under existing law, a provisional ballot may be counted if the voter returns with acceptable photo or non-photo ID or by signature matching. This bill would also provide a free nondriver's license for anyone who requests one for voting. Under existing law, a free nondriver's license is only available to a person who lacks any other form of ID.
  • Change absentee ballot applications processes by:
    • Requiring that absentee ballot applications include either the voter's driver's license number or the last four digits of the voter's social security number, in addition to existing requirements of including the voter's name, address, mailing address, and absentee voting excuse.
    • Prohibiting anyone, including an election authority, from sending an unsolicited absentee ballot application or from soliciting a person to obtain an absentee ballot application.
  • Prohibit any election authority from accepting any funding, grants, or gifts from any source other than the state of Missouri or a political subdivision of the state. This provision specifically prohibits election authorities from accepting federal funds unless approved by a concurrent resolution of the general assembly. Existing law is silent as to whether these funds can be accepted.
  • Increase or alter the power of watchers and challengers by:
    • Requiring that challengers and watchers be permitted to observe all stages of the election process, including certification of voting systems, testing of equipment, absentee in-person voting, canvassing, voter appeals, vote tabulation, ballot transport, audits, and recounts. Under existing law, watchers are only explicitly permitted to observe voting, vote counting, and absentee ballot processing and counting.
    • Allowing watchers and challengers to challenge any ballot or any voter's qualifications to vote. Under existing law, watchers and challengers are only permitted to challenge a voter's qualifications to vote.
    • Prohibiting any election authority from barring a duly appointed watcher from a polling place or removing a watcher from a polling place during times when the watcher is entitled to be there. Under existing law, which remains unchanged on this point, an election judge may ask the watcher or challenger to cease disruption or leave the polling place if the watcher or challenger interferes with the orderly process of voting or is guilty of any misconduct or legal violation.
    • Creating a new criminal penalty for election authorities who bar or remove a watcher from a polling place or otherwise violate the rights of a watcher or challenger.
    • Allowing watchers and challengers to bring in voting lists when observing the voting process.
    • Requiring election authorities to designate observation areas for challengers and watchers that are between 3-6 feet from tables where voters check in to vote or register to vote.

    • Allow review via issuing voter registration cards or by using postal service contractors via the postal service's National Change of Address program. Under existing law, such a review can only be accomplished by house-to-house or mailed confirmations.
    • Clarify that removal from a voter list may only occur after a voter fails to respond to a confirmation notice and a voter fails to engage in voter activity before the second general election after the date of the notice. Under existing law, the voter must vote, not just engage in voter activity, during the two election cycles period.
    • Require election authorities to investigate the qualifications of any voter who has not engaged in voter activity or has transferred their registration in the past two years.     • Allowing any voter to petition an election authority or the secretary of state for an audit of a particular election. BILLSUMMARY: Creates new provisions relating to reapportionment and redistricting in certain political subdivisions.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 5, 2022, would create criteria for redistricting local political subdivisions. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require populations as nearly equal as practicable, with no deviation of more than 5%.
  • Require that redistricting be conducted in accordance with the U.S. Constitution and federal law, specifically the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
  • Prohibit any redistricting that results in a denial or abridgment of the right to vote on account of race or color or that results in any such protected group having less opportunity to participate in the political process or to elect representatives of their choice.
  • Require the consideration of the following factors, which are specifically subordinate to the previous criteria:
    • Contiguity.
    • Compactness.
    • Preservation of communities of interest.

Under existing law, people who are convicted of disenfranchising offenses may only regain the right to vote if they receive a supportive vote from two-thirds of the legislature, a pardon, or, after completion of probation, have their civil rights restored via action by the governor. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Restore voting rights to a person after they complete:
    • Incarceration, if they are not sentenced to parole, but irrespective if they are sentenced to probation following incarceration,
    • Probation, if they have not been sentenced to incarceration at all, or
    • Parole, if they are sentenced to parole after incarceration.
  • Require a person who registers to vote after completing confinement to register to vote with a copy of their certificate of restoration issued by the department of corrections, parole board, or court of original jurisdiction.
  • Require that the secretary of state regularly access information from the department of corrections and parole board to prepare regular reports to local election officials of people convicted of disenfranchising crimes in their county.
  • Require that election commissioners, registrars, and poll managers receive training on registering people to vote after restoration of rights.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on June 21, 2022, would:

  • Establish a Class H felony covering threatening or attempting to threaten any person for voting or attempting to vote, voting or attempting to vote for or against a particular candidate, registering to vote, urging or aiding individuals to vote or attempt to vote as permitted by law, and exercising lawful powers or duties as an election official. The following specific acts would be considered threatening:
    • Knowingly challenging a person's right to vote on fraudulent or spurious grounds
    • Engaging in mass, indiscriminate, and groundless challenging of voters solely for the purpose of preventing voters from voting or to delay the process of voting or the lawful and orderly administration of an election
    • Fraudulently advising any person that they are not eligible to vote or are not registered to vote when in fact that person is eligible or registered to vote
  • Establish a Class H felony covering an employer's enclosing candidate campaign materials with an employee's pay and an employer's expressing or implying that continued employment or pay is dependent on voting or not voting or voting or not voting for a particular candidate.
  • Establish a Class A1 misdemeanor covering intimidating or coercing or attempting to intimidate or coerce any person for voting or attempting to vote, for voting or attempting to vote for or against a particular candidate, urging or aiding any persons to vote or attempt to vote as allowed by law, and exercising any lawful powers or duties as an election official.
  • Permit individuals aggrieved by a violation of the above criminal prohibitions to seek an injunction, restraining order, or any other order in state court.
  • Establish that individuals who are victims or illegal threats or intimidation as established by the bill to seek attorneys fees and restitution. Restitution funds recovered would be used for voter education purposes.

Last updated June 22, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on January 5, 2022, would change the first date that ballots may be mailed from 35 days before Election Day to 22 days before Election Day. It would also move the earliest date to request an absentee ballot in person from 30 days before Election Day to 22 days before Election Day. Additionally, the bill would permit a voter to designate an agent to return a ballot on the voter's behalf. Under existing law, a voter may only designate an agent to request a ballot for the voter, and third party return is neither authorized nor prohibited.

Last Updated January 6, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2022, would create a new felony for anyone who intentionally manipulates election results for certain races by bribery, extortion, threat, or fraud.

Last updated January 7, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2022, would include emergency responders deployed to a declared state of emergency as a category of people who are permitted to simultaneously register to vote and apply for all ballots in a calendar year through the federal postcard application or a personal letter. Under existing law, only UOCAVA voters are permitted to do both simultaneously. This bill would also permit emergency responders to request an early voting ballot by fax beginning 45 days prior to Election Day. Election officials must send the ballot if the request is received by noon on Election Day. The emergency responder voter must complete an oath swearing, under penalty of perjury, that they have not and will not vote another ballot in the relevant election.

Last Updated January 7, 2022

This bill, as enacted on April 19, 2022, retains most of the provisions of the previous version of the bill. Unless otherwise noted below, the provisions described in this commentary were retained unchanged from the previous version of the bill. The bill, as amended, makes numerous changes across many areas of Nebraska's election law. Specifically, the bill:

  • Permits voters who are emergency responders serving outside of their county of residence for the period beginning 45 days before Election Day to request an absentee ballot (called an "early voting ballot" in Nebraska) by fax or email and to return the ballot by any transmission method authorized by the Secretary of State. Under existing law, such voters could use the state's no-excuse absentee voting procedures only.
  • Authorizes voters who are members of the state National Guard and are ordered into active service to vote by applying for a ballot using a federal postcard application, thus aligning the voting options of National Guard members with UOCAVA voters. Under existing law, National Guard members in service could use the state's no-excuse absentee voting procedures only.
  • Imposes new requirements on absentee ballot drop boxes, including securing the box to the ground, being locked, and being ADA-compliant. The bill also requires local election officials to notify the Secretary of State of each drop box's location in advance. The bill also requires drop boxes to be accessible until the deadline for return of ballots, with collections from each box at least once per business day. Finally, the bill, in a provision added by the most recent amendment, requires the Secretary of State to promulgate rules and regulations to carry out the drop box requirements imposed by the bill. These are new requirements, regulating matters not previously addressed by statute.
  • Expands and revises voters' options to receive a replacement mail ballot, in either a traditional or vote-by-mail election. Specifically, the bill:
    • Allows voters to request a replacement mail ballot by fax or email as well as by mail or in-person. Existing law only allowed requests in person or by mail.
    • Specifies the deadline to request a replacement mail ballot as 6 p.m. on the second Friday before the election instead of "close of business" on that day.
    • Newly requires the voter's signature on the replacement ballot request, if returned by mail, fax, or email, to be verified before the replacement ballot is sent. Existing law did not have this requirement.
  • Clarifies that the deadline for receiving ballots in all elections except special elections conducted by mail is 7:00 p.m. on Election Day for jurisdictions in the Mountain time zone, and 8:00 p.m. on Election Day for jurisdictions in the Central time zone. This was already the existing deadline for receipt of ballots, but this provision provides additional clarification.
  • Makes changes to the maintenance and use of the voter lists by:
    • Mandating that election officials remove people from voter lists if they are notified by the DMV that the person has changed their state of residence by surrendering their Nebraska license or state ID. This is a new item in the existing list of mandatory reasons for removing a voter from the voter list.
    • Requiring any person requesting use of the voter list to state their reason for requesting the list.
    • Directing the secretary of state to make the voter list available to each jury commissioner. Under existing law, the jury commissioner could access the voter list upon request only.
    • Requiring any person who has a voter list to disclose any breach of the information on that list to an election official immediately.
  • Prohibits funding of elections from any source other than governmental entities or subdivisions and prohibits election officials from soliciting, accepting, or using grants or donations from any private entity except in-kind contributions of food or use of building space. This provision is modified from the previous version of the bill, which explicitly allowed funding from governmental sources, including the federal government. The enacted bill is silent as to whether election administrators can accept funding from the federal government.
  • Prohibits foreign nationals from funding ballot questions. This provision was added by the most recent amendment to the bill.
  • Directs the Secretary of State, in addition to their other duties, to support the day-to-day operations of elections officials and to oversee and review the actions of local elections commissioners.
  • Authorizes election commissioners to appoint election workers who reside outside the county, if no in-county appointees are available, provided that such workers live in vote by mail counties or, if not, that such appointment is approved by the secretary of state. Under existing law, only residents of a jurisdiction could be appointed as election workers in that district.
  • Requires any person distributing voter registration applications or early voting applications by mail to use a form prescribed by the secretary of state making clear that the application was not sent from an elections officials. State voter registration agencies are exempted from this requirement. Under existing law, no such disclosure is required. This provision is substantially similar to a provision in a previous version of the bill, but the notice required by the person distributing the election material has been reworded.
  • Permits any person who cannot write their name or mark because of a disability to use instead:
    • A mark written by another person, provided that such other person writes their own name, address, and signature.
    • An impression made by a signature stamp.
      Under existing law, a voter unable to write their name had to have another person sign for them, with no requirement that the third party assistant identify themself.
  • Creates an electioneering boundary for drop boxes of 200 feet.

  • Requires notice to be posted in a physical location by 1:00 p.m. on Election Day of the date and time when the canvassing board will convene. There is no notice requirement of canvassing board meetings under existing law.

    Several provisions that appeared in earlier versions of the bill were removed from the bill by previous amendments and were not enacted into law. These provisions would have:

    • Required that local election officials who maintain a list of voters who requested early voting ballots remove voters from the list upon the voter's request, upon a return of the voter's application as undeliverable, or if the voter has not requested an early voting ballot or has not voted in two consecutive general elections.
    • Created an exit poll boundary of 20 feet from a drop-box.

    This bill contains provisions dealing with recounts, ballot initiatives, and recall elections, including criminal penalties related to improper conduct of recall elections, that are not tracked by Voting Rights Lab.

Last Updated December 6, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2022, would expand the existing misdemeanor of failing to perform duties imposed by the state's election act to include such a failure by a member of a governing body of any political subdivision who is subject to a duty under the election act.

Last updated January 27, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2022, would prohibit private funding for any election, and would restrict funding sources for elections to appropriations from federal, state, or local government. The bill would explicitly permit in-kind contribution of food and beverages for election workers and in-kind donations, in whole or in part, of building use.

Last updated January 27, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on January 19, 2022, would prohibit counting boards from beginning to count any ballots, including early voting ballots and absentee ballots, until after the close of the polls on Election Day. Under existing law, counting of early ballots can begin 24 hours before polls open on Election Day.

Last Updated January 22, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 19, 2022, would change various ID requirements to register and vote. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require voters to attach a copy of a photo ID or a copy of a utility bill, bank statement, paycheck, government check, or other government document dated within the previous sixty days along with their absentee ballot application. Applications submitted without a copy of ID would be rejected.

  • Change the documents required for newly registering voters. The bill would require all new registrants to provide acceptable ID confirming the voter's identity and address. If a voter uses a nonphoto ID, such as a utility bill, bank statement, paycheck, government check, or other government documents, it must be dated within sixty days before it is presented as ID. Under existing law, certain first-time voters, if they had previously voted for a federal office in the county, were not required to submit ID. Existing law did not require a specific date for nonphoto ID.

Last Updated February 7, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 20, 2022, would authorize local election officials to maintain ballot drop boxes for the return of voted ballots. Under existing law, jurisdictions with vote-by-mail elections must have drop boxes, but there is no statutory provision for drop boxes in other jurisdictions. In practice, some jurisdictions that do not conduct vote-by-mail elections offer drop boxes. For jurisdictions offering drop boxes, this bill would:

  • Require that drop boxes be available beginning on the sixth Friday before Election Day in a statewide primary or general election, and beginning on the fourth Friday before Election Day in any special election. Drop boxes would be required to be available until the close of the polls on Election Day.
  • Require collection of ballots from drop boxes at least once every business day.
  • Mandate that drop boxes be accessible and compliant with the ADA.
  • Require that drop boxes be secured to the ground and locked.
  • Require local election officials to inform the secretary of state as to the location of each drop box at least 42 days before Election Day.

  • Require local election officials to develop a procedure for secure collection and transport of ballots from drop boxes.

Last Updated January 22, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2022, would change the body in charge of redistricting and how members are chosen. Specifically, this bill would:

  • Direct the legislature to create a screening committee once every ten years beginning in 2031 comprised of nine legislative members with no more than five belonging to the same party. Action by this screening committee requires a six-person vote. This screening committee shall appoint a redistricting commission.
  • Create a method of establishing a redistricting commission, with three commissioners from the largest political party in the state, three commissioners from the second largest political party in the state, and three commissioners not affiliated with either party. The screening committee shall advertise to the public and make a pool of applicants. They may conduct interviews prior to selection. The screening committee shall select two members of each group at random and may choose the third member of each category based on qualifications.
  • Direct each to-be-established redistricting commission to begin work on or before April 1 in each year following a decennial census and shall recommend maps setting forth district boundaries by August 1 in the same year. To accomplish this, the commission may retain employees, consultants, and legal counsel. Before recommending maps, the commission must hold at least one public meeting in each congressional district, with the maps available at least seven days prior to the first such meeting. The commission may only recommend maps on a vote of at least 2 commissioners from each of the three groups of commissioners.
  • The legislature has final approval of maps but may not redraw maps. If a map is rejected, the commission shall redraw the map and resubmit it to the legislature.
  • Establish criteria for redistricting, listed in descending order of priority:
    • compliance with federal law,
    • contiguous districts,
    • making districts as nearly equal in population as possible,
    • ensuring that the right to vote is not abridged on the basis of race or language,
    • minimizing division of political subdivisions,
    • not intentionally favoring or disfavoring any incumbent or party.
  • Clarify that all proceedings of all committees and commissions regarding redistricting must be conducted in public with a remote viewing option.
  • Establish personal qualifications and disqualifications for serving on the commission.

  • Create a private cause of action in any registered voter to compel compliance with the provisions of the bill.

    Last updated January 7, 2022.

This proposed amendment to the state constitution, as amended on March 16, 2022, would provide that only citizens of the United States and citizens of New Hampshire, defined as being individuals who are domiciled and have their primary residence in New Hampshire, have the right to vote. Under existing law, "every inhabitant of the state of 18 years of age and upwards shall have an equal right to vote in any election."

This provision was newly amended into this proposed amendment. The previous version of the amendment would have permitted 17 year olds to vote in primaries if they were going to turn 18 before the corresponding general election.

Last Updated May 25, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 5, 2022, would amend the state constitution to require the Attorney General to prosecute whenever there is clear and convincing evidence an election fraud has been committed. If the Attorney General failed to bring the clear and convincing evidence to a grand jury, the Attorney General would be removed from office. Existing law has no comparable provision.

Last updated February 10, 2022.

This bill, as introduced January 5, 2022, would ban the use of tabulation equipment for the counting of votes and require that all elections be conducted using paper ballots.

Last updated January 24, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on January 5, 2022, would prohibit mailing a ballot to a voter unless the voter applied for the ballot and the voter's application was approved. In effect, this prohibits mail ballot elections. Under existing law, New Hampshire does not conduct any elections by mail, nor does existing law have a similar prohibition.

Last Updated January 24, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 5, 2022, would require voters who are not affiliated with a political party to join a party at least 120 days before the state primary, if the voter wishes to vote in the primary. Similarly, it would prohibit voters affiliated with a party from changing parties between the first Wednesday in June and the state primary. Finally, it would require people to be members of a party for at least six months before running as a candidate for that party. Under existing law, unaffiliated voters may join a party for the purposes of voting in the party's primary as late as Election Day, and people do not have to be members of a party for any particular time to run as candidates in that party.

Last Updated March 21, 2022

This bill, as enacted on July 1, 2022, directs election officials to position challengers where the challenger is able to see and hear the hand-counting of ballots and maintain a line of sight on any electronic ballot counting device.

A previous version of the bill would have required that election administrators permit challengers to stand not more than six feet of the location where ballots are hand counted and to permit them to maintain a line of sight on any electronic ballot counting device.

Last updated October 4, 2022.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on April 28, 2022, would bring the code into compliance with a state supreme court decision overturning a 2018 law. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Repeal the requirement that a voter carry out a verifiable act, or acts, establishing their intent to maintain a domicile in the state, stating instead that domicile for voting purposes is a question of intention and fact.
  • Repeal the differentiated registration requirements for voter registering on Election Day or in the 30 days before Election Day, compared to before that period. Under existing law, which has been enjoined, individuals could not register to vote without documentary proof of their qualifications more than 30 days before an election and within 30 days of an election were required to provide documentation post-election.
  • Permit the identity of a voter without photo ID at the polling place to be verified by another registered voter who does possess photo ID with them at the polling place. A voter could not verify the identities of more than two voters at the same election.
  • Permit municipal supervisors of the voter checklists to use nonpublic information to verify the qualifications of an applicant for registration who does not possess documentary proof at the polling place.
  • Permit registrants to verify their qualifications via a "qualified voter affidavit." Under existing law, which has been enjoined, documentary proof of identity, age, domicile, and citizenship was required for registration.
  • Permit the secretary of state to establish a process whereby first-time voters who failed to present photo ID while registering to vote could respond to identity verification letters via email or text message. Under existing law, responses to identity verification letters must be "written."
  • Repeal the requirement that the department of motor vehicles send notice to all individuals who attested to their qualifications rather than submitting documentation that they are required to obtain a New Hampshire driver's license within 60 days of becoming a state resident.
  • Direct the secretary of state to amend the voter registration form to collect voluntary additional information for contacting a voter post-election if necessary, including but not limited to phone number, email address, vehicle information, employer information, social media accounts, or a friend or relative's name and address.
  • Direct the secretary of state to amend the voter registration form to allow for the documentation of voter verification either by an election official or by another voter.
  • Repeal provisions regarding the Interstate Voter Registration Crosscheck Program.
  • Make non-substantive changes to the voter registration form.

Previous versions of this bill contained several provisions that were amended out of the current version. These provisions would have:

  • Clarified that establishing residence for voting purposes is not conclusive of an individual's residence for other purposes.
  • Required that individuals registering to vote more than 30 days before Election Day attest that they did not possess, and could never possess, proof of domicile before they could be permitted to register by signing an affidavit in lieu of documentation.
  • Established a domicile affidavit to be signed by individuals registering on Election Day or within 30 days of Election Day who do not have in their possession proof of domicile.
  • Permitted registrants more than 30 days before Election Day to present a wider array of documents to establish domicile, including any "reasonably similar documentation" to the enumerated forms of documentation, if they do not have an enumerated form of ID in their possession.
  • Repealed the authority of supervisors of checklists to request that law enforcement visit the address of an individual who registered within 30 days of Election Day without documentary evidence of their domicile in order to verify that the registrant does indeed live at that address.
  • Repealed the presumption that anyone who has lived in the state for 30 or fewer days is in the state temporarily.
  • Repealed requirements that local election officials, and potentially the attorney general and secretary of state, conduct post-election investigations into registrants who claimed they could not offer documentary proof of residency.
  • Shifted responsibility for investigating individuals who registered on Election Day and did not provide proof of identity, if a mailing intended to verify the voter's identity was returned as undeliverable, from the secretary of state to the attorney general.
  • Required the secretary of state to join ERIC.

Last Updated May 11, 2022

This bill, as introduced on January 5, 2022, would:

  • Allow the state senate to refer allegations of voter fraud to the state supreme court for the hearing of witnesses and evidence prior to the allocation of presidential and vice-presidential electors.
  • Require allocation of presidential and vice-presidential electors to be proportionate to the percent of the vote received in the state.

Last Updated February 9, 2022

This bill, as introduced January 5, 2022, would:

  • Require all election officers appearing on the ballot, except clerks, to remain in the areas at polling places designated for electioneering except when they are casting their own ballots. Violation of this prohibition would be a misdemeanor. Under existing law, election officials who are on the ballot are barred from electioneering while conducting their duties, and violating this prohibition is a misdemeanor, however, existing law does not require that such candidate-officials remain in the area designated for electioneering even when they are not actively electioneering.
  • Disqualify a municipality's moderator, selectman, inspector of election, and supervisor of the checklist from performing duties as an election official for an election in which they appear on the ballot. Under existing law, individuals holding such positions were exempted from a general prohibition against candidates serving as election officials.
  • End the disqualification of clerks who are on the ballot at a given election from handling marked ballots and counting votes.
  • Bar municipal moderators from going behind the guardrail at a polling place during an election at which they are on the ballot, and permit municipal clerks to do so. Under existing law, moderators who appear on the ballot are exempted from the general prohibition from candidates' going behind the guard rail.

Last updated January 24, 2022.

This bill, as introduced January 5, 2022, would require a "forensic audit" of the results of the November 2020 general election in Merrimack County. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Establish an audit team comprised of representatives selected by each audited town, the state house of representatives, and the state senate. The audit team would then select a third-party technical lead.
  • Require the audit to expand to cover the entire state if the audited number of votes for any candidate deviated by over 500 votes from the results as certified.

Last updated February 9, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on January 5, 2022, would require the speaker of the house of representatives to appoint "an independent third party" to conduct a "forensic audit" of the certified results of the November 3, 2020, election. The bill does not describe what qualifications the third party must have, or what the "forensic audit" would involve, but its focus is broad. The reviewing party must submit a report detailing their findings, including "anomalies or discrepancies in voter data, ballot data, or tabulation" to the legislature, the governor, and the state library on or before November 1, 2022.

The bill expressly authorizes the Secretary of State to receive and disburse private funds for the "forensic audit" and does not provide an appropriation.

Last updated January 6, 2022.

This bill, as enacted on June 17, 2022, provides that a person requesting a copy of the voter checklist for a given municipality may receive a physical or electronic copy in the format of their choosing. Under existing law, statute provided only that the clerk "shall furnish one or more copies" of the list, without expressly authorizing delivery in electronic form.

Last Updated July 7, 2022

This bill, as introduced January 5, 2022, would

  • Require absentee voters to include a photocopy of proof of identity and residence in the outer absentee ballot envelope. Under existing law, no such documentation is required.
  • Direct moderators to contact absentee voters who fail to include the required documentation with their ballot. Voters would have until the close of polls on Election Day to provide the moderator with the required documentation. The moderator would reject the ballot if documentation was not received by the close of polls. Existing law does not provide for any type of cure process for defective absentee ballots.

The bill also contains provisions regarding election equipment, ballot paper, the chain of custody of voted ballots, and the publication of ballot images that are not tracked by the Voting Rights Lab.

Last Updated March 24, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced January 5, 2022, would establish procedures for casting provisional ballots for voters without qualifying ID. Voters who cast provisional ballots would be required to return to the polling place where they cast their provisional ballot and provide sufficient documentation of identity before the moderator has finished counting votes. Such voters would also be required to produce a receipt given to them when they cast their provisional ballot.

Under existing law, voters who do not have appropriate proof of identity at their polling place are permitted to cast a regular ballot after completing a challenged voter affidavit and are not required to provide proof of identity at any point.

Last Updated January 11, 2022

This bill, as introduced January 5, 2022, would establish provisional ("affidavit") voting for same-day registrants and voters whose names do not appear on the rolls on Election Day. Such voters would complete new registration forms, and their ballots would be set aside. Upon the close of polls, the municipal clerk would review these ballots and associated documentation for accuracy and completeness before counting them. Under existing law, such voters cast regular ballots, and the ballots and associated documentation are only subject to scrutiny if the voter is challenged while at the polling place.

Last updated March 23, 2022.

This bill, as enacted on July 8, 2022:

  • Requires the state attorney general to investigate misconduct by election officials. Under existing law, the attorney general had broad authority to investigate violations of election law at their discretion.
  • Requires the attorney general to remove the voting rights of election officials convicted of misdemeanor election misconduct, in accordance with the state constitutional provision providing for the disenfranchisement of individuals convicted of "willful violation of the election laws."
  • Requires the attorney general to provide 45 days notice to the relevant jurisdiction before assessing civil penalties related to an election official's negligent failure to perform their duties, and give the jurisdiction an opportunity to respond. Existing law required the attorney general to give notice prior to imposing a fine, but did not specify a timeline.The bill also creates an express right for jurisdictions to appeal the imposition of a civil penalty to the superior court.

Last updated August 15, 2022.

This bill, as introduced January 5, 2022, would require public colleges and universities in the state to charge in-state tuition rates to all students who are registered voters in the state. Under existing law, there is no link between voter registration and tuition rates.

Last Updated January 10, 2022

This bill, as enacted on June 17, 2022, requires high schools to include voter registration, when deemed appropriate, in the development of education plans for students with disabilities. Under existing law, there was no requirement that high schools provide any voter registration programming.

Last Updated June 27, 2022

This bill, as amended on February 16, 2022, would draw new state senate districts based on the results of the 2020 census. These districts were amended from the previous version of the bill.

Last updated February 17, 2022.

This bill, as amended on March 24, 2022, would draw new executive council districts based on the results of the 2020 census. These districts were amended from the previous version of the bill.

Last updated March 29, 2022.

This bill, as introduced January 5, 2022, would establish criteria for redistricting. Districts would have to be:

  • Contiguous.
  • Respectful of existing political boundaries, to the extent practicable.
  • Drawn in compact shapes, avoiding jagged edges and extensions.
  • Considerate of the integrity of communities of interest, defined to include but not be limited to, racial, ethnic, economic, social, cultural, geographic, or historic identities, and to exclude relationships with political parties or a political candidate.
  • Not unduly favorable or disfavorable towards any political party, incumbent, candidate, racial group, or language group.

Last updated January 10, 2022.

This bill, as introduced January 5, 2022, would:

  • Eliminate the requirement that absentee ballots cast in person at clerks' offices or returned in person to clerks' offices after being received in the mail be placed in an outer ballot envelope. Existing law requires that all absentee voters to place their affidavit envelopes inside an outer envelope, although it is not made explicit that ballots contained in affidavit envelopes returned in person without an outer envelope would be rejected.
  • Permit election officials to open outer envelopes purporting to contain absentee ballots immediately upon receipt. Under existing law, officials may not open outer until Election Day. These provisions were retained from the previous version of the bill. The amended version also contains a provision that was not in the previous version. This provision would modify the absentee ballot request form to require the voter provide their address next to their signature.

Last Updated March 28, 2022

This bill, as enacted on June 17, 2022:

  • Creates a Class B felony for the use or threat of force, violence, or any tactic of coercion or intimidation to knowingly discourage, interfere with, or compel any election officer or worker from engaging in or completing duties related to an election.
  • Establishes a default penalty of a civil fine of between $250 and $1000 for any violation of the election code for which a different penalty is not specified.
  • Creates a new civil penalty for an election official negligently failing to perform their duty or negligently performing their duty so as to hinder the conduct of elections, through imposition of a $250-1000 fine and restitution damages, assessed on the employer jurisdiction. The state attorney general must notify the employer of its intent to seek the penalty and of the opportunity to negotiate settlement.
  • Modifies civil penalties for the destruction of political advertising.

Last Updated July 7, 2022

This bill, as enacted on June 16, 2022:

  • Creates a new category of provisional ("affidavit") ballots for certain voters who register at the polls on Election Day and do not meet ID verification requirements. Affidavit ballots must be accompanied by a postage-paid voter verification letter, which is given to the voter and must be returned with a copy of required ID within 10 days for the ballot to be certified. The bill also sets out requirements for preliminary and certified tabulation of provisional ballots. Under existing law, any voter who did not meet the ID verification requirements was required to submit a challenged voter affidavit attesting to their identity and be photographed by election officials, and subsequently voted a regular ballot.
  • Requires officials to check the statewide voter database to try to verify the identities of voters who do not meet the ID requirements, and requires the secretary of state to provide training on how to do so. If a voter's identity cannot be verified through the database, the voter must execute a challenged voter affidavit, be photographed, and cast an affidavit ballot.
  • Requires the secretary of state to report individuals who cast an affidavit ballot and do not return the verification letter, or do not provide a copy of required ID, to the state attorney general's office for investigation of potential election crimes.
  • Requires election workers attesting to the identity of a voter in lieu of the voter providing ID to provide specific notations regarding their role and name, and specifies that ID affirmations are made under penalty of perjury.
  • Directs the secretary of state to develop informational materials regarding how to obtain free voter ID documents.

Last Updated August 29, 2022

This bill, as amended on March 24, 2022, would expand absentee voting eligibility to cover illness and other medical conditions that prevent a voter from being able to cast a vote in person on Election Day. Under existing law, physical disability is the only medical excuse. This provision was newly amended into this version of the bill.
A previous version of the bill contained several provisions that were amended out of this version. These provisions would have:

  • Established no-excuse absentee voting and, by extension, early voting at clerks' offices. Under existing law, voters must have a qualifying excuse in order to apply for an absentee ballot.
  • Established no-excuse absentee voter registration. Under existing law, voter registration must be completed in person unless the voter is disabiled or temporarily absent from their municipality of residence.
  • Permited moderators to begin opening outer envelopes containing absentee ballots on the Thursday, Friday, Saturday, or Monday before Election Day. Challenges would have to be made at this time. Under existing law, outer envelopes may not be opened until Election Day.
  • Repealed signature-matching provisions that have been blocked by state courts.

The bill also provides an exception for when a law enforcement officer is called by the election officials to assist in a specific emergency at a polling place or at a senior residential center. This provision was modified from the previous version of the bill, which would not have addressed senior residential centers.
  • Prohibit law enforcement officers from serving as members of a district election board unless they are off-duty. The bill would also prohibit law enforcement officers from serving as authorized challengers located within their jurisdiction of law enforcement service with the exception that officers who are candidates on the ballot may serve as challengers if otherwise authorized by law. A law enforcement officer may not remain within 100 feet of a polling location except for the act of voting, unless the officer's personal residence is within 100 feet of a polling place. This provision has been modified from the previous version of the bill to condition the limitation on service as a challenger to the officer's jurisdiction.
  • Prohibit ballot drop boxes to be placed within 100 feet of the entrance or exit of a law enforcement agency. Existing drop boxes in certain locations would be exempt from this prohibition. The previous version of the bill did not include the exemption for certain existing drop boxes.
  • Prohibit electioneering activity within 100 feet of a drop box. A person who violates this provision may be charged with a disorderly persons offense. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Allow a county to open only the drop box nearest the office of the municipal clerk and the drop box at the county board of elections office during a municipal, school board, or special election. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

Note: 2020 A.B. 4655, which is identical to this bill, was enacted on January 18, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on June 20, 2022, would add new processes for removing deceased people from the voter registration list. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the municipal officer in charge of death records to give the county clerk the monthly file of death data the officer currently gives to the commissioner of registration only. The data would continue to be sent to the commissioner of registration as well.
  • Require the State Registrar of Vital Statistics to file with the county clerk the annual data the Registrar currently gives to the commissioner of registration only. The data would continue to be sent to the commissioner of registration as well.
  • Require the clerk, as well as the commissioner, to investigate and determine if any registered voters in the county died. The clerk would give the commissioner the findings of any investigation by the clerk. Under existing law only the commissioner investigates.
  • Require a commissioner of registration to transfer a deceased voter's registration to the death file upon receiving a properly completed and notarized form from the next of kin affirming the death of the deceased registrant and a copy of the deceased registrant's death certificate. The form would have to be filed in person with the commissioner or the clerk of the county in which the deceased person was registered. Existing law has no comparable provision.
  • Require a commissioner of registration to transfer a deceased voter's registration to the death file upon receiving a properly completed and notarized form from the Director of the Division of Veterans' Healthcare Services or a nursing home administrator that reports the death of a facility resident who was a registered voter. Existing law has no comparable provision.
  • Require the commissioner of registration shall transfer the deceased registrant's voter registration record to the death file upon receipt of a properly completed and notarized form from a funeral director that is accompanied by the deceased registrant's death certificate. The funeral director may deliver the form and certificate to the commissioner or the county clerk.

Last updated June 21, 2022

This bill, as introduced on June 20, 2022, attempts to protect election officials and workers by enabling them to keep their personal information in records maintained by the Division of Elections off of the internet, and by creating misdemeanors. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the Division of Elections to remove election workers' personal information from records that are available on the internet, if the election worker submits a written request supported by evidence that they are an election worker and why they believe the dissemination of the personal information contained in the records on the Internet poses an imminent and serious threat to the safety of the election worker. Existing law has no comparable provision.
  • Define the personal information to be protected as a person's:
    • home address,
    • home telephone number,
    • personal mobile telephone number,
    • personal email address,
    • photograph,
    • directions to a person's home, and
    • a photograph or description of a person's home, vehicle, or vehicle license plate.
  • Create two misdemeanors that prohibit a person who is not an election official from, in writing, through electronic means:
    • intimidating, threatening, coercing, or attempting to do any of those, to any election official or election worker in the discharge of their duties.
    • attempting to induce any election official to violate or refuse to comply with the election official's duty or any law regulating the same.
  • Create a misdemeanor that prohibits a person who is not an election official from knowingly and willfully preventing an election official or election worker from performing official duties.
  • Create a misdemeanor to prohibit any person from knowingly making available on the Internet personal information about an election official or an election official's immediate family if the dissemination of personal information poses an imminent and serious threat to the safety of the election official or the election official's immediate family and the person making the information available on the Internet knows or reasonably should know of the imminent and serious threat.
  • Create a presumption that the dissemination of the personal information of an election official or their immediate family poses an imminent and serious threat to their safety if a federal, state, or local law enforcement agency has issued a safety advisory or warning for election officials that is in effect and applies to the election official.

Last updated June 21, 2022.

  • Repeal a prohibition on police officers serving as challengers at polling places or remaining or standing within 100 feet of a polling place.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on September 22, 2022, would establish the John R. Lewis Voting Rights Act of New Jersey. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Prohibit any jurisdictions from prescribing or maintaining voting or election policies that unnecessarily deny or abridge the right vo toe, including methods of election that have the effect or impairing the ability of members of a protected class ro elect candidates of their choice. Any policy that burdens the right to vote would have to be narrowly tailored to promote a compelling policy justification supported by substantial evidence.
  • Establish a preclearance regime whereby jurisdictions that have been subject to court orders or enforcement actions under this law, the federal Voting Rights Act of 1965, or relevant portions of the U.S. constitution, would be required to seek approval from the Division on Civil Rights in the Office of the Attorney General or a state court before making any changes to election procedures.
  • Require that all statutes, rules, and regulations, including all local laws or ordinances related to the franchise, be construed liberally in favor of protecting the right of voters to have their ballot cast and counted, ensuring that eligible individuals are not impaired in registering to vote, and ensuring that voters of race, color, and language minority groups have equitable access to fully participate in registering to vote and voting.
  • Require language assistance and translated voting materials to language minority groups when 4000 individuals or 2% of the population of a jurisdiction (but no less than 300 individuals) are citizens of voting age with limited English proficiency.
  • Permit the attorney general, impacted individuals, or organizations whose membership includes impacted individuals, to file a lawsuit in state court based on a violation of the provisions of the bill.

Last updated November 15, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on May 26, 2022, attempts to protect election officials and workers by enabling them to keep their personal information in records maintained by the Division of Elections off of the internet, and by creating misdemeanors. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the Division of Elections to remove election workers' personal information from records that are available on the internet, if the election worker submits a written request supported by evidence that they are an election worker and why they believe the dissemination of the personal information contained in the records on the Internet poses an imminent and serious threat to the safety of the election worker. Existing law has no comparable provision.
  • Define the personal information to be protected as a person's
    • home address,
    • home telephone number,
    • personal mobile telephone number,
    • personal email address,
    • photograph,
    • directions to a person's home, and
    • a photograph or description of a person's home, vehicle, or vehicle license plate.
  • Create two misdemeanors that prohibit a person who is not an election official from, in writing, through electronic means:
    • intimidating, threatening, coercing, or attempting to do any of those, to any election official or election worker in the discharge of their duties.
    • attempting to induce any election official to violate or refuse to comply with the election official's duty or any law regulating the same.
  • Create a misdemeanor that prohibits a person who is not an election official from knowingly and willfully preventing an election official or election worker from performing official duties.
  • Create a misdemeanor to prohibit any person from knowingly making available on the Internet personal information about an election official or an election official's immediate family if the dissemination of personal information poses an imminent and serious threat to the safety of the election official or the election official's immediate family and the person making the information available on the Internet knows or reasonably should know of the imminent and serious threat.

  • Create a presumption that the dissemination of the personal information of an election official or their immediate family poses an imminent and serious threat to their safety if a federal, state, or local law enforcement agency has issued a safety advisory or warning for election officials that is in effect and applies to the election official.

    Last updated June 16, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced May 26, 2022, would dramatically change both mail and in-person voting by imposing identification requirements on both voting methods and by sharply shortening the time voters have to apply for and return mail ballots. In addition, it would change the voter registration deadline for November general elections only, requiring people to register sooner than otherwise required to vote in those elections.

Specifically, the bill would impose very restrictive ID requirements on both in-person and mail voting by:

  • Requiring voters to show their driver's license or state ID plus their Social Security card to vote in person. The clerk would examine the documents and only if satisfied that they are valid proof of identification, would the clerk issue the voter a ballot. Existing law does not require voters to show a physical ID to vote in person.
  • Requiring people who vote by mail to include a copy of their driver's license or state ID plus their Social Security card with their ballot. Existing law does not require ID copies to vote by mail.
  • Requiring voters who moved within the county but failed to properly update their voter registration to provide their driver's license or state ID and the voter's Social Security card when submitting a related affirmation regarding their change of address. Existing law expressly prohibits requiring an identifying document in this context.

  • Requiring the identification used to vote be added to the voter's registration record in the statewide registration database.

    The bill would restrict voting by mail by:


  • Changing the deadline to apply to receive a ballot by mail to 14 days before the election. Under existing law, the deadline is seven days before the election.
  • Changing the deadline to apply in person to pick up a mail ballot to 3 p.m. eight days before the election. Under existing law, the deadline is 3 p.m. on the day before the election.

  • Changing the deadline to return a mail ballot to seven days before Election Day. Under existing law, voters have until the close of polls on Election Day to return their mail ballots in person. If returned by mail, a ballot will be timely if it is postmarked by Election Day and received by election officials within 144 hours of the closing of the polls, or, if the ballot is not postmarked but is received by mail, it is received within 48 hours of the polls closing.

    Finally, the bill would require people wishing to vote in a November general election to register on or before the immediately preceding October 1. Under existing law, the registration deadline for all elections is 21 days before the election.

Last Updated June 17, 2022

  • Require the State Registrar of Vital Statistics to file with the county clerk the annual data the Registrar currently gives to the commissioner of registration only. The data would continue to be sent to the commissioner of registration as well.

  • Require a commissioner of registration to transfer a deceased voter's registration to the death file upon receiving a properly completed and notarized form from the next of kin affirming the death of the deceased registrant and a copy of the deceased registrant's death certificate. The form would have to be filed in person with the commissioner or the clerk of the county in which the deceased person was registered. Existing law has no comparable provision.
  • Require a commissioner of registration to transfer a deceased voter's registration to the death file upon receiving a properly completed and notarized form from the Director of the Division of Veterans' Healthcare Services or a nursing home administrator that reports the death of a facility resident who was a registered voter. Existing law has no comparable provision.

  • Require the commissioner of registration shall transfer the deceased registrant's voter registration record to the death file upon receipt of a properly completed and notarized form from a funeral director that is accompanied by the deceased registrant's death certificate. The funeral director may deliver the form and certificate to the commissioner or the county clerk.
