BILLSUMMARY: Proposes to amend the constitution of New Mexico to provide for the creation of an independent redistricting commission to develop redistricting plans for congressional districts, state legislative districts and the districts of other districted state offices.
VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as amended on February 10, 2022, proposes a constitutional amendment that would create an independent, bipartisan redistricting commission to draw and adopt redistricting plans. Under existing law, the legislature conducts redistricting. The amendment makes minor changes to the previous version of the bill, as detailed below. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Authorize the commission to draw state legislative districts and federal congressional following each federal decennial census, using the following criteria:
    • Equal population (within certain margins, which were altered by the amended version of the bill).
    • Based upon federal decennial census data and other reliable sources of demographic data.
    • Compliance with federal and state law.
    • No dilution to any protected minority's voting strength, although race may not be the predominant consideration and traditional, race-neutral redistricting principles cannot be subordinated to racial considerations.
    • Single-member districts only.
    • No splitting precincts.
    • Contiguous and compact districts.
    • Preservation of communities of interest.
    • Political and geographic boundaries, including boundaries of Indian nations, tribes, and pueblos.
    • Preservation of the core of existing districts.
  • Require the commission to hold public hearings throughout the state before and after proposing plans.

  • Comprise members who have not run for office, been lobbyists, or worked for a campaign, party, or PAC recently. The state ethics commission selects 38 nominees, with bipartisan legislative leaders getting a chance to strike nominees, and the state ethics commission making the final selection.

    Last updated February 11, 2022.

HISTORY: {"date":"02/10/2022","summary":"From HOUSE Committee on GOVERNMENT, ELECTIONS AND INDIAN AFFAIRS:  Do pass","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on February 3, 2022, remains mostly unchanged from the previous version of the bill, except as noted below. This bill would change existing election laws and would specifically:

  • Establish same-day registration for Election Day. Under existing law, same-day registration is only available during the early voting period. Same-day voter registration would be available at all Election Day voting locations to voters who affirm that they have not previously voted in this election and who provide an ID with the voter's name, photograph, and address, or two separate IDs, one with the voter's name and photograph and one document, from an approved list, that contains the voter's address. The same documentation is required to register to vote under existing law, but is not required to vote in person on Election Day.
  • Require counties to establish vote centers for all statewide elections. Under existing law, such vote centers are authorized but not required. Vote centers must have real-time access to the electronic voter management system, which will allow all voters to vote a regular ballot. The bill would also require that all polling places established in the 2021 polling place resolution shall operate as a vote center for statewide elections in 2022 and 2023.
  • Require the secretary of state to develop a uniform list maintenance procedure to cancel voter registrations for voters who:
    • have voted in another state after registering in New Mexico,
    • are listed as deceased in the social security master death index, or
    • have obtained a driver's license or ID card in another state.
  • Prohibit local election officials from modifying early voting hours or locations without secretary of state approval and notice to voters. (EV Other)
  • Change requirements for absentee ballot applications to:
    • Prohibit anyone except election officials from distributing absentee ballot applications, but specifically authorizing third parties to direct voters to the website where voters can access an online absentee ballot application.
    • Require that mailed applications must be postmarked by 14 days before Election Day to be timely. Under existing law, absentee ballot applications must be made by the Thursday before Election Day.
    • Require local election officials to send a notice to a voter's registered address if they receive an absentee ballot application requesting the ballot be sent to a different address than the one on file.
    • Require that, for any absentee ballot applications rejected as untimely, local election officials send a notice of the rejection and a list of early voting locations and Election Day polling places in the county.
    • Clarifying that replacement ballots are not subject to the same deadline for issuance as new ballots.
  • Change requirements for absentee ballots, to:
    • Require voters to include their signature and the last four digits of their social security number on the absentee ballot envelope. Under existing law, the voter's name, address, year of birth, and signature were the only data required.
    • Authorize only those drop boxes which are under the supervision of an election official or county employee. Existing law requires drop boxes to be monitored by video surveillance, but it is unclear whether such surveillance would satisfy the "supervision" requirement of this provision.
    • Permit local election officials to collect ballots from drop boxes once every three days and on Election Day, rather than daily as required under existing law.
    • Create new processing procedures for received absentee or vote by mail ballots to require that election workers immediately check the last four digits of the voter's social security number upon receipts and send a voter whose ID number does not match notice of the defect and cure information. Cure, under this provision, would follow existing procedure. In addition, the absentee board would be required to randomly sample absentee ballots to determine if the verification process was correctly conducted. The bill would also prohibit separating inner and outer envelopes before the election board confirms the county clerk's verification process.
    • Permit absentee ballot processing and counting to begin at 9:00 a.m. on Election Day. Under existing law, it cannot begin until after the close of the polls. Absentee vote counters would be required to recess no later than 11:00 on Election Day and continue their work only between 9:30 a.m. and 9:30 p.m. on subsequent days.
    • Expand the definition of who qualifies as immediate family to return an absentee ballot to include domestic partners, grandchildren, grandparents, or other people with whom the voter has a continuing personal relationship.
    • Require that voters who applied for an absentee ballot but wish to vote in person must vote at a vote center. Under existing law, voters could go to their polling place or a vote center.
  • Change the qualifications for poll workers to require fewer conditions on 16- and 17-year-old poll workers and to require that elections judges be put on teams with people of different political parties.
  • Change requirements, qualifications, and authority for challengers and watchers to:
    • Require that challengers must be voters in a precinct in the county where they are appointed.
    • Prohibit challengers who have previously been removed from service as a challenger, watcher, or election or canvass observer.
    • Require that they attend training sessions provided by local election officials based on a curriculum created by the secretary of state.
    • Prohibit challengers and watchers from photographing ballots or voter information. The amended version of the bill specifically permits challengers and watchers to observe the last four digits of a voter's social security number and the voter's signature on an absentee ballot envelope.
    • Prohibit challengers and watchers from recording audio or video in a polling place.
    • Be allowed access to see and hear the election board and to speak with the presiding judge to ask questions and advise as to problems.
    • Require that messengers meet the same qualifications as challengers, watchers, and election observers. This provision was not in the previous version of the bill.
  • Revises existing post-election audits rules to require a full hand recount of certain races in certain precincts.
  • Require a re-tabulation if local election officials find previously unaccounted-for paper ballots, absentee ballots, provisional ballots, and ballots with write-in votes.
  • Require additional voter education, including:
    • Requiring the secretary of state to mail a notification to each voter, except those whose election mail has been returned as undeliverable, at least 42 days before each statewide election with details of how to vote in the election.
  • Change the way that election equipment is evaluated and certified by opening the process of inspecting electronic voting machines to the public.
  • Require that federal elections funds be deposited into a state fund for appropriation by the legislature.
  • Impose additional requirements on local election officials, including:
    • Requiring county canvassers to report final vote counts separated by method of voting, total ballots requested, returned, accepted, or rejected from UOCAVA voters, and total provisional ballots accepted and rejected.
    • Requiring preservation of paper ballots for 22 months after federal elections and 10 months after all other elections.
    • Requiring the secretary of state to establish educational certificates for clerks and entitling clerks and deputy clerks to additional pay for holding certificates of various levels. This provision did not appear in the previous version of the bill.
    • Requiring that any election official who verifies absentee and mail ballots must meet the requirements to be a challenger, watcher, or election observer. This provision did not appear in the previous version of the bill.
  • Expand who has access to the absentee ballot register from only county political parties to include candidates, political committees, and state political parties.
  • Create new election crimes or change existing election crimes, for:
    • Unlawful possession of a key to a drop box, which would be a felony.
    • Establishing, designating, or operating any container as a ballot drop box by a person not authorized by the election code, which would be a felony.
    • Altering the absentee ballot register, which would be a felony.
    • Narrowing the existing misdemeanor of obstructing the polling place, by permitting additional people access to the polling place and thus making fewer people potentially liable for the offense.
  • Expanding the address confidentiality program so that household members of a person who has address confidentiality may also be granted address confidentiality.
  • Creating a voter education and elections task force to examine and recommend best practices regarding voter registration, maintenance of voter rolls, existing election systems, voting modernization, ballot tracking and delivery, and interagency data sharing.

This bill also includes provisions regarding elections appropriations, referendum petitions, campaign finance, the candidate nomination process, appointments to vacant offices, the primary process, and other provisions not tracked by Voting Rights Lab. Some of these provisions were amended by the most recent version of the bill.

Last Updated September 5, 2025

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on February 10, 2022, would make a number of changes to existing election law. In doing so, it retains many of the provisions of previous versions of the bill, though it also removes some of the provisions that appeared in the previous version. The provisions that the amendment retains from the previous version of the bill would:

  • Create automatic voter registration at the motor vehicle division and the human services department. The bill would have automatically transmitted a registrant's information to election officials, who would be required to send the person, if eligible, a notice that they will be registered to vote unless they affirmatively opt out of registration. This bill also includes a provision, not in previous versions of the bill, requiring that a person whose information is transmitted for automatic voter registration be notified, without being given an opportunity to opt out of the transmission, during their transaction. Previous versions of the bill would also have provided that only those voters who knowingly and willfully took voluntary action to register to vote with knowledge that the person is ineligible could potentially be charged with any election crimes. This bill does not limit criminal liability in this manner but does provide that if a person who is not eligible becomes registered to vote, the remedy is removal of that person from the voter rolls.
  • Automatically restore voting rights to people disenfranchised because of a felony conviction immediately after release from incarceration. Under existing law, such voters' voting rights were only restored after completion of probation or parole. In addition, the bill would facilitate restoration of rights for formerly disenfranchised people by:
    • Requiring the corrections department to provide such voters with an opportunity to register at the time when the person is preparing for release.
    • Requiring data sharing from the corrections department to the secretary of state.
    • Requiring the secretary of state to update a voter's eligibility upon receipt of information from the corrections department.
    • Creating a presumption that any person who appears in person to register to vote is not disenfranchised based on incarceration.
  • Allow voters who register online to use their driver's license or state ID number when registering. Under existing law, the only ID number an online registrant can provide is a full social security number.
  • Create a permanent absentee voter list that would allow to the voter to receive a ballot in every election in which the voter is eligible to vote, indefinitely. Voters would be removed from the permanent absentee voting list if they:
    • Fail to vote in two consecutive elections, including at least one general election.
    • Have mail returned to the county clerk as undeliverable from their registration address.
    • Cancel their voter registration.
    • Move outside the county in which they are registered.
    • Request to be removed from the permanent absentee voter list.
  • Require every county to have at least two monitored drop boxes, except that counties must have at least as many drop boxes as they have early voting locations. A previous version of the bill would have required counties to have only one monitored drop box per county. The bill would also:
    • Allow local governments, school districts, and community colleges to request additional monitored drop boxes in their jurisdictions, which the local election official would be required to evaluate and respond to.
  • Require local election officials to consider written requests from Indian nations, tribes, and pueblos for drop boxes sited on their land.
  • Approve requests for vote centers (called "voter convenience centers" in New Mexico) on Indian nation, tribal, or pueblo land if:
    • Any voter in the county can use the location.
    • The location meets location requirements for other vote centers.
    • The county clerk provides federally mandated language translators.
    • The Indian nation, tribe, or pueblos provides the facility and services for the vote center.
  • Change the procedures for processing mailed ballots or ballots deposited in a drop box. These ballots would be accepted until 7:00 p.m. on Election Day and election officials would be required to mark the date of receipt on the outer envelope. Within one day of receipt, election officials would be required to verify the presence of the voter's signature on the ballot and confirm that the last four digits of the voter's social security number match the information on file. The bill also would require local election officials to notify voters of any deficiencies and provide an opportunity to cure the deficiency. These provisions codify the existing notice and cure provisions for absentee and vote-by-mail ballots from administrative regulations and judicial decisions into statutory law.
  • Create an Election Day school holiday. The previous version of the bill created a general statewide holiday on Election Day.

  • Change eligibility to hold office after a felony conviction, in provisions not tracked by Voting Rights Lab.

    The provisions that were in previous versions of the bill that are no longer in the current version of the bill would have:


  • Created automatic voter registration via Indian nations, tribes, or pueblos who collect sufficient information to determine voter eligibility. The previous version of the bill would have required the state to enter into a memorandum of understanding to require these bodies to participate in automatic voter registration. Under existing law, such nations, tribes, and pueblos are not automatic voter registration agencies. The current version of the bill removes these provisions in their entirety, instead only creating automatic voter registration at the motor vehicle division and the human services department as described above.
  • Permitted 16-year-olds to vote in local or municipal elections after registration. Under existing law, voters must be 18 years old, except that 17-year-olds may vote in a primary if the voter will be 18 by the time of the general election associated with that primary. Under the current version of the bill, only people who are 18 years old on the day of an election, primary or general, may vote in that election.
  • Allowed voter list maintenance activities to resume the Monday after Election Day. Under existing law, such activities resume 35 days after Election Day. Since this provision was removed entirely from the amended version of the bill, existing law would continue to control.
  • Created provisions for siting voting locations if the governing body of an Indian nation, tribe, or pueblo has declared a state of emergency. There are no similar provisions under existing law, and the current, amended version of the bill removes this provision altogether.
  • Permitted polling places on Indian nation, tribal, or pueblo lands to be eliminated or consolidated only as provided in the Native American Voting Rights Act. Under existing law, which would continue under the amended version of the bill, these polling places could only be closed with the written agreement of the nation, tribe, or pueblo where the polling place is located.
  • Changed certain drop box requirements regarding collection of ballots from drop boxes and creating a new offense for any person to possess a key to a drop box or to create a drop box other than the county clerk or the clerk's designees.
  • Eliminated statutory specifications detailing the contents of the sworn statement on the absentee ballot envelope, and potentially eliminate the requirement that the voter sign this statement under penalty of perjury.

  • Made changes to the petition process in provisions not tracked by Voting Rights Lab. Previous versions of the bill made changes to the petition process in provisions that no longer appear in the current, amended version of the bill.

Last Updated March 25, 2022

This bill, as amended on February 17, 2022, makes significant changes to the previous version of the bill. The provisions of the previous version of the bill are still retained in this amendment and would:

  • Expand the definition of intimidation for the existing felony offense to include intimidation directed at the secretary of state, county clerks, and municipal clerks.

  • Expand election intimidation to include intimidation directed at employees and agents of the secretary of state, employees and agents of a county clerk, and employees and agents of a municipal. Under existing law, only members of precinct boards, voters, challengers, and watchers are included in the definition of intimidation.

    The bill, as amended, makes numerous additions to these retained provisions. These new provisions would:


  • Repeal statutory restrictions prohibiting a person convicted of a felony from voting until after they have completed sentencing terms, including probation and parole. This would have the effect of ending disenfranchisement based on conviction entirely, since the New Mexico state constitution does not impose independent restrictions on the franchise based on convictions, but instead only authorizes such impositions to be imposed statutorily.
  • Designate all sites that were designated as polling places in 2021 as voter convenience centers for all statewide elections in 2022 and 2023.
  • Create a Native American Voting Rights Act, which would
    • Allow any Indian nation, tribe, or pueblo to request voter convenience centers on or near the land of the Indian nation, tribe, or pueblo, and provide deadlines for such requests. Voter convenience centers will only be granted if all voters in the county have access to the site, if the site meets requirements for voter convenience centers, and if the county clerk can provide federally mandated language translators. Approved voter convenience centers cannot be consolidated or eliminated without the written agreement of the Indian nation, tribe, or pueblo where the site is located.
    • Allow any Indian nation, tribe, or pueblo to request early voting locations on or near the land of the Indian nation, tribe, or pueblo and provide deadlines for such requests. The county clerk must provide at least one alternative or mobile location on or near the land of the Indian nation, tribe, or pueblo after receiving such a request, but the site must be accessible to any voter in the county, must meet requirements for early voting locations, and must have federally mandated language translators. Such locations may operate for less than the full early voting period, as agreed by the local election official and the Indian nation, tribe, or pueblo.
    • Allow any Indian nation, tribe, or pueblo to request a monitored, secured drop box on or near the land of the Indian nation, tribe, or pueblo and provide deadlines for such requests. Local election officials must review the population of the Indian nation, tribe, or pueblo, the distance voters living there have to travel to vote, and the availability of nearby drop boxes and early voting locations. The election official must respond in writing. If the request is denied, the Indian nation, tribe, or pueblo may appeal to the secretary of state, who may place a drop box in response to the appeal.
    • Permit voters to register using the name and/or address of a government or official building on Indian nation, tribe, or pueblo land, based on a list of such buildings that the secretary of state would be required to compile and maintain.
    • Require that, during redistricting, local governments request from each Indian nation, tribe, or pueblo information about the internal political boundaries so that precinct boundaries can be adjusted accordingly.
    • Prevent a declared state of emergency being used as a basis for closing polling places on Indian nation, tribe, or pueblo lands or modifying days and times of voting with the written agreement of the Indian nation, tribe, or pueblo.
    • Require that, during a declared state of emergency, an Indian nation, tribe, or pueblo may request alternative voting locations and Election Day polling places later than they would otherwise be permitted to make such a request.
    • Require the secretary of state to reimburse local election officials for costs incurred by the local election official for complying with the Native American Voting Rights Act.
  • Change the powers of challengers, watchers, and observers by:
    • Prohibiting them from photographing ballots and voter information.
    • Prohibiting them from making audio or video recording in a polling place.
    • Mandating that they be within sufficient sight and sound of an election board to hear the conduct of the board's duties.
    • Authorize them to speak with certain election workers to ask questions or advise of breaches of the election code, provided that doing so does not interfere with the administration of the election.
  • Change provisions regarding special elections, which are conducted fully absentee under existing law. Specifically, the bill would provide that voters whose "voter notifications" are returned as undeliverable will not automatically receive a mailed ballot in a special election. It would also require mailed ballots to include information about the recommended mailing deadline based on return times for the U.S. Postal Service.
  • Alter the existing address confidentiality provisions to allow household members to receive address confidentiality if they live with a person who is entitled to address confidentiality. This provision would also end address confidentiality for anyone who does not comply with the Intimate Partner Violence Survivor Suffrage Act.
  • Expand the existing offense of obstructing the polling place to include willfully blocking access to a monitored, secured drop box. This provision also clarifies who has authorized access to polling places and drop boxes and thus cannot commit polling place obstruction.
  • Narrow the existing offense of unlawful possession of alcoholic liquors to decriminalize possessing alcohol within 200 feet of a polling place during an election. The bill would retain the aspects of the offense that criminalize an election board member using or possessing alcohol while performing official duties.
  • Create an Election Day holiday for students and staff at public schools.

  • Detail how local appropriations for election administration should be handled.

This bill, as introduced on May 13, 2022, would make numerous, disparate changes to the election code to increase transparency and voting access. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require local boards of election to allow a voter to vote at any polling place in their county and require the State Board of Elections to issue related rules. The county boards would be prohibited from reducing polling places simply because voters could use any of them. Under existing law, voters must vote at the correct polling place, although they may vote in the wrong election district at that polling place. If they appear at the wrong polling place and complete a provisional (affidavit) ballot, the ballot will not count.
  • Require local boards of election to allow all voters to use any early voting location in their county. Under existing law, boards of election can assign voters to specific early voting sites under certain conditions.
  • Require local boards of election to provide accessible polling places. Under existing law, voters whose polling place is inaccessible to them are allowed to vote at any other polling place that offers the same ballot.
  • Require the online ballot tracking system to include instructions on how the voter can cure their rejected ballot if the reason it was rejected can be cured.
  • Require local boards to publicly propose poll sites at least 30 days before an election and allow the public to comment on the proposal. Nonetheless, the board would retain the power to change poll sites at any time without public comment, provided five days' notice is given to voters as existing law requires. The bill would additionally require that to the extent the board has voters' contact information, it must provide notice of a changed polling place by email and text as well.
  • Require local boards of election to give notice about an upcoming primary election at least 30 days in advance. The notice must be available in all major languages spoken in the county and prominently placed on the county's website. The State Board of Elections, starting at least 25 days before the election, must use its website and social media to notify voters of the election and direct them to the county's online notice. The local board would similarly be required to promote the information using its social media. The local board's notice must include:
    • the deadline to register to vote in that election.
    • the hours and date of the election.
    • the public office(s) and party positions to be filled.
    • the mail ballot request deadline and the mail ballot return deadline.
    • dates and times of early voting.
    • sample ballots.
    • a mechanism for a voter to determine their polling place.
  • Allow the committee on open government to appoint election watchers.
  • Require every board or body authorized to designate places to register voters to consistently have registration instructions prominently displayed on its website.
  • Make boards of elections public bodies subject to open meeting rules.
  • Change rules relating to reporting results. Specifically, unofficial results released after the close of polls would be posted by election district and category, specifically early in-person, Election Day, mail, military, overseas, affidavit, and write-in. Within 24 hours of the close of polls, all results must be released for ballots tabulated by 6 a.m. the day after Election Day. The results must be updated at least every 24 hours thereafter until all the results are tabulated. The board must make the results available on its website as a downloadable spreadsheet. When the election results are certified, the final results must be posted with the detail required for the unofficial returns. The board of elections would be required to issue rules to maximize data transparency while ensuring data security and voters' privacy. Existing law does not include this specificity, both as to how returns should be detailed, and when.
  • Require local boards of election to hold a public hearing within two weeks of certifying election results to allow voters and non-voters to give feedback. Meetings would be recorded and reasonably accessible for anyone who wishes to participate in person or virtually.

  • Make changes to rules governing the testing of equipment, designing ballots, paper ballots, and ballot custody that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

Specifically, the bill would:

  • Replace the four-person, bipartisan State Board of Elections that the Governor appoints with an elected Secretary of Elections. Candidates for Secretary cannot be affiliated with any political party when they file their nominating papers but must be registered New York voters. Candidates would follow the independent candidate nominating rules.

  • Give the Secretary new powers not allocated to the current State Board, namely, the power to:

    • issue regulations stating minimum qualifications for local commissioners of elections, requiring that appointments of local commissioners be made on the basis of merit, and enforcing such regulations in court where necessary.
    • create mandatory training programs for local elections commissioners, and for other state and local elections staff where the secretary shall deem necessary.
    • facilitate shared staffing among the state board of elections, local boards of elections, and local municipal and county governments, including creating regional elections supervisors within the state board.
    • provide guidance and assistance with recruitment and training of poll workers.
    • provide grants to allow local boards of elections to improve the administration of their elections.
    • remove local election officials for good cause. Specifically, the Secretary could remove someone "for incompetence, misconduct, or other good cause, provided that prior to removal, such election commissioner shall be given a written copy of the charges against him or her and have an opportunity to be heard in his or her defense, and provided that the decision by the secretary of election to remove a commissioner may be overruled by order of the governor."

This bill, as introduced on May 20, 2022, would make numerous, disparate changes to the election code to increase transparency and voting access. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require local boards of election to allow a voter to vote at any polling place in their county and require the State Board of Elections to issue related rules. The county boards would be prohibited from reducing polling places simply because voters could use any of them. Under existing law, voters must vote at the correct polling place, although they may vote in the wrong election district at that polling place. If they appear at the wrong polling place and complete a provisional (affidavit) ballot, the ballot will not count.
  • Require local boards of election to allow all voters to use any early voting location in their county. Under existing law, boards of election can assign voters to specific early voting sites under certain conditions.
  • Require local boards of election to provide accessible polling places. Under existing law, voters whose polling place is inaccessible to them are allowed to vote at any other polling place that offers the same ballot.
  • Require the online ballot tracking system to include instructions on how the voter can cure their rejected ballot if the reason it was rejected can be cured.
  • Require local boards to publicly propose poll sites at least 30 days before an election and allow the public to comment on the proposal. Nonetheless, the board would retain the power to change poll sites at any time without public comment, provided five days' notice is given to voters as existing law requires. The bill would additionally require that to the extent the board has voters' contact information, it must provide notice of a changed polling place by email and text as well.
  • Require local boards of election to give notice about an upcoming primary election at least 30 days in advance. The notice must be available in all major languages spoken in the county and prominently placed on the county's website. The State Board of Elections, starting at least 25 days before the election, must use its website and social media to notify voters of the election and direct them to the county's online notice. The local board would similarly be required to promote the information using its social media. The local board's notice must include:
    • the deadline to register to vote in that election.
    • the hours and date of the election.
    • the public office(s) and party positions to be filled.
    • the mail ballot request deadline and the mail ballot return deadline.
    • dates and times of early voting.
    • sample ballots.
    • a mechanism for a voter to determine their polling place.
  • Allow the committee on open government to appoint election watchers.
  • Require every board or body authorized to designate places to register voters to consistently have registration instructions prominently displayed on its website.
  • Make boards of elections public bodies subject to open meeting rules.
  • Change rules relating to reporting results. Specifically, unofficial results released after the close of polls would be posted by election district and category, specifically early in-person, Election Day, mail, military, overseas, affidavit, and write-in. Within 24 hours of the close of polls, all results must be released for ballots tabulated by 6 a.m. the day after Election Day. The results must be updated at least every 24 hours thereafter until all the results are tabulated. The board must make the results available on its website as a downloadable spreadsheet. When the election results are certified, the final results must be posted with the detail required for the unofficial returns. The board of elections would be required to issue rules to maximize data transparency while ensuring data security and voters' privacy. Existing law does not include this specificity, both as to how returns should be detailed, and when.
  • Require local boards of election to hold a public hearing within two weeks of certifying election results to allow voters and non-voters to give feedback. Meetings would be recorded and reasonably accessible for anyone who wishes to participate in person or virtually.

  • Make changes to rules governing the testing of equipment, designing ballots, paper ballots, and ballot custody that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

Last Updated May 23, 2022

An Ohio drivers license or non-driver ID can contain a former address.

Under existing law, voters may provide a current and valid photo identification, a military identification, or a copy of a current utility bill, bank statement, government check, paycheck, or other government document that shows their current address.

  • Allow voters whose absentee ballots have been received by election officials to cast a provisional ballot on Election Day and have that ballot be counted rather than their absentee ballot. Under existing law, voters whose ballots have been received are not permitted to cast any ballot in person on Election Day.
  • Establish a system for the granting of no-cost photo IDs with ID numbers to any individual age 17 or older who applies for one at the DMV. Under existing law, free IDs are only available to individuals who are unemployed and disabled veterans.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on April 6, 2022, would make stricter voter ID requirements to vote in-person, absentee, register to vote, and apply for absentee ballots, along with other changes to existing election law. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require photo ID to vote at the polls, both on Election Day and during in-person absentee voting. Under existing law, voters must provide ID, but certain forms of non-photo ID, like current utility bills, government checks, paychecks, and other government documents, are also accepted. This bill would require that any person who lacks photo ID must vote a provisional ballot that can only be verified by providing an ID number (Ohio driver's license, state ID, or the last four digits of the voter's social security number) or copy of their photo ID within seven days after Election Day.
  • Narrow what types of photo ID are accepted. Under existing law, photo ID must be a single, unexpired document issued by the government that includes the voter's name, address, and photograph, but a driver's license or state ID is a permissible type of ID even if the address on it does not match the address in the poll book. This bill would require that driver's licenses be issued by the state of Ohio to constitute valid ID. The bill would also require a voter whose address on their driver's license or state ID does not match the pollbook to produce a second type of ID that shows the voter's current address. The permitted types of these secondary IDs are:
    • a current utility bill,
    • a bank statement,
    • a government check
    • a paycheck, or
    • another government document, other than a notice of voter registration.
  • Change the ID requirements to request an absentee ballot. Under existing law, absentee ballot applicants must provide either their driver's license number or the last four digits of their social security number. Alternatively, under existing law, voters may provide a copy of other forms of ID, including military IDs, current utility bills, bank statements, government checks, paychecks, or other government documents. This bill would require absentee ballot applicants to provide both the last four digits of their social security number and either the number of their Ohio driver's license or state ID or a copy of their photo ID, front and back. The bill would also eliminate the existing alternatives to providing driver's licenses and social security numbers. This bill explicitly applies these provisions to UOCAVA voters as well.
  • Change the ID requirements to vote an absentee ballot. Under existing law, absentee voters must provide either their driver's license number or the last four digits of their social security number. This bill would require absentee voters to provide both the last four digits of their social security number and either the number of their Ohio driver's license or state ID or a copy of their photo ID, front and back. Ballots not containing both items would be rejected, although voters could use the existing notice and cure process to provide the missing information so that the ballot could be counted. This bill would also apply these ID requirements to UOCAVA voters and supervised voting.
  • Expand the opportunities to vote for voters who appear to vote in person after requesting or casting an absentee ballot. Under existing law, voters who have requested an absentee ballot but whose absentee ballot was not received by election officials may cast a provisional ballot at the polls. This bill would provide that any voter who requested an absentee ballot, regardless of whether it was received, may cast a provisional ballot in person. These ballots would be counted if either:
    • Election officials do not receive the voter's absentee ballot by the deadline, ten days after Election Day, or
    • Election officials timely receive the absentee ballot but must reject it for a signature mismatch.
  • Change the documents required for voter registration. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Change the ID numbers accepted for voter registration. Under existing law, voters were required to provide a driver's license number. This bill would specify that only Ohio driver's license numbers will be accepted. The bill would also permit registrants to use a state ID number in addition to a driver's license number.
    • Eliminate the requirement that the photo ID provided in the registration be current and valid.
  • Narrowing the documents accepted for voters who move to a different address within a precinct and want to update their registration on Election Day. Under existing law, such voters may show several types of photo and nonphoto ID that contain their name and current address. This bill would require the voter to show photo ID but eliminate the language requiring that such ID contain the voter's name and current address.
  • Create free state ID for all people over age 17 who apply for free ID.
  • Require in-person voters, both on Election Day and during in-person absentee voting, to sign the voter's name in the poll book. Under existing law, the voter need not sign the book but instead must write their name and address.
  • Permit ballots voted via the in-person absentee process to be recorded by a voting machine or scanned by automatic tabulating equipment before the close of the polls on Election Day, but explicit prohibit tabulating or counting those ballots before the close of the polls on Election Day. Under existing law, the exact timing for pre-processing and counting of ballots is not specified.

  • Require the DMV to report monthly on the number of free IDs issued and allocate state and local responsibility for related expenses.

Last Updated April 7, 2022

This bill, as enacted on May 9, 2022, increases criminal investigation and potential prosecution related to voter registration. Specifically, the bill:

The local board must then "immediately" notify the county district attorney of the identified voters.

This bill, as created by the conference committee on May 12, 2022, after differing drafts passed both chambers, would require that state and local elections be conducted according to state law, and create a process to bifurcate state and federal elections if federal action for federal elections would substantially modify or supersede Oklahoma election law. Specifically:

  • The Attorney General, with the concurrence of the Secretary of the State Election Board, could determine that federal law, regulation, order, or other official action would substantially modify or supersede Oklahoma voter registration or election administration laws and procedures if the determination is in writing and states the reasons for the determination.
  • If the Attorney General makes such a determination, the bill creates an 11-member committee to propose changes to the time, place, and manner of conducting elections for state, county, and other non-federal offices. The committee would submit its recommendations to the President Pro Tempore of the Senate, the Speaker of the House of Representatives, and the Governor within 60 days of the Attorney General's determination. Although one section of the bill clearly states this 60-day deadline, other provisions give the Legislature two weeks after the determination to name the committee members and give the committee members two months after their first meeting to create their recommendations.
  • For the recommendations to become operative, the Legislature would enact them in the same manner as other legislation. However, if the Legislature is not in session when the determination is made, then the committee may temporarily modify election dates and other associated dates and deadlines to ensure that no other election in this state is held on the same date as a special or regular election for federal office. Such modifications shall expire on January 1 of the year following the next regularly scheduled general election.

  • The committee would be comprised of eight legislators, the Governor, or designee, the Attorney General, or designee, and the chair of the District Attorneys Council, or designee. The Secretary of the State Election Board or designee and a secretary of a county election board chosen by the Secretary of the State Election Board would attend meetings in an advisory capacity. The eight legislators would be:

    • four members of the Oklahoma State Senate, at least one of whom shall be a member of the minority party, appointed by the President Pro Tempore of the Senate, and
    • four members of the Oklahoma House of Representatives, at least one of whom shall be a member of the minority party, appointed by the Speaker of the House of Representatives.

    This version of the bill is a substantial reworking of it, although the purpose remains the same. One provision in prior versions limited voters who registered pursuant to a federal process to federal elections only. While that rule could result from the committee process created by this bill, the provision has been removed from this version.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 7, 2022, would grant the Secretary of the State Election Board new power to audit county voter list maintenance and to regulate election equipment. The bill would also create two legislative committees, one of which would appoint the other, and that latter committee would be given authority to do limited post-election audits and election security assessments.

Specifically, with regard to the Secretary of the State Election Board, the bill would:

  • Give the Secretary authority to audit any county's list of registered voters to ensure accuracy. The Secretary would give the county election board at least five business days' notice. The audits would verify:
    • that a registered voter is alive,
    • that a registered voter currently resides within the jurisdiction of the county election board, and
    • that a registered voter is entitled to vote.
  • If names are found that do not meet that criteria, the Secretary would instruct the county election board to remove the names. The Secretary could conduct a second audit to ensure the names were removed. If a county election board did not cooperate with the audit, the Secretary would be authorized to withhold funds from it.
  • Give the Secretary exclusive authority to promulgate rules for the use of election equipment, machines, programs, and systems involved with the tabulation and counting of votes.
  • Require the Secretary to require vendors entering into contracts with election authorities to allow the examination and testing of election equipment, machines, programs, and systems by the office or its employees or agents. The State Election Board may examine and test hardware or software and may engage in penetration testing of such vendor-provided equipment.
  • Prohibit the State Election Board from approving any equipment, machine, program, or system that is capable of Internet connection but would allow systems that allow data transfer by disk or another physical drive.
  • Authorize the Secretary to forbid the use of specified election equipment, machines, programs, or systems. County election boards that fail to comply would be subject to an injunction by any court of proper jurisdiction and to the payment of any court costs and attorney fees to the State Election Board.

With regard to the legislative committees, the bill would:

  • Create the Joint Committee on Elections comprised of seven state senators appointed by the President Pro Tempore of the Senate and seven state representatives appointed by the Speaker of the House of Representatives. Both of these leaders are Republicans, and the bill has no requirement that any Democrats be included on the Joint Committee. The Joint Committee would then appoint a 20-person "Election Integrity Committee" which would be evenly bipartisan. The 16 members would be chosen from each of the eight Congressional districts, one from each party in each district, and four would be chosen at large, two from each party.
  • Require the Election Integrity Committee, every general election day, to randomly audit two precincts. One would be in the largest five precincts and one will be in the smallest one hundred, each case by the number of votes received. At least two citizen volunteers would be present.
    • If the audit showed by clear and convincing evidence a discrepancy in the vote count likely to affect the outcome of any local, state, or federal election, a second audit would be conducted by two independent teams. If the second audit confirmed discrepancies, a statewide election investigation would be conducted that involved a statutory recount. The recount would be funded through a mechanism the bill would create. The results would be public, and any candidate could use an audit report to file an election contest.

  • Require the Election Integrity Committee to conduct a comprehensive risk assessment of each county election board in the state. The risk assessment could be conducted by an outside entity and would identify security risks, the magnitude of such risks, and areas that require safeguards. The risk assessment would include:

    • Load testing and stress testing to ensure that the online voter registration system has sufficient capacity to accommodate foreseeable use, including during periods of high-volume website use in the week before the voter registration deadline.
    • Screening computers and networks used to support the online voter registration system for malware and other vulnerabilities.
    • Evaluating database infrastructure, including software and operating systems, to fortify defenses against cyber attacks.
    • Identifying any anticipated threats to the security and integrity of data collected, maintained, received, or transmitted by the online voter registration system.

    Finally, the bill would create a revolving fund for the State Election Board called the "Election Integrity Fund". The State Election Board could use the money for authorized purposes.

This bill, as enacted on May 20, 2022, makes changes to several aspects of the election code. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires watchers observing the official count to appear in person and forbids them from appearing via electronic devices. Existing law authorized watchers "at any place where an official count is being conducted," but did not include express requirements to appear in person.
  • Expands the criminal offense of "absentee ballot harvesting" to include distributing an absentee ballot application or request to a voter using the official letterhead of a candidate or elected official. Engaging in, or directing, illegal ballot harvesting is a misdemeanor offense for less than ten ballots, and a felony offense for ten or more ballots. Under existing law, the absentee ballot harvesting offense included conduct related to ballots only, not applications.

  • Makes changes relating to ballots and canvassing. Specifically, the bill:

    • Requires paper ballots for all voters, except that each voting location must provide a way for any voter who requires assistance due to blindness, disability, or illiteracy to cast a ballot privately and independently.
    • Requires any statewide election system run by the Secretary of the State Election Board and implemented on or after January 1, 2023, to report election results by precinct, including in-person early votes and absentee votes. Existing law had no comparable provision regarding precinct data.
    • Prohibits devices or equipment used by the State Election Board or a county election board to count or tabulate ballots from connecting to the Internet, except that the equipment would be able to make a secure network connection between the State Election Board and a county election board to send and receive voter registration or election-related data. Existing law had no comparable provision.

  • Required election boards in possession of documents that appear to be evidence of voter registration or voting crimes to notify the Attorney General, in addition to the district attorney for the county or counties involved. Existing law only requires referral to appropriate district attorneys.

This bill, as enacted on May 20, 2022, requires voters to provide an ID number on an absentee ballot application, which must match an ID number that appears on their voter registration, if any. Under existing law, a voter did not need an ID number to apply for an absentee ballot. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires voters who apply for an absentee ballot by electronic means to provide their name, birth date, and an identification number, all of which must match their voter registration record for acceptance. If any of the required data does not match voter records, the applicant must be informed and instructed to contact their local election board. Voters who do not have a birthdate or ID number in their voter registration record may not use the electronic application process.
  • Requires applicants whose registration is inactive, or who meet certain criteria for potential address changes, to confirm their address prior to submitting an electronic absentee ballot application. Existing law required address confirmation for these voters before being issued a ballot for in-person absentee voting or when applying for an absentee ballot generally, but did not expressly require address confirmation before the electronic application process.
  • Requires voters who apply for an absentee ballot in person, by mail, or by fax, to provide their name, birth date, and the ID number included in their voter registration record, if any. All required information must match the voter's record for the application to be accepted. This bill, as enacted on May 23, 2022, changes various voter registration and list maintenance processes. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires voter identification cards to be sent to a voter's physical address, if the address is valid to receive mail delivery. If a voter's residence address is not a valid address for mail delivery, the card will be sent to the mailing address provided on the voter registration application. Existing law did not specify when officials were permitted or required to send voter ID cards to a voter's mailing address.
  • Requires, rather than permits, a voter's registration to be canceled due to notice from the voter, death, conviction for a felony, judicial determination of mental incapacity, registration in another county or state, or failure to respond to an address confirmation mailing and not voting in two federal general election cycles. The bill also adds a new mandatory cancellation ground, for the surrender of a voter's driver's license to the state's Department of Public Safety upon being issued a license in another state.
  • Specifies that registration in another jurisdiction or surrender of an Oklahoma driver's license on receiving a license from another state constitute confirmation from the voter to cancel their registration due to change in residence. The bill also removes voters who have surrendered their Oklahoma license and become licensed in another state from the list of voters who are sent address confirmation notices during biennial list maintenance.
  • Requires an address confirmation notice to be sent to anyone registered to vote at the same residence address as five or more other voters, as part of biennial list maintenance. To count as the same address, the street name, street direction, street type, street post direction, street number, building number or apartment number, and zip code must match. Existing law did not have a similar requirement.
  • Requires a list of voter registrations that were canceled during the previous 24 months, and the reason for the cancellation, to be made available to the public. Existing law had no similar provision.

Existing law required the Department of Health to send a monthly list of deceased Oklahoma residents but did not specify requirements or limitations on specific identifying information.
  • Requires, rather permits, cancellation of a voter's registration on receipt of the voter's death certificate.
  • Requires the State Election Board and county election boards to keep the records from the Department of Health confidential, even in response to an Open Records Act request. Existing law did not have a similar provision.
  • Requires the publicly available voter registration list to indicate all voters for whom a first-class mailing from the state or local election board was returned undeliverable. Existing law did not have a similar provision.

  • Requires completion of an address confirmation form, when voting in person or by mail, by all inactive voters, voters identified as possibly having moved using National Change of Address data, voters with incomplete or invalid addresses as defined by the bill, and voters who have had a voter identification card returned as undeliverable. Under existing law, only inactive voters and voters who had been identified as possibly having moved were required to submit an address confirmation form prior to voting.

This bill, as introduced on February 7, 2022, would enable people who were disenfranchised due to a felony conviction to regain their voting eligibility sooner. Specifically, the bill would add the following triggers for automatic restoration of voting eligibility:

  • The voter's sentence has been discharged.
  • The voter received a commutation that reduced the sentence to time served.
  • The voter received a commutation for a crime that has been reclassified from a felony to a misdemeanor.
  • The voter has been granted a pardon.

Under existing law, eligibility is restored when a person has fully served their sentence of court-mandated calendar days, including any term of incarceration, parole, or supervision, or completed a period of probation ordered by any court. That trigger for automatic restoration would remain for whenever any of the new triggers do not apply.

This bill, as introduced on February 7, 2022, would create a cure process for absentee ballot certificates enabling ballots to be counted instead of rejected, and create rules that apply during a state of emergency. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Allow county election boards to begin opening and reviewing absentee ballots returned by mail 30 days before Election Day.
  • Provide that, if a ballot certificate is rejected for any reason, the board would be required to notify the voter by mail, and if available, email, or phone. In addition, the board would update the voter's record in the Oklahoma Voter Portal to note the rejection. The notice sent by mail would include a cure form that would instruct the voter to complete and return the cure form by mail or in person by Election Day, along with whatever else is needed to address the issue. Under existing law, voters do not have an opportunity to address issues with their absentee ballots.
  • Provide that if the reason for the rejection is the voter's printed name or signature is missing, in addition to the cure form, the voter must show valid iD with information matching their registration record, or have the signature or printed name verified by notarization. In case of emergency, a copy of such ID could be mailed with the cure affidavit. Incapacitated voters could continue to use two witnesses.
  • Require the State Election Board to issue necessary materials and instructions.
  • Provide that signatures cannot be deemed to be mismatched because of substituting initials for a first or middle name or both. Under existing law, Oklahoma does not match signatures on the ballot certificate to signatures on file, nor does the bill mandate such a process.
  • Create ballot verification rules that apply if a state of emergency declared by the Governor is in effect within the 45 days before a scheduled election:
    • A voter may sign the absentee ballot affidavit and attach a photocopy of a form of valid identification instead of having their signature verified.
    • A voter who is normally able to have their signature witnessed by two witnesses may instead sign the absentee ballot affidavit and include a photocopy of a form of valid identification.
    • In the event an absentee voting board is prohibited from entering a nursing facility or veterans center due to restrictions related to the state of emergency, then the secretary of the county election board may allow the absentee voting board to deliver the absentee ballots to a designated official at the nursing facility or veterans center. The designated nursing facility or veterans center official would be required to sign an oath acknowledging the duties and responsibilities of the absentee voting board, and then may carry them out.

This bill, as introduced on February 7, 2022, would require a "forensic audit" of the 2020 election. The bill would:

The bill does not identify any processes for the reviewers to follow, nor provide for any oversight by the State Election Board.

This bill, as introduced on February 7, 2022, would substantially change how absentee ballots are applied for and what voters must do to have their ballots successfully counted. The bill would end no-excuse absentee voting, require copies of photo ID to apply for and return absentee ballots, in addition to signature matching, and witnesses/notarization. The bill would also change other aspects of election administration relating to voting by mail.

Specifically, concerning applying for mail ballots, the bill would:

  • Limit voters' ability to choose to vote by mail by ending no-excuse absentee voting. Instead, to vote by absentee ballot a voter would be required to attest that they expect to be out of the jurisdiction on Election Day and on all early voting days, or that they have a disability preventing their attendance at the polls.
  • Require voters to apply for a mail ballot for each election in which they wish to vote by mail. Under existing law, one application can cover all elections in a calendar year.
  • Require voters to apply not less than 10 days before Election Day. Under existing law, voters must apply by 5 p.m. on the third Monday before Election Day.
  • Require a "wet ink" signature on absentee ballot applications, and require them to be returned by hand to an election official or by mail. Currently, voters may request an absentee ballot through an online portal maintained by the State Election Board.
  • Provide that if a voter cannot sign and instead uses a mark, their mark must be witnessed. No one would be allowed to witness more than one absentee ballot request form per election unless doing so for an immediate family member. The bill would impose a civil penalty of $500/violation. Under existing law, a witness is not required to apply for an absentee ballot.
  • Require election officials to verify the signature on the application against one on file, as well as review the ID. Under existing law, signatures on the ballot application are not reviewed.
  • Require voters to include a copy of photo identification with their application, or the number of their state driver's license or ID card. Acceptable ID would have to indicate if the person is a citizen if the ID types are issued to both citizens and non-citizens. Alternatives to ID would be prohibited. Allowed ID types would be:
    • Driver license,
    • State non-driver ID card,
    • Current (non-expired) U.S. passport,
    • United States military ID,
    • Tribal government ID,
    • ID issued by a state government, or
    • College or university ID.
  • Facilitate people acquiring state ID by offering free ID with a proper application and by providing appropriate transportation from a person's home if they have physical or other disabilities that prevent them from getting to the office or motor license agent, or generally providing proving "such other assistance as is necessary to ensure" a person can get an ID.
  • Prohibit a government official or entity from sending absentee ballot applications to voters who have not requested them, and prohibit prefilling any information required of the voter.

  • Prohibit anyone other than a voter, a person assisting a physically disabled elector, a common carrier charged with returning the ballot application, an election official, or a law enforcement official in the course of an investigation from returning or handling a voter's completed absentee ballot application.

    The bill would change how voters complete and return their ballots. Specifically, the bill would:


  • Expand a voter's options for verifying their mail ballot by allowing a voter to choose to have a witness for their ballot certificate signature instead of a notary. Under existing law, a voter's certificate signature must be notarized. If a voter chooses to use a witness instead of a notary, the witness must include their printed name, address, and telephone number.
  • Limit people to witnessing only one ballot signature per election, except that a person could witness an unlimited number of ballots for their immediate family members. A person witnessing ballots in violation of this restriction would be subject to a civil penalty of $500/violation. Existing law limits how many ballots a person can notarize.
  • Require voters to submit a copy of valid ID or the number from their driver's license or state ID with their ballot. Existing law does not require ID as well as notarization.

  • Require election officials to provide a bipartisan team for each precinct to assist individuals who are seeking to cast an absentee ballot from a hospital, nursing home, or other such facility or who, due to physical limitation or handicap, require assistance in returning an absentee ballot in the appropriate format.

    The bill would change how ballots are counted and rejected, as well as change other aspects of election administration. Specifically, the bill would:


  • Require ballots to be stored until the close of polls on Election Day. Ballots would then be canvassed non-stop until all accepted ballots are counted.
  • Require ballots to be rejected if:
    • The certificate is not signed by the voter. Under existing law ballots are rejected for this reason.
    • The voter's signature does not match one on file. Under existing law, the signature on the ballot certificate is not matched to a reference signature, the notarization is enough.
    • The voter's signature is not notarized or witnessed, and if witnessed, the witness failed to provide a signature, printed name, address, and phone number. Under existing law, a ballot is rejected if it is not notarized.
    • The required ID is missing. Under existing law, voters are not required to provide ID.
  • Require election officials to investigate if an absentee ballot request form or an absentee ballot is returned undeliverable. The officials must determine the eligibility, qualifications, and validity of the voter's registration and registration address.
  • Forbid the creation of a permanent absentee ballot list or a permanent absentee ballot application list.
  • Forbid mailing all voters ballot applications or ballots.
  • Require absentee ballots to have a watermark on the ballot and a barcode or microchip that ensures the ballot can only be counted once.
  • Require all envelopes used to deliver mail ballots to voters and used by voters to return ballots to have a barcode or microchip that allows the ballot to be tracked.
  • Require election officials to maintain a list of absentee ballots provided to registered voters, including the date the application for the absentee ballot was received.
  • Require the voter registration systems at the local and state level to allow for real-time reporting of absentee mail ballot requests, transmittal and receipt of ballots, or the check-in of early voters.
  • Suggest county election offices scan and provide absentee ballot information to state election authorities within 24 hours of the request, transmission, and return of all absentee or mail ballots.

  • Suggest absentee ballot information from locality or county election offices be uploaded or transmitted to state election databases electronically and made available to political campaigns or the public for review.

BILLSUMMARY: Proposes amendment to Oregon Constitution establishing Citizens Redistricting Commission to adopt redistricting maps for Senate, House of Representatives and United States Congress.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced, would amend the state constitution to create a 12-person Citizens Redistricting Commission with equal representation of the two major political parties and people affiliated with neither. The selection process would be highly specified. The bill would set forth specific criteria for drawing districts and involving the public. The commission would adopt the final plans, or if it failed to do so or the plans it adopted were challenged, the state Supreme Court would.

The existing process has the Legislature draw the maps, which are then reviewed by the state Supreme Court. Under the existing process, the criteria specified by the bill are not required.

The bill would provide the following selection process to staff the Commission:

  • The Secretary of State, no later than August 15 in years ending in nine, would begin the process of recruiting the 12 commissioners who would need to meet certain criteria to ensure their partisan leanings and their independence from political parties, candidates, office holders, and political committees. The applicants would be winnowed to eliminate those with conflicts of interest by a panel of administrative law judges who also had to meet certain criteria. If the pool of applicants includes more than 300 people registered with the largest party, more that 300 with the second largest, and more than 300 registered with neither, the panel would randomly select 300 of each.
  • By March 15 of a year ending in zero, the Secretary would publicize the remaining names along with their applications, and by May 15, the panel would give the Secretary of 50 people from each pool with the most relevant analytical and other skills and who demonstrate an appreciation for and reasonably reflect the state's diversity, or if there are fewer than 50, only those.
  • By July 5 the Secretary would randomly select two from each pool, and by August 15 those six would choose two more from each pool, with at least four yes votes required for each new person, and those four votes must include at least one from each group.

Commission members would serve until the succeeding commission is chosen, or until they are removed for cause by the Governor according to a specified process, and would be subject to conflict of interest rules both during and after their service.

The Commission would create districts by:

  • Conducting an open and transparent process enabling full public participation. All records relating to redistricting, and all data considered by the Commission would be public records, and would be posted in a manner that ensured immediate and widespread access. The Commission would hold at least 10 public hearings across the state before proposing redistricting plans, and at least five after proposing plans. Remote testimony would be allowed at the hearings.
  • Using specified criteria for Congressional and state legislative districts, namely:
    • Compliance with the U.S. Constitution and federal law
    • Population equality, as nearly as practicable
    • Geographic contiguity
    • To the extent practicable, and if possible without conflicting with federal law, equal population, and geographic contiguity, respecting geographic integrity and minimizing the division of a city, county, local neighborhood, government jurisdiction or community of interest or other contiguous population that shares common social and economic interests and is cohesive for purposes of its effective and fair representation.
    • To the extent practicable, and if possible without conflicting with federal law, equal population, and geographic contiguity, achieve competitiveness.
  • Not doing any of these:
    • considering where office holders or candidates live
    • favoring or discriminating against an office holder or candidate
    • creating a district with the purpose or effect of diluting the voting strength of any language or ethnic identity group.
  • Adopting final maps by August 15 of the year ending in one, and issuing a report that explains the basis on which the commission established the districts, responded to public input, and achieved compliance with the criteria.To adopt final maps requires at least seven yes votes reflecting at least one vote from each of the three groups. Any registered voter could petition the Supreme Court to review the maps by September 1. If the Court approves the maps, they would go into effect. If the Court rejects one or more maps, they would be sent to the Commission for revision, then re-submitted to the Court. The process would repeat until final maps were approved, except that the Court would have to approve final maps by December 31.

  • If the Commission fails to meet the August 15 deadline, four or more commissioners including at least one person in each group would submit a plan to the Supreme Court by August 29, and the Court would pick among the plans offered based on their compliance with the criteria, and that map would go into effect. The Court would have to decide by December 31.
