This bill, as introduced on January 4, 2022, proposes a constitutional amendment to change the method of reapportionment after the federal decennial census from a legislative committee to a citizen's committee. Under existing law, reapportionment is conducted by a five-member legislative committee, comprising the majority and minority leaders of each chamber of the state legislature, and a chairperson selected unanimously by the other four members. Specifically, this bill would:

  • Create a citizen's commission to conduct reapportionment based on the federal decennial census in 2022, and subsequently in the years following the census in all future censuses. The membership of this commission would be comprised of people who have been Pennsylvania residents for at least five years and who have submitted applications to the Secretary of the Commonwealth to serve, selected as follows:
    • two members appointed by the Senate majority leader,
    • two members appointed by the Senate minority leader,
    • two members appointed by the House majority leader,
    • two members appointed by the House minority leader,
    • two members appointed by county governments in Pennsylvania, where each county receives one vote, and each appointee is a member of a different major political party, and
    • one member appointed by the judges of the Commonwealth Court, who must be a former judge.
  • Require the citizen's commission to to prepare a preliminary reapportionment plan for the sent and the house and file those with the Secretary of the Commonwealth. A plan can preliminarily be adopted by a 2/3 vote of the members of the commission. Within 14 days after the plan is preliminarily adopted, anyone can file exceptions with the commission, which can be adopted for up to 14 days after that. A proposed reapportionment plan can then be adopted by a 2/3 vote of the commission members.
  • Require the senate to review the proposed senate reapportionment plan and house to review the proposed house reapportionment plan. The plans can be adopted by each chamber without action by the other chamber or the governor. The bill also provides a process for revisions by the citizen's commission based on certain actions taken by the legislative chambers.
  • Require the secretary of the commonwealth to publish any plan adopted by the commission in every legislative district.
  • Authorize appeals from the adopted reapportionment plans within 30 days after their adoption by any aggrieved person, which shall be directly filed with the state supreme court.
  • Create a process for what happens when apportionment plans are not timely created and adopted.

  • Appropriate funds for the compensation and expenses of members of the commission and other operating expenses.

    Last updated January 5, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on January 10, 2022, would create a designated early voting period and specify the conduct of early voting. Under existing law, a voter is permitted to vote an absentee ballot (which includes both excuse-only "absentee ballots" and no-excuse "mail-in ballots" in Pennsylvania) in-person, but there is no specific designated process for early voting. Specifically, this bill would:

  • Create an early voting period beginning on the thirtieth day before Election Day and ending on the day before Election Day, including every intervening Saturday and Sunday.
  • Establish early voting hours of either 8:30-4:30 or 9:00-5:00 on weekdays, 9:00-12:00 on Saturdays, and 10:00-4:00 on Sundays, except that beginning eight days before Election Day, the early voting locations must be open from at least 9:00 a.m.-7:00 p.m. every day. Early voting locations must remain open for at least 8 hours on any holidays during the early voting period.
  • Establish minimum numbers of early voting locations. In a county with a population over 250,000, there must be at least one permanent early voting location in each of the three largest municipalities in the jurisdiction, except that any municipality with over 80,000 residents must have at least two permanent early voting locations during the early voting period. Counties with between 100,000 and 250,000 residents must have at least one permanent early voting location. The bill also requires that any county containing a municipality with a population over 100,000 must establish at least permanent polling places.
  • Set standards for early voting locations. The county may use the county board's main office or other sites, provided that all early voting locations must be at least 1.5 miles apart, except in municipalities with over 500,000 residents. Public buildings must be made reasonably available as early voting locations without charge. In addition, counties may establish temporary polling places for early voting, which are not subject to the days and hours schedule required of other early voting locations.
  • Create Election Day-style voting by requiring that each county provide voting booths with voting machines and other suitable equipment during the early voting period.
  • Require that each county board maintain a list of voters who vote during the early voting period, which list must be delivered to the judges of election in each election district.

  • Require that early voting locations and schedules be published in a newspaper and posted physically and online at least a week before the early voting period begins and weekly during the early voting period.

This bill, as introduced on January 14, 2022, would explicitly require signature verification for absentee ballots (which includes both "absentee ballots" and "mail-in ballots" in Pennsylvania) and would create a notice and cure provisions for signatures mismatches. The bill would require local election officials to notify voters by mail, email, phone, or text of the mismatch. The voter could cure the mismatch within six days of receiving the notice, by providing, in person or by electronic means:

  • Proof of identification and affidavit affirming that the voter is the person who sent the absentee ballot.

  • An affidavit affirming that the voter is the person who the absentee ballot and further affirming the the voter lacks ID due to indigency.

    Under existing law, local election officials are required to verify the voter's proof of identification when canvassing absentee ballots. The Pennsylvania Supreme Court has ruled that this does not require signature verification. Pennsylvania does not have an existing statewide notice and cure process for defects in absentee ballots.

This bill, as introduced on January 14, 2022, would change the time for pre-canvassing all absentee ballots (which includes "absentee ballots" and "mail-in ballots" in Pennsylvania). Activities that local election officials would be permitted to do include opening ballots, voiding ballots whose envelopes contain information about the voter's identity, political affiliation, or candidate preference, removing ballots, and counting, computing, and tallying votes on absentee ballots. This bill, as introduced on April 25, 2022, would propose a constitutional amendment to prohibit the legislature from establishing absentee voting for any reason other than the excuses currently permitted by the constitution, and expressly prohibit establishing any form of early voting. Existing constitutional law requires the legislature to provide for absentee voting for voters who will be absent on Election Day due to obligations to their duties, occupation, or business, or due to illness or physical disability, observance of a religious holiday, or Election Day duties related to county employment. There is no express constitutional limitation on the establishment of absentee voting for other reasons or on early voting generally, and existing statutory law provides for early voting through the "mail-in ballot" process.

This bill, as introduced on April 25, 2022, would make changes to voter eligibility and voter ID requirements, eliminate a voting method, make changes to voter registration and absentee voting, and increase state oversight of elections. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Repeal early voting and no-excuse absentee voting by eliminating the "mail-in ballot" voting process. Under existing law, this process permits all voters to receive and cast a mail-in ballot, without providing an excuse, for any primary or election held in the state. Because in-person request and return of a "mail-in ballot" constitutes the existing early voting system, this provision would effectively repeal early voting statewide.
  • Repeal disenfranchisement for individuals who have been incarcerated for a felony conviction within the last five years. While existing statutory law prohibits voter registration within five years of incarceration for a felony, note that the waiting period was struck down by a state appellate court in 2000. Since that time, restoration of voting rights has generally occurred, with an exception for election crime convictions, upon release from incarceration.
  • Change voter ID requirements by eliminating some currently accepted forms of ID and adding two new ones, and making the new requirements applicable to all voters, including those voting an absentee ballot. Specifically, the bill would eliminate the use of photo ID cards issued by municipalities to their employees, by higher education institutions and care facilities, and those issued by the Department of Transportation that are within 12 months of their expiration date. The bill would also require that acceptable ID issued by the state or federal government must include a signature, in addition to the existing requirements of the voter's name and photo. New forms of accepted ID would be a voter registration card with a scannable registration number and signature, and any ID issued by the Secretary of State for the purpose of voting, which includes the voter's photo and signature. The bill would make these requirements expressly applicable to all voters, and repeal existing provisions that permit absentee voters to provide a driver's license number or last four digits of their Social Security number, or other form of specified documentation showing a name and photo.
  • Make changes to voter registration requirements and processing. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Move the voter registration deadline from 15 days before an election, to 30 days before.
    • Permit online applications for voter registration, a party designation change, or a name or address change to be conducted online through a link provided on the secretary of state's website. The voter would be required to sign the application electronically. While existing law does not expressly provide for online applications, the process has been available to voters since 2015.
    • Add a new requirement for voter registration applications to include the last four digits of the applicant's Social Security number, and deem applications incomplete if the number is missing. Voters without a Social Security number would be permitted to confirm their identity through an "alternate record." The bill would also require the registration form to request the applicant's driver's license or DMV ID card number, but would expressly prohibit rejection of applications if this data is missing.
    • Require election officials to verify the last four digits of an applicant's Social Security Number, and license or DMV ID number if provided, when processing a voter registration application.
    • Move the deadline for officials to reject a voter registration application from at least 10 days before an election, to at least 25 days before.
    • Require the voter ID card issued to voters upon registration to include a scannable identification code or strip. Existing law does not contain a similar requirement.
    • Require the department of transportation to retain all voter registration information submitted through the driver license application process, for the expressly limited purpose of supporting audit measures. Existing law does not contain a similar provision.
    • Require the department of transportation to enter into an agreement with the secretary of state to match information in the voter registration system with information in the department of transportation database to verify the accuracy of voter registration information. Existing law does not contain a similar provision.
    • Require the department of transportation to enter into an agreement with the commissioner of social security to verify the Social Security number provided in a voter's registration application. Existing law does not contain a similar provision.
    • Allow a voter who has an active protection from abuse order against another person to have the voter's year of birth changed in the voter registry. Existing law does not contain a similar provision.
    • Specify that election officials must provide public notice of additional voter registration locations, other than the clerk's office, at least 30 days before the location's opening. Under existing law, notice is required "within reasonable time."
  • Make changes to absentee voting. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Prohibit the counting of an absentee ballot if the ballot declaration does not include a date, or a signature matching the elector's signature on record. Existing law requires officials to compare ballot declarations with the voter file and determine a declaration is "sufficient" for the ballot to be counted, but does not expressly require rejection due to missing dates or unmatched signatures.
    • Require election officials to separate out absentee ballots that are returned in person and appear to violate the election code, and record the date and time of their receipt and the voter's identity. Officials would be required to determine whether the ballot violates any statutory provisions, and only direct those ballots in compliance to be canvassed. Existing law has no express provisions regarding ballot verification upon in-person delivery.
  • Establish a Bureau of Election Audits within the existing Office of the Auditor General, and specify requirements for regular audits of all elections, the state voter registration list, and election systems and processes.
  • Prohibit the Secretary of State and county boards of elections from accepting any private donations for the purposes of operating an election, employing staff, equipping a polling place or for voter education or outreach. Existing law does not contain a similar prohibition.

  • Require each county board of elections to record in the electronic voter registration system whether a registrant voted and the method each voter used to vote. A copy of the record would be required to be included with the certified election results. The bill would also require return boards to investigate apparent discrepancies between the total number of voters in a district and votes recorded, and would authorize recount procedures and the exclusion of district returns if discrepancies were found. Existing law does not contain a similar requirement.

This bill, as introduced on May 27, 2022, would change several aspects of voting by mail. The bill would give voters less time to apply for mail ballots, give election officials more time to process and count returned mail ballots, and allow voters to address issues with their ballot certificate that would otherwise prevent their ballot from counting. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Change the deadline to apply to receive a mail-in ballot (no-excuse mail ballot) in the mail to the fourteenth day before Election Day, while leaving the current application deadline of 5 p.m. on the first Tuesday before the primary or general election for in-person applications for mail-in ballots. People applying in person would be required to show ID to receive the ballot, but their ballot would still be subject to the same verification process that all mail-in ballots.
  • Change the deadline to apply to receive an absentee ballot (excuse required mail ballot) to the fourteenth day before Election Day instead of the existing deadline of the first Tuesday before Election Day. Nonetheless, people may apply for an absentee ballot after that deadline if their excuse occurred after the deadline or if their disability, illness, business, duties, or occupation prevented them from applying on time. Such voters can apply through the close of polls but must support their application with a sworn statement explaining why they missed the deadline.
  • Change the pre-canvass process for both types of mail ballots by:
    • Requiring the county board of elections to meet no earlier than seven days before Election Day to pre-canvass all ballots received before the meeting. Under existing law, this meeting cannot be held until 7 a.m. on Election Day.
    • Allowing one authorized representative of each candidate, of the county chairperson of each political party, and another of each political party, to attend the pre-canvass meeting. Under existing law, the county chairs are not allowed to appoint watchers.
    • Requiring election officials to give these representatives "meaningful access to view and observe the entire process of pre-canvassing or canvassing." The county board of elections would be required to designate an official to respond to concerns reported by an authorized representative. Existing law has no parallel requirements.
    • Requiring the Department of State to establish a procedure for an authorized representative to report a concern arising from a pre-canvass meeting and then investigate and report on the concern raised. Existing law has no parallel requirements.
    • Requiring the county board of elections to record the pre-canvassing and canvassing meetings with audio and visual recordings, and store them as an encrypted file. The recording may be posted on the county's publicly accessible Internet website in the encrypted format. The password or encryption software may be distributed as necessary. Existing law has no parallel requirements.
  • Change the ballot counting timeline for both types of mail ballots so that counting begins no earlier than the close of polls and no later than 8 a.m. the day after the election. Under existing law, mail ballots may be counted starting any time between the close of polls and the third day after the election.
  • Create a cure process to enable mail voters to address certain issues with their ballot certificates so their ballots can be counted. Existing law does not give voters notice or an opportunity to cure such issues.
    • Issues that can be cured are incomplete, unsigned, or undated certificates.
    • The county board would give notice of the issue to the voter by mail, email, telephone, or text message that their ballot will not be counted unless the voter addresses the issue before the close of polls on Election Day.

  • Require the county board to place and seal an absentee ballot or mail-in ballot that does not have a ballot envelope or has unidentifiable marks on the envelope into an empty official election ballot envelope and secure the envelope with the other removed official election ballot envelopes to be tabulated. Existing law has no parallel requirement.

Last Updated June 7, 2022

This bill, as introduced on June 7, 2022, would create new election crimes prosecutors, an election offense hotline, and give watchers viewing the processing and counting of mail ballots greater access. Existing law does not have comparable provisions.

Concerning election law enforcement, the bill would:

  • Require the Attorney General to appoint an independent prosecutor with experience prosecuting election law violations at least 90 days before each primary election. The appointment would be subject to the approval of a majority of the state senate. The independent prosecutor would:
    • Review election complaints received by the Department of State and the county boards of elections for elections until the next independent prosecutor is appointed.
    • Coordinate election oversight efforts with each level of law enforcement.
    • Publish a report following each election during their term of service. Each report would include the total number of complaints filed with which entities, a summary of how each complaint was investigated, and recommendations to the General Assembly, the Department of State, and county boards of elections for reducing future complaints. These reports would be public records.
  • Designate each county's district attorney of a county or their designee as the county's election integrity officer. The election integrity officer would work with its respective county board of elections, director of elections, and judge of elections to develop chain of custody procedures and internal control procedures to:
    • Ensure the integrity of elections.
    • Prevent fraud and illegal voting.
    • Recommend data analytic tools to prevent fraud and illegal voting.
    • Ensure that proper evidence can be developed to prosecute violations of Federal and State election laws.
  • Require the Secretary of the Commonwealth to:
    • Maintain an election crimes hotline. All of the information received through the hotline would be automatically transmitted to the independent prosecutor.
  • Provide annual election law training to district attorneys and their employees.

  • Require county boards of elections to cooperate with the election integrity officer in their county to review election complaints the board receives and to include the officer in all correspondence related to the conduct of the election.

    Concerning authorized watchers of mail ballot processing and canvassing, the bill would:


  • Require county boards of election to:
    • Make audio and visual recordings of the pre-canvass and canvass meetings but make them available only after the close of the polls.
    • Provide authorized watchers at the pre-canvass and canvass of mail ballots with meaningful access to view and observe the entire process of pre-canvassing or canvassing activities, including allowing them to easily read the text on any ballot or envelope at any point in the process.
    • Designate an official to respond to issues reported by authorized watchers.
  • Require the Department of State to establish a procedure for authorized watchers to report any concerns arising from any pre-canvass meeting.

  • Require the Department of State and county boards of elections to investigate and report on any concerns raised in each election. All information regarding the oversight of elections generated by the watchers and the investigations of their allegations would be turned over to the independent prosecutor.

This bill, as amended on April 6, 2022, would retain many of the provisions of the previous version of the bill that would require an overhaul of the state's voter management software (called SURE in Pennsylvania) and system to meet certain specifications. Unless noted below, the provisions described are retained from the previous version of the bill. The changes provided by this bill that impact voter access and election administration would:

This bill, as enacted on June 7, 2022, creates no-excuse absentee voting, changes the verification process for absentee ballots (called "mail ballots" in Rhode Island), changes voter list maintenance practices, and changes accessibility standards for absentee voting. Specifically, the bill:

  • Creates no-excuse absentee voting, in place of the excuse-required absentee voting system provided by existing law. Along with eliminating excuse requirements, and making various related conforming changes, the bill:
    • Allows voters to request an absentee ballot electronically through the portal created by other provisions of the bill.
    • Changes the absentee ballot certifying envelope to require voters to affirm that they have not and will not vote elsewhere in this election. Under existing law, voters certified instead that they were not qualified to vote elsewhere.
    • Permits the state board of elections to promulgate regulations allowing for the acceptance of mail ballot applications via drop boxes.
  • Eliminates the requirement that absentee ballots envelopes be notarized or witnessed, and instead requires only the voter's signature on the absentee ballot envelope. In addition to various conforming changes, the bill also:
    • Eliminates a lack of witnesses or notary signatures as a reason to reject a ballot.
    • Repeals the existing felony of falsely notarizing or witnessing a voter signature.
    • Repeals the existing law permitting any candidate to inquire into any notary or witness who witnesses more than 50 voters' signatures.
  • Mandates the use of absentee ballot drop boxes. Every municipality must have at least one drop box placed outside the office of the board of elections. Drop boxes must be:
    • available beginning 20 days before Election Day
    • available 24 hours a day, seven days a week, if outside a municipal building or during normal business hours if inside a municipal building
    • available on Election Day until the close of the polls
    • accessible to persons with disabilities
    • monitored by a video surveillance system
    • identified by location on the websites of both the state and local boards of elections
  • Creates an online application for absentee ballots using a form similar to the existing paper ballot application form. This application requires an electronic signature made under penalty of perjury as to the truth of the application. Voters utilizing this system are required to provide their date of birth and ID number (either state driver's license or state ID). The online form must be available in any language required by federal or state voting rights laws, and compliant with federal disability requirements.
  • Changes the deadline to request an accessible ballot from 45 days before Election Day to 21 days before Election Day, and allows such requests to be made through the electronic voter registration portal created by other provisions of the bill.
  • Adds long-term residents of nursing homes to the list of voters who are eligible to receive an absentee ballot application automatically for every election.
  • Changes voter list maintenance procedures by:
    • Requiring the secretary of state to update the central voter list for address changes based on information from the United States Postal Service's National Change of Address program four times annually. Under existing law, these updates were required once every two years.
    • Requiring the secretary of state to update the central voter list for deceased voters on monthly receipt of the federal Social Security Administration's master death list or state vital statistics data. Existing law required monthly updates based solely upon information from state data.
    • Requiring the secretary of state to maintain a list in the central voter list of all voters who automatically receive absentee ballot applications.
    • Setting a deadline that all voter list maintenance activities end no later than 90 days before any state election.

  • Requires the secretary of state to provide a public hotline with voting information in multiple languages.

Under existing law, a commission with a different makeup and different criteria draws maps that are then adopted by the legislature. Specifically, this bill would:

  • Create a seven-member commission, appointed by legislative leaders of both parties and by the state ethics commission.     • Create contiguous districts.
    • Comply with all applicable federal law.
    • Draft district plans based on the most recent federal decennial census data in addition to other reliable sources of demographic data.
    • Not consider political parties or incumbency.
    • Not consider partisan data, unless required to ensure compliance with federal law.
    • Not dilute communities of interest.
    • Not intentionally preserve the cores of existing districts, unless all other requirements are satisfied.
    • Ensure equal population as much as possible, and only permit deviations in population based on federal law, tribal government considerations, avoiding dilution of communities of interest, avoiding fragmentation of existing governmental subdivisions, and preserving the core of existing districts.
    • Adopt plans that are most compact based on metrics set forth in the statute.
    • Write evaluations of each adopted plan setting forth the compliance with the criteria set forth in the statute as well as the ability of racial and language minorities to elect their candidates of choice, partisan fairness, and the preservation of communities of interest.
  • Authorize the legislature to adopt one of the plans proposed by the commission.

  • Create a right of appeal in any person who submitted testimony at one of the commission's public hearings, granting initial review to the state supreme court.

This bill, as introduced on March 4, 2022, would change voter registration, voter list maintenance, in-person early voting, and absentee voting processes, would create new voting crimes, and would change other aspects of voting law in the state. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Change voter registration requirements in several ways by:
    • Requiring that voters must be residents of the state and their voting district for at least 60 days before being entitled to vote in any election, whether presidential, federal, state, or local. Under existing state law, and in accordance with existing federal law, a 30-day residency period is required for voters.
    • Changing the standard for determining residence for voting purposes by requiring that a person's residence for voting is their full-time domicile. The words "full-time" do not appear in existing law.
    • Stating that only people who claim Rhode Island as their state income tax jurisdiction shall be allowed to vote in the state. This is a new requirement.
    • Requiring that all voters must produce at least one of the following IDs: a valid driver's license, a state ID card with a photograph, or a U.S. passport.
    • Requiring that election officials send a signature form to any voter who registers to vote online, which the voter must return.
  • Change voter list maintenance practices by:
    • Requiring any realtor representing a seller in a sale of residential property to deliver a form confirming the sale and the identity of the new owners to local election officials. This is a new requirement.
    • Requiring managers of residential rental property to quarterly submit a list of all the tenants who have moved out to local election officials. Local election officials must pay such property managers $10 for every vacated unit reported. This is a new requirement.
    • Requiring that the department of health inform the board of elections of every death within 20 days after the death. The secretary of the state would be required to remove such voters from the rolls within five days after receipt of such notice. Under existing law, the department of health sends this information to the secretary of state monthly, and the secretary of state then notifies local election officials, who remove voters from the rolls.
  • Create in-person early voting for a period beginning 14 days before Election Day and ending on Election Day. Under existing law, voters may only vote early in person if they apply for an emergency absentee ballot and cast it at their local board of canvassers office. It is unclear whether this bill creates an early voting process available to all voters or just creates a standardized process for voters with an absentee voting excuse who are eligible under existing law. Early voting under this bill must:
    • Take place in a location designated by local election officials, which must be accessible.
    • Be available from 7:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. every day during the period, including Saturdays and Sundays.
    • Require each early voting location to produce a list of voters who cast ballots there the previous day, including returned absentee ballots. This list must be available to both the public and local election officials.
  • Change the process of applying for and sending absentee ballots (called "mail ballots" in Rhode Island), by:
    • Requiring that a voter's signature on their application for an absentee ballot be verified before the absentee ballot can be sent to the voter. Under existing law, no signature verification of the absentee ballot application is required.
    • Requiring election officials to send a voter an absentee ballot within five days of receipt of the voter's absentee ballot application.
    • Requiring that absentee ballots be sent no earlier than 30 days before Election Day. Under existing law, there is no specified earliest date for sending absentee ballots.
  • Change requirements for return of absentee ballots by:
    • Changing the deadline for receipt of absentee ballots from UOCAVA voters to the close of the polls on Election Day. Under existing law, UOCAVA voters' ballots are counted if received by 4:00 p.m. on the seventh day after Election Day, while other voters' ballots are counted only if received by the close of the polls on Election Day. This bill would also clarify that ballots that are mailed, returned to voting locations or election officials' offices, or returned to drop boxes all must be returned by the close of the polls on Election Day.
    • Requiring that absentee ballot drop boxes be inside a governmental building subject to supervision during its hours of access. The bill would further require that drop boxes be continuously monitored by people approved by local election officials during the hours when the drop box is accessible for return of ballots.
  • Prohibit governmental units from accepting financial or in-kind donations from any private individuals or third parties for election expenses.
  • Extend the notice that local election officials are required to give to candidates of absentee ballot processing and counting to include local candidates and parties. Under existing law, notice must only be given to state and federal candidates and parties.
  • Require that all state IDs include a large "FN barcode" across the face, which would indicate that the holder is a foreign national ineligible to vote. The barcode would be used to prevent the ID's use in voter registration or voting.

  • Create a new elections crimes by:

    • Creating a new felony for any person who willfully violates voter registration requirements, submits false documents, or unlawfully manipulates the voter registration process.
    • Creating a new misdemeanor for ballot harvesting, which is not defined, although the bill defines a ballot harvester as a person who is associated with a candidate, campaign, or political party, who has a vested or financial interest in the outcome of a campaign, or who coordinates or plans ballot harvesting activities including collection and delivery of absentee ballots and absentee ballot applications. The bill does allow voters to designate a member of their family or a medical designee (provided the medical designee has no ties to ballot harvesting) to return their ballot if they are unable to do so because of illness, disability, or infirmity. The bill also would require the state chair recognized political parties to designate members of a team to collect ballots from nursing homes or congregate care facilities.

Last Updated April 13, 2022

BILLSUMMARY: Creates a redistricting commission to act every ten (10) years to adopt a redistricting plan for all general assembly and congressional districts that would require the approval of the general assembly and the governor, sets forth requirements and prohibitions for creating district plans, allows public participation and allows for a possible right of appeal of the plan, to the state supreme court.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 1, 2022, would create a state redistricting commission to conduct redistricting of federal congressional districts and state legislative districts following each federal decennial census. Under existing law, districts are drawn and approved by the legislature. This new commission would:

  • Create district plans composed of single-member districts. The plans must comply with federal laws and be composed of contiguous territory. The commission must also consider the following factors when creating plans:
    • equality of population, with no more than 5% deviation in state legislative districts.
    • consideration of tribal governments,
    • non-dilution of communities of interest, and
    • avoiding the fragmentation of existing governmental subdivisions. The commission would be prohibited from:
    • considering if the district is favorable towards a political party,
    • considering if the district is favorable towards an incumbent,
    • using partisan data, such as voting history or party registration, except to the extent required to comply with federal law,
    • creating a plan that intentionally dilutes representation of communities of interest, and
    • creating a plan that preserves the cores of existing districts, unless all other requirements are met.
  • Adopt three to five district plans during each redistricting cycle. The commission must select the most compact plans, based on two metrics described in the bill.
  • Be allowed to consider federal decennial census data and other reliable sources of demographic data.
  • Hold at least six public meetings throughout the state before issuing plans and at least six public hearings throughout the state after issuing plans.

  • Comprise seven members, with two appointed by bipartisan legislative leaders, two appointed by the state ethics commission, and a commissioner appointed by the state ethics commission who must be a retired judge. The bill also sets forth various anti-corruption qualifications for membership.

    The bill also includes provisions relating to passage of the plans and legal challenges to the plans. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the legislature to consider the plans adopted by the commission and pass one plan for each district type (federal congressional, state senate, state congressional) without amendment. If the legislature fails to do so, the plan that the commission rated as most compact shall be presented to the governor for approval without amendment.

  • Create a right of action for any person who submitted a comment at a public hearing of the commission asking for a review of a plan adopted by the commission. The appellant. has the burden to demonstrate that the district plan violates applicable law, is arbitrary or capricious, or is not supported by substantial evidence. The court cannot modify the plan, but may only affirm or annul a plan.

    Last updated March 3, 2022.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 10, 2022, would alter the state's existing automatic voter registration system by requiring different procedures depending on how an applicant certifies their citizenship status. Under existing law, all qualified individuals are automatically registered to vote during DMV transactions, unless they choose to opt-out during the transaction, if they provide proof of identity and residence and certify through documentation or a declaration that they are citizens. This bill would:

  • Limit automatic voter registration at the DMV to only those applicants who present documentation of citizenship, and change the opt-out process. For individuals who provide citizenship documentation, voter registration information would be automatically transmitted to election officials, who would subsequently send a notice of registration to the applicant. If the applicant failed to decline registration within 14 days of receipt of that notice, the applicant would be registered to vote. Under existing law, automatic voter registration requires only certification of citizenship, not documentation, and the DMV must provide the opportunity to opt-out during the transaction itself.
  • End automatic voter registration for individuals who do not present affirmative documentary proof of citizenship at the DMV, and instead provide an opt-in streamlined registration process for these applicants. Individuals whose documentation neither proves or disproves citizenship would be given the option to register if they certify their citizenship status, which may be done by declaration, but would not be automatically enrolled.
  • Prohibit automatic voter registration or streamlined voter registration at the DMV for any individual who fails to certify, by documentation or declaration, that they are a U.S. citizen, and expressly prohibit the agency from offering the opportunity to register to individuals who have documented their non-citizenship. Existing law requires certification of citizenship for registration at the DMV, but does not include an express prohibition on offering registration when documentation of non-citizenship has been provided.
  • Expand which additional agencies beyond the DMV may offer automatic voter registration, by permitting agencies to do so if they either collect documentary proof of citizenship or can verify citizenship by database matching or other means deemed reliable by the Secretary of State. Existing law limits automatic voter registration to only those non-DMV agencies that verify citizenship through documentation. The bill would also require non-DMV agencies that process transactions for multiple individuals eligible for registration to register each individual according to the procedures applicable to the DMV process.

  • Permit agencies that are not authorized to offer full automatic voter registration to make automatic updates to voter registration address information, if the Secretary verifies that the agency collects sufficient information to do so.

Last Updated May 23, 2022

This bill, as introduced on March 10, 2022, would facilitate voting opportunities for certain incarcerated people. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Allow any "specially qualified voter" to request an absentee ballot (called a "mail ballot" in Rhode Island), even if the person has not previously voted. A specially qualified voter is one who is:
    • Incarcerated in a Rhode Island jail or prison for any reason other than conviction of a felony.
    • Domiciled in Rhode Island.
    • Otherwise qualified to vote.
  • Require the department of corrections to designate a "jail voting coordinator" to facilitate voting by qualified incarcerated people. Among other responsibilities, the coordinator would be required to submit a plan to the secretary of state detailing how the requirements of this bill would be implemented.
  • Require the department of corrections to post voting information in all correctional facilities in the place normally used for posting notices.

  • Create a new right to submit a complaint to the secretary of state for any incarcerated person eligible to vote under this bill whose access to voting has been denied.

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2022, would create a standing joint legislative committee to examine election integrity issues. Specifically, the committee created by the bill would:

  • Recommend three counties to undergo audits of their 2020 primary and general election results and absentee ballot signatures. If a pattern of election law discrepancies is revealed by these audits, the new committee would have the authority to recommend additional issues to be audited and/or an audit of the 2020 election statewide.
  • Examine and report annually upon election security issues, including:
    • voter access to ballot tracking,
    • data storage and security of election hardware and software,
    • the accuracy and security of election processes, particularly canvassing and precanvassing processes,
    • statewide uniformity of election processes,
    • the judiciary's role in the election process, including the U.S. Supreme Court's upholding of the state's absentee ballot witness requirement before the 2020 general election, and
    • other election-related issues.
  • Be composed of three members of the state senate appointed by the senate president, including at least one member of the largest minority party, three members of the state house appointed by the house speaker, including at least one member of the largest minority party, and one governor appointee.

Last updated February 9, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2022, would create a committee to examine the conduct and results of the 2020 general election. The committee would report findings and recommendations to the state general assembly by the end of 2022. Specifically, the committee created by the bill would:

  • Examine irregularities in precinct results compared to previous elections.

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2022, would amend the definition of domicile for voting purposes to make clear that a person who enters another state, county, or municipality and votes in such other location has changed their domicile for voting purposes. For general purposes, registering to vote in a new location is considered an act indicating a change in domicile. The bill would also remove certain factors from consideration in deciding whether a person has changed their domicile for voting purposes, including:

  • the voter's address on legal and financial documents,
  • the voter's address for club or organizational membership, and

  • a voter's temporary relocation due to medical care.

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2022, would change certain aspects of applying for and voting absentee ballots. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require voters to provide an ID number on their absentee ballot application, defined as either the voter's voter registration notification number, driver's license number, or state issued identification card number. This bill would require that the envelope be designed so as to obscure the voter's ID number from view. If an applicant fails to include their ID number, their ballot will be treated as a provisional ballot. Under current law, absentee ballot applicants are not required to provide any ID number.
  • Change the dates on which a person may request an absentee ballot application, with requests for applications only being allowed from 78 days before an election to 11 days before an election. Under current law, absentee ballot applications can be requested at any time during the calendar year of the election in which the voter wishes to vote absentee.
  • Require that the address in the voter's absentee ballot application be the same address as is on file in the state election commission's voter registration system. Under current law, the applicant need only include their current address. If a voter wishes their ballot be mailed to an address other than their on-file address, the request must be made in writing, signed by the voter, and include the voter's ID number.
  • Prohibit a person from serving as a witness on more than five absentee ballot applications.
  • Require that return envelopes included with all absentee ballots be marked "return to sender" to prevent forwarding. Existing law is silent about forwarding return envelopes for absentee ballots.

  • Prohibit a person from requesting "absentee applications for more than qualified electors in addition to himself."

Last Updated February 2, 2022

This bill, as introduced January 31, 2022, would establish early voting, same-day registration, and automatic voter registration, encourage voter registration, and establish an independent redistricting commission. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Establish a seven-day early voting period from 30 to 3 days before Election Day. Each early voting center would have to be open on no fewer than three Saturdays. Under existing law, there is no early voting.
  • Establish same-day registration on Election Day and during early voting for "a seven-day period beginning on the second Saturday before the election and ending on the first Saturday before the election." Under existing law, the registration deadline is 30 days prior to an election.
  • Establish automatic voter registration at the Department of Motor Vehicles for individuals processing drivers license or non-driving ID applications. Applicants would be registered automatically unless they declined to be registered by following instructions received in the mail post-transaction. Under existing law, individuals can affirmatively choose to have their DMV paperwork function as a voter registration form, however they may be required to provide additional information or signatures beyond what is required as part of their DMV transaction.
  • Facilitate voter registration, including by formerly disenfranchised individuals. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Direct the Department of Corrections and the Department of Probation, Parole and Pardon Services to inform individuals who have been disenfranchised due to criminal convictions that they will become eligible to vote after completing all of the terms of their sentences.
    • Require the automatic reinstatement of the registrations of individuals who were registered prior to their disenfranchisement, and the transmission of disenfranchised individuals' information to election officials.
    • Require all the State Department of Education, the State Election Commission, and the county boards of voter registration and elections to ensure that all high school students 17 and older complete voter registration forms, with an option for some students to opt out.

The bill would also establish a redistricting commission, an area not tracked by Voting Rights Lab.

Last Updated May 10, 2022

This bill, as amended on April 21, 2022, would:

  • Establish an early voting period. Specifically:
    • Early voting would be available at between one and seven early voting centers in each county.
    • Early voting would be available from at least 8:30 a.m. to 6 p.m. from Monday to Saturday for the two-week period immediately preceding an election, except that for elections other than statewide general elections, county election officials would determine whether to provide Saturday hours.
    • Sunday early voting would be prohibited
    • For a primary runoff where timing would not permit the standard early voting period, the executive director of the state election commission would determine the days of voting.
    • These provisions would not apply to presidential preference primaries.
  • Restrict absentee voting. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require that ballots be either mailed or hand-delivered to an elections employee at the main election office during office hours, effectively prohibiting the use of ballot drop boxes. Existing law is silent on drop boxes.
    • Require that if a voter or a voter's authorized representative returns an absentee ballot in person, they must present a photo ID or the election official may not accept the ballot.
    • Require voters to provide the last four digits of their social security numbers on their request for an absentee ballot application. Existing law contains no such requirement, although the last four digits of a voter's Social Security number are required to request an absentee ballot application online.
    • Move forward the absentee application deadline from the 4th day before an election to the 11th day.
    • Prohibit the return of more than five completed ballots in addition to one's own. Violation of this prohibition would be a felony punishable by imprisonment of up to five years or a fine of between $100 and $1000.
    • Require that voters be outside their county of residence for the entire early voting period in order to be eligible to vote absentee on that basis. Under existing law, a voter is eligible to request an absentee ballot if they will be outside the county on Election Day.
    • Eliminate the absentee-qualifying excuse of having had a death in the family within a three day period before the election.
    • Limit the applicability of the absentee excuse covering persons confined to a jail or pretrial facility to voters who will be confined to such facility for the entire early voting period. Under existing law, a voter so confined is eligible to request an absentee ballot regardless of the specific timeframe of their confinement.
    • Prohibit campaign volunteers from requesting an absentee ballot on a voter's behalf as an authorized representative. Under existing law, only paid campaign workers who are compensated for their time are prohibited from serving as authorized representatives.
    • Require that authorized representatives requesting an absentee ballot on behalf of a voter be disclosed on the voter's application, including their address, date of birth, and relationship to the voter, and the voter's date of birth and the last for digits of their social security number.
    • Prohibit an individual from requesting absentee ballot applications for more than five additional voters per election.
    • Establish a felony for a person to provide, offer to provide, or accept anything of value in exchange for requesting, collecting, or delivering an absentee ballot.
    • Prohibit election officials from providing voters with absentee ballot applications or absentee ballots except in response to a request as provided for in the election code.
  • Make other changes to absentee voting. These provisions would:
    • Permit processing of absentee ballots to begin at 7 a.m. on the second day before Election Day. Under existing law, processing may not begin until 9 a.m. on Election Day.
    • Permit tabulation of absentee ballots to begin at 7 a.m. on Election Day. Under existing law, tabulation may not begin until 9 a.m. on Election Day.
    • Establish a felony for the intentional premature release of absentee ballot results by an election official, worker, candidate, or watcher, punishable by a fine of up to $1000 or imprisonment of not more than five years.
    • Guarantee that candidates and any appointed watchers have a right to be present for the examination of absentee ballot envelopes and the opening of envelopes, at a reasonable distance to ensure both the right to observe and the secrecy of the ballots.
    • Facilitate in-person voting by individuals who have requested absentee ballots by allowing such voters to cast provisional ballots at early vote centers or on Election Day, which would be counted so long as their absentee ballot is not received. Under existing law, individuals who have been sent absentee ballots may not vote in person unless they present to the officials at their polling place a certificate from county election officials stating that they turned in an unvoted absentee ballot.
    • Require that absentee ballots incorporate security features that do not render them identifiable.
  • Change how elections are administered in the state. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require that the governor's appointments to the state election commission be confirmed by the state senate. In the aftermath of the 2020 election, legislators have objected to pro-voter measures advocated for by the governor's appointees to the election commission and the commission's executive director..
    • Require that the commission's selection for its executive director be confirmed by the state senate.
    • Require that race, gender, and other geographic and demographic factors be considered in the selection of members of the state election commission to assure nondiscrimination, inclusion, and representation to the greatest extent possible of all segments of the population of the state.
    • Prohibit the state election commission from issuing emergency regulations.
    • Grant the president of the senate and speaker of the house of representatives, on behalf of their respective bodies, the right to intervene in state court action challenging the validity of any election law or policy and, in federal court, the authority to intervene, file a brief, provide written or oral evidence or argument, within the rules of federal procedure, regardless of whether or not another state actor is a party to the case.
    • Direct the state election commission and attorney general to notify the legislative leaders within 24 hours of receipt of service of a complaint challenging the validity of any election law or policy.
    • Expand the supervision of county election officials by the state election commission to include compliance with "standardized processes" prescribed by the commission. Under existing law, supervisory authority extends to compliance with state and federal law and commission "policies" and "procedures."
  • Elevate several crimes from misdemeanors to felonies. These crimes would include:
    • Fraudulent registration
    • Multiple voting
    • Impersonating another person in order to vote
    • Willful violation of their duties by an election official or manager
  • Facilitate voter list maintenance. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Direct the department of motor vehicles to provide to the executive director of the state election commission a monthly report of all non-U.S. citizens who are issued a driver's license or non-driver ID, including their name, social security number where applicable, and date of birth.
    • Direct county probate courts to provide to the executive director of the state election commission a monthly report of all individuals age 18 or older who have been declared mentally incapacitated. This list would include the name, county of residence, social security number, and date and place of birth of any relevant person.
    • Require the bureau of vital statistics to provide the executive director of the state election commission with a monthly report of all persons eighteen or older who have died outside of the state. Under existing law, such list must only contain those who died within the state.
    • Direct the executive director of the state election commission to conduct an annual general list maintenance program.
    • Require that individuals be removed from the list of eligible voters within seven days of receipt of information that they are not qualified. Under existing law, there is no prescribed timeline for removal.
    • Add not being a U.S. citizen to the list of reasons for which the state election commission can remove an individual from the list of qualified voters.
    • Establish that a voter can only be removed from the roles due to a change in residence if their new residence is outside their county of registration and with written confirmation from the voter.
  • Prohibit the state election commission and county boards of registration and elections from receiving, accepting, or expending gifts, donations, or funding from private individuals, corporations, partnerships, trusts, or any third party not provided through ordinary state or county appropriations.
  • Make other changes to election law. These provisions would:
    • Elevate fraudulent registration crimes from a misdemeanor to a felony with a fine of not less than $1000 and imprisonment of not more than five years.
    • Elevant multiple voting at the same election from a "misdemeanor" punishable by up to three years imprisonment to a felony with a penalty of a fine between $1000 and $5000 and imprisonment of not more than five years.
    • Expand the scope of the electioneering crime to cover early voting locations.
    • Direct the executive director of the state election commission to promulgate regulations governing voter registration by private entities.

Absentee ballot requests made before May 31, 2022, in accordance with the law as of April 21 would be exempt from the application requirements established by this bill.

The bill also contains provisions related to election equipment and candidate ballot access that are not tracked by Voting Rights Lab.

    • Expands the supervision of county election officials by the state election commission to include compliance with "standardized processes" prescribed by the commission. Under existing law, supervisory authority extended only to compliance with state and federal law and commission "policies" and "procedures."
  • Elevates several crimes from misdemeanors to felonies. These crimes include:
    • Fraudulent registration
    • Multiple voting
    • Impersonating another person in order to vote
    • Willful violation of their duties by an election official or manager
  • Facilitates voter list maintenance. Specifically, the bill:
    • Directs the department of motor vehicles to provide to the executive director of the state election commission a monthly report of all non-U.S. citizens who are issued a driver's license or non-driver ID, including their name, social security number where applicable, and date of birth. The first report must include a retrospective list of all DMV transactions with non-citizens.
    • Directs county probate courts to provide to the executive director of the state election commission a monthly report of all individuals age 18 or older who have been declared mentally incapacitated. This list must include the name, county of residence, Social Security number, and date and place of birth of any relevant person.
    • Requires the bureau of vital statistics to provide the executive director of the state election commission with a monthly report of all persons 18 or older who have died outside of the state. Under existing law, such list was only required to contain those who died within the state.
    • Directs the executive director of the state election commission to conduct an annual general list maintenance program.
    • Requires that individuals be removed from the list of eligible voters within seven days of receipt of information that they are not qualified. Under existing law, there was no prescribed timeline for removal.
    • Adds not being a U.S. citizen to the list of reasons for which the state election commission can remove an individual from the list of qualified voters.
    • Establishes that a voter can only be removed from the rolls due to a change in residence if their new residence is outside their county of registration and with written confirmation from the voter.
  • Prohibits the state election commission and county boards of registration and elections from receiving, accepting, or expending gifts, donations, or funding from private individuals, corporations, partnerships, trusts, or any third party not provided through ordinary state or county appropriations.

Makes other changes to election law. These provisions:

  • Expand the scope of the electioneering crime to cover early voting locations.
  • Direct the executive director of the state election commission to promulgate regulations governing voter registration by private entities.

The bill also contains provisions related to election equipment and candidate ballot access that are not tracked by Voting Rights Lab.

This bill, as introduced on February 2, 2022, would change post-election audit procedures. These audits would be to confirm that ballots have been accurately counted. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create a new, additional audit process by allowing the secretary of state to select the county election commissions that must conduct an audit. The secretary of state will select three counties to audit after August elections and six counties after November elections.
  • Allow the secretary of state to choose whether each county subject to the new audit process conducts either:
    • A "risk-limiting" audit where the number of ballots to be reviewed is chosen by statistical analysis,
    • A "traditional" audit, where bipartisan teams of election officials hand count randomly chosen ballots, or
    • A "performance" audit, where some undesignated person or entity reviews the procedures followed to conduct the election.
  • Create a pilot audit program for the November 2022 elections where Williamson County's elections will be audited using the new, additional audit process prescribed by this bill.
  • Require that each county not selected for a random audit by the secretary of state and not required to conduct a mandatory results-confirming audit must conduct a mandatory performance audit after certification. In addition, the secretary of state will randomly select six counties where their performance audit will be conducted by the state. These audits will examine, at a minimum, the procedures for absentee ballots, including requests, transmittal, and returns.
  • Alter the existing audit process required in every county using optical scan tabulators. Under existing law, this audit of the top race in the election occurs in a set number of precincts (depending on county size) immediately after the polls close. The vote totals from one tabulator shall be compared to the vote totals obtained from a different tabulator. If there is a discrepancy of greater than 1%, more precincts must be audited and, in addition, a hand count may also be ordered. This bill would maintain this structure but would allow additional races to be audited. The bill also requires that the results of the hand count, if any, are the results to be certified.

  • Add additional security features that may be included with absentee ballots, which are already required to be watermarked.

This bill, as enacted on February 2, 2022, changes post-election audit procedures. These audits are to confirm that ballots have been accurately counted. Specifically, the bill:

    • A "traditional" audit, where bipartisan teams of election officials hand count randomly chosen ballots, or
    • A "performance" audit, where some undesignated person or entity reviews the procedures followed to conduct the election.
  • Requires that each county not selected for a random audit by the secretary of state and not required to conduct a mandatory results-confirming audit must conduct a mandatory performance audit after certification. In addition, the secretary of state will randomly select six counties where their performance audit will be conducted by the state. These audits will examine, at a minimum, the procedures for absentee ballots, including requests, transmittal, and returns.
  • Alters the existing audit process required in every county using optical scan tabulators. Under existing law, this audit of the top race in the election occurs in a set number of precincts (depending on county size) immediately after the polls close. The vote totals from one tabulator shall be compared to the vote totals obtained from a different tabulator. If there is a discrepancy of greater than 1%, more precincts must be audited and, in addition, a hand count may also be ordered. This bill would maintain this structure but would allow additional races to be audited. The bill also requires that the results of the hand count, if any, are the results to be certified.
  • Adds additional security features that may be included with absentee ballots, which are already required to be watermarked.

  • Creates a pilot audit program for 2022 elections where Williamson County's elections will be audited.
