This bill, as amended on February 23, 2022, would improve Utah's existing cure process, making it more likely more eligible voters will be able to ensure their ballots count. In addition, it would improve the accessibility of the state's mail ballot election system. Most of these provisions were in the previous version. The February 23 amendments enabled parties and candidates to help voters cure their ballots, and slightly delayed certain record keeping requirements. Specifically, as amended on February 24, the bill would:

  • Require election officers to provide a method of accessible voting to disabled people who are not able to vote by mail, and include information about that method with ballots and on their website. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Define what it means for a ballot envelope signature to correspond generally, and require the Director of Elections to issue regulations. The regulations would define more precisely what corresponding signatures are, require election worker training and certification regarding the signature comparison criteria and processes, and specify an Americans with Disabilities Act-compliant method for disabled voters to verify their ballots when their disability causes inconsistent signatures. Existing law merely requires election officials to determine if the signatures correspond. This provision was in the previous version of the bill, except that the previous version provided the new signature match process would begin January 1, 2024. Under the amended bill, the changes would take effect when the law does.
  • Provide that if the reason the voter's ballot certificate signature does not correspond with the one on file is the voter has a disability, the voter may include related information in the affidavit. If the affidavit discloses a disability, the election officer must follow the new rules for accessible verification. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law has no comparable provision.
  • Require the notice of a defect to include a copy of the cure affidavit, or if the notice is by email or text, a link to the affidavit on the county clerk's website. If the notice is by phone, whether in conversation or by voice message, it must include arrangements for the voter to receive a copy of the affidavit. Existing law does not require the affidavit to be provided with the notice.
  • Improve the timeline and methods for giving voters notice of a ballot certificate issue. Specifically, the election officer would give notice:
    • by any means within 24 hours after the ballot is rejected, and if the voter does not cure the issue within the 24 hours after the ballot is rejected, the election officer would be required to give additional notice.
    • by phone, mail, and SMS text message, if the election officer has the voter's relevant contact information, within one business day after that 24 hour period ends.
    • by mail within two business days after the ballot is rejected.

      These provisions were in the previous version of the bill. Under existing law, notice is given by phone, email, and text within one business day, and by mail within two business days, only if the ballot is rejected before Election Day. If the election official rejects the ballot on Election Day, they have up to the seventh day after the election to give notice. If the ballot is rejected after Election Day and before the end of the canvass, the election official has seven days after the canvass to give notice.
  • Create an additional way a voter can cure an issue with their ballot envelope besides completing and returning the cure affidavit. Specifically, if the election officer or their employee communicates directly with the voter, the voter provides identifying information to the officer or their employee that they verify using the voter's voter registration file, and the election officer maintains written documentation of that communication and information, the voter's ballot counts. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law only allows cure by affidavit.
  • Require election officials to enable political parties and candidates to help voters cure their ballots. Specifically, election officials would be required to disclose the name and address of each voter whose ballot has been rejected and not yet cured to a political party or candidate that requests the information within one business day of the request. The information would be disclosed for voters whose registration record is kept confidential under other provisions of law. This is a new provision. Existing law does not have a comparable requirement.
  • Require the election official to record in the statewide voter registration database any initial rejection of a ballot within one business day of rejecting the ballot, any resolving of the issue causing the ballot rejection, within one business day after resolution.
  • Require the election official to include in the canvass report a final report on rejected and resolved ballots, starting January 1, 2024. This is a modified provision. Under the previous version, this provision would take effect immediately. Specifically, the report would include:
    • the number rejected because the voter did not sign.
    • the number rejected because the voter's signature did not correspond with the one on file.
    • the number of voters who reported the lack of signature correspondence stemmed from their disability.
  • Provide that an election official's willful failure to comply with the notice and cure process and related reporting is a willful neglect of duty, a felony, and generally expand that felony, which currently applies to poll workers, to apply to election officers as well. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

  • Require the publicly available voting history record include the reporting on the disposition of rejected ballots and the reasons for their rejections. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

Last Updated February 28, 2022

This bill, as enacted on March 22, 2022, prohibits private funding of elections, expands drop box requirements, and makes numerous other changes to election law. Specifically, the bill:

  • Prohibits an election officer from soliciting, accepting, or using any funds for an election if they were donated by any person other than a government entity. Existing law did not include a prohibition against the solicitation or use of private election funds.
  • Creates new drop box rules. Specifically, the bill:
    • Requires an election officer to place at least one ballot drop box in each municipality in the area in which the election officer has jurisdiction and permits the officer to place additional drop boxes in the officer's jurisdiction. Existing law permitted an election officer to place a ballot drop box in the officer's jurisdiction but did not require it.
    • Requires an election officer to provide 24-hour video surveillance of each unattended ballot drop box and post related signage. Existing law did not contain a similar provision.
    • Appropriates $500,000 to assist counties and cities with obtaining the video surveillance equipment for ballot drop boxes.
    • Requires at least two poll workers to be present when a poll worker collects ballots from a ballot drop box and delivers them to the place where they will be opened and counted. Relatedly, the bill requires an election office to ensure a specific chain of custody for the ballots. Existing law permitted an election officer to authorize two or more poll workers to remove ballots from a drop box, but did not require them. In addition, existing law required an election official to ensure procedures were followed to document a ballot chain custody for other ballot types, but not for ballots placed in a drop box.
  • Clarifies that the prohibition against voting more than once at any election includes voting in a state outside of Utah. Existing law simply prohibited an individual from voting more than once at any one election.
  • Requires an election officer to use all available resources to determine whether an individual is registered to vote, or votes, in more than one state or precinct. If the election officer identifies such an individual and believes the individual has committed election fraud, the bill requires them to report discrepancies to law enforcement or a prosecutor. Existing law did not impose a comparable duty on election officers.
  • Requires each county clerk, within 30 days of processing a voter registration form, to provide to the voter instructions on how the voter may sign up to receive electronic ballot status notifications through the state ballot tracking system. Existing law required the county clerk to provide instructions only if the voter did not opt to receive electronic ballot status notifications on the voter registration form.
  • Requires an individual who did not provide valid voter identification at the time of registering to vote to provide such identification before voting by mail or in person. If the election officer determines that a voter voting by mail is required to show valid voter identification, the bill allows them to give the voter instructions to sign up for the ballot tracking system as part of the notice about identification. Under existing law, all in-person voters were required to show ID to vote and all accepted forms of ID were sufficient to complete a voter's registration if ID were needed for that purpose. Existing law did not address the ballot tracking system in this context.
  • Requires the Lieutenant Governor to conduct an annual audit of the voter registration database, share the results with each county clerk, and verify that the clerk addresses any concerns and fulfills necessary training. Beginning in 2023, the Lt. Governor must report the results of the audit to the Government Operations Interim Committee biannually. Existing law did not contain a similar provision.
  • Requires the Lieutenant Governor and the county clerk to ensure that a record of each time a person accesses a voter database is made and stored for at least 22 months. Existing law did not have a similar provision.
  • Requires the director of elections within the Office of the Lieutenant Governor to make rules applicable to election officials regarding ballot security and requires election officers to certify that they abide by such security rules and that they maintain the voter registration list in compliance with applicable law. This certification must be included with all election returns provided to a board of canvassers. Existing law did not contain a similar provision.
  • Allows the legislative auditor general to make copies of ballots and election returns as part of a legislative audit, but forbids the auditor general from examining, making copies, or keeping copies of a ballot in a manner that identifies who cast the ballot. Existing law did not contain a similar provision.

  • The bill also has provisions relating to ballot printing, election equipment security, servicing, and design that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

    On February 15, 2022, the original version of this bill was replaced with a substitute bill, and numerous provisions were deleted. The deleted provisions would have:


  • Required all first-time voters choosing to vote in person to show their Utah driver's license or a Utah identification card. Other forms of photo ID would not be accepted.
  • Required all first-time voters choosing to vote by mail to include a copy of their Utah driver's license or a Utah identification card. Other forms of photo ID would not be accepted.
  • Required people voting by mail to write their Utah driver's license number, state ID number, or the last four digits of their Social Security number on their ballot return envelope.
  • Rejected any mail ballot returned without the ID number on the ballot envelope or without a copy of ID inside, if it was required. Similarly, mail ballots would be rejected if a provided number did not match one on file.
  • Allowed a voter whose mail ballot was rejected on an ID or ID number basis to use the existing cure process to address the issue.

  • Required a voter who received assistance in voting or completing the return envelope to include in the return envelope a statement identifying the individual, their relationship to the voter, and whether the individual was paid for the assistance. The individual who assisted the voter would have had to sign the statement.

Last Updated June 14, 2022

This bill, as introduced on February 10, 2022, would fundamentally change Utah elections by ending universal mail voting. Instead, people would be required to have an excuse to vote absentee. In addition, the bill adds ID requirements to mail voting and provisional ballot counting, eliminates drop boxes, and makes other changes throughout the election code. Specifically, the bill would:

  • End mail ballot elections except for referenda challenging local tax laws. Under existing law, voting by mail is the primary method of elections in Utah.
  • Require an excuse to vote by mail. Under existing law, all voters may vote by mail. Under the bill, voters would qualify to apply to vote absentee if they cannot vote in person during early voting or on Election Day:
    • due to a disability,
    • due to the individual's age,
    • due to anticipated hospitalization or other anticipated medical treatment, or
    • because the individual will be outside Utah during early voting and on election day.
  • Require applications to vote by mail include a copy of the voter's photo ID and be received 45 days before the election. Under existing law, people do not apply for mail ballots.
  • Require voters to return their absentee ballots by mail, and relatedly repeal provisions authorizing drop boxes for mail ballot return. As a consequence, the bill would narrow an existing misdemeanor by repealing references to ballot drop boxes, and would make other conforming changes throughout the code.
  • Require voters returning absentee ballots to enclose a copy of their photo ID with their ballot when returning it. Under existing law, a voter signs the certificate under oath but does not need to enclose an ID.

  • Expand an existing misdemeanor to prohibit possessing another person's completed voter registration form within 150 feet of the polling place, unless they live in the same household as the voter, are otherwise authorized by law to assist the voter with delivering their ballot, or their possession of the completed form is pursuant to federal law, or the person possessing it is a postal worker or election official acting in their official capacity.

  • Mandate a post-election audit of the accuracy of electronic vote tabulators conducted by an independent auditor chosen by the Lieutenant Governor. This bill, as enacted on March 24, 2022, makes various changes to poll watching rules, and improves transparency by requiring substantially more disclosure of ballot statistics than required by existing law. Specifically, the bill:

    • Adds signature matching to the processes watchers may observe. This is a new provision that was not in the previous version of the bill.
    • Requires any ballot adjudication, or upload of votes from a voting machine or scanner, that is conducted on a computer screen to be projected onto a screen that is large enough to be viewed by each watcher. Counties with fewer than 31,000 residents are exempt from this requirement. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill did not exempt the small counties.
    • Prohibits a watcher from recording any of the activity they are allowed to observe if the recording would reveal a vote or otherwise violate a voter's privacy or a voter's right to cast a secret ballot. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law prohibited a watcher from "electronically recording" such activity.
  • Creates a new requirement that county clerks must post on their website their upcoming schedule for verifying and canvassing ballots, beginning at least three days before the mailing of ballots and continuing through the first day of the canvass.   • Requires county clerks to post on their website certain ballot statistics when they finish processing ballots, beginning on the day the clerk starts mailing ballots and every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, ending on the Friday before the election, except that statistics need not be posted on Monday if no related activity occurred on the Saturday or Sunday. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law had no similar requirement. Specifically, the clerk must post:
    • the number of ballots in the county clerk's possession. Of those, the clerk must post:
    • the number of ballots that have not yet begun processing
    • the number of ballots in process
    • the number of ballots processed
  • Requires the election officer to post and update certain data, beginning the Friday after the election and every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday thereafter until the last day of the canvass. If no ballot processing happens on a Saturday or Sunday, the totals do not need to be updated on Monday. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill would have required the data to be posted beginning the day after the election, and would have required the data to be posted at 5 p.m. each time. Specifically, the election officer must post and update:
    • the election officer's best estimate of the number of ballots received to date. This is a modified provision. The previous version required a precise count. Under existing law, the election officer was required to post this information on the day after the election, and was permitted, but not required, to post this information thereafter.
    • the number of those ballots that have been rejected and not yet cured. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • the number of unprocessed provisional ballots. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • the number of ballots that need to be adjudicated, but have not yet been. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • the number of ballots awaiting duplication. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • the number of ballots that have been duplicated. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

The bill also repeals the requirement that officials make a public report on the day after the election of the number of in-person ballots received, and repeals permissive authority for officials to report updated totals of received ballots through the date of the canvass. These provisions were in the previous version of the bill.

Governor requires. This log would be maintained as ballot replication occurs. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

This bill, as introduced on February 24, 2022, would modify the state's existing redistricting process but not fundamentally change it. The most substantial changes would relate to the process of finalizing a plan for the Legislature's consideration, the required criteria for and transparency of the Legislature's process to adopt its plan instead, and the creation of a way for residents to challenge an enacted plan. Under both the bill and existing law, an independent redistricting commission tries to draw maps for the Legislature's consideration, but the Legislature may reject the plans and adopt its own. The bill would:

  • Change the process for developing and submitting redistricting plans to the Legislature. Specifically:
    • The bipartisan independent redistricting commission would draw plans using specified criteria and public input gathered during at least seven public hearings across the state. Within 30 days of the last public hearing, the commission would attempt to agree on up to three plans with the support of at least five of its seven members. If the commission agrees on a plan or plans, it would submit them to the Legislature. Under existing law, the commission must hold similar public hearings but has only 14 days after the last public hearing to attempt to agree to three plans that each has the support of five of the seven members. If the commissioners agree, they would submit the plans to the Legislature.
    • If at least five commissioners cannot agree to at least one plan, the commission would submit at least two plans with bare majority support to the Chief Justice of Utah Supreme Court. At least one of those plans would need to be supported by the commissioner appointed jointly by the leadership of the majority political party in the Senate and the leadership of that party in the House. Another plan would need to be supported by the commissioner appointed jointly by the leadership of the minority political party in the Senate and the leadership of that party in the House. The Chief Justice would select up to three of the plans and submit them to the Legislature. Under existing law, if at least five commissioners cannot agree to three plans, the commission would submit plans to the Legislature that have majority support. At least one plan's majority must include the person appointed jointly by the Senate President and the Speaker of the House. Another plan's majority must include the person appointed jointly by the minority party's leadership in the Senate and the House. The Chief Justice has no role under existing law.
    • When the commission submits plans to the Legislature, it must also submit a report detailing how the plans comply with the criteria required by the bill. These submissions must be made at least 10 days before the Legislature votes on the plan(s). The Legislature would then vote on the plan without amendment, and if the Legislature rejects the plan, the Legislature could create its plan. Under existing law, the legislative redistricting committee must hold a public hearing on the plan and take public comment on the plan, but the committee and Legislature do not have to vote on it. After failing to adopt a commission-submitted plan the Legislature may adopt its own.
  • Create a new process for the Legislature to adopt its plans if it rejects the commission's plans. Specifically, the Legislature would:
    • Be required to follow the same criteria the commission did in drawing plans. Under existing law, the independent commission must follow certain criteria, but the Legislature is not similarly bound.
    • Make its plan available to the public, including on the internet, not less than 10 calendars before adopting it. The plan must be available in a way that allows the public to assess its compliance with the redistricting criteria, and submit comments on it. Existing law imposes no similar requirement.
    • Issue "a detailed written report" explaining why it rejected the commission's plan and why its plan better satisfies the redistricting criteria. The Legislature would issue this report no less than seven calendar days after enacting its plan. The commission could, by majority vote, issue public statements, assessments, and reports responding to the Legislature's actions. Existing law imposes no similar requirement.
  • Impose criteria that both the commission and the Legislature would need to follow when drawing plans. Specifically, they would have to consider, in this order of priority:
    • Adhering to the U.S. Constitution and federal law, including, to the extent required, achieving equal population among districts using the most recent Census. Under existing law, the commission must comply with the U.S. Constitution and federal law, use the most recent Census, ensure that Congressional districts do not deviate in population by more than 1% and other district types not deviate by more than 10%
    • Minimizing the division of municipalities and counties, giving first priority to minimizing the division of municipalities and second priority to minimizing the division of counties. Under existing law, the commission must define and follow a criterion relating to minimizing the division of municipalities and counties. Existing law does not rank preserving municipalities over counties and does not rank criteria more generally.
    • Creating districts that are geographically compact. Existing law requires the commission to draw reasonably compact districts.
    • Creating districts that are contiguous and that allow for the ease of transportation throughout the district. Existing law requires the commission to draw contiguous districts but does not address ease of transportation.
    • Preserving traditional neighborhoods and local communities of interest. Existing law requires the commission to define and apply a standard for preserving communities of interest.
    • Following natural and geographic features, boundaries, and barriers. Existing law allows the commission to define and apply a standard for following these features.
    • Maximizing boundary agreement among different types of districts. Existing law does not address this criterion.
  • Prohibit the consideration of certain kinds of data or priorities. Specifically, the commission and Legislature could not:
    • Divide districts in a manner that purposefully or unduly favors or disfavors any incumbent elected official, candidate, or prospective candidate for elective office, or any political party. Existing law does not have a similar prohibition.
    • Use partisan political data and information, such as partisan election results, voting records, political party affiliation information, and residential addresses of incumbent elected officials and candidates or prospective candidates for elective office. Under existing law, the commission could choose to define and follow a standard that prohibited considering these factors.
  • Require the Legislature and commission would use judicial standards, the best available data, and scientific and statistical methods, including measures of partisan symmetry, to assess whether a plan meets the criteria. This requirement is explicitly exempted from the prohibition on using partisan data. Existing law does not have a similar provision.
  • Require the Legislature and commission to make computer software and information and data concerning proposed redistricting plans reasonably available to the public so that the public has a meaningful opportunity to review redistricting plans and assess their compliance with the criteria. Existing law does not have a similar provision.

  • Create a private right of action to enable people to challenge a redistricting plan the Legislature adopts. Existing law has no similar provision. Specifically:

    • Any person who resides or is domiciled in the state, or whose executive office or principal place of business is in the state, would be able to sue in a court of competent jurisdiction without posting a bond.
    • The court would assess if the enacted plan complied with the redistricting standards, procedures, and requirements, and if not, the court would enjoin the plan, barring its implementation. The court could also issue a temporary restraining order or preliminary injunction while the litigation was pending.
    • If the plaintiff prevailed, the court would order the defendant to pay attorneys' fees, expert witness fees, and related costs.
    • If the court determines the plaintiff brought the case for an improper purpose, or their claims were frivolous, the court would order the plaintiff to pay the defendants' legal fees and related costs.
    • Governmental immunity would be waived to enable these suits and fee orders.

    Last updated March 11, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on January 12, 2022, would end no-excuse absentee voting by mail in Virginia and replace it with excuse-only absentee voting by mail, and no-excuse absentee voting in person. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create excuse-only absentee voting in person by allowing only those people who meet one of the following criteria to vote absentee by mail:
    • A person who will be absentee from the city or county on Election Day for business or personal travel.
    • A uniformed, active duty service member temporarily residing outside of the U.S., or the spouse of such a person, if they will be absent on Election Day.
    • A higher education student or their spouse who will be absent on Election Day.
    • A person with a disability who is unable to go to the polls on Election Day because of the voter's disability, illness, or pregnancy.
    • A person incarcerated awaiting trial or after a misdemeanor conviction.
    • An election official or election worker.
    • A person who cannot go to the polls on Election Day because the voter has primary responsibility for the care of an ill or disabled family member who is confined at home.
    • A person who has a religious obligation on Election Day.
    • A person who will be away from home at work on Election Day for at least 11 hours of the 13 hours that polls are open.
    • A law enforcement office, firefighter, volunteer firefighter, search and rescue personnel, or EMS personnel.
    • A designee of a political party or candidate who is the party or candidate's representative inside a polling place on Election Day.
    • A person granted a protective order.
  • Creating an in-person absentee voting period of two tiers, with a longer period for people with an excuse and a shorter people for people who do not meet one of the enumerated excuses.
    • Absentee voters with a valid excuse could vote absentee in-person from 45 days before Election Day to the second Friday before Election Day.
    • Any voter, regardless of whether they have a valid excuse, could vote absentee in-person from the second Saturday before Election Day until 5:00 p.m. on the Saturday before Election Day.

  • Change the makeup of the state board of elections.   • Require a tiebreaker board member. Under existing law, the board consists of five members, so a tiebreaker member is unnecessary, however, this version of the bill requires the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Virginia to designate a retired Virginia circuit court judge to serve as the tiebreaker for the eight member board for a one year term, but who would otherwise have non voting privileges. This is a new provision that was not included in the previous version of the bill.

Under existing law, any adjudication of incapacity leads to a voter losing the eligibility to vote.

    • A person who has a religious obligation on Election Day.
    • A person who will be away from home at work on Election Day for at least 11 hours of the 13 hours that polls are open.
    • A law enforcement office, firefighter, volunteer firefighter, search and rescue personnel, or EMS personnel.
    • A designee of a political party or candidate who is the party or candidate's representative inside a polling place on Election Day.
    • A person granted a protective order.

If the signatures are deemed not to match, the ballot will be processed as a provisional ballot and will not be counted unless the voter completes a cure affidavit and provides a copy of their ID before noon on the third day after Election Day. This bill would require notice to the voter of the mismatch via email, text message, phone call, and, for ballots returned more than seven days before Election Day, mail.

  • End the permanent absentee voting list for all voters and only allow voters who are eligible for an absentee ballot because of disability or illness to file an annual application to receive ballots for all elections for the calendar year. The first time such a voter applies for an annual application, the application must be signed by the voter's physician or religious practitioner that the voter is eligible for an absentee ballot on the grounds of disability or illness.   • Evaluate the potential for partisan pressure and influence in state and local election decision-making.
  • Review funding provided by state and local governments.

  • Develop objective performance metrics for state and local election officials.

This bill, as introduced January 11, 2022, would establish enhanced criminal penalties for certain serious threats made against election officials and other public officials with the intent to influence the targeted individual's official conduct or in retaliation for previous official conduct. Such threats would be punishable by a term of imprisonment of up to three years, a fine of up to $1000, or both. Under existing law, such conduct would be punishable by a term of imprisonment of up to one year, a fine of up to $1000, or both.

Last updated April 18, 2022.

This bill, as enacted on March 17, 2022, expands the misdemeanor offense of electioneering, requires each county auditor to issue rules designating the entrance and exits for each voting location, gives election officials more flexibility to site a required vote center in certain circumstances, and requires county auditors to operate vote centers in their offices. Specifically, the bill:

  • Expands the locations at which electioneering is prohibited to include:
    • inside student engagement hubs,
    • within 100 feet of the entrance of a vote center or student engagement hub, and
    • within 25 feet of a drop box.
      Existing law only prohibited electioneering inside vote centers.
  • Requires the county auditor to designate by rule the entrance and exit for each voting location and to post signage. Existing law did not have a comparable provision.
  • Prohibits electioneering using amplified sound from further away than the physical boundaries if the electioneering can be understood within the electioneering-free zones. Existing law did not address amplified electioneering.
  • Clarifies that the electioneering restrictions cannot be construed to limit or otherwise restrict the access of an authorized political party observer to a voting center, student engagement hub, or ballot drop box to observe the election process. Existing law did not contain a similar provision.

  • Requires county auditors to open a vote center - providing voter registration, ballots, a ballot drop box, and other voting resources - in the auditor's office, or at the division of elections if it is in a separate location from the office. Existing law required vote centers to be located in public buildings, but did not specify specific locations, and required auditors to register voters in person at the auditor's office and the division of elections if it was located in a different city.

Last Updated September 20, 2022

HISTORY: {"date":"01/10/2022","summary":"To HOUSE Committee on STATE GOVERNMENT & TRIBAL RELATIONS","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 10, 2022, would require all voting be done manually, on specially watermarked paper ballots, and all ballot counting be done by hand. The bill would make several related changes to the election code, including:

  • repealing the secretary of state's authority to certify electronic voting machines or ballot tabulators, including accessible machines for disabled voters.
  • repealing the requirement that election officials offer accessible voting machines at each vote center.
  • repealing the ability of localities to receive grants to upgrade their election equipment.
  • repealing the ability of UOCAVA voters to return ballots by fax or email.
  • requiring ballot canvassers to reject ballots that lack the special watermark, or are returned by email or fax.
  • repealing the ability of voters to obtain a replacement ballot by telephone request, by mail, or electronically, leaving only the option of obtaining a replacement ballot in person.

  • requiring all counts, recounts, and audits be done by hand.

    Unrelated to the elimination of electronic voting and ballot tabulation, the bill would also require ballot canvassers to reject ballots returned by mail that have a missing or illegible postmark. Existing law, which requires ballots that are returned by mail to be postmarked on or before Election Day, treats a ballot with a missing or illegible postmark that is received after Election Day as returned on the day the ballot declaration is signed. As a result, this provision functionally shortens the ballot return deadline for these ballots.

Last Updated February 1, 2022

HISTORY: {"date":"01/10/2022","summary":"To HOUSE Committee on STATE GOVERNMENT & TRIBAL RELATIONS","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 10, 2022, would cancel the voter registration of anyone who has not provided documentary proof of citizenship, and would require such proof to register going forward. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require county auditors to do a one-time review of the voter registration list to determine which registered voters in their county also have enhanced driver's licenses or state IDs, which require proof of citizenship to receive.
  • Require the auditors to cancel the registration of any voter that does not have an enhanced license or ID.
  • Require the auditors to send notice to the cancelled voters, informing them that they may prove citizenship and re-register.

  • Require new registrants, including those using the online voter registration system, to prove citizenship as part of their registration.

    • People who wish to register online would be able to with an enhanced driver's license or ID number, but not a regular one. Existing law allows people to use any Washington driver's license or ID. People who wish to use tribal ID to use the online system may only do so if the system is able to access both a copy of their signature, which is required under existing law, and proof that they are citizens, which would be new.
    • When a county auditor receives a paper application, they would be required to determine if the applicant has an enhanced license or ID. If not, the auditor would be prohibited from processing the registration, but would be required to contact the applicant to request proof of citizenship. If the applicant provides the proof, the auditor would immediately register the voter.

    Valid proofs of citizenship would be:


  • A valid United States passport
  • A United States certificate of naturalization
  • A United States department of state consular report of birth abroad

  • An original, certified birth certificate from a United States birth place, issued by a city, county, state, or territory, that contains all of the following:

    • Full name and date of birth,
    • Place of birth, which must be a United States location,
    • A registrar's raised, embossed, impressed, or multicolored seal,
    • A control or file number that the issuing authority can confirm,
    • A registrar's signature, and
    • The date the certificate was filed with the registrar's office.

    These documents could not be used to prove citizenship:


  • Birth certificates from Puerto Rico issued before July 1, 2010, and

  • Washington wallet-sized birth registrations.

Last Updated January 11, 2022

BILLSUMMARY: Concerns the timely processing of updated voter registration information.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 10, 2022, would make timing changes to maintaining the statewide voter registration database and require county auditors to take "forensic images" of the database. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the county auditor to update voter registration information in the statewide voter registration database as soon as practicable and no later than the next business day after receiving the new information.
  • Require the county auditor to "capture a forensic image of the voter registration database both before and after updating a voter's registration information in the database." The bill does not define a "forensic image".
  • Require election officials doing same day registration to update voter registration information in the statewide voter registration database as soon as practicable and no later than the next business day, and to capture a "forensic image" of the database both before and after updating.

  • Require voter registration agencies and the department of licensing to send voter registration applications to the secretary of state or the appropriate county auditor within one business day instead of existing law's three business day deadline.

    Last updated January 10, 2022.

This bill, as enacted on March 24, 2022, prohibits public disclosure of a voter's signature, phone number, and email address on ballot envelopes, ballot declarations, and ballot envelope signature correction forms. The Secretary of State is authorized, but not required, to issue rules to allow in-person inspection of unredacted ballot envelopes, ballot declarations, and signature correction documents.

HISTORY: {"date":"02/03/2022","summary":"To HOUSE Committee on STATE GOVERNMENT & TRIBAL RELATIONS","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 2, 2022, would create a new "forensic audit" process for general elections, limit the existing audit processes to special elections and primaries while modifying the requirements, prevent certification of election results until audits are complete, shift a significant amount of election authority from the Secretary of State to the State Auditor, including giving the State Auditor a role in certifying elections. The bill would also change voter list maintenance practices and authority, deeming the county voter registration lists authoritative instead of the state list, and otherwise transferring election authority from the Secretary of State to county auditors.

Regarding "forensic audits" for general elections beginning in 2022, the bill would:

  • Create the state election audit board, comprised of the State Auditor, or the auditor's authorized designee, four randomly selected election observers representing four geographic locations throughout the state, and two precinct committee officers, one Democrat and one Republican. A board would serve for one general election cycle, beginning in 2022. The audit would be completed within 30 days of Election Day and must be completed before the certification of the results.
  • Require the audit board to contract with "an impartial, nonpartisan, and bonded third-party audit vendor" to conduct a "forensic audit" of the relevant general election. No vendor could be used more than once every three years.
  • Specify that the forensic audit would include a manual hand count audit to determine the vote total to be used in certifying the election.
    • The hand count would include every ballot in every precinct in the 10 most populous counties and in at least 10 percent of the precincts in all other counties, randomly selected.
    • If the hand count total is different than the tabulated total, a second hand count would be done. If it matches the first hand count, the hand count results would be used to certify the election. Similarly, if the second hand count matches the tabulated total, that result would be used for certification. If none of the three match, then the audit board would investigate and determine the accurate count before the date of certification.
    • In addition, the vendor would reconcile the county's ballot totals, specifying totals from ballot production through canvass completion. The vendor would also reconcile the number of registered voters for the general election being audited, the number of ballots mailed, received, accepted, rejected, and duplicated, the number of provisional ballots, the number of counted ballots, and the number of final votes cast.
  • Specify that the forensic audit would include a review of the voter registration database. The third-party audit vendor would create a log of voter registrations added to the database, revisions made to existing registrations, and cancellations, made between January 1st of the year being audited and the date the audit began.
    • The log would include the name of each person who modified the voter registration database, the location from which they modified the database, what specifically was modified, and how the modification was done. The log would also include the source of information relied upon to make the modification. The third-party audit vendor would be required to verify the source's legitimacy and check for any invalid entries, revisions, or cancellations.
    • The third-party audit vendor would also search for duplicate entries using a comparison of the name, date of birth, and valid state-issued identification number.
  • Specify the audit would include the voting systems used in the election to ensure proper setup, calibration, maintenance, and function of these systems.
  • Require the audit vendor to video the proceedings and follow procedures relating to pens, worker clothing, inspecting ballots to confirm they were completed by people.
  • Require the audit vendor to capture myriad "forensic images" before and after the election and audit them.
  • Require the state election audit board and the third-party audit vendor to investigate any affidavits or complaints concerning the general election being audited, even if they were submitted to a county auditor, the state auditor, or the secretary of state.
  • Require the audit vendor to determine who authorized, and what procedures were followed for, sending out unsolicited absentee voter ballot applications in each general election. Under existing law, Washington conducts its elections by mail and voters do not apply for ballots.
  • Require the county auditor to do detailed ballot-related record keeping and use specified materials.

  • Require each county and its election officials, election employees, and election volunteers shall cooperate with the audit vendor, or be subject to subpoena, warrant, criminal prosecution, or civil penalty. Counties would be subject to a minimum fine of $5,000 per day of refusal. Intentionally and knowingly committing fraud during any part of the election or audit process would be a felony. Fines would be collected by the state auditor, and the attorney general would be authorized to enforce the fines. Fines would be put in a special fund to finance these activities. Prosecutions would be by county prosecutors.

    With regard to auditing primary and special elections, the bill would modify the existing audit process to require counties to use two of four methods, instead of one, would increase the amount of equipment being audited and require the audits to be open to observation by officially appointed observers and the general public.

    The bill would give the State Auditor election authority it does not currently have:


  • Authority relating to results certification, audit design, election equipment, cybersecurity, petition validation, and chains of custody from the Secretary of State.

  • Authority relating to duplicating ballots from the county board of canvassers.

    The bill would change voter registration list maintenance practices by


  • Shifting authority from the Secretary of State to County Auditors by designating the county voter registration list as the definitive list, and resolving any discrepancies between it and the state list in favor of the county.
  • Eliminating the Secretary's authority to coordinate the state database with other states', and require the Secretary to give the auditor updated information derived from coordinating the state database with the other allowed databases. In addition, the bill would repeal the requirement that the database comply with the federal Help America Vote Act.
  • Requiring the Secretary to screen voter registrations against databases to verify Washington residency. Existing law has no equivalent requirement.

  • Requiring voter list maintenance no later than 60 days before Election Day focused on identifying voters who moved using change of address information from the Postal Service, and on voters who died, using both state data and data from the Social Security Administration. Under current law, these processes happen at different times and do not include data from the Social Security Administration.

    Finally, the bill would restrict who a voter could choose to return their ballot for them, change ballot processing timelines, and create a new reason to reject ballots. Specifically, the bill would:


  • Require all ballots to be processed and counted before midnight on the seventh day after the election. Under existing law, ballots postmarked on or before Election Day are timely, and voters have until the day before results are certified to cure issues with their ballot envelope. Under existing law, a general election must be certified within 21 days, and other election types are generally 10 to 14 days.
  • Require the rejection of any ballot lacking a newly required watermark.
  • Restrict a voter's choices as to who may return their completed, sealed ballot for them. Specifically, a voter could only choose their spouse, family member, legal guardian, or other person they have had an in-person continuous relationship with of 12 months or more. Voters would be expressly prohibited from choosing an organization or other entity.

  • Create a felony to enforce the restriction on third-party return.

Last Updated March 2, 2022

BILLSUMMARY: Concerns dates and timelines associated with the operation of the state primary and elections.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced January 11, 2022, would move the state's primary from August to May, triggering a cascade of other date changes. Although Voting Rights Lab does not track the timing of primaries, one of the date changes relates to the timeline and process to alter election precincts, which we do track.

The bill changes precinct boundary revisions in two ways. Under the bill:

  • the deadline to alter precinct boundaries in the ordinary course would become seven days before candidates may begin to file their candidacies for the primary, instead of 14 days before the filing window opens. For offices that will be filled at the next regular general election, because of the shift in the primary's date, the time frame in which precinct boundaries must remain static is sharply increased despite making the deadline closer to the filing window. Specifically, the bill would open the filing window on the fourth Monday in February, instead of the Monday two weeks before Memorial Day. The filing window, and thus deadline to change precincts for a special election, would continue to depend on the special election's date.

  • the county auditor must propose precinct boundary changes up to 45 days before the candidacy filing window opens. The county legislative authority may use those 45 days to modify, or reject the proposal. If the county takes no action, the temporary changes take effect. Existing law does not provide a parallel timeline. Instead it requires enough time before the deadline to honor the necessary procedural steps.

    Last updated January 11, 2022.

Specifically, the Redistricting Commission would be required to make a redistricting plan publicly available at least 72 hours before voting to approve the plan. Once the plan has been made publicly available, the commission would be required to debate and vote on any amendments in open session. Last, the commission would be required wait at least 24 hours after any amendments are adopted before the commission could vote on final approval of the plan. Existing law does not have this requirement. The commission completing the 2020 redistricting took actions that would be prohibited by this bill, although the bill's prospective focus would leave the 2020 redistricting intact.

BILLSUMMARY: Concerns Washington Voting Rights Act, makes changes concerning vote dilution, certain protected citizens, requirements of specified superior courts, and related remedies.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as engrossed on February 10, 2022, would create a temporary preclearance regime for various election law changes to prevent discrimination, revise the existing prohibitions against vote dilution, and create a state data repository that could be used to identify discrimination. The engrossed bill is substantially the same as the versions recommended by committees on January 26 and February 7 and is significantly narrower than the version introduced on January 10, 2022. The only significant difference between the February 7th committee bill and the bill engrossed on February 10th is that the engrossed bill repeals the preclearance provisions on June 30, 2029.

Preclearance Provisions

The engrossed bill would create a process for a "covered jurisdiction" to seek preclearance for a "covered practice" through June 30, 2029. Existing law has no comparable provisions. Specifically:

  • A covered jurisdiction could seek preclearance by filing for a declaratory judgment in Thurston County superior court or, if the jurisdiction is located within Thurston county, King county superior court, or by submitting the covered practice to the state Attorney General for a certification of no objection. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. As introduced, the bill allowed covered jurisdictions to seek preclearance in any county superior court. Olympia, the state capital, is located in Thurston County.
  • If the Attorney General objects, refusing to grant preclearance, the jurisdiction can appeal to the Thurston County superior court. If the Attorney General does not object, an affected voter may appeal to any superior court. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. As introduced, the bill would have allowed the jurisdiction to appeal to any county's superior court.

  • When deciding these cases, the court or the Attorney General must block the proposed practice unless it determines that:

    • it would not violate the anti-vote dilution provisions, and
    • it would not result in the diminution of the ability of a protected class to participate in the electoral process or elect candidates of their choice such that the covered practice does not have the purpose or effect of diminishing the ability of any citizen on account of race, color, or membership in a language-minority group to do so.
      This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

    The covered jurisdictions would be:

  • A political subdivision that meets two criteria:
    • First, it must have at least one racial, ethnic, or language minority group which is at least 10 percent of its voting-age population, as determined every fifth calendar year by the Secretary of State in consultation with the Attorney General, the office of financial management, and other relevant agencies, using the most recent American community survey data. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. As introduced, the bill would have required the determination to be made every year.
    • Second, it must be a city with at least 10,000 residents, a county with at least 50,000 residents, or be a port district. The Secretary of State would notify those counties, cities, and towns that meet both criteria, and the Attorney General would publish a list of them on a website established and maintained for this purpose.
  • A school district with at least 2,000 students. .
  • A political subdivision which, within the previous 25 years, has become subject to a court order or government enforcement action based upon a finding of any violation of this chapter, the federal Voting Rights Act, the Fifteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution, or a voting-related violation of the Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution.
  • A political subdivision that, within the previous five years, has failed to comply with its obligations to provide data or information to the statewide repository created by this bill.

  • A political subdivision which, within the previous 25 years, has become subject to at least three court orders or government enforcement actions based upon a finding of any violation of state or federal civil rights law or the Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution concerning discrimination against members of a protected class.

    This definition of covered jurisdiction was in the previous version of the bill. As introduced, the bill did not specify a subset of political subdivisions to which the language requirement applied and did not include school districts without the language requirement, but otherwise included this definition.

    Covered practices would be:

  • Any change to the method of election of members of a governing body by adding seats elected at large or by converting seats elected from a single-member district to at-large seats or seats from a multi-member district. This provision was in the bill as introduced.
  • Any change, or series of changes within 12 months, to the boundaries of the covered jurisdiction that reduces by more than five percentage points the proportion of the jurisdiction's voting-age population that is composed of members of a single racial or language-minority group, as determined by the most recent American community survey data. This provision was in the bill as introduced.
  • Any change to the boundaries of election districts in the covered jurisdiction. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. As introduced, the bill also included changes in the boundaries of the covered jurisdiction itself.
  • Any change that restricts the ability of any person to provide interpreter services to voters or which limits non-English voting materials. This provision was in the bill as introduced.

  • Any change to the covered jurisdiction's plan of government, including a change to or in the framing of a jurisdiction's charter. This provision was in the bill as introduced.

    Vote Dilution Provisions

    The engrossed bill would expand and revise existing vote dilution prevention provisions primarily by changing various aspects of vote dilution litigation and expanding plaintiffs' cost recovery options. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Change the substance of vote dilution litigation by:
    • Providing that no single factor is dispositive or necessary to establish a vote dilution violation. This provision was in the bill as introduced. Existing law has no comparable provision.
    • Focusing on polarized voting. This provision was in the bill as introduced. Existing law relates to racially polarized voting.
    • Defining a protected class as including a cohesive coalition of members of different racial, ethnic, or language minority groups. This provision was in the bill as introduced. Existing law has no comparable provision.
  • Expand who may bring enforcement actions, and the timing of enforcement actions by:
    • allowing an organization whose membership includes or is likely to include a voter who resides in the challenged political subdivision to bring an enforcement action. This provision was in the bill as introduced. Under existing law, only a voter who resides in the challenged political subdivision may sue.
    • clarifying that a cohesive coalition of different protected classes may file a vote dilution action jointly if they demonstrate that the combined voting preferences of the multiple protected classes are polarized against the rest of the electorate. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Under existing law, plaintiffs looking to join together must meet that standard, but existing law simply speaks of "members" of different protected classes rather than a "cohesive coalition" of them.
  • Change remedies to vote dilution claims by:
    • repealing language expressly giving the court authority to order the jurisdiction to draw or redraw district boundaries, or to appoint a person to do so. Instead, the bill would provide that If the court orders a district-based remedy, the court must approve proposed district boundaries before their implementation, expressly determining that the proposed district boundaries will not have a dilutive effect on the protected class. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Under existing law, the court must approve proposed boundaries before implementation but need not determine that the new boundaries will not have a dilutive effect.
    • providing that in tailoring a remedy, the court must consider proposed remedies by the parties and not defer to the remedy proposed by the political subdivision. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law does not have a comparable provision.
    • prohibiting a judge from ordering a remedy that has a dilutive effect on the protected class. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law does not have a comparable provision.

  • Expand plaintiffs' ability to recover costs for enforcement actions, by:

    • providing that if plaintiffs succeed in using the existing notice process to achieve a remedy without a lawsuit, they can recover costs up to $50,000.
    • providing that to establish a plaintiff "prevailed" in litigation and is thus able to recover costs and fees, a plaintiff does not need to achieve relief or favorable judgment. Instead, they may demonstrate that they succeeded in altering the political subdivision's behavior to correct a claimed harm, including, but not be limited to, the subdivision's adopting a new method of electing a governing body, modifying district boundaries, or amending a voting rule or qualification. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.

    Data Collection and Reporting

    The bill would create a statewide repository at the University of Washington to assist the state and political subdivisions with evaluating whether and to what extent existing voting and elections practices are consistent with the public policies in the election code, with implementing best practices to achieve those policies, and to investigate potential violations. All of these provisions were in the previous version of the bill. Specifically:

  • The repository would be managed by a University of Washington employee who has doctoral-level expertise in demography, statistical analysis, and electoral systems, and who would be appointed by the Governor. This is a modified provision. As introduced, this director of the repository would have been required to be a faculty member. This director would appoint such staff as are necessary to implement and maintain the repository. Those staff would also provide nonpartisan technical assistance to political subdivisions, scholars, and the general public.
  • Staff would prepare any estimates by applying the most advanced, peer-reviewed, and validated methodologies.
  • The repository would be publicly available, online, except for any data, information, or estimates that identify individual voters.
  • The repository would include at least 12 years of the following data:
    • Estimates of the total population, voting-age population, and citizen voting-age population by race, ethnicity, and language-minority groups, broken down to the election district and precinct level on a year-by-year basis for every political subdivision in the state, based on data from the United States census bureau, American community survey, or data of comparable quality collected by a public office.
    • Election results at the precinct level for every statewide election and every election in every political subdivision.
    • Regularly updated voter registration lists, voter history files, voting center locations, ballot drop box locations, and student engagement hub locations for every election in every political subdivision.
    • Contemporaneous maps, descriptions of boundaries, and shapefiles for election districts and precincts.
    • Ballot rejection lists, curing lists, and the reasoning for ballot rejection for every election in every political subdivision.
    • Apportionment plans for every election in every political subdivision.
    • Any other data that the director deems advisable to maintain in furtherance of the purposes of the election code.
  • The Secretary of State would, upon certifying each election's results and completing the voter history file, send the data to the director, who would have to add it to the repository within 30 business days. The data would include:
    • Election results at the election district level,
    • Contemporaneous voter registration lists,
    • Voter history files,
    • Maps, descriptions, and shapefiles for election districts, and
    • Lists of vote centers and student engagement hubs.

  • On or before January 1, 2023, and every fifth year thereafter, the repository would publish on its website, and transmit to the state for dissemination to the county auditors, a list of political subdivisions required by federal law to assist members of language-minority groups, and in which languages. Each county auditor would then transmit the list described herein to all political subdivisions within their jurisdiction.

    Numerous provisions that were in the bill as introduced have been amended out of it. The removed provision would have:

  • Defined a political subdivision as presumptively in violation of the vote dilution prohibitions and created a standard for the subdivision to rebut the presumption. This provision was removed by committee on January 26.
  • Provided that evidence concerning elections of the governing body of the challenged political subdivision is more probative than evidence concerning other elections. Statistical evidence would have been deemed more probative to establish the existence of polarized voting than nonstatistical evidence. This provision was removed by committee on January 26.
  • Identified a nonexclusive list of other factors which help prove a vote dilution violation, and clarified that evidence of those factors concerning the state, private actors, or other political subdivisions in the geographic region could have been considered but would have been less powerful than evidence concerning the political subdivision itself. This provision was removed by committee on January 26.
  • Identified factors relevant to shaping a vote dilution remedy, but which could not have been used to prevent finding a violation. This provision was removed by committee on January 26.
  • Limited arguments a political subdivision could have used to defend against a vote dilution claim. Specifically, a political subdivision could not use partisanship, or characteristics that are a proxy for partisanship, as a defense. This provision was removed by committee on January 26.
  • Declared that the data, information, and estimates maintained by the repository would be granted a rebuttable presumption of validity by any court concerning any preclearance or vote dilution claim. This provision was removed by committee on January 26.
  • Allowed suit 50 days after serving notice of an alleged violation to the political subdivision. This provision was removed by committee on February 7. Existing law allows suit after 90 days.

  • Included as a covered practice any change that reduces or relocates voting centers or ballot drop boxes in the covered jurisdiction or on a Native reservation, except where permitted by law in the event of an emergency. This provision was removed by committee on February 7.

This bill, as substituted and recommended by committee on January 26, 2022, would expand automatic voter registration in the state. The committee's changes will not be effective until the Senate adopts them, but it is the form of the bill moving forward. The discussion below addresses the committee substitute, and indicates how it differs from the introduced version. As substituted by committee on January 26, 2022, the bill would change how Washington's automatic voter registration system at the Department of Licensing (the state's DMV) works, in ways that expand who will be automatically registered, without changing the existing requirement that the system register only people who prove they are U.S. citizens as part of the DMV transaction. Second, it would revise the voter registration process done by the state health exchange, however, these changes would no longer convert the process into a fully automatic one, nor would the state Medicaid agency be required to automatically register its applicants. As introduced, the bill would have changed existing law in both of those ways.

Revising Automatic Registration at the Department of Licensing
The bill, as substituted by committee, would:

  • Provide that the Department of Licensing must allow people to use the automated system to be registered to vote, or update their registration if they are qualified and the Department's records demonstrate the person is qualified, has all the information necessary, and a signature record, regardless of the type of permit, license, or ID that they are applying for, updating or renewing. Under existing law, automatic registration is limited to people doing transactions relating to enhanced licenses or identification cards, which require proof of citizenship to obtain.
  • Expand these new provisions further by covering pre-registering 16 and 17 year olds automatically. As introduced, the bill made this same change but through slightly different drafting. Under existing law, the existing system is scheduled to expand to these teenagers on January 1, 2023, which is the date this bill would take effect.
  • Require the Department of Licensing, in consultation with the Secretary of State, to determine which documents accepted for driver's license transactions prove U.S. citizenship, prove non-citizenship, or do not demonstrate citizenship status either way. This provision was in the bill as introduced.
  • Require the Department of Licensing to implement an electronic information system that allows it to determine, at the time of the individual's driver's license transaction, whether the individual is currently registered or pre-registered to vote. This provision was in the bill as introduced.
  • Require the Department to take different actions for people who are not already registered or pre-registered, depending on what an individual's transaction documents indicate about their citizenship status. These provisions were in the bill as introduced. Specifically:
    • If the transaction involves an enhanced drivers license/ID or the person has submitted a document proving citizenship for a different type of transaction, the Department would automatically register them. Existing law only automatically registers people doing enhanced license/ID transactions.
    • If the person produces a document proving non-citizenship, the Department would not offer a registration opportunity, automatic or otherwise. Existing law does not have a comparable explicit provision. Under existing law, people who are not doing a transaction that requires them to prove citizenship are simply offered the opportunity to affirmatively choose to register.
    • If the person produces documents that do not indicate citizenship status, they would not be automatically registered, but would be asked if they are a citizen and wish to register. If they answer both questions affirmatively, their information would be electronically transmitted to the Secretary of State. This process is part of existing law, but existing law does not limit who is offered the opportunity in the same way.
    • The Department would also be required to give people who participate in the address confidentiality program a way to participate that will not breach their confidentiality. This provision was in the bill as introduced. Existing law does not have a similar provision.
  • Require the Department, once it has determined that a person should be automatically registered, their registration automatically updated, or, the person has affirmatively requested to be registered or have their registration updated, to, at least daily, send to the Secretary the potential voter's name, address, date of birth, gender, driver's license number, signature image, language preference if known, and the date on which the registration or update was submitted. This provision was in the bill as introduced. Existing law provides for data transmission but does not specify the datapoints nor require the transmission to be daily.
  • Require the Secretary of State, within 30 days of receiving the information from the Department, to cause county auditors to send the voter a voter registration acknowledgment notice by nonforwardable mail. This is a modified provision. As introduced, the bill would have required the Secretary to cause the notice to be sent within 10 days.
  • Provide that if the voter returns the form affirmatively declining to:
    • update their registration, the Secretary would revise the registration list accordingly.
    • become registered, the Secretary would remove them from the list and the person will be deemed to have never registered. However, if the voter casts a ballot in an election before the declination form is received by the Secretary, the declination form will have no force or effect.
      These provisions were in the bill as introduced. The existing process allows people to opt out of voter registration during the transaction, not by a later-mailed form.

  • Require the Secretary of State to cause verification notice to be promptly sent to any applicant whose application is incomplete. The verification notice must require the applicant to provide the missing information. If the applicant provides the required information within 45 days, they would be registered. If they do not, they would not be. This provision was in the bill as introduced. Existing law requires the same notice, deadline, and consequences, but simply states that the auditor will send the notice, not that the Secretary will cause the notice to be sent.

    Revising Registration Through the Health Benefit Exchange
    As substituted by committee, the bill would revise the existing process at the health benefit exchange, but no longer convert the process into a fully automated one by removing the existing requirement that an applicant opt-in to the process, nor create a similar system at the Medicaid agency, changes that the bill as introduced would have made. The committee's bill would change the existing process by:


  • Requiring the health benefit exchange to expand its existing, streamlined opt-in registration process to applicants who are 16 or 17 years old. As introduced, the bill would have included applicants of this age, but would have converted the existing process to a fully automatic, opt-out registration process, and would have required a similar process at the state Medicaid agency.
  • Adding to the information existing law requires the health benefit exchange to send to the Secretary. Specifically, the exchange would additionally send the application date, and, if known, the applicant's language preference, and any other necessary information. As introduced, the bill would have required the application date, language preference if known, and the last four digits of an applicant's Social Security number (SSN4).
  • Limiting who the existing streamlined process to applicants that the health benefit exchange verifies are citizens, but does not specify how they must verify citizenship status. Existing law does not specify who verifies the citizenship of applicants.
  • Requiring the Secretary of State to use the information sent by the health benefit exchange and health care authority to register or pre-register people to vote, or to update their registrations, and to cause a registration confirmation notice be sent to applicants that is substantially similar in form and process to the one used for Department of Licensing applicants. As introduced, the bill similarly referenced the Department's notice and process, but the details of that notice and process were different. Under existing law, all voters who are newly registered or have had their registrations newly updated are sent a notice that is substantially similar to the one required by the bill.
  • Requiring the health benefit exchange to work with the Secretary to obtain signature images from the Department of Licensing or through other means. This is a modified provision. As introduced, this provision also applied to the Medicaid agency. Existing law does not contemplate signature options other than the Department of Licensing.

  • Requiring the exchange, and the Secretary to create a similar process for participants in the address confidentiality program that protects their confidentiality. This provision is modified. As introduced, it also applied to the state Medicaid agency. Existing law has no comparable provision.

    Revising the Automatic Voter Registration Process at Other Agencies
    The bill would change the existing process for expanding automatic voter registration to other state agencies. Specifically, the bill would:


  • Allow applicants to attest to the truth of the information they provide without a signature. Existing law requires attestation by signature.
  • Require reliable verification of citizenship information by database match or by manual verification by the agency during the client transaction. Existing law requires verification using Social Security Administration data or manual verification during the transaction.
  • Provide that the governor, in consultation with the Secretary of State, may decide whether other state agencies that collect names, addresses, dates of birth, and citizenship data may engage in automatic registration, only automatic registration updates, or neither. Any authorized process would have to be substantially similar to the processes used by the Department of Licensing. The process under existing law would allow a potential voter or registrant to opt out of registering or updating their registration during the transaction.

  • Provide that the governor, in consultation with the Secretary of State, could decide to have local or federal agencies offer automatic registration through a similar process, provided that those agencies consent.

    Revising the Notice Sent to All People with New Registrations or Registration Updates. The bill as revised by committee removes language creating special notice procedures for automatically registered or updated voters involving a swifter timeline, extra information, and a special return envelope, and instead revises the existing notice procedures for all voters in similar ways. Under existing law, county auditors send all new voters or newly updated voters a simple acknowledgement notice with their new information by non-forwardable mail within 60 days of the change. The committee bill would:


  • Require auditors to send the notice within 30 days, instead of 60.

  • Require the notice to include:

    • a pre-addressed, postage prepaid return envelope for the voter to decline registration or the registration update.
    • a statement, in all languages required by federal law, explaining that the person has been registered to vote, setting forth the qualifications to vote in this state, instructing the person that if they are not qualified or they do not want to be registered, they should decline to register, and that they may unregister at any time.
    • information about how they can gain more information and assistance in their preferred language.
