This bill, as introduced on January 10, 2022, would require the Washington state patrol to do a "survey" of the accuracy of the signature matching done to validate ballots in the upcoming 2022 election, require reporting of election crime prosecutions, require the state to give county auditors access to a new database for registration list maintenance, would change the registration process at the department of licensing (the DMV equivalent), and provide free enhanced licenses or IDs to poor applicants. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require a "survey" of 5,000 to 10,000 randomly selected ballot envelope signatures per county, depending on the number of registered voters in the county. The "survey" would include "a comparison to measure the accuracy of signatures on voter registrations against signatures on ballot return envelopes." The bill does not impose any signature match training requirements on the state patrol, nor indicate how the comparisons would be done. Existing law requires that everyone doing signature matching as part of ballot canvassing be trained, and sets forth rules about what constitutes a match, which are further supplemented by detailed regulations. The state patrol would report the results of the survey to the legislature and the secretary of state by December 1, 2023.
  • Require the Washington association of prosecuting attorneys to compile and report on cases brought to enforce the election code. The report would be a list of the number of cases referred to prosecutors in the preceding 12 months with a description of the allegations and circumstances, the number of prosecutions initiated based on the referrals, and the current status or ultimate outcome of those cases. The bill does not identify to whom the report must be given, or how it should be published.
  • Require the secretary of state to provide each county auditor free access to a legal research data service that includes death and court records covering the United States to assist in the list maintenance program.
  • Change the process to register voters at the department of licensing who are not being automatically registered as part of an enhanced license or enhanced ID transaction. Instead of simply verbally affirming to the department employee that the person wishes to register and is a U.S. citizen, the employee would present the applicant with a signature pad on which they can affirm their eligibility, including citizenship, and sign. Thereafter, as with existing law, the employee would electronically transmit the applicant's data to the secretary of state for registration.

  • Require the department of licensing to issue enhanced licenses or IDs for free to applicants who have a gross family income of 200 percent of the federal poverty level or less. The bill explains that these IDs involve proving citizenship but that poor people face a barrier in obtaining them. The bill does not link the free IDs enabling poor people to be automatically registered, or helping them vote in person instead of using the ballot they are mailed, or facilitating their use of same day registration, but the provision could help poor people in all three election-related ways.

BILLSUMMARY: Makes it unlawful for public officials and candidates to knowingly make false statements and claims regarding the election process or results of elections conducted within the state.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 13, 2022, is a response to "false claims regarding the validity of the 2020 election." The bill states that such claims are "damaging, but such claims are even more damaging when made by elected officials", cites the events of January 6, 2021, and proposes a new crime for elected officials making such claims.

Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create a gross misdemeanor for an elected official or candidate who has filed for public office who, in relation to any election conducted in the state:
    • "knowingly makes false statements or claims regarding the election process or election results,"
    • "which statements or claims are made for the purpose of undermining the election process or election results and"
    • "are directed to inciting or producing imminent lawless action and"
    • "such statements or claims produce such action".
  • Define the elements of the crime so that:
    • "knowingly makes false statements or claims" would means public statements or claims for which there is no proof or evidence. The bill provides that prosecutor would have to prove that the elected official or candidate knowingly made them.
    • "undermining the election process or election results" would mean the elected official or candidate intended to deceive the public regarding the election process or results of an election conducted in the state, interfered with a voter's ability to cast their ballot, intimidated a voter, or deterred a voter from voting freely.

  • Remove from office anyone convicted of that crime.

This bill, as introduced on February 15, 2022, would allow any candidate contesting election results to require a "full forensic physical and cyber audit" of election results whenever the margin of victory is equal to or greater than the number of absentee ballots. If the Wisconsin Elections Commission, the Attorney General, or the relevant district attorney decide that, based on the review, election threats, election bribery, or election fraud occurred, then the elections would be null and void and the Governor would be required to order a new one.     • A complete examination, including by using "kinematic artifact detection," of all physical ballots.
    • A physical canvass, and an examination of whether county clerks and election officials, including volunteers, followed election rules and regulations mandated by the county.
    • Measures to ensure transparency, including broadcasting audit proceedings by live stream on the Internet.

This bill, as introduced on February 16, 2022, would give the Legislature a direct role in implementing federal election administration guidance, directives, and funds. In addition, it would require the Wisconsin Election Commission (WEC) to retain as counsel both a Republican lawyer and a Democratic lawyer chosen by legislative leaders. None of these provisions have analogs in existing law. Finally, the bill would add data gathering and reporting requirements for municipal, county, and state election officials, both to the public and the Legislature. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require any agency of Wisconsin government, defined in a way that reaches throughout the executive, legislative, and judicial branches of government, that receives a directive or guidance relating to elections from the federal Department of Justice or other federal executive branch agency, to give the directive or guidance, and any communications with the federal agency relating to it, within 48 hours to:
    • the Senate Majority Leader,
    • the Senate Minority Leader,
    • the Speaker of the Assembly,
    • the Assembly Minority Leader,
    • the chairpersons of the standing committees with jurisdiction concerning elections, and
    • the co-chairpersons of the Joint Committee for Review of Administrative Rules.
  • Prohibit any such agency from implementing any such directive or guidance unless the Joint Committee on Review of Administrative Rules approves, either affirmatively, or by failing to schedule a meeting to review the rules within 30 days of receiving notice of the guidance.

The bill would also add rules relating to the disbursement of federal funds for elections. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Prohibit the Governor from disbursing federal election funds to the WEC until the WEC establishes a plan to spend them, submits the plan to the Legislature's Joint Committee on Finance, and the Joint Committee approves the plan either affirmatively or by failing to schedule a meeting to review the plan with 14 working days. If the committee schedules a meeting to review the plan, the Governor and WEC could act only with the approval of the committee.

  • Require the bipartisan Wisconsin Election Commission (WEC) to have bipartisan legal counsel chosen by the legislative leadership of the two major political parties.

    The bill would also add additional voter registration and voting statistics gathering and reporting to that required by existing law. Some of the new reporting requirements would relate to municipal clerks or local boards of election commissions, and some would relate to county clerks and county boards of election commissioners.

    The local officials would be required to report to the WEC and the relevant county clerk or county board of election commissioners, within 30 days of a primary or general election that included a state or federal office, or a statewide referendum, for their municipality:


  • The number of registered voters residing in the municipality on the day of the election.
  • The number of voters who registered to vote beginning on the day of the immediately preceding primary or election and ending on the day of the most recent primary or election.
  • The number of voters who voted absentee ballots by mail.
  • The number of voters who voted absentee ballots in person (early voters).
  • The total number of absentee ballots returned by voters that were not counted, and the reasons why.
  • The number of voters casting ballots at the polling place on Election Day.
  • The number of voters casting provisional ballots, and the number of such ballots not counted because they did not provide the requisite ID in time.
  • The total number of defective ballots that election officials recreated, with a separate itemization of such ballots cast by military and overseas electors, damaged ballots, and ballots recreated for other reasons.
  • The location of each residential care facility and qualified retirement home to which the municipality dispatched special voting deputies, and the number of ballots cast by their residents using special voting deputies.
  • The number of voters whose personally identifiable information on the official registration list maintained by the WEC did not match the personally identifiable information maintained by the department of transportation, beginning on the day of the immediately preceding primary or election and ending on the day of the most recent primary or election, along with a description of each mismatch, and the number of such voters whose registration status was changed from eligible to ineligible.

County election officials would be required to submit an electronic report to the WEC no later than 30 days after each election at which a state or national office is filled or a statewide referendum is held, including any special election:

  • The approximate number of voters in each municipality in the county that the municipal clerk certified to the clerk or board when making their ballot request, and the related number of ballots requested.
  • The number of ballots that the county or board distributed to each municipality in the county.
  • The number of ballots distributed to each municipality that were ultimately cast in the election.
  • The number of ballots that election inspectors rejected, the reasons for rejection, and the number of ballots that were remade by election inspectors and cast.
  • The number of unused ballots.
  • Any other action that the county took to reconcile the total number of ballots with the number of votes cast.
  • An explanation of any discrepancy between the number of ballots ordered by municipalities and the number distributed to them, and of any discrepancy between the number of ballots distributed and the number cast or rejected.

The bill would also impose data reporting and storage requirements on the WEC. Specifically, the bill would require the WEC to:

  • Publish the information in these reports in an easily accessible format on its internet site.
  • Submit each county's report, within 7 days of receiving it, to the Senate Majority Leader, the Senate Minority Leader, the Speaker of the Assembly, the Assembly Minority Leader, the co-chairpersons of the standing committees with jurisdiction concerning elections, and the Legislative Audit Bureau. The Bureau would review the report and, within 30 days, report its findings and recommendations to the Legislature, including a description of any discrepancies it found and an explanation of those discrepancies it received from local election officials.
  • Require the WEC to archive, on the first day of each month, an electronic copy of the official registration list as it appeared on the last day of the previous month and retain that copy for no less than 22 months.

This bill, as introduced on February 16, 2022, would make major changes to how voters apply for and return absentee ballots, how clerks handle absentee ballots, and smaller but significant changes to voter registration.

Concerning changing absentee ballot applications, the bill would:

  • Eliminate an exemption to the rule that a voter include a copy of their photo ID when applying for an absentee ballot. Under existing law, a voter who submitted a copy of their photo ID when applying for an absentee ballot once, and has not moved nor changed their name, need not submit a copy of their ID again when they apply. The bill would repeal that exception and instead require these voters to submit a copy of their ID with each application.
  • Require all voters who wish to vote absentee, including voters attempting to vote early in person, to complete a standalone absentee ballot application with specified data fields before the clerk can give them a ballot. Wisconsin conducts early voting by in-person absentee voting, and thus the form would have to be completed by early voters as well as people requesting a ballot be mailed to them. Current practice integrates the application with the voter's certificate for in-person absentee voters. After the 2020 general election, that integrated form was challenged by litigation brought on behalf of President Trump, asserting that ballots cast without a separate, standalone application form should be invalidated. The form the bill would require would ask for at least:
    • The voter's municipality and county of residence.
    • The voter's name, date of birth, and contact information, including as applicable their telephone number, fax number, and email address.
    • The street address of the voter's legal voting residence.
    • The election at which the voter intends to vote absentee.
    • Whether the voter is a military or overseas voter.
      *The voter's confidential identification serial number if they are in the address confidentiality program
    • The lawful method by which the voter prefers to receive the absentee ballot.
    • Whether the voter is hospitalized for purposes of a special absentee procedure.
  • Create a class 1 felony to punish any clerk who issued an absentee ballot to a voter who did not complete such an application first, including in-person early voters.
  • Reduce the number of elections a voter can apply to receive ballots for with a single application to a single primary and general election pair. Under existing law, a voter can apply to receive ballots for every election in a calendar year.
  • Prohibit municipal clerks, county clerks, or county boards of election commissioners from sending absentee ballot applications or ballots to anyone who has not applied for them. Existing law requires an application before sending out ballots but has no similar prohibition on sending unrequested ballot applications. In 2020, the Wisconsin Election Commission (WEC) sent absentee ballot applications to all voters.
  • Require voters applying for an absentee ballot by fax or email to include a copy of their original written signature with the application, including in PDF form.

  • Prohibit political committees from giving voters mail ballot applications that have a return address other than the municipal clerk or local board of commissioners.

    Concerning clerk and voter handling of absentee ballots, the bill would:


  • Limit who a voter could choose to return their completed, sealed ballot for them. Existing law is silent on who may deliver a ballot for a voter. Under the bill, a voter could return their ballot, or could choose:
    • a member of their immediate family, defined as spouses, siblings, parent and child, and grandparent and grandchild.
    • their legal guardian.
    • any registered voter they designate in writing, provided that no one can return more than two ballots not their own for anyone not immediate family per election, and the person cannot be a candidate nor compensated to return the ballot.
  • Create a felony to punish a person who returned a voter's ballot in violation of these restrictions.
  • Restrict the locations a voter may return their completed ballot to the office of the municipal clerk, an alternate ballot site, or the voter's polling place on Election Day. Under existing law, voters must return their ballots to the clerk, and the WEC has interpreted that statute as giving the clerk discretion to decide how to receive the ballots. Relying on that interpretation, clerks have used drop boxes throughout their municipalities.
  • Prohibit clerks from preprinting or stamping their initials on absentee ballot envelopes, and instead require them to handwrite their initials.

With regard to voter registration, the bill would:

  • Require a person to have a driver's license, state ID, or Social Security number to register to vote. Under existing law, a person who attests to having neither kind of number but who is otherwise eligible can register to vote.
  • Require WEC to maintain a version of a completed online voter reg application that has the voter's electronic signature

  • Allow people to return a voter registration application by a for-profit commercial delivery service.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 16, 2022, would create a voter registration list maintenance compliance program and election law compliance program overseen and enforced by the Legislature's Joint Committee on Finance and the Secretary of Administration by maintaining or reducing the relevant agencies' appropriations and employee levels. The Secretary of Administration is appointed by the Governor. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the Wisconsin Elections Commission (WEC) to submit to the Joint Committee and the Secretary, no later than 15 days after each spring election, a report that details all list maintenance data sharing failures in the preceding 12 months committed by the Department of Transportation, the Department of Corrections, the Department of Health Services or State Registrar, and the WEC itself, about the data it receives from the Electronic Registration Information Center (ERIC).
  • Require the Secretary, no later than ten days after receiving the report, to request that the Joint Committee maintain these agencies' funding or eliminate one or more full-time equivalent employees from any of the agencies, or to lapse or maintain appropriated funds for those agencies.
  • Provide that after receiving the Secretary's request, the Joint Committee could choose to act on the request to lapse funds or reduce employees if:
    • concerning the agencies other than the WEC, the Joint Committee finds that the department or departments failed to comply with applicable election laws, including the list maintenance data sharing program failures.
    • concerning the WEC, the Joint Committee finds that the commission failed to comply with any election law, including relating to ERIC data, or provided erroneous guidance to municipal clerks or other election officials. The Joint Committee would be able to lapse from an appropriation up to an amount equal to $50,000 for each day of noncompliance or provision of erroneous guidance, as determined by the Joint Committee.

  • Provide that if the Joint Committee takes no action within 45 days, the Secretary's request would lapse.

    Last updated February 17, 2022.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 16, 2022, would add jury summonses to the data sources used for voter registration list maintenance, and would require the Wisconsin Election Commission to refer voters to the Attorney General or local law enforcement for criminal investigation if someone is registered to vote or voted and either lacks eligibility for citizenship reasons or does not live at their registration address.

The bill would require each clerk of court to send to the appropriate municipal clerk or local board of elections commissioners, and to the Wisconsin Elections Commission, any juror summons returned that asserted the potential juror was not a citizen or did not live in the circuit for which they were called for jury duty. When the Commission receives such notices, it would be required to determine if such person is a registered voter or has voted. If the Commission determines that the prospective juror is a registered voter and/or has voted, and either lacks eligibility or does not meet the residency requirements for their registration, the Commission would remove their name from the registration list. The Commission would then send notice to both the voter and either the district attorney or Attorney General.

Under existing law, the WEC generally notifies local clerks of registrations to cancel or potentially cancel, rather than cancel them itself, and canceled registrations are not removed from the list, they are marked "ineligible".

Last updated February 17, 2022.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 16, 2022, would change all of the rules and elections processes relating to absentee voters who are deemed "indefinitely confined". Under existing law, indefinitely confined voters do not have to submit a copy of their photo ID when they apply for an absentee ballot, can attest to their status by checking a box on the existing absentee application, and continue to receive absentee ballots for every election without further application. Indefinitely confined status became very controversial in 2020 because of uncertainties around how the pandemic should relate to that status, and was litigated in multiple ways. The bill would change the rules relating to indefinitely confined voters by:

  • Further specifying and limiting who can claim indefinitely confined status. To apply, a person must be unable to travel independently without significant burden because of frailty, physical illness, or a disability that will last longer than one year. Existing law simply says a person must be indefinitely confined due to age, physical illness, infirmity, or disability for an indefinite period.
  • Clarifying that existence of an outbreak or epidemic of a communicable disease in a voter's community does not qualify the voter as indefinitely confined.
  • Requiring voters to use a special application to apply to join the list and receive absentee ballots.
  • Requiring indefinitely confined voters applying for the first time to join the list and receive an absentee ballot to:
    • provide a copy of their photo ID if they possess proof of identification and are not using the online application.
    • provide the number of a current and valid operator's license or ID, along with their name and date of birth if they are using the online application, so long as the Wisconsin Election Commission (WEC) can successfully use that information to verify their identity.
    • attest, in language created by the WEC, to their indefinitely confined status, include the last four digits of their Social Security number, and authorize the WEC to use that number to verify their identity. This attestation would have to be supported by another attestation by someone who is a citizen and at least 18 years old. This last option would only be available to indefinitely confined voters who do not possess photo ID and who are not using the online application.
  • Changing how a voter is removed from the indefinitely confined list. In addition to the reasons the bill does not impact, a voter could be removed if:
    • they fail to cast and return a ballot for a spring election or a general election and they do not renew their application by responding to a notice sent by the clerk within 30 days. Under existing law, the clerk sends the notice any time a voter fails to cast and return a ballot, including after a primary.
    • they vote in person. Existing law does not address this.
    • the clerk receives reliable information that the voter is no longer indefinitely confined because of frailty, physical illness, or a disability that will last longer than one year. Under existing law, the clerk can remove someone upon reliable information that they no longer qualify as indefinitely confined.

  • Creating a new misdemeanor to punish falsely making any statement to qualify as indefinitely confined. Existing law does not have a similarly narrowly tailored crime, however, an existing felony punishes lying to the municipal clerk or local board of election commissioners or any other election official, and an existing misdemeanor punishes falsely making a statement to obtain an absentee ballot.

    In addition to these changes, the bill would require the WEC to facilitate the removal from the list anyone who joined during the period beginning on March 12, 2020, and ending on November 3, 2020. March 12, 2020, is when Governor Evers ordered people to stay at home to minimize the risks posed by Covid-19.

Last Updated February 17, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 16, 2022, would change how the Wisconsin Elections Commission (WEC) responds to complaints that it receives about violations of election law and how it reports on those complaints, and also creates a performance audit of electronic voting systems to be done according to WEC rule from randomly selected units after each general election.

With regard to complaints about election law violations, the bill would:

  • Require the WEC to resolve each complaint within 60 days unless two-thirds of the WEC vote to extend the time by another 60 days, which it could do twice. During that time, the WEC would decide, by a two-thirds vote whether to dismiss the complaint, initiate an investigation, or grant the relief, in whole or in part, that has been requested. If the WEC does not dismiss the complaint, it must investigate it or refer it to the Attorney General or a district attorney. Existing law does not have comparable provisions, although it already provides for the WEC to refer appropriate matters to the Attorney General or district attorney.
  • Allow a person who alleges that an action of the WEC either violated or resulted in a violation of election law to sue in any county where the alleged violation occurred without filing a complaint with the WEC first. Under existing law, people may sue after the WEC completes its process.
  • Change how the WEC reports on its investigations. The bill would require the WEC, within 30 days of resolving a complaint, to give the complaint, with all names and other personally identifiable information redacted, and documentation of complaint's resolution, to the state legislators representing the area where the alleged violation occurred or is occurring, and to the co-chairs of the legislative committees with jurisdiction over elections. Existing law does not have comparable provisions.
  • Require an additional, annual report of the WEC's investigations, that would:
    • Include the number of complaints filed with the WEC, a description of each complaint, and a description of the WEC's responses.
    • Include the number of investigations undertaken by the WEC and a description of them.
    • Include the number of informal reports, including from the election crimes hotline, a description of the general categories of concerns expressed.
    • Be submitted to the Governor and the chief clerk of each house of the Legislature no later than January 31. Under existing law, the WEC files a different annual report with officers that includes a description of each investigation it undertook since the last report. The bill would eliminate the requirement to include the investigations information in that annual report.
  • Require the WEC to testify about this report before the legislative committees with jurisdiction over elections and provide a copy of this report to county and municipal clerks and local boards of election commissioners.
  • Require the WEC to issue rules specifying procedures for its consideration and handling of all formal complaints and informal reports of possible violations of election laws that the commission receives, including reports received via the toll-free hotline.

With regard to electronic voting equipment audits, the bill would:

  • Require a performance audit of the performance of electronic voting systems used in at least 4 reporting units in the city of Milwaukee, at least 4 reporting units in the city of Madison, at least one reporting unit in each of the 20 other largest municipalities, and at least 5 percent of the reporting units in all other municipalities combined. These audits would be completed by November 30 following a general election.
  • Require the WEC to issue rules that
    • establish an error rate for the performance audit
    • establish a process that provides for a random selection of reporting units, and other than the units required for specific jurisdictions, ensures distribution across the state and units that have at least 10 votes cast in them. Finally, the process would provide that the county clerk would oversee the counting of ballots by hand in connection with the audits as a part of the county canvass.
  • Require the Legislative Audit Bureau to analyze the results of the audits and report to the Legislature recommendations for improving the audits and, if needed, improvements to the accuracy of the voting systems. The Bureau would report its analysis and recommendations by January 15.

  • Require the municipal clerk, if a recount is happening, to print and make available for each recount paper copies of all absentee ballot applications received electronically.

    Last updated February 17, 2022.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 17, 2022, would change the absentee ballot certificate and its review in ways that appear likely to lead to additional ballots being disqualified, change the processes relating to election activities in residential care facilities, both during ordinary times and pandemics, prohibit private funding of election administration, and create new election crimes, among other changes to election administration.

The bill would change absentee ballot certificates and their review by:

  • Requiring absentee ballot certificates to include 12 different fields relating to the voter's name and address, and the voter's witness and their address, and requiring clerks to reject ballots if one or more of those fields is blank. Thus the ballot must be rejected if the voter or their witness omitted their municipality, but did include their zip code. Under existing law, ballots must be rejected if the witness's address is incomplete, or more generally if the certificate is improperly completed or missing.
  • Requiring a clerk who determines a voter completed the certificate improperly or returned the ballot without the certificate to post notice of the defect in the voter's information page in the online voter registration system, and allowing the clerk to attempt to notify the voter by other means. Under existing law, the clerk has no similar duty or authorization, although existing law does allow the clerk to return the ballot to the voter whenever time permits to allow the voter to address the issue. The bill maintains that option.

  • Forbidding anyone other than the voter or witness to correct a defect in the certificate, and creating a misdemeanor to enforce the prohibition. Under existing Wisconsin Election Commission (WEC) guidance in place since 2016, clerks are allowed to correct certain errors relating to the witness's address. Clerks have relied on that guidance to ensure that eligible voters' otherwise valid ballots are counted since 2016. Continuing to do so, under this bill, would be a crime.

    The bill would change election activities at retirement homes and residential care facilities by:


  • Prohibiting such a facility from denying access to special voting deputies unless the facility is closed to the public due to a public health emergency or is closed to the public because of an infectious disease incident. To close access, the administrator of the facility would document the issue and inform the municipal clerk or local board of election commissioners. Existing law does not have a similar provision. In the 2020 election, the inability of special voting deputies to access these facilities, and the WEC's guidance that, when access was denied, ballots could be mailed to residents who requested them, proved controversial.
  • Allowing a new kind of special voting deputy, called "personal care voting deputies" to be appointed to supervise absentee voting at the facility whenever traditional special voting deputies are denied access. Any other employee of the facilities could not assist residents with voting in any way other than distributing ballots in their unopened envelopes to residents who had requested them. The personal care voting deputies would be subject to certain rules:
    • They must be people employed or retained by the facility and must be registered to vote in Wisconsin.
    • They cannot assist anyone with registering to vote, only completing absentee ballots. Thus Wisconsin's same-day registration procedure would not be available if personal care voting deputies are used.
    • They must take a training course the bill requires the WEC to create for them.
    • Before helping anyone vote, they must take an oath that they are qualified, understand the proper absentee voting procedure and have read the governing law, understand the penalties for failing to follow the law, and that they must fully and fairly implement the absentee voting law. Finally, the oath must include an acknowledgment that the individual realizes that any error could result in the voter's ballot being rejected and that absentee voting is a privilege and not a constitutional right.
    • They must complete a form that includes their name, the name of each voter they assisted, the type of assistance they provided to each, and the information on the form on the ballot return envelope. This form must be separate from the absentee ballot certificate and delivered to the municipal clerk or local board of election commissioners.
    • At least two personal care voting deputies must be appointed, of different political parties if possible.
  • Changing the timeline for absentee voting deputies to visit facilities. The bill would require the special voting deputies to arrange one or more times to visit the facilities by the 11th working day before Election Day and require the visit to be no later than the 6th working day before the election. Under existing law, these deadlines are the 6th working day and the Monday before Election Day, respectively.
  • Allowing the municipal clerk or the local board of election commissioners to mail ballots to those voters at those facilities who requested them no later than 5 p.m. on the Friday before Election Day if special voting deputies were denied access twice due to a public health emergency or incident of infectious disease. Existing law does not have a similar provision.
  • Requiring the facility to give notice of the days and times the voting deputies will offer voting to each relative of the facility for whom the facility has contact information. Under existing law, relatives must request such notice.

  • Creating new class 1 felonies to prohibit any employee from coercing a resident to register or not register to vote, or to apply to vote absentee or not, to complete their absentee ballot or not, or to vote for or against any person or ballot measure. "Coerce" is not defined.

    The bill would change multiple other aspects of election administration, including prohibiting private funding of elections, prohibiting certain people from being election officials, and other changes. Specifically, the bill would:


  • Prohibit certain types of people from serving as election officials. Existing law has no equivalent. Specifically, these people would be prohibited:
    • People employed by a candidate committee, legislative campaign committee, political action committee, independent expenditure committee, political party, recall committee, or referendum committee, as those terms are defined by law.
    • People employed by a political organization are required to register with the Federal Elections Commission.
    • People employed by an issue advocacy group.
  • Prohibit an official or agent of a state agency, county, or municipality from:
    • seeking or receiving any donation or grant of private resources for purposes of election administration, except as expressly authorized under state law.
    • entering into a contract related to election administration that includes any requirement governing election administration or the transfer of any duty or power related to election administration to a person not authorized by state law to have it.
      Violations of these prohibitions would be a felony.
  • Prohibit anyone other than an election official or a vendor of an approved electronic voting system from performing any election administration task.

  • Allow the absentee ballot canvass to temporarily stop as the result of a natural disaster, if an inspector is ill or otherwise incapacitated, or if the physical condition of the canvass location is unsuitable for continuing the canvass. Under existing law, it must be continuous until finished.

    The bill would also create new felonies that could be committed by election officials. Specifically, all of these would become felonies:


  • Intentionally assisting or causing the casting or counting of a vote or the receipt of a registration that is invalid for any reason.
  • Intentionally assisting or causing the rejection of or failure to otherwise count a valid vote or the rejection of a valid registration.
  • Intentionally failing to promptly report a violation under this subsection to the commission and to the district attorney for the county in which the violation occurred. Under existing law, municipal clerks must report violations.

  • Assisting in counting or tabulating votes unless the person is a state resident who is a trained election official and has signed and returned the official oath.

Last Updated July 20, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 16, 2022, would change voter registration list maintenance practices substantially, create a process to reduce lines to vote and provide for clerk training, equipment testing, and clerk vacancy filling procedures.

Specifically, the bill would change list maintenance practices by:

  • Changing how data is shared the Wisconsin Elections Commission (WEC) and the Department of Transportation, Department of Corrections, and the Office of Vital Statistics by:
    • Requiring the WEC and the Office Vital Statistics to enter an agreement that enables the Office to access the voter registration list daily and match the personally identifiable information of voters to the people for whom Vital Statistics has death records. When the Office finds a match, it would immediately notify the WEC of the name, date of birth, date of death, and place of death of the person. Under existing law, the WEC and municipal clerks have a general duty to check vital statistics records to identify deceased voters.
    • Requiring the WEC and the Department of Transportation to enter an agreement that expands their existing data sharing. Under the bill, the agreement would enable the Department to access the voter registration list and compare it to its database of driver's licenses and state IDs daily. The Department would notify the WEC whenever the comparison identifies people who appear to have moved because they updated their address on their driver's license or state ID. Under existing law, the Department and the WEC are required to enter an agreement only to enable them to verify a voter's registration when the voter registers or updates their registration.
    • Requiring the WEC and the Department of Corrections to enter an agreement under which the Department would give a list of people disenfranchised by a felony conviction daily. Under existing law, the Department provides a list of such people to the WEC on a continuous basis.
    • Requiring the data-sharing agreements between the WEC and these agencies to be updated every two years.
  • Requiring the WEC to request information from the Electronic Registration Information Center (ERIC) on a specific schedule. Under existing law, the WEC would simply enter a data-sharing agreement and comply with it. Under the bill, the WEC would request information every 90 days, except:
    • Once a year, the WEC would request information about eligible, but unregistered voters.
    • After an election for a national office, the WEC would request information regarding registered voters who may have voted multiple times in the same election.
  • Changing how information that suggests a voter moved is handled by shifting responsibility to the WEC and changing the consequences to a voter's registration in certain instances. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require the WEC to act on reliable information that a registered voter moved by mailing the voter a notice by 1st class mail stating the source of the information. Under existing law, the municipal clerk or local board of election commissioners acts on change of address information. The bill would further provide that the local election official would act on change of address information only if the WEC did not also receive the information.
    • Mark more voters ineligible, because if the WEC learns the voter moved within the municipality the WEC would mark the voter's registration ineligible, as well as change the voter's registration status if the voter moved out of the municipality. Under existing law, the local election official updates a registration if the voter moves within the municipality and sends the voter a confirmation notice, and marks a voter ineligible only if they move outside the municipality or fail to respond timely to the notice.
    • Provide that for this purpose, information received from ERIC would be considered reliable. Existing law has no equivalent provision. Removing voters based on the ERIC movers list has been the subject of litigation in Wisconsin.

  • Requiring both the WEC and the local election officials to change registrations to ineligible when they are identified using these practices. Under existing law, only the local election official has this duty.

    The bill would reduce the risk of Election Day lines to vote. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the chief inspector at each polling place to submit an incident report to the municipal clerk or local board of election commissioners documenting each time voters waited in line to vote for at least an hour.

  • Require the governing body or board of election commissioners of a municipality, after an election, to address such incidents by taking all necessary steps, including establishing additional polling places, to prevent a recurrence.

    The bill also contains myriad other administrative provisions. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create new duties for the WEC relating to training municipal clerks, reviewing election forms at least once every 4 years for accessibility, usability, clarity, and readability, and updating them as needed.
  • Create processes relating to municipal clerk vacancies.

  • Require certain testing of election equipment, and for that equipment to be unable to connect to the internet.

    Last updated February 17, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on February 16, 2022, would impose legislative oversight on guidance issued by Wisconsin Elections Commission (WEC) by enabling Legislature's Joint Committee for Review of Administrative Rules to review the WEC's guidance documents and confirm that they are guidance, or determine that they are rules and must be withdrawn and, if the WEC wants, formally promulgated. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the WEC to submit, weekly, to the Legislature's Joint Committee for Review of Administrative Rules all guidance that it issued in the previous week.
  • Provide that the Joint Committee may determine that a particular guidance is in fact a rule under the Wisconsin administrative procedures act and must be promulgated as such.
  • Provide that if the Joint Committee decides a piece of guidance is a rule, the WEC will withdraw it and notify local election officials of the determination, and that the guidance is withdrawn and is no longer applicable.
  • Provide that the WEC may promulgate the guidance as an emergency rule, if allowable under the relevant law.
  • Require all guidance documents that the commission provides to municipal clerks to include a disclaimer that provides the definition of "guidance document" and indicates that a guidance document does not have the force of law.

  • Provide that the WEC must submit to the Joint Committee for review of administrative rules all guidance documents that the commission provided to municipal clerks beginning on January 1, 2020, and ending on the effective date of the provision.

    Last updated February 17, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on February 17, 2022, would create new duties to track and refer allegations of election fraud or misconduct. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require each municipal clerk and local board of election commissioners to keep a record of all election fraud or misconduct complaints at an election.
  • Require these officials to submit a report detailing each allegation to the Wisconsin Election Commission (WEC) and to the relevant county district attorney within 14 days after the election.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 25, 2022, would create an automatic voter registration system, create new crimes aimed at protecting voters, improve language accessibility, and make other changes to election administration. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create an automatic registration system with the Department of Transportation (DOT) that includes a wholesale effort to register voters and update their registration. The WEC would be required to report on its progress in doing the wholesale effort by July 1, 2023, and attempt to complete it by July 1, 2025. Specifically, the bill would require the Department of Transportation to transfer to the Wisconsin Election Commission (WEC) its entire database of current license and state ID holders, and to the extent, people provided it, copies of any documentation of their citizenship as part of getting their license or ID. If a person opted out of voter registration while doing their transaction with the DOT, their data would not be included. The WEC would compare the data to its existing voter registration list, and then:
    • If the person is already registered, but there is a discrepancy between the registration and the DOT database, the WEC would attempt to contact them and resolve the issue. If the WEC did not successfully contact the voter, the WEC would resolve the discrepancy in favor of the registration record.
    • If the person is not yet registered and the WEC can confirm their eligibility using the DOT data and any other reliable data the WEC can obtain, the WEC would register them. After registering someone to vote, the WEC would send them a multilingual notice to the voter to enable them to opt-out of being registered or to request a confidential listing.
    • If the person had been registered but their registration was marked ineligible because they failed to vote for four years and did not respond to a notice, and the person has neither moved nor changed their name, the WEC would contact the voter to determine if the voter wanted to change their registration to eligible. If the WEC did not successfully contact them, the voter's registration would remain ineligible.
  • Require the WEC to send a voter notice at their last known address whenever removing them from the registration list or changing their status to ineligible, except if the voter requested the change. Under existing law, notice is required if the change is for an address reason and is explicitly not required when canceling a registration due to death. Notice to the voter is not specifically addressed if the reason is a felony conviction or adjudication of mental incapacity.
  • Require the Department of Transportation to give the WEC information from its drivers' license and state ID database for registration list maintenance purposes continuously and no less than monthly.
  • Expand early voting by requiring election officials to allow anyone in line at the time voting is to end to vote.
  • Create a way for people to seek an injunction to stop deceptive election practices and create a related felony. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Define "deceptive election practices" as a person, acting under color of law or otherwise, intentionally inducing another person to refrain from registering or voting at an election by knowingly providing that person with false election-related information. "Election-related information" would be information about the date, time, place, or manner of conducting an election, eligibility to vote generally, a specific voter's registration status or eligibility, or the explicit endorsement by any person of a candidate at an election.
    • Allow an impacted person to seek an injunction in the relevant circuit court.
    • Allow an impacted person to complain to the WEC, which would be required to promptly investigate, and if the WEC determines the complaint is meritorious, refer the complaint to an appropriate prosecutor, disseminate accurate information,
    • Require the WEC to report to the Legislature about any such complaints and its actions after every general election.
    • Define engaging in deceptive election practices with the intent to prevent any person from exercising the right to vote in an election as a felony.
  • Create a new felony crime of voter suppression. The bill would define voter suppression as knowingly attempting to prevent or deter another person from voting or registering to vote based upon fraudulent, deceptive, or spurious grounds or information. In addition to the criminal penalty, any voter would be allowed to sue for any legal or equitable relief to stop voter suppression, and a prevailing plaintiff could recoup attorneys' fees and costs. The bill would specify two acts as inherently voter suppression, but not limit the crime to them:
    • Challenging another person's right to register or vote at an election based upon information the person knows is false.
    • Attempting to induce another person to refrain from registering or voting by providing that person with information the person knows is false.
  • Expand and narrow the existing felony of election threats and increase its severity. In addition to the criminal penalty, any voter would be allowed to sue for any legal or equitable relief to stop election threats, and a prevailing plaintiff could recoup attorneys' fees and costs. Concerning the definition of the crime, the bill would:
    • Expand one provision to enable it to be committed by using "any tactic of coercion or intimidation," and enabling it to be committed by impacting a voter's registration decision instead of only their voting decision.
    • Narrow one provision to replace a prohibition on "any act" that has the threatening effect with a requirement that a person to use, or threaten to use, force, violence, restraint, or any tactic of coercion or intimidation to compel to have that impact.
  • Create a voter's bill of rights and require its posting and dissemination.
  • Improve language accessibility by:
    • Requiring the municipal clerk or board of election commissioners in jurisdictions that are required to provide multilingual election information and materials by federal law to contact and coordinate with organizations that advocate for such language speakers to ensure that each polling place in the jurisdiction adequately serves the needs of those individuals.
    • Allowing any voter to sue for legal or equitable relief to enforce multilingual notice requirements or the requirements to post the voters' bill of rights or other materials. Prevailing plaintiffs would be able to recover attorneys' fees and costs.
    • Creating a civil penalty of $500/violation for municipal clerks or executive directors of boards of election commissioners who fail to provide required multilingual election materials.
  • Require the WEC, county clerks, and municipal clerks to maintain the privacy of voters' phone numbers and email addresses.

  • Require the WEC to improve its election administration manual by adding certain content and features.

Last Updated March 2, 2022

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 25, 2022, would enable people who have been disenfranchised for a felony conviction to regain their right to vote much sooner than under existing law.

Under the bill, they would regain their right to vote upon their release from incarceration. In addition, they would not lose their right to vote if they are convicted but placed on probation that does not involve incarceration. If they are incarcerated because of a violation of parole or probation, they would lose their right to vote during that incarceration. Finally, the bill would require training of corrections employees and election officials, as well as notice to people released from incarceration.

Under existing law, people disenfranchised for a felony conviction regain their right to vote when they complete incarceration, parole, and/or probation.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 10, 2022, would amend the state constitution to make major changes to the state's redistricting process. Under the bill, the Legislative Research Bureau would prepare the redistricting plans, receiving advice from a new Redistricting Advisory Commission. The Bureau would present plans to the Legislature, which could enact or reject them. If the Legislature rejected two plans, it could create its own, but any such plan would need to be approved by three-fourths of the Legislature. Under existing law, the Legislature draws and adopts maps with few constraints other than those imposed by the U.S. Constitution and federal law. To the extent constraints are imposed, they are in the state constitution. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the Bureau to propose redistricting plans that comply with certain criteria, then embody them in legislation that it submits to the Legislature. Any draft maps, along with the data sets used to create the maps, would be open to public inspection and copying and made available on the Internet site of the Bureau as soon as the maps are produced. The districts the Bureau draws would be required to meet these criteria:
    • Congressional districts would have as equal a population as practicable while complying with the Voting Rights Act of 1965, and state legislative districts could not vary in population by more than 10% unless necessary to comply with the Voting Rights Act of 1965. While the U.S. Constitution and the Voting Rights Act apply to redistricting generally, they are not referenced in the current constitutional redistricting provisions or redistricting statutes.
    • District boundaries would coincide with ward boundaries, and to the extent consistent with population and federal law, coincide with the boundaries of political subdivisions. Minimizing the division of political subdivisions would be required. Under current constitutional provisions, Assembly districts must follow county, precinct, town, or ward lines, consist of contiguous territory, and be in as compact form as practicable. Senate districts must be composed of three Assembly districts comprising convenient contiguous territory.
    • Districts would be composed of convenient contiguous territory. Areas that meet only at the points of adjoining corners would not be contiguous. Under current constitutional provisions, Assembly districts must follow county, precinct, town, or ward lines, consist of contiguous territory, and be in as compact form as practicable. Senate districts must be composed of three Assembly districts comprising convenient contiguous territory.
    • Districts would be compact in form, meaning square, rectangular, or hexagonal to the extent permitted by natural or political boundaries. The bill includes ways of determining relative compactness. Under current constitutional provisions, Assembly districts must follow county, precinct, town, or ward lines, consist of contiguous territory, and be in as compact form as practicable. Senate districts must be composed of three Assembly districts comprising convenient contiguous territory.
    • Districts could not be drawn with the intent or result of denying or abridging the equal opportunity of racial or language minorities to participate in the political process or diminishing the ability of racial or language minorities to elect representatives of each minority group's choice, whether by the group or by voting in concert with other persons. Current redistricting rules do not have comparable provisions beyond the requirements of federal law.
    • Districts could not be drawn to favor a political party, incumbent legislator or member of Congress, or other person or group or, except to the extent required to augment or dilute the voting strength of a language or racial minority group. In drawing districts, the Bureau could not consider the residence addresses of incumbent legislators or members of Congress. Current redistricting rules do not have comparable provisions beyond the requirements of federal law.
    • Congressional districts would contain only whole state senate districts, to the extent complying with other criteria allows. Current redistricting rules do not have a comparable provision.
    • Except to test the "efficiency gap" and the competitiveness of each district, which the bill requires the Bureau to do, the Bureau could not consider the political affiliations of registered voters or previous election results. Demographic information could only be used as needed to meet the various redistricting requirements. Current redistricting rules do not have a comparable provision.
  • Create a five-member Redistricting Advisory Commission. No analog exists under current law. The majority leader of the senate and the speaker of the assembly would each appoint one person, and the minority leaders in each house would appoint one each. The four members would then choose the fifth. The Commission would:
    • If requested to do so by the Bureau, provide direction concerning any decision for which no clearly applicable guideline is provided.
    • Oversee the work of Bureau employees engaged in preparing a redistricting plan and would be able to enter into contracts for hiring experts to assist in the preparation of such plans, if three-fourths of the commission approves. Similarly, the Commission would be able to terminate a contract employee only with the approval of three-fourths of its members.
    • Upon delivery by the Bureau of a bill embodying a redistricting plan, make available to the public at the earliest feasible time copies of the bill, maps illustrating the plan, a summary of the criteria, a statement of the population of each district included in the plan and the relative deviation of each district population from the ideal district population.
    • As expeditiously as reasonably possible after the Bureau delivers its bill, schedule and conduct public hearings on the plan. No more than one public hearing could be held in the city of Madison, and at least one public hearing would be held in each Congressional district of the state.
    • Following the hearings, promptly submit to the Legislature a report summarizing information and testimony from the hearings.
  • Create a process for the Legislature to follow once it receives the Bureau's bills. Specifically:
    • No less than seven days after receiving the Commission's report following the public hearings, one chamber would vote on the Bureau's bills without amendment. If the bill passed, it would be sent to the other chamber for a similar vote. If the bills failed to pass both chambers, the chief clerk of the chamber(s) that rejected the bills would give the Bureau the chamber's reasons for rejecting the bills.
    • The Bureau would then create new plans, reflecting the reasons to the extent possible while complying with the redistricting criteria, and submit new bills to the Legislature within 21 days of the first bills' rejection. The Legislature would be required to vote on the new bills, without amendments, within seven days.
    • If the Legislature again rejects the bills, the process would be repeated, but this time the Legislature would be allowed to amend the Bureau's third set of bills. The passage of the third set of bills would need the approval of three-fourths of all the members elected in each house.

  • Establish an evidentiary rule for litigation challenging a redistricting plan brought based on an excessive population variance among senate or assembly districts established in the plan, the Legislature would have the burden of justifying any variance over 10 percent between the population of a senate or assembly district and the applicable ideal district population. If an action was brought challenging a Congressional redistricting plan based on an excessive population variance among congressional districts, the Legislature would have the burden of justifying any variance over 1 percent between the population of a Congressional district and the applicable ideal district population.

    Last updated March 14, 2022.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 3, 2022, would change voter registration list maintenance practices substantially, create a process to reduce lines to vote and provide for clerk training, equipment testing, and clerk vacancy filling procedures.

Specifically, the bill would change list maintenance practices by:

  • Changing how data is shared the Wisconsin Elections Commission (WEC) and the Department of Transportation, Department of Corrections, and the Office of Vital Statistics by:
    • Requiring the WEC and the Office Vital Statistics to enter an agreement that enables the Office to access the voter registration list daily and match the personally identifiable information of voters to the people for whom Vital Statistics has death records. When the Office finds a match, it would immediately notify the WEC of the name, date of birth, date of death, and place of death of the person. Under existing law, the WEC and municipal clerks have a general duty to check vital statistics records to identify deceased voters.
    • Requiring the WEC and the Department of Transportation to enter an agreement that expands their existing data sharing. Under the bill, the agreement would enable the Department to access the voter registration list and compare it to its database of driver's licenses and state IDs daily. The Department would notify the WEC whenever the comparison identifies people who appear to have moved because they updated their address on their driver's license or state ID. Under existing law, the Department and the WEC are required to enter an agreement only to enable them to verify a voter's registration when the voter registers or updates their registration.
    • Requiring the WEC and the Department of Corrections to enter an agreement under which the Department would give a list of people disenfranchised by a felony conviction daily. Under existing law, the Department provides a list of such people to the WEC on a continuous basis.
    • Requiring the data-sharing agreements between the WEC and these agencies to be updated every two years.
  • Requiring the WEC to request information from the Electronic Registration Information Center (ERIC) on a specific schedule. Under existing law, the WEC would simply enter a data-sharing agreement and comply with it. Under the bill, the WEC would request information every 90 days, except:
    • Once a year, the WEC would request information about eligible, but unregistered voters.
    • After an election for a national office, the WEC would request information regarding registered voters who may have voted multiple times in the same election.
  • Changing how information that suggests a voter moved is handled by shifting responsibility to the WEC and changing the consequences to a voter's registration in certain instances. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require the WEC to act on reliable information that a registered voter moved by mailing the voter a notice by 1st class mail stating the source of the information. Under existing law, the municipal clerk or local board of election commissioners acts on change of address information. The bill would further provide that the local election official would act on change of address information only if the WEC did not also receive the information.
    • Mark more voters ineligible, because if the WEC learns the voter moved within the municipality the WEC would mark the voter's registration ineligible, as well as change the voter's registration status if the voter moved out of the municipality. Under existing law, the local election official updates a registration if the voter moves within the municipality and sends the voter a confirmation notice, and marks a voter ineligible only if they move outside the municipality or fail to respond timely to the notice.
    • Provide that for this purpose, information received from ERIC would be considered reliable. Existing law has no equivalent provision. Removing voters based on the ERIC movers list has been the subject of litigation in Wisconsin.

  • Requiring both the WEC and the local election officials to change registrations to ineligible when they are identified using these practices. Under existing law, only the local election official has this duty.

    The bill would reduce the risk of Election Day lines to vote. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the chief inspector at each polling place to submit an incident report to the municipal clerk or local board of election commissioners documenting each time voters waited in line to vote for at least an hour.

  • Require the governing body or board of election commissioners of a municipality, after an election, to address such incidents by taking all necessary steps, including establishing additional polling places, to prevent a recurrence.

    The bill also contains myriad other administrative provisions. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create new duties for the WEC relating to training municipal clerks, reviewing election forms at least once every 4 years for accessibility, usability, clarity, and readability, and updating them as needed.
  • Create processes relating to municipal clerk vacancies.

  • Require certain testing of election equipment, and for that equipment to be unable to connect to the internet.

    Last updated February 10, 2022.

Governor Evers vetoed this bill on April 8, 2022.

This bill, as introduced on February 3, 2022, would have changed the absentee ballot certificate and its review in ways that appeared likely to lead to additional ballots being disqualified, changed the processes relating to election activities in residential care facilities, both during ordinary times and pandemics, prohibited private funding of election administration, and created new election crimes, among other changes to election administration.

The bill would have changed absentee ballot certificates and their review by:

  • Requiring absentee ballot certificates to include 12 different fields relating to the voter's name and address, and the voter's witness and their address, and requiring clerks to reject ballots if one or more of those fields is blank. Thus the ballot would have been rejected if the voter or their witness omitted their municipality, but did include their zip code. Under existing law, ballots must be rejected if the witness's address is incomplete, or more generally if the certificate is improperly completed or missing.
  • Requiring a clerk who determined a voter completed the certificate improperly or returned the ballot without the certificate to post notice of the defect in the voter's information page in the online voter registration system, and allowing the clerk to attempt to notify the voter by other means. Under existing law, the clerk has no similar duty or authorization, although existing law does allow the clerk to return the ballot to the voter whenever time permits to allow the voter to address the issue. The bill maintains that option.

  • Forbidding anyone other than the voter or witness to correct a defect in the certificate, and creating a misdemeanor to enforce the prohibition. Under existing Wisconsin Election Commission (WEC) guidance in place since 2016, clerks are allowed to correct certain errors relating to the witness's address. Clerks have relied on that guidance to ensure that eligible voters' otherwise valid ballots are counted since 2016. Continuing to do so, under this bill, would be a crime.

    The bill would have changed election activities at retirement homes and residential care facilities by:


  • Prohibiting such a facility from denying access to special voting deputies unless the facility is closed to the public due to a public health emergency or is closed to the public because of an infectious disease incident. To close access, the administrator of the facility would have had to document the issue and inform the municipal clerk or local board of election commissioners. Existing law does not have a similar provision. In the 2020 election, the inability of special voting deputies to access these facilities, and the WEC's guidance that, when access was denied, ballots could be mailed to residents who requested them, proved controversial.
  • Allowing a new kind of special voting deputy, called "personal care voting deputies" to be appointed to supervise absentee voting at the facility whenever traditional special voting deputies had been denied access. Any other employee of the facilities could not assist residents with voting in any way other than distributing ballots in their unopened envelopes to residents who had requested them. The personal care voting deputies would have been subject to certain rules:
    • They must be people employed or retained by the facility and must be registered to vote in Wisconsin.
    • They cannot assist anyone with registering to vote, only completing absentee ballots. Thus Wisconsin's same-day registration procedure would not be available if personal care voting deputies are used.
    • They must take a training course the bill requires the WEC to create for them.
    • Before helping anyone vote, they must take an oath that they are qualified, understand the proper absentee voting procedure and have read the governing law, understand the penalties for failing to follow the law, and that they must fully and fairly implement the absentee voting law. Finally, the oath would state that the individual realizes that any error could result in the voter's ballot being rejected and that absentee voting is a privilege and not a constitutional right.
    • They must complete a form that includes their name, the name of each voter they assisted, the type of assistance they provided to each, and the information on the form on the ballot return envelope. This form must be separate from the absentee ballot certificate and delivered to the municipal clerk or local board of election commissioners.
    • At least two personal care voting deputies must be appointed, of different political parties if possible.
  • Changing the timeline for absentee voting deputies to visit facilities. The bill would have required the special voting deputies to arrange one or more times to visit the facilities by the 11th working day before Election Day and require the visit to be no later than the 6th working day before the election. Under existing law, these deadlines are the 6th working day and the Monday before Election Day, respectively.
  • Allowing the municipal clerk or the local board of election commissioners to mail ballots to those voters at those facilities who requested them no later than 5 p.m. on the Friday before Election Day if special voting deputies were denied access twice due to a public health emergency or incident of infectious disease. Existing law does not have a similar provision.
  • Requiring the facility to give notice of the days and times the voting deputies will offer voting to each relative of the facility for whom the facility has contact information. Under existing law, relatives must request such notice.

  • Creating new class 1 felonies to prohibit any employee from coercing a resident to register or not register to vote, or to apply to vote absentee or not, to complete their absentee ballot or not, or to vote for or against any person or ballot measure. "Coerce" is not defined.

    The bill would have changed multiple other aspects of election administration, including prohibiting private funding of elections, prohibiting certain people from being election officials, and other changes. Specifically, the bill would have:


  • Prohibited certain types of people from serving as election officials. Existing law has no equivalent. Specifically, these people would have been prohibited:
    • People employed by a candidate committee, legislative campaign committee, political action committee, independent expenditure committee, political party, recall committee, or referendum committee, as those terms are defined by law.
    • People employed by a political organization required to register with the Federal Elections Commission.
    • People employed by an issue advocacy group.
  • Prohibited an official or agent of a state agency, county, or municipality from:
    • seeking or receiving any donation or grant of private resources for purposes of election administration, except as expressly authorized under state law.
    • entering into a contract related to election administration that includes any requirement governing election administration or the transfer of any duty or power related to election administration to a person not authorized by state law to have it.
      Violations of these prohibitions would have been felonies.
  • Prohibited anyone other than an election official or a vendor of an approved electronic voting system from performing any election administration task.

  • Allowed the absentee ballot canvass to temporarily stop as the result of a natural disaster, if an inspector is ill or otherwise incapacitated, or if the physical condition of the canvass location is unsuitable for continuing the canvass. Under existing law, it must be continuous until finished.

    The bill would also have created new felonies that could be committed by election officials. Specifically, all of these would have become felonies:


  • Intentionally assisting or causing the casting or counting of a vote or the receipt of a registration that is invalid for any reason.
  • Intentionally assisting or causing the rejection of or failure to otherwise count a valid vote or the rejection of a valid registration.
  • Intentionally failing to promptly report a violation under this subsection to the commission and to the district attorney for the county in which the violation occurred. Under existing law, municipal clerks must report violations.

  • Assisting in counting or tabulating votes unless the person is a state resident who is a trained election official and has signed and returned the official oath.

Last Updated July 20, 2022
