VRLANALYSIS:
Governor Evers vetoed this bill on April 15, 2022, and the Senate failed to override it on May 17, 2022.

This bill, as amended on February 22, 2022, would have changed how the Wisconsin Elections Commission (WEC) responds to complaints that it receives about violations of election law and how it reports on those complaints, and also would have created a performance audit of electronic voting systems to be done according to WEC rule from randomly selected units after each general election.

With regard to complaints about election law violations, the bill would have:

  • Required the WEC to resolve certain complaints it receives within 60 days unless two-thirds of the WEC vote to extend the time by another 60 days, which it could have done twice. During that time, the WEC could have decided, by a two-thirds vote to grant the relief, in whole or in part, that had been requested, to investigate the complaint, or to refer it to the Attorney General or a district attorney. The two-thirds threshold requires bipartisan votes and is the general requirement for WEC action. If two-thirds of the WEC could not agree on any of those actions, the WEC would have dismissed the complaint. This provision would not apply to certain kinds of complaints the WEC received from a voter. Existing law does not have comparable provisions, although it already provides for the WEC to refer appropriate matters to the Attorney General or district attorney.
  • Required the WEC to resolve complaints from voters that ask the WEC to require their local election administrators to act differently because the voter believes their current behavior is illegal or an abuse of discretion within 60 days unless two-thirds of the WEC voted to extend the time by another 60 days, which it could do twice. During that time, the WEC could have decided, by a two-thirds vote to grant the relief, in whole or in part, that has been requested. If the WEC failed to extend the period or grant the relief, the complaint would have been dismissed.
  • Allowed a person who alleges that an action of the WEC either violated or resulted in a violation of election law to sue in any county where the alleged violation occurred without filing a complaint with the WEC first. Under existing law, people may sue after the WEC completes its process.
  • Changed how the WEC reports on its investigations. The bill would have required the WEC, within 30 days of resolving a complaint, to give the complaint, with all names and other personally identifiable information redacted, and documentation of the complaint's resolution, to the state legislators representing the area where the alleged violation occurred or is occurring, and to the co-chairs of the legislative committees with jurisdiction over elections. Existing law does not have comparable provisions.
  • Required an additional, annual report of the WEC's investigations, that would have:
    • Included the number of complaints filed with the WEC, a description of each complaint, and a description of the WEC's responses.
    • Included the number of investigations undertaken by the WEC and a description of them.
    • Included the number of informal reports, including from the election crimes hotline, and a description of the general categories of concerns expressed.
    • Been submitted to the Governor and the chief clerk of each house of the Legislature no later than January 31. Under existing law, the WEC files a different annual report with such officers that includes a description of each investigation it undertook since the last report. The bill would have eliminated the requirement to include information relating to investigations in that annual report.
  • Required the WEC to testify about this report before the legislative committees with jurisdiction over elections and provide a copy of this report to county and municipal clerks and local boards of election commissioners.
  • Required the WEC to issue rules specifying procedures for its consideration and handling of all formal complaints and informal reports of possible violations of election laws that the commission receives, including reports received via the toll-free hotline.
  • Required a performance audit of the performance of electronic voting systems used in at least four reporting units in the city of Milwaukee, at least four reporting units in the city of Madison, at least one reporting unit in each of the 20 other largest municipalities, and at least five percent of the reporting units in all other municipalities combined. These audits would have been completed by November 30 following a general election.
  • Required the WEC to issue rules that:
    • established an error rate for the performance audit
    • established a process that provides for a random selection of reporting units, and other than the units required for specific jurisdictions ensures distribution across the state and units that have at least 10 votes cast in them.
    • provided that the county clerk would oversee the counting of ballots by hand in connection with the audits as a part of the county canvass.
  • Required the Legislative Audit Bureau to analyze the results of the audits and report to the Legislature recommendations for improving the audits and, if needed, improvements to the accuracy of the voting systems. The Bureau would have reported its analysis and recommendations by January 15.

  • Required the municipal clerk, if a recount is happening, to print and make available for each recount paper copies of all absentee ballot applications received electronically.

Governor Evers vetoed this bill on April 8, 2022.

This bill, as amended on February 22, 2022, would have changed all of the rules and elections processes relating to absentee voters who are deemed "indefinitely confined". Under existing law, indefinitely confined voters do not have to submit a copy of their photo ID when they apply for an absentee ballot, can attest to their status by checking a box on the existing absentee application, and continue to receive absentee ballots for every election without further application. Indefinitely confined status became very controversial in 2020 because of uncertainties around how the pandemic should relate to that status, and was litigated in multiple ways.

The bill would have changed the rules relating to indefinitely confined voters by:

  • Further specifying and limiting who could claim indefinitely confined status. To apply, a person would have had to be unable to travel independently without significant burden because of frailty, physical illness, or a disability that is expected to last longer than one year. This is a modified provision. The previous version provided that the disability "will last longer than one year." Existing law simply says a person must be indefinitely confined due to age, physical illness, infirmity, or disability for an indefinite period.
  • Clarifying that existence of an outbreak or epidemic of a communicable disease in a voter's community does not qualify the voter as indefinitely confined. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Requiring voters to use a special application to apply to join the list and receive absentee ballots. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Under existing law, people check a box on the existing application to apply.
  • Requiring the ordinary absentee ballot application form to inform voters of the indefinitely confined application. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
  • Changing the rules relating to proving identity when indefinitely confined voters apply for the first time to join the list and receive absentee ballots. Under existing law, these voters either provide a copy of their photo ID in the same way as all absentee voting applicants, or they have their ballot witness attest to their identity as part of their witnessing of the ballot. Under the amended bill:
    • the voter could have provided the number of a current and valid operator's license or ID, along with their name and date of birth, so long as the Wisconsin Election Commission (WEC) can successfully use that information to verify their identity. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • the voter could have provided a copy of their photo ID if they possess proof of identification and do not successfully submit a state ID or driver's license number. This is provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • the voter could have attested, in language created by the WEC, to their indefinitely confined status, included the last four digits of their Social Security number (SSN4), and authorized the WEC to use that number to verify their identity. This last option would only be available to indefinitely confined voters who do not possess photo ID and who do not successfully submit a state ID or driver's license number. A voter using this approach would have been required to support their application further with an attestation by someone who is a citizen and at least 18 years old. This person would be attesting to the identity of the indefinitely confined voter, not their indefinitely confined status. This provision was in the previous version of the bill.
    • the clerk processing the application would have indicated on the new form that the voter complied with the identification requirement by one of these methods. This is a new provision.
  • Changing how a voter is removed from the indefinitely confined list. All of these provisions were in the previous version of the bill. In addition to the reasons the bill does not impact, a voter could have been removed if:
    • they failed to cast and return a ballot for a spring election or a general election and they did not renew their application by responding to a notice sent by the clerk within 30 days. Under existing law, the clerk sends the notice any time a voter fails to cast and return a ballot, including after a primary.
    • they voted in person. Existing law does not address this.
    • the clerk received reliable information that the voter is no longer indefinitely confined and cannot travel independently without significant burden because of frailty, physical illness, or a disability that will last longer than one year. This is a modified provision. The previous version of the bill lacked part of the new definition of indefinitely confined. Under existing law, the clerk can remove someone upon reliable information that they no longer qualify as indefinitely confined.

  • Creating a new misdemeanor to punish falsely making any statement to qualify as indefinitely confined. This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law does not have a similarly narrowly tailored crime, however, an existing felony punishes lying to the municipal clerk or local board of election commissioners or any other election official, and an existing misdemeanor punishes falsely making a statement to obtain an absentee ballot.

    In addition to these changes, the bill would have required the WEC to facilitate the removal from the list anyone who joined during the period beginning on March 12, 2020, and ending on November 3, 2020. March 12, 2020, is when Governor Evers ordered people to stay at home to minimize the risks posed by COVID-19. This provision was in the previous version of the bill

This bill, as introduced on February 3, 2022, would have required the Wisconsin Elections Commission (WEC) to attempt to verify the citizenship status of everyone on the voter registration list 60 days before absentee ballots are mailed for every election by:

  • Comparing the Department of Transportation (DOT)'s driver's license and state ID database.

  • Checking the systematic alien verification for entitlements database maintained by the federal Department of Homeland Security.

    The bill does not indicate what data points must match for the WEC to determine that a non-citizen identified in either process is the same person as a registered voter.

Separately, the bill would have required the DOT to put "Not valid for voting purposes" on the driver's license or state ID it issues to anyone the DOT knows is not a U.S. citizen.

This bill, as introduced on February 3, 2022, would have made major changes to how voters apply for and return absentee ballots, how clerks handle absentee ballots, and smaller but significant changes to voter registration.

Concerning changing absentee ballot applications, the bill would have:

  • Eliminated an exemption to the rule that a voter must provide a copy of their photo ID when applying for an absentee ballot. Under existing law, a voter who submitted a copy of their photo ID when applying for an absentee ballot once, and has not moved nor changed their name, need not submit a copy of their ID again when they apply. The bill would have repealed that exception and instead required these voters to submit a copy of their ID with each application.
  • Required all voters who wish to vote absentee to complete a standalone absentee ballot application with specified data fields before the clerk could give them a ballot. Wisconsin conducts early voting by in-person absentee voting, and thus the form would have had to be completed by early voters as well as people requesting a ballot be mailed to them. Current practice integrates the application with the voter's certificate for in-person absentee voters. After the 2020 general election, that integrated form was challenged by litigation brought on behalf of President Trump, asserting that ballots cast without a separate, standalone application form should be invalidated. The form the bill would have required would ask for at least:
    • The voter's municipality and county of residence.
    • The voter's name, date of birth, and contact information, including as applicable their telephone number, fax number, and email address.
    • The street address of the voter's legal voting residence.
    • The election at which the voter intends to vote absentee.
    • Whether the voter is a military or overseas voter.
    • The voter's confidential identification serial number if they are in the address confidentiality program.
    • The lawful method by which the voter prefers to receive the absentee ballot.
    • Whether the voter is hospitalized for purposes of a special absentee procedure.
  • Created a class 1 felony to punish any clerk who issued an absentee ballot to a voter who did not complete such an application first, including in-person early voters.
  • Reduced the number of elections a voter can apply to receive ballots for with a single application to a single primary and general election pair. Under existing law, a voter can apply to receive ballots for every election in a calendar year.
  • Prohibited municipal clerks, county clerks, or county boards of election commissioners from sending absentee ballot applications or ballots to anyone who has not applied for them. Existing law requires an application before sending out ballots but has no similar prohibition on sending unrequested ballot applications. In 2020, the Wisconsin Election Commission (WEC) sent absentee ballot applications to all voters.
  • Required voters applying for an absentee ballot by fax or email to include a copy of their original written signature with the application, including in PDF form.

  • Prohibited political committees from sending voters mail ballot applications that have a return address other than the municipal clerk or local board of commissioners.

    Concerning clerk and voter handling of absentee ballots, the bill would have:


  • Limited who a voter could choose to return their completed, sealed ballot for them. Existing law is silent on who may deliver a ballot for a voter. As a result of pending litigation, this silence has been interpreted as a prohibition on anyone returning another's ballot. Prior to the litigation, the reverse interpretation was applied. Voters could choose who they wished to return their ballots. Under the bill, a voter could return their ballot, or could have chosen:
    • a member of their immediate family, defined as spouses, siblings, parent and child, and grandparent and grandchild.
    • their legal guardian.
    • any registered voter they designated in writing, provided that no one can return more than two ballots not their own for anyone not immediate family per election, and the person cannot be a candidate nor compensated to return the ballot.
  • Created a felony to punish a person who returned a voter's ballot in violation of these restrictions.
  • Restricted the locations a voter may return their completed ballot to the office of the municipal clerk, an alternate ballot site, or the voter's polling place on Election Day. Under existing law, voters must return their ballots to the clerk. Although the WEC had interpreted that statute as giving the clerk discretion to decide how to receive the ballots, which allowed clerks to use drop boxes throughout their municipalities, the litigation has prohibited using drop boxes unless they are at the clerk's office or an early voting location.
  • Prohibited clerks from preprinting or stamping their initials on absentee ballot envelopes, and instead require them to handwrite their initials.

With regard to voter registration, the bill would have:

  • Required a person to have a driver's license, state ID, or Social Security number to register to vote. Under existing law, a person who attests to having neither kind of number but who is otherwise eligible can register to vote.
  • Required the WEC to maintain a version of a completed online voter registration application that has the voter's electronic signature.

  • Allowed people to return a voter registration application by a for-profit commercial delivery service.

Last Updated October 18, 2022

This bill, as introduced on February 3, 2022, would have increased the Wisconsin Elections Commission (WEC)'s use of the Department of Transportation (DOT)'s database of driver's licenses and state IDs in voter registration list maintenance. Specifically, the bill would have required the WEC to compare a voter's personally identifiable information to the DOT database no later than ten days after a person registers to vote or updates their registration, and if the WEC determined there was a match between a person issued a license or ID and a registered voter, but a discrepancy in the details of the information in the two databases, take an action depending on the discrepancy:

  • Correct a discrepancy, if there is only one, such as a common variation in the voter's name, like a nickname, or a missing suffix, and the WEC is able to correct the discrepancy based on reliable information.
  • Send a notice to the voter informing them of a discrepancy the WEC cannot correct, or of two or more discrepancies. The notice would explain that the voter's registration would be suspended unless the voter corrects all the discrepancies within 30 days of the notice's mailing.
  • Change a voter's status from eligible to ineligible if they fail to correct the discrepancies in the 30 days.
  • Keep a permanent record of each discrepancy and how it was resolved.

The bill would have allowed the WEC to delegate to local election officials the duties to correct discrepancies, contact voters, and change registration status.

This bill, as introduced on February 3, 2022, would have given the Legislature a direct role in implementing federal election administration guidance, directives, and funds. In addition, it would have required the Wisconsin Elections Commission (WEC) to retain as counsel both a Republican lawyer and a Democratic lawyer chosen by legislative leaders. None of these provisions have analogs in existing law. Finally, the bill would have added data gathering and reporting requirements for municipal, county, and state election officials, both to the public and the Legislature. Specifically, the bill would have:

  • Required any agency of Wisconsin government, defined in a way that reaches throughout the executive, legislative, and judicial branches of government, that receives a directive or guidance relating to elections from the federal Department of Justice or other federal executive branch agency, to give the directive or guidance, and any communications with the federal agency relating to it, within 48 hours to:
    • the Senate Majority Leader,
    • the Senate Minority Leader,
    • the Speaker of the Assembly,
    • the Assembly Minority Leader,
    • the chairpersons of the standing committees with jurisdiction concerning elections, and
    • the co-chairpersons of the Joint Committee for Review of Administrative Rules.
  • Prohibited any such agency from implementing any such directive or guidance unless the Joint Committee on Review of Administrative Rules approves, either affirmatively, or by failing to schedule a meeting to review the rules within 30 days of receiving notice of the guidance.

The bill would also have added rules relating to the disbursement of federal funds for elections. Specifically, the bill would have:

  • Prohibited the Governor from disbursing federal election funds to the WEC until the WEC establishes a plan to spend them, submits the plan to the Legislature's Joint Committee on Finance, and the Joint Committee approves the plan either affirmatively or by failing to schedule a meeting to review the plan with 14 working days. If the committee scheduled a meeting for the purpose of reviewing the plan, the Governor and WEC could act only with the approval of the committee.

  • Required the bipartisan WEC to have bipartisan legal counsel chosen by the legislative leadership of the two major political parties.

    The bill would also have added additional voter registration and voting statistics gathering and reporting to that required by existing law. Some of the new reporting requirements would have related to municipal clerks or local boards of election commissions, and some would have related to county clerks and county boards of election commissioners.

    The local officials would have been required to report to the WEC and the relevant county clerk or county board of election commissioners, within 30 days of a primary or general election that included a state or federal office or a statewide referendum, for their municipality:


  • The number of registered voters residing in the municipality on the day of the election.
  • The number of voters who registered to vote beginning on the day of the immediately preceding primary or election and ending on the day of the most recent primary or election.
  • The number of voters who voted absentee ballots by mail.
  • The number of voters who voted absentee ballots in person (early voters).
  • The total number of absentee ballots returned by voters that were not counted, and the reasons why.
  • The number of voters casting ballots at the polling place on Election Day.
  • The number of voters casting provisional ballots, and the number of such ballots not counted because they did not provide the requisite ID in time.
  • The total number of defective ballots that election officials recreated, with a separate itemization of such ballots cast by military and overseas electors, damaged ballots, and ballots recreated for other reasons.
  • The location of each residential care facility and qualified retirement home to which the municipality dispatched special voting deputies, and the number of ballots cast by their residents using special voting deputies.
  • The number of voters whose personally identifiable information on the official registration list maintained by the WEC did not match the personally identifiable information maintained by the Department of Transportation, beginning on the day of the immediately preceding primary or election and ending on the day of the most recent primary or election, along with a description of each mismatch, and the number of such voters whose registration status was changed from eligible to ineligible.

County election officials would have been required to submit an electronic report to the WEC no later than 30 days after each election at which a state or national office is filled or a statewide referendum is held, including any special election, that detailed:

  • The approximate number of voters in each municipality in the county that the municipal clerk certified to the clerk or board when making their ballot request, and the related number of ballots requested.
  • The number of ballots that the county or board distributed to each municipality in the county.
  • The number of ballots distributed to each municipality that were ultimately cast in the election.
  • The number of ballots that election inspectors rejected, the reasons for rejection, and the number of ballots that were remade by election inspectors and cast.
  • The number of unused ballots.
  • Any other action that the county took to reconcile the total number of ballots with the number of votes cast.
  • An explanation of any discrepancy between the number of ballots ordered by municipalities and the number distributed to them, and of any discrepancy between the number of ballots distributed and the number cast or rejected.

The bill would also have imposed data reporting and storage requirements on the WEC. Specifically, the bill would have required the WEC to:

  • Publish the information in these reports in an easily accessible format on its internet site.
  • Submit each county's report, within 7 days of receiving it, to the Senate Majority Leader, the Senate Minority Leader, the Speaker of the Assembly, the Assembly Minority Leader, the co-chairpersons of the standing committees with jurisdiction concerning elections, and the Legislative Audit Bureau. The Bureau would have reviewed the report and, within 30 days, reported its findings and recommendations to the Legislature, including a description of any discrepancies it found and any explanation of those discrepancies it received from local election officials.

  • Archive, on the first day of each month, an electronic copy of the official registration list as it appeared on the last day of the previous month and retain that copy for no less than 22 months.

This bill, as amended on February 24, 2022, was substantially expanded in scope. As introduced on February 7, the bill would have provided whistleblower protections to municipal clerks. While that provision remains in the amended bill, the amended bill would also change how and when absentee ballots are canvassed, and when absentee ballots are initially mailed to voters. All of those provisions are new to this bill. Specifically, as amended, the bill would:

  • Protect municipal clerks who lawfully report, or are believed to have reported, witnessing what the clerk reasonably believed to be election fraud or irregularities. The bill defines lawfully reported to mean any disclosure not expressly prohibited by state or federal law, rule, or regulation. The bill does not define "irregularities." This provision was in the previous version of the bill. Existing law does not have a comparable provision.
  • Allow municipalities that have not adopted a resolution to count absentee ballots at a "central count" location to nonetheless adopt an ordinance to allow their municipal clerk to canvass absentee ballots the day before Election Day using some of the processes followed by central count municipalities. Before adopting the ordinance, the municipality would communicate with the Wisconsin Elections Commission concerning the process. This is a new provision. Under existing law, absentee ballots are canvassed beginning on Election Day, and municipalities must either count them at polling places or central count locations.
  • Specify processes for municipalities that canvass absentee ballots starting the day before Election Day, either as central count communities or as municipalities adopting a more limited process. Under the bill, these municipalities would:
    • give at least 60 days' notice of where and when canvassing would happen and allow the same rights of observation granted for in-person voting. Under existing law, central count municipalities need to give only 48 hours' notice, and those municipalities already grant watchers in-person voting access.
    • begin canvassing absentee ballots beginning at 7 a.m. the day before the election. Central count municipalities, only, would be required to continue canvassing until they run out of ballots or 8 p.m. on the day before the election, whichever comes first. Central count municipalities would then reconvene at 7 a.m. on Election Day and continue canvassing until all ballots received by 8 p.m. that day have been canvassed. Under existing law, ballots may be canvassed beginning at 7 a.m. on Election Day, and the canvass must begin by 10 p.m. on election night.
    • report to the county clerk, at 7 a.m., noon, and 8 p.m. on both the day before the election and the day of the election, the total number of absentee ballots returned, the total canvassed, and the total that remain to be counted. The county clerk would post the totals on their internet site. Existing law requires the county clerk to post certain canvassing reporting on its website, but not this information.
    • secure election equipment and ballots upon the recess of the canvass the night before the election following certain procedures. If signs of tampering were found the next morning, the bill would require notification of the Commission, provide for a recount of absentee ballots in that municipality using existing recount procedures, and/or require the replacement of election equipment.
    • not tabulate absentee ballots before the later of the completion of the canvass or the closing of the polls, in all municipalities. Existing law has similar provisions, except that under existing law canvassing does not begin until Election Day.
  • Create a felony to prohibit a person from intentionally acting in a manner that would give him or her the ability to know or provide information on the accumulating or final results from the canvassed ballots before the later of the canvass completion or the close of polls.
  • Create a new felony to punish an election official or member of the board of absentee ballot canvassers in a central count municipality for willful neglect of or refusal to perform any of their absentee ballot duties. Under existing law, willful neglect of or refusal to perform duties is punishable by disqualification to act as an election official for five years.
  • Require all municipalities, regardless of when they began canvassing absentee ballots, to report certain ballot statistics to their county clerk at 9 p.m. on Election Day and every hour thereafter. Specifically, they must report:
    • the total number of ballots, including absentee ballots, that have been cast.
    • the total number of ballots that have been canvassed.
    • the total number of ballots that remain to be canvassed.
  • Require clerks to send out mail ballots to UOCAVA voters by the 45th day before Election Day, and to all other voters no later than the 21st day before Election Day. Under existing law, ballots are sent no later than the 47th day before Election Day.
  • Require disclosure of electronic election equipment testing, including of tabulators, on a municipality's internet site, if the municipality has one. Under existing law, such disclosure must be published in newspapers.

  • Make multiple conforming changes and changes to the nominating process for independent candidates that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 17, 2022, would create an automatic voter registration system, create new crimes aimed at protecting voters, improve language accessibility, and make other changes to election administration. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create an automatic registration system with the Department of Transportation (DOT) that includes a wholesale effort to register voters and update their registration. The WEC would be required to report on its progress in doing the wholesale effort by July 1, 2023, and attempt to complete it by July 1, 2025. Specifically, the bill would require the Department of Transportation to transfer to the Wisconsin Election Commission (WEC) its entire database of current license and state ID holders, and to the extent people provided it, copies of any documentation of their citizenship as part of getting their license or ID. If a person opted out of voter registration while doing their transaction with the DOT, their data would not be included. The WEC would compare the data to its existing voter registration list, and then:
    • If the person is already registered, but there is a discrepancy between the registration and the DOT database, the WEC would attempt to contact them and resolve the issue. If the WEC did not successfully contact the voter, the WEC would resolve the discrepancy in favor of the registration record.
    • If the person is not yet registered and the WEC can confirm their eligibility using the DOT data and any other reliable data the WEC can obtain, the WEC would register them. After registering someone to vote, the WEC would send them a multilingual notice to the voter to enable them to opt-out of being registered or to request a confidential listing.
    • If the person had been registered but their registration was marked ineligible because they failed to vote for four years and did not respond to a notice, and the person has neither moved nor changed their name, the WEC would contact the voter to determine if the voter wanted to change their registration to eligible. If the WEC did not successfully contact them, the voter's registration would remain ineligible.
  • Require the WEC to send a voter notice at their last known address whenever removing them from the registration list or changing their status to ineligible, except if the voter requested the change. Under existing law, notice is required if the change is for an address reason and is explicitly not required when canceling a registration due to death. Notice to the voter is not specifically addressed if the reason is a felony conviction or adjudication of mental incapacity.
  • Require the Department of Transportation to give the WEC information from its drivers' license and state ID database for registration list maintenance purposes continuously and no less than monthly.
  • Expand early voting by requiring election officials to allow anyone on line at the time voting is to end to vote.
  • Create a way for people to seek an injunction to stop deceptive election practices and create a related felony. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Define "deceptive election practices" as a person, acting under color of law or otherwise, intentionally inducing another person to refrain from registering or voting at an election by knowingly providing that person with false election-related information. "Election related information" would be information about the date, time, place, or manner of conducting an election, eligibility to vote generally, a specific voter's registration status or eligibility, or the explicit endorsement by any person of a candidate at an election.
    • Allow an impacted person to seek an injunction in the relevant circuit court.
    • Allow an impacted person to complain to the WEC, which would be required to promptly investigate, and if the WEC determines the complaint is meritorious, refer the complaint to an appropriate prosecutor, disseminate accurate information,
    • Require the WEC to report to the Legislature about any such complaints and its actions after every general election.
    • Define engaging in deceptive election practices with the intent to prevent any person from exercising the right to vote in an election as a felony.
  • Create a new felony crime of voter suppression. The bill would define voter suppression as knowingly attempting to prevent or deter another person from voting or registering to vote based upon fraudulent, deceptive, or spurious grounds or information. In addition to the criminal penalty, any voter would be allowed to sue for any legal or equitable relief to stop voter suppression, and a prevailing plaintiff could recoup attorneys' fees and costs. The bill would specify two acts as inherently voter suppression, but not limit the crime to them:
    • Challenging another person's right to register or vote at an election based upon information the person knows is false.
    • Attempting to induce another person to refrain from registering or voting by providing that person with information the person knows is false.
  • Expand and narrow the existing felony of election threats and increase its severity. In addition to the criminal penalty, any voter would be allowed to sue for any legal or equitable relief to stop election threats, and a prevailing plaintiff could recoup attorneys' fees and costs. Concerning the definition of the crime, the bill would:
    • Expand one provision to enable it to be committed by using "any tactic of coercion or intimidation," and enabling it to be committed by impacting a voter's registration decision instead of only their voting decision.
    • Narrow one provision to replace a prohibition on "any act" that has the threatening effect with a requirement that a person to use, or threaten to use, force, violence, restraint, or any tactic of coercion or intimidation to compel to have that impact.
  • Create a voter's bill of rights and require its posting and dissemination.
  • Improve language accessibility by:
    • Requiring the municipal clerk or board of election commissioners in jurisdictions that are required to provide multilingual election information and materials by federal law to contact and coordinate with organizations that advocate for such language speakers to ensure that each polling place in the jurisdiction adequately serves the needs of those individuals.
    • Allowing any voter to sue for legal or equitable relief to enforce multilingual notice requirements or the requirements to post the voters' bill of rights or other materials. Prevailing plaintiffs would be able to recover attorneys' fees and costs.
    • Creating a civil penalty of $500/violation for municipal clerks or executive directors of boards of election commissioners who fail to provide required multilingual election materials.
  • Require the WEC, county clerks, and municipal clerks to maintain the privacy of voters' phone numbers and email addresses.

  • Require the WEC to improve its election administration manual by adding certain content and features.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 9, 2022, would amend the state constitution to make major changes to the state's redistricting process. Under the bill, the Legislative Research Bureau would prepare the redistricting plans, receiving advice from a new Redistricting Advisory Commission. The Bureau would present plans to the Legislature, which could enact or reject them. If the Legislature rejected two plans, it could create its own, but any such plan would need to be approved by three-fourths of the Legislature. Under existing law, the Legislature draws and adopts maps with few constraints other than those imposed by the U.S. Constitution and federal law. To the extent constraints are imposed, they are in the state constitution. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the Bureau to propose redistricting plans that comply with certain criteria, then embody them in legislation that it submits to the Legislature. Any draft maps, along with the data sets used to create the maps, would be open to public inspection and copying and made available on the Internet site of the Bureau as soon as the maps are produced. The districts the Bureau draws would be required to meet these criteria:
    • Congressional districts would have as equal a population as practicable while complying with the Voting Rights Act of 1965, and state legislative districts could not vary in population by more than 10% unless necessary to comply with the Voting Rights Act of 1965. While the U.S. Constitution and the Voting Rights Act apply to redistricting generally, they are not referenced in the current constitutional redistricting provisions or redistricting statutes.
    • District boundaries would coincide with ward boundaries, and to the extent consistent with population and federal law, coincide with the boundaries of political subdivisions. Minimizing the division of political subdivisions would be required. Under current constitutional provisions, Assembly districts must follow county, precinct, town, or ward lines, consist of contiguous territory, and be in as compact form as practicable. Senate districts must be composed of three Assembly districts comprising convenient contiguous territory.
    • Districts would be composed of convenient contiguous territory. Areas that meet only at the points of adjoining corners would not be contiguous. Under current constitutional provisions, Assembly districts must follow county, precinct, town, or ward lines, consist of contiguous territory, and be in as compact form as practicable. Senate districts must be composed of three Assembly districts comprising convenient contiguous territory.
    • Districts would be compact in form, meaning square, rectangular, or hexagonal to the extent permitted by natural or political boundaries. The bill includes ways of determining relative compactness. Under current constitutional provisions, Assembly districts must follow county, precinct, town, or ward lines, consist of contiguous territory, and be in as compact form as practicable. Senate districts must be composed of three Assembly districts comprising convenient contiguous territory.
    • Districts could not be drawn with the intent or result of denying or abridging the equal opportunity of racial or language minorities to participate in the political process or diminishing the ability of racial or language minorities to elect representatives of each minority group's choice, whether by the group or by voting in concert with other persons. Current redistricting rules do not have comparable provisions beyond the requirements of federal law.
    • Districts could not be drawn to favor a political party, incumbent legislator or member of Congress, or other person or group or, except to the extent required to augment or dilute the voting strength of a language or racial minority group. In drawing districts, the Bureau could not consider the residence addresses of incumbent legislators or members of Congress. Current redistricting rules do not have comparable provisions beyond the requirements of federal law.
    • Congressional districts would contain only whole state senate districts, to the extent complying with other criteria allows. Current redistricting rules do not have a comparable provision.
    • Except to test the "efficiency gap" and the competitiveness of each district, which the bill requires the Bureau to do, the Bureau could not consider the political affiliations of registered voters or previous election results. Demographic information could only be used as needed to meet the various redistricting requirements. Current redistricting rules do not have a comparable provision.
  • Create a five-member Redistricting Advisory Commission. No analog exists under current law. The majority leader of the senate and the speaker of the assembly would each appoint one person, and the minority leaders in each house would appoint one each. The four members would then choose the fifth. The Commission would:
    • If requested to do so by the Bureau, provide direction concerning any decision for which no clearly applicable guideline is provided.
    • Oversee the work of Bureau employees engaged in preparing a redistricting plan and would be able to enter into contracts for hiring experts to assist in the preparation of such plans, if three-fourths of the commission approves. Similarly, the Commission would be able to terminate a contract employee only with the approval of three-fourths of its members.
    • Upon delivery by the Bureau of a bill embodying a redistricting plan, make available to the public at the earliest feasible time copies of the bill, maps illustrating the plan, a summary of the criteria, a statement of the population of each district included in the plan and the relative deviation of each district population from the ideal district population.
    • As expeditiously as reasonably possible after the Bureau delivers its bill, schedule and conduct public hearings on the plan. No more than one public hearing could be held in the city of Madison, and at least one public hearing would be held in each Congressional district of the state.
    • Following the hearings, promptly submit to the Legislature a report summarizing information and testimony from the hearings.
  • Create a process for the Legislature to follow once it receives the Bureau's bills. Specifically:
    • No less than seven days after receiving the Commission's report following the public hearings, one chamber would vote on the Bureau's bills without amendment. If the bill passed, it would be sent to the other chamber for a similar vote. If the bills failed to pass both chambers, the chief clerk of the chamber(s) that rejected the bills would give the Bureau the chamber's reasons for rejecting the bills.
    • The Bureau would then create new plans, reflecting the reasons to the extent possible while complying with the redistricting criteria, and submit new bills to the Legislature within 21 days of the first bills' rejection. The Legislature would be required to vote on the new bills, without amendments, within seven days.
    • If the Legislature again rejects the bills, the process would be repeated, but this time the Legislature would be allowed to amend the Bureau's third set of bills. The passage of the third set of bills would need the approval of three-fourths of all the members elected in each house.

  • Establish an evidentiary rule for litigation challenging a redistricting plan brought based on an excessive population variance among senate or assembly districts established in the plan, the Legislature would have the burden of justifying any variance over 10 percent between the population of a senate or assembly district and the applicable ideal district population. If an action was brought challenging a Congressional redistricting plan based on an excessive population variance among congressional districts, the Legislature would have the burden of justifying any variance over 1 percent between the population of a Congressional district and the applicable ideal district population.

    Last updated March 10, 2022

BILLSUMMARY: Creates the Independent Redistricting Commission of the Joint Committee on Government and Finance.
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 12, 2022, would create an independent redistricting commission for federal congressional and state legislative districts, which would create a redistricting plan for final approval by the legislature. Members of the redistricting commission will be designated by legislative leaders of the majority and minority party and the state chairs of the two largest political parties. The members may not be lobbyists, elected officials, or state party officers. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require that redistricting considerations for the commission include, in order of priority:
    • Creating a grid-like pattern with districts of equal population, which are then altered as necessary to accommodate additional goals.
    • Compliance with existing state and federal law.
    • Equal population, to the extent practicable.
    • Compact and contiguous districts.
    • District lines use visible geographic features, political boundaries, and undivided census tracts, to the extent practicable.
    • Competitive districts should be favored.
    • Geographic integrity of political subdivisions and communities of interest.
    • Avoiding oddly shaped districts.
    • Avoiding division of counties, or minimizing division if a division is necessary.
    • Party registration and voting history data must be excluded from the initial map-drawing process, but may be used to test maps for compliance with the other goals.
    • Incumbency may not be considered.
    • Demographic information, other than population, cannot be considered except as required by other laws.
  • Mandate that the redistricting commission create a 30-day public comment period with a public hearing in each federal congressional district and with the opportunity for online comment.
  • Set the deadline for map drawing as April 1 in each year ending in one, except that this deadline may be moved back commensurately with any delay in delivery of census data.

  • The legislature must bring the commission's plan to a vote within three months after the plan is approved by the commission. If the legislature doesn't pass the redistricting plan, the commission must create a second plan considering the legislature's reasons for rejection of the initial plan. The second plan must be voted on by the legislature within two months of its approval by the commission. That process continues until such time a redistricting plan is approved by the legislature.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 17, 2023, would expand Alaska's limited same-day registration to every election conducted by the state, and offer it on Election Day and during early voting. The bill would also facilitate mail voting by verifying mail ballots through signature matching, offering voters an opportunity to cure signature issues, enabling them to join a permanent mail voting list, and prepaying ballot return postage. Existing law requires voters to have their ballot certificate signature notarized or witnessed, apply for mail ballots every year, and gives voters no notice of a ballot certificate issue that will prevent their ballot from being counted, much less an opportunity to address it. Finally, the bill would create comprehensive ballot tracking, improve ballot language access, make conducting a universal mail ballot election easier, change the voter registration form, and set minimum poll worker pay.

With regard to same-day registration, the bill would expand same-day registration to all elections conducted by the state, and offer it during early voting and on Election Day. Under existing law, people may register and then immediately vote only for the offices of President and Vice-President. The bill would provide that:

  • Voters who same-day register must cast ballots that are verified on the spot, such as in-person mail ballots (called "in-person absentee", in Alaska), or ballots that can be verified before counting, such as a provisional ballot (called a "questioned ballot" in Alaska), or a special needs ballot. Under existing law, voters who register at a voting location and then cast presidential ballots must vote provisional ballots.
  • Voters who same-day register must sign an affidavit attesting that they meet Alaska's 30-day residency-before-registration requirement because they will have lived in the state and the state house district in which they are voting for the 30 days before the election. They must sign that affidavit in front of an election official at the voting location, who will witness the signature. Voters who have moved within the state and meet the residency requirement at their new address may use the same-day registration process to update their address and vote an in-person mail, provisional, or special needs ballot appropriate to their new address. Under existing law, voters who complete mail ballots, including in person, must have their signature witnessed, but no voters are required to complete a similar affidavit. Also under existing law, voters who transfer their registration to a new precinct or a new state house district within 30 days of an election must vote provisional ballots appropriate for their new address.
  • Voters who same-day register must document their residency by showing:
    • a physical or electronic copy of identification issued by the federal government, the state, a municipality, a tribal government, or a secondary or postsecondary school that displays the applicant's Alaska residence address or
    • a utility bill, bank statement, paycheck, government check, or other government document dated not more than 60 days before the registration or reregistration and displaying the applicant's name and Alaska residence address.
  • The envelope for an in-person absentee ballot, provisional ballot, or special needs ballot, which is used to register the voter, must include space for the voter to affiliate with a political party if they choose and related instructions. Under existing law, the envelope for provisional and in-person absentee ballots already includes the information needed to register, and in the case of presidential same-day registration is so used. However, existing law does not address special needs ballots in this context, nor does it require the envelope to include the opportunity to affiliate with a party.
  • Election officials would be required to staff early voting locations with one or more registration officials.

  • Municipalities would be required, for certain local elections, to allow people not on the statewide voter registration list within 30 days of the election, to register and then vote, but only on an in-person mail, provisional, or special needs ballot. The bill would make a conforming change by repealing a provision of municipal law.

    The bill would facilitate voting by mail (called "absentee voting" in Alaska) by:


  • Repealing the requirement that a voter have their signature on the ballot certificate notarized or witnessed, instead requiring that the voter's signature be matched against a signature in their registration record. Only voters' signatures on ballots that voters received by mail would be verified by signature match. Mail ballots received and cast in person would be considered verified by the voter ID the voter was required to show to receive the ballot in person.
    • For the ballots requiring signature matching, the bill would require the Director to issue regulations creating a signature verification process that includes signature comparison software, and would require the Director to provide signature match training, including the use of the software, to election officials who had that role. Election officials would be prohibited from deciding that a voter's signature did not match simply because the voter used initials or a common nickname as part of their signature.
  • Creating a cure process to enable mail voters to address ballot certificate signature issues and enable their ballot to be counted. Specifically, if a mail voter's ballot is rejected because they forgot to sign the ballot certificate, their certificate signature was deemed not to match a signature on file, or their record lacked a signature for comparison:
    • the Director would be required, within 24 hours, to attempt to send deficiency notices by email, text, or phone, if the voter has any such contact information on file. Within 48 hours and not later than five days after Election Day, the Director would be required to mail the notice by first class, nonforwardable mail to the address on the voter's registration record.
    • the required deficiency notice would include an explanation, a form for the voter to return with a copy of acceptable in-person voter ID, and a signature for verification. The mailed notice must include a printed copy of the form, but the form must also be available in a format that can be completed and returned electronically.
    • the ballot would be counted if the completed form, signature, and ID copy are received by the Division within 14 days after Election Day, and the ballot is otherwise valid.
    • the Division would add the signature to the voter's registration record if the voter provides a missing signature or cures a nonmatching signature.
    • if a voter returns the cure form and indicates that they did not vote a mail ballot, the Division would send a copy of the ballot certificate signature and the voter's file signatures to the Alaska Attorney General for investigation.
  • Enabling any voter to join a list to receive a mail ballot for every upcoming election automatically. Voters would be removed from the list if their ballot were returned undeliverable, or if they did not vote their mail ballot for four years. Under existing law, certain voters are allowed to join a list to automatically receive mail ballot applications.
  • Allowing voters to request mail ballot materials in any language the state is required by federal law to offer, so long as the request is made at least 45 days before the election.
  • Providing prepaid return postage for mail ballot voters. Under existing law, postage is the voter's responsibility. The bill would make a conforming change to an election crime to explicitly exempt prepaid postage from the definition of things of value that could be considered prohibited bribes to a vote.
  • Creating comprehensive ballot tracking. Although existing law does not require the Division to offer ballot tracking, the Division through its website allows a voter to check if their absentee ballot application was accepted or if a correction is needed, if the ballot was mailed, or if the ballot was received. The existing tracking system on the state website does not include information on whether the voter's ballot was counted. Under the bill, the Director would be required to offer a free online system that a voter could use easily with a mobile device that would enable a voter to
    • confirm that the voter's ballot has been sent by the division.
    • track the date of the ballot's delivery to the voter.
    • confirm the division's receipt of the voter's ballot.
    • determine whether the voter's certificate has been reviewed.
    • determine whether the voter's ballot has been counted. Relatedly, the bill would repeal certain existing requirements relating to post-election notices to voters about their ballots' rejection.
    • receive the information necessary to cure a ballot rejected for a missing or mismatched signature.
  • Allowing mail ballot verification to begin 10 days before Election Day. Under existing law, verification may begin seven days before Election Day.

  • Prohibiting a voter's party affiliation from being disclosed on the ballot envelope.

    The bill would make changes to the standard voter registration process. Specifically, the bill would:


  • Revise the voter registration form to:
    • offer applicants the opportunity to pick, from the written languages in which federal law requires Alaska to offer election materials, which language they would like to receive ballots and other materials. The Division would provide the applicant with such materials until the voter's registration is inactivated or canceled, or the Division is no longer required by federal law to offer election materials in that language. If election materials are not available in the applicant's language of choice, the Division would be required to inform the applicant and allow them to choose another language.
    • allow a voter to submit an electronic signature instead of signing the paper or making their mark on it, according to a process to be created by the Alaska Division of Elections by regulation.
    • change the warning related to a false statement on the form so that it reads subjection to prosecution under the election code or for perjury, instead of saying prosecution for a misdemeanor. Perjury is a felony. As the bill does not amend the definition of perjury nor specifically and newly apply it to registration forms, this provision appears to be a conforming change to reflect the current state of the law.
    • inform the voter that if they are registered to vote in another jurisdiction, the Director of the Division of Elections will inform the chief elections officer in that jurisdiction and request that the voter's registration in that jurisdiction be canceled.

  • Allow voters to register when they complete an online application for a mail ballot, repealing existing law's specific prohibition against the practice. Under existing law, people applying for a mail ballot using a paper form are allowed to register to vote as part of the mail ballot application, and voters are separately able to register to vote online.

    The bill would make myriad changes to in-person voting. Specifically, the bill would:


  • Provide in-person voters with language access by:
    • requiring the Division, at each polling place, to provide the language assistance required by federal law in a manner that enables each voter to participate effectively in the electoral process.
    • requiring an election supervisor to post at each polling place information regarding the availability of language assistance in English and all other languages federal law requires language assistance be provided in the jurisdiction.
  • Improve notice of precinct or polling place changes by requiring the public notice to include mailing affected voters two written notices of the change in addition to the notice to local officials, in newspapers, on the Divison's website, and in the voter's pamphlet. Under existing law, the Division needs to mail only one notice to voters.
  • Set minimum election worker pay.
  • Prohibit showing a photo, video, or another image of one's ballot or another voter's ballot within 200 feet of the entrance to a polling place in an attempt to persuade a person to vote for or against a candidate, proposition, or question. However, showing such an image for any other purpose, including to the public on social media, would not be prohibited, nor would a voter needing assistance be prohibited from showing their ballot to the person assisting them. Under existing law, people are simply prohibited from attempting to persuade voters to vote for or against candidates, propositions, or questions in that zone, without reference to ballot images, and showing one's marked ballot to an election official or any other person is flatly prohibited.
  • Require properly designated early voting locations that offer in-person mail ballots to remain used as such for all elections unless it becomes unavailable or the Director determines in writing that the location is no longer appropriate, and makes the written determination public.
  • Clarify that a person who goes to an early voting location that offers Election-Day ballots who is unable to show voter ID, verify their address, and/or sign the poll book would be allowed to vote an in-person absentee ballot under the rules that apply to that process.

  • Require the chairperson of any political party, party committee, candidate, organized group, or organization that existing law allows to appoint poll watchers to sign the appointing certificate for each watcher. Under existing law, the election board or data processing review board may require watchers to show written proof of their appointment, but it need not be signed by the appointing authority's chairperson. The bill would also repeal the ability of a candidate to appoint one watcher in each precinct and counting center during a primary, special primary, or special election.

    The bill would expand the Division's ability to mail ballots to all voters instead of offering in-person voting. Under existing law, the Division may only send universal mail ballots for entire elections, and only if the election is not a general, party primary, or municipal election, or held concurrently with such an election. Recently the special primary to fill Representative Don Young's seat was conducted with universal mail ballots. The bill would allow the Division to mail ballots to all voters in specific jurisdictions during an election that is otherwise being conducted in a traditional manner. Specifically, the bill would allow the Division to choose to mail ballots to all voters in:


  • An unincorporated community with a population of 750 or less if the director determines that, because of an inability to hire election workers, facilitating organized in-person voting in the community is unreasonable.

  • An area affected or threatened by a disaster for which the governor has issued a disaster declaration due to a natural disaster, epidemic, explosion, riot, an outbreak of disease or a credible threat of an imminent outbreak of disease, or an enemy or terrorist attack or a credible threat of an imminent enemy or terrorist attack.

    Finally, the bill has miscellaneous other provisions that would:


  • Require the Division to recommend to the legislature ways to expand early voting in rural communities and low-income neighborhoods by November 1, 2025.
  • Update unofficial return reporting and hand count auditing to reflect the adoption of ranked-choice voting by requiring unofficial results to include, for each candidate, the subsequent candidate rankings selected by the voters who ranked that candidate as the voters' first choice, and the hand count audit to show voters' rankings for each candidate on the ballot.
  • Simplify the election code by referring to all locations at which people may vote in person before Election Day as "early" voting locations. Under existing law, the term early voting refers to locations where people may vote on Election-Day-style ballots, and locations at which people vote in-person mail ballots are referred to as "absentee voting stations."

  • Require the Director to begin immediately issuing regulations, but otherwise provide that the bill takes effect January 1, 2024.

Last Updated January 18, 2023

This bill, as amended on May 15, 2024, would create a notice and cure process for mail ballots, eliminate the existing witness signature requirement for mail ballots, and change voter list maintenance practices. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create a notice and cure process for mail ballots and make conforming changes related to the creation of that process. Existing law requires that a ballot be rejected if the ballot certificate is missing a signature or the insufficient voter ID has been provided, but does not require notice to a voter of a defect, or the opportunity to correct it. The bill would require the following:
    • Election officials would be required to notify the voter of a ballot defect within 24 hours by email, text, and/or telephone call, and to send notice by mail within 48 hours (but not later than five days after Election Day).
    • Notice would be required to include a form through which the voter could provide a signature or copy of voter ID, for return by mail or electronically.
    • A defective ballot would be counted only if the voter returned a properly completed form within 14 days after Election Day.
  • Eliminate the existing requirement that a voter have a notary or witness observe while they complete their mail ballot and sign their ballot envelope, and make conforming changes related to the elimination of the requirement. Under existing law, a voter casting a mail ballot must do so in the presence of an individual qualified to administer oaths, such as a notary public, commissioned officer of the armed forces, district judge or magistrate, United States postal official, or registration official. If such a witness is not reasonably accessible, a mail ballot may be witnessed by any individual over the age of 18 and that individual must sign the ballot and provide their birthdate.
  • Expand the categories of voters who receive an address confirmation notice during annual list maintenance of the voter roll, and shorten the timeframe for inactivating a registration. Under existing law, notice is sent to voters who (1) have had mail returned to election officials as undeliverable in the last two years, or (2) have not contacted the Election Division in the last two years, or (3) have not voted or appeared in vote in the last two general elections. The bill would:
    • Expand the categories of voters that receive a confirmation notice to include to voters who, in the last two years, have registered to vote in another state, obtained a license in another state, served as a juror in another state, received resident benefits in another state, or have established residency in another state. The bill would also modify the existing requirements by requiring that notice go to voters who have both failed to contact the Election Division in the last two years and not voted or appeared to vote in the last two general elections. Under existing law, officials must send notice to voters who meet either criterion, rather than both.
    • Require that confirmation notices be sent by forwardable mail and email if available. Under existing law, initial confirmation notice must be sent by non-forwardable mail only.
    • Require officials to inactivate a voter's registration if the voter fails to respond to the confirmation notice within 45 days. Under existing law, officials may only inactivate a voter's registration if (1) an initial confirmation notice is returned as undeliverable, and the voter has not contacted the election division or voted or appeared to vote in the last four years; and (2) the voter fails to respond to a second confirmation notice, sent by forwardable mail, within 45 days.
    • Require the new provisions go into effect on July 1, 2025.
  • Require the Division of Elections to adopt a new routine list maintenance process for the voter roll, to review data breaches and the number of registered voters compared to individuals eligible to vote in the state; the names of voters who are deceased, disenfranchised due to a felony conviction, or otherwise ineligible to vote; and individuals registered to vote in another state. The bill would specify data sources for the review, require "a best practice voter registration system to improve identity matching," and require a report of the review to the legislature at the state of each session. These requirements would go into effect on July 1, 2025.
  • Prohibit officials from rejecting a special needs ballot voted by a qualified voter with a disability for an administrative error, provided that the voter complies with the voting process rules.
  • Require the director of elections to develop a process to allow a voter to cancel their registration in person or electronically. Existing law is silent on this issue but in practice, voters may cancel their registration by contacting their regional elections office or by mail or email.
  • Require the director of elections to publish notice of any data breach of confidential voter registration records and report details to the president of the Senate and speaker of the House of Representatives within 30 days of discovering the breach. There is no similar requirement under existing law. The bill would also newly require the Division of Elections to develop a cybersecurity program for the voter list and provide cybersecurity training to election officials.
  • Prohibit knowingly using deepfakes ("synthetic media") in election-related communication with the intent to influence an election, and create a civil right of action for a "person who is harmed" by a communication that violates the prohibitions. The bill would set out definitions for the elements of the action, including affirmative defenses. The bill would also provide that a claim for defamation due to synthetic media brought by a candidate is a per se claim.

The bill also contains several provisions related to topics that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

Previous versions of the bill contained provisions that were amended out of this version. Those provisions would have:

  • Created same day registration, provided that the voter supplied a declaration stating that they established residency at least 30 days before Election Day in the state and the House district in which they sought to vote.
  • Required officials to send registration confirmation notices to voters who had not voted or appeared to vote in the last two years, rather than in the last two general elections as provided by existing law.
  • Required the director of elections to conduct a risk-limiting audit of selected election results after the ballot counting review but before the certification.
  • Allowed an individual who claimed to be a registered voter, but for whom there was no evidence of registration in the precinct, to vote an absentee, special needs, or questioned ballot.
  • Required the director of elections to transfer the registration of a voter from one precinct to another within a house district when requested by the voter even if the request was made within 30 days of an election. If a request was made within 30 days of an election, the voter could vote an absentee, special needs, or questioned ballot.
  • Required a mail ballot be rejected if it was returned by mail and had no postmark.

Last Updated July 9, 2024

This bill, as introduced on March 22, 2023, would create new election crimes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create two new ways to commit the felony of unlawful interference with an election. The bill would make it a felony for a person to:
    • Intentionally open or tamper with a signed mail ballot certificate (called "absentee ballot certificate" in Alaska), sealed mail ballot envelope, or package of ballots without express authorization from the Director of the Division of Elections.
    • Intentionally breach, hack, alter, or tamper with election machinery, including a tabulator, a program, a system, a server, or software used to verify identity, count or tabulate, or manage or control an election function.
  • Create the felony of election fraud. A person would commit election fraud if they commit any form of the felony of unlawful interference with an election with the intent to change the outcome of an election.

  • Create a new way for election officials to commit the felony of election official misconduct in the first degree. Specifically, it would be a felony for an election official to knowingly disclose, share, or report to a person who is not an election official election results, returns, or any confidential election data before the polls close on Election Day.

Last Updated March 24, 2023
