VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 22, 2023, would:

  • Allow people voting by mail to complete their ballot certificate without having their signature notarized or witnessed. Existing law requires the voter's signature to be notarized or, if a notary is not reasonably available, to be witnessed by someone who is at least 18 years old.
  • Create a cure process to enable registered voters whose mail ballots would otherwise be rejected to address the issue causing the ballot rejection. Issues that could be remedied would be (1) a missing signature on the ballot certificate, or (2) a failure to enclose ID documentation if the voter is voting for the first time and failed to provide sufficient identifying information when registering to vote. The cure process would:
    • Require the Director to immediately make a reasonable effort to contact the voter, explain the ballot deficiency, explain how the deficiency may be cured, and inform the voter of the deadline to cure the ballot. Within 48 hours and not later than five days after election day, the Director would send a notice of deficiency by first class, nonforwardable mail to the address on the voter's registration record and by electronic mail to the voter's electronic mail address if the voter has provided one. If the voter has provided a telephone number, the Director would attempt to notify the voter of the deficiency by telephone call or text message to the voter's telephone number.
    • Provide that the notice of deficiency include a form for the voter to confirm that they returned a ballot and provide a copy of ID documentation sufficient to vote in person. The mailed notice would include a paper copy of the form, and the Director would be required to also make the form available in a format that can be completed and returned electronically.
    • Require the voter to return the form and ID documentation within 14 days after Election Day.
  • Create comprehensive mail ballot tracking. While existing law does not require ballot tracking, the Division of Elections' website currently enables voters to learn if their mail ballot application has been received and approved or rejected and if their mail ballot has been sent to them or received back from them. The bill would require the Division to build or procure from a third party a tracking system that is free to voters, mobile-friendly, online, and uses multi-factor authentication. The tracking system would be required to enable voters to:
    • Confirm that the voter's ballot has been sent by the Division
    • Track the date of the ballot's delivery to the voter
    • Confirm the division's receipt of the voter's ballot
    • Determine whether the voter's certificate has been reviewed
    • Determine whether the voter's ballot has been counted
    • Provide the information necessary to cure a rejected ballot.
    • Learn why their ballot was rejected, if it was rejected.
  • Require the Director to make instructions on how to use the online multi-factor authentication system for tracking absentee ballots available to voters.
  • Create an election offense telephone hotline. The Director of the Division of Elections would be required to establish a toll-free election offense hotline to receive reports of election offenses, publicize its availability, and encourage the public to report voter misconduct or other election offenses. The bill would require the hotline to be continuously staffed during the hours an absentee voting station or an early voting location is open, and for 24 hours after the time the polls open on Election Day. From 24 hours after the polls open until all election results are certified, the Director would be required to ensure an election official is available to respond to such calls. Publicizing the hotline would include putting the phone number on voting machines, ballot envelopes, and other election materials in a manner the Director determines will provide maximum public notice of the hotline and include at least two conspicuous notices in each polling place.
  • Empower the Legislative Council to contract with and appoint technical subject matter experts to conduct full forensic audits of election data, algorithms, software, and equipment, including precinct tabulators, storage devices, voting machines, and vote tally systems. The Division would be required to provide the technical subject matter expert full supervised access to all election data, algorithms, software, and equipment, including precinct tabulators, storage devices, voting machines, and vote tally systems. The Legislative Council is a 14-member body evenly divided between the members of the House and Senate, appointed by the President of the Senate and the Speaker of the House, and must include at least one member of the minority major party from each chamber. The current Legislative Council has ten Republican members, three Democratic ones, and one unaffiliated member.
  • Require ballots to have a security identifier, such as a watermark, or a seal, and require ballots to be rejected if they lack the identifier. "Security identifier" would include an election official's signature.
  • Require the Director to issue regulations developing a cybersecurity program to protect voter registration records and enable the division to detect and recover from cyberattacks. The program would be required to include cybersecurity training for election officials. The director would also be required to develop a nonpublic list of registered voters whose numerical identifiers have been released in a breach of data.
  • Clarify that if an early voter does not show the required voter ID documentation, they may vote a provisional ballot (called "questioned ballot" in Alaska.)

  • Create ballot chain of custody, election equipment, and document retention rules Voting Rights Lab does not track.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 17, 2023, would facilitate mail voting by making it easier to complete a mail ballot, give voters notice of ballot certificate defects and an opportunity to address them so that their ballots will count, and create comprehensive ballot tracking. The bill would also create new election security requirements focused on cybersecurity, chains of custody, and tabulator testing, while also creating a voter fraud hotline. Finally, the bill would empower an at least nominally bipartisan legislative committee to hire "technical subject matter experts" to conduct "forensic audits" of essentially everything connected to election administration.

Specifically, concerning mail voting, the bill would:

  • Repeal the requirement that mail voters (called "absentee voters" in Alaska) have their signature on their ballot certificate on the ballot envelope notarized or witnessed.
  • Create a cure process to enable a mail voter who failed to sign their ballot or who, being a first-time voter that registered to vote without providing a verified driver's license or Social Security number, failed to include the ID required to complete their voter registration. Specifically, the bill would:
    • require the Director of the Alaska Division of Elections to immediately make a reasonable effort to contact the voter, explain the ballot deficiency and how to cure it, and inform the voter of the cure deadline. Within 48 hours and not later than five days after Election Day, the Director would be required to send notice by first class, nonforwardable mail to the address on the voter's registration record and by email if the voter has provided an electronic mail address. If the voter has provided a telephone number, the Director shall attempt to notify the voter of the deficiency by telephone call or text message.
    • require the notice to include a form for the voter to confirm that the voter returned a ballot to the division and to provide a copy of in-person voter ID. Notice by mail would include a printed copy of the form, but the Director would also be required to make the form available in a format that could be completed and returned electronically.
    • require a voter to return the form and ID within 14 days after Election Day, or their ballot will not count.
  • Create mail ballot tracking by requiring the Director to establish or purchase from a third party an online, mobile-friendly, free tracking system that verifies a voter's identity using a multi-factor authentication system and allows a voter to:
    • confirm that the voter's ballot has been sent by the division
    • track the date of the ballot's delivery to the voter
    • confirm the Division's receipt of the voter's ballot
    • determine whether the voter's certificate has been reviewed
    • determine whether the voter's ballot has been counted
    • learn the process by which the voter may cure the lack of signature or verify their identity if the signature on the voter's ballot was missing
    • learn the reason the voter's ballot was not counted, if the ballot was not counted.
  • Allow a mail ballot that is returned by mail but lacks a postmark or is postmarked after Election Day to be counted if the ballot envelope is marked with a tracking barcode sufficient to verify the ballot was mailed on or before Election Day.

  • Make a conforming change to confirm that early voters who fail to show the required voter ID may vote a provisional ballot (called a "questioned ballot" in Alaska).

    Concerning election crimes and election security, the bill would:


  • Require the Director and/or the Division to:
    • establish a toll-free election offense hotline to receive telephone calls reporting election offenses under this chapter, and to publicize its availability and encourage its use. The publicity must include posting the number on voting machines, ballot envelopes, and other election materials, and giving each election board notices to conspicuously post in each polling place. The hotline would be required to be continuously staffed during the hours an absentee voting station or early voting location is open, and for 24 hours after the polls open on Election Day. From 24 hours after the polls open until all election results are certified, the Director would be required to ensure an election official is available to respond to calls made to the hotline.
    • issue regulations creating a chain of custody system to account for every ballot, absentee ballot certificate and envelope, and paper record of an electronically generated ballot that accounts for their location and who has their custody from the time the ballot is produced to the expiration of the 22 month post-election record retention period. Relatedly, the bill would require unused and spoiled ballots to be marked void and secured, rather than destroyed.
    • issue regulations creating a cybersecurity program to defend voter registration records, including training of election officials. In addition, the Director would be required to create a nonpublic list of registered voters whose numerical identifiers were released in a data breach and "exercise caution to protect election integrity."
    • conduct a "routine forensic examination" of each ballot tabulator before and after each election, prohibit a tabulator from being connected to an internet or cellular network from 24 hours before polls open on Election Day until 14 days after polls close, and require tabulator data to be transferred to a separate storage device for transmission. In addition, the Division would be required to develop and apply strict chain-of-custody protocols for precinct tabulators and the separate storage device.
    • Require ballots to have a watermark, seal, or another security identifier, and forbid counting any ballot that lacked it. The signature of an election official would qualify as a security identifier.

  • Empower the Legislative Council to contract with and appoint "technical subject matter experts" to "conduct full forensic audits of election data, algorithms, software, and equipment, including precinct tabulators, storage devices, voting machines, and vote tally systems." The bill would require the Division to provide any such expert "full supervised access" to all such data and equipment. The Legislative Council is a 14-legislator committee, composed of the Senate President and six Senators the President appoints, the Speaker of the House, and six Representatives the Speaker appoints. Each chamber's delegation must include at least one member of each of the two major parties.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 17, 2023, would create new election felonies. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create new ways to commit the class C felony of unlawful interference with an election. Under existing law, five different kinds of conduct constitute the crime. Under the bill, those five would remain, and a person would also commit that felony:
    • if they intentionally open or tamper with a signed absentee ballot certificate, sealed absentee ballot envelope, or package of ballots without express authorization from the Director of the Alaska Division of Elections, or
    • if they intentionally breach, hack, alter, or tamper with election machinery, including a tabulator, a program, a system, a server, or software used to verify identity, count or tabulate, or manage or control an election function.
  • Create a new Class B felony, called "election fraud." A person would commit election fraud if they committed unlawful interference with an election with the intent to change the outcome of an election.

  • Create a new way for an election official to commit the class C felony of election official misconduct in the first degree. Under existing law, three kinds of conduct can constitute the crime. The bill would add as a fourth knowingly disclosing, sharing, or reporting to a person who is not an election official election results, returns, or any confidential election data before the close of polls on Election Day.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 17, 2023, would both facilitate and restrict voting by mail. In addition, it risks criminal investigation of innocent conduct. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require a voter's signature on the ballot certificate to be matched against the voter's signature in voter registration records, while preserving existing law's requirement that the voter's signature be notarized or witnessed. Despite the notary or witness signature, if the voter's signature is determined not to match, the ballot would be rejected unless the voter cured the signature issue.
    • The signature matching would be done by the district absentee ballot counting board using a process created by regulations issued by the Director of the Alaska Division of Elections that includes signature comparison software. The bill would require training for officials who did signature matching and would prohibit officials from deciding a signature did not match solely because the voter substituted initials or a common nickname for part of their signature.
  • Create a cure process to address missing or mismatched signatures. Specifically, if a voter's mail ballot certificate is not signed, the signature is determined not to match a signature in the voter's record, or the voter does not have a signature on record:
    • the Director must send the voter notice by first class, nonforwardable mail within 48 hours but not later than two days after Election Day, and if the information is in the voter's record, by email, telephone call, or text.
    • the notice must include an explanation of the issue, a form, and instructions. The form would allow the voter to confirm that the voter returned a ballot, provide an ID sufficient to register to vote, and provide a signature. To successfully cure the issue, the voter would need to return the form, ID, and signature to the Division by the 14th day after Election Day. If the voter successfully cured a missing or mismatched signature, the Division would be required to update the voter's record to include the cure signature.
    • if the voter simply fails to return the form by the deadline, or returns the form and indicates that they did not return the ballot to the Division, the ballot will be rejected and copies of the certificate signature and reference signatures will be sent to the Alaska Attorney General for investigation.
  • Create comprehensive ballot tracking and electronic voter registration record access. The Director would be required to establish a free online system available through the Division's website and easily used on a mobile device that:
    • would allow a voter to confirm the Division mailed their ballot, track the date of the ballot's expected delivery, confirm the Division received the returned ballot, determine if their ballot certificate has been reviewed, determine whether their vote has been counted, learn if their signature was missing or was believed not to match, how to cure that signature issue, and determine if their ballot was not counted, why.
    • would allow an election official to access the names and political affiliations of all active and inactive voters on the master voter registration list who registered to vote by mail or with the assistance of a voter registration agency.
  • Require the state to pay the return postage for mail ballots. Under existing law, voters are required to pay the postage to return a ballot.
  • Create a permanent mail voting list so that any voter may choose to automatically receive a mail ballot for every election thereafter. A voter would be removed from the list if a ballot sent to the voter is returned undeliverable or the voter does not vote a mail ballot for four years. Under existing law, certain voters are allowed to join a list to receive mail ballot applications automatically.
  • Authorize certain people to provide voters with ballot return assistance and make it a class A misdemeanor for anyone else to knowingly possess another voter's ballot. Existing Alaska law is silent on ballot return assistance. The bill would authorize:
    • a family member of the voter.
    • a caregiver of the voter.
    • a registered voter who is an employee of a 501(c)(3) organization and is collecting the ballot on behalf of that organization.
    • election officials, postal workers, or private delivery service workers, provided they are performing official duties.

  • Limit the types of ID a voter who registered by mail without including a verified driver's license, state ID, or last four digits of their Social Security number can include with their mail ballot to complete their registration. Under the bill, a voter would no longer be allowed to use a current utility bill, bank statement, paycheck, government check, or another government document that shows the name and current address of the voter. Acceptable forms of ID would be limited to a driver's license, state identification card, current and valid photo identification, birth certificate, passport, or a hunting or fishing license. This change is essentially a conforming change to match acceptable ID types to those allowed by the voter registration portion of the election code.

Last Updated January 31, 2023

This bill, as enacted on August 5, 2023, creates new requirements related to the Department of Corrections, concerning registration verification and ID issued to returning citizens. Specifically, the bill:

  • Adds Dept. of Corrections data to the mandated sources for verifying registration application information provided to voter registration agencies. Previous law required verification through data from the Dept. of Administration (DMV-equivalent) and the Dept. of Revenue only.

  • Requires that the Dept. of Corrections "ensure" that upon discharge from incarceration, individuals have a valid state ID, and requires that the agency issue an ID to those without one at that time. Under previous law, the Department was required only to "assist" a returning citizen in obtaining an ID. The bill keeps in place the existing requirement that officials must pay the application fee for a newly issued state ID.

Last Updated August 21, 2023

This bill, as amended and passed by the Senate State Affairs Committee on May 2, 2023, would enable voters to register through Election Day, change verifying mail ballots to signature matching with cure instead of requiring voters to have their signature notarized or witnessed, improve the state's ballot tracking system, enable voters to join a mail voting list, provide prepaid postage to return mail ballots, require mail ballot counting to start before Election Day, and make other changes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Allow voters to register year-round and vote in any election, implicitly extending same-day registration to all elections. Existing law requires people to register to vote 30 days before Election Day, except that voters may use same-day registration to vote for Presidential and Vice-Presidential races. When registering within the 30 days before Election Day or on Election Day, the voter would be required to complete a ballot type that is only counted after the information about the voter is verified, such as an in-person mail ballot (called "absentee ballot"), a provisional ballot (called "questioned ballot"), or a special-needs ballot. Existing law provides that same-day registrants complete provisional ballots. Relatedly, the bill would allow registration address updates within the 30 days before Election Day if the voter completes a ballot type that undergoes verification before counting.
  • Change how mail ballots (called "absentee ballots" in Alaska) are verified to rely on signature matching instead of having the voter's signature on the ballot certificate notarized or witnessed. Mail ballots completed in person would be exempt from signature verification, as the voter receives the ballot only after showing ID documentation. Relating to signature verification of mail ballots, the bill would:
    • Require the Director of the Division of Elections to issue regulations to create a signature verification process.
    • Require the Director to create signature match training including the use of signature match software.
    • Declare that signatures cannot be ruled inconsistent simply because the voter used a common nickname or an initial.
    • Require election officials to reject ballots when the voter's signature on their ballot certificate is not consistent with a signature in their registration records.

  • Create a cure process that would enable voters to address issues with their mail ballot certificates that would otherwise cause their votes to be rejected. The process would enable voters to address a missing signature, an inconsistent signature, or the voter's failure to provide identification, as certain first-time voters are required to do. Voters would also be able to verify their ballot using the cure process if their registration record does not contain a signature against which the ballot certificate signature could be compared. To cure, voters would be required to sign and return a form and support it with a copy of identification sufficient to vote in person by the 14th day after Election Day.

    To enable cure, the Division would be required to give prompt notice to the voter of the issue that must be cured. If the voter has provided the Division with an email address or phone number, the Division must attempt to contact the voter by email, text, and/or phone call within 24 hours of rejecting the ballot. The Division must also mail notice to the voter within 48 hours of rejecting the ballot, but only through the fifth day after Election Day. The notice would include a description of the issue, the process to cure it, and the form the voter must complete and return. The bill would require the Division to offer an electronic method for the voter to complete the cure process.

    If a voter returns the cure form and indicates that they did not cast the ballot, the Division would forward the ballot signature and any file signatures for the voter to the Attorney General for investigation.


  • Improve the state's ballot tracking system. Ballot tracking is not currently required by statute, but the Division of Elections currently enables voters to use its website to learn if their absentee ballot application was accepted or if a correction is needed, if the ballot was mailed, or if the ballot was received. The tracking system on the state website does not include information on whether the voter's ballot was counted, however, existing law requires the Division to mail a notice of rejection after the election. The bill would require the Division to offer a system that is free, mobile-friendly, and enables a voter to:
    • confirm that the voter's ballot has been sent by the division
    • track the date of the ballot's delivery to the voter
    • confirm the division's receipt of the voter's ballot
    • determine whether the voter's certificate has been reviewed
    • determine whether the voter's ballot has been counted
    • provide the information necessary to cure a rejected ballot
    • learn the reason the voter's ballot was not counted, if the ballot was not counted.
  • Change rules relating to rejecting ballots in additional ways. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Allow a ballot's timeliness to be demonstrated by a ballot tracking code in addition to a postmark.
    • Require rejecting a ballot received by mail after Election Day if the voter dated their signature after Election Day. Existing law requires a ballot to be rejected if it is not attested to on or before Election Day.
    • Provide that certain errors by an election official or a special needs voter's representative would not cause the special needs voter's ballot to be rejected
    • Provide that unless the Division has evidence that a voter who returned multiple ballots intended to have multiple ballots counted, the Division should count a ballot that is not an absentee, questioned, or special needs ballot and reject any other ballot, or, if all the multiple ballots are one of those ballot types, to count the ballot in the first envelope it reviews and reject any other.
  • Enable voters to join a mail voting list when they apply for a mail ballot. Once on the list, a voter would be automatically mailed a ballot for each election until either a ballot is returned undeliverable or the voter fails to return a mail ballot for four years. Existing law allows voters to apply for a mail ballot for all elections in a calendar year with one application, and allows certain voters to be sent a mail ballot application for every election.
  • Provide prepaid return postage for mail ballots. Existing law requires voters to pay the postage. Relatedly the bill would revise an existing crime to clarify that giving a voter prepaid postage would not be a violation of the crime.
  • Require the counting of mail ballots to begin at least seven days before Election Day, and require the first results to be reported to the district absentee counting board by the close of polls on Election Day. Existing law requires ballot counting to begin at the close of polls.
  • Create new language access rules to implement federal law. Specifically, the bill would require the Division to offer election materials in languages required by federal law and in-person assistance in those languages by:
    • Enabling a person, when registering to vote, to designate one of the required languages as the language in which they wish to receive election materials, and have that request remain valid until their registration is made inactive or canceled, or the language is no longer required by federal law.
    • Enabling a person who did not so select a language when registering to request a mail ballot in a covered language, provided that they make the request at least 45 days before Election Day.
    • Requiring the Division to provide federally-required in-person voting language assistance, and to post notices about the availability of the assistance in all polling places.
  • Change the rules relating to when a person is a resident of Alaska for voter registration purposes, and how a voter's residency may be challenged. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Define a voter's residence as that place in which the person's physical habitation is fixed, and to which, whenever absent, the person has a definite, articulable, and reasonable plan to return. Existing law defines residence as that place in which the person's habitation is fixed, and to which, whenever absent, the person has the intention to return. The bill would also clarify that a person loses their Alaska residence when they establish residence in another state, and eliminate a limitation that a change of residence is made solely by removal and intent to remain in another place.
    • Change the process of challenging a voter's residence. The bill would allow a person to challenge a voter's residence by providing evidence that the voter has established residence in another state or elsewhere in the state, or evidence that the person does not meet the definition of resident. The challenge would be made according to a process the bill requires the Director to create by regulation. Existing law provides that a voter's registration address is presumptive evidence of their voting residence that can only be challenged if the voter notifies the Director in writing that the voter moved.
  • Revise address-based list maintenance to change when notices are sent, to whom they are sent, and how they are sent. These notices can result in the cancellation of registrations. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require notices to be sent to voters (1) whose mail has been returned to the Division in the two years preceding the address list maintenance process, have not contacted the Division of Elections in those two years, and did not vote or appear to vote in those two years or (2) after registering to vote in Alaska and in the two years preceding the address confirmation process, moved based on the National Change of Address program or did any of these in another state: registered to vote, received a driver's license or registered a vehicle, received public assistance, served on a jury, obtained a resident's hunting or fishing license, paid state resident tuition for a public university, received a homestead or residential property tax exemption, or received any other benefit available only to a state resident. Existing law provides for such mailers to people who had mail returned to the Division as undeliverable in the preceding two years, who had not contacted the Division in the preceding two years, or who had not voted or appeared to vote in the two preceding general elections.
    • Make voters' registrations inactive if they fail to respond to the notice within 45 days, and relatedly, revise the notice to explain that the voter's registration will be inactivated unless the voter responds within 45 days. Existing law inactivates registrations if a voter has not contacted the Division, voted, or appeared to vote in the four years, an address confirmation notice is returned undeliverable, and the voter fails to respond to a forwardable address confirmation notice within 45 days.
    • Require the Director to send the required address confirmation notice by forwardable mail instead of non-forwardable mail, and to send it to a voter's email address as well as by mail, if the Director has the voter's email address.
  • Make changes to election observation and ballot challenges. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Allow a candidate, or an organization or organized group with authorization from the Director, to appoint at least one watcher for each location where ballots or envelopes are reviewed or counted in a precinct or counting center.
    • Require the documentation that a person has been appointed as a watcher to be signed by the respective chairperson of the precinct party committee, party district committee, state party chairperson, organization or organized group, or candidate.
    • Require the Director to create by regulation a process and a timeframe for a person present at the ballot counting review to challenge the decision of whether to count an absentee, special needs, or questioned ballot. The process must allow a reasonable amount of time to make a challenge.
    • Allow international election observers if they are invited by the U.S. Department of State and meet other qualifications, but deny them the ability to challenge voters or ballots.
  • Provide that if the official registration list indicates that an in-person voter received or voted a mail ballot, they must surrender the mail ballot or complete a provisional ballot instead of a regular ballot. This provision is in the nature of clarification, as existing law does not address the situation but the Division of Elections has indicated in the past that a person who received a ballot in the mail could vote in person.
  • Require the Director to provide secure ballot drop boxes for elections conducted by mailing all voters a ballot. In addition, the bill would specify that for a municipality with over 20,000 residents, the Director must place one box for each 20,000 residents in locations that ensure the boxes are accessible to the most possible voters. When picking locations, the Director would be allowed but not required to consult with municipalities, school districts, tribal organizations, and nonpartisan civic organizations. If practicable, the bill would also require the Director to place a drop box at each Division regional office. Finally, the bill would also require the Director to issue regulations specifying the criteria for siting drop boxes and their security requirements, and providing that the boxes are open 24/7 during the 10 days before an election, closing at 8 p.m. on Election Day. Existing law is silent on the use of secure ballot drop boxes, but the Division has offered them during elections on a small scale.
  • Change the standard voter registration process and form to enable a voter to register using an electronic image of their signature according to a process created by the Division by regulation.
  • Require the Director of the Division of Elections to create a process to allow a voter to cancel their registration in person or electronically, and require the information about the process to be posted at each polling place and on the Division's website.
  • Revise the prohibition against electioneering and a prohibition against a voter displaying their completed ballot to enable voters to take and share ballot selfies, provided they do not use them for impermissible electioneering.
  • Require risk-limiting audits, a cybersecurity program, and otherwise address topics not tracked by the Voting Rights Lab, such as certain lobbying reports, financial disclosure reports, the offices of the Alaska Public Offices Commission, and political signage.

Two provisions were removed by the amendments. One would have revised the voter registration form to notify the voter that the Director will notify election officials in a jurisdiction where the voter was previously registered so the voter's registration there may be canceled. Another would have required the Director to create by regulation a process and a timeframe for a campaign or organized group that sponsors or opposes an initiative, referendum, or question to challenge the decision to count or reject an absentee, special needs, or questioned ballot.

Last Updated May 3, 2023

Bill version 3/7/23: This bill, as introduced on March 7, 2023, would automatically restore the voting rights of people disenfranchised for felony convictions when they have completed their sentences, create the ability to do community service instead of paying court costs and fees, require notice to election officials when certain voters' rights are restored, and make other related changes to election law. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Restore the voting rights of people who meet all of the qualifying criteria after a review of documentation showing the criteria are met. Under existing law, a person must apply for restoration, but as under the bill, if all of the criteria are met, the application must be granted.
    • The Board of Pardons and Paroles would be required to review the record to determine if a person has met the criteria for restoration when a person has been released upon completion of sentence, been pardoned, or successfully completed probation or parole and has been released from compliance by the ordering entity.
    • Within 14 calendar days of that review, the reviewing officer would issue a report determining whether or not the person met all the criteria for restoration and submit it to their executive director. Within 14 days of the executive director certifying the report, the individual would be notified if they met the criteria. If they met the criteria, the Board of Pardons and Paroles would restore the person's right to vote. If the criteria had not been met, the person would be informed what they must do to meet the criteria. The person could submit a written request for the state to re-review whenever the person believes the criteria have been met.
  • Set out the criteria that must be met before voting rights are restored. To have their rights restored, a person must have:
    • Paid all restitution, fines, fees, and court costs ordered by the sentencing court at the time of sentencing, or, paid all restitution and fines, and either complied with an approved payment plan for the court costs and fees for one year or complied with an approved community service plan for one year. Existing law does not allow for restoration while on a payment plan or doing community service for court costs and fees.
    • Been released upon completion of sentence, been pardoned, or successfully completed probation or parole and has been released from compliance by the ordering entity. Existing law imposes a similar requirement.
  • Require the Board of Pardons and Paroles, after restoring a person's right to vote, to take certain steps:
    • If the person has an address known to the Board, provide the Secretary of State with that address and the date upon which the Board restored their voting rights. Upon receipt of the information, the Secretary of State shall notify the individual and the board of registrars of the county in which the individual resides of the date upon which the board restored his or her right to vote. If the person was previously registered to vote, the board of registrars would be required to add the individual's name to the poll list and notify the individual of the date that he or she is eligible to vote. If the person was not registered to vote before their conviction, they would be required to register before voting. Under existing law, all people whose voting rights are restored must register to vote, and the Board and Secretary do not have similar notice requirements.
    • If the individual does not have an address, the Board would be required to post the person's name on their website, and would not need to notify the Secretary of State.
  • Provide that when a newly restored person registers to vote, they would not be required to submit documentation of their rights restoration. Under existing law, when registering, a newly restored person must submit a copy of their Certificate of Eligibility to Register to the relevant board of registrars. The certificate is issued as part of the current process but would no longer be issued under the bill.
  • Require the Board of Pardons and Paroles and the Secretary of State to jointly develop and post on their websites a form and instructions for any individual who, before the bill's effective date, was been released upon completion of sentence, pardoned, or successfully completed probation or parole and was released from compliance by the ordering entity to ask that their eligibility be reviewed using the process the bill creates. The form and website posting would be required by September 1, 2024.
  • Require the circuit clerk of the court in which any outstanding fines, court costs, fees, or restitution are owed to apply payments in a specific order of priority. Existing law does not appear to have a similar provision, however, courts can order restitution to be paid in particular ways, and perhaps sentencing documents may direct how payments are apportioned. The bill would apply payments in this priority order:
    • To any restitution owed on a disenfranchising case.
    • To any fines owed on a disenfranchising case.
    • To any restitution owed on a non-disenfranchising case.
    • To any fines, court costs, or fees owed on a non-disenfranchising case.
  • Revise the language describing convictions for which automatic restoration is not available to eliminate "impeachment" but not otherwise change which crimes are in the category.
  • Require the Board of Pardons and Paroles to create a community service program by December 31, 2023, to develop options and requirements for individuals who are indigent to engage in community service to offset the payment of court costs and fees. No person could be required to participate in the program.
    • Participants would earn credit towards their fees and court costs at the federal minimum wage rate.
    • An individual demonstrating economic hardship could petition the board to participate in a community service plan to offset the payment of court costs and fees.
    • The community service program would set guidelines for the design of community service plans under the program.
    • The Board would annually report to the Legislative Council to consider the nonprofit programs offered to individuals by the Board, the use of resources, and the success or shortcomings of the program.

This bill, as amended on March 2, 2023, amends several statutes under which governmental entities are required to give notice related to elections. Under the bill, a governmental entity giving notice of a change of a vote center location, notice of an election, or notice of the exhibition of election equipment should publish the notice on a website. This bill, as enacted on April 7, 2023, makes several changes to voter registration, voter ID, and list maintenance requirements, through amendments to Amendment 51 of the state constitution and statutory law. Note: Amendment 51 sets out detailed requirements for voter registration, and authorizes further amendment by direct legislative action (without submitting changes to the electorate for approval, as generally required for constitutional amendments).

Specifically, in changes to Amendment 51 of the state constitution, the bill:

  • Requires the secretary of state to ensure the "security and accuracy" of the statewide voter registration list. Existing law, which the bill does not change, requires county registrars to cancel registrations on various grounds, but did not expressly require ongoing list maintenance by the secretary. Under the amendment, the secretary is required to:
    • Cooperate with other states and jurisdictions to compare registered voters, voter history, and voter registration lists
    • Establish and implementing a system for the verification of voter registration applicants' citizenship status
    • Use Social Security Administration data to assist in the removal from the registration list of dead voters
    • Establish a process for address verification
    • Keep voter registration information confidential and allowing local officials limited access as needed to administer elections
    • Provide annual reports to the legislature on the accuracy of the voter rolls
  • Requires that the voter registration application inform the applicant that if the application is being collected by a third-party organization, the organization may be unable to deliver it to the registrar by the deadline of thirty days before the next election and the applicant may return the form in person or by mail. The form must also inform the applicant of the process to track receipt of the form by the secretary.
  • Adds US citizenship to the express requirements for voter registration, and requires cancellation of the voter registration of a non-US citizen. Existing constitutional law includes U.S. citizenship among the qualifications for electors, but had no comparable provisions expressly regarding registration.
  • Permits the legislature to designate a state entity as having authority to investigate election fraud. Previous law authorized investigation of this conduct by the prosecuting attorney only.
  • Expressly provides that any public employee who violates a provision of voter registration laws commits a misdemeanor and upon conviction must be removed from their position. Under previous law, the misdemeanor and removal provision for violation of the Amendment's requirements applied only to any public official or election official.
  • Expands accepted forms of voter ID, by allowing voters to use a student photo ID issued by a trade school in the state. Previous law permitted use of a student ID from an accredited postsecondary school in the state only. The bill also expressly specifies that all forms of voter ID must include the voter's "legal name." Under previous law, the requirement was the voter's "name."
  • Amends some reporting requirements for voter registration agencies

In changes to statutory law, the bill:

  • Requires the State Board of Election Commissioners to perform an annual audit of voter registration data, and report the data on its website.

Last Updated May 3, 2023

This bill, as enacted on March 21, 2023, makes several changes related to an application for a mail ballot. Specifically, the bill:

  • Creates a new misdemeanor offense for a county clerk or other election official distributing an unsolicited application for a mail ballot or an unsolicited mail ballot to a voter. Previous law prohibited both actions, but did not have a criminal penalty.
  • Requires that an application for a mail ballot be completely blank when delivered to a voter except for the information that may be automatically populated by the voter registration system.
  • Requires an individual picking up a mail ballot for a voter to provide a state-issued or federal-issued photo identification when doing so. Previous law required the presentation of a current, valid photo ID, but did not specify state or federal forms.
  • Requires that if a voter has assistance completing an application for a mail ballot, the assistant must provide their name, address, and signature on the application.

Last Updated March 27, 2023

This bill, as enacted on April 4, 2023, changes the qualifications and duties of poll watchers. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires the State Board of Election Commissioners to establish a training program for poll watchers and develop training materials regarding poll watcher duties, rights, and responsibilities.
  • Specifies that poll watchers may represent a county or state political party with a candidate on the ballot. Previous law permitted representation of a party with a candidate, but did not specify that the party must be a county or state entity. The bill also permits watchers to represent county or state political parties that are seeking to pass or defeat a ballot measure. Previous law, which the bill does not change, permitted watchers representing a "group" advocating for or against a ballot measure, but had no express provision for parties doing so.
  • Requires a watcher to be a registered voter in the state, complete the training program created by the State Board of Election Commissioners, and wear identification while serving. Previous law had no comparable provisions.
  • Specifies procedures for poll watchers at courthouses, early voting locations, vote centers, polling locations, mail ballot processing locations, ballot tabulation locations, and audit and recount locations. New requirements specify observation areas at each location and require "uniform and nondiscriminatory access to observe all stages of the election process." These provisions expand on more general provisions in previous law, which remain in place, that authorize watchers to be "present" for various election processes.
  • Expressly permits poll watchers to bring in voter lists and challenge a ballot for review.
  • Forbids a watcher from:
    • Wearing campaign material while serving,
    • Interfering with a voter, or
    • Hindering or preventing the performance of the duties of any election official.
  • Authorizes officials to expel a poll watcher who engages in prohibited activity for the duration of the election.
  • Creates a misdemeanor offense for using force, intimidation, harassment, or coercion to interfere with a registered voter's ability to vote, an election official's duties, or a poll watcher's duties.

Last Updated April 10, 2023

This bill, as enacted on March 16, 2023, requires all state and county election officials receiving any "new federal election guidance" by phone, electronic means, mail, or in person, to submit the material to the Secretary of State within two days of receipt. Federal election guidance is defined as any federal directive, guidance, or communication relating to elections. The bill also designates the Secretary of State as the "custodian" of all the specified guidance, and requires them to submit an annual report of the material to the legislature.

Last updated April 6, 2023.

This bill, as enacted on March 16, 2023, makes changes to laws concerning complaints of election law violations. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires officials to provide notice to an individual who alleges a violation of election law or voter registration law, but whose complaint does not otherwise comply with all procedural requirements, and to permit correction of the complaint within ten days. Under previous law, notice and the opportunity to amend were required for "a complaint," with no specific criteria related to subject matter.
  • Requires the State Board of Elections to make an offer of settlement on a complaint before holding a public hearing.
  • Clarifies that the deadline to submit a complaint alleging an election law violation to the State Board of Elections is thirty days after the deadline to certify an election, not thirty days after the certification itself.

Last updated April 10, 2023.

This bill, as enacted on March 30, 2023, changes the laws concerning the acceptance of mail ballots sent by voters outside of the United States. Under previous law, the mail ballot of a voter outside the United States could be counted if it arrived as late as ten days after the election, as long as the ballot was applied for at least 30 days before the election and signed, dated, postmarked, and mailed by the voter no later than Election Day. Under the bill, the ballot will be accepted regardless of whether the voter applied at least 30 days before the election. The bill also removes the requirement that the ballot be dated by the voter.

Last Updated April 10, 2023

This bill, as enacted on April 11, 2023, establishes the Election Integrity Unit within the office of the Attorney General and creates new civil penalties for misconduct related to elections and voting. Specifically, the bill:

  • Establishes the Election Integrity Unit within the office of the Attorney General, with the purpose of aiding the Secretary of State and State Board of Election Commissioners in their duties "related to the investigation of election crimes and the security of elections." The unit is required to:
    • Establish and administer the Arkansas Election Integrity Database, a database to track all alleged violations, complaints, and investigations of election law.
    • Receive and respond to complaints of election law violations, including by forwarding the complaints to the State Board of Election Commissioners or to an appropriate prosecuting attorney.
    • Oversee the attorney general's election fraud hotline.
    • Institute civil proceedings for the purpose of enforcing state election laws related to elections and voting.
  • Instructs the State Board of Election Commissioners to notify the Election Integrity Unit upon receipt of a complaint of an election law violation. The board must forward a complaint to an appropriate prosecutor if their investigation of the complaint leads them to believe probable cause exists to find that an election law has been violated. Under previous law, this finding only resulted in the board holding a hearing. Finally, the bill requires the board to submit annual reports regarding all closed investigations from the prior year to the governor, attorney general, and Joint Performance Review Committee.
  • Permits a prosecuting attorney having jurisdiction over an election law violation to appoint an attorney from the Attorney General's office as a "special deputy prosecuting attorney" whose power to prosecute is derived from the prosecuting attorney.
  • Authorizes the Attorney General to initiate civil actions if they believe someone has engaged or is about to engage in any conduct constituting misdemeanor or felony offenses related to elections and voting, and creates a new civil penalty of at least $1,000 per violation for engaging in such conduct.

Last updated April 19, 2023.

This bill, as introduced February 8, 2023, would extend early voting in the state and provide additional protections for workers seeking to exercise their right to vote. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Extend the early voting period. Under the bill, the early voting period would begin 30 days before Election Day, instead of 15 days before Election Day as under existing law.
  • Extend the hours in which early voting is offered. Under existing law, early voting is offered from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. on each weekday of early voting except for the Monday before the election, when early voting is offered from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Under this bill, early voting on weekdays would be offered:

    • from 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. on every other weekday during the early voting period except for the Monday before the election, and
    • from 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. on the Monday before the Election.
    • Require employers to give each employee who is a registered voter 8 hours of paid leave to be used during the early voting period or on Election Day for all elections. An employer who failed to comply with this requirement would be subject to conviction of a misdemeanor. Under existing law, employers must schedule their employees in a manner that permits them to vote on Election Day, but the existing statute does not address early voting and employers are not required to give employees leave for voting purposes.

Under existing law, a voter who completes an application for a mail ballot who resides within the county in which they are registered to vote will only receive a ballot for one election cycle. A voter who completes an application for a mail ballot who does not reside within the county in which they are registered to vote, a voter residing in a long-term care or residential care facility, or a voter with a disability will receive a ballot for each election held in the next year.

Under this bill, each type of voter would receive a ballot for one election cycle, but could opt into having the application apply for each application held in the next year.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on March 29, 2023, would change the process for tabulating mail ballots and create a cure process. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Provide that mail ballots can begin to be tabulated or counted no earlier than 8:30 a.m. on Election Day. The county board of election commissioners would be instructed to complete the count of mail ballots and early votes (with some exceptions for ballots coming from overseas) before beginning to count election day votes.
  • Require a mail ballot to be treated as a provisional ballot when required materials are placed inside the inner absentee envelope instead of within the outer envelope. Under existing law, the materials are moved to the larger envelope while preserving the secrecy of the ballot, and the ballot is treated as a regular ballot.
  • Require a mail ballot to be treated as a provisional ballot when the voter fails to provide the required voter identification with the ballot.
  • Create a cure process for ballots designated as provisional under the bill to permit the voter to address the deficiency not later than noon on the Monday after the election. The voter would be required to be notified of the deficiency no later than 48 hours after the voter's mail ballot is designated as provisional.
  • Require election officials processing mail ballots to compare all ballot materials returned, other than the ballot itself, to check whether the voter's name, address, date of birth, and signature are comparable. Existing law only requires an election official to compare the name, address, date of birth, and signature of the voter's mail ballot application with the voter's statement and, for first-time voters who registered by mail, the first-time voter's identification document.
  • Require mail ballot materials to be transmitted to the county board of election commissioners for additional review if any materials are missing, the voter's name, residential voting address, date of birth, and signature do not compare, or if the information of an agent who delivered the ballot on the voter's behalf does not match the information on the voter statement. Under existing law, the ballot would typically be treated as a provisional ballot. The board would then perform a similar evaluation process of the ballots. If the board concludes that the ballot can be approved to be counted, the voter must be notified within 48 hours that curing the ballot is no longer necessary.
  • Require a county board of election commissioners to file a complaint with the State Board of Election Commissioners if the county board believes a mail ballot was fraudulently submitted.

Last Updated April 3, 2023

This bill, as enacted on February 24, 2023, expands the accepted excuses for voting by mail ballot, to include voters will be engaged in religious observance or discipline during the entire 12-hour Election Day voting period.

Last Updated March 1, 2023

This bill, as enacted on March 21, 2023, requires the counting of ballots to be complete within 24 hours after the polls close, and specifies that "no significant breaks" may take place in the counting process. Previous law provided that after the polls close, poll workers must "continue the count to completion," but did not expressly address a counting deadline or breaks. The bill also requires county boards to ensure that there is more than one worker present to continue the count if a poll worker becomes sick or incapacitated.

The bill makes various additional changes to areas of election law that Voting Rights Lab does not track, concerning the compatibility of paper ballots and tabulating machines.

Last updated March 27, 2023.

This bill, as enacted on March 21, 2023, prohibits any state or county employee or official from accepting any non-public money to be used for the purpose of conducting elections or otherwise conducting the employee or official's duties. Under previous law, this prohibition only applied to a county board of election commissioners.

Last updated March 27, 2023.

This bill, as enacted on March 21, 2023, prohibits the use of drop boxes for the return of a mail ballot and explicitly requires all mail ballots not returned by mail to be hand-delivered to the office of the county clerk. Previous law provided no guidance on the use of drop boxes, but generally required ballots returned in person to be delivered to the physical office of the county clerk only.

Last Updated March 27, 2023

This bill, as enacted on April 11, 2023, newly authorizes the State Board of Election Commissioners to conduct an extensive election integrity review process, requires an additional mandatory audit of certain election results, and creates a new criminal offense for forging a voter's signature on voting materials. Specifically, the bill:

  • Authorizes the State Board of Election Commissioners to:
    • Conduct, at the Board's discretion, a comprehensive election integrity review of "election related documents and records," in odd-numbered years following an election. If undertaken, the review must be made of counties randomly selected at a public meeting (unless two-thirds of the board conclude that a particular county needs to be investigated). The review may include investigation into errors and fraudulent activity in voter registration records, mail ballot fraud, and/or the accuracy and integrity of certified election results.
    • File a complaint within three years of an alleged felony violation of election law, felony violation of voter registration law, or violation that may impact the accuracy of an election result. Note: The provision does not specify the body to which the Board's "complaints" may be filed.
  • Requires the State Board to conduct an audit of results for each presidential preference primary, in addition to the audit required under existing law for results of every general election.
  • Creates a felony offense for forging the signature of a voter on a registration application, application for a mail ballot, or mail ballot voter statement.

Last updated April 25, 2023.

This bill, as enacted on March 30, 2023, changes certain requirements for the use of vote centers (polling places where any registered voter in a county may vote on Election Day, regardless of their specific precinct assignment). Specifically, the bill:

  • Changes requirements for the location of vote centers for runoff elections. Under previous law, officials were generally required to locate vote centers in the same place for consecutive elections. Under the bill, in a runoff election in a county that exclusively uses voting centers, but in which only certain precincts in the county will be voting:
    • Vote centers must be located within a precinct where voters are eligible to vote in the runoff.
    • If no vote center is located within a precinct that will be voting in the runoff, a new vote center for the runoff must be established either within the precinct or at the county seat.
  • Changes the deadlines by which officials may change the location of a vote center. Previous law provided that no vote center location could be changed less than 30 days before an election, except in the event of an emergency. Under the bill, in a preferential primary election or general election, officials may not change vote center locations less than 60 days before, except for emergencies. The 30 day deadline remains in place for all other elections. The bill also permits a county board to establish a new vote center less than 30 days before an election if a majority of the board determines that existing vote centers do not adequately serve the county's needs. Previous law had no comparable provision.

Last updated April 11, 2023.

    • irregularities in precinct or voting center results
    • inadequacy of or irregularity in documentation required to be maintained as prescribed by this title
  • Require the election official to respond with the requested explanation and documentation within 20 days.
  • Allow the individual who requested the explanation and documentation, if dissatisfied with the response, to make follow up requests, and require the election official to respond within 10 days.
  • Allow the individual who made the requests, if still dissatisfied, to make a written request to the Secretary of State regarding their requests and the election official's responses.
  • Require the Secretary of State, upon receipt of the request, to review it and request additional information from the election official. The election official would have 30 days to respond. If the Secretary was not satisfied with the response, the Secretary would be allowed to audit the claimed actions, irregularities, or inadequacies. The election official would be required to cooperate.

  • Require the Secretary to notify the election official of their findings. The official would have 30 days to remedy any matters specified in the Secretary's findings, or face a civil penalty of up to $500 for each unresolved finding.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on February 16, 2023, would make major changes to various core election procedures. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Shorten the time voters have to return mail ballots by requiring all mail ballots to be returned not later than three days before Election Day. Under existing law, voters have until 7 p.m. (the close of polls) on Election Day.
  • Require all early ballots, which include mail ballots, to be counted on Election Day before 7 p.m. (the close of polls), with the results released after 8 p.m. on Election Day. Under existing law, early ballots, including mail ballots, are counted after being verified, including before and after Election Day.
  • Repeal provisions authorizing the Secretary of State to issue the Elections Procedure Manual. The Manual is a regulatory document with the force of law, drafted by the Secretary of State and approved by the Governor and Attorney General. Under existing law, the Secretary is charged with issuing these rules to maximize "correctness, impartiality, uniformity and efficiency" for voting and election procedures throughout the state.
  • Limit electronic voting machines and their use to disabled voters, and otherwise expressly require use of paper ballots. Under existing law, counties may freely use properly-certified electronic voting machines.
  • Limit use of ballot tabulators to mail ballots and disabled voters' ballots, and otherwise expressly require tabulation of ballots by hand. Existing law allows ballot tabulators for all vote types.
  • Change rules relating to election precincts and polling places. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require election precincts to have no more than 1,000 voters assigned to them when drawn. Existing law does not impose a cap.
    • Eliminate vote centers. Under existing law, counties may offer vote centers in addition to, or instead of, precinct polling places.
    • Eliminate counties' ability to consolidate polling places for various reasons, and require at least one polling place per precinct.
    • Require two years' prior notice to voters before relocating a polling place.
    • Require the use of schools and government buildings as polling places, and repeal provisions establishing grounds for a school administrator to deny a request for the school to serve as a polling place.
    • Eliminate most reasons a county could open an emergency polling place, allowing an emergency polling place only when an act of God renders a previously-designated polling place unusable.
    • Repeal authorization for election officials to mail presidential primary ballots to all voters in precincts with fewer than three hundred voters rather than open a polling place in the precinct.

Note: the bill would also make what appear to be partial edits to the election code relating to mail ballot elections, mail ballots, and early voting. It is unclear whether these changes would have an operational impact, if passed as currently drafted.

Last Updated March 2, 2023

This bill, as amended on February 16, 2023, would make major changes to core aspects of Arizona election law. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Eliminate in-person early voting. Under existing law, voters may choose to vote in person beginning 27 days before Election Day.
  • Eliminate vote centers by requiring voters to vote at precinct polling places. Under existing law, counties can choose to offer vote centers in addition to or instead of precinct polling places.
  • Require all voters to show a valid state-issued identification document to receive a ballot. Under existing law, other forms of identification are allowed.
  • Require all ballots to be counted by hand and repeal the hand count audit.
  • Repeal the explicit authority of the Elections Procedures Manual to address counting practices at central count locations. The Manual is a regulatory document that standardizes election practices statewide that is drafted by the Secretary of State and must be approved by the Governor and Attorney General.

  • Rename mail ballots "absentee ballots" but otherwise does not change mail voting. Existing law calls mail ballots "early ballots".

    The previous version of the bill did not substantively change Arizona election law. All of the provisions in the amended version are new.

HISTORY: {"date":"02/21/2023","summary":"From HOUSE Committee on RULES:  Do pass constitutional and in proper form","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on February 16, 2023, would make voter ID more restrictive, create civil penalties for voter registration organizations, strip county recorders of most election duties, and require all ballots to be counted by hand, among other changes. All of the provisions in the bill are new. Prior to the amendment, the bill made non-substantive changes to the election code. Specifically, the amended bill would:

  • Restrict in-person voting by making voter ID document rules more restrictive. The bill would require voters to present valid state-issued ID to receive a ballot. Under existing law, additional ID types are authorized.
  • Create a civil penalty of $50,000 for a non-governmental organization that fails to timely return completed voter registration forms, and a $1,500/form civil penalty for each form an employee, contractor, or volunteer for a non-governmental organization unlawfully alters. The bill would also clarify that a person or organization registering voters using blank forms they get from election officials are subject to a misdemeanor for failing to properly return completed forms.
  • Strip county recorders of most of their election duties and reassign the duties to the county board of supervisors. Under the bill, recorders would be responsible only for providing ballots, pens, tables, and other equipment as necessary for the various polling places. Under existing law, recorders have duties relating to early voting (in-person and by mail), ballot verification, and voter registration, among other duties.
  • Require all ballots to be counted by hand with returns made within 24 hours after the polls close. Under existing law, tabulators are allowed, and unofficial returns are released after polls close and updated regularly as ballots are counted.
  • Require all voting to happen in person on Election Day at the voter's election precinct polling place except for voting by absentee ballot. The bill does not make numerous amendments to the code that would be necessary, such as repealing in-person early voting, eliminating vote centers, or changing mail voting to absentee voting.
  • Prohibit counties from requiring voters and election workers to wear masks, be vaccinated, or be tested for a virus as a condition of entering a polling place or other voting or tabulating location.

  • Prohibit ranked-choice voting. Ranked choice voting is not currently used in Arizona.

HISTORY: {"date":"01/23/2023","summary":"Additionally referred to HOUSE Committee on RULES","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 12, 2023, would:

  • End felony disenfranchisment.
  • Allow in-person early votes to be tabulated without having the voter's signature on the ballot envelope matched against one in their voter record, and relatedly prohibit watchers from challenging such ballots on that basis. Under existing law, in-person early voters show the same ID to receive a ballot that Election Day voters do. Nonetheless, the signature on their ballot certificate is matched against signatures on file and if deemed not to match, will be rejected unless cured.
  • Extend the early voting period to the day before Election Day. Under existing law, early voting ends on the Friday before Election Day, but counties can open emergency vote centers or other emergency voting options to serve people who, because of a reason that occurred after early voting ended, cannot vote on Election Day.
  • Require county recorders to offer early voting at their offices and to offer any other locations as the Elections Procedures Manual (EPM) prescribes. Under existing law, the statute says recorders "may" offer early voting at their offices, but the EPM, which has the force of law, requires recorders to offer early voting at least in their offices.
  • Allow mail voters to cure a missing signature on their ballot certificate until the fifth business day after an election with a federal office and until three business days after for other elections. Under existing law, ballot certificates with signatures deemed not to match one in the voter's record have that cure deadline, but missing signatures must be cured by the close of polls on Election Day.
  • Expand who is eligible for voting with special election boards by including qualified voters who are "physically confined" and explicitly allow people in pretrial detention to request such a board. Under existing law, only qualified voters who are ill or have a disability are eligible for such boards.
  • Provide that if a provisional ballot is rejected because the voter was not registered, the information on the provisional ballot envelope must be used to register them for future elections. Relatedly, the bill requires the envelope to request all necessary information to register someone.
  • Require all unofficial results transmitted to the Secretary of State to include estimates of the numbers of early, Election Day, and provisional ballots that remain uncounted.
  • Create a risk-limiting audit pilot program by:
    • appropriating $100,000 in each of fiscal years 2023-23, and 2024-25 to fund a grant program to enable officers in charge of elections to conduct risk-limiting audits.
    • allowing officers in charge of elections to conduct risk-limiting audits for the 2024 general election rather than the existing hand count audit required by statute.
    • requiring the Secretary to report their plan for distributing these grants to the joint legislative budget committee on or before March 31, 2024
    • requiring the Secretary to report to the President of the Senate and the Speaker of the House on any findings and recommendations relating to risk-limiting audits on or before March 31, 2025.

  • Make other changes not specifically tracked by Voting Rights Lab relating to election equipment testing and security, international observers, and election officer certificates.

Last Updated January 13, 2023
