HISTORY: {"date":"01/23/2023","summary":"Additionally referred to HOUSE Committee on RULES","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 12, 2023, would expand the early voting period by extending it to the day before Election Day, change rules for siting and staffing vote centers, and make small changes to other sections of the election code. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Expand the early voting period to allow early voting to be offered through the day before Election day, provided that early voting will end earlier if needed to ensure that precinct registers and other election materials are revised for Election Day to indicate which voters requested a mail ballot ("early ballot" in Arizona), which have already voted, and which have inactive registrations. Under existing law, early voting ends at 5 p.m. on the Friday before Election Day, although emergency voting is allowed after that through 5 p.m. on the day before Election Day. The bill would preserve the emergency voting option in any jurisdiction that ends early voting before that time.
  • Limit county recorders' discretion to open early voting sites by requiring the county board of supervisors to specifically authorize the county recorder or other officer in charge of elections to establish additional sites. Under existing law, a specific resolution is not required for the recorder to open additional sites, and only county recorders, not other officers in charge of elections, are allowed to site them. The bill would allow recorders or other officers in charge of elections to make changes to the approved early voting sites, notifying the board and the public as soon as possible.
  • Create "early voting drop-off centers", defined as a facility in which any voter in the county may return a voted mail ballot (called "early ballot" in Arizona) to a lawful custodian for voted ballots. Under existing law, voters may return their voted mail ballots to early and Election Day voting locations, drop boxes if offered, and by mail. Drop box use is not specifically addressed in existing statute, however, the Elections Procedures Manual, which has the force of law, explicitly authorizes their use.
  • Expand and clarify rules relating to vote centers, by:
    • Allowing any officer in charge of elections, upon a specific authorizing resolution of the county board of supervisors, to use vote centers in lieu of, or in addition to, precinct polling places, both for early voting and on Election Day. Under existing law, only a county recorder may be so empowered.
    • Clarifying that early voting locations may be vote centers, and that Election Day polling places are subject to the laws applicable to polling places. Under existing law, vote centers have been offered for both early and Election Day voting.
    • Providing that a vote center can be used as a ballot replacement location in a mail ballot election.
  • For Arizona's limited universal mail ballot elections, change the rules relating to voters obtaining replacement ballots. The bill would require the county recorder or other officer in charge of elections to set up one or more locations in the appropriate jurisdiction, instead of existing law's requirement that one central location be offered. In addition, the bill would require a voter seeking a replacement ballot to sign an affidavit attesting that they had not cast their original ballot. Under existing law, the voter must attest that the original ballot was lost, spoiled, destroyed, or not received.
  • Authorize a voter to put their completed provisional ballot into the provisional ballot envelope and then the ballot box. Under existing law, only an election official is so authorized.

  • Create a new section of code providing for "voting center election boards" and their qualifications without addressing the existing section of code that provides for such boards. Under the bill and existing law, the county board of supervisors must appoint election boards for each vote center consisting of inspectors, marshals, judges, and clerks of election, but the details of their appointment and who may serve on such boards differ slightly. Specifically, under the bill, a voting center election board would:

    • consist of at least one inspector, one marshal, and as many judges or clerks as deemed necessary. Existing law provides for one inspector, one marshal, two judges and as many clerks as deemed necessary.
    • require different political parties to be represented within each voting center election board generally, and specifically require an equal number of inspectors in the various voting centers in a county to be members of the two largest parties. Under existing law, strict bipartisan balance across offices and within vote centers is required.
    • require vote center election workers to be qualified voters of the county. Under existing law, election workers for precinct polling places must be voters of the precinct in which they serve unless an insufficient number of them are available, and for vote centers, workers must be voters in the state.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 12, 2023, would create automatic voter registration, create same-day voter registration, revise standard voter registration processes, extend the early voting period, empower Native Americans in siting voting locations on their lands, and give mail voters more time to return their ballots. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create automatic voter registration at the DMV for every person who provides proof of U.S. citizenship during the course of applying for, renewing, or correcting a driver's license or state identification, updating their residence address or name, or obtaining a duplicate, reissuance, or replacement of a driver's license or state ID. Existing law forbids automatic voter registration. In creating automatic voter registration, the bill would:
    • Require the DMV to electronically transmit at least the eligible voters' name, residence address or location, date of birth, and signature to the Secretary of State to register or update the registration of such people.
    • Require the Director of the DMV and the Secretary, after consulting with all county recorders, to adopt rules to implement the system.
    • Require the Secretary to evaluate implementing automatic voter registration at other agencies, specifically including the Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System Administration. Such agencies would be required to have, or acquire, the ability to collect and transmit electronic signatures. The Secretary would be authorized to designate additional agencies as automatic voter registration agencies, and once designated, an agency would not be able to lose that designation.
    • Require all automatic voter registration agencies, including DMV, to accept Tribal identification numbers and nontraditional residential addresses, including addresses that can be identified by mile markers, or geographic or other identifying features. Automatic voter registration agencies would be required to transmit voter registration to the Secretary on the day it was received by the agency. The Secretary would promptly re-transmit the data to the appropriate county recorders, after removing the information of individuals in the address confidentiality program, or who the Secretary has information indicating the individual is not eligible to register.
    • Require county recorders, on receipt of voter registration information from the Secretary, to determine if the person is already registered, and if so, whether their registration is inactive or needs updating. If the registration information is the same but the registration is inactive, the recorder would make the registration active. If the person is not registered, the county recorder would determine if the information received includes enough to register to vote. If the information is insufficient, the recorder would send the potential voter an incomplete registration notice explaining what more is needed and a postage-prepaid return form. If the person completes their registration by the close of polls on Election Day and the recorder confirms their eligibility, the registration would be effective from the date the information was collected by the source agency. For each eligible person who is not registered or needs their registration updated, the recorder would register them or update their registration, and send the person a nonforwardable automatic voter registration notice.
    • Require the automatic voter registration notice to include an explanation of voter eligibility requirements, a statement that if the person should decline registration using the enclosed form and postage prepaid return envelope if they are not eligible, a statement of the penalties for false registration, and assurance that a decision to decline will be confidential and that the identity of the source agency will be confidential as well. The return form would be required to enable the individual to decline registration, join the permanent mail voting list (called "active early voting list" in Arizona), and affiliate with a political party. If an already registered voter is affiliated with a party, the automatic process would not change their affiliation unless the voter indicates the change on the form. The notice would also include information about the address confidentiality program.
    • Protect people from prosecution for false registration simply for failing to return the opt-out form by redefining, and thus narrowing, the felony.
    • Protect people from prosecution for the felony of illegal voting by providing a person must vote or attempt to vote knowing that they are not eligible to vote. In addition, if a voter's registration is processed as valid by the state, the registration would be presumed to have been officially authorized and the person would not be subject to penalty.
    • Provide that for the fourteen days after a recorder mails an individual an automatic voter registration notice, the person is considered a pending registrant. If the person does not opt out using the return form, their registration will take effect. Pending registrants are allowed to vote regular ballots in any election occurring in the 14-day window for opting out.
    • Require the DMV to report to the Secretary annually on the program and require the Secretary to publish the information on the Secretary's website. The DMV and any other source agency would be required to publish information about the program on their websites and post signage in their locations.
  • Create same-day registration on Election Day and during early voting. Existing law specifically prohibits same-day registration. Under the system created by the bill:
    • Eligible people would be able to prove residency to register with any in-person voter ID document that includes their name and current address, a government check, paycheck, or another government document that shows the name and current address of the voter, or a student identification card for an educational institution in this state.
    • The Secretary of State, after consulting with all county recorders, would establish in the Elections Procedures Manual a verification process for voters who register on or close to Election Day to ensure efficient eligibility verification can happen at a voting location.
    • Voters who engage in same-day registration will cast regular ballots unless their registration has not been verified. Voters whose registration is not confirmed on the spot would cast ballots that would count if their ineligibility is not confirmed by the end of provisional ballot processing.
    • Voters not affiliated with a political party would be allowed to participate in a presidential primary by affiliating with that party at the voting location.
    • The registration process would be prohibited from being more restrictive or burdensome than the standard voter registration process.
  • Revise standard voter registration processes. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Repeal the requirement that a person is a resident of Arizona 29 days before the election.
    • Revise registration at the DMV (called Department of Transportation in Arizona) to provide that a person who reports a change of residential or mailing address or a change of name, and who in the same transaction does not provide documentation of non-citizenship, would be offered an opportunity to register to vote. The updated name and/or address information would be transmitted to the Secretary of State, who would then send the information to the appropriate county recorder only if the relevant individual is already registered to vote. Existing law provides this opportunity to people applying for driver's licenses or renewals only.
    • Revise online voter registration to require the system to allow a person to register or update their registration without a driver's license or state ID, and with any proof of U.S. citizenship that is valid under Arizona law. Moreover, the system must accept nontraditional residential addresses. These rules would apply to online registration offered by any agency. Existing law does not require online voter registration, but the service is offered by the Secretary of State's office.
    • Revise the voter registration form to inform applicants that if they do not provide the required documentary proof of citizenship they will be eligible to vote in federal races only. The existing form states that applications not accompanied by documentary proof of citizenship will simply be rejected.
    • Change the rules relating to inactivating a voter's registration so that failure to respond to an address confirmation mailing does not result in inactivation. Additionally, the bill would repeal existing law's requirement that a voter who fails to respond to such a mailing must provide affirmation or confirmation of their address to vote.
    • Add as a method of providing documentary proof of citizenship an official notification from any government agency in Arizona that the agency has received such proof for the voter registration applicant.
    • Clarify that people who registered to vote before December 8, 2004, are deemed to have provided satisfactory proof of citizenship and do not need to resubmit such proof. This clarification reflects the Arizona law before the enactment of laws in 2022 that created ambiguity about whether such registrants needed to provide such documentation. The bill would also clarify that proof of registration in another Arizona county could be proof of citizenship.
  • Create new rules for siting polling places on Native land. Specifically, when determining precinct boundaries, polling places, vote centers, early voting locations, and hours, the county board of supervisors or officer in charge of elections in each county would be required to notify all Tribes within the county, allow the tribes to participate in the process, and cooperate and coordinate all aspects of the determinations with the Tribes. For each election, at least one precinct and one polling place, vote center, or early voting location on the lands of each Tribe in the county at a location selected by the Tribe unless the Tribe certifies it has no members in the county. The chosen locations must be accessible to voters on at least a temporary basis, and if not, the officer in charge of elections must provide alternative voting procedures for voters unable to access the location. The bill would create a special cause of action and related procedures to enforce these rules. Existing law does not have comparable provisions.
  • Expand the early voting period until 5 p.m. on the day before Election Day, provided that voting locations will close sooner if necessary to revise precinct registers and other election materials for Election Day use. Under existing law, early voting ends at 5 p.m. on the Friday before Election Day.
  • Change rules relating to returning mail ballots (called "early ballots" in Arizona). Specifically, the bill would:
    • Allow more time for voters to return their mail ballots by allowing them to be postmarked by the close of polls on Election Day and received within five business days after a general election that includes a federal office and three business days for any other election. Existing law requires mail ballots to be received by election officials by the close of polls on Election Day. The bill would make a conforming change to the cure period for such ballots.
    • Prohibit requiring an ID or any other requirement to return a mail ballot in person that is not required to return it by mail.

  • Require risk-limiting audits and revise campaign finance laws, areas of election law Voting Rights Lab does not track.

Last Updated March 22, 2023

This bill, as introduced on January 12, 2023, would end voting by mail except for military and overseas (UOCAVA) voters or voters temporarily residing out of state. The bill would require the legislature to provide people who are in Arizona, but who are unable to go to the polls, an alternate method of voting that ensures ballot secrecy to the greatest extent possible. The out-of-state and UOCAVA voters would be required to have a "certified witness" attest that the voter voted in the absence of others and did not show anyone the ballot before putting it in the envelope. Election officials would be required to ensure the mail ballot was sent to the correct address and the voter is a resident and registered voter of the state.

Under existing law, any Arizona voter may choose to vote by mail in any election, and as many as 80% of voters do. Moreover, election officials verify mail ballots ("early ballots" in Arizona) using signature matching. Voters are not required to have their signature witnessed or notarized.

Last Updated January 16, 2023

This bill, as introduced on January 12, 2023, would repeal no-excuse mail voting and limit the opportunity to vote by mail to qualified voters who:

  • Are confined and physically unable to go to the polls, including people confined to their homes, a nursing home, hospital, jail, or other facility due to the voter's illness, disability, age, infirmity, incarceration, or any other reason,
  • Expect to be absent from their precinct when the election is held, including UOCAVA voters, or

  • Are blind or visually impaired.

    Because in-person early voting in Arizona is done by applying for and casting mail ballots (called "early ballots" in Arizona), requiring an excuse to vote a mail ballot effectively eliminates in-person early voting as well.

    The bill would also declare that:


  • While Federal law is supreme and thus any conflict would invalidate state law, any conflict must be interpreted as narrowly as possible, seeking to preserve secrecy in voting to the greatest extent possible.

  • The invalidated provision or provisions must be deemed reformed to the extent necessary to conform to applicable law and they and the other provisions interpreted to give the maximum effect to the intent of the bill.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on February 16, 2023, would end early voting, eliminate vote centers, restrict mail voting, make voter ID more restrictive, strip county recorders of most of their election duties, eliminate tabulators, and create new civil fines for people and organizations who do voter registration drives but don't turn in completed forms rapidly enough. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Restrict in-person voting by eliminating early voting and vote centers. The bill would require all voting to occur on Election Day at voters' precinct polling places, except for mail voting, which the bill would call "absentee ballots" and existing Arizona law calls "early ballots." Under existing law, voters may cast ballots in person beginning 27 days before Election Day, and county boards of supervisors may authorize the use of vote centers in addition to, or in lieu of, precinct polling places. Relatedly, the bill would change the rules relating to siting polling places and drawing precincts. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Cap each precinct at 1500 voters the day the precincts are drawn. Existing law does not provide a cap.
    • Prohibit county boards of supervisors from changing polling place locations unless affected voters are given notice by mail at least two years in advance. Under existing law, counties must give notice of polling place changes 33 days before an election.
    • Restrict counties' ability to open emergency polling places to only in response to an act of God rendering an ordinary polling place unusable.
    • Prioritize using schools as polling places and repeal provisions that allowed schools to opt out of being polling places.
    • Repeal rules relating to documenting and minimizing voter wait times.
  • Restrict in-person voting by making voter ID document rules more restrictive. The bill would require voters to present valid state-issued ID to receive a ballot. Under existing law, additional ID types are authorized.
  • Restrict in-person voting by eliminating electronic voting machines except as necessary to serve disabled voters. Under existing law, electronic voting machine use is not similarly restricted. The bill would also eliminate the use of e-pollbooks.
  • Restrict mail voting by allowing only voters with an approved excuse to choose to vote by mail. Under existing law, any Arizona voter has the freedom to choose to vote by mail. The bill would allow these excuses to justify voting by mail:
    • the voter expects to be outside the state at the time of the election.
    • the voter is physically unable to go to the polls because the voter is hospitalized or in a nursing home.
    • the voter has a visual impairment.
    • the voter is an absent uniformed services voter or overseas voter or a spouse or household member of the absent uniformed services voter or overseas voter.
  • Restrict mail voting by shortening the time voters mail apply to receive a ballot. The bill would require applications to receive a ballot in the mail to be received by 5 p.m. on the 14th day before the election, instead of 5 p.m. on the 11th day before the election. Moreover, the bill would eliminate the ability of a voter to pick up a mail ballot in person. Under existing law, a voter could go to the election official's office, show voter ID documentation, and receive and vote a mail ballot.
  • Restrict mail voting by requiring voters to return their ballots sooner, no later than three days before Election Day. Under existing law, voters have until 7 p.m. on Election Day, the close of polls, to return their ballots.
  • Restrict mail voting by repealing the "Active Early Voters List". Under existing law, voters may join this list and automatically receive ballots in the mail for every election thereafter until they request to leave the list or one of the other triggers to leave the list occurs.
  • Strip county recorders of most of their election duties and reassign the duties to the county board of supervisors. Under the bill, recorders would be responsible only for providing ballots, pens, tables, and other equipment as necessary for the various polling places. Under existing law, recorders have duties relating to early voting (in-person and by mail), ballot verification, and voter registration, among other duties.
  • Restrict ballot tabulation by requiring all mail ballots to be counted on Election Day before 7 p.m. and provide that results cannot be released before 8 p.m. Under existing law, mail ballots are verified and counted before and after Election Day.
  • Restrict ballot tabulation by prohibiting tabulator use for in-person votes, requiring all ballots to be counted by hand, and requiring ballots to be sorted by precinct before and after counting. Under existing law, tabulators are allowed, and ballots cast at vote centers are not sorted by precinct before and after counting. Existing law authorizes a "hand-count audit" for each election to verify the accuracy of the tabulators. Having eliminated tabulators for most ballots, the bill would repeal the hand-count audit.
  • Allow tabulators to count absentee ballots, but at only one county absentee ballot counting center. Under existing law, counties may use more than one central counting location and may use tabulators for all types of ballots.
  • Eliminate the Elections Procedures Manual, which under existing law functions as a regulatory document with the force of law. Under existing law, it is drafted by the Secretary of State, but must be reviewed and approved by the Attorney General and the Governor to take effect.
  • Create a civil penalty of $50,000 for a non-governmental organization that fails to timely return completed voter registration forms, and a $1,500/form civil penalty for each form an employee, contractor, or volunteer for a non-governmental organization unlawfully alters. The bill would also clarify that a person or organization registering voters using blank forms they get from election officials are subject to a misdemeanor for failing to properly return completed forms.
  • Prohibit election officials from mailing all presidential primary voters in precincts with fewer than 300 voters instead of opening a polling place.
  • Prohibit counties from requiring voters and election workers to wear masks, be vaccinated, or be tested for a virus as a condition of entering a polling place or other voting or tabulating location.
  • Prohibit ranked-choice voting. Ranked choice voting is not currently used in Arizona.

  • Make changes to ballot paper, sample ballot mailing, and other changes not tracked by the Voting Rights Lab.

Last Updated February 23, 2023

This bill, as introduced on January 12, 2023, would change the rules for election contests to expand the grounds to file contests, expand allowed discovery, delay a hearing, and require appeals to be directly heard by the Arizona Supreme Court. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Expand the grounds for election contests on account of illegal votes to include votes in which the chain of custody is broken and early votes that have inconsistent signatures or personal information. Although existing law does not directly address inconsistent signatures as a ground for an election contest, the issue has been raised in such litigation.
  • Expand discovery dramatically. Under existing law, parties have a general right to inspect ballots, which in recent contests has involved samples of all the voted ballots. The bill would expand the right to inspection and other discovery rights by:
    • Providing that the parties to the contest have the right to physically examine all physical ballots and physical ballot images, any early ballot envelopes, and voters' registration records. The court would be required to allow "ample time to the parties for a thorough examination of these materials" and would be forbidden from restricting the examination in any manner.
    • Provide that the parties have the right to "full discovery on any matter that could pertain to the election in any way." The court would further be required to liberally construe parties' discovery rights, and the parties themselves would be required to "make every attempt not to limit discovery." Existing law has no similar provisions.
    • Allow each party the right to depose up to 10 people. The election contest code has no similar provision.
    • Clarifying that an organization or entity can be deemed by a party as the person to inspect ballots as existing law currently allows and that "person" could provide a rotating series of individuals to do the ballot inspection.
  • Delay a hearing on the contest by requiring it to happen not later than 20 days after the contest was filed, rather than the 10 days after that existing law provides.

  • Require any appeals of an election contest trial to be filed directly with the Arizona Supreme Court within 10 days after the final trial judgment issues, with a response filed within five days, and a reply within three days after that. The Court would then schedule a hearing within five days of full submission of the papers, and would be required to render a decision within five days after that. Under existing law, appeals are made to the lower appellate court first.

    Last updated January 26, 2023

Governor Katie Hobbs vetoed this bill on May 19, 2023. As passed by the Legislature, this bill would have increased the ability of political parties to observe the verification of mail ballot signatures and imposed new related requirements for ballot handling and record-keeping. Specifically, the bill would have:

  • Required county recorders and other officers in charge of elections to allow representatives of the two major parties to observe each stage of the signature verification process for mail ballots ("early ballots"), in-person early ballots, provisional ballots, and conditional provisional ballots. Under existing law, political parties have no expressly designated role during the signature verification process but may appoint challengers who may challenge any of these ballot types on multiple grounds.
  • Required officers in charge of elections to allow these observers to be as close as six feet to the process so they can reasonably, comfortably, and clearly view the contents of any screens or monitors used to display information or other materials related to signature verification. Such reasonable, comfortable, and clear visibility would also have been required for observers watching screens that are not in the same area in which the signature verification is occurring. The bill would have also clarified that if the election worker is working from home, the observers are not allowed in their home. Existing law does not have a comparable provision.
  • Prohibited observers from noting, transcribing, or otherwise holding or disclosing any voter's personal identifying information, including their month and day of birth, driver's license number, nonoperating identification license number, father's name, mother's maiden name, state and county of birth, the records that contain a voter's signature, and the voter's email address.
  • Required the officer in charge of elections to maintain a log of election board workers and employees at each stage of the signature and affidavit verification process. The log would have identified all election board workers and employees involved in each phase of review and provide for full accounting and disclosure of the total number of signature verifications performed by each election board worker and employee. The log would also have been required to disclose the determination made by each election board worker and employee, including: the name of the election board worker, the date the signature review was conducted, the batch numbers, the total number of signature verifications performed and the total number of signatures accepted, rejected, sent for further review, and the final determination made at subsequent phases or levels of review. These logs would have been updated daily and made available daily to any political party and all candidates on request. Existing law requires lists to be maintained of challenged voters, the challenge grounds, and challenge resolutions. These lists are public records. Existing law also provides for chain of custody documentation relating to ballots but does not include these details.
  • Created a felony offense for violation of the bill's provisions.

Provisions were amended out of the bill. Those provisions would have:

  • Imposed a "nondiscretionary duty" on the county attorney to file charges for violations of the bill's provisions.
  • Authorized observers to challenge ballot affidavits that do not appear to meet signature standards and created a new process for reviewing those challenges. Existing law allows observers from political parties to challenge ballots on the ground that the person is not a qualified voter or they have already voted, but does not expressly permit challenges based on signature standards alone. Existing law also provides, in provisions that would not have been altered by the bill, that challenges must be made in writing and include specific grounds, and that officials must notify a voter by mail within 24 hours of the opportunity to appear to defend the challenge to their ballot.
  • Required, if the ballot affidavit is cured, that the process and means for curing, as well as the name of the person curing, be documented. The unopened ballot would then be sent back to the challenge review board for final confirmation. Under existing law, the county recorder is in charge of the cure process and cure determinations.

This bill, as engrossed on February 28, 2023, would create a process for registered voters in pre-trial detention to vote using a narrow and highly specified process only. The bill would provide that if the process is not followed exactly, or if the law is struck down in court, eligible, registered voters in pre-trial detention cannot vote. The process created by the bill involves voters requesting to vote, and then an election official, accompanied by poll watchers, delivering the voter a ballot, waiting for the voter to vote, and then bringing the completed ballot back to the election official office for processing.

Specifically, the bill would provide that:

  • An eligible voter in pre-trial detention could vote if they make a written request to vote at least 180 days before the election that includes their full name, signature, and place of detention. A jail officer would be required to deliver a request to the officer in charge of elections within five calendar days.
  • The officer in charge of elections would notify political parties about the voting requests and the date the officer intends to bring ballots, so the parties can send observers. The parties would be required to notify the officer in charge of elections at least 10 days before the scheduled voting process who the poll watchers would be.
  • The jail would set aside a special area without cameras except that election officials and political party watchers may bring their cell phones.
  • The voter would be required to show an ID document or documents sufficient to vote in person at the polls and which prove their U.S. citizenship. Providing documentary proof of citizenship is not a necessary step for in-person voting in any other context. Arizona voters provide such proof when they register, or they are only allowed to vote "federal-only" ballots. The bill would prohibit giving voters in pre-trial detention federal-only ballots.
  • After being given a ballot, they would be observed voting, but their votes would be secret. The election official and poll watchers would be forbidden from speaking while the voter has the ballot until after it has been sealed in the envelope. Jail officials could only speak to the voter to give commands unrelated to voting and only if absolutely necessary. Once the ballot was sealed, the poll watchers and the voter would be required to sign certificates validating the voting process.
  • Specific chain of custody practices must be followed.
  • Ballots cast by pre-trial detainees would be rejected if any portion of the process was not strictly followed. Any qualified voter in the state could sue to enforce strict compliance with the process.
  • Government employees or contractors who violate this process would be guilty of a class 3 felony.
  • If any portion of the bill were found invalid by a court, people in detention would not be allowed to vote at all.

  • If federal detention facilities did not strictly follow these processes, their detainees would not be allowed to vote either.

    Before a February 16 amendment adopted by committee and then the House on February 28, the bill did not substantively change election law.

Governor Katie Hobbs vetoed this bill on May 19, 2023. As passed by the Legislature, the bill would have made voters' names, addresses, birth years, and precinct numbers public before and after each election, as well as whether they voted in the election. The bill would also have required the public disclosure of ballot images and related information. Exceptions would have applied to people in confidentiality programs and precincts with less than 25 voters. Existing law does not have similar requirements, but does have rules for sharing voter registration list data that are more restrictive than the process the bill would have created. Some of the restrictions may apply to the data the bill would have disclosed. Finally, the bill would have given people two additional days to file election contests. Specifically, the bill would have:

  • Required the county recorder to send a list of the names, home addresses, years of birth, and precinct numbers of every eligible registered voter, active or inactive, to the Secretary of State at least 10 days before Election Day. The Secretary would have been required to immediately post the information in a convenient downloadable format on a secure website the bill would require the Secretary to create. People participating in address confidentiality programs or living in a precinct with 25 or fewer registered voters would not have had their information exposed but would be included only as a total number of voters in a precinct. Under existing law, precinct voter lists for Election Day use must be prepared at least 10 days before Election Day and made available to state and county political party chairs eligible to request them. Those lists contain the same information as shared by the bill, plus mailing addresses, phone numbers, party affiliation, date of registration, occupation if given, four years of voting history, and all data relating to early voting, including ballot requests and returns.
  • Required the county recorder or other officer in charge of the election, no later than 48 hours after the delivery of the official county canvass, to send the Secretary for immediate posting on the same website for all precincts with more than 25 registered voters:
    • the same information for the people who voted in the election. For precincts with 25 registered voters or less, the total number of voters would be included.

This bill, as introduced on February 6, 2023, would eliminate early voting by allowing only people who will be away from their precinct on Election Day to vote a ballot early in person, limit mail voting to people who will be out of state for the fifteen days before Election Day through Election Day, require identification numbers and a notary's signature on mail ballot certificates, facilitate challenging mail ballots, shorten deadlines to return mail ballots and to cure them, and otherwise restrict voting access. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Eliminate early voting, instead requiring a voter to have an excuse to vote a ballot early, in person, and eliminate all locations for such voting except the county recorder's office, which would be required to offer it starting 15 days before Election Day. Under existing law, all voters may opt to vote early in person, and each county board of supervisors may authorize the county recorder to open as many early voting locations as the county deems appropriate. Early voting must be offered at the recorder's office beginning 27 days before Election Day.
  • Require voters to justify voting by mail or early in person with an excuse.
    • Voters would only be allowed to vote early in person if they expect to be absent from their precincts on Election Day and so attest on the application. Under existing law, any voter is free to choose to vote early in person.
    • To receive a ballot in the mail, voters must attest that they expect to be outside the state on Election Day and the fifteen days prior, and provide a temporary out-of-state address to receive the ballot. No other voters would be allowed to vote by mail. Under existing law, any voter is free to choose to vote by mail.
    • Voters who cannot come to the polls for other, specific reasons, could so attest and have a special election board bring a ballot to them so they could vote early in person. The voters eligible for this process are those confined to home, a nursing home, a hospital, or another facility due to age, illness, disability, infirmity, incarceration, or another reason. Voters who cannot appear at the polls on Election Day due to confinement would be required to vote using this procedure. As part of the procedure, the voter would use a privacy screen, and the bipartisan team who brings the ballot would each sign affidavits attesting that the voter completed the ballot without assistance and in secrecy. Under existing law, this basic voting method is available for these people, but such voters are also able to vote by mail. Moreover, existing law does not require special election board workers to sign the affidavits the bill would require.
  • Require voters to include the last four digits of their Social Security number (SSN4) on the application for a mail ballot, whether receiving it by mail or in person.
  • Require voters who are completing mail ballots to have their signature on the ballot certificate notarized, and the notary must attest that the voter voted the ballot without assistance and outside the view of any other person. Because both ballots received in the mail and ballots completed early in person are called "early ballots" in Arizona, this requirement appears to apply to both mail and in-person early votes. Such voters would also be required to put their SSN4 and their birthdate on the ballot certificates. If any of this information is missing or incorrect, the ballot would be rejected, although voters would be given notice about issues with birthdates and SSN4s and an opportunity to cure them. Under existing law, voters do not put their birthdates or SSN4s on ballot certificates, nor do they need their signatures notarized. Ballots are verified by signature matching, and missing or mismatched signatures are subject to cure. The bill would retain signature matching and cure for those reasons.
  • Shorten the mail ballot return deadline by requiring voters to return completed ballots no later than three days before Election Day. Under existing law, mail ballots must be returned by the close of polls on Election Day.
  • Give voters less time to cure issues with their ballot certificates by changing the cure deadline for ballots with missing or incorrect birthdates and SSN4s or mismatched signatures to the day before Election Day. Under existing law, birthdates and SSN4s are not part of mail ballot verification, and mismatched signatures can be cured until the fifth business day after Election Day for elections involving a federal office and the third business day after Election Day for all other elections. The bill would not change the deadline to cure a missing signature, which would remain 7 p.m. on Election Day.
  • Expand the ability to challenge mail ballots, whether returned by mail or voted in person. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Authorize the county political party, early election boards, and party observers to challenge ballots on the grounds of inconsistent signatures or unmatching last four digits of social security numbers or dates of birth.
    • Require election officials to give party observers and early election challengers full access to view in detail the signature and information review process, including seeing the ballot envelope signature and reference signatures as well as the information on the envelope and the corresponding reference information.
    • Require election officials, at the request of the county political party, to give the party a copy of all early ballot envelopes along with all reference signatures and information for all accepted ballots before removing those ballots from their privacy envelopes in sufficient time for the county political party to challenge any unmatched signatures or information.
  • Require all early (both in-person and returned by mail) votes to be counted by Election Day by 7 p.m. but not released until after 8 p.m. on Election Day. Polls close at 7 p.m. on Election Day.
  • Eliminate vote centers on Election Day. Under existing law, counties are allowed to offer vote centers in addition to, or instead of, precinct-based polling places.
  • Eliminate emergency vote centers. Under existing law, the period between 5 p.m. on the Friday before Election Day and 5 p.m. on the day before Election Day is known as the emergency voting period, and counties must offer a method to vote during that time period to voters, who, for a reason that occurred after 5 p.m. on that Friday, cannot vote on Election Day. Emergency vote centers are an explicit option. Although the authorization for emergency vote centers would be repealed by the bill, and the early voting period changed to cover the emergency voting period, the bill would preserve the requirement that counties offer some voting method to such voters.
  • Eliminate the permanent mail voting list (called "active early voting list" in Arizona) by repealing it entirely. Under existing law, any voter can join the list at any time and automatically receive ballots in the mail for every election.
  • Repeal code authorizing candidates, political committees, and other organizations to distribute, collect, and submit mail ballot applications and repeal code regulating those activities.
  • Limit UOCAVA procedures:
    • UOCAVA ballot applications could be made by mail, email, or through the Secretary of State's website. Under existing law, applications could be made by internet or fax.
    • UOCAVA ballots could be sent to such voters by mail or email only. Existing law allows for transmittal by internet, fax, or other electronic means.
    • UOCAVA voters would be required to return their completed ballots by mail. Existing law allows them to return ballots by fax or electronic format.
  • Repeal the ability of special districts to conduct special district elections by mailing ballots to all eligible voters. Under existing law, special districts may notify the officer in charge of elections and seek the county board of supervisors' permission to conduct their elections with universal mail ballots, and if permission is granted, conduct the election according to processes specified in the election code. This bill would repeal the approval process for conducting special district elections with universal mail ballots, but not the part of the code that names the special districts allowed to conduct their elections that way.
  • Repeal the part of the code that specifies how nonpartisan elections may be conducted by mailing ballots to all eligible voters.

  • Change procedures for during presidential primaries (called "presidential preference elections" in Arizona). Specifically, the bill would:

    • Eliminate the ability of the officer in charge of elections to mail ballots to all voters in precincts with fewer than 300 active voters.
    • Eliminate early voting

    • Eliminating the option for a voter to deposit their ballot in a drop box at the voting location, requiring counties to offer the previously optional process, as modified by the bill, and requiring all voters to use the modified process. Implicitly, because the bill did not provide for a person to return another voter's ballot to an Election Day voting location as current law allows, the removed provisions appeared to prohibit such return.
    • Requiring voters who successfully show in-person voter ID, to remove their mail ballot from the envelope, put the envelope in a designated drop box, surrender their mail ballot for spoiling, and become an in-person voter, checking in, receiving a regular ballot, and feeding it into the tabulator.
    • Requiring voters who do not successfully show in-person voter ID to remove their mail ballot from the envelope, put the envelope in a designated drop box, surrender their mail ballot for spoiling, and become an in-person voter, checking in, and receiving a provisional ballot. The provisional ballot would have counted only if the voter later provided an in-person voter ID as existing law requires.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on March 1, 2023, would restrict ballot drop boxes and voting options. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Prohibit election officials from offering unmonitored drop boxes unless the drop box is:
    • Inside a voting location while polls are open and election staff is present and monitoring the box to ensure compliance with all applicable laws, or
    • Inside a county office or other facility used by the officer in charge of elections and election staff is present and monitoring the drop box.
  • Allow election officials to offer an outdoor drop box, including one open 24 hours a day, if:
    • Two or more election workers with equal representation of the two largest political parties in this state monitor the outdoor ballot drop box from 8:00 a.m. until 5:00 p.m.
    • The officer in charge of elections operates a video recording system for the ballot drop box that includes night vision filters and motion activated markers in the recordings, that is monitored live by an election worker from 5:00 p.m. until 8:00 a.m., that is equipped with a publicly available live feed, and that provides for stored video recordings for at least twenty-four months.
  • Appropriate $1,000,000 for disbursement to counties to reimburse:
    • Relocating ballot drop boxes from facilities at which video recording is otherwise prohibited by law.
    • Providing for personnel to monitor the overnight video feed of ballot drop boxes.
    • Developing or acquiring appropriate infrastructure for live video and recording of ballot drop boxes in rural areas.
  • Prohibit election officials from allowing a voter to receive and vote a ballot from a vehicle or other conveyance unless required to by the Americans with Disabilities Act or other federal law. This restriction would apply to early and Election Day voting.

Existing statutes do not directly address drop boxes, however, they are authorized without these restrictions in the Elections Procedures Manual, which has the force of law. Neither existing statutes nor the Manual specifically addresses voting from vehicles, but the Manual does authorize a variant called "curbside voting" for voters with disabilities when a polling place is not accessible.

Governor Katie Hobbs vetoed this bill on June 20, 2023. As passed by the Legislature, the bill would have increased the distribution of voter registration information, created a new way to be removed from the list of voters automatically mailed a ballot each election, revised aspects of the hand count audit process primarily aimed at ensuring sufficient staffing, and revised challenger appointment powers to facilitate appointing challengers and expand what activity they may observe. Specifically, this bill would have:

  • Broadened the access the public has to voter registration information without changing what information in voters' records is kept confidential, and removed protections against the redistribution of the data. The bill would have:
    • allowed access for any non-commercial purpose, while existing law limits the use of voter information to purposes relating to a political or political party activity, a political campaign, or an election, for revising election district boundaries, or for any other purpose specifically authorized by law.
    • required officers in charge of elections to provide electronic access to the information and specifically authorize the public posting of properly received information. People seeking copies of the list would be required to establish an electronic profile, attest the information will be for noncommercial use, and pay the fees required under existing law. Other than the fees, these provisions would be new. Existing law prohibits the public posting of the information.
    • repealed limits on the redistribution of the data. Specifically, the bill would repeal the existing prohibition against any person possessing part of all of the official voter registration list permitting its use, sale, purchase, or other transfer except for authorized uses. In addition, the bill would have repealed the existing prohibition against distributing, posting, or otherwise providing internet access to any portion of the information except as otherwise authorized by the code.
  • Created a new way a voter may be removed from the permanent mail voting list (called "active early voting list" in Arizona). Specifically, the bill would have allowed a voter to make a verbal request that includes information sufficient to verify the voter's identity. The bill did not define what information would be sufficient. The voter registration information the bill would have allowed to be shared more easily includes a voter's name in full, title, party preference, date of registration, residence address, mailing address (if different), zip code, birth year, phone number (if available), and occupation (if available).
  • Expanded the locations challengers appointed by political parties may access and expand parties' power to appoint them. Specifically, the bill would have:
    • added a voting center and a location at which electronic ballot processing occurs as locations where challengers may act, and required election officials to enable challengers to see the electronic vote adjudication board's activities.
    • added any third-party vendor location that processes returned affidavit envelopes on behalf of the county, subject to specified notice rules. "Affidavit envelopes" includes both mail ballot envelopes and provisional ballot envelopes.
    • provided that if the county party chairperson failed to appoint challengers, the state party chairperson could, and if they failed, the legislative district chairperson could. Existing law in the Elections Procedures Manual provides similar access, however, the successive appointment powers would be new.
  • Provided that any new signature images submitted for comparison with the voter's registration record cannot contain any indication of the voter's political party. Existing law does not have this requirement.
  • Revised aspects of the existing hand count audit. Specifically:
    • The county officer in charge of the election would have been required to publish the times, locations, and procedures of the hand count on the county website no later than a week before Election Day. Existing law does not have that requirement.
    • The county officer in charge of the election would have been prohibited from creating procedures that are not expressly authorized by statute.
    • Political parties would have had new, earlier deadlines to designate people to perform the hand count, and the designation process would change slightly. As under existing law, if an insufficient number of people are appointed by 5 p.m. on the Thursday before Election Day or if an insufficient number of designated people report to the hand count, the hand count would not occur.
    • More than 75 percent of the hand counters could have belonged to the same political party if a recognized party provides an insufficient number of qualified people. Existing law prohibits conducting the hand count with more than 75 percent of the counters being affiliated with the same party.
    • The county would have been required to make the hand count results available on its website as well as provide them to the Secretary of State for publication on the Secretary's website. Existing law requires only publication by the Secretary.
    • Observer access and live streaming rules for proceedings at the counting center would have applied to the hand count locations. The bill would also have clarified that the process is under the direction of the county board of supervisors or other officer in charge of the election.
  • Repealed and re-enacted provisions requiring counties to offer early ballot tracking effective December 31, 2023.

Beginning in January of the even-numbered year, if a new manual is not approved, the Secretary would be required to provide an annotated version of the previous manual reflecting any new or revised laws and applicable court decisions. VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 26, 2023, would create automatic voter registration at the DMV (called the Department of Transportation in Arizona). Under existing law, voter registration services are offered at the DMV, but automatic voter registration is prohibited. Specifically, the bill would provide that people applying for driver's licenses or state IDs, or the renewal or update of either, would be automatically registered to vote upon completing and submitting the application. The DMV would send county recorders the registration information, and the recorders would then send the new registrants information on how to decline to be registered. If a person does not decline within 21 days of the mailing, they would be presumed to be properly registered. A person who is not qualified to register but who unknowingly registered through this process would not be guilty of specific false registration or false swearing felonies.

Last Updated January 31, 2023

This bill, as amended on March 28, 2023, would make voters' names, addresses, birth years, and precinct numbers public before and after each election, as well as whether they voted in the election. The bill would require the public disclosure of ballot images and related information as well. Exceptions would apply to people in confidentiality programs and precincts with less than 25 voters. Existing law does not have similar requirements, but does have rules for sharing voter registration list data that are more restrictive than the process created by the bill. Some of the restrictions may apply to the data disclosed by the bill. Finally, the bill would give people two additional days to file election contests. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the county recorder to send a list of the names, home addresses, years of birth, and precinct numbers of every eligible registered voter, active or inactive, to the Secretary of State at least 10 days before Election Day. The Secretary would be required to immediately post the information in a convenient downloadable format on a secure website the bill would require the Secretary to create. People participating in address confidentiality programs or living in a precinct with 25 or fewer registered voters would not have their information exposed but would be included only as a total number of voters in a precinct. Under existing law, precinct voter lists for Election Day use must be prepared at least 10 days before Election Day and made available to state and county political party chairs eligible to request them. Those lists contain the same information as shared by the bill, plus mailing addresses, phone numbers, party affiliation, date of registration, occupation if given, four years of voting history, and all data relating to early voting, including ballot requests and returns.
  • Require the county recorder or other officer in charge of the election, no later than 48 hours after the delivery of the official county canvass, to send the Secretary for immediate posting on the same website for all precincts with more than 25 registered voters:
    • the same information for the people who voted in the election. For precincts with 25 registered voters or less, the total number of voters would be included.
    • unaltered images of all ballots used in the tabulation of the election. An adjudicated or duplicated ballot image would be sent together with the original ballot image. These images would be suppressed in a precinct with 25 or fewer registered voters, but the total number of images would be included.
    • the cast vote record in a sortable format. Only the total number of cast vote records would be included for a precinct with 25 or fewer registered voters. "Cast vote record" would be defined as the electronic records available within an election management system that show how the votes were cast on each anonymous ballot for each race and that allow for verification of the accumulated vote totals for each candidate or issue together with a summary report for each batch for counties whose election management system does not tie images of electronically adjudicated ballots to underlying original ballot images. For precincts with 25 people or less, the number of cast vote records would be included.
  • Require any person wishing to access the secure website and download the voter and voting information to provide the Secretary:
    • Their name, address, email address, phone number, and proof of identity.
    • A declaration signed by the person stating that the person will not use the information for commercial purposes, alter the images in information in any manner, or use the information or images for voter intimidation.
  • Prohibit commercial use of the newly public data. This prohibition would be enforced with a new felony. Existing law provides that the voter information in the precinct voter lists, and more generally, information derived from registration forms, may be used only for purposes relating to (1) political party activity, a political campaign, or an election, (2) for revising election district boundaries, or (3) for any other purpose specifically authorized by law, and may not be used for a commercial purpose. Existing law also restricts the redistribution of voter data. Specifically, any person in possession of a precinct register or list, in whole or part, or any reproduction of a precinct register or list, shall not permit the register or list to be used, bought, sold, or otherwise transferred for any unauthorized purpose. Moreover, existing law prohibits a person in possession of information derived from voter registration forms or precinct registers from distributing, posting, or otherwise providing access to any portion of that information through the internet. These existing restrictions are enforced with a felony.
  • Prohibit election officials from altering or adding voter data as part of a security measure.
  • Protect the Secretary, county recorder, or other officer in charge of elections from liability for any personally identifying information, handwritten statements, and other notations made or provided by the voter that are included in the ballot images.

  • Allow people seven days after the completion of the canvass to file election contests, not five.

This bill, as introduced on January 27, 2023, would allow an "enterprise" to be criminally prosecuted for knowingly communicating false information about where, when, how, or if people can vote. If convicted, the enterprise could be dissolved. In addition, an impacted voter could sue for an injunction. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create a felony forbidding an "enterprise" from using any means to knowingly communicate to a registered voter false information intended to impede the voter's right to vote and that relates to any of:

    • the voter's precinct, polling place or voter registration status.
    • the voter's eligibility to register or vote.
    • the voter's status on the active early voting list.
    • information regarding early or mail-in ballots.
    • information on how to obtain a ballot.
    • information on how to vote or the location of an on-site early voting location, voting center or emergency voting center or any other location at which a person may vote or register to vote, including the office of the county recorder or other officer in charge of elections.
  • Create a civil cause of action to enable a registered voter to whom such false information to sue for a court order against the enterprise communicating the false information.
  • Give the Attorney General and county attorneys the authority to investigate and prosecute alleged violations.
  • Provide that a conviction for the felony is grounds for dissolution.

  • Define "enterprise" as

    • any corporation, partnership, association, labor union or other legal entity.
    • any group organized under section 527 of the internal revenue code.
    • any group of persons who are associated in fact although not a legal entity.

This bill, as amended on June 13, 2023, would enable more eligible voters' timely ballots to be counted, would make ballot images and cast vote records public, and extend the deadline to file election contests. Specifically, the amended bill would:

  • Enable more eligible voters' timely ballots to be counted by:
    • Ending the double verification of in-person early voters' ballots imposed by existing law. In Arizona, in-person early voters show voter ID and receive mail ballots (called "early ballots") which they then complete, seal in ballot return envelopes, and sign the voter certificate on the envelope. Those signatures are later verified by signature matching. The bill would exempt mail ballots completed in person after showing voter ID from that signature matching process.
    • Allowing voters to return completed ballots that they had received in the mail to early voting locations, show voter ID, and have their ballot deemed ready for counting without later signature verification. Existing law allows counties to offer a process to voters returning such ballots to Election Day voting locations to show voter ID and then feed their ballots into tabulators.
  • Make ballot images and the cast vote record public after the primary and general election and not later than 48 hours after the certification of results by the approval of the official county canvass. The images and records would be submitted by the county officer in charge of the election to the Secretary of State, who would immediately post them on a secure website in a convenient downloadable format. The bill would also:
    • Hold the Secretary and the county officer in charge of the election harmless for any information or notations made by voters that are included in the ballot images.
    • Require the Secretary to create and administer an electronic portal to receive requests for and provide access to the images and records. A person requesting access would be required to provide their name, address, email address, and telephone number and attest that they will not alter or misrepresent the images or records or use the information to reveal how a person voted. The Secretary would be required to verify the requester's identity.
    • Create a felony for violations of that attestation.
  • Require election officials to make the chain of custody log for early ballots returned at voting locations on Election Day available for inspection by the public, the political parties, committees representing ballot measures on the ballot, and the candidates on the ballot within forty-eight hours after Election Day.
  • Extend the time to file election contests to seven days after the completion of the canvass, instead of the current five days.

The June 13 amendments removed provisions that were in the previous version of the bill. Those provisions would have:

  • Enable election officials to pick up certain mail ballots returned to voting locations on Election Day before the close of polls.
  • Specified details of a process for voters and election officials to follow when voters are showing ID to have their completed mail ballot bypass signature matching verification.

Amendments on March 22 removed provisions that would have:

  • Eliminated ballot return assistance by expanding a felony to prohibit voters from choosing anyone to return their ballots for them.
  • Shortened the time voters have to return mail ballots.
  • Required voters returning their mail ballots after 5 p.m. on Friday to use voter ID to avoid having their ballot ballots verified by signature matching.

Governor Katie Hobbs vetoed this bill on June 21, 2023. As passed by the Legislature, this bill would have expanded the early voting period, ended the double verification of in-person early ballots, and changed the rules and processes for returning and verifying mail ballots (called "early ballots" in Arizona.) Specifically, the bill would have:

  • Allowed in-person early voting to be offered through the day before Election Day unless the county recorder or other officer in charge of the election is unable to revise precinct registers and other election material in a timely manner for Election Day use. If the registers and election materials cannot be timely updated, early voting would end at 7 p.m. on the Friday before Election Day. Under existing law, early voting must end by 5 p.m. on the Friday before Election Day.
  • Ended the requirement that mail ballots completed in person after showing in-person voter ID undergo signature match verification. These ballots would be stamped "ID verified" by election officials and put into a ballot box dedicated to such ballots.
  • Changed the deadline for dropping off a mail ballot in the ordinary manner to 7 p.m. on the Friday before Election Day instead of the close of polls on Election Day.
  • Created a new process for dropping off a mail ballot between 7 p.m. on the Friday before Election Day and the close of polls on Election Day. Specifically:
    • If the voter returned their ballot to a voting location after 7 p.m. on the Friday before Election Day, the voter would have been required to show ID documentation sufficient to vote in person and sign the poll book before depositing their ballot. If the voter showed such ID, their ballot would have been stamped "ID verified" and put into the ballot box dedicated to such ballots. If the voter did not show such ID, they would be required to present such ID to the county recorder or other officer in charge of elections not later than the fifth business day after the election if a federal office is on the ballot or the third business day after any other election. If the voter did not return with such ID their ballot would have been rejected.
    • If the voter's family member, household member, or caregiver returned the ballot for the voter after 7 p.m. on the Friday before Election Day, the voter would have been required to appear and present ID documentation sufficient to vote in person to the county recorder or other officer in charge of elections not later than the fifth business day after the election, if a federal office is on the ballot, or the third business day after any other election. If the voter did not return with such ID their ballot would have been rejected.
    • If the voter's county offers the process, on Election Day, the voter could have either shown in-person ID documentation and fed their mail ballot into a tabulator or surrendered the mail ballot and completed a provisional ballot. Under existing law, even if the county offers the process, the voter can simply drop off their ballot rather than use the process. The bill would have eliminated that option.
  • Required election officials to maintain a tally of ID-verified ballots supported with an affidavit.
  • Allowed ID-verified mail ballots to be picked up from polling places on Election Day before the close of polls, provided that certain chain of custody procedures are followed. Existing law does not allow for the pickup of mail ballots returned to polling places before the close of polls.

Last Updated June 21, 2023

Governor Katie Hobbs vetoed this bill on June 20, 2023. As passed by the Legislature, this bill would have changed rules relating to poll watchers for both in-person voting and mail ballot processing, both in terms of who may appoint them and the access they must be granted. (In Arizona, both mail ballots and in-person early ballots are called "early ballots" and both are sealed in affidavit envelopes the voter signs. "Early ballots" are later processed by signature matching.) Specifically, the bill would have:

  • Required early ballot processing watchers to be registered Arizona voters and prohibited candidates on the ballot from serving as watchers. Similar rules apply to watchers of in-person voting under existing law.
  • Created rules for poll watcher conduct during early ballot processing. Neither existing law nor the Elections Procedures Manual has similar provisions. The bill would have:
    • Provided that watchers may not approach an election official's table or equipment any closer than reasonably necessary to properly perform their observation functions.
    • Prohibited watchers from obstructing the administration of the election, early election board procedures, or ballot processing.
    • Required watchers to pose questions regarding procedures directly to the supervisor of the early election board.
    • Required watchers to bring their own materials and necessities.
    • Clarified that each watcher must be allowed to observe election officials' conduct.
  • Created rules for poll watcher conduct during in-person voting. These rules are similar to rules in the Election Procedures Manual, but the bill addressed more topics and with greater specificity than those rules. The bill would have:
    • Provided that watchers may not approach an election official's table, equipment, check-in stations, or the voting booths any closer than reasonably necessary to properly perform their observation functions.
    • Allowed challengers to observe the conduct of voters and election officials, including the set up of the voting location before polls open and the closeout procedures after voting ends.
    • Prohibited watchers from obstructing the administration of the election or the voting process. Relatedly, watchers would have been prohibited from interacting with a voter.
    • Required watchers to pose questions regarding polling place procedures directly to the inspector at the voting location or the officer in charge of the election.
    • Allowed watchers to enter and observe all polling places in the county in which the watcher is designated.
    • Required watchers to bring their own materials and necessities.
    • Prohibited candidates from serving as watchers.
  • Made conforming changes to provide that rules for watching in-person voting apply at vote centers as well as at precincts.
  • Created rules for observing at ballot counting centers. The bill would have:
    • Prohibited watchers from approaching an election official's table or equipment any closer than is reasonably necessary to properly perform their functions.
    • Prohibited watchers from obstructing the administration of any election or procedure.
    • Allowed each watcher to observe the conduct of election officials.
    • Required each watcher to provide their own materials and necessities.
    • Required watchers to pose any questions regarding procedures directly to the supervisor at the counting center or the officer in charge of elections for resolution.
  • Allowed each candidate for federal office, during general elections only, to appoint one poll watcher at each counting center. If multiple candidates for the U.S. House of Representatives in a single party name observers for the same counting center, one would have been drawn by lot to observe. Under existing law, representatives of political parties, the public, a candidate for nonpartisan office, or a political committee in support of or opposed to a ballot proposition may appoint observers to serve at counting centers.
  • Required observers at counting centers to be registered voters in Arizona.

The February 28, 2023 amendment removed several provisions from the bill. Those provisions would have prescribed rules for poll watcher access and behavior that are broadly similar to ones imposed by the Elections Procedures Manual.

Last Updated June 21, 2023

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on March 21, 2023, was rewritten. The amended bill would create a process for preventing the canvass of the results of a primary or general election, other than a presidential election, and for holding a new election instead. The prior version also involved invalidating the results of an election and holding a new one, but it targeted large counties only and had fundamentally different provisions.

As amended, the bill would prohibit the county board of supervisors, the county recorder, and the county officer in charge of elections from canvassing of a primary or general election and require a new election to be held if an election official for that election violated election law or the Elections Procedures Manual and all of these occur:

  • Voters in the county are disenfranchised as a result of at least one of the following occurring:
    • Voters wait more than ninety minutes outside of a voting location.
    • An election official for that election violated election law or the Elections Procedures Manual ("EPM").
    • The ballot chain of custody is not maintained as prescribed by election law or the EPM.
  • Voters complete and submit, within five days after Election Day, affidavits alleging facts that support a claim of 90 minute or more waits, an election official violating election law or the EPM, or the failure to maintain the ballot chain of custody as prescribed by election law or the EPM. The bill specifies the affidavit form.
  • A sufficient number of voters submit completed affidavits to the relevant clerk of the superior court to require action by a superior court judge. for Maricopa County, the only county with at least one million registered voters, one thousand voter affidavits would be sufficient. For all other counties, 250 voter affidavits would be.
  • Within five days after the deadline to submit affidavits, a superior court judge orders the canvass to be delayed and appoints a special master to examine the submitted affidavits to confirm the necessary facts. The court would be required to order the canvass delayed and appoint a special master if a sufficient number of submitted affidavits are confirmed. The special master would be a certified Arizona election officer who conducts elections in a county other than the county affected by the court's orders.

  • The court would be required to declare the election to be a failed election if the court confirms the truth of a sufficient number of the affidavits. If the court declares the election to be a failed election and orders the county board of supervisors to call another election within sixty days after the court's declaration, the election would be supervised by the special master.

    The county board of supervisors, county recorder, and county officer in charge of elections would be required to hold a new primary or general election if so ordered by the court. Any member of the board of supervisors who violates the provisions of the bill would forfeit that office.

    Last updated March 22, 2023
