This bill was vetoed by Governor Gavin Newsom on September 22, 2024. As passed by the legislature, the bill would have required the secretary of state to operate a pilot program that would provide grants to San Benito, San Mateo, and Santa Cruz counties to facilitate voting at city or county jails for all eligible incarcerated individuals, including registration and voting by mail ballot, provisional ballot, or replacement ballot, for any statewide primary and general election from 2026 through 2028. The bill would also have permitted, but not required, participating counties to provide voting access for local and special elections.

Specifically, the bill would have:

  • Required that the program offer registration and voting opportunities for all applicable elections and that information about voting procedures be posted on the county's elections website.
  • Required that eligible individuals be provided the opportunity to vote a regular, provisional, or replacement ballot using an accessible voting machine "that provides for a private and independent voting experience."
  • Required compliance with federal accessibility requirements related to disability and language, and the provision of voting- and election-related materials required by state law, "to the maximum extent feasible."
  • Provided that state protections related to voter intimidation and electioneering apply to voting sites under the program.
  • Required facilities to develop procedures for voting during lockdowns and during administrative segregation or other restrictions.
  • Specified that in-person voting in a jail facility may not count toward a jurisdiction's number of required polling places or vote centers required under existing law.
  • Required voting to begin at any time from the 29th day before an election through Election Day. Each county would have been required to provide at least eight hours of cumulative voting in each jail facility during the relevant period, which could occur over one or more days, and would have been required to make its best efforts to offer more than the minimum of eight hours of voting time and provide at least 13 cumulative hours of voting time.
  • Required each participating county to designate an employee as a voting coordinator to ensure compliance with the program, including specified duties, and require the secretary of state to provide relevant training.
  • Required a local election official to evaluate the program after every election conducted in the program and to report the results to the secretary of state. The report would have included statistics that measure different outcomes from the election, a description of challenges in implementing and administering the program, recommendations for future models of the program.
  • Required the secretary of state to submit the post-election report to the legislature, and post it on the agency website.
  • Set the end date for the program at January 1, 2030.

A previous version of the bill also included a provision that was amended out before passage by the legislature, which would have permitted officials responsible for the safety of incarcerated individuals to deviate from required procedures if they were deemed impractical, unsafe, or if adherence would undermine the goal of increasing voter participation. Officials would have been required to list any such deviations in the program report provided to the secretary of state.

This bill was vetoed by Governor Gavin Newsom on September 22, 2024. As passed by the legislature, the bill would have expanded access to voting information for non-English speakers. Specifically, the bill would have:

  • Required the Secretary of State by March 1 of each year following a presidential election, starting with March 1, 2025, to determine the number of residents of voting age in each county and precinct who are members of a single language minority group (a group of 10,000 or more people of voting age in a county or five percent of the voting-age population) and who lack sufficient skills in English to vote without assistance.
  • Required the secretary of state to make publicly available on their website a list of languages used by single language minority groups, with at least one of the following:
    • Ten thousand or more individuals in a county of voting age who lack sufficient skills in English to vote without assistance
    • Five percent of all Native American voting age residents on a reservation who lack sufficient skills in English to vote without assistance so long as that number is more than five percent of all residents of the reservation.
    • Three percent or more of voting age residents of a particular county or precinct who lack sufficient skills in English to vote without assistance.
  • Allowed interested citizens or organizations to provide the secretary of state with information that gives the secretary of state sufficient reason to believe that there is a need to provide translated ballots in another language, and would allow the secretary of state, if they find a significant need, to provide translated ballots in the applicable language.
  • Required that the existing law requiring the secretary of state to provide specific elections and voting materials in designated minority languages go into effect on January 1, 2028.
  • Required that the existing law allowing a mail voter to request by facsimile a copy of their ballot in the language of their preference and to have it provided to them via mail or email remain in effect until January 1, 2028. The secretary of state would also be required to not expand the categories of covered languages for the purpose of providing translated ballots via facsimile from March 1, 2025 until January 1, 2028.
  • Required that the determinations and findings made by the secretary of state regarding whether it is appropriate to provide election materials in other languages, as required under existing law, be made by March 1 of each year following a presidential election until January 1, 2028.

Previous versions of the bill contained provisions that have been amended out. Those provisions would have:

  • Required the Secretary of State, for each statewide election, to:

  • Required county election officials whose county contained a single language minority group in one or more identified languages, for each election, to:

These materials would have included the county voter guide. Relatedly, the county would have been required to provide translated materials to voters who indicated a language preference for one of the languages and ensured the translated voter guide was on the county's website.
    • Create a dedicated internet website address where voters could find all available translated voting materials in that language created in the state.
    • Make at least two direct contacts with voters to inform them of the upcoming election and promote the toll-free voter assistance hotline.
    • Establish a language accessibility advisory committee of representatives of language minority communities no later than October 1, 2025, and have the committee meet no less than quarterly thereafter.
    • Report to the secretary of state the number of voters who indicated a language preference, by language.

This bill, as enacted on October 10, 2023, creates a new misdemeanor offense for voting or attempting to vote in an election in both California and another state if the election is held on the same date. The crime does not apply if one of the elections requires voters to be landowners only, or otherwise does not require voters to be residents of the jurisdiction conducting the election.

Last updated October 18, 2023

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on June 14, 2023, would clarify and expand two felonies to protect election equipment that election officials uniquely have access to, although the crimes are generally applicable. The bill would also make changes to election record retention, chains of custody documentation, and other aspects of election administration that the Voting Rights Lab does not track. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Clarify the existing felony that prohibits someone, before or during an election, from interfering or attempting to interfere with the secrecy of voting or ballot tally software program codes, by further defining "interferes or attempts to interfere with". Specifically, the bill would explain that "interferes or attempts to interfere with, includes but is not limited to, knowingly, and without authorization, providing unauthorized access to, or breaking the chain of custody to, certified voting technology during the lifecycle of that certified voting technology or any finished or unfinished ballot cards."
  • Expand an existing felony so that it prohibits knowingly, and without authorization, making or having in the person's possession credentials, passwords, or access keys to a voting machine that has been adopted and will be used in elections in California. Existing law prohibits such knowing and unauthorized making or possessing of a key to such a voting machine.

Provisions amended out of the bill on April 6, 2023, would have created new felonies to prohibit:

  • Knowingly, and without authorization, makes or has in the person's possession copies of electronic data. The bill defines electronic data as "voting technology software, operating systems, databases, firmware, drivers, and logs."
  • Knowingly, and without authorization, providing unauthorized access to, or breaking the chain of custody to, certified voting technology during the lifecycle of that technology, or any finished or unfinished ballot cards.

Last updated June 15, 2023

This bill, as amended on April 12, 2023, would end felony disenfranchisement in California and facilitate voting by incarcerated eligible voters. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Repeal statute sections disenfranchising people who are incarcerated in prison for a felony conviction. The bill reflects the need to amend the state constitution first, providing that disenfranchisement would end when voters ratify a related constitutional amendment.
  • Facilitate voting by eligible incarcerated people. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Provide that eligible incarcerated individuals retain the right to vote by mail based on their last voluntary address prior to incarceration, unless their last voluntary address was out of state.
    • Provide that the election official administering the election at the person's last voluntary address is responsible for giving the incarcerated voter all of the mail ballot election materials in the manner and time otherwise required by law. The voter would be responsible for informing the election official where they are incarcerated.

Last Updated April 24, 2023

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on June 27, 2023, would require the Secretary of State to seek an agreement with the federal Social Security Administration to make death statistics available to the Secretary. After reaching an agreement, the Secretary would be required to issue regulations governing the electronic transfer of those death statistics. Beginning January 1, 2026, the Secretary and county election officials would be required to use the Social Security death statistics to cancel the registrations of deceased voters. Under existing law, the Secretary is required to issue similar regulations for using death data from the state Department of Health Services.

Last updated July 5, 2023

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on October 8, 2023, repeals a moot section of the election code that authorized Los Angeles County to conduct a unique variant of the universal mail ballot election process created by the Voter's Choice Act, and makes conforming changes. That portion of the election code was written explicitly as an interim stage of converting to Voter's Choice Act elections, and Los Angeles County began conducting Voter's Choice Act elections in November 2020.

The bill also contains additional provisions related to topics that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

Last Updated March 6, 2024

This bill, as introduced on February 6, 2023, proposes an amendment to the California Constitution that would eliminate its requirement that the Legislature disenfranchise people convicted of felonies while they are serving a state or federal prison term. Passage of the bill would be the first step in amending the constitution. After the bill's passage, it would be put on the ballot for voters to ratify.

Last updated February 9, 2023.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on October 10, 2023, requires election officials to give voters notice of defects with their mail ballot by telephone, text message, or email if such contact information is in the voter's record, and expressly requires officials to leave a voicemail for voters who do not answer a telephone call. Under existing law, election officials were permitted, but not required, to send phone, text, or email notifications, in addition to mandatory notice by mail.

Last Updated October 18, 2023

This bill was vetoed by Governor Gavin Newsom on September 29, 2024. As passed by the legislature on September 5, 2024, the bill would have authorized the secretary of state to establish "preapproved registration" for eligible individuals, as part of the state's existing automatic registration (AVR) process at the driver licensing agency, and made other changes to general AVR procedures.

Specifically, the bill would have:

  • Authorized the secretary of state to establish a process for "preapproved registration" of individuals applying for a driver's license, including steps for a resident to "activate" their preapproved registration. Individuals would be preapproved if they:
    • Were not registered or pre-registered at the time of their license application
    • Declined to become registered during the transaction
    • Provided documentation of U.S. citizenship and voting age during the transaction
    • Were not enrolled in an address confidentiality program
    • Received notice of their preapproved status, and the option to "activate" registration at a later date
  • Prohibited the licensing agency from providing applicants who showed documentation of non-U.S. citizenship with the opportunity to attest to eligibility for voter registration. Existing law has no express prohibition concerning these applicants.
  • Expressly required that the secretary of state and licensing agency jointly develop a process by which the agency may determine whether an applicant is currently registered or pre-registered to vote, and permitted the secretary to meet the requirement by providing the voter list daily. Existing law does not specifically require the transmission of current registration status information.
  • Required the transmission of application information from the licensing agency to the secretary of state only if data indicates the applicant is not registered or pre-registered, or if their status cannot be determined. Existing law requires the agency to transfer information for "each person who submits a driver's license application."
  • Removed the requirement that the AVR process provide the opportunity for an applicant to join the state's permanent mail voter list. As of 2021, the state automatically provides a mail ballot to all active voters.
  • Specified an effective date for the bill's provisions of the earlier of January 1, 2030, or five days after agency officials determine that technical infrastructure required is functional, and permitted action related to the requirements starting January 1, 2025.

Previous versions of the bill contained provisions that were amended out prior to passage by the legislature. Those provisions would have:

  • Changed the opt-out process for AVR based on whether an applicant provided documentation of citizenship. Existing law provides for "front end" AVR, in which all applicants are given the opportunity to opt out of registration during the license transaction. Under a previous version of the bill, applicants showing citizenship documentation in the course of business with the agency would have been provided "back end" AVR, with the opportunity to opt out provided after the transaction by mailed notice. The previous version would also have required that the voter list include a notation of citizenship documentation for AVR-registered voters, and would have expressly provided that the new AVR process did not create a new affirmative documentation requirement for voter registration generally.
  • Required the secretary of state and DMV to develop procedures to "ensure" that a driver's license, identification card, or other identifying information from an applicant was sufficiently evaluated to determine whether that applicant was eligible to register or pre-register to vote.
  • Expanded the existing safe harbor provision for individuals erroneously registered through the AVR process, by requiring notice to the applicant and documentation of agency responsibility for an error.
  • Expanded the implementation of AVR by requiring the secretary of state to assess which existing voter registration agencies collect sufficient information from applicants for new and updated registrations in the regular course of business, and scheduling the implementation of AVR as applicable. Previous provisions would also have authorized the secretary to develop procedures for processing agency records with an electronic image of the applicant's signature.

Last Updated October 10, 2024

HISTORY: {"date":["10/08/2023","10/08/2023"],"summary":["Signed by GOVERNOR","Chaptered by Secretary of State.  Chapter No. 2023-611"],"meta":["[]","[]"],"order":[1,0]}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on October 8, 2023, provides express definitions for various elements of the felony offense for interfering with (1) election officers’ administration of elections and the vote canvass, or (2) a voter exercising their right to vote. Prior law did not include definitions of any elements of the offense. The bill:

  • Defines “officers holding an election or conducting a canvass" as including, but not limited to, the secretary of state as the chief elections officer, and their staff, as it relates to performance of any of their duties related to administering the provisions of the Elections Code, and elections officials and their staff, including temporary workers and poll workers, and members of a precinct board, in their performance of any duty related to assisting with holding an election or conducting a canvass.
  • Defines "holding an election or conducting a canvass" as including, but not limited to, the election observation process governed by the Elections Code and applicable regulations adopted by the secretary.
  • Defines "voting at an election" as including, but not limited to, voting in person at a polling place, the office of the elections official, or satellite locations and voting by mail and returning a voted ballot.

Prior versions of the bill included an additional provision that was amended out prior to enactment. That provision would have created a new felony offense for making, hiring, or arranging for any other person to make use of or threaten to make use of any force, violence, or tactic of coercion or intimidation to prevent or attempt to prevent:

  • An elections official or their staff, including temporary workers and volunteers, from performing any duty related to conducting an election or canvass.
  • A member of the precinct board from performing any duty related to assisting with conducting an election or canvass.
  • The secretary of state as the chief elections officer, or their staff, from performing any duties related to administering the provisions of the code.

Last updated March 6, 2024.

HISTORY: {"date":"02/01/2024","summary":"In SENATE.  Returned to Secretary of Senate pursuant to Joint Rule 56","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 17, 2023, would change the automatic voter registration system at the DMV. Specifically, the bill would provide for two parallel systems of automatic voter registration, one for people whose documents submitted for the DMV transaction prove that they are U.S. citizens, and one for people whose documents neither prove nor disprove U.S. citizenship. The latter group would be served by the existing automatic registration process, which gives voters the option to decline registration as part of their transaction with the DMV. The new process would apply to the people who incidentally prove citizenship and would give the opportunity to decline registration through a notice mailed to the voter after their DMV transaction. The bill would also confirm that a person whose documents prove they are not a U.S. citizen would not be registered using either process. Similarly, people who participate in address confidentiality programs would not have their information transmitted to the Secretary.

The bill would also revise the registration update process. The DMV would identify applicants who are already registered to vote, and then send their information to the Secretary as the Secretary directs so their registrations could be updated as needed. To facilitate the update process, the Secretary would either give the DMV a daily copy of the statewide voter registration list or, jointly with the DMV, create a method for DMV to access the information. If a voter's name or address has changed based on the DMV information, the Secretary would update the voter's record ad activate their registration if necessary. The relevant county election official would send the voter notice by forwardable mail, along with a postage-paid preaddressed return form by which the person could verify or correct the information. Existing law provides that automatic voter registration information must be used to update registrations, but does not require the DMV to prescreen for existing registrations, nor does it specify the notice the bill requires.

Finally, the bill would mandate language access for the automatic voter registration notices sent to voters, expand protections for ineligible people accidentally registered in this process, and enable the Secretary of State to create automatic voter registration or registration updates at other agencies in the future.

Specifically, the bill would create a new automatic registration system for people who are not currently registered to vote, who apply for a driver's license, and who, as part of that application, submit documents demonstrating U.S. citizenship and sufficient age to register.

  • For those people, the DMV would electronically send information about the person to the Secretary of State, including:
    • Name.
    • Date of birth.
    • Either or both their residence address and mailing address.
    • Digitized signature
    • Telephone number, if available.
    • Email address, if available.
    • The language in which the person conducted the transaction with the department.
    • Other information specified in regulations implementing this chapter.
  • An existing misdemeanor prohibiting disclosure of information received from the DMV as part of the existing automatic voter registration process would be expanded to include improper disclosure of the information received pursuant to the new process.
  • The existing requirement that the Secretary of State process the information received from the DMV and determine whether the person is or will be eligible to vote or not and then complete or reject registration would be expanded to include the new automatic registration process.

  • When a voter's information is sent under the new automatic process and the Secretary confirms the person's eligibility to vote, the appropriate county elections official would send a specific notice to the voter by nonforwardable mail to their address of record, along with a postage-paid preadressed return form the voter could use to decline registration, pick a party, and select a language preference. The notice would detail the eligibility requirements to register and the penalties for falsely registering, and instruct people to decline registration if they did not meet the requirements. If the notice is returned undeliverable, the county elections official would send a forwardable address confirmation notice. If the form is returned by the voter, the county elections official would act accordingly.

    Finally, the bill would require the Secretary of State to prescribe the form of various notices, and ensure that each county that must provide election materials in languages other than English provides the notices in the relevant languages as well. The Secretary would be required to issue related rules.

    The bill would require the Secretary of State and the DMV to develop procedures to ensure that transmitted information is sufficiently reviewed to determine eligibility and protect against erroneous registrations or preregistrations. If the Secretary or DMV realize they have made an error and registered an ineligible person, they would contact the person and give them a letter asserting the Secretary, DMV, or both were responsible for the error A copy of the letter would be kept on file and made available to the person upon request. However, if clear and convincing evidence shows that the ineligible person committed a registration crime, the Secretary and the DMV would not provide such a letter.

    The bill would also create a process through which the Secretary can convert voter registration agencies into automatic voter registration agencies for new registrations, registration updates, or both if the agencies collect sufficient information when interacting with the public for non-registration reasons.

Last Updated February 24, 2023

HISTORY: {"date":"02/27/2023","summary":"From HOUSE Committee on STATE, CIVIC, MILITARY and VETERANS AFFAIRS: Postponed indefinitely","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 31, 2023, would enable certain small counties to apply to the Secretary of State to open fewer voter service centers than existing law requires, and would allow other small counties to use an employee to serve as an election worker during a general election. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Allow counties with between 10,000 and 37,500 active voters to apply to the Secretary of State for permission to open fewer than the required number of voter service centers for a general election. Existing law requires such counties to open one during the early voting period, and three on Election Day. The application would be made as part of the election plan existing law requires counties to submit to the Secretary, and must include data showing how many voters used the required voter service centers compared to the county's available resources, and demonstrating the number of required centers are not necessary, even after considering the required equitable siting factors. The Secretary would be required to develop detailed guidelines for the applications, specifying the data that must be included, and would be required to decide whether to allow the voter service center reduction as part of approving the county's election plan.

  • Allow counties with fewer than 37,500 active voters to appoint one member of the county clerk and recorder's staff to serve as one of the three required election judges at a voter service center during a partisan election.

    Last updated February 1, 2023

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 2, 2023, would create an elaborate system of verifying voter identity based on distributed ledger technology, digital tokens, and specialized election workers that do not have analogs as elections are currently conducted in the state. The in-person voter check in and voting process would be changed to use the technology, including having a voter attach a token to their completed ballot before depositing the ballot in a ballot box. For mail voters, the bill would require election officials to notify each voter upon receipt of the completed mail ballot, and when the voter responded confirming their ballot, the official would then attach a token to that mail ballot. If the voter did not respond to the official's contact, their ballot would be rejected. Only ballots with tokens attached could be counted.

Last Updated February 10, 2023

This bill, as enacted on June 6, 2023, makes numerous changes to Colorado election law, related to voting access on tribal lands, access to polling centers on college campuses, voting by eligible incarcerated voters, use of digital voter ID, rules for the counting of mail ballots, rules for poll watchers, and other changes. Specifically, the bill:

  • Expands access to voter registration and in-person voting locations on tribal lands. The bill:
    • Permits a tribe to provide the Secretary of State with a list of tribal members eligible to vote in an election for the purpose of automatic new registrations and registration updates. If the information is complete, including citizenship verification, the Secretary will send the individuals' information to the relevant counties for registration, pre-registration, or update. Similar to the state's automatic voter registration process, the bill requires that individuals registered or pre-registered through the tribal list program be sent an information package that enables them to opt out of becoming registered, or to choose to affiliate with a political party.
    • Expands the number of days a tribe can request a voter service and polling center be open on their lands. The bill allows a tribe to request either two or four days of in-person voting at a voter service and polling center within the boundaries of their land. If two days, the days would be Election Day and the day before. If four days, the days would be Election Day, the day before, the Saturday before, and the Friday before. Previous law allowed a tribe to request only Election Day and the day before.
  • Requires a voter service and polling center to be located on the campus of each institution of higher education in the state with at least 2,000 students for general elections, coordinated elections, and presidential primaries. Previous law only required this for public institutions. This provision will take effect on January 1, 2024.
  • Requires that in a county that has issued electronic tablets to eligible incarcerated voters, the county include in its plan to offer voting at county jails or detention centers how the county clerk and the sheriff will use the tablets to facilitate voter registration, ballot delivery, and ballot return. The plan must also include the number of confined eligible voters who registered and/or voted in the last November election.
  • Permits any form of identification used for an elections purpose to be presented in a digital format.
  • Requires counties with a population of 10,000 or more to begin counting mail ballots no later than four days before Election Day. Previous law only specified that the counting may begin 15 days before the election.
  • Modifies rules for poll watchers and observation of ballot counting:
    • Specifies the number of watchers political parties can appoint for various election processes during primaries, general elections, and Congressional vacancy elections, subject to a general rule that the number of watchers permitted in a room at one time is subject to space limitations and local safety codes. Previous law did not include these specifics. Each appointment must be made using a standardized form created by the Secretary of State, rather than county forms as existing law provides. Under the bill, each party can appoint (1) at each central count facility, one watcher per central count process, and in any case not less than one watcher for every 10 election judges, (2) during signature verification, one watcher for every four election judges, (3) at each voter service and polling center, one watcher or one watcher per voter service and polling center process.
    • Provides that candidates in a primary are entitled to appoint a watcher in each voter service and polling center and each place where votes are counted in each county in which they are a candidate. Previous law allows such candidates to "appoint some person to act on their behalf in every precinct."
    • Prohibits watchers from taking pictures or recording videos during their service in any place where election activities are conducted and a voter's confidential or personal information is visible.
    • Requires ballot duplication to be done by a bipartisan team of election workers, rather than be done in front of two witnesses as previous law required.
  • Modifies rules related to drop boxes and polling location sites:
    • Specifies the frequency with which ballots must be collected from drop boxes.
    • Allows counties to establish drop boxes at houses of worship. Previous law neither required nor prohibited such placement and allows counties to open drop boxes beyond those required at their discretion.
    • Allows a polling location or drop-off location to be located in a multi-use facility where alcohol is served as long as the alcohol is served in a separate area of the facility. Previous law simply prohibited siting polling places and drop-off locations in a room where alcohol is served.
  • Repeals a law that requires a person's residence, for purposes of voter registration, to be the same as the residence given by the person for vehicle registration and state income tax purposes.
  • Repeals the misdemeanor offense for an individual knowingly voting or offering to vote at a polling place in which they are not qualified to vote.
  • Changes how voters not affiliated with a political party receive ballots for a primary election. The bill repeals an option for such voters to specify a party preference and receive that party's primary ballot and instead, specifies that all such voters should receive a mailing that contains the ballots of all of the major political parties.
  • Permits a county with fewer than 15,000 active registered voters to appoint two election judges for each polling location during a partisan election. Existing law requires three.
  • Specifies that a county clerk or other designated election official must update the voter registration system to reflect that voters have cured their ballot deficiency within 24 hours after receiving the voter's cure documentation.
  • Permits a voter to bring their cell phone into a polling place as long as the voter does not conduct a phone call, take pictures, or record video while in the polling place, other than to call the multilingual ballot hotline or take images of themselves or their own ballot. Existing law was silent as to cell phones in the polling place.

The bill also makes extensive changes in multiple areas of election law not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, including candidate qualifications, recounts, campaign contributions, and the form of a ballot.

Note: Previous versions of the bill contained additional provisions that were amended out before enactment. These provisions would have:

  • Repealed the section of code authorizing a voter who is 17 years of age on the date of a primary election to vote in that election if the voter will be 18 by the time of the associated general election. This provision was removed from the bill on April 28, 2023, leaving the existing authority intact. However, the April 28 amendments did not remove sections 5 and 6 of this bill, which would revise the affirmation for people who are registering to vote and revise the rules for sharing information from the voter registration list to reflect eliminating the ability of a 17-year-old person to vote in the primary.
  • Expanded the number of drop boxes counties were required to site on college campuses by mandating a box for each campus of a state school that had at least 1,000 students. Existing law requires siting a drop box on such a campus with at least 2,000 students. This provision was amended out on April 19, 2023, after committees had considered expanding it to all schools with at least 1,000 students, not simply state schools.
  • Clarified technological requirements for an accessible voting system.

Last Updated September 21, 2023

This bill, as enacted on June 7, 2023, newly establishes in-person early voting and changes the deadline for standard voter registration. Specifically, the bill:

  • Creates an early voting process and sets out requirements for its administration. The bill:
    • Establishes an early voting period beginning on the 15th day before an election and ending the 2nd day before an election, with a total period of 14 days. For presidential preference primaries and special elections, the early voting period will be four days.
    • Requires that early voting be available from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. each day, and from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. on the Tuesday and Thursday prior to the election.
    • Requires prior authorization from the secretary of state for designation of early voting locations, and sets out requirements for changes to locations.
    • Allows municipalities with populations of over 20,000 to hold a public hearing to designate additional early voting locations.
    • Allows same-day registration during early voting for general elections, as is provided on Election Day for all elections under existing law.
    • Requires unaffiliated voters to register with a party by noon on the day before the start of early voting in order to vote early in a partisan primary. Unaffiliated voters will be permitted to affiliate with a party and vote in a primary at the polls on the date of a primary as is allowed under existing law.
    • Requires municipalities to post early voting location information on their websites.
    • Sets out additional requirements for the administration of early voting sites, education regarding early voting for voters and election officials, handling of early voting ballots, and other related procedures, and makes conforming changes throughout various provisions.
  • Moves the standard voter registration deadline from the seventh to the eighteenth day before an election, and makes conforming changes to reflect the change.

The bill also contains additional provisions related to aspects of election law that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

A previous version of the bill contained a provision that was amended out prior to enactment that would have required municipalities with populations of over 45,000 to apply to the secretary of state for permission to establish additional early voting locations and did not establish a procedure for smaller municipalities.

Last Updated August 14, 2023

AUTHORNAME: Joint Committee on Government Administration and Elections
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 16, 2023, would make changes to "absentee" mail ballot voting procedures, including creation of a notice and cure process for missing ballot signatures, paid postage for mail ballot return, and new ballot processing requirements. Specifically the bill would:

  • Create a notification and cure process for ballot envelopes missing voter signatures. Registrars would be required to make best efforts to notify voters whose unsigned ballots are received by the municipal clerk before 6 p.m. on Election Day and inform them of their options. The bill would permit voters to provide a ballot signature until the close of polls at 8 p.m. at the clerk's office, or vote in person at their polling place. Existing law does not provide a notice and cure process for missing ballot signatures.
  • Require prepaid postage, funded by the state, on mail ballot envelopes. Under existing law, voters are responsible for providing postage on mail ballot envelopes.
  • Require preprocessing of mail ballots upon delivery by municipal clerks. Under existing law, ballot envelopes are not checked until after the close of polls on Election Day.
  • Allow the counting of mail ballots to begin at 6 p.m. on Election Day. Under existing law, mail ballots cannot be counted until the close of polls at 8 p.m.

Last Updated February 23, 2023

This bill, as enacted June 27, 2023, requires municipal clerks to begin retrieving mail ("absentee") ballots from drop boxes on a daily basis as soon as ballots are issued. Under existing law, clerks were not required to retrieve ballots on a daily basis until 29 days before Election Day.

Last updated July 13, 2023.

This bill, as amended on April 12, 2023, would:

  • Allow election officials and workers to prevent their residential addresses from being subject to freedom of information requests, so long as they provide a business address, or, if they do not have one, the address of the office of the registrar of voters. Such requests would have to be in writing and would be effective for 90 days at a time with the possibility of extension for an additional 90 days if the municipality determined that there was good cause.
  • Create a class D felony covering any person who harasses or intimidates, or attempts to harass or intimidate, any election worker in the performance of any duty, including through publicly disclosing or threatening to publicly disclose personal identifying information of such election worker, when doing so interferes with the orderly process of voting.

Last updated May 22, 2023.

This bill, as enacted on June 12, 2023, contains the state general budget for July 1, 2023, to June 30, 2025. Included in the budget is a state voting rights act modeled on the federal Voting Rights Act of 1965. The relevant provisions establish certain explicit protections for historically disenfranchised groups, a cause of action for impacted individuals and groups representing them, and a preclearance regime for proposed changes to election laws or practices in covered municipalities. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires preclearance by the secretary of state or the superior court for the district of Hartford before certain covered jurisdictions are permitted to make certain electoral changes. A covered jurisdiction is one that:
    • Has, in the past 25 years, been subject to any court order or governmental enforcement action based on a violation of the right to vote or protected class discrimination set forth of this bill, the federal Voting Rights Act, state or federal civil rights laws, or the 14th or 15th Amendments to the U.S. Constitution,
    • Has failed to provide data to the statewide database established by this bill in the previous five years,
    • Has disproportionate arrest rates of protected class members based on metrics set forth in this bill in the previous ten years,
    • Has, in the last ten years, enacted or implemented a covered policy without attaining preclearance, or
    • Contains at least 1000 eligible voters of any protected class, or in which covered members constitute at least 10% of the voting eligible population, and in which, during the prior 10 years, the percentage of eligible voters who participated in any general election for any municipal office is less than 10% below the percentage of all the voters in the municipality that participated.
  • Requires that a covered jurisdiction seek approval before it enacts changes to its laws or policies regarding:
    • Redistricting
    • Method of election
    • Form of government
    • Annexation, incorporation, dissolution, consolidation, or division of the municipality
    • Removal of individuals from voter lists or other activities concerning the voter list
    • Admission of voters
    • Number, location, or hours of polling places
    • Assignment of districts to polling place locations
    • Assistance offered to voters in a protected class
    • Any other matter identified for preclearance by the Secretary of State following formal rulemaking.
  • Directs the secretary of state or the superior court, when considering a preclearance request, to provide notice of the proceedings, provide an opportunity for comment by interested parties, and render a decision within enumerated time frames. Preclearance may only be granted if the policy will not diminish the ability of voters in a protected class to participate in the electoral process or elect their preferred candidates.
  • Explicitly prohibits any voting laws or practices that result in the denial or abridgment of the right to vote for a person in a protected class. This includes laws and practices that impair the ability of voters in a protected class to elect candidates of their choice or to influence the outcome of elections. The bill also prohibits methods of election that impair the ability of voters in a protected class to elect candidates of their choice or to influence the outcome of elections. Laws and practices that violate this provision include, but are not limited to:
    • At-large elections in municipalities with racially polarized voting or when this method of voting, based on the totality of circumstances, impairs the ability of voters in a protected class to elect candidates of their choice or to influence the outcome of elections.
    • District-based elections or alternative methods of elections in which the candidates of choice for voters in a protected class would usually be defeated if the municipality has racially polarized voting or when this method of voting, based on the totality of circumstances, impairs the ability of voters in a protected class to elect candidates of their choice or to influence the outcome of elections.

A voter who fails to return the card is to be moved to inactive status, meaning they will be removed from the rolls if they remain on inactive status for two consecutive general elections. This bill, as amended on June 13, 2024, would amend the Delaware Constitution to establish an in-person early voting period, allow all voters to choose to vote by mail, and codify the criteria for joining the permanent mail voting list for certain categories of voters. Specifically, the bill would amend the constitution to:

  • Establish a ten-day early voting period including the Saturday and Sunday immediately prior to an election. Legislation establishing an early voting period has been enacted by the legislature before being blocked by courts as being outside what is permitted under the state constitution.
  • Allow all voters to request a mail ballot. Under existing law, voters must have a qualifying excuse in order to vote by mail. Legislation establishing no-excuse mail voting has been enacted by the legislature before being blocked by courts as being outside what is permitted under the state constitution.
  • Allow voters to apply to join a permanent mail voting list if they meet certain criteria including sickness or physical disability; caring for a relative who requires constant care due to illness disability, or injury; or certain types of public service that causes a voter to be outside their jurisdiction for an extended period of time. Permanent mail voters would have to affirm their continued eligibility each time they cast a mail ballot. This tracks existing statutory law.
  • Codify that all voters may request mail ballots for all elections in a given election cycle via a single form. This is already the case under statutory law.
  • Require mail voters to sign an affirmation that their vote was free from improper influence.

Last Updated June 17, 2024

This bill, as amended on June 11, 2024, would amend the state constitution to:

  • Establish automatic restoration of voting rights for individuals disenfranchised due to felony convictions following release from incarceration. Under existing law, automatic restoration does not occur until the completion of all parts of the sentence, including probation and parole.
  • Eliminate the authority of the legislature to impose a loss of voting rights as a penalty for given crimes beyond what is required by the constitution.
  • End permanent disenfranchisement for public corruption and sexual crimes, bringing the rights-restoration process for these crimes in line with all other disenfranchising convictions.
  • Make conforming changes to federal law by repealing a literacy test for voting and changing the minimum voting age from 21 to 18.

This constitutional amendment, if adopted this legislative session, would have to additionally be adopted in the subsequent legislative session in order to go into effect.

This bill, as introduced on February 6, 2023, would expand the jurisdiction of the Office of Statewide Prosecution to enable it to successfully prosecute more cases investigated by the Office of Election Crimes and Security. Some cases that the statewide office has attempted to prosecute have been dismissed because the office lacked jurisdiction, and local prosecutors must bring the cases. The bill would:

  • Allow the statewide prosecutors to investigate and prosecute any crime involving a more specified list of election-related crimes. Existing law allows them to investigate and prosecute "any crime involving voter registration, voting, or candidate or issue petition activities". The bill would specify that the office could investigate and prosecute any crime involving:
    • Voting in an election in which a candidate for a federal or state office is on the ballot,
    • Voting in an election in which a referendum, an initiative, or an issue is on the ballot,
    • The petition activities of a candidate for a federal or state office,
    • The petition activities for a referendum, an initiative, or an issue,
    • Voter registration, or
    • any attempt, solicitation, or conspiracy to commit any of the crimes specifically enumerated above.

  • Expand the scope of the statewide prosecutors' jurisdiction by providing the office will have investigatory and prosecutorial power "when any such offense is affecting, or has affected, two or more judicial circuits" in addition to the power to investigate and prosecute "when any such offense is occurring, or has occurred, in two or more judicial circuits as part of a related transaction, or when any such offense is connected with an organized criminal conspiracy affecting two or more judicial circuits."

This bill, as introduced on March 7, 2023, would assist people who have been disenfranchised by felony convictions in determining whether they have paid all the restitution, fines, and fees and have otherwise completed their full sentence so that their right to vote has been restored. Specifically, the bill would:
*Require the Florida Commission on Offender Review ("Commission") to develop and maintain a database of each such disenfranchised person that includes:

  • Name and other personal identifying information
  • The remaining length of any term of supervision ordered by a court as a part of his or her sentence.
  • The remaining amount of any restitution owed to a victim as ordered by a court as a part of his or her sentence.
  • The remaining amount due of any fines or fees that were initially ordered by a court as a part of his or her sentence or as a condition of any form of supervision, including, but not limited to, probation, community control, or parole.
  • The completion status of any other term ordered by a court as a part of his or her sentence.

  • Any other necessary information.

    • Require the Department of State, the Department of Corrections, clerks of the circuit courts, county comptrollers, and the Board of Executive Clemency to monthly provide to the Commission the information which is required for the database.
    • Require the Department of Management Services, acting through the Florida Digital Service, to provide any technical assistance necessary to develop and maintain the database.
    • By July 1, 2024, require the Commission to present a comprehensive plan to build the database to the Governor and the Legislature.
    • By July 1, 2026, require the Commission to make the database available to the public on a website and update it monthly.
    • Provide that, notwithstanding any law to the contrary, a person who registers to vote or who votes in reasonable reliance on information contained in the database indicating that his or her voting rights have been restored has an affirmative right to register and to vote and may not be charged with a violation of any criminal law of this state related to fraudulently voting or registering to vote.

    Last updated March 7, 2023

This bill, as introduced on March 7, 2023, would provide language assistance to certain limited-English speakers. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require a supervisor of elections or a political subdivision administering an election to provide language assistance to a limited English-proficient voter if, based on data from the American Community Survey or comparable data:
    • More than two percent of the voting-age residents are members of a single language minority group and limited English-proficient voters, if that percentage equals 300 or more people,
    • More than 4,000 of the voting-age residents of voting age are members of a single language minority group and limited English-proficient voters, or
    • For an election held in a political subdivision that contains any part of a Native American reservation, more than 2 percent of the Native American voting-age residents of voting age are members of a single language minority group and limited English-proficient voters.
  • Require the assistance to consist of:
    • Election materials in the covered language(s) that are the same quality as comparable English language election materials, including, but not limited to, ballots, sample ballots, mail ballots, mail ballot requests, voting guides, voting instructions, voter registration applications and materials, polling place signage, and notices, electronic communications, and websites containing election-related information.
    • Manual translation of the materials whenever possible. Automatic translation services would only be allowed when manual translation is not possible.
    • A language assistance hotline. Each relevant supervisor of elections would be required to operate and provide public notice of a language assistance hotline that is staffed during early voting hours, all hours during which a polling place is open on Election Day, and all hours of the period after Election Day during which a voter may cure a vote-by-mail ballot or provisional ballot deficiency.
    • Signage at the main office and branch offices of the supervisor, making printed materials available to voters, and posting information on the supervisor's public website that publicizes the availability of the translated materials, including the translated addresses and operating hours of early voting sites, secure ballot intake station locations, and polling places.
    • Translated versions of any English language sign or poster or notice displayed or distributed to voters in the same way the English versions are.
    • Translated redistricting information.
  • Allows a limited English-proficient voter to sue a supervisor of elections or a political subdivision for a declaratory judgment and injunctive relief to enforce the language assistance requirements. The court would grant the requested relief upon finding that the violation was unreasonable or an abuse of discretion.
  • Require this assistance to be provided in all languages required by the federal Voting Rights Act and explicitly includes a group of people whose primary language is Haitian-Creole or Brazilian-Portuguese.

  • Define "limited English-proficient voter" to mean a member of a covered language minority group who does not speak or understand English adequately to participate in the electoral process. A person who has not completed the fifth grade would be presumed to not speak or understand English adequately to participate in the electoral process.

Last Updated March 8, 2023

This bill, as introduced on March 7, 2023, would make major changes throughout the election code, including creating same-day and automatic voter registration, making several changes to mail voting including creating a permanent mail voting list, and numerous smaller changes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create same-day registration on Election Day and during early voting by allowing eligible people to complete a voter registration application and then immediately cast a ballot.
  • Create automatic voter registration at DMV, with the option to decline registration as part of the transaction.
  • Make multiple changes to mail voting. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Create a permanent mail voting list by allowing voters to apply once and then receive mail ballots for every ensuing election until they ask to leave the list.
    • Facilitate completing and returning mail ballots by prepaying the ballot return postage and allowing the voter to choose whether they want their ballot verified by matching their signature to one on file or matching the last four digits of their Social Security number (SSN4) to their voter record. The cure process would be expanded to enable voters to cure mismatched SSN4s.
    • Repeal the ability of voters and candidates to challenge mail ballots as illegal due to a defect in a ballot certificate.
    • Facilitate in-person pick up of mail ballots by repealing restrictions on who a voter may designate in writing to pick up the ballot and how many a properly designated person may pick up, and restrict in-person ballot pick up by requiring it to be done by the 11th day before Election Day instead of the 9th day before.
    • Add a layer of ballot tracking by requiring election officials to add a voter's email address to their file when a voter includes it on the mail ballot application, email the voter to confirm their application was received and when the voter should expect their ballot, and email the voter when the official receives the returned mail ballot. Existing law imposes those requirements on applications filed by uniformed and overseas voters only. Existing law also provides for ballot tracking, which each county offers. The bill would also allow anyone who timely applies for a mail ballot but does not receive it to use the federal write-in mail ballot currently available only to uniformed and overseas voters.
  • Make the Secretary of State elected for four-year terms, rather than appointed by the Governor and serving at the Governor's pleasure.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on April 19, 2023, would make significant, disparate changes to election law. The bill would change rules for requesting mail ballots (called vote-by-mail ballots in Florida), change aspects of voter registration, including imposing new rules and fines on voter registration organizations, change voter registration list maintenance processes including data sources, frequency, and the cancellation process, revise certain election crimes, require signature match training, and myriad other changes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Revise rules relating to requesting mail ballots, both to receive them by mail and to pick them up in person or through an agent. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Reduce the time voters have to apply to receive a ballot in the mail by setting the deadline as the 12th day before Election Day instead of the 10th day as provided by existing law.
    • Limit a voter's ability to pick up a ballot in person. Specifically, a voter or their designee could pick up a mail ballot only after ballots have been mailed, which must be done by the 10th day before an election, and would not allow a ballot to be picked up in person during mandatory early voting or on Election Day unless the voter attests to an emergency that prevents them from voting in person, whether early or on Election Day. Existing law allows a voter to pick up a ballot through the close of polls without limiting the start to after ballot mailing, and allows their designee to pick one up starting nine days before the election through Election Day.
    • Require the Department of State to provide a uniform statewide application by October 1, 2023. Under existing law, each county has their own form.
    • Require a supervisor of elections to cancel a standing request for a mail ballot if non-forwardable mail to the voter is returned undeliverable. Under existing law, a voter may request all ballots for a general election cycle with a single application. If a voter's request is canceled for returned mail and the voter again requests a mail ballot, they would be required to confirm their address.
    • Require a supervisor to update a voter's record to include any ID number the voter includes on their mail ballot application that is not already in their record. Existing law requires a voter to include a driver's license number, state ID number, or the last four digits of their Social Security number on their application, and requires the supervisor to verify that number against numbers in the voter's record.
  • Add a disclaimer to the voter registration information cards that supervisors of elections issue to voters who register or update their voter registration that says "This card is for information purposes only. This card is proof of registration but is not legal verification of the eligibility to vote. It is the responsibility of a voter to keep his or her eligibility status current." In 2023, the state prosecuted people for voting illegally because their felony conviction had rendered them ineligible to vote. In their defense the voters said that they had no intention of illegally voting, they thought their voting rights had been restored, and pointed out they had successfully registered and received their voter information cards.
  • Impose new rules and fines on voter registration organizations. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require voter registration organizations that are not subsidiaries of political parties to register with the state each general election cycle. This provision would take effect January 1, 2025. Existing law requires organizations to register but does not require re-registration after each election cycle.
    • Require voter registration organizations to attest that each person working for them who collects or handles voter registration forms has not been convicted of a felony violation of the election code or certain identity-theft-type felonies. The bill would impose a fine of $50,000 for any such person collecting or handling voter registration forms for the organization. Existing law has no similar requirement or fine.
    • Require voter registration organizations to attest that each person collecting or handling registration forms for them is a U.S. citizen. The bill would impose a fine of $50,000 for each non-citizen collecting or handling voter registration forms for the organization. Existing law has no similar requirement or fine.
    • Require voter registrations to issue a receipt to each applicant. The receipt would be designed by the Division of Elections and would include at a minimum the applicant's name, date the application was received, name of the organization, name of the registration agent, applicant's political party affiliation, and county in which the applicant resides. Existing law does not require such receipts.
    • Require voter registration organizations to turn applications in within 10 days of receiving them. Existing law requires them to be turned in within 14 days.
    • Raise fines on voter registration organizations who turn in completed applications late from $50 total/application to $50/day late, capped at $2,500/application. If the lateness was willful, the bill would raise the penalty to $2,500/application up from $250/application.
    • Raise fines on voter registration organizations for turning in completed applications after the registration deadline from $100/application to $100/day late, up to $5,000/application. If the lateness was willful, the bill would raise the penalty to $5,000/application from $500/application.
    • Raise the fine a voter registration organization can face if one of its registration agents alters an application without the applicant's consent to $5,000/application, up from $1,000.
    • Impose a fine of $50/application if a voter registration application mails or otherwise provides an applicant with a partially filled out voter registration application.
    • Raise the aggregate fines an organization could face in one year to $250,000, up from $50,000.
    • Create a felony prohibiting a person working for a voter registration organization from making copies of voter registration applications they receive, or to retain information like the voter's ID number or signature, other than to complete the voter's registration.
  • Change voter registration list maintenance relating to addresses in multiple ways including targeting an address type, increasing the frequency of data sharing, change data requirements, and altering certain mailing and notice requirements. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require supervisors of elections to annually review registration records looking for people registered at addresses that "may not be an address of legal residence". If the supervisor has reasonable belief a voter is registered at an address that is not a legal residential address, the supervisor would be required to begin the existing registration cancellation process which involves notice to the voter. Existing law does not address whether a residential address is an "address of legal residence", nor does the bill define what such an address is. Homeless voters and often, people who live on Indigenous lands, do not have traditional addresses.
    • Require the DMV to send the Department of State information weekly about people who surrendered their FL driver's license or state ID because they were issued one in another state. The bill would also revise what information must be transferred, requiring the DMV to send each person's name, last known FL address, out-of-state address, date of birth, sex, last four digits of their Social Security number, the FL driver's license or state ID number, and if available, the address and state in which the person is now licensed. Existing law requires the data to be sent monthly, does not require all of these data points and asks for full Social Security numbers.
    • Require county clerks of courts to send to their county supervisors of elections information from responses to jury summons returned in the previous week that indicated the potential voter had moved, and would require the information to include the last four digits of the person's Social Security number. Existing law requires the information to be sent to the Department of State on a monthly basis, and requires full Social Security numbers.
    • Repeal a requirement that an address confirmation mail be sent to a voter's residential address, even if the voter has a different mailing address, such as a P.O. Box, on file.
    • Repeal a provision that required supervisors of elections to send a second address confirmation card if the voter did not respond within 30 days. The bill would retain existing requirements to send a second confirmation if the first is returned undeliverable without forwarding information. Relatedly, the bill would repeal a notice in address confirmation mailers that instructs voters that if they have not moved, they must respond to the card within 30 days.
    • Require annual list maintenance to be started no later than April 1 and finish no later than 90 days before a federal election. Existing law does not require a similar starting time frame.
    • Provide that if the Department of State decides that a county has not done required address list maintenance, the Department must coordinate with the supervisor to ensure the maintenance is done. Existing law requires the Department to take over and do the maintenance in such a situation.
  • Change voter registration list maintenance relating to death, felony convictions, mental incompetence to increase the frequency of data sharing, revise the data shared, and revise who receives the data. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Allow the Department of State to use any of the listed data sets to check for deceased voters, rather than require it to check all of them, as provided by existing law.
    • Increase the frequency that the Department of Health sends death data to the Department of State to weekly instead of monthly.
    • Give supervisors of elections seven days to cancel a deceased voter's registration based on a death certificate or data received from the DMV. Existing law requires immediate cancellation based on a death certificate and requires the DMV to send death data to the Department of State on a monthly basis. The bill would require the DMV to send the death data to the Department on a weekly basis.
    • Require supervisors of elections to get weekly data from their counties' court clerks to identify people convicted of a felony in the preceding week whose voting rights were not restored and use that data to cancel registrations using the existing cancellation process. Existing law requires court clerks to send such data to the Department of State monthly.
    • Require the Department of Law Enforcement to give weekly data to the Department of State about people convicted of felonies. Existing law requires this data to be given "in a time and a manner that allows the [Department of State] to meet its obligations under state and federal law."
    • Require the Commission on Offender Review to give the Department of State weekly instead of bimonthly data about people whose voting rights have been restored.
    • Require the Department of Corrections to report to the Department weekly about people placed in their custody and/or supervision for felony convictions in the preceding week. Existing law requires reports about such people to be made "in a time and a manner that allows the [Department of State] to meet its obligations under state and federal law."
  • Revise the data-sharing requirements on DMV regarding sending non-citizenship data to the Department of State. The bill would require DMV to send weekly data about people who, during the previous week, presented evidence of non-US citizenship. Existing law does not similarly cabin the data DMV must send, and requires it to be sent monthly. The bill also requires the DMV to send additional data points about each person while asking for the last four digits of each person's Social Security number instead of their whole Social Security number.
    • Require clerks of courts to give supervisors of elections and the Department of State weekly data on people who were declared mentally incapacitated, rather than give the data monthly to the Department of State. The bill would require that for each person, the clerk would include their name, address, date of birth, race, sex, and if available, driver's license, state ID, and/or Social Security number. Existing law requires a list of such people but does not specify the data points to be shared.
    • Provide that supervisors of elections must act on data from any government agency that identifies a voter as potentially ineligible. Existing law allows supervisors to act based on information from other sources than those listed in the code and does not limit those sources to government agencies.
    • Provide that if the Department of State decides a county has not done the required list maintenance, the Department must coordinate with the supervisor to ensure the supervisor does it. Existing law requires the Department to do the maintenance instead in such a situation.
  • Revise the voter registration cancellation process, primarily with regards to notices and timing. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Revise the initial notice sent to voters in a registration cancellation process to inform them that if they attempt to vote in person during the cancellation process, they will be required to vote a provisional ballot, and if they attempt to vote by mail, their ballot may not be accepted, until the completion of the cancellation process and a determination that they were in fact eligible.
    • Allow a supervisor of elections, if the mailed cancellation notice is returned as undeliverable, to publish the second notice on their or the county's website instead of in a newspaper. This notice would be required within 14 days of receiving the returned notice. Existing law does not set a deadline for publishing the second notice. The bill would also revise the second notice to include information about voting provisionally or having a mail ballot not be accepted while the cancellation process is ongoing, and to notify the voter that they have the right to a hearing if they dispute the basis of their ineligibility. Existing law requires notice of the voter's hearing right in the initial notice only.
    • If a voter does not respond to a cancellation notice within 30 days, set a seven day deadline for supervisors to make a final eligibility determination, specifying that the seven days begin after the voter's time to respond ends. The supervisor would then be required to cancel the voter's registration within seven days of determining ineligibility. Existing law requires the determination and cancellation but does not provide such deadlines.
    • If a voter responds to the notice and disputes the information but does not request a hearing, require the supervisor to make a decision within 30 days. If they cancel a voter's registration, the bill would require the supervisor to notify the voter and inform them of their right to appeal. Existing law merely requires the supervisor to determine the voter's eligibility and cancel ineligible voters.
    • If a voter responds and requests a hearing, the supervisor would be required to schedule it and issue notice within 7 days, and then hold the hearing within 30 days of the notice. The voter would be allowed to request an extension for good cause if they can't attend the scheduled date. The supervisor would be required to make a decision on eligibility within seven days of the hearing. If the supervisor cancels the registration, they would be required to tell the voter of their right to appeal. Existing law does not specify these timing requirements nor the notice of appeal rights.
    • Allow all notice in the cancellation process that would have been given by publication in a newspaper to be made by publication on the supervisor's or county's website instead.
  • Revise election crimes. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Revise the crime of voting more than once in an election to make it easier to prosecute and clarify that the crime covers voting more than once in the same county, voting in more than one county, and voting in Florida and in another state/territory.
    • Revise the crime of voting a fraudulent ballot to exclude provisional ballots cast by people in the cancellation process.
    • Direct supervisors of elections to report findings about illegal registrations and illegal voting to the office of Election Crimes and Security instead of the Florida Elections Commission.
  • Change aspects of signature matching by requiring training, changing the process, and certain notices. Florida validates mail and provisional ballots using signature matching. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require the Department of State to create rules for signature matching and training, and require anyone who performs signature matching to be trained.
    • Provide that the most recent signature is the first comparator, but allows older signatures "from previous registration updates" to be used for secondary or tertiary reviews.
    • Include petition signatures in the code section on signature matching.
    • Set details of timing of publishing notice to voters to update signatures, and allow that notice to be on the supervisor of elections' website instead of published in a newspaper.
    • End the requirement that the Department of State include information about signature matching when communicating with voters. The bill would leave in place the requirement that supervisors of elections include the information.
  • Change canvassing mail ballots to provide that when two or more mail ballots are returned in one mailing envelope the ballots must be rejected. Existing law does not address this situation.
  • Reduce the notice given to voters when their polling place changes. The bill would require notice by mail and by publication in any of the following: newspaper, supervisor's website, or county's website. Existing law requires notice by mail and publication in both the newspaper and on the supervisor's website. In addition, the bill would provide that when a supervisor of elections makes a temporary change of a polling place they do not need to mail new voter information cards to affected voters. Existing law does not address this situation.
  • Require supervisors to segregate the provisional ballots of people whose registrations are in the cancellation process if possible.
    • Require supervisors to maintain geographic information systems-compatible maps of precincts and change details of drawing precincts.
  • Revise multiple aspects of election law not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, such as voting and election data gathering and reporting, campaign finance rules, candidate oaths, ballot names, and other topics.

This bill, as introduced on March 8, 2023, would assist people who have been disenfranchised by felony convictions in determining whether they have paid all the restitution, fines, and fees and have otherwise completed their full sentence so that their right to vote has been restored. Specifically, the bill would:
*Require the Florida Commission on Offender Review ("Commission") to develop and maintain a database of each such disenfranchised person that includes:

  • Name and other personal identifying information
  • The remaining length of any term of supervision ordered by a court as a part of his or her sentence.
  • The remaining amount of any restitution owed to a victim as ordered by a court as a part of his or her sentence.
  • The remaining amount due of any fines or fees that were initially ordered by a court as a part of his or her sentence or as a condition of any form of supervision, including, but not limited to, probation, community control, or parole.

    • Require the Department of Management Services, acting through the Florida Digital Service, to provide any technical assistance necessary to develop and maintain the database.
    • By July 1, 2024, require the Commission to present a comprehensive plan to build the database to the Governor and the Legislature.
    • By July 1, 2026, require the Commission to make the database available to the public on a website and update it monthly.
    • Provide that, notwithstanding any law to the contrary, a person who registers to vote or who votes in reasonable reliance on information contained in the database indicating that his or her voting rights have been restored has an affirmative right to register and to vote and may not be charged with a violation of any criminal law of this state related to fraudulently voting or registering to vote.
