This bill, as introduced on March 7, 2023, would provide language assistance to certain limited-English speakers. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require a supervisor of elections or a political subdivision administering an election to provide language assistance to a limited English-proficient voter if, based on data from the American Community Survey or comparable data:
    • More than two percent of the voting-age residents are members of a single language minority group and limited English-proficient voters, if that percentage equals 300 or more people,
    • More than 4,000 of the voting-age residents of voting age are members of a single language minority group and limited English-proficient voters, or
    • For an election held in a political subdivision that contains any part of a Native American reservation, more than 2 percent of the Native American voting-age residents of voting age are members of a single language minority group and limited English-proficient voters.
  • Require the assistance to consist of:
    • Election materials in the covered language(s) that are the same quality as comparable English language election materials, including, but not limited to, ballots, sample ballots, mail ballots, mail ballot requests, voting guides, voting instructions, voter registration applications and materials, polling place signage, and notices, electronic communications, and websites containing election-related information.
    • Manual translation of the materials whenever possible. Automatic translation services would only be allowed when manual translation is not possible.
    • A language assistance hotline. Each relevant supervisor of elections would be required to operate and provide public notice of a language assistance hotline that is staffed during early voting hours, all hours during which a polling place is open on Election Day, and all hours of the period after Election Day during which a voter may cure a vote-by-mail ballot or provisional ballot deficiency.
    • Signage at the main office and branch offices of the supervisor, making printed materials available to voters, and posting information on the supervisor's public website that publicizes the availability of the translated materials, including the translated addresses and operating hours of early voting sites, secure ballot intake station locations, and polling places.
    • Translated versions of any English language sign or poster or notice displayed or distributed to voters in the same way the English versions are.
    • Translated redistricting information.
  • Allows a limited English-proficient voter to sue a supervisor of elections or a political subdivision for a declaratory judgment and injunctive relief to enforce the language assistance requirements. The court would grant the requested relief upon finding that the violation was unreasonable or an abuse of discretion.
  • Require this assistance to be provided in all languages required by the federal Voting Rights Act and explicitly includes a group of people whose primary language is Haitian-Creole or Brazilian-Portuguese.

  • Define "limited English-proficient voter" to mean a member of a covered language minority group who does not speak or understand English adequately to participate in the electoral process. A person who has not completed the fifth grade would be presumed to not speak or understand English adequately to participate in the electoral process.

Last Updated March 8, 2023

This bill, as introduced on March 7, 2023, would revise voter registration list maintenance procedures relating to death, felony conviction, and mental incapacity, and would create an affirmative defense to registration and illegal voting crimes based on the state allowing ineligible people to register. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the Department of State to:
    • Adopt procedures by January 31, 2024, to ensure it reviews the data it receives relating to deaths, felony convictions, and judicial determinations of mental incapacity. Existing law requires the Department to review the data.
    • Provide all such information to county supervisors of elections as soon as possible, but no later than one month after receipt. Existing law requires the Department to notify supervisors after making initial determinations that registered people are no longer eligible to vote.
    • After a supervisor of elections determines that a registered voter is ineligible because their voting rights have not been restored post-conviction and cancels their registration, to immediately notify the voter of their ineligibility, the basis for that determination, information regarding the outstanding terms of their sentence, information explaining rights restoration, and instruction for seeking restoration. The notice must also include contact information for a person who can answer questions. This notice must be made by email, text message, telephone, and certified mail. Existing law requires supervisors of elections to give notice to voters as part of the registration cancelation process.

  • Create an affirmative defense to certain registration and voting crimes. Specifically, the bill would provide that in a criminal action related to voting or registering to vote, it is an affirmative defense that:

    • the person who registers to vote or casts a ballot was authorized if the Department of State, a supervisor, or a state agency that had access to information indicating the person's potential ineligibility to vote, or
    • the person was provided a voter information card by the Department.

    In 2020 people who mistakenly believed their voting rights had been restored successfully registered to vote, voted, and then faced criminal charges.

This bill, as introduced on March 7, 2023, would require sentencing scoresheets to include a new notice to the person being sentenced that details the constitutional and statutory provisions relating to the loss and restoration of voting rights based on felony convictions.

Last updated March 8, 2023

Note: This law is the subject of litigation that could impact the enforceability of some of its provisions. On July 3, 2023, two provisions of this law were enjoined by a U.S. District Court. The enjoined provisions relate to third-party voter registration organizations and are noted below. For the current status of the litigation, see Florida State Conference of Branches and Youth Units of the NAACP, et al., v. Byrd, 4:23-cv-215, U.S. Dist. Ct. FL N.D.

This bill, as enacted on May 24, 2023, makes numerous changes to a wide array of voting and election procedures, including voter registration and requirements for registration drives, processes related to requesting mail ballots ("vote-by-mail ballots") and verification of returned ballots, voter list maintenance processes, definitions of certain election crimes, and others.

Regarding voter registration generally, the bill mandates changes to voter registration cards, effective July 1, 2023. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires voter information cards to newly include the following statement: "This card is for information purposes only. This card is proof of registration but is not legal verification of the eligibility to vote. It is the responsibility of a voter to keep his or her eligibility status current. A voter may confirm his or her eligibility with the Department of State."
  • Requires cards to include a link to the local election administration website, where polling locations are listed.
  • Expressly provides that temporary changes to polling locations do not require reissuing voter registration cards.

Regarding voter registration organizations, the bill imposes various new rules and penalties for prohibited conduct. As noted below, two of these provisions were preliminarily enjoined on July 3, 2023. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires voter registration organizations that are not subsidiaries of political parties to register with the state each general election cycle. This provision would take effect on November 6, 2024. Previous law required organizations to register but did not require re-registration after each election cycle.
  • Requires voter registration organizations to attest that each person working for them who collects or handles voter registration forms has not been convicted of a felony violation of the election code or myriad other felonies. The bill imposes a fine of $50,000 for any such person collecting or handling voter registration forms for the organization. Previous law had no similar requirement or fine.
  • Requires voter registration organizations to attest that each person collecting or handling registration forms for them is a U.S. citizen. The bill imposes a fine of $50,000 for each non-citizen collecting or handling voter registration forms for the organization. Previous law had no similar requirement or fine. This provision has been preliminarily enjoined.
  • Requires voter registrations to issue a receipt to each applicant. The receipt would be designed by the Division of Elections and would include at a minimum the applicant's name, the date the application was received, the name of the organization, the name of the registration agent, the applicant's political party affiliation, and county in which the applicant resides. Previous law did not require such receipts.
  • Requires voter registration organizations to turn applications in within 10 days of receiving them, and makes a conforming change to the voter registration application. Previous law required them to be turned in within 14 days.
  • Raises fines on voter registration organizations that violate requirements for handling applications:
  • For turning in completed applications later than 10 days after receipt, the fine is raised from $50 total per application to $50 per each day late, capped at $2,500 per application. For "willfully" making a late return, the bill raises the penalty from $250 per application to $2,500 per application.
    • For turning in completed applications after the state's registration deadline, the fine is raised from $100 per application to $100 per each day late, up to $5,000 per application. For "willfully" making a late return after the registration deadline, the bill raises the penalty from $500 per application to $5,000 per application.
    • For willfully failing to submit an application to the appropriate election official for the applicant's residence, the fine is raised from $1,000 per application to $5,000 per application.
    • For the above infractions, the bill raises the aggregate fine for violations in a calendar year from $50,000 to $250,000.
  • For altering an application without the applicant's consent, the fine is raised from $1,000 to $5,000 per application.
  • For mailing or otherwise providing an individual with a registration application that is pre-filled with any of the applicant's information, the bill creates a new fine of $50 per application.
  • Creates a new felony offense for an individual working for a voter registration organization making copies of voter registration applications they receive, or retaining information such as the voter's ID number or signature, other than to complete the voter's registration. This provision has been preliminarily enjoined.

Regarding mail ballot voting, the bill revises rules relating to requesting mail ballots, both to receive them by mail and to pick them up in person or through an agent. Specifically, the bill:

  • Reduces the time voters have to apply to receive a ballot in the mail by setting the deadline as the 12th day before Election Day instead of the 10th day as provided by previous law.
  • Limits a voter's ability to pick up a ballot in person. Specifically, a voter or their designee may pick up a mail ballot only after ballots have been mailed, which must be done by the 10th day before an election, and may not pick up a ballot in person during mandatory early voting or on Election Day unless they attests to an emergency that prevents them from voting in person, whether early or on Election Day. Mandatory early voting continues through the third day before Election Day. Previous law allowed a voter to pick up a ballot through the close of polls without limiting the start to after ballot mailing, and allowed their designee to pick one up starting nine days before the election through Election Day.
  • Requires the Department of State to provide a uniform statewide mail ballot application by October 1, 2023. Under previous law, each county had its own form.
  • Requires a supervisor of elections to cancel a standing request for a mail ballot if non-forwardable mail to the voter is returned undeliverable. If a voter's request is canceled for returned mail and the voter again requests a mail ballot, they would be required to confirm their address.
  • Requires a supervisor to update a voter's record to include any ID number the voter includes on their mail ballot application that is not already in their record. Existing law required a voter to include a driver's license number, state ID number, or the last four digits of their Social Security number on their application, and required the supervisor to verify that number against numbers in the voter's record.
  • Defines "immediate family" of a voter or designee, for the purpose of mail voting rules, as the spouse, parent, child, grandparent, grandchild, or sibling of the individual, or the same relations of the individual's spouse.

Regarding the verification process for mail ballots and mail ballot canvassing, the bill:

  • Changes aspects of signature matching by requiring training, changing the matching process, and revising certain notices. Florida validates mail and provisional ballots using signature matching. Specifically, the bill:
    • Requires the Department of State to create rules for signature matching and training, and requires anyone who performs signature matching to be trained.
    • Provides that the most recent signature is the first comparator, but allows older signatures "from previous registration updates" to be used for secondary or tertiary reviews.
    • Includes petition signatures in the code section on signature matching.
    • Sets details of the timing of publishing notice to voters to update signatures, and allows that notice to be on the supervisor of elections' website instead of published in a newspaper.
    • Ends the requirement that the Department of State include information about signature matching when communicating with voters. The bill leaves in place the requirement that supervisors of elections include the information in their communications with voters.
  • Changes canvassing mail ballots to provide that when two or more mail ballots are returned in one mailing envelope the ballots must be rejected. Previous law did not address this situation.

Regarding polling places, the bill:

  • Reduces the notice given to voters when their polling place changes. The bill requires notice by mail and by publication in any of the following: newspaper, supervisor's website, or county's website. Previous law required notice by mail and publication in both the newspaper and on the supervisor's website. In addition, the bill provides that when a supervisor of elections makes a temporary change of a polling place they do not need to mail new voter information cards to affected voters. Previous law did not explicitly address this situation.
  • Requires public, tax-supported buildings to be made available for use as early voting locations as well as for polling places if requested by the supervisor of elections. Previous law imposes this requirement for polling places only.
  • Requires supervisors to segregate the provisional ballots of people whose registrations are in the cancellation process if possible.
    • Requires supervisors to maintain geographic information systems-compatible maps of precincts and change details of drawing precincts.

Regarding list maintenance procedures, the bill makes numerous changes for processes related to voter addresses, removal under various criteria, and the cancellation process. Specifically, the bill:

  • Changes list maintenance procedures related to voter addresses, including targeting an address type, increasing the frequency of data sharing, changing data requirements, and altering certain mailing and notice requirements. The bill:
    • Requires supervisors of elections to annually review registration records looking for individuals registered at addresses that "may not be an address of legal residence." If the supervisor has reasonable belief a voter is registered at an address that is not a legal residential address, the supervisor is required to begin the existing registration cancellation process which involves notice to the voter. Previous law did not address whether a residential address is an "address of legal residence," nor does the bill define what such an address is.
    • Requires the DMV to send the Department of State information weekly about people who surrendered their FL driver's license or state ID because they were issued one in another state. The bill also revises what information must be sent, requiring the DMV to send each person's name, last known FL address, date of birth, sex, last four digits of their Social Security number, the FL driver's license or state ID number, and if available, the address and state in which the person is now licensed. Previous law required the data to be sent monthly, did not require all of these data points, and included full Social Security numbers.
    • Requires county clerks of courts to send to their county supervisors of elections information from responses to jury summonses returned in the previous week that indicated the potential juror had moved, and would require the information to include the last four digits of the person's Social Security number. Previous law required the information to be sent to the Department of State on a monthly basis, and required full Social Security numbers.
    • Repeals a requirement that an address confirmation mail be sent to a voter's residential address, even if the voter has a different mailing address, such as a P.O. Box, on file.
    • Repeals a provision that required supervisors of elections to send a second address confirmation card if the voter did not respond within 30 days. The bill retains existing requirements to send a second confirmation if the first is returned undeliverable without forwarding information. Relatedly, the bill repeals a notice in address confirmation mailers that instructs voters that if they have not moved, they must respond to the card within 30 days.
    • Requires annual list maintenance to be started no later than April 1 and finish no later than 90 days before a federal election. Previous law did not require a similar starting time frame.
    • Revises a list maintenance process to involve returned non-forwardable return-if-undeliverable address confirmation requests only. Previous law included any such returned mail.
  • Changes list maintenance procedures relating to death, felony convictions, and mental incompetence to increase the frequency of data sharing, revise the data shared, and revise who receives the data. Specifically, the bill:
    • Increases the frequency that the Department of Health sends death data to the Department of State to weekly instead of monthly.
    • Requires that supervisors of elections cancel a deceased voter's registration within seven days of issuance of a death certificate. Previous law required immediate cancellation based on a death certificate.
    • Requires the DMV to send death data to the Department of State on a weekly basis. The data to be sent would include the voter's name, address, date of birth, last four digits of their Social Security number, Florida driver's license number or Florida identification card number, and date of death. Previous law did not require the DMV to send death data to the Department.
    • Requires clerks of courts to give the Department of State and the supervisors of elections in their relevant jurisdictions weekly data identifying people convicted of a felony in the preceding week whose voting rights were not restored and requires the supervisors to use that data to cancel registrations using the existing cancellation process. The Department must assist supervisors in identifying their voters who were convicted outside their county. Previous law required court clerks to send such data to the Department of State monthly.
    • Requires the Department of Law Enforcement to give weekly data to the Department of State about people convicted of felonies. Previous law required this data to be given "in a time and a manner that allows the [Department of State] to meet its obligations under state and federal law."
    • Requires the Commission on Offender Review to give the Department of State weekly instead of bimonthly data about people whose voting rights have been restored.
    • Requires the Department of Corrections to report to the Department weekly about people placed in their custody and/or supervision for felony convictions in the preceding week. Previous law required reports about such people to be made "in a time and a manner that allows the [Department of State] to meet its obligations under state and federal law."
  • Revises the data-sharing requirements on DMV regarding sending non-citizenship data to the Department of State. The bill requires DMV to send weekly data about people who, during the previous week, presented evidence of non-US citizenship. Previous law did not similarly cabin the data DMV must send, and required it to be sent monthly. The bill also requires the DMV to send additional data points about each person while asking for the last four digits of each person's Social Security number instead of their whole Social Security number.
    • Requires clerks of courts to give supervisors of elections and the Department of State weekly data on people who were declared mentally incapacitated, rather than give the data monthly to the Department of State only. The bill would require that for each person, the clerk include their name, address, date of birth, race, sex, and if available, driver's license, state ID, and/or Social Security number. Previous law did not specify the data points to be shared.
    • Provides that supervisors of elections must act on data from any government entity that identifies a voter as potentially ineligible. Previous law allowed supervisors to act based on information from other sources than those listed in the code and did not limit those sources to government entities.
  • Revises the voter registration cancellation process, primarily concerning notices and timing. Specifically, the bill:
    • Revises the initial notice sent to voters in a registration cancellation process to inform them that if they attempt to vote in person or by mail during the cancellation process, they will be required to vote a provisional ballot or have their ballot treated as one, until the completion of the cancellation process and a determination that they were in fact eligible. The notice would further instruct the voter that to ensure their ballot is counted, the voter must provide the supervisor of elections with evidence of their eligibility within two days of Election Day.
    • Allows a supervisor of elections, if the mailed cancellation notice is returned as undeliverable, to publish the second notice on their or the county's website instead of in a newspaper. This notice must be published within 14 days of receiving the returned notice. Previous law did not set a deadline for publishing the second notice. The bill also revises the second notice to include information about voting provisionally or having a mail ballot not be accepted while the cancellation process is ongoing, and to notify the voter that they have the right to a hearing if they dispute the basis of their ineligibility. Previous law required notice of the voter's hearing right in the initial notice only.
    • If a voter does not respond to a cancellation notice within 30 days, the bill sets a seven-day deadline for supervisors to make a final eligibility determination, specifying that the seven days begin after the voter's time to respond ends. The supervisor must then cancel the voter's registration within seven days of determining ineligibility. Previous law required the determination and cancellation but does not provide such deadlines.
    • If a voter responds to the notice and disputes the information but does not request a hearing, the bill requires the supervisor to make a decision within 30 days. If they cancel a voter's registration, the bill would require the supervisor to notify the voter and inform them of their right to appeal. Previous law merely required the supervisor to determine the voter's eligibility and cancel ineligible voters.
    • If a voter responds and requests a hearing, the bill requires the supervisor to schedule it and issue notice within 7 days, and then hold the hearing within 30 days of the notice. The voter could request an extension for good cause if they could not attend the scheduled date. The supervisor must make a decision on eligibility within seven days of the hearing. If the supervisor cancels the registration, they must tell the voter of their right to appeal. Previous law did not specify these timing requirements nor the notice of appeal rights.
    • Allows all notices in the cancellation process that would have been given by publication in a newspaper under previous law to be made by publication on the supervisor's or county's website instead.

Regarding election crimes and enforcement, the bill:

  • Alters the crime of voting more than once in an election to specify that the crime includes voting more than once in the same county, voting in more than one county, and voting in Florida and another state/territory. Existing law defines the offense as willfully voting more than one ballot "at any election," with no further detail. The bill also expressly provides that prosecution for the offense does not require establishing which ballot was cast first.
  • Narrows the crime of voting a fraudulent ballot to exclude provisional ballots cast by voters in the cancellation process.
  • Directs supervisors of elections to report findings about illegal registrations and illegal voting to the Office of Election Crimes and Security instead of the Florida Elections Commission.

The bill also contains numerous provisions related to aspects of election law that are not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, including voting and election data gathering and reporting, resign-to-run rules, campaign finance rules, candidate oaths, ballot names, and other topics.

Multiple provisions were amended out of the bill on April 20, 2023. Those provisions would have:

  • Created a felony for harassing election workers.
  • Limited the addresses to which a certain address confirmation mailer is sent.
  • Required voters with inactive registrations who appear to vote to confirm their address and required supervisors of elections to reactivate a registration if the voter signs a candidate or state or local petition.
  • Made clarifying changes relating to the Office of Election Crimes and Security created in 2022 and revised during the February 2023 special session. Specifically, the bill would have:
    • Clarified the jurisdiction of the Office by providing that any "alleged election irregularity" it investigates must relate to violations of the Florida Election Code and any rule issued thereto.
    • Authorized the Office to make referrals of investigated matters for further legal action to the Department of Law Enforcement, the Office of Statewide Prosecution, and the state attorney with jurisdiction
    • Required a statewide prosecutor who received such a referral to investigate the complaint promptly and thoroughly, undertake any related criminal action as justified by law, and report to the Office on the results, including the final disposition of the complaint.
    • Provided that if the statewide prosecutor does not prosecute for any reason, that decision is not binding on any other law enforcer with jurisdiction.
  • Allowed supervisors of elections to offer early voting on the third Sunday before Election Day or the Sunday before if the election involves a state or federal office but not both. Existing law already designates the Sunday before Election Day as an optional early voting day but does not authorize early voting on the third Sunday before.
  • Required people who are registering to vote in Florida for the first time and who the Department of State verifies lack a driver's license, state ID, or Social Security number to vote in person unless they are covered by an exception under existing law. Existing law requires such voters to provide additional ID documentation before voting for the first time, but does not limit them to voting in person.

Additional provisions were amended out of the bill on April 26, 2023. Those provisions would have:

  • Provided that if the Department of State decides that a county has not done required list maintenance, the Department must coordinate with the supervisor to ensure the maintenance is done. Existing law, no longer modified by the bill, requires the Department to take over and do the maintenance in such a situation.
  • Allowed the Department of State to use any of the listed data sets to check for deceased voters, rather than require it to check all of them, as provided by existing law.

Last Updated September 21, 2023

This joint resolution, as introduced on March 7, 2023, proposes an amendment to Florida's constitution to allow for the recall of elected county officials, which includes county supervisors of elections. To successfully amend the constitution, this resolution would need to pass both chambers of the legislature with 60% of the vote, and then be ratified by voters by a similar margin. If the constitution were amended by this resolution, the legislature would then enact implementing legislation.

Last updated March 8, 2023

This bill, as introduced on January 9, 2023, would change requirements for runoff elections by moving these elections to further out from an initial election, and requiring additional runoff early voting. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Move runoffs to the Tuesday of the sixth week after an initial election. Under existing law, runoffs are held 28 days (four weeks) after an election.
  • Move the latest start date for counties to begin offering runoff early voting from 8 days before the election to 15 days before. Along with this new deadline, the bill would leave in place the requirement that runoff early voting begin "as soon as possible."
  • Require that counties offer early voting on the second and third Saturdays before a runoff or primary. Existing law does not require Saturday early voting for runoff elections and has no express requirement regarding primary elections.

Last Updated February 27, 2023

This bill, as introduced on January 9, 2023, would direct the Secretary of State to establish a secure electronic voting internet portal through which voters with visual disabilities could complete a ballot electronically and either return the completed ballot by email or print the completed ballot to mail to election officials.

Last Updated January 17, 2023

This bill, as amended on February 9, 2023, would:

  • Establish new, burdensome chain-of-custody documentation requirements for voted ballots and other election material. Among the requirements, the bill would mandate use of numbered seals on ballot boxes, records including the signature, date, and time for any individual handling ballots, and the presence of a poll official for any handling of voted ballots.
  • Require that drop boxes be closed in a manner that prevents the insertion of ballots at times when early ("advance") voting is not taking place. Existing law requires only that the drop boxes be "closed" during such times.
  • Clarify that mail ("absentee") ballots may be issued and mailed to qualified applicants within 25 days of Election Day. Existing law states that ballots are to be sent "not less than 25 days" prior to an election in order to establish a date by which election officials must begin sending ballots.

Last Updated March 6, 2023

This bill, as introduced on February 14, 2023, would grant counties the discretion to offer "advance" early voting on the Saturday and Sunday immediately preceding an election. Under existing law, early voting must end on the Friday before an election.

Last Updated February 27, 2023

This bill, as amended on February 27, 2024, would:

  • Allow voters accompanied by one or more children age three or under to vote immediately upon arriving at an early voting location or at an Election Day polling place between 9:30 a.m. and 4:30 p.m. without waiting in line.
  • Lower the age above which a voter may bypass the lines at a voting location from 75 to 70.
  • Remove the requirement that a voter with a disability must require assistance in voting in order to bypass the lines at a voting location.

Last updated March 4, 2024.

This bill, as introduced on February 22, 2023, would allow county election superintendents to allow voters to appear at any precinct in the county on Election Day, effectively creating a vote center model without new, dedicated vote centers. Under existing law, voters must appear at their assigned precinct in order to vote on Election Day.

Last updated February 27, 2023.

This bill, as introduced on February 28, 2023, would:

  • Empower the state election board to hire investigators.
  • Establish the state election board as a "separate and distinct budget unit" from the secretary of state's office.
  • End the secretary of state's role as a non-voting ex officio member of the state election board.
  • Empower the state elections board to appoint a full-time executive director who would be the ex officio secretary of the board and serve at the pleasure of the board, and require the executive director to prepare annual reports for the governor and legislature detailing the activities of the board of elections over the previous year.

Last updated March 6, 2023.

This bill, as introduced on March 6, 2023, would:

  • Establish an option for county superintendents to conduct all primaries and general elections by universal mail ballot to all active registered voters. The bill would also establish procedures for voters to request that a "special absentee ballot" be sent to an alternate address. Other rules applicable to the processing of mail ballots would apply. Counties that opted into this system of voting would be required to open vote centers during the early voting period from 7 a.m. 18 days before an election and ending at 7 p.m. on the day of the election. Under generally applicable law, early voting ends the Saturday before an election.
  • Repeal code sections establishing a process through which the state election board can suspend and replace election superintendents.
  • Establish same-day voter registration on Election Day by moving the deadline for registration to the close of business on Election Day. Under existing law, the registration deadline is the fifth Monday before an election.
  • Eliminate ID number requirements for mail ballot requests, instead requiring only that voters provide sufficient information for officials to identify them, and the address to which they want a ballot mailed.
  • Eliminate ID number requirements for mail ballot envelopes, requiring only that voters sign an attestation.
  • Repeal restrictions on distribution of unrequested mail ballot applications by election officials and third parties.
  • Move the last possible date on which counties must begin offering runoff early voting from the second Monday before the runoff election to the third Monday before.
  • Clarify that early voting may not be held on the Saturday following a Thursday or Friday holiday or on the Saturday preceding a Sunday or Monday holiday.
  • Require signature matching between mail ballot applications and voters' registration cards.
  • Require signature matching between mail ballot envelopes and voters' registration cards and mail ballot applications.
  • Allow counties to establish unlimited drop boxes with no hour restrictions until the close of polls on Election Day. Under existing law, counties may only establish drop boxes at election offices and early voting sites, and the boxes may only be usable during hours when voting is taking place.
  • Limit each registered voter to challenging at most ten other voters' registrations during a 24-month period. Under existing law, voters may make unlimited challenges.
  • Repeal the requirement that challenges to voters' registrations must be heard within 10 business days.
  • Modify the automatic voter registration system to eliminate the ability of an agency customer to opt out of registration and to require all DDS customers to attest to whether or not they are eligible to register to vote. Under existing law, agency customers may opt out of registration during their transaction with the automatic voter registration agency.
  • Allow 16 and 17 year olds with valid Georgia driver's licenses or non-driver ID cards, who would be eligible to register to vote but for their ages, to pre-register on the website of the secretary of state. Under existing law, pre-registration is available beginning at 17.5 years old.
  • Change the range in which officials must begin mailing out ballots from 29-25 days prior to an election to 49-45 days before.
  • Allow placement of voting locations on public and private university campuses and direct county officials to consider placement of voting locations on or near the campuses of any historically black colleges or universities within their jurisdiction.
  • Repeal the prohibition on mobile polling facilities when there is no declared emergency necessitating their use.
  • Repeal the requirement that there be "imminent peril" before the state election board may adopt emergency rules or regulations and that such emergency rules be in "strict and exact compliance" with the election code.
  • Expand the date range during which mail ("absentee") ballot applications may be accepted by officials from 78-11 days prior to an election to any time within 180 days of an election, although ballots could not be issued or mailed on the day prior to an election.
  • Shorten the window for emergency mail ballots from beginning 10 days before the election to 5 days before.
  • Repeal a provision authorizing removal of voters from the roles based on flags from ERIC that they may have moved.
  • Repeal the requirement that the state election board and secretary of state, or their staffs, provide at least five business days' notice to the legislative judiciary committees prior to entering into any consent agreement or consent order relating to the election code.
  • Eliminate the inactive list for voters who have failed to respond to address confirmation notices within 30 days.
  • End the requirement that a runoff election take place if the winner of an initial election receives over 45% of the vote.
  • Close primaries to individuals who designate an affiliation with that party at least 10 days before the start of early ("advance") voting. Under existing law, any individual can vote in either party's primary election.
  • Establish Election Day as a state holiday.
  • End the use of "special run-off ballots" on which UOCAVA voters could rank candidates in anticipation of a potential runoff election.
  • Prohibit opening outer ballot envelopes until the opening of polls on Election Day. Under existing law, such envelopes may be opened beginning at 8 a.m. on the third Monday prior to Election Day, and ballots may be run through scanners beginning at that time.
  • Repeal provisions allowing for the public watching of mail ballot processing.
  • Repeal a prohibition on giving, offering to give, or participating in the giving of money or gifts, defined to include food and water, to a voter at a polling place.
  • Establish countywide vote centers, requiring that all voters be allowed to cast a regular ballot at any polling place or registration office in their county of residence. Under existing law, voters may not cast ballots outside their precincts, except that voters who arrive at the incorrect precinct after 5 p.m. and will not be able to travel to their proper precinct before the close of polls are permitted to cast provisional ballots.
  • Move runoff elections back two weeks from the 28th day after an initial election to the Tuesday of the sixth week following an initial election.
  • Expand the existing felony of voter intimidation to include patrolling or observing within 1000 feet of a polling place, early voting location, or drop box while openly carrying a firearm or other weapon.
  • Repeal the felony prohibition on unauthorized return of another's ballot.
  • Narrow the felony crime of attempting to induce a voter to show how they marked their ballot to only include activity prior to the depositing of the ballot.
  • Expand an existing felony regarding preventing poll workers from performing their duties to include using or threatening force or violence in a manner manner that would prevent a reasonable poll officer or election official from executing their, materially interrupting or improperly interfering with the execution of a poll worker or election official's duties, or acting in any other manner to intimidate any poll worker or election official from faithfully performing his or her duties. This bill, as amended on February 22, 2024, would:

  • Repeal automatic voter registration. The bill would require voters to affirmatively opt in to voter registration when they receive or renew their driver's license. Currently, Georgia residents are automatically registered during such DMV transactions unless they choose to opt out or fail to sign the voter registration application. The bill would declare that all applicants must be U.S. citizens and Georgia residents.
  • Establish standards for adjudication of challenges to voter registrations. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Provide that challenge proceedings are not governed by the standard rules of civil practice or rules of evidence. Evidence presented would simply have to be "persuasive and reliable."
    • Provide that a registered voter's name appearing in the U.S. Postal Service change of address database would be sufficient evidence to sustain a challenge of a voter's registration, except that temporary absence due to enrollment as a student, service in the armed forces, or relocation for government service would not be allowable bases to challenge a registration and such data could not be used as the sole basis for a challenge within 45 days of an election. Existing law allows for challenges to voters' registration but does not provide for how such challenges are to be adjudicated. Officials have generally required that a challenger have personal knowledge regarding a challenged individual in order to sustain the challenge.
  • Modify rules for determining residency. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Automatically deem a voter to have changed their residence if they register to vote in another state, county, municipality, or legislative district. Individuals who register elsewhere then return to their original place of residence would be required to re-register upon their return. The bill would also expressly deem ownership or rental of a post office box insufficient to constitute residency in a jurisdiction.
    • Authorize registrars to use, in addition to currently permitted sources, U.S. Postal Service change of address information, professionally aggregated datasets, and other factors that registrars may reasonably deem necessary to determine in good faith that an applicant is qualified, including a sworn statement by any individual, in determining whether to accept an application for voter registration. The bill would also repeal the provision that establishes a registrar's decision regarding a voter's residence is presumptive evidence of that residence.
    • Assign the county courthouse as the voter residency for individuals who are homeless and without a permanent address.
  • Modify election review requirements, requiring that local superintendents conduct "tabulation or risk limiting audits" for all elections. Under existing law, superintendents are required to conduct "precertification tabulation" audits and are not required to audit results of primary elections.
  • Prohibit the awarding of attorney fees to the prevailing party in an election contest if the contest was brought in good faith.
  • Eliminate the criteria required for use of paper ballots, and instead permit counties, with permission from the state board of elections, to conduct elections by paper ballot at their discretion. Existing law provides that paper ballots may be used only if use of voting machines is "not possible or practicable."
  • Create a new misdemeanor offense for county and municipal election officials willfully neglecting or refusing to call an election when required to do so by law.
  • Expand an existing felony offense by specifying that it is unlawful to willfully prevent any poll officer or other election official from performing their duties or to intimidate any poll officer or election official from performing their duties as required by law. Existing law does specify 'other election officials' or expressly prohibit intimidation of such officials.

  • Require that any individual employed or retained by a county election superintendent to undertake election-related duties be a U.S. citizen and be "judicious, intelligent, and upright." Existing law requires these qualifications for poll officers only.

    The bill also contains additional provisions making minor changes that Voting Rights Lab does not track.


An earlier version of this bill contained a provisions that was amended out of this version. One of the provisions would have expanded existing prohibitions on Saturday early voting when the Saturday is a holiday, follows a holiday on the preceding Thursday or Friday, or precedes a holiday on the following Sunday or Monday. Under existing law, early voting is prohibited if such a Saturday is the second Saturday before a primary or election. The bill would have prohibited early voting on this day if it is the first or second Saturday before a primary, election, or runoff. Note: Depending on the early voting period determined for a particular runoff, this provision could have potentially prevented early voting on the Saturday following Thanksgiving, for general election runoffs. The bill would have repealed provisions allowing for the use of ballot dropboxes. The bill would have reduced the criteria for minimum number of voting booths required at a polling place, by changing the requirement from one machine per 250 registered voters to one machine per 250 registered voters who have not already cast a ballot prior to Election Day. The bill would have required secure storage of ballots after printing, with access to the storage space limited to specified individuals. The bill would have required chain of custody documentation for the transport of unvoted ballots to and from precincts. The bill would have required that, following certification, all election materials be available for electronic inspection by the public via high-resolution images. The bill would have specified that ballots and other election documents preserved under seal by a municipal clerk following an election must be retained in such a manner that they cannot be altered, amended, damaged, modified, or mutilated. The bill would have allowed members of county boards of elections to serve on performance review boards appointed by the state board of elections to evaluate other county boards of elections. Existing law requires performance review boards to be made up of "local election officials." The bill would have modified the disclaimer that must be included on mail ballot applications distributed by third parties to include the address of the distributing individual or organization address. The bill would have moved the deadline for county officials to report the breakdown of ballots cast in the election to the secretary of state and the public, from 10 p.m. on the day of an election to 11:59 p.m.

This bill, as enacted on May 3, 2023:

  • Expands the existing prohibition on the use of private funds for election administration. Under previous law, superintendents and boards of registrars were barred from accepting funding, grants, or gifts, from any source other than county, municipal, state, or federal government entities. The bill now:
    • Expressly prohibits county and municipal governments, government employees, and election officials from soliciting, taking, or accepting private funds for election administration, with the exception of donation of locations for voting locations, free services, or goods less than $500 in value.
    • Prohibits counties and municipalities, in addition to superintendents and boards of registrars, from accepting grants or gifts for election administration from unauthorized sources, and limits authorized sources to only the state of Georgia or federal government.
    • Creates a new felony offense for violating the newly expanded ban on the use of private funds, punishable by a minimum term of imprisonment of one year and a minimum fine of $10,000.
  • Deems the state election board a separate and distinct budget unit from the office of the secretary of state, attached to that agency "only for administrative purposes," and expressly provides that the board is not under the jurisdiction of the secretary and is not a division of the agency.
  • Authorizes the state election board to appoint an executive director, who serves "at the pleasure of the board," and to determine the director's compensation. The bill specifies that the executive director shall serve as the secretary of the board ex officio but is not a voting member, and sets out various details regarding the duties of the position.

A previous version of the bill contained a provision that was amended out before enactment. That provision would have removed the secretary of state as an ex-officio nonvoting member of the state election board.

This bill, as introduced on March 20, 2023, would clarify procedures around challenges to voter registrations. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require that challenges be made at least 45 days before the start of early ("advance") voting.

    • Not 18 years old and will not be by the next primary, election, or runoff
    • Not a citizen of the United States
    • Convicted of a felony offense without having had their rights restored
    • Declared ineligible due to mental incompetency
    • Not a resident at the residential address in the registration record
  • Require that a challenger alleging that a voter does not live at their address of registration submit evidence that they exercised due diligence in verifying the information alleged by providing the challenged voter's actual address or by performing at at least two of the following acts:
    • Sending a letter with return service requested to voter's residential and mailing address
    • Searching telephone directories to determine whether the voter maintains a telephone listing in the county
    • Searching county property records to see if the challenged voter owns property in the county.
    • Searching the statewide voter registration database to see whether the voter has registered at another address in the state.
  • Require challengers to provide a signed affidavit swearing that based on personal knowledge and belief the challenged voter is neither qualified to vote nor lives at the address on their registration card.
  • Provide that a challenge based on voter address will only be entertained if it is alleged that the actual residence of the challenged voter is outside the precinct of their registration address.

  • Direct the secretary of state to prepare a challenge form and stipulate that all documents relating to challenges are public records.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 20, 2023, would require people to provide documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote, require video surveillance of drop boxes, increase the required number of voter service centers, and increase the frequency of address-based voter registration list maintenance. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require people to provide documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote, except that everyone already registered when the bill, if it became law, took effect, would be deemed to have provided satisfactory evidence of citizenship and would not be required to provide citizenship documentation unless the person is changing voter registration from one county to another. Under U.S. Supreme Court precedent and federal law, people cannot be required to provide documentary proof of citizenship to vote in federal elections. Acceptable documentation would include:
    • The number of the applicant's driver's license or state ID from Hawaii or another state if the identification indicates that the person has provided satisfactory proof of United States citizenship.
    • A legible photocopy of the applicant's birth certificate that verifies citizenship to the satisfaction of the county clerk.
    • A legible photocopy of pertinent pages of the applicant's United States passport identifying the applicant and the applicant's passport number or presentation to the county clerk of the applicant's United States passport.
    • A presentation to the county clerk of the applicant's United States naturalization documents or the number of the certificate of naturalization. If only the number of the certificate of naturalization is provided, the applicant would not be registered until the number of the certificate of naturalization is verified with the United States immigration and naturalization service by the county clerk.
    • Other documents or methods of proof that are established pursuant to the immigration reform and control act of 1986.
    • The applicant's bureau of Indian affairs card number, tribal treaty card number, or tribal enrollment number.
  • Require 24-hour video surveillance of ballot drop boxes. Existing law simply requires drop boxes to be "securely maintained."
  • Require one voter service center per precinct. Under existing law, each county must open one for the entire voting period, and county clerks have the discretion to open as many more as needed to meet the needs of their voters.

  • Increase the frequency and types of address-based voter registration list maintenance. Specifically, the bill would:

    • Require county clerks to send all election mailings except sample ballots by nonforwardable first-class mail. If the mail is returned undelivered, the clerk would be required to send a follow-up notice within three weeks of receiving the returned mail. The follow-up notice could be sent to either the voter's registration address or the forwarding address provided by the U.S. Postal service. The follow-up notice would inform the voter to revise their registration information online or return a new voter registration form to the county clerk within 35 days their registration status would be changed to inactive. Under existing law, the registrations of people whose election mail is returned undeliverable and who do not timely respond to a follow-up confirmation mailing are marked inactive.
    • Provide that if a voter updates their registration with a residence outside the county where they had been registered to vote, the county clerk must forward that information to the clerk in the new county, and if the information indicates the voter moved out of state, the county clerk must cancel the registration. Existing law provides for county clerks to notify each other regarding transferring voters' registration and provides that clerks must cancel the registration of anyone no longer eligible to vote in Hawaii, which would include people who have moved out of state.
    • Require the county clerk to revise voter registration records and send notices to impacted voters whenever the clerk is notified that a government agency has changed the name of any street, route number, post office box number, or other address designation.
    • Require the county clerk to use U.S. Postal Service change of address information every month to revise voter registrations and send address confirmation mailers to voters. Depending on how the voter responds, their registration will be updated or their status changed to inactive. If the voter does not return the address confirmation notice and their registration is made inactive, the registrant would be required to provide affirmation of confirmation of their address in order to vote.

Last Updated January 30, 2023

This bill, as introduced February 20, 2023, would change procedures concerning the challenging of a voter's registration and the acceptance of a ballot voted by mail. Specifically, the bill would:

The bill repeals a requirement requiring a mail ballot to be rejected if it appears that the signature on the affidavit is not that of the voter.

This bill, as introduced on March 1, 2023, would make significant changes to Iowa election law, greatly expanding access to the ballot in a variety of ways, including automatic rights restoration for individuals convicted of felonies, limiting cancellation of registration, extending the mail ballot voting period, and permitting later delivery of mail ballots, among other changes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the governor to immediately restore the right to vote to an individual convicted of a felony other than murder. Iowa currently has no provision for automatic rights restoration in law, though the governor issued an executive order in 2020 which provides for this to occur. Individuals convicted of murder would still be permitted to apply to the governor to have their voting rights restored.
  • Add the following documents to the list of acceptable documents for proving a voter's identity:
    • A social security card.
    • A birth certificate.
    • A document for receiving public assistance.
    • A supplemental nutrition assistance program card.
    • A Medicare or Medicaid card.
    • A hunting or fishing license.
    • A university or college identification card.
    • A government or other employer identification card.
    • A paycheck.
    • A debit or credit card.
    • A utility bill in print or electronic format.
    • Any other form of identification approved by the Iowa state association of county auditors.
  • Extend the mail voting period by:
    • Changing the first day of the mail voting period from the 20th day before the election to the 40th day.
    • Permitting a mail ballot to be counted if delivered to the commissioner's office no later than the Monday following the election, if postmarked by the day before the election. Existing law only permits a mail ballot to be counted if received by the commissioner's office before the polls close on Election Day.
  • Improve access to drop boxes for mail ballots. A county commissioner would be permitted to establish any number of drop boxes, and a commissioner of a county with a population of at least 25,000 would be required to establish at least one drop box per 25,000 residents. Existing law permits the establishment of only a single drop box per county.
  • Allow a county commissioner of elections to establish absentee voting stations without first receiving a petition and requires a county commissioner of elections to establish an absentee voting station on the Saturday before an election at a public building.
  • Remove provisions limiting who may return a mail ballot on behalf of another person. The bill would remove the requirements that such an agent:
    • Be a registered voter,
    • May not be the voter's employer, an agent thereof, an officer or agent of the voter's union, or a person acting as an agent for a political party or committee,
    • Only return a ballot for a voter who is unable to do so due to blindness or other disability.
  • Strikes a provision canceling a voter's voter registration if the voter has been marked inactive and not voted in two consecutive general elections.

This bill, as introduced on March 1, 2023, would potentially have a dramatic impact on the ability of most voters to have their votes counted. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require, before a voter at a polling place may deposit their ballot into a tabulation machine or have it placed into a ballot box, that two challengers of opposing parties swear under penalty of perjury (a felony) that they have personal knowledge that the ballot was cast in secret and only by the voter authorized to cast the ballot. This provision would make it impossible to cast a ballot unless two challengers of opposing parties were present at the polling place and observing each voter throughout the ballot marking process. In the event that this were true, the bill also would permit a challenger to refuse to make a sworn statement at the challenger's discretion, which in turn would legally prevent a voter from having their ballot counted.

  • Require, before a mail ballot may be counted, that two challengers of opposing parties swear under penalty of perjury (a felony) that they have personal knowledge that the ballot was cast in secret and only by the voter authorized to cast the ballot. This provision would make it impossible for a mail ballot to be accepted unless the challengers were present when the mail voter marked the ballot, or otherwise independently verified that the ballot was cast in secret.

    The bill additionally makes no amendment to other provisions of law which may result in a voter casting their ballot not entirely in secret, such as provisions permitting a voter with disabilities to receive assistance in marking their ballot.


Last Updated March 2, 2023

This bill, as enacted on June 1, 2023, repeals the requirement that the state registrar use information from the Electronic Registration Information Center (ERIC) to update information in the state voter registration system. Provisions left in place require the registrar to "cross-reference" data from other states to maintain the voter list, but statutory law no longer specifically mandates accessing ERIC.

The bill also includes provisions related to precinct caucuses that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

A previous version of the bill contained a tracked provision related to caucus procedures that was amended out prior to enactment. That provision would have required a voter to be a member of the party for at least 70 days before the caucus in order to participate.

This bill, as introduced February 21, 2023, would create a new process under which a voter's registration can be challenged by a voter in another county and clarify rules regarding the creation and use of voter registration lists. Specifically, the bill would:

The state registrar of voters would be required to create a form to be used for this purpose. A challenger would not be required to attend a hearing held regarding the challenge. This bill, as introduced January 11, 2023, would repeal the statutory provisions that disenfranchise individuals during imprisonment for a felony offense. Note that in addition to existing statutory law, the Illinois state constitution expressly disenfranchises individuals during incarceration as well, and would require separate procedures for amendment.

Last Updated January 17, 2023

This bill, as introduced January 11, 2023, would restore voting rights after conviction for a criminal offense within 14 days and require facilitation of registration and mail voting during incarceration, and would streamline the mail ballot request process during registration for all voters. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Restore voting rights to an individual convicted of a felony, or otherwise under sentence in a correctional institution or jail, 14 days following their conviction. The bill would expressly apply the restoration provision to all individuals under any form of state supervision or custody, including those owing court fines or fees, and expressly prohibit the denial of voting rights due to prior criminal conviction. Existing constitutional law mandates disenfranchisement upon conviction of a felony, and under existing statutory law, voting rights are restored upon completion of a sentence of incarceration.
  • Require local election authorities to coordinate with correctional agencies to facilitate voting by mail from each correctional institution in the state. Each correctional institution would be required to provide voter registration applications, applications to vote by mail, ballots received from election authorities, and all other election materials, including voter education materials. The bill would also require distribution of voting related materials upon release from custody.
  • Clarify that a person confined in a county jail located in a county other than the one where the person is entitled to vote may only vote by mail.
  • Establish a confined voter's residence for purposes of voting as their last place of residence before confinement.
  • Establish a task force to monitor implementation of the bill.
  • Provide generally that an individual completing a voter registration application be informed of the option to vote by mail, and allow that individual to request that their voter registration application be treated as a simultaneous application for a ballot to be voted by mail. The bill would also require provision of registration applications and mail ballots in non-English languages, in locations covered by federal or local language access requirements.

Last Updated January 24, 2023

This bill, as amended on March 7, 2023, would require public universities, public community colleges, and other institutions of higher education that receive state money to adopt a policy for awarding academic credit or a non-credit alternative to a person who serves as an election judge. An election judge who receives academic credit would be ineligible for monetary compensation for their service.

Last Updated March 8, 2023

This bill, as introduced January 11, 2023, would require each election authority in the state, before the 2024 primary election, to establish procedures for curbside and drive-through voting and to designate a phone number that can be used for voter assistance purposes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require each election authority, if a parking lot is available at a polling place, to establish procedures for curbside or drive-through voting ("in-vehicle assisted voting") for voters who have a disability, are with an infant under one year old, or are aged 80 or older. Voters seeking this assistance would be required to complete an affidavit establishing their eligibility and would be required to vote a paper ballot. Existing law permits an authority to offer curbside voting with no eligibility restrictions, but does not require it to be offered.
  • Require each election authority to designate a phone number, which a voter may call to receive assistance with curbside or drive-through voting. The election authority would also have discretion to permit a voter to send a text message to a designated phone number. The bill would require notice of the number to be posted on the door of polling places and on voter registration cards that list a polling location.
  • Specify that the phone number established under the bill may also be used to report an individual who is acting in an intimidating or unlawful manner inside or outside of the polling place. The election judge or authorized volunteer answering the call would be required to determine whether assistance could be provided, and inform the caller.

This bill, as introduced January 12, 2023, would create a mail ballot tracking system to be operational no later than January 1, 2024. Specifically, the bill would:

This bill, as introduced January 12, 2023, would change processes for the maintenance of voter registration lists, related to the death or address update of voters. Specifically, the bill would:

The bill would also newly require parties who issue death certificates to submit records to the county clerk within seven days of a death, and require clerks and coroners to certify their compliance with reporting requirements on a quarterly basis to county boards.

  • Permit any individual to request that clerks provide evidence of records and reports related to list maintenance for the death or address update of voters, and create a new civil cause of action for enforcement of requests by injunction or declaratory relief.

Last Updated January 30, 2023

This bill, as introduced January 12, 2023, would require a voter to present photo identification or a voter identification card when desiring to vote in person. Under existing law, a person desiring to vote in Illinois must provide only their name and residence. Specifically, the bill would:

    • a copy of the State or federal tax return filed by the applicant for the previous calendar year,

    • a W-2 for the preceding calendar year.
  • Permit voters who are indigent or who have a sincere religious objection to being photographed to sign an affidavit attesting to that fact in lieu of providing photo ID, and require them to vote a provisional ballot These voters would not be required to provide additional information for verification of their registration for their ballot to be counted, but may do so within seven days. The bill would also permit voters who are otherwise unable to present photo identification or a voter identification card to cast a provisional ballot, but these voters would be required to present photo identification or a voter identification card to the county clerk or board of elections within 10 days of an election for the ballot to be counted.

This bill, as introduced on January 12, 2023, would make several procedural changes to voter registration and voter list maintenance practices. Specifically, the bill would:

Failure to appear would cause automatic cancellation of the voter's registration.

  • Allow documents that demonstrate a person's citizenship and voting age to be used to support a dual-purpose application (one that serves as either an application to register to vote or an application to change the voter's registered residential address or name). Under existing law, only identification documents meeting REAL ID standards may serve as the basis for a dual-purpose application. This bill would also allow documents that are silent as to citizenship to serve as the basis for a dual-purpose application. The bill makes clear that an identity document that affirmatively shows a person's noncitizen status cannot be the basis for a voter registration application.
  • Eliminate all provisions suggesting that an applicant may opt out of automatic voter registration at the time of the transaction, and instead reinforce that the only mechanism for opting out is after the transaction, in response to a notice sent by election officials.
  • Eliminate requirements that the registration agency inform an applicant of qualifications to vote, the penalties for false application, how automatic registration works, and that declining to register is confidential and does not affect the services a person is otherwise seeking to receive.

Last Updated February 28, 2023

This bill, as introduced February 7, 2023, would provide opportunities for individuals younger than 18 years of age to preregister to vote and otherwise participate in the democratic process. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create pre-registration for minors. The bill would permit an individual who is 16 years of age to preregister to vote. The registration would be "held in abeyance" by the election authority until the individual reached voting age.
  • Provide that an individual who is 17 years of age and will be 18 on the date of the next general or consolidated election is permitted to circulate a petition.

Last Updated February 27, 2023

This bill, as enacted on August 4, 2023, makes a number of changes to Illinois election law across a variety of issue areas. Specifically, the bill:

  • Changes the rules under which election authorities are required to supply each voter with an application to be permanently placed on vote by mail status. Under existing law, an election authority was required to provide each voter with the application before each election and notify them of how to apply. Under the bill, the election authority is no longer be required to do this for a voter if:
    • The voter is already on the permanent mail voting list,
    • The election is taking place in an odd-numbered year, or
    • The voter has opted out of receiving the notification
  • Requires any jurisdiction with a population of 500,000 or more to establish at least two vote centers where eligible voters can cast a ballot regardless of the precinct in which they are registered. Existing law only required one, at the office of the local election authority or in the biggest municipality. The bill also requires curbside voting to be offered at all vote centers.
  • Requires an election authority, if it changes the location of a polling place less than 10 days before an election, to immediately notify the township committeeperson, ward committeeperson, or precinct committeepersons, as applicable.
  • Permits preregistration for eligible individuals, starting at 16 years old. Existing law permits 17 year olds to vote in primary elections if they will be 18 by the time of the related general election, but did not otherwise provide for pre-registration. The bill also makes related changes to allow for pre-registration of minors.
  • Requires local election officials to send to the State Board information about mail ballots rejected for any reason, within one day of the rejection, including the voter's name and address. Officials must provide the information to State or local political committees within one day of their request.
  • Requires notifications of proposed constitutional amendments to be published in the "digital equivalents" of newspapers, as well as in newspapers directly as required by existing law. The bill also requires proposed constitutional amendments to be placed at the top of a ballot.
  • Extends the tenure of the Access to Voting for Persons with Disabilities Advisory Task Force, by requiring the entity be dissolved July 1, 2025, instead of January 1, 2024, as provided for under existing law.
  • Establishes a task force to study possible changes to voting systems and the implementation of ranked-choice voting.
  • Establishes a task force to study the plausibility and security of sending voters their ballots electronically, to be voted and returned electronically.
  • Requires the statewide voter registration list to be synchronized with the vote by mail, early vote, and rejected ballot information maintained by each election authority at least every 24 hours.
  • Makes Election Day a state holiday.

The bill also contains provisions pertaining to areas of law not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, including rules concerning the composition of certain party committees and rules for ballot lettering.

Last Updated September 18, 2023

This bill, as introduced on February 10, 2023, would place restrictions on the use of private, nongovernmental funding to conduct elections. Under the bill, the state board of elections would be responsible for regulation and oversight of such funds given to an election authority for the purpose of running an election. An election authority would be prohibited from applying for or requesting any such funds from any source. Funds controlled by the state board of elections would be required to be disbursed in proportion to the total population of a jurisdiction within an election authority.

Last Updated June 9, 2023

Under existing law, an election authority is required to provide each voter with the application before each election and notify them of how to apply. Under the bill, the election authority would no longer be required to do this for a voter if:

  • The voter is already on the permanent mail voting list,
  • The election is taking place in an odd-numbered year, or

This bill, as introduced on February 10, 2023, would authorize election authorities to elect to provide mail voting options or on-premises voting options to physically incapacitated voters. Under existing law, election authorities must provide on-premises voting at veteran's homes, hospitals, nursing homes, and other facilities to physically incapacitated voters.

Under existing law, the provision is only applicable to an election held in 2022 and is scheduled to be repealed July 1, 2023.

This bill, as amended on March 20, 2023, would disenfranchise individuals convicted of a vote fraud offense for a period of ten years and would also enact certain election worker protections. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Define an election worker as:
    • an individual who serves as the secretary of state, an employee of the election division, a member of the commission, a precinct election officer, a member of a county election board, a member of a county board of elections and registration, a member of a board of registration, a circuit court clerk, an employee of the office of a circuit court clerk, a member of a town election board, a student precinct election officer, individual who serves under IC 3-6-6-39, a challenger or pollbook holder, or a watcher,
    • an individual appointed to an absentee voter board as an absentee ballot counter or courier,
    • an individual who works or volunteers at a precinct or vote center under the supervision of another election worker.
  • Clarify that the existing felony offense for obstructing or interfering with an election officer applies to any election worker as defined by the bill.
  • Creates a felony offense for any individual who takes certain threatening or coercive actions with the intent of unlawfully influencing an election worker.
  • Disenfranchise individuals convicted of a vote fraud offense for a period of ten years following the date of conviction, regardless of whether they are imprisoned for the offense. The individual would be unable to register to vote and any existing registration would be canceled. Under existing law, individuals convicted of any criminal offense are disenfranchised only during their period of incarceration.

The bill also contains additional provisions related to aspects of election law that Voting Rights Lab does not track, such as payments to county clerks and the electronic display of a sample or provisional ballot at a polling place.
