This bill, as introduced January 10, 2023, would make changes to multiple areas of Indiana election law. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Prohibit the use of drop boxes for delivery of a ballot voted by mail. Existing law permits the delivery of a ballot to a drop box if the drop box is under the physical control and supervision of the county election board at the time the ballot is deposited.
  • Create a new felony offense for voting twice in the same state election with the intent that both ballots be counted. The bill would also create a new felony offense for casting a ballot in Indiana and in another state for a federal office with intent that both ballots be counted.
  • Increase the offense level for battery of an election worker from a misdemeanor to a felony if the battery is committed against the election worker while they are engaged in official duties or if bodily fluid or waste is placed on the worker.
  • Prohibit any individual providing a voter with a mail ballot application from highlighting or making any other marks on the application that may "prompt or confuse" the voter.
  • Permit the training given by county election boards to precinct election officers to be given in person, online, or via video. Existing law does not specify any particular method of training instruction.
  • Expressly define an "election worker" within the election code, and expressly provide within the criminal code that election workers are included within the definition of "public official."
  • Direct the Interim Study Committee on Elections to study "all issues relating to making voting by absentee ballot by mail as secure as in-person voting."

This bill, as introduced January 11, 2023, would establish automatic voter registration at the DMV ("Bureau of Motor Vehicles Commission" in Indiana). Under the bill, the DMV would be required to modify its application forms to permit anyone applying to obtain or renew a driver's license, permit or state identification card to provide the information necessary to register to vote, or to update the individual's registration. An individual completing the DMV application would be given an opportunity to opt out of registration at the time of the transaction.

Last Updated February 2, 2023

This bill, as enacted on May 1, 2023, makes various changes to mail ballot voting, including limiting unsolicited applications for mail ballots and imposing new ID number requirements for ballot applications. Specifically, the bill:

  • Specifies that an agency of the state or a political subdivision may not provide an individual with a mail ballot application unless requested by the individual or by the individual's family member. Previous law was silent as to election officials issuing voters unsolicited applications.
  • Requires the mail ballot application form to "request" the applicant to provide the last four digits of their social security number and either their driver license number, state identification card number, or unique voter identification number, or provide a photocopy of acceptable photo identification under existing law. The form must also notify the applicant that failure to submit ID numbers matching their voter registration record may cause a delay in receiving their mail ballot. Under previous law, the voter was requested to provide the last four digits of their social security number, but this was not required.
  • Permits a voter submitting a request for a mail ballot in an electronic format to submit one of the following in order to access the application: the last four digits of the voter's social security number, the voter's driver license number, state identification card number, or unique voter identification number. Under previous law, a voter was required to provide either their driver license number or unique voter identification number in order to access the ballot application.
  • Establishes a process for county election boards to enable voters to cure defects in mail ballot requests, including procedures for voters whose applications fail to include an identification number requested under the bill. Under previous law, county boards were required to notify voters when a ballot application is rejected, including the reason, but there were no specific requirements for a cure process.
  • Requires the bureau of motor vehicles to supply the secretary of state with driver's license numbers, identification card numbers, and the last four digits of social security numbers for the purpose of matching those numbers to voter registration records, or for updating voter registration records.

A previous version of the bill included a provision that was amended out on March 20, 2023, prior to enactment. That provision would have required a voter to meet the conditions for a qualifying excuse for mail ballot voting during the entire early voting period and on Election Day, to be eligible for a mail ballot. Under existing law, a voter is eligible to receive a mail ballot if they will meet a qualifying excuse condition on Election Day alone.

Last Updated September 15, 2025

This bill, as enacted on May 4, 2023, makes extensive but mostly technical changes to Indiana election law. Specifically, the bill:

  • Expands the scope of a provision that permits a civil penalty to be imposed on a precinct election officer who fails to complete a required duty. The bill expands this provision to also apply to an absentee voter board member, or a person who counts absentee ballots.
  • Permits some opposed local candidates to serve as a precinct election officer upon the unanimous vote of the entire membership of the county election board.
  • Requires the identification of voter registration addresses that are potentially nonresidential to confirm whether a registrant could possibly live there before accepting the registration.
  • Permits a voter's signature to be updated in their voter record from several sources maintained by a county election board, such as a poll list.
  • Allows a person to apply for voter registration with a form other than the most recent version.
  • Provides that precincts may contain more than the statutorily prescribed number of residents if the precinct is located in a vote center county.
  • Requires a circuit court clerk who receives an application for a mail ballot from a voter not registered to vote in the clerk's county to forward the application on an expedited basis to the clerk of the county where the voter is registered, if applicable.
  • Clarifies that a voter designated as an absent uniformed services voter, an overseas voter, or a voter with print disabilities has that designation cleared on January 1st of each year.
  • Permits a voter voting by mail who is required to provide additional documentation in order to vote by mail to provide the documentation by 6 p.m. on Election Day for their ballot to be counted non-provisionally. Previous law required the documentation be provided by noon on Election Day. The bill also, however, eliminates the possibility of the ballot being counted provisionally if the documentation is provided after 6 p.m. on Election Day.

The bill also makes extensive changes to areas of election law not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, particularly with respect to requirements for candidates.

Last Updated May 12, 2023

This bill, as introduced January 17, 2023, would add a student ID card from most postsecondary educational institutions in Indiana as an acceptable form of voter identification. The bill would also require those institutions to modify their student ID cards to ensure they contain the student's photograph, the student's name as it appears on their voter registration record, and an expiration date.

This bill, as introduced January 17, 2023, would increase the punishment for the offense of intimidation if the offense is committed against an election worker and the threat is related to the person's status or official duties as an election worker. Under the bill, the offense would become a Level 5 felony. Under existing law, the offense would be a Class A misdemeanor under most circumstances.

This bill, as introduced on January 17, 2023, would create same-day voter registration for every election statewide. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require same-day registrants to meet all voter eligibility requirements and provide all of the following:
    • A voter registration form witnessed by two poll workers from different political parties (or one poll worker and the precinct inspector if there are not two poll workers from different parties)
    • Proof of residence, in the form of a current photo ID, a current utility bill, bank statement, government check, paycheck, or other government documents that shows the name and address of the applicant, or a statement by any other voter in the precinct corroborating the voter's residency, who must provide an approved ID and must sign the statement in the presence of two poll workers from different political parties (or one poll worker and the precinct inspector if there are not two poll workers from different parties). Individuals who cannot immediately provide proof of residence would be permitted to re-enter the polling place later to provide documentation, or would otherwise be required to file a copy of the required documentation in the county registration office or the precinct election board for their ballot to be counted.
    • An affirmation signed by the voter including a statement that the voter has not already voted in the election
  • Require all same-day registrants to vote a provisional ballot.
  • Require the county voter registration office to add the name of same-day registrants to the registration record of the county. If a notice mailed to a same-day registrant in the course of adding that person to the county records is returned as undeliverable, the county voter registration office would be required to follow the existing steps to remove the person from the registration rolls.

This bill, as introduced January 19, 2023, concerns requirements for establishing residence for purposes of Indiana election law. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Repeal the provision that permits a voter to establish a presumption of an asserted residency if they provide a statement under penalty of perjury. The bill would instead expressly provide that such a statement is not sufficient alone to prove residency, and would require voters to provide evidence of their intention to abandon a previous residence and reside at a new location, to meet a preponderance of evidence standard. Documentation would be required to show the voter's name and asserted address, such as a current photo ID, utility bill, paycheck, or government document.
  • Expressly provide that a person who registers to vote in another state loses residence in Indiana for purposes of election law. Existing law provides that an individual may not have residence both inside and outside the state, but does not expressly deny residency due to out-of-state voter registration.

This bill, as introduced on January 17, 2023, would require myriad state agencies to offer voter registration services, including submitting completed applications to state and county election officials. Specifically, the bill would require:

    • The Kansas Department for Aging and Disability Services

  • The Departments and supervisory agencies above to inform people for whom they lack citizenship documentation that the people must provide such documentation to complete their voter registration. Existing law requires that registration applicants provide documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote, however, that provision has been permanently enjoined.

This bill, as introduced on January 18, 2023, would revise certain voter registration list maintenance practices relating to non-citizenship. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Prohibit public agencies from sharing information with federal courts for the purpose of federal courts creating jury lists unless the courts agree to notify the county election officer for the county in which a potential juror resides whenever a potential juror refuses jury service on the ground that the potential juror is not a U.S citizen. The court would be required to include the potential juror's name and address.
  • Require state jury commissioners to notify the county election officer of a county in which a potential juror resides whenever a potential juror declines jury service on the ground that the potential juror is not a U.S. citizen. The notice would be required to include the potential juror's name and address.

This bill, as enacted on April 24, 2023, creates new, special processes for a state-run presidential primary in 2024, with regard to voter registration and mail voting. Under previous law, the political parties conduct their own nomination processes. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires individuals to register to vote by the 31st day before the election, instead of the 21st day before as generally applicable election law requires.
  • Requires mail ballot applications (called "advance voting" applications in Kansas) to be received by the 30th day before Election Day. Under generally applicable election law, applications may be filed up to the Tuesday before Election Day.
  • Requires mail ballots to be returned by the close of polls on Election Day regardless of return method. Under generally applicable election law, mail ballots are due by the close of polls if hand-delivered, and must be postmarked on or before Election Day and received by the third day after Election Day if returned by mail.
  • Requires the county canvass of the primary to be no later than eight days after the election, and includes the presidential primary in the post-election audit process generally applicable election law requires. Under previous law, counties were required to canvass the results of a presidential primary on the Friday after the election, or the Monday thereafter if the county election officer so chose and provided notice of the change.
  • Sets a March 19, 2024 date for the presidential primary.

  • Requires the state canvass of the 2024 presidential primary to be held on or before April 12, 2024.

    The bill also contains additional provisions that Voting Rights Lab does not track, including changes to candidate filing requirements.

    Previous versions of the bill included provisions related to drop boxes that were amended out prior to enactment. These provisions, amended out on March 24, 2023, would have required the Secretary of State to consult with county election officers prior to adopting rules and regulations for the use of mail ballot drop boxes located anywhere other than in a county election office or satellite early voting site (called "satellite advance voting site" in Kansas). The regulations would have been required to address at a minimum the dates, times, and locations for the use of such boxes.

This bill, as introduced on January 18, 2023, would prohibit anyone other than an election official from mailing voters applications for mail ballots (called "advance ballots" in Kansas), and enforce that prohibition by expanding an existing misdemeanor. Under existing law, people domiciled in Kansas are allowed to send voters such applications, and the misdemeanor applies only to people domiciled outside of the state.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on February 22, 2023, would shorten the time voters have to return their mail ballots (called "advance ballots" in Kansas) and would expressly authorize mail ballot drop boxes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require mail ballots to be received by the close of polls on Election Day, regardless of whether the voter is returning the ballot by mail or hand delivery. Under existing law, mail ballots returned by mail must be postmarked on or before Election Day and received by election officials by the third day after Election Day, whereas ballots returned by hand must be received by the close of polls on Election Day.

  • Include county-maintained ballot drop boxes and satellite election offices as places mail ballots may be received up to the close of polls on Election Day. Existing law only mentions county election offices or polling places as places to return ballots. Existing law generally does not address ballot drop boxes, although in 2020 both the Governor and the Secretary of State supported their use and provided funding for counties to acquire two each.

Last Updated February 23, 2023

This bill, as introduced on January 18, 2023, would limit and regulate mail ballot drop box use outside of county election offices or other early voting locations (called "satellite advance voting sites" in Kansas). These drop boxes would be called "remote drop boxes". Existing law does not address drop boxes of any type, however, both the Governor and Secretary of State encouraged their use in 2020 and provided funding for two per county.

Specifically, the bill would:

  • Limit counties to offering one remote drop box per 30,000 registered voters or portion thereof. Based on 2021 data, only 20 of Kansas' 105 counties have a total population of 30,000 or more.
  • Require remote drop boxes to be closed whenever the county election office is closed, "except as otherwise provided." The bill provides for drop boxes to remain open on Election Day until polls close and any voters in line at the close of polls have deposited their ballots, but otherwise does not address when drop boxes may be open.
  • Require remote drop boxes to be under visual surveillance of an election office employee or video cameras. If a box is monitored by video surveillance, the video must be recorded and the camera positioned to capture the face of the person depositing the ballots. The video must be retained for a year, be a public record, and be provided upon request to any candidate whose name is on the ballot in the county in which the drop box is located.
  • Require signage near the remote box's opening making clear the legal restrictions on returning ballots and the penalties for violating them. Under existing law, anyone the voter designates in writing may return the voter's ballot for them, but a person may not return more than a total of 10 ballots. Depending on the violation, returning a ballot illegally is either a misdemeanor or a felony.

  • Require the Secretary of State to adopt rules and regulations to implement and enforce the drop box rules. The rules and regulations would be required to direct all ballots collected from remote drop boxes to be preserved separately from all other ballots.

This bill, as amended on February 22, 2023, would make changes to disparate areas of the election code, impacting who has election administration authority, when people can be asked to confirm they want to keep receiving mail ballots, poll watcher appointments and observation powers, election crimes, and other topics. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Shift and clarify election administration authority by:
    • specifying the roles of the Secretary of State and county election officers in conducting elections. The Secretary would oversee the conduct of statewide elections as chief election officer, responsible for assisting and advising county election officers. County election officers would be, for their respective counties, the sole public officer responsible for planning, conducting, and coordinating elections held in their county.
    • broadening the pool of people the Secretary of State could appoint as election commissioner, who is the chief election officer in the large counties whose elected county clerk does not serve in that role. The bill would repeal the existing requirement that the appointee must have been a qualified voter and resident of the county at least two years prior to their appointment but would require the appointee to become a resident of the county within six months of taking the oath of office.
    • broadening the pool of people who could be appointed to be county clerk, the chief election officer in most Kansas counties, in case the elected clerk leaves office before the end of their term. Under the bill, any qualified voter in the state could be appointed, whereas existing law requires an appointee to be a qualified voter of the county.
    • prohibiting people from serving as county election officers if they have been convicted of an election crime in Kansas or its equivalent in another jurisdiction.
    • allowing the Secretary of State to dismiss a complaint alleging violations of the federal Help America Vote Act without a requested hearing if, after reviewing the complaint and giving all inferences to the complainant, the Secretary decides the complaint does not allege facts that assert a violation.
    • prohibiting county election offices and/or their employee or agents from creating, disclosing, or allowing someone else to create or disclose, an image of the hard drive of any electronic or electromechanical voting system, optical scanning equipment, or any other voting system that contains a hard drive component without the written consent of the Secretary.
  • Change rules relating to the appointment and powers of poll watchers.
    • Remove the ability of any precinct committee person to appoint poll watchers or to automatically be one themselves, although they could be appointed by someone who has the power to appoint watchers.
    • Increase the number of poll watchers that state and county political party chairpeople may each appoint from one to two.
    • Authorize poll watchers to observe recounts and audits as well as the other activities they may observe under existing law.
    • Require all poll watchers to carry identification supplied by the county election officer that identifies the authority under which the person has been appointed a poll watcher, and show it upon the request of an election officer. Under existing law, only candidates and precinct committee people are required to have such identification and show it upon request. Because violations are a misdemeanor under existing law, by expanding who must carry and show ID this provision expands the misdemeanor.
    • Revise the prohibition on people other than voters and election officers allowed by law to be within three feet of voting booths, voting machines, or any table being used by any election board to allow the supervising judge to expand such distance beyond three feet as needed.
  • Create new ways to commit the felony of "electronic or electromechanical voting system or electronic poll book fraud", specifically:
    • accessing without authorization or facilitating the unauthorized access to electronic or electromechanical voting system equipment, electronic poll book equipment, computer programs, operating systems, firmware, software or ballots, or
    • knowingly publishing or causing to be published any password or other confidential information relating to electronic or electromechanical voting system equipment, electronic poll book equipment, computer programs, operating systems, firmware, or software
  • Create new ways to commit the felony of optical scanning equipment fraud, specifically:
    • accessing without authorization or facilitating the unauthorized access to optical scanning equipment, or
    • knowingly publishing or causing to be published any password or other confidential information relating to optical scanning equipment
  • Provide that if a voter who is not affiliated with a political party casts a provisional partisan ballot in a primary, canvassers must count the votes for offices or issues that unaffiliated voters were eligible to vote for. Existing law requires the partial counting of ballots in other situations but does not address this one.
  • Make small changes to the rules for elections involving universal mail ballot elections by:
    • Removing two special district types relating to sewage disposal from the list of 16 special jurisdictions allowed to conduct elections by universally mailing ballots to eligible voters.
    • Clarifying that the cure process available to voters voting by mail in a traditionally conducted election also applies to voters in an election involving universally mailed ballots by adding conforming provisions to the universal mail ballot section of the election code. Existing law generally provides that traditional election mail ballot rules apply to universal mail ballot elections.
  • Clarify that a county election officer cannot mail a ballot to a voter who did not apply for one unless the voter is on the permanent mail voting list or the election includes universally mailed ballots. Under existing law, county election officers do not appear to have the discretion to mail ballots without an application outside of those two circumstances.
  • Improve public notice of election information by:
    • Requiring county election officers to publish notice of the places, dates, and deadline for voter registration on the county election website as well as in newspapers as existing law requires. The website notice would remain up until the day after the close of registration.
    • Requiring counties to post notice of the election on the county's election office website at least 30 days before an election and remain on the site through the day after the election, in addition to the existing requirement to publish a notice in a newspaper once at least 15 days before an election.
  • Change the rules for drawing precincts to prohibit redrawing between January 1 of a year ending in 0 and the time the legislature has been redistricted in a year ending in two, except for certain enumerated reasons. Under existing law, the prohibition begins January 1 of a year ending in 7 and continues through the same endpoint.

  • Make various changes to recounts, regular audits, and bond, political party officer, and other specialty election types that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

    The February 13, 2023 amendment removed a provision that would have allowed election officials to do a mailing that could remove voters from the permanent mail voting list (called "permanent advance voting list" in Kansas) if they failed to vote in two consecutive general elections, instead of waiting until after the voter failed to vote in four consecutive general elections.

This bill, as introduced on February 7, 2023, would make voter registration continuous and enable people to use same-day registration on Election Day and during early voting. The bill contains conflicting provisions as to how same-day registration would work and imposes documentary proof of citizenship requirements on same-day registrants.

Specifically, the bill would:

  • Repeal the registration deadline. Under existing law, voters must register at least 20 days before Election Day to vote in an election.
  • Allow registration to be offered until 9 p.m. on the three business days before Election Day. Existing law allows these late hours for registration on the three business days before the close of registration.
  • Allow registration at voting locations on Election Day and during early voting. Section 1 of the bill provides that same-day registrants would be allowed to vote regular ballots unless a reason other than their registration's timing required them to vote a provisional ballot. Section 2 of the bill requires such voters to complete provisional ballots and provides that the provisional ballots must count unless it was not properly cast or the person had already voted.
  • Require people doing same-day registration to complete a registration card, make an oath on a form created by the Secretary of State, and provide proof of residence. The county election officer would mail a nonforwardable certificate of registration to the voter.

  • Provide that if the person must provide documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register, they may either show a U.S. passport or a copy of one of the documents authorized by the election code. If using a passport, that would be recorded on their provisional ballot envelope. Otherwise, they would be able to put a copy of one of the other documents in a special envelope attached to the provisional ballot envelope or can bring, mail, or electronically submit such a copy to the county election officer before the meeting of the board of canvassers. The voter would be given the information needed to submit the documentation. Existing Kansas statutes require registrants to provide documentary proof of citizenship to register, however, those provisions have been permanently enjoined and are not enforced. Nonetheless, the bill provides that same-day registrants who do not provide such documentation would have their registrations and provisional ballots rejected.

This bill, as enacted on April 24, 2023, makes several disparate changes to the election code. The changes clarify election administration authority, improve various notices by requiring website posting in addition to newspaper publication, create new ways to commit felonies relating to election equipment, and make other smaller changes to election law areas tracked by the Voting Rights Lab. The bill also makes myriad changes to election law topics not tracked by VRL, such as write-in candidacies, nominations, recall elections, recounts, and election equipment, among other topics. Specifically, the bill:

  • Clarifies the relative roles of the Secretary of State and county election officers by specifying their duties, and restricts who may become a county election officer. Previous law did not have comparable provisions. The bill provides that:
    • The Secretary is responsible for assisting and advising county election officers in conducting elections in compliance with federal and state laws and rules and regulations. Separately and in addition, the bill provides the Secretary can dismiss a complaint relating to the federal Help America Vote Act without holding a hearing if after giving all inferences to the complainant and consulting on such complaint with the Attorney General, the Secretary determines the complaint fails to allege facts that assert a violation
    • Each county election officer is the sole public officer responsible for planning, conducting, and coordinating elections held within such officer's county. The county officer is responsible for ensuring that all such elections comply with federal and state laws, rules, and regulations.
    • No person shall serve as a county election officer if such person has been convicted of any crime in the election code, or of any substantially similar crime in any other jurisdiction
  • Changes county-level election administration by changing the threshold and process for choosing a commissioner of elections to administer county elections instead of the elected county clerk. Specifically, the bill:
    • Requires an election commissioner to be appointed by the Secretary of State in counties with a population exceeding 125,000 as certified to the Secretary by the Division of the Budget. Previous law required the Secretary to make the appointment in a county with at least 130,000 residents but required an election commissioner instead of the county clerk in all counties with at least 100,000 thousand residents. Neither section of the prior law specified how the population was determined. Four of the 105 counties in Kansas exceed the new 125,000-person threshold, and Douglas County, at about 119,000 residents, is close.
    • Requires a search committee with specified membership to identify, interview, and recommend three people from which the Secretary would appoint the commissioner. The committee would include the chairperson of the board of county commissioners or their designee, a representative of the county's HR department, and three representatives from the Secretary's office.
    • Changes the qualifications for county election commissioners so that they must have been Kansas residents at least two years before being appointed, and must be a resident of the relevant county on the day they file their oath of office. Previous law required them to be a qualified elector and resident of the county for at least two years prior to appointment.
    • Provides that in a county in which an election commissioner has been appointed, drawing all precinct boundary lines is their responsibility exclusively. Previous law specified that only the election commissioners in counties with a population between 140,000 and 220,000 had such exclusive authority. Based on current population numbers, only the election commissioners in Wyandotte and Shawnee Counties were so empowered.
  • Improves notice of upcoming elections by:
    • Requiring notice to be published in newspapers at least 30 days before the election instead of at least 15 days before, or in the case of special elections, instead of at least 10 days before.
    • Requiring notice of elections to be published on the county election office website starting 30 days before the election and lasting through the day after the election.
  • Improves notice relating to voter registration availability and deadlines by requiring an existing notice to be published on the county election officer's website as well as in the newspaper. The website notice must remain up until the day after the registration closes.
  • Improves general voter-facing communications by requiring certain documents and information to be published on the county election officer's website. Previous law required election officials to "furnish" the information and documents.
  • Creates new ways to commit the existing felony of electronic or electromechanical voting system or electronic poll book fraud. Specifically, the following conduct now constitutes the crime, as well as the previously criminalized conduct:
    • accessing without authorization or facilitating the unauthorized access to electronic or electromechanical voting system equipment, electronic poll book equipment, computer programs, operating systems, firmware, software or ballots, or
    • knowingly publishing or causing to be published any password or other confidential information relating to electronic or electromechanical voting system equipment, electronic poll book equipment, computer programs, operating systems, firmware, or software;
  • Creates new ways to commit the existing felony of optical scanning equipment fraud. Specifically, the following conduct now constitutes the crime, as well as the previously criminalized conduct:
    • accessing without authorization or facilitating the unauthorized access to optical scanning equipment, or
    • knowingly publishing or causing to be published any password or other confidential information relating to optical scanning equipment.
  • Requires county election officers to create a backup copy of the hard drive of any electronic or electromechanical voting system, optical scanning equipment, or any other voting system that contains a hard drive component. Such backup copies shall be created immediately prior to and immediately after any system updates, repairs, or improvements and prior to and after each general election. The county election officer shall maintain such backup copies in a secured location for not less than 22 months. Creating or disclosing any other such copy or image would be prohibited without the written consent of the Secretary of State.
  • Requires election officials reviewing a ballot cast in a partisan primary by an unaffiliated voter to count the votes for the offices or issues for which the unaffiliated voter was eligible to vote. Previous laws and regulations did not expressly address this situation.
  • Expressly provides that election officials must provide voters in Kansas' limited universal mail ballot elections with notice and an opportunity to cure a missing or mismatched signature on their ballot envelope certificate. The previous law had a general requirement that laws applicable to mail voting in traditional elections also applied to universal mail ballot elections, and the regulations implementing the cure process specified by traditional election mail voting law expressly applied to universal mail ballot elections already.
  • Prohibits a county election officer from mailing a ballot to a voter unless the voter applied for the ballot, is on the state's mail voting list, or the election is a universal mail ballot election. Previous law required an application but did not expressly prohibit mailing a ballot without an application.
  • Revises removing a voter from the state's limited mail voting list based on a person's failure to vote so that the confirmation notice is set whenever a person fails to vote in four consecutive general elections. Previous law required those four consecutive general elections to be held on the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November in each even-numbered and odd-numbered year. Relatedly, the bill redefines "general election" so it includes a special election to fill a vacancy at which an officer is finally elected instead of only elections on the specified November Tuesday.
  • Defines "special election" so that it includes universal mail ballot elections, and provides that special elections generally may be held on the same day as a general or primary election but not within 45 days of one. The universal mail ballot election code nonetheless prohibits conducting such an election on the same day as another election, unless the mail ballot election relates to piercing a tax cap.

This bill, as introduced on February 16, 2023, would shorten the mail ballot return deadline, require all ballots to be counted by hand, make a huge range of election records publicly available before an election is certified, give the Legislature a role in certain rule making by the Secretary of State, and expand existing audits and recounts. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Shorten the mail ballot return deadline to 7 p.m. on Election Day (the close of polls) from postmarked on or before Election Day and received within three days after. In Kansas, mail ballots are called "advance ballots."
  • Require all ballots to be counted by hand. Under existing law, counties may use tabulators.
  • Require all available election records to be made available for public inspection at least 72 hours before any election is certified, including any audit or recount records, and also after an election. Election records would be broadly defined to include without limitation chain-of-custody documents, polling books, drop-box surveillance videos, paper ballots or electronic or paper copies of ballots, advance voting records or election audit or recount records. Records would be exempt from public release if they may by themselves or in combination with other records connect a particular voter with a particular ballot.
  • Require the Secretary of State to issue rules relating to hand counting ballots, audits, and recounts according to a special process. Specifically, the bill would provide that:
    • The Secretary would give notice to the chair of the Legislative Coordinating Council within one business day of issuing the rules.
    • The chair would call a meeting of the Council to review the rules.
    • The rules could be approved or revoked at any time by concurrent resolution of the Legislature, or if it is adjourned for three or more days, by the Council.
    • The rules would be deemed approved unless and until revoked. If an election is 30 calendar days or fewer away, revocation must occur within three calendar days or the rules will be in effect for that election.
  • Expand the scope and frequency of audits required by existing law, while also requiring them to be done by hand. The bill would require that audit to be live streamed and recorded. The bill would change the scope and frequency of audits by:
    • Requiring statewide and state legislative races to be audited if the margin of victory is within 2.5% of the votes tallied on election night, instead of 1% as existing law requires.
    • Requiring the audit to include 25% of precincts instead of 10% as existing law requires.
    • Requiring the Secretary of State to expand the audit to all precincts if an unresolved discrepancy exists between the unofficial results and the audit. Existing law authorizes the Secretary to include additional precincts if a discrepancy exists.
  • Expand who may request a recount of an election in two ways. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Allow any member of the county board of canvassers to call for a recount if they determine that there are manifest errors in the poll books of any election board which might make a difference in the result. Under existing law, a majority of the county board of canvassers must so determine.
    • Expand the election types for which any person who voted can demand a recount to be any election, instead of any "question submitted" election.

  • Make changes relating to the audit threshold, ballot paper, chains of custody, and recount processes that the Voting Rights Lab does not track.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 16, 2023, would restrict mail voting in multiple ways, both expand and limit in-person early voting, require public posting of election-related materials before election results are certified, and make other changes throughout the election code.

The bill would restrict mail voting by requiring voters to justify their decision to vote by mail with an approved excuse and in some cases, a doctor's note, notarize their signature on their ballot application and ballot certificate, shorten the time voters have to return their mail ballots, and eliminate an existing option to return a mail ballot by prohibiting drop boxes. The bill would also make it harder to join the limited permanent mail voting list and easier to be removed from it. Kansas calls mail ballots "advance ballots." Specifically, the bill would restrict voting by mail by:

  • Changing the mail ballot application process. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Restrict voting an "advance ballot" by mail to registered voters with a permanent or temporary disability or illness that prevents them from voting in person. If the person is asserting a permanent or temporary disability, they must include with their application a written statement from a doctor attesting to their disability and that the disability prevents them from voting in person. Under existing law, all voters have the freedom to choose to vote by mail.
    • Allow anyone to file a complaint with the Attorney General alleging that a person violated the excuse requirement, and would require the Attorney General to file a civil action against them. Under existing law, people may complain to the Attorney General if someone who is not a state resident mails a mail ballot application, and the Attorney General may file an action. The fine is $20 per application mailed. Existing law appears aimed at people and organizations distributing mail ballot applications to voters, while the bill appears to revise this section to apply it to voters returning completed applications.
    • Require a voter's signature on a mail ballot application to be notarized. Under existing law, voters must include an ID number or a copy of photo identification with their mail ballot application, a requirement that would remain in place.
    • Retain the requirement that a voter's application signature be verified against signatures on file, despite the notarization requirement. Moreover, election officials would be prohibited from using signature-matching software as part of the verification process. Under existing law, such software may be used.
    • Require organizations collecting mail ballot applications from voters to turn them in within two days of receiving them or the applications would be voided. Existing law does not void applications based on when organizations submit them.
    • Increase the penalty for distributing mail ballot applications without required disclosures or otherwise violating the rules to a felony from a misdemeanor, and narrow the exception to the rules to exclude entities required to provide information concerning elections and voting procedures by federal law and the official protection and advocacy for voting access agency designated under the federal Help America Vote Act.
    • Require approval of each application to be noted on the application and require a record of each application and its approval to be publicly available.
    • Allow mail ballot applications to be filed 93 days before an election. Existing law allows for 90 days before an election.
  • Changing the ballot completion and return process. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require mail voters to have their signature on the ballot certificate notarized. Under existing law, ballots are verified by comparing the voter's signature on the ballot envelope with their signature on file.
    • Prohibit ballot drop boxes outside of county election offices. Existing law does not specifically address ballot drop boxes, however, in the 2020 election both the Secretary of State and Governor encouraged their use and provided funding to all counties to acquire and use two.
    • Shorten the time a voter has to return their mail ballot to 7 p.m. on Election Day, the close of polls, and further require that if the voter mails their ballot back, it must be mailed no later than the Tuesday that is three weeks before Election Day. Under existing law, mail ballots must be postmarked on or before Election Day and received within three days of Election Day.
    • Require voters mailing their completed mail ballots to election officials to use a level of service that not only documents when their ballot was mailed but also allows the voter to verify the ballot was delivered. Voters do not face a similar responsibility under existing law. The Secretary of State offers ballot tracking on their website without the voter needing to use a specific delivery service.

  • Restrict the permanent mail voting list. Under existing law, any person having a permanent disability or an illness that has been diagnosed as a permanent illness may apply to join the list and thereafter automatically receive a ballot in the mail. The bill would:

    • Require disabled voters applying to join the permanent mail voting list to include a doctor's note with their application that attests to their disability and that the disability prevents the voter from voting in person. Under existing law, a voter's attestation under penalty of perjury is sufficient.
    • Remove voters from the permanent mail voting list if they fail to vote in two consecutive general elections. Under existing law, voters are removed from the list if they fail to vote in four consecutive general elections. Kansas holds general elections each year.

    The bill would make changes to in-person voting as well. Specifically, the bill would:


  • Expand the mandatory early voting period. The bill would require early voting to begin 10 days prior to an election while allowing it to begin as soon as the 23rd day before an election. Under existing law, early voting must begin seven days before an election but can begin as soon as 20 days before.
  • Limit where early voting may be offered to the central county election office. Under existing law, county election officials may open satellite offices to offer early voting.
  • Prohibit precincts from having more than 1,000 people based on the most recent census data and allow new precincts to be created whenever necessary to maintain that cap.
  • Require polling places to be within precincts and prohibit countywide vote centers. The only way two precincts may be served by the same polling place is if one precinct has fewer than 20 voters.
  • Expand employees' right to up to two hours of paid leave from work to go vote. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Expand the right to time off to vote to include the option to vote in person early. Under existing law, employees have the option to have paid time off to vote on Election Day only.
    • Increase the penalty on employers for not providing such leave to a level 3 felony instead of a class A misdemeanor.

  • Require the county election officer to staff polling places with sheriff's deputies on Election Day both during voting and the initial canvass at the polling place.

    The bill would make voter registration applications public, give the Legislature a role in certain regulations, impose deadlines on ballot counting, require the Secretary of State to post a lot of election materials online before election results can be certified, and make other changes to the elections code. Specifically, the bill would:


  • Require county election officers to make applications for voting registration available for public inspection. The bill does not require the redaction of any information on those applications, which can include sensitive information such as driver's license numbers.
  • Provide that for certain election-related rulemaking, the Secretary of State would advise the Legislature and the chair of the Legislative Coordinating Council of the proposed adoption of a rule or regulation. The chair would then call a meeting of the council to review the proposal and would advise the Legislature of the results. The rule or regulation could be revoked at any time by concurrent resolution of the Legislature or, when the Legislature is adjourned for three or more calendar days, by the Council.
  • Require the canvasses of mail ballots and Election Day voting to be reported to county election officials by midnight of the day after the election. Existing law does not have a similar requirement.
  • Require the Secretary of State to post all election-related materials, broadly defined, on their website at least 72 hours before a general election in even-numbered years is certified. The counties would provide the Secretary with election-related material from all precincts in an organized fashion. "Election-related materials" would include without limitation copies of all chain-of-custody documents, ballots, mail ballot envelope images, ballot-definition files, system log files, cast-vote records, ballot images, chain-of-custody documents for all parts of the voting process and any surveillance videos of dropboxes, election offices, collection of ballots, counting of ballots or storing of ballots. Under existing law, poll workers give county election officials all election supplies, all voted ballots, all ballots unused, spoiled, void, or objected to, along with all tally sheets, poll books, abstracts, and all other books and records in the possession of the election board.
  • Require county election officers to produce a report providing a full accounting of the number of advance ballots mailed, received, accepted, rejected, missing, and destroyed for each election, accompanied by a declaration signed by the county election official attesting to the accuracy of the report.
  • Require the Secretary of State to publish the unofficial results only after receiving the initial canvass from every precinct and prohibit anyone from publishing results before all results have been reported to the Secretary. Existing law does not require publishing the results sooner, but as the Kansas Election Standards on Canvassing note, counties generally release results promptly and on a rolling basis as a public service.

  • Make November general election days state holidays.

    • During the 30 calendar days before an election, the Secretary would not be allowed to issue a new rule, regulation, or determination that impacts the election unless an emergency is approved by the Legislative Coordinating Council. If the Secretary is reasonably unable to give prior notice of the rule, the determination or rule would take effect when the Secretary gives such notice and would remain in effect for the election unless either the Legislature or Legislative Coordinating Council revokes it within three calendar days after the day they received notice from the Secretary.
    • At all other times, the Secretary is to provide prior notice to the Legislature and the Legislative Coordinating Council of a proposed determination or a proposed rule or regulation adoption. The chair of the Council would call a meeting to review the proposal. The proposed determination, rule, or regulation could take effect and remain in force unless and until either the Legislature or the Council revokes it. The Legislature could revoke a determination, rule, or regulation at any time by concurrent resolution. If the Legislature is not in session or adjourned for at least three calendar days, the Council could revoke the Secretary's rule, regulation, or determination.
  • Require all ballots to be marked by hand. Existing law allows the use of ballot-marking voting machines. Federal law requires that disabled voters be given accessible voting options which include ballot-marking voting machines.

This bill, as introduced on March 21, 2023, would establish special rules for presidential primary elections that are more restrictive than generally-applicable election law provides. Under existing law, the political parties conduct their own nomination processes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require people to register to vote in a presidential primary at least 31 days before an election. Existing law allows people to register through the 21st day before Election Day.
  • Shorten the time voters have to submit applications for mail ballots (called "advance voting ballots" in Kansas) for presidential primaries by requiring them to be delivered to election officials by the 30th day before Election Day. Under existing law, the deadline is the Tuesday before Election Day. The bill would require ballots to be mailed to voters who successfully apply 14 days before the presidential primary. Under existing law, ballots are mailed 20 days before the election.
  • Shorten the time voters have to return their mail ballots by setting the deadline as the closing of polls on Election Day. Under existing law, ballots must be postmarked on or before Election Day and are timely if received by the third day after the election.
  • Prohibit county election officials from offering early voting for presidential primaries earlier than the Tuesday before Election Day. Under existing law, counties may choose to offer early voting before that Tuesday.
  • End the ability of voters who are not affiliated with a political party to choose to affiliate at a voting location and vote that party's primary ballot. Unaffiliated voters would be required to pick a party by the close of registration. This provision would apply to all primaries, not just presidential primaries.

The bill would make various changes relating to voter registration, most significantly by creating same-day registration. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create same-day registration on Election Day. To use the process, an eligible person would complete a registration application form, present proof of residency, and make a written oath of eligibility specified by the bill. People who do all three would be issued a regular ballot. People who do not provide the required documentation would be issued a provisional ballot and, for the provisional ballot to count, would be required to present sufficient identification within two business days after a state primary or municipal election or within six days following a state election. Same-day registration would not be available for purposes of voting at an annual or special town meeting, nor could it be used to change party affiliation for a primary or general election. Proof of residence would be defined as one of the following, so long as it includes the applicant's name and the address for which they are registering:
    • a valid photo identification including, but not limited to, a Massachusetts driver's license or other state-issued identification card or
    • other documentation demonstrating the name and address where the applicant lives including, but not limited to, a copy of a current utility bill, bank statement, government check, residential lease agreement, wireless telephone statement, paycheck, other government document or correspondence, a current student fee statement or another document from a post-secondary educational institution that verifies the student's current address.
  • Create enforcement provisions relating to same-day registration. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require either the Attorney General or the relevant district attorney to investigate credible information or allegation of illegal voter registration, or credible information or allegation of illegal multiple voting.
    • Provide that violations of the same-day registration provisions could be prosecuted using existing felonies, namely felony illegal registration, felony illegal voting or attempted illegal voting, and felony illegal excuse-based mail voting.
  • Require the Secretary of the Commonwealth to give the election officers at each polling location, to the extent possible, access to the statewide voter registration list.
  • Expand the confidentiality of voter registration information by providing that, with one exception, all information in the statewide voter registration list is confidential, not simply voters' names and addresses. State party committees, statewide candidate committees, state ballot question committees, the jury commissioner, the adjutant general, and anyone else authorized by regulation would be allowed access to the information after entering a licensing agreement with the Secretary. Under existing law, these entities have access to the information without a licensing agreement.

  • End regular registration at 5 p.m. rather than 8 p.m.

    The bill would change the availability of early in-person voting in multiple ways. Specifically, the bill would:


  • Restrict the availability of in-person early voting by:
    • Limiting early voting to state general elections, while allowing localities to offer it during their annual town meetings. Under existing law, early voting must be offered for all state and federal primaries and general elections, and federal special elections, and localities have the option to offer it for local elections not held on the same day as a state or federal election.
  • Shortening the early voting period for November even-year general elections. The bill would provide that early voting begins on the second Saturday before Election Day and continues through the close of business on the Friday before the Election. Under existing law, early voting must be offered during that time period for primaries and federal special elections, but for even-year November general elections, early voting begins a week earlier, on the third Saturday before Election day.
  • Expand the availability of early voting by increasing the hours early voting must be offered in municipalities with fewer than 40,000 registered voters. The bill would require early voting to be offered on weekdays during all regular business hours of the municipal clerk in all communities, eliminating the existing ability of these municipalities to offer early voting during a percentage of their regular business hours. The bill would also require expanded weekend hours in smaller communities based on their size. Specifically, in municipalities with:
    • Fewer than 5,000 registered voters, the bill would require at least two hours of early voting on each weekend day. Existing law requires at least four hours per weekend and allows all four to be on a single weekend day.
    • Between 5,000 and 19,999 registered voters, the bill would require at least four hours each weekend day. Existing law requires communities with between 5,000 and 24,999 registered voters to offer at least six hours each weekend, all of which could be on one day.
    • Between 20,000 and 39,999 registered voters, the bill would require at least five hours each weekend day. Existing law requires communities with between 25,000 and 39,999 registered voters to offer at least four hours each weekend day.
    • Between 40,000 and 74,999 registered voters, the bill would require at least six hours each weekend day, and for larger communities, at least eight hours each weekend day. Existing law imposes the same requirements.

  • Repeal some siting requirements for early voting locations. Specifically, the bill would repeal language of existing law that requires election officials who open additional early voting locations to consider, to the extent feasible, diverse geographic locations and whether such sites would have an impact on access to the polls on the basis of race, national origin, disability, income, or age.

    The bill would make changes to all aspects of mail voting. Specifically, the bill would:


  • Expand the availability of no-excuse mail voting by requiring local election officials to offer it for all elections. Existing law allows municipalities to choose not to offer early voting for elections involving only local offices and issues and exempts annual and special town meeting votes.
  • Repeal code provisions requiring the Secretary, before each election, to send a no-excuse mail ballot application, along with a pre-addressed, prepaid postage return envelope, to all voters who had not yet applied for such a ballot.
  • Repeal code provisions requiring local election officials to send a no-excuse mail ballot application with each registration confirmation card mailed to a voter who newly registered or updated their registration.
  • Repeal code provisions that require the no-excuse mail ballot package to include both prepaid return postage and, to the extent feasible, a barcode to facilitate verifying the date of mailing.
  • Repeal provisions relating to electronic mail ballot applications and ballots, and replace them with an advisory committee on the implementation of an accessible vote-by-mail process. The advisory committee would study the resources needed and the feasibility of providing an accessible online vote-by-mail process accommodating voters with physical disabilities who wish to vote a no-excuse mail ballot, including the application process, electronic delivery, and electronic return of ballots for voters with disabilities who are unable to mark a paper ballot. The advisory committee would report to the legislature by February 1, 2024. The repealed provisions require mail voting to be accessible for people with physical disabilities, require the Secretary of the Commonwealth to offer an online application portal, and require electronic applications to be signed in a manner substantially similar to a handwritten signature.
  • Allow voters to return their completed mail ballot to a secure drop box in any municipality, not simply to one in the municipality in which they are registered to vote.
  • Repeal a provision of code mandating that mail ballots cast by eligible voters must count even if the voter became ineligible after voting, such as by dying.
  • Repeal provisions of code requiring public notice of, and public observation of, mail ballot pre-processing.
  • Require no-excuse mail ballots to be sent to voters as soon as they are available but no later than 28 days before Election Day. Existing law simply provides that they must be sent as soon as they are available.
  • Clarify the deadline to apply to receive a ballot in the mail, excuse-based or no-excuse, by setting the deadline as 5 p.m. on the seventh day before Election Day, instead of by that time on the fifth business day before Election Day. In most situations, those deadlines would be the same.

  • Change the mail ballot return deadline for both excuse-based and no-excuse mail ballots slightly. The bill would set the deadline as the close of polls on Election Day for any election that is not a federal general election and would set it for those elections as postmarked on or before Election Day and received within three days after Election Day. Existing law sets the deadlines similarly, except that it defines the mailed on or before Election Day deadline as applying to biennial state elections, which are held in even-numbered years like federal general elections are, and existing law provides that the postmark, if legible, is evidence of timely mailing.

    The bill would change other aspects of election administration. Specifically, the bill would:


  • Repeal language authorizing the state to participate in the Electronic Registration Information Center.
  • Improve notice to voters regarding polling place locations. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require local election officials to send voters notices by mail and, to the extent possible, by email and reverse 911, when their polling places have been designated and when they have been changed. Local election officials would also be required to post the information on municipal websites. Existing law requires public posting of polling place information, but does not require it to be on a website nor does it require direct contact of voters unless their polling place changed, and then only mail notice is required.
    • Require local election officials to publish all polling locations, dates, and hours not less than seven days prior to an election on the city or town's website, if any, and by printed notice in certain public buildings, and on the website of the Secretary of the Commonwealth. Existing law does not require posting on the internet.

  • Shift responsibility for assigning law enforcement to early voting locations from the discretion of election officers to local government.

    The bill contains other provisions to change the timing of primaries and other provisions not tracked by the Voting Rights Lab. Note, the bill also contains provisions that purport to change existing law but which propose changes that were enacted in 2022.

Last Updated March 17, 2023

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 16, 2023, would give the Secretary of the Commonwealth special powers relating to elections during emergencies and require contingency planning.

In emergency situations that make conducting an election, town meeting, or administering an election deadline unsafe and contrary to the public interest, the Secretary could twice postpone elections or extend deadlines up to 45 days each time and would be granted additional powers. The provides that any actions taken by the Secretary would be subject to judicial review if an appropriate lawsuit is filed. Specifically, the Secretary would have emergency authorization including, but not limited to:

  • Providing procedures for the orderly conduct of elections.
  • Postponing the date of any caucus, primary, special primary, preliminary, election, special election, or town meeting in the affected area, subject to the time limit on postponements.
  • In the case of municipal elections, postponing or suspending the election, including a caucus or preliminary, after consulting local election officials and the chief executive of the municipality. These postponements would be subject to the cumulative 90-day time limit.

  • Postponing or extending the qualifying periods for candidates seeking municipal, county, or statewide office, subject to the time limit on postponements.

    The bill would also require the Secretary of the Commonwealth to adopt, by rule or regulation, an elections emergency contingency plan that gives specific direction to state and local elections officials when an election has been suspended or delayed due to an emergency or alternate voting procedures are necessary. The contingency plan would address, but not be limited to:


  • Providing procedures for state and local elections officials to follow when:
    • an election has been suspended or delayed to ensure notice of the suspension or delay to the proper authorities, the electorate, the media, poll workers, and the custodians of polling places.
    • election deadlines are postponed or extended to ensure notice of the suspension or delay to the proper authorities, the electorate, candidates, and the media.
  • Providing procedures for the release and certification of election returns and documents relating to the election to the Secretary's office for elections suspended or delayed and subsequently rescheduled.

  • Providing alternate voting procedures for local election officials and voters to follow when election emergencies exist that may affect the ability to vote at a polling place and to ensure notice of the procedures to the proper authorities, the electorate, candidates, and the media.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 16, 2023, would enable eligible voters who are incarcerated to vote by facilitating their registration and their voting by mail, and would facilitate the registration and voting of people whose voting rights will be restored by giving them information and registration assistance. Existing law has no similar provisions. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Designate correctional facilities as voter registration agencies.

  • Require correctional facilities to give eligible prisoners mail ballot application forms upon request, and either provide an appropriate return envelope and postage or send the completed application to the appropriate city or town clerk responsible for processing absentee ballot request applications in the county where the requester claims residence.

    For people who were disenfranchised by a felony conviction and incarceration, the bill would:


  • Prior to the expiration of a prisoner's term, the superintendent or administrator of the state or county correctional facility would, in writing, notify the prisoner whose term expires that his or her voting rights shall be restored upon discharge.
  • Provide that as part of the release process leading to the discharge of a person who has been disfranchised because of a felony conviction, the correctional facility would provide that person with a voter registration form and a declination form, and offer that person assistance in filling out the appropriate form. Unless the registrant refuses to permit it to do so, the correctional facility would provide the registrant with a sufficient size envelope and postage stamps, or transmit the completed voter registration form to the appropriate city or town. The Secretary of the Commonwealth would be required to ensure that these people were pre-registered and upon release, registered to vote.
  • Facilitate accurate voter registration lists by requiring each administrator of a state or county correctional facility to, on or before the fifteenth day of each month, transmit to the Secretary of the Commonwealth 2 lists. The first list would identify people convicted of a felony who, during the preceding period, became ineligible to vote because of their incarceration, while the second list would identify people convicted of a felony who, during the preceding period, became eligible to vote because of their discharge from incarceration. Each list would contain the following information for each person:
    • name
    • date of birth
    • date of entry of judgment of conviction,
    • sentence, and
    • last 4 digits of their Social Security number, or driver's license number, if available.
  • Require the Secretary to ensure that persons who have become eligible to vote because of their discharge from incarceration face no continued barriers to registration or voting resulting from their felony convictions.
  • Require judges to advise defendants of the following when applicable: "You are hereby advised that the acceptance by this court of your plea of guilty, plea of nolo contendere, or admission to sufficient facts will result in loss of the right to vote only if and for as long as you are incarcerated and your voting rights are restarted upon discharge." The court shall advise such defendant during every plea colloquy at which the defendant is proffering a plea of guilty, a plea of nolo contendere, or an admission to sufficient facts in any matter considered to be a disenfranchising felony. If a defendant's plea or admission is accepted but the defendant was not given such notice, the defendant could move to vacate the plea and instead plead not guilty.

  • Require the Secretary to develop and implement a program to educate: attorneys, judges, election officials, each superintendent of a state correctional facility, each administrator of a county correctional facility, the Department of Correction and corrections officials including parole and probation officers, and members of the public, ensuring that:

    • Judges are informed of their obligation to notify defendants facing disfranchisement of the potential loss and restoration of their voting rights.
    • The Department of Correction and county correctional facilities are prepared to help eligible voters in their custody obtain absentee ballots, including providing sufficient size envelopes and postage stamps for mailing, or by forwarding their completed absentee ballot application to the appropriate elections official. The education program would also ensure that the Department of Correction and county correctional facilities are also prepared to assist those convicted of a felony with registration to vote in anticipation of their discharge, including providing the registrant with sufficient size envelope and postage stamps or by forwarding his or her completed voter registration forms to the appropriate election official.
    • The language on voter registration forms makes clear that people who have been disqualified from voting because of felony convictions regain the right to vote when they are discharged from incarceration.
    • The Department of Correction is prepared to transmit to the state secretary the information specified in this section.
    • Probation and parole officers are informed and prepared to notify probationers that their right to vote is restored.
    • Accurate and complete information about the voting rights of people who have been charged with or convicted of crimes, whether disenfranchising or not, is made available through a single publication to government officials and the public.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 16, 2023, would revise voter registration list maintenance procedures to disconnect them from an annual census that Massachusetts does, change provisions relating to inactive registration status, and tweak provisions related to canceling registrations. As under existing law, the bill's process would have the local election officials create and maintain registration lists for their jurisdictions which the Secretary of the Commonwealth would then reflect in the statewide registration system. Also as under existing law, local election officials would add people to the list who register and correct any errors, maintain the confidentiality of certain voters' information, and would remove people from the list only in certain circumstances.

Under the bill, local election officials would not remove anyone from the list except if:

  • The voter so requests in writing. Existing law has a similar provision.
  • They receive notice from the city or town clerk that the voter has died. Existing law has a similar provision.
  • They receive official written notice that the voter is incarcerated after conviction of a felony, is disqualified by law because of corrupt practices in respect to elections, or is under guardianship that prohibits voting. Existing law does not have a similar provision, although it does have a general direction to local election officials to revise and correct the list in accordance with any facts they may have presented to them.
  • They find that the voter is illegally or incorrectly registered after complaint, notice, and hearing. This process is in existing law, but cancellation for this reason is not separately itemized in the list maintenance section.

  • The voter no longer resides in their city or town, as determined by a process the bill creates. Existing law provides for cancellation of voter registration when the person has moved out of the jurisdiction.

    Under the bill, the inactive voter list would be different. Inactive status is assigned to voters who election officials believe have moved out of their jurisdiction, under both the bill and existing law, but the bill would change aspects of the list's operation. Specifically:


  • The process for joining the inactive list would change. Under the bill, at any time except during the 90 days immediately before a presidential or regular state primary or biennial state election, registrars would shift a voter's registration to the inactive voters list if they receive information that the voter no longer resides in their city or town from certain itemized sources. Under existing law, registrations are made inactive when voters fail to respond to an annual census notice for two consecutive years and do not vote in those two years. Under the bill, the information sources that trigger a shift to the inactive list would be:
    • change-of-address information supplied by the United States Postal Service or its licensee.
    • the Electronic Registration Information Center, Inc.
    • official notice that the voter has registered to vote in another jurisdiction.

  • Whenever a local election official shifts a voter registration to the inactive list under the bill, they would mail notice to the voter at their registration address. The notice would inform the voter that they may be removed from the voting list if the voter fails to respond and does not vote during the period ending with the second biennial state election following the notice's mailing. The notice would:

    • be postage prepaid.
    • contain a pre-addressed and postage-prepaid return card.
    • be sent by forwardable mail.
    • instruct the voter to return the card before the last day to register if the voter did not change residence from the city or town.
    • contain additional information about remaining eligible to vote, as prescribed by the Secretary.

    Under existing law, the second annual census notice that is sent to a voter--the one immediately before putting the voter on the inactive list--has all of these features. The bill would change the warning in that census notice so that it warns that a failure to respond might result in a fine, rather than placement on the inactive list and possible registration cancellation.


  • A voter with an inactive registration would be allowed to vote on a regular ballot upon the voter's written affirmation of continued residence in the city or town.
  • A voter registration would be reactivated if the person:
    • Notifies the registrar in writing that they continue to reside in the city or town,
    • Votes,
    • Applies for a mail ballot,
    • Signs a nomination paper or petition for a ballot question, or
    • Performs any other official election-related act, using an address in their city or town.

  • If a voter on the inactive list fails to take any of those actions through two biennial state elections after the notice was mailed, their registration would be canceled and the voter would be sent a forwardable notice. Existing law has similar provisions.
