VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 13, 2023, would:

  • Establish same-day voter registration during early voting and at a precinct on Election Day. Registrants would be required to present proof of name and residence and sign an affidavit. Registrants without proof of residence would be permitted to cast a provisional ballot that would only be counted if they returned within 2 business days of a primary or 6 days after a general election to present proof of residence to the municipal clerk.
  • Limit the placement of voters on the inactive list to registered voters about whom the registrar has received information that the voter no longer lives in their municipality using U.S. Postal Service change-of-address information (NCOA), the Electronic Registration Information Center (ERIC), or official notice that the voter has registered in another jurisdiction. Under existing law, voters can be placed on the inactive list, which can trigger a removal process, for failure to vote or appear in the annual town register for two consecutive years.
  • Require that upon credible information or allegation of illegal voter registration, or credible information or allegation of illegal multiple voting, registrars must proceed under receive and evaluate the complaint, and the attorney general or the appropriate district attorney investigate the information or allegation. Under existing law, local election and law enforcement officers are charged with investigating complaints of illegal or incorrect registrations.
  • Require an agent of the secretary of state to inspect every polling place at least every four years in order to ensure compliance with state and federal disability accessibility laws and relevant regulations issued by the secretary.
  • Establish a process for removal from the voter rolls based on incarceration for a felony conviction. Under existing law, individuals incarcerated for felony convictions are disenfranchised but there is no statutory process for removing them from municipal voter lists.
  • Establish the possibility of a fine for failure to respond to an annual address confirmation notice for two consecutive years.

Last Updated December 12, 2025

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 16, 2023, would end in-person early voting unless municipalities choose to offer it, site polling places near campuses, create a permanent mail voting list open to all voters, require drop boxes, and make other changes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • End mandatory in-person early voting for state and federal elections by repealing the requirement that municipalities offer it. Instead, municipalities could choose to offer in-person early voting for any election. Existing law allows municipalities to expand in-person early voting to local elections not held on the same day as a state or federal election but requires them to offer it in all other elections.
  • Require the board of elections in cities and towns to site at least one polling place within one mile of any public or private institution of higher education located within the geographical limits of the city or town, including without limitation any community college.
  • Create a permanent mail voting list open to all voters. Voters could join the list when registering to vote, or at any time by completing a special form or by using the ballot application portal on the State Secretary's website. The ability to join when registering would be offered on the standard registration form and as part of the automatic voter registration process. Voters could leave the list at any time by making a written request to the State Secretary or by using the online ballot application portal. Under existing law, voters with permanent physical disabilities can apply to join a list to be sent an application for an absentee ballot for each election.
  • Require the State Secretary to mail to all registered voters a permanent mail voter status request form by June 30, 2024, that includes a postage-prepaid return envelope pre-addressed to the local election official.
  • Require each municipality to offer at least 1 secured municipal ballot drop box in a public location that is accessible to voters for not less than 12 hours each day, including business hours. Municipalities would maintain these drop boxes starting on the earliest date that ballots become available to voters through the close of polls on Election Day. Municipalities with more than 25,000 registered voters would be required to offer one drop box per 25,000 registered voters. A municipality with fewer than 5,000 voters in excess of any 25,000 registered voter increment could seek a waiver from the State Secretary of the requirement to maintain an additional secured municipal ballot drop box for such population.
  • Require local governments to site the drop boxes by prioritizing, to the extent feasible:
    • proximity to public transportation and availability of parking
    • equitable distribution across population centers
    • access for persons with disabilities and
    • use of public buildings.
  • Change the deadline to mail a completed ballot back to election officials by allowing a time mailed ballot two more days to reach election officials. Specifically, if the ballot is mailed on or before Election Day, it would be timely if it is received by election officials by 5 p.m. on the fifth day after Election Day. Under existing law, the ballot must arrive by 5 p.m. on the third day after Election Day.
  • Revise the requirement that employers give an employee who is eligible to vote time off to vote if the employee requests it. Specifically, the bill would enable the employee to take two paid hours off to vote at any time during the early voting period or on Election Day. The bill would deem it unlawful for any employer to interfere with or deny the employee's ability to take the time, including by treating the voting leave as a negative factor in any employment action such as an evaluation, promotion, disciplinary action, or termination. Existing law limits the opportunity to the first two hours after polls open on Election Day, and does not provide protections against employer misconduct. Under both the bill and existing law, the employee must request the time.

  • Make staffing police officers at polling places optional instead of required as under existing law.

Last Updated March 27, 2023

HISTORY: {"date":"02/08/2024","summary":"From JOINT Committee on JUDICIARY: Accompanied Study Order S2612","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 16, 2023, would create felonies to attempt to protect election workers. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create a felony prohibiting a person from knowingly harassing, threatening, coercing, or intimidating an election worker, or attempting to do such acts, with the intent to impede or interfere with them while they are engaged in the performance of their duties or with the intent to retaliate against them because of their performance of their official duties.
    • The bill clarifies that the felony would include, but not be limited to, conduct or acts conducted in person, by gesture, verbally, by mail, and by use of an electronic communication device including, but not limited to, electronic mail, internet communications, cell phone communications, instant messages, and facsimile communications.
  • Create a felony to prohibit a person from knowingly making available on the internet personal information about an election worker or family members of an election worker if the dissemination of personal information promotes harassment, threats, coercion, and intimidation or poses an imminent and serious threat to the safety of the election worker or their family member.
  • Define key terms for the crimes. Specifically:
    • "Election worker" would apply to any person working full-time, part-time, or under contract, whether paid or unpaid, for the Commonwealth of Massachusetts or any municipality and who is performing duties and activities in connection with, and in the furtherance of, the administration of elections.
    • "Election duties" would apply to duties and responsibilities required or authorized by law to administer and conduct elections.
    • "Family members" would apply to an election worker's spouse, child, parent, or any person residing in their same household.
    • "Personal information" would apply to an election worker's home address, personal phone number(s), personal email address, personal motor vehicle, motor vehicle number plate, a photograph of the election worker, their home, and their motor vehicle.

  • Set the punishment for these crimes:

    • For the first offense, imprisonment for not more than four years or by a fine of not more than $10,000 or both.
    • For any subsequent conviction, imprisonment for not more than ten years or by a fine of not more than $25,000 or both.

Last Updated March 27, 2023

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2023, would impose new restrictions on voting by mail by:

  • Requiring people who vote by mail to have their signature on their ballot certificate witnessed.
  • Requiring election officials to match the voter's signature to one in their registration record in accordance with regulations the bill would require the State Board of Elections to issue.

  • Rejecting ballots with mismatched signatures or unwitnessed signatures.

    The bill would exempt UOCAVA voters from the witness requirement.

Last Updated January 12, 2023

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2023, would require in-person voters to show a photo ID document before receiving a ballot, and create a misdemeanor prohibiting voting or attempting to vote using a fake ID. Under existing law, election workers verify a voter's identity without requesting a document. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require in-person voters to show an acceptable ID document to receive a regular ballot. Voters who fail to show the required ID documentation would be required to vote a provisional ballot. Accepted ID types would be:
    • a valid government-issued photo identification, or
    • a valid nongovernment-issued photo identification, and
    • a current utility bill, bank statement, paycheck, government check, or another government document that states the voter's name and address.

  • Create a misdemeanor to prohibit voting or attempting to vote under a false form of identification.

Last Updated January 19, 2023

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2023, would create "curbside voting", a process of voting at a designated outside location under the observation of election judges, to facilitate voting by certain people who are disabled, unable to enter the polling place, pregnant, or face health risks for entering it. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Authorize these groups of people to use curbside voting:
    • voters with disabilities recognized by the federal Americans with Disabilities Act
    • voters physically unable to enter the polling place
    • pregnant voters
    • voters likely to have their health harmed by entering the polling place
    • voters authorized to make the request by the state board in the interest of public health and safety.
  • Require each local board of elections to offer curbside voting within 150 feet of these locations during the entire time polls are open:
    • each early voting center during early voting, and
    • at the office of the local board of election on Election Day, or if that is not practicable, at each polling place the State Board of Elections delegates in collaboration with the local board. Curbside voting locations would be required to be designated at least six months before a primary.
  • Require the curbside voting process to enable voters to mark their ballots secretly and without assistance unless the voter requests help. Curbside voters would use paper ballots. If a voter eligible for curbside voting wished to use a ballot marking device, they would need to enter the polling place. Once a voter marked their paper ballot, the election judge would put the completed ballot in the ballot box or scanner inside the polling place, and if scanned, would give the voter a receipt, if practicable.
  • Require local boards to:
    • post signage at curbside voting locations informing voters of its availability, who is eligible, and how to request the service,
    • ensure that curbside voters are timely provided the same information given to people voting inside,
    • provide an area that allows voters to get campaign literature.
    • maintain records of each use of curbside voting

  • Require certified voting systems to be able to accommodate curbside voting.

Last Updated January 19, 2023

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2023, would improve elderly and disabled voters' in-person voting experience. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require election worker training to include oral and written instruction in the various ways an election judge may assist or accommodate elderly and disabled voters, including providing individualized accommodations at a voter's request or the request of a person accompanying the voter who needs assistance.
  • Require the State Board of Elections to develop signage that allows each polling place to inform voters of the available assistance and accommodations using standardized language while enabling polling places to customize the sign if not every method is available at a specific polling place, and

  • Require polling places to post the signage prominently at the entrances to the polling place and near the check-in table.

    Last updated January 19, 2023

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2023, would enable voters who are not affiliated with a party to participate more easily in Maryland's closed primary system by allowing them to affiliate with a party by 5 p.m. on the day before early voting starts. All other voters wishing to join a party to vote in its primary must affiliate by the 21st day before Election Day, which is eight days earlier than the day before early voting starts and is the day regular voter registration ends.

Last Updated January 19, 2023

This bill, as enacted on April 7, 2023, changes the process for establishing polling places, creates a public comment process for proposed changes to polling place locations, and creates a misdemeanor offense for intimidating individuals voting by mail.

Regarding the designation of polling places, the bill:

  • Requires that, at least six months before each statewide primary election, each local board submit a polling place plan to the State Board of Elections for approval. The plan must include:
    • Evidence that the plan complies with statutory requirements for polling sites,
    • An analysis of how to maximize voter participation in each precinct, and
    • For proposals to reduce the total number of separate buildings used as polling places from the total number used in the 2018 general election, eight additional categories of data, including information about specific locations, transportation and disability accessibility, voting methods used in the precinct and voter population, and impact on "historically disenfranchised communities" (defined by the bill as "racial, ethnic, or socioeconomic groups that have historically been subject to voter suppression efforts").
  • Requires the State Board to approve a polling place plan if the plan complies with the requirements of the bill and existing law, and will not negatively affect access to voting for historically disenfranchised communities. The bill also expressly requires the Board to reject any plan that does not meet these requirements.
  • In the case of a rejected polling place plan, requires a local board to submit a revised plan within 15 days after the rejection.

Regarding the process for changes to polling place locations, the bill creates a new public participation process that boards must engage in prior to taking action, unless changes are being made as the result of an emergency within the 21 days before Election Day. For polling place changes in the ordinary course, the bill:

  • Prohibits local boards from voting on changes to polling place locations unless they have first held a meeting to discuss the proposed change and provided the opportunity for interested individuals and organizations to testify at the meeting.
  • Requires local boards to maintain a contact list of individuals and organizations who wish to be notified about polling place changes and enable people and organizations to join that list.
  • Requires local boards to provide written notice at least 14 days before a board meeting to vote on changes to (1) the groups and individuals on the list, and (2) the mayor, county executive, county commissioner(s), county council member(s), municipal council member(s), and members of the Maryland General Assembly who are elected by voters using either the current or proposed polling location.

Regarding criminal penalties, the bill creates a new misdemeanor offense for influencing or attempting to influence, by using force, threat, or other prohibited conduct, a voter's decision to vote by means other than going to the polls (e.g., voting by mail). Under previous law, which the bill leaves in place, this offense was limited to interference with a voter's decision to "go to the polls to cast a vote."

The bill also includes provisions that change the date of Baltimore primaries, an aspect of election law that the Voting Rights Lab does not track.

Previous versions of the bill contained provisions that were amended out prior to enactment. Those provisions would have:

  • Required local boards that operated fewer polling places in 2022 than in the 2018 general election (in violation of statutory prohibitions against such reductions) to provide, for each relevant precinct, the same data as required in any polling plan that proposes reducing locations for future elections.
  • Authorized state officials to deny public access to election and voting records normally open to the public for five working days if (1) the request to inspect the records was received in the period beginning 90 days before Election Day through the certification of the election's results, and (2) the official custodian believed that inspection would cause substantial injury to the public interest by impairing the ability of the board of elections to prepare for the election. The provision would have required the custodian to petition the circuit court for continued denial of inspection within five working days of denying access, and set out the specific criteria for judicial review.

Last updated May 3, 2023

This bill, as introduced on January 30, 2023, would require each county board of education to post on its website a link to the voter registration webpage maintained on the website of the State Board of Elections or of the local board of elections of that county.

Last Updated February 8, 2023

This bill, as enacted on April 24, 2023, creates statutory requirements for a cure process for mail ballots (called "absentee ballots" in Maryland), requires local boards of election to start processing mail ballots before the start of early voting, sets a timeline for mailing ballots, and makes other changes to the election code. Specifically, the bill:

  • Creates statutory requirements for a cure process for mail ballots. The state's existing cure process was established by administrative rules promulgated under the State Board's general regulatory power, but previous statutory law had no specific requirements for these rules. By statute, the bill now:
    • Requires a local board of elections to review the mail ballot certificate "promptly" after receiving the returned ballot to determine whether the voter's signature is present. Existing law had no comparable requirement, although existing regulations make clear that local boards may confirm whether a voter signed the oath before canvassing ballots.
    • Requires the State Board to issue regulations mandating local boards to give a voter notice that their mail ballot is missing a signature as soon as practicable after discovering the omission, but not later than three business days after determining the signature was missing. This requirement is identical to existing regulations. The Board's rules must also allow a voter to (1) provide a signature through a digital picture message sent by email or phone, and (2) communicate with a local board about their missing signature through multiple options, including e-mail, an accessible online portal, a mailed form, and an in-person visit to the local board office. Existing Board regulations allow a voter to provide a signature by email, mail, in-person visit to the local board, or other means offered by the State Board.
    • Sets the deadline for voters to provide a missing signature by 10 a.m. on the 10th day after Election Day. The existing regulations do not set a deadline.
  • Requires local boards to record the receipt of a mail ballot in the statewide voter registration system and make the information available in the ballot tracking system as soon as possible but no later than two business days after receipt of a ballot provided by mail, and no later than four business days after receipt of a ballot provided by internet or by fax. Previous law provided for ballot tracking but did not include a deadline for entering data.
  • Requires local boards of election to begin processing mail ballots eight business days before the first day of early voting, unless the local board is granted a waiver due to the low volume of ballots received by that board or because such early processing is not practicable due to resource or other constraints. Mail ballot tallying is permitted during preprocessing, but the bill prohibits mail ballot tabulation before the opening of polls on Election Day and prohibits the release of mail vote totals before the close of polls. Under previous law, boards of elections could not open ballot envelopes before 8 a.m. on the Wednesday after Election Day, and existing regulations begin the canvass on Thursday after Election Day.
  • Requires local boards to send out mail ballots by the 43rd day before an election to those voters who applied for a mail ballot at least 60 days before the election. For voters who request a ballot less than 60 days before an election, the bill leaves in place the existing requirement that mail ballots be sent "as soon as practicable" after the request is received.
  • Requires local boards, if a voter returned more than one ballot, to count the first legally sufficient ballot and reject any others. Previous law required the local board to reject a provisional ballot if the voter cast more than one ballot, and in the event of receiving more than one mail ballot from a single voter, to count only the one with the latest properly signed oath.
  • Makes technical and conforming changes to various definitions for terms in the election code.

The bill also contains additional provisions related to topics that Voting Rights Lab does not track, including changes to reporting of election results and timing of primary elections.

Last Updated May 3, 2023

This bill, as introduced on February 1, 2023, would allow certain individuals living overseas to register to vote and vote in Maryland using certain processes but not others. Under existing law, if an individual never resided in Maryland, they are not considered a resident and cannot vote there. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Allow U.S. citizens born abroad who never lived in the U.S. to register to vote in the county that their parents lived in before moving abroad and vote if:
    • They have a parent or legal guardian who is registered to vote in Maryland or lived in Maryland before moving abroad and was either registered to vote in Maryland, was eligible to register in Maryland, or would have been eligible to register in Maryland had they been older, and
    • They have neither established a domicile in another state nor registered to vote in another state.
  • Provide that a person who qualifies as an "overseas voter" as defined in federal law and who lived in Maryland before moving abroad may register in the county they lived in before moving abroad only if they have not established a domicile in another state and is not registered to vote in another state.
  • Require overseas voters to register using the federal postcard application.

Last Updated September 3, 2026

This bill, as introduced on February 3, 2023, would require the Governor to certify the results of a presidential election based on the returns of the election delivered to the Governor. Existing law implies the Governor must do so, but the bill would make the requirement explicit.

Last updated February 9, 2023

This bill, as introduced on February 3, 2023, would shorten the early voting period to five days and eliminate voting on Saturday. Under existing law, the eight day early voting period runs from the second Thursday before Election Day through the Thursday before Election Day, and includes offering voting on both the Saturday and Sunday in that period. The bill would move the start date of the early voting period to the second Sunday before Election Day, and would leave the last day as the first Thursday before Election Day.

Last Updated February 8, 2023

HISTORY: {"date":"03/10/2023","summary":"To SENATE Committee on EDUCATION, ENERGY, AND THE ENVIRONMENT","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on March 7, 2023, would empower the State Board of Elections to remove the State Administrator of Elections without cause upon the vote of four of the five commissioners and provide that the terminated State Administrator cease working immediately. Under existing law, four members can vote to remove a State Administrator for cause after notice and an opportunity to be heard, and the Administrator would remain in office until the new Administrator was appointed and confirmed by the Maryland Senate. Requiring at least four votes ensures bipartisanship, as the State Board has three members of one major political party and two of the other.

As amended, the bill would also provide that the State Administrator serve a four-year term starting on August 1, that the State Administrator as of June 1, 2023, would have to leave office on July 31, 2023, unless they are appointed to the term starting on August 1.

Last updated March 8, 2023

This bill, as introduced on February 10, 2023, would allow voters who are checking in to vote in person to use an ID document to identify themselves instead of the existing process in which they state the month and day of their birth, which is then verified against their registration record. Using an ID document would not be required, the existing process would remain fully available. Voters who preferred to use an ID document could present any of the following:

  • The voter's voter registration card
  • The voter's valid Maryland driver's license

  • Any identification card that contains a photograph of the voter and is issued to the voter by:

    • a political subdivision of the state,
    • any unit of a political subdivision of the state,
    • the state, or
    • the federal government.

Last Updated February 10, 2023

This bill, as introduced on February 10, 2023, would enable candidates to get a list of voters who requested absentee ballots, including the voters' email addresses if available, on the same terms and conditions that voter registration lists may be requested.

Last Updated February 15, 2023

This bill, as introduced on February 10, 2023, would create misdemeanors to protect election officials from interference with their work or having their personal information put on the internet in certain circumstances, and would create a process for election officials to request the Department of Assessments and Taxation to redact personal information relating to the officials the Department ordinarily includes in a public real estate database it publishes on the internet. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create a misdemeanor to prohibit inducing an election official to violate or to refuse to comply with their official duties or any law or regulation regulating their official duties or threatening, coercing, or intimidating the election official with the intent to (1) impede or interfere with the election official performing their official duties or (2) retaliate against the election official for performing their official duties.
    • This crime would not apply to an enforcement action brought by an election official against an election judge for a violation of law, a regulation adopted by the state board, or an election judge's oath.
  • Create a misdemeanor to prohibit a person from posting on the internet personal information regarding an election official or a member of an election official's immediate family if the person knows or reasonably should know that the dissemination of the personal information poses an imminent and serious threat to the safety of the election official or a member of an election official's immediate family.
    • "Personal information" would mean home address, home or personal mobile telephone number, pager number, personal e""mail address, a photograph of the individual, directions to, photograph of, or description of the individual's home, personal vehicle or license plate, or immediate family member's personal vehicle or license plate.
    • "Immediate family" would mean a spouse, child, or parent, or an individual who lives in the same residence.
  • Enable people employed by a county, a municipality, the state board of elections, or a local board of elections to perform election duties to ask the Department of Assessment and Taxation to redact personal information from the real property assessment database the department makes publicly available online if they are threatened. Poll workers and other temporary employees would not be eligible for this protection. Both "personal information" and "immediate family" would be defined as they are for the new misdemeanor. Specifically, if the inclusion of covered election workers' personal information in the database poses an imminent and serious threat to them or their immediate family, they may submit a redaction request on a form created by Department that includes:
    • A statement that their personal information is in the database, its disclosure poses an imminent and serious threat to them, and they fear for their safety or the safety of their immediate family,
    • Evidence that their information is in the public database and they are employed as an election worker,
    • The address the election worker wants redacted from the database,
    • An attestation that all the information in the request is true,
    • The election worker's signature and the date the request was signed, and
    • A voluntary release and waiver of all future claims against the state that may arise from the request except for a claim based on gross negligence.

  • Require the Department, on receipt of such a request, to review it and after confirming it is properly completed, redact the information and reject requests to review or release a copy of the redacted information unless the person asking has been specifically authorized by the bill to make the request. The redaction would be valid for two years unless the election worker cancels the request sooner by submitting a signed request. These people would be allowed by the bill to request the redacted information if they attest that they are in the category of people allowed to make a request and support their attestation with evidence:

    • a party to the record,
    • a settlement service,
    • a title insurance company or agency,
    • a mortgage servicer or a mortgage servicer's qualified agent, or
    • a licensed attorney who is engaged in a real estate matter.

    Last updated February 16, 2023

This bill, as introduced on February 10, 2023, would create a voting rights act aimed at regulating the elections and voting-related policies of counties and municipalities to ensure that voting rights are protected generally, and provide specific protections for certain classes of voters. The bill provides protections against vote dilution, requires preclearance, requires language access, prohibits voter intimidation, creates a statewide database of election data to enable discrimination detection and further best practices, and facilitates enforcement with special litigation processes.

As a threshold matter, the bill would declare that state and local laws, rules, regulations, charters, and ordinances must be construed liberally in favor of:

  • Protecting the right to cast a ballot
  • Ensuring that eligible voters are not impaired in registering to vote or voting, including having their votes counted

  • Ensuring protected class voters equitable access to opportunities to register to vote and vote.

    The anti-vote dilution provisions focus on protected classes that engage in racially polarized voting. "Protected class" would mean a class of citizens who are members of a race, color, or language minority group, as referenced in the federal Voting Rights Act. "Racially polarized voting" would mean voting in which there is a divergence between the candidate or electoral choice preferred by protected class voters and the candidate or electoral choice preferred by other voters. This section of the bill would:

  • Declare that a local government may not deny, impair, or diminish the right to vote of protected class members through any:
    • qualification for eligibility to be a voter or other prerequisite to voting, or
    • ordinance, regulation, or other law regarding the administration of elections, or any standard, practice, procedure, or policy.
  • Define as violations of that prohibition:
    • implementation of a prerequisite to voting, a rule relating to election administration, or any policy that results or will result in any disparity or reduction in voter participation, voting access, or ability to participate in the political process among protected class members, or which, based on the totality of the circumstances, results in any impairment of the opportunity or ability of protected class members to participate in the political process, elect candidates of their choice, or otherwise influence election outcomes.
    • enactment of a prerequisite to voting, a rule relating to election administration, or any policy that has the purpose or effect of diminishing the ability of any protected class voter to participate in the electoral process or elect their preferred candidates.
  • Prohibit a local government from using a method of election that has the effect, or is partially motivated by the intent, of impairing protected class voters' ability to participate in the political process, elect candidates of their choice, or otherwise influence election outcomes by diluting or abridging their votes.
  • Define as violations of that prohibition:
    • Implementing an at-large method of election where racially polarized voting by protected class voters occurs, or based on the totality of the circumstances, the opportunity or ability of protected class voters to participate in the political process, elect candidates of their choice, or otherwise influence election outcomes is impaired.
    • Implementing a district-based or another method of election where the candidates or electoral choices of protected class members would usually be defeated and either racially polarized voting by protected class voters occurs or based on the totality of the circumstances, the opportunity or ability of protected class voters to participate in the political process, elect candidates of their choice, or otherwise influence election outcomes is impaired.
    • Implementing any method of election that has the purpose of, or will have the effect of, diminishing the ability of any protected class voter to participate in the electoral process or elect the preferred candidates of choice of the protected class member.

  • Create a pre-lawsuit process to speed the implementation of remedies. The bill would:

    • Require potential plaintiffs to send a notification letter to the relevant local government asserting a possible violation prior to filing suit. A suit would be delayed for 50 days after sending the letter.
    • Allow local governments to forestall suit by adopting a resolution within 60 days of such a letter being sent. The resolution would affirm the local government's intent to enact and implement a remedy, establish specific measures it would take, and provide a schedule for taking them. A suit could not be filed for 90 days after such a resolution was adopted.
    • Create a process for the Civil Rights Division of the Office of Attorney General ("Civil Rights Division") to review and then accept or reject remedies proposed by the local government.
    • Allow parties that sent a notification letter to submit a detailed reimbursement claim from the local government for the costs of producing and sending the letter up to a cumulative total of $50,000, if the process successfully resolves the violation.
    • Allow parties to seek preliminary relief notwithstanding this pre-suit process if an election impacted by the violation is scheduled within 120 days. The preliminary relief would be granted if the court decides the party is more likely than not to succeed on the merits and it is possible to implement an appropriate remedy before the election. Nonetheless, if the action is dismissed or withdrawn because of the local government's enactment or implementation of a remedy or the approval of the Civil Rights Division of a remedy, the parties could only seek reimbursement for costs relating to the notification letter.

    If the notice letter process failed and the case went forward in court, the bill would:

  • Specify what evidence a court must consider and must not consider when determining if racially polarized voting in a local government election occurs, or if candidates or electoral choices preferred by protected class voters would be usually defeated.
  • Specify what factors a court may and may not consider in determining whether, based on the totality of the circumstances, a denial or impairment of the opportunity or ability of protected class members to participate in the political process, elect candidates of their choice, or otherwise influence election outcomes.
  • Require courts, after finding a violation, to order remedies tailored to address the violation. Such remedies could not diminish the ability of protected class members to participate in the political process, elect candidates of their choice, or otherwise influence election outcomes. The court would be required to consider remedies proposed by any parties, but prohibited from giving deference or priority to a remedy because it was proposed by the local government.
  • Authorize the court to impose remedies that are inconsistent with any other provision of state or local law if that state or local law would otherwise prevent the court from ordering an appropriate remedy. Remedies could include:
    • a district-based method of election,
    • an alternative method of election, including proportional ranked-choice voting, cumulative voting, or limited voting,
    • new or revised districting plans,
    • elimination of staggered elections,
    • reasonably increasing the size of the legislative body
    • additional voting hours or days
    • additional polling locations
    • additional means of voting, such as voting by mail or additional opportunities to return ballots
    • ordering special elections
    • requiring expanded opportunities for the admission of voters
    • requiring additional voter education
    • restoring or adding people to a voter registry
    • the court retaining jurisdiction, and if so, the court must preclear any new or change to prerequisites to voting or standards, practices, or procedures. The court could allow such changes only after finding that they do not have the purpose and would not have the effect of impairing or diminishing the right to vote on the basis of protected class membership.

  • Require local governments to hold detailed public hearings including specified notice processes before enacting and implementing either:

    • a new method of election to replace an at-large method
    • a new districting plan proposed after being sued or threatened with suit for an alleged violation of this bill or the federal Voting Rights Act.

    The bill would require "covered jurisdictions" to get permission before implementing any "covered policies", a process called "preclearance." A covered jurisdiction would have a choice about how to get preclearance for a covered policy. The jurisdiction could either submit the policy to the Civil Rights Division of the Attorney General's office or to the court for Anne Arundel County. If a covered jurisdiction failed to seek preclearance for a covered policy, the bill would enable individuals, organizations, and the Civil Rights Division to enjoin the covered policy until it is precleared. A special preclearance process would be developed for use during emergencies. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create a preclearance process at the Civil Rights Division. To use this process the covered jurisdiction would submit the policy to the Division. Thereafter:
    • The Division would post the covered policy on its website within 10 days and solicit public comment. Depending on the type of policy, the period of public comment would be 5, 10, or 20 business days. The Division would review the policy and the public comments in making its determination. The Division could seek more information from the covered jurisdiction, and the jurisdiction would bear the burden of proof that the covered policy should be approved.
    • The Division would approve, conditionally approve, or reject the policy. If the Division conditionally approves the policy, it could then reject the policy, but the rejection would need to be within 60 days of the receipt of the policy. If the Division fails to act within the deadlines imposed by the bill, the policy would be deemed approved.
    • The Division would only be able to reject a policy if it determined that the policy is more likely than not to diminish the opportunity or ability of protected class members to participate in the political process and elect candidates of their choice or otherwise influence the outcome of elections, or that the policy is more likely than not to violate the bill. A decision to preclear or reject a covered policy would not be admissible in a future challenge to covered policy.
    • Denials of preclearance could be appealed to the Supreme Court of Maryland.
  • Create a preclearance process at the Circuit Court for Anne Arundel. The covered jurisdiction would submit the policy in writing and contemporaneously send the policy to the Civil Rights Division. If the Division isn't contemporaneously served, the policy would be automatically denied. Assuming notice is given as required, thereafter:
    • The covered jurisdiction would have the burden of proof, just as in the other process.
    • The court could deny preclearance only if it determined that the policy is more likely than not to diminish the opportunity or ability of protected class members to participate in the political process and elect candidates of their choice or otherwise influence the outcome of elections, or that the policy is more likely than not to violate the bill, just as in the other process. A decision to preclear or reject a covered policy would not be admissible in a future challenge to a covered policy.
    • The court would be required to rule on preclearance within 60 days, but if it does not, the policy could not be implemented until preclearance is affirmatively granted.
    • Denials would be appealed under the ordinary rules of appellate procedure, however, it would be expedited.
  • Authorize the State Board of Elections, in consultation with the Civil Rights Division, to adopt regulations creating an expedited, emergency preclearance process if a covered policy occurs during or immediately before an election as a result of a disaster, emergency, or other exigent circumstances. Preclearance through such a process would be preliminary and could be revoked by the Civil Rights Division within 60 days of receipt of the covered policy.
  • Authorize plaintiffs to seek an injunction to prevent the implementation of a covered policy that was not submitted for preclearance.
  • Define "covered jurisdiction" as any local government:
    • that within the immediately preceding 25 years, became subject to a court order or government enforcement action based on a violation of this bill, the federal Voting Rights Act, the 15th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, or a voting-related violation of the 14th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.
    • that within the immediately preceding 25 years, became subject to at least three court orders or government enforcement actions based on a finding of a violation of a federal or state civil rights law or the 14th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution concerning discrimination against members of a protected class.
    • where the combined misdemeanor and felony arrest rate of members of any protected class consisting of at least 10,000 voting-age citizens or whose members are at least 10% of the citizen voting-age population served by the local government exceeds the proportion that the protected class constitutes of the citizen voting-age population served by the local government by at least 20% at any point in within the immediately preceding 10 years.
    • where, based on data made available by the U.S. Bureau of the Census, the dissimilarity index of any protected class of at least 25,000 voting-age citizens or whose members are at least 10% of the voting-age population of the local government has been more than 50 with respect to the race, color, or language minority group that is a majority within the local government at any point in the immediate preceding 10 years.
    • or a local board of elections in a county that is a covered jurisdiction.

  • Define "covered policy" as a new or modified local government qualification for admission as a voter, prerequisite to voting, or a regulation, ordinance, standard, practice, procedure, or policy concerning:

    • a change to the method or dates of election of a governing body or an elected school board
    • a change to the boundaries of election districts or wards, including changes made under a decennial redistricting
    • a change to the form of government for a local government
    • an annexation, incorporation, dissolution, consolidation, or division of a local government
    • a change to voter registration list maintenance or other activities concerning the cancelation or denial of voter registration
    • a change to the assignment of a voting precinct, polling place, or drop box location, including the relocation of voters, the relocation or reduction of hours of any polling place or ballot drop box, or the reduction or consolidation of polling places or ballot drop boxes,
    • a change to translation or interpretation services in any language other than English, including the creation or distribution of voting materials in any language other than English,
    • a change to assistance to voters with disabilities, including the creation or distribution of voting materials for voters with disabilities, or
    • any additional subject matter that the state board, in consultation with the civil rights division, may identify for inclusion by regulation if the civil rights division determines that any qualification for admission as a voter, prerequisite to voting, or any ordinance, regulation, standard, practice, procedure, or policy concerning the subject matter may have the effect of impairing or diminishing the right to vote of any protected class voter.

    The bill would require language assistance. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the State Board of Elections to make certain determinations of language assistance for non-native English speakers using the American Community Survey or equivalent data, and then using those determinations, publish on its website on or before January 1, 2024, and every three years thereafter, a list of each local government election that requires non-English language-related assistance and the kind of assistance required.
  • Require the State Board to issue regulations relating to how it will make the determinations of language assistance needs, and to include a process through which the public can propose languages for evaluation.
  • Require local governments to competently provide the required language assistance and materials on their website and in physical materials, including
    • registration and voting notices
    • election-related forms and instructions
    • ballot and other materials relating to the electoral process.
    • bilingual poll workers where available.

  • Enable lawsuits both to enforce the language assistance provisions and to enable local governments to provide English-only materials. The court would allow English-only materials if it found the State Board's determination of need was arbitrary and capricious, or an abuse of discretion.

    The bill would create a statewide election database and information office to assist state and local governments with evaluating current election laws and practices for consistency with the voting rights protections in the bill, implementing best practices, and investigating potential infringements on the right to vote. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create the Statewide Election Database and Information Office within the State Board of Elections. The Office would be headed by a Director, who would be responsible for the operation and administration of the Office and oversee a staff provided by the State Board. The Director would be an employee of the State Board, appointed by the Governor, and must hold an advanced degree from an accredited university and have expertise in demography, statistics, and electoral systems. The Office would maintain, in an electronic format, at least 12 years of elections-related data using the most advanced, peer-reviewed, and validated methodologies. The Office would make the data publicly available on the State Board's website for free, except that information that would identify individual voters would be redacted. The data would include:
    • estimates of the total population, voting age population, and citizen voting age population by race, color, and language minority group, broken down annually to the precinct level for each local government
    • election results at the precinct level for state and local government elections
    • regularly updated voter registration lists, geocoded locations for each registered voter, and other voter records, including voter history files for each election in each local government
    • districting plans and precinct boundaries for each election in each local government,
    • geocoded locations of polling places and ballot drop boxes for each election in each local government, and a list or description of the districts or geographic areas served by each polling place or ballot drop box location, and
    • any other information that the director determines advisable to maintain in furtherance of the purposes of the office and this title.
  • Require the authority responsible for administering a local election to transmit data to the Office on the certification of election results and the finalization of other voter records, specifically:
    • the election results at the precinct level
    • contemporaneous registration lists
    • voter records or voter history files
    • election district and precinct boundaries and
    • lists of polling place and ballot drop box locations and lists or descriptions of the districts or geographic areas served by the locations.
  • Require state agencies identified by the Director as possessing necessary information to provide it once a year to the Director, or more frequently if requested by the Director.

  • Authorize the Director to provide nonpartisan technical assistance to local governments, researchers, and members of the public seeking to use the resources of the statewide database.

    The bill would create new prohibitions on voter intimidation and obstruction, identify conduct that would automatically violate the prohibitions, and enable impacted people to sue. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Prohibit a person, whether acting under the color of law or otherwise, from engaging in acts of intimidation, deception, or obstruction that interferes with an individual's right to vote.
  • Define as violations of that prohibition:
    • the use of force or threats to use force, or the use of any other conduct to practice intimidation that causes or will reasonably have the effect of causing interference with an individual's right to vote,
    • the knowing use of a deceptive or fraudulent device, contrivance, or communication that causes or will reasonably have the effect of causing interference with any individual's right to vote, or
    • interference with access to a polling place, a ballot drop box, or an office or a place of business of an election official or a voter or an election official in a manner that causes or will reasonably have the effect of causing interference with any individual's right to vote or any delay in voting or the voting process.

  • Enable plaintiffs to sue over alleged violations in the circuit court for Anne Arundel County and provide that if the court finds a violation:

    • The court must order appropriate, tailored remedies that could include additional time to vote
    • The person who committed or aided the violation would be liable for any damages awarded by the court, including nominal damages for any violation and compensatory or punitive damages for any willful violation.

    Finally, the bill would empower enforcement of all of the provisions in the bill by creating certain litigation rules and enabling parties to recover costs and fees. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Enable any of these parties to file suit to enforce any of the provisions in the bill:
    • an aggrieved person
    • an organization whose membership includes or is likely to include aggrieved persons,
    • an organization whose mission would be frustrated by a violation of this section,
    • an organization that would expend resources to fulfill its mission as a result of a violation of this section, or
    • the Civil Rights Division.
  • Give enforcement actions expedited proceedings and automatic calendar preference.
  • Direct courts to grant preliminary injunctions relating to upcoming elections if the party is more likely than not to succeed on the merits, and it is possible to implement an appropriate remedy that would resolve the alleged violation in the upcoming election

  • Allow the prevailing party to recover reasonable attorneys' fees and litigation costs, including expert witness fees and expenses. However, a state or local government would not be awarded costs or fees unless the court decides the action was frivolous, unreasonable, or without foundation. When the state or local government is the opposing party, a party would be defined as prevailing if as a result of the action the government yields some or all of the relief sought.

    Last updated February 22, 2023

This bill, as enacted on April 24, 2023, sets statewide minimum pay for poll workers and mandates a poll worker recruitment campaign. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires boards of elections to pay poll workers at least $50 per required training session and pay new election workers at least $250/day for each early voting day or Election Day worked. Experienced election workers must be paid at least $100/day more than new workers. Local governments must appropriate sufficient funds to enable local boards of elections to pay wage minimums, and local boards may pay above the minimum, as permitted by local appropriations. Previous law provided wage minimums for only select counties in the state, in each case lower than the bill now requires, and did not expressly require compensation for training.
  • Requires the State Board of Elections to reimburse local boards $50 of the extra $100 paid to returning workers.

  • Requires the State Board to develop a marketing campaign to recruit poll workers that targets diverse populations, including multilingual people, and must give the campaign to local boards.

This bill, as introduced on February 10, 2023, would require the State Board of Elections to issue rules that would enable a voter to prevent their registration information and voting history from being sold to a person other than an employee or vendor of the State Board or of a local board of elections.

This bill, as introduced on January 27, 2023, would create a misdemeanor to punish willfully and knowingly casting a ballot in a general election in more than one state in one year.

Last updated January 27, 2023

This bill, as enacted on April 24, 2023, creates statutory requirements for a cure process for mail ballots (called "absentee ballots" in Maryland), requires local boards of election to start processing mail ballots before the start of early voting, sets a timeline for mailing ballots, and makes other changes to the election code. Specifically, the bill:

  • Creates statutory requirements for a cure process for mail ballots. The state's existing cure process was established by administrative rules promulgated under the State Board's general regulatory power, but previous statutory law had no specific requirements for these rules. By statute, the bill now:
    • Requires a local board of elections to review the mail ballot certificate "promptly" after receiving the returned ballot to determine whether the voter's signature is present. Existing law had no comparable requirement, although existing regulations make clear that local boards may confirm whether a voter signed the oath before canvassing ballots.
    • Requires the State Board to issue regulations mandating local boards to give a voter notice that their mail ballot is missing a signature as soon as practicable after discovering the omission, but not later than three business days after determining the signature was missing. This requirement is identical to existing regulations. The Board's rules must also allow a voter to (1) provide a signature through a digital picture message sent by email or phone, and (2) communicate with a local board about their missing signature through multiple options, including e-mail, an accessible online portal, a mailed form, and an in-person visit to the local board office. Existing Board regulations allow a voter to provide a signature by email, mail, in-person visit to the local board, or other means offered by the State Board.
    • Sets the deadline for voters to provide a missing signature by 10 a.m. on the 10th day after Election Day. The existing regulations do not set a deadline.
  • Requires local boards to record the receipt of a mail ballot in the statewide voter registration system and make the information available in the ballot tracking system as soon as possible but no later than two business days after receipt of a ballot provided by mail, and no later than four business days after receipt of a ballot provided by internet or by fax. Previous law provided for ballot tracking but did not include a deadline for entering data.
  • Requires local boards of election to begin processing mail ballots eight business days before the first day of early voting, unless the local board is granted a waiver due to the low volume of ballots received by that board or because such early processing is not practicable due to resource or other constraints. Mail ballot tallying is permitted during preprocessing, but the bill prohibits mail ballot tabulation before the opening of polls on Election Day and prohibits the release of mail vote totals before the close of polls. Under previous law, boards of elections could not open ballot envelopes before 8 a.m. on the Wednesday after Election Day, and existing regulations begin the canvass on Thursday after Election Day.
  • Requires local boards to send out mail ballots by the 43rd day before an election to those voters who applied for a mail ballot at least 60 days before the election. For voters who request a ballot less than 60 days before an election, the bill leaves in place the existing requirement that mail ballots be sent "as soon as practicable" after the request is received.
  • Requires local boards, if a voter returned more than one ballot, to count the first legally sufficient ballot and reject any others. Previous law required the local board to reject a provisional ballot if the voter cast more than one ballot, and in the event of receiving more than one mail ballot from a single voter, to count only the one with the latest properly signed oath.
  • Makes technical and conforming changes to various definitions for terms in the election code.

The bill also contains additional provisions related to topics that Voting Rights Lab does not track, including changes to reporting of election results and timing of primary elections.

Last Updated May 2, 2023

This bill, as introduced on February 3, 2023, would require the Department of Legislative Services to do a study on the creation of an electronic ballot return system, and the State Board of Elections to propose legislation reflecting the results. The study report would be due on or before December 1, 2023, and the State Board would be required to propose legislation by January 1, 2024. The study must consider:

  • The impact on disabled, uniformed, and overseas voters of being required to return paper ballots.
  • Best practices for accessibility and security of electronic ballot return
  • The integration of such a system with the State's existing election infrastructure, including cost of implementation and any changes to election law that are necessary
  • Which voters are eligible for electronic ballot return in the states that offer it

  • The mechanism to opt in to electronic ballot return

This bill, as introduced on February 6, 2023, would require voters to present photo ID documentation to receive an in-person ballot, whether on Election Day or during early voting. Voters who do not present satisfactory ID documentation would be required to cast provisional ballots. Under existing law, voters are identified by stating the month and day of their birth and having that information checked against registration records. The bill would also create a new misdemeanor prohibiting attempting to vote or voting using a fake ID.

Under the bill, these ID documents would be accepted:

  • A valid government-issued photo ID, or

  • Both:

    • a valid non-government-issued photo ID, and
    • a current utility bill, bank statement, paycheck, government check, or another government document that states the voter's name and address.

his bill, as introduced on February 6, 2023, would allow certain U.S. citizens living overseas to register and vote in Maryland elections. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Allow an overseas voter who previously resided in Maryland to register and vote in federal, state, and local elections in the Maryland county where the voter last resided before leaving the United States, if the voter was eligible to register before leaving or would have been eligible but for age. This bill, as enacted on April 24, 2023, changes the procedures for removal of the State Administrator of Elections by the State Board of Elections. This bill, as introduced on February 6, 2023, would create a misdemeanor to protect county election officials, narrow grounds for rejecting mail ballots (called "absentee ballots" in Maryland), narrow who may apply to receive a ballot by internet, set a deadline for mail ballots to be sent to voters, and require the State Board of Elections to develop certain plans and reports. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create a misdemeanor to prohibit a person from knowingly and willfully making a threat to take the life of, kidnap, or cause physical injury to a county election director. An existing misdemeanor prohibits the same conduct against other public officials, including state and local officials.
  • Narrow an existing ground for rejecting mail ballots. The bill would require ballots to be counted despite stray marks, blemishes, or writing on the ballot unless the mark is clearly an identifying mark intentionally placed on the ballot for the purpose of identifying it. Stray marks and blemishes would include a tear, fold, food spill, or errant punctuation. Existing law authorizes ballot rejection only if the ballot is intentionally marked with an identifying mark that is clearly evident and placed on the ballot for the purpose of identifying the ballot but lacks the detail provided by the bill.
  • Reduce options for receiving a mail ballot by eliminating ballot delivery by fax and limiting who is eligible to receive a ballot by internet delivery. Existing law authorizes ballot delivery by fax and allows any voter to receive a ballot by internet. Under the bill, only these voters could receive a ballot by internet:
    • Uniformed and overseas voters
    • Disabled voters unable to mark a ballot independently by hand
    • A voter with a medical emergency or who is hospitalized
    • A voter who has an unforeseen and short-notice travel commitment
    • Any other voter who would be unable to vote if the voter could not receive a mail ballot electronically.
  • Require mail ballots to be sent to voters not later than 47 days before the election. Existing law does not specify a ballot mailing deadline.
  • Require the State Board of Elections, by January 31, 2024, to develop and implement strategies to inform voters about voting by mail and the rare circumstances in which internet ballots may be requested. The State Board would also be required to report on the plan and its implementation to the Legislature by that date.
  • Require the State Board to analyze election data within 90 days of primary and general election days in 2024 and 2026 to determine why voters cast provision ballots and report the analysis to the Legislature.

  • Make changes to presidential elector certificates and related processes, as well as circuit court judge elections and election equipment purchasing that Voting Rights Lab does not track.
