This bill, as introduced on February 8, 2023, would create a voting rights act aimed at regulating the elections and voting-related policies of counties and municipalities to ensure that voting rights are protected generally, and provide specific protections for certain classes of voters. The bill provides protections against vote dilution, requires preclearance, requires language access, prohibits voter intimidation, creates a statewide database of election data to enable discrimination detection and further best practices, and facilitates enforcement with special litigation processes.

As a threshold matter, the bill would declare that state and local laws, rules, regulations, charters, and ordinances must be construed liberally in favor of:

  • Protecting the right to cast a ballot
  • Ensuring that eligible voters are not impaired in registering to vote or voting, including having their votes counted

  • Ensuring protected class voters equitable access to opportunities to register to vote and vote.

    The anti-vote dilution provisions focus on protected classes that engage in racially polarized voting. "Protected class" would mean a class of citizens who are members of a race, color, or language minority group, as referenced in the federal Voting Rights Act. "Racially polarized voting" would mean voting in which there is a divergence between the candidate or electoral choice preferred by protected class voters and the candidate or electoral choice preferred by other voters. This section of the bill would:

  • Declare that a local government may not deny, impair, or diminish the right to vote of protected class members through any:
    • qualification for eligibility to be a voter or other prerequisite to voting, or
    • ordinance, regulation, or other law regarding the administration of elections, or any standard, practice, procedure, or policy.
  • Define as violations of that prohibition:
    • implementation of a prerequisite to voting, a rule relating to election administration, or any policy that results or will result in any disparity or reduction in voter participation, voting access, or ability to participate in the political process among protected class members, or which, based on the totality of the circumstances, results in any impairment of the opportunity or ability of protected class members to participate in the political process, elect candidates of their choice, or otherwise influence election outcomes.
    • enactment of a prerequisite to voting, a rule relating to election administration, or any policy that has the purpose or effect of diminishing the ability of any protected class voter to participate in the electoral process or elect their preferred candidates.
  • Prohibit a local government from using a method of election that has the effect, or is partially motivated by the intent, of impairing protected class voters' ability to participate in the political process, elect candidates of their choice, or otherwise influence election outcomes by diluting or abridging their votes.
  • Define as violations of that prohibition:
    • Implementing an at-large method of election where racially polarized voting by protected class voters occurs, or based on the totality of the circumstances, the opportunity or ability of protected class voters to participate in the political process, elect candidates of their choice, or otherwise influence election outcomes is impaired.
    • Implementing a district-based or another method of election where the candidates or electoral choices of protected class members would usually be defeated and either racially polarized voting by protected class voters occurs or based on the totality of the circumstances, the opportunity or ability of protected class voters to participate in the political process, elect candidates of their choice, or otherwise influence election outcomes is impaired.
    • Implementing any method of election that has the purpose of, or will have the effect of, diminishing the ability of any protected class voter to participate in the electoral process or elect the preferred candidates of choice of the protected class member.

  • Create a pre-lawsuit process to speed the implementation of remedies. The bill would:

    • Require potential plaintiffs to send a notification letter to the relevant local government asserting a possible violation prior to filing suit. A suit would be delayed for 50 days after sending the letter.
    • Allow local governments to forestall suit by adopting a resolution within 60 days of such a letter being sent. The resolution would affirm the local government's intent to enact and implement a remedy, establish specific measures it would take, and provide a schedule for taking them. A suit could not be filed for 90 days after such a resolution was adopted.
    • Create a process for the Civil Rights Division of the Office of Attorney General ("Civil Rights Division") to review and then accept or reject remedies proposed by the local government.
    • Allow parties that sent a notification letter to submit a detailed reimbursement claim from the local government for the costs of producing and sending the letter up to a cumulative total of $50,000, if the process successfully resolves the violation.
    • Allow parties to seek preliminary relief notwithstanding this pre-suit process if an election impacted by the violation is scheduled within 120 days. The preliminary relief would be granted if the court decides the party is more likely than not to succeed on the merits and it is possible to implement an appropriate remedy before the election. Nonetheless, if the action is dismissed or withdrawn because of the local government's enactment or implementation of a remedy or the approval of the Civil Rights Division of a remedy, the parties could only seek reimbursement for costs relating to the notification letter.

    If the notice letter process failed and the case went forward in court, the bill would:

  • Specify what evidence a court must consider and must not consider when determining if racially polarized voting in a local government election occurs, or if candidates or electoral choices preferred by protected class voters would be usually defeated.
  • Specify what factors a court may and may not consider in determining whether, based on the totality of the circumstances, a denial or impairment of the opportunity or ability of protected class members to participate in the political process, elect candidates of their choice, or otherwise influence election outcomes.
  • Require courts, after finding a violation, to order remedies tailored to address the violation. Such remedies could not diminish the ability of protected class members to participate in the political process, elect candidates of their choice, or otherwise influence election outcomes. The court would be required to consider remedies proposed by any parties, but prohibited from giving deference or priority to a remedy because it was proposed by the local government.
  • Authorize the court to impose remedies that are inconsistent with any other provision of state or local law if that state or local law would otherwise prevent the court from ordering an appropriate remedy. Remedies could include:
    • a district-based method of election,
    • an alternative method of election, including proportional ranked-choice voting, cumulative voting, or limited voting,
    • new or revised districting plans,
    • elimination of staggered elections,
    • reasonably increasing the size of the legislative body
    • additional voting hours or days
    • additional polling locations
    • additional means of voting, such as voting by mail or additional opportunities to return ballots
    • ordering special elections
    • requiring expanded opportunities for the admission of voters
    • requiring additional voter education
    • restoring or adding people to a voter registry
    • the court retaining jurisdiction, and if so, the court must preclear any new or change to prerequisites to voting or standards, practices, or procedures. The court could allow such changes only after finding that they do not have the purpose and would not have the effect of impairing or diminishing the right to vote on the basis of protected class membership.

  • Require local governments to hold detailed public hearings including specified notice processes before enacting and implementing either:

    • a new method of election to replace an at-large method
    • a new districting plan proposed after being sued or threatened with suit for an alleged violation of this bill or the federal Voting Rights Act.

    The bill would require "covered jurisdictions" to get permission before implementing any "covered policies", a process called "preclearance." A covered jurisdiction would have a choice about how to get preclearance for a covered policy. The jurisdiction could either submit the policy to the Civil Rights Division of the Attorney General's office or to the court for Anne Arundel County. If a covered jurisdiction failed to seek preclearance for a covered policy, the bill would enable individuals, organizations, and the Civil Rights Division to enjoin the covered policy until it is precleared. A special preclearance process would be developed for use during emergencies. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create a preclearance process at the Civil Rights Division. To use this process the covered jurisdiction would submit the policy to the Division. Thereafter:
    • The Division would post the covered policy on its website within 10 days and solicit public comment. Depending on the type of policy, the period of public comment would be 5, 10, or 20 business days. The Division would review the policy and the public comments in making its determination. The Division could seek more information from the covered jurisdiction, and the jurisdiction would bear the burden of proof that the covered policy should be approved.
    • The Division would approve, conditionally approve, or reject the policy. If the Division conditionally approves the policy, it could then reject the policy, but the rejection would need to be within 60 days of the receipt of the policy. If the Division fails to act within the deadlines imposed by the bill, the policy would be deemed approved.
    • The Division would only be able to reject a policy if it determined that the policy is more likely than not to diminish the opportunity or ability of protected class members to participate in the political process and elect candidates of their choice or otherwise influence the outcome of elections, or that the policy is more likely than not to violate the bill. A decision to preclear or reject a covered policy would not be admissible in a future challenge to covered policy.
    • Denials of preclearance could be appealed to the Supreme Court of Maryland.
  • Create a preclearance process at the Circuit Court for Anne Arundel. The covered jurisdiction would submit the policy in writing and contemporaneously send the policy to the Civil Rights Division. If the Division isn't contemporaneously served, the policy would be automatically denied. Assuming notice is given as required, thereafter:
    • The covered jurisdiction would have the burden of proof, just as in the other process.
    • The court could deny preclearance only if it determined that the policy is more likely than not to diminish the opportunity or ability of protected class members to participate in the political process and elect candidates of their choice or otherwise influence the outcome of elections, or that the policy is more likely than not to violate the bill, just as in the other process. A decision to preclear or reject a covered policy would not be admissible in a future challenge to a covered policy.
    • The court would be required to rule on preclearance within 60 days, but if it does not, the policy could not be implemented until preclearance is affirmatively granted.
    • Denials would be appealed under the ordinary rules of appellate procedure, however, it would be expedited.
  • Authorize the State Board of Elections, in consultation with the Civil Rights Division, to adopt regulations creating an expedited, emergency preclearance process if a covered policy occurs during or immediately before an election as a result of a disaster, emergency, or other exigent circumstances. Preclearance through such a process would be preliminary and could be revoked by the Civil Rights Division within 60 days of receipt of the covered policy.
  • Authorize plaintiffs to seek an injunction to prevent the implementation of a covered policy that was not submitted for preclearance.
  • Define "covered jurisdiction" as any local government:
    • that within the immediately preceding 25 years, became subject to a court order or government enforcement action based on a violation of this bill, the federal Voting Rights Act, the 15th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, or a voting-related violation of the 14th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.
    • that within the immediately preceding 25 years, became subject to at least three court orders or government enforcement actions based on a finding of a violation of a federal or state civil rights law or the 14th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution concerning discrimination against members of a protected class.
    • where the combined misdemeanor and felony arrest rate of members of any protected class consisting of at least 10,000 voting-age citizens or whose members are at least 10% of the citizen voting-age population served by the local government exceeds the proportion that the protected class constitutes of the citizen voting-age population served by the local government by at least 20% at any point in within the immediately preceding 10 years.
    • where, based on data made available by the U.S. Bureau of the Census, the dissimilarity index of any protected class of at least 25,000 voting-age citizens or whose members are at least 10% of the voting-age population of the local government has been more than 50 with respect to the race, color, or language minority group that is a majority within the local government at any point in the immediate preceding 10 years.
    • or a local board of elections in a county that is a covered jurisdiction.

  • Define "covered policy" as a new or modified local government qualification for admission as a voter, prerequisite to voting, or a regulation, ordinance, standard, practice, procedure, or policy concerning:

    • a change to the method or dates of election of a governing body or an elected school board
    • a change to the boundaries of election districts or wards, including changes made under a decennial redistricting
    • a change to the form of government for a local government
    • an annexation, incorporation, dissolution, consolidation, or division of a local government
    • a change to voter registration list maintenance or other activities concerning the cancelation or denial of voter registration
    • a change to the assignment of a voting precinct, polling place, or drop box location, including the relocation of voters, the relocation or reduction of hours of any polling place or ballot drop box, or the reduction or consolidation of polling places or ballot drop boxes,
    • a change to translation or interpretation services in any language other than English, including the creation or distribution of voting materials in any language other than English,
    • a change to assistance to voters with disabilities, including the creation or distribution of voting materials for voters with disabilities, or
    • any additional subject matter that the state board, in consultation with the civil rights division, may identify for inclusion by regulation if the civil rights division determines that any qualification for admission as a voter, prerequisite to voting, or any ordinance, regulation, standard, practice, procedure, or policy concerning the subject matter may have the effect of impairing or diminishing the right to vote of any protected class voter.

    The bill would require language assistance. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the State Board of Elections to make certain determinations of language assistance for non-native English speakers using the American Community Survey or equivalent data, and then using those determinations, publish on its website on or before January 1, 2024, and every three years thereafter, a list of each local government election that requires non-English language-related assistance and the kind of assistance required.
  • Require the State Board to issue regulations relating to how it will make the determinations of language assistance needs, and to include a process through which the public can propose languages for evaluation.
  • Require local governments to competently provide the required language assistance and materials on their website and in physical materials, including
    • registration and voting notices
    • election-related forms and instructions
    • ballot and other materials relating to the electoral process.
    • bilingual poll workers where available.

  • Enable lawsuits both to enforce the language assistance provisions and to enable local governments to provide English-only materials. The court would allow English-only materials if it found the State Board's determination of need was arbitrary and capricious, or an abuse of discretion.

    The bill would create a statewide election database and information office to assist state and local governments with evaluating current election laws and practices for consistency with the voting rights protections in the bill, implementing best practices, and investigating potential infringements on the right to vote. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create the Statewide Election Database and Information Office within the State Board of Elections. The Office would be headed by a Director, who would be responsible for the operation and administration of the Office and oversee a staff provided by the State Board. The Director would be an employee of the State Board, appointed by the Governor, and must hold an advanced degree from an accredited university and have expertise in demography, statistics, and electoral systems. The Office would maintain, in an electronic format, at least 12 years of elections-related data using the most advanced, peer-reviewed, and validated methodologies. The Office would make the data publicly available on the State Board's website for free, except that information that would identify individual voters would be redacted. The data would include:
    • estimates of the total population, voting age population, and citizen voting age population by race, color, and language minority group, broken down annually to the precinct level for each local government
    • election results at the precinct level for state and local government elections
    • regularly updated voter registration lists, geocoded locations for each registered voter, and other voter records, including voter history files for each election in each local government
    • districting plans and precinct boundaries for each election in each local government,
    • geocoded locations of polling places and ballot drop boxes for each election in each local government, and a list or description of the districts or geographic areas served by each polling place or ballot drop box location, and
    • any other information that the director determines advisable to maintain in furtherance of the purposes of the office and this title.
  • Require the authority responsible for administering a local election to transmit data to the Office on the certification of election results and the finalization of other voter records, specifically:
    • the election results at the precinct level
    • contemporaneous registration lists
    • voter records or voter history files
    • election district and precinct boundaries and
    • lists of polling place and ballot drop box locations and lists or descriptions of the districts or geographic areas served by the locations.
  • Require state agencies identified by the Director as possessing necessary information to provide it once a year to the Director, or more frequently if requested by the Director.

  • Authorize the Director to provide nonpartisan technical assistance to local governments, researchers, and members of the public seeking to use the resources of the statewide database.

    The bill would create new prohibitions on voter intimidation and obstruction, identify conduct that would automatically violate the prohibitions, and enable impacted people to sue. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Prohibit a person, whether acting under the color of law or otherwise, from engaging in acts of intimidation, deception, or obstruction that interferes with an individual's right to vote.
  • Define as violations of that prohibition:
    • the use of force or threats to use force, or the use of any other conduct to practice intimidation that causes or will reasonably have the effect of causing interference with an individual's right to vote,
    • the knowing use of a deceptive or fraudulent device, contrivance, or communication that causes or will reasonably have the effect of causing interference with any individual's right to vote, or
    • interference with access to a polling place, a ballot drop box, or an office or a place of business of an election official or a voter or an election official in a manner that causes or will reasonably have the effect of causing interference with any individual's right to vote or any delay in voting or the voting process.

  • Enable plaintiffs to sue over alleged violations in the circuit court for Anne Arundel County and provide that if the court finds a violation:

    • The court must order appropriate, tailored remedies that could include additional time to vote
    • The person who committed or aided the violation would be liable for any damages awarded by the court, including nominal damages for any violation and compensatory or punitive damages for any willful violation.

    Finally, the bill would empower enforcement of all of the provisions in the bill by creating certain litigation rules and enabling parties to recover costs and fees. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Enable any of these parties to file suit to enforce any of the provisions in the bill:
    • an aggrieved person
    • an organization whose membership includes or is likely to include aggrieved persons,
    • an organization whose mission would be frustrated by a violation of this section,
    • an organization that would expend resources to fulfill its mission as a result of a violation of this section, or
    • the Civil Rights Division.
  • Give enforcement actions expedited proceedings and automatic calendar preference.
  • Direct courts to grant preliminary injunctions relating to upcoming elections if the party is more likely than not to succeed on the merits, and it is possible to implement an appropriate remedy that would resolve the alleged violation in the upcoming election

  • Allow the prevailing party to recover reasonable attorneys' fees and litigation costs, including expert witness fees and expenses. However, a state or local government would not be awarded costs or fees unless the court decides the action was frivolous, unreasonable, or without foundation. When the state or local government is the opposing party, a party would be defined as prevailing if as a result of the action the government yields some or all of the relief sought.

This bill, as introduced on February 13, 2023, would revise automatic voter registration processes at the DMV (called the Motor Vehicle Administration in Maryland) and at the Maryland Health Benefit Exchange ("Exchange") to create a process for new registrations for people whose transaction-related documentation or database match demonstrate their U.S. citizenship. In addition, the bill would create new registration update processes, would authorize the State Board of Elections to identify additional agencies for automatic voter registration, and authorize special processes for participants in address confidentiality programs Specifically, the bill would:

  • Limit the existing automatic voter registration process at the DMV to individuals who are not registered to vote and have not provided documentary proof of citizenship.
  • Limit the existing automatic voter registration process at the Exchange to individuals who are not registered to vote and whose citizenship cannot be verified through an electronic database match.
  • Require the DMV to maintain an electronic information system that allows it to determine, at the time a person applies for a transaction, whether the person is registered to vote. If a person is registered to vote, the DMV would electronically transmit the voter registration information of that person to the State Board of Elections.
    • If the information shows the voter's registration information is correct, the State Board would note the date of the update in the voter registration list, and if the voter's registration was inactive, activate it.
    • If the information shows the voter's address or name has changed, the State Board would update their registration and if applicable, activate it. Within five days after receiving the voter registration information from the DMV, the State Board would send the voter an automatic voter registration update notice by nonforwardable mail that included a postage-prepaid form to return to make corrections. If the voter affirmatively corrects the update in writing, the State Board would update their registration. The State Board would also be required to provide an electronic means for a voter to update their registration.
    • The bill authorizes the State Board to delegate some or all of these responsibilities to the local boards of elections.
  • Require the DMV to classify each type of document it accepts as proof of identity as a document that proves U.S. citizenship, proves non-citizenship, or neither.
  • Prohibit the DMV from offering registration to, or transferring the information of, a person whose documents prove they are not U.S. citizens.
  • Create a new automatic registration process at DMV for people who affirmatively demonstrate citizenship as part of their transaction. Specifically, the new process would be used at DMV for any transaction in which the person is not yet registered to vote, provides a document as part of their transaction that demonstrates U.S. citizenship, and they are at least 16 years old and a resident of Maryland. DMV would be authorized but not required to create a process to review prior transaction documents to see if an applicant previously submitted proof of U.S. citizenship if in the current transaction a voter's documents do not demonstrate citizenship or noncitizenship. In this process, once the State Board receives the voter's information and confirms no other information indicates the person is not qualified to vote:
    • The State Board would send the applicant an automatic voter registration notice by nonforwardable mail within 5 days after receiving their voter registration information, and if the applicant does not affirmatively decline registration within 21 days of the mailing, would cause them to be an active voter in the statewide voter registration list. The applicant will be deemed registered as of the date of their DMV transaction. If the applicant affirmatively declines, the State Board would remove them from the statewide voter registration list. The State Board would be authorized to delegate these responsibilities to local boards of elections.
    • The automatic voter registration notice would be in a form prescribed by the State Board and would include notice (1) that the person will be registered to vote if they do not decline, (2) of the qualifications to register, the penalties for false registration, and an instruction to decline registration if the person is not eligible to register, (3) that registration is voluntary and does not affect the availability of services or benefits, (4) that the applicant must pick a political party to participate in a party primary, but can register without affiliation, and (5) of how to pick a party electronically and get more information. The notice would enable the applicant to decline registration and select a political party.
    • If a voter who is automatically registered nonetheless does not appear on the election register, they may either use same-day registration or vote a provisional ballot, which will count as long as the person did not affirmatively decline to register before they cast the provisional ballot.
  • Create a new automatic registration process at the Health Benefit Exchange for people who the Exchange reliably confirms are U.S. citizens through an electronic database match as part of the eligibility determination process, and the people are at least 16 years old and reside in Maryland. If a person attests to non-citizenship, the Exchange would not offer a registration opportunity. In the new process, the Exchange would transmit the applicants' voter registration information to the State Board, and the State Board would determine if the applicant was already registered to vote.
    • If the applicant was already registered, the State Board would do the same registration update process the bill creates for already registered applicants from the DMV.
    • If the applicant is not already registered, the State Board would use the same automatic voter registration process the bill creates for applicants from the DMV who are not yet registered to vote.
    • The Exchange's automatic voter registration processes are subject to federal laws and regulations impacting the exchange, and the bill provides that the processes may be modified by the State Board and the Exchange as needed to comply with federal law.
  • Authorize the State Board to:
    • Identify additional state, federal, or local agencies that, in the regular course of business, reliably verify applicants' citizenship by verifying documents or through an electronic database match, and with the consent of the agency, implement the procedures for automatic voter registration created by the bill
    • Identify additional state, federal, or local agencies that, in the regular course of business, reliably collect sufficient information to update the voter registration information of applicants currently registered to vote in the state, and with the consent of the agency, implement the procedures for automatic voter registration updates created by the bill.
  • Acknowledge that participants in address confidentiality programs need special processes, and authorize the DMV, Exchange, and State Board to create them.

Prior law provided for limited access to a permanent mail voter list for voters over 65 years old or with a disability, starting in February 2024. The bill eliminates these criteria, making the list available to all voters (as of its effective date of December 31, 2025).
  • Restricts the ability of officials to remove voters from the permanent mail voting list by eliminating failure to vote by mail ballot for one general election as a reason for removal.

A previous version of this bill contained additional provisions that were amended out before enactment. These provisions would have:

  • Allowed voters to enroll in the permanent mail voter list by the same means available for requesting a mail ballot and on the voter registration form.
  • Ended the practice of removing a voter from the permanent mail voter list when they were put on inactive status.
  • Modified the existing mail ballot tracking system to require automatic notifications to voters at certain stages of the ballot process, establish a statewide telephone hotline for ballot status inquiries, and to require clerks to provide ballot status information to voters over the phone.

Last Updated March 6, 2024

This bill, as introduced on April 24, 2023, would require state legislative acquiescence before new federal funding could be accepted or used for election administration unless otherwise required by federal or state law. Election officials would have to provide 30 days' notice of their intention to accept new federal funding, and the legislature would then have 30 days to either approve or reject the funding, with failure to act being presumed approval.Violations of this prohibition would be a civil violation punishable by a fine up to the amount of funds inappropriately accepted or disbursed plus an additional $1000.

Last updated May 1, 2023.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on April 28, 2023, would prohibit public officials from soliciting or accepting from any person a contribution, donation or anything else of value for purposes of conducting state or local elections, requiring that all costs and expenses relating to state or local elections be paid for with public funds. A violation of this prohibition would be a Class C felony.

Last updated May 1, 2023.

This bill, as enacted on June 26, 2023:

  • Changes the deadline for implementation of an online voter registration system from November 1, 2023, to January 1, 2024.
  • Changes the deadline for implementation of a permanent mail voter ("ongoing absentee status") list for voters over 65 and who self-identify as having a disability from November 1, 2023, to February 1, 2024.
  • Moves forward the deadline by which an individual must request to inspect mail ballot applications and envelopes before they are counted, from 9 a.m. the day of counting to 4 p.m. the day before. The bill also expressly grants the secretary of state authority to adopt rules for the inspection of mail ballot applications and envelopes before they are processed.
  • Requires voters on the address confidentiality list to submit voter registration applications to the secretary of state. Prior law required these voters to apply to their local registrar, and authorized registrars to contact the secretary to verify the voter's eligibility to register in the jurisdiction. The bill also requires the secretary to issue mail ballots to these voters for state elections, and requires local clerks to do so for local elections.
  • Restricts still photography in polling places of individuals other than the photographer themselves, to outside the guardrail enclosure. Under prior law, only videography was so restricted.
  • Moves forward the registration deadline for UOCAVA voters, from 5 p.m. the day before Election Day to 12 p.m. the day before.

The bill also includes additional provisions related to recounts, candidates, and political parties that are not tracked by Voting Rights Lab.

Last Updated March 6, 2024

This bill, as enacted on November 30, 2023, creates new offenses for individuals who intimidate election officials or prevent them from conducting election-related duties. Specifically, the bill:

  • Defines "election official" as a public officer, public employee, election inspector, member of the board of state canvassers, member of a board of county canvassers, member of an absent voter counting board, or a county, city, or township clerk who has a duty to perform in connection with an election.
  • Creates a new offense for any individual who:
    • Intimidates an election official because of their status as an election official, with the specific intent of interfering with the performance of their election-related duties
    • Prevents an election official from performing their duties
  • Classifies these offenses as misdemeanors, unless the individual has been convicted of one of these offenses at least twice before, in which case a subsequent offense would be a felony.
  • Specifically exempts "constitutionally protected activity" from the offense, such as reporting, protesting, and lobbying.

Last updated December 7, 2023.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on September 27, 2023, would delay the start of a program under which an "eligible member" may return a mail ballot electronically, and would also modify the program. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Define an eligible member as a member of a uniformed service on active duty (or the member's spouse) or a member of the merchant marine (or the member's spouse) who is absent from the United States due to the member's service.
  • Delay the start of a program under which an eligible member may return the member's ballot electronically. The program is scheduled to begin January 1, 2024, and under the bill this implementation would be delayed until September 1, 2025.
  • Modify the program to require the member to also return the member's physical ballot when the member returns an electronic copy. Under rules required to be adopted by the secretary of state, the member's ballot would be counted if the electronic ballot is received no later than 8 p.m. on Election Day. The member would still be required to send the physical copy of the ballot, and if received by the 6th day after Election Day, the physical ballot would be the copy that is officially counted.

Last Updated October 27, 2023

This bill, as introduced on March 9, 2023, would require a voter's photograph to be part of the voter's qualified voter file, and would require each voter to be compared against the photograph when appearing to vote. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the most recent digital photo of a voter, obtained from DMV records, to be a part of each voter's qualified voter file. The photos would be exempt from public disclosure. Existing law requires voters to present photo ID or an affidavit to vote in person, but does not require digitized images as part of a voter's registration record.
  • Require that electronic poll books include a voter's digitized signature and digital photo, if contained in their registration file.
  • Require an election official to compare the voter with their digital photographic image or photo image in the electronic poll book, in addition to the existing requirement for voters to present photo ID, and for officials to compare a voter's ballot application and digitized signatures. If the voter does not appear to be the person in the photograph, or the voter's signature does not appear to match the signature in the voter's file, the voter must be challenged.

Last Updated April 26, 2023

This bill, as introduced on March 22, 2023, would add a current concealed pistol license as a form of voter identification.

Last Updated March 23, 2023

This bill, as introduced on May 3, 2023, would require challengers to wear a badge that identifies them as a challenger while serving. The bill also provides procedures for recording a challenger's time of service and for recording the resolution of a challenge made by the challenger.

Last Updated July 31, 2023

This bill, as introduced on May 3, 2023, would require the Secretary of State to develop a training program regarding the processes and procedures on election day and the powers, rights, and duties of election challengers. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the Secretary of State to create a comprehensive training program regarding the processes and procedures on election day and the powers, rights, and duties of election challengers.
  • Require each county clerk and the secretary to offer the training program to each political party, incorporated organization, or organized committee of interested citizens wishing to appoint challengers in an election during the period beginning not earlier than 100 days before the election and not later than 45 days before the election.
  • Permit a party or organization that completes the training to offer the same program to each person that the party or organization wishes to appoint as a challenger in the election. The party or organization would be required to issue each person who completed the training a certificate of completion, the presentation of which would be a prerequisite to service in the election.
  • Require comprehensive recordkeeping by the secretary of which parties, organizations, and persons have completed the training.
  • Impose a civil penalty, including a fine of not more than $2,500, on a party or organization that issues a certificate of completion to a person who has not completed the training.

Last Updated July 31, 2023

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on October 24, 2023, would require the Department of Corrections to provide incarcerated individuals with a document that states their eligibility to vote once released from confinement, provides 'specific information' on the registration process and how to vote on Election Day, or vote early in-person or by mail ballot, and lists regular election dates. The bill would require the secretary of state to create a document meeting the requirements, for distribution by the department.

The bill also contains provisions making non-substantive changes and changes that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

Last Updated March 4, 2024

This bill, as enacted on November 7, 2023, removes a requirement that a ballot must be processed as a challenged ballot if cast by a voter who has registered to vote within 14 days of the election or on Election Day, and has provided an alternative form of proof of identity and/or proof of residency for registration. Such ballots must now be processed as regular ballots.

Last Updated February 27, 2024

This bill, as enacted on November 7, 2023, permits the hire, or causing the hire of, a car or other transportation to transport voters to an election, by eliminating the misdemeanor offense for doing so. Under prior law, the only exception to the offense was hiring transport for voters who were “physically unable to walk” to the voting location.

Last updated February 27, 2024.

This bill, as enacted on November 30, 2023, lowers the age for voter pre-registration to 16 years old. Under prior law, eligible residents could register before age 18 only if they would be age 18 on the date of the next election. Specifically, the bill:

  • Permits pre-registration for eligible individuals between 16 and 17 and �� years old. The voter registration system must notify local officials when a pre-registered individual reaches 17 and �� years old, and officials must then issue the registrant a voter ID card.
  • Requires the secretary of state and Department of Education to coordinate to establish a voter education and outreach program regarding pre-registration, including providing registration materials to all public high school students. The secretary must also carry out annual outreach to all eligible minors who have applied for a driver's license or state ID card.
  • Deems voter file information for pre-registered voters confidential and not subject to public disclosure until the individual is 17 and 1/2 years old.
  • Permits local officials to change information in the voter file within the seven days before an election and on Election Day, by eliminating the prohibition against doing so.

Last Updated February 27, 2024

This bill, as enacted on November 30, 2023, requires the secretary of state to create and maintain an online mail ballot application system. To use the system, voters with a digital signature on file with the secretary must confirm their identity by providing their name, complete driver license or state personal identification card number, full date of birth, last four digits of their Social Security number, and eye color. A voter whose digital signature is not on file must upload a photograph of their physical signature via the online application portal.

Last Updated February 27, 2024

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on June 13, 2023, requires the secretary of state to establish an electronic system by which mail ballot voters can use a website or mobile application to track the status of their application and returned ballot. These statutory provisions would codify a constitutional amendment enacted in 2022, which requires the establishment of "a state-funded system to track submitted absent voter ballot applications and absent voter ballots." Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the secretary of state to establish an electronic system that provides the following information to voters:
    • The date a mail ballot application was received and the date the application was accepted, if applicable. If rejected, the system would be required to state the reason and instructions for curing the error, and the date when the application was ultimately accepted.
    • The date the mail ballot was sent to the voter by mail or electronically, and whether the ballot was returned as undeliverable.
  • The date the voter's ballot was received by the clerk, whether it was accepted (including the date of acceptance) or rejected, and instructions and the deadline for curing a defective ballot. The system would also be required to provide an update to the voter if the defect is cured and will be counted.
  • Allow a voter to opt in to receive email or text notifications from the system with updates on their application and ballot. The bill would designate this information confidential, and exempt it from public disclosure.

Last Updated March 4, 2024

This bill, as enacted on November 21, 2023, no longer contains any provisions tracked by Voting Rights Lab.

Previous versions of the bill contained tracked provisions that would have codified requirements for in-person early voting, following a state constitutional amendment in 2022 that required nine days of early voting before statewide and federal elections. The provisions were ultimately enacted in Senate Bill 367, and were subsequently amended out of this bill. The deleted provisions would have:

  • Required municipalities to offer nine consecutive days of in-person Election Day-style early voting for each statewide or federal election. For all other elections, municipalities would have been permitted, but not required, to offer in-person early voting.
  • Prohibited any polling place or early voting site from being located in a building owned or leased by an elected official, a candidate, or a person regulated under the Michigan campaign finance act.
  • Permitted municipalities in the same county to enter into an agreement to hold early voting jointly, and permitted municipalities to enter into an agreement with their county to have the county conduct early voting for the municipality.
  • Permitted an early voting site to differ from an Election Day polling place by permitting an early voting site to serve more than six precincts or to serve more than one municipality.
  • Required the secretary of state to undertake responsibility for implementation of early voting, including through the issuance of instructions and guidance, the procurement of necessary equipment, creating model agreements and voting plan templates, and evaluating and approving new technologies.
  • Required municipalities to file an early voting plan with the county clerk at least 120 days before the first statewide or federal election in each even-numbered year.
  • Required clerks to provide ample notice to all affected voters when a polling place or early voting site is designated or changed.
  • Prohibited early voting results from being reported until after the polls close on Election Day, and created a new felony offense for violating the prohibition.

Last Updated February 29, 2024

This bill, as enacted on July 18, 2023, changes statutory requirements regarding the use of drop boxes for return of a mail ballot or mail ballot application. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires each municipality in the state to provide at least one drop box for mail ballots and applications, and for municipalities with over 15,000 registered voters to provide at least one drop box for every 15,000 voters. These provisions codify requirements for drop boxes that were adopted into the state constitution in November 2022. The bill expressly permits local officials to provide additional drop boxes at their discretion, subject to all relevant requirements. Previous law had no requirements for the number of drop boxes required in each municipality.
  • Requires that municipalities ensure drop boxes are distributed "equitably," according to specific criteria, and to provide information of drop box locations to the secretary of state, for posting on the agency's website. Previous law did not specify criteria for locating drop boxes, and had no requirement for reporting locations to the secretary.
  • Requires the secretary of state to facilitate the procurement, distribution, repair, and video monitoring of drop boxes at no cost to the municipality (with the exception of costs for video data storage). Previous law was silent as to which entity must bear the cost of drop boxes.
  • Requires the video monitoring of drop boxes installed after October 1, 2020, for the 75 days before an election and on Election Day. Beginning in 2026, video monitoring is required of all drop boxes, regardless of when they were installed, for the 75 days before an election and on Election Day. Previous law required video monitoring for boxes ordered or installed after October 1, 2020 only.

Last Updated August 14, 2023

HISTORY: {"date":"12/13/2024","summary":"In SENATE. Read third time. Passed SENATE. *****To HOUSE for concurrence","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on June 13, 2023, would modify the definition of "identification for election purposes." Specifically, the bill would:

  • Broaden the list of educational institutions whose student photo identification cards constitute acceptable ID for voting.
  • Add a current photo identification card issued by a local government as acceptable ID for voting.

A previous version of the bill would have required that a current military photo identification card must be issued by the federal or state government and a current tribal photo identification card must be issued by a tribal government to be acceptable voter ID, and would have required that a current state government issued photo identification card, other than a driver's license or state identification card, is only valid if issued by the state of Michigan. Those provisions were amended out of the bill on June 13, 2023.

Last Updated June 15, 2023

This bill, as enacted on July 18, 2023, creates a permanent mail voter list, codifying a 2022 amendment to the state constitution. Although previous law did not expressly address permanent mail ballot requests, the mail ballot application in use at the time of this bill's enactment allowed voters to join a mail ballot application list and receive an application for a mail ballot for each election. Specifically, the bill:

  • Permits any registered voter to submit an application to receive a mail ballot ("absent voter ballot") by mail for all future elections. Once a voter is established as a permanent mail voter, officials must send the voter a mail ballot for each election until the application is rescinded.
  • Establishes the following as circumstances under which permanent mail voter status can be rescinded:
    • At the voter's request
    • If the voter is no longer qualified to vote in Michigan
    • The clerk receives reliable information that the voter moved out of Michigan or moved within Michigan without updating their registration address
    • The voter fails to vote for six consecutive years
  • Specifies that a voter may retain their permanent mail voter status if they change their residence within the state and update their voter registration accordingly.
  • Requires clerks to contact permanent mail voters no later than 60 days before a presidential primary election to permit them to request a ballot for their party of choice. The clerks must also make an effort at voter outreach to remind voters that if they fail to request a ballot for their party of choice, they will not receive a primary election ballot for that party.
  • Permits destruction of ballots containing a federal office and presidential primary ballot selection forms 22 months after an election. Previous law generally required retention of all ballots for 30 days after a final determination of an election, with limited exceptions. The bill would also reduce preservation requirements for other election materials from 2 years to 22 months.

The bill also makes various technical changes throughout multiple provisions, with no impact on substantive law.

Last Updated August 14, 2023

HISTORY: {"date":"06/15/2023","summary":"To SENATE Committee on ELECTIONS AND ETHICS","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on June 14, 2023, makes extensive changes to the mail ballot process, including by establishing a cure process for a mail ballot application or mail ballot that is defective. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create a cure process for a mail ballot that is rejected because the signature on the absent voter ballot return envelope is missing or does not agree sufficiently with the voter's signature on file. The clerk would be required to notify the voter of the rejection and of all information relevant to the cure process, and the voter would have until 5 p.m. on the third day after the election to correct the deficiency. Signatures may only be deemed not to agree if the signature differs in "significant and obvious respects" from the voter's signature on file.
  • Permit an applicant to cure a defective application for a mail ballot if the application was rejected because the signature did not match "sufficiently" or the application was unsigned. Notification must advise the voter that they have until the 4th day before the election to cure the deficiency and still receive a mail ballot.
  • Require the development of a cure form through which a voter can correct a deficiency in their mail ballot or mail ballot application. The form could be received and returned electronically, in person, or through the mail. The secretary of state would also be authorized to develop other methods by which a voter could cure a defect.
  • Require, beginning 45 days before an election, that clerks verify or reject applications for a mail ballot (and notify the applicant of a curable defect) by the next business day. Beginning 5 days before the election, clerks would be required to verify or reject the applications (and notify the applicant of a curable defect) on the day of receipt.
  • Expressly permit concurrent submission of a registration application and an application for a mail ballot. If this is done on Election Day, the bill requires the voter to cast their ballot in the municipal clerk's office.
  • Require municipal clerks to provide an application form for a mail ballot upon request in person, by mail, or by e-mail. The bill also expressly provides that the secretary of state or any county or municipal clerk is permitted to send unsolicited mail ballot applications to registered voters.
  • Permit the electronic submission of an application for a mail ballot. The secretary of state would be responsible for developing an electronic form. The bill further provides that a voter's digital signature from their driver's license or state ID card would constitute an acceptable signature for submission of the electronic application.
  • Provide that a signed mail ballot application form may only be in the possession of the applicant, a member of the applicant's immediate family, a person residing in the applicant's household, a registered voter chosen by the applicant, or a person handling mail or election official acting within the scope of their job. If the registered voter chosen by the applicant returns the application on the applicant's behalf, that person must sign the application accordingly.
  • Permit a voter to request that their mail ballot be sent to a different address than the voter's registration address or to a post office box.
  • Provides, in accordance with language added to the Michigan constitution in 2022, that a single application for a mail ballot may be used as an application for all elections in a single year. The application form would also contain a checkbox that would allow a voter to request to be put on a permanent mail voter list.
  • Require a voter to present ID if applying in person for a mail ballot. A voter who does not have ID must sign an affidavit to that effect.
  • Guarantees the right, as added to the Michigan constitution in 2022, to have the government pay for postage for both a mail ballot application and the ballot itself.
  • Require a clerk, upon receiving an untimely application for a mail ballot, to immediately notify the applicant that the application was untimely and advise them of how else they can vote in the election. The clerk would still be required to process the application for all future elections to which it may apply. The bill also would place an obligation on clerks to forward an application sent to the wrong clerk and to advise an applicant accordingly.

Last Updated June 16, 2023

This bill, as enacted on July 19, 2023, changes rules concerning the consolidation of precincts. Specifically, the bill:

  • Permits a municipality with 5,000 or fewer voters to consolidate into a single precinct. Previous law allowed consolidation only if the municipality had 2,999 or fewer voters.
  • Raises the limit generally on the number of registered voters who may be within one precinct from 2,999 to 5,000.
  • Repeals a provision of law that required a minimum number of voting machines based on the number of registered voters in a precinct.

Last updated August 14, 2023.

This bill, as introduced on June 8, 2023, would make a number of changes to criminal offenses connected to an application for a ballot to be voted by mail. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Repeal an existing misdemeanor offense for making a false statement on an application for a mail ballot and replace it with a felony offense for knowingly submitting an application containing false information or a forged signature.
  • Create a felony offense for an individual who completes and submits (or causes the submission of) an application for a mail ballot for another person without that person's consent, if the action is not otherwise authorized by statute.
  • Create a felony offense for an individual who completes and submits (or causes the submission of) an application for a mail ballot with intent to obtain multiple mail ballots for one voter.

Last Updated June 12, 2023

This bill, as introduced on June 14, 2023, would require Michigan to terminate its membership in the Electronic Registration Information Center (ERIC) and would prohibit the state from rejoining.

Last Updated June 15, 2023

This bill, as introduced on June 14, 2023, would permit the establishment of "election day vote centers" to facilitate the casting and tabulating of ballots cast by voters who register or update their registrations on Election Day and make several changes to mail ballot procedures. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Permit a municipality that had at least 500 same-day registrants in at least one of the last two November general elections to establish an "election day vote center" not later than 90 days before an election.
  • Establish an election day vote center as a polling place for individuals registering to vote on Election Day. The voter would be permitted to register, cast their ballot, and insert it directly into the tabulator, and would otherwise be entitled to the same protections as any voter voting at their precinct polling place.
  • Permit mail voters to deliver their mail ballots to a polling place or an early voting site to directly insert their ballot into the tabulator. A voter who does this would be required to present ID or sign an affidavit attesting that they do not have ID. Some exceptions would be made to this for a municipality that is unable to program a tabulator to directly receive such ballots.
  • Limit the time period during which a mail voter may request that their ballot, if not already tabulated, be spoiled. Under existing law, this request can be made as late as the Friday before Election Day. Under the bill, the deadline would be a week earlier.
  • Clarify, in accordance with changes made to the state constitution in 2022, that postage for returning a mail ballot is prepaid by the government.
  • Make adjustments to procedures for the verification of mail ballots by clerks and election inspectors, including through establishment of a process under which mail ballots may be tabulated as early as eight days before Election Day.

Last Updated June 20, 2023

This bill, as introduced on June 15, 2023, would codify in statute a change made to the Michigan constitution in 2022 under which voters have the right to in-person Election Day-style early voting for at least nine days before a federal or statewide election. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Establish Election Day-style early voting, and require each municipality to offer it for each statewide or federal election. An early voting site would be required to be open for at least 8 hours per day on at least 9 consecutive days of early voting beginning on the second Saturday before a statewide or federal election and ending on the Sunday before the election. Municipalities would also be permitted to offer early voting for elections that are not statewide or federal elections.
  • Establish that a publicly owned or controlled building, including a municipal building or school building, must be used as a polling place or early voting site unless it is not possible or convenient to use a publicly owned or controlled building for that purpose.
  • Require that central polling places may only be established if their use will not result in significantly increased travel times or delays for voters.
  • Permit municipalities in the same county to enter into an agreement to hold early voting jointly, and permit municipalities to enter into an agreement with their county to have the county conduct early voting for the municipality. The bill would also provide guidance for the minimum provisions necessary to include in a municipal or county agreement, the rules for its duration, and the methods for withdrawing from it.
  • Permit an early voting site to differ from an Election Day polling place by permitting an early voting site to serve more than 6 precincts or to serve more than one municipality.
  • Require the secretary of state to undertake responsibility for implementation of early voting, including through the issuance of instructions and guidance, the procurement of necessary equipment, creating model agreements and voting plan templates, and evaluating and approving new technologies.
  • Require municipalities to file an early voting plan with the county clerk no later than February 15 in a year when a November election is held (and no later than December 1 of the preceding year if the November election is a presidential election). The plan would be required to provide sufficient details describing the processes created to conduct early voting.
  • Require that the site of each early voting location be finalized no later than 60 days before the election.
  • Require electronic tabulating equipment to be used at each early voting site.
  • Require the board of election commissioners to verify the count of ballots after each day of early voting, including a hand count of the number of ballots cast. The early voting clerk or early voting site supervisor would be responsible for securing all early voting equipment at the end of each day of early voting.
  • Create a felony offense for intentionally disclosing an election result from an early voting site before 8 p.m. on election day.
  • Forbid the offering of voter registration services at an early voting site.

Last Updated June 23, 2023

This bill, as introduced on June 28, 2023, would require the secretary of state to mail a notice to each registered voter after the federal census is completed to inform the voter of the methods for updating their address. A voter whose address has changed would be required to update their address information via one of these methods.

Last Updated June 29, 2023

This bill, as introduced on June 28, 2023, concerns the use of a juror qualifications questionnaire for voter list maintenance. Under the bill, if an individual is sent the questionnaire but it is returned as undeliverable or the recipient indicates that their current address is different from the address to which the questionnaire was sent, the county clerk would be required to immediately notify the secretary of state. The secretary would then be required to send the individual a confirmation notice if the individual is a registered voter. Failure to respond to the confirmation notice would result in the voter being required to affirm their current address at their polling place before being permitted to vote, and failure to vote in two consecutive November elections following the failure to return the confirmation notice would result in the voter's registration being canceled.

Last Updated June 29, 2023

This bill, as introduced on June 28, 2023, would require the Secretary of State, beginning in 2024, to mail confirmation notices to voters who have not voted in the last six years. A voter receiving a confirmation notice would be instructed to sign and return it to confirm their address. A voter failing to do so within 30 days would then be sent another notice, which they would have 30 days to sign and return - failure to respond to this second notice would result in the voter's registration status being marked as challenged. The voter would then be required to affirm their current address at their polling place before being permitted to vote, and their registration would be canceled if they fail to vote or "engage in voter-related activity" within two general elections of the date the second notice is sent.

Last Updated June 29, 2023

This bill, as introduced on June 28, 2023, would require any data or report received from an multistate voter list maintenance program concerning the current residence and registration status of electors to be shared with the chairs of the legislative committees on elections, to the extent permitted by the membership agreement.

Last Updated June 29, 2023

This bill, as enacted on November 30, 2023, expands the existing automatic voter registration (AVR) process, including the designation of new participating agencies and creating automatic pre-registration. The bill will take effect June 30, 2025. Specifically, the bill:

  • Adds two new required agencies to the AVR system. Under the bill, AVR will be provided by the Department of Health and Human Services to all eligible residents applying for Medicaid coverage, and the Department of Corrections to all eligible individuals being released from its custody. The secretary of state and the Department of Corrections will be required to ensure that an individual is not registered to vote until they have been released on parole or discharged after completing their maximum sentence.
  • Authorizes the secretary of state to designate additional automatic voter registration agencies if they collect information sufficient to confirm the eligibility for a voter to register in the regular course of their business. Under prior law, AVR was only authorized at motor vehicle offices.
  • Enables an Indigenous nation or tribe in the state to request the secretary of state's approval to allow one of its governing bodies to electronically submit the information required for the purpose of registering and pre-registering tribal members to vote. If an Indigenous nation or tribe's governing body collected sufficient information to verify an individual's eligibility to register, then the Secretary is authorized to enter a memorandum of understanding with them permitting automatic registering and pre-registering.
  • Mandates that the secretary of state develop procedures for processing electronic records received from AVR agencies or from Indigenous nations or tribes without a digitized image of the applicant's signature.
  • Creates automatic pre-registration, using the same procedures for automatic voter registration, for any individual who meets the qualifications to pre-register.
  • Requires officials to provide the opportunity to opt out of automatic voter registration after a transaction, rather than during the transaction as required under prior law. Notice must be sent by mail and include information regarding declining registration, the affirmative duty to decline if ineligible to vote, and information on how to cast a mail ballot. The bill also sets out requirements for processing returned notices.
  • Requires the name of any automatically registered voter be electronically forwarded to the local clerk. The voter file must indicate that the person was automatically registered.
  • Expressly prohibits automatic registration of an applicant with documentation of non-U.S. citizenship. The bill leaves in place the provision allowing AVR for individuals who have not provided affirmative documentation of American citizenship if they indicate they are a United States citizen on the transaction application.
  • Creates a presumed defense to prosecution for a person not entitled to vote but who votes or attempts to vote after being automatically registered. The defense does not apply if the person knowingly or willfully made false statements to get registered. Prior law protected only those ineligible individuals who were automatically registered from prosecution, not those who actually voted or attempted to vote.
  • Requires the secretary of state to publicly release monthly data reports related to automatic voter registration.
  • Requires the secretary of state to develop procedures to implement the registration of persons who have previously declined automatic voter registration.

Last Updated March 5, 2024

This bill, as enacted on November 30, 2023, makes minor clarifications and changes to the automatic voter registration (AVR) process at the DMV during driver's license transactions. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires that when an applicant's information will be used for voter registration or pre-registration, any printed notice given to them must state that their information will be used for such purposes and that the printed notice serves as a receipt verifying their voter registration application. Prior law had no comparable provision.
  • Specifies that an individual applying for a driver's license must disclose their citizenship during automatic registration transactions only. Prior law provided that citizenship status is required for AVR transactions, but did not expressly state the requirement is "only" for such.
  • Provides that only for applications for driver's licenses in which the applicant indicates that they are a citizen of the United States must the applicant be offered the option to decline using the application for voter registration.
