VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 14, 2023, would improve access to the ballot for absent uniformed services voters and overseas voters. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Expand a program under which absent uniformed services voters would be able to return their mail ballots electronically. The program is scheduled to begin January 1, 2024 under existing law. Under the bill:
    • The program would expand to include overseas voters.
    • Policies and procedures for administering this program, currently required to be promulgated by Secretary of State rule, would be added to statute. The procedures would mostly consist of security measures and ensuring that voters returning their ballots electronically are actually absent from their home.
  • Permit a mail ballot from an absent uniformed service voter or overseas voter to be received as late as six days after Election Day. This extension could be increased by a day for each day after the prescribed deadline that the clerk failed to send the ballot. The Michigan Constitution was amended in 2022 to permit a mail ballot from an absent uniformed service voter or overseas voter to be received as late as six days after Election Day, so this change would resolve the contradiction in statute.

Last Updated April 21, 2023

This bill, as enacted on May 1, 2023, codifies the extension of the deadline for receipt of a mail ballot sent by a uniformed or overseas voter. Under previous statute, mail ballots were required to be received by the close of the polls on Election Day in order to be counted. However, this provision was contradicted by language added to the Michigan Constitution in 2022, which requires that a ballot mailed by a uniformed or overseas voter be considered timely if received not later than 6 days after the election if postmarked on or before Election Day. This bill codifies this constitutional requirement. The bill also specifies that if a ballot postmark is missing or unclear, the ballot is timely if the ballot return envelope or the voter certificate are dated on or before Election Day by the voter.

Last Updated May 4, 2023

This bill, as enacted on July 18, 2023, requires the Secretary of State to establish an electronic system for mail ballot tracking. These provisions codify a November 2020 amendment to the state constitution, which requires the establishment of "a state-funded system to track submitted absent voter ballot applications and absent voter ballots." Under previous law, jurisdictions with access to the state's ballot tracking system were required to provide online access to their voters, but participation was not required.

Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires the Secretary of State to establish an electronic system, accessible by a website or mobile application. The system must inform voters of (1) when their mail ballot application was received and accepted, or if rejected, the reason for rejection and steps to cure the defect, (2) when election officials have sent the mail ballot to the voter, (3) when the mail ballot has been received by election officials and accepted, or if rejected, the reason for rejection and steps to cure the defect.
  • Requires the tracking system to offer the option to receive notifications by email or text. The bill specifies that an email address or telephone number supplied by a voter for this purpose is not considered public information, and prohibits their disclosure by unauthorized individuals.

Last Updated August 14, 2023

This bill, as enacted on July 18, 2023, codifies in statute a change made to the Michigan constitution in 2022 under which voters have the right to in-person Election Day-style early voting for at least nine days before a federal or statewide election, among other changes. Specifically, the bill:

  • Establishes Election Day-style early voting, and requires each municipality to offer it for each statewide or federal election. An early voting site would be required to be open for at least 8 hours per day on at least 9 consecutive days of early voting beginning on the second Saturday before a statewide or federal election and ending on the Sunday before the election. Beginning in 2026, this would be permitted to extend until the Monday before the election, ending no later than 4 p.m. Clerks otherwise desiring to extend the early voting period would be permitted to do so, but could not begin early voting before the 29th day before an election.
  • Permits a municipality to offer early voting for an election that is not a statewide or federal election at the municipality's discretion. If offered for such an election, the early voting period must otherwise comply with the rules set forth in the bill, except that the requirement to offer early voting for at least 8 hours per day on at least 9 consecutive days would not apply.
  • Prohibits any polling place or early voting site from being located in a building owned or leased by an elected official, a candidate, or a person regulated under the Michigan campaign finance act. Existing law only prohibits polling places from being located in a building owned by a candidate or by a person that is a sponsor of a political committee or independent committee. The bill would also require a public building to be used as a polling place unless not possible or convenient.
  • Permits municipalities in the same county to enter into an agreement to hold early voting jointly, and permits municipalities to enter into an agreement with their county to have the county conduct early voting for the municipality. The bill also provides guidance for the minimum provisions necessary to include in a municipal or county agreement, the rules for its duration, and the methods for withdrawing from it.
  • Requires clerks to provide ample notice to all affected voters when a polling place or early voting site is designated or changed. The site of each early voting location would be required to be finalized no later than 60 days before the election.
  • Prohibits any polling place or early voting site from being located in a building owned or leased by an elected official, a candidate, or a person regulated under the Michigan campaign finance act. Existing law only prohibits polling places from being located in a building owned by a candidate or by a person that is a sponsor of a political committee or independent committee. The bill would also require a public building to be used as a polling place unless not possible or convenient.
  • Requires early voting sites to use electronic tabulation equipment.
  • Requires municipalities to file an early voting plan with the county clerk at least 120 days before the first statewide or federal election in each even-numbered year. The county clerk would then be required to file an early voting plan with the secretary of state not later than 110 days before the election. The plan would be required to provide sufficient details describing the processes created to conduct early voting.
  • Prohibits early voting results from being reported until after the polls close on Election Day. A person who violated this prohibition would commit a felony.
  • Permits a municipality that had at least 500 same-day registrants in at least one of the last two November general elections to establish an "election day vote center" not later than 90 days before an election. An election day vote center would be used as a polling place for individuals registering to vote on Election Day. The voter would be permitted to register, cast their ballot, and insert it directly into the tabulator, and would otherwise be entitled to the same protections as any voter voting at their precinct polling place.
  • Permit mail voters to deliver their mail ballots to a polling place or an early voting site to directly insert their ballot into the tabulator. A voter who does this would be required to present ID or sign an affidavit attesting that they do not have ID. Some exceptions would be made to this for a municipality that is unable to program a tabulator to directly receive such ballots.
  • Permits a municipality to enter into an agreement to combine boards for the counting of mail ballots with another municipality in the same county.

The bill also contains provisions not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, including ballot marking instructions.

Last Updated November 22, 2023

This bill, as amended on June 14, 2023, would create a permanent mail voter list, as required under language added to the state constitution in 2022. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Permit any registered voter to submit an application to receive an absent voter ballot by mail for all future elections. Once a voter is established as a permanent mail voter, they must be sent a mail ballot for each election until the application is rescinded.
  • Establish the following as circumstances under which permanent mail voter status can be rescinded:
    • At the voter's request,
    • If the voter is no longer qualified to vote in Michigan,
    • The clerk receives reliable information that the voter moved out of Michigan or moved within Michigan without updating their registration address, or
    • The voter fails to vote for six consecutive years.
  • Specify that a voter may retain their permanent mail voter status if they change their residence within the state and update their voter registration accordingly.
  • Require clerks to contact permanent mail voters no later than 60 days before a presidential primary election to permit them to request a ballot for their party of choice. The clerks would also be required to make an effort at voter outreach to remind voters that if they fail to request a ballot for their party of choice, they will not receive a primary election ballot for that party.
  • Prescribe rules for the retention and destruction of ballots containing a federal office and of presidential primary ballot selection forms that require them to be retained for 22 months.

Last Updated June 15, 2023

This bill, as enacted on July 18, 2023, makes various changes related to voting by mail ballot ("absent voter ballot"), including changes to the notice and cure processes, and paid postage requirements. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires the Secretary of State to develop a "cure form" through which a voter can correct a signature-related deficiency on their mail ballot application or completed ballot. The form must be able to be received and returned electronically, in person, or through the mail. The Secretary is also authorized to develop other methods by which a voter may cure a defect. Existing law permitted voters to cure a ballot with a non-matching signature, but did not require development of a standard form, or cure procedures for ballot applications.
  • Sets out specific requirements for when clerks must provide voters notice of a defect in a mail ballot application or completed ballot, depending on when the defect is determined.
  • Changes procedures for the return and processing of completed mail ballots. Specifically, the bill:
  • Requires that clerks provide prepaid return postage for mail ballots. This provision codifies a requirement established by amendment of the state constitution in 2022.
    • Shifts the duty of signature matching to verify mail ballots from the board of inspectors of election, to city and township clerks. The bill specifies that signatures may only be deemed not to agree if the signature differs in "significant and obvious respects" from the voter's signature on file. Previous law required signature "comparison" but did not specify criteria.
    • Modifies the existing notice and cure process for voters to address missing or mismatched signatures. Clerks must notify the voter that their ballot has been rejected by telephone, email, or text if possible, or otherwise by mail. The notice must provide information about how to cure the defect, including the deadline to do so. The bill also extends the previous cure deadline to 5 p.m. on the third day after the election. Previous statutory law required that notice be issued to voters if a ballot was rejected by 8 p.m. on the day before Election Day, with no specific notice methods required, and state policy permitted cure until 8 p.m. on Election Day.
    • Repeals the requirement that a mail ballot obtained in person without the voter showing required ID must be processed as a "challenged ballot." The bill retains the existing requirement that such voters must provide an affidavit that they do not have identification, but no longer requires the ballot to be deemed "challenged."
  • Changes procedures for applying to receive a mail ballot. Specifically, the bill:
    • Permits a mail ballot applicant whose application is rejected because their signature did not match records "sufficiently" or the application was unsigned, to cure the defect. Notification must advise the voter that they have until the 4th day before the election to cure the deficiency and still receive a ballot by mail. Previous law required clerks to notify applicants that their application had been rejected due to a non-matching or missing signature, but did not provide for a specific cure process.
    • Expressly permits concurrent submission of a registration application and an application for a mail ballot, and expressly provides that voters who do so in person on Election Day must vote the mail ballot in the municipal clerk's office. Previous law provided for same-day registration on Election Day or when voting early in person by mail ballot, but did not have an express provision generally allowing the practice for mail ballot applications.
    • Expressly requires municipal clerks to provide voters with the state's mail ballot application form in person, by mail (with a prepaid return envelope), or by e-mail, per the voter's request. Previous law required clerks to provide an application form "on a verbal or written request," but did not require electronic delivery of the form or prepaid return postage for mailed forms. The bill also expressly provides that the Secretary of State or any county or municipal clerk is permitted to send unsolicited mail ballot applications, including with prepaid return postage, to registered voters.
    • Permits voters to submit an application for a mail ballot by email and by using the online application process provided by the Secretary of State, in addition to the existing options to submit a request by mail or in person. The bill further provides that a voter's digital signature from their driver's license or state ID card can be used to meet the signature requirement for a ballot request.
    • Requires a clerk to immediately notify a voter if their mail ballot application is received after the deadline to send out ballots (5 p.m. on the Friday before Election Day), and they have not otherwise received one, to inform the voter that the application has been rejected as untimely. The notice must advise the voter of alternative methods of voting in the election, and must be made by any means available, including by phone, email, text message, or mail. Applications rejected as untimely for the immediate election must still be processed for future elections, if the voter has indicated a request to receive mail ballots indefinitely. The bill also requires clerks to notify voters and/or forward applications when an application has been submitted to the wrong jurisdiction.

  • Creates a permanent mail voter list by providing, in accordance with an amendment to the Michigan constitution in 2022, that a single application for a mail ballot may be used as an application for all elections in a single year, or for all future elections, and amending the application accordingly. Under previous practice, Michigan's mail ballot application allowed voters to join a list to receive a ballot application for each election, but not to automatically receive a ballot directly.

    The bill also includes numerous technical and conforming changes to provisions with no substantive impact on the law.


Last Updated October 17, 2023

This bill, as amended on June 14, 2023, concerns the use of drop boxes for deposit of a mail ballot or mail ballot application. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require each municipality in the state to establish at least one drop box for mail ballots. If the municipality has 15,000 or more voters, it must establish at least one drop box for every 15,000 voters in the municipality. The municipality would be responsible for ensuring that the placement of drop boxes is equitable.
  • Instruct the secretary of state to assist municipalities in the procurement, distribution, repair, and video monitoring of drop boxes at no cost to the municipality (the secretary would not bear the cost of video data storage). The secretary of state would also be required to post the location of each drop box on the website of the department of state.
  • Specify that a drop box may be used for the deposit of a mail ballot application in addition to a mail ballot.
  • Require drop boxes to be accessible 24 hours a day during the 40 days preceding Election Day and until 8 p.m. on Election Day. Collection from the drop boxes would be required to happen any day the clerk's office is open for business beginning 35 days before Election Day.
  • Require drop boxes to be affixed to the ground or another stationary object.
  • Require the video monitoring of drop boxes installed after October 1, 2020 for the 75 days before an election and on Election Day. Beginning in 2026, require the video monitoring of all drop boxes for the 75 days before an election and on Election Day.

Last Updated June 15, 2023

This bill, as enacted on July 18, 2023, expands the types of accepted voter ID. Specifically, the bill:

  • Broadens the types of student ID accepted for voting, to include IDs issued by professional and vocational educational institutions. Under previous law, accepted student IDs were limited to those issued by a high school or higher education institution granting accredited degrees or certificates.
  • Permits the use of a current photo identification card issued by a local government, in addition to the existing accepted IDs from federal, tribal, and state government.

A previous version of the bill contained additional provisions that were amended out on June 14, 2023. These provisions would have required that an acceptable current military photo identification card must be issued by the federal or state government and a current tribal photo identification card must be issued by a tribal government, and would have required that a current state government issued photo identification card, other than a driver's license or state identification card, is only valid if issued by the state of Michigan.

Last Updated August 18, 2023

This bill, as enacted on November 30, 2023, makes a minor change to precinct size and consolidation rules. House Bill 4702, enacted on July 19, 2023, raised the maximum precinct size from 2,999 active registered voters to 5,000 voters. This bill:

  • Lowers the maximum precinct size by one, from 5,000 active voters to 4,999.
  • Makes a corresponding change to lower the criteria for consolidating precincts, from 5,000 active registered voters in a jurisdiction, to 4,999 voters.

A previous version of this bill included tracked provisions that were amended out prior to enactment. These provisions would have:

  • Required a minimum number of voting machines, based on the number of active registered voters in a voting precinct.
  • Required local officials to consider only the number of active registered voters when determining whether to divide precincts, by eliminating the existing alternative option to consider the total of active and inactive voters.

The bill also includes an additional provision related to candidate disclosure requirements that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

Last updated February 29, 2024.

This bill, as enacted on November 30, 2023, permits a county, city, or township clerk to offer an online or otherwise electronic application process for the position of poll worker (“precinct election inspector”). Prior law required poll worker applications to be completed in the applicant’s own handwriting.

Last updated February 29, 2024.

This bill, as introduced on June 13, 2023, would permit the establishment of "election day vote centers" to facilitate the casting and tabulating of ballots cast by voters who register or update their registrations on Election Day and make several changes to mail ballot procedures. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Permit a municipality that had at least 500 same-day registrants in at least one of the last two November general elections to establish an "election day vote center" not later than 90 days before an election.
  • Establish an election day vote center as a polling place for individuals registering to vote on Election Day. The voter would be permitted to register, cast their ballot, and insert it directly into the tabulator, and would otherwise be entitled to the same protections as any voter voting at their precinct polling place.
  • Permit mail voters to deliver their mail ballots to a polling place or an early voting site to directly insert their ballot into the tabulator. A voter who does this would be required to present ID or sign an affidavit attesting that they do not have ID. Some exceptions would be made to this for a municipality that is unable to program a tabulator to directly receive such ballots.
  • Limit the time period during which a mail voter may request that their ballot, if not already tabulated, be spoiled. Under existing law, this request can be made as late as the Friday before Election Day. Under the bill, the deadline would be a week earlier.
  • Clarify, in accordance with changes made to the state constitution in 2022, that postage for returning a mail ballot is prepaid by the government.
  • Make adjustments to procedures for the verification of mail ballots by clerks and election inspectors, including through establishment of a process under which mail ballots may be tabulated as early as eight days before Election Day.

Last Updated June 20, 2023

This bill, as amended on June 26, 2024, would establish certain protections in recognition of the right to vote and other constitutional guarantees, and would assert that the state intends all election law to be construed in a manner that encourages electoral participation and intends that members of minority groups have equal access to participate. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Assert that all laws of the state are intended to be construed in a manner that favors the lawful exercise of the vote by eligible voters, the counting of those votes, and accessibility of the electoral process.
  • Prohibit any agency or local government of the state from imposing any qualification on a person's ability to vote, adopting any prerequisite to voting or any regulation or ordinance impacting the administration of elections, or imposing any standard, practice, procedure, or policy inconsistent with the goals of electoral participation and equal access to the process. The bill creates a rebuttable presumption that certain activities, including failure to provide translated voter materials, closing a polling place in a manner likely to disproportionately impact a protected class, or changing a local government (including through annexation or dissolution) in a way likely to disproportionately impact a protected class.
  • Prohibit any local government from using any method of election that has the effect of impairing the opportunity of protected class members to elect candidates of the protected class member's choice, or otherwise diluting their votes. The bill provides guidelines and general principles for how to conclude whether this has occurred.
  • Provide general guidelines for how to determine if a protected class has had their right to vote impaired, when viewing the totality of the circumstances. The bill also provides procedures for commencing an action against a local government alleging a violation of a right guaranteed under the bill. The bill would also permit local governments to adopt resolutions to remedy alleged violations. Such a resolution would be sent to the secretary of state to determine if the remedy proposed would solve the problem.
  • Require covered jurisdictions to obtain preclearance for covered policies from the secretary of state or the court of claims. The secretary would make an annual determination of which jurisdictions are covered for this purpose based on a set of rules intended to encompass recent violators of the bill or local governments otherwise engaging in activities inconsistent with the bill's stated goals. A covered policy would be any new or modified qualification for admission as an elector, prerequisite to vote, or any law or regulation of any kind impacting access to the ballot.
  • Permit a voter with disabilities, or an organization that advocates for such voters, to bring an action requesting that a monitor be appointed for elections conducted by a local government having recently engaged in activity that negatively impacts access to the ballot for voters with disabilities. The monitor, if appointed, would be granted authority to take actions to protect the voting rights of these individuals within the local government's jurisdiction.

The bill would take effect only if Senate Bills 401, 402, and 403 are also passed into law.

A previous version of the bill would have created a voter education fund in the state treasury, administered by the department of civil rights. That provision was amended out of the bill on June 18, 2024.

Last Updated August 9, 2024

This bill, as amended on June 26, 2024, would require the Secretary of State, not later than November 5, 2025, to enter into an agreement with one or more public universities in Michigan to create a voting and elections database and institute. The purpose of the database and institute would be to aggregate all elections and voting data available to the public from local governments (who would be required to share their data) and to foster research on existing laws and on election best practices. All data would be maintained electronically and all relevant election and voting data and records for at least the previous 12-year period would be required to be made available for study.

The bill would only take effect if Senate Bills 401 and 403 are also passed.

Last Updated July 24, 2024

This bill, as amended on June 26, 2024, would require local governments to provide language assistance to voters. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require local governments to provide language assistance to voters if one of the following conditions is met:
    • Before January 1, 2030, at least 5% of eligible voters or at least 10,000 eligible voters in that local government's jurisdiction speak a non-English language and have limited English proficiency
    • Beginning January 1, 2030, at least 600 eligible voters in that local government's jurisdiction (or at least 100 if that comprises at least 2.5% of the voting-eligible population in that government) that speak a non-English language and have limited English proficiency
  • Require a county to provide language assistance to voters if a local government required to do so enters into an agreement with the county under which the county will conduct early voting for the local government.
  • Require the secretary of state to track and share which jurisdictions are covered by these provisions, and the relevant languages, at least biannually. The secretary would also be required to create the necessary documents for language assistance for elections in all covered languages. A language access advisory council would be created within the secretary's office to advise on how to implement the law.
  • Instruct the director of elections to keep local governments up to date with whether they are required to provide language assistance under the law.
  • Require a prospective plaintiff to notify the local government or secretary of state, as appropriate, before filing a civil action alleging that a local government failed to provide effective language assistance to attempt to create a written plan to address the issue. Such a lawsuit could be filed by the attorney general, an affected voter, or an affected entity. The local government would then be required to provide effective language assistance in that language (including translated materials and live interpretation if possible), and the attorney general, an affected voter, or an affected entity could bring an action in court to request appropriate remedies if the jurisdiction failed to provide effective language assistance.

The bill would only take effect if Senate Bill 401 and Senate Bill 402 are also passed.

Last Updated August 8, 2024

This bill, as amended on June 26, 2024, would:

  • Permit a voter who is unable to enter a polling place to request to vote their ballot curbside at a polling place by requesting that assistance in advance or sending another person inside the polling place to request assistance on their behalf, or through any other method deemed appropriate by election officials. The bill would:
    • Require that two election officials from opposing political parties deliver the voter's ballot, wait while the voter casts the ballot, then take it inside to be tabulated and return to confirm the tabulation to the voter.
    • Require curbside voting to be offered at all hours a polling place or early voting site is open.
  • Provide that an individual is permitted to provide food, entertainment, warmth, or other necessities to persons waiting in line to vote.
  • Permit a voter to have language assistance while voting from any individual chosen by the voter to assist the voter in participating in the electoral process.
  • Require the secretary of state to provide notice on the secretary's website within 5 days of receiving notice from a local government of any of the following:
    • a change in location of a polling place, ballot dropbox, or other voting location
    • any change in voting hours during regular or early voting, or changes to an early voting plan
    • the results of an election audit, selection of a voting system, establishment of a counting board, or changes to a district
  • Repeal a provision of law requiring a primary election ballot to be spoiled, and the voter prevented from voting in that primary, if the voter shows the ballot to another person in a way likely to reveal how the voter voted.

The bill would take effect only if Senate Bills 401 and 403 are also passed.

The bill would also make changes in areas of law not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, including notice requirements for certain ballot language or for the inspection of election equipment.

A previous version of the bill would have made additional changes. Those provisions were amended out of the bill on June 18, 2024. Those provisions would have:

  • Provided that a nonprofit or nonpartisan entity, other than a political committee, may provide transportation for voters. The bill would accordingly have also repealed a criminal statute that prohibits this practice. These provisions were enacted by another bill, H.B. 4568.
  • Repealed a misdemeanor offense that prohibits the publication of anonymous "false, deceptive, scurrilous, or malicious" statements about political candidates.

Last Updated August 9, 2024

This bill, as enacted on November 7, 2023, delays the start date for election officials to provide for electronic return of ballots by UOCAVA and merchant marine voters (and their spouses). Prior law required officials to offer electronic ballot return to these voters by January 1, 2024. Under the bill, the deadline is now September 1, 2025.

Last Updated February 29, 2024

This bill, as enacted on November 22, 2023, makes a minor change to the requirements for consolidating election precincts, by permitting consolidation in localities with up to 4,999 active registered voters, rather than up to 5,000 as required by prior law.

Note: Enacted Senate Bill 374 included this same change, among other minor changes to precinct size requirements.

Last updated February 29, 2024.

This bill, as enacted on November 22, 2023, makes a minor change to the requirements for maximum election precinct size, by capping precincts at 4,999 active registered voters, rather than 5,000 as required by prior law.

Note: Enacted Senate Bill 374 included this same change, among other minor changes to precinct size requirements.

Last updated February 29, 2024.

This bill, as enacted on November 30, 2023, modifies the state's online voter registration system by allowing use of an alternative form of identification, requiring digital signature images, and removing certain ID restrictions. The bill will take effect June 30, 2025. Specifically, the bill:

  • Permits an eligible person to register to vote online by providing the last four digits of their Social Security number if they do not possess a valid ID number. Under prior law, online voter registration was available for voters who have a Michigan driver's license or state ID.
  • Requires the voter registration interface to authenticate the identity of those who provide only the last four digits of their Social Security number by verifying that number, the person's full name, and their date of birth.
  • Requires people applying to register online to submit a digital signature image and assent to use of the signature for registration purposes if one is not already in their voter file. The bill allows a registered voter to submit a new or additional signature and require their identity to be authenticated before the signature is added to their voter file. Prior law required a voter's assent to use their digital signature if it is captured or reproduced by the secretary of state but did not expressly mandate submission of a digital signature. This bill also requires the secretary of state to develop a process for submitting high-quality digitized signature images.
  • Removes provisions in existing law that prohibit use of the electronic voter registration interface by individuals who:
    • Have only an expired driver's license or state ID
    • Order a duplicate driver's license or state ID the same day as submitting an electronic voter application

HISTORY: {"date":"05/05/2023","summary":"Filed with Secretary of State. Chapter No. 34","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on May 5, 2023, makes various changes to election law, including establishing automatic voter registration at multiple state agencies, creating a permanent mail voter list, and creating new criminal offenses for conduct related to intimidation and interference with voting and registration. Specifically, the bill:

  • Creates an automatic voter registration system in the state. Specifically, the bill:
    • Requires that eligible individuals be registered to vote when submitting an application for a driver's license, instruction permit, or state identification card to the Department of Public Safety, for medical assistance under the program administered by the commissioner of human services or MinnesotaCare, or for benefits or services from a participating state agency. Under the bill, the governor has sole discretion to determine whether an additional state agency would be an appropriate partner in the program.
    • Requires automatic updates to the voter registration record if an applicant for services provides a different name or address than listed on their existing registration.
    • Requires the relevant state agencies to change their application forms as necessary to accommodate these changes, including by obtaining evidence that the applicant is a United States citizen. The agencies must keep and submit data on the program to the Secretary of State, who must publish a monthly report detailing the number of registrants.
    • Requires "prompt" notice by mail after an automatic registration transaction that the individual may decline their new or updated registration. Applicants who opt-out within 20 days of completing the application would not be registered (or have their record updated).
  • Establishes a permanent mail voter list that allows voters who apply for "permanent absentee voter status" to receive a mail ballot for all elections and modifies the standard registration application form to allow for enrollment. Under previous law, a person placed on the permanent absentee ballot list was mailed a mail ballot application for each election, rather than a ballot. A conforming change is also made to permit the ballot board, when examining a voter's name and address on a signature envelope to determine whether the ballot should be counted, to compare the information against voter record or ballot application. Previous law permitted comparison against the application only.
  • Permits an eligible individual who is age 16 years or older to preregister to vote by direct application or through automatic registration procedures. The bill exempts pre-registered individuals from prosecution under the state's illegal voter registration statute, and exempts their information from disclosure on the registered voters list until they turn 18. Under previous law, pre-registration was available only if the individual would have been 18 or older at the time of the next scheduled election.
  • Creates new misdemeanor offenses for:
    • intimidating a person in an attempt to compel the person to register or not register to vote, to vote or not vote, or to vote for or against a candidate or ballot question
    • intimidating a person to impede that person's efforts to "encourage" another person to participate in the electoral process (e.g., assistance with registration, casting a ballot, travel to a polling place)
    • causing deceptive information to be transmitted by any means within 60 days of an election with the intent to impede or prevent another person from exercising that person's right to vote, if the person making the transmission knows the information is materially false
    • intentionally interfering with voter registration or voting
    • intentionally aiding or compelling an individual to commit or attempt a voting intimidation or interference offense, or conspiring to do so or have someone else do so
  • Authorizes the Attorney General, election officials, or any injured party to bring a civil cause of action, with penalties of up to $1,000 per violation, for any injuries they incur due to prohibited intimidation or interference conduct.
  • Requires the Secretary of State or a county auditor to contract with a translator to provide election materials at polling places in the three most commonly-spoken non-English languages in the state, and additional languages as determined by specified state demographic criteria and/or by request. In a precinct with 20%+ language minority voters, an election judge fluent in a particular language must also be present at a polling place if ten or more voters make a request, via the Secretary or county auditor, for interpretation services at least 30 days before the election. The Secretary is also responsible for providing copies of the translated election materials on the agency website.
  • Explicitly provides that a voter registration application that does not contain the revisions required by the bill will still be valid if provided to the voter before the bill goes into effect.

The bill also contains additional provisions related to areas of election law that Voting Rights Lab does not track, including campaign finance.

A previous version of the bill included several provisions that were amended out before enactment. These provisions would have moved forward the restoration of voting rights of persons disenfranchised due to felony convictions, and created new notice requirements for impacted individuals. The provisions were amended out of the bill on February 15, 2023, likely due to the advancement of H.B. 28, which contains similar provisions.

Last Updated October 23, 2023

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced January 19, 2023, would change procedures related to the state's early voting process. Procedures related to early voting by in-person "absentee" mail ballot would remain in place, but the bill would expand Election Day-style early voting. Specifically, the bill would :

  • Require Election Day-style early voting for federal, state, and county elections beginning 30 days before Election Day and ending at 5 p.m. on the third day before Election Day. Existing law authorizes local election officials to offer Election Day-style early voting during the seven days before an election (in-person absentee is available during the 46 days before), ending at 5 p.m. the day before an election. As under existing law, early voting must be offered in the office of the county auditor or municipal clerk, and may be offered at additional designated locations.
  • Expand the hours that Election Day-style early voting is offered. The bill would require the process to be available 8 a.m. - 4:30 p.m. on weekdays, 8 a.m. - 8 p.m. on at least one weekday, and 10 a.m. - 5 p.m. on the two Saturdays before an election. Existing law requires early voting (of both types) to be offered from 10 a.m. - 3 p.m. on Saturday and until 5 p.m. on the day before an election, but is otherwise silent as to specific hours.
  • Require each polling location for early voting to offer at least one voting station and one ballot marking device for disabled voters. Existing law is silent as to specific accessibility requirements.
  • Require local election officials to provide notice of the days, times, and locations for early voting at least 14 days before the voting period begins, by posting information on their website or in a newspaper.
  • Authorize local election officials to offer Election Day-style early voting for city elections that are not run along with federal, state, or county elections, by adoption of resolution, if the municipal clerk meets certain equipment requirements.
  • Require election authorities, in elections that are subject to new provisions for Election Day-style early voting, to offer in-person "absentee" mail voting from 8 a.m. to noon on the day before Election Day. For elections that would not be subject to the new provisions, clerks' offices must be open for in-person absentee voting from 10 a.m. - 3 p.m. on Saturday and until 5 p.m. on the day before the election. Under existing law, the latter requirements apply to clerk office hours during the early voting period, regardless of election type.
  • Expand multiple existing felonies for third party conduct related to absentee voting, by applying the prohibitions to the early voting process and materials, as well.
  • Repeal existing statutory provisions concerning the optional Election Day-style "alternative" procedure for early voting. The bill would also define "early voting" as a distinct process from "absentee voting," and make conforming changes throughout provisions.

Last Updated February 8, 2023

HISTORY: {"date":"01/19/2023","summary":"To HOUSE Committee on ELECTIONS FINANCE AND POLICY","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced January 19, 2023, would change the state's voter ID requirements. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require documentary proof of identity, in the form of voter ID, in many situations where it is not currently required, by:
    • Requiring photo ID and proof of residence to vote in person. Under existing law, voters affirm their identity and residence under penalty of perjury but are not required to provide documentation.
    • Requiring anyone lacking proof of ID or proof of residence when voting in person to cast a provisional ballot. Provisional ballots would only be counted if a voter presents photo ID and documents proving their residence within seven days after Election Day, unless the voter attempts to procure these documents but is unable to and attests to that fact.
    • Requiring photo ID for anyone registering to vote on Election Day. Under existing law, photo ID is typically required but can be waived if a registered voter or residential facility employee signs an oath affirming the voter's identity, based on the affiant's personal knowledge.
    • Requiring photo ID for any person applying to vote at the time they return an absentee ballot or a mail ballot. This provision would require that the voter show the witness signing the voter's absentee ballot photo ID to demonstrate their identity. Under existing law, the voter needed to only show the witness proof of residence. This provision would also require the witness to provide their own driver's license number, state ID number, voter ID number, the last four digits of their social security number, or a statement that they do not have any of these numbers. Ballots lacking this information would be rejected.
    • Expanding the types of ID numbers required on absentee ballot applications, absentee ballot envelopes, and mail ballot envelopes to include voter ID numbers. Under existing law, applicants must provide their driver's license number, state ID number, the last four digits of their social security number, or a statement that they do not have any of these ID numbers. This bill would require that the voter's ID number be verified and reject any application with an invalid ID number.
    • Providing free voter ID cards to any person who lacks a driver's license or state ID card. Applicants would be required to provide information including the last four digits of the applicant's social security number (or a certification that they do not have one), proof of citizenship, and proof of name, date of birth, identity, and residence address before obtaining a free voter ID card. Voter ID cards would have a unique ID number, the person's name, date of birth, address, signature, and photograph, and the card would have to be replaced if the voter's name or address changed. This bill would also provide that people who need a certified vital record can obtain the record for free if the person attests that it is to obtain a voter ID card.
    • Requiring the secretary of state to conduct a public education campaign regarding the new ID requirements of this bill and the availability of free voter ID.
  • Prohibit compensation for the solicitation, collection, or acceptance of mail ballot applications from voters if the compensation is tied to the number of applications.
  • Repeal a provision of law that permits a voter to designate an agent to return the voter's mail ballot.
  • Require any early voting location established by a county to be open for the same days and hours that the county auditor's office is open for early voting during the entire early voting period.
  • Require an individual assisting a voter voting in person with their ballot to provide their name, address, and telephone number, and create a felony offense for assisting a voter with a ballot in a manner not authorized by law.
  • Add unduly influencing a person to register to vote or to apply for a mail ballot to the definition of the offense of unduly influencing a voter, and increasing the punishment for that offense from a misdemeanor to a felony.
  • Add bribing a person to register to vote or to apply for a mail ballot to the definition of the offense of bribing a voter.
  • Require the secretary of state to annually report to legislative leadership their proposed legislation, which, according to this bill, should only be legislation that would codify matters that would otherwise be adopted through administrative rulemaking.
  • Extend the timeframe for canvassing ballots after primaries and elections.
  • Make additional conforming changes to other sections of the election code.

Last Updated February 23, 2023

HISTORY: {"date":"01/26/2023","summary":"To HOUSE Committee on ELECTIONS FINANCE AND POLICY","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced January 20, 2023, would create new photo ID requirements for in-person voting, same-day registration, provisional ballots, and mail ballot voting, among other changes. Existing law does not require voters to show ID to vote in person, and has less onerous documentation requirements for other voting-related activities than those set out in the bill. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Define accepted forms of "documentary proof of identity and residence" for use as voter ID. Accepted forms of ID would be limited to:
    • an unexpired state driver's license, state ID, or voter ID card, with photo and current residence
    • valid US military ID, with photo and current residence
    • unexpired tribal ID, with photo and current residence
    • receipt for a driver's license, state ID, or voter ID card, with photo and current residence (if receipt lacks photo, this must be accompanied by (1) a license, state ID, or voter ID that is expired or shows prior address, (2) a US passport, (3) a photo ID issued by the state or federal government, (4) a student ID issued by a postsecondary institution that has provided an enrollment list to election authorities, or (5) a tribal ID)
    • a US passport, tribal ID, or US military card that has a photo but does not have the voter's current address, plus one of the following with their address: (1) utility bill or work services order, (2) bank statement, (3) high school transcript, (4) college or university transcript issued by institution in the state, (5) unemployment stub, (6) statement from long-term health care facility, (7) insurance policy, (8) federal or state tax return, (9) property tax statement, (10) vehicle title, (11) property deed or title, (12) SSI statement, (13) mortgage document, (14) lease agreement, (15) unexpired professional license, (16) unexpired Selective Service card, (17) current military orders, (18) cell phone bill, or (19) game or fishing license.
    • for students, a state license, state ID, or voter ID card issued by any state that includes a photograph, and a current fee statement showing state residence
    • for residential facility residents, a license or state ID card, and a certification of residence through the state's official form
  • Require an accepted form of photo ID to vote in person. Under existing law, in-person voters must affirm their identity and residence under penalty of perjury, but are not required to provide documentation.
  • Require in-person voters who lack an accepted form of photo ID to cast a provisional ballot, and set out procedures related to provisional ballot voting and verification. A provisional ballot would only be counted if the voter presents required photo ID within seven days after Election Day, unless they have attempted to procure the documents and were unable to, and attest to that fact. Existing law does not provide for the use of provisional ballots.
  • Require an accepted form of photo ID for same-day registration on Election Day. Under existing law, same-day registrants are required to provide proof of residence only, by presenting a driver's license, state ID, student ID and enrollment list/fee statement, or tribal ID, but this documentation requirement can be waived if a registered voter or residential facility employee signs an oath affirming the voter's identity, based on the affiant's personal knowledge. Under the bill, same day registrants who could not provide acceptable photo ID would only be permitted to vote a provisional ballot.
  • Require mail ballot voters to show an accepted form of photo ID to their ballot witness, who must note the specific type on the ballot certificate. Voters who have attempted to procure accepted ID and been unable to do so would be permitted to execute an affidavit asserting the explanation, which must be signed in the presence of the witness. Under existing law, mail ballot voters who are already registered must provide an ID number on the ballot certificate, but are not required to present any documentation to their witness. For mail voters who are applying to register along with their completed ballot, existing law requires these voters to provide proof of residence only. The bill would also require a ballot witness to provide their own driver's license number, state ID number, voter ID number, the last four digits of their social security number, or a statement that they do not have any of these numbers. Ballots lacking this information, or any information required on the ballot certificate, would be rejected.
  • Expressly require election administrators to verify the identification numbers provided by a mail ballot applicant, and reject any application with a number that is not verified. Existing law requires verification of ID numbers by the Secretary of State for electronic mail ballot applications, but does not have an express requirement for applications otherwise submitted.
  • Provide for free voter ID cards to any person who lacks a driver's license or state ID card. Applicants would be required to provide information including a social security number (or a certification that they do not have one), proof of citizenship, and a photo ID (unless they have a religious objection) to obtain a free voter ID card. Voter ID cards would have a unique ID number, the person's name, date of birth, address, signature, and photograph, and would have to be replaced prior to use for voting if the voter's name or address change. The bill would also provide that people who need a certified vital record can obtain the record for free if the person attests that it is to obtain a voter ID card. Use of a voter ID card number would be permitted throughout election provisions where a driver's license or state ID number is accepted under existing law.
  • Require the Secretary of State to conduct a public education campaign regarding the new photo ID requirements and availability of free voter ID cards.
  • Require the Secretary of State to report to legislative leadership, by January 2024, proposed legislation to codify any election-related matters currently subject to administrative rulemaking that could be enacted into statutory law. For matters that are not practicable in statutory law, the Secretary must propose legislation that directs specific changes in administrative rules such that no interpretation of the law is required of the Secretary and the good cause rulemaking exception would be appropriate if authorized by the legislature.
  • Extend the timeframe for canvassing ballots after primaries and elections.

  • Make various conforming changes to other sections of the election code.

    The bill also contains additional provisions related to topics that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

  • Change requirements for registering to vote by mail by:

    • Eliminating the requirement that voters who are simultaneously registering to vote and returning an absentee ballot present proof of residence to the witness for the absentee ballot.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced February 1, 2023, would change the state's voter ID requirements. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require documentary proof of identity, in the form of voter ID, in many situations where it is not currently required, by:
    • Requiring photo ID and proof of residence to vote in person. Under existing law, voters affirm their identity and residence under penalty of perjury but are not required to provide documentation.
    • Requiring anyone lacking proof of ID or proof of residence when voting in person to cast a provisional ballot. Provisional ballots would only be counted if a voter presents photo ID and documents proving their residence within seven days after Election Day, unless the voter attempts to procure these documents but is unable to and attests to that fact.
    • Requiring photo ID for anyone registering to vote on Election Day. Under existing law, photo ID is typically required but can be waived if a registered voter or residential facility employee signs an oath affirming the voter's identity, based on the affiant's personal knowledge.
    • Requiring photo ID for any person applying to vote at the time they return an absentee ballot or a mail ballot. This provision would require that the voter show the witness signing the voter's absentee ballot photo ID to demonstrate their identity. Under existing law, the voter needed to only show the witness proof of residence. This provision would also require the witness to provide their own driver's license number, state ID number, voter ID number, the last four digits of their social security number, or a statement that they do not have any of these numbers. Ballots lacking this information would be rejected.
    • Expanding the types of ID numbers required on absentee ballot applications, absentee ballot envelopes, and mail ballot envelopes to include voter ID numbers. Under existing law, applicants must provide their driver's license number, state ID number, the last four digits of their social security number, or a statement that they do not have any of these ID numbers. This bill would require that the voter's ID number be verified and reject any application with an invalid ID number.
    • Providing free voter ID cards to any person who lacks a driver's license or state ID card. Applicants would be required to provide information including the last four digits of the applicant's social security number (or a certification that they do not have one), proof of citizenship, and proof of name, date of birth, identity, and residence address before obtaining a free voter ID card. Voter ID cards would have a unique ID number, the person's name, date of birth, address, signature, and photograph, and the card would have to be replaced if the voter's name or address changed. This bill would also provide that people who need a certified vital record can obtain the record for free if the person attests that it is to obtain a voter ID card.
    • Requiring the secretary of state to conduct a public education campaign regarding the new ID requirements of this bill and the availability of free voter ID.
  • Prohibit compensation for the solicitation, collection, or acceptance of mail ballot applications from voters if the compensation is tied to the number of applications.
  • Repeal a provision of law that permits a voter to designate an agent to return the voter's mail ballot.
  • Require any early voting location established by a county to be open for the same days and hours that the county auditor's office is open for early voting during the entire early voting period.
  • Require an individual assisting a voter voting in person with their ballot to provide their name, address, and telephone number, and create a felony offense for assisting a voter with a ballot in a manner not authorized by law.
  • Add unduly influencing a person to register to vote or to apply for a mail ballot to the definition of the offense of unduly influencing a voter, and increasing the punishment for that offense from a misdemeanor to a felony.
  • Add bribing a person to register to vote or to apply for a mail ballot to the definition of the offense of bribing a voter.
  • Require the secretary of state to annually report to legislative leadership their proposed legislation, which, according to this bill, should only be legislation that would codify matters that would otherwise be adopted through administrative rulemaking.
  • Extend the timeframe for canvassing ballots after primaries and elections.
  • Make additional conforming changes to other sections of the election code.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced February 2, 2023, would make various changes to election law, including establishing automatic voter registration at multiple state agencies, changing the date for restoration of voting rights following conviction for a felony offense, creating a permanent mail voter list, and creating new criminal offenses for conduct related to intimidation and interference with voting and registration. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create an automatic voter registration system in the state. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require that a person be registered to vote, if eligible, at the time the person submits an application for a driver's license, instruction permit, or state identification card to the Department of Public Safety, for medical assistance under the program administered by the commissioner of human services or MinnesotaCare, or for benefits or services from a participating state agency. The governor would have sole discretion to determine whether an additional state agency would be an appropriate partner in the program.
    • Require automatic updates to the voter registration record if an applicant for services provides a different name or address than listed on their existing registration.
    • Require the relevant state agencies to change their application forms as necessary to accommodate these changes, including by obtaining evidence that the applicant is a United States citizen. The agencies would be required to keep and submit data on the program to the secretary of state, who would publish a monthly report detailing the number of registrants.
    • Require "prompt" notice by mail after an automatic registration transaction that the individual may decline their new or updated registration. Applicants who opt-out within 20 days of completing the application would not be registered (or have their record updated).
    • Set the effective date for automatic registration provisions at July 1, 2023.
  • Move forward the restoration of voting rights of persons disenfranchised due to felony convictions, and create new notice requirements for impacted individuals. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Restore the right to vote upon release from incarceration for a felony conviction, or upon sentencing if no incarceration is imposed. Under existing law, voting rights are restored upon "discharge," which includes serving any period of probation, parole, or supervised release.
    • Require the secretary of state to develop a publication about the voting rights of persons charged with or convicted of a crime and make that publication widely available.
    • Require each correctional facility in the state to designate an official to provide notice of the restoration of voting rights to each person convicted of a felony upon release from incarceration, and a registration application. The bill would also require probation officers and supervised release agents to do the same.
  • Establish a permanent mail voter list that allows voters who apply for "permanent absentee voter status" to receive a mail ballot for all elections. Under existing law, a person placed on the permanent absentee ballot list is mailed a mail ballot application for each election, rather than a ballot. A conforming change is made to permit the ballot board, when examining a voter's name and address on a signature envelope to determine whether the ballot should be counted, to compare the information against voter record or ballot application. Existing law only permits comparison against the application.
  • Permit an individual who is age 16 years or older to preregister to vote. These pre-registered individuals would be protected from prosecution under the state's illegal voter registration statute, and their information would not be included on the public information list of registered voters until they turn 18. Under existing law, a person under the age of 18 may preregister to vote, but only if they will be 18 or older at the time of the next scheduled election.
  • Create new misdemeanor offenses for:
    • intimidating a person in an attempt to compel the person to register or not register to vote, to vote or not vote, or to vote for or against a candidate or ballot question
    • intimidating a person to impede that person's efforts to "encourage" another person to participate in the electoral process (e.g., assistance with registration, casting a ballot, travel to a polling place)
    • causing deceptive information to be transmitted by any means within 60 days of an election with the intent to impede or prevent another person from exercising that person's right to vote, if the person making the transmission knows the information is materially false
    • intentionally interfering with voter registration or voting
    • intentionally aiding or compelling an individual to commit or attempt a voting intimidation or interference offense, or conspiring to do so or have someone else do so
  • Authorize the attorney general and election officials to bring a civil cause of action, with penalties of up to $1,000 per violation, for any injuries they incur due to prohibited intimidation or interference conduct
  • Require the secretary of state or a county auditor to contract with a translator to provide election materials at polling places in Spanish, Hmong, and Somali, and additional languages as determined by specified state demographic criteria and/or by request. In a precinct with 20%+ language minority voters, an election judge fluent in a particular language must also be present at a polling place if ten or more voters make a request, via the secretary of state or county auditor, for interpretation services at least 30 days before the election.

The bill also makes changes to areas of election law that Voting Rights Lab does not track, including campaign finance.

This bill, as introduced February 13, 2023, would create new photo ID requirements for in-person voting, same-day registration, provisional ballots, and mail ballot voting, among other changes. Existing law does not require voters to show ID to vote in person, and has less onerous documentation requirements for other voting-related activities than those set out in the bill. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Define accepted forms of "documentary proof of identity and residence" for use as voter ID. Accepted forms of ID would be limited to:
    • an unexpired state driver's license, state ID, or voter ID card, with photo and current residence
    • valid US military ID, with photo and current residence
    • unexpired tribal ID, with photo and current residence
    • receipt for a driver's license, state ID, or voter ID card, with photo and current residence (if receipt lacks photo, this must be accompanied by (1) a license, state ID, or voter ID that is expired or shows prior address, (2) a US passport, (3) a photo ID issued by the state or federal government, (4) a student ID issued by a postsecondary institution that has provided an enrollment list to election authorities, or (5) a tribal ID)
    • a US passport, tribal ID, or US military card that has a photo but does not have the voter's current address, plus one of the following with their address: (1) utility bill or work services order, (2) bank statement, (3) high school transcript, (4) college or university transcript issued by institution in the state, (5) unemployment stub, (6) statement from long-term health care facility, (7) insurance policy, (8) federal or state tax return, (9) property tax statement, (10) vehicle title, (11) property deed or title, (12) SSI statement, (13) mortgage document, (14) lease agreement, (15) unexpired professional license, (16) unexpired Selective Service card, (17) current military orders, (18) cell phone bill, or (19) game or fishing license.
    • for students, a state license, state ID, or voter ID card issued by any state that includes a photograph, and a current fee statement showing state residence
    • for residential facility residents, a license or state ID card, and a certification of residence through the state's official form
  • Require an accepted form of photo ID to vote in person. Under existing law, in-person voters must affirm their identity and residence under penalty of perjury, but are not required to provide documentation.
  • Require in-person voters who lack an accepted form of photo ID to cast a provisional ballot, and set out procedures related to provisional ballot voting and verification. A provisional ballot would only be counted if the voter presents required photo ID within seven days after Election Day, unless they have attempted to procure the documents and were unable to, and attest to that fact. Existing law does not provide for the use of provisional ballots.
  • Require an accepted form of photo ID for same-day registration on Election Day. Under existing law, same-day registrants are required to provide proof of residence only, by presenting a driver's license, state ID, student ID and enrollment list/fee statement, or tribal ID, but this documentation requirement can be waived if a registered voter or residential facility employee signs an oath affirming the voter's identity, based on the affiant's personal knowledge. Under the bill, same day registrants who could not provide acceptable photo ID would only be permitted to vote a provisional ballot.
  • Require mail ballot voters to show an accepted form of photo ID to their ballot witness, who must note the specific type on the ballot certificate. Voters who have attempted to procure accepted ID and been unable to do so would be permitted to execute an affidavit asserting the explanation, which must be signed in the presence of the witness. Under existing law, mail ballot voters who are already registered must provide an ID number on the ballot certificate, but are not required to present any documentation to their witness. For mail voters who are applying to register along with their completed ballot, existing law requires these voters to provide proof of residence only. The bill would also require a ballot witness to provide their own driver's license number, state ID number, voter ID number, the last four digits of their social security number, or a statement that they do not have any of these numbers. Ballots lacking this information, or any information required on the ballot certificate, would be rejected.
  • Expressly require election administrators to verify the identification numbers provided by a mail ballot applicant, and reject any application with a number that is not verified. Existing law requires verification of ID numbers by the Secretary of State for electronic mail ballot applications, but does not have an express requirement for applications otherwise submitted.

Applicants would be required to provide information including a social security number (or a certification that they do not have one), proof of citizenship, and a photo ID (unless they have a religious objection) to obtain a free voter ID card. This bill, as amended on April 11, 2023, would make various changes to election law, including establishing automatic voter registration at multiple state agencies, creating a permanent mail voter list, and creating new criminal offenses for conduct related to intimidation and interference with voting and registration. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create an automatic voter registration system in the state. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require that a person be registered to vote, if eligible, at the time the person submits an application for a driver's license, instruction permit, or state identification card to the Department of Public Safety, for medical assistance under the program administered by the commissioner of human services or MinnesotaCare, or for benefits or services from a participating state agency. The governor would have sole discretion to determine whether an additional state agency would be an appropriate partner in the program.
    • Require automatic updates to the voter registration record if an applicant for services provides a different name or address than listed on their existing registration.
    • Require the relevant state agencies to change their application forms as necessary to accommodate these changes, including by obtaining evidence that the applicant is a United States citizen. The agencies would be required to keep and submit data on the program to the secretary of state, who would publish a monthly report detailing the number of registrants.
    • Require "prompt" notice by mail after an automatic registration transaction that the individual may decline their new or updated registration. Applicants who opt-out within 20 days of completing the application would not be registered (or have their record updated).
  • Establish a permanent mail voter list that allows voters who apply for "permanent absentee voter status" to receive a mail ballot for all elections. Under existing law, a person placed on the permanent absentee ballot list is mailed a mail ballot application for each election, rather than a ballot. The standard voter registration application form would be modified accordingly. A conforming change is made to permit the ballot board, when examining a voter's name and address on a signature envelope to determine whether the ballot should be counted, to compare the information against voter record or ballot application. Existing law only permits comparison against the application.
  • Permit an individual who is age 16 years or older to preregister to vote. These pre-registered individuals would be protected from prosecution under the state's illegal voter registration statute, and their information would not be included on the public information list of registered voters until they turn 18. Under existing law, a person under the age of 18 may preregister to vote, but only if they will be 18 or older at the time of the next scheduled election.
  • Create new misdemeanor offenses for:
    • intimidating a person in an attempt to compel the person to register or not register to vote, to vote or not vote, or to vote for or against a candidate or ballot question
    • intimidating a person to impede that person's efforts to "encourage" another person to participate in the electoral process (e.g., assistance with registration, casting a ballot, travel to a polling place)
    • causing deceptive information to be transmitted by any means within 60 days of an election with the intent to impede or prevent another person from exercising that person's right to vote, if the person making the transmission knows the information is materially false
    • intentionally interfering with voter registration or voting
    • intentionally aiding or compelling an individual to commit or attempt a voting intimidation or interference offense, or conspiring to do so or have someone else do so
  • Authorize the attorney general and election officials to bring a civil cause of action, with penalties of up to $1,000 per violation, for any injuries they incur due to prohibited intimidation or interference conduct
  • Require the secretary of state or a county auditor to contract with a translator to provide election materials at polling places in the three most commonly-spoken non-English languages in the state, and additional languages as determined by specified state demographic criteria and/or by request. In a precinct with 20%+ language minority voters, an election judge fluent in a particular language must also be present at a polling place if ten or more voters make a request, via the secretary of state or county auditor, for interpretation services at least 30 days before the election. The secretary of state would also be responsible for providing copies of the translated election materials available on the secretary's website.
  • Explicitly provide that a voter registration application that does not contain the revisions required by the bill would still be valid if provided to the voter before the bill goes into effect.

A previous version of the bill included several provisions that would have moved forward the restoration of voting rights of persons disenfranchised due to felony convictions, and create new notice requirements for impacted individuals. These provisions were amended out of the bill on March 1, 2023, likely due to the passage of H.B. 28, which contains similar provisions. The bill also makes changes to areas of election law that Voting Rights Lab does not track, including campaign finance.

Last Updated April 25, 2023
