This bill, as introduced January 20, 2023, would create new photo ID requirements for in-person voting, same-day registration, provisional ballots, and mail ballot voting, among other changes. Existing law does not require voters to show ID to vote in person, and has less onerous documentation requirements for other voting-related activities than those set out in the bill. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Define accepted forms of "documentary proof of identity and residence" for use as voter ID. Accepted forms of ID would be limited to:
    • an unexpired state driver's license, state ID, or voter ID card, with photo and current residence
    • valid US military ID, with photo and current residence
    • unexpired tribal ID, with photo and current residence
    • receipt for a driver's license, state ID, or voter ID card, with photo and current residence (if receipt lacks photo, this must be accompanied by (1) a license, state ID, or voter ID that is expired or shows prior address, (2) a US passport, (3) a photo ID issued by the state or federal government, (4) a student ID issued by a postsecondary institution that has provided an enrollment list to election authorities, or (5) a tribal ID)
    • a US passport, tribal ID, or US military card that has a photo but does not have the voter's current address, plus one of the following with their address: (1) utility bill or work services order, (2) bank statement, (3) high school transcript, (4) college or university transcript issued by institution in the state, (5) unemployment stub, (6) statement from long-term health care facility, (7) insurance policy, (8) federal or state tax return, (9) property tax statement, (10) vehicle title, (11) property deed or title, (12) SSI statement, (13) mortgage document, (14) lease agreement, (15) unexpired professional license, (16) unexpired Selective Service card, (17) current military orders, (18) cell phone bill, or (19) game or fishing license.
    • for students, a state license, state ID, or voter ID card issued by any state that includes a photograph, and a current fee statement showing state residence
    • for residential facility residents, a license or state ID card, and a certification of residence through the state's official form
  • Require an accepted form of photo ID to vote in person. Under existing law, in-person voters must affirm their identity and residence under penalty of perjury, but are not required to provide documentation.
  • Require in-person voters who lack an accepted form of photo ID to cast a provisional ballot, and set out procedures related to provisional ballot voting and verification. A provisional ballot would only be counted if the voter presents required photo ID within seven days after Election Day, unless they have attempted to procure the documents and were unable to, and attest to that fact. Existing law does not provide for the use of provisional ballots.
  • Require an accepted form of photo ID for same-day registration on Election Day. Under existing law, same-day registrants are required to provide proof of residence only, by presenting a driver's license, state ID, student ID and enrollment list/fee statement, or tribal ID, but this documentation requirement can be waived if a registered voter or residential facility employee signs an oath affirming the voter's identity, based on the affiant's personal knowledge. Under the bill, same day registrants who could not provide acceptable photo ID would only be permitted to vote a provisional ballot.
  • Require mail ballot voters to show an accepted form of photo ID to their ballot witness, who must note the specific type on the ballot certificate. Voters who have attempted to procure accepted ID and been unable to do so would be permitted to execute an affidavit asserting the explanation, which must be signed in the presence of the witness. Under existing law, mail ballot voters who are already registered must provide an ID number on the ballot certificate, but are not required to present any documentation to their witness. For mail voters who are applying to register along with their completed ballot, existing law requires these voters to provide proof of residence only. The bill would also require a ballot witness to provide their own driver's license number, state ID number, voter ID number, the last four digits of their social security number, or a statement that they do not have any of these numbers. Ballots lacking this information, or any information required on the ballot certificate, would be rejected.
  • Expressly require election administrators to verify the identification numbers provided by a mail ballot applicant, and reject any application with a number that is not verified. Existing law requires verification of ID numbers by the Secretary of State for electronic mail ballot applications, but does not have an express requirement for applications otherwise submitted.
  • Provide for free voter ID cards to any person who lacks a driver's license or state ID card. Applicants would be required to provide information including a social security number (or a certification that they do not have one), proof of citizenship, and a photo ID (unless they have a religious objection) to obtain a free voter ID card. Voter ID cards would have a unique ID number, the person's name, date of birth, address, signature, and photograph, and would have to be replaced prior to use for voting if the voter's name or address change. The bill would also provide that people who need a certified vital record can obtain the record for free if the person attests that it is to obtain a voter ID card. Use of a voter ID card number would be permitted throughout election provisions where a driver's license or state ID number is accepted under existing law.
  • Require the Secretary of State to conduct a public education campaign regarding the new photo ID requirements and availability of free voter ID cards.
  • Require the Secretary of State to report to legislative leadership, by January 2024, proposed legislation to codify any election-related matters currently subject to administrative rulemaking that could be enacted into statutory law. For matters that are not practicable in statutory law, the Secretary must propose legislation that directs specific changes in administrative rules such that no interpretation of the law is required of the Secretary and the good cause rulemaking exception would be appropriate if authorized by the legislature.
  • Extend the timeframe for canvassing ballots after primaries and elections.

  • Make various conforming changes to other sections of the election code.

    The bill also contains additional provisions related to topics that Voting Rights Lab does not track.


Last Updated February 8, 2023

This provision would require that the voter show the witness signing the voter's absentee ballot photo ID to demonstrate their identity. This provision would also require the witness to provide their own driver's license number, state ID number, voter ID number, the last four digits of their social security number, or a statement that they do not have any of these numbers. Ballots lacking this information would be rejected.

Under existing law, applicants must provide their driver's license number, state ID number, the last four digits of their social security number, or a statement that they do not have any of these ID numbers. This bill would require that the voter's ID number be verified and reject any application with an invalid ID number.
    • Providing free voter ID cards to any person who lacks a driver's license or state ID card. Applicants would be required to provide information including the last four digits of the applicant's social security number (or a certification that they do not have one), proof of citizenship, and proof of name, date of birth, identity, and residence address before obtaining a free voter ID card. Voter ID cards would have a unique ID number, the person's name, date of birth, address, signature, and photograph, and the card would have to be replaced if the voter's name or address changed. This bill would also provide that people who need a certified vital record can obtain the record for free if the person attests that it is to obtain a voter ID card.
    • Requiring the secretary of state to conduct a public education campaign regarding the new ID requirements of this bill and the availability of free voter ID.

The bill would also require, rather than permit, institutions who enroll students receiving state aid to provide an enrollment list to election officials, to the extent permitted under federal law. This bill, as introduced February 10, 2023, would make various changes to election law, including establishing automatic voter registration at multiple state agencies, changing the date for restoration of voting rights following conviction for a felony offense, creating a permanent mail voter list, and creating new criminal offenses for conduct related to intimidation and interference with voting and registration. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create an automatic voter registration system in the state. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require that a person be registered to vote, if eligible, at the time the person submits an application for a driver's license, instruction permit, or state identification card to the Department of Public Safety, for medical assistance under the program administered by the commissioner of human services or MinnesotaCare, or for benefits or services from a participating state agency. The governor would have sole discretion to determine whether an additional state agency would be an appropriate partner in the program.
    • Require automatic updates to the voter registration record if an applicant for services provides a different name or address than listed on their existing registration.
    • Require the relevant state agencies to change their application forms as necessary to accommodate these changes, including by requiring applicants to present documentary proof that the applicant is a United States citizen. The agencies would be required to keep and submit data on the program to the secretary of state, who would publish a monthly report detailing the number of registrants.
    • Require "prompt" notice by mail after an automatic registration transaction that the individual may decline their new or updated registration. Applicants who opt-out within 20 days of completing the application would not be registered (or have their record updated).
    • Set the effective date for automatic registration provisions at July 1, 2023.
  • Move forward the restoration of voting rights of persons disenfranchised due to felony convictions, and create new notice requirements for impacted individuals. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Restore the right to vote upon release from incarceration for a felony conviction, or upon sentencing if no incarceration is imposed. Under existing law, voting rights are restored upon "discharge," which includes serving any period of probation, parole, or supervised release.
    • Require the secretary of state to develop a publication about the voting rights of persons charged with or convicted of a crime and make that publication widely available.
    • Require each correctional facility in the state to designate an official to provide notice of the restoration of voting rights to each person convicted of a felony upon release from incarceration, and a registration application. The bill would also require probation officers and supervised release agents to do the same.
  • Establish a permanent mail voter list that allows voters who apply for "permanent absentee voter status" to receive a mail ballot for all elections. Under existing law, a person placed on the permanent absentee ballot list is mailed a mail ballot application for each election, rather than a ballot. A conforming change is made to permit the ballot board, when examining a voter's name and address on a signature envelope to determine whether the ballot should be counted, to compare the information against voter record or ballot application. Existing law only permits comparison against the application.
  • Permit an individual who is age 16 years or older to preregister to vote. These pre-registered individuals would be protected from prosecution under the state's illegal voter registration statute, and their information would not be included on the public information list of registered voters until they turn 18. Under existing law, a person under the age of 18 may preregister to vote, but only if they will be 18 or older at the time of the next scheduled election.
  • Create new misdemeanor offenses for:
    • intimidating a person in an attempt to compel the person to register or not register to vote, to vote or not vote, or to vote for or against a candidate or ballot question
    • intimidating a person to impede that person's efforts to "encourage" another person to participate in the electoral process (e.g., assistance with registration, casting a ballot, travel to a polling place)
    • causing deceptive information to be transmitted by any means within 60 days of an election with the intent to impede or prevent another person from exercising that person's right to vote, if the person making the transmission knows the information is materially false
    • intentionally interfering with voter registration or voting
    • intentionally aiding or compelling an individual to commit or attempt a voting intimidation or interference offense, or conspiring to do so or have someone else do so
  • Authorize the attorney general and election officials to bring a civil cause of action, with penalties of up to $1,000 per violation, for any injuries they incur due to prohibited intimidation or interference conduct
  • Require the secretary of state or a county auditor to contract with a translator to provide election materials at polling places in Spanish, Hmong, and Somali, and additional languages as determined by specified state demographic criteria and/or by request. In a precinct with 20%+ language minority voters, an election judge fluent in a particular language must also be present at a polling place if ten or more voters make a request, via the secretary of state or county auditor, for interpretation services at least 30 days before the election.

The bill also makes changes to areas of election law that Voting Rights Lab does not track, including campaign finance.

This bill, as introduced January 5, 2023, would make sweeping reforms to Missouri election law, including creating no-excuse mail voting, establishing automatic voter registration, and ending the disenfranchisement of most persons convicted of a criminal offense, among other changes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Allow voters to vote by mail ballot during the entire voting period without requiring a qualifying excuse, by repealing existing excuse requirements and authorizing the use of "absentee" mail ballots if a voter believes they may be prevented from going to the polls on Election Day. Under existing law, mail ballot voting without an excuse is permitted only by casting an "in-person absentee ballot" in the two weeks prior to Election Day.. The bill would additionally facilitate mail voting by:
    • Permitting the establishment of an online application process for mail ballots, including submission of an electronic signature.
    • Repealing the prohibition on an individual, group, or party soliciting a voter to obtain a mail ballot application, and the prohibition on pre-filling of voter information on an application.
    • Removing a requirement that an in-person applicant for a mail ballot submit their request no later than 5 p.m. the day before the election. The bill is silent on the new deadline to apply in-person, suggesting that as long an in-person applicant must only comply with the deadline to return the ballot.
    • Permitting any voter to apply for a mail ballot for both a primary election and subsequent general election, with a single application. Existing law limits this option to UOCAVA voters. The bill would also require election officials to inform any registration or mail ballot applicant of the reason for rejecting an application. Under existing law, rejection notice is required only to UOCAVA voters.
    • Eliminating unique mail ballot application requirements for new residents.
    • Eliminating the requirement that mail ballots be witnessed by a notary or election official.
    • Extending the deadline for a ballot by mail to be returned, by requiring ballots to be counted if they are postmarked by Election Day and received within seven days of the election. Under existing law, a ballot voted by mail must be returned no later than the close of polls on Election Day.
    • Creating an online tracking system for ballots voted by mail. The tracker would indicate if the voter's ballot has been received, if the ballot has been counted, and, if the ballot has not been counted, the reason it has not been counted. The tracker would additionally provide instructions on how to cure the defect by the 7th day after the election.
  • Create automatic voter registration. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require the secretary of state to use driver's license information, nondriver's license information, tax records, school enrollment records, or any other records practicable for determining voter eligibility to create lists of recommended persons for voter registration and deliver the lists to local election authorities.
    • Require each election authority receiving a list to send, within two months of receiving the list, a notice to each eligible person to inform them of their impending automatic voter registration, and allow the person an opportunity to opt out.
    • End disenfranchisement of individuals after conviction of a felony, during their sentence of incarceration, probation, or parole. The bill would leave in place disenfranchisement requirements related to conviction for any offense connected with the right of suffrage.
    • Establish same-day voter registration, and permit registration on or before an election day at any election authority or polling place, any location otherwise established for registration by the Secretary of State, or online. Under existing law, voters must generally be registered by any method no later than the fourth Wednesday (27 days) before Election Day.
    • Add a photo ID issued by a school or employer to the list of acceptable voter ID.
  • Repeal a provision in existing law that prohibits an individual, other than a governmental entity or a person paid by a governmental entity, from being paid for soliciting voter registration applications. Additionally, the bill would:
    • Require individuals to register with the secretary of state as a voter registration solicitor only if the person is paid or otherwise compensated for soliciting ten or more voter registration applications. Under existing law, registration is required if an individual solicits ten or more registration applications, and may not be paid or otherwise compensated to do so unless by a governmental entity. Note that this provision would, in effect, also narrow the existing felony offense for failing to register as a registration solicitor of ten or more applicants, by making it apply only if the solicitor was compensated for 10+ applications.
    • Require an individual registering as a voter registration solicitor to indicate whether they expect to be compensated for soliciting voter registration applications, and if so, identify the payor.

This bill, as introduced January 12, 2023, would make several changes to Missouri election law related to voting by provisional ballot, election crimes, voter registration drives, and other areas. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Permit an individual voting early through the in-person "absentee" mail ballot process to cast a provisional ballot if they do not possess accepted voter ID but are otherwise eligible to vote. Under existing law, voters are only permitted to cast a provisional ballot under these circumstances when voting at a polling place.
  • Permit a voter to cast a provisional ballot in any election when their eligibility cannot be determined by the precinct register, if they provide ID or an affidavit. Under existing law, provisional ballot provisions for such voters apply only to elections for federal or statewide officers or statewide issues.
  • Creates a new felony offense for "tampering with an election official," by doing any of the following with the purpose of harassing or intimidating an election official in performance of their official duties:
    • threatening or causing harm to the official or their family,
    • using force, threats, or deception against the official or their family,
    • attempting to cause an election official to violate election law,
    • engaging in harassing or alarming behavior toward an election official, including stalking, or
    • disseminating the personal information of an election official or their family.
  • Expressly exempt governmental entities who solicit voter registrations, or persons paid or compensated by a governmental entity to solicit voter registrations, from the existing requirement that individuals who solicit more than ten voter registration applications must register with the government each election cycle.
  • Prohibit posting or displaying the list of applicants for a mail ballot due to permanent disability, and require the list be kept confidential to the extent possible under the law.

  • Expand the existing misdemeanor offense for prohibited activity, including electioneering and polling, at a polling site. The bill would prohibit this activity during the early voting period, in addition to Election Day, and expand the zone of prohibited conduct from 25 feet outside a polling place building, to 100 feet.

This bill, as introduced January 18, 2023, would clarify certain aspects of the verification process for mail ballots and create a cure process for certain types of ballot defects. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the election authority to "promptly" provide notice to a voter whose mail ballot has been rejected for any reason provided by law, including information about the required procedures to cure the defect. Voters would have until the end of the provisional ballot verification period (i.e., the third day after the election) to cure ballot problems. For a failure to complete a statement on the ballot envelope, a failure to sign the oath, an invalid signature, or a failure to have the signature verified, the cure process would require voters to submit an affidavit and a copy of an accepted form of voter ID. This bill, as introduced January 4, 2023, would modify various provisions of Missouri election law, including laws affecting the use of electronic voting machines, the mailing and counting of ballots, and requiring the state to withdraw from the Electronic Registration Information Center. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require voters to use paper ballots in each election, which must be counted by hand. Voters with disabilities would still be able to use an electronic voting system that complies with the relevant provisions of federal law, but must submit a request to the secretary of state to be added to a database containing the names of each voter authorized to vote on an accessible system. The secretary would be required to distribute the names in the database to each election authority every thirty days.
  • Forbid the state from entering into any agreement which requires the secretary of state to share voter registration data in the secretary's possession, including the Electronic Registration Information Center. Existing contracts would be permitted to continue until complete, but could not be renewed. The secretary would still be permitted to coordinate with other states to verify the accuracy of voter registration data, but only if the coordination is conducted by the secretary.
  • Permit an election authority to begin counting absentee ballots as they are received, instead of the time polls open on election day, as under existing law. The election authority would also be able to begin counting ballots voted in-person as they are received, instead of after the polls close on Election Day, as under existing law. The election authority would not be permitted to make the tally publicly available until all such ballots have been counted in the jurisdiction.
  • Permit any registered voter who was eligible to vote in an election to file an election contest challenging the results. Under existing law, such contests can only be filed by candidates.
  • Eliminate a felony prohibiting wilfully tampering or damaging voting machines or marking devices with the intent to impair their functioning, mislead any voter, or destroy or change the count or record of votes on such machines. While other provisions of the bill would sharply limit the number of such machines in use during an election, ones available to disabled voters would remain.
  • Require that any absentee ballot mailed to a voter be postmarked from the same county as the election authority mailing the ballot.
  • The bill also makes changes to areas of election law that the Voting Rights Lab does not track, such as modifications to the process by which political parties appoint election judges, rules for ballot production, rules for retention of ballot materials, and quicker availability of voter participation data.

Last updated on February 28, 2023.

Under existing law, voters have no opportunity to address defects with their ballot certificates that cause their votes to be rejected. Existing law also simply states that a ballot must be rejected if "the statements on any ballot envelope have not been completed." Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create a cure process by:
    • Requiring an election authority to notify a voter if their absentee ballot is rejected, including the reason for the rejection and the process and deadline for addressing the issue that triggered the rejection.
    • Enabling a voter to cure certain defects by submitting an affidavit to the election authority, along with a copy of acceptable voter ID, before the end of the period for verifying provisional ballots. The affidavit would affirm that the ballot was submitted by the voter, is the voter's ballot, and that the voter is registered and qualified to vote in the election.
    • Allowing the voter to use that process to cure a failure to complete a statement on the ballot envelope, to sign the oath, an invalid signature, or failure to have the voter's signature notarized.

  • Clarify the reasons a ballot could be rejected to include:

    • failing to sign the oath
    • the signature does not appear to be valid
    • the oath has not been verified as provided by law
    • any other reason for rejection provided by law
    • the voter is determined to be ineligible.

The bill clarifies that in the absence of such a court order, the person is eligible to register to vote. Reasonable accommodations may be made during the registration process for the person, as needed.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 4, 2023, would create the Missouri Elections Sovereignty Act. These provisions would impose significant changes to existing law, with various new procedures for election administration. The provisions would:

  • Assert the State's authority to regulate state and local elections.
  • Bifurcate state and federal elections when there are differences in regulations for time, place and manner of holding elections.
  • Exempt state and local elections from federal regulation to the extent permitted by the U.S. Constitution.
  • Require any state agency or agent that receives communication regarding election laws from the Department of Justice or other federal agency to notify the governor and General Assembly within five days. This section would expire on Feb. 1, 2025.
  • Require any entity involved in state election administration that intends to implement any federal election guidance on state elections to notify the General Assembly at least 30 days before implementation. All implementation of federal guidance would require approval by the Assembly, which could consist of abstaining from a legislative vote within 30 days of the notification. The Act would impose a fine of $5,000 for violations of these provisions, to be accrued every 30 days until the implementation was withdrawn. This section would expire on Feb. 1, 2025.

  • Require any official election administrator who intends to accept or disburse federal election funds to notify the General Assembly of this intent at least 30 days before accepting the funds, or, if the funds have already been accepted, 30 days before the funds are disbursed. Acceptance of funds would be subject to legislative approval, which could consist of abstaining from a vote within 30 days of notification. The Act would impose a fine of the amount of the federal funds plus $1,000 for violation of the provisions. This section would expire on Feb. 1, 2025.

Currently voters may choose to participate in any party's primary. Specifically, the bill would require affiliated voters to change their affiliation no later than 23 weeks before Election Day to be eligible in the new party's primary election. Existing law permits changes to party affiliation at any time. A newly registered voter may vote in a primary election if the voter registers to vote and declares their affiliation no later than 4 weeks before the primary, which is concurrent with the general deadline to register to vote.

The bill would also make related changes to areas of election law that Voting Rights Lab does not track, including details for the closed primary process and the timing of affiliation requirements for candidates for office.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced January 4, 2023, would make several changes to Missouri election law across a number of issue areas. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Permit a person voting absentee in person to cast a provisional ballot if the person does not possess a valid identifying document but is otherwise eligible to vote. Under existing law, such a person would only be permitted to cast a provisional ballot under these circumstances if they voted at a polling place.
  • Expand the applicability of certain provisions of law permitting a voter to cast a provisional ballot if the voter claims to be registered and eligible to vote in an election, but whose eligibility cannot immediately be established by examining the precinct register. Under existing law, these provisions apply only to elections for federal or statewide officers or statewide issues, the bill would expand this to any public election.
  • Creates the felony criminal offense of tampering with an election official. A person commits this offense if the person, with the purpose of harassing or intimidating an election official in performance of their official duties:
    • threatens or causes harm to the official or their family,
    • uses force, threats, or deception against the official or their family,
    • attempts to cause an election official to violate election law,
    • engages in harassing or alarming behavior toward an election official, including stalking, or
    • disseminates the personal information of an election official or their family.
  • Expressly exempt governmental entities who solicit voter registrations, or persons paid or compensated by a governmental entity to solicit voter registrations, from the requirement under existing law for any person who solicits more than ten voter registration applications to register with the government each election cycle.
  • Clarify that any list of persons applying for an absentee ballot on the grounds of permanent disability shall be kept confidential to the extent possible under the law.

  • Expand the applicability of the misdemeanor offense of engaging in electioneering activities in an improper manner. The bill would require a person to refrain from electioneering within 75 feet of a polling place on election day or during the absentee voting period. Under current law, electioneering is forbidden within 25 feet of a polling place and only on election day.

    The bill would also make changes to areas of election law that the Voting Rights Lab does not track, such as the filing date for candidates.

This bill, as introduced on January 4, 2023, would create in-person early voting and alter mail ("absentee") voting processes and deadlines. Specifically, the bill would:

    • Permitting voting at the registrar's office, or an alternative location designated by the registrar, during regular business hours.
    • Requiring notice of early voting hours to be posted in public places at least eight days before the early voting period begins.
    • Requiring the registrar's office to be open from 8:00 a.m. to noon on the two Saturdays preceding Election Day.

This bill, as amended on March 31, 2023, would increase the maximum imposed penalties for a variety of elections-related crimes, and create a new felony offense for unlawfully denying an individual the right to vote. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Raise the maximum penalty for the following crimes to 3 years in the state penitentiary and a fine of up to $5,000:
    • Disposing of ballots before they are counted or giving access to a ballot box to an unauthorized person, by a poll manager. Under existing law, the penalty is imprisonment up to one year and/or a $3,000 fine.
    • Conducting an election, by a poll manager, without locking and securing the ballot box as directed by law, or opening and reading ballots given to them to be deposited in the ballot box, by a poll manager. Under existing law, the penalty is imprisonment up to one year and/or a $1,000 fine.
    • Offering a voter a bribe to vote in a certain way. Under existing law, the penalty is imprisonment up to one year and/or a $1,000 fine.
    • Refusal or neglect by an election commissioner or registrar to perform their duties regarding the registration of voters, knowingly permitting a person to sign a false affidavit or otherwise violate the election code, or making a false statement on a registration certificate. Under existing law, the penalty is up to one year imprisonment and/or a $1,000 fine.
  • Raise the penalties for the following crimes to not less than two years nor more than seven years in the state penitentiary and a fine of up to $10,000:
    • Knowingly making or consenting to a false entry on the voter list, stuffing the ballot box with illegitimate ballots, removing ballots from the ballot box except as prescribed by law, or by any act or omission "designedly" destroy or change ballots as given by voters. Under existing law, the penalty is imprisonment up to five years and/or a $5,000 fine.
    • Voting while not qualified, voting in multiple locations in one election, or voting in a primary runoff after having voted in a different party's initial primary. Under existing law, the penalty for (1) unqualified voting is up to one year imprisonment and/or a $1000 fine, (2) for voting multiple times is one year imprisonment and/or a $1,000 fine (or up to five years' imprisonment and/or a $5,000 fine), and (3) for prohibited primary runoff voting, up to six months' imprisonment and/or a $500 fine.
  • Knowingly voting in any election in multiple jurisdictions with the intent to have more than one vote counted. Under existing law, the penalty is imprisonment up to five years and/or a $1,000 fine.
  • Raise the penalties for the following crime to not more than 15 years in the state penitentiary and/or a fine of up to $10,000:
  • Willfully tampering with or damaging a voting machine or tabulation device. Under existing law, the penalty is imprisonment up to 10 years and/or a $5,000 fine.
  • Raise the penalties for the following crime to up to 7 years in the state penitentiary and a fine of up to $7,500:
    • Basing the compensation of a person who is assisting voters in marking mail ballots on the number of ballots cast by individuals receiving assistance who cast mail ballots.
  • Raise the penalties for the following crime to not less than seven years in the state penitentiary, a fine of up to $5,000, or both:
    • Procuring or endeavoring to procure a vote, or the influence of another person over voters, by means of violence or threats. Under existing law, the penalty is imprisonment up to one year and/or a $3,000 fine.
  • Raise the maximum fine imposed for the following crime to $7,500:
    • Offering a prize, cash award, or other item of value in order to encourage or discourage voting. Under existing law, the penalty is a fine up to $5,000.
  • Create a new felony offense for denying a person the right to vote for a reason that is not provided in law. This felony would be punishable by a fine of up to $5,000, 10 years imprisonment by the department of corrections, or both.

The bill would also make conforming changes to mail ballot materials, to reflect changes to maximum penalties for mail ballot vote fraud, and to repeal moot provisions specific to elections held in 2020.

A previous version of the bill contained a provision, which was amended out of this bill, that would have increased the penalty for voting outside one's district of domicile from up to one year in county jail and/or a $1000 fine to as much as 20 years in the state penitentiary and/or a fine of up to $20,000.

This bill, as amended on April 17, 2023, would require the Secretary of State to establish procedures for verifying the citizenship of people newly applying to register as voters. The process would use the identity-verifying information on the application, whether the applicant's driver's license number, state ID number, last four digits of their Social Security number, or other ID accepted from the people who lack the other three types of ID. After the process, an applicant's citizenship status would be deemed verified, not yet verified, or noncitizen. Noncitizens could not register or vote, but the bill would require election officials to accept and process the registration applications of people whose citizenship status was not yet verified. Nonetheless, the amendment removed a provision requiring the Secretary to adopt rules that would enable people whose citizenship status was pending to vote. Finally, the bill would require the DMV to adopt rules as needed to facilitate this process.

Because the bill no longer provides an explicit path for people to vote while their citizenship verification is deferred to future rulemaking, this bill restricts voting access. Federal law provides that people may vote in federal elections after attesting to their U.S. citizenship. Moreover, Texas used DMV data to verify the citizenship of registered voters, but improperly canceled citizens' registrations because the state did not focus on when DMV received documentation indicating non-citizenship and when people registered. As a result, people who naturalized before registering were impacted. Another factor that impacts whether eligible people are improperly impacted by eligibility verification is how careful the process of matching the person applying to register to vote with the person identified as a non-citizen is.

    • to update the elector's voter information file and registration status accordingly, if the person returns the form to correct or provide additional voter information.
    • to add the person to the permanent mail voting list if the person returns the completed application.
  • Require the Secretary of State to establish security requirements for the interagency information exchanges, and require the Secretary, the DMV and the Department of Public Health and Human Services to agree on various aspects of information transfer. The Secretary and the agencies would also be authorized to issue needed rules and regulations.
  • Require the Secretary of State to report annually, publicly, on how many people had their information transferred by the two agencies, and of those, how many were registered, had their registrations updated or reactivated, and how many declined registration.

  • Provide that the transfer of information of an ineligible applicant is not a violation of various crimes and that an ineligible person who was nonetheless automatically registered would not be guilty of a crime unless the applicant took intentional, voluntary action to register to vote knowing that the applicant was not eligible to register to vote.

Last Updated February 23, 2023

This bill, as introduced on February 24, 2023, would restrict voting by mail by requiring voters to justify voting by mail with a specified excuse, shorten the deadline to apply to receive a ballot in the mail, and end the state's existing permanent mail voting list by requiring voters to request to receive mail ballots every two years. Despite Montana offering in-person early voting by allowing people to vote a mail ballot in person, this bill would not restrict that option to people with an excuse. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require voters to have an excuse to vote by mail. These people could vote by mail:
    • Uniformed and overseas voters,
    • Voters in a nursing home or long-term care facility, or who are homebound, hospitalized, or on vacation on Election Day, or
    • Voters who may be absent from their election district on Election Day.
  • Shorten the time to apply for a mail ballot (called an "absentee ballot" in Montana) by setting the deadline at seven days before Election Day, instead of noon on the day before.
  • Eliminate the emergency voting procedure existing law offers voters who, because of an illness or health emergency occurring between 5 p.m. of the Friday preceding the election and before the close of polls, cannot appear at the polls. The procedure involves the person requesting a mail ballot and election officials bringing it to the voter in person.
  • End the permanent mail voting list by requiring everyone to request mail ballots every two years while limiting the ability to request mail ballots to those with one of the named excuses. Under existing law, any voter may join the list and may remain on it so long as they do not move or become disqualified from voting.

Last Updated February 27, 2023

This bill, as introduced on February 24, 2023, would potentially shorten the early voting period by five days, limit the ways a voter can re-activate their inactive registration, prohibit third parties from pre-filling information on a voter registration form, and require the elected county clerk and recorder to be a county's election administrator. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Change the beginning of early voting from 30 days before Election Day to "at least 25 days" before Election Day.
  • Restrict how a voter may reactivate their inactive registration by requiring them to vote or apply for a mail ballot with no information on their application pre-filled by a third party and, in either case, to complete a voter registration form with their new address. Under existing law, a person may reactivate their registration by
    • Voting or applying for a mail ballot,
    • Notifying the county election administrator in writing of their new address, OR
    • Completing a registration activation form provided by the county election administrator.

  • Require the elected county clerk and recorder to be a county's election administrator. Under existing law, a county governing body may appoint a different election administrator. The bill would limit a county government's ability to appoint an election administrator to when the county clerk has resigned, been recalled, died, or has become mentally or physically incapacitated. In those situations, the county government could appoint someone to serve until a replacement is elected.

    Last updated February 27, 2023

This bill, as enacted on May 22, 2023, creates new criminal offenses related to voting and registration, and specifies penalties for certain existing offenses. Enforcement of the registration crime has been blocked by a federal court. Specifically, the bill:

  • Creates a new misdemeanor for voting in Montana more than once at any election or voting both in Montana and in another state or territory in the same or equivalent elections, except that a voter may also vote in a special district election in which a person or voter is entitled to vote. The bill defines "equivalent elections" as elections that have the same date for in-person voting or primaries for candidates for general elections that will have the same date for in-person voting, except that the term would not include a special district election held simultaneously with another election. Previous law stated, "No person may vote more than once at an election." The bill revises the wording of this existing crime to state "An elector may not vote more than once at an election," and adds the new offense as a separate, additional provision.
  • Creates a new misdemeanor for purposefully remaining registered to vote in more than one place in this state or another state at any time, unless related to involvement in special district elections. The section creating the crime further provides that "A person or elector previously registered to vote in another county or another state shall provide the previous registration information on the Montana voter registration application." On April 24, 2024, a federal court granted a preliminary injunction, temporarily blocking this provision of the bill. 
  • Specifies that the penalty for the existing misdemeanors relating to double voting is imprisonment for up to 18 months, a fine of up to $5,000, or both. Existing law deemed the offenses misdemeanors but did not specify the penalty.

Last Updated May 28, 2023

This bill, as introduced on March 24, 2023, would create "an election security team" whose duties would be to oversee a hand count of all ballots cast in the 2024 and 2026 general elections within a year of those elections and evaluate the implementation and execution of the security measures adopted as part of the hand count to determine whether the measures were properly followed by county election administrators. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create an eight-person election security team, with one member appointed by each of the Governor, State Auditor, Secretary of State, Supreme Court, House of Representatives Majority Leader, House of Representatives Minority Leader, Senate Majority Leader, and Senate Minority Leader.
  • Empower the team to:
    • ensure that an independent, full hand count of all ballots cast in all precincts in the state is conducted within a year of the election.
    • hire and oversee a team to conduct the full hand count.
    • report the results of the full hand count to the county election administrators and the Secretary of State's office.
    • evaluate the implementation and execution of the security measures adopted as part of ensuring the hand count to determine whether the measures were properly followed by county election administrators.

  • Appropriate $100,000 for each of the two hand counts required.

    Last updated March 30, 2023

This bill, as amended on March 30, 2023, would create a special investigative and prosecutorial regime for election-related crimes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the Attorney General's office (called the "Department of Justice" in Montana) to designate a prosecutor to assist the Commissioner of Political Practices ("Commissioner") with prosecutions of certain election crimes, including but not limited to ones involving county attorneys, county officials, or employees, or if the county attorney is unavailable when the complaint comes in.
  • Require the designated prosecutor to be available to both the Commissioner and county attorneys the week before an election, on Election Day, and after the election as required to review and process alleged violations.
  • Allow the designated prosecutor to work on non-election matters but prosecuting election cases would take priority over all of their other duties.
  • Require the Commissioner to designate an investigator who is qualified by education, training, experience, and high professional competence in criminal investigative procedures, to process and investigate certain election law complaints as directed by the commissioner of political practices and work with the designated state prosecutor, county attorney, and/or the Commissioner for the duration of all cases.
  • Allow election officials and individuals to file complaints of election law violations to the Office of the Commissioner of Political Practices or through a special case management system the bill requires the Commissioner, in conjunction with the Secretary of State and the Department of Justice, to create. The case management system would allow election law complaints to be filed and processed.
  • Require the Commissioner to investigate if the alleged violation relates to election law the Commissioner enforces under existing law. If the Commissioner substantiates the allegation, the Commissioner would notify and consult with the county attorney in the jurisdiction within which the violation allegedly occurred. Based on that consultation, the Commissioner would refer the case to either that attorney or the designated state prosecutor. Either as part of or after that consultation, the county attorney could refer the case to the designated state prosecutor if, after review, the county attorney decides the case is too complicated or there is a conflict of interest.
    • The receiving prosecutor would immediately review the case and decide whether prosecution is appropriate. If not, the prosecutor would notify the Commissioner and the complainant, and update the case management system. If a prosecution is undertaken by the designated state prosecutor or the Commissioner, the state would bear the costs of the prosecution and receive any fines and forfeitures that result.
  • Require the Commissioner to similarly consult about and refer potential violations of false swearing, official misconduct, and similar crimes that the Commissioner uncovers while investigating crimes in their purview.
  • Ensure that the designated state prosecutor, county attorney, and Commissioner have the necessary investigative and prosecutorial powers needed.
  • Require the Commissioner, local government employees, and local officials with relevant duties or information to cooperate with any prosecution. A refusal to assist with investigations of prosecutions would be defined as a violation of misdemeanor official misconduct.
  • Set as a general statute of limitations for prosecuting these complaints one year after the occurrence of the facts giving rise to the allegation, unless a different limit is otherwise provided by law.
  • Require at least one district court of the state to remain open on Election Day to receive and review emergency petitions brought by the designated state prosecutor, a county attorney, or the Commissioner. The bill would provide that the court would have personal jurisdiction over anyone with sufficient minimum contacts with Montana for the purpose of these cases.
  • Require the Commissioner to adopt rules to implement the bill.
  • Appropriate $170,000 to the Office of the Commissioner of Political Practices to contract with the Department of Justice to dedicate the prosecutor and to fund the development of the case management system.

  • Require the Office of the Commissioner of Political Practices to make an annual written report to the Legislature that details:

    • the number of complaints received
    • the number of complaints investigated
    • the number of complaints not investigated and the reason why they were not investigated
    • the number of prosecutions resulting from complaints and investigations and
    • the outcomes of the prosecutions.

    The amendments significantly changed aspects of the bill's previous approach to handling election law allegations, most notably by replacing the Secretary of State's office with the Commissioner of Political Practices. That said, the basic structure created by the amended bill is very similar.

    Last updated March 31, 2023

This bill, as introduced on January 2, 2023, would repeal the "Ballot Interference Prevention Act" which was permanently enjoined in 2020 and not enforced since then. The enjoined law had restricted voters' ability to give their completed, sealed ballots to someone else to return for them in ways the court held violated Native voters' constitutional rights.

Last Updated January 3, 2023

This bill, as enacted on May 1, 2023, establishes new definitions for "election worker" and "election official," and creates a new misdemeanor offense for certain types of interference with officials conducting an election. Specifically, the bill:

  • Defines an election official as an election administrator, election deputy, or election judge, and defines an election worker as someone appointed by an election official to perform election support duties.

  • Expands the existing misdemeanor offense of "interference with officials," and creates a new offense for certain types of misconduct. Under previous law, the interference offense comprised interfering with "officers" holding an election or conducting a canvass so as to prevent the election or canvass from being fairly held and lawfully conducted. Under the bill, the offense now extends to misconduct against election officials or election workers, rather than officers alone. It also newly criminalizes obstructing, impairing, or hindering the election or canvass, in addition to conduct to "prevent" either one.

    Last updated May 25, 2023

This bill, as enacted on March 25, 2023, caps the size of precincts at 2,500 voters, and authorizes adjusting precinct boundaries under certain conditions when the cap is pierced between regular redistricting periods. Specifically, the bill:

  • Caps the number of people per election precinct at 2,500 registered voters. Previous law required only that each county establish a "convenient" number of election precincts, "equalizing the number of electors in each precinct as nearly as possible." The bill leaves this general guideline in place, along with the new cap.
  • Requires precincts to be redrawn to bring the registered voters under the cap only if the number of people who move within its borders reaches at least 3,750 registered voters. Under previous law, precincts were redrawn only because of redistricting, and could be redrawn at any time except within 100 days of an election. The bill preserves these aspects of previous law.

  • Provides that if a precinct reaches 3,750 voters, redrawing it may be delayed if the level is reached during a year with a federal election. Redrawing the precinct must take place the following year.

Last Updated May 3, 2023

This bill, as enacted on May 1, 2023, prohibits use of private funding for election administration. Specifically, the bill:

  • Prohibits the state, the Secretary of State, a county, a municipality, or the officers or employees of those entities, from soliciting, accepting, using, or disposing of a donation from an individual or a corporation to fund conducting an election, and expressly mandates that all costs and expenses relating to conducting elections must be paid for with public funds. The prohibition does not apply to in-kind donations of a polling place, volunteer services, or goods worth less than $100.
  • Specifies that the private funding prohibition does not prevent Tribal Nations from donating space to be used as a polling location or election office, or from using their funds, funds from other tribes, or public funds including state or federal funds for election purposes. The bill also expressly permits nonprofit organizations and corporations to spend their money on their own election-related initiatives.
  • Creates a new felony offense for purposefully or knowingly violating the prohibition on private funding for election expenses.

The bill also includes provisions that Voting Rights Lab does not track, related to private funding to other state institutions such as universities and public hospitals.

Last updated May 3, 2023

This bill, as introduced on January 18, 2023, would further restrict when election officials can choose to mail all voters ballots for a specific election. The bill would end election officials' ability to choose to universally mail ballots for a city election, and instead require that the Legislature specifically authorize election officials to universally mail ballots whenever the officials wish to conduct a special federal, state, or city election that way. In addition, the bill would require the Legislature's authorization to be by the affirmative vote of three-quarters of each chamber. Under existing law, election officials do not need the Legislature's permission to universally mail ballots for city elections, and for special federal and state elections, the permissive threshold is ordinary majorities.

Last Updated January 23, 2023

This bill, as introduced on February 1, 2023, would require all election records in the Secretary of State's office and other specified election records to be preserved for seven years, and would create a felony to enforce that requirement. Under existing law, certain of the records must be maintained for one year, others for 22 months, and, given the breadth of the retention requirement proposed in the bill, others may not be subject to any record retention periods or may be subject to different ones.

Last updated February 6, 2023

This bill, as amended on March 1, 2023, would give election administrators the power to remove poll workers (called "election judges" in Montana) for cause in certain circumstances, would change the rules for appointing poll workers, and make certain other changes to the election code. (In Montana, the "election administrator" is the county clerk and recorder unless the county commissioners have appointed someone else.) Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create a process for an election administrator to remove a poll worker for cause. Existing law does not have similar provisions. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Allow an election administrator to make a complaint about a poll worker to the political party county central committee that nominated them. The complaint could be for violating the election code in any way, including not fulfilling their duties, or for tampering with ballots, voting systems, or any other election materials or equipment. This process would not apply if the election administrator's complaint is about an election official or poll worker who is reporting malfeasance or potential malfeasance of official rules for how an election is being conducted.
    • Following a verbal warning to the poll worker and with the agreement of the presiding officer of the central committee that nominated the poll worker, the election administrator may remove, replace, or reassign an election judge who causes a disruption in a polling location or willfully disobeys the election code.
  • Require any complaint about an election administrator to be submitted to the county attorney. Existing law does not have a similar provision.
  • Require poll workers to attend training before serving, and provide that anyone who takes the training may serve on election-related boards "provided for in rule". Existing law makes the training optional and does not link the training to serving on election boards.

  • Change the rules for appointing poll workers. Specifically:

    • At least 135 days before the primary election in even-numbered years, the election administrator would notify the county central committees of political parties of the requirement to submit a list of poll worker nominees. Existing law does not include this requirement.
    • At least 45 days before the election, the central committees must submit a list of registered voters qualified to be poll workers. All of these nominees must be considered eligible to serve as poll workers or chief poll workers after completing required training unless they have been convicted of violating Montana election laws. Existing law provides the 45-day deadline, but not the qualification provision. Any potential poll worker determined ineligible must be notified in writing of the exclusion and its basis.
    • Require the election administrator to use all certified trained poll workers on such lists before seeking additional judges, and if the list does not include sufficient names to fill all vacancies, require the election administrator to ask for more before appointing anyone else to a vacancy. Existing law merely states that those on the lists not initially appointed must be given to the election administrator to use in filling vacancies.
    • Require counting boards to include members from each political party that submitted lists and apply this requirement to general elections as well as primary elections. Counting boards are composed of three people eligible to be poll workers, and count ballots starting as early as the day before Election Day. Existing law imposes this multi-party requirement on poll workers only.
    • Require the election administrator to provide a full list of the certified and appointed poll workers to each political party central committee at least 30 days before the primary and general elections in even-numbered years and notify them of any changes by the close of business on the day of the change. Existing law does not have a similar requirement.

    The March 1, 2023 amendments removed provisions. Those provisions would have:

  • Required complaints about county clerks to be heard and decided by the county board of supervisors and required their decisions to be made public.
  • Required election administrators to honor any request from a political party county central committee that a specific qualified poll worker be appointed to a specific precinct or counting board.
  • Prohibited a chief poll worker from presiding over more than one precinct.

  • Changed the random sample audit to remove an exemption for counties that do not use tabulators and make other changes not tracked by Voting Rights Lab.

    Last updated March 6, 2023

This bill, as introduced on February 20, 2023, would require all ballots to be counted by hand in all elections. Existing law authorizes the use of approved tabulators.

Last updated February 22, 2023

This bill, as introduced on February 21, 2023, would sharply limit a voter's choices for mail ballot return assistance and put an improperly returned mail ballot at risk of rejection. (Mail ballots are called "absentee ballots in Montana.) The bill amends provisions of Montana law that were permanently blocked by litigation on the basis that they too severely restricted voting rights, particularly of Native voters who often rely on ballot collection to vote. The bill would amend the unenforceable provisions to make them even more restrictive, with one exception: the bill would lift the 6-ballot cap on how many ballots an authorized person could return. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Allow voters to give their completed, sealed ballot to an election official, a postal worker, or a family member. A family member would be defined as a spouse, a person related by blood or adoption within the second degree, an individual related to the voter's spouse by affinity or adoption within the second degree, or the legal guardian of a voter. The enjoined provisions allowed voters to choose a caregiver, family member (defined as related to the voter by blood, marriage, adoption, or legal guardianship), household member, or acquaintance.
  • Require a person who is returning another voter's ballot to sign a statewide ballot collection and conveyance registry to be created by the Secretary of State for each ballot they deliver. The person would be required to provide their name, address, phone number, their relationship to the voter, the date the ballot was "conveyed", the voter's name and address, and hand in a form signed by the voter granting the person permission to return the ballot for them. The election official receiving the ballot would be required to match the voter's signature on the form with the voter's signature in their registration record and on the mail ballot. The enjoined law contained a less restrictive version of these provisions. People were required to sign a registry providing similar information but voters did not have to sign a permission slip for the person returning their ballot, and the registry did not need to be statewide, created by the Secretary.
  • Allow anyone to receive abstracts and reports derived from the registry from either the Secretary or a local election administrator upon payment of a fee, provided the information is for non-commercial use. The enjoined law had no similar provision.
  • Create a misdemeanor to prohibit collecting another voter's ballot except as authorized by the bill, punishable by a fine of $500. Each ballot improperly collected would be a separate violation. Under the enjoined law, violations of different limitations on ballot return than the bill would impose are not criminal but are subject to a $500 per ballot fine.

  • Provide that any ballot returned in violation of these provisions would be treated as a provisional ballot.

Last Updated February 22, 2023

This bill, as introduced on February 22, 2023, would change who is in charge of administering elections in counties with a population over 50,000 people from the county recorder and clerk to an election administrator hired by the county government. In 2021, six of Montana's 56 counties were that large. The hired election administrator would be prohibited from holding elected office or any positions within a political party, and if hired after July 1, 2023, would be required to have three or more years of experience in administering elections. Under existing law, any county may choose another official to administer elections or appoint an election administrator instead of the county clerk and recorder.

Last updated February 23, 2023

This bill, as introduced on February 22, 2023, would require counties to complete counting votes within three hours of polls closing on Election Day, create an enforcement mechanism, add a postmark deadline for mail ballots in addition to the existing received-by-close-of-polls deadline, require a residency affidavit for uniformed and overseas voters, and make other changes to the election code that Voting Rights Lab does track, relating to election equipment testing and record retention. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require counties to count votes on Election Day and continue counting until all available ballots that can be legally counted have been tabulated except for pending unresolved resolution board ballots, provisional ballots, and military overseas ballots. Counties would be required to complete the count within three hours.
  • Require the Secretary of State to place any county clerk and recorder who fails to meet the 3-hour tabulation requirement under their direct supervision for two years. During the 2-year supervision period, the county clerk and recorder would work with the Secretary of State's office to revise county election policies and procedures to ensure the 3-hour tabulation requirement is met for all future elections.
  • Require the Secretary of State to adopt implementing rules but prohibit the Secretary from adopting rules that violate or contradict the bill. In addition, the bill would provide that if any of these requirements are violated through regulation, rule process, contract, agreement, settlement, or executive order, the Secretary of state or the Governor, whichever is responsible for the violation, is liable for any action taken in a civil action brought by the Commissioner of political practices, the county attorney, or by an individual member of the public. The statute of limitations for the violation would be 6 years.
  • Require mail ballots returned by mail to be postmarked by no later than the day before Election Day, as well as received by the close of polls on Election Day. The bill would also require the voter's return address on the mail ballot return envelope.

  • Require UOCAVA voters to submit a signed affidavit confirming their residency of record is in Montana.

Last Updated February 23, 2023

This bill, as introduced on February 23, 2023, would enable people to affiliate with a political party when they register to vote, and allow only people affiliated with a political party to vote in a party's primary election. The bill would make conforming changes throughout the code and create rules for when voters may participate in a primary after changing their affiliation. Under existing law, people do not affiliate with a party through voter registration and primaries are open to all voters.

Last Updated February 24, 2023

This bill, as enacted on May 19, 2023, makes changes to voter registration list maintenance related to voters' addresses. Specifically, the bill:

  • Includes all voters in the address-based list maintenance processes by removing an exception that applied to mail ballot voters who had recently confirmed their address.
  • Requires a county election official, when the voter fails to return an address confirmation form within 30 days, to cooperate with the Secretary of State and the DMV to verify the voter's address. If the county official cannot confirm the voter's address, the voter's registration must be made inactive. Under previous law, election officials had no duty to attempt to confirm the voter's address after a voter failed to respond to the address confirmation notice.

Previous versions of the bill contained a provision that was amended out prior to enactment. This provision would have required voters whose registrations became inactive to appear in person at their county election office to provide proof of their address.

Last Updated September 6, 2023

This bill, as enacted on October 3, 2023, appropriates state funds for the 2023-2024 fiscal year, including various provisions related to election administration. Specifically, the bill:

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 8, 2023, would:

  • Require counties to offer early ("one-stop") voting on each Saturday during the early voting period and move back the end of early ("one-stop") voting from 3 p.m. on the Saturday before an election 5 p.m. on that day. Under existing law, weekend early voting is offered at the discretion of county officials.
  • Establish new crimes and civil penalties meant to protect voters. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Create a Class H felony for threatening or attempting to threaten a person for voting or attempting to vote, voting or attempting to vote for or against a particular candidate, registering to vote, urging or aiding any individuals to vote or attempt to vote as allowed by law, or exercising any lawful powers or duties as an election official or enlisting another person to do the same.
    • Create a Class H felony for knowingly challenging another's right to vote on fraudulent or spurious grounds, engaging in "mass, indiscriminate, and groundless" challenging of voters for the purposes of preventing or delaying their voting or interfering with the orderly administration of an election, or fraudulently advising any person that they are not eligible or registered.
    • Create a Class A1 misdemeanor for intimidating or coercing, or attempting to intimidate or coerce, any person for voting or attempting to vote, voting or attempting to vote for or against a particular candidate, registering to vote, urging or aiding any individuals to vote or attempt to vote as allowed by law, or exercising any lawful powers or duties as an election official or enlisting another person to do the same.
    • Create a Class H felony for various actions employers could take in order to influence the votes of their employees.
    • Establish a private cause of action allowing any victim of the established crimes to seek preventative relief and attorney's fees.
    • Establish a restitution fund which individuals convicted of violations of the above prohibitions could be ordered by a court to pay funds into. The fund would then be used for voter education campaigns.
    • Explicitly authorize the state board of elections and district attorneys to investigate, prosecute, and seek penalties for violations of the created crimes.
    • Define "coerce," "intimidate," and "threaten" as used in this section, and establish that a person will be deemed to have committed such acts if they should have known or reasonably should have known that their actions would produce such an effect.
  • Explicitly authorize online voter registration whereby the voter could either authorize transfer of an image of their signature from another state agency to the board of elections or provide an electronic image of an ink signature and repeal language prohibiting the use of "electronically captured" signatures for voter registration. An online registration system currently exists through the DMV.

  • Modify voter list maintenance processes to provide more protection to voters. Specifically, the bill would:

    • Require that there be a match between the name and last four digits of the social security number between a death record and a voter registration before a county board of elections could cancel the registration. If the social security number was missing from the records, the registration could not be canceled until there was a match between the name, complete date of birth, and other identification information.
    • Require the board of elections to attempt to contact a voter by email or phone, if the registration record contains such information, before canceling a registration due to an unreturned address confirmation mailer.
    • Require that a voter must fail to respond to an address confirmation mailing for at least 60 days before cancellation of the registration can take place. Existing law does not define a time period for "failure" to respond.
    • Prohibit boards of elections from canceling a voter's registration based solely on failure to return an address confirmation mailing without first attempting to confirm the voter's address by other means.
    • Direct the board of elections to establish an online portal through which a voter who has received an address confirmation mailing could confirm their address.

    The bill also contains provisions relating to redistricting that are not tracked by Voting Rights Lab.


Last Updated March 15, 2023

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on April 4, 2023, would:

  • Establish a mail ("absentee") ballot receipt deadline of the close of polls at 7:30 p.m. on Election Day. Under existing law, ballots postmarked by Election Day can be received until 5 p.m. on the third day after an election.
