The legislature overrode Governor Roy Cooper's veto of this bill on October 10, 2023. As enacted, the bill makes wide-ranging changes to voting and election administration, including changes to mail voting, early voting, poll observers, same-day registration, voter challenges, voter list maintenance, use of private funds, and other areas of election law.

Regarding "absentee voting" (mail voting), the bill:

  • Restricts mail voting through changes to ballot return methods and timing, and to the witness requirement. Specifically, the bill:
    • Changes the deadline for receipt of all mail ballots to 7:30 p.m. on Election Day (or the close of polls, if extended past 7:30 p.m.). Under existing law, mail ballots were deemed timely if returned in person by 5 p.m. on Election Day, or if returned by mail, postmarked by Election Day and received by 5 p.m. three days after Election Day.
    • Explicitly prohibits ballot drop boxes, requiring that ballot delivery to early voting locations must be hand delivery to an official. Existing law was silent on drop boxes, and they were not generally used.
    • Requires witnesses who sign a voter's mail ballot envelope to also print their names. Failure by a witness to print their name will be a reason for rejecting a ballot if the signature is not legible.
  • Codifies a cure process for mail ballot envelopes that are not signed by the voter, were signed in the wrong place, or do not include required photo ID, and are received by the county board of elections by the deadline. Deficiencies must be cured by the close of business on the day before canvass, as was required under existing law. Officials will be required to contact voters with deficient ballot envelopes in writing and by email and/or phone if the voter provided that information. Missing ID documentation or attestations can be submitted by email. While there was an existing cure process under board of elections guidance, these rules predate the implementation of the state's current voter ID requirement, and as such do not provide for cure of missing ID documentation.
  • Requires mail ballot applications to contain optional fields for a voter's phone number and email address to facilitate contacting the voter for cure.
  • Expands opportunities to challenge voters' mail ballots by allowing challenges to any mail ballot cast in a voter's county and allowing challenges up to the fifth business day after an election. Under existing law, voters could only challenge ballots cast by voters in their precinct.
  • Requires that mail ballots received prior to Election Day be counted on Election Day. Existing law required only that officials meet to begin counting mail ballots at 5 p.m. on Election Day.
  • Requires election officials to provide, either on election board websites or in voter mailings, mail ballot information including the date that mail ballots are available, the ballot application deadline, ballot return requirements, and the return deadline.
  • Establishes a pilot program for use of signature verification software, to be carried out in 10 counties for the 2024 primary election.

Regarding early voting, the bill:

  • Modifies procedures for early voting to conform with Election Day procedures, including those related to:
    • General requirements for the voting process and receiving a ballot, eliminating the requirement that early voters complete a mail ballot application
    • Challenge processes, including allowing individuals to challenge any early voter in their county as opposed to only within their precinct as is the case under existing law
    • Appointment of election officials at early voting polling places
  • Changes terminology throughout the code to eliminate references to "one-stop" early voting locations and references to ballots cast during early voting as "absentee" ballots, except for retrievable absentee ballots cast by same-day registrants.
  • Requires that ballots cast in person during early voting be reported separately from mailed ballots and that the certified list of in-person early voters be public record. Existing law had no comparable provision.
  • Sets out new express requirements for recording early votes and transmitting information to precincts for Election Day.
  • Establishes rules for counting of early ballots electronically or by hand.

Regarding use of private funds for election administration, the bill:

  • Prohibits the state board, county boards of elections, and county commissions from accepting private contributions, whether directly or in kind, for the administration of elections other than the use of space for polling locations and certain specified expenses.

Regarding same-day registration, the bill:

  • Recodifies the same-day registration process, which is available only during early voting. Code provisions regarding same-day registration were repealed by 2013 H.B. 589, but this bill was blocked from going into effect by a federal appeals court in 2016. The new code section largely mirrors existing requirements, except that the bill requires removing retrievable ballots cast by same-day registrants if a single address confirmation mailing is returned as undeliverable within a certain timeframe. Existing law provided for discarding ballots and cancelling registrations if two confirmation mailings were returned as undeliverable, which in practice often could not occur before the certification process was complete.

Regarding rules for polling place observers, the bill:

  • Expressly permits observers appointed by political parties to take notes, listen to conversation between voters and poll workers, move freely around the polling place, leave and reenter the voting enclosure, communicate by phone outside the voting enclosure, and witness any setup and teardown procedures at the polling place.
  • Expressly permits observers to take photos inside the voting place before and after the voting period. Existing law stated that observers could "attend" voting places, but did not specify permitted conduct.
  • Prohibits observers from looking at or recording any voter's ballot, impeding access to the polling place, interfering with poll workers' duties, engaging in electioneering, and making phone calls while in the voting place. Existing law prohibited impeding the voting process in any manner, and interfering, communicating with, or observing a voter casting a ballot, and prohibited electioneering, but was not otherwise specific.
  • Permits the state board of elections to require that observers wear identification.
  • Permits student election assistants to be present inside the voting enclosure, along with other authorized observers.
  • Creates a procedure for the removal of an observer who engages in prohibited conduct, including requiring a showing of evidence, issuance of a warning, an opportunity to correct misconduct, and an appeals process. Existing law had no comparable provisions.
  • Removes the requirement that observers "have good moral character," and changes the deadline for reporting names of observers to election officials, to noon on the business day before the observer will serve. Existing law required notification prior to 10 a.m. on the fifth day before an election. The bill also makes minor changes to which election official must receive notice of different types of observers.

Regarding polling place procedures generally, the bill:

  • Requires precinct officials to maintain a log of all individuals who enter a polling place other than appointed observers and runners and minor children accompanying a voting parent, including names, addresses, and signatures. Existing law had no comparable provision.
  • Specifies that appeals brought by the state board of elections to a challenge determination are to be held in the county superior court where the challenge originated. Existing law had no similar provision.
  • Requires election officials to record voter names, voting methods, and type of voter ID submitted, for voters who appear to vote for the first time after having registered by mail. The information collected is to be deemed a public record.
  • Requires the state and county boards of election to carry out a "robust" public education campaign regarding voter ID requirements.

Regarding voter list maintenance, the bill:

  • Establishes procedures for identifying and removing registered voters believed to not be U.S. citizens. Specifically, the bill:
    • Directs state superior court clerks to transfer to the state board of elections on a semi-annual basis the name, address, and reason for disqualification of each individual who requests to be excused from jury duty on the basis that they are not qualified. These lists will not be public records.
    • Directs the state board of elections, within 30 days of receipt of such a list, to identify registered voters who potentially self-identified as not being a U.S. citizen, consulting information available in state and federal databases and distribute a list of potential matches to the proper county boards of elections.
    • Directs county boards of elections, within 30 days of receiving a report from the state board, to send a written notice of cancellation to the registered voter. If the voter does not respond within 30 days, their registration will be canceled. If the voter contests their removal, the chair of the county board will enter a challenge to the registration and a hearing will take place.
    • Requires the state board of elections to provide the state bureau of investigation and the relevant district attorney with a copy of any investigation regarding a naturalized citizen found to have voted prior to becoming a U.S. citizen.
  • Requires that voter list maintenance for death, disenfranchising convictions, and change of address be conducted at least once a week. Under existing law, updates for death and convictions were required monthly, while no timeline was prescribed for changes of address.
  • Makes explicit that non-voting can be a trigger for sending a voter an address confirmation mailing. Under existing law, non-voting was a trigger in practice but the code stated only that mailings are to be sent to voters whose address "has not [been] confirmed by another means."
  • Commissions a study on the feasibility of replacing the statewide voter registration system, to allow for improved coordination between agencies for list maintenance and voter registration processes.

Regarding primary election procedures, the bill:

  • Eliminates the discretion of state political parties to exclude unaffiliated voters from their primary elections.
  • Ends the practice of holding non-federal primary runoffs seven weeks after the initial primary election, making all primary runoffs 10 weeks after the initial primary, as federal runoffs already were under existing law.

Regarding criminal and civil enforcement of election crimes, and retention of election materials, the bill:

  • Creates two new Class 1 misdemeanor offenses for:
    • Impersonating an election official in the course of duties in registering voters or administering an election
    • Affixing or printing an identifier to a mail ballot request form, unless the individual is a state or county board of elections employee
  • Adds a mens rea element to the felony offense for voting when disenfranchised due to a criminal conviction. Existing law defined the offense as voting "without having been restored" to voting eligibility. Under the bill, the offense is defined as voting after disenfranchisement "knowing" that such eligibility had not been restored.
  • Requires the state board of elections to refer suspected violations of election law to the state bureau of investigations. Under existing law, such referrals were to be made to the attorney general or proper district attorney.
  • Expressly charges the state bureau of investigations with investigating all cases arising from fraud in connection with elections in the state. Existing law charged the state board of elections with investigating violations of election law, but otherwise had no specific express delegation of investigative duty for election fraud.
  • Requires officials to retain and preserve voted ballots, challenged ballots, election results tapes, and executed ballot applications for a period of 22 months after an election or as required by in federal law, whichever is greater.

Regarding presidential and vice-presidential electors, the bill:

  • Requires that certificates of ascertainment regarding the appointment of presidential and vice-presidential electors sent by the governor to the Archivist of the United States contain a security feature for the purpose of verifying their authenticity and be sent by the most expeditious method available. Existing law required transmission by registered mail.

The bill also contains additional provisions related to topics that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

Previous versions of the bill contained provisions that were amended out prior to passage of the final version of the bill. These provisions would have:

  • Permanently required county boards of elections to use electronic verification software to compare signatures on mail ballot envelopes to signatures on file, effective September 2024.
  • Required the state board of elections to establish and implement a two-factor authentication process to be used to verify mail ballots before they could be opened and counted.
  • Modified same-day registration to allow voters who met documentation requirements to cast regular ballots while requiring those who did not meet the requirements to cast provisional ballots that would be rejected unless the voter provided documentation before the end of canvassing.
  • Made mail ballot certificates subject to public inspection at weekly meetings of county boards of elections at which mail ballot envelopes are verified.

The legislature overrode Governor Roy Cooper's veto of this bill on October 10, 2023. As enacted, the bill:

  • Changes the makeup of the state board of elections. Specifically, the bill:
    • Reconstitutes the state board of elections, establishing an eight-member board with the two major political parties' leaders in both legislative chambers appointing two members each. The legislative leaders must be provided with lists of potential appointees by each major party's state chairs but are not obligated to appoint from those lists. The four-year terms for the new board will begin on January 1, 2024. Under existing law, the governor appointed all members of the five-member board from lists provided by both party chairs, with three coming from the governor's own party and two from the other major political party.
    • Grants the legislature the authority to select a member of the state board of elections to serve as chair if the board does not select its own chair within 30 days of the appointment of new members. For 2024 only, the legislature will have appointment authority if a chair is not selected by January 10. Existing law did not specify what is to happen if the board fails to select a chair.
    • Grants the legislature the authority to appoint an executive director for the state board of the board does not fill the position by June 15 of an odd-numbered year or within 30 days of the appointment of new board members or the position becoming vacant. For 2024 only, the legislature has appointment authority if an executive director is not selected by January 10. Existing law did not specify procedures for when the board failed to appoint an executive director.
    • Makes conforming changes to shift vacancy-filling and limited removal authority from the governor to the legislative leader whose appointee is in question.
    • Repeals a provision allowing the governor to remove and replace a member of the board who failed to attend a meeting and thereby prevented a quorum from being obtained for three consecutive days.
  • Changes the makeup of county boards of elections. Specifically, the bill:
    • Reconstitutes the county boards of elections, establishing four-member boards with the two major political parties' leaders in both state legislative chambers appointing one member each. The legislative leaders must be provided with lists of potential appointees by each major party's state chairs but are not obligated to appoint from those lists. Each county board will be responsible for selecting a chair from among its membership. Under existing law, each county had a five-member board of elections with four members appointed by the state board of elections from lists provided by state party chairs and one member appointed by the governor to serve as chair.
    • Grants the legislature the authority to appoint chairs of county boards of elections if a board fails to select a chair within 15 days from the date new members are appointed or within 30 days of a vacancy. For 2024 only, the legislature has appointment authority if a chair is not selected by January 10. Existing law did not specify what is to happen if a county board does not select a chair.
    • Grants county boards of commissioners the authority to fill vacancies for county directors of elections. Under existing law, county boards of elections submitted recommendations to the state board's executive director for approval.
    • Ends the ability of the executive director of the state board of elections to override a recommendation from a county board of commissioners on how to fill a vacancy in the office of county director of elections.
    • Prohibits individuals who have held elected or party office, held certain campaign positions, are candidates for office, or are a relative of a candidate for office from serving on a county board.
  • Changes the functioning of the state board of elections. Specifically, the bill:
    • Changes the state board of elections from an independent agency to part of the office of the Secretary of State for administrative purposes. The board continues to be authorized to exercise its prescribed statutory powers independently of the Secretary of State. Existing law expressly prohibited the board from being placed within any administrative department of state government.
    • Lowers the threshold required for the state board of elections to order carrying out a new election from four of five members to five of eight members. This authority is limited to specific circumstances set out in existing law that the bill does not change.
    • Shifts emergency authority from the executive director of the state board of elections to the board as a whole, although the board is authorized to delegate its emergency authority to the executive director or any other individual.
    • Shifts responsibility from the governor to the legislature, for approval of an Attorney General recommendation that the state board of elections retain private counsel.
    • Repeals a requirement that mandatory criminal background checks conducted for prospective county board of elections employees are shared with the state board of elections.
    • Requires that criminal background check reports regarding potential appointees for the position of executive director of the state board be provided to the relevant legislative committees considering the appointment.
    • Repeals a requirement that the state board provide recommendations regarding UOCAVA voting to the governor, limiting such recommendation-making to the legislature as is already required by law.
  • Specifies that mail voters claiming to have a reasonable impediment to obtaining a qualifying photo ID must provide a driver's license number or the last four digits of their Social Security numbers. Existing law imposed such a requirement on mail voters who had a qualifying ID but could not attach a photocopy but was unclear regarding voters who did not possess a qualifying ID document.

The bill also changes procedures around candidate qualification for presidential preference primary elections, candidate disclosures, and other non-election policies that are not tracked by Voting Rights Lab.

This bill, as enacted on April 6, 2023, prohibits the governor from issuing an executive order or suspending or amending a provision in a statute, order, or rule relating to a state or local requirement regarding the required minimum number of physical polling places.

Note: In 2020, responding to conditions of the Covid-19 pandemic, the governor issued an executive order allowing all counties to conduct the June 2020 primary by mailing all voters a ballot application and waiving the requirement for at least one in-person voting location. This bill prohibits such executive action.

This bill, as enacted on March 27, 2023, gives voters more time to cure a mismatched signature on a mail ballot, and gives election officials more time to count mail ballots and perform other duties. Specifically, the bill:

  • Changes the deadline for curing a signature defect on a mail ballot from six days after the election to thirteen days after the election. Cure must be made by the close of the canvassing board meeting on that day.
  • Allows county auditors to start scanning mail ballots in a "mail ballot election" three business days before Election Day, rather than the day before Election Day as the previous law provided. A "mail ballot election" is one in which the auditor sends all voters a mail ballot application.
  • Changes the deadline for auditors to provide a certified abstract of a primary or general election to the Secretary of State, from the eighth day after an election to thirteen days after.

  • Removes the adjective "electronic" from references to "voting systems" and "voting devices" in several sections of the code. This edit does not appear to prohibit the use of electronic voting machines, however.

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2023, would require people to provide documentary proof of their U.S. citizenship before being allowed to vote. Under existing law, documentary proof of citizenship is not required, and under U.S. Supreme Court precedent cannot be required of people voting for federal offices. The bill is not explicit about whether the proof of citizenship would be required once or every time a person votes. While North Dakota does not require people to register before voting, but it does maintain a "central voter file" and the bill would provide that after a person submits proof of citizenship, the information would be added to the central voter file. Nonetheless as written the bill suggests that documentary proof of citizenship, like documentary proof of identity, would be required each time a person votes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require voters to provide documentary proof of citizenship before receiving a ballot. All of these documents, in either paper or electronic format, would be accepted:
    • A driver's license or nondriver's identification card issued by the North Dakota Department of Transportation which indicates the cardholder is a citizen.
    • A legible photocopy of the individual's birth certificate that verifies citizenship.
    • An unexpired United States passport or a legible photocopy of pertinent pages of the individual's United States passport identifying the individual and the individual's passport number.
    • The individual's United States naturalization documents or the number of the certificate of naturalization. If only the number of the certificate of naturalization is provided, the individual's ballot must be held aside until the proper election official can verify with the United States citizenship and immigration services that naturalization is complete.
    • Other documents or methods of proof established pursuant to the Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986.
    • The individual's bureau of Indian affairs card number, tribal treaty card number, or tribal enrollment number.

  • Allow voters who do provide the required voter ID but not documentary proof of citizenship may vote a provisional ballot that will only be counted if the voter returns with the proof of citizenship either to the polling place while polls remain open or to the election officer conducting the election before the canvassing board meeting held 13 days after Election Day. The same option to return with needed documentation would be provided to voters who have provided documentary proof of citizenship but did not show the required voter ID. Under existing law, voters who do not show the required voter ID document are offered a provisional ballot and must return with ID on the same deadlines without regard to documentation of citizenship.

Last Updated January 19, 2023

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2023, could restrict the use of secure drop boxes for mail ballots. Under existing law, county auditors have the discretion to designate places of deposit that voters may use to return their ballots through 5 p.m. the day before Election Day, without further requirements. The bill would further:

  • Require drop boxes to be "under the control of the local election official at all times", but the bill does not define what "under the control of" means.
  • Require ballots to be collected from a drop box at least once per day.

This bill, as introduced on January 16, 2023, would limit the use of vote centers and make changes to how certain mail ballots are counted. Specifically, the bill would limit Election Day vote centers to five precincts each, requiring voters to go to assigned vote centers, rather than allowing vote centers to serve all voters in a county as existing law provides. This limitation is related to provisions of the bill that would prevent electronic pollbook use during Election Day voting. The bill would also require mail ballots postmarked five days before Election Day or less to be verified and counted during the meeting of the canvassing board, rather than at the time returns are canvassed.

Last updated March 8, 2023

This bill, as enacted on April 6, 2023, changes procedures for meeting voter ID requirements. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires a voter who shows a driver's license or state identification that indicates they are not a citizen of the United States, but asserts they are a citizen, to vote a provisional ballot that will only be counted if the voter provides a driver's license or state ID that no longer reflects noncitizenship to the election official responsible for the election to the canvassing board meeting on the 13th day after the election. Existing law was silent as to voters in these circumstances. Note: The bill includes the disclaimer that this section does not affect "any associated consent decree or administrative rules adopted related to a consent decree consented to or enacted before August 1, 2023."
  • Allows any voter who was required to vote provisionally because they failed to show a valid ID to provide the needed ID by print or electronic means. Existing law required that these voters "show" valid ID to an election official, but did not specify the means.

This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2023, would require people to show documentary proof of citizenship before receiving a ballot. The bill would also change processes at the DMV so that any non-citizen who is issued a driver's license is instructed to update DMV within 45 days of naturalizing. The DMV would report that change in citizenship status to the Secretary of State to update the central voter file. Under existing law, people are not required to present documentary proof of citizenship to receive a ballot. Existing U.S. Supreme Court precedent prevents voters in federal elections from being required to show such proof. Although North Dakota does not require voters to register before receiving and casting ballots, it does maintain a central voter file that is for preventing and determining voter fraud, and generating information, including pollbooks, reports, inquiries, forms, and voter lists.

This bill, as enacted on March 22, 2023, expands who may be an election observer, defines what access observers must be granted in polling places, and expands the misdemeanor offense for obstructive conduct at a polling place. Specifically, the bill:

  • Allows "any individual," except a candidate on the ballot being voted at the relevant polling place, to be an election observer, if they inform the election inspector of their intent to do so. Previous law provided for election observers, but did not expressly permit "any" individual to serve. The bill also revises the requirement that observers wear a badge of "the" organization they are representing, to instead require a badge for "any" such organization.
  • Provides that each election observer in a polling place must be positioned where they can plainly view and hear the occurrences of the polling place, without infringing on voter privacy. Previous law required that observers must have "uniform and nondiscriminatory access to all stages of the election process," but did not provide further detail regarding their position.

  • Expands the existing misdemeanor offense for obstructing a voter, and includes new conduct in the offense. Specifically, the bill defines the offense as causing a disturbance, breaching the peace, or obstructing a qualified voter or a poll worker who is on the way to or at a polling place. Previous law limited the obstruction offense to obstructing a qualified voter on the way to a polling place.

This bill, as introduced on January 16, 2023, would repeal the part of the election code under which jurisdictions may choose to send all eligible voters an application for a mail ballot and offer potentially limited in-person voting on Election Day, although one or more in-person voting sites must be offered. Under existing law not addressed by the bill, election officials have the discretion to mail ballot applications to all voters, and the number of in-person voting locations is discretionary.

This bill, as introduced on January 16, 2023, would:

  • Empower an election official to determine that a ballot or any other material, voting system, or device is not in sufficient compliance with the law or established criteria and standards, and require the Secretary of State to decertify such ballot, materials, voting system, or device. The bill would further provide that if a decertified voting system becomes in sufficient compliance with law or established criteria or standards, the Secretary must recertify it according to existing rules. Under existing law, the Secretary of State, not any election official, may determine non-compliance, and having done so, may decertify the system in addition to directing the proper changes to be made.
  • Require, after polls are closed, a hand count of tabulated ballots to ensure the number of ballots equals the number as shown on the machines' report and the number of voters who checked in to vote. If the total number of ballots does not match, recounts must occur until the numbers match. Ballots could not be moved from the polling place to perform this count match or otherwise before it is complete, unless good and substantial reasons exist, as defined by the Secretary of State before the election. Any relocation of the ballots would be subject to chain of custody rules and be publicly disclosed. Under existing law, the ballot number reconciliation involves only the total produced by the machine compared to the number of voters who checked in, the good and substantial reasons for relocating the ballots do not need to be pre-determined by the Secretary of State, and the part of the election code being amended does not address chain of custody rules.

This bill, as introduced on January 23, 2023, would allow voter information in the central voter file to be publicly accessible without limitation on the information's use and make changes that the Voting Rights Lab does not track, such as banning electronic poll books. This bill, as introduced January 10, 2023, would require a voter to present photo identification at many stages in the electoral process, and would curtail the use of mail voting in Nebraska. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require an individual to present qualifying photographic identification (or a copy) to be able to register to vote, to vote in person during early voting or on Election Day, or when applying for or returning a mail ballot. A voter unable to present photo ID when voting in person would only be permitted to vote a provisional ballot, and would need to present voter ID within a week of Election Day for their ballot to be counted.
  • Define qualifying photographic identification as:
    • A Nebraska driver's license or state identification card that is not expired or has been expired less than sixty days,
    • A valid Nebraska photographic voter identification that is not expired or has been expired less than sixty days,
    • A United States Passport that is not expired or has been expired less than sixty days, or
    • A valid tribal identification issued by a recognized Indian tribe.
  • Waive the fee for a state ID card, and for a certified copy of a birth record for a voter seeking to obtain a state ID card, for a voter who needs photo ID for voting purposes but who does not have a driver's license.
  • End no-excuse mail voting in the state, and only allow a voter to vote by mail if the voter is handicapped with a qualifying condition or is a member of the armed forces of the United States or the Nebraska National Guard. These voters would be required to submit a request for a mail ballot each election.
  • Establish a felony offense for a voter who uses a fake ID for purposes of voting, a felony offense for an election official who scans a voter's ID into an electronic system, and a misdemeanor offense for election officials who fail to properly verify a voter's eligibility.
  • End the system under which certain special elections are conducted entirely by mail. The bill would also repeal a requirement that an election authority, if the authority maintains a secure drop box for voted ballots during a special election, allow at least one such drop box to remain accessible for the entire mail voting period.

This bill, as enacted on June 1, 2023, creates new statutory requirements for photo ID to vote in person and by mail, implementing an amendment to the Nebraska constitution approved by the voters in 2022. Specifically, the bill:

  • Defines "valid photographic identification" as:
    • A document issued by the United States, the Department of Defense, Department of Veterans Affairs, the U.S. military, a Native American tribe, or by Nebraska, a Nebraska state agency, or a political subdivision or college within the State of Nebraska that includes the person's name and photo
    • A hospital, assisted-living facility, nursing home, or any other skilled care facility record containing the person's name and photo.
  • Requires an individual to present valid photographic identification when appearing to vote in person during early voting or on Election Day. A voter who does not present photo ID, even if the person has a reasonable impediment to obtaining ID or a religious objection to being photographed, would be required to vote provisionally. Previous law did not require a voter to present ID in order to vote.
  • Requires a voter unable to present photo ID when voting to present photo ID no later than the Tuesday following Election Day or sign a reasonable impediment certification (in a form designed by the Secretary of State) for their provisional ballot to be counted. Reasonable impediments under the bill include illness or disability, lack of documents required to obtain photo ID, or a religious objection to being photographed (the bill also includes procedures for maintaining a list of religious objectors).
  • Creates new voter ID requirements for mail ballot voters. Specifically, the bill:
    • Requires a voter applying for a mail ballot in-person to present photo ID, and for mailed requests, requires the applicant to include either a photocopy of their valid photographic identification, the number from their Nebraska drivers license or state ID card, or their reasonable impediment certification. Previous law only required basic identifying information.
    • Requires mail voters to also meet ID requirements when returning their voted ballot. If a returned mail ballot does not meet ID requirements, election officials must notify the voter by the day after Election Day that they must cure the defect by the following Tuesday for the ballot to be counted.
  • Requires conforming changes to the mail ballot envelope related to the new voter ID requirements, including a voter's oath that includes notice of criminal penalties for false statements.
    • Creates exceptions to the mail ballot ID requirements for UOCAVA voters and emergency response providers located outside their home county.
    • Sets out conforming requirements for mail ballot verification and processing, related to new ID rules.
  • Requires the Secretary of State to develop a process, in cooperation with the Attorney General and the DMV, to use any information in the Secretary's possession or available to their office to match and verify the citizenship of each voter. The bill specifies that this information may not be used for any purpose other than list maintenance.
  • Mandates a public awareness campaign to ensure voters are advised of the new photo ID requirements.
  • Waives the fee for a state identification card or copy of a birth record for a person who needs one for voting purposes.

A previous version of this bill prior to enactment comprised entirely different provisions across a wide variety of elections topics, only some of which were tracked by Voting Rights Lab. Amendments to the bill on May 22, 2023, stripped all of these provisions from the bill.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced January 17, 2023, would create extensive new voter ID requirements in the state of Nebraska. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require a voter to present valid photographic identification when the voter wishes to vote in person, whether during early voting or on Election Day. A voter who does not present ID would be required to complete an affidavit asserting their right to vote, and would commit a felony if the document is falsified. A voter completing the affidavit would only be permitted to vote provisionally, and their ballot would only be counted if they presented valid photographic identification within seven days of Election Day.
  • Define "valid photographic identification" as any of the following:
    • A document issued by the United States or by Nebraska, that shows the individual's name and photograph, and has an expiration date that has either not passed or only passed after the most recent statewide general election.
    • A document issued by the United States Department of Defense, the United States Department of Veterans Affairs or its predecessor, the Veterans Administration, a branch of the uniformed services, or a Native American Indian tribe or band recognized by the United States Government that displays the individual's name and photograph and either has no expiration date or an indefinite expiration date.
    • A document issued by Nebraska that shows the individual's name and contains a digital image of an affidavit explaining the individual's religious objection to being photographed, the individual's signature, and either has no expiration date or an indefinite expiration date.
  • Incorporate the verification of voter identification into the registration process.
  • Require a voter requesting a mail ballot to include either the identification number of their valid photographic identification (if issued by the state of Nebraska) or a photocopy of it, if requesting by mail. A voter requesting a mail ballot in person would also be required to present valid photographic identification. The same requirements would apply when returning the ballot, and to an agent who requests a mail ballot on another voter's behalf.
  • Waive the fee for a state identification card or certified birth record for an individual who needs one to obtain photo ID for voting purposes.
  • Require the Secretary of State to conduct a public awareness campaign to help voters understand the identification requirements imposed by the bill.

Last Updated March 1, 2023

This bill, as introduced January 17, 2023, makes several changes to Nebraska election law to facilitate voting by mail. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the election commissioner or county clerk to contact a mail ballot voter by text or email, if known, to confirm that the voter's mail ballot was received, the date of its receipt, whether or not the ballot was accepted, and if applicable, the reason for its rejection.
  • Permit an individual to access the official application for a ballot to be voted by mail via the website of the Secretary of State.
  • Require the election commissioner or county clerk to include a postage-paid return envelope with each ballot to be voted by mail.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced January 18, 2023, would make significant changes to Nebraska's election laws, including by requiring identification to vote in person and establishing automatic voter registration at the Department of Motor Vehicles. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require voters, beginning in 2026, to present a form of identification to be permitted to cast a ballot in person during early voting and on Election Day. Under existing law, voters are generally required only to state their name and address for in-person voting. Under the bill, accepted identification would expressly not be required to be current or unexpired, or to have an exact name or address match, gender marker, or signature, and must be one of the following documents:
    • A driver's license or learner's permit issued by a state or territory of the United States,
    • A state identification card issued by a state or territory of the United States,
    • An identification card issued by a high school or postsecondary educational institution accredited by an accrediting agency or state approval agency recognized by the United States Secretary of Education,
    • An identification card issued by an agency of the United States, including a United States passport and an identification card issued by a branch of the armed forces of the United States,
    • An identification card issued by a political subdivision of the State of Nebraska,
    • An employee identification card from any branch, department, agency, or entity of the United States Government, state, county, municipality, board, or authority of the state,
    • A tribal identification card from any federally recognized tribe in the United States,
    • A social security card,
    • A medicare or medicaid identification card,
    • A United States citizenship certificate,
    • A United States naturalization certificate,
    • A certified birth record issued by a government bureau of vital statistics or board of health in the United States, District of Columbia, Guam, Puerto Rico, or Virgin Islands,
    • A certificate of Birth Abroad (FS-545 or DS-1350) issued by the United States Department of State,
    • A report of Birth Abroad of a United States Citizen (FS-240) issued by a United States Embassy,
    • A certified adoption certificate from a federal court,
    • An identification card provided by a shelter for the homeless,
    • A hunting, fishing, or concealed carry license issued by the State of Nebraska, or
    • A hospital, nursing home, or other skilled care facility record.
  • Require the DMV and Secretary of State to make accommodations to provide voters with qualified identification in advance of an election, including by accommodating online requests, expanding DMV hours prior to an election, and issuing qualifying ID at election offices, mobile units, libraries, and non-profits. Election commissioners and county clerks would also be required to increase staffing, training, and seating to avoid long lines on Election Day.
  • Require a voter who does not present required identification when voting in person to cast a provisional ballot. The ballot would only be counted if the voter presented qualifying identification to the election office in person, or by mail, email, or fax, by the end of business on the Tuesday after Election Day. The bill would permit an exception to the identification requirement for provisional ballot verification for voters who can instead present a declaration of identity, a declaration of poverty (including identity and financial inability to obtain required ID) or religious objection to being photographed, with signed acknowledgement that a false claim of eligibility to vote is a criminal offense.
  • Expressly provide that voter ID is not required for a voter to request a mail ballot to be sent to a specific address, for an agent to request a mail ballot on the voter's behalf, or for voters to cast ballots on-site at care facilities.
  • Waive fees for a state identification card for an individual who does not have a driver's license and will be of voting age at the next election. The bill would also waive fees for a birth record for an individual who needs their birth record for voting purposes.
  • Establish automatic voter registration at the Department of Motor Vehicles. Under existing law, an individual conducting a transaction at the DMV must be offered an opportunity to register to vote or to update their existing registration. The bill would require instead that the individual's information be automatically forwarded to the proper voter registration authority unless the individual indicates that they wish to opt out at the time of the transaction or that they are not a U.S. citizen. The bill would also expressly provide that submission of a registration application for an ineligible applicant will not constitute an unlawful statement or attempt to register, unless the individual willfully and knowingly takes affirmative steps to register knowing they are ineligible to do so.
  • Expand authorization for use of universal mail ballots (sent automatically to all registered voters), by eliminating the limitation that officials may only do so in counties with less than 10,000 residents. The bill would retain the requirement that local officials must apply to the Secretary of State for approval to send universal mail ballots, setting out compliance with various conditions.
  • Permit a voter to request a mail ballot by online application on the website of the Secretary of State.
  • Establish a permanent mail voting list.
  • Newly require an election commissioner or county clerk to:
    • Advise a voter who requests a mail ballot of their receipt of the request, and of their receipt of the voter's returned mail ballot, and
    • Include a postage-paid return envelope with each mail ballot sent.
  • Require the secretary of state to conduct a public awareness campaign about voter identification documentation requirements.
  • Expressly state the legislature's "intent" to ensure sufficient funding is provided to bring all polling sites into compliance with federal law on access for individuals with disabilities.

Last Updated February 23, 2023

This bill, as introduced January 18, 2023, would make changes to voter identification and registration requirements. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require photographs of voters be used to verify their identity when they appear to vote. If a photograph of a voter is not stored in the electronic poll book, the voter would be required to show identification in a form determined by law before casting a ballot.
  • Give a person obtaining or updating a DMV record a more explicit opportunity to opt out of registering to vote or updating their registration during the transaction.   • Create a misdemeanor for an officer who uses voter registration records for any purpose other than voter registration, election administration, or enforcement of the Election Act.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced January 5, 2023, would submit a constitutional amendment to the voters to remove the constitutional requirement that persons convicted of felonies be disqualified to vote "unless restored to civil rights." The bill would leave in place disqualifications for mental incapacity and convictions for treason. Note that this amendment, if passed, would remove the constitutional mandate for disenfranchisement due to felony convictions other than treason, but would not repeal or prohibit statutory provisions that do so.

Last updated January 19, 2023.

This bill, as introduced on January 4, 2023, would:

  • Repeal the requirement that an individual carry out verifiable acts carrying out an intent to establish and maintain a domicile in order to be eligible to vote.
  • Repeal the requirement that applicants for registration provide documentary evidence of their qualifications or attest that none exists by completing a qualified voter affidavit.
  • Define domicile as "that place, more than any other, where [the voter] sleep[s] most nights of the year, or to which [they] intend to return after a temporary absence."
  • Repeal the requirement that an applicant for registration in the final 30 days before an election use a special form, retaining that form only for registration on Election Day.
  • Establish a Domicile Affidavit for same-day registrants to use in lieu of documentary evidence of domicile.
  • Allow same-day registrants who do not have an approved photo ID to establish their identity via "any reasonable means," including other forms of photo ID or verification by another registered voter.
  • Remove the requirement that the secretary of state mail letters to all new registrants within 30 days of an election informing them that new New Hampshire residents must get a New Hampshire driver's license without 60 days of becoming a resident of the state.
  • Direct the secretary of state to cease participating in Crosscheck and to prepare a report for legislators regarding potentially joining ERIC.
  • Modify the statutory definitions of resident, for all purposes, to require that an individual claiming residence have an intention to stay in a given place "for the indefinite future."
  • Shift responsibility for investigating certain suspected cases of fraudulent voting from the secretary of state to the attorney general.
  • Establish that a claim of domicile for voting purposes is not conclusive evidence of a voter's residence for any other legal purpose.
  • Make conforming changes to the application for registration.

Last Updated January 24, 2023

  • Modify the mail ballot application form to restate other qualifying excuses without substantively changing them

This bill, as introduced on November 20, 2023, would establish same-day voter registration during early voting and on Election Day. Specifically, the bill would:

The bill would create an exception permitting a registration to be effective for a person who appears at an unassigned polling place within their county, if the registration is otherwise valid. Under existing law, a voter casting a provisional ballot has until the second business day after the election to provide sufficient proof of identification.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on June 27, 2023, would make a number of changes to the existing automatic voter registration (AVR) process and designate additional mandatory participating agencies. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Add two new required agencies to the AVR system. Under the bill, AVR would be provided by the Department of Corrections to all eligible individuals being released from its custody, and by the Division of Medical Assistance and Health Services to all eligible residents applying for its program (Medicaid). Under existing law, AVR is only required at the Motor Vehicle Commission, with other state agencies authorized to implement AVR if the Secretary of State verifies that they already collect information sufficient to determine a person's eligibility to vote.
  • Expand the information that the Motor Vehicle Commission must transmit to the Secretary of State to include: name, date of birth, address, driver's license or state ID number, county residence, citizenship status, signature as a digitized image, and, if available, telephone number and email address. Existing law requires the transmission of "information necessary for voter registration," but does not itemize specific requirements.
  • Prohibit transmission of information from the Commission to election officials for participants in the Address Confidentiality Program. Existing law, which the bill would leave in place, requires the Commission to provide notice that victims of domestic violence or stalking may decline registration or register without disclosing their address, but does not expressly prohibit transmission of data for individuals in the program.
  • Expressly state that the Motor Vehicle Commission is not authorized to request documents proving citizenship solely for voter registration purposes. However, a person who provides documentation that conclusively shows they are not a citizen will not be given the opportunity to register.
  • Mandate that information regarding a person's decision to decline to register remain confidential and be used only for election administration purposes.
  • Mandate that new registrants be provided notice by mail after the transaction, including information about declining registration and choosing party affiliation. Existing law has no express requirements for such notice. Under the bill, the notice would be required to include:
    • Disclosure of the requirement that information regarding a choice not to register is confidential.
    • A pre-addressed, postage-paid form that allows them to affiliate with a political party or decline to be registered.
    • Information on how to prevent disclosure of their address.
    • Translations of required information into English and Spanish, as well as any language that is the primary language of five percent or more of the population of the county where notice is mailed.
  • Enumerate the procedure following a return of the notice.
    • A person who declines to register will have their registration canceled.
    • A person who returns the notice and affiliates with a political party is considered affiliated with that party the day the information is received.
    • A person who returns the notice without selecting any options or providing new information will remain registered to vote.
  • Mandate that the Secretary of State develop procedures for processing electronic records received from an AVR agency other than the Commission without a digitized image of the applicant's signature.
  • Create an affirmative defense to prosecution for a person not entitled to vote but who votes or attempts to vote after being automatically registered. The defense does not apply if the person knowingly or willfully made false statements to get registered. Existing law only protects ineligible individuals who were automatically registered from prosecution for "false registration," not those who actually voted or attempted to vote.
  • Alter the criteria for additional AVR agencies by permitting agencies to offer AVR if they collect sufficient information to determine voting eligibility through either direct review of documents or through database verification. Existing law requires collection of information through documents alone.
  • Make conforming changes throughout the code to reference voter's ability to be registered electronically from the Motor Vehicle Commission.

Last Updated September 28, 2023

This bill, as enacted on March 30, 2023, makes various changes to multiple aspects of the voting process, including restoring the voting rights of people convicted of felonies upon their release from incarceration, creating automatic voter registration, modifying same-day registration processes, creating a permanent mail voting list, creating rules for drop boxes, establishing the "Native American Voting Rights Act" to facilitate registration and voting on Indigenous land, modifying the criminal offense of misuse of voter data, and making election days school holidays.

Regarding voting rights restoration, the bill ends disenfranchisement earlier for many voters by restoring voting rights automatically after incarceration, and facilitates voting by formerly incarcerated people. Specifically, the bill:

  • Limits disenfranchisement due to a felony conviction to only the period of imprisonment. Under previous law, voting rights were restored upon completion of the terms of a suspended or deferred sentence, unconditional discharge from a correctional facility, completion of all conditions of parole or supervised probation, or the overturn of conviction on appeal.
  • Repeals the requirement that clerks must cancel a voter's registration upon conviction for a felony, and instead deems registered voters "ineligible" to vote while incarcerated. As a result, once a registered individual is released from custody, they are immediately eligible to vote without re-registering.
  • Provides that during the reentry phase of an inmate's sentence, if the inmate is a voter or qualified to be one, they must be given the opportunity to register or update their registration as part of a transaction with DMV, prior to release. If the person does not do a transaction with DMV at that time, they must be given access to the online voter registration system, or if that is not possible, a paper registration form. Previous law did not have a comparable provision.
  • Provides that notwithstanding an individual's status in the voter registration system, appearing personally before an official authorized to perform registration establishes a presumption that the individual meets the "requirement of non-imprisonment" required for registration. The bill also repeals the requirements under previous law regarding notice by the court or corrections officials to the Secretary of State when an individual has completed their sentence, and repeals the requirement that officials must issue, and clerks must accept, a "certificate of completion" to establish restoration of voting rights after imprisonment.

Regarding automatic voter registration, the bill creates an automatic voter registration process at the DMV and creates a mechanism for instituting automatic voter registration at other state agencies and at Indigenous nation, tribal, and pueblo agencies. Under previous law, registration was available at the DMV, but required an applicant to affirmatively opt in to the process. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires the DMV to check the voter registration database to see if an individual is already registered if, as part of their DMV transaction, the person provides a document that proves their U.S. citizenship. If the individual is not already registered, they will be registered, offered an opportunity to affiliate with a political party, and informed that the county clerk will mail them information about how to decline registration.
  • Requires the DMV to send the Secretary of State automatically registered voters' information within seven days of their transactions. The Secretary must forward the information to the relevant county clerk, who must then send the person a nonforwardable notice that they have been registered. The notice must include:
    • A postage-prepaid and pre-addressed return card the person may use to decline registration or affiliate with a political party.
    • An explanation of voter eligibility requirements, a statement of the penalties for registering when not eligible, and an instruction to decline registration if the person is not eligible.
    • A statement that the decision to decline and the agency at which the registration transaction occurred will be confidential.
    • Information on how a person may become a participant in the confidential address program.
    • An opportunity to request a mail ballot for the next statewide election.
  • Requires automatic updates to existing voter registrations when a voter indicates a change of address during a DMV transaction.
  • Limits criminal liability related to automatic registration. The bill specifies that unless an ineligible individual "knowingly and willfully takes voluntary action to register," the automatic transfer of their data or their failure to decline registration does not constitute unlawful registration. The bill also provides that if an ineligible individual is automatically registered and subsequently votes, they have not committed the false voting offense unless they knowingly and willfully took action to register or to vote with the knowledge they were not eligible.
  • Limits traditional voter registration agency activity at the DMV to only those individuals who are not automatically registered during a transaction.
  • Authorizes the Secretary of State to designate additional automatic voter registration agencies, subject to the requirement that additional agencies must collect sufficient information for the registration process (expressly including verification of citizenship by documentation or database records).
  • Authorizes the Secretary of State to enter a memorandum of understanding with any Indigenous nation, tribe, or pueblo that collects sufficient information to do a DMV-style automatic registration process, at their discretion to enter such an agreement.
  • Permits a state agency or Indigenous nation, tribe, or pueblo that collects all the necessary information for automatic voter registration but not a digitized signature, to provide automatic voter registration, and directs the Secretary to create a process to obtain a signature. The process must include options such as mailing a signature request, uploading a signature through an electronic system, providing a signature on a mail ballot envelope, or providing one at an early voting location or polling place.

Regarding same-day registration, the bill expands ID types that may be used to complete the process, expands the number of days the process is available during a special election, and removes references to "business hours" when discussing availability during early voting. Specifically, the bill:

  • Expands the accepted forms of ID documentation that can be used to register or update a registration at a voting location. Under the bill, the voter may use a physical ID document issued by the federal government, a state government, a federally recognized Indigenous nation, tribe, or pueblo, or an educational institution that contains the voter's name and photograph, and either includes the voter's registration address or is paired with another document that shows the voter's name and registration address, such as a utility bill. Under previous law, a voter was required to show a New Mexico driver's license or state identification card, any document that contains an address in the county together with a photo identification card, or a current valid student photo identification card from a post-secondary educational institution in New Mexico accompanied by a current student fee statement that contains the student's address in the county.
  • Allows individuals seeking to vote in a special election to use the same-day registration process through the close of polls on Election Day. Under previous law, same-day registration for a special election was available during early voting through the last business day in the week before Election Day.
  • Allows individuals to use same-day registration during a statewide election at the county clerk's office or any early or Election Day voting location, provided that the Secretary of State establishes procedures to ensure that a registration officer can review the information before the person votes. Under previous law, voters could use the process at the county clerk's office during the regular hours and days of business during the early voting period, or at an additional alternative early voting location during the regular hours and days of business during the early voting period. Moreover, previous law further restricted the process outside of the clerk's office during early voting by allowing it only where the clerk had designated a specific registration officer.

Regarding voter registration assistance at state agencies, the bill expressly requires the state's Human Services Department to develop procedures, with the approval of the Secretary of State, to ensure that all benefits programs include the opportunity for enrollees to register or update registration without duplication of information. Previous law required that state agencies make registration available to residents, but did not include specific requirements for benefits programs.

Regarding permanent mail voting lists, the bill creates a list open to all voters except uniformed and overseas voters, participants in the Intimate Partner Violence Survivor Suffrage Act, and voters with out-of-state mailing addresses. The list must contain the voter's name, year of birth, address, and precinct. Specifically, the bill:

  • Allows voters to join the list by completing a paper or online application and submitting it to the county clerk.
  • Requires the county clerk to send mail ballots to voters on the list for each election, in the first batch of mailed ballots, until a voter leaves the list.
  • Requires the county clerk to send each voter on the list, at least 49 days before each statewide election, a notice reminding the voter they will be mailed a ballot and informing the voter of how to leave the list if they wish. The notice must be sent by nonforwardable mail with return postage prepaid.
  • Removes voters from the list under certain circumstances. If a voter is removed from the list, the county clerk must attempt to contact and notify the voter of their removal. A voter must be removed from the permanent mail voting list if:
    • The voter fails to return the mail ballot in two consecutive elections, including at least one general election.
    • A mailed ballot or other election mail sent to the voter's mailing address was returned undeliverable.
    • The voter's registration is canceled.
    • The voter updates their registration to an address outside the county.
    • The voter requests to leave the list.

Regarding mail ballot drop boxes ("monitored secure containers"), the bill:

  • Requires each county to have at least two drop boxes. Clerks may request a waiver from the Secretary of State for the requirement, on the grounds of geographic or security constraints. Clerks may also request approval from the Secretary for the use of additional drop boxes as needed. Previous law provided for the use of drop boxes, but did not include specific requirements regarding their number.
  • Authorizes political subdivisions, including municipalities, school districts, and community colleges, to make a written request to a clerk for one or more drop boxes on or near the boundaries of the subdivision. This request must be made between the second Tuesday of March and the second Tuesday of April of any year. In considering a request, the clerk must evaluate the population in and near the area requested, the distance voters have to travel to get to the nearest monitored secured container, and the number of such containers and early voting sites on or near the area of request, and must respond in writing within 30 days. If the clerk rejects the request, the political subdivision may appeal to the Secretary, who is authorized to place a drop box at their discretion. If a subdivision's request for a drop box is approved, it must provide the necessary facility and services for its use.

Regarding election administration in Indigenous nations, tribes, and pueblos, the bill creates the "Native American Voting Rights Act," which permits use of official buildings on Indigenous lands for registration and mail ballot delivery, sets out rules for precinct drawing on Indigenous land, creates processes for Indigenous officials to request early voting locations, Election Day voting locations, and drop boxes, and requires state funding for compliance with all requirements. In addition to these changes, the bill also relocates into the Act existing provisions that create special rules relating to early and Election Day voting sites that apply when the president, governor, or governing body of an Indigenous nation, tribe, or pueblo has declared a state of emergency or has invoked emergency powers. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires the Secretary of State to create a list of government and official buildings on Indigenous lands at which residents can designate their voter registration address and request delivery of their mail ballots. The list must include the buildings' common names and mailing addresses and would be distributed to every county clerk with Indigenous lands in their jurisdiction. If the clerk receives a voter registration certificate or application for a mailed ballot that lists such a building, the clerk is prohibited from rejecting the certificate or application for lack of a mailing address. If the certificate or application is otherwise proper, the clerk must mail the ballot and balloting materials to that address. Previous law provided that if a voter registration applicant lived in an area lacking a specific physical address, they were required to substitute a mailing address along with a description indicating where they live.
  • Requires the board of county commissioners, whenever it is adjusting precinct boundaries for any group of census blocks that are on Indigenous land, to obtain from each nation, tribe, or pueblo the internal and external political boundaries provided to the U.S. census bureau. The board of county commissioners must adjust the precinct boundaries to match, and the Secretary of State must reject any precinct map that does not conform.
  • Permits Indigenous nations, tribes, and pueblos to make written requests for voting locations and ballot drop boxes from county clerks. Requests must be made at specific times, depending on the type of request. Specifically:
    • A request for an Election Day voting site during the next general election cycle must be made between the second Tuesday in March and the second Tuesday in April of each even-numbered year. Thus a request for an Election Day voting site for the November 2024 general election must be made in the March-April window in 2022.
    • A request for an early voting location during a current election cycle may be made at two different times. The first opportunity is between the second Tuesday in March and the second Tuesday in April of each odd-numbered year. The second opportunity is between January 1 of the year of the general election and the date that the Secretary of State issues the proclamation for the election, and is only open to nations, tribes, and pueblos that had not yet requested one. Thus a request for an early voting site for the November 2024 general election may be made in the March-April window in 2023, or between January 1, 2024, and the last Monday in January, or January 29, 2024. Under previous law, a request for an early voting location was required to be made by the first Monday in November of an odd-numbered year.
    • A request for a drop box for the 2023 regular local election may be made by July 15, 2023, and for any other election, between the second Tuesday in March and the second Tuesday in April.
  • Requires the county clerk to consider the nation, tribe, or pueblo's request for an Election Day polling place when submitting recommendations to the board of county commissioners for the biennial Election Day polling place resolution establishing voter convenience centers for the upcoming election. The clerk must consider the distance voters must travel to get to the nearest Election Day voting location and the number of early voting locations and ballot drop boxes located on or near Indigenous land. When the clerk submits their Election Day polling place resolution to the board of county commissioners, the clerk is required to inform the board of any written requests received from Indigenous nations, tribes, or pueblos. Once the resolution is adopted, the bill prohibits eliminating or consolidating an Election Day voting location on Indigenous land without the written agreement of the nation, tribe, or pueblo on whose land the voting location is sited. Previous law had a similar rule for consolidation, but the additional new provisions did not have parallels in prior law. The bill also sets out requirements for these Election Day voting locations. Previous law did not have similar provisions for Election Day voting sites but did have generally similar rules for early voting locations on Indigenous lands. Specifically, an Election Day voter convenience center may only be sited as requested if:
    • Any voter of the county may vote at the location.
    • The location conforms to the requirements for Election Day polling places.
    • The county clerk provides federally mandated language translators at the Election Day polling places.
    • If the voting location is on Indigenous land, the nation, tribe, or pueblo provides the facility and services for the polling place.
  • Requires the county clerk to respond to the nation, tribe, or pueblo's request for an early voting location by siting at least one on or near the nation, tribe, or pueblo land. Previous law required clerks to site a requested location on Indigenous land, without the option to site it "near" Indigenous land. The site is otherwise required to meet the same conditions as under previous law required, which parallel those the bill imposes on Election Day voting sites on Indigenous lands. When responding to the written request, the clerk must evaluate the population on the Indigenous land, the distance voters must travel, and the number of early voting locations and ballot drop boxes located on or near Indigenous land.
  • Creates a process for the county clerk to consider an Indigenous nation, tribe, or pueblo's request for drop boxes, and an appeal process for the Indigenous requestors if the clerk denies the request. Specifically, the bill:
    • Requires the county clerk to evaluate the population on the Indigenous land, the distance voters must travel, and the number of early voting locations and ballot drop boxes located on or near Indigenous land, and respond in writing to the nation, tribe, or pueblo within 30 days of receiving the request.
    • Allows an Indigenous nation, tribe, or pueblo to appeal a denial of their request to the Secretary of State by giving the Secretary the original written request, the clerk's rejection letter, and any response the nation, tribe, or pueblo made to that letter. The Secretary is authorized to site a drop box on Indigenous land as requested, at their discretion.
    • Requires any drop box sited on or near Indigenous land to comply with all requirements for such containers in the election code. If on Indigenous land, the Indigenous nation, tribe, or pueblo must provide the facility and services necessary for the container.
  • Requires the Secretary of State to pay for all necessary and reasonable expenses incurred by county clerks to comply with provisions of the Act.

Regarding criminal penalties for misuse of voter data, the bill:

  • Modifies the felony of unlawful use of voter data, mailing labels, or special voter lists. The previous crime prohibited the knowing and willful use of such information for purposes prohibited by the Voter Records System Act. Under the bill, the crime now specifically prohibits:
    • selling, loaning, providing access to, or otherwise surrendering of voter data, mailing labels, or special voter lists by a person for purposes prohibited by the Election Code
    • causing voter data, mailing labels or special voter lists or any part of the voter data, mailing label or special voter lists that identifies, or that could be used to identify, a specific voter or the voter's name, mailing, or residence address to be made publicly available on the internet or through other means

Regarding election day holidays, the bill makes every general election and regular local election a school holiday for students and staff at public schools.

Previous versions of the bill also included provisions that were amended out prior to enactment:

  • On February 27, 2023, a provision was amended out that would have created the role of "Tribal absentee ballot assistant" to facilitate collecting and returning mail ballots completed by voters on Indigenous nation, tribe, and pueblo lands.
  • On March 30, 2023, multiple provisions were amended out, concerning the use of voter data. These provisions would have changed the definitions of various categories of data use, and would have prohibited an individual who requests voter data from transferring, copying, sharing, or conveying the data to any person outside the requesting party's agency or organization, or making the information accessible to the general public on the internet or through other means.

Last Updated September 21, 2023

This bill, as introduced February 6, 2023 would make amendments to laws concerning ballots voted by mail and election board compensation, among other changes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require a request for a mail ballot, from a voter other than a federally qualified elector, to be received no later than fourteen days before Election Day. Under existing law, an application for a mail ballot is timely if received up to the Thursday immediately preceding the election.
  • Require the county clerk to send a "notice of mailed ballot" to a voter's registration address if the voter requests a mail ballot to be sent to another address. The bill would also require a rejection notice be sent to a voter whose request for a mail ballot is rejected.
  • Require all applications for a mail ballot to be submitted on either the official paper form or via the secretary of state's official web portal.
  • Increase the maximum allowable compensation for members of an election board (presiding judge, election judges, and election clerks) from $200 per election day to $400.

This resolution, as introduced February 6, 2023, would propose an amendment to the state constitution to permit any voter to request the ballot of any single political party conducting a state-funded primary election, regardless of whether the voter's registration indicates an affiliation with that party. Under existing statutory law, only voters affiliated with a party are permitted to vote in that party's primary election. The proposed amendment would permit a party to opt out of the open-primary system if the party administers and pays all costs associated with the nomination process.

The bill would additionally remove voter names and addresses from the copy of entries made in the absentee ballot register distributed to party chairs during an election.
