This bill, as enacted on March 30, 2023, makes extensive changes to New Mexico election law related to vote centers, mail ballot procedures, and a wide variety of other election processes. Specifically, the bill:

  • Mandates, rather than permits, the use of vote centers ("voter convenience centers") in statewide elections. The bill also includes a temporary provision that requires all polling place locations established for elections in 2021 to operate as voter convenience centers for all statewide elections in the 2023 calendar year.
  • Alters procedures and requirements for mail ballot voting. Specifically, the bill:
    • Changes the mail ballot application deadline for non-UOCAVA voters, from the Thursday before the election to the 14th day before the election. The bill also requires that a notice of requested ballot be sent to a voter's registration address if the clerk receives a request to send the voter's mail ballot to a different address, and establishes a cure process for a defective application.
    • Expressly requires that if a form is issued by the secretary of state for any election-related process only that form may be used, and expressly limits mail ballot applications to only the state's online portal or the official application form.
    • Requires voters using a mail ballot to provide the last four digits of their social security number and their signature as "identification" on the return ballot envelope. Previous law required voters to provide their name, registration address, and date of birth as identification. Note: For the 2020 general election, temporary legislation required mail ballots to include a voter's social security number, and permanent state regulations subsequently promulgated this requirement.
    • Permits any member of a mail voter's household to return a mail ballot on the voter's behalf, and expands the definition of "immediate family" permitted to return a ballot, by including domestic partners, grandparents and grandchildren, and a "person with whom the voter has a continuing personal relationship." Previous law permitted third party return by only a voter's caregiver, spouse, child, parent, or sibling. The bill also requires the mail ballot return envelope to include a notice stating who may return a ballot.
    • Permits a voter who applied for a mail ballot or was sent a mail ballot that has not yet been received by the clerk as of Election Day to vote in person. Under previous law, voters who requested a mail ballot could vote in person only if they did not receive or return the ballot. As under previous law, these voters are permitted to vote a regular ballot if there is real-time synchronization between the clerk and polling location. If there is not, these voters are required to vote a provisional paper ballot.
    • Creates a comprehensive cure process for missing signatures, and missing or non-matching social security numbers, on mail ballots. Voters have until the Friday following Election Day to correct errors. While previous statutory law did not provide for a cure process, state regulations required notice and opportunity to cure these ballot defects.
    • Specifies requirements for recess of the absent voter election board, if they do not complete processing ballots by 11 p.m. on election night, including the provision of law enforcement for overnight supervision of uncounted mail ballots and video surveillance. Previous law had no comparable provisions.
    • Prohibits clerks from mailing a voter a replacement mail ballot within seven days of an election, unless the voter is enrolled in the confidential substitute address program. Previous law had no deadline for mailing a replacement ballot, and expressly exempted such ballots from the standard issuance deadline of the Friday before an election. The bill also specifies procedures for request of a replacement ballot for participants in the address confidentiality program.
    • Makes minor changes to requirements for the operation of drop boxes, including deadlines for posting their location prior to an election, signage regarding third-party return rules, and frequency of ballot collection by officials.
    • Creates new felony offenses for possessing the key to a ballot drop box without permission and for any individual other than the secretary of state or county clerk to provide or operate a drop box. The bill also specifies that the felony offense of unlawful possession of a mail ballot includes the establishment, designation, or operation of an authorized receptacle to receive mail ballots and entering information into the absentee register.
    • Expands the existing misdemeanor offense of obstructing the polling place to include willfully blocking access to a ballot drop box. The bill also expands the categories of authorized individuals who are exempt from the prohibition of coming within 50 feet of a polling place.
    • Establishes that an application by a UOCAVA voter for a mail ballot is effective as an automatic application for all elections in the current cycle. Previous law limited the types of elections for which an application would apply in a single election cycle. The bill also permits a UOCAVA voter to submit a request for a ballot as late as three days before Election Day if the voter provides information permitting secure electronic delivery. Previous law required all UOCAVA ballot requests to be received by the standard mail ballot deadline (as noted above, this bill changes that deadline from Thursday before an election to the 14th day before an election).
  • Extends early voting hours to permit voting to begin as early as 7:00 a.m. and continue as late as 9:00 p.m., and requires at least eight consecutive hours of voting access each day. Previous law required early voting to be conducted during the ordinary business hours of the county clerk's office. The bill also deletes the provision requiring early voting on the Saturday before an election to be available specifically from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. County clerks must publicize early voting hours not less than 90 days before the election, after which point the county clerk may not modify the hours without seeking permission from the secretary of state. Previous law had no comparable provision regarding notice.
  • Changes list maintenance procedures by instructing the secretary of state to develop a general program for county clerks to investigate and identify voters who may be eligible to have their voter registration canceled. The program must provide standard procedures for the cancellation of registration of a voter confirmed to have voted in another state, moved to another state, or died. Previous law, which the bill leaves in place, required only that the secretary maintain a manual of best practices for investigating and reconciling information for voter list maintenance, including "safeguards" to prevent erroneous removal.
  • Permits clerks to process voter registration applications that were submitted after the deadline to register for an election starting on the Monday after the election, as opposed to 35 days after the election as required by previous law.
  • Modifies requirements for service as a member of the election board, or as an election watcher or challenger. Specifically, the bill:
    • Mandates training for election watchers and challengers. The bill also requires a watcher to be a voter in the state, rather than a voter in the precinct where they are appointed as required by previous law. The bill leaves in place the requirement that challengers be voters in the precinct where they are appointed.
    • Prohibits the domestic partner of a candidate in an election, or the partner's parent, from serving on an election board, or as an election challenger, watcher, or observer. This prohibition is in addition to the existing prohibition on service in these roles by other family members.
    • Disqualifies a person as a challenger, watcher, or election observer if the person has accepted an appointment to serve as an election board member in the same election, or has been unanimously removed from service by an election board in the current or most recent election.
    • Increases the maximum compensation of election board members and messengers from $200 per election day to $400 and specifies that they must be paid for undergoing training.
  • Requires the secretary of state, 42 days before each general election, to send a notice to all voters including the date of the election, a list of early voting and Election Day voting locations, and ways to obtain further information.
  • Establishes an "elections security program" within the office of the bureau of elections. The program's responsibilities include advising the secretary of state, county clerks, and other elections officials of voting system and cybersecurity requirements.
  • Requires service of process to the secretary of state for any action challenging a provision or procedure of the Election Code, regardless of whether the secretary is a party to the action.
  • Changes procedures related to confidentiality of voter addresses. Specifically, the bill:
    • Permits public officials to designate their home address as confidential, in election- or financial-related disclosures made to the secretary of state or county clerks. Under previous law, confidentiality of voter registration address information was generally restricted to individuals experiencing the threat of domestic violence.
    • Permits an applicant to the confidential substitute address program to include members of their household on an application, and deems these additional individuals as separate participants. If currently enrolled in the program, participants are required to add new household members within ten days (the same notification period required for name and address changes).
    • Authorizes officials to decertify an individual from the address confidentiality program if they fail to comply with the provisions of the Intimate Partner Violence Survivor Suffrage Act. Among other provisions, the Act requires voting by mail only.
  • Expressly permits cure of an issue that has caused a provisional ballot to be rejected during the period up to and including the appeal process for rejection.

The bill also makes extensive changes to various areas of election law not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, including requirements for candidates, primary election procedures, ballot design and preparation, processing of paper ballots, canvassing procedures, data disclosure rules, voting machine requirements, and others.

This bill, as introduced on March 1, 2023, would reduce the amount of time voters have to mail their completed ballots to election officials, and make a conforming change to the felony prohibiting a third party from failing to return a voter's ballot for them on time. VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 15, 2023, would overhaul how elections in Nevada are conducted. The bill would require in-person voters to show a photo ID to receive a ballot and end Nevada's practice of mailing all active voters a ballot for all elections. Instead, the bill would require voters to have an excuse to vote by mail and to apply for the ballot. The bill would also change other aspects of voting by mail, such as the ballot return deadline, how a voter may return their ballot, and more.

The bill would change how election officials verify the identity of in-person voters. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require in-person voters to provide "proof of identity" to receive a ballot. The bill would define "proof of identity" to mean a document or identity card that:

    • Is issued by this State, the United States, or a federally recognized Indian tribe.
    • Shows the name, signature, and recognizable photograph of the person to whom the document or identity card is issued.
    • If issued by Nevada, has an expiration date no more than four years before the date of the election.

    Under existing law, in-person voters are identified by signing the poll book and having a poll worker compare their signature on the voter registration application. If the poll worker does not believe the signature matches, among the other ways to confirm the voter's identity, the voter may show an allowed ID document containing their signature and have their signature matched against that document. Existing law allows the voter to offer any form of ID issued by a governmental agency that includes the voter's signature and either their picture or their description. Specifically allowed documents included the voter registration card issued to the voter, a driver's license, a Nevada state ID, and a military ID.


  • Require voters who are challenged as not being who they say they are to provide "proof of identity". Existing law allows a challenged voter to show any official ID with a photograph or to bring a person who is at least 18 years old and has a photo ID to the election official and have that person vouch for them.
  • Require a voter who does not provide "proof of identity" to vote a provisional ballot. To have the ballot counted, the voter would be required to provide such proof to the county or city clerk by 5 p.m. on the Friday after Election Day.
  • Require the DMV to issue an identification card without charge to a person who:
    • Complies with the general requirements to receive an ID.
    • Provides proof they are a registered voter.
    • Attests they are experiencing financial hardship. The DMV would not be allowed to ask for proof beyond the attestation.

  • Create new exceptions to the general rule that certain first-time voters who registered by mail or computer must vote in person. The bill would allow such a person to vote by mail if they submit a written request for a mail ballot with their signature notarized or they request the mail ballot in person at the office of the county clerk.

    The bill would fundamentally change voting by mail by ending the practice of universally mailing ballots to all voters. Instead, the bill would:


  • Provide that only a person unable to vote in person because of an illness or disability resulting in confinement in a hospital, sanatorium, dwelling, or nursing home may apply for a mail ballot (called "absent ballot" by the bill). The deadline to apply would be 5 p.m. on the 14th day before Election Day. If a voter becomes suddenly hospitalized, seriously ill, or called away from home after the deadline for requesting a mail ballot, they would use a slightly different application process but could apply for a mail ballot through 5 p.m. on Election Day. Polls close at 7 p.m.
  • Require qualified voters who want a mail ballot to give the appropriate county clerk a written request. These mail ballot requests would be available for public inspection, and a county clerk who allows a person to copy information from them would be immune from civil or criminal liability for any damage caused by the distribution of that information unless they knowingly and willingly allowed a person to copy the information who intends to use the information to further an unlawful act.
  • Require the written requests to include as applicable:
    • The name, address, and signature of the registered voter requesting the ballot.
    • The name, address, and signature of the person designated by the registered voter to obtain, deliver and return the ballot for the registered voter.
    • A brief statement of the illness or disability of the registered voter or of facts sufficient to establish that the registered voter was called away from home after the time had elapsed for requesting the ballot.
    • If the registered voter is confined in a hospital, sanatorium, dwelling, or nursing home, a statement that he or she will be confined therein on the day of the election.
    • Unless the person designated to carry the ballot will mark and sign it on behalf of the registered voter, a statement signed under penalty of perjury that only the registered voter will mark and sign the ballot.
  • Allow a registered voter with a disability to use the system for approved electronic transmission established by the Secretary of State to request a ballot.
  • Allow a voter with an appropriate excuse to use a single application to request ballots for all elections in the calendar year of the request, and allow a voter with an appropriate excuse to request to be mailed ballots for all elections going forward. After making such a request, the voter would continue to receive ballots until their registration became inactive, was canceled, or a ballot was returned undeliverable.
  • Create a felony to prohibit fraudulently requesting a mail ballot in the name of another person or inducing or coercing another person to do so.
  • Allow a county clerk who did not mail a ballot to a domestic voter as required to send that voter the ballot electronically. The voter would complete and return the ballot either in the ordinary way or by approved electronic method.
  • Require a mail voter to include the last four digits of their Social Security number on the ballot return envelope. Existing law does not require voters to include an ID number with their ballot. Notably, the bill does not require election officials to verify the number, reject ballots with a missing number, or notify voters if there is an issue with the number.
  • Change the mail ballot return deadline. The bill would require ballots returned by mail to be postmarked at least three days before Election Day and be received by the seventh day after the election. Ballots received by mail in that window without a postmark would be deemed timely mailed. Under existing law, ballots must be postmarked on or before Election Day and received by election officials by 5 p.m. on the fourth day after the election, or if not postmarked but received by mail, by 5 p.m. on the third day after. Ballots returned by hand must be returned by the close of polls on Election Day under both the bill and existing law.
  • Limit a voter's options to return their ballot by eliminating the requirement that all jurisdictions offer voters ballot drop boxes, and possibly prohibiting the use of ballot drop boxes altogether by requiring voters to return ballots by mail or by hand delivery "to the county clerk."
  • Restrict ballot return assistance and enforce the restrictions with a new felony. Under existing law, a voter has the freedom to choose anyone to return their ballot for them. The bill would:
    • Require a voter to return their own mail ballot or give it to a member of their immediate family to return.
    • Require an immediate family member who is returning their relative's ballot to indicate, under penalty of perjury, that they are an immediate family member of the voter and that the voter asked them to return their ballot.
    • Prohibit an immediate family member from returning more than two relatives' ballots each election.
    • Create a class E felony to enforce these restrictions.
  • Change the signature matching and cure processes.
    • For signature matching, the bill would provide for human review of signatures only, while existing law allows the use of signature matching technology, provided that any rejected signature is also reviewed by people. The human review process is essentially the same under the bill and existing law, but existing law provides detail on what constitutes "a reasonable question of fact" that the voter's signature does not match one on file.
    • To cure a mismatched signature, the bill would eliminate detail about how and when to contact the voter, and how a voter can cure. The basic language requiring the clerk to contact the voter and confirm that they voted the ballot is the same in the bill as in existing law. The bill does not provide a specific deadline for this process. Under existing law, the deadline is 5 p.m. on the sixth day after the election.
    • To cure a missing signature, the bill would require the clerk to contact the voter and require the voter to provide a signature by the seventh day after the election. The bill would require the clerk to prescribe procedures for contacting the voter, for the voter to submit a signature, and for the cured ballots to be delivered for counting. Existing law provides such procedures and sets a deadline for cure of 5 p.m. on the sixth day after the election.
  • Change mail ballot counting processes.
    • Under the bill, mail ballots would be counted no sooner than four working days before Election Day. Under existing law, the process may begin 15 days before Election Day. The bill creates an optional new type of counting board called an absent ballot central counting board. The processes for storing ballots before counting and other details are slightly different depending on whether the optional board is used. Under existing law, mail ballot central counting boards process the mail ballots.
    • Under the bill, the election board doing the counting must compare the voter's signature on the ballot envelope against their signature on their application to register to vote. The bill does not provide steps if the signature does not match. Existing law does not require this second verification of the voter's signature. The original signature match process done by the county clerk uses, if necessary, every signature in the voter's file.
    • The bill would require the count to be completed by the seventh day after Election Day.
  • Clarify that an existing felony against voting in the name of another person includes voting a mail ballot in their name.

  • Require people who distribute mail ballot applications to at least 500 voters in the six months before an election to follow certain rules. Specifically, such people:

    • Must use the Secretary of State mail ballot application form, and add to the top of it the person's name and a specified disclaimer.
    • Must, at least 28 days before distributing forms, notify the county clerks of any counties in which the person will distribute forms approximately how many forms they will distribute and on which date distribution will begin.
    • Must not return or offer to return to the county clerk a form they mailed to a voter, and must not mail a form to a voter less than 35 days before the election.

    The bill also includes provisions relating to mail voting that would not change existing law, such as the timeline to mail ballots to voters entitled to receive them, the requirement that domestic mail ballot return envelopes be postage prepaid, special paperwork for anyone who assists a voter with completing their ballot, the process for voting in person after receiving a mail ballot, and other topics. Finally, the bill would make conforming changes throughout the code.

This bill, as introduced on March 17, 2023, would create an "Election Crimes Unit" within the Elections Division of the Office of the Secretary of State. The Unit would create means of receiving complaints about "election irregularities" and either investigate complaints or refer them to the Attorney General. The Unit would also report on its activities to the Governor and Legislature. Finally, the Unit's powers would be in addition to existing investigative and enforcement mechanisms for election law violations, and its creation would not limit the authority of any other agency or political subdivision of the State authorized by law to investigate or prosecute violations of election law. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create an Election Crimes Unit composed of:
    • A Director appointed by the Secretary of State, and
    • Within the limits of legislative appropriations, a number of investigators and other staff that the Secretary of State determines are necessary to carry out the duties of the Unit.
  • Require the Unit to create ways to receive complaints about election irregularities. Specifically, the bill would require the Unit to:
    • Establish and administer a statewide complaint system to allow any person who believes that there has been an election irregularity to notify the Unit in writing using a Secretary of State-prescribed form.
    • Maintain a 24-hour, toll-free statewide hotline by which any person can report an alleged election irregularity.
    • Receive and review any complaints, notices, or reports concerning allegations of election irregularities submitted to the Secretary of State.
  • Define "election irregularity" as a violation of any provision of election law except those applicable to uniformed and overseas voters and campaigns.
  • Require the Unit to act on complaints it receives. Specifically, if, after reasonable inquiry, there is reasonable suspicion that an election irregularity has occurred, the Unit may:
    • Conduct an investigation concerning the alleged election irregularity, or
    • Refer the alleged election irregularity to the Attorney General.
  • Require the Unit to report on its activities or before January 15 of each odd-numbered year to the Governor and the Director of the Legislative Counsel Bureau for transmittal to the Legislature. Specifically, the report must include:
    • The number of complaints, notices, and reports received and reviewed by the Unit, the number of investigations initiated by the Unit, and the number of referrals made to the Attorney General.
    • For each alleged election irregularity identified by the Unit, the report must include the source of the alleged election irregularity, its nature, the county in which it allegedly occurred, and the current status of any investigation, referral, or prosecution concerning the alleged election irregularity.

  • Require county clerks to report certain incidents to the Secretary of State in addition to reporting to the relevant district attorney as current law requires. Specifically:

    • Any violations by field registrars, who conduct voter registration.
    • Any verified challenges to a person's right to vote, and any withdrawal of a challenge.
    • Any violation of the election code relating to tampering with mechanical voting devices and ballot-counting computer programs.

This bill, as introduced on March 22, 2023, would provide additional opportunities for voters to opt out of receiving a mail ballot for every election, and would revise the automatic voter registration process to allow a person to opt out of registering or updating their registration during their non-voting transaction with the agency. This bill, as enacted on June 15, 2023, requires the Secretary of State to create an elections procedures manual at least once every two years to ensure correctness, impartiality, uniformity, and efficiency in Nevada elections. The manual must be consistent with law and regulation, and the Secretary must submit it to the Legislative Commission for approval at least every four years. The Secretary may make changes to the manual without the Commission's approval only if the changes are not substantively related to administering an election. The Legislative Commission is an evenly bipartisan body of 12 legislators, six from each house. The Commission supervises the Legislative Counsel Bureau and takes action when the Legislature is not in session.

The Secretary must train each county clerk and city clerk on election procedures including the manual. Each clerk could require any of their deputies or employees to attend the training course as well. The Secretary must provide funding for clerks to attend, but not for clerks' deputies or employees. While clerks would be required to take the course in odd-numbered years if possible, if not, they would attend the class the next year.

A previous version of the bill required the Attorney General, not the Legislative Commission, to approve the manual.

This bill, as amended on April 24, 2023, would require each person who administers a county or city jail to establish a policy on or before January 1, 2024, that ensures that a prisoner who is a registered voter may vote in any primary, general, or special election for which they are eligible.

The bill would require the policy to ensure incarcerated registered voters can vote to:

  • Be developed in coordination with the county clerk and, if applicable, the city clerk
  • Be consistent with the provisions of this title relating to elections
  • Ensure the safety of any election board officer or other person who assists in the conduct of voting at the jail
  • Ensure the secrecy of the ballot, including, without limitation, the mail ballot of each prisoner.

The bill would also require each person who administers a county or city jail to submit a copy of their policy to the Secretary of State and to the Legislature by October 1 of each odd-numbered year. If a special election is held, each person who administers a county or city jail would also be required to submit a copy of the policy to the Secretary of State at least 30 days before the date of the special election. Finally, the bill would require the Secretary of State to adopt implementing regulations.

Several provisions were amended out of this version of the bill. Those provisions would have required jails to offer in-person voting and all related services including same-day registration on Election Day, and applied all the rules for polling places to jail voting except that no member of the general public would have been allowed to observe voting at a jail without the approval of the sheriff for a county jail or the administrator of the city jail, as applicable.

This bill, as enacted on June 9, 2023, creates new requirements related to in-person and electronic voting access for Indigenous Peoples. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires the Secretary of State to allow Indigenous voters living on Indigenous lands to use the system of approved electronic transmission established for uniformed and overseas voters to both register to vote and vote.
  • Requires county and city clerks to schedule meetings with Indigenous Peoples located in whole or in part within their jurisdictions to "discuss" plans for election administration, no later than August 1 of each odd-numbered year. The meeting may address, without limitation:
    • The establishment and operation of polling places, temporary branch polling places, or ballot drop boxes within Indigenous land and the size requirements for any such polling places and temporary branch polling places.
    • The dates and times of the upcoming elections for which polling places, temporary branch polling places, or ballot drop boxes may be established.
    • The deadlines in existing law for a Tribe to ask the county to establish polling places, temporary branch polling places, or ballot drop boxes on their land for the next election cycle.
    • Responsibilities for the recruitment of election board officers.
    • Any other information relating to the establishment of polling places, temporary branch polling places, and ballot drop boxes.
  • Requires election officials to hold additional meetings no later than September 1 of each odd-numbered year to confirm any details relating to the establishment of polling places, temporary branch polling places, and ballot drop boxes. This meeting may address, without limitation:
    • Whether the Tribe will request or has requested to establish any polling places, temporary branch polling places, or ballot drop boxes within their lands and the size requirements for any such polling places and temporary branch polling places.
    • The days and hours of any polling place or temporary branch polling place established within their lands.
    • Election board officers for any polling place or temporary branch polling place established within their lands.
    • The deadlines relating to the next regularly scheduled election cycle for The Tribe to submit a request for these voting services under state law.
    • On an ongoing basis during the year of an election, if a Tribe elects to establish any polling places or temporary branch polling places within their lands.
  • Provides that if a county or city clerk is unable to make contact with a Tribe to carry out the meeting requirements, the clerk may contact the Secretary of State to facilitate contact. Similarly, if a county or city clerk has not contacted a Tribe as required, a representative of the Tribe may contact the Secretary of State to facilitate contact. Finally, the tribal liaison designated by the Office of the Secretary Of State may assist the county clerk or a tribe to facilitate any contact required.

Previous versions of the bill contained provisions that were amended out prior to enactment. These provisions would have authorized Indigenous tribes to request that the Secretary of State approve use of tribal ID cards for access to the state's online voter registration and voter information portal.

This bill, as introduced on March 8, 2023, would create a strict photo ID requirement to vote in person, require the DMV to issue free ID to indigent voters, require voters to include an ID number or a new affidavit with their mail ballot, and repeal the cure process related to verifying mail ballots through signature matching. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require voters to show a photo ID document to receive a ballot in person unless the person is a resident of certain facilities like nursing homes. The bill would define acceptable ID as a document provided by the administrator of a licensed residential facility to a resident of that facility attesting to their identity and residency, or an identity card that:
    • Is issued by this State, the United States, or a federally recognized Indian tribe,
    • Shows the name, signature, and a recognizable photograph of the person to whom the document or identity card is issued, and
    • If the document or identity card is issued by Nevada, bears an expiration date that is not earlier than 4 years before the date of the election.
  • Require a person who does not show the required ID document when voting in person to cast a provisional ballot, and require that person to provide an acceptable by five p.m. on the Friday after Election Day to have the provisional ballot counted.
  • Require the DMV to issue a free ID to a person who is a registered voter, does not possess an acceptable voter ID, attests that they are experiencing financial hardship, and files an application that includes proof of their registered voter status. The bill prohibits DMV from requiring proof of financial hardship.
  • Require voters to either put an ID number on their mail ballot return envelope or include an affidavit signed under penalty of perjury attesting to their identity. Acceptable ID numbers would be the last four digits of the person's Social Security number or a driver's license or state ID number. Existing law requires neither step. Mail ballots are verified by matching a voter's signature to one in their registration record.
  • Change how mail ballots are verified to require the election official to verify the ID number or the affidavit, as applicable, instead of verifying the voter's signature on the ballot certificate. The bill does not specify how the affidavit is to be verified.

  • Repeal the cure process designed to address unsigned mail ballots or mail ballots with mismatched signatures. The bill does not create a cure process for a mismatched ID number, a missing number and/or affidavit, or a non-verified affidavit.

This bill, as introduced on March 8, 2023, would clarify that automatic voter registration is only available to U.S. citizens of appropriate age and require the DMV to add a legend to the driver's license or state ID of anyone whose documents did not affirmatively demonstrate U.S. citizenship. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Clarify that automatic voter registration at the DMV does not apply to the type of license that can be issued to undocumented immigrants. Existing law authorizes automatic voter registration only when the person provides sufficient information to verify eligibility, including citizenship.
  • Clarify that automatic voter registration at any agency does not apply to any person who includes any of a list of documents that demonstrate non-U.S. citizenship or age under 17 years. Existing law authorizes automatic voter registration only when the person provides sufficient information to verify eligibility, including citizenship and age. The list of disqualifying documents would be:
    • A Permanent Resident Card, Alien Registration Receipt Card, Form I-551, or any temporary version of such documents issued by the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services of the Department of Homeland Security,
    • An employment authorization document issued by the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services of the Department of Homeland Security using Form I-765 or I-766,
    • An arrival and departure record issued by the United States Customs and Border Protection of the Department of Homeland Security using Form I-94,
    • A nonimmigrant visa issued by the United States Department of State, or
    • Any birth certificate, driver's license, or identification card which indicates that the person is not 17 years of age or older as of the date of the application.

The DMV would also give such people a notice that only citizens of the United States are eligible to register to vote.

    • Maintain a 24-hour, toll-free statewide hotline by which any person can report an alleged election irregularity.

This bill, as enacted on June 14, 2023, fundamentally changes how counties offer voting access to Indigenous voters on Indigenous lands by requiring county and city clerks to establish an Election Day polling place, ballot drop box, and an early voting location on Indigenous land within their jurisdiction unless the relevant Tribe opts out by submitting written notice to the relevant clerk by certain dates. Under existing law, Tribes must request such voting access by certain deadlines, and such access is not guaranteed.

Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires county and city clerks to establish, at a location approved by an Indigenous Tribe, an Election Day polling place and ballot drop box on the Tribe's land unless the Tribe opts out by the deadline. The bill also allows Tribes to request additional locations by the same deadline. Any approved locations must satisfy standard polling place and ballot drop box siting criteria. To opt out, the Tribe would give notice to the county or city clerk by certain dates depending on the type of election involved. Previous law required Indigenous Tribes to request a polling place, ballot drop box, or both by the same dates the bill would set for opting out. Previous law also allowed the county or city clerk to refuse to open an Election Day polling place that was properly requested if the clerk offered early voting on the Tribe's land. The bill repeals that provision of existing law.
  • Sets the deadlines for a Tribe to opt out of the mandatory polling place and drop box or to request additional polling places or drop boxes as follows:
    • For a primary, January 15th of the year of the primary. Previous law required Tribes to request voting access by March 1 of the primary year.
    • For a presidential preference primary, September 15 of the year before the primary. Previous law set the deadline to request voting access as the first Friday in November of the year before the primary.
    • For a general election, June 15 of the year of the election. Previous law set the deadline to request voting access as August 1 of the year of the election.
  • Requires Indigenous Tribes who are not opting out to give the county or city clerk certain information by the opt-out deadline. If a Tribe does not submit the information by the deadline, that failure is deemed a decision to opt out of having a polling place or ballot drop box established on Tribal lands. Specifically, the Tribe must submit to the clerk and the Tribal liaison designated by the Secretary of State:
    • The location or locations for the polling place and ballot drop box.
    • Whether the Tribe will select registered voters to be appointed to act as election board officers to staff the polling place.
    • The proposed days and hours for the operation of the polling place.
  • Requires the county or city clerk to continue establishing one or more polling places and ballot drop boxes within the boundaries of the Indigenous lands unless and until the Tribe opts out. Under previous law, once the county or city clerk establishes one or more Election Day polling places or ballot drop boxes on Tribal lands, the clerk must continue to do so unless otherwise requested by the Tribe.
  • Requires county and city clerks to establish early voting and a ballot drop box at location(s) approved by an Indigenous Tribe on their lands unless the Tribe opts out, and allows more to be established if the Tribe timely requests them. The opt-out and additional early voting site request deadlines would be the same as for polling places. Any approved locations must satisfy standard early voting siting criteria. Previous law required Indigenous Tribes to request an early voting place by the same dates as set for polling place requests in existing law. Previous law also allowed the county or city clerk to refuse to open an early voting location that was properly requested if the clerk determines that establishing the site is not logistically feasible. The bill repeals that provision of previous law.
  • Requires Indigenous Tribes who are not opting out of an early voting site to give the county or city clerk certain information by the opt-out deadline. If a Tribe does not submit the information by the deadline, that failure would be deemed a decision to opt out of having an early voting site established on Tribal lands. Specifically, the Tribe must submit to the clerk and the Tribal liaison designated by the Secretary of State:
    • The location or locations for the early voting site.
    • Whether the Tribe will select registered voters to be appointed to act as election board officers to staff the early voting site.
    • The proposed days and hours for the operation of the early voting site.
  • Requires the county or city clerk to continue to establish one or more early voting sites within the boundaries of the Indigenous lands unless and until the Tribe opts out. Under previous law, once the county or city clerk establishes one or more early voting sites on Tribal lands, the clerk must continue to do so unless otherwise requested by the Tribe.

Governor Joe Lombardo vetoed this bill on June 1, 2023. As passed by the Legislature, this bill would have changed certain aspects of challenging in-person voters and allowed county clerks to start the early voting count earlier than allowed by existing law. Numerous provisions of the bill as introduced were amended out prior to final passage. As passed by the Legislature, the bill would have:

  • Required voters who are challenged as not residing at their registration address to provide "satisfactory identification" in addition to attesting to their residence. The bill would have defined satisfactory identification as including without limitation any of these documents that show the voter's current residential address:
    • A current and valid Nevada driver's license or identification card
    • A military identification card
    • A tribal identification card
    • A utility bill
    • A bank or credit union statement
    • A paycheck
    • An income tax return
    • A statement concerning the mortgage, rental, or lease of a residence
    • A motor vehicle registration
    • A property tax statement
    • Any other document issued by a governmental agency.
  • Prohibited people from using in-person voting challenges to challenge a person's right to vote by mail.
  • Allowed the county clerk to order the appropriate election board to begin counting early voting returns on or after the first day of early voting, and require the early voting count to begin not later than 8 a.m. on Election Day. Existing law requires such count to be publicly conducted after 8 a.m. on Election Day.

Provisions amended out of the bill on April 24, 2023, would have:

  • Given both the Governor and the Secretary of State special election-related powers during a declared state of emergency. The powers could be used for the whole state or a portion of the state, depending on the scope of the emergency. Specifically, if the Governor or Legislature declares a state of emergency or a disaster, and the emergency or disaster directly and substantially impacts an election, either the Governor or the Secretary could have:
    • Rescheduled a primary, special election, or presidential preference primary.
    • Extended the deadline to return mail ballots
    • Extended the deadline to cure signatures on mail ballots
    • Required additional polling places
    • Relocated polling places.
  • Given county and city clerks, with the approval of the Secretary of State, the authority to extend the hours for which polls are open for an extraordinary situation.
  • Created a new felony to try to protect election workers.
  • Changed other rules for challenging in-person voters. The bill would have:
    • Required challenges to be in writing.
    • Allowed voters who have been challenged as not residing at their registration address and who cannot provide satisfactory identification which contains proof of their residential address to complete a provisional ballot.
    • Allowed voters who have been challenged as not being the person they assert themselves to be and who do not respond by providing photo ID or a person who has an ID and can vouch for them to complete a provisional ballot.
  • Changed aspects of canvassing election results and certifying winners.

  • Added new requirements relating to risk-limiting audits, changed how recounts are triggered, and changed aspects of election contests, all of which are areas of election law Voting Rights Lab does not track.

Last Updated June 5, 2023

This bill, as introduced on March 27, 2023, would require in-person voters to show photo ID to receive a ballot, end Nevada's practice of mailing ballots to all active voters each election and instead require people to apply for mail ballots, require people voting by mail to include an ID number on their ballot return envelope and use that number to verify the ballot instead of signature matching, shorten the mail ballot return deadline, restrict ballot return assistance, and make other changes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require in-person voters to show a photo ID issued by a state, the U.S., or a federally recognized Tribe that includes the voter's name and signature to receive a ballot, unless the voter lives in a licensed residential facility "for the dependent", in which case a document provided by the administrator of the facility is sufficient. If the ID document used is a Nevada driver's license or state ID, it must not have expired. Under existing law, in-person voters can verify their identity without providing documentation by providing personal information orally or in writing that the election worker can verify with the registration record. To facilitate voters meeting the new ID documentation requirement, the bill would:
    • Require the DMV to issue a free voter identification card to a person who documents that they are a registered voter, does not have an ID document that meets the requirements, and attests they have a financial hardship. The bill would prohibit the DMV from requiring the person to document their hardship. The free ID would show the person's name, address, date of birth, sex, height, weight, eye color, photograph, and signature. The ID would remain valid as long as the person is registered to vote and lives at the address on the card. The Secretary of State would be required to consult with the DMV and issue implementing regulations.
  • Require people who appear to vote in person but do not present the required ID document to vote a provisional ballot. For the provisional ballot to count, the voter must provide the required ID to the county or city clerk by 5 p.m. on the Friday after Election Day.
  • End Nevada's practice of mailing all active voters a ballot for all elections unless they opt out of receiving one. Instead, the bill would require people to apply for a mail ballot.
  • Create rules for applying for a mail ballot. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Set a deadline to apply for a mail ballot of 5 p.m. on the 14th calendar day before Election Day.
    • Authorize voters with disabilities to apply using the approved electronic transmission system the Secretary offers uniformed and overseas voters.
    • Create a felony to prohibit fraudulently requesting a mail ballot in the name of another person or inducing or coercing another person to do so.
    • Require ballots to be mailed to voters who requested them as soon as ballots for their precincts are available.
    • Prohibit mailing a requested ballot if the voter's registration became inactive or was canceled after the request. Under existing law, ballots are not automatically mailed to inactive voters or unregistered voters.
  • Shorten the deadline to return a completed mail ballot to the close of polls on Election Day. Existing law requires completed mail ballots returned by hand to be delivered by the close of polls, but provides ballots returned by mail must be postmarked on or before Election Day and received not later than 5 p.m. on the fourth day after Election Day, or if not postmarked, by 5 p.m. on the third day after Election Day.
  • Require mail voters to add an ID number to their mail ballot return envelope. Specifically, voters would need to write in the last four digits of their Social Security number or their driver's license number or state ID number. Mail ballot return envelopes would be revised to include space for the information and a flap to conceal it.
  • Require election officials to verify the ID number on returned ballots against the numbers in a voter's registration record. If the voter did not provide a number or did not do so in the manner required by law, the clerk must contact the voter and advise them how to provide the ID number by 5 p.m. on the 6th day after Election Day. If a voter does not cure the missing or improperly applied number on time, their ballot would be rejected. The bill does not indicate if voters who transpose a number or otherwise make a mistake with their ID number have the ability to cure that error. Existing law requires election officials to verify ballots using signature matching, and provides a cure process for missing and mismatched signatures.
  • Restrict ballot return assistance and enforce the restrictions with a felony. Although a voter could authorize anyone they wished to return their ballot for them, the authorized person would face new rules and restrictions. The Secretary of State would be required to issue implementing rules. Under the bill, an authorized person would be:
    • Required to attest under penalty of perjury on a form created by the county clerk that the voter authorized them to return the ballot, and the date on which the voter authorized them. Existing law does not have this requirement.
    • Limited to returning 30 ballots for any election. Existing law does not have this requirement.
    • Required, if returning the ballot by mail, to mail it by the next to last day of early voting, or if the authorized person received the ballot three or fewer days before the end of early voting, before the deadline established by the U.S.P.S. to ensure delivery by the close of polls.
    • Required, if returning the ballot by personal delivery, by the day before Election Day, or if the authorized person received the ballot three or fewer days before Election Day, by the close of polls. Existing law requires an authorized person to return a ballot by hand delivery on this timeline, and requires a person returning a voter's ballot by mail to ensure it is postmarked on or before Election Day.
    • Required, after the election, to submit a report to the Secretary of State that identifies each voter for whom the person returned a ballot. Existing law does not have a similar requirement.
  • Require the Secretary of State to create a form affirmation for voters who request a mail ballot and then appear to vote in person but do not surrender the mail ballot. Otherwise, the list of documents addressed in the bill is the same as that allowed under existing law. Specifically, a voter who proved identity with a Nevada DMV-issued photo ID that showed a previous address could have proved residency and completed the same-day registration process using any of these that show the voter's current address:

This bill, as amended on January 11, 2024, would fundamentally restructure how elections are administered in New York City. The bill would remake the New York City Board of Elections (NYC BOE) into a two-person bipartisan body and reallocate its powers between the Board and a reconceived Executive Director appointed by the Mayor of NYC, the Speaker of the NYC Council, and the NYC Public Advocate. Under existing law, the NYC BOE is a 10-member, evenly bipartisan body that chooses its own executive director and a deputy executive director whose duties are to "supervise the operations of the board elections under the supervision of such board." Instead of that apparent total overlap, the bill would explicitly limit the role of the NYC BOE and empower the executive director. The bill would also make smaller changes that impact boards of elections throughout the state. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Immediately end the terms of the ten current commissioners, shrink the board to two commissioners, and require the county committees of the two major parties within New York City to nominate replacements within 60 days. The New York City council would hold a public hearing on the nominees and confirm two of them. The two commissioners chosen would be required to come from different major parties and be from different counties. Under existing law, the ten-member board is evenly bipartisan with two members from each New York City county nominated by the county committees of the two major parties and approved by the city council without a public hearing.
  • Provide that the New York City Board of Elections will have an executive director selected following a nationwide search for qualified and experienced candidates who will serve a four-year term. Nonetheless, the bill also provides that the two commissioners of the NYC BOE may make at least three party recommendations of executive director candidates, and if they make less than three, then members of the New York City Council affiliated with the party that recommended less than three may make nominations by a majority vote of their caucus. Candidates would need to meet local officer qualifications plus merit qualifications specified by the State Board of Elections. The final decision would be by a majority vote of the Mayor, Speaker, and Public Advocate provided that if the decision is not unanimous the Mayor must be in the majority. The three appointing authorities could remove an executive director for cause, and, if acting jointly with the NYC BOE commissioners, without cause.
  • Define the powers of the NYC BOE. The NYC BOE would:
    • Advise the executive director on matters of policy, but in general exercise no executive power and perform no executive or administrative functions, nor make individualized employment decisions, nor make decisions about the registration, pre-registration, enrollment, or qualifications of any specific voter or applicant, nor exercise day-to-day supervision of the executive director. Notwithstanding those general rules, the bill allocates the board certain specific powers and allows the board to delegate more to the executive director.
    • Have the specific power and duty to make determinations regarding: (1) the nomination and designation of candidates for public office and party positions, (2) the form and content of ballots including the determination of candidates and questions to appear on it, (3) concerning challenges to voter registration and applications of voters unlawfully denied the right to register, and (4) concerning the adoption and use of voting machines or systems, in each case as specified in cited sections of the elections code
    • Have the specific power and duty to: adopt resolutions eliminating meetings for local registration, canvass and certify election results and perform all functions of the board of canvassers in the city of New York, issue subpoenas and administer oaths, and approve certain specified contracts.
  • Define the powers of the executive director. The executive director would be the chief executive officer and would have the powers and duty to:
    • appoint, and at their pleasure remove, a deputy director, clerks, voting machine technicians, custodians, and other employees, fixing their number, prescribing their duties, fixing their titles and rank, and establishing their salaries within the amounts appropriated therefor in the expense budget of the city of New York.
    • create written policies and procedures for employees in consultation with the NYC Department of Citywide Administrative Services that specify job duties and qualifications, protect whistleblowers from retaliation, provide training, open hiring, performance evaluations,
    • exercise all the powers and duties delegated to boards of elections and the NYC BOE, except those powers reserved to it, expressly including all matters relating to the qualifications of voters, voter registration and enrollment, registration cancellation, change of voter status, creating and altering election districts, places of registration, and polling places, and in all other matters.
  • Require the executive director to make regular reports to the NYC BOE at their public meetings, allowing for public comment, and to issue an annual report on the performance of the NYC BOE as an agency in the preceding year. The executive director and the two election commissioners would report to the New York City Council in a public hearing.
  • Require the board to track and report key voting and election administration data, including:
    • turnout by election district,
    • average wait times by poll site and district,
    • call volume by poll site and types of complaints received,
    • the frequency and use of different voting methods,
    • the rates of and reasons for ballot rejections, and
    • language interpreter staffing by language and poll site.

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2023, would revise certain voter registration deadlines to give voters more time to register. In 2022, New York changed the in-person voter registration deadline from 25 days before Election Day to 10 days before, and mail registrations to postmarked by the 15th day before Election Day and received by the 10th day before but did not make conforming changes throughout the code. This bill would finish updating registration deadlines to reflect the 2022 law and make additional process improvements. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Provide that a person can register to vote at the DMV or any other voter registration agency (VRA) through the 12th day before an election, provided that the agency delivers the registration application to the board of elections by the 10th day before. Existing law ends registration through a VRA on the 25th day before an election. Relatedly, the bill would require the state's VRAs to deliver voter registration forms received after the 20th day before an election and by the 12th day before to deliver them to the appropriate board of elections as soon as practicable and not later than the 10th day before the election. Under existing law, the window for accelerated delivery is 30-25 days before the election, and the deadline for VRAs to turn in the forms is 20 days before an election.
  • Revise the voter registration form so that its instructions accurately inform voters to return the form to a board of elections at least 10 days before the election, and if mailing the form, that it must be postmarked at least 15 days before the election.
  • Require boards of election to process voter registration forms more quickly. The bill would require a local board of elections to verify an applicant's identity as soon as practicable and not later than seven days after receiving the application. Under existing law, the board of elections must verify the applicant's identity "promptly" and not later than 21 days after receiving the application.
  • Provide that a local board of elections that receives a registration application from a voter residing outside the board's jurisdiction must electronically forward that registration form to the correct board of elections on the same day that it is received. Existing law requires such a board to forward the form "forthwith" without a specific deadline or transmission format.
  • Require address updates received 15 days before an election to be completed before the election. Existing law provided such updates must be completed if received 20 days before an election.
  • Require boards of elections to reactivate voter registrations by Election Day if a voter takes an action that should reactivate their registration by the 10th day before Election Day. Existing law requires reactivation if the voter takes action by the 20th day before.
  • Require boards of election to notify people whose voter registration applications the board is rejecting not later than seven days before an election happening at least 10 days after the application was filed. Under existing law boards were required to notify voters of the rejection at least 10 days before an election happening at least 25 days after the application was filed.
  • Make conforming changes for UOCAVA voters so their registration deadline and the deadline to affiliate with a party are 10 days before the election, not 25 days before.

  • Allow an unaffiliated voter who was registered by automatic voter registration at least 10 days before the election to affiliate a voting location and participate in the primary. Existing law requires the automatic registration to have occurred at least 25 days before the election. Relatedly, a voter would be allowed to correct their affiliation through the 10th day before a primary instead of 25 days before. Note, this deadline is for correcting an erroneous record only. Changing affiliation has a much earlier deadline. Finally, the bill would revise the deadline for distributing a supplemental list of voters affiliated with political parties to the 10th day before a primary, instead of existing law's 15-days-before deadline.

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2023, purports to create a mail ballot tracking system. However, in 2022 New York enacted a similar bill, which this bill does not address. The details of the system proposed by the bill are similar but not identical to the new law. The most notable differences are that the bill's system would provide greater information relating to curing a ballot, existing law provides notice that the voter's ballot was returned to the board of elections as undeliverable, and existing law requires local boards of election to create their own systems integrated with the state system and accessible on the local boards' websites, whereas the bill simply authorizes local tracking systems in addition to the state system.

Specifically, the bill would require the State Board of Elections to create a mail ballot tracking system to enable a voter to determine whether their local board of elections has:

  • Received the voter's request for a mail ballot (called "absentee ballot" in New York). Existing law requires the tracking system to provide this information.
  • Approved or rejected the request, and if rejected, why. Existing law requires the tracking system to provide this information.
  • Mailed or delivered an absentee ballot to the voter. Existing law requires the tracking system to also include the date of the mailing or delivery, and the expected date of delivery.
  • Received the voter's completed mail ballot. Existing law requires the tracking system to provide this information, and also notify the voter if the ballot was returned to the board of elections as "undeliverable".
  • Counted or rejected the voter's completed ballot, and if rejected, why. Existing law requires the tracking system to provide this information.

  • Determined that the ballot envelope is subject to a cure, the deadline to submit the cure, and how to obtain information about the cure from the applicable board of elections, if applicable. Existing law requires the tracking system to enable the voter to learn that their board of elections determined their ballot envelope was subject to a cure.

    This bill would also authorize county boards of election or the New York City Board of Elections to offer their own tracking systems, for their own voters only, in addition to the State Board of Elections system the bill would create. Existing law requires such local systems, and for those systems to be integrated with the state system.

This bill, as enacted on March 24, 2023, revises certain voter registration deadlines to give voters more time to register. In 2022, New York changed the in-person voter registration deadline from 25 days before Election Day to 10 days before, and mail registrations to postmarked by the 15th day before Election Day and received by the 10th day before but did not make conforming changes throughout the code. This bill completes the implementation of new registration deadlines with changes to reflect the 2022 law and makes additional process improvements. Specifically, the bill:

  • Permits voter registration at the DMV or any other voter registration agency (VRA) through the 12th day before an election, provided that the agency delivers the registration application to the board of elections by the 10th day before. Previous law ended registration through a VRA on the 25th day before an election. Relatedly, the bill requires the state's VRAs to deliver voter registration forms received after the 20th day before an election and by the 12th day before to deliver them to the appropriate board of elections as soon as practicable and not later than the 10th day before the election. Under previous law, the window for accelerated delivery was 30-25 days before the election, and the deadline for VRAs to turn in the forms was 20 days before an election.
  • Revises the voter registration form so that its instructions accurately inform voters to return the form to a board of elections at least 10 days before the election, and if mailing the form, that it must be postmarked at least 15 days before the election.
  • Requires boards of election to process voter registration forms more quickly. The bill requires a local board of elections to verify an applicant's identity as soon as practicable and not later than seven days after receiving the application. Under previous law, the board of elections was required to verify the applicant's identity "promptly" and not later than 21 days after receiving the application.
  • Provides that a local board of elections that receives a registration application from a voter residing outside the board's jurisdiction must electronically forward that registration form to the correct board of elections on the same day that it is received. Previous law requires such a board to forward the form "forthwith" without a specific deadline or transmission format.
  • Requires address updates received 15 days before an election to be completed before the election. Previous law provided that such updates must be completed if received 20 days before an election.
  • Requires boards of elections to reactivate voter registrations by Election Day if a voter takes an action that should reactivate their registration by the 10th day before Election Day. Previous law required reactivation if the voter took action by the 20th day before.
  • Requires boards of election to notify people whose voter registration applications the board is rejecting not later than seven days before an election happening at least 10 days after the application was filed. Under previous law, boards were required to notify voters of the rejection at least 10 days before an election happening at least 25 days after the application was filed.
  • Makes conforming changes for uniformed and overseas voters so their registration deadline and the deadline to affiliate with a party are 10 days before the election, not 25 days before.
  • Allows an unaffiliated voter who was registered by automatic voter registration at least 10 days before the election to affiliate a voting location and participate in the primary. Previous law requires automatic registration to have occurred at least 25 days before the election.
  • Allows a voter to correct their affiliation through the 10th day before a primary instead of 25 days before. Note, this deadline is for correcting an erroneous record only. Changing affiliation has a much earlier deadline.

  • Revises the deadline for distributing a supplemental list of voters affiliated with political parties to the 10th day before a primary, instead of the previous law's 15-days-before deadline.

  • Authorizing aggrieved individuals to enforce their rights in court.
  • Creating a presumption that if any superintendent, employee, or agent of a correctional facility by commission or omission intentionally frustrates the ability of eligible incarcerated people to register and vote, an election law violation has occurred that may be enforced in court by any aggrieved persons, an organization whose membership includes aggrieved persons or members of a protected class, an organization whose mission, in whole or in part, is to ensure voting access, or the attorney general. That section of code allows multiple remedies including nominal, compensatory, or punitive damages.

The bill would facilitate registration and voting by incarcerated eligible people through three different measures. One involves expanding an existing program in which election workers bring mail ballots to residential facilities, distribute them, collect them, and return them to the board of elections, as well as provide any needed assistance to the people voting them.     • Expand the window of time in which boards of elections may bring mail ballots to residential facilities to start 21 days before Election Day and expand the possible hours to between 7 a.m. and 8 p.m. Existing law allows the process to occur beginning thirteen days before Election Day and sets the possible hours as between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m.

In addition, the election workers would be required to bring assistive devices and any reasonable accommodations for disabled voters, as well as interpretive resources and personnel for those in need of language assistance. Completed mail ballot applications would be treated as an application to receive a ballot in person, rather than to have a ballot mailed to the applicant.
    • Require boards of elections, when serving a correctional facility in this program, to provide voter registration forms and mail ballots for voters not eligible to vote in the jurisdiction covered by the local board, in accordance with a written procedure the board would be required to adopt. The correctional facility's superintendent, administrator or director, or their designated democracy officer or agent would be required to countersign the procedures, and the local board of elections would be required to submit them to the State Board of Elections at least 90 days before the election. This bill, as enacted on August 4, 2023:

  • Allows voters who will be away from their district during the period when mail ballots are universally sent to receive an early "absentee" ballot. Under the bill, these voters may obtain their ballot in person or by mail starting on the 43rd day before an election. Previous law permitted voters to request an absentee ballot, but did not provide for delivery earlier than the regular ballot delivery period of the 20th-14th day before Election Day.
  • Removes the ability of a county clerk to cancel a voter's registration upon receiving written evidence that the voter has registered to vote in another county in Oregon. The bill leaves in place other existing grounds for registration cancellation, including written notice that a voter has registered in another state. Existing law provides elsewhere that registering to vote in a new county within the state constitutes an update of the voter's existing registration.
  • Expressly guarantees each voter the right to vote and the right to a secret ballot, and expressly prohibits election officials from disclosing information that would reveal how an individual voted in an election.
  • Changes the timing of notifications provided to a voter who makes a written complaint to the Secretary of State or Attorney General alleging a violation of election law. Under previous law, the Secretary or Attorney General were required to notify the person who is the subject of the complaint within three days of receiving the complaint, or ten days if there are more than 10 subjects. Under the bill, notification is only required if the official determines that an investigation is necessary, and the notification periods begin with such a determination.
  • Requires the annual security plan submitted by each county clerk to the Secretary of State to include, in addition to existing requirements, security procedures for ensuring the integrity of printed ballots, cybersecurity procedures for the process of casting and tallying ballots, and anything else required by Secretary of State rule.
  • Permits a voter to include a family member residing with them in a request for non-disclosure of their address information by a clerk.
  • Requires voter signatures to be available as public records, for inspection in the office of the chief elections officer.

The bill also contains provisions relating to areas of law not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, including rules concerning campaign contributions.

A previous version of this bill contained additional provisions that were amended out prior to enactment. Those provisions would have created new felony offenses for harassment and aggravated harassment of an election worker. These provisions were amended out of the bill on May 30, 2023.

    • Alteration of information on a petition signature sheet
    • Payment based on signatures obtained on nominating petition or voter registration card

    • Prohibited distribution of ballots

  • Expressly include among the violations subject to a $10,000 penalty, an election official's knowing failure to comply with a rule, instruction, or interpretation of law made by the Secretary of State.

  • Increase the civil penalties associated with the following election offenses for a second or subsequent violation:

    • Payment based on signatures obtained on nominating petition or voter registration card
    • Prohibitions relating to circulation, filing or certification of initiative, referendum or recall petition
    • Payment for signing or not signing initiative, referendum or recall petition, sale or purchase of signature sheets
    • Alteration of information on petition signature sheet
    • Use of threats and intimidation for the purpose of extorting money

    • An individual voting or offering to vote in any election knowing they are not entitled to vote

    • Supplying false information when applying for a federal-only ballot
    • Illegal alteration of an absent elector application
    • Illegal acts relating to voting machines or vote tally systems
    • Under some circumstances, undue influence to affect registration, voting, candidacy, signing petitions or solicitation of money or other benefits
    • Prohibited distribution of ballots
    • Premature release of vote tally
    • False statement, oath or affidavit
    • Requesting a ballot in a name other than the person's own name
    • Voting or attempting to vote more than once at any election held on the same date
    • Voting or attempting to vote both in an election held in this state and in another state on the same date
    • Wilfully altering or destroying a ballot cast at an election or the returns of an election
    • Willfully placing a fraudulent ballot among the genuine ballots

This bill, as introduced on March 10, 2023, would create "Election-Day style" early voting during the 15 days before Election Day. Under existing law, people may vote early in person by applying for and casting a no-excuse mail ballot at the office of the county board of elections. The current form of early in-person voting begins as soon as ballots become available, no later than the second Tuesday before Election Day, and ends the Tuesday before Election Day. Instead of that process, the bill would:

  • Require county boards of elections to offer Election-Day style early voting during the 15 days before Election Day at uniform days and hours countywide.
  • Require such early voting to be offered at the main office of the county board and elsewhere, but would not require a specific number of sites. The county board would have the discretion to decide how many locations to open.
  • Require eight hours of early voting on each weekday the county board offers early voting, such hours to begin no earlier than 7 a.m. and end no earlier than 7 p.m.
  • Require a minimum of eight aggregate hours on each of the two weekends in the early voting period. County boards could choose to offer those hours all on a Saturday, Sunday, or both.
  • Prohibit county boards from tabulating results before the close of polls on Election Day, but require them to keep track of voting by precinct in a way that prevents people from voting twice during early voting or once during early voting and again on Election Day.
