This bill, as introduced on March 10, 2023, would eliminate grounds for rejecting timely mail ballots cast by eligible voters, authorize and regulate ballot drop boxes, change the deadline to apply to receive a ballot in the mail, and rename the list voters may join to receive a ballot application each year without otherwise changing the rules relating to the list. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Eliminate grounds for rejecting mail ballots. Specifically, so long as the ballot certificate is otherwise properly executed, the bill would require election officials to count:
    • Ballots with unsigned ballot certificates. Currently, some counties attempt to contact voters and allow them to address this issue by the close of polls.
    • Ballots returned without a secrecy envelope (colloquially known as "naked ballots"). Currently, some counties attempt to contact voters and allow them to address this issue by the close of polls.
    • Ballots with undated or misdated signatures on ballot certificates. Currently, some counties attempt to contact voters and allow them to address this issue by the close of polls.
  • Authorize and regulate ballot drop boxes, but would not require their use. Existing statutes do not address drop boxes, however, the Secretary of the Commonwealth issued guidance relating to them in 2020 and they have been used in some counties. If a county board of elections decides to offer ballot drop boxes, the bill would:
    • Require notice to voters at least 30 days before Election Day with signage at the county board's office and other locations, on the board's website, and in the materials mailed to voters with their ballots. These notices would include information about each location, its hours of operation, accessibility, and other topics.
    • Require each drop box to be fully ADA-compliant and in a well-lit, fixed location. Boxes would also need to be tamper-resistant, locked, and secured.
    • Require county boards of election to monitor the boxes when they are open either in person or by video and require video recordings to be retained for a year.
    • Allow county boards of elections to decide when their drop boxes would be open, subject to certain minimum parameters. Specifically, boxes would need to open no later than 30 days before Election Day and be open on Election Day, and in the five days before Election Day must be open at least one weeknight and at least one weekend time period.
    • Require ballots to be collected from the boxes by two county employees, at least one of whom is assigned to the board of elections. The other may be a member of law enforcement. A chain of custody log would be required.
  • Shorten the time to apply to receive a ballot by mail by requiring such applications to be received by the board of elections by the 12th day before Election Day. Existing law allows voters to apply for mail ballots through 5 p.m. on the Tuesday before Election Day. The bill would keep that deadline for in-person applications for mail ballots.

  • Rename the permanent absentee voter list and the permanent mail-in voter list the "annual absentee voter list" and "annual mail-in ballot list".

This bill, as introduced on March 14, 2023, would create the "Future Voter Program" to facilitate the registration and pre-registration of 16 and 17-year-old students.     • Provide all students who will be 18 by the next general election an opportunity to register to vote online in the classroom.
    • Make voter registration applications available in the classroom.
  • Require the Secretary of the Commonwealth, in consultation with county commissions, to:
    • Enable students who are 16 years old to pre-register to vote electronically through the Department of State's website. Such students would be required to use their driver's license or state ID number if they have one, and the last four digits of their Social Security number if they do not. The Secretary would be required to use that information to get an electronic copy of the students' signatures from the DMV.
    • Keep pre-registrations in pending status and securely stored separately from the statewide voter registration list until students turn 18 and are added to the registration list. Pre-registrations would not be publicly disclosable the way voter registrations are.
    • Allow county commissions access to the pre-registration data so they may send the future voters notices about their registration status or other voter registration information.

  • Require county commissions to notify students whose registration or pre-registration applications are incomplete and require them to submit the missing information.

This bill, as introduced on March 27, 2023, would create Election-Day style early voting without changing the availability of in-person mail voting, which is how Pennsylvania currently offers in-person early voting.   • Create a 30-day Election-Day style early voting period. Under existing law, voters may complete a mail ballot in person at county board of elections' offices beginning when ballots are available. Even if litigation is ongoing, in-person mail voting must begin no later than two weeks before Election Day. During the 30-day Election-Day-style early voting period the bill would create, early voting locations would be open for the days and times a county board of elections chooses within these parameters:
    • All early voting sites in a county must be open for the same days and hours.

    • 500,000 or more residents, the county board would be required to open at least four early voting locations
    • 250,000-499,999 residents, the county board would be required to open at least three early voting locations
    • 100,000-249,999 residents, the county board would be required to open at least two early voting locations

This bill, as introduced on June 14, 2023, would make major changes throughout the election code, including provisions to:

  • Change mail voting rules to increase ID requirements, shorten deadlines, regulate drop boxes, create a cure process, and make other changes. Because of the changes, the bill would eliminate same-day registration during early voting.
  • Change timelines and processes for counting mail ballots and certifying election results.
  • Repeal and recodify voter registration requirements, making some changes to deadlines and other rules and explicitly authorizing the online voter registration system the Department of State created administratively.
  • Revise voter ID documentation rules and require the state to issue certain free IDs.
  • Create law enforcement roles, create new election crimes including one intended to protect election officials, and generally double the penalties for election crimes.
  • Create Election Day-style early voting and repeal the existing in-person mail ballot early voting process.
  • Re-allocate election authority and duties among the Legislature, the Department of State, county boards of elections, and the Pennsylvania Election Law Advisory Board.
  • Create an election results and election processes auditing regime housed in the office of the Auditor General.
  • Make myriad other revisions to the election code (including some provisions that are not tracked by Voting Rights Lab).

Concerning mail voting, the bill would:

  • Require more information to apply for a mail ballot (both excuse-based "absentee ballots" and no-excuse "mail-in ballots"). The bill would require an applicant to include at least two of the following numbers on their application: the last four digits of the applicant's Social Security number (SSN4), their Pennsylvania driver's license number, and the voter's voter registration number. Under existing law, an applicant must include either their SSN4 or their driver's license/state ID number, or if they have neither, enclose a copy of an unexpired photo ID. If they do not, they will be issued a ballot but the ballot will not be counted unless the voter provides the required ID in time.
  • Change the deadline to apply for a mail ballot to fifteen days before Election Day instead of the Tuesday before. Relatedly, the bill would change the window for emergency applications to cover situations arising after the 15th day before Election Day rather than ones arising after the Tuesday before.
  • Change the timeline for election officials to distribute mail ballots to people who properly applied for them. The bill would require distribution to begin the day after voter registration ends. Under existing law, ballots are distributed as soon as ballots are certified and available. The change proposed by the bill would eliminate same-day registration during the early voting period, as early voting is conducted by in-person application for, and completion of, a mail ballot. Also relating to ballot distribution, the bill would require county boards of elections to investigate the circumstances of any mail ballot returned to the board as undeliverable, and to send a notice to a voter's registration address if the voter applies for a mail ballot to be sent anywhere other than their registration address.
  • Authorize and regulate "ballot return locations." Existing law does not address drop boxes or other variations of ballot return locations. The Secretary of State issued guidance relating to drop boxes, and many jurisdictions used them in 2020. The bill would:
    • Require each county to maintain at least one, which could be the county board of elections' office, and authorize counties to open one more per each 100,000 residents.
    • Limit the days and hours of ballot return locations to 7 a.m. through 8 p.m. on the seven days prior to an election.
    • Require ballot return locations to be monitored by two poll workers, one from each major party, and by video recording. If a poll worker is not available, the location would be prohibited from opening. The recording would be maintained for two years and available to the public.
    • Require the poll workers to review "the identification of each individual returning a ballot consistent with the provisions of this act". Pennsylvania law contains voter ID provisions that have been enjoined and are not enforced. The poll workers would also be required to review the ballot envelope certificate to ensure that it is complete, signed, and dated.
    • Expressly allow household members, as reflected by their having the same registration address, to return each others' ballot. The poll workers would be required to review ballot addresses every time someone returns more than one ballot to ensure compliance with the household requirement. Existing law does not allow household members to return ballots for each other.
    • Require the poll workers to set aside any ballot and document they believe was completed or returned in violation of the act. Only if the county board is satisfied that such ballots do not violate the could the ballots be counted.
    • Require the locations to be equitably distributed, designated at least 30 days in advance, be fixed for the entire seven-day period, and meet the requirements of polling places. Once in-person early voting as created by the bill began, the bill would require ballot return locations to be set up only at early voting locations.
    • Prohibit the state from reimbursing counties for opening ballot return locations.
  • Create a requirement that the voter's signature on their mail ballot certificate match the voter's signature on file and authorize the use of software to do signature verification. If the voter's signature is missing, does not match, or the ballot certificate is otherwise incomplete, the ballot will be rejected unless the voter cures the issue using a process created by the bill.
  • Create a cure process for mail ballots. The bill would require election officials to give voters notice of the issue that will prevent their ballot from counting and allow voters to address the issue through the close of polls on Election Day. Issues that could be addressed would be a missing signature, a mismatched signature, an undated signature, failure to provide the required ID, or an otherwise incomplete ballot certificate. To cure, the voter would need to go to the board of elections in person to complete the missing information or provide the board with an electronic, paper, or fax copy of identification and a specified affirmation, or a different affirmation that includes an attestation of indigence and a lack of ID. If a voter returns a ballot with an incurable defect, such as a missing privacy sleeve or a privacy sleeve marked with identifying information, election officials would direct them to vote a provisional ballot in person or apply for an emergency mail ballot. Under heavily litigated existing law, counties may choose to offer a cure process, and some do.
    • Require the Secretary of the Commonwealth to create and maintain a mail ballot tracking system that includes the status of an application for a mail ballot and the dates on which the applied-for ballot is prepared, mailed, received back, pre-canvassed, and canvassed. The Pennsylvania Department of State currently offers a ballot tracking system but existing law does not address it.
  • Repeal the ability of a voter to join a permanent mail voting list and expressly forbid the state or a county from maintaining such a list. Relatedly, the bill would repeal the ability of a voter to use a single application to request a ballot for each election in a single year. The bill would require voters to apply for a mail ballot for each election in which they wish to vote by mail.
  • Require third parties who distribute excused-based mail ballot applications to indicate on the form that it was not distributed by a county or the Department of State and require forms to be blank when distributed.
  • Prohibit mailing a ballot to a voter who did not request one, or registering a person to vote who did not submit a valid application. Existing law requires an application to receive a mail ballot and to register to vote.

Concerning timelines and processes related to counting ballots and certifying election results, the bill would:

  • Begin processing completed mail ballots sooner by requiring at least two pre-canvassing meetings prior to Election Day to pre-canvass all mail ballots received by the time of the meeting. Pre-canvassing meetings would be limited to being between 7 a.m. and 11 p.m. on the five days prior to Election Day and on Election Day while polls are open. Existing law prohibits pre-canvassing before 7 a.m. on Election Day.
  • Require mail ballots to be canvassed sooner by requiring the canvass to begin upon the close of polls. Existing law provides that canvassing may happen no sooner than the close of polls, but need not begin until the third day after the election.
  • Require county boards of elections to canvass or pre-canvass all mail ballots received prior to Election Day by no later than 9 p.m. on Election Day, and all those received on Election Day prior to the close of polls by 2 a.m. on the day after Election Day. In addition, precinct returns excluding provisional ballots, UOCAVA ballots, and mail ballots set aside for further review would be due by 6 a.m. on the day after the election. A county's reimbursement for election costs would be conditioned on meeting these deadlines. Existing law authorizes much later counting and reporting, but conditions a specific grant program on beginning pre-canvassing of mail ballots as early as allowed by state law.
  • Change the rules for appointing observers of mail ballot pre-canvassing and canvassing and specify the access observers must be granted. The bill would:
    • Allow a political party county chairperson to appoint an observer. Existing law allows candidates and political parties to appoint one representative each.
    • Require election officials to give observers "meaningful access to view and observe the entire process", including enabling observers to "easily read the text on any ballot or envelope at any point in the process." Election officials would have to designate an official to respond to issues reported by observers.
    • Require pre-canvassing and canvassing meetings to be recorded but make the recording available to the public only after the close of polls on Election Day.
  • Change the timeline for county boards of elections to submit unofficial results to the Secretary of the Commonwealth. The bill would require the unofficial results to be submitted incrementally and as often as practicable until complete. Existing law requires unofficial returns to be submitted by 5 p.m. on the Tuesday following the election. The bill would also require the public internet posting of various unofficial results and election statistics.
  • Create a new step in the results certification process. The bill would require election officials to determine if the number of ballots cast in any district exceeds the number of voters recorded as participating in the election in that district. If that kind of discrepancy exists, an investigation would be triggered and no votes from that district could be counted until the discrepancy is resolved. If the discrepancy is not resolved in specific ways, election officials would be empowered to exclude the district's votes, either as to all offices, candidates, questions, and parties or as to the particular race impacted by the excess.
  • Extend the county boards of elections' deadline for certifying the results of an election to the fourth Friday after an election, instead of the third Monday as set by existing law. The bill would also require that certification to include a complete record of each registered voter in the county on the date of the election that includes whether each one voted and if so, by which method they voted.
  • Require the Secretary of the Commonwealth to proclaim the results of the election within three days after receiving all the returns from all the counties. Existing law requires the Secretary to proclaim the results but does not set a deadline.

Concerning voter registration, the bill would recodify voter registration law in a new code location, and make various substantive changes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require voter registration applicants to include the last four digits of their Social Security number on the form, and if an applicant doesn't, the bill would deem the application incomplete. If an applicant does not have a Social Security number, they could confirm their identity with an alternate record. The bill would require space on the voter registration form for the four digits and for a driver's license or state ID number but provides that a missing state ID number would not render the application incomplete. Existing statutes do not require space for these ID numbers although the current form provides space for them. Relatedly, the bill would explicitly require election officials to verify the applicant's ID number as part of approving their registration. The bill would also require counties that are connected to the statewide voter registration database to search that database for duplicate/former registrations of new applicants.
  • Change voter registration deadlines to give applicants two weeks less to register. The bill would require valid applications to be received by the appropriate registration commission 30 days before the election, instead of 15 days before. Relatedly, the bill would require election officials to reject voter registration applications no later than 25 days before the next election, or five days after the application deadline. Existing law allows rejections until the 10th day before an election, again, five days after the application deadline.
  • Explicitly authorize the Department of State to offer online voter registration, and forbid any other application or third-party interface from being approved or used for voter registration. The Department of State currently offers online voter registration, a practice that existing statutes do not address. The bill would also make minor changes to notice requirements for in-person registration, and add record retention and requirements for data-sharing agreements to the section on voter registration at the DMV.
  • Add language to the voter registration code creating an address confidentiality program for voters who have an active protection for abuse order. Under existing law and policy, such victims can participate in an address confidentiality program that includes their voter registration record.
  • Add a requirement that the voter identification card mailed to each successful applicant include a "scannable identification code or strip".

Concerning voter ID documentation, the bill would:

  • Define "proof of identification" for any voter, presumably for both in-person and mail voters, as:
    • the voter's driver's license. The bill does not reference the expiration date of the driver's license, but generally requires photo IDs, including those issued by the state, to be unexpired. The existing, unenforced law does not separately list driver's licenses, instead more generally authorizing a document issued by the Department of Transportation that is not more than 12 months expired. The existing law also offers mail voters the option of using a driver's license number to validate their mail ballot.
    • in the case of a voter who has a religious objection to being photographed, a copy of a valid-without-photo driver's license or a valid-without-photo identification card issued by the Department of Transportation. The existing, unenforced law includes this option for in-person voters and a copy of such a document for mail voters.
    • military ID. Existing, unenforced law allows these IDs as well.
    • the voter's voter registration card created by the bill and issued by county boards of elections,
    • a photo ID created by the bill and issued by the Secretary of the Commonwealth,
    • an affidavit provided to a voter by elections officers, on which the voter affirms their identity, including their signature and the last four digits of their Social Security number. The unenforced existing law offers mail voters the option to validate their ballot using the last four digits of their Social Security number but does not offer a Social Security number option for in-person voters.
    • a document that shows the name and photograph of the voter, includes an expiration date, is not expired, and is issued by the U.S. government, the State of Pennsylvania, a municipality of Pennsylvania to an employee, an accredited college or university in Pennsylvania, or a care facility in Pennsylvania. The unenforced existing law allows a similar option for in-person voters and a copy of such a document for mail voters who lack a current and valid driver's license or Social Security number. The bill would also define "care facility.".
  • Require the Secretary of the Commonwealth to issue a free, durable photo identification card for voting to any registered voter who requests one.
  • Require county boards of election to provide each registered voter in their county with a durable voter registration card, including a scannable identification code and a likeness of a registered elector's signature. The county boards would be required to issue one to all registered voters within one year of the effective date of the bill, and thereafter to all voters registering for the first time or updating their registration, or upon the request of a voter. If the card is returned as undeliverable, the county board would be required to investigate, including by contacting the voter.

Regarding election crimes, the bill would create new offenses and penalties, and allocate new election law enforcement duties. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create a new felony to enforce the prohibition on collecting completed, sealed ballots and returning them for the voters unless the person returning the ballot is a household member of the voter. Existing law generally requires voters to return their own ballot, although disabled voters may designate someone to return their ballot, and special rules apply in emergencies.
  • Create a new misdemeanor to attempt to protect election workers. Specifically, a person would commit the new misdemeanor if they directly or indirectly use or threaten to use any force, violence, or restraint, or inflict or threaten to inflict any injury, damage, harm, or loss, or in any other manner practices intimidation or coercion upon or against any election official, administrator, judge of elections, or poll worker in the course of their duties in administering an election.
  • Double the penalties for election crimes wholesale. Although some of the penalties thereby become more typical of felonies, the bill does not reclassify any misdemeanors as felonies.
  • Create a new independent prosecutor for elections and expand the election-related duties of district attorneys. The Attorney General would nominate a prosecutor with experience in election violations for Senate approval before each primary, who would review all election complaints, report on their resolution, and receive cooperation from the Department of State and county boards. District attorneys would serve as “election integrity officers” unless on the ballot, and the Secretary of the Commonwealth would be required to maintain a fraud reporting hotline and provide public education.

Concerning early voting, the bill would:

  • Create Election Day-style early voting using vote centers starting with the 2025 primary election. Each county would be required to have at least one, and an additional one per 100,000 up to a cap of five required vote centers. The vote centers would open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. each day starting on the second Friday before Election Day and ending on the Wednesday following, for a total of six days. Vote centers could only be established in certain kinds of public buildings, would need to be equitably distributed, and their locations fixed at least 30 days before early voting started. Early voting locations would need to be monitored 24/7 including by video recording throughout the early voting period.
  • Repeal the ability of a voter to request and receive a mail ballot in person. This repeal would end in-person early voting as currently conducted in Pennsylvania.

Concerning the allocation of legal authority over election administration, the bill would reallocate authority among the Legislature, Department of State, county boards of elections, and the Pennsylvania Election Law Advisory Board in ways that add numerous explicit duties, and would eliminate discretion to do a non-enumerated act. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Deem the Legislature supreme and grant it special standing to enforce election law. The bill would:
    • Declare that Article 1, Section 5 of the U.S. Constitution and Article VII of the Pennsylvania Constitution vest authority for prescribing election law in the General Assembly.
    • Provide for special standing in lawsuits challenging the election code as unconstitutional, allowing the Senate or House to intervene if approved by their respective bodies, without waiving any legal privileges or immunities. The bill specifies that neither chamber is a necessary party and cannot be named in such actions, while preserving the potential standing of the chambers or individual legislators in cases involving impairment of their unique powers.
  • Specify additional duties of the Secretary of the Commonwealth beyond the new duties the bill imposes relating to voter IDs, audits, election crime hotline, and private election grants as discussed in other sections of this summary. The exhaustive specification that includes codifying actions the Secretary had previously taken, like offering ballot tracking, is then followed by an express limitation on the Secretary's discretion. The bill would explicitly require the Secretary:
    • To obtain and maintain uniformity in the interpretation and implementation of election laws, and provide uniform standards for the accurate and uniform implementation of voter registration laws and records.
    • To retain and make publicly available any communications relating to election administration sent between the department and at least three county election directors.
    • To take actions relating to voter registration list maintenance, including seeking death records, participating fully in ERIC, using National Change of Address data, and reporting new Pennsylvania registrations to states where the people had previously been registered.
    • To develop a uniform application for registered voters to update their signature of record or to provide a medical doctor's assessment of signature inconsistency due to a medical condition.
    • To actively collect the data necessary to scrutinize the effectiveness of election laws and provide technical assistance to election directors.
    • To submit the official instructions and procedures manual prescribed by the Pennsylvania Election Law Advisory Board to the Legislative Reference Bureau by December 31 of each odd-numbered year.
    • To develop the training prescribed by the Election Law Advisory Board and offer it free of charge to any individual required to complete it, and to reimburse counties for the cost of required annual training. Relatedly, the bill would repeal a requirement that the Secretary of the Commonwealth develop a voluntary professional certification and poll worker training program for county election officials in consultation with the county board of elections.
    • To maintain a public Internet website using a .gov domain name that adheres to generally accepted accessibility standards and post information required by election law on it. The bill would add to the information existing law requires by requiring the Secretary to post (1) the list of registered voters in each county and statewide at least five days before an election and (2) a record of registered voters and their participation in the election before the proclamation of the election results. A physical copy of the voter participation record required would be required to be retained for five years.
  • Expressly limit the Secretary of the Commonwealth's discretion. The bill would authorize the Secretary, in addition to expressly stated responsibilities in existing law or added by the bill, to perform only such other duties relating to elections explicitly authorized by the election code and prohibit any other action. Existing law simply empowers the Secretary to perform such other duties as may be prescribed by law.
  • Require the Department of State to report to the Legislature on each election, not later than 75 days after the election. The report's content is highly specified by the bill, detailing the numbers of various types of ballots, ballot challenges, ballot return methods, and many other aspects of election administration.
  • Sharply limit the powers of the county boards of elections. The bill would:
    • Repeal county boards' existing power to make and issue such rules, regulations, and instructions not inconsistent with law as necessary for the guidance of voting machine custodians, election officers, and voters.
    • Authorize county boards to "follow and obey rules, regulations, and instructions as are included for each election in the manual of operations.".
    • Prohibit county boards from any actions or duties relating to elections not explicitly authorized by the election code or by the manual of operations.
  • Explicitly grant county boards of elections specific new powers not otherwise mentioned in this summary. The bill would authorize or require counties to:
    • Cancel the registration of a voter whose registration matches a deceased person in first name, last name, date of birth, and last four digits of their Social Security number. After cancellation, the local commission would mail the presumably deceased voter notice of the cancellation.
    • Enter an agreement with Pennsylvania courts to receive a record of any county resident that asserted ineligibility for jury service, and to investigate the registration status of any registered voter who asserted ineligibility to be a juror on the basis of non-U.S. citizenship.
    • Include the election integrity officer created by the bill in all correspondence related to the conduct of the election.
    • Implement the minimum voter education standards and conduct additional nonpartisan education as necessary. Each board would be required to report on their voter education efforts to the Pennsylvania Election Law Advisory Board by December 31 of each general election year.
    • Capture and store voter signatures for signature matching, purchase specified electronic poll books and provide each election district with at least one accessible voting machine.
    • Review polling places with wait times of 30 minutes or more to eliminate such waits in the future.
  • Create siting and other requirements for any satellite county election office a county board of elections wishes to open.

Under existing law, mail ballots must be received by the close of polls regardless of the method of return. If a county board receives a ballot from another county's voter, the county board would be required to forward the ballot to the correct board no later than the eighth day after the election.
  • Require and regulate ballot drop boxes. In addition to the bill's requirements, the bill would authorize the Department of State to issue guidance, rules, or regulations establishing the criteria to implement the drop box provisions, including for siting drop boxes, security requirements, and the dates and times drop boxes must be open. Existing law does not address drop boxes, but in 2020 the Secretary of the Commonwealth issued guidance on their use and some counties use them. Under the bill:
    • Each county would establish one official drop box site for every 30,000 registered voters in the county, and any county with fewer voters would be required to have at least one.
    • Before Election Day, drop boxes may open on the first day ballots are mailed, but at a minimum, must be open to the public beginning on the Friday before Election Day, during the normal business hours of each official ballot drop site location. The county board would set the days and hours for each box, and post the information at a conspicuous place at each drop box location and on the publicly accessible Internet website of the county. On Election Day, county boards would keep drop boxes open for at least eight hours and until 8 p.m., the close of polls. A voter in line at 8 p.m. would be allowed to deposit their ballot.
    • Drop box locations would be staffed by on-site employees, such as municipal buildings, county buildings, libraries, and fire stations.
    • Drop boxes may be indoors or outdoors, but must remain in view of on-site staff, visually or by video monitoring, or both.
    • Drop box locations must be convenient, offer parking, and be accessible for disabled voters.
    • County boards of elections would develop and maintain a drop box security plan that they file with the Secretary of the Commonwealth.
  • Create rules for replacement ballots. Under the bill, a voter may obtain a replacement ballot if the original ballot is destroyed, spoiled, lost, or not received by them. Replacement ballots could be sent as late as the fifth day before Election Day and would be made available at the office of the county board or at one central location designated by the county board in the election district in which the election is conducted. These rules would apply:
    • The voter would complete and sign a replacement ballot request form under oath that their mailed ballot was destroyed, spoiled, lost, or not received.
    • The replacement ballot request may be made electronically, by telephone, in writing, in person, or by other means designated by the department.
    • If the request is made without the form, the form would be made available to the voter along with the replacement ballot.
    • The county board would verify the registration of the voter, ensure that they have not returned another ballot, record the request, note in the district register that the elector has requested a replacement ballot, mark the outer return envelope to indicate it contains a replacement ballot, and mail or otherwise deliver the ballot to the voter.
    • Upon receipt of a voted replacement ballot, the county board would verify that a completed and signed replacement ballot request form has been received by the county board or is included with the voted replacement ballot. The ballot could not be processed unless the county board received the completed form.
    • If the county board determines that a voter to whom a replacement ballot has been issued has voted more than once, only the first ballot received by the county board would count. The board would provide the voter's name to the Department for further review.
  • Require election officials to start processing ballots sooner. No earlier than the seventh day before Election Day, the county board would be required to begin pre-canvassing the ballots received before the meeting, subject to public notice and access by poll watchers. Under existing law, pre-canvassing cannot start before 7 a.m. on Election Day and is not required to start then.
  • Expand an existing misdemeanor relating to violations of mail ballot provisions to include the provisions created by the bill.

  • Add a new warning to ballots: "ANY PERSON WHO, BY USE OR FORCE OR OTHER MEANS, UNDULY INFLUENCES AN ELECTOR TO VOTE IN ANY PARTICULAR MANNER OR TO REFRAIN FROM VOTING IS SUBJECT TO CRIMINAL PENALTIES UPON CONVICTION, INCLUDING IMPRISONMENT OR A FINE, OR BOTH."

This bill, as introduced on March 15, 2023, would increase the number of poll watchers candidates may appoint, increase the election types for which candidates and parties may appoint poll watchers, expand who can serve as poll watchers, increase the access poll watchers have, and increase the severity of a few election crimes. Specifically the bill would:

  • Increase the number of poll watchers who may be appointed for each election by allowing candidates to appoint three poll watchers instead of two per election district.
  • Increase the election types for which candidates and political parties may appoint poll watchers by allowing both candidates and parties to appoint watchers for primary, general, municipal, and special elections. Under existing law, candidates may appoint watchers for primaries, and parties may appoint watchers for general, municipal, and special elections.
  • Expand who may serve as poll watchers by allowing anyone registered to vote in Pennsylvania to serve anywhere in the state. Under existing law, poll watchers must be registered voters of the county in which they are serving.
  • Increase the access and power of poll watchers have by:
    • After polls close, allowing them into the closed area at each polling place where ballots are being counted while prohibiting them from interfering with the counting of ballots. Under existing law, watchers must remain outside the closed area.
    • Adding "at any facility where votes are collected" to the locations at which watchers are allowed to challenge voters. Under existing law, watchers may challenge voters at polling places.
    • Specifying that watchers observing mail ballot pre-canvassing must be allowed a clear line of sight to view and hear the proceedings at a distance of six feet or less, that does not impede the ability of the person canvassing ballots from carrying out the person's duties. Under existing law, watchers are simply permitted to "remain in the room" in which mail ballots are being pre-canvassed.
  • Increase the penalty for certain election crimes. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Raise the penalty from misdemeanor to second degree misdemeanor, doubling the potential fine and length of incarceration, for any election official refusing to permit overseers, watchers, attorneys, or candidates to act. In addition, the bill would add the penalty of forfeiting or repaying any compensation for election services rendered.
    • Raise the penalty from misdemeanor to second degree misdemeanor, doubling the potential fine and length of incarceration, for hindering or delaying an election official in the performance of their duties.
    • Raise the penalty from misdemeanor of the second degree to misdemeanor of the first degree, doubling the potential fine and increasing the potential incarceration from two yeast to three, for voter intimidation. This bill, as introduced on April 17, 2023, would expand the duties of the bipartisan Pennsylvania Election Law Advisory Board, give the Attorney General new election crime prosecution duties, and double penalties for dozens of election crimes. The Election Law Advisory Board, created in 2020, studies Pennsylvania election law and recommends improvements. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Expand the duties of the Election Law Advisory Board to include:
    • Establishing and collaborating with a working group of county election officials from a minimum of ten counties to prescribe rules to achieve and maintain the maximum degree of accuracy, impartiality, uniformity, and efficiency of the procedures for voting and producing, distributing, collecting, counting, tabulating and storing of ballots.
    • Adopting rules regarding the return of unused ballots, ballot requests, voted ballots, and other election materials to and from an absent uniformed services voter as defined by federal law. These rules would be issued in an "official instructions and procedures manual" that the Advisory Board would be required to issue by December 31 of each odd-numbered year. Prior to its issuance and no later than October 1 of an odd-numbered year, the Advisory Board would submit the Manual to the Governor and the Legislature. The Advisory Board would be required to include a citation to state law for each rule.
    • Establishing standards for annual training requirements for all county election officers, poll workers, watchers, and judges of elections. Training to fulfill the requirements would be conducted online by the Department of State and would be made available on all business days.
    • Developing and publicizing standards for nonpartisan voter education. The standards would address, at a minimum: (1) voter registration, (2) balloting procedures, by mail and polling place, (3) voter rights and responsibilities, (4) distribution of sample ballots, and (5) public service announcements.
    • Receiving reports from county boards of elections, reexamining the voter education standards, and modifying the standards to incorporate successful voter education programs and techniques.
  • Require poll watchers to complete training developed by the Advisory Board. Existing law does not require such training.
  • Require the Attorney General to appoint an independent prosecutor to review election complaints received by the Department of State and the county boards. This bill, as introduced on September 7, 2023, would permit an individual who is 16 years of age but not yet 18 years of age to pre-register to vote. Under existing law, pre-registration is allowed only if the individual will be 18 by Election Day. Specifically, the bill would:

This bill, as introduced on October 13, 2023, would establish same-day voter registration on Election Day and create related criminal enforcement measures. Under existing law, same-day registration is only available during the early voting period. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Permit a person to register to vote on the day of any primary, municipal or general election by appearing at the polling place in the district where they reside, completing a registration card, making an oath, and proving their residence by presenting a valid driver's license or approved documentation.
  • Make registration cards and forms for oaths available at each polling place and require the completed registration cards to be sent to the county board.
  • Require judges of elections to conduct same-day registration, and require judges to record the number of people who attempt to register but cannot provide proof of residence.
  • Require written notice to be mailed to a voter if a county board finds that the voter's Election Day registration is "substantially deficient." The bill specifies that a registration is not deficient solely because the person who provided proof of residence was ineligible to do so.
  • Require county boards to send notice to a random sample of at least 25 percent of voters registered on Election Day within 10 days of the election. County boards would also be required to mail registration verification notices to all voters registered on Election Day as soon as practicable and notify the district attorney and the Department of State if they do not receive satisfactory proof of a person's eligibility to vote.
  • Create new second degree misdemeanor offenses for conduct related to improper voter registration. Existing law includes various misdemeanor and felony offenses for improper registration by applicants and officials processing applications, some of which overlap with the new offenses set out in the bill. Specifically, the bill would create offenses for:
    • Causing an ineligible person's name to be registered to vote.
    • Causing a person's name to be registered in order to vote in multiple elections or to vote in an election district where the person does not reside.
    • Misrepresenting a person's identity when attempting to register to vote.
    • A judge of elections allowing an unregistered voter to vote in any election.
    • Aiding, abetting, counseling or procuring another person to commit one of these crimes.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on April 7, 2023, would alter the state's existing automatic voter registration system by requiring different procedures depending on whether the documents the person submits with their DMV transaction demonstrate U.S. citizenship or not. Under existing law, all qualified individuals are automatically registered to vote during DMV transactions, unless they choose to opt out during the transaction, if they provide proof of identity and residence and certify through documentation or a declaration that they are citizens. This bill would:

  • Limit automatic voter registration at the DMV to only those applicants who present documentation of citizenship, and change the opt-out process. For individuals who provide citizenship documentation, voter registration information would be automatically transmitted to election officials, who would subsequently send a notice of registration to the applicant. The bill would also allow the DMV to look at its records to determine if the individual had previously submitted documentation demonstrating U.S. citizenship even if they did not during the current transaction. If the DMV found such documentation, the DMV would also send the person's information to election officials, triggering the same notice. If the applicant failed to decline registration within 14 days of receipt of that notice, the applicant would be registered to vote. Under existing law, automatic voter registration requires only certification of citizenship, not documentation, and the DMV must provide the opportunity to opt out during the transaction itself.
  • End automatic voter registration for individuals who do not present affirmative documentary proof of citizenship at the DMV, and instead provide an opt-in streamlined registration process for these applicants. Individuals whose documentation neither proves nor disproves citizenship would be given the option to affirmatively choose to register by certifying their citizenship status, which may be done by declaration.
  • Provide that if the DMV has access to information to determine whether someone is already registered to vote and determines that an applicant is already registered, then the DMV would treat the transaction as a registration update and would send the person's information to election officials without regard to whether the person provided citizenship documentation in their DMV application.
  • Exempt from automatic registration people who are doing a DMV transaction using their business address rather than their residential address. Such people would be offered the opt-in streamlined registration process.
  • Prohibit automatic voter registration or streamlined voter registration at the DMV for any individual who fails to certify, by documentation or declaration, that they are a U.S. citizen, and expressly prohibit the agency from offering the opportunity to register to individuals who have documented their non-citizenship. Existing law requires certification of citizenship for registration at the DMV, but does not include an express prohibition on offering registration when documentation of non-citizenship has been provided. Nonetheless, existing law expressly contemplates registration of eligible individuals only.
  • Expand which additional agencies beyond the DMV may offer automatic voter registration, by permitting agencies to do so if they either collect documentary proof of citizenship or can verify citizenship by database matching or other means deemed reliable by the Secretary of State. Existing law limits automatic voter registration to only those non-DMV agencies that verify citizenship through documentation. The bill would also require non-DMV agencies that process transactions for multiple individuals eligible for registration to register each individual according to the procedures applicable to the DMV process.

  • Permit agencies that are not authorized to offer full automatic voter registration to make automatic updates to voter registration address information, if the Secretary verifies that the agency collects sufficient information to do so.

Last Updated April 10, 2023

This bill was amended on March 2, 2023 to replace all of its provisions with new ones. As amended on March 2, 2023, the bill addresses appointing poll watchers and poll watcher access, whereas the prior versions of the bill address voter registration list maintenance. Specifically, the amended bill would:

  • Create new rules for polling place poll watchers and the access they must be granted. The bill would also create a misdemeanor to enforce the new rules. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Allow any candidate, party, or ballot question committee to have a poll watcher present at any polling place to observe the voting and counting process. Candidates on the ballot at a polling place cannot serve as poll watchers and may only be present to cast their ballot. Under existing law, any person except a candidate on a ballot may observe voting and counting. This authorization would be repealed by the bill. In addition, under existing law for primaries, each candidate, each slate of national convention delegates and alternates, and each side of any ballot issue to be voted on may have one poll watcher at each polling place. For a general election, each political party, each independent candidate, each slate of presidential electors, and each side of any ballot issue to be voted on may have a poll watcher. If space at the polling place allows, more poll watchers may be allowed.
    • Require the polling place observation area to be between three and six feet from the table at which voters announce their name and address to be issued a ballot, and positioned to permit any poll watcher to plainly see and hear all public aspects of the voting process. Existing law does not address the observation distance from the voter check-in table but does mandate that poll watchers be able to plainly see and hear what is done within the polling place.
    • Create a class 2 misdemeanor to enforce these observation rules.
  • Enable poll watchers to observe the process of sorting, validating, and counting ballots and create a misdemeanor to enforce the rules. Existing law does not provide for this access.
    • Poll watchers would be required to keep a reasonable distance from ballots and identification information to protect the privacy of voters.
    • No record associating an individual voter with a ballot would be allowed to be created.
    • The State Board of Elections to promulgate rules setting the number of poll watchers allowed for the sorting, validating, and counting of ballots.
    • The bill would create a class 2 misdemeanor to enforce these rules.
  • Provide that a meeting of a recount board must be open to the public. Members of the general public would be required to keep a reasonable distance from ballots. A violation of these rules would be a Class 2 misdemeanor.

The March 3, 2023 amendment removed all the prior provisions of the bill. Those provisions would have:

  • Required the Secretary of State to match voter registration records in the statewide voter registration file with the death records maintained by the Social Security death index, and the Social Security Administration master death file, as well as the records maintained by the Department of Health. Existing law requires searching for deceased voters using the Department of Health data only.
  • Required the Secretary to perform the searches for deceased voters and people convicted of felonies each month. Existing law does not require a specific timetable.

Provisions that were amended out of the bill on February 3, 2023, would have:

  • Canceled inactive registrations after one general election cycle of inactivity instead of two,

This bill, as enacted on March 21, 2023, makes several changes to mail voting (called "absentee voting" in South Dakota), including prohibiting the use of ballot drop boxes and creating several new criminal offenses related to ballot handling and voter assistance. Specifically, the bill:

  • Prohibits county auditors from using ballot drop boxes and creates a new class 2 misdemeanor offense for violations of the provision. While previous law was silent on drop boxes, some South Dakota counties used them in 2020.
  • Creates a new misdemeanor offense for county auditors failing to comply with certain mail ballot signature processing rules.
  • Specifies that the room occupied by the mail ballot counting board must be open to poll watchers to observe the process of sorting, validating, and counting mail ballots, and requires poll watchers to keep a "reasonable distance" from ballots and identification information to protect the privacy of mail voters. The bill enforces these rules with a new class 2 misdemeanor. Previous law required only that the room for ballot processing must be open "to any person for the purpose of observing the counting process."
  • Creates new misdemeanor offenses for creating a record associating a voter with a particular ballot during either the processing mail ballots, or during observation by poll watchers of mail ballot processing.
  • Increases the offense level of existing misdemeanors for paying people to assist voters on a per-voter basis, and/or for receiving such payment, from class 2 to class 1 misdemeanors.
  • Requires election officials to reject mail ballots returned by voters who, by the time polls open, are no longer eligible to vote due to death, felony conviction, or mental incapacity. Under previous law, officials were required to reject ballots for a change in a voter's eligibility due to death only.
  • Expands the availability of a special process in which election officials bring mail ballots to nursing homes and similar facilities to enable residents to vote so it is available during primaries as well as general elections. In addition, the bill requires the State Board of Elections to issue rules prescribing how the county auditor will conduct voting at such institutions.
  • Prohibits distributing mail ballot applications that have the voter's name and registration address prefilled, unless the person doing the prefilling is:
    • authorized to request a mail ballot for a voter,
    • assisting a voter who requires assistance because of an inability to read or write, blindness, or other physical disability, or
    • in charge of the election and sending an absentee ballot application to a voter who requested it.
  • Requires election officials to keep records of authorized individuals picking up mail ballots on behalf of a voter. Previous law did not explicitly require such recordkeeping.
  • Creates a new misdemeanor offense for a candidate to serve as voter's "authorized messenger" for receiving or returning a mail ballot, with narrow exceptions. Previous law prohibited this conduct, but did not impose a criminal penalty for violations.
  • Prohibits mailing a voter a properly requested mail ballot after the Monday before Election Day.
  • Requires election officials to mark mail ballot envelopes with the date of receipt.

  • Specifies that mail ballots returned after the close of polls to the office of the person in charge of election must not be opened or counted. Previous law addressed late return to a polling place only or to the absentee counting board only.

This bill, as introduced on February 1, 2023, would require voters to justify their choice to vote by mail with an excuse. Existing law gives all voters the freedom to vote by mail. In addition, the bill would prohibit county auditors from using ballot drop boxes or allowing anyone else to use them in their jurisdiction. The bill would create a misdemeanor to enforce the drop box ban. Existing law does not specifically address drop boxes. A couple of counties used them in 2020 but they are not generally used in the state. Finally, by requiring an excuse to vote a mail ballot (called an "absentee ballot" in South Dakota), the bill would end early voting. In-person early voting is only offered as in-person mail ballot voting.

Under the bill, a person would qualify to vote by mail if:

  • The voter expects to be or may be absent outside the county, state, or the United States on the day that any election is held,
  • The voter is within the county on the day of the election, but will be unable to cast a ballot at the polling place in the voter's election district because of:
    • permanent or total physical disability,
    • illness,
    • temporary physical disability,
    • the observance of a religious holiday pursuant to the tenets of a voter's religion,
  • resident attendance at a school, college, or university, or
    • the nature and hours of the voter's employment, or

  • The voter is an absent uniformed services voter or an overseas voter.

Finally, the bill would require the Secretary to send county auditors monthly lists of deceased voters in their counties.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 25, 2023, would revise voter registration list maintenance processes in multiple ways, primarily focused on identifying voters who moved or who are not citizens. The bill would also add new address-focused steps to processing new registrations. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the Secretary of State to ensure that the statewide voter registration file database can electronically communicate with other state agency databases and allow exchanges and comparisons of information. Once the statewide registration database has this capability, the Secretary would be required to look for voters who moved or who are not citizens each month by comparing the registration database with the databases maintained by the departments of human services, public safety, and social services, in coordination with secretaries of those departments. The information for each voter would include name, date of birth, and if available, the last four digits of the individual's Social Security number. If matches are identified, the bill would:
    • Require the Secretary to inform relevant county auditors of changes to voters' addresses or citizenship information.
    • Require county auditors to do an address verification process for a person identified as having moved, and to notify the county's state's attorney of any registered voters whose citizenship information changed.
  • Require the Secretary of State to use national change of address data every quarter and require the county auditors to do the address confirmation process for identified voters. Existing law requires this data to be used in every odd-numbered year.
  • Authorize the Secretary of State to cooperate with any other state to compare voter lists to identify individuals who are registered to vote in more than one state.
  • Authorize the Secretary of State and each county auditor to contract with commercial data companies, including credit reporting agencies, to verify and audit information in voter registration lists, including citizenship status and residence.

  • Require each county auditor to do a list maintenance process aimed at identifying voters who have moved, sending them address confirmation notices, and canceling registrations depending on the responses to the notices. Existing law requires similar but not identical processes that this bill does not address. Under the bill, if an auditor has evidence that a voter has moved, the auditor would mail a notice to that individual requesting confirmation that they have not moved. Existing law requires such a notice using national change of address data, and a similar notice to voters who have not voted, returned a confirmation card, or updated their registration in four years. Under the bill, the county auditor would remove the individual from the master registration file if the individual fails to:

    • Respond to the notice and vote in the registered precinct at least once during four consecutive years covering two general elections, or
    • Update the voter's registration with the auditor and vote at least once during four consecutive years covering two general elections.

    Under existing law, voters who fail to respond to the confirmation notices have their registrations marked inactive, and inactive registrations are canceled if the voters fail to vote in two consecutive general elections.

  • Require county auditors to do the address confirmation process if election officials receive other information showing a voter moved, died, or is otherwise ineligible to vote.
  • Require each county auditor to update the county's voter registration file twice a year, including no less than 60 days before a general election. Existing law does not have a comparable provision.
  • Create additional duties for processing a new registration application. Specifically, the bill would require each county auditor to:
    • Compare the address on each new voter registration application with county tax records to verify that the address is a residence, and not a commercial, industrial, vacant, or government property. Existing law has no similar provision.
    • Check the master registration file against the information in county tax records to verify how many people are registered at a given residence to look for anomalies.

  • Determine if a voter registration application for an individual at the same address and similar name as another registered voter reflects a duplicate registration, and if so, notify the Secretary of State. Existing law requires the Secretary to review the statewide list for duplicates and notify county auditors of duplicates, and existing regulations require that review to be at least annual and specify what is considered a duplicate record.

    Last updated February 8, 2023

This bill, as enacted on March 21, 2023, imposes a 30-day residency requirement to register to vote. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires individuals to have maintained their residence in South Dakota for at least 30 days before applying to register. Previous law did not impose a residency duration requirement.
  • Redefines residence as the place in which a person is domiciled as shown by an actual fixed permanent dwelling, establishment, or any other abode to which the person returns after a period of absence. Previous law defined residence as the place in which a person has fixed his or her habitation and to which the person, whenever absent, intends to return. The bill also expressly provides that an individual retains residency in the state "until another residence has been gained."
  • Requires voters to vote in the election precinct in which they are registered. Note: Existing law, which the bill leaves in place, provides that notwithstanding any other provision of law, jurisdictions may use vote centers at which all voters in the jurisdiction may vote. In such a case, the entire jurisdiction is designated as a precinct.

  • Requires the voter registration form to include a certification with an attestation made under penalty of perjury to each of the eligibility requirements, including the new 30 day residency requirement. This bill, as enacted on March 21, 2023, makes several changes to voter registration and registration list maintenance processes. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires the State Board of Elections to issue rules determining how voter registration records are matched to death data and felony conviction data to identify registrations that must be canceled. Previous law authorized the State Board to issue rules but did not require it.
  • Requires each clerk of court, within 15 days of the close of each month, to forward to the county auditor information on any individual excused from jury service due to having moved, conviction for a felony, declaration of mental incompetence, death, or non-U.S. citizenship. Auditors must review the county's registration file to see if these individuals are registered and remove any voters who are on the clerk's list due to any listed reason (other than having moved), subject to certain confirmation requirements.
  • Requires the county auditor to cancel the registration of a person based on an obituary. Previous law authorized but did not require cancellation using obituary information.
  • Requires the county auditor to match voter registration records, on a monthly basis, with death records from the state Department of Health, the Social Security death index, the Social Security Administration master death file, and felony convictions maintained by the Unified Judicial System, and cancel the registrations of identified ineligible voters. Previous law did not require matching against the Social Security lists, nor did it specify the election official who must do the matching.
  • Permits voters to request a county auditor to remove their name from the registration list, and requires the State Board to issue a form for voters to do so. If such a request is made less than fourteen days before an election, the removal of the individual's name is effective on the day after the election. Previous law had no express provision for requesting removal from the voter registration file.
  • Requires the county auditor, before providing a registration list to precincts as required under existing law, to certify to the Secretary of State that all registrations that need to be canceled have been canceled, based on the information the auditor has received through that date. The bill also requires the State Board of Elections to prescribe the certification form to certify the list's accuracy. Previous law had no comparable certification requirements.
  • Requires the Secretary of State to submit an annual report to the State Board of Elections, providing the number of registrations canceled due to inactivity, felony conviction, mental incompetence, or moving to another jurisdiction. The Board is authorized to determine the form and content of the report, and the Secretary is required to post the report on the agency website.
  • Changes details of voter registration processing. Specifically, the bill:
    • Requires the State Board of Elections to issue rules determining technical parameters for verifying driver's licenses and Social Security numbers. Previous law authorized the State Board to issue rules but did not require it.
    • Requires the auditor to save an electronic copy of the index card the auditor creates from UOCAVA requests for mail ballots. Previous law requires the paper index card to be attached to the master registration file.
    • Permits voters to revise their voter registration record to add or correct their phone number or email by completing a new registration card. Previous law did not address changes to a voter's phone number or email address. In addition, if new registrants leave the party affiliation field blank, the bill requires county officials to register them as having "no party affiliation." Under previous law, if a new registrant did not pick a party, auditors were directed to register them as either "independent" or "no party affiliation."
  • Requires the county auditor or the person responsible for a local election to publish notice of voter registration opportunities and deadlines on their website unless the jurisdiction does not have an official website. Previous law required notice to be published in official newspapers.
  • Requires the Secretary of State to post voter registration statistics on their website on the first business day of every month and on the date of any primary, general, runoff, or special election in the state, and requires the State Board to issue related rules. Previous law did not have a similar provision.

  • Requires the State Board of Elections to issue cyber security rules for the voter registration file. Previous law did not have a similar provision.

    The bill also contains additional provisions making technical and conforming changes throughout the code.

    Previous versions of the bill contained a provision that was amended out on February 23, 2023, prior to enactment. That provision would have authorized the county auditor to contact voter registration applicants by phone or email to collect missing registration information preventing the processing of a registration application, as well as mailing them a nonforwardable notice. Existing law requires a nonforwardable mail notice and does not address other contact methods.

Last Updated April 25, 2023

This bill, as introduced on March 10, 2023, would make extensive changes to Texas election law, including by changing eligibility for mail voting, shortening the early voting period, creating and strengthening criminal offenses, eliminating the use of electronic voting systems, and more. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Remove being 65 years of age or older on Election Day as grounds to vote a ballot by mail.
  • Replace the existing early voting period with a period of 9 consecutive days of voting, culminating with Election Day. Under existing law, the early voting period generally starts 17 days before Election day and continues through the fourth day before Election Day.
  • Create a felony offense for a voter who votes curbside without meeting the eligibility requirements.
  • Decrease the maximum population of a county election precinct (subject to exceptions existing in current law) to 2,000 from 5,000 registered voters.
  • Specify that the required distribution of election supplies to each election judge includes delivery of enough ballots for all registered voters in the precinct, plus one percent. The bill further specifies that if this requirement is not met, the election administrator or office responsible may be removed and the election itself would be required to be reconducted.
  • Increase the severity of the offense of obstructing delivery of election supplies from a misdemeanor to a felony.
  • Require ballot printers to be located in the state of Texas and follow strict chain of custody procedures to keep their contracts.
  • Require ballots to be designed for hand marking, be difficult to counterfeit, and not contain any markings undecipherable by the human eye. An elections administrator would commit a misdemeanor if they fail to comply with these requirements. Ballots would also be required to be numbered sequentially. The bill would additionally repeal the entire title of the Election Code concerning voting systems.
  • Remove authorization for a political party or candidate to distribute unsolicited applications for a mail ballot.
  • Require ballots to be counted by hand by bipartisan teams. The counting would be required to be filmed, and if technically feasible, live-streamed, and the recordings would be required to be freely and publicly available. The bill would set a recommended time frame of three hours to complete the count. Election materials would also be required to be under constant video surveillance.
  • Establish a new procedure under which the election could not be certified until the public has a 30-day period to examine the recording of the counting for errors. If an error is identified, the bill would create a comprehensive process for reviewing and correcting the error, including the ability for voters to file a suit to resolve a disputed error and recall or removal of officials who refuse to correct an error in the count.
  • Provide for mail ballots to be delivered to the precinct in which the voter would have voted, to be counted with ballots voted in-person.
  • Create a misdemeanor offense for an election official who modifies any election practice or procedure in a way not authorized by statute. The modification would be subject to injunctive relief or mandamus, and would become a felony if done more than once.
  • Create a misdemeanor offense for an election officer who alters a voter's ballot in any way.
  • Require the widespread public posting of election results by precinct.
  • Clarify procedures for the voiding and destruction of misprinted ballots.
  • Repeal the countywide polling place program. The bill would allow a voter to vote in a polling place in an adjoining precinct.
  • Repeal provisions of law requiring a person who assists seven or more voters by providing transportation to the polling place to complete forms providing their personal information.
  • Expand an existing prohibition on siting a polling place at the residence of a candidate or a candidate's family to include a business location. The bill would also prohibit a polling place from being located in a movable structure.
  • Require that a room in a public building in which an election is being conducted be used solely for that purpose during the election and be capable of being locked and fully secured if an election judge is not present.
  • Provide extensive procedures for an election judge to follow if the judge believes that some election materials or supplies have been compromised.
  • Require more frequent updates from an election judge of how many people have voted.
  • Expand the prohibition on using a device to record sound or video near a voting station to encompass the area within 100 feet of the entrance to a voting station and exempt watchers from the requirement. Violation of this would result in a misdemeanor.
  • Require a physical paper poll list. Provisions permitting an electronic poll list, combination form, or signature roster would be repealed.

This bill, as enacted on June 18, 2023, facilitates voting by persons with disabilities. The bill:

  • Instructs the early voting clerk to do the following if a voter submits an application for a mail ballot containing a defect, not later than the second day after discovering the defect:
    • Determine whether it would be possible for the voter to correct the defect and return a corrected application before the applicable deadline
    • If so, either return the application to the voter or send a new application, with instructions for correcting the defect. Existing law only requires the clerk to send a new application, and only if the defective application was received at least 18 days before Election Day.
    • E-mail or telephone the voter if it would not be possible for the voter to mail a corrected application in time to meet the applicable deadline. The clerk should instruct the voter that they can come to the clerk's office to correct the defect before the deadline or, if possible, correct the defect using the online tool.

This bill, as introduced on March 10, 2023, would make a wide variety of changes to Texas election law, including changing the eligibility requirements to vote a mail ballot, requiring paper ballots for all voters, and changing procedures for curbside voting, among other changes. Specifically, the bill would:

Under existing law, a voter voting curbside may request that a person accompanying them to the polling place "select" the voter's ballot and deposit it in the ballot box. This bill would remove that possibility, and instead allow a voter who requests to be assisted in marking their ballot to be helped by two election officers. Anyone physically able accompanying the voter would be required to exit the vehicle while the voter votes unless assisting the voter in marking their ballot.

  • Specify that notwithstanding any law to the contrary, the county clerk or commissioners court, as applicable, should determine the number of polling places needed during an "election period" and cause that number of polling places to be open during the election period. Note that "election period" is not a defined term under the bill or under current Texas election law.

  • Require, rather than permit, the Secretary of State to publish tabulation reports. The bill would require the publication to be on the secretary's website. County clerks would also be required to post precinct results on their websites, and the Secretary would be required to investigate and resolve any discrepancies.
  • Repeal provisions of law requiring a person who assists seven or more voters by providing transportation to the polling place to complete forms providing their personal information.
