This bill, as enacted on March 14, 2023, makes changes to ballot accessibility and ballot verification and cure processes in the state. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires election officers to provide a method of accessible voting to disabled people who are not able to vote by mail, and include information about that method with ballots and on their website.
  • Requires the Director of Elections to issue regulations concerning signature matching criteria and processes, and poll worker certification and training requirements, for verification of mail ballots. Regulations must include an Americans with Disabilities Act-compliant method for disabled voters to verify their ballots when their disability causes inconsistent signatures. The bill also expressly requires poll workers to implement the regulations to determine if a voter's signatures are "reasonably consistent," when verifying ballots. Previous law merely required poll workers to determine if a voter's ballot and registration signatures "correspond."
  • Makes various changes to the cure process for rejected ballots. The bill:
    • Requires election officials to give notice of rejection to the voter no later than the second business day after the day the ballot is rejected, regardless of the method by which notice is given. If a ballot is rejected for arriving late, or another reason that cannot be cured, officials would have 30 days after either Election Day or the rejection decision to provide notice. Under previous law, notice was required to be given within a single business day if given by email or text message, within two business days if given by email or phone, and within seven days if the ballot was rejected on or after Election Day.
    • Requires that notice of non-matching signatures include a copy of the cure affidavit, or if the notice is by email or text, a link to the affidavit on the county clerk's website. If the notice is by phone, whether in conversation or by voice message, it must include arrangements for the voter to receive a copy of the affidavit. Previous law did not require notice of non-matching signatures to include a cure affidavit.
    • Amends the cure affidavit to permit voters to indicate that their signatures do not match due to disability, and to attest to the ability to provide documentation and provide contact information. If the affidavit discloses a disability, election officers must follow the newly required rules for accessible verification. Previous law had no comparable provision.
  • Requires election officials to record in the statewide voter registration database any initial rejection of a ballot within one business day of rejecting the ballot, and any resolution of the issue causing the ballot rejection, within one business day after resolution. Previous law had no comparable provision.
  • Requires election officials to include in the canvass report data on rejected and resolved ballots. Specifically, the report must include:
    • the number of ballots rejected because the voter did not include a signature
    • the number rejected because the voter's signature did not correspond with the one on file
  • Expands the existing felony offense for "willful neglect of duty or corrupt conduct" to include conduct by election officers, and expressly provides that an election official's willful failure to comply with provisions concerning mail ballot voting constitutes an offense. Under previous law, the offense was limited to misconduct by poll workers.
  • Requires that if, in accordance with law, an election officer discloses the names of voters whose ballots have been rejected but not yet resolved, that the disclosure be made only on the election officer's publicly available website.

Last Updated March 22, 2023

This bill, as enacted on March 13, 2023, makes minor changes to certain voter notice statutes and permits additional officers to receive a voter registration form. Specifically, the bill:

The bill also requires notice of the election, including the date, voting times, and polling place or drop box locations to be distributed five days before Election Day, rather than two days before Election Day as under previous law.

This bill, as enacted on March 20, 2023, alters rules for accessing voter registration data and disclosure of voter registration data for "protected individuals." Specifically, the bill:

This bill, as enacted on March 15, 2023, expands the authority of the Lt. Governor, as the state's chief elections officer, and changes requirements related to list maintenance, mail ballot cure processes, and other aspects of election administration. Specifically, the bill:

  • Modifies and specifies the powers of the Lt. Governor, in their role as the chief elections officer of the state, by newly providing for:
    • Express rulemaking authority for voter list maintenance procedures and mail ballot voting procedures (and additional areas noted below).
    • Full access to examine and copy all records and documents in an election officer's custody.
    • The right to attend any meeting and closely observe any process related to elections.
    • The authority to give orders, having the full force of law, to election officers who are in violation of election law. The bill expressly limits judicial authority to overturn these orders, setting out specific standards for reversal.
    • The authority to design and provide training for election officers. The bill also sets out various requirements for the substance of training, and requirements for election officers to complete training within certain timeframes.
    • Authority to make recommendations for improvements in audit processes.
  • Changes requirements related to voter list maintenance. Specifically, the bill:
    • Specifies that the Lt. Governor's voter list maintenance procedures must include weekly review of voter name and address data from driver's license records, weekly review of data for deceased residents, and monthly review of data for incarcerated individuals and data from other states regarding registered individuals. Previous law required ongoing maintenance of the voter registration list based on information from voters, government entities, and other states, but did not specify the frequency for review or detail procedures.
    • Requires the Lt. Governor's website to provide information about maintenance requirements, including compliance with review deadlines by local clerks.
    • Requires clerks to utilize list maintenance tools to identify duplicate registrations at least once a month, and to identify inactive registrations for removal once a year. Previous law had no comparable provisions. The bill also specifies that for apparent address changes within a county, clerks must send a confirmation notice within 31 days of obtaining information of the change, and eliminates the requirement that notice be sent on a postage prepaid, preaddressed return form. For address changes to a different county, the bill leaves in place the paid postage requirement (and no specific deadline for issuing notice).
    • Clarifies that a voter may not be removed from the voter registration roll "solely" for failure to vote in an election.
    • Requires, rather than permits, a clerk to mark a voter as inactive after sending the voter a confirmation notice. As provided under existing law, inactive voters have the privileges of regular voters, but do not receive regular mailings and are not taken into consideration when election supply distribution is calculated.
  • Changes verification and cure processes for mail ballots. Specifically, the bill:
    • Specifies that election workers comparing signatures to determine whether to accept or reject a mail ballot must judge whether the signatures are "reasonably consistent." Previous law required the workers to determine whether the signatures "correspond" and "match." The bill also requires the Lt. Governor's office to promulgate rules to establish the criteria for signature matching, and related training and certification requirements.
    • Requires election officials to give notice of ballot rejection to the voter no later than the second business day after the day the ballot is rejected, for any method of notice, if the reason for rejection can be cured. If a ballot is rejected for arriving late, or another reason that cannot be cured, officials would have 30 days after either Election Day or the rejection decision to provide notice. Under previous law, notice was required to be given within a single business day if given by email or text message, within two business days if notice is given by email or phone, and within seven days if the ballot is rejected on or after Election Day.
    • Specifies procedures for verifying the identity of voters with defective ballots. Previous law required that a mail ballot be counted if the voter provides a cure affidavit or the clerk is otherwise able to "confirm" their identity, but did not set out additional requirements.
    • Requires election officers to carry out "regular" audits of signature comparisons, to include review of 1% of all comparisons and training as needed based on results. Officials must report audit information to the Lt. Governor and board of canvassers.
    • Mandates that the Driver License Division study options for improving the quality of signatures used for signature verification in an election.
    • Includes the record of voters contacted to cure a ballot in the definition of "election returns."
  • Changes requirements related to accessibility for disabled voters. Specifically, the bill:
    • Expressly requires officials administering an election by mail ballot to provide an accessible method of voting for disabled voters unable to vote by mail.
    • Enables disabled mail ballot voters whose disability renders their signature inconsistent to prevent their ballots from being disqualified for non-matching signatures. The bill revises the affidavit voters sign to address election officials' determination that their ballot envelope signature did not match their reference signature to include a checkbox with the language "I am a voter with a qualifying disability under the Americans with Disabilities Act that impacts my ability to sign my name consistently. I can provide appropriate documentation upon request. To discuss accommodations, I can be contacted at __." The director of elections must also make rules that provide for an alternative means of verifying the signature of people who check the box.
  • Changes requirements for custody and processing of ballots. Specifically, the bill:
    • Sets out requirements for initial count, storage, and record keeping for voted ballots.
    • Requires all ballot processing to occur in the presence of at least one other election official, and all processing be monitored by recorded video. Review of video recordings is limited to specified officials, or other parties only by court order.
    • Authorizes the Lt. Governor to promulgate rules related to ballot custody, verification audits, and final ballot reconciliation.
  • Specifies that 24-hour video surveillance of a ballot drop box must be recorded, and sets out requirements for preservation of recordings. The bill also limits review of video recordings to specified officials, or other parties only by court order.

The bill also makes amendments to areas of election law Voting Rights Lab does not track, including technological methods and reporting requirements for the counting of ballots.

This bill, as introduced February 21, 2023, would end universal mail voting in the state of Utah. Specifically, the bill would:

This bill, as enacted on March 14, 2023, changes certain rules related to voter residency requirements and procedures for uniformed and overseas voters. Specifically, the bill:

  • Allows a voter who moves within the state to remain resident for voting purposes at their previous address for 30 days after the move. Previous law provided that individuals lose their place of residence once they have established another one, with no carve-out for the period following relocation.
  • Expressly allows an individual who is homeless to establish a "non-traditional" location (including a location without a structure) as their principal place of residence for voting purposes. Previous law was silent as to residency requirements for homeless individuals.
  • Requires election officials to have "reasonable and articulable grounds" to investigate a voter's asserted residency, and specifies certain evidence that meets the standard. If the grounds are met, officials are authorized to require additional information from the voter to confirm their residence. Previous law had no comparable provision regarding the specific standard of review for residency challenges.
  • Changes the definition of a "covered voter" for the purposes of the state's Uniformed Military and Overseas Citizen Voting Act (UOCAVA). Under previous law, covered voters included only (1) uniformed or overseas voters currently registered in the state, and (2) uniformed individuals who are resident in Utah and otherwise eligible to vote. The bill alters the category to comprise voters who meet all voting eligibility requirements unrelated to residency, are not registered anywhere other than Utah, and are absent on the day of the election because they are:
    • a uniformed service voter,
    • temporarily residing outside the United States,
    • a foreign United States citizen who established residency in Utah prior to moving abroad and has not since registered or established residency in another state, or
    • a foreign United States citizen who has never registered to vote in a state other than Utah never established a principal place of residence in the United States, and whose parent, legal guardian, spouse, or domestic partner established the parent's, legal guardian's, spouse's, or domestic partner's most recent United States principal place of residence in Utah.

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2023, would end same-day registration, require voters to show photo ID to vote, sharply shorten the early voting period, eliminate drop boxes, shorten the ballot return deadline, and make other changes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • End same-day registration, both on Election Day and during early voting, by limiting the people eligible to use the service to uniformed and overseas voters.
  • Require in-person voters to show a photo ID to receive a regular ballot. People who do not show such an ID document would be given provisional ballots. Relatedly, the bill would require the state Department of Elections to enable local general registrars to create photo voter ID cards that would include the voter's signature to give to voters who would otherwise lack photo ID that included a signature. Voters would be given these IDs for free. The bill would also require the DMV to assist with the production of these IDs. Under existing law, voters have non-photo ID document options and can sign an affidavit under penalty of perjury instead of showing an ID document. Only people who do not show any accepted ID document and refuse to sign the affidavit are issued provisional ballots.

The bill would also repeal election officials' authority to offer early voting on Sundays. The bill would maintain the requirement that early voting be offered on the Saturday before Election Day.

Voters applying for a ballot by mail must include their SSN4 on their ballot application, but existing law exempts in-person voters from needing to include that information on their ballot application.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2023, would make major changes to in-person voting, mail voting, and voter registration. The bill would end same-day registration, require voters to show photo ID to vote, eliminate early voting, require voters to have an excuse to vote by mail, eliminate the state's permanent mail voting list, end curbside voting, repeal online voter registration and end pre-registration for people who are 17 years old but will be 18 by the general election, including ending their ability to vote in a primary or special election held before the general election. The bill would also make smaller changes to voter registration list maintenance. Finally, the bill would create a new process for investigating and prosecuting foreign interference in Virginia elections and impose certain requirements on voting machines, provisions Voting Rights Lab does not track.

The bill would make major changes to in-person voting. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Eliminate early voting by repealing the provisions that authorized it. Existing law allows voters to cast mail ballots in person beginning 45 days before Election Day and continuing through the Saturday before Election Day, with two Saturdays required and Sundays authorized if counties choose to offer Sunday voting.
  • Eliminate curbside voting by repealing the provisions that authorized it. Under existing law, voters who are at least 65 years old or who are disabled may vote by going to a polling place but not inside it -- election officials will bring the ballot to them.

  • Require in-person voters to show a photo ID to receive a regular ballot. People who do not show such an ID document would be given provisional ballots. Relatedly, the bill would require the state Department of Elections to enable local general registrars to create photo voter ID cards that would include the voter's signature to give to voters who would otherwise lack photo ID that included a signature. The bill would also require the DMV to assist with the production of these IDs. Finally, the bill would require that driver's licenses and state IDs issued to non-citizens have "not an acceptable voter ID" printed on them. Under existing law, voters have non-photo ID document options and can sign an affidavit under penalty of perjury instead of showing an ID document. Only people who do not show any accepted ID document and refuse to sign the affidavit are issued provisional ballots. Existing law does not provide for free photo IDs, nor does it require the voter ID language to be on non-citizen identification.

    The bill would make significant changes to voter registration, registration crimes, and voter registration list maintenance. Specifically, the bill would:


  • End same-day registration, both on Election Day and during early voting, by limiting the people eligible to use the service to uniformed and overseas voters.
  • Repeal the code provisions requiring the state to offer an online voter registration system.
  • Change voter registration at the DMV so that online transactions with the DMV do not prompt voter registration.
  • Repeal the code provisions that allow people who are 17 years old to register to vote if they will be 18 by the general election, including ending their ability to vote in a primary or special election held before the general election.
  • Increase the penalty for existing crimes relating to voting and voter registration and criminalize new conduct as felonies. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Raise the penalty for illegal voting to a Class 4 felony, up from a Class 6 felony.
    • Raise the penalty for intentionally registering to vote at more than one residence to a Class 4 felony, up from a Class 6 felony.
    • Create new registration-related crimes and make all of the Class 4 felonies. The new crimes would prohibit any person who without lawful authority (1) and with the intent to deceive, makes or alters any registration application or any record accompanying such application, (2) willfully and knowingly furnishes or possesses any registration application or related records with the knowledge or intention that it be used to deceive, (3) possesses any registration application or related record knowing it to have been stolen, or (4) in any way handles any registration application or related record for any purpose of deception.
  • Require the state Department of Elections to perform list maintenance practices that cannot be done within 90 days of a federal election to be done within 30 days before any primary or general election that does not have any federal races. Existing law has no similar requirement. In addition, the bill would require the Department to cancel duplicate registrations.

  • Revise the voter registration form to ask if anyone claims the applicant as a dependent for tax purposes, and if so, where such person lives. Relatedly, the bill would make the domicile and place of abode of the person who claims a voter registration applicant as a dependent the presumed residence of the registration applicant. This presumption could be rebutted.

    The bill would restrict mail voting by requiring voters to justify voting by mail with an excuse, and by eliminating the permanent mail voting list. Under existing law, any voter may choose to vote by mail without justifying their decision, and any voter may choose to join a list of voters who are automatically sent ballots each election. Specifically, the bill would:


  • Allow only voters with an authorized excuse to vote by mail. These people would be authorized:
    • Any registered voter who, because of work, personal business, or vacation, will be out of their county or city on Election Day.

    • Uniformed and overseas voters and their spouses.
    • Disabled, hospitalized, or pregnant voters who cannot go to the polls on Election Day because of their disability, hospitalization, or pregnancy.
    • Incarcerated voters who are awaiting trial or convicted of misdemeanors and thus retained their voting rights, provided their trial or release date is scheduled on or after the third day before Election Day. If a person is in pretrial detention and is a resident of the county in which they are confined, they can request to be taken to vote in person on Election Day if they did not have an opportunity to vote absentee or if their trial date was postponed.
    • Any person who is a member of an electoral board, registrar, election officer, or custodian of voting equipment.
    • Any registered voter who is unable to go in person to the polls because they are primarily and personally responsible for the care of an ill or disabled family member who is confined at home.
    • Any registered voter who is unable to go in person to the polls because of an obligation occasioned by their religion.
    • Any person who will be at work and commuting to and from his home and work for 11 or more hours of the 13 hours that the polls are open
    • Law-enforcement officers, firefighters, search and rescue personnel, or emergency medical services personnel,

    • People who have been granted court orders of protection.

Voters would be contacted by email, text message, or phone call, and by mail if the ballot was returned at least seven days before the election, and could submit a cure affidavit and a copy of an ID in order to have their ballot counted. Under existing law, missing signatures can be cured by providing a signature without providing ID.
    • Establish a system where mail ballot envelopes must be either notarized, or, if witnessed by someone other than a notary, include a copy of the voter's photo ID. Under existing law, mail ballot envelopes must be signed by a witness but do not need to be notarized or include a copy of an ID.
    • Change the deadline for mail ballots to receipt by the close of polls at 7 p.m. on Election Day. Under existing law, ballots postmarked by Election Day may be received until noon on the third day after Election Day.

This bill, as introduced on January 10, 2023, deals with audits, by requiring an audit of 2020 election results and creating a process for citizen-initiated audits going forward. Specifically, the bill would:

    • number of absentee ballot applications received and approved,
    • number of absentee ballots returned and canvassed,
    • number of provisional ballots of each type,
    • number of absentee ballot applications submitted by people who were not registered voters but for whom a timely voter registration application was later received,
    • number and timing of voter registration applications within 30 days of Election Day,
    • number of incidents where an absentee ballot was sent to the wrong address, was voted by a person other than the voter, and number of times an absentee ballot was returned in an unauthorized manner, and a review of actions taken in response to any of these situations,
    • review of issues with the electronic voting system,
    • review of audit logs,
    • review of changes to election equipment within 45 days before Election Day,
    • review of inconsistent treatment of absentee ballots received after the close of the polls on Election Day,
    • review of inconsistent processing of incomplete absentee ballots,
    • review of inconsistent treatment of authorized representatives and observers due to political affiliation,
    • review of issues with drop boxes, and
    • review of inconsistent treatment of absentee ballots depending on the manner of return.
  • Permit residents of a city or county to demand a forensic audit of an election by gathering a petition with at least 1,000 resident signatures within seven days after certification of election results.
    • Audits would review all materials, equipment, and procedures, be open to the public, and be conducted by "a qualified and independent third party."
    • The results of the audience would be presented to a jury of randomly selected residents, which would have the power to determine whether the election results are valid or not.
    • If the jury invalidated the election, vacancies would be filled pursuant to existing procedures.

This bill, as enacted on April 13, 2023, amends Washington's Voting Rights Act to expand who can bring enforcement actions and make other related changes. Specifically, the bill:

  • Clarifies that when a court determines if a violation of the act occurred, no single factor is dispositive or necessary. Existing law does not have a similar provision.
  • Revises and adds certain definitions:
    • Revises the definition of "polarized voting" so that case law regarding the enforcement of the federal Voting Rights Act no longer defines "polarized voting." Moreover, the new definition provides that polarized voting could be engaged in by a coalition of protected classes, not simply by a protected class.
    • Revises the definition of "protected class" to clarify that the protected class must be in the state of Washington.
    • Adds a definition of "cohesive," which is used when describing coalitions of protected classes and what they must prove.
  • Expressly authorizes coalitions, organizations, and tribes to serve as potential parties for enforcement of the act, and requires that coalitions taking enforcement action must prove the coalition as a whole is cohesive, not that each group within the coalition is cohesive. The bill also specifies that recognition of these potential plaintiffs does not eliminate the requirement for any party to establish standing under Washington law.
  • Revises remedies and the remedy process to:
    • Include as a possible remedy, if the protected class or one of the protected classes subject to alleged vote dilution is based on Indigenous status, increasing the number of elected officials on a county commission.
    • Clarify that a court may order appropriate remedies upon the stipulation of the parties, not only upon finding a violation.
    • Clarify that the court must consider remedies proposed by the parties but cannot give deference to the remedy proposed by the political subdivision.
    • Require the court, if ordering a district-based remedy, to determine that the proposed boundaries do not violate the state's voting rights act. Previous law simply required the court to approve the districts before their implementation, which the bill preserves.
  • Allows parties whose pre-lawsuit notice resulted in a court-approved remedy without a lawsuit to make a demand for reimbursement from the political subdivision of the costs for the research necessary to do the process. Reimbursement must be based on documented expenses and capped at $50,000. Previous law prohibited awarding fees or costs unless a civil action was filed and the plaintiffs prevailed.

  • Increases prevailing plaintiffs' ability to recoup costs and fees related to enforcing the act. Specifically, the bill:

    • Explicitly permits plaintiffs to recoup reasonable fees and costs for pre-litigation expenses incurred to bring the suit.
    • Deems a plaintiff a "prevailing" party if they demonstrate they succeeded in altering the political subdivision's behavior to correct a claimed harm, whether or not the lawsuit achieved relief or favorable judgment. "Altering the political subdivision's behavior" includes without limitation, adopting a new method of electing a governing body, modifying district boundaries, or amending a voting rule or qualification. Previous law had no similar provision.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 9, 2023, would attempt to protect election officials from certain types of harassment by redefining the crimes and making them felonies instead of misdemeanors if committed against election officials. In addition, the bill would provide that if an election official is a victim of one of the types of harassment they would be eligible to participate in an existing address confidentiality program. These changes build on ones enacted in 2022, which made committing cyber harassment against an election official a felony and enabled election official victims of that crime to join the address confidentiality program.

With regard to criminal harassment, the bill would redefine the crime and make it a felony instead of a misdemeanor if the victim is an election official performing official duties at the time the threat is made, or the person harasses an election official because of an action taken or decision made by the election official while performing official duties. "Election official" would include any Secretary of State staff member or county auditor staff member, whether temporary, part-time, or full-time, whose duties relate to voter registration or the processing of votes. Election official victims of the redefined crime, and any family members living with them, would be able to join the address confidentiality program administered by the Secretary of State that allows people to have a designated address in certain public records including driver's licenses. Harassment would be redefined as a person with the intent to harass or intimidate any other person, and under circumstances not constituting cyber harassment, making a communication that:

  • Uses any lewd, lascivious, indecent, or obscene words, images, or language, or suggests the commission of any lewd or lascivious act,
  • Contains a threat to inflict bodily injury immediately or in the future to the person threatened or to any other person, or
  • Contains a threat to damage, immediately or in the future, the property of the person threatened or of any other person,
  • Contains a threat to subject the person threatened or any other person to physical confinement or restraint, or
  • Contains a threat to maliciously do any other act which is intended to substantially harm the person threatened or any other person with respect to the threatened person's physical or mental health or safety, and
  • With respect to any of those communications:
    • Would cause a reasonable person to suffer emotional distress or to fear for the safety of the person threatened, or
    • Reasonably caused the threatened person to suffer emotional distress or fear for the threatened person's safety, and
    • The fear from the threat must be a fear that a reasonable election official would have under all the circumstances. Threatening words would not constitute harassment if it is apparent to the election official that the person does not have the present and future ability to carry out the threat.

The bill would also revise the crime of cyber harassment that was revised in 2022 to make it a felony if committed against an election official, defining election officials similarly as in harassment. Under the bill, a person is guilty of cyber harassment if the person, with intent to harass or intimidate any other person, and under circumstances not constituting harassment, makes an electronic communication to that person or a third party and the communication:

  • Uses any lewd, lascivious, indecent, or obscene words, images, or language, or suggests the commission of any lewd or lascivious act,
  • Contains a threat to inflict bodily injury immediately or in the future on the person threatened or to any other person,
  • Contains a threat to damage, immediately or in the future, the property of the person threatened or of any other person,
  • Contains a threat to subject the person threatened or any other person to physical confinement or restraint, or
  • Contains a threat to maliciously do any other act which is intended to substantially harm the person threatened or any other person with respect to the threatened person's physical or mental health or safety, and

  • With respect to any of those communications,

    • Would cause a reasonable person to suffer emotional distress or to fear for the safety of the person threatened, or
    • Reasonably caused the threatened person to suffer emotional distress or fear for the threatened person's safety.

The bill would also make myriad changes to other voter registration processes, and clarify challenge processes.

Regarding automatic voter registration, the bill would:

  • Require county auditors to send people whose information has been received through the automatic registration process an "automatic voter registration acknowledgment notice package." That package must include:
    • A postage-prepaid, pre-addressed return form by which the individual may decline to be registered to vote or decline the update. Relatedly, the bill repeals the requirement that a person doing an enhanced license or ID transaction at the DMV be informed that their information will be used for registration and given an opportunity to opt out of being registered.
    • A statement explaining that the person has become registered or preregistered to vote, as appropriate, setting forth the qualifications to vote and instructing the individual that if they do not meet the qualifications to return the notice and affirmatively decline in writing to register. The statement would also inform the person that if they wish to cancel their voter registration at any time, they may contact their county auditor.
    • Instructions regarding how an individual can obtain more information about the notice and assistance in the individual's preferred language.
    • An acknowledgment notice.
    • Any other information required by the secretary of state.
  • Expand and clarify the requirement that the Secretary of State or county auditors send notices "to acknowledge a voter registration transaction" to address automatic voter registration specifically. The notices would be required to be sent by first-class, nonforwardable mail:
    • after an automatic registration application and/or after a residential address change, in addition to after a "voter registration transaction". Furthermore, the notice would be newly required to include the registrant's precinct and any other information required by the Secretary.
    • by the auditor within five days of receiving an automatic voter registration, automatic registration update, or automatic reactivation of an inactive voter from the DMV. This notice would include the "automatic voter registration acknowledgment notice package." Notices for non-automatic registration transactions would be required within 60 days. Existing law does not distinguish between confirmation notices sent to automatic registration applicants and traditional applicants. Both types must be sent notices within 60 days.
  • Provide that a person's automatic registration takes effect 21 days after the transaction that led to their registration occurred, provided that the person does not decline to register. For the 15 days after the person was mailed the automatic voter registration acknowledgment notice package, their registration would be classified as "pending." If the automatic registration is for a new registration, and the person does not decline to register within 15 days of being mailed the package that includes the declination card, the county auditor must add them to the voter registration list at that time.
  • Make changes to crimes relating to automatic voter registration. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Create a new gross misdemeanor to prohibit a state or county employee tasked with assisting the public with voter registration from intentionally registering ineligible voters.
    • Eliminate a safe harbor for automatically registered ineligible voters. Specifically, the bill would repeal a provision that an ineligible person who was nonetheless automatically registered to vote and subsequently votes or attempts to vote is not guilty of a specific registration crime, unless they willfully and knowingly voted or attempted to vote knowing that they are ineligible. Nonetheless, existing law provides a different safe harbor against the crime of unqualified registration for automatically registered ineligible voters in the absence of a knowing violation.
  • Require the DMV to send the Secretary automatic voter registration information daily. Existing law merely requires "in an expedited manner."
    • If the information relates to an existing voter registration and does not change the voter's name, residence, or mailing address, the auditor would be authorized but not required to send an acknowledgment notice to the voter.
    • If the information is for a new registration or updates any element of an existing registration, the auditor would be required to update the record and, if the update affects the voter's name, residence, or mailing address, send the voter an automatic voter registration acknowledgment package within five days of the voter's registration transaction.
  • Require DMV to display information about automatic voter registration services for people applying for enhanced licenses or ID cards. The information must be visible to a person while they do their license transaction, either as a sign or a placard handed to the voter for their review. The information must be available in the various languages required of state agencies.

  • Authorize automatic voter registration to anyone applying for any government service that requires proof of citizenship for that service. The application must also include their name, residential address, mailing address if different, date of birth, and signature attesting to the accuracy of that information. Under existing law, automatic voter registration is offered to people applying for an enhanced driver's license or enhanced identification card, either of which requires proof of citizenship.

    Regarding standard voter registration processes, the bill would:


  • Create a felony by providing that a person or organization collecting voter registration forms that intentionally does not transmit the forms to an election office may be prosecuted under the felony statute prohibiting willful violation of any provision of the election code regarding the conduct of mail ballot primaries or elections. Under existing law, such people or organizations must turn in voter registration forms within five business days, but violations of that provision are not clearly punishable by the existing felony.
  • Revise the requirements for voter registration to clarify that a person must include their mailing address if it is different from their residential address and that citizenship may be proven either by attesting to it on the voter registration form or by providing citizenship proof as part of a different government transaction.
  • Expand the information that DMV must send to the Secretary of State for each person who requested voter registration to include:
    • any language preference information collected
    • any phone number and email address provided by the voter
    • digital images of documents proving citizenship, if applicable
  • Enable people who are reactivating their inactive registrations by voting to receive a regular ballot applicable to their current address. Existing law requires them to be given a regular ballot applicable to their inactive registration's address. The bill would also require the voter's registration to be updated as part of reactivating it, and would acknowledge that a person whose registration had been lawfully canceled could re-register and vote a regular ballot for their current address. Existing law does not explicitly require updates as part of reactivation and contains provisions for people whose registrations were lawfully canceled that are no longer relevant because Washington offers same-day registration.
  • Revise the maintenance of the statewide voter registration list to:
    • eliminate the requirement that it be coordinated with the administrative office of the courts, an essentially conforming change to reflect that voting eligibility is restored after release from incarceration.
    • clarify that the database must be screened against other available government databases to identify voters who are ineligible due to serving a sentence of total confinement as the result of a felony conviction or a court finding of mental incompetence. Existing law requires screening for people ineligible due to a felony conviction or mental incompetence.
    • require county auditors to allow address change information to be transferred from their system to the statewide list.
  • Require county auditors to cancel an inactive registration before the end of the normal two-general-election period when receiving information that an inactive voter died or moved out of state.
  • Clarify that designated voter registration agencies must offer voter registration services to every client 16 years or older.
  • Expand the required content of a confirmation notice to ask the voter to provide, if relevant, a new residence address for voting or information that they no longer live in the state. Existing law only requires the notice to ask the voter to confirm they continue to live at their registration address and desire to continue to use that address for voting purposes.
  • Make a voter's month and day of birth confidential, allowing only their year of birth to be included in the publicly available registration record. Existing law allows access to a voter's full birthdate.

  • Expand the definition of "Election official" pertaining to voter registration to include the staff of state agencies or offices providing voter registration services.

    Finally, the bill would revise the rules relating to challenges to a person's right to vote to:


  • Allow auditors or canvassing boards to allow voters and/or challengers to appear at hearings virtually using video telecommunications technology. Existing law requires personal appearance or affidavit testimony but does not expressly authorize virtual appearances.
  • Clarify that if a challenge is sustained on any basis other than the voter's address, the voter's registration will be canceled as well as their ballot rejected, and if the voter has moved within the state, their registration will be updated to reflect the new address and votes in any races on their ballot that the voter is eligible to vote for at the new address will count.
  • Conform challenges based on a person's felony conviction to current law restoring eligibility upon release from incarceration.
  • Clarify with cross-references the boundaries of mental incompetency- and address-based challenges, and further clarify the address-based challenge process. A person challenging a voter on the basis that the voter does not live at their registration address would no longer be required to attempt to contact the challenged voter, and it would no longer be considered evidence that a voter moved if the challenger visited the voter's residential address and contacted people there, or obtained an affidavit from a person who owns or manages the property, or is employed at that address. Evidence types would be expanded to include that the challenger searched other states' voter registration databases for the challenged voter.
  • Clarify that all challenged ballots must be resolved before the certification of the election, regardless of whether they can affect a person's vote in the particular election. Existing law required "challenged ballots" to be resolved, but the bill adds "all".

  • Make non-substantive and conforming changes throughout the election code.

    • digital images of documents proving citizenship, but only if requested by the Secretary for a specific voter.
  • Enables people who are reactivating their inactive registrations by voting to receive a regular ballot applicable to their current address. Previous law required them to be given a regular ballot applicable to their inactive registration address. The bill also requires the voter's registration to be updated as part of reactivating it, and acknowledges that a person whose registration had been lawfully canceled could re-register and vote a regular ballot for their current address. Previous law did not explicitly require updates as part of reactivation and contained provisions for people whose registrations were lawfully canceled that are no longer relevant because Washington offers same-day registration.
  • Revises the maintenance of the statewide voter registration list to:
    • eliminate the requirement that it be coordinated with the administrative office of the courts, an essentially conforming change to reflect that voting rights are restored after release from incarceration.
    • clarify that the database must be screened against other available government databases to identify voters who are ineligible due to serving a sentence of total confinement as the result of a felony conviction or a court finding of mental incompetence. Previous law required screening for people ineligible due to a felony conviction or mental incompetence.
    • require county auditors to cancel an inactive registration before the end of the normal two-general-election period when receiving information that an inactive voter died or moved out of state.
    • expand the required content of an address confirmation notice to ask the voter to provide, if relevant, a new residence address for voting or information that they no longer live in the state. Previous law only required the notice to ask the voter to confirm they continue to live at their registration address and desire to continue to use that address for voting purposes.
  • Provides that if a person submits a document proving that they are not U.S. citizens as part of a DMV transaction, the licensing agent would not offer them voter registration services. The DMV, in consultation with the Secretary of State, would determine which types of documents demonstrate non-citizenship.
  • Clarifies that designated voter registration agencies must offer voter registration services to every client 16 years or older.
  • Makes a voter's month and day of birth confidential, allowing only their year of birth to be included in the publicly available registration record. Previous law allowed access to a voter's full birthdate.
  • Creates a felony by providing that a person or organization collecting voter registration forms that intentionally does not transmit the forms to an election office may be prosecuted under the felony statute prohibiting willful violation of any provision of the election code regarding the conduct of mail ballot primaries or elections. Under previous law, such people or organizations must turn in voter registration forms within five business days, but violations of that provision were not clearly punishable by the existing felony.
  • Clarifies that an existing misdemeanor prohibiting various registration misconduct by county auditors and registration assistants also applies to the conduct of government agency employees providing voter registration services under state or federal law.
  • Expands the definition of "Election official" pertaining to voter registration to include the staff of state agencies or offices providing voter registration services.

Finally, the bill revises the rules relating to challenges to a person's right to vote to:

  • Allow auditors or canvassing boards to allow voters and/or challengers to appear at hearings virtually using video telecommunications technology. Previous law required personal appearance or affidavit testimony but did not expressly authorize virtual appearances.
  • Conform challenges based on a person's felony conviction to current law restoring eligibility upon release from incarceration.
  • Specify with cross-references the boundaries of mental incompetency- and address-based challenges, and further clarify the address-based challenge process.
  • Change how a person challenging a voter on the basis that the voter does not live at their registration address demonstrates that they exercised due diligence to verify where the voter lived. The bill eliminates the existing requirement that the challenger attempt to contact the challenged voter including by visiting the address and, if unable to contact the voter at the address, obtaining and submitting an affidavit from a person who owns or manages the property, or is employed at that address. Instead, the challenger is required, in addition to other measures required by existing law, to search the voter registration database of another state to determine if the voter is registered in any other state.
  • Provide that if a voter is challenged based on their residential address, the voter may update their registration address or re-register through the close of polls on Election Day. Previous law gave the challenged voter the same remedies, but one less day, requiring them to update or re-register by the day before the election.
  • Specify how to address a ballot from a challenged voter:
    • If a challenge is received before the voter's ballot is returned, the ballot must be held until the challenge is resolved. Previous law provided that the ballot must be treated as a challenged ballot, but did not include this specificity. If the voter has moved within the state, their registration will be updated to reflect the new address, and votes in any races on their ballot that the voter is eligible to vote for at the new address will count.
    • If a challenge is received after the voter's ballot has been returned, the challenge would not impact that ballot. However, the challenge would continue until it was resolved.
  • Specify that all challenged ballots must be resolved before the certification of the election, regardless of whether they can affect a person's vote in the particular election. Previous law required "challenged ballots" to be resolved, but the bill would add "all".
  • Specify that if a challenge is sustained on any basis other than the voter's address, the voter's registration will be canceled as well as their ballot rejected.
  • Allow county auditors to remove challenge information from their websites 45 days after the relevant election is certified, but requires auditors to retain the information for the relevant retention period and disclose it upon request. Previous law did not have a similar provision, instead addressing only posting the information on the auditor's site within 72 hours of receiving the challenge.

  • Make non-substantive and conforming changes throughout the election code.

    The February 15, 2023 amendment removed a provision from the bill that would have eliminated an existing safe harbor for automatically registered ineligible voters and removed a provision that would have classified a new, automatically submitted registration as "pending" for the 15 days after the person was mailed the automatic voter registration acknowledgment notice package.

This bill, as introduced on May 25, 2023, would require military voters to provide their military ID numbers to receive a mail ballot (called "absentee ballot" in Wisconsin) and would require municipal clerks to verify that number before counting the voter's ballot. If the voter does not include their number on their application, the clerk would be required to make a good faith effort to contact the voter to request the number. If the clerk cannot verify the number before the 4 p.m. on the Friday following the election, the military voter's ballot will not count, however, the clerk would be required to continue trying to verify the number so that the military voter can use the number to vote in future elections. Once verified, a military voter who has not moved or changed their name since providing their number would only be required to provide it every six years, rather than every election. The bill also requires the mail ballot certificate to be edited to include space for the clerk to enter their initials to indicate the ID number verification process has been completed.The bill would take effect in time for the presidential election in 2024.

Under existing law, military voters are exempt from the standard voter ID rules that apply to other voters. Those rules require non-military voters to provide a copy of photo identification to receive a ballot, unless they had previously submitted such an ID and had not moved or changed their name, or certain other exceptions apply. Leading up to the November, 2022 election, a clerk in Milwaukee fraudulently applied for military voters' absentee ballots asserting that they did so to expose a vulnerability in the system. Verification of military ID numbers would require the cooperation of the military, a federal entity.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on November 7, 2023, would make a number of election law changes, including permitting mail ballots to be canvassed early in certain municipalities, creating new felonies related to mail ballot canvassing, and changing notice requirements after a determination of incompetence. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require boards of absentee ballot canvassers, for most elections, to begin canvassing mail ("absentee") ballots the day before Election Day in municipalities that have ordinances establishing such boards. Existing law prohibits canvassing mail ballots until Election Day. The bill would also require the boards to publicly convene from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. the day before Election Day and prohibit the tallying of canvassed mail ballots until close of polls on Election Day.
  • Require the board of absentee ballot canvassers to secure specified election equipment and material with tamper-evident security seals in a double-locked location. If there is evidence of tampering, the board would not be allowed to resume canvassing until the equipment is replaced and tested.
  • Require the local clerk or local board of election commissioners to provide the county clerk or county board of election commissioners with a statement of the total number of mail ballots returned and the total number of ballots canvassed at three designated times on the day before the election and on Election Day. Existing law does not include a similar provision for reporting at specific times of day.
  • Eliminate the option of counting ballots cast at polling places at a central counting station.
  • Create a felony for acting in a manner that would give one the ability to know or provide information on the tallied results from the ballots canvassed under the bill before close of polls on Election Day.
  • Create a felony for a member of a municipal board of absentee ballot canvassers or other election official who willfully neglects or refuses to perform any of their duties required under the bill or existing law regarding canvassing absentee ballots. Under existing law, this offense is punishable by disqualification to act as an election official.
  • Require that at 10 p.m. on the night of the election, and every hour thereafter until the canvass is complete, each municipal clerk provide the county clerk with updated numbers of how many ballots have been canvassed and how many remain to be canvassed. These figures would be required to be quickly posted on the county clerk's publicly available website and on the website of the municipal board of election commissioners, if that board exists (currently, only Milwaukee has such a board).
  • Require a court to notify the Election Commission (the Commission) by email after a determination of a voter's incompetence so that the Commission can change the voter's status to inactive and place them on the ineligible voter list. The Commission would have three business days to make the change. The bill would also provide that if a court reviews a determination of incompetency and restores the voter's right to vote, the court should email the Commission, which would then have three business days to notify the voter that they have regained their eligibility and must re-apply to vote to register. An appointed guardian of an ineligible voter would be required to report a change of address to the court within three days, and the court would immediately be required to email the Commission. Existing law does not include provisions imposing deadlines on the court or the Commission following changes in a voter's eligibility status.

A previous version of the bill contained several provisions that were amended out on November 7, 2023. Those provisions would have:

  • Prohibited any local clerk who has lawfully reported (or is believed to have reported) election fraud or irregularities from being discharged, disciplined, demoted or discriminated against.
  • Required the Commission to verify the citizenship of all voters on the official registration list as soon as practicable using information from the Department of Transportation.

This bill, as introduced on October 31, 2023, would address an array of voting and election issues, including automatic voter registration, voter intimidation and suppression, polling place postings, the election manual, a voter bill of rights, and the withholding of voluntarily-provided voter information. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create automatic voter registration at the DMV. Automatic voter registration is not available under current law. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require the Elections Commission (the Commission) and the Department of Transportation (the Department) to enter an agreement allowing the Department to transfer specified personally identifiable information to the Commission. The Commission would be required to maintain the confidentiality of information it receives.
    • Require the Commission to obtain the full name of each individual issued a driver's license or state ID as well as their date of birth, license or identification number, address history, proof of citizenship and a statement from the Department indicating that it verified their citizenship. Under the bill, there would be an initial transfer of information of all people whose information is already on file and the Department would continue to transfer information to the Commission at least monthly.
    • Require the Commission to enter the name of an individual on the registration list if it concludes that they are eligible but not registered to vote.
    • Require the Commission to mail a notice advising that a person has been registered and that they may request to have their name removed from the registration list and how to do so. Under the bill, the notice must be in English, Spanish and any other language spoken by a significant number of residents.
    • Require that a notice of removal be sent to a voter if the Commission removes their name from the register without their request to do so, unless the person's death is verified.
    • Permit a person to file a request with the Commission to exclude their name from the registration list.
    • Require the Commission to report to the appropriate legislative standing committee on its progress in implementing the registration system by July 1, 2025. The report would also be required to include an assessment of the feasibility and desirability of adding more registration agencies, including the following departments: Health Services, Children and Families, Workforce Development, Revenue, Safety and Professional Services, and Natural Resources. The list would also include the University of Wisconsin System, the Technical College System Board, and technical colleges.
  • Change criminal and civil enforcement for offenses related to voter intimidation and suppression. Under existing law, it is a Class I felony to use or threaten force to compel a person to vote, refrain from voting, or vote for or against a particular candidate or issue. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Create a Class D felony for intentionally preventing a person from voting or registering to vote in an election by providing them false information. Under the bill, a victim of this offense may bring an action for injunctive relief in the circuit court of the county where the alleged violation occurs. The Commission would be required to create a report of any complaints of deceptive election practices and post a copy on its website.
    • Create a Class E felony for knowingly attempting to prevent or deter another person from voting or registering to vote based upon "fraudulent, deceptive or spurious" grounds. Under the bill the violation includes challenging another person's right to register or vote based on knowingly false information as well as attempting to prevent a person from registering or voting by providing them false information.
  • Change requirements for polling place postings. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Permit the Commission to authorize (in writing) alternative means of providing notice to voters of the information that must be posted if the alternative is at least as effective as posting. Under existing law, materials must be positioned so that they are readily observed by voters waiting in line or entering the polling place.
    • Require the local clerk and board of election commissioners in jurisdictions that are federally required to provide voting materials in a language other than English to contact and coordinate with organizations that advocate for the rights of people who speak that language. The bill would also require notices to be provided in that language and that the jurisdiction "endeavor to ensure" at least one elected official at each polling place speaks that language.
    • Subject any local clerk or executive director of a board of elections commissioners who fails to ensure compliance with this provision to no more than a $500 per violation.
  • Change requirements to the election manual. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require that the manual be written in clear and unambiguous language, indexed by subject, and contain specific examples of common problems at polling places on election day and procedures for resolving them. Current law requires the election manual to be written so as to be understood by the general public.
    • Require that the manual include explanations on procedures for a variety of polling place issues.
    • Subject any local clerk or executive director of a board of elections commissioners who fails to ensure compliance with this provision to of no more than a $500 penalty per violation. Existing law does not include a similar provision.
  • Create a voter bill of rights that local clerks and boards of election commissioners would be required to post at each polling place. The list would include a voter's right to:
    • Vote if registered and eligible to vote.
    • Inspect a sample ballot before voting.
    • Cast a ballot if in line when the polling place closes or, if voting by in-person absentee ballot on the last day for which such voting is allowed, when the municipal clerk's office closes.
    • Cast a secret ballot.
    • Get help casting a ballot if disabled.
    • Get help voting in a language other than English as provided by law.
    • Get a new ballot, up to three ballots in all, if the voter makes a mistake on the ballot.
    • Cast a provisional ballot as provided by law.
    • Have the voter's ballot counted accurately.
    • Vote free from coercion or intimidation.
    • Report any illegal or fraudulent election activity.
  • Require local clerks to withhold the telephone number and email address of a voter from public inspection.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on October 23, 2023, would address an array of voting and election issues, including automatic voter registration, voter intimidation and suppression, polling place postings, the election manual, a voter bill of rights, and the withholding of voluntarily-provided voter information. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create automatic voter registration at the DMV. Automatic voter registration is not available under current law. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require the Elections Commission (the Commission) and the Department of Transportation (the Department) to enter an agreement allowing the Department to transfer specified personally identifiable information to the Commission. The Commission would be required to maintain the confidentiality of information it receives.
    • Require the Commission to obtain the full name of each individual issued a driver's license or state ID as well as their date of birth, license or identification number, address history, proof of citizenship and a statement from the Department indicating that it verified their citizenship. Under the bill, there would be an initial transfer of information of all people whose information is already on file and the Department would continue to transfer information to the Commission at least monthly.
    • Require the Commission to enter the name of an individual on the registration list if it concludes that they are eligible but not registered to vote.
    • Require the Commission to mail a notice advising that a person has been registered and that they may request to have their name removed from the registration list and how to do so. Under the bill, the notice must be in English, Spanish and any other language spoken by a significant number of residents.
    • Require that a notice of removal be sent to a voter if the Commission removes their name from the register without their request to do so, unless the person's death is verified.
    • Permit a person to file a request with the Commission to exclude their name from the registration list.
    • Require the Commission to report to the appropriate legislative standing committee on its progress in implementing the registration system by July 1, 2025. The report would also be required to include an assessment of the feasibility and desirability of adding more registration agencies, including the following departments: Health Services, Children and Families, Workforce Development, Revenue, Safety and Professional Services, and Natural Resources. The list would also include the University of Wisconsin System, the Technical College System Board, and technical colleges.
  • Change criminal and civil enforcement for offenses related to voter intimidation and suppression. Under existing law, it is a Class I felony to use or threaten force to compel a person to vote, refrain from voting, or vote for or against a particular candidate or issue. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Create a Class D felony for intentionally preventing a person from voting or registering to vote in an election by providing them false information. Under the bill, a victim of this offense may bring an action for injunctive relief in the circuit court of the county where the alleged violation occurs. The Commission would be required to create a report of any complaints of deceptive election practices and post a copy on its website.
    • Create a Class E felony for knowingly attempting to prevent or deter another person from voting or registering to vote based upon "fraudulent, deceptive or spurious" grounds. Under the bill the violation includes challenging another person's right to register or vote based on knowingly false information as well as attempting to prevent a person from registering or voting by providing them false information.
  • Change requirements for polling place postings. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Permit the Commission to authorize (in writing) alternative means of providing notice to voters of the information that must be posted if the alternative is at least as effective as posting. Under existing law, materials must be positioned so that they are readily observed by voters waiting in line or entering the polling place.
    • Require the local clerk and board of election commissioners in jurisdictions that are federally required to provide voting materials in a language other than English to contact and coordinate with organizations that advocate for the rights of people who speak that language. The bill would also require notices to be provided in that language and that the jurisdiction "endeavor to ensure" at least one elected official at each polling place speaks that language.
    • Subject any local clerk or executive director of a board of elections commissioners who fails to ensure compliance with this provision to no more than a $500 per violation.
  • Change requirements to the election manual. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require that the manual be written in clear and unambiguous language, indexed by subject, and contain specific examples of common problems at polling places on election day and procedures for resolving them. Current law requires the election manual to be written so as to be understood by the general public.
    • Require that the manual include explanations on procedures for a variety of polling place issues.
    • Subject any local clerk or executive director of a board of elections commissioners who fails to ensure compliance with this provision to of no more than a $500 penalty per violation. Existing law does not include a similar provision.
  • Create a voter bill of rights that local clerks and boards of election commissioners would be required to post at each polling place. The list would include a voter's right to:
    • Vote if registered and eligible to vote.
    • Inspect a sample ballot before voting.
    • Cast a ballot if in line when the polling place closes or, if voting by in-person absentee ballot on the last day for which such voting is allowed, when the municipal clerk's office closes.
    • Cast a secret ballot.
    • Get help casting a ballot if disabled.
    • Get help voting in a language other than English as provided by law.
    • Get a new ballot, up to three ballots in all, if the voter makes a mistake on the ballot.
    • Cast a provisional ballot as provided by law.
    • Have the voter's ballot counted accurately.
    • Vote free from coercion or intimidation.
    • Report any illegal or fraudulent election activity.
  • Require local clerks to withhold the telephone number and email address of a voter from public inspection.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on November 15, 2023, would make a number of election law changes, including permitting mail ballots to be canvassed early in certain municipalities, creating new felonies related to mail ballot canvassing, changing notice requirements after a determination of incompetence, establishing whistleblower protections for local clerks, and requiring citizenship verification by the Elections Commission. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require boards of absentee ballot canvassers, for most elections, to begin canvassing mail ("absentee") ballots the day before Election day in municipalities that have ordinances establishing such boards. Existing law prohibits canvassing mail ballots until Election Day. The bill would also require the boards to publicly convene from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. the day before Election Day and prohibit the tallying of canvassed mail ballots until close of polls on Election Day.
  • Require the board of absentee ballot canvassers to secure specified election equipment and material with tamper-evident security seals in a double-locked location. If there is evidence of tampering, the board would not be allowed to resume canvassing until the equipment is replaced and tested.
  • Require the local clerk or local board of election commissioners to provide the county clerk or county board of election commissioners with a statement of the total number of mail ballots returned and the total number of ballots canvassed at three designated times on the day before the election and on Election Day. Existing law does not include a similar provision for reporting at specific times of day.
  • Eliminate the option of counting ballots at a central counting station.
  • Change the timeline for the sending of mail ballots. Under existing law, ballots must be sent no later than the 47th day before most elections (or within one business day, if not received by the 47th day). Under the bill, ballots would not be required to be sent until the 21st day before the election for non-UOCAVA voters.
  • Create a felony for acting in a manner that would give one the ability to know or provide information on the tallied results from the ballots canvassed under the bill before close of polls on Election Day.
  • Create a felony for a member of a municipal board of absentee ballot canvassers or other election official who willfully neglects or refuses to perform any of their duties required under the bill or existing law regarding canvassing absentee ballots. Under existing law, this offense is punishable by disqualification to act as an election official.
  • Require a court to notify the Election Commission (the Commission) within one business day after a determination of a voter's incompetence so that the Commission can change the voter's status to inactive and place them on the ineligible voter list. The bill would permit a person to vote again upon presenting documentation that a court has restored their right to vote or permit the voter to cast a provisional ballot if they are unable to present such documentation. The Commission would have no more than one business day to change the voter's status back to active on the official registration list and remove them from the ineligible voter list. An appointed guardian of an ineligible voter would be required to report a change of address to the court within 10 business days, and the court would have one business day to notify the Commission. Existing law does not include provisions imposing deadlines on the court or the Commission following changes in a voter's eligibility status.
  • Require the circuit court clerk to notify the county clerk or board of election commissioners and the elections commission of any prospective juror whose returned juror qualification form indicates they are not qualified for jury service due to residence or citizenship status. The bill would also require the Commission to remove a prospective juror from the voter registration list and send notice to them and the district attorney or attorney general of the commission's action if it is determined that they are not qualified to vote.
  • Prohibit any local clerk who has lawfully reported (or is believed to have reported) election fraud or irregularities from being discharged, disciplined, demoted or discriminated against.
  • Require the Commission to verify the citizenship of all voters on the official registration list as soon as practicable using information from the Department of Transportation.

  • Prohibited any person from distributing a mail ballot application by any means, unless requested by a voter.
  • Created a new misdemeanor offense for violating the prohibition.

This bill, as enacted on March 9, 2023, shortens the period for early voting both in person and by mail, by prohibiting clerks from distributing mail ballots more than 28 days before an election for all voters other than UOCAVA voters. Under previous law, clerks were permitted to distribute mail ballots to all voters, for voting in person or by mail, up to 45 days before an election. The bill also amends provisions of election law not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, including technological requirements for electronic voting systems and rules for the counting of ballots.

Last Updated February 20, 2024

VRLANALYSIS:

  • Require the absentee ballot manager to allow voters who receive the notice to cure any of these defects no later than the last business day before Election Day:
    • Voter failed to sign the affidavit
    • Voter address on the affidavit does not match the address on the ballot application
    • Order of envelopes is incorrect

    • Voter failed to note their reason for voting absentee

Last Updated February 19, 2024

This bill, as amended on April 2, 2024, would:

  • Allow voters who have moved to a new address in a different precinct to travel to the correct precinct for their current address and cast a provisional ballot that permits the voter to update their address immediately. Election officials who direct a voter to a new polling location may give the voter a pass that will limit their wait time at the new precinct.
  • Allow voters who assert that they are at the correct polling location to cast a provisional ballot. Election officials may challenge the provisional ballot and state their grounds for their belief the voter is ineligible to vote at that location.

Last Updated April 5, 2024

This bill, as enacted on May 15, 2024:

  • Expands the list of offenses deemed crimes of "moral turpitude" that result in disenfranchisement, to include:

    • Compelling street gang membership
    • Aggravated stalking
    • Domestic violence in the first and second degrees
    • Domestic violence by strangulation or suffocation
    • Elder abuse

Last updated May 21, 2024.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 6, 2024, would create mandatory early in-person voting opportunities for all registered Alabama voters. Existing law does not provide early in-person voting available to all registered voters. The bill would:

  • Require early voting centers to be open at least four days but no more than six days in the week immediately preceding Election Day. Each county would have the option to determine which days the early voting center would be open.
  • Require early voting centers to be open from 9 A.M. to 5 P.M. on weekdays and Saturdays, and from 1 P.M. to 5 P.M. on Sundays.

Last Updated February 19, 2024

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 6, 2024, would create no-excuse absentee voting to allow any registered voter to apply for and cast an absentee ballot. Existing law limits eligibility for absentee voting to voters who meet one of a few statutory criteria. The bill would make conforming changes to the form of the absentee ballot affidavit to remove requirements for a voter to note their reason for voting an absentee ballot.

Last Updated February 19, 2024

This bill, as enacted on May 15, 2024:
