    • Distributes the material within 90 days of an election
    • Intends the distribution to harm the reputation or electoral prospects of a candidate, and intends the distribution to deceive voters and to influence their voting patterns
  • Exempts conduct from the criminal offense if the media contains a disclaimer; constitutes satire or parody; or was distributed by certain broadcasting providers in certain circumstances.
  • Creates a civil right of action for a permanent injunction against the prohibited conduct. An action may be brought by:
    • The attorney general
    • An individual depicted in the media
    • A candidate for office who has been injured by the deceptive media

Last Updated February 27, 2024

HISTORY: {"date":"02/22/2024","summary":"To HOUSE Committee on CONSTITUTION, CAMPAIGNS AND ELECTIONS","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 22, 2024, would create new requirements for processing provisional and mail ballots that are improperly marked and cannot be read by the ballot counter during the vote canvass. Existing law has no express provisions concerning provisional and mail ballots that cannot be read by counters. For these ballots, the bill would:

  • Require the canvassing board to attempt to determine the voters choice on the ballot.
  • Require that if the voters choice can be determined by the canvassing board and is approved by the probate judge present, the improper ballot be marked as spoiled, and a new ballot completed properly reflecting the voters choice.
  • Require that if it is impossible to determine the voters choice, the ballot must not be counted.

Last Updated March 19, 2024

This bill, as enacted on March 20, 2024, creates new restrictions on the mail ballot application process, and new related criminal offenses. The bill:

  • Expressly prohibits individuals from returning a completed mail ballot application on behalf of someone else, unless they have been designated to do so by a voter who requires emergency treatment by a physician within five days of an election. Prior law provided for return by the applicant, but did not expressly state that third party return of an application was prohibited.
  • Creates a new Class A misdemeanor for violations of the prohibition against returning a mail ballot application on behalf of a voter.
  • Prohibits the distribution of mail ballot applications with any field pre-filled other than selecting the election for which the application is intended to apply.
  • Prohibits giving or receiving payment or gifts in exchange for distributing, requesting, collecting, prefilling, completing, obtaining, or delivering another voter's mail ballot application. Prior law contained no such prohibition.
  • Creates a new Class B felony for making prohibited payments for handling mail ballot applications, and a Class C felony for receiving prohibited payments.
  • Specifies that a voter who requires assistance to vote due to blindness, disability, or inability to read or write may receive assistance from another individual of their choosing other than their employer, an agent of their employer, or an agent or officer of their union. Under prior law, voters were permitted to receive assistance from an individual of their choosing, if the voter and the witness signed the application themselves. The bill leaves this general provision in place, alongside the new restriction for voters with disabilities.
  • Modifies the requirements for the mail ballot application form by:
    • Prohibiting officials from accepting handwritten applications other than the official form, as was permitted by prior law.
    • Specifying that all information needed to complete the enumerated fields is required to be provided by the voter. Prior law required that the form contain certain fields but did not explicitly require that they all be completed for an application to be accepted.
    • Requiring applicants to certify that they have not been convicted of a disenfranchising crime or, if they have, that their voting rights have been restored.
    • Specifying that the voters signature on the application is given under penalty of perjury.
  • Exempts voters using the process established by the Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act from the above restrictions.

A previous version of the bill contained provisions that were amended out before enactment. These provisions would have:

  • Imposed the same restrictions on the return of mail ballots that the bill applies to mail ballot applications, with violations being a Class A misdemeanor.
  • Authorized certain family members, household members of at least six months, certain election officials, and certain parties related to probate court to request, apply for, and return mail ballots and mail ballot applications on behalf of the voter.

Last Updated March 25, 2024

This bill, as introduced on February 29, 2024, would modify the process for restoration of voting rights after a criminal conviction, for individuals released from custody or supervision before October 1, 2024. Under existing law, all disenfranchised individuals must apply for a Certificate of Eligibility after meeting the requirements for restoration, and must present the Certificate to then register to vote. The bill would:

  • Require the Board of Pardons and Paroles and the secretary of state to develop a form for individuals released or pardoned before October 1, 2024, to request review of their eligibility for restoration and to make the form available online.
  • Require the board to post online the name of every individual whose right to vote has been restored and the county in which they were last registered or in which they resided.
  • Require the board to provide the secretary of state with the address and date of restoration for every individual whose right to vote has been restored, and require the secretary to then notify the relevant registrar of the date of restoration.
  • Require the registrar to add the individual's name to the poll list if that individual was previously registered, and notify the individual that they are eligible to vote.

Last updated on March 22, 2024.

This bill, as introduced on February 29, 2024, would facilitate restoration of voting rights after disenfranchisement for a criminal conviction, by eliminating the existing application-based process and instead requiring state review of eligibility upon release or pardon. Under existing law, individuals must apply for a Certificate, by no specific procedure, upon release from incarceration, probation, or parole, or receiving a pardon, and show that they (1) have no pending state/federal felony charges, and (2) have paid all court-ordered financial obligations. If granted, these voters must present the Certificate to a registrar to register to vote. The bill would:

  • Eliminate the application process to receive a Certificate of Eligibility for restoration, and instead require officials to review an individuals eligibility for restoration upon release from custody or supervision, or grant of a pardon. The bill would also require officials to develop a form for individuals released or pardoned before October 2024 to request review of their eligibility, and to make the form available online.
  • Eliminate the requirement that restored individuals present a Certificate of Eligibility to a clerk to register, and instead provide that if an applicant meets the restoration criteria, (1) previously registered individuals are deemed eligible to vote, and (2) individuals without prior registration are permitted to do so.
  • Establish that if the Board of Pardons and Paroles cannot verify that an applicant has met one of the restoration criteria, it must be deemed as met.
  • Require, among the criteria for restoration, that an individual must have paid an amount equal to all fines, costs, fees, and restitution ordered by the court. Existing law requires that an applicant has paid these assessments.
  • Require the Board to issue its initial draft report on applications within 30 days of making its review, rather than within 30 days of receiving an application as required under existing law.
  • Expressly require that if state review for restoration results in a denial of eligibility, the notice issued to the individuals must include information about measures the applicant must take to meet the criteria. The bill also specifies that notice must be provided within 14 calendar days. Existing law states only 14 days.
  • Include convictions in foreign courts in provisions relevant to disenfranchisement and restoration. While existing law provides for disenfranchisement for a conviction in foreign country that would constitute a qualifying offense under state law, the existing restoration provisions only expressly address convictions in state and federal courts.
  • Permit restoration of voting rights for individuals convicted of impeachment and subsequently pardoned, if the pardon specifically provides so. Under existing law, both treason and impeachment are exempted from the general rule that allows for restoration after a pardon where specifically provided for.
  • Make conforming and non-substantive changes to various provisions to reflect the new requirements.

Last updated on March 25, 2024.

This bill, as introduced on February 29, 2024, would remove certain offenses from the list of convictions resulting in disenfranchisement. Under the bill, the following crimes would no longer be considered crimes of moral turpitude and therefore conviction of those crimes would no longer disqualify someone from voting:

  • Trafficking in cannabis, cocaine, or other illegal drugs
  • Burglary
  • Theft of property
  • Robbery
  • Forgery

Last updated on March 13, 2024.

HISTORY: {"date":"01/22/2024","summary":"Additionally referred to HOUSE Committee on RULES","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 10, 2024, would authorize the expansion of the early voting period, change procedures related to vote centers, and make minor changes to mail ballot return locations, emergency early voting, mail ballot elections, and provisional voting. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Authorize the expansion of the early voting period and provide for use of vote centers and ballot drop-off centers for early voters. The bill would:
    • Expand the availability of early voting by permitting county recorders to offer early voting during the three days immediately preceding an election. Early voting would be required to end by whatever time is necessary to allow for updating voter records to reflect all requested mail ballots ('early ballots'), voted mail ballots, and inactive voters, by Election Day. Under existing law, early voting ends on the Friday before an election.
    • Authorize the use of vote centers during early voting, by the same county board resolution process applicable to their use for Election Day voting. Under existing law, early voting must be available at the county recorder office only, and recorders may designate additional locations as needed.
    • Permit county boards to authorize local election officials to establish 'early voting drop-off centers' in addition to designated polling places, where any voter in the county may deliver a completed mail ballot to a ballot custodian. Existing statutory law provides for drop-off locations for ballots in special district mail ballot elections, and the current Elections Procedures Manual permits local officials to offer drop-boxes in regular elections.
    • Authorize local officials to make changes to approved early voting locations, and require notice to the public and county board 'as soon as is practicable.' Existing law is silent as notice of changes to early voting locations.
  • Change various general requirements concerning vote centers. The bill would:
    • Specify that authority related to establishing and operating vote centers includes 'officers in charge of elections,' as well as county recorders. While the current Elections Procedures Manual refers to the 'officer in charge of elections,' existing statutory law refers specifically to county recorders.
    • Deem vote centers as 'polling places' subject to all applicable requirements as such, and deemed them ballot replacement locations for mail ballot elections.
    • Require county boards to appoint a voter center election board for each location, and set out requirements for staff consistent with those applicable to designated polling places.
  • Provide that emergency voting procedures are available between the Friday and Monday before an election if early voting has ended in the county, to reflect the bill's provision for in-person early voting on the three days before Election Day. Under existing law, emergency procedures are available between 5 p.m. on Friday and 5 p.m. on Monday before an election, as in-person early voting ends on Friday.
  • Make minor changes to replacement ballot procedures in special district mail ballot elections. The bill would:
    • Require local officials to provide one or more locations in the appropriate jurisdiction for voters to get a replacement mail ballot. Existing law requires the county recorder to provide only one ballot replacement center in a central location.
    • Eliminate the requirement that a voter can only obtain a replacement ballot if their original ballot was lost, spoiled, destroyed, or not received, and instead require only a sworn statement that the ballot was not cast.
  • Expressly allow voters casting a provisional ballot to place the completed ballot in the ballot box. Existing law specifies that an election official must place the ballot into the box.

Last Updated February 8, 2024

HISTORY: {"date":"01/22/2024","summary":"Additionally referred to HOUSE Committee on RULES","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 10, 2024, would create automatic voter registration, create same-day voter registration, revise standard voter registration processes, extend the early voting period, empower Native Americans in siting voting locations on their lands, and give mail voters more time to return their ballots. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create automatic voter registration at the DMV for every person who provides proof of U.S. citizenship during the course of applying for, renewing, or correcting a driver's license or state identification, updating their residence address or name, or obtaining a duplicate, reissuance, or replacement of a driver's license or state ID. Existing law forbids automatic voter registration. In creating automatic voter registration, the bill would:
    • Require the DMV to electronically transmit at least the eligible voters' name, residence address or location, date of birth, and signature to the Secretary of State to register or update the registration of such people.
    • Require the Director of the DMV and the Secretary, after consulting with all county recorders, to adopt rules to implement the system.
    • Require the Secretary to evaluate implementing automatic voter registration at other agencies, specifically including the Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System Administration. Such agencies would be required to have, or acquire, the ability to collect and transmit electronic signatures. The Secretary would be authorized to designate additional agencies as automatic voter registration agencies, and once designated, an agency would not be able to lose that designation.
    • Require all automatic voter registration agencies, including DMV, to accept Tribal identification numbers and nontraditional residential addresses, including addresses that can be identified by mile markers, or geographic or other identifying features. Automatic voter registration agencies would be required to transmit voter registration to the Secretary on the day it was received by the agency. The Secretary would promptly re-transmit the data to the appropriate county recorders, after removing the information of individuals in the address confidentiality program, or who the Secretary has information indicating the individual is not eligible to register.
    • Require county recorders, on receipt of voter registration information from the Secretary, to determine if the person is already registered, and if so, whether their registration is inactive or needs updating. If the registration information is the same but the registration is inactive, the recorder would make the registration active. If the person is not registered, the county recorder would determine if the information received includes enough to register to vote. If the information is insufficient, the recorder would send the potential voter an incomplete registration notice explaining what more is needed and a postage-prepaid return form. If the person completes their registration by the close of polls on Election Day and the recorder confirms their eligibility, the registration would be effective from the date the information was collected by the source agency. For each eligible person who is not registered or needs their registration updated, the recorder would register them or update their registration, and send the person a nonforwardable automatic voter registration notice.
    • Require the automatic voter registration notice to include an explanation of voter eligibility requirements, a statement that if the person should decline registration using the enclosed form and postage prepaid return envelope if they are not eligible, a statement of the penalties for false registration, and assurance that a decision to decline will be confidential and that the identity of the source agency will be confidential as well. The return form would be required to enable the individual to decline registration, join the permanent mail voting list (called "active early voting list" in Arizona), and affiliate with a political party. If an already registered voter is affiliated with a party, the automatic process would not change their affiliation unless the voter indicates the change on the form. The notice would also include information about the address confidentiality program.
    • Protect people from prosecution for false registration simply for failing to return the opt-out form by redefining, and thus narrowing, the felony.
    • Protect people from prosecution for the felony of illegal voting by providing a person must vote or attempt to vote knowing that they are not eligible to vote. In addition, if a voter's registration is processed as valid by the state, the registration would be presumed to have been officially authorized and the person would not be subject to penalty.
    • Provide that for the fourteen days after a recorder mails an individual an automatic voter registration notice, the person is considered a pending registrant. If the person does not opt out using the return form, their registration will take effect. Pending registrants are allowed to vote regular ballots in any election occurring in the 14-day window for opting out.
    • Require the DMV to report to the Secretary annually on the program and require the Secretary to publish the information on the Secretary's website. The DMV and any other source agency would be required to publish information about the program on their websites and post signage in their locations.
  • Create same-day registration on Election Day and during early voting. Existing law specifically prohibits same-day registration. Under the system created by the bill:
    • Eligible people would be able to prove residency to register with any in-person voter ID document that includes their name and current address, a government check, paycheck, or another government document that shows the name and current address of the voter, or a student identification card for an educational institution in this state.
    • The Secretary of State, after consulting with all county recorders, would establish in the Elections Procedures Manual a verification process for voters who register on or close to Election Day to ensure efficient eligibility verification can happen at a voting location.
    • Voters who engage in same-day registration will cast regular ballots unless their registration has not been verified. Voters whose registration is not confirmed on the spot would cast ballots that would count if their ineligibility is not confirmed by the end of provisional ballot processing.
    • Voters not affiliated with a political party would be allowed to participate in a presidential primary by affiliating with that party at the voting location.
    • The registration process would be prohibited from being more restrictive or burdensome than the standard voter registration process.
  • Revise standard voter registration processes. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Repeal the requirement that a person is a resident of Arizona 29 days before the election.
    • Revise registration at the DMV (called Department of Transportation in Arizona) to provide that a person who reports a change of residential or mailing address or a change of name, and who in the same transaction does not provide documentation of non-citizenship, would be offered an opportunity to register to vote. The updated name and/or address information would be transmitted to the Secretary of State, who would then send the information to the appropriate county recorder only if the relevant individual is already registered to vote. Existing law provides this opportunity to people applying for driver's licenses or renewals only.
    • Revise online voter registration to require the system to allow a person to register or update their registration without a driver's license or state ID, and with any proof of U.S. citizenship that is valid under Arizona law. Moreover, the system must accept nontraditional residential addresses. These rules would apply to online registration offered by any agency. Existing law does not require online voter registration, but the service is offered by the Secretary of State's office.
    • Revise the voter registration form to inform applicants that if they do not provide the required documentary proof of citizenship they will be eligible to vote in federal races only. The existing form states that applications not accompanied by documentary proof of citizenship will simply be rejected.
    • Change the rules relating to inactivating a voter's registration so that failure to respond to an address confirmation mailing does not result in inactivation. Additionally, the bill would repeal existing law's requirement that a voter who fails to respond to such a mailing must provide affirmation or confirmation of their address to vote.
    • Add as a method of providing documentary proof of citizenship an official notification from any government agency in Arizona that the agency has received such proof for the voter registration applicant.
    • Clarify that people who registered to vote before December 8, 2004, are deemed to have provided satisfactory proof of citizenship and do not need to resubmit such proof. This clarification reflects the Arizona law before the enactment of laws in 2022 that created ambiguity about whether such registrants needed to provide such documentation. The bill would also clarify that proof of registration in another Arizona county could be proof of citizenship.
  • Create new rules for siting polling places on Native land. Specifically, when determining precinct boundaries, polling places, vote centers, early voting locations, and hours, the county board of supervisors or officer in charge of elections in each county would be required to notify all Tribes within the county, allow the tribes to participate in the process, and cooperate and coordinate all aspects of the determinations with the Tribes. For each election, at least one precinct and one polling place, vote center, or early voting location on the lands of each Tribe in the county at a location selected by the Tribe unless the Tribe certifies it has no members in the county. The chosen locations must be accessible to voters on at least a temporary basis, and if not, the officer in charge of elections must provide alternative voting procedures for voters unable to access the location. The bill would create a special cause of action and related procedures to enforce these rules. Existing law does not have comparable provisions.
  • Expand the early voting period until 5 p.m. on the day before Election Day, provided that voting locations will close sooner if necessary to revise precinct registers and other election materials for Election Day use. Under existing law, early voting ends at 5 p.m. on the Friday before Election Day.
  • Change rules relating to returning mail ballots (called "early ballots" in Arizona). Specifically, the bill would:
    • Allow more time for voters to return their mail ballots by allowing them to be postmarked by the close of polls on Election Day and received within five business days after a general election that includes a federal office and three business days for any other election. Existing law requires mail ballots to be received by election officials by the close of polls on Election Day. The bill would make a conforming change to the cure period for such ballots.
    • Prohibit requiring an ID or any other requirement to return a mail ballot in person that is not required to return it by mail.

  • Repeal disenfranchisement for individuals convicted of a felony offense.
  • Expand the early voting period by moving the end of the period from 5 p.m. on the Friday before an election, to 5 p.m. on the Monday before. While the bill would not expressly require early voting hours during the weekend before Election Day, existing law permits local election officials to offer weekend voting. The bill would also repeal the provision that provides for emergency early voting between the last Friday and Monday before an election, as the general deadline for all voters would now be Monday.
  • Remove the specific requirement that a voter must make a request by 5 p.m. on the eleventh day before an election to receive a mail ballot ("early ballot") for delivery by mail. Under the bill, only the calendar day would be left in place as the deadline.
  • Expressly require the county recorder to establish on-site early voting locations at the recorder's office and elsewhere, as prescribed in the current Elections Procedures Manual. Existing statutory law permits, but does not require, in-person early voting.
  • Expressly permit county recorders to count a mail ballot voted in-person without conducting signature verification, if the voter presented the required ID to receive the ballot. Existing law requires signature verification for all mail ballots, regardless of whether they are voted in person or returned by other methods.
  • Expressly provide for notice and cure procedures for voters who return a mail ballot with a missing signature. While such a procedure is currently required under the state's Elections Procedures Manual, statutory law requires notice and cure for an inconsistent signature only.
  • Expand the category of voters who can request personal delivery of a mail ballot, to include those who are physically confined and in pre-trial detention. Existing law only allows those who become ill or "become a person with a disability" to request personal ballot delivery.
  • Require the secretary of state to allow a "limited number" of international observers to observe any statewide or federal election. Existing law has no comparable requirement.
  • Require, rather than permit, the county recorder to provide voters with the opportunity to update their voter registration at any on-site early voting location.
  • Require that if a county recorder determines that a provisional ballot voter is not properly registered to vote, the information from the ballot must be used to register the individual for subsequent elections. This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2024, would change the rules for election contests to expand the grounds to file contests, expand allowed discovery, delay a hearing, and require appeals to be directly heard by the Arizona Supreme Court. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Expand the grounds for election contests on account of illegal votes to include votes in which the chain of custody is broken and early votes that have inconsistent signatures or personal information. Although existing law does not directly address inconsistent signatures as a ground for an election contest, the issue has been raised in such litigation.
  • Expand discovery dramatically. Under existing law, parties have a general right to inspect ballots, which in recent contests has involved samples of all the voted ballots. The bill would expand the right to inspection and other discovery rights by:
    • Providing that the parties to the contest have the right to physically examine all physical ballots and physical ballot images, any early ballot envelopes, and voters' registration records. The court would be required to allow "ample time to the parties for a thorough examination of these materials" and would be forbidden from restricting the examination in any manner.
    • Provide that the parties have the right to "full discovery on any matter that could pertain to the election in any way." The court would further be required to liberally construe parties' discovery rights, and the parties themselves would be required to "make every attempt not to limit discovery." Existing law has no similar provisions.
    • Allow each party the right to depose up to 10 people. The election contest code has no similar provision.
    • Clarifying that an organization or entity can be deemed by a party as the person to inspect ballots as existing law currently allows and that "person" could provide a rotating series of individuals to do the ballot inspection.
  • Delay a hearing on the contest by requiring it to happen not later than 20 days after the contest was filed, rather than the 10 days after that existing law provides.
  • Require any appeals of an election contest trial to be filed directly with the Arizona Supreme Court within 10 days after the final trial judgment issues, with a response filed within five days, and a reply within three days after that. The Court would then schedule a hearing within five days of full submission of the papers, and would be required to render a decision within five days after that. Under existing law, appeals are made to the lower appellate court first.

Last updated on January 15, 2024.

    • Four election officers appointed by the Secretary of State, not more than two of which may be members of the same political party.

The report would be made to the Governor, the Arizona Senate President, the Arizona Speaker of the House, the chairs of the respective Senate and House committees with jurisdiction, and the Secretary of State. The report would be due on or before January 1, 2025, and each year thereafter.

This bill, as enacted on February 9, 2024, shortens the cure period for mail ballots, codifies existing signature verification procedures, creates an ID-based ballot verification process as an alternative to signature verification, extends the early voting period by two hours, and makes other changes to election administration. Specifically, the bill:

  • Changes the timing for the curing of a signature defect on a mail ballot for elections held in 2024, 2025, and 2026. For a primary, general, or special election involving a federal office, the cure period is now five calendar days, instead of five business days as under prior law. For all other elections in those years, the cure period is three business days. The bill also requires the county recorders office to be open on the Friday and the weekend before and after a primary, general, or special election involving a federal office.
  • Enacts into statute the signature verification process for mail ballots that is currently in place under the authority of the Arizona secretary of states signature verification guide. Under the bill:
    • A person verifying a mail ballot must manually examine the broad characteristics of a signature at first, and if discrepancies appear, then examine the more specific local characteristics. The process would then be repeated if discrepancies continue to be found.
    • Officials must reject an electronic signature that uses a typed font.
    • An exact match is unnecessary, and evaluators need not examine broad and local characteristics one at a time.
  • Creates a new alternative to signature matching verification for mail ballots, beginning in 2026, under which a voter may present a valid form of identification when returning a mail ballot and the ballot is deemed ID Verified. Such ballots would not require signature verification in order to be counted. The bill also makes several conforming changes throughout various provisions to reflect the new ID option.
  • Requires the county recorder or other election official in charge of elections to provide daily updates to the political parties entitled to continued representation on the state ballot of a list of all voters whose mail ballots have been rejected due to signature issues. The bill also requires daily updates of voters who voted with a conditional provisional ballot.
  • Sets new deadlines for canvassing certain elections. Under prior law, counties were required to complete their canvass between six and twenty days after the election. Under the bill, the requirement is completion by not later than the second Monday after a primary election and the third Thursday after a general election, with no flexibility in either case to postpone the canvass to account for missing returns. The secretary of state is required to complete its canvass by no later than the third Thursday after a primary election and the third Monday after a general election, with no flexibility to postpone canvassing a general election to account for missing returns. The timing for a city, town, or school district to canvass an election remains at between six and twenty days after the election.
  • Changes the timeline for verifying that a provisional voter did not vote elsewhere or by mail ballot. For a general, primary, or special election with federal offices on the ballot, the deadline is changed from 10 days after the election to five days. For all other elections, the deadline shifts from five business days to three business days.
  • Extends early in-person voting by two hours. Under prior law, in-person early voting concluded at 5 p.m. on the Friday before an election. Under the bill, voting hours are extended to 7 p.m. The bill makes a conforming change to the timeline for emergency voting.
  • Requires the Department of Administration to coordinate with state agencies and counties to provide state-owned facilities for use as a voting location when requested by the officer in charge of elections.

The bill also makes changes in areas of law not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, including changes to the process of generating sample ballots for primary elections, and requirements for recounts and results reporting.

While not expressly requiring the state to withdraw from the Electronic Registration Information Center (ERIC), the bill's provisions would likely prohibit the state from remaining a member. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Prohibit the state or any political subdivision, through the end of 2025, from being a member of any multistate voter registration list maintenance organization that requires the sharing of confidential voter information, including drivers license or Social Security numbers. Beginning in 2026, if the secretary of state intends to join such an organization, the secretary would be required to submit the plan to the appropriate committee of the legislature for approval and provide public notice. The secretary would also not be permitted to join such an organization if it required as a condition of membership to conduct a voter registration program not specifically authorized by Arizona law.
  • Prohibit the state or any political subdivision from joining any organization that "imposes any duty on this state" not required by state law, including the mailing of registration forms to eligible residents.

Last updated April 1, 2024.

HISTORY: {"date":"03/07/2024","summary":"Additionally referred to SENATE Committee on RULES","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on February 28, 2024, would eliminate no-excuse mail ballot voting and in-person early voting, eliminate the use of regular and emergency vote centers, and shorten the period to cure mail ballot defects, among other changes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Eliminate no-excuse mail voting, and limit voting by mail to only:
    • Students attending school out of state, with documentation
    • Voters temporarily residing out of state, with documentation
    • Voters traveling out of state on Election Day, with documentation
    • Elderly voters and voters with a disability
    • UOCAVA voters
  • Eliminate in-person early voting. Existing law requires elections officials to offer in-person early voting at each county recorder's office during the period when mail ballots are available, and permits officials to operate additional locations at their discretion.
  • Prohibit the use of vote centers and emergency vote centers, by eliminating existing provisions that grant local officials the authority to do so.
  • Expressly prohibit officials from using vote centers, in-person early voting locations, or 'another similar method of voting,' and expressly require that all in-person voting take place at precinct polling locations with ballots that have been printed before delivery to the location.
  • Prohibit the consolidation of election precincts based on early voter turnout, by eliminating the existing authority for local officials to do so. The bill would also eliminate the existing authority for establishing emergency vote centers.
  • Shorten the period to cure mail ballot issues, by moving the deadline to two business days after Election Day. Under existing law, voters have until five calendar days after a primary, general, or special election that includes a federal office to cure mail ballot issues, and until the third business day otherwise.
  • Move the start date to begin sending mail ballots to voters earlier, from at least 27 days before an election to at least 34 days before.
  • Move earlier the start date for counties to begin the election canvass, to no later than 12 days after Election Day. Under existing law, the canvass for a primary election must begin no later than the second Monday after the election, and canvass for a general election must begin no later than the third Thursday following Election Day. The bill would also require the secretary of state to canvass state elections no later than 14 days after Election Day. Under existing law, the secretary must canvass a primary by the third Thursday following the election, and a general election by the third Monday after Election Day.

Last Updated March 4, 2024

HISTORY: {"date":"02/07/2024","summary":"Held in HOUSE Committee on MUNICIPAL OVERSIGHT AND ELECTIONS","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as introduced on January 11, 2024, would propose a referendum to amend the state's statutory provisions regarding signature verification of mail ballots. The proposed provisions would set out express requirements for verification that match the guidelines set out in the secretary of state's 2020 Signature Verification Guide, including specific guidance for matching 'broad' and 'local' signature characteristics. Existing statutory law requires officials to verify that a mail ballot signature is 'consistent' with the voter's signature on file, but does not specify criteria for verification.

Adoption of the proposed statutory provisions would require approval of the referendum by a majority of voters at the next general election.

Last Updated February 2, 2024

HISTORY: {"date":"05/09/2024","summary":"Additionally referred to SENATE Committee on RULES","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as amended by the Senate Committee on Elections on March 18, 2024, would propose a referendum to amend statutory provisions to:

  • Eliminate no-excuse mail voting. Under the proposed provision, eligibility to vote by mail ballot would be limited to the following voters:
    • 65 years of age or older
    • Residing outside the state and enrolled in a college or university outside the state
    • Absent uniformed services or overseas voters under federal law
    • Active duty military members and their families not covered under the federal UOCAVA law
    • A person with a disability
  • Require counties with populations of over 500,000 to open precinct-based polling places with no more than 1,000 registered voters in each precinct. Under existing law, which the resolution would leave in place for all other counties, officials may choose to open countywide voting centers in lieu of precinct polling places, and there is no statutorily prescribed precinct size.
  • Shorten the in-person early voting period by moving the start date from the 27th day before an election to the 11th day before. The last day of early voting would continue to be the Friday before an election.
  • Expressly allow in-person early voting by voters who already requested mail ballots, from the Tuesday before Election Day until the end of early voting, and via the emergency voting process on the Monday before Election Day.
  • Make conforming changes throughout the code, including changing the terminology for mail voting from "early voting" to "absentee voting."

Adoption of the proposed statutory provisions would require approval of the referendum by a majority of voters at the next general election.

A previous version of the resolution contained provisions that were amended out of the current version. These provisions would have:

  • Eliminated in-person early voting. Under existing law, all voters may cast ballots in person prior to Election Day.
  • Eliminated all use of vote centers. Under existing law, in addition to specifically designated polling places, county boards of supervisors are authorized to establish vote centers where any voter in the county may cast a ballot.

Last Updated July 9, 2024

This resolution, as amended on June 15, 2024, would propose a referendum to create new restrictions on foreign funding of election administration and create new reporting and enforcement provisions. Specifically, the resolution's proposed changes would:

  • Prohibit any government entity from using money or in-kind goods or services donated by a foreign government or any foreign nongovernmental source for election administration.
  • Prohibit giving, accepting, or using money or in-kind goods or services contributed by a foreign government or nongovernmental source to influence the outcome of an election or a ballot measure.
  • Require vendors supplying election-related services to certify under penalty of perjury that they have not received donations from a foreign source. Entities would be required to submit documentation quarterly, and the secretary of state would be required to monitor compliance and post certifications on the agency website.
  • Create a new misdemeanor offense for knowingly failing to provide an accurate initial or updated certification.
  • Create a civil right of action for the attorney general or any qualified elector and any state official to enforce the new certification requirements.

Final enactment of the changes proposed by this legislative resolution would require passage by the current session of the legislature, and subsequent approval by a majority of voters at the next general election.

Previous versions of the bill contained additional provisions that were amended out of this version. Those provisions would have:

  • Expanded the existing prohibition of private funds for election-related purposes to include in-kind goods and services. Existing law prohibits any city, town, county, school district, or other public body from receiving or expending private money for preparing for, administering, or conducting an election (including registration).
  • Required local officials to perform on-site tabulation of all ballots cast at polling locations during early voting and on Election Day, beginning in 2026. The only exception to the requirement would have been provisional, misread, or write-in ballots.
  • Increased restrictions on the return of a completed mail ballot to a polling place. Beginning 2026, the resolution would have:
    • Required all voters returning a completed mail ballot at a polling place on Election Day to present an accepted form of voter ID, and to have their ballot tabulated on site. The resolution would also have eliminated the use of affidavit envelopes for mail ballots requested in-person at a voting site.
    • Moved the deadline earlier for the deposit of completed mail ballots to polling places, from 7 p.m. on Election Day to 7 p.m. on the Friday before Election Day. If a county board designated the recorder's office as an emergency voting location, mail ballot delivery would have also been permitted at that location on the Saturday, Sunday, and Monday before the election.

Last Updated August 20, 2024

This bill, as introduced on January 8, 2024, would require the Secretary of State and each county recorder to post on their websites a list of all events where they or their staff attend and provide voter registration services within 24 hours after the event. The bill would require the post to include (at minimum) the event's location, title, and all affiliated organizations. Existing law requires events to be listed within 24 hours but does not specify minimum information to be included or that the requirement applies to events attended by staff.

Last Updated January 9, 2024

This bill, as introduced on January 8, 2024, would change third-party distribution requirements for mail ("early") ballot applications and permanent mail voting list applications as well as modify certain signature matching requirements. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Permit only a political party, a county recorder, or an election official to distribute, collect, and return mail ballot applications or permanent mail voting list applications. Under the bill, certain special taxing districts would be exempt from these restrictions. Existing law authorizes candidates, political committees, or organizations to distribute, collect, and return the forms.
  • Prevent a voter's signature from being the sole exemplar used for comparison, including ballot verification, if the signature is on a pre-printed request to revise a voter's registration or apply for a mail ballot and the pre-printed form is not an official one. Existing law does not have a similar limitation.

Last Updated January 8, 2024

Governor Hobbs vetoed this bill on April 23, 2024. As passed by the legislature, it would have specified procedures for poll watchers and observers. Specifically, the bill would have:

  • Specified requirements for challengers during observation of mail ballot processing. Existing law provides only for the number of challengers and sets out procedural requirements for making a challenge. The bill would have:
    • Limited challengers to approaching only as close to proceedings as "reasonably necessary" to perform their function.
    • Required that challengers raise questions directly to the senior election official on site.
    • Required challengers to be registered voters in the state.
    • Prohibited candidates from serving as challengers.
  • Specified requirements for challengers and party representatives at in-person voting locations. Existing law provides only for the number of observers allowed and prohibits challengers from entering a voting booth (other than to mark their own ballot). The bill would have:
    • Permitted parties to appoint representatives to be present at voting centers, as well as precinct places as allowed by existing law.
    • Permitted observers to be present at all polling places in the county where they were designated.
    • Permitted observers to be present during set-up and close out of the voting location.
    • Prohibited observers from interacting with voters.
    • Prohibited candidates from serving as challengers.
    • Limited observers to approaching only as close "reasonably necessary" to perform their function, and required questions be raised directly to the senior election official on site.
  • Specified requirements for observers at vote counting centers. The bill would have:
    • Permitted, during a general election only, a candidate for federal office to designate an observer to be present at vote counting centers. Existing law permits only representatives of each political party and the public to observe the vote counting process.
    • Required observers to be registered voters in the state.
    • Limited observers to approaching only as close "reasonably necessary" to perform their function, and required questions be raised directly to the senior election official on site.
  • Made non-substantive changes to terminology in various provisions.

Last updated on May 14, 2024.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on February 27, 2024, would prohibit in-person early voting, end no-excuse mail voting, and eliminate the use of voting centers, expressly requiring that all in-person voting be conducted at precinct locations. The bill would also significantly tighten voter ID rules, among other changes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Eliminate in-person early voting and the use of voting centers at which all voters in a county can cast a ballot. All in-person voting would be required to be conducted on Election Day at the voter's specific precinct.
  • End no-excuse mail voting, by limiting mail ballots to UOCAVA voters, voters who are temporarily residing outside the state, and students attending school outside the state.

Under existing law, a voter who does not possess an approved form of unexpired photo ID may prove their identity through two alternative documents, including utility bills, vehicle registrations, and other documents bearing their name and address. This bill would require each voter to present a photo ID in order to vote without exception, and would repeal laws permitting a voter without ID to vote a provisional ballot.
  • Require election workers to post the precinct voter tally into a publicly viewable database upon completion of the count.
  • Eliminate the authority of public school principals to deny a request for their school to be used as a polling place, by repealing the existing provision that grants this discretion.
  • Require all ballots to contain "ballot fraud countermeasures,' including the use of colored and/or fluorescent threads.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 22, 2024, would create same-day registration and automatic voter registration at the Department of Transportation (DMV). Under existing law, both registration processes are prohibited. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create same-day registration on Election Day and during early voting. Eligible people would complete a voter registration form and be allowed to vote a provisional ballot in any election other than a partisan primary. Twenty-nine or more days after registering, the voter would be allowed to participate in partisan primaries and could vote a regular ballot in all elections. If registering on Election Day, the person would be required to provide proof of residence.
  • Generally allow registration during the 28 days before Election Day, provided that a person registering in that window of time can only vote a provisional ballot until an election 29 or more days after the person registered. Under existing law, registration closes 29 days before Election Day.
  • Create automatic voter registration at the DMV for anyone applying for a driver's license or state ID or the renewal or update of either. The DMV would give the applicants' information to the relevant county recorders, who would in turn mail notices to the applicants of their registration and the process to decline registration. If a person does not decline within 21 days of the notice's mailing, that person would be registered to vote.
  • Revise two election felonies to provide that a person who is not qualified to register to vote but who unknowingly becomes registered through the automatic voter registration process did not commit either crime.

HISTORY: {"date":"02/05/2024","summary":"Additionally referred to SENATE Committee on RULES","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 29, 2024, and entitled "The Arizona State Voting Rights Act," would provide protections from unequal access to voting and political participation based on a voter's race, income level, gender, disability, national origin, language ability, age, sexual orientation, or religion. The bill would:

  • Declare that members of the protected classes mentioned above are entitled to an equal opportunity for voting and political participation as that enjoyed by all other voters. The bill would prohibit the implementation of laws or rules impairing the rights of the protected classes.
  • Provide members of the protected classes and organizations composed of such members standing to seek enforcement of the act's provisions in court.
  • Define "covered political subdivisions" as subdivisions in which two percent of the population or 4,000 people of voting age are members of a single language minority and speak English "less than very well." If a political subdivision includes a tribal nation, the two percent analysis is applied to the tribal nation.
  • Require covered political subdivisions to provide voting materials (including registration forms, ballot applications, instructions, and ballots) and notices in each covered language.
  • Require each covered political subdivision to provide at least one election official at each voting location that speaks each covered language.
  • Subject covered political subdivisions to a $5,000 fine for each affected voter for failure to comply with the provisions of the act.
  • Prohibit the state or any political subdivision from implementing any procedure that provides any of the protected classes of equal opportunities for voting and political participation.
  • Create a rebuttable presumption that any regulation that impairs the participation of a protected class within the 90 days before an election is a violation of the act's provisions and allows members of the protected class to seek judicial relief.
  • Authorize courts to provide additional voting hours or days, additional voting locations or methods, voter education, or the restoration of names to the voting rolls when necessary to remedy regulations that unlawfully impair the rights of voters in the protected classes.


Last Updated September 5, 2025

HISTORY: {"date":"03/12/2024","summary":"Additionally referred to HOUSE Committee on RULES","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as engrossed on March 6, 2024, would newly require public disclosure of active voters' names, addresses, birth years, and precinct numbers, before and after each general election, as well as ballot images and related information. Some exceptions would apply to people in confidentiality programs, precincts with fewer than 25 voters, UOCAVA voters, and voters with visual impairments. Existing law does not have similar requirements, but does have rules for sharing voter registration list data that are more restrictive than the bills provisions, some of which may apply to the data the bill would disclose. The bill would also provide two additional days to file election contests.

Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the county recorder to send a list of the names, home addresses, years of birth, and precinct numbers of every eligible registered voter, active or inactive, to the secretary of state at least 10 days before a general election. The secretary would be required to create a website on which the information must be posted immediately, in a convenient downloadable format. Voters participating in address confidentiality programs or living in a precinct with 25 or fewer registered voters would not have their information disclosed, but would be included in the total number of voters in a precinct. Under existing law, precinct voter lists for Election Day use must be prepared at least 10 days before Election Day and made available to state and county political party chairs eligible to request them. Those lists contain the same information as shared by the bill, plus mailing addresses, phone numbers, party affiliation, date of registration, occupation if given, four years of voting history, and all data relating to early voting, including ballot requests and returns.
  • Require the county recorder or other officer in charge of the election, no later than 48 hours after the delivery of the official county canvass, to send the secretary for immediate posting on the same website for all precincts with more than 25 registered voters:
    • The same information for the people who voted in the election. For precincts with 25 registered voters or fewer, the total number of voters would be included.
    • Unaltered images of all ballots used in the tabulation of the election. An adjudicated or duplicated ballot image would be sent together with the original ballot image. These images would be suppressed in a precinct with 25 or fewer registered voters, but the total number of images would be included. Exceptions to this requirement would also be made for UOCAVA voters and for voters who use a large-format or braille ballot.
    • The cast vote record in a sortable format. Only the total number of cast vote records would be included for a precinct with 25 or fewer registered voters. "Cast vote record" would be defined as the electronic records available within an election management system that show how the votes were cast on each anonymous ballot for each race and that allow for verification of the accumulated vote totals for each candidate or issue together with a summary report for each batch for counties whose election management system does not tie images of electronically adjudicated ballots to underlying original ballot images. For precincts with 25 registered voters or fewer, the number of cast vote records would be included.
  • Require any person wishing to access the secure website and download the voter and voting information to provide the secretary:
    • Their name, address, email address, phone number, and proof of identity.
    • A declaration signed by the person stating that the person will not use the information for commercial purposes, alter the images in information in any manner, or use the information or images for voter intimidation.
  • Prohibit commercial use of the newly public data or intentional alterations of images or information received under the bill, and create a new felony offense for violating the prohibition. Existing law provides that the voter information in the precinct voter lists, and more generally, information derived from registration forms, may be used only for purposes relating to (1) political party activity, a political campaign, or an election, (2) for revising election district boundaries, or (3) for any other purpose specifically authorized by law, and may not be used for a commercial purpose. Existing law also restricts the redistribution of voter data. Specifically, any person in possession of a precinct register or list, in whole or part, or any reproduction of a precinct register or list, shall not permit the register or list to be used, bought, sold, or otherwise transferred for any unauthorized purpose. Moreover, existing law prohibits a person in possession of information derived from voter registration forms or precinct registers from distributing, posting, or otherwise providing access to any portion of that information through the internet. Violation of these existing provisions is a felony offense under current law.
  • Prohibit election officials from altering or adding voter data as part of a security measure.
  • Protect the secretary, county recorder, or other officer in charge of elections from liability for any personally identifying information, handwritten statements, and other notations made or provided by the voter that are included in the ballot images.
  • Allow the filing of an election contest within seven days after the completion of the canvass to file election contests. Under existing law, contests must be filed within five days.

This bill, as introduced on January 29, 2024, would automatically restore voting rights to people disenfranchised by felony convictions upon their completion of probation or absolute discharge from the Department of Corrections or absolute discharge from prison in another state, or federal prison. Under existing law, automatic restoration of voting rights is only available to first-time offenders who have completed probation or have been absolutely discharged and, in either case, have fully paid restitution. This bill, as amended on February 8, 2024, would make extensive modifications to rules for the acceptance of mail ballots and the certification of election results, among other changes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Change the timing for the curing of a signature defect on a mail ballot. Under existing law, ballots must be cured no later than the fifth business day after the election. Under the bill, this would be shortened to the fifth calendar day. The bill would require the county recorder's and city or town clerk's office to be open on the weekend before and after a primary, general, or special election involving a federal office.
  • Enact into statute the signature verification process for mail ballots that is described in the Arizona Secretary of State's signature verification guide. The bill would require a person verifying a mail ballot to "manually" examine the "broad characteristics" of a signature at first, and if discrepancies appear, then examine the more specific "local characteristics." The process would then be repeated if discrepancies continue to be found. The bill would also require that an electronic signature that uses a "typed font" be rejected.
  • Create a new process under which a person, beginning in 2026, may present a valid form of identification when returning a mail ballot. A ballot returned in this manner would be considered "ID Verified" and would not require signature verification in order to be counted. The bill would make several conforming changes to statute to reflect this.
  • Prohibit early election boards and recorders from accessing an aggregate complete results file or from producing a report of aggregate results before Election Day. These officials would only be permitted to produce a partial results report to internally prepare for a hand count audit or for logic and accuracy testing. Results, whether complete or partial, would not be permitted to be released until the earlier of all precincts reporting or one hour after polls close on Election Day. The relevant officer would be required to post all system log files on its website within 48 hours of the completion of tabulation to prove compliance with these rules.
  • Require a county recorder to count the number of early ballots returned on Election Day and post that number on their website with the last unofficial results released on election night. Under existing law, a county recorder is only required to do this if practicable.
  • Require the county recorder or other election official in charge of elections to provide daily updates to the political parties qualified for continued representation on the state ballot of a list of all voters whose mail ballots have been rejected due to signature issues.
  • Set new dates for canvassing certain elections. Under existing law, counties must complete their canvass between six and twenty days after the election; this would change to not later than the second Monday after a primary election and not later than the third Thursday after a general election, with no flexibility in either case to postpone the canvass to account for missing returns. The secretary of state would be required to complete its canvass no later than the third Thursday after a primary election and no later than the third Monday after a general election, with no flexibility to postpone canvassing a general election to account for missing returns.
  • Require a county to send official returns to the secretary of state after a primary election on the 13th day after the election instead of the 14th day as under current law. The bill would also require returns for all primary and general elections to be sent by both electronic and physical means and permit the secretary of state to initiate a canvass with the electronic copy if it contains verification that a physical copy has also been sent.
  • Impose a 24-hour deadline after the last county canvass is received for the secretary of state to certify to a court the facts showing that a recount is required.
  • Permit a partial hand count to begin before an electronic tabulation during a recount has been completed. Under existing law, the partial hand count occurs after electronic tabulation. The secretary of state would also be required to conduct logic and accuracy testing of automatic tabulation equipment to be used in a recount within two calendar days of a court's order for a recount.
  • Change the timeline for verifying that a provisional voter did not vote elsewhere or by mail ballot. For a general, primary, or special election with federal offices on the ballot, the deadline would be changed from ten days after the election to five days; for all other elections, it would shift from five business days to three business days.
  • Extend early in-person voting by two hours. Under existing law, in-person early voting concludes at 5 p.m. on the Friday before an election. Under the bill, this would be extended to 7 p.m. The bill would make a conforming change to the timeline for emergency voting.
  • Shift the date of the 2024 primary election to July 30.
  • Require the department of administration to coordinate with state agencies and counties to provide available and appropriate state-owned facilities for use as polling places.

  • Adjust petition signature requirements to be based on the number of qualified voters in the jurisdiction as of October 1st in the previous year, rather than January 2 of the current year as under existing law.

    The bill also makes changes in areas of law not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, including changes to the process of generating sample ballots for primary elections and deadlines for determining which parties are entitled to continued representation on state ballots.

Existing law includes various criminal offenses for use of threats of force to influence voting, and possession of a firearm or unauthorized presence of uniformed individuals near a polling place.     • Voting or attempting to vote
    • Urging or aiding any person to vote

    • Their status as a past or present participant in the administration of elections
  • Establishes a legal presumption that a person is engaging in voter intimidation if they are openly carrying a firearm or imitation firearm while observing or interacting with the specified election-related activities or interacting with or observing a person due to their status as a past or present participant in the administration of elections.
  • Creates a new civil right of action for individuals, election officials, and the attorney general, for violations of the provisions, with remedies of equitable relief or money damages.

  • The nature of the changes or updates or the reason for cancellation

The in-person voter check in and voting process would be changed to use the technology, including having a voter attach a vote tracking number to their completed ballot before depositing the ballot in a ballot box. For mail voters, the bill would require election officials to notify each voter upon receipt of the completed mail ballot, and when the voter responded confirming their ballot, the official would then attach a vote tracking number to that mail ballot. If the voter did not respond to the official's contact, their ballot would be rejected. Only ballots with vote tracking numbers could be counted.

This bill, as enacted on May 31, 2024:

  • Requires county officials to establish, at minimum, one day of in-person voting for confined voters on any day between the 15th and 4th day before Election Day at the county jail or detention center. The bill requires in-person voting to be available for at least six hours. Prior law permitted eligible incarcerated individuals to vote by mail, but had no requirement for in-person early voting at detention facilities.
  • Requires county sheriffs to designate at least one individual to facilitate voting for incarcerated voters at county and local detention centers and require the designee to coordinate with the county clerk and recorder. Prior law required only that the county clerk and recorder "make efforts" to coordinate with the sheriff or designee to facilitate voting.
  • Specifies certain duties of the county sheriff's designee. Those duties include:
    • Ensuring that notice of the date and time of in-person voting is provided to confined individuals and that they may register to vote during in-person voting.
    • Ensuring that confined individuals who wish to verify or change their voter registration or register to vote have reasonable access to the resources to do so.
    • Establishing a location at the county jail or detention center for incarcerated voters to return their mail ballots, which must be collected by a team of bipartisan election judges. The bill requires the designee to provide incarcerated voters with information regarding methods for returning ballots, deadlines, and where in the jail ballots must be returned.
    • Establishing a process for incarcerated voters to have the opportunity to cure a deficiency on their mail ballots.
  • Creates a new civil penalty for a sheriff or designee failing to comply with the provisions for coordinating voting at county jails or detention centers, in the amount of $5,000 per violation.
  • Requires the secretary of state to create training materials to be used by county clerks and recorders to provide training and assistance for staff facilitating the voting process at detention facilities.

A previous version of the bill included a provision that was amended out prior to enactment. This provision would have created a new misdemeanor offense for detention officials failing to carry out their duties related to in-person voting at facilities.

Last Updated July 17, 2024

This bill, as enacted on June 6, 2024, expands drop box availability on college campuses, modifies requirements for requesting emergency replacement ballots, authorizes voters who have not met state residency requirements to cast provisional ballots in presidential elections, lowers the age for pre-registering to vote from 16 to 15 years old, and makes a number of other minor changes to election law. Specifically, the bill:

  • Expands drop box availability by requiring each county to establish a drop box on each campus of an institution of higher education located in that county that has 1,000 or more enrolled students. Prior law required drop boxes on the campuses of state institutions having at least 2,000 enrolled students. The bill also repeals a provision for determining the number of students enrolled in an institution of higher education that was applicable during the COVID-19 pandemic.
  • Authorizes county officials to request a waiver from the secretary of state exempting their county from existing drop box collection requirements. Under the bill, if the waiver is approved the clerks must arrange for the collection of ballots by a bipartisan team of poll workers from all exempt drop box locations once they are open at least once each week after the initial mailing of ballots.
  • Makes minor changes to requirements for "emergency voting." Under prior law, voters could request a replacement ballot for emergency voting if they are unable to vote in person on Election Day due to (1) their confinement, or that of an immediate family member, to their residence or a hospital on Election Day, or (2) emergency conditions, such as a natural disaster, arising after the deadline when ballots are mailed. These emergency ballots were required to be requested before 5 p.m. on Election Day, and returned by 7 p.m. that day. The bill:
    • Removes the requirement that emergency replacement ballots be requested by 5 p.m. on Election Day. The bill does not specify a new request deadline, leaving in place only the requirement that the ballot be returned by 7 p.m.
    • Specifies that for a voter to be eligible due to an immediate family member's confinement to a hospital or place of residence on Election Day, they must require the voter's "care or constant presence." The bill also specifies that for emergency conditions, such as a natural disaster, emergency voting is available if eight or fewer days before Election Day the voter is unable to vote in person because of the event.
    • Expands eligibility to voters who, on Election Day (1) are members of a religion that forbids secular activity, or (2) are employed as a first responder, member of law enforcement, or healthcare worker, and are unable to leave their work location or unable to return to their residence county.
  • Permits a registered voter who will not have been a Colorado resident for at least 22 days prior to a presidential general election to cast a provisional ballot that enables them to vote in the presidential election only. Previous law included a general 22-day residency requirement for voters.
  • Lowers the age for an individual to pre-register to vote from 16 to 15 years old. The bill also repeals a provision that allows pre-registered 17-year-olds to vote in a primary election or presidential primary election if they will be 18 by the upcoming general election.
  • Specifies that the county clerk and recorder are the chief election officials for counties and requires them to set operational hours for their respective offices. Previous law did not expressly include similar declarations.
  • Requires the secretary of state to administer a pilot program allowing county election officials in counties with 10,000 to 37,500 active voters and that meet certain eligibility requirements to request a waiver of the requirement to designate at least three voter service and polling centers on Election Day, and instead designate two.
  • Requires the secretary of state to approve or deny applications from political subdivisions to purchase new electromechanical voting systems within 30 days of receiving applications.

The bill also includes provisions not covered by the Voting Rights Lab, including provisions related to appropriations, audits, candidate nominations, campaign practices, party committees, presidential electors, removal of county election judges by political parties, ranked choice voting, and recounts.

Last Updated July 11, 2024
