This bill, as enacted on June 6, 2024, makes numerous changes to election law, including new requirements for requesting a mail ballot, increased security measures for drop boxes, minor changes to mail ballot processing, later deadlines for designation of early voting locations, increased criminal and civil penalties for misconduct towards voters and election workers, and new routine voter list maintenance procedures. Specifically, the bill:

  • Changes various procedures related to requesting a mail ballot. The bill:
    • Requires that applications for replacement mail ballots be completed only by the voter themselves and that replacement mail ballots only be provided in person to the voter or mailed directly to the voter at their designated mailing address.
    • Requires mail ballot applications to include the year for which the application's use is authorized and prohibits distribution, use, and acceptance of forms not authorized for use in the current year. Prior law did not require that applications be made for use exclusively in a given year.
    • Prohibits local officials from providing more than five mail ballot applications at a time to any individual more than 90 days prior to the issuance of mail ballots. Prior law contained no such limitation.
    • Expands assisted access to mail ballots by permitting a voter who is a patient in a nursing home within six days of the close of polls of an election to appoint a designee to deliver their ballot to them. Prior law limited the use of designee to voters who are unavailable due to unforeseen illness or physical disability or in a hospital.
    • Limits removal of a voter from the state's limited permanent mail voting list following annual address confirmation mailings, to only those voters whose notice is returned as undeliverable. Under prior law, removal was also required if a voter failed to affirmatively respond to the notice.
  • Creates new requirements for security and operation of drop boxes. The bill:
    • Requires each municipality to make daily video recordings of all drop boxes starting from the first day of issuance of mail ballots through the end of the election. Recordings must be publicly available as soon as practicable, and in no case later than five days after Election Day. Prior law had no comparable requirement.
    • Authorizes the secretary of state to adopt regulations concerning the use, placement, positioning, and recording of secure drop boxes.
    • Requires the municipal clerk to retrieve mail ballots from drop boxes at the close of each election, in addition to each weekday as required prior law.
  • Makes minor changes to requirements for processing mail ballot applications and completed ballots. The bill:
    • Requires local officials to use the statewide centralized voter registration system when checking mail ballot applications or returned ballots against registered voter lists. Prior law contained no such requirement.
    • Requires that if any voter returns more than one mail ballot, the ballot received latest must be counted and any other ballots rejected. Prior law generally required counting of the latest mail ballot issued to a voter (for UOCAVA voters, officials were required to count the ballot with the latest postmark).
    • Requires local election officials to note on outer envelopes of each returned mail ballot the method by which the ballot was returned and to provide a report after each election to the secretary of state. Prior law did not require officials to track how mail ballots are received.
  • Moves deadlines for finalizing early voting locations closer to the day of elections. Under the bill, local officials must certify proposed locations to the secretary of state at least 60 days before any primary or election, and the secretary must approve or disapprove proposals at least 45 days before. Prior law required proposals be submitted at least 120 days before a regular election or primary (20 days before a special election or presidential primary), and determinations be made at least 90 days prior (11 days before a special election or presidential primary).
  • Prohibits the presence of individuals other than voters casting their votes, election officials, and unofficial checkers, at designated polling places and locations for early voting, same-day registration, and ballot counting. Prior law had no comparable provision.
  • Expands criminal and civil penalties related to misconduct against voters and election workers. The bill:
    • Expands the existing class D felony offense for influencing or attempting to influence a voter to "stay away from any election," with the intent of disenfranchising the voter. Under the bill, prohibited conduct also includes influencing a voter to "otherwise refrain from voting," and expressly applies to voting by mail, at a drop box, or in person at all voting locations.
    • Expands the existing class C felony for willfully and fraudulently suppressing or destroying any vote or ballot, to expressly include any vote given or cast by mail, deposit in a drop box, or in person at all voting locations.
    • Creates a new class C felony offense for influencing or attempting to influence, by force, threat, or harassment, any election worker in the performance of any election-related duty.
    • Creates a new class A misdemeanor offense for any individual who, with intent to terrorize, alarm, or improperly influence any election worker in the performance of their duties, publicly discloses personal identifying information about that election worker.
    • Creates new civil rights of action for election workers to enforce the prohibitions set out in the new criminal offenses.
  • Requires new periodic voter list maintenance procedures. The bill:
    • Requires the secretary of state to review the voter list at least annually to identify voters who are registered in more than one or town or registered more than once in the same town, and to submit a list of potentially duplicative registrations to the relevant local clerks. Prior law permitted, but did not require, the secretary to review the list at their discretion for voters registered in more than one town, and to notify local clerks.
    • Requires the state's jury administrator to provide the secretary of state with the list of qualified jurors, and requires the secretary to use the list to verify information provided by online voter registration applicants.
  • Permits election officials to request non-disclosure of their residential address in records provided to the public. The procedure is available to municipal clerks, registrars of voters, deputy registrars of voters, election officials as defined by statutory law, primary officials, and audit officials.
  • Requires the secretary of state to review processes by which ballots are translated into non-English languages as required by state and/or federal law, and to submit a one-time report regarding prevention of mistranslations to the legislature.
  • Requires the State Elections Enforcement Commission to refer complaints regarding violations of election law to the chief state's attorney within 90 days of a determination that probable cause exists if the commission has not issued a decision regarding the complaint. The chief state's attorney must submit reports to the legislature regarding the status of any enforcement actions related to referred complaints. Prior law did not require such referrals.

The bill also includes numerous provisions not tracked by Voting Rights Lab.

Several provisions from previous versions of the bill were amended out of the current text prior to enactment. They would have:

  • Required that all state court litigation against election officials be brought in the district of Hartford, rather than the superior court district where the alleged violation occurred.
  • Prohibited the use of the voter registration list for personal or commercial purposes, including harassment of any individual, advertising or marketing products or services, or reproduction of such data for public consumption.

Last Updated October 23, 2024

This bill, as amended on April 15, 2024, would establish the Municipal Election Accountability Board ("the Board") and grant the Board the authority to hear complaints regarding irregularities in municipal election administration and to impose a range of levels of oversight over municipalities based on its determinations. Under the bill:

  • There would be four possible levels of oversight by the Board of a municipality's election administration:
    • Tier 1 municipalities would be required to develop a plan to mitigate the issues leading to Board oversight, fulfill training requirements, and distribute training materials.
    • Tier 2 municipalities would be subject to Tier 1 oversight, plus a requirement to be in regular contact with the Board regarding compliance with the mitigation plan and training requirements.
    • Tier 3 municipalities would be subject to oversight by an election monitor appointed by the Board, who would be authorized to conduct inspections, inquiries and investigations related to any duty or responsibility under the election code performed by a municipal official; have access to all records, data and material maintained by or available to municipal election officials; and immediately report to the Secretary of the State any irregularity or impropriety in the performance responsibilities by municipal election officials. The municipality would be required to provide the monitor with any office space, supplies, equipment and services necessary to properly carry out their duties.
    • Tier 4 municipalities would have all election administration functions taken over by the Board,
  • The secretary of state, State Elections Enforcement Commission, and superior court judges could refer complaints to the Board, which would hold hearings and issue determinations. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Grant the secretary of state and the State Elections Enforcement Commission authority to make referrals to the Board when they are of the opinion that a reasonable likelihood of irregularity or impropriety in the administration of any election exists, based on a formal or informal complaint.
    • Grant superior court judges the authority to make referrals to the Board based on matters before their court when they are of the opinion that a reasonable likelihood of irregularity or impropriety in the administration of any election exists.
    • Require the Board to hold review hearings within 10 days of receiving a referral, and to make a determination regarding oversight of elections in a municipality within five days of the hearing, including whether oversight is necessary, which tier of oversight is necessary, and for how long oversight is necessary.
  • The Board would be comprised of:
    • The secretary of state or their designee, who would chair the board
    • The executive director of the State Elections Enforcement Commission or their designee
    • Nine members appointed by the secretary of state with the advice and consent of the legislature
    • The state comptroller or their designee
    • One individual admitted to practice law in the state with expertise in election administration
    • Two certified election moderators of different parties, selected by the secretary of state with the advice and consent of the legislature from a list of five recommendations provided by the Registrars of Voters Association of Connecticut
    • Two registrars of voters of different parties, selected by the secretary of state with the advice and consent of the legislature from a list of five recommendations provided by the Registrars of Voters Association of Connecticut
    • Two town clerks of different political parties selected by the secretary of state with the advice and consent of the legislature from a list of five recommendations provided by the Connecticut Town Clerks Association
    • Two chief elected municipal officials of different political parties selected by the secretary of state with the advice and consent of the legislature from a list of five recommendations provided jointly by the Connecticut Conference of Municipalities and the Connecticut Council of Small Towns
    • Four individuals with with expertise in election administration or election law selected by each major party's legislative leader in each chamber of the legislature

Last updated July 24, 2024.

This bill, as enacted on October 23, 2024, directs the Department of Elections to ensure that all polling places are accessible to individuals with disabilities, in compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act, and have adequate and accessible parking spaces. The bill requires that these accessibility features be available to voters for any election held in the state.
This requirement does not apply in the case of a natural disaster or other emergency that renders a polling site unsafe or unusable, as determined by the election commissioner, or when the commissioner determines that no accessible polling place is available and the Department of Elections cannot make a polling place temporarily accessible. In such an instance, the commissioner would be required to ensure that any voter with a disability assigned to an inaccessible polling place would be reassigned to an accessible polling place or provided with an alternative means for casting a ballot on Election Day, upon request of the voter.
The bill additionally allows a person to file an administrative complaint if they have information that the Department has not complied with the accessibility requirements.

The bill leaves in place the general existing requirement, for cases other than registration updates, that individuals who do not indicate a party affiliation must be registered without an affiliation.

  • Allow counties to count ballots by hand at the precinct level. Under existing law, ballots must be counted using electronic or electromechanical tabulators.
  • Prohibit the Department of State (the Department) from approving the use of tabulators that are produced entirely or partially in a foreign country. The bill would also prohibit tabulators that incorporate hardware or software designed, produced, owned or licensed by an entity that is owned, operated or majority-controlled by a foreign company or a domestic company registered in another county or owned by a person who is not a U.S. citizen. If enacted, the bill would effectively ban the ballot tabulators currently in use in Florida.
  • Require the Department to make copies of program codes, operator manuals and voting system software available to the public on the Department’s website at least three months before an election in which it will be used. Existing law does not require such publication.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 9, 2024, is titled the "Florida Voting Rights Act," and would make significant changes throughout the election code, including creating same-day and automatic voter registration, creating a permanent mail voting list, modifying the mail voting process, developing a database for disenfranchised individuals, and establishing the Florida Voting Rights Act Commission to enforce various new prohibitions against voter suppression and dilution. The bill would also disband the Office of Election Crimes and Security, repeal recently enacted prohibitions on third-party voter registration organizations and private funding for election expenses, and make various additional minor changes to the code. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create same-day voter registration on Election Day and during early voting by allowing eligible residents to complete voter registration applications and then immediately cast a ballot. The bill would leave in place the existing deadline for standard registration, which is 29 days before Election Day.
  • Create automatic voter registration during license or ID applications, renewals, or updates at the DMV, with individuals given the option to decline registration during the transaction. The bill does not specify an implementation date for the new AVR process. Under existing law, individuals may opt to initiate or renew voter registration at the DMV, but there is no automatic procedure.
  • Create a permanent mail voting list, by providing that any valid application for a mail ballot is sufficient to receive a mail ballot for all elections, unless the voter indicates a specific period or withdraws their request. Under existing law, voters who submit a valid mail ballot application receive mail ballots for all elections through the end of the calendar year of the next general election only.
  • Make changes to mail voting requirements to provide for slightly earlier delivery of ballots to voters and facilitate pick-up and return of ballots. The bill would:
    • Move the deadline earlier for officials to send mail ballots to voters, from the 10th day before an election to the 11th day before.
    • Require officials to provide a postage-paid return envelope for all mail ballots.
    • Provide voters with the to submit the last four digits of their Social Security number, rather than a signature, on the mail ballot certificate.
    • Repeal the existing provision that limits third parties to picking up no more than two mail ballots per election on behalf of a voter, unless the ballots are for their immediate family. The bill would also eliminate the requirement for written authorization from the voter and an affidavit from the third party when collecting mail ballots for others.
    • Reduce restrictions on drop boxes ("secure ballot intake stations") by eliminating the requirement that drop boxes located elsewhere than the office of the supervisor be used only during early voting hours, and eliminating the requirement that all drop boxes be monitored in person by supervisor office staff.
    • Repeal the existing penalty against county supervisors for violating requirements related to drop boxes. Under existing law, supervisors are subject to a $25,000 fine.
  • Permit voters who appear to vote and person and claim to be registered, but are not on the voter list, to vote a provisional ballot at any polling place in the county if they claim to be a county resident. Existing law permits provisional voting only when the voter asserts they are resident in the specific precinct where they have appeared to vote. The bill also makes conforming changes to require canvassing boards to determine whether the voter appeared in the correct county, rather than precinct, when determining whether to count the provisional ballot.
  • Disband the Office of Election Crimes and Security by repealing the provisions that establish and authorize its operations. Under existing law (enacted in 2022), the Office operates within the Department of State, and is authorized to review complaints and undertake preliminary investigations of alleged violations of the election code and "election irregularities." The Office must also make an annual report to the legislature detailing the scope and status of its investigations.
  • Repeal provisions (enacted in 2023) establishing strict requirements and penalties for voter registration assistance provided by third-party voter registration organizations, and reduce remaining penalties for certain conduct. The bill would:
    • Eliminate requirements that third parties affirm their status regarding certain past felony convictions and citizenship status, and eliminate the $50,000 fine for handling registration applications if disqualified on either ground. [Note: The citizenship requirements were temporarily enjoined in July 2023.] The bill would also repeal the automatic expiration of organizations' registration credentials at the end of each election cycle, and the requirement that organizations provide a receipt for applications they receive to submit.
    • Require that organizations deliver registration applications within 14 days after an applicant has completed the form, rather than 10 days as required under existing law.
  • Reduce fines related to timely handling of applications. For failing to submit an application within the required period, the bill would lower the basic penalty to $50, and the penalty for willful violation to $250. Under existing law, the penalties are $50 per day (up to $2,500), and $2,500 for a willful violation. For applications collected from an applicant before the registration deadline but returned after it passes, the penalty would be reduced to $100, or $500 for a willful violation. Under existing law, the penalty is $100 per day (up to $5,000), or $5,000 for a willful violation.
    • Reduce the penalty for willful failure to return an application to the proper jurisdiction, from $5,000 to $1,000. The total aggregate penalty would also be reduced from $250,000 to $1,000.
    • Eliminate the penalty against a voter registration organization if someone acting on their behalf is convicted of altering an application. Under existing law, organizations are liable for a fine of $5,000 per each altered application.
    • Eliminate the prohibition on third party organizations providing registration applications with any information pre-filled.
    • Eliminate the mandate for a form that elicits information from individuals who claim to have been registered by a third party organization but do not appear in the voter list, and eliminate the directive for administrative rules "to ensure the integrity of the registration process."
  • Repeal the prohibition on using private funds for election related expenses.

    • Require regular information sharing between the Department of State, Department of Corrections, state judiciary, and others, to maintain the accuracy of the database.
    • Expressly provide that an individual who registers or votes in reliance on database information has an affirmative right to do so, and may not be charged with a criminal offense for improper registration or voting.

    • Oversight of the newly created Florida Voting and Elections Database and Institute, for the maintenance of public elections and voting data and records. The Commission would be required to enter into an agreement with one or more universities to maintain and administer the system.

This bill, as introduced on January 9, 2024, would increase requirements for verifying identity and citizenship status during voter registration and voting, and increase requirements related to routine and on-going voter list maintenance procedures. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Expand general requirements for determining eligibility for voter registration applications. The bill would:
    • Require officials to use 'all available data sources' when determining whether a registration applicant is ineligible to register due to defects in their application, or for disqualifications such being deceased, convicted of a disenfranchising felony, etc.
    • Require that, in considering an applicant's driver's license, eligibility for voter registration be verified by comparing information from 'all available sources,' including records from the Department of State, to determine if the license (1) is classified as a non-citizen license, (2) has been surrendered by an individual who has moved out of state, or (3) was issued to an individual who is now deceased. Existing law has no comparable provision.
  • Require extensive verification of citizenship status for voter registration. Under existing law, applicants affirm their citizenship by checking a box on the registration form, and officials must only confirm 'the authenticity or nonexistence' of the applicant's driver's license, state ID, or Social Security number to process the application. Under the bill:
    • For applicants using a driver's license or state ID card number, election officials would be required to verify that the ID was not obtained using non-United States citizen documentation, and affirmatively determine that the applicant is classified as a U.S. citizen in DMV records. If non-citizen documentation was used to obtain the ID, officials would be required to use 'every possible means' to determine whether the person became a naturalized citizen after obtaining their driver's license. The bill would expressly prohibit acceptance of any voter registration application if non-United States citizenship status is indicated, and require documentation of steps taken to confirm an applicant's status.
    • For applicants using a Social Security number, officials would be required to use 'all possible means' to verify citizenship status, and these voters would be required to present their Social Security card before voting for the first time (in addition to a form of voter ID otherwise required under existing law). If a voter's Social Security card includes a work restriction, they would be required to cast a provisional ballot and provide proof of citizenship for their ballot to be counted.
    • For applicants using neither a driver's license, state ID card, or Social Security number, the bill would require officials to use "all possible means" to verify citizenship status, and would specify that those means include data from the courts, Department of Corrections, or other government agency that collects citizenship data. If no findings indicate non-citizenship, the application would be considered valid.
  • Modify the statewide voter registration application by including a field that elicits the last four digits of a person's Social Security number. Existing law requires fields for a driver's license or state ID card number only.
  • Require elections officials who determine that a false affirmation has been knowingly made on a registration application, to refer the information to the Office of Election Crimes and Security. Existing law has no comparable provision.
  • Change criteria and special ID requirements for certain voters, depending on their registration method. Under existing law, individuals who (1) register by mail, (2) have never voted previously in Florida, and (3) have been verified as never having obtained a Florida driver's license, state ID card, or a Social Security card, must provide ID before casting a ballot. Accepted forms of ID include photo IDs already required of all voters to cast a ballot, or in the alternative, a utility bill, bank statement, government check, paycheck, or other government ID, if they include the voter's name and current address. The bill would:
    • Apply special ID requirements before voting to any individual who registers by any method other than at a DMV office, rather than only individuals who registered by mail and who meet the other two criteria.
    • Change the accepted types of ID to verify registration, to include (1) a U.S. passport, (2) a U.S. birth certificate, (3) U.S. naturalization papers, (4) consular record of birth abroad, or (5) a Social Security card that does not contain a work restriction. These forms of ID must be accompanied by an 'acceptable identification' containing the voter's name and photo, which is limited to a: (1) debit or credit card, (2) military ID, (3) student ID, (4) retirement center ID, (5) public assistance ID, (6) Veterans Affairs ID, (7) concealed carry license, (8) or government employee ID. Under existing law, these forms of ID (which are currently accepted as voter ID for all voters) are sufficient alone to satisfy the registration verification requirement, as is a neighborhood association ID.
    • Eliminate the use of a utility bill, bank statement, government check, paycheck, or other government ID, if they include the voter's name and current address, for registration verification, and instead deem them acceptable only as proof of address, if dated within the last two months.
    • Eliminated the existing exemption from these registration verification ID requirements for individuals over 65 years old.
    • Require individuals who are exempt due to physical disability, or are members of the military or Merchant Marine, and their spouses/dependents, to provide documentation of their status to claim the exemption. Existing law does not include any documentation requirement for the exemption.

  • Require new procedures for voter registration at the DMV, related to citizenship status and identity verification. The bill would:
    • Expressly limit voter registration services at the DMV to individuals classified as U.S. citizens.
    • Require a wet signature on a registration application form completed at the agency. Under existing law, an electronic signature alone is required.
    • Require the DMV to offer non-U.S. citizens the opportunity to register when they obtain citizenship, and provide such information with license renewal notices.

    • Require the DMV to notify the Department of State when a driver's license has been made invalid due to a notification of death or issuance of a driver's license in another state, and when an ID or license has been obtained with documentation of non-citizenship. Under existing removal procedures, notification of a voter's death would result in immediate removal from the list, and non-citizenship would trigger a mailed notice prior to removal. The bill would deem DMV notice of an out-of-state license as a 'written request' for removal, which would also result in immediate removal with no prior notice to the voter.
    • Require the DMV to make weekly reports of license surrender, death, and non-citizenship status to the Dept. of State, and make the information available to election officials online or by written query. Existing law has no comparable provisions.
  • Require new periodic list maintenance procedures by local election officials. Under existing law, the only periodic list maintenance requirement is an annual review of the list to confirm the accuracy of voter addresses. The bill would:
    • Require 'bulk list maintenance' at least quarterly, comparing DMV reports and 'other sources' that would identify voters who are not U.S. citizens, have moved out of state, are deceased, or are otherwise ineligible to vote.
    • Require an analysis of the voter database at least quarterly, to determine addresses with more registered voters than allowed by applicable zoning regulations. The bill would also include the related requirement that the Dept. of State's database of valid residential addresses must include the maximum number of occupants for each address, per applicable zoning restrictions.
  • Modify list maintenance procedures related to determining a voter's eligibility, following a reported change of address or receipt of other information. The bill would:
    • Require local officials to verify a voter's general eligibility status 'using all available data sources' when the voter provides notice of an address change. Under existing law, the eligibility of a voter is not re-verified upon an address update.
    • Require officials to act on information from any 'credible source' regarding a voter's ineligibility for ongoing list maintenance. Existing law requires action on information from any governmental entity only. The bill also specifies that a voter's surrender of their driver's license provides grounds for ineligibility.
    • Define 'credible source' as an affidavit from a group living facility manager, homeowner association manager, or county resident, if verified with information from the DMV, county tax records, or 'other credible sources.' Credible sources would also include Social Security Death Index information, if the Social Security number matches the voter's and the information is verified by the DMV.

  • Require third-party voter organizations to provide affirmations that each person collecting applications may not knowingly solicit non-citizens to register to vote and must incorporate citizenship status and other eligibility requirements in their screening questions and provide anyone who is not a U.S. citizen with instructions on how to register after becoming a citizen. Existing law requires an affirmation that the registration organizer has not been convicted of certain felonies and is a U.S. citizen, but does not include any statements concerning the citizenship status of individuals solicited to register.
  • Expand the type of information on the voter list subject to disclosure as a public record, to include the method of an individual's registration and the type of identifying number used to apply. Under existing law, the 'place' of registration and ID numbers are confidential and exempt from disclosure.
  • Require instructions on how to cancel voter registration to be prominently displayed on any website that instructs voters on how to update their voter registration information.
  • Require the Dept. of State to adopt rules prescribing minimum standards for non-partisan voter education on the importance of updating a voter's registration and mailing address and canceling a voter's registration upon moving out of state, in addition to existing topics.     • Eliminate the requirement that five days' notice be given to the legislative judiciary committees before the state election board or secretary of state enters into any agreement or settlement that limits, alters, or interprets provisions of the election code.

    • Eliminate the felony for observing a person casting their ballot, with the exception of authorized assistants, individuals under 12 years old, or any minor child of the observed voter. This bill, as enacted on May 6, 2024, specifies the process for voter registration challenges, removes the secretary of state as a non-voting member of the State Election Board, more clearly defines residency for voting purposes, and requires changes to certain election administration processes and equipment. The bill:

  • Specifies the process for challenges to voter registrations. Specifically, under the bill:
    • Probable cause to sustain a challenge to a voter's registration expressly includes, but is not limited to, a voter having died, a voter registering to vote or obtaining a homestead exemption in another jurisdiction, or being registered at a non-residential address. Prior law did not provide any standard for determining probable cause for voter challenges.
    • A voter appearing in the U.S. Postal Services National Change of Address data is insufficient to sustain a challenge unless there is additional evidence that the voter has lost their residency in their jurisdiction of registration.
    • Challenges are not allowed against voters based on absence or presence in a jurisdiction while enrolled at a college, university, or other institution of learning within the state or against residents who move to D.C., another federal territory, or a foreign country to engage in government service.
    • Challenges made within 45 days of an election cannot be heard until after the election.
  • Removes the secretary of state as a non-voting member of the State Election Board.
  • Specifies requirements related to voter residency. Under the bill:
    • Voters who are homeless and without a fixed permanent address must use the address of the county clerk's office as their mailing address when registering to vote.
    • Voters who register to vote in another state, county, municipality, or legislative district are deemed to have changed their residency to that place and those who return to a jurisdiction after having lived and registered to vote somewhere else must update their voter registrations. The bill also specifies that ownership or rental of a post office box may not be grounds to establish residency in that jurisdiction. Prior law provided only that voters do not lose their residency for voting purposes if they go to another state, county, or municipality temporarily and with the intention to return, unless they register to vote or perform other acts indicating a desire to change citizenship and residence.
    • County registrars are expressly permitted to take into account information from the U.S. Postal Service's change of address program in making residency determinations.
  • Allows counties with under 5,000 registered voters to use paper ballots for in person voting in county-only elections with approval from the State Election Board. Under prior law, all in-person voting was done on a machine.
  • Requires that election results from in-person early voting and mail ballots received and verified by the day before an election must be reported by 8 p.m. on Election Day or within an hour of the close of polls, whichever occurs later. Prior law did not mandate a timeline for results reporting.
  • Requires, beginning in 2026, that the human-readable text portion of a paper ballot indicating the voter's selection constitute the official vote read by tabulators in determining election results. The bill specifies that a machine mark may only be used for tabulation if it clearly denotes the voters selection and does not use a QR code, bar code or similar coding. Existing practice in the state is to use QR codes or bar codes for tabulation purposes.
  • Directs the secretary of state to establish a pilot program for the auditing of paper ballot images using the human-readable text portion of the ballot rather than QR codes.
  • Imposes new requirements on officials to document access to and storage of voted mail ballots beginning in 2025.

The bill also contains provisions not tracked by Voting Rights Lab regarding regulation of members of the State Board of Elections, equipment procurement, ballot access, and election dates.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 18, 2024, would tighten various security requirements in Hawaii's elections. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Specify that ballot packages would only be sent to registered voters who request a ballot. Under existing law, ballots are sent to all registered voters.
  • Require any mailing sent by a county clerk to a voter, other than a sample ballot, to be sent via nonforwardable mail. If the mailing is returned as undeliverable, the clerk would then be required to send a follow-up notice to the forwarding address on file with USPS; if the voter does not update their registration within 35 days of that notice being sent, the voter's registration would be changed to inactive.
  • Require county clerks to use USPS data to proactively identify voters whose addresses may have changed. If a voter appears to have moved within the county, the clerk should update the registration accordingly and send the voter notice; a voter who fails to confirm the changes within 35 days or otherwise update their registration would have their registration changed to inactive. The voter could reactivate their registration by confirming their address. If the voter does not vote for two consecutive general federal elections, their registration would be canceled. A voter who moved out of the county should be sent information on how to register at their new address.
  • Require county clerks to reject any registration applicant that does not provide proof of US citizenship. Under the bill, acceptable proof of citizenship would include certain drivers licenses, a birth certificate or passport, naturalization documents, tribal documents, or any other document established as proof of citizenship under federal law. This would not apply retroactively.
  • Require 24-hour video monitoring of ballot drop boxes.
  • Require at least one voter service center per precinct.

Last Updated February 2, 2024

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 18, 2024, would replace Hawaii's universal mail ballots with a system under which all voters must cast their ballots in person for a regularly scheduled primary or general election. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Establish a process for selecting polling places, including what types of buildings are considered suitable and how to consolidate precincts during an emergency, and establish procedural rules for the conduct of in-person voting. Voters would be required to provide identification if requested by a precinct official.
  • Create a process for in-person same-day registration at absentee polling places, which must be open beginning ten days before the election. Voter service centers would no longer be available.

  • Establish rules for watchers at a precinct polling place or an absentee polling place.
  • Permit elections other than a regularly scheduled primary or general election to remain vote-by-mail.

This bill, as introduced on January 22, 2024, would impose new security requirements for voting systems and expand the felony of election fraud. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require a voting system to be under constant video surveillance, other than when in use by voters. Records of the video would need to be retained for at least twenty-five months.
  • Require a voting system to be stored under key card access security, and revoke access of anyone convicted of an election fraud offense involving the leaking of passwords or other confidential information related to a voting system.
  • Make modifications to the felony offense of election fraud, including defining the following acts as election fraud:
    • creating, permitting any person to create, or disclosing to any person an image of a hard drive of any voting system component without authorization
    • knowingly publishing or causing to be published passwords or other confidential information relating to an electronic voting system without authorization
  • accessing or attempting to access the voter registration system, erasing any name, figure, or word on the voter register or a voter service center roster of voters, removing or destroying the voter register or a voter service center roster of voters; or erasing or removing any part of the voter register or a voter service center roster of voters
  • tampering with a ballot box or other receptacle for ballots, or tampering with or permitting access to a voting system, without authorization

Under the bill, if a person is absent from their habitation for "a prolonged period of time," the absence would create a rebuttable presumption that the person intends to establish a new residence in the place where they have been for that period.

Under Hawaii law, a voter service center is a location at which a voter can drop off their mail ballot, vote in person if necessary, and receive any other necessary election services.
  • Permit an applicant for voter registration to provide their University of Hawaii student ID card number or a copy of the card as an alternative to a driver license or state ID card number.
  • Require the state's chief to conduct a study on how best to improve youth participation in elections.

Last Updated January 17, 2024

Existing law also provides that a mail ballot be sent to a voter no earlier than 20 days before the election.
  • Create an electronic tracking system by which voters can verify that their voted ballot has been received. The bill would require voter registration cards and mail ballots to include information on how to use the tracking system.

This bill, as enacted on May 8, 2024:

  • Requires an individual designated by a voter to return the voter's mail ballot to issue the voter a receipt. Under prior law, receipts were required only upon request of the voter.
  • Makes a minor adjustment to the deadline for certain voter registration forms. If the deadline to register to vote before an election is the day after Thanksgiving, as may be the case for a runoff election, the bill changes the deadline to the next day the office of the county commissioner of elections or state commissioner of elections is open. Under prior law, the deadline was shifted to the Monday after Thanksgiving.
  • Requires a county commissioner of elections to:
    • Hold training for all election personnel before each election. Under prior law, training was mandatory before primary and general elections, but was otherwise optional.
    • Certify its compliance with various requirements within 20 days of every election. Under prior law this was only required after a general election.
    • Provide the state commissioner of elections, not later than 10 days before an election, with the date, time, and location of equipment testing, the date and location where the election notice will be published, and the date that election personnel training will be conducted.
  • Requires a recount board to include in its written report a full tally and accounting of ballots reviewed by the board.
  • Requires the state commissioner of elections to conduct an unofficial canvass of election results after regular city, regular school, primary, and general elections. Prior law required the unofficial canvass only after a general election. The commissioner is also required under the bill to include an explanation if any precinct is not reported in the unofficial canvass.

  • Defines intentionally hindering, interfering with, or preventing an election official in the performance of the election official’s duties as a misdemeanor.
  • Defines intentional dissemination of an election official’s private information, or that of an official’s family or household member, in a manner that poses an imminent and serious threat, as a misdemeanor.

The bill would also move slightly earlier the start of the mail voting period, by allowing officials to begin issuing mail ballots 22 days before an election, rather than 20 days before as provided by existing law.
  • Prohibit the use of a ballot drop box for returning a mail ballot, by repealing existing provisions that permit their use.
  • Provide that a ballot is considered defective if its voter verification number does not match the voters registration number, and require notice and opportunity to cure the defect under existing rules. The bill would also repeal the provision that deems a ballot defective if the voters ballot signature does not match that on file. In 2019, a judicial order permanently enjoined the use of signature matching in the state.
  • Require the state registrar to contract with a third-party vendor to develop or provide a program to allow the registrar to verify the status of records in the statewide voter registration file and identify ineligible voters on an ongoing basis.
  • Allow voters in the address confidentiality program who are living in a shelter to provide the shelter name and contact information in lieu of a physical address, if the facility is known to the program. The bill would also permit voters in the program to request the secretary of state hold their mail for up to 30 days, and would authorize the secretary to remove individuals from the list if they receive reliable information that the voter has died.
  • Modify various technical requirements relating to the materials sent to a mail voter.
  • Prohibit the use of ranked choice voting in the state. Existing law requires that voters may not vote for more than one candidate, but does not expressly prohibit ranked choice voting.

The bill also would make changes in areas of law not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, including candidate eligibility.

Last Updated March 18, 2024

This bill, as introduced on January 9, 2024, would impose numerous substantial changes on Indiana elections that would limit voter access and threaten voter privacy. The bill would:

  • Prohibit in-person early voting. Existing law allows up to 28 days of early voting (in-person absentee voting).
  • Limit the availability of absentee voting to members of the military, voters with disabilities, voters working the polls on Election Day, UOCAVA voters, and voters age 65 or older. Existing law provides several other reasons for absentee voting, including absence from the precinct on Election Day, confinement due to illness or injury, work schedule, religious observance, and unavailability of transportation to the polls.
  • Require absentee voters to include a copy of their photo ID and the last four digits of their Social Security number with their returned ballot for verification purposes. Existing law requires election officials to compare the ballot signature with the voter's signature on file for verification.
  • Move the absentee ballot return deadline to noon on Election Day. Existing law allows voters to return ballots until 6 P.M. on Election Day.
  • Require all elections to be conducted on paper ballots designed and printed in Indiana. The ballots must include a watermark and a unique serial number. Polling locations must have one accessible voting system to comply with the requirements of HAVA.
  • Require election officials to count the paper ballots by hand beginning at 7 A.M. on Election Day.
  • Require election officials to open and count mail-in ballots at precinct locations beginning at noon on Election Day. Under existing law, mail-in ballots may be verified by county officials on receipt.
  • Require ballot counting at precinct locations to be recorded and live streamed. Voters at polling locations must place completed ballots in a transparent ballot box.
  • Require each precinct worker to affirm the final vote totals, be present for the calling in of results to the county board, and receive a copy of the final vote totals. The county board must announce election results on the night of the election.
  • Require the use of paper pollbooks
  • Deem voted ballots as not confidential records. Election officials must maintain election records at secure county-owned facilities. Only the county clerk and a member of the opposing political party may have access to the stored records.
  • Allow all Indiana citizens to inspect and copy voter lists, pollbook signatures, voter histories, absentee voting applications and signatures, chain of custody records, and ballots (except those belonging to individuals in the address confidentiality program).
  • Require the Secretary of State to select randomly 10 counties for a post-election hand recount following each election.
  • Require the Secretary of State to maintain a statewide public voter database. The Secretary must reconcile the list monthly with various named databases and any other database the Secretary "deems useful."
  • Prohibit vote centers and internet voting.
  • Limit absentee ballot return to the voter or an immediate family member. Existing law also allows a voter to name an attorney-in-fact for ballot return.
  • Require voter registration applications to include an undefined "proof of citizenship" and the voter's signature.
  • Prohibit third party organizations from conduction voter registration activities.
  • Prohibit staffed and unstaffed drop boxes. Existing law allows staffed drop boxes.
  • Prohibit the use of digital ID for voter ID purposes.
  • Prohibit anyone from sending a voter an absentee ballot application unless the voter requests one.
  • Create a Class A misdemeanor for any violation of the provisions of the bill. Additionally, any person convicted of a violation would be ineligible to register or vote for 10 years following conviction.
  • Require the Attorney General to create an "Elections Crime Unit" to investigate allegations of election law violations. The Unit would have jurisdiction throughout Indiana, but would not limit the jurisdiction of local officials to investigate and prosecute election law violations. The Unit would administer an election fraud hotline and would submit an annual report to the legislature.

This bill, as enacted on April 27, 2024, makes changes to numerous aspects of voting and election administration, including expanding access to excuse-required in-person early voting, facilitating delivery of mail ballots to alternate addresses, facilitating mail voting for incarcerated individuals, and others. Specifically, the bill:

  • Expands eligibility for excuse-required in-person early voting. Excuse-required in-person early voting is available during the six days before the general early voting period, which comprises the Thursday, Friday, and Saturday before Election Day. The bill:
    • Includes any voter who is unable to vote in person at the polls on Election Day or to vote during the general early voting period, due to being absent from their county. Under prior law, only UOCAVA voters were eligible for excuse-required in-person early voting if they would be absent for regular early voting and on Election Day, and all other voters had to meet more specific criteria.
    • Removes the requirement under existing law for a pregnant voter in their last trimester to complete a form attesting to the facts of their pregnancy to be eligible for excused in-person absentee voting.
  • Adds specific requirements for delivery of mail ballots to an address outside the voter's county of residence. The bill:
    • Requires mail ballots to be sent to specific locations for certain voters who qualify for ballot delivery outside the county. Prior law had no express provisions regarding which alternative addresses are permitted. Under the bill, (1) for students temporarily residing outside of their county of residence, delivery is required to either their residence or the current address at the educational institution at which they are enrolled as a student, (2) for eligible incarcerated voters, delivery is required to the correctional facility where the voter was in custody at the time the application for the mail ballot was submitted, (3) for voters receiving inpatient or residential care, delivery is required to the facility where the voter is receiving care.
    • Allows voters who request ballots mailed to addresses outside the county to contact their clerk and have those ballots canceled if they wish to subsequently receive a ballot at another address.
  • Facilitates mail ballot requests and ballot assistance for eligible incarcerated voters. The bill:
    • Specifies that eligible incarcerated voters must be provided with telephone access to request a mail ballot.
    • Adds jail employees to the list of individuals allowed to possess a mail ballot belonging to another person for the purpose of providing assistance.
  • Expands the list of individuals permitted to handle a voter's mail ballot to include employees providing medical or healthcare assistance in various healthcare facilities. Prior law limited such assistance to "caregivers" only at these locations.
  • Requires officials to inform UOCAVA voters that they must utilize a federal write-in absentee ballot if their military-overseas ballot application is received after the deadline of seven days before an election.
  • Permits county boards to remove a voter if the voter submits a change of county residence through the form available on the State Board of Elections website. Prior law provided for removal following notice from a voter "in writing," but did not specify use of the form.
  • Expands the existing felony offense for tampering with election equipment to include prohibited activity with an e-poll book or election administration system. The bill defines such a system as "any computer-based information technology" used by the state in the administration of elections.
  • Repeals a provision that generally prohibits the names of mail voters from being disclosed.
  • Authorizes the State Board of Elections to enter into agreements with other governmental agencies to further voter list maintenance practices. The bill expressly limits "intergovernmental agreements" to those with the "sole purpose" of removing ineligible voters, and prohibits any commercial or third-party use of data.
  • Requires the county boards of elections to establish the voting place for each precinct by January 15, instead of September 20, of each year. The bill also specifies that county boards have the authority to designate voting places for Election Day and all days of early voting. Prior law granted authority for the boards to designate voting places but did not expressly state the voting periods to which the authority applies.
  • Requires that precinct consolidation petitions from the county boards of elections to the State Board of elections to be submitted at least 120 days before a primary election. Prior law did not include a deadline for submitting petitions. The bill also specifies that, beginning January 1, 2025, any approved petition applies for the entire year, but the county board may petition the State Board to amend the petition no later than 120 days before an election.
  • Specifies that video recordings of election equipment and ballot boxes are only subject to the Kentucky Open Records Act during the 60 days after an election and may be disposed of after those 60 days or upon completion of any investigation or litigation, whichever is later. The bill also specifies that during the period when voting equipment and ballot boxes are locked, the keys must remain with the county clerk. Under prior law, the keys remained with the county board of elections and were then returned to the county clerk after the period they were required to be locked.

The bill also includes provisions not covered by the Voting Rights Lab, including provisions related to candidates, electioneering, and meeting locations for presidential electors.

This bill, as introduced on March 11, 2024, would require early voting to be conducted on every day of the week during the early voting period. Existing law only requires early voting to be conducted Monday through Saturday during the early voting period.

Last Updated March 11, 2024

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 11, 2024, would extend the early voting period. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require early voting to be conducted from the 21st day to the 7th day before any election. Under existing law, early voting is conducted from the 14th day to the 7th day before most elections, and the 18th day to the 7th day before a presidential election.
  • Require early voting to be conducted on every day of the week during the early voting period. Existing law only requires early voting to be conducted Monday through Saturday during the early voting period.

Last Updated March 11, 2024

This bill, as introduced on March 11, 2024, would provide for increases in compensation for certain election workers. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Increase compensation for:
    • a commissioner-in-charge on election day, from $250 to $300
    • a commissioner-in-charge who serves in more than one precinct, from $350 to $400
    • a commissioner who received a certificate of instruction for taking a general course of instruction for commissioners, from $100 to $150
    • a commissioner who received a certificate of instruction for taking a specialized course of instruction for commissioners-in-charge, commissioners, and alternate commissioners, from $200 to $250
    • a commissioner who is uncertified, from $35 to $85
    • a commissioner who serves during early voting, from $150 to $200 per day
  • Authorize the secretary of state to pay up to $150 per day of assistance to a commissioner who serves in an election held within one year of an emergency declared by the governor.
  • Authorize a parish board commissioner to be paid for service during a recount. The bill would also increase parish board commissioner compensation from $50 to $100, and authorizes the secretary of state to approve increased compensation of up to $150 for parish board commissioners ($100 under current law).

Last updated March 11, 2024.

This bill, as enacted on May 8, 2024, requires a curator to mail a certified copy of a judgment of interdiction for mental incompetence, or a judgment modifying or terminating such an interdiction, to the appropriate registrar of voters within 15 days of the judgment. In doing so, the curator would be required to provide the interdicted individual's date of birth and the last four digits of their Social Security number "to ensure the proper person is removed" from the voter rolls.

Existing law requires the cancellation of voter registration for a person adjudged mentally incompetent, but did not provide specific requirements for notice to election administrators.

Last updated May 23, 2024.

This bill, as enacted on May 28, 2024, restricts third-party return of mail ballots by prohibiting any person from returning more than one completed mail ballot by any means, except for return by a voter's immediate family member. Prior law prohibited returning more than one mail ballot by hand delivery, but did not impose any limitations on third-party ballot return by mail or other means.

Last Updated July 17, 2024

This bill, as enacted on June 10, 2024, prohibits individuals who are required to register as a sex offender or child predator from serving as an early voting commissioner.

Last updated July 18, 2024.

This bill, as enacted on June 19, 2024, creates new requirements for third-party voter registration organizations and new criminal penalties related to their activities. The bill:

  • Requires third-party voter registration organizations to register with the secretary of state. Organizations would not be required to register if they are providing access to the state's electronic registration application only and are not capturing any applicant information. Under prior law, individuals or entities undertaking registration drives were permitted, but not required, to register.
  • Creates a new criminal offense for filling out information on another individual's voter registration application, except as expressly permitted by law. The offense is a misdemeanor for the first charge, and a felony for second and subsequent charges.
  • Modifies the elements of the criminal offense for a third party failing to submit a completed registration form on time (charged as a misdemeanor for a first offense, and felony for second or subsequent offenses). Under prior law, the offense comprised failing to return the form within 30 days of receipt from the applicant. Under the bill, the offense now comprises failing to return the form by the earlier of the 30th day after the form is received or the day before the registration deadline for the next election.

Last Updated July 18, 2024

This bill, as enacted on June 3, 2024, changes the affiliation deadline to vote in committee elections for political parties, from 30 days before the election to the general registration deadline (i.e., 20 days before an election for electronic registration and 30 days before an election for all other methods).

Last Updated July 18, 2024

This bill, as enacted on June 19, 2024, creates a new criminal offense for an existing prohibition on witnessing multiple mail ballots, and specifies new witness requirements. Specifically, the bill:

  • Creates a misdemeanor-level criminal offense for witnessing more than one mail ballot of a voter who is not an immediate family member. Prior law prohibited this conduct, but had no criminal offense for violating the prohibition.
  • Specifies that a witness to a mail ballot must be at least 18 years old. Prior law did not set out any criteria for who may witness a voter's ballot.
  • Requires a mail ballot witness to provide their mail address on the ballot certificate. Prior law had no comparable provision. The bill expressly provides that failure to include this address may not constitute grounds for challenging the ballot.

Last Updated July 18, 2024

This bill, as enacted on May 28, 2024, makes minor changes to removal of voters from the registration list, disclosure of mail ballot information, and eligibility for serving as an election commissioner. Specifically, the bill:

  • Removes a requirement that the registrar confirm a voter's death with the Office of Vital Records before removing a voter's name from the rolls based on an obituary. Prior law required removal "if the notice provides sufficient information to properly identify the voter" and the information was confirmed. Under the bill, such notice is sufficient grounds for removal alone.
  • Shifts the duty of removing an inactive voter from the rolls from the registrar to the Department of State.
  • Requires a voter to sign a statement requesting to be removed from the voter registration list. Prior law required submission of a statement, but did not require the voter's signature.
  • Expands the prohibition on disclosure of mail ballot information. Under prior law, officials were prohibited from disclosing a voter's mail ballot application or information until the voted ballot had been returned by the voter. Under the bill, the prohibition is extended to the status of the mailed ballot, as well as the application, and through the time at which the voted ballot is accepted by the registrar.
  • Prohibits a commissioner who is removed from that role for cause from serving as a commissioner in any future election. Under prior law, service was prohibited for twelve months after removal for cause.

The bill also makes changes in areas of law not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, including campaign finance and candidate disqualification.

Last updated July 25, 2024.

This bill, as introduced on March 18, 2024, would create an exception to the general rule that a person who registered to vote by mail and has not previously voted in their current parish must vote in person. The bill would permit such a person to vote by mail if the person is incarcerated but otherwise remains eligible to vote.

Last Updated March 19, 2024

This bill, as enacted on June 11, 2024, imposes new restrictions on election officials with respect to federal elections directives, guidance, and funds. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires an election official who receives a federal directive or guidance pertaining to elections that is not published on the secretary of state's website to notify the secretary of state within five business days if they wish to implement the directive or guidance. If the secretary of state wishes for the directive or guidance to be implemented the secretary must then notify the legislature within five business days. The same requirements apply if the official is offered new federal funding for the purpose of conducting elections.
  • Prohibits an election official from implementing any federal directive or guidance pertaining to elections, or from accepting or dispersing new federal elections funds, unless the action is explicitly required by law or the implementation is approved by the legislature (explicitly or through 30 days of inaction). The secretary of state must consult with the legislature on such an action, and both chambers' relevant committees must agree to approve the action.
  • Permits the secretary of state to temporarily implement new federal guidance or funding within 90 days of a state of emergency by publishing the directive or authorization on the secretary's website and notifying the legislature. An order issued in a state of emergency must expire within 30 days.
  • Authorizes the attorney general to pursue any available legal means to enjoin an elections official from accepting and dispersing federal election funds in violation of state law, and to recover expended funds.
  • Explicitly exempts any funding disbursed pursuant to the Help America Vote Act or other funding for which federal or state law requires dispersal.
  • Requires the secretary of state to make an annual report to the legislature of requests submitted to the secretary under the bill and of the source and amount of any federal funding received for election administration purposes.

Last updated July 22, 2024.

This bill, as enacted on June 11, 2024:


  • Requires each registrar of voters to assign voters to each voting district in their parish not later than the 58th day before an election. Prior law required assignments be done not later than the 51st day before an election.
  • Moves the deadline later for local registrars' annual canvass of voters, from June 30th to July 31st.

The bill also makes extensive changes in areas of law not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, including campaign finance and candidate qualifications.


A previous version of the bill contained an additional provision that was amended out prior to enactment, which would have moved the early voting period for most elections earlier by several days.

Last Updated January 13, 2025

This bill, as enacted on June 19, 2024, makes minor changes to oversight of boards of election supervisors during ballot processing and to public notice of board meetings, and creates new restrictions on recording activity related to voting machines and ballot processing. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires a local board, if conducting its counting and verification duties on Election Day without a majority of its members present, to receive approval from the commissioner of elections to select a sufficient number of commissioners to assist. Prior law authorized the members present to select parish board commissioners to assist without the commissioner's approval. The bill also requires the board to seek approval from the commissioner of elections to appoint a parish board commissioner to serve as a board member as needed when the board cannot locate an alternate designee or appointee.
  • Changes notice requirements for parish board meetings to require 24 hours' actual notice of all meetings. Prior law required 24 hours' written public notice of any meeting, exclusive of Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays.
  • Prohibits the live broadcasting or recording of the preparation, testing, inspecting, sealing, or locking of voting machines, and the preparation, verification, counting, and tabulation of mail ballots and early ballots.

Last Updated July 23, 2024

Governor Jeff Landry vetoed this bill on May 30, 2024.

This bill, as enrolled on May 22, 2024, would have provided that a person with a valid Louisiana driver's license or state ID card who requires internet access or other assistance could complete the online voter registration application in person at their parish registrar's office.

Last Updated May 31, 2024

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 11, 2024, changes the voter eligibility requirements for persons convicted of a felony. Specifically, the bill would change the timing under which a person convicted of a felony becomes eligible to register to vote. Under existing law, a person convicted of a felony regains the right to vote, even if technically remaining under an order of imprisonment, if they have not been incarcerated for the offense in the past five years. (A person is considered to still be "under an order of imprisonment" when out on probation, supervision, or parole.) Under the bill, the person's right to vote would not be restored until the person is no longer under an order of imprisonment.

The bill would make various conforming changes to statutes regarding the administrative requirements for the change in restoration timing.

Last updated March 18, 2024.

This bill, as enacted on May 28, 2024:

  • Prohibits assisting more than one voter with completing a mail ballot, other than an immediate family member. While the bill does not expressly create a specific criminal offense for violating the limit, individuals assisting with a ballot must sign an acknowledgment certificate, and this signature may serve as the required witness signature for a mail ballot. The bill, and other legislation enacted this session, creates a new criminal offense for witnessing more than one mail ballot, except for immediate family members (charged as a misdemeanor for the first offense, and felony for subsequent offenses).
  • Increases the early voting period for nursing home residents, by moving the start date to two weeks before the beginning of regular early voting. Under prior law, this period began one week before the beginning of regular early voting.
  • Specifies that a witness to a mail ballot must be at least 18 years old. Prior law required mail ballots to be witnessed, but did not set out any criteria for who may do so.
  • Requires a mail ballot witness to provide their mail address on the ballot certificate. Prior law had no comparable provision.

Last Updated July 24, 2024

This bill, as introduced on March 11, 2024, concerns the offense of filing or maintaining a false public record. The bill would expand the definition of a false public record, for purposes of that offense, to include a voter registration application containing a false statement that the applicant is a citizen of the United States. A person convicted of the offense would commit a misdemeanor.

Last updated March 12, 2024.

This bill, as introduced on March 11, 2024, proposes a constitutional amendment under which the attorney general would gain authority to institute, prosecute, or intervene in any criminal action or proceeding concerning a felony election offense.

Last updated March 18, 2024.
