VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 11, 2024, would permit a parish registrar of voters to use a database of customers of publicly owned utilities to verify the addresses of registered voters. The utility would be required to provide an updated list once a quarter. If a voters address on the list provided by the utility does not match the voters registration address, the registrar would send a confirmation notice as provided under current law.

Last updated March 11, 2024.

This bill, as enacted on May 28, 2024, creates new prohibitions and criminal offenses for certain distribution or return of mail ballot applications, limits eligibility for the permanent mail voter list, and creates new information requirements for providing assistance to a voter at the polling place. Specifically, the bill:

  • Creates new prohibitions on the distribution and return of mail ballot applications. The bill prohibits:
    • Any person, unless otherwise authorized by law, from distributing an application form for a mail ballot to a person who did not request one. If a state of emergency is declared within 45 days of an election, the secretary of state is authorized to determine whether applications may be sent to displaced residents, and must notify the legislature within 10 days of the distribution. Prior law was silent as to unsolicited distribution of applications.
    • Any person other than an immediate family member of a voter submitting the voter's completed mail ballot application by any means, including by mail. Prior law had no restrictions on third-party return of an application.
  • Creates criminal offenses for violating the new prohibitions on unsolicited distribution and third-party return of mail ballot applications (charged as a misdemeanor for a first offense, and felony for subsequent offenses).
  • Restricts eligibility for the permanent mail voter list, by excluding formerly eligible individuals in the Special Program for Handicapped Voters and those at least 65 years old. Under the bill, an application for mail ballots from these voters is now valid for a maximum of four years only. Remaining eligibility for the permanent mail voter list is limited to voters with documented disabilities and those in the state's address confidentiality program.
  • Increases information requirements for providing assistance to a voter at a polling place. Under prior law, election officials were required to write the voter's name in the register, and the name of the individual assisting. Under the bill, the voter or their assistant must now complete a "voter assistance form," providing the assistant's name, address, and relationship to the voter, and an attestation of whether they were paid for providing the assistance.

Last Updated July 24, 2024

This bill, as enacted on May 28, 2024, deems mail ballots with missing certificate information as challenged, and sets out processing requirements for these ballots. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires that any mail ballot with a ballot certificate that is missing information and is not cured by the voter in accordance with existing law be treated as a challenged ballot. The bill specifies that a ballot may not be treated as challenged solely because the voter indicates that they do not know their mother's maiden name. Prior law generally required a proactive challenge of a ballot from a candidate or their representative, a member of the board, or a registered voter, but had no clear provisions concerning the outcome for a ballot that lacked certain information but was not proactively challenged.
  • Requires that if the challenge is sustained, the board must not count the ballot, and sets out requirements for notice to the voter. Under existing law, "at least a majority of the members of the board shall hear and determine the validity of any ballot challenged."
  • Requires the secretary of state to provide for a "uniform, standard process" for determining challenges to ballots with missing certificate information. The bill also requires the secretary to provide for the pre-printing of certain information on mail ballot certificates, including the date of the election.

Last Updated July 24, 2024

This bill, as enacted on May 28, 2024, requires the tabulation and counting of a mail or early voting ballot cast by a voter who dies before Election Day. Prior law was silent as to processing such ballots.

Last Updated July 24, 2024

This bill, as enacted on June 11, 2024, permits the parish executive committee of a political party that has at least 25% of the state's registered voters as affiliated members to appoint watchers and "super watchers" in the parish if one of the party's nominees is on the ballot. Specifically, the bill permits the parish executive committee to appoint:

  • An early voting watcher at each early voting location in the parish, as space permits. The chairman of the party's state central committee is authorized to make these appointments if the party has no parish executive committee in that parish.
  • One "super watcher" per 50,000 voters, up to a maximum of five super watchers, for each parish holding an election in which one of the party's candidates is on the ballot. The chairman of the party's state central committee is authorized to make these appointments if the party has no parish executive committee in that parish.

Last updated July 24, 2024.

This bill, as enacted on June 10, 2024:

  • Requires local registrars to record the reason for the rejection of a mail or early voting ballot in the state voter registration computer system.
  • Requires the secretary of state to maintain records of the number and reason for all rejected ballots, and include the information in their post-election statistical data on the agency website.

A previous version of this bill contained additional provisions that were amended out prior to enactment. These provisions would have:

  • Removed the existing requirement that voters provide their mother's maiden name as part of identifying information for voter registration, a mail ballot application, and the mail ballot certificate. For voters submitting an affidavit as an alternative to required voter ID for in-person voting, the previous version of the bill would have required the voter's address in place of the maiden name.
  • Required written notice from local election officials to the voter and the secretary of state if a voter cast an early ballot using an ID affidavit (as an alternative to presenting ID) and the affidavit was rejected.

Last Updated July 24, 2024

This bill, as enacted on May 28, 2024, creates a new criminal offense for election fraud or forgery, charged as a misdemeanor-level offense for first violation and felony-level offense for subsequent violations. The prohibited conduct includes:

  • Voting or attempting to vote more than once in one election
  • Voting or attempting to vote if unqualified to vote, or influencing another to do so if the voter would be unqualified or the vote would be fraudulent
  • Registering or voting, or attempting to do so, in another person's name or under a false identity
  • Forging another person's name on any document required under Louisiana election law
  • Procuring or submitting a voter registration application that the person knows to be false or fraudulent
  • Forging, altering, or destroying any document required under Louisiana election law without authorization
  • Possessing an official ballot in violation of Louisiana election law
  • Possessing another's registration certificate with intent to violate Louisiana election law
  • Copying a voter's submitted registration application without legal authority to do so

Last updated July 24, 2024.

This bill, as enacted on June 11, 2024:

  • Requires, in a code section describing voter registration using the state's form, that applicants provide proof of citizenship. The bill does not specify implications, if any, for applicants using the federal form, which does not require proof of citizenship, and also does not specify what constitutes proof of citizenship for this purpose. Under prior law, applicants were required to attest to their U.S. citizenship, among other eligibility requirements, but were not required to submit specific proof.
  • Expressly prohibits voter registration by any person who is not a U.S. citizen. While prior law included citizenship as a qualification for registration, it did not contain a comparable provision.

Last Updated July 25, 2024

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on May 30, 2024, would change procedures related to maintenance of local voter registration lists, and the criteria for inactive voter status and removal from the voter list. The bill would:

  • Repeal the requirement that local voter registrations lists be generated from data in the annual state census, and instead require registrars to compile and maintain registration information with data from the affidavit registration form, the state's online registration portal, and automatic voter registration transactions at the DMV.
  • Require registrars to inactivate a voter's registration only upon notice of an address change from the USPS or Electronic Registration Center (ERIC), and set out requirements for notice to the voter. Under existing law, a voter's registration is made inactive if they fail to respond to a state census mailing for two consecutive years. Under the bill:
    • If data from the USPS or ERIC indicates an address change within the voter's current town or city, the registrar would be required to update, rather than inactivate, the registration record. Existing law has no provision for automatic updates based on address change information.
    • Inactivating a voter's registration would be prohibited within 90 days of a presidential or regular state primary or biennial state election. Existing law has no comparable provision.
  • Expand the types of action that return an inactive voter to active status. Under existing law, voters rejoin the active list by responding to an inactive notice, or appearing to vote and providing an affirmation of residence. Under the bill, an inactive voter would also be returned to active status if they do any of the following:
    • Notify the registrar in writing of their continued residence in the city or town
    • Apply for a mail ballot
    • Sign a nomination paper or petition for a ballot question
    • Perform any other election-related act using an address in their city or town
  • Expressly provide that a voter in inactive status may vote a regular ballot if they provide an affirmation of their continued residence in the jurisdiction. While this process is available under existing state policy, it is not codified in statutory law.
  • Modify slightly the existing grounds for removing a voter from the registration list. The bill would:
    • Require removal upon determination that the voter is no longer resident in the jurisdiction, per data from the USPS or ERIC. The bill would also eliminate the requirement that voters be removed upon receipt of change of address information from the DMV.
    • Keep in place existing requirements for removal if (1) the registrar receives notice of a voter's death via the monthly report sent from local clerks to election officials, (2) the registrar receives documentation from another jurisdiction of the voter's registration, (3) the voter's registration is found to be invalid, or (4) a voter has not responded to an inactivation notice and has not voted in the following two biennial state elections. The bill would also specify removal upon official notice of imprisonment, disqualification for certain election-related offenses, or limitations under guardianship, which are provided for in substantive provisions elsewhere in existing law.
  • Eliminate the requirement that the registrar make the inactive voters list available for public inspection.
  • Establish new requirements for oversight of compliance with federal and state accessibility requirements for voters with disabilities. The bill would:
    • Require officials from the secretary of state's office to inspect each polling place and early voting site at least once every four years to ensure compliance with federal and state accessibility laws.
    • Require the inspector to report every compliance failure to the secretary and the city or town clerk, and require local officials take immediate action to ensure access and submit a written compliance plan within five days.
    • Authorize the secretary of state to order compliance with the new procedures, and grant them authority to bring civil actions for enforcement.
    • Require the secretary to provide a written annual report on "all activities" relevant to the requirements, to both bodies of the state legislature.

Last Updated June 17, 2024

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on April 3, 2024, would

  • Make a minor change to reporting requirements of court clerks to state election administrators, concerning individuals convicted of a felony. Under existing law, clerks are required to report monthly which individuals had been convicted of a felony and are"currently serving" a term of imprisonment. Under the bill, the report would now be required to list individuals who have been sentenced to imprisonment for a felony with commitment papers.
  • Require the State Board to adopt regulations that establish an appeals process for the designation of a public building as an early voting center, including certain specific procedures. Existing law does not provide for an appeals process.

Last updated on October 17, 2024.

This bill, as introduced on January 10, 2024, would authorize an additional method for a voter to confirm their identity at a polling place. The bill would permit a voter to present their voter registration card, a valid Maryland driver's license, or any photo ID issued by the state government, federal government or any unit of a political subdivision. Under existing law, a voter may establish their identity only by stating the month and day of their birth, which is then compared to the information listed in the election register.

Last Updated January 31, 2024

This bill, as introduced on January 10, 2024, would require in-person voters to show a photo ID document before receiving a ballot, and create a misdemeanor prohibiting voting or attempting to vote using a fake ID. Under existing law, election workers verify a voter's identity without requesting a document. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require in-person voters to show an acceptable ID document to receive a regular ballot. Voters who fail to show the required ID documentation would be required to vote a provisional ballot. Accepted ID types would be:
    • a valid government-issued photo identification, or
    • a valid nongovernment-issued photo identification, and
    • a current utility bill, bank statement, paycheck, government check, or another government document that states the voter's name and address.
  • Create a misdemeanor offense for voting or attempting to vote under a false form of identification.

Last Updated January 19, 2024

This bill, as introduced on January 10, 2024, would establish requirements related to mail "absentee" ballot signatures. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the state board to establish guidelines for the verification of signatures on mail ballot envelopes.

  • Prohibit a local board from counting a mail ballot or removing a mail ballot from the return envelope or the ballot return envelope unless the envelope is signed by the voter and a witness and the voter's signature is verified by the local board. Under the bill, the witness signature requirement would not apply to mail ballots voted and returned by active duty military members serving overseas or their spouses (if the spouse or dependent lives overseas). Existing law does not include any similar provisions.

    This bill would be an emergency measure which if passed by three-fifths of all members elected to each chamber would take effect upon enactment.


Last Updated January 31, 2024

This bill, as introduced on January 12, 2024, would authorize voters who are unaffiliated with a political party to request to affiliate with a party at an early voting center during a primary election and vote a provisional ballot. Existing law does not include a similar provision.

Last Updated January 31, 2024

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 24, 2024, would:

  • Permit minors who are 15 years and 9 months old to register to vote. The bill would not change the voting age. Existing law permits pre-registration by people who are 16, and allows people who are 17 to vote in a primary if they will be 18 by the date of the general election.
  • Require the county Election Director to send registered voters who become eligible to vote a notice of their eligibility to vote in the next primary election as well as information related to available voting methods, early voting centers, and polling places. Existing law does not include a similar provision.

Last Updated January 25, 2024

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 22, 2024, would require the State Board to carry out performance evaluations of the state administrator of elections and the election director of each local board, and require the election director to oversee voting system equipment security. Existing law has no comparable provisions. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the State Board of Elections to evaluate the performance of the state administrator of elections at least annually.
  • Require the state administrator to evaluate the election director of each local board and provide the evaluation to the local board at least annually.
  • Require each local election board to confer with the state administrator in appointing an election director.
  • Require the election director to manage the storage, security, maintenance, and preparation of voting system equipment. The bill would also require the election director to notify the state administrator and local board within 24 hours of any security violation, significant attempted security violation, or damage to the office, warehouse, or materials used to conduct an election. Existing law is silent as to authority over these duties.

The bill also contains additional non-substantive changes that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

Last updated on October 17, 2024.

This bill, as enacted on April 25, 2024:

  • Requires the governor to declare the winner in presidential and congressional elections "consistent with the returns received" through the certified vote canvass. Prior law required the governor to "ascertain and enumerate the number of votes cast for each candidate," but did not include an express mandate to do so consistent with the canvass. The bill also expressly requires the governor to issue and transmit a certificate of presidential results as required by federal law, and to publish on the State Board's website a signed and issued proclamation declaring the name of each elected candidate. Prior law, which the bill repeals, required publication in newspapers.
  • Creates new procedures related to vote canvassing by local boards of election. The bill:
    • Requires the state administrator to review any statements of dissent from local canvass members regarding an election result or compliance with election law, and submit the dissent to the State Board of Canvassers for a determination. The bill also requires the state board to keep a record of all dissent determinations. Prior law required that dissents be filed with the local board and recorded by the state board, but did not require review or a determination on their claims.
    • Requires local boards to consult with the state administrator when investigating irregularities in documents or records produced in an election. Prior law required investigation by local boards alone.
  • Changes procedures for the statewide canvass and the administration of the State Board of Canvassers. The bill:
    • Moves the deadline earlier for beginning the statewide canvass for all elections except special congressional primaries, to within 30 days of an election. Under prior law, the deadline was within 35 days. The bill also makes gubernatorial primaries subject to the general canvassing rules, rather than subject to the special rules for congressional special primaries as they were under prior law.
    • Requires, for the canvass in all elections, that the State Board of Canvassers review certified statements from local boards within one day of convening, and provides that if the board determines by clear and convincing evidence that a statement is "inaccurate," the state board must reject the statement and "ascertain the accurate election results." The board must provide the State Board of Elections with a written statement of its reasons for rejecting a local board's statement, including the evidence on which it's based. Prior law required only that the state board "prepare statewide election results for each candidate and question, based on the certified copies of the statements made by the boards of canvassers," with no express provision for rejecting statements and making independent determinations.
    • Specifies that the state administrator must transmit certified election results to the governor within three days of receipt. Prior law required delivery within 30 days.
    • Authorizes the board to adopt regulations governing the certification of election results.

This bill, as introduced on January 31, 2024, would create the “Maryland Voting Rights Act of 2024” aimed at regulating the elections and voting-related policies of counties and municipalities to ensure that voting rights are protected generally, and provide specific protections for certain classes of voters. The bill provides protections against vote dilution, requires preclearance, requires language access, prohibits voter intimidation, creates a statewide database of election data to enable discrimination detection and further best practices, and facilitates enforcement with special litigation processes.

As a threshold matter, the bill would declare that state and local laws, rules, regulations, charters, and ordinances must be construed liberally in favor of:

  • Protecting the right to cast a ballot
  • Ensuring that eligible voters are not impaired in registering to vote or voting, including having their votes counted

  • Ensuring protected class voters equitable access to opportunities to register to vote and vote.

    The anti-vote dilution provisions focus on protected classes that engage in racially polarized voting. "Protected class" would mean a class of citizens who are members of a race, color, or language minority group, as referenced in the federal Voting Rights Act. "Racially polarized voting" would mean voting in which there is a divergence between the candidate or electoral choice preferred by protected class voters and the candidate or electoral choice preferred by other voters. This section of the bill would:

  • Declare that a local government may not deny or impair the right to vote of protected class members through any:
    • qualification for eligibility to be a voter or other prerequisite to voting,
    • ordinance, regulation, or other law regarding the administration of elections, or any standard, practice, procedure, or policy, or
    • action or inaction
  • Define as violations of that prohibition:
    • implementation of a prerequisite to voting, a rule relating to election administration, or any policy that results or is intended to result in any disparity or reduction in voter participation, voting access, or ability to participate in the political process among protected class members, or which, based on the totality of the circumstances, results in any impairment of the opportunity or ability of protected class members to participate in the political process, elect candidates of their choice, or otherwise influence election outcomes.
    • enactment of a prerequisite to voting, a rule relating to election administration, or any policy that has the purpose or effect of diminishing the ability of any protected class voter to participate in the electoral process or elect their preferred candidates.
  • Prohibit a local government from using a method of election that has the effect, or is partially motivated by the intent, of impairing protected class voters' ability to participate in the political process, elect candidates of their choice, or otherwise influence election outcomes by diluting or abridging their votes.
  • Define as violations of that prohibition:
    • Implementing an at-large method of election where racially polarized voting by protected class voters occurs, or based on the totality of the circumstances, the opportunity or ability of protected class voters to participate in the political process, elect candidates of their choice, or otherwise influence election outcomes is impaired.
    • Implementing a district-based or another method of election where the candidates or electoral choices of protected class members would usually be defeated and either racially polarized voting by protected class voters occurs or based on the totality of the circumstances, the opportunity or ability of protected class voters to participate in the political process, elect candidates of their choice, or otherwise influence election outcomes is impaired.
    • Implementing any method of election that has the purpose of, or will have the effect of, diminishing the ability of any protected class voter to participate in the electoral process or elect the preferred candidates of choice of the protected class member.

  • Create a pre-lawsuit process to speed the implementation of remedies. The bill would:

    • Require potential plaintiffs to send a notification letter to the relevant local government asserting a possible violation prior to filing suit. A suit would be delayed for 50 days after sending the letter.
    • Allow local governments to forestall suit by adopting a resolution within 60 days of such a letter being sent. The resolution would affirm the local government's intent to enact and implement a remedy, establish specific measures it would take, and provide a schedule for taking them. A suit could not be filed for 90 days after such a resolution was adopted.
    • Create a process for the attorney general to review and then accept or reject remedies proposed by the local government.
    • Allow parties to seek preliminary relief notwithstanding this pre-suit process if an election impacted by the violation is scheduled within 120 days. The preliminary relief would be granted if the court decides the party is more likely than not to succeed on the merits and it is possible to implement an appropriate remedy before the election. Nonetheless, if the action is dismissed or withdrawn because of the local government's enactment or implementation of a remedy or the approval of the attorney general of a remedy, the parties could only seek reimbursement for costs relating to the notification letter.

    If the notice letter process failed and the case went forward in court, the bill would:

  • Specify what evidence a court must consider and must not consider when determining if racially polarized voting in a local government election occurs, or if candidates or electoral choices preferred by protected class voters would be usually defeated.
  • Specify what factors a court may and may not consider in determining whether, based on the totality of the circumstances, a denial or impairment of the opportunity or ability of protected class members to participate in the political process, elect candidates of their choice, or otherwise influence election outcomes.
  • Require courts, after finding a violation, to order remedies tailored to address the violation. Such remedies could not diminish the ability of protected class members to participate in the political process, elect candidates of their choice, or otherwise influence election outcomes. The court would be required to consider remedies proposed by any parties, but prohibited from giving deference or priority to a remedy because it was proposed by the local government.
  • Authorize the court to impose remedies that are inconsistent with any other provision of state or local law if that state or local law would otherwise prevent the court from ordering an appropriate remedy. Remedies could include:
    • a district-based method of election,
    • new or revised districting plans,
    • elimination of staggered elections,
    • reasonably increasing the size of the legislative body
    • additional voting hours or days
    • additional polling locations
    • additional means of voting, such as voting by mail or additional opportunities to return ballots
    • ordering special elections
    • requiring expanded opportunities for the admission of voters
    • requiring additional voter education
    • restoring or adding people to a voter registry
    • the court retaining jurisdiction, and if so, the court must preclear any new or change to prerequisites to voting or standards, practices, or procedures. The court could allow such changes only after finding that they do not have the purpose and would not have the effect of impairing or diminishing the right to vote on the basis of protected class membership.

  • Require local governments to hold detailed public hearings including specified notice processes before enacting and implementing either:

    • a new method of election to replace an at-large method
    • a new districting plan proposed after being sued or threatened with suit for an alleged violation of this bill or the federal Voting Rights Act.

    The bill would require "covered jurisdictions" to get permission before implementing any "covered policies", a process called "preclearance." A covered jurisdiction would have a choice about how to get preclearance for a covered policy. The jurisdiction could either submit the policy to the attorney general's office or to the court for Anne Arundel County. If a covered jurisdiction failed to seek preclearance for a covered policy, the bill would enable individuals, organizations, and the attorney general to enjoin the covered policy until it is precleared. A special preclearance process would be developed for use during emergencies. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create a preclearance process at the attorney general’s office. To use this process the covered jurisdiction would submit the policy to the Division. Thereafter:
    • The Division would approve, conditionally approve, or reject the policy. If the Division conditionally approves the policy, it could then reject the policy, but the rejection would need to be within 60 days of the receipt of the policy. If the Division fails to act within the deadlines imposed by the bill, the policy would be deemed approved.
    • The attorney general would only be able to reject a policy if it determined that the policy is more likely than not to diminish the opportunity or ability of protected class members to participate in the political process and elect candidates of their choice or otherwise influence the outcome of elections, or that the policy is more likely than not to violate the bill. A decision to preclear or reject a covered policy would not be admissible in a future challenge to covered policy.
    • Denials of preclearance could be appealed to the Appellate Court of Maryland.
  • Create a preclearance process at the Circuit Court for Anne Arundel. The covered jurisdiction would submit the policy in writing and contemporaneously send the policy to the Civil Rights Division. If the Division isn't contemporaneously served, the policy would be automatically denied. Assuming notice is given as required, thereafter:
    • The covered jurisdiction would have the burden of proof, just as in the other process.
    • The court could deny preclearance only if it determined that the policy is more likely than not to diminish the opportunity or ability of protected class members to participate in the political process and elect candidates of their choice or otherwise influence the outcome of elections, or that the policy is more likely than not to violate the bill, just as in the other process. A decision to preclear or reject a covered policy would not be admissible in a future challenge to a covered policy.
    • The court would be required to rule on preclearance within 60 days, but if it does not, the policy could not be implemented until preclearance is affirmatively granted.
    • Denials would be appealed under the ordinary rules of appellate procedure, however, it would be expedited.
  • Authorize plaintiffs to seek an injunction to prevent the implementation of a covered policy that was not submitted for preclearance.
  • Define "covered jurisdiction" as any local government:
    • that within the immediately preceding 25 years, became subject to a court order or government enforcement action based on a violation of this bill, the federal Voting Rights Act, the 15th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, or a voting-related violation of the 14th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.
    • that within the immediately preceding 25 years, became subject to at least three court orders or government enforcement actions based on a finding of a violation of a federal or state civil rights law or the 14th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution concerning discrimination against members of a protected class.
    • where the combined misdemeanor and felony arrest rate of members of any protected class consisting of at least 10,000 voting-age citizens or whose members are at least 10% of the citizen voting-age population served by the local government exceeds the proportion that the protected class constitutes of the citizen voting-age population served by the local government by at least 20% at any point in within the immediately preceding 10 years.
    • where, based on data made available by the U.S. Bureau of the Census, the dissimilarity index of any protected class of at least 25,000 voting-age citizens or whose members are at least 10% of the voting-age population of the local government has been more than 50 with respect to the race, color, or language minority group that is a majority within the local government at any point in the immediate preceding 10 years.
    • or a local board of elections in a county that is a covered jurisdiction.

  • Define "covered policy" as a new or modified local government qualification for admission as a voter, prerequisite to voting, or a regulation, ordinance, standard, practice, procedure, or policy concerning:

    • a change to the method or dates of election of a governing body or an elected school board
    • a change to the boundaries of election districts or wards, including changes made under a decennial redistricting
    • a change to the form of government for a local government
    • an annexation, incorporation, dissolution, consolidation, or division of a local government
    • a change to voter registration list maintenance or other activities concerning the cancelation or denial of voter registration
    • a change to the assignment of a voting precinct, polling place, or drop box location, including the relocation of voters, the relocation or reduction of hours of any polling place or ballot drop box, or the reduction or consolidation of polling places or ballot drop boxes;
    • a change to translation or interpretation services in any language other than English, including the creation or distribution of voting materials in any language other than English;
    • a change to assistance to voters with disabilities, including the creation or distribution of voting materials for voters with disabilities; or
    • any additional subject matter that the state board, in consultation with the civil rights division, may identify for inclusion by regulation if the civil rights division determines that any qualification for admission as a voter, prerequisite to voting, or any ordinance, regulation, standard, practice, procedure, or policy concerning the subject matter may have the effect of impairing or diminishing the right to vote of any protected class voter.

    The bill would require language assistance. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the State Board of Elections to make certain determinations of language assistance for non-native English speakers using the American Community Survey or equivalent data, and then using those determinations, publish on its website on or before January 1, 2024, and every three years thereafter, a list of each local government election that requires non-English language-related assistance and the kind of assistance required.
  • Require the State Board to issue regulations relating to how it will make the determinations of language assistance needs, and to include a process through which the public can propose languages for evaluation.
  • Require local governments to competently provide the required language assistance and materials on their website and in physical materials, including
    • registration and voting notices
    • election-related forms and instructions
    • ballot and other materials relating to the electoral process.
    • bilingual poll workers where available.

  • Enable lawsuits both to enforce the language assistance provisions and to enable local governments to provide English-only materials. The court would allow English-only materials if it found the State Board's determination of need was arbitrary and capricious, or an abuse of discretion.

    The bill would create new prohibitions on voter intimidation and obstruction, identify conduct that would automatically violate the prohibitions, and enable impacted people to sue. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Prohibit a person, whether acting under the color of law or otherwise, from engaging in acts of intimidation, deception, or obstruction that interferes with an individual's right to vote.
  • Define as violations of that prohibition:
    • the use of force or threats to use force, or the use of any other conduct to practice intimidation that causes or will reasonably have the effect of causing interference with an individual's right to vote,
    • the knowing use of a deceptive or fraudulent device, contrivance, or communication that causes or will reasonably have the effect of causing interference with any individual's right to vote, or
    • interference with access to a polling place, a ballot drop box, or an office or a place of business of an election official or a voter or an election official in a manner that causes or will reasonably have the effect of causing interference with any individual's right to vote or any delay in voting or the voting process.

  • Enable plaintiffs to sue over alleged violations in the circuit court for Anne Arundel County and provide that if the court finds a violation:

    • The court must order appropriate, tailored remedies that could include additional time to vote
    • The person who committed or aided the violation would be liable for any damages awarded by the court, including nominal damages for any violation and compensatory or punitive damages for any willful violation.

    Finally, the bill would empower enforcement of all of the provisions in the bill by creating certain litigation rules and enabling parties to recover costs and fees. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Enable any of these parties to file suit to enforce any of the provisions in the bill:
    • an aggrieved person
    • an organization whose membership includes or is likely to include aggrieved persons;
    • an organization whose mission would be frustrated by a violation of this section;
    • an organization that would expend resources to fulfill its mission as a result of a violation of this section; or
    • the attorney general
  • Give enforcement actions expedited proceedings and automatic calendar preference.
  • Direct courts to grant preliminary injunctions relating to upcoming elections if the party is more likely than not to succeed on the merits, and it is possible to implement an appropriate remedy that would resolve the alleged violation in the upcoming election
  • Allow the prevailing party to recover reasonable attorneys' fees and litigation costs, including expert witness fees and expenses. However, a state or local government would not be awarded costs or fees unless the court decides the action was frivolous, unreasonable, or without foundation. When the state or local government is the opposing party, a party would be defined as prevailing if as a result of the action the government yields some or all of the relief sought.

This bill, as introduced on February 7, 2024, would revise automatic voter registration processes at the DMV (called the Motor Vehicle Administration in Maryland) and at the Maryland Health Benefit Exchange ("Exchange") to create a process for new registrations for people whose transaction-related documentation or database match demonstrate their U.S. citizenship. In addition, the bill would create new registration update processes, would authorize the State Board of Elections to identify additional agencies for automatic voter registration, and authorize special processes for participants in address confidentiality programs Specifically, the bill would:

  • Limit the existing automatic voter registration process at DMV and at the Maryland Health Benefit Exchange to people who are not yet registered to vote and:
    • At the DMV, either use documents for their transactions that do not indicate citizenship or non-citizenship, or do not use any documents.
    • At the Health Benefit Exchange, the applicant's citizenship can not be reliably verified through an electronic database match and the applicant has not attested to non-citizenship.
  • Require the DMV to maintain an electronic information system that allows it to determine, at the time a person applies for a transaction, whether the person is registered to vote. If a person is registered to vote, the DMV would electronically transmit the voter registration information of that person to the State Board of Elections.
    • If the information shows the voter's registration information is correct, the State Board would note the date of the update in the voter registration list, and if the voter's registration was inactive, activate it.
    • If the information shows the voter's address or name has changed, the State Board would update their registration and if applicable, activate it. Within five business days after receiving the voter registration information from the DMV, the State Board would send the voter an automatic voter registration update notice by non-forwardable mail that included a postage-prepaid form to return to make corrections. If the voter affirmatively corrects the update in writing, the State Board would update their registration. The State Board would also be required to provide an electronic means for a voter to update their registration.
    • The bill authorizes the State Board to delegate some or all of these responsibilities to the local boards of elections.
  • Require the DMV to classify each type of document it accepts as proof of identity as a document that proves U.S. citizenship, proves non-citizenship, or neither.
  • Prohibit the DMV from offering registration to, or transferring the information of, a person whose documents prove they are not U.S. citizens.
  • Create a new automatic registration process at DMV for people who affirmatively demonstrate citizenship as part of their transaction. Specifically, the new process would be used at DMV for any transaction in which the person is not yet registered to vote, provides a document as part of their transaction that demonstrates U.S. citizenship, and they are at least 16 years old and a resident of Maryland. DMV would be authorized but not required to create a process to review prior transaction documents to see if an applicant previously submitted proof of U.S. citizenship if in the current transaction a voter's documents do not demonstrate citizenship or non-citizenship. In this process, once the State Board receives the voter's information and confirms no other information indicates the person is not qualified to vote:
    • The State Board would send the applicant an automatic voter registration notice by nonforwardable mail within 5 days after receiving their voter registration information, and if the applicant does not affirmatively decline registration within 21 days of the mailing, would cause them to be an active voter in the statewide voter registration list. The applicant will be deemed registered as of the date of their DMV transaction. If the applicant affirmatively declines, the State Board would remove them from the statewide voter registration list. The State Board would be authorized to delegate these responsibilities to local boards of elections.
    • The automatic voter registration notice would be in a form prescribed by the State Board and would include notice (1) that the person will be registered to vote if they do not decline, (2) of the qualifications to register, the penalties for false registration, and an instruction to decline registration if the person is not eligible to register, (3) that registration is voluntary and does not affect the availability of services or benefits, (4) that the applicant must pick a political party to participate in a party primary, but can register without affiliation, and (5) of how to pick a party electronically and get more information. The notice would enable the applicant to decline registration and select a political party.
    • If a voter who is automatically registered nonetheless does not appear on the election register, they may either use same-day registration or vote a provisional ballot, which will count as long as the person did not affirmatively decline to register before they cast the provisional ballot.
  • Create a new automatic registration process at the Health Benefit Exchange for people who the Exchange reliably confirms are U.S. citizens through an electronic database match as part of the eligibility determination process, and the people are at least 16 years old and reside in Maryland. If a person attests to non-citizenship, the Exchange would not offer a registration opportunity. In the new process, the Exchange would transmit the applicants' voter registration information to the State Board, and the State Board would determine if the applicant was already registered to vote.
    • If the applicant was already registered, the State Board would do the same registration update process the bill creates for already registered applicants from the DMV.
    • If the applicant is not already registered, the State Board would use the same automatic voter registration process the bill creates for applicants from the DMV who are not yet registered to vote.
    • The Exchange's automatic voter registration processes are subject to federal laws and regulations impacting the exchange, and the bill provides that the processes may be modified by the State Board and the Exchange as needed to comply with federal law.
  • Authorize the State Board to:
    • Identify additional state, federal, or local agencies that, in the regular course of business, reliably verify applicants' citizenship by verifying documents or through an electronic database match, and with the consent of the agency, implement the procedures for automatic voter registration created by the bill
    • Identify additional state, federal, or local agencies that, in the regular course of business, reliably collect sufficient information to update the voter registration information of applicants currently registered to vote in the state, and with the consent of the agency, implement the procedures for automatic voter registration updates created by the bill.

  • Require the DMV to maintain an electronic information system that allows it to determine, at the time a person applies for a transaction, whether the person is registered to vote. If a person is registered to vote, the DMV would electronically transmit the voter registration information of that person to the State Board of Elections.
    • If the information shows the voter's registration information is correct, the State Board would note the date of the update in the voter registration list, and if the voter's registration was inactive, activate it.
    • If the information shows the voter's address or name has changed, the State Board would update their registration and if applicable, activate it. Within five days after receiving the voter registration information from the DMV, the State Board would send the voter an automatic voter registration update notice by non-forwardable mail that included a postage-prepaid form to return to make corrections. If the voter affirmatively corrects the update in writing, the State Board would update their registration. The State Board would also be required to provide an electronic means for a voter to update their registration.
  • The bill authorizes the State Board to delegate some or all of these responsibilities to the local boards of elections.
  • Require the DMV to classify each type of document it accepts as proof of identity as a document that proves U.S. citizenship, proves non-citizenship, or neither.
  • Prohibit the DMV from offering registration to, or transferring the information of, a person whose documents prove they are not U.S. citizens.
  • Create a new automatic registration process at DMV for people who affirmatively demonstrate citizenship as part of their transaction. Specifically, the new process would be used at DMV for any transaction in which the person is not yet registered to vote, provides a document as part of their transaction that demonstrates U.S. citizenship, and they are at least 16 years old and a resident of Maryland. DMV would be authorized but not required to create a process to review prior transaction documents to see if an applicant previously submitted proof of U.S. citizenship if in the current transaction a voter's documents do not demonstrate citizenship or noncitizenship. In this process, once the State Board receives the voter's information and confirms no other information indicates the person is not qualified to vote:
    • The State Board would send the applicant an automatic voter registration notice by non- forwardable mail within 5 days after receiving their voter registration information, and if the applicant does not affirmatively decline registration within 21 days of the mailing, would cause them to be an active voter in the statewide voter registration list. The applicant will be deemed registered as of the date of their DMV transaction. If the applicant affirmatively declines, the State Board would remove them from the statewide voter registration list. The State Board would be authorized to delegate these responsibilities to local boards of elections.
    • The automatic voter registration notice would be in a form prescribed by the State Board and would include notice (1) that the person will be registered to vote if they do not decline, (2) of the qualifications to register, the penalties for false registration, and an instruction to decline registration if the person is not eligible to register, (3) that registration is voluntary and does not affect the availability of services or benefits, (4) that the applicant must pick a political party to participate in a party primary, but can register without affiliation, and (5) of how to pick a party electronically and get more information. The notice would enable the applicant to decline registration and select a political party.
  • Create a new automatic registration process at the Health Benefit Exchange for people who the Exchange reliably confirms are U.S. citizens through an electronic database match as part of the eligibility determination process, and the people are at least 16 years old and reside in Maryland. If a person attests to non-citizenship, the Exchange would not offer a registration opportunity. In the new process, the Exchange would transmit the applicants' voter registration information to the State Board, and the State Board would determine if the applicant was already registered to vote.
    • If the applicant was already registered, the State Board would do the same registration update process the bill creates for already registered applicants from the DMV.
    • If the applicant is not already registered, the State Board would use the same automatic voter registration process the bill creates for applicants from the DMV who are not yet registered to vote.
    • The Exchange's automatic voter registration processes are subject to federal laws and regulations impacting the exchange, and the bill provides that the processes may be modified by the State Board and the Exchange as needed to comply with federal law.
  • Authorize the State Board to:
    • Identify additional state, federal, or local agencies that, in the regular course of business, reliably verify applicants' citizenship by verifying documents or through an electronic database match, and with the consent of the agency, implement the procedures for automatic voter registration created by the bill
    • Identify additional state, federal, or local agencies that, in the regular course of business, reliably collect sufficient information to update the voter registration information of applicants currently registered to vote in the state, and with the consent of the agency, implement the procedures for automatic voter registration updates created by the bill.
  • Acknowledge that participants in address confidentiality programs need special processes, and authorize the DMV, Exchange, and State Board to create them.

This bill, as introduced on January 29, 2024, would create the “Maryland Voting Rights Act of 2024” aimed at regulating the elections and voting-related policies of counties and municipalities to ensure that voting rights are protected generally, and provide specific protections for certain classes of voters. The bill provides protections against vote dilution, requires preclearance, requires language access, prohibits voter intimidation, creates a statewide database of election data to enable discrimination detection and further best practices, and facilitates enforcement with special litigation processes.

As a threshold matter, the bill would declare that state and local laws, rules, regulations, charters, and ordinances must be construed liberally in favor of:

  • Protecting the right to cast a ballot
  • Ensuring that eligible voters are not impaired in registering to vote or voting, including having their votes counted

  • Ensuring protected class voters equitable access to opportunities to register to vote and vote.

    The anti-vote dilution provisions focus on protected classes that engage in racially polarized voting. "Protected class" would mean a class of citizens who are members of a race, color, or language minority group, as referenced in the federal Voting Rights Act. "Racially polarized voting" would mean voting in which there is a divergence between the candidate or electoral choice preferred by protected class voters and the candidate or electoral choice preferred by other voters. This section of the bill would:

  • Declare that a local government may not deny or impair the right to vote of protected class members through any:
    • qualification for eligibility to be a voter or other prerequisite to voting,
    • ordinance, regulation, or other law regarding the administration of elections, or any standard, practice, procedure, or policy, or
    • action or inaction
  • Define as violations of that prohibition:
    • implementation of a prerequisite to voting, a rule relating to election administration, or any policy that results or is intended to result in any disparity or reduction in voter participation, voting access, or ability to participate in the political process among protected class members, or which, based on the totality of the circumstances, results in any impairment of the opportunity or ability of protected class members to participate in the political process, elect candidates of their choice, or otherwise influence election outcomes.
    • enactment of a prerequisite to voting, a rule relating to election administration, or any policy that has the purpose or effect of diminishing the ability of any protected class voter to participate in the electoral process or elect their preferred candidates.
  • Prohibit a local government from using a method of election that has the effect, or is partially motivated by the intent, of impairing protected class voters' ability to participate in the political process, elect candidates of their choice, or otherwise influence election outcomes by diluting or abridging their votes.
  • Define as violations of that prohibition:
    • Implementing an at-large method of election where racially polarized voting by protected class voters occurs, or based on the totality of the circumstances, the opportunity or ability of protected class voters to participate in the political process, elect candidates of their choice, or otherwise influence election outcomes is impaired.
    • Implementing a district-based or another method of election where the candidates or electoral choices of protected class members would usually be defeated and either racially polarized voting by protected class voters occurs or based on the totality of the circumstances, the opportunity or ability of protected class voters to participate in the political process, elect candidates of their choice, or otherwise influence election outcomes is impaired.
    • Implementing any method of election that has the purpose of, or will have the effect of, diminishing the ability of any protected class voter to participate in the electoral process or elect the preferred candidates of choice of the protected class member.

  • Create a pre-lawsuit process to speed the implementation of remedies. The bill would:

    • Require potential plaintiffs to send a notification letter to the relevant local government asserting a possible violation prior to filing suit. A suit would be delayed for 50 days after sending the letter.
    • Allow local governments to forestall suit by adopting a resolution within 60 days of such a letter being sent. The resolution would affirm the local government's intent to enact and implement a remedy, establish specific measures it would take, and provide a schedule for taking them. A suit could not be filed for 90 days after such a resolution was adopted.
    • Create a process for the attorney general to review and then accept or reject remedies proposed by the local government.
    • Allow parties to seek preliminary relief notwithstanding this pre-suit process if an election impacted by the violation is scheduled within 120 days. The preliminary relief would be granted if the court decides the party is more likely than not to succeed on the merits and it is possible to implement an appropriate remedy before the election. Nonetheless, if the action is dismissed or withdrawn because of the local government's enactment or implementation of a remedy or the approval of the attorney general of a remedy, the parties could only seek reimbursement for costs relating to the notification letter.

    If the notice letter process failed and the case went forward in court, the bill would:

  • Specify what evidence a court must consider and must not consider when determining if racially polarized voting in a local government election occurs, or if candidates or electoral choices preferred by protected class voters would be usually defeated.
  • Specify what factors a court may and may not consider in determining whether, based on the totality of the circumstances, a denial or impairment of the opportunity or ability of protected class members to participate in the political process, elect candidates of their choice, or otherwise influence election outcomes.
  • Require courts, after finding a violation, to order remedies tailored to address the violation. Such remedies could not diminish the ability of protected class members to participate in the political process, elect candidates of their choice, or otherwise influence election outcomes. The court would be required to consider remedies proposed by any parties, but prohibited from giving deference or priority to a remedy because it was proposed by the local government.
  • Authorize the court to impose remedies that are inconsistent with any other provision of state or local law if that state or local law would otherwise prevent the court from ordering an appropriate remedy. Remedies could include:
    • a district-based method of election,
    • new or revised districting plans,
    • elimination of staggered elections,
    • reasonably increasing the size of the legislative body
    • additional voting hours or days
    • additional polling locations
    • additional means of voting, such as voting by mail or additional opportunities to return ballots
    • ordering special elections
    • requiring expanded opportunities for the admission of voters
    • requiring additional voter education
    • restoring or adding people to a voter registry
    • the court retaining jurisdiction, and if so, the court must preclear any new or change to prerequisites to voting or standards, practices, or procedures. The court could allow such changes only after finding that they do not have the purpose and would not have the effect of impairing or diminishing the right to vote on the basis of protected class membership.

  • Require local governments to hold detailed public hearings including specified notice processes before enacting and implementing either:

    • a new method of election to replace an at-large method
    • a new districting plan proposed after being sued or threatened with suit for an alleged violation of this bill or the federal Voting Rights Act.

    The bill would require "covered jurisdictions" to get permission before implementing any "covered policies", a process called "preclearance." A covered jurisdiction would have a choice about how to get preclearance for a covered policy. The jurisdiction could either submit the policy to the attorney general's office or to the court for Anne Arundel County. If a covered jurisdiction failed to seek preclearance for a covered policy, the bill would enable individuals, organizations, and the attorney general to enjoin the covered policy until it is precleared. A special preclearance process would be developed for use during emergencies. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create a preclearance process at the attorney general’s office. To use this process the covered jurisdiction would submit the policy to the Division. Thereafter:
    • The Division would approve, conditionally approve, or reject the policy. If the Division conditionally approves the policy, it could then reject the policy, but the rejection would need to be within 60 days of the receipt of the policy. If the Division fails to act within the deadlines imposed by the bill, the policy would be deemed approved.
    • The attorney general would only be able to reject a policy if it determined that the policy is more likely than not to diminish the opportunity or ability of protected class members to participate in the political process and elect candidates of their choice or otherwise influence the outcome of elections, or that the policy is more likely than not to violate the bill. A decision to preclear or reject a covered policy would not be admissible in a future challenge to covered policy.
    • Denials of preclearance could be appealed to the Appellate Court of Maryland.
  • Create a preclearance process at the Circuit Court for Anne Arundel. The covered jurisdiction would submit the policy in writing and contemporaneously send the policy to the Civil Rights Division. If the Division isn't contemporaneously served, the policy would be automatically denied. Assuming notice is given as required, thereafter:
    • The covered jurisdiction would have the burden of proof, just as in the other process.
    • The court could deny preclearance only if it determined that the policy is more likely than not to diminish the opportunity or ability of protected class members to participate in the political process and elect candidates of their choice or otherwise influence the outcome of elections, or that the policy is more likely than not to violate the bill, just as in the other process. A decision to preclear or reject a covered policy would not be admissible in a future challenge to a covered policy.
    • The court would be required to rule on preclearance within 60 days, but if it does not, the policy could not be implemented until preclearance is affirmatively granted.
    • Denials would be appealed under the ordinary rules of appellate procedure, however, it would be expedited.
  • Authorize plaintiffs to seek an injunction to prevent the implementation of a covered policy that was not submitted for preclearance.
  • Define "covered jurisdiction" as any local government:
    • that within the immediately preceding 25 years, became subject to a court order or government enforcement action based on a violation of this bill, the federal Voting Rights Act, the 15th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, or a voting-related violation of the 14th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.
    • that within the immediately preceding 25 years, became subject to at least three court orders or government enforcement actions based on a finding of a violation of a federal or state civil rights law or the 14th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution concerning discrimination against members of a protected class.
    • where the combined misdemeanor and felony arrest rate of members of any protected class consisting of at least 10,000 voting-age citizens or whose members are at least 10% of the citizen voting-age population served by the local government exceeds the proportion that the protected class constitutes of the citizen voting-age population served by the local government by at least 20% at any point in within the immediately preceding 10 years.
    • where, based on data made available by the U.S. Bureau of the Census, the dissimilarity index of any protected class of at least 25,000 voting-age citizens or whose members are at least 10% of the voting-age population of the local government has been more than 50 with respect to the race, color, or language minority group that is a majority within the local government at any point in the immediate preceding 10 years.
    • or a local board of elections in a county that is a covered jurisdiction.

  • Define "covered policy" as a new or modified local government qualification for admission as a voter, prerequisite to voting, or a regulation, ordinance, standard, practice, procedure, or policy concerning:

    • a change to the method or dates of election of a governing body or an elected school board
    • a change to the boundaries of election districts or wards, including changes made under a decennial redistricting
    • a change to the form of government for a local government
    • an annexation, incorporation, dissolution, consolidation, or division of a local government
    • a change to voter registration list maintenance or other activities concerning the cancelation or denial of voter registration
    • a change to the assignment of a voting precinct, polling place, or drop box location, including the relocation of voters, the relocation or reduction of hours of any polling place or ballot drop box, or the reduction or consolidation of polling places or ballot drop boxes;
    • a change to translation or interpretation services in any language other than English, including the creation or distribution of voting materials in any language other than English;
    • a change to assistance to voters with disabilities, including the creation or distribution of voting materials for voters with disabilities; or
    • any additional subject matter that the state board, in consultation with the civil rights division, may identify for inclusion by regulation if the civil rights division determines that any qualification for admission as a voter, prerequisite to voting, or any ordinance, regulation, standard, practice, procedure, or policy concerning the subject matter may have the effect of impairing or diminishing the right to vote of any protected class voter.

    The bill would require language assistance. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the State Board of Elections to make certain determinations of language assistance for non-native English speakers using the American Community Survey or equivalent data, and then using those determinations, publish on its website on or before January 1, 2024, and every three years thereafter, a list of each local government election that requires non-English language-related assistance and the kind of assistance required.
  • Require the State Board to issue regulations relating to how it will make the determinations of language assistance needs, and to include a process through which the public can propose languages for evaluation.
  • Require local governments to competently provide the required language assistance and materials on their website and in physical materials, including
    • registration and voting notices
    • election-related forms and instructions
    • ballot and other materials relating to the electoral process.
    • bilingual poll workers where available.

  • Enable lawsuits both to enforce the language assistance provisions and to enable local governments to provide English-only materials. The court would allow English-only materials if it found the State Board's determination of need was arbitrary and capricious, or an abuse of discretion.

    The bill would create new prohibitions on voter intimidation and obstruction, identify conduct that would automatically violate the prohibitions, and enable impacted people to sue. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Prohibit a person, whether acting under the color of law or otherwise, from engaging in acts of intimidation, deception, or obstruction that interferes with an individual's right to vote.
  • Define as violations of that prohibition:
    • the use of force or threats to use force, or the use of any other conduct to practice intimidation that causes or will reasonably have the effect of causing interference with an individual's right to vote,
    • the knowing use of a deceptive or fraudulent device, contrivance, or communication that causes or will reasonably have the effect of causing interference with any individual's right to vote, or
    • interference with access to a polling place, a ballot drop box, or an office or a place of business of an election official or a voter or an election official in a manner that causes or will reasonably have the effect of causing interference with any individual's right to vote or any delay in voting or the voting process.

  • Enable plaintiffs to sue over alleged violations in the circuit court for Anne Arundel County and provide that if the court finds a violation:

    • The court must order appropriate, tailored remedies that could include additional time to vote
    • The person who committed or aided the violation would be liable for any damages awarded by the court, including nominal damages for any violation and compensatory or punitive damages for any willful violation.

    Finally, the bill would empower enforcement of all of the provisions in the bill by creating certain litigation rules and enabling parties to recover costs and fees. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Enable any of these parties to file suit to enforce any of the provisions in the bill:
    • an aggrieved person
    • an organization whose membership includes or is likely to include aggrieved persons;
    • an organization whose mission would be frustrated by a violation of this section;
    • an organization that would expend resources to fulfill its mission as a result of a violation of this section; or
    • the attorney general
  • Give enforcement actions expedited proceedings and automatic calendar preference.
  • Direct courts to grant preliminary injunctions relating to upcoming elections if the party is more likely than not to succeed on the merits, and it is possible to implement an appropriate remedy that would resolve the alleged violation in the upcoming election
  • Allow the prevailing party to recover reasonable attorneys' fees and litigation costs, including expert witness fees and expenses. However, a state or local government would not be awarded costs or fees unless the court decides the action was frivolous, unreasonable, or without foundation. When the state or local government is the opposing party, a party would be defined as prevailing if as a result of the action the government yields some or all of the relief sought.

This bill, as introduced on November 7, 2024, would make changes to several aspects of voting procedures. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Allow a municipality or county that is party to an early voting municipal agreement to change the days, hours, and locations for early voting no later than 60 days before an election. Any changes would need to be submitted as an addendum to the original agreement, signed by the county and municipal clerk, and submitted to the secretary of state. Existing law allows other aspects of early voting municipal agreements to be amended upon agreement of the parties, but is silent on this particular issue. Existing law also provides that early voting sites must be finalized no later than 60 days before Election Day.
  • Require the clerk of each municipality to notify the Bureau of Elections at least 50 days before an election of the days, hours, and location of each early voting site. The Bureau of Elections would be required to post that information in a "conspicuous place" in the clerk's office and on the municipality's website, if available. Under existing law, after an early voting site is approved, the clerk must notify registered voters directly but the law is silent on notifying the Bureau of Elections.
  • Require each city or township clerk to establish ballot drop box locations no later than 75 days before an election. Existing law is silent on when ballot drop box locations must be determined. However, existing law provides that ballot drop boxes must be video monitored by the municipal clerk beginning 75 days before each election.
  • Allow a registered voter to update their registration in person at the city clerk's office from the 14th day before an election through Election Day. Under existing law, individuals who are not registered to vote may do so at the clerk's office during this timeframe.
  • Require the secretary of state to send an annual notice to all UOCAVA voters on the permanent mail voter list to confirm that the voter remains an absent uniformed services voter or overseas voter.
  • Require that a UOCAVA voter on the permanent mail voter list remain on the list if any of the following occur:
    • The voter responds to the notice and confirms their status as a UOCAVA voter and either updates their registration or does not update their registration.
    • The notice is not returned as undeliverable.

  • Require the clerk to remove a UOCAVA voter from the permanent mail ballot voter list if:

    • The voter responds to the notice stating that they are no longer a UOCAVA voter
    • The notice is returned as undeliverable
    • The city or township clerk "otherwise determines" that the voter is no longer a UOCAVA voter.

    Under existing law, a voter on the permanent mail voter list can be removed from the list for the following reasons: (1) the voter submits a signed request to be removed from the list, (2) the voter is no longer qualified to vote in the state, (3) the secretary of state or clerk receives "reliable information" that the voter has moved without updating their address or has moved to another state, or (4) the voter has not voted for six consecutive years.


  • Require mail ballot applications to allow voters to request mail ballots for any election, certain elections, or all elections in that calendar year. Under existing law, a voter may request mail ballots for a primary election or for all elections that year.
  • Require the Board of Elections to verify mail ballots by comparing the ballot number on the ballot stub with the ballot number on the face of the return envelope or with the ballot number listed in the qualified voter file. If the ballot numbers do not match or the ballot stub is missing without explanation, the ballot must be processed as a challenged ballot. Under existing law, the Board of Elections is only required to compare the ballot number on the stub with the ballot number on the envelope. Existing law specifies that the ballot must be counted if the numbers match but does not specify how to treat ballots with unmatched numbers.
  • Require municipal clerks to determine how many voting booths are needed at a polling place. Under existing law, at least one booth must be provided at a polling place and no less than one voting booth per 100 registered voters in that precinct.
  • Eliminate the requirement that voting booths have walls that are at least six feet high but would leave in place the requirement that voting booths be built in such a manner that the voter is concealed from all other individuals.

The bill also includes numerous provisions not tracked by Voting Rights Lab.

    • a current mortgage, lease, or rental agreement
