This bill, as amended on December 10, 2024, makes numerous changes to Michigan election law, mostly surrounding the role of election watchers ("challengers"). Specifically, the bill would:

  • Clarify the role of election watchers ("challengers") during elections. Specifically, the bill would:
    • More clearly enumerate the rights and responsibilities of a challenger, and specify prohibited conduct, codifying existing practice.
    • Specify the locations at which a challenger may be present: a city or township clerk's office during the 40 days before election day and on election day, an election day precinct polling place, an election day vote center, an early voting site, an absent voter counting place, or a combined absent voter counting place.
    • Specify the maximum number of challengers appointed by an entity are permitted to be present at each type of site.
    • Expand, from 30 to 60 days, the maximum time during which an incorporated nonprofit organization or organized committee of interested citizens may inform a clerk of its intention to appoint challengers.
    • Require challengers to be credentialed by their appointing authority, again codifying existing practice.
    • Clarify that for-profit organizations are not permitted to appoint challengers.
  • Codify an existing practice under which a "challenger liaison" is required to be present at any location where challengers are permitted to ensure challengers comply with the law.
  • Clarify the requirements for an affidavit submitted by a person challenging another voter's registration. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require a clerk to evaluate the reliability of a challenge before acting on it. Under existing law, a clerk must notify a voter who is the subject of a challenge upon receipt of the challenging affidavit. Under the bill, the clerk would be required to first evaluate the reliability of the affidavit and discard the challenge if the information therein is unreliable. The bill would therefore also include changes to the information required to be included in a challenge by making it more extensive.
    • Specify that a challenge to a voter's registration must be submitted by a registered voter in the same municipality having personal knowledge of the voter's alleged ineligibility. Under existing law, any registered voter in the municipality may file a challenge.
    • Change the requirements for canceling a voter's registration following a challenge. Under existing law, a challenged voter has their registration canceled after 30 days of a notice being sent unless the voter proves their qualifications. HISTORY: {"date":"05/17/2024","summary":"Filed with Secretary of State. Chapter No. 112","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on May 17, 2024, creates the "Minnesota Voting Rights Act," which sets out new prohibitions and enforcement mechanisms for voter suppression and vote dilution. The bill also makes changes to various existing areas of election law, including expanding eligibility to serve as a mail ballot witness, facilitating voter registration and voting access for unhoused and student voters, expanding language accessibility for certain election materials, moving vote canvassing procedures forward, and establishing new requirements for maintenance and public use of the voter registration list.

Specifically, the bill:

  • Creates the "Minnesota Voting Rights Act." The Act:
    • Prohibits any political subdivision or government official or entity from adopting or enforcing any law or rule of any kind that would result in (1) voter suppression, defined as a disparity in voter participation, access to voting opportunities, or the opportunity or ability to participate in the political process between a protected class and other members of the electorate, or a denial or abridgement of the right to vote by a member of a protected class, or (2) vote dilution, defined as impairing the equal opportunity or ability of members of a protected class to nominate or elect candidates of their choice as a result of diluting the vote of members of that protected class.
    • Specifies factors for a court to consider in determining whether voter suppression or vote dilution has occurred.
    • Creates a civil right of action for the attorney general, a county attorney, or an individual or entity aggrieved by a violation to obtain remedies for voter suppression or vote dilution, and sets out procedural requirements for claims.
    • Requires any law, rule, charter provision, or local ordinance or code concerning voting rights to be liberally construed in favor of the protection of voting rights.
    • Authorizes changes to polling places if necessary to remedy or prevent a violation of the prohibitions on voter suppression or vote dilution.
  • Expands criteria for who may serve as a witness for a mail ballot. Under prior law, only a registered voter in Minnesota or a notary public (or other person authorized to administer oaths) could witness a voter's mail ballot. The bill removes the "registered voter in Minnesota" option and instead permits ballots to be witnessed by any U.S. citizen 18 years of age or older.
  • Permits a voter to submit an electronic application for a mail ballot for any election other than a town election held in March. Under prior law, electronic applications were permitted for a federal, state, or county election only.
  • Facilitates voter registration for unhoused individuals and students. The bill:
    • Modifies voter registration forms to permit a voter to provide a physical description of their residence if it has no street address. The bill specifies that a registration application is not invalid if used on a form that was printed before the bill took effect.
  • Specifies requirements for certain forms of student ID accepted for same-day registration.
  • Expands mandatory voter registration outreach at public schools to include providing applications to students who are eligible for pre-registration. Prior law required providing applications only to those students who would be eligible to vote at the next election.
  • Requires election officials to establish an early voting location for at least one day on or near a school campus for state general elections and odd-year city general elections, at the request of the school or student government. Institutions must provide on-campus housing for at least 100 students to be eligible to make a request, and requests must meet certain procedural requirements set out by the bill.
  • Expands requirements related to language accessibility for election materials. The bill:
    • Requires the secretary of state to designate language-minority districts by January 1 of each year, rather than 90 days before an election as under prior law. The bill also specifies that the secretary must provide example ballots in non-English languages for state elections. Prior law did not specify election types.
    • Requires translations of voting instructions and sample ballots into multiple languages if a language-minority district contains multiple language groups constituting at least three percent of the population, and requires the secretary of state and county auditors to maintain a list of the districts on their respective websites.
  • Moves certain canvassing processes forward, and specifies certain counting procedures for in-person and mail ballots. The bill:
    • Reduces the county canvassing period by two days, from the 3rd-10th day after the election, to the 3rd-8th day. The bill also moves the meeting date of the state canvassing board from the third Tuesday after an election to the 16th day after an election, and moves several other post-election processes forward.
    • Requires election judges in precincts using ballot tabulators to immediately prepare the summary statement once the final count of ballots agrees with the number of ballots to be counted.
    • Specifies the timing for the counting and processing of mail ballots received after 3 p.m. on Election Day.
  • Requires new procedures for list maintenance concerning deceased voters, and specifies limits on use of the voter list by the public. The bill:
    • Requires the secretary of state to determine if any of the persons listed on the Social Security Death Index or reported as deceased by the vital records department of another state are registered to vote and prepare a list of those registrants for each county auditor. Prior law permitted, but did not require, doing so.
    • Prohibits individuals who access the voter list from disseminating the list on the internet in any searchable format, or selling, loaning, or otherwise providing access to the list to other persons except within the person's own organization for election or law enforcement purposes.
  • Itemizes the information that must be included in the restoration of voting rights notice provided to individuals on release from incarceration. Prior law set out template language for the notice, which provided less detail regarding registration and voting requirements.
  • Specifies the definition of "personal information" for purposes of the criminal offense of disseminating personal information of an election official.

The bill also makes extensive changes in areas of law not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, including procedures for contesting elections, and campaign finance and redistricting requirements.

Last Updated July 25, 2024

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 3, 2024, would change rules for provisional and mail voting for certain voters and make modifications to criminal statutes involving voting. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Expand the applicability of certain provisions of law permitting a voter to cast a provisional ballot if the voter claims to be registered and eligible to vote in an election, but whose eligibility cannot immediately be established by examining the precinct register. Under existing law, these provisions apply only to elections for federal or statewide officers or statewide issues, but the bill would expand this to any public election.
  • Clarify that any list of persons applying for a mail ballot on the grounds of permanent disability shall be kept confidential to the extent possible under the law.
  • Change a provision that permits a covered (UOCAVA) voter to submit their registration and vote at a polling place on Election Day by moving the location for this process to the office of the election authority.
  • Expand a provision that permits interstate former residents and new residents to vote by mail ballot by permitting them to do so in person at the office of the election authority on Election Day.
  • Create the felony criminal offense of tampering with an election official. A person commits this offense if the person, with the purpose of harassing or intimidating an election official in performance of their official duties:
    • threatens or causes harm to the official or their family,
    • uses force, threats, or deception against the official or their family,
    • attempts to cause an election official of their family to violate election law,
    • engages in harassing or alarming behavior toward an election official, including stalking, or
    • disseminates the personal information of an election official or their family.
  • Expand the applicability of the misdemeanor offense of engaging in electioneering activities in an improper manner. The bill would require a person to refrain from electioneering within 25 feet of a polling place on election day or during the absentee voting period. Under current law, electioneering is forbidden only on election day.

The bill also modifies statutes in areas of law not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, including candidate filing deadlines and electronic delivery of a notice of election.

"Voter activity" would include registering to vote, voting in an election, signing a petition to form a new political party, signing a petition for the nomination of an independent candidate for office, or signing an initiative petition. Under existing law, a voter is included in an address confirmation process if they did not vote or transfer their registration in the preceding four years.
  • Create a duty for election authorities to cancel registration due to a change of address based on the voter's written request or failure to respond to a cancellation notice or engage in "voter activity" in the following two general elections. Existing law does not impart a duty on election authorities to cancel registrations on the occurrence of those conditions. Instead, it prohibits the cancellation of a voter's registration due to a change of address unless the voter requests or the voter fails to respond to the cancellation notice or did not vote for two general election cycles after the notice.
  • Make any "voter activity" within the time period between the issuance of a notice of registration cancellation and the following two general elections sufficient to avoid cancellation of registration. Under existing law, a person must vote to avoid cancellation.

This bill, as amended on June 26, 2024, would propose a state constitutional amendment expanding North Carolina's voter ID requirement, to constitutionally require presentation of photo ID for all forms of voting. Existing constitutional law expressly requires photo ID for voting in person only. Under existing statutory law, most mail voters are also required to include a copy of a qualifying photo ID when returning a mail ballot.

Adoption of the proposed amendment requires passage by three-fifths of the legislature and approval by a majority of voters.

The legislature overrode Governor Cooper's veto of this on December 11, 2024. As enacted, the bill transfers administration of the State Board of Elections from the secretary of state's office to the Department of the State Auditor as of July 1, 2025, and shortens various time periods related to mail voting, curing mail ballots, and verification of provisional ballots, among other changes. Specifically, the bill:

  • Transfers administration of the State Board of Elections from the secretary of state's office to the state auditor as of July 1, 2025. The bill grants the state board authority to exercise its powers "independently," except that budgeting functions must be performed under the "direction and supervision" of the auditor. The bill:
    • Terminates the current terms of the members of the state board on April 1, 2025, and requires new terms of office for the board to begin May 1 following a presidential election. The bill also specifies 2025 term end and start dates for county boards of election.
    • Authorizes the auditor to make appointments to the state board and to fill vacancies. Prior law assigned this authority to the governor.
    • Authorizes the state auditor to appoint the chair of each county elections board. Prior law assigned this authority to the governor.
  • Moves the deadline earlier for mail ballot applications, to receipt by local officials on the second Tuesday before the election. Under prior law, the receipt deadline was the Tuesday before the election.
  • Moves the deadline earlier for providing documents to cure a defective mail ballot, or to verify a provisional ballot cast without required voter photo ID, to 12 p.m. on the third business day after an election. Under prior law, the deadline to provide this documentation was the ninth day after an election. The bill also expressly requires a voter whose registration application includes an ID number that cannot be verified to provide ID by this deadline, for their provisional ballot to be counted. Prior law did not specify a deadline for these voters.
  • Requires that the county board meeting to count mail ballots be "continuous until completed," and expressly prohibits members from leaving the counting place except for "unavoidable necessity." The bill permits a supplemental counting meeting for UOCAVA ballots only, and requires officials to announce the tally of mail ballots no later than the third day after the election. Prior law granted boards discretion to hold additional meetings for ballot counting on the day after an election and the day before the canvass.
  • Requires provisional ballots to be counted no later than 5:00 p.m. on the third business day after the election. Under prior law, the general deadline for this count was any time before the ballot canvass.
  • Requires precinct officials to use a log provided by the state board to track all voter assistants who enter a polling location. Prior law required recording this information, but did not specify use of a state board document to do so.
  • Prohibits the attorney general from taking a position on behalf of the state that is contrary to or inconsistent with the position of the legislature in litigation involving the validity or constitutionality of an act of the legislature or a provision of the state constitution.

The bill also makes extensive changes in other areas of law not covered by Voting Rights Lab.

This bill, as introduced on January 11, 2024, would make changes across a variety of elections-related statutes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the election commissioner or county clerk to verify the driver's license or state identification card data of a person applying for a mail ballot before sending the voter a mail ballot.
  • Extend the deadline to apply for a mail ballot in an election other than a statewide primary or general election from thirty days before the election to fifteen days before the election.
  • Require the Secretary of State to make all necessary adjustments to the citizenship-verification process of registered voters to ensure that no person is removed from the rolls in violation of law.
  • Require the Secretary of State to obtain a digital copy of each voter's photograph from the Department of Motor Vehicles.
  • Tighten the requirements for a person claiming to have a reasonable impediment to obtaining a photo ID. The bill would clarify that existing reasonable impediments are only valid if they prevent the voter from obtaining a photo ID, not from presenting it. The bill would also require that the election commissioner or county clerk verify that a voter claiming to have a reasonable impediment does not, in fact, have a current driver's license or state ID card.
  • Permit election workers to decline to be compensated and instead redirect those funds for election worker recruitment.
  • Limit each state or county political party to one monthly request for a free copy of the list of registered voters.

The bill also makes changes to areas of law not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, including filing requirements for candidates.

This bill, as introduced on January 16, 2024, would narrow the amount of time Nebraska voters have to complete a mail ballot or vote early. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require ballots to be sent to mail voters at least twenty-two days before a statewide primary or general election. Existing law requires them to be sent at least thirty-five days before such an election.
  • Permit a voter who knows they will be absent from their county of residence on Election Day to cast their ballot in person in the office of the election commissioner or county clerk as early as twenty-two days before an election. Existing law permits this as early as thirty days before an election.

This bill, as introduced on January 17, 2024, concerns interference with election officials and threats made against them. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the secretary of state to issue a report every presidential election year of threats made against the secretary or any other election official in the state, including any instance of AI deep fakes to disseminate misinformation.
  • Create a new misdemeanor offense for obstructing, hindering, or otherwise interfering with the secretary of state or any other official administering an election, or preventing such a person from occupying from any place they need to be present in order to conduct their duties.
  • Create a new misdemeanor offense for disseminating the home address of the secretary of state or any other official administering an election without their consent and with intent to facilitate the commission of an offense, or with reckless disregard for the fact that an offense might occur due to the dissemination.
  • Create a new misdemeanor offense for using an AI deep fake to disseminate election misinformation. The bill would also authorize a cause of action for injunctive relief against a person who violates this section.

  • Create a felony offense for the following conduct:

    • Knowingly removing or destroying a registration list or polling place roster or preventing any voter from voting.
    • Knowingly accessing or attempting to access the statewide voter registration systems except for conducting official duties.
    • Knowingly creating or permitting disclosure of an image of the hard drive of any voting system component by a local clerk without permission of the Secretary of State.
    • Knowingly publishing passwords or other confidential information related to an electronic voting system.
  • Create a class A misdemeanor for knowingly publicizing the personal information of an election official, officer, or worker, their family or household member without consent if it is known that publication of the information poses an imminent and serious threat to their safety.
  • Create a class B misdemeanor for election officials who fail to comply with the requirements to keep all components of voting systems in a location secured by key card access or similar entry logging system and to ensure that the log is maintained as an election record for 25 months following the date of any entry.

Last updated March 20, 2024.

This bill, as amended on May 16, 2024, would tighten documentation requirements for voter registration and photo ID requirements to vote, by eliminating the use of provisional "affidavit ballots." The bill would:

  • Require all applicants for voter registration to provide documentary proof of citizenship, age, domicile, and identity. Under existing law, registrants may submit an affidavit attesting to their qualifications in lieu of providing documentation.
  • Require the secretary of state to coordinate with various state agencies to use data contained in state databases on Election Day to provide real-time verification of first-time registrants who have not provided sufficient documentation.
  • Repeal a provision that permits a voter to cast a provisional ballot (affidavit ballot) without ID. Under existing law, voters registered in advance of Election Day who lack qualifying ID may cast a regular ballot after signing an affidavit and having their photo taken or having an election worker attest to their identity, and Election Day registrants without photo ID may cast provisional (affidavit) ballots that are counted if they present a photo ID to election officials within seven days after the election.
  • Permit a person aggrieved by the decision of an election official that prevents the person from voting to cast a ballot pending judicial review. Under the bill, such ballots would be kept separate from regular ballots, and a voter would have to obtain a ruling from a superior court for the ballot to be counted. The bill would require a superior court hearing such a dispute to make an effort to resolve the dispute before noon on the last day for candidates to request a recount.
  • Allow a person completing a voter registration application to provide a nondrivers picture identification card number as an alternative to providing a driver's license number.
  • Repeal code provisions related to affidavit ballots, to conform with the bill's elimination of their use.

Last Updated May 23, 2024

This bill, as introduced on January 3, 2024, would create a new civil penalty of up to $5,000 for any election officer who violates any election law. Existing law creates civil penalties for a number of voting violations but does not specify penalties applicable to election officers only.

The bill would define "synthetic media'' as "any form of media including text, image, video or sound, fully or partially created or modified through the use of artificial intelligence algorithms." Existing law does not include a similar provision.
  • Create a class B felony for a second or subsequent conviction of unlawful distribution of election-related synthetic media if the previous conviction(s) occurred within the previous 5 years or the complaint alleges that the media was distributed with the purpose of provoking violence.

  • Requires all in-person voters to present photo ID in order to cast a ballot, by repealing existing provisions that (1) allowed for a voter's identity to be confirmed by an election moderator, checklist supervisor, or clerk, and (2) allowed for casting a provisional ballot (affidavit ballot) without ID. Under prior law, voters registered in advance of Election Day who lacked qualifying ID were permitted to cast a regular ballot after signing an affidavit and having their photo taken or having an election worker attest to their identity, and Election Day registrants without photo ID were permitted to cast provisional (affidavit) ballots that would be counted if they presented a photo ID to election officials within seven days after the election.

This bill, as introduced on January 3, 2024, would change New Hampshire statute with regard to ballot reconciliation. Specifically, the bill would:

This bill, as introduced on January 9, 2024, is titled the "John R. Lewis Voting Rights Act of New Jersey". The bill enshrines protections to ensure equality of political participation for voters of racial, color and language minority groups. The bill would:

  • Prohibit any political subdivision from implementing a practice that abridges the rights to political participation of any protected class of eligible voters who are members of a race, color, or language-minority group. This prohibition extends to any method of election that abridges the rights of a protected class.
  • Authorize courts to implement appropriate remedies for abridgment of the rights of protected classes, including changes to the time, days, locations, and methods of elections, additional voter education, expanded voter registration, and add persons back to voter rolls. Courts may retain jurisdiction as necessary to ensure the remedies are implemented.
  • Require localities to give members of protected classes a meaningful opportunity to participate in the redistricting process.
  • Give members of protected classes and organization composed of members of protected classes standing to sue for enforcement of the act's provisions.
  • Require potential plaintiffs to send a locality a letter at least 50 days prior to filing suit, during which time the locality may take steps to remedy the alleged violation.
  • Require localities to provide voting materials in languages other than English if 2% of the voting age population or 4,000 people are members of a single-language minority.
  • Require covered entities to preclear regulations about many election-related practices with the Division on Civil Rights or a court. The bill defines covered entities as localities who have been subject to court orders related to civil rights violations in the last 25 years, localities with certain crime rate data, and localities with certain dissimilarity indexes.
  • Prohibit any person acting under color of law from intimidating, deceiving, or obstructing the rights of voters.

HISTORY: {"date":"10/24/2024","summary":"From SENATE Committee on STATE GOVERNMENT, WAGERING, TOURISM AND HISTORIC PRESERVATION","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on June 26, 2024, would:

  • Create a fourth degree felony offense for a natural person knowingly or recklessly disclosing or soliciting "deceptive audio or visual media" within 90 days of an election with the intent to deceive a voter with false information about a candidate, election, or public question. A second or subsequent violation would be a third degree felony.
  • Create a civil right of action for voters to seek injunctive or equitable relief to enjoin distribution of deceptive media, and a right of action for candidates whose likenesses are used in such media against the content creator.
  • Create an exception to the offense for content that:
    • Consists of "solely de minimis" alterations of a person's image or appearance
    • Contains a disclaimer stating "This work contains manipulated images or sound," subject to certain requirements
    • Is "clearly identified" as a work of deceptive audio or visual media and is disclosed in connection with criticism, comment, satire, parody, news reporting, teaching, scholarship, or research
    • Is provided to law enforcement or in response to a court order, or in furtherance of investigation of certain other criminal offenses
  • Exempt the following entities from the offense:
    • Interactive computer service providers, cloud services providers, commercial developers or providers of artificial intelligence technology, if they are not they are not deemed to be a publisher, speaker, or information content provider under federal law.
    • Advertising platforms on which deceptive media appears, including broadcasting stations, cable services, radio stations, telecommunications carriers, and television stations, as defined by federal law; billboards, internet websites, mobile applications, video streaming services, newspapers, magazines, publications, or any other advertising channels or mediums whose role in dissemination is limited to selling time or space, or who are prohibited by federal law from "censoring" content.
    • News providers that routinely carry news and commentary of general interest and that provide prohibited deceptive media "solely for the purpose of disseminating newsworthy facts," including broadcasting stations, programmers, or producers, websites, video streaming services, regularly published newspapers, magazines, or other periodicals of general circulation. If the deceptive nature of the media is "known or verified," the news source must provide a disclaimer identifying it as such.

Previous versions of the bill contained provisions that were amended out of this version. Those provisions would have:

  • Created a misdemeanor offense for engaging in prohibited conduct with deceptive audio or visual media.
  • Established slightly different exemptions from criminal liability for internet service providers or developers, and for advertisers.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on January 8, 2026, would create the "John R. Lewis Voter Empowerment Act of New Jersey." Specifically the bill would:

  • Prohibit any state agency, local election office, or political subdivision from enacting or implementing any voting qualification, prerequisite to voting, law, ordinance, standard, or policy that results in a denial or abridgement of the right of members of a protected class to vote. It would specifically prohibit policies that burden the right to vote for any individual on the basis of disability.
  • Prohibit any local election office or political subdivision from using any method of election that would impair the equal opportunity of protected class members in the political process.
  • Prohibit local governments from taking any action or failing to take any action, including implementing, imposing, or enforcing any qualification for qualification for eligibility to vote or any law, ordinance, regulation, standard, practice, procedure, or policy regarding the administration of elections that is intended to result in impairing voter participation among a protected class.
  • Create a set of factors to be analyzed to determine if violations of the bill have occurred.
  • Authorize courts to implement appropriate remedies for abridgment of the rights of protected classes, including transitioning to an alternative method of election, changes to the days, locations, and methods of elections, additional voter education, expanded voter registration, and adding voters back to voter rolls. Courts may retain jurisdiction as necessary to ensure the remedies are implemented.
  • Require localities to give members of the public opportunities to participate in the redistricting process. Localities must also conduct additional outreach to limited English proficient communities so that they may participate in the process.
  • Give members of protected classes and organizations composed of members of protected classes standing to sue for enforcement of the act's provisions.
  • Require potential plaintiffs to send a locality a letter at least 50 days prior to filing suit, during which time the locality may take steps to remedy the alleged violation.
  • Require localities to provide voting materials in languages other than English if more than two percent of the voting age population, but no fewer than 100 individuals, speak a language other than English and have limited proficiency in English or more than 4,000 individuals speak a language other than English and have limited proficiency in English.
  • Require "covered entities" to preclear regulations about many election-related practices with the newly established Division of Voting Rights within the Department of the Treasury (the "Division."). The bill defines covered entities as any political subdivision that has been subject to court orders related to civil rights violations in the last 15 years, localities with certain arrest rate data, localities with certain dissimilarity indexes, localities with certain poverty rates, localities with certain voter participation rates, localities that failed to provide voter data to the New Jersey Voting and Elections Institute in the last three years, and localities that enacted a policy without obtaining preclearance in the past 25 years.
  • Create a process for a covered entity to obtain preclearance from the Division.
  • Provide the attorney general with authority to investigate or enforce provisions of the bill.
  • Require the attorney general to engage in public education efforts to inform the voting eligible population about their voting rights, including which populations are protected classes, which languages access materials are available, and any causes of action and avenues of redress available under the bill.
  • Prohibit any person from intimidating, deceiving, or obstructing the rights of voters.
  • Require the attorney general to provide an annual report on voting rights and election-related matters, including summaries of actions taken to enforce the provisions of the bill.
  • Specify that the provisions of the bill would take effect on July 1, 2026.

The bill also contains additional provisions related to topics that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

This bill, as amended on December 18, 2025, would expand automatic voter registration to additional agencies, change existing automatic voter registration practices at the Motor Vehicle Commission (MVC), and change automatic voter registration related requirements at other state agencies. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Establish automatic voter registration at additional state agencies. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require the Division of Assistance and Health Services in the Department of Human Services to serve as an automatic voter registration agency. Under existing law, the only agency required to provide automatic voter registration is the MVC.
    • Require the Department of Corrections to serve as an automatic voter registration agency for otherwise eligible individuals scheduled to be released from incarceration. Under existing law, individuals scheduled to be released must be provided a non-driver identification card. The bill would newly require those individuals additionally be provided an opportunity to register to vote at the time they are provided a non-driver identification card. The individual's registration would not be effective until their release from incarceration. To be registered, the individual would also be required to identify a place of residence within the state where the individual will reside upon release from incarceration.
    • Use the process established to facilitate the removal of a person's voter registration if requested during an automatic voter registration transaction.
  • Divide the existing automatic voter registration process at the MVC into separate processes based on whether documentation provided in the course of the agency transaction establishes U.S. citizenship. Under existing law, there is a single process for all agency customers, regardless of whether they show proof of citizenship. Specifically, under the bill:
    • When individuals provide documentation establishing U.S. citizenship during the course of business with the MVC, the county commissioner of registration would register the individual and send them by non-forwardable mail a notice that they could return in order to decline to be registered, affiliate with a political party, or join the permanent mail voter list. The notice would include a postage-paid pre-addressed return envelope.The notice would explain voter eligibility requirements and penalties for submission of a false application and include the required information in English, Spanish, and any language that is the primary language of five percent or more of the registered voters in that county. A new registrant through this process would not be registered to vote until their information was received and processed by the county commissioner of registration, with the effective date being the date of the person's application with the MVC.
    • When an MVC customer does not provide documentation establishing U.S. citizenship or the documentation provided during the agency process does not establish U.S. citizenship, they would be required to affirmatively select or decline voter registration as a necessary condition to complete their MVC application. The chief administrator would be required to ensure that the information necessary for voter registration was collected from the application and promptly transmitted to the secretary of state if the applicant selects the option to register to vote.
    • Any individual, who at the time of the transaction provides a document proving that they are not a U.S. citizen, would not be offered the opportunity to register to vote.
  • Allow agencies (other than the MVC) that collect and verify voter eligibility information from databases to serve as automatic voter registration agencies. Under existing law, only agencies that collect voter eligibility information from documents are allowed to offer automatic voter registration.
  • Prohibit the chief administrator from transmitting information for any person who is a participant in the address confidentiality program. There is no similar provision under existing law.
  • Specify additional components of the MVC automatic voter registration process. The bill would:
    • Expressly provide for automatic registration updates through the MVC for name and address changes, including for voter list maintenance purposes by county election commissioners. Existing law already provides for certain updates to registration through the automatic registration process, but does not set out specifics and does not direct the use of change of address information from the MVC for list maintenance by local officials.
    • Direct the secretary of state and MVC to develop procedures for the MVC to identify whether a customer is already registered to vote.
    • Specify what information must be transmitted to the secretary of state, including telephone number and email address. Existing law does not itemize data.

A previous version of this bill contained provisions that would have directed the secretary of state to develop procedures for processing electronic voter registration records received from automatic voter registration agencies (other than the MVC) that do not contain a digitized image of the applicant's signature, and provisions that would expanded safe harbor protections for persons registered erroneously through automatic voter registration. Those provisions were amended out of the bill on December 15, 2025.

The bill would leave in place the provision in existing law that invests members of the election board with "all the powers and duties of constables of this State in criminal matters."
  • Allow election officials or the police department to assign police officers to any district board whenever they deem it "necessary" to do so, and eliminate the existing provisions that expressly prohibit doing so. Under existing law, requests for police officer presence may be made only for assistance with a specific emergency, allegation of criminal conduct, or a disturbance. In such cases, the district board must notify the county board of elections or superintendent of elections of the police presence who must promptly notify the secretary or state. Under the bill, officials would be authorized to assign police to "enforce the election laws, maintain order, peace and quiet during the hours of registry and election," as well the existing authority to assist with transportation of election materials. Officers would be prohibited from performing duties of a board member or challenger at the location where they were dispatched.
  • Permit increased presence of police officers at the polling place in election-related roles. The bill would:
    • Allow police officers to serve as challengers at a polling place, by removing the prohibition on doing so.
    • Remove the requirement that officers may only serve on an election board if they are off-duty.
  • Create a new felony offense ("crime of the fourth degree") for an officer violating the prohibition on wearing their uniform or carrying an exposed weapon while serving in an election-related role.
  • Allow election officials to locate a mail ballot drop box inside, or within 100 feet of an entrance or exit, of a police station, by removing the existing prohibition on doing so.
  • Allow police officers, whether in or out of uniform, to remain or stand within 100 feet of a polling place during an election, by removing the prohibition on doing so.

This bill, as introduced on May 2, 2024, would create a new photo ID requirement for in-person and mail voting, and would expand the authority of challengers to inspect ID documents. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require all voters to present photo ID when voting in person, or provide a copy of photo ID when voting by mail ballot, as of January 1, 2025. Under existing law, voters do not need to present ID to vote. Accepted ID would be limited to:
    • A New Jersey driver's license or non-driver's ID card, or
    • Any document that (1) includes the name of voter, (2) includes the voter's photograph, (3) has an expiration date that has not expired or expired only after the date of the most recent election, (4) was issued by the federal government or the state of New Jersey
  • Allow a voter who does not provide photo ID due to a religious objection to being photographed to complete a sworn affidavit regarding their religious objection, as an alternative to presenting ID.
  • Allow voters who do not present an accepted form of voter ID, or an affidavit of religious objection, to vote a provisional ballot. Under existing rules for verifying a provisional ballot, voters would have until the second day after the election to provide ID or the affidavit for the ballot to be counted.
  • Require the examination of voter ID on Election Day to occur in full view of the challengers.
  • Authorize members of an election board and challengers to examine any document concerning proof of identification.
  • Apply the existing challenge procedure to voters whose voter ID or religious objection affidavit is challenged as invalid. Under the procedure, the voter must provide an affidavit of qualifications, and a "provisional document" to establish identity. The bill would eliminate a driver's license as an accepted provisional document, but would otherwise preserve the existing list: (1) a sample ballot which lists the voter's name and address; (2) an official federal, State, county or municipal document which lists the voter's name and address; (3) a utility or telephone bill or tax or rent receipt dated; or (4) a piece of mail postmarked, on or after the 60th day before the day of the election at which the voter is challenged.
  • Authorize the secretary of state, rather than the attorney general, to determine which forms of ID are accepted for individuals who registered by mail and are voting for the first time. The bill would also require the secretary, rather than the attorney general, to maintain records related to voter identification.
  • Require the DMV to provide free ID to any eligible resident who requests ID for voting purposes and submits an affidavit of indigence. Existing law does not provide for any form of free ID.
  • Exempt voters entitled to vote by mail under UOCAVA or under other federal laws from the photo ID requirements.
  • Make conforming and non-substantive changes to various provisions to reflect the new requirements.

Under prior law, such markings did not count as a vote for the candidate.
  • Requires the secretary of state, in consultation with the county board of elections in each county, to establish uniform guidelines to assist the county board and the district boards in their assessment of the validity of marks made.

This bill, as enacted on January 12, 2026, changes New Jersey's "front-end opt out" automatic voter registration process to a "back-end opt out" process when applying for certain forms of ID, expands the list of agencies who can conduct automatic voter registration, and makes other changes to automatic voter registration procedures. Specifically, the bill:

  • Allows any state agency, except for the Motor Vehicle Commission ("MVC"), that the secretary of state verifies already collects sufficient information, including through documents or database verification, that would provide proof of eligibility to establish automatic voter registration. The bill eliminates the requirement that the secretary of state comply with these requirements but would require each county commissioner of registration to comply with them. Under previous law, only an agency that collects documents that provide proof of eligibility could serve as an automatic voter registration agency.
  • Requires the secretary of state and chief administrator to jointly develop a process by which the MVC, upon obtaining an individual's full name, date of birth, driver's license or state ID number, and address, uses the information from the statewide voter registration system to determine whether that individual is already registered to vote in the state.
  • Requires the MVC and any other state agency that has implemented automatic voter registration to send any change of name or residence information received during a transaction with a registered voter to the secretary of state for the purpose of updating the voter's registration. Under previous law, change of residence information was required to be sent in written format to the commissioner of registration, made via phone call to the commissioner, or by completing a change of residence notice online from the secretary of state. Specifically, the bill requires:
    • The secretary of state to send that information to the commissioner of registration in the individual's county of residence
    • The county commissioner of registration to update that voter's registration information and to transfer that individual's registration file if inactive to the active file, and to send that voter by forwardable mail, a notice of the change and a postage paid pre-addressed return form by which the voter could correct the information.
    • The county commissioner, upon receiving a notice from a voter that a change was made in error, to immediately correct the voter's information in the statewide voter registration system.
  • Changes the MVC's front-end opt out automatic voter registration process to a back-end opt out process when applying for certain forms of ID. Specifically, the bill requires the MVC to automatically transmit sufficient information, including the voter's signature as a digitized image, to the secretary of state to conduct voter registration for each individual who completes an application for a REAL ID license, REAL ID card, and each related update, renewal, or change of address. The MVC may not transmit information for any applicant who has provided documentation that they are not a U.S. citizen. Specifically, the bill requires the secretary of state to:
    • Register individuals who applied for a REAL ID license, REAL ID card, or updated their information, based on information received from the MVC or other participating agencies unless the individual has demonstrated that they are not eligible to vote or are a member of the Address Confidentiality Program. 
    • Send the voter a notice by non-forwardable mail informing them they have been registered with instructions on how to declare a party affiliation, apply for mail-in ballots, or decline registration and request that their registration be removed from the statewide voter registration system. The notice would state the penalties for submission of a false application and state that if the individual declines registration that the request will remain confidential. The notice must be in English, Spanish, and any other language spoken by at least five percent of the registered voters in the county. The voter's registration would be deemed effective as of the date of their application with the MVC.
    • Electronically transmit a voter's information to the appropriate county commissioner of registration. If the information transmitted is an updated name or change of address for a registered voter, the county commissioner of registration would be required to update that voter's registration information. 
  • Requires the commissioner of registration to remove a voter's registration from the statewide voter registration system if that individual returns a notice declining to be registered. If that individual votes in an election after the transfer of their record but before the notice is returned, that individual would remain registered to vote.
  • Repeals the requirement that an individual's notice form declining to be registered not be considered a government record pursuant to the law concerning access to government records.
  • Changes the existing front-end opt out automatic voter registration system, which would only apply to individuals applying for standard licenses, standard ID cards, examination permits, probationary driver's licenses, and related updates or renewals. The bill requires that individuals engaging in those transactions affirmatively agree or decline the automatic voter registration. Under previous law, an individual would be registered unless they specifically declined the automatic voter registration.
  • Requires that upon implementation of online voter registration, voter registration information received from an application online for the renewal of a driver's license or ID card be collected and automatically transmitted to the secretary of state.
  • Requires the Department of Corrections, the secretary of state, and the MVC to coordinate to ensure that eligible individuals scheduled to be released from incarceration who are provided an opportunity to receive a non-driver ID card in advance of release are also provided voter registration opportunities as part of the ID card application. That individual would be allowed to preregister to vote if they have identified a place of residence within the state where they will reside following their release from incarceration. That individual would not be registered until they were released from incarceration.
  • Repeals a provision requiring a voter to receive a confirmation notice in the mail if they update their party affiliation when updating an existing voter registration.

Previous versions of the bill contained provisions that were amended out of this version. Those provisions would have:

  • Required the MVC to automatically transmit sufficient information to conduct voter registration for each person who completed a voter registration transaction with the MVC to the secretary of state.
  • Required the secretary of state and the chief administrator to jointly determine which documents are acceptable to demonstrate that an individual is a United States citizen.
  • Required the secretary of state to develop procedures for processing electronic records received from an agency without a digitized image of the applicant's signature. An individual whose registration record did not contain a digitized image of their signature would not be allowed to vote until a signature was obtained.
  • Required notices sent to voters who were automatically registered to vote to provide information and procedures for any individual wishing to prevent disclosure of their street address.
  • Provided that an individual who was not entitled to vote and who became registered to vote as a result of a transaction with the MVC and voted or attempted to vote would be presumed to have an affirmative defense to prosecution.
  • Extended back-end opt out automatic voter registration to the Division of Medical Assistance and Health Services in the Department of Human Services. Specifically, the bill would have required the Division of Medical Assistance to electronically transmit voter registration information to the secretary of state for each individual who applied to the New Jersey Medical Assistance and Health Services Program who was of sufficient age and was "externally verified" as a U.S. citizen as part of an application with the agency.

This bill, as introduced on January 9, 2024, is titled the "John R. Lewis Voting Rights Act of New Jersey". The bill enshrines protections to ensure equality of political participation for voters of racial, color and language minority groups. The bill would:

  • Prohibit any political subdivision from implementing a practice that abridges the rights to political participation of any protected class of eligible voters who are members of a race, color, or language-minority group. This prohibition extends to any method of election that abridges the rights of a protected class.
  • Authorize courts to implement appropriate remedies for abridgment of the rights of protected classes, including changes to the time, days, locations, and methods of elections, additional voter education, expanded voter registration, and add persons back to voter rolls. Courts may retain jurisdiction as necessary to ensure the remedies are implemented.
  • Require localities to give members of protected classes a meaningful opportunity to participate in the redistricting process.
  • Give members of protected classes and organization composed of members of protected classes standing to sue for enforcement of the act's provisions.
  • Require potential plaintiffs to send a locality a letter at least 50 days prior to filing suit, during which time the locality may take steps to remedy the alleged violation.
  • Require localities to provide voting materials in languages other than English if 2% of the voting age population or 4,000 people are members of a single-language minority.
  • Require covered entities to preclear regulations about many election-related practices with the Division on Civil Rights or a court. The bill defines covered entities as localities who have been subject to court orders related to civil rights violations in the last 25 years, localities with certain crime rate data, and localities with certain dissimilarity indexes.
  • Prohibit any person acting under color of law from intimidating, deceiving, or obstructing the rights of voters.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on April 8, 2024, would create the "John R. Lewis Voter Empowerment Act of New Jersey." Specifically the bill would:

  • Prohibit any state agency, local election office, or political subdivision from enacting or implementing any voting qualification, prerequisite to voting, law, ordinance, standard, or policy that results in a denial or abridgement of the right of members of a protected class to vote. It would specifically prohibit policies that burden the right to vote for any individual on the basis of age, disability, sexual orientation, including gender identity and gender presentation, or criminal history.
  • Prohibit any local election office or political subdivision from using any method of election that would impair the equal opportunity of protected class members in the political process.
  • Create a set of factors to be analyzed to determine if violations of the bill have occurred.
  • Authorize courts to implement appropriate remedies for abridgment of the rights of protected classes, including transitioning to an alternative method of election, changes to the days, locations, and methods of elections, additional voter education, expanded voter registration, and adding voters back to voter rolls. Courts would be permitted to retain jurisdiction as necessary to ensure the remedies are implemented.
  • Require localities to give members of the public opportunities to participate in the redistricting process. Localities would also be required to conduct additional outreach to limited English proficient communities so that they may participate in the process.
  • Give members of protected classes and organizations composed of members of protected classes standing to sue for enforcement of the act's provisions.
  • Require potential plaintiffs to send a locality a letter at least 50 days prior to filing suit, during which time the locality may take steps to remedy the alleged violation.
  • Require localities to provide voting materials in languages other than English if more than two percent of the voting age population, but no fewer than 100 individuals, speak a language other than English and have limited proficiency in English or more than 4,000 individuals speak a language other than English and have limited proficiency in English.
  • Require "covered entities" to preclear regulations regarding many election-related practices with the attorney general or a court. The bill defines covered entities as any political subdivision that has been subject to court orders related to civil rights violations in the last 25 years, localities with certain arrest rate data, localities with certain dissimilarity indexes, localities with certain poverty rates, localities with certain voter participation rates, localities that failed to provide voter data to the New Jersey Voting and Elections Institute in the last three years, and localities that enacted a policy without obtaining preclearance in the past 25 years.
  • Create a process for a covered entity to obtain preclearance from the attorney general.
  • Provide the attorney general with authority to investigate or enforce provisions of the bill.
  • Require the attorney general and secretary of state to engage in public education efforts to inform the voting eligible population about their voting rights, including which populations are protected classes, which languages access materials are available, and any causes of action and avenues of redress available under the bill.
  • Prohibit any person from intimidating, deceiving, or obstructing the rights of voters. Any individual or organization impacted by a violation of this bill can bring an action in court.

  • Establish the New Jersey Voting and Elections Institute at a public university to maintain and administer a database of elections and voting data that is available to the public.

    The bill also contains additional provisions related to topics that Voting Rights Lab does not track.


Last Updated April 9, 2024

  • Allow election officials or the police department to assign police officers to any district board whenever they deem it "necessary" to do so, and eliminate the existing provisions that expressly prohibit doing so. Under existing law, requests for police officer presence may be made only for assistance with a specific emergency, allegation of criminal conduct, or a disturbance. In such cases, the district board must notify the county board of elections or superintendent of elections of the police presence who must promptly notify the secretary or state. Under the bill, officials would be authorized to assign police to "enforce the election laws, maintain order, peace and quiet during the hours of registry and election," as well the existing authority to assist with transportation of election materials. Officers would be prohibited from performing duties of a board member or challenger at the location where they were dispatched.
  • Permit increased presence of police officers at the polling place in election-related roles. The bill would:
    • Allow police officers to serve as challengers at a polling place, by removing the prohibition on doing so.
    • Remove the requirement that officers may only serve on an election board if they are off-duty.
  • Create a new felony offense ("crime of the fourth degree") for an officer violating the prohibition on wearing their uniform or carrying an exposed weapon while serving in an election-related role.
  • Allow election officials to locate a mail ballot drop box inside, or within 100 feet of an entrance or exit, of a police station, by removing the existing prohibition on doing so.
  • Allow police officers, whether in or out of uniform, to remain or stand within 100 feet of a polling place during an election, by removing the prohibition on doing so.

The bill would also make conforming and non-substantive changes to various provisions to reflect the new requirements.

  • Require the examination of voter ID on Election Day to occur in full view of the challengers.
  • Authorize members of an election board and challengers to examine any document concerning proof of identification.

Under the procedure, the voter must provide an affidavit of qualifications, and a "provisional document" to establish identity. The bill would eliminate a driver's license as an accepted provisional document, but would otherwise preserve the existing list: (1) a sample ballot which lists the voter's name and address; (2) an official federal, State, county or municipal document which lists the voter's name and address; (3) a utility or telephone bill or tax or rent receipt dated; or (4) a piece of mail postmarked, on or after the 60th day before the day of the election at which the voter is challenged.

Specifically, the bill would:

This bill, as introduced on March 26, 2024, would guarantee the voting rights of eligible incarcerated individuals by providing the ability to register and vote, enforceable in court. As part of this guarantee, the bill would create two methods for incarcerated eligible voters to vote by mail ballot and authorize local boards of election to offer two days of early voting at correctional facilities.

Specifically, the bill would guarantee the right of eligible incarcerated people to vote by:

  • Declaring that people who are eligible to register to vote and vote and who are detained, confined, or committed to a correctional facility are "entitled to the free exercise and enjoyment of the elective franchise without discrimination or preference."
  • Requiring the Department of Corrections to issue regulations directing each facility to ensure the timely delivery, and to facilitate the timely return if applicable, of all official election mail, forms, notices, or communications to any individual detained or confined at such facility and that non-partisan plain language educational materials about the voting rights of individuals currently incarcerated and formerly incarcerated are included in the inmate handbook or similar materials and reentry resources.
  • Requiring the rules and regulations established for the government of any correctional facility to recognize the right of qualified detained or incarcerated individuals to register and vote. Such rules would be required to allow access to electronic personal voter registration or voter registration by application, and allow access to mail balloting services ("absentee balloting services" in New York) through the electronic mail ballot application transmittal system or by paper application. The rules for both voter registration and mail voting would be required to best effect this spirit and intent while being consistent with the proper discipline and management of the correctional facility.
  • Requiring the superintendent of each correctional facility to cooperate with the board of elections in developing and implementing a plan to facilitate at least one method of voter access for all persons eligible to vote who are detained or confined at each such facility, including making available space and reasonable accommodations.
  • Requiring the same registration and voting access be given to people who are in solitary confinement.
  • Authorizing aggrieved individuals to enforce their rights in court.
  • Creating a presumption that if any superintendent, employee, or agent of a correctional facility by commission or omission intentionally frustrates the ability of eligible incarcerated people to register and vote, an election law violation has occurred that may be enforced in court by any aggrieved persons, an organization whose membership includes aggrieved persons or members of a protected class, an organization whose mission, in whole or in part, is to ensure voting access, or the attorney general. That section of code allows multiple remedies including nominal, compensatory, or punitive damages.

One involves expanding an existing program in which election workers bring mail ballots to residential facilities, distribute them, collect them, and return them to the board of elections, as well as provide any needed assistance to the people voting them.   • Expand an existing program in which election workers bring mail ballots to nursing homes and other residential facilities. Some of the changes to the program would be specific to correctional facilities, and some would apply to all residential facilities. The bill would:

  • Specify automatic voter registration procedures for individuals who submit applications for a driver's license, driver's license renewal, ID card, or any renewal, recertification, or re-examination transaction, or any change of address or name. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require DMV officials to electronically transmit certain personal information to the state board of elections if during a transaction they conclusively determine a person is old enough to register or pre-register to vote and is a U.S. citizen. The personal information would include: name, date of birth, driver's license or state ID number, residence, mailing address, citizenship status, copy of signature, date of the transaction. The bill would also require DMV officials to collect a person's gender, email, phone number, if available. The bill would prohibit DMV officials from transmitting information of participants in the address confidentiality program.
    • Require DMV officials and the state board of elections to jointly determine which documents conclusively demonstrate United States citizenship. Nothing under the bill would be construed to require voters to present proof of citizenship for voter registration.
    • Require county or city election officials to promptly send a notice to automatically registered or pre-registered voters informing them of their option to decline such registrations and that a decision to decline would remain confidential. Officials would be required to cancel the registration of anyone who declines. Under the bill, the notice must offer voters the opportunity to enroll with a political party and advise them that only enrolled members of a party may vote in that party's primaries. The notice would also include information for voters who wish to prevent disclosure of their address.
    • Repeal a provision in existing law that limits an "application for services or assistance" to an application for a driver's license, a driver's license renewal, or an identification card issued by the DMV.
  • Specify automatic voter registration procedures for individuals who apply for or re-enroll in Medicaid. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require officials at the department of health and the county and city departments of social services to automatically and electronically send certain personal information to the state board of elections to facilitate registration and pre-registration of individuals to vote if they are of sufficient age and are externally verified as U.S. citizens. The personal information would include: name, date of birth, driver's license or state ID number, residence, mailing address, citizenship status, copy of signature, date of the transaction. The bill would also require DMV officials to collect a person's gender, email, phone number, if available. Existing law declares these departments as designated automatic voter registration agencies beginning January 1, 2024.
    • Specify that if necessary to comply with federal law, before sending a person's information to the state board of elections, department officials must notify the person by mail within 15 days of the transaction that they may decline their registration by using the postage paid pre-addressed return form. A voter would be registered to vote for an election if their information is sent to the county or city board 10 days before an election.
  • Require officials to mail a second notice regarding party affiliation if no response is received within 45 days after notice is sent to automatically registered voters who did not designate a political party.

This bill, as enacted on January 8, 2025, expands audit requirements; authorizes electronic voter registration at the DMV during transactions; expands requirements for third-party assistance to voters; and prohibits pre-filling of voter registration and mail ballot applications, among other changes. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires election officials to conduct post-election audits after declaring the official results of any election. Prior law required post-election audits only after general elections and primary elections held in even-numbered years.
  • Allows residents to electronically register to vote or update their voter registration during transactions at the Bureau of Motor Vehicles (DMV equivalent). In addition to the new electronic process, the bill also leaves in place prior law that requires the agency to provide paper registration forms, with the express provision that the agency is not required to provide assistance in completing them.
  • Requires DMV officials to send electronic records to the secretary of state within 24 hours of new voter registrations or updates. The bill specifies rules for transmitting the information including:
    • Prohibiting a direct electronic connection between the office of the registrar or a deputy registrar and the statewide voter registration database
    • Requiring the secretary of state or Board of Elections to verify any voter registration information before it is added to the statewide voter database
    • Requiring each electronic record to be date stamped
  • Expands requirements for voters to obtain third-party assistance with voting-related activities. Prior law permitted voters to use third party assistance for casting an Election Day or early voting ballot, with certain parties excepted, if they declared they were unable to do so otherwise due to blindness, disability, or illiteracy. Under the bill:
    • In addition to casting a ballot, third-party assistance requirements are expressly applicable to voter registration and updates, requesting and completing a mail ballot, casting a provisional ballot, or completing any other voting-related form.

In addition to the new general prohibition, the bill also leaves in place prior law that prohibits certain public officials from entering certain information on a registration application.

This bill, as introduced on April 8, 2024, would make extensive changes to Ohio election law related to voter list maintenance, voter registration, voting systems, and mail voting. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Implement new list maintenance requirements. Specifically the bill would:
    • Require boards of elections to make a notation in the record of any individual flagged its system as being a non-citizen.
