    • Require boards of elections to send a person identified by its system as not being a U.S. citizen a confirmation notice and cancellation notice within 15 days to confirm citizenship. If no response is received in 15 days, the board would be required to send a second confirmation notice. The bill would require officials to cancel the registration of a voter who does not respond with the necessary proof of citizenship within 30 days of the first confirmation letter. The bill also requires the board to forward the matter to the prosecuting attorney for investigation. Existing law does not include similar provisions.
    • Require the secretary of state to obtain records from the U.S. postal service, the bureau of motor vehicles, the U.S. social security administration, and other state and federal agencies, institutions of higher education, county property records, and any other available databases for the purpose of generating reports required by law and to make the resources available to local boards of elections.
    • Require the boards of elections to remove individuals who are not eligible to vote from the database. The bill would prohibit officials from canceling a voter's registration solely because the information does not conform to records in another database.
    • Require the director of health, probate judges, and clerks of each court of common pleas to provide on a monthly basis to the secretary of state the social security numbers and dates of birth in addition to the name and address of individuals who have died, been adjudicated incompetent, or convicted of disenfranchising crimes, respectively. Such monthly reports are required under existing law, but current law does not require the inclusion of social security numbers and dates of birth.
    • Require canceled voter registration records to be subject to disclosure as public records.
    • Permit a voter's registration to be updated only as a result of their actions in submitting a voter registration update form.
  • Modify the voter registration application process. Voters would be required to provide a signature and declare under penalty of election falsification that they are United States citizens and meet the requirements for being a voter. The bill would require the application form to specify the criminal penalty for election falsification. Existing law does not require the application form to include such declarations.
  • Establish new requirements for voter registration agencies. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Define "voter registration agency" to include the secretary of state or a board of elections, the registrar of motor vehicles or deputy registrar, a designated agency, a public high school or vocational school, a public library, the office of the treasurer, or a probate court or court of common pleas. Existing law does not define voter registration agencies. The bill would make conforming changes throughout the code replacing "designated agency" with "voter registration agency".
    • Require all voter registration agencies, except for the board of elections or the secretary of state, to designate a person to serve as a voter registration program coordinator. Under existing law, this requirement only applies to designated agencies.
    • Require training programs for coordinators at voter registration agencies to include instruction on how to explain voter qualifications to applicants.
    • Require voter registration agencies to provide residents who apply for voter registration with an information sheet explaining the qualifications to register and vote in the state. The bill would require agency officials to provide such information to an applicant before providing them with a voter registration application. The bill would specify exact language that must be included in the information sheet.
    • Repeal a provision that prohibits officials from rejecting a registration, change of residence or change of name form solely because the person registering the applicant failed to sign their name or name their employer.
  • Implement changes to the statewide voter registration database. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require officials to ensure that the servers and other equipment be physically located in a facility in the state that is under the control of the secretary of state.
    • Require anyone who has authority to create, modify, or cancel a record in the database be a U.S. citizen and a resident of the state without a criminal record involving dishonesty, moral turpitude, or any violation of immigration laws.
    • Prohibit officials from including in the statewide voter registration database any photograph of a voter or any image of a voter's signature.
    • Require the database to include a voter's voting activity for the current calendar year and at least the last 19 years. Existing law does not specify how far back the voting history must extend.
    • Require the database to include a unique voter registration identification number for each voter's registration record.
    • Require the auditor of the state to conduct an audit of the database and of three counties' voter registration systems each year. The bill would also require the auditor to conduct additional audits if requested by the secretary of state or the appropriate board of elections.
    • Require officials to provide additional voter information from the statewide voter registration database to be available on the state website, including: the voter's registration record ID number and whether the voter's registration is subject to cancellation and the date on which the registration may be canceled.
    • Require the statewide voter registration database website to allow users to access information concerning individual voters, generate reports regarding individuals whose registrations have been canceled, duplicate registrations, individuals who have received confirmation notices and not responded.
  • Require board of election officials to use the voter registration system to do the following:
    • Verify the voter registration form includes all required information
    • Verify the person's full name and ensure the name is entered into the voter registration system in a manner that complies with state directives.
    • Verify the person's date of birth and verify that the person will be 18 years or older by the next general election.
    • Verify the person's residence is a valid address and ensure that the address is entered into the voter registration system in a standardized format recognized by the U.S. postal services and complies with state directives.
    • Verify the person is a U.S. citizen by comparing their information to the DMV database; the systematic alien verification for entitlements services; or a database that contains information derived from a person's (1) valid and expired passports or (2) certified copies of United States birth certificates, certification of reports of birth, consular reports, certificates of citizenship, or certificates of naturalization.
    • Verify the person is living using death records and any other database available to the board of elections or the secretary of state.
  • Modify mail voting application requirements. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require a voter to provide their full name as it appears on their Ohio driver's license or state ID, or if they do not have one, their name as it appears on their social security card. Existing law requires a voter's name, but does not include a provision mandating that the name match any other identification.
    • Require a voter to provide the last four digits of a voter's social security number if they do not have a state driver's license or ID. Under existing law a voter may present one of the following: Ohio driver's license or state ID, the last four digits of their social security number, or a copy of their photo identification. The bill would also repeal the third option.
    • Make conforming changes to the identification envelope voter statement.
  • Authorize each county to adopt hand-counted paper ballots for use in elections instead of voting machines by approval of the board of elections, the board of county commissioners, or by a vote by the majority of voters in the county.
  • Require the secretary of state to appoint a board of voting system examiners. Under the bill, members of the board must be U.S. citizens and residents of the state without criminal records or any influence or control of entities outside the United States. Under existing law, the board is known as the "board of voting machine examiners" and there are no similar qualification restrictions related to criminal history or citizenship. The bill would also require the board of voting system examiners to seek a review from a cybersecurity reviewer before recommending a system.
  • Prohibit the use of a voting system if the secretary of state, any official in the office of the secretary of state, any member of the board of voting systems examiners, any person who conducts cyber security assessments of the voting system, or any relative of one of these listed individuals has a pecuniary interest in or affiliation with the voting system.

This bill, as introduced on May 15, 2024, would modify the process for officials to verify information in voter registration records, specify procedures for voters to correct their registration record after receiving a confirmation notice, and require the secretary of state to issue reports identifying discrepancies in voter registration records in each county. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Modify the confirmation notice process and repeal certain existing confirmation notice provisions. The bill would specify that if the board of elections sends an acknowledgment notice and is still unable to verify a voter's address, then the board must proceed with the confirmation notice process. The board would be required send a confirmation notice and mark the voter's name in the official registration records to indicate that the voter must vote by provisional ballot when:
    • The board is unable to verify a voter's address. Under the bill, if the voter provides a valid address to the board before the voter appears to vote, the board must correct the registration and remove the requirement that the voter cast a provisional ballot.
    • The board receives a report from the secretary of state indicating that the board must verify the voter's driver's license or state ID, the last four digits of their social security number, or the voter's residence address. Under the bill, if the voter provides a driver's license, state ID, or the last four digits of their social security number (confirmed by the secretary of state), before the next time they appear to vote, the board must remove the requirement that the voter cast a provisional ballot. If the provisional ballot has already been cast, the voter must provide an acceptable state ID, the last four digits of their social security number, or a correction to their registration record (confirmed by the secretary of state) on the provisional ballot affirmation or appear in person within four days after Election Day and provide one of those forms of ID for the ballot to be counted.
  • Redefines "confirmation notice" to mean a "notice sent by a board of elections, on a form prescribed by the secretary of state, to a registered elector to confirm the registered elector's current address, name, or other information required for registration." Existing law requires the notice to confirm address only. Additionally, the bill would require the notice to be sent by forwardable mail accompanied by a pre-addressed, postage prepaid envelope that meets the requirements of the National Voter Registration Act of 1993.
  • Require the secretary of state to use information from state databases and the U.S. social security administration to send a report to each board of elections a weekly report identifying voter registration in each county where any of the following apply:
    • The record is missing an Ohio driver's license or state ID number or the last four digits of a social security number.
    • The record contains an Ohio driver's license but the number is not in the records of the bureau of motor vehicles or the number in the DMV records is not associated with the name and date of birth in the DMV records.

This bill, as introduced on February 5, 2024, would create a cure process for absentee ballot certificates enabling ballots to be counted instead of rejected, and create rules that apply during a state of emergency. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Allow county election boards to begin opening and reviewing absentee ballots returned by mail 30 days before Election Day.
  • Provide that, if a ballot certificate is rejected for any reason, the board would be required to notify the voter by mail, and if available, email or phone. In addition, the board would update the voter's record in the Oklahoma Voter Portal to note the rejection. The notice sent by mail would include a cure form that would instruct the voter to complete and return the cure form by mail or in person by Election Day, along with whatever else is needed to address the issue. Under existing law, voters do not have an opportunity to address issues with their mail ballots.
  • Provide that if the reason for the rejection is the voter's printed name or signature is missing, in addition to the cure form, the voter must show valid ID with information matching their registration record, or have the signature or printed name verified by notarization. In case of emergency, a copy of such ID could be mailed with the cure affidavit. Incapacitated voters could continue to use two witnesses.
  • Require the State Election Board to issue necessary materials and instructions.
  • Provide that signatures cannot be deemed to be mismatched because of substituting initials for a first or middle name or both. Under existing law, Oklahoma does not match signatures on the ballot certificate to signatures on file, nor does the bill mandate such a process.
  • Create ballot verification rules that apply if a state of emergency declared by the Governor is in effect within the 45 days before a scheduled election:
    • A voter may sign the absentee ballot affidavit and attach a photocopy of a form of valid identification instead of having their signature verified.
    • A voter who is normally able to have their signature witnessed by two witnesses may instead sign the absentee ballot affidavit and include a photocopy of a form of valid identification.
    • In the event an absentee voting board is prohibited from entering a nursing facility or veterans center due to restrictions related to the state of emergency, then the secretary of the county election board may allow the absentee voting board to deliver the absentee ballots to a designated official at the nursing facility or veterans center. The designated nursing facility or veterans center official would be required to sign an oath acknowledging the duties and responsibilities of the absentee voting board, and then may carry them out.

This bill, as amended on October 17, 2023, no longer includes provisions that are tracked by Voting Rights Lab. The provisions removed by the amendments would have:

  • Ended the rejection of ballots caused by the voter failing to date or misdating their signature on the ballot certificate. Existing law, a combination of statute and judicial rulings, requires counting some misdated ballots and rejecting others and requires rejecting undated ballots. Under existing law, the date of the ballot signature is not relevant to the determination of a ballot's timeliness.
  • Required the county board of elections to notify voters within 24 hours if their mail ballot declaration is unsigned and that their ballot will be rejected unless the issue is resolved by six days after Election Day. The bill would have required this notice to be given by email, telephone, or text message. Voters could have cured the issue by signing and returning an affidavit, either in person or returning an electronic, fax, or mail to the county board of elections. Existing law neither requires nor prohibits such notice, and some counties offer the service.
  • Redefined the "pre-canvass" of mail ballots. The bill would have defined "pre-canvass" as the inspection and opening of all envelopes containing mail ballots, removing ballots from the envelopes, and preparing those ballots for scanning. The preparation for scanning would include unfolding, straightening, and duplicating if the ballot is damaged in some way that prevents it from being scanned but where the voter's intent is still clear. If the equipment used by the county board of elections permits a ballot to be scanned without tabulating votes, the pre-canvass can include scanning ballots. Existing law defines "pre-canvass" as the counting, computing, and tallying of the votes reflected on the ballots.
  • Authorized county boards of elections to begin pre-canvassing mail ballots three days before Election Day. Existing law allows pre-canvassing to start no earlier than 7 a.m. on Election Day.

Bill version 1/10/2024: This bill, as introduced on January 10, 2024, would change existing law for mail voting (which, in Pennsylvania, includes both excuse-required ("absentee") voting and no-excuse ("mail-in") voting), modify the process for challenging mail ballots, and create a related misdemeanor offense. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require all mail ballots to be submitted by 5:00 p.m. the Friday prior to a primary or election. Under existing law, all mail ballots must be received in the office of the county board of elections no later than 8 p.m. on the day of the primary or election.
  • Modify the mail voting process by authorizing a person to vote at their polling place after receiving a mail ballot. Under the bill, their original ballot would be voided. The bill would specify that a ballot with the letter "x" on its face or has the word "spoiled" on its face must not be counted. Under existing law, a person may only vote at the polling place by provisional ballot unless they return their mail ballot and sign a statement under penalties relating to unsworn falsification to authorities.
  • Modify the process and grounds for challenging mail ballots. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require the local election board to examine the declaration on each envelope labeled "Official Absentee Ballot" that is not set aside and compare it with the excuse-required mail voter lists. The bill would require the election board to announce the names on the mail ballots and to give watchers an opportunity to challenge the mail voters on the grounds that they are not a qualified voter or were within the district when polls were open and able to appear.
    • Require the local election board to examine the declaration on each envelope labeled "Official Mail-in Ballot" that is not set aside and compare it to the information contained in no-excuse mail voting lists. The bill would require the election board to announce the name of the voters and to give watchers an opportunity to challenge the mail voters on the grounds that they are not a qualified voter or they voted in person.
    • Require any challenged ballots under either process to be marked as "challenged" along with the reason for the challenge. The unopened envelope would not be counted, but would be sent to the county board for them to make a decision regarding the ballot.
    • Require a notice of hearing to be provided "where possible" to all mail voters challenged and to each attorney, watcher or candidate who made the challenge. The bill would require the time of the hearing to be no later than seven days after the date of the challenge and require the testimony at the hearing to be stenographically recorded and made part of the record.
    • Provide for an appeal process. The bill would require an appeal to a decision by the county board to be made within 2 days of their decision.
  • Modify the process obtaining an emergency mail ballot. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require a voter to complete and file an application with the court of common pleas in the county where they are qualified to vote an emergency application, or a letter or other signed document with the necessary information. Under existing law the person applies to the county board of elections.
    • A person would be qualified if they (1) became physically disabled or ill between 5:00 p.m.on the first Friday before an election and 8:00 p.m. the day of the election; or (2) due to their occupation, would be necessarily absent from the municipality and could not have reasonably known on or before 5:00 p.m. the Friday before an election.
    • Require an emergency ballot to be submitted by 8:00 p.m. on the date of the election.
    • Require voters to include supporting affidavits from their attending physician verifying their physical disability or illness. The bill would also require voters absent due to their occupation or business to submit a supporting affidavit. Existing law does not include a similar provision.
    • Require the judge to issue the emergency ballot to a qualifying voter, and authorize the judge to give the mail ballot to an authorized representative who is designated in writing by the voter. In the event that the voter is not able to get assistance from an authorized representative, the judge would be required to direct a deputy sheriff (or a constable) to deliver the ballot to the voter and return the completed ballot.
    • Require any person assisting a voter to declare in writing that assistance was rendered.
    • Declare that it would be a violation of the emergency voting provision for an undesignated person to provide assistance in marking a voter's ballot or a designated person fails to execute a declaration that assistance was received.
  • Establish "temporary registration cards" that would indicate a voter is a mail voter. The bill would require the county board of elections to maintain a file containing duplicate temporary registration cards for every voter who has received a mail ballot.
  • Require any mail ballot to be set aside and declared void if it contains any extraneous marks or identifying symbols other than the words "Official Absentee Ballot" or "Official Mail-in Ballot".
  • Create a misdemeanor offense for knowingly assisting another person who is not a qualified voter in filling out a mail ballot or a mail ballot application.
  • Specify that a county board of elections shall not pay compensation to an election judge who willfully fails to deliver by 2:00 a.m. the day following an election certain items, including envelopes; supplies, including all un-cast provisional ballots; and returns, including all provisional ballots, election supplies, provisional ballots, mail-in ballots and absentee ballots. This bill, as introduced on February 2, 2024, would alter the state's existing automatic voter registration system by requiring different procedures depending on whether the documents the person submits with their DMV transaction demonstrate U.S. citizenship or not. Under existing law, all qualified individuals are automatically registered to vote during DMV transactions, unless they choose to opt out during the transaction, if they provide proof of identity and residence and certify through documentation or a declaration that they are citizens. This bill would:

  • Limit automatic voter registration at the DMV to only those applicants who present documentation of citizenship, and change the opt-out process. For individuals who provide citizenship documentation, voter registration information would be automatically transmitted to election officials, who would subsequently send a notice of registration to the applicant. The bill would also allow the DMV to look at its records to determine if the individual had previously submitted documentation demonstrating U.S. citizenship even if they did not during the current transaction. If the DMV found such documentation, the DMV would also send the person's information to election officials, triggering the same notice. If the applicant failed to decline registration within 14 days of receipt of that notice, the applicant would be registered to vote. Under existing law, automatic voter registration requires only certification of citizenship, not documentation, and the DMV must provide the opportunity to opt out during the transaction itself.
  • End automatic voter registration for individuals who do not present affirmative documentary proof of citizenship at the DMV, and instead provide an opt-in streamlined registration process for these applicants. Individuals whose documentation neither proves nor disproves citizenship would be given the option to affirmatively choose to register by certifying their citizenship status, which may be done by declaration.
  • Provide that if the DMV has access to information to determine whether someone is already registered to vote and determines that an applicant is already registered, then the DMV would treat the transaction as a registration update and would send the person's information to election officials without regard to whether the person provided citizenship documentation in their DMV application.
  • Exempt from automatic registration people who are doing a DMV transaction using their business address rather than their residential address. Such people would be offered the opt-in streamlined registration process.
  • Prohibit automatic voter registration or streamlined voter registration at the DMV for any individual who fails to certify, by documentation or declaration, that they are a U.S. citizen, and expressly prohibit the agency from offering the opportunity to register to individuals who have documented their non-citizenship. Existing law requires certification of citizenship for registration at the DMV, but does not include an express prohibition on offering registration when documentation of non-citizenship has been provided. Nonetheless, existing law expressly contemplates registration of eligible individuals only.
  • Expand which additional agencies beyond the DMV may offer automatic voter registration, by permitting agencies to do so if they either collect documentary proof of citizenship or can verify citizenship by database matching or other means deemed reliable by the Secretary of State. Existing law limits automatic voter registration to only those non-DMV agencies that verify citizenship through documentation. The bill would also require non-DMV agencies that process transactions for multiple individuals eligible for registration to register each individual according to the procedures applicable to the DMV process.

This bill, as introduced on March 21, 2024, would require each county Board of Voter Registration and Elections to conduct a post-election hand count audit of at least ten percent of polling places in the county after every contested statewide party primary and general election. Under existing law, the executive director of the State Election Commission must conduct reviews, audits, or post election analysis to ensure compliance with applicable federal or state law or State Election Commission policies, and the Commission currently requires hand count audits for all state level and federal level elections.

The bill would codify express statutory requirements for a hand count audit process that would:

  • Apply to contested races only.
  • Count all votes cast, including mail ballots and ballots cast during early voting.
  • Take place in precincts in each county that have been randomly selected by the Board
  • Prioritize races with a narrow margin of victory.
  • Include at least three contested races, and if feasible and applicable, must include the presidential race and one statewide office.
  • Provide at least 24 hours' notice to the public of the upcoming audit on the State Election Commission website and county Board website, including the date, time, and location of the audit. The audit must also be conducted within 24 hours of the close of polls on Election Day unless that time falls on a Sunday.
  • Allow candidates or their representatives, party representatives, poll watchers, and observers to be permitted access to observe all aspects of the process.
  • Be conducted by teams composed of at least four individuals selected by the Board with advice and consent of the county chair of each political party involved in the audited election. Participants in the audit could not be regular salaried Board members or staff.
  • Allow the public to observe ballots during the process at all times.
  • Report a discrepancy between the post-election audit results and the tabulated vote counts of .0001% or greater. Specifically, those results must be:
    • Reported to the State Election Commission and the Office of the Inspector General by the director of the county Board.
    • Investigated for election system tampering by a forensic audit team appointed by the Inspector General which shall examine all hardware, software, and internet connectivity used by the audited precincts.
    • Followed by a hand recount of all vote totals for all races in all precincts in the affected county prior to certifying results. Those results must be reported to the county Board of Canvassers and all political party chairpersons as the final election results. The bill would expressly provide that failing to report a discrepancy as required constitutes the existing felony offense of "corrupt conduct of an election officer."
  • Identify and immediately revoke any vote recorder with an error rate of .001 percent or greater. Under existing law, a vote recorder may be revoked only if it can no longer be used accurately and efficiently.

This bill would also require each county Board to create electronic versions of various election-related records, including the voter registration list, and make them available to registered voters for no cost upon request.

Under these provisions, a number of poll watchers were permitted for each candidate in a primary election, and for each political party and independent candidate in a general election.

This bill, as amended on February 1, 2024, would make changes to criminal offenses involving threats or obstruction of public servants (a category which, for purposes of the bill, includes a person conducting an election). Specifically, the bill would:

  • Modify the existing misdemeanor offense of "threats to influence official action" to a more expansive offense of "threat against a public servant, party official, or voter to influence or retaliate against an official action or a political action." Specifically, the bill would:
    • Expand the list of entities against whom a threat qualifies as a crime under the statute, including a family or household member or an entity in which a person has an interest.
    • Clarify that a threat qualifies as an offense under the statute if it is intended to retaliate for an official or political action. Under existing law, a threat only qualifies if it is intended to influence an official or political action.
    • Increase the penalty under the statute to a felony if the actor’s conduct includes an attempt to inflict bodily injury, or actually results in such injury.
  • Modify the existing offense of interference with a public servant's performance of an official function to increase the severity of the offense from a misdemeanor to a felony if the actor’s conduct includes an attempt to inflict bodily injury, or actually results in such injury.
  • Define denial of a public servant’s use of public property as its own separate misdemeanor offense. Under existing law, a person who willfully denies a public servant lawful movement, use, or entry of public property commits the misdemeanor of interference with a public servant’s performance of an official function.

    • A higher education student or their spouse who will be absent on Election Day.
    • A person with a disability who is unable to go to the polls on Election Day because of the voter's disability, illness, or pregnancy.
    • A person incarcerated awaiting trial or after a misdemeanor conviction.
    • An election official or election worker.
    • A person who cannot go to the polls on Election Day because the voter has primary responsibility for the care of an ill or disabled family member who is confined at home.
    • A person who has a religious obligation on Election Day.
    • A person who will be away from home at work on Election Day for at least 11 hours of the 13 hours that polls are open.
    • A law enforcement office, firefighter, volunteer firefighter, search and rescue personnel, or EMS personnel.
    • A designee of a political party or candidate who is the party or candidate's representative inside a polling place on Election Day.
    • A person granted a protective order.
  • Create an in-person absentee voting period of two tiers, with a longer period for people with an excuse and a shorter period for people who do not meet one of the enumerated excuses.
    • Absentee voters with a valid excuse could vote absentee in-person from 45 days before Election Day to the second Friday before Election Day.
    • Any voter, regardless of whether they have a valid excuse, could vote absentee in-person from the second Saturday before Election Day until 5:00 p.m. on the Saturday before Election Day.
  • End the permanent absentee voting list for all voters and only allow voters who are eligible for an absentee ballot because of disability or illness to file an annual application to receive ballots for all elections for the calendar year. The first time such a voter applies for an annual application, the application must be signed by the voter's physician or religious practitioner that the voter is eligible for an absentee ballot on the grounds of disability or illness. Local election officials shall send a blank application to voters who received annual absentee ballots in the previous year by December 15 of the year that is ending.
  • Restrict same day voter registration by repealing a provision that allows all voters to register in person up to and including Election Day at their local general registrar office or at their polling place. The bill would only permit uniformed service members, individuals residing temporarily out of the country, and the spouse or dependent of those two groups of individuals.
  • Eliminate the option for Election Day voters to sign a sworn statement in lieu of providing ID to vote a regular ballot. Voters who lack ID would instead be required to vote a provisional ballot, which could only be counted if the voter presents a photo ID to the electoral board by noon on the third day after Election Day. Under existing law, a provisional ballot may be counted if the voter shows an ID document or signs a sworn statement that they are the voter they claim to be.
  • Require early ("in-person absentee") voters to provide photo ID to obtain or return a mail ballot in person. Under existing law, a voter can obtain or return a mail ballot by presenting an ID (including a non-photo ID) or by signing a sworn statement that they are the voter they claim to be.
  • Require all IDs to have a photo and be current, repealing existing provisions allowing for the use of certain non-photo ID documents such as utility bills, bank statements, government checks, paychecks, and other government documents, along with non-photo student IDs.
  • Require the Department of Elections to provide voter photo IDs for free to any voters who do not have an otherwise acceptable photo ID. The bill would also require the DMV to assist in providing voter photo ID.
  • Repeal provisions that allow for the use of drop-off locations for returning mail ballots. The bill would also repeal provisions related to central absentee voter precincts.
  • Require the general register of each locality to publish on its official website each month a list of all registered voters added or removed from each precinct in the general in the locality and the reason for each change. The general registrar would also be required to publish on its website a list of all qualified and registered voters in each precinct on the first day that registration records are closed for the election.

This bill was vetoed by Governor Glenn Youngkin on May 17, 2024. As passed by the legislature, the bill would have made extensive updates to voter list maintenance process. Specifically, the bill would have:

  • Required the Department of Elections to exchange voter registration lists with border states and use the information to identify duplicate registrations, voters who no longer live in the state, and individuals who are not entitled to be registered to vote.
  • Prohibited the use of voter data received from another state or jurisdiction or through a list comparison if the data file did not include a unique identifier for each individual. The bill would have define a unique identifier as a persons full social security number, DMV number or any data field that can be reliably linked to a single person. Existing law does not include a similar provision requiring unique identifiers.
  • Specified the events that initiate the confirmation notification process. The process would have been initiated if:
    • A voter provided an address on a candidate or referendum petition that differs from the address in the voter registration system.
    • Certain documents were sent to a registered voter and returned by the U.S. Postal services as undeliverable, including an acknowledgement of registration, acknowledgement of transfer to a new address, mail ballot or mail ballot application, notification regarding precinct reassignment, notification of change of address, or any official voter registration or election mail.
  • Required the Department of Elections to compare the contents of lists related to voters who have been convicted of certain crimes, are noncitizens, or are deceased to the list of registered voters and determine a confidence score based on a specified point system. The Department would have only transmitted a voters registration record if the match included a confidence score of at least 80. Then, the registration would have been canceled.
  • Removed the deadline by which general registrars must delete certain voters from the record of registered voters. Existing law requires the action to be taken no later than 30 days after notification from the Department of Elections. The bill would have also repealed the provisions requiring the Department to promptly provide certain list maintenance information to general registrars.
  • Repealed a provision setting a deadline by which general registrars must delete certain voters from the record of registered voters. Existing law requires the action to be taken no later than 30 days after notification from the Department of Elections. The bill would have also repealed the provisions requiring the Department to promptly provide certain list maintenance information to general registrars.
  • Authorized the Department of Elections to exchange voter lists with bordering states for the purpose of identifying possible duplicate voters or voters who have moved.
  • Required the Department to conduct a regular list maintenance process using data from the U.S. Postal Service's National Change of Address (NCOA) program.
    • Voters identified as having moved within the same city or county of registration would have been sent a confirmation notice at their new address.
    • Voters identified as having moved outside their city or county of registration would have been sent a confirmation notice at their last known address.
    • Voters who failed to return the confirmation notice would have been moved to inactive status.
    • Voters moved to inactive status could have moved back to active status by notifying election officials of a change of address, responding to an address confirmation notice, voting or attempting to vote, or transferring their voter registration to another county.
    • Voters who remained on inactive status through two federal election after the initial status change would have had their registrations canceled.
  • Added a persons DMV customer ID number to the list of information that must be included in the weekly list of deceased individuals provided to the Department from the State Registrar of Vital Records. The bill would have created a similar requirement for the monthly list the Central Criminal Records Exchange provides to the Department regarding individuals convicted of felony offenses.
  • Created a process for a voter to cancel their own registration. The bill would have required the voter to submit a written and signed authorization to the general registrar.

The bill would require the general registrar to send a mail notice to any resident whose information does not match, and the resident would be required to correct the information or present a qualifying form of identification in order to be registered. Existing law does not require verification via the Social Security Administration.
  • Specify that an individual who is provisionally registered to vote must cast a provisional ballot, which would not be counted unless the voter presents a valid photo ID by noon on the third day after the election. Existing law does not include a similar provision.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 9, 2024, would require all in-person voters to show photo ID to receive a ballot, eliminating currently-accepted types of non-photo voter ID and the ability of a voter to sign an affidavit in lieu of showing ID. Under the bill, voters who do not show photo ID would be given a provisional ballot. For the provisional ballot to count, the voter would be required to submit a copy of acceptable photo ID by noon on the third day after the election. Existing law imposes a similar rule, but the current forms of non-photo ID and affidavit also enable the provisional ballot to count. The bill would further require the Department of Elections to issue free photo IDs to people who lack one of the other forms of ID accepted and require the Department of Motor Vehicles to assist the Department of Elections in that effort.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 10, 2024, would establish a strict photo ID requirement for in-person voters. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Eliminate the option for Election Day voters to sign a sworn statement in lieu of providing ID to vote a regular ballot. Voters who lack ID would instead be required to vote a provisional ballot, which could only be counted if the voter presents a photo ID to the electoral board by noon on the third day after Election Day. Under existing law, a provisional ballot may be counted if the voter shows an ID document or signs a sworn statement that they are the voter they claim to be.
  • Require early ("in-person absentee") voters to provide photo ID to obtain or return a mail ballot in person. Under existing law, a voter can obtain or return a mail ballot by presenting an ID (including a non-photo ID) or by signing a sworn statement that they are the voter they claim to be.
  • Require all IDs to have a photo and be current, repealing existing provisions allowing for the use of certain non-photo ID documents such as utility bills, bank statements, government checks, paychecks, and other government documents, along with non-photo student IDs.
  • Require the Department of Elections to provide voter photo IDs for free to any voters who do not have an otherwise acceptable photo ID. The bill would also require the DMV to assist in providing voter photo ID.

Last Updated January 10, 2024

This bill, as introduced on January 10, 2024, would limit in-person voter registration by only permitting voters to register in person "up to" the day of an election at the general registrar office in the locality where they reside. Existing law permits in-person voter registration "up to and including" Election Day at a voter's local registrar or the polling place for the precinct in which they reside.

Last Updated January 10, 2024

This bill was vetoed by Governor Glenn Youngkin on May 17, 2024. As passed by the legislature, the bill would have prohibited the use of voter data received from other states without unique identifiers, required an annual review of all sources of data used for list maintenance, required voter registration challenges to be brought in state court only, and repealed existing provisions regarding challenges brought to the general registrar. Specifically, the bill would have:

  • Prohibited the use of voter data received from another state or jurisdiction or through a list comparison if the data file did not include a unique identifier for each individual. The bill would have defined a unique identifier as a voter's full Social Security number, DMV number, or any data field that can be reliably linked to a single person. Existing law requires officials to compare data received from other states, but does not specify matching criteria.
  • Required the Department of Elections to conduct an annual review of all sources of data used for list maintenance in order to determine the reliability of data used from each source, and include this information in its annual report to the Committees on Privileges and Elections. The bill would have also moved the deadline for making the report from October 1 to August 1.
  • Required that challenges to voters' registrations be brought in state court only, by repealing the existing authorization to also bring challenges to the general registrar. The bill would have set out requirements for court procedure for challenges, including 15 days notice to the challenged voter, exemption from formal pleading rules, first docket priority, and the right to appeal to the Court of Appeals. Existing law does not specify procedures for judicial adjudication of registration challenges.
  • Repealed existing provisions setting out notice, determination, and appeal procedures for registration challenges brought to the general registrar, corresponding to the bill's elimination of this venue for challenges.

Last updated on May 23, 2024.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 10, 2024, would require the general registrar to process the list of people convicted of felonies within 28 to 21 days before Election Day instead of 21 to 14 days beforehand. The bill would also modify notice procedures by requiring the general register to mail notice to anyone known to have been convicted of a felony prior to canceling their registrations. Under the bill, the person would have 14 days to submit evidence that their right to vote has been restored, and an additional notice would be sent to any person whose registration is canceled after failure to respond. Existing law requires notice to be sent out after the person’s registration has been canceled only.

Last updated on January 17, 2024.

This bill was vetoed by Governor Glenn Youngkin on May 17, 2024. As passed by the legislature, the bill would have made extensive updates to voter list maintenance process. Specifically, the bill would have:

  • Required the Department of Elections to exchange voter registration lists with border states and use the information to identify duplicate registrations, voters who no longer live in the state, and individuals who are not entitled to be registered to vote.
  • Prohibited the use of voter data received from another state or jurisdiction or through a list comparison if the data file did not include a unique identifier for each individual. The bill would have define a unique identifier as a persons full social security number, DMV number or any data field that can be reliably linked to a single person. Existing law does not include a similar provision requiring unique identifiers.
  • Specified the events that initiate the confirmation notification process. The process would have been initiated if:
    • A voter provided an address on a candidate or referendum petition that differs from the address in the voter registration system.
    • Certain documents were sent to a registered voter and returned by the U.S. Postal services as undeliverable, including an acknowledgement of registration, acknowledgement of transfer to a new address, mail ballot or mail ballot application, notification regarding precinct reassignment, notification of change of address, or any official voter registration or election mail.
  • Required the Department of Elections to compare the contents of lists related to voters who have been convicted of certain crimes, are noncitizens, or are deceased to the list of registered voters and determine a confidence score based on a specified point system. The Department would have only transmitted a voters registration record if the match included a confidence score of at least 80. Then, the registration would have been canceled.
  • Removed the deadline by which general registrars must delete certain voters from the record of registered voters. Existing law requires the action to be taken no later than 30 days after notification from the Department of Elections. The bill would have also repealed the provisions requiring the Department to promptly provide certain list maintenance information to general registrars.
  • Repealed a provision setting a deadline by which general registrars must delete certain voters from the record of registered voters. Existing law requires the action to be taken no later than 30 days after notification from the Department of Elections. The bill would have also repealed the provisions requiring the Department to promptly provide certain list maintenance information to general registrars.
  • Authorized the Department of Elections to exchange voter lists with bordering states for the purpose of identifying possible duplicate voters or voters who have moved.
  • Required the Department to conduct a regular list maintenance process using data from the U.S. Postal Service's National Change of Address (NCOA) program.
    • Voters identified as having moved within the same city or county of registration would have been sent a confirmation notice at their new address.
    • Voters identified as having moved outside their city or county of registration would have been sent a confirmation notice at their last known address.
    • Voters who failed to return the confirmation notice would have been moved to inactive status.
    • Voters moved to inactive status could have moved back to active status by notifying election officials of a change of address, responding to an address confirmation notice, voting or attempting to vote, or transferring their voter registration to another county.
    • Voters who remained on inactive status through two federal election after the initial status change would have had their registrations canceled.
  • Added a persons DMV customer ID number to the list of information that must be included in the weekly list of deceased individuals provided to the Department from the State Registrar of Vital Records. The bill would have created a similar requirement for the monthly list the Central Criminal Records Exchange provides to the Department regarding individuals convicted of felony offenses.
  • Created a process for a voter to cancel their own registration. The bill would have required the voter to submit a written and signed authorization to the general registrar.

Last updated on May 23, 2024.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on February 9, 2024, would:

  • Require the DMV to send to the Department of Elections (Department) information necessary determine whether a registered voter has changed their name or address any time the voter comes to the DMV to (1) get a new or renewed driver's license or ID, or (2) change their address on an existing driver's license or ID. The bill would require the Department to send a voter's registration record to the appropriate general registrar if the information shows the voter has moved to a new address within the state and treat it as a request for transfer. Likewise, if information indicates a voter's legal name has changed, the information would be sent to the general registrar and treated as a notice of name change. A voter would receive information on how to correct a notice of name or address change. Existing law does not include a similar provision.

  • Require the Department to send information from the voter registration record to the DMV to determine whether a customer is registered to vote. If the Department could not determine whether a person is registered, the DMV would initiate the automatic registration process.

    A previous version of this bill included provisions that were amended out of the original text. Those provisions would have required the DMV to ask residents during a transaction whether they are already registered to vote before presenting them with the option to decline automatic voter registration. Existing law does not require the DMV to ask about a resident's current voter registration status. Additionally, the bill would have required the DMV to send to the Department of Elections the information of any person who indicates that they are already registered to vote.


Last Updated February 28, 2024

This bill, as enacted on April 17, 2024:

  • Expands the existing felony election offense for hindering or preventing an election, or attempting to do so. Under existing law, the offense comprises using bribery, intimidation, threats, coercion, or other means in violation of the election laws to (1) willfully, (2) hinder or prevent "officers of election" at any polling place, voter satellite office, or other location being used by a locality for voting purposes, from holding an election. Under the bill, the prohibited conduct must now (1) be both wilful and intentional, and (2) hinder or prevent "an election official or the employee of an election official from administering elections," or attempt to do so.
  • Expands eligibility for the voter address confidentiality list to include current and former election officials and current and former presidential electors.

Previous versions of the bill included additional provisions that were amended out prior to enactment. These provisions would have:

  • Included election officials and their employees among the protected categories for the definition of hate crimes, and made conforming changes for elevating various offenses as a result.
  • Created a felony offense for interfering with a presidential elector carrying out their duties.
  • Created a civil cause of action for election officials and their employees, and presidential electors, to apply for preventative relief against conduct meeting the elements for the criminal offense of interference with their duties.

Last Updated May 7, 2024

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on April 4, 2024, expands the category of voters with disabilities who are eligible to vote outside the polling place. Under prior law, outside voting was available only to voters over the age of 65, and those with a permanent or temporary physical disability or an injury. The bill eliminates the requirement that a disability be "physical," permitting a voter with any disability to vote outside. The bill also requires all election officers to receive training on providing assistance to voters outside of the polling place.

Last updated on April 19, 2024.

Governor Glenn Youngkin vetoed this bill on March 8, 2024. As passed by the legislature, it would have required the Commissioner of Elections to submit an application for the state to join the Electronic Registration Information Center (ERIC). The bill would also have required the Commissioner to execute any membership agreement, pay any associated fee, and take any necessary steps to maintain good standing with ERIC. Virginia is not currently a member of ERIC.

Last updated on March 11, 2024.

VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as introduced on January 10, 2024, would amend the state constitution to:

  • Establish that individuals convicted of felonies shall have their right to vote automatically restored upon release from incarceration. Under existing law, the voting and other civil rights of individuals convicted of felonies can only be restored by an act of the governor "or other appropriate authority."
  • Modify language regarding mental capacity to vote by requiring a specific judicial finding that an individual lacks the capacity to understand the act of voting before being disenfranchised. Under existing law, all individuals "adjudicated to be mentally incompetent" are disenfranchised.

  • Declare that, other than enumerated exceptions, "[e]very person who meets the[ ] qualifications shall have the fundamental right to vote in the Commonwealth, and such right shall not be abridged by law."

    If enacted by the legislature, this resolution would need to be enacted again by the subsequent legislature (2025-26 session) and then ratified by a vote of the public before the constitution was amended to incorporate its terms.

Last updated on January 10, 2024.

This bill, as introduced on January 3, 2024, would prohibit the knowing possession of firearms at polling places, with exceptions for firearms carried for law enforcement purposes by federal or state law enforcement officers and for firearms carried in the course of performing one's official duties as a state or federal employee. Violations of this prohibition would be a crime punishable by not more than one year of imprisonment, a fine of not more than $1000, or both.

Last updated January 4, 2024.

This bill, as enacted on March 26, 2024:

  • Creates a new felony offense for harassing an election official, and defines such officials as including any staff member of the office of the secretary of state or staff member of a county auditor's office whose duties relate to voter registration or processing votes, regardless of whether the member is employed on a temporary or part-time basis. Under prior law, the general offense of harassment was elevated from a misdemeanor to a felony offense only if directed to certain individuals working in the criminal justice system, or for certain forms of harassing conduct.
  • Expands eligibility for the state's address confidentiality program to include election officials targeted for generally prohibited threats or harassment, and members of their households. Under prior law, election officials and household members were eligible for the program only if they were targeted for cyber harassment.

The bill also includes additional minor changes related to topics that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

Last Updated April 16, 2024

This bill, as enacted on March 13, 2024, requires county auditors who receive address change information indicating that a voter has moved to another county in the state, to notify the auditor in the new county of the voter's relocation. That auditor must then update the voter's registration with the new address and send notice to the voter of the change. Under prior law, auditors receiving change-of-address information for a move to another county were required to place the voter in inactive status and send notice and a registration form to all of the voter's known addresses.

The bill also makes numerous technical and non-substantive changes throughout various provisions.

Last updated on April 12, 2024.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 8, 2024, would:

  • Require the secretary of state to provide certain counties with voting related materials in languages besides English, including registration or voting notices, forms, instructions, ballots, or any other materials or information related to the electoral process. The following criteria must be met to be a covered county:
    • At least two and one-half percent of voting age individuals or those who are qualified to vote are members of a single language minority group and have limited English proficiency, and the illiteracy rate of those citizens exceeds the national illiteracy rate for those who speak that language or,
    • The county contains all or part of an Indian reservation and at least two and one-half percent of the Indigenous or Alaska Native citizens living in the reservation are of voting age or qualified to register to vote and are members of a single language minority group. They must also have limited English proficiency and the illiteracy rate of those individuals must exceed the national illiteracy rate for those who speak that language.
  • Require the secretary of state to establish a grant program to provide funding to counties that do not qualify as covered counties to provide materials or information related to the electoral process in a language other than English.

Last Updated January 18, 2024

This bill, as introduced on January 8, 2024, would effectively end disenfranchisement of people convicted of an offense in Washington. Under the state constitution, a person must lose the right to vote after conviction of an "infamous crime." Current state statute defines an infamous crime as a felony punishable by death or imprisonment, and deprives persons convicted of an infamous crime of the right to vote while incarcerated for that offense. Under this bill, an infamous crime would be redefined as one punishable by death. Since the death penalty has been abolished in the state, this would effectively end disenfranchisement of persons convicted of an offense.

Last updated January 12, 2024.

This bill, as introduced on January 8, 2024, would require public high schools to observe "National Voter Registration Day" on the third Thursday of September in each year. The bill also changes certain existing requirements concerning voter registration outreach to eligible high school students. The bill would:

  • Require all high schools give all eligible students 16 or older the opportunity to register to vote by paper application or online on National Voter Registration Day. Existing law requires high school to give students 18 or older these opportunities on "Temperance and Good Citizenship Day", which is observed on January 16.
  • Require the superintendent of public education to provide voter registration materials to high schools by August 1 of each year. Existing law requires the superintendent to provide these materials by December 1 of each year.

Last Updated February 19, 2024

This bill, as introduced on January 8, 2024, would require the secretary of state to provide an online system through which voters could print replacement ballots and update their voter registrations. These services are available online although they are not required by law.

Last Updated January 16, 2024

This bill, as enacted on March 13, 2024, expands existing election-related offenses, mandates digital intrusion detection systems for certain counties, and creates protocols for the certification of election results. Specifically, the bill:

  • Expands the existing felony offense for defacing, removing, or destroying supplies or materials intended for use at a voting center to enable voting, to also include acts against materials used for an election office, ballot counting area, ballot storage area, or election system.
  • Creates a new felony offense for an unauthorized person accessing or assisting with unauthorized access to an election system, voting center, election office, ballot counting or storage area. The bill also expands the existing felony offense for tampering with or damaging voting machines to include illegal access or assisting in access to these locations.
  • Expands the existing felony offense for misconduct by election officials in the performance of their duties, to include providing unauthorized access to a person or entity to physical locations, or electronic or physical access to election software or hardware used in any element of conduct of an election.
  • Expands the existing misdemeanor offense for prohibited conduct at a voting center to include interfering with the operation of the center by engaging in unauthorized access or handling of ballots, or unauthorized access to any voting equipment or election systems. Under prior law, the offense was limited to certain electioneering activities and obstructing a voting center or drop box to prevent free access.
  • Expands the existing misdemeanor offense for destroying, altering, defacing, concealing, or discarding completed voter registration forms or signed ballot declarations to include voted ballots.
  • Prohibits the touching of ballots, ballot materials, or election systems by observers at counting centers during the processing of ballots, and expressly states that unauthorized contact constitutes a criminal offense under existing provisions.
  • Requires each county to install an intrusion detection system that passively and continuously monitors the network for malicious traffic. The bill requires the system to include a security team with access to cyber incident responders to assist the county during a malicious attack, and requires the county auditor or the county IT director to notify the secretary of state and the attorney general of malicious activity in specified circumstances. Under prior law, which the bill leaves in place, the manufacturer or distributor of election equipment certified by the secretary of state must report certain breaches of security, but there was no mandate for counties to digitally monitor systems directly.
  • Permits the secretary of state, in the event that a county canvassing board refuses to certify election results, to examine the records, ballots, and results of an election and certify the results within two business days after the certification deadline.

Last updated on March 27, 2024.

HISTORY: {"date":"03/07/2024","summary":"By order of Resolution","meta":["[\" Returned to SENATE. Placed on Third Reading.\"]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on January 31, 2024, would modify the grounds on which an individual may challenge another individual's right to vote and specify the process for resolving challenges. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Allow voter registration challenges if the challenger has personal knowledge that the challenged voter has registered to vote more recently in another state, is not a United States citizen, or will not be 18 years old on Election Day. Existing law permits challenges based on residency, mental incompetence, or felony disenfranchisement only.
  • Authorize the county auditor to dismiss a challenge if the challenged voter is qualified to vote or their registration is inactive, and require the county auditor to determine whether a challenge is in proper form within 10 business days of receiving it. Existing law allows a county auditor to dismiss a challenge if it is not in proper form or the factual basis does not meet the legal qualifications for a challenge. Additionally, the bill specifies that voters with inactive registrations do not receive ballots and are not subject to voter registration challenges.
  • Require the county auditor to attempt to resolve a challenge by contacting the challenged voter, searching the statewide voter registration database, or determining for a challenge that includes an out-of-state address whether the voter's registration in the other state or Washington was more recent. Existing law does not include a provision with specific instructions for resolving challenges. The bill would also require county auditors to publish the affidavit of unresolved voter challenges on their website within 10 days of receipt, as opposed to the existing requirement of seventy-two hours.

Last updated on February 20, 2024.

This bill, as enacted on March 26, 2024, expands the required outreach by auditors to voters who need to cure ballots, adds new requirements related to signature matching, and specifies how canvassing meetings must be made accessible to the public. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires the secretary of state to adopt and regularly review statewide standards for signature matching to verify ballots, and publish a manual for dissemination to local election officials. The secretary must develop tools to ensure compliance, which may include random comparisons of signature matches. The bill also requires signature matching training materials to be publicly available. Prior law required signature verification and training for ballot processors, and administrative rules provided some guidance concerning matching criteria, but statutory law did not have an express requirement that the secretary establish statewide standards and oversee compliance.
  • Requires initial notice to a voter for a missing or non-matching ballot signature to be made by telephone, text, or email, if possible, in addition to the existing requirement of sending notice by mail. The bill also expressly requires officials to leave a voicemail if the voter does not answer a telephone call related to a missing or non-matching ballot signature.
  • Sets an earlier deadline for the existing requirement to contact a voter by telephone in certain circumstances. Under prior law, telephone notification was required if a ballot with a missing or mismatched signature is received within three business days of the final meeting of the canvassing board, or if the voter did not respond to initial notification by mail by that time. The bill requires telephone contact if either occurs within five business days of the final meeting. For mismatched signatures only, the bill also expressly requires officials to attempt contact by text or email, as well as by phone.
  • Requires that a ballot be counted if the signature on a ballot declaration is "not the same" because the voter's name "has changed" from the signature on a registration file, so long as the handwriting is "clearly the same." The requirement under prior law was to count such ballots if the mismatch is due to the voter's name being "different" than the registration file record.
  • Requires that if an auditor provides electronic means for submission of a ballot declaration, the auditor establish appropriate privacy and security protocols that ensure that the information transmitted is received directly and securely by the auditor for the sole purpose of verifying the signature on the voters ballot. Prior law had no comparable provision.
  • Requires that if a voter's ballot is rejected in two consecutive primary or general elections due to a mismatched signature, the auditor contact the voter to request that the voter update their signature for the voter's registration file.
  • Requires revision of the ballot declaration form by June 1, 2025, to include a statement informing voters that the signature on the declaration will be compared to the signature in the voter's registration file.
  • Requires county auditors to develop a "community outreach plan" to educate voters on processes for signature verification, signature updates to the voters file, and cure for challenged ballots.
  • Requires the secretary of state to develop forms for curing incomplete ballot declarations and updating voter signatures, in various languages required of state agencies. Forms must include the oath and warning language on voter registration forms, and be provided at the auditor's office and online.
  • Requires the county auditor to publish on its website the names of all canvassing board members who received training on statewide standards for signature verification and the dates on which the training was completed. While prior law provided that all personnel assigned to verify signatures must receive training on statewide standards for signature verification, it did not require that this information be available to the public.
  • Requires the county canvassing board to conduct meetings at times and locations that are accessible to the public "to ensure that the public is informed and able to attend or observe" and for the times and locations of those meetings to be published in libraries, other community locations throughout the county, and on the county's website. Prior law only provided that county canvassing board meetings be public.
  • "Encourages" the secretary of state to amend the voter registration application to include multiple signature blocks, to assist with signature matching for ballot declarations. The bill also "encourages" auditors to contact all voters for signature updates, following certification of a general, primary, or presidential primary election result.

The bill also contains additional provisions related to topics that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

Last Updated July 11, 2024

This bill, as enacted on March 15, 2024, establishes a pilot program under which any county in the state may apply to the secretary of state to test a new method for verifying that a ballot was filled out and returned by the intended voter, as an alternative to the existing signature verification process. Specifically, the bill:

  • Permits any county to submit a plan to the secretary of state under which the county would use an alternate verification method for ballots. An application submitted by a county must include a description of the alternate methods, the manner in which the plan would be implemented, and the election for which it would be used. Only special elections are permitted.
  • Requires any method used under the pilot project to allow a voter to submit clear evidence and attest that their ballot is their own and to establish criteria for verification. The method must also be compatible with the centralized voter registration list.
  • Requires that any voter whose signature on their ballot matches a signature of the voter in their registration file has their ballot counted, as under the standard system, regardless of whether the voter attempted to participate in the alternate verification method.
  • Sets the expiration of the program at January 1, 2029.

Last Updated April 16, 2024

VRLANALYSIS:

This bill, as introduced on February 2, 2024, would make a change to certain voter ID requirements. Under existing law, a voter in Wisconsin may use an unexpired, dated college ID card for voter ID purposes if concurrently submitted with proof that the person is currently enrolled in that college. However, a federal court ruled that the additional requirement to submit proof of enrollment was not constitutional. This bill changes current law to comply with that ruling, and also permits a voter to present an expired college ID card for voter ID purposes if concurrently submitted with proof that the person is currently enrolled in that college. Each state university would be required to issue new cards that comply with the law.

This bill, as prefiled on January 3, 2024, would separate the existing felony offense of intimidation into two separate offenses. Under existing law, a person commits intimidation by using or threatening to use force against an election official or voter with intent to impede the electoral process, or soliciting campaign donations through using or threatening to use force. This bill, as introduced on January 21, 2025, would:

Specifically, the bill would require the governor to appoint two members of each of the two political parties whose candidate for governor received the highest number of votes in the most recent gubernatorial election. Under existing law, the governor is required to appoint two members of each of the two political parties or political groups with the largest number of registered voters at the time of the most recent gubernatorial election.
  • Specify that a candidate for office that does not affiliate with a political party would still be entitled to appoint a watcher at a counting center. The bill would make nonsubstantive and conforming changes because of this requirement.
