This bill, as amended on May 14, 2025, would eliminate the existing witness requirement for mail ballots; create a new statewide notice and cure process for mail ballots; create same-day registration and permit registration within 30 days of an election; extend the early voting period; and make additional changes to voting procedures and election administration. 


Concerning the completion, return, and verification of mail ballots, the bill would:

  • Eliminate the requirement that a voter complete their mail ballot in the presence of a notary or witness, and instead require the voter only to sign and date the ballot. Under the bill, the date listed on the certificate must be on or before Election Day for the ballot to be counted. Existing law requires voters to have their mail ballots witnessed by an individual qualified to administer oaths, such as a notary public, unless one is not reasonably accessible. In that case, the voter may use anyone over 18 years old. The witness must sign the ballot attesting that the voter cast the ballot on the date shown. In addition, the voter must include an identifier, which can be their birthdate. 
  • Create a cure process for ballots that are rejected due to a missing signature or insufficient voter identification. Existing law does not provide for any cure process. The new cure process would require the following: 
    • The director of elections would be required to immediately make a reasonable effort to contact the voter, explain the ballot deficiency, explain how the deficiency may be cured, and inform the voter of the deadline to cure the ballot. 
    • Notice to the voter would be required within 24 hours by email, text, and/or phone if possible, and within 48 hours but no later than five days after Election Day by first class, non-forwardable mail. 
    • For a defective ballot to be cured and counted, the voter would be required to return the completed form sent with the notice of deficiency electronically or by mail within 14 days of the election, confirm that they returned a ballot, provide a signature, and include a copy of their photo ID, and the ballot must otherwise be valid. 
    • If the voter returns the cure form indicating that they did not return a ballot, the director would be required to send the signature on the mail ballot and in the voter's file to the attorney general for investigation. 
  • Modify requirements concerning the timeliness of postmarked mail ballots. Under existing law, if a ballot is postmarked, it may only be counted if the postmark is dated on or before Election Day, and the ballot is received by the tenth day after the election. The bill would eliminate this postmark requirement, and instead provide that mail ballots without a postmark, or with a postmark after Election Day, may not be counted unless the ballot is marked with (1) a postal service barcode indicating it was mailed on or before ElectionDay, or (2) a Division of Elections barcode indicating the same.  
  • Require officials to provide a pre-addressed, postage prepaid return envelope for mail ballots. Existing law is silent as to return postage for mail ballots, and in practice, voters must pay for return by mail. The bill would also expressly prohibit identification of a voter's party affiliation on the ballot envelope. Existing law has no comparable provision. 
  • Move the start of mail ballot verification and counting earlier, to no less than 10 days before Election Day. Under existing law, ballot verification must begin no later than seven days before Election Day, and counting must begin at 8 p.m. on Election Day. The bill would also require the count of mail ballots to be made by 8 p.m. on Election Day. Existing law has no deadline for reporting a first count. 
  • Make conforming changes throughout the code consistent with the new provisions. 

Concerning standard and same-day registration, the bill would: 

  • Create same-day registration (SDR), and permit registration by any method during the 30 days before Election Day for all elections. Under existing law, same-day registration is available only for the purposes of voting for president and vice president of the United States. For all other elections, registration ends 30 days before Election Day and registrants after this time are not permitted to vote in that election. Under the bill, individuals registering within 30 days of an election or on Election Day would be required to:
    • Provide a declaration stating that they established residency at least 30 days before the date of the election in the state and the house district in which they seek to vote. 
    • Cast only an in-person mail ballot, special needs ballot, or questioned ballot. Election officials would be expressly prohibited from rejecting a ballot from such voters on the grounds that the voter is not on the official registration list for that election. The bill would also allow SDR voters to declare a political party affiliation when voting their ballot. 
  • Modify the rules for determining residence for voter registration by:
    • Defining residence as the place of "physical habitation," for which when the person is absent they have an "articulable and reasonable plan" for return. Under existing law, the definition is for a place of habitation, for which the person has an "intention" to return when absent.
    • Eliminating the existing provision that defines a change of residence as requiring an act of removal joined with the intent to remain in another place. 
    • Expressly requiring loss of residence status when residence is established in another state. Existing law specifies loss of residence for voting in another state, and provides that there can be only one residence, but does not otherwise directly address establishing residence elsewhere.  
  • Require officials to provide registration applicants with the option to request election materials in certain available non-English languages. 
  • Expressly allow registration applicants or their agent to provide an electronic signature when applying by mail, fax, scanning, or other electronic means. Existing law has no comparable provision.
  • Require officials to develop a process to allow a voter to cancel their registration electronically or in person, and to prominently display instructions on how to cancel registration at each polling place. Existing law has no comparable provision. 
  • Require the director of elections to develop a cybersecurity program to "defend" voter registration records from cyber attacks and security breaches. 

Concerning the request of mail ballots and alternative ballots, the bill would:

  • Expand the period for special needs ballot requests, by moving the start date to the 30 days before an election. Under existing law, these requests are accepted beginning 15 days before. The bill would also expressly provide that a special needs ballot may not be rejected due to errors by the voter's representative or election officials, if the ballot is otherwise valid. Existing law has no comparable provision.
  • Apply existing requirements for voter certificates for in-person mail ballots and questioned ballots to special needs ballots, and require the form to include instructions for designating party affiliation.  
  • Require officials to provide mail ballot materials in other languages, as a conforming change to a new requirement to do so for all election materials. 

Concerning in-person early voting, the bill would:

  • Extend the early voting period by moving the first day of voting earlier, from the 15th day before an election to the 20th day before. As under existing law, the voting period would end the day before Election Day. Existing law provides for both "early voting" and "in-person absentee" voting during the early voting period, depending on the voting location's access to the state's voter database. Under the bill, the new earlier start date would apply for in-person requests of a mail ballot from an elections official or at an early voting location (in-person absentee voting), and for the early voting process.
  • For the "early voting" method, permit voters who cannot provide required voter ID or verification of residence to vote a mail ballot by the "in-person absentee" method, which would later be verified prior to counting. . NB: Existing provisions for in-person absentee voting, which the bill does not change, also require presentation of an accepted form of voter ID.  
  • Move the deadline earlier for designation of early voting locations, from 15 days before Election Day to 30 days before.

Concerning voter list maintenance, the bill would:

  • Expand the categories of voters who receive an address confirmation notice during annual list maintenance of the voter roll, and shorten the timeframe for inactivating a registration. The bill would:
    • Modify and expand the categories of voters that receive a confirmation notice. Under existing law, non-forwardable notice is sent to voters who (1) have had mail returned to election officials as undeliverable in the last two years, or (2) have not contacted the Election Division in the last two years, or (3) have not voted or appeared in vote in the last two general elections. Under the bill, notice would be sent to voters who: 
      • Had mail returned to the election division within the last two years, or
      • Have not contacted the division and have not voted or appeared to vote within the last two years, or
      • (1) Registered to vote in another state, (2) received a driver's license in another state, (3) registered a vehicle in another state, (4) received public assistance from another state, (5) served on a jury in another state, (6) obtained a resident hunting or fishing license in another state, (7) paid the state resident tuition rate for a public university in another state, (8) received a homestead or residential property tax exemption in another state, or (9) received a benefit available only to residents of another state
    • Require that confirmation mailings be sent by forwardable mail, rather than non-forwardable mail as required under existing law, and by email.  
    • Require voters to respond to the initial confirmation notice within 45 days to maintain their active registration status. Existing law requires officials to notify voters that their registration will be made inactive only after (1) an initial confirmation notice is returned as undeliverable, and (2) the voter has not contacted the division, voted, or appeared to vote in the past four calendar years. If the voter does not respond within 45 days, their registration is inactivated, and subject to cancellation. 

Concerning polling place procedures, the bill would:

  • Permit voting by in-person mail ballot, special needs ballot, or questioned ballot for voters who:
    • Re-register, or transfer their registration within a house district, within 30 days of an election. Under existing law, these voters were subject to the general registration deadline of 30 days before an election. 
    • Claim to be a registered voter but for whom no evidence of registration can be found to vote. Under existing law, these individuals must vote a questioned ballot and the board of directors must determine whether the voter is registered in the house district before counting the ballot.
    • Have lived in a municipality for at least 30 days but not registered within the jurisdiction, and wish to vote in a municipal election except for election for specific districts. The bill would also repeal the requirement that individuals be registered at an address in a municipality to qualify to vote in municipal elections.
  • Require the division to provide a voter with election materials in a language in which the division is required to provide materials under federal law. The division would be required to notify a voter when materials in their designated language are not available and allow them to designate another language.
  • Expressly require language assistance at polling places, consistent with federal law, and require officials to post notice of available assistance at each location. 
  • Repeal a requirement that specifies provision of voting booths that are at least six feet in height. 
  • Require an election official to advise an individual seeking to vote in person that if their name appears on the registration list as having received or voted a mail ballot, they may surrender their mail ballot for destruction or cast a questioned ballot. If the voter does not surrender their mail ballot, they would be allowed to vote a questioned ballot only. 
  • Allow, during a challenge to a voter's qualifications, the challenger to rebut the presumptive evidence of the voter's residence by providing evidence that the voter has established residence in another state or place, or is not a resident. Under existing law, the address of a voter on the voting list is presumptive evidence of their residence, negated only by the voter's written notification of a change, and voters challenged as ineligible may provide a sworn affirmation of their qualification to vote. 
  • Expressly specify that compensation for election board members may only be reduced from the set rate by regulation. Existing law has no comparable provision. 

Concerning election observers and facilitation of voting access for rural communities, the bill would:

  • Narrow the role of political party representatives in the ballot counting process by permitting them to observe counting, rather than to assist as provided by existing law. 
  • Require the elections director to employ five rural community liaisons responsible for collaborating with tribes, municipalities, corporations, regional nonprofit corporations, and other community organizations to facilitate access to early and mail voting in rural areas of the state and ensure that rural areas of the state are fully staffed. 

The bill also contains additional provisions related to topics that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

  • Required an individual registering in the 30 days before Election Day or on Election Day to provide a specified form of ID with the applicant's name and address. Under existing law, applicants must provide an Alaska driver's license, ID card, or the last four digits of their Social Security number.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 22, 2025, would eliminate automatic voter registration, shorten the early voting period, move the deadline earlier for receipt of mail ballots, change voter list maintenance practices, make changes to mail ballot processing procedures, redefine a voter's residence for purposes of voter registration, and expand the circumstances in which elections can conduct an election by mail. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Eliminate automatic voter registration, by repealing the provisions currently providing for the process through applications to the Permanent Fund Dividend, and make conforming changes to reflect the repeal.
  • Shorten the early voting period from a total of 15 days to 10 days, by moving the end date to five days before Election Day. Under existing law, early voting is available "for 15 days before an election." Under the bill, the period would begin on the 15th day before an election and end five days before.
  • Move the receipt deadline earlier for return of a mail ballot, to the close of business on Election Day, and make conforming changes. Under existing law, a completed mail ballot is timely if postmarked no later than Election Day and received by the close of business on the tenth day after the election. 
  • Expand the categories of voters who receive an address confirmation notice during routine list maintenance of the voter roll, and shorten the timeframe for inactivating a registration. Under existing law, notice is sent to voters who (1) have had mail returned to election officials as undeliverable in the last two years, or (2) have not contacted the Election Division in the last two years, or (3) have not voted or appeared in vote in the last two general elections. The bill would:
    • Expand the categories of voters that receive a confirmation notice to include to voters who, in the last two years, became ineligible to receive a Permanent Fund dividend or obtained a driver's license in another state.
    • Require that confirmation notices be sent by forwardable mail. Under existing law, initial confirmation notice must be sent by non-forwardable mail only.
    • Require officials to inactivate a voter's registration if the voter fails to respond to the confirmation notice within 45 days. Under existing law, officials may only inactivate a voter's registration if (1) an initial confirmation notice is returned as undeliverable, and the voter has not contacted the election division or voted or appeared to vote in the last four years; and (2) the voter fails to respond to a second confirmation notice, sent by forwardable mail, within 45 days.
  • Eliminate the requirement that an individual have the intention to return home for the purposes of determining a voter's residence, and make conforming changes.
  • Require officials to provide a pre-addressed, postage prepaid return envelope to voters requesting a mail ballot. Existing law is silent as to return postage for mail ballots, and in practice, voters must pay for return by mail.
  • Allow absentee voting officials to send ballots to election supervisors via electronic transmission as a means of "mail service." Under existing law, those ballots must be sent by the most expeditious mail service, which does not include any electronic methods.
  • Increase the amount of time election officials have to process mail ballots before an election. The bill would require the election supervisor to review all voter certificates of absentee ballots received by that date no less than 10 days before an election. Under existing law, the election supervisor must review them no less than seven days before an election.
  • Expand the elections that may be conducted by mail ballot, to include an election for a community with a population of 750 or less. Under existing law, elections by mail are permitted only for those elections held at a time other than when the general, primary party, or municipal election is held.

The bill also contains additional provisions related to topics that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

Last Updated February 12, 2025

This bill, as introduced on January 24, 2025, would: 

  • Require that all ballots be tabulated, counted, and the election be certified by 11:59 p.m. on Election Day. Under existing law, ballots may not be counted before 8 p.m. on Election Day and the election must be certified no later than the 15th day following the election. The bill would make conforming and non-substantive changes because of this change.
  • Allow the director of elections to delay the certificate of results of the election in order to receive and count ballots. 
  • Would require that all ballots be "delivered" to the director after counting rather than mailed.
  • Shorten the timeframe for early voting. The bill would require that early voting begin 15 days before an election and end the Saturday immediately preceding Election Day. Under existing law, early voting is available for 15 days before an election and ending on Election Day.
  • Require mail ballots to be postmarked and received on or before Election. Under existing law, mail ballots must be mailed no later than Election Day and received by the close of business on the 10th day after the election.
  • Move up the return deadline for mail ballots from overseas. The bill would require mail ballots returned from qualified overseas voters to be received no later than the close of business on Election Day. Under existing law, those bellows must be received no later than the close of business on the 10th day following a primary election or special primary election and the 15th day following a general election or special election.
  • Require the director to send a mail ballot and other voting materials to a UOCAVA voter at least 60 days before the election if the voter submits an application to the division at least 60 days in advance. If the voter submitted an application at least 45 days before an election, the director would be required to send them a mail ballot at least 45 days in advance, as is required under existing law.


Last Updated March 10, 2025

This bill was vetoed by Governor Mike Dunleavy on April 30, 2026. The bill, as amended on March 23, 2026, would have created a cure program for rejected ballots; made changes to accepted forms of voter ID; required new routine list maintenance procedures and modified the existing annual procedure; created new criminal and civil penalties related to elections; and made various other changes. 


Concerning mail ballot voting, the bill would:

  • Create a cure process for mail ballots that are rejected due to a missing voter or witness signature or insufficient voter identification. Under existing law, voters are notified when their mail ballot is rejected, but there is no statewide process for curing defects. Under the new process: 
    • If a ballot is rejected, officials must "immediately make a reasonable effort" to contact the voter explaining the ballot deficiency, how the deficiency may be cured, and the deadline to cure the ballot. Notice must be sent within 24 hours by email and/or telephone call and text, if contacts were provided, and within 48 hours (and no later than five days after Election Day) by mail. The notice must include a printed form for the voter to provide required information for ballot verification, and officials must also make a cure form available for electronic submission.
    • The cure deadline would be 10 days after Election Day, and a rejected ballot would be counted if the voter confirmed that they returned a ballot, and provided a signature and copy of voter ID, and the ballot was otherwise valid. 
    • If the voter indicates on the cure form that they did not return a ballot, the bill would authorize the director of elections to send the signature on the return ballot to the attorney general for investigation.
  • Require officials to provide mail ballot voters with a postage-paid return envelope. Under existing law, voters must pay for postage to return a mail ballot.
  • Move the receipt deadline earlier for all mail ballots returned from outside the U.S. or by UOCAVA voters, to the 10th day after an election. Under existing law, the receipt deadline is the 10th day after a primary or special primary, and the 15th day after a general election or special election. 
  • Move the start of mail ballot processing earlier, from seven days before Election Day to 12 days before. 
  • Require the director of elections to create a procedure for challenging mail ballots, special needs ballots, and questioned ballots during the counting process, that provides a "reasonable amount of time" to submit a challenge. Existing law is silent as to a challenge process. 
  • Require officials to provide an online ballot tracking system that allows voters to know the date a ballot was sent out by officials, delivered, and received back by officials; whether the ballot was counted; and steps required to cure a defective ballot. The bill would specify that any vendor for the system must be a business incorporated in the U.S., and that the system must use multi-factor authentication. Online ballot tracking is not required under existing law, but the state currently provides information online as to delivery and return of ballots, and provides notice to a voter when a ballot is rejected.  
  • Specify that for the existing requirement that completed mail ballots be delivered by local officials to election supervisors for processing "by the most expeditious mail service," such service includes delivery by optical scanning and electronic transmission.

Concerning voter ID, the bill would:

  • Change the list of accepted ID for voter registration and casting a ballot.
    • For registration, the bill would eliminate use of a hunting or fishing license, and add tribal ID to accepted ID. The bill would leave in place the remaining forms of accepted ID: driver's license; state ID card; current and valid photo ID; birth certificate; passport; or waiver of the ID requirement by a registration official who knows the identity of the voter.
    • For voting in person (and certain first-time mail ballot voters), the bill would eliminate use of a hunting or fishing license, and add tribal ID to accepted ID. The bill would leave in place some remaining forms of accepted ID: driver's license; state ID card; current and valid photo ID; birth certificate; passport. The bill would also repeal existing language allowing the use of a utility bill, bank statement, government check, or other government document showing the voter's name and current address, the document must be dated within the previous 60 days. Existing law requires only that these documents be "current."

Concerning voter list maintenance, the bill would:

  • Permit the Division of Elections to use information provided by the Department of Revenue to conduct voter roll maintenance. Existing law has no comparable provision. The bill would also require the Division to submit an annual report to the governor, state secretary, and chief clerk of the House of Representatives annually detailing the number of permanent fund dividend applicant records shared with the division; the effect that shared permanent fund dividend applications had on voter roll maintenance and on election integrity; and security measures taken to protect voter information.
  • Expand the categories of voters who receive an address confirmation notice during annual list maintenance of the voter roll, and shorten the timeframe for inactivating a registration. Under existing law, non-forwardable notice is sent to voters who (1) have had mail returned to election officials as undeliverable in the last two years, or (2) have not contacted the Election Division in the last two years, or (3) have not voted or appeared in vote in the last two general elections. The bill would:
    • Modify the existing categories of voters receiving notice by requiring confirmation from voters who have not contacted the election division in the last two years and also have not voted or appeared in vote in the last 28 months, rather than each category of voters separately, as required under existing law. The bill also expressly provides that registering to vote does not constitute "contact" with the division. Existing law specifies various actions that constitute contact, but is silent as to registration.
    • Expand the categories of voters that receive a confirmation notice to additionally include voters who: 
      • During the last 28 months, (1) registered to vote in another state, (2) received a driver's license in another state, (3) registered a vehicle in another state, (4) received public assistance from another state, (5) served on a jury in another state, (6) received a homestead or residential property tax exemption in another state, or (7) received a benefit available only to residents of another state.
    • Require that confirmation notices be sent by forwardable mail and to the voter's email address, if available. Under existing law, initial confirmation notice must be sent by non-forwardable mail only. 
    • Require officials to inactivate a voter's registration if the voter fails to respond to the confirmation notice or provides an incomplete or ambiguous response within 45 days, and require notice to state the response deadline. Under existing law, officials may only inactivate a voter's registration if (1) an initial confirmation notice is returned as undeliverable, and the voter has not contacted the election division or voted or appeared to vote in the last four years; and (2) the voter fails to respond to a second confirmation notice, sent by forwardable mail, within 45 days.
  • Require new routine list maintenance procedures, in addition to the existing annual address confirmation process. The bill would require the adoption of regulations to review voter registrations and update the master register, and direct the Division of Elections to:
    • Review the list for deceased voters, voters convicted of a felony involving moral turpitude, voters not qualified to vote, voters registered to vote in another state, whether the number of registered voters on the master list exceeds the number of eligible voters in the state, and voter registration information data breaches. 
    • Gather and examine available data from other states and information from the USPS forwarding databases, motor vehicle records, Department of Corrections records, property and sales tax records, U.S. Social Security Administration databases, jury duty records, national change of address records, and similar records. 
    • Annually audit the master register in consultation with an external, nationally recognized subject-matter expert. The division would be required to publish a report describing the audit by April 1 of each year.
    • Specify requirements for notice to voters under the removal provisions, and authorize the division to contact a voter and request information from the voter to determine their residence, in addition to issuing a required notice. 

Concerning voter registration, the bill would:

  • Expand grounds for challenges to a voter based on their residence. Under existing law, the address of a voter on their registration record is presumptive evidence of their voting residence, and may only be negated by the voter changing their residence in writing. Under the bill, the presumption may also be rebutted by providing evidence to the division that the voter has established residence in another country, state, or place in Alaska.
  • Require officials to post data about any breach of confidential voter information, and specify the scope and timing for such reports. 
  • Repeal a provision allowing an elections official to substitute a mailing address provided by a voter for the Permanent Fund Dividend program as the mailing address for the voter's registration record. 


Concerning criminal and civil penalties related to elections, the bill would:

  • Create a new class C felony for intentionally opening or tampering with a submitted mail ballot or package of ballots without express authorization from the director or intentionally breaching, hacking, altering, or tampering with election machinery. 
  • Create a new class C felony for knowingly disclosing, sharing, or reporting official election results, returns, or any confidential election data to an individual who is not an election official before the close of polls on Election Day.
  • Prohibit the use of "synthetic media" in electioneering activity with the intent to influence an election, and create a private right of action for individuals harmed by its use. The bill would set out definitions for prohibited and exempt conduct, defenses, and forms of relief. 

Concerning election outreach, data security, and observation of counting processes, the bill would:

  • Require the elections director to employ a rural community liaison responsible for collaborating with tribes, municipalities, corporations, regional nonprofit corporations, and other community organizations to facilitate access to early and mail voting in rural areas of the state and ensuring that rural areas of the state are fully staffed.

Previous versions of the bill contained additional provisions that were amended out of this version. Those provisions would have:

  • Eliminated the existing witness requirement for voting a mail ballot, and instead require that voters provide a signature and date on the ballot for verification.   • Created a permanent mail voting list. Under existing law, a voter can request a mail ballot for a specific election or for all elections in that calendar year, and certain voters may request delivery of an automatic mail ballot application each year.
  • Required the provision of secure ballot drop boxes and require the director of elections to adopt regulations governing their use and location. While existing law is silent as to use of drop boxes, they have been available for some past elections.
  • Created same-day voter registration for all elections and extended the general registration period to include the 30 days before Election Day. Voters registered within 30 days or on Election Day would have been required to vote an absentee, special needs, or questioned ballot.   • Allowed preregistration for individuals who were at least 16 years of age. Existing law permits eligible residents to register within 90 days of their 18th birthday, but does not otherwise provide for preregistration.

  • Specified that a mail ballot without a postmark or postmark after Election Day is timely only if marked with a USPS or Division of Elections tracking barcode verifying that the ballot was mailed on or before Election Day. Existing law provides that if a ballot is postmarked, it must be marked on or before Election Day, with no requirement related to barcode data.
  • Required the Division of Elections to permit a voter registration applicant to choose their desired language from a list of possible language options for election-related materials, and specified related requirements for language accessibility. 
  • Set out specific requirements for the location and number of ballot drop boxes.
  • Required an election official to advise an individual seeking to vote in-person that if their name appeared on the registration list as having received or voted a mail ballot, they may surrender their mail ballot for destruction or cast a questioned ballot.   • Permitted a voter who has changed the place in which their physical habitation is fixed to continue to vote in the senate district or judicial district that includes the individual's former place of physical habitation if that voter has an articulable and reasonable plan to remain in or return to that senate or judicial district.

This bill, as introduced on February 3, 2025, would restore the right to vote to individuals convicted of most felonies, change the existing restoration process from an application-based system to automatic restoration, allow all voters to vote by mail, create a cure process for defects on mail ballots, and would create the Alabama Voting Rights Act and the Alabama Voting Rights Act Commission. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Allow voters who have lost their right to vote by reason of conviction of a felony, except for individuals convicted of treason or impeachment, to automatically have their right to vote restored upon completion of their sentence. Under existing law, individuals who are eligible to have the right to vote restored must apply and be granted a certificate of eligibility to register to vote. The bill would make conforming and nonsubstantive changes because of this change.
  • Repeal the requirement that an individual re-register to vote upon having their right to vote restored if the individual had previously registered to vote.
  • Repeal the requirement that an individual pay all fines, fees, court costs, and ordered restitution prior to restoration.
  • Repeal the requirement that an individual have no criminal felony charges pending against them in order to have their right to vote restored.
  • Allow individuals convicted of the following offenses to have their right to vote restored:
    • Murder
    • Rape in any degree
    • Sodomy in any degree
    • Sexual abuse in any degree
    • Incest
    • Sexual torture
    • Enticing a child to enter a vehicle for immoral purposes
    • Soliciting a child by computer
    • Production of obscene matter involving a minor
    • Production of obscene matter
    • Parents or guardians permitting children to engage in obscene matter
    • Possession of obscene matter
    • Possession with intent to distribute child pornography.
  • Allow any voter to vote by mail. Under existing law, a voter can only vote by mail if they meet of the following requirements: 1) they expect to be out of town on Election Day; 2) they have a physical illness or infirmity which prevents their attendance at the polls; 3) they expect to work a shift which has at least 10 hours that coincide with voting hours; 4) they are enrolled as a student outside the county of their personal residence; 5) they are a member of the military, their spouse or dependent is a member of the military, or are qualified to vote by mail via UOCAVA; 6) they were appointed as an election officer or poll watcher at a location other than their regular polling place;7) they are a caregiver for a family member to the second degree of kinship by affinity or consanguinity and the family member is confined to their home; 8) they are incarcerated but have not been convicted of a felony involving moral turpitude. The bill would leave in place the existing requirement that a voter provide a reason for voting by mail even though anyone can do so. The bill would make nonsubstantive and conforming changes because of this change. One of the conforming changes would be the elimination of emergency mail voting.
  • Require the secretary of state to create a form for voters to fill out when they wish to vote by mail.
  • Repeal the statute making it unlawful for an individual to knowingly distribute a mail ballot application to a voter that is prefilled with the voter's name or any other information required on the form.
  • Allow a voter to submit an application to vote by mail via a designee delivering the application in person or via designee mailing the application in addition to the existing methods. Under existing law, a voter must deliver or mail their application themselves. The bill would make nonsubstantive and conforming changes because of this change. One of the conforming changes would be the repeal of a provision making it a crime to deliver an application to vote by mail on behalf of another voter.
  • Require the mail voting election manager ("absentee election manager") to examine any affidavit envelope and determine if it contains a defeat that would require curing. They would be required to allow a voter to cure any of the following defects:
    • A missing signature
    • Address on affidavit that does not match the address on the application
    • Envelopes out of order
    • Affidavit is not properly witnessed or notarized
    • The voter failed to indicate their reason for voting by mail. Under existing law, voters cannot cure defects with their mail ballots.
  • Require the mail voting election manager to notify a voter of any defects within two business days of receipt. The manager would also be required to provide instructions on how to cure the defect and notify the voter that they have until the last business day before the election to cure the defect. The secretary of state would be required to implement rules to carry out these requirements.
  • Create the Alabama Voting Rights Act, which would do the following:
    • Prohibit any local government, state agency, or state official from implementing procedures that results in a disparity among members of a protected class in election participation
    • Prohibit any local government from employing a method of election that has the effect of, or is motivated in part by, the intent to impair the ability of members of a protected class from participating in the political process 
    • Allow any individual aggrieved by a violation of this bill or organization whose membership includes individuals aggrieved by this a violation of this bill, or the attorney general to file an action to enforce compliance.
    • Create a covered policy for covered jurisdictions subject to preclearance by the commission or the Fifteenth Judicial Circuit. The bill would set forth the requirements for the process, including notifying jurisdictions, and any appeals process.
      • The commission would be required to determine at least annually which governmental entities are covered jurisdictions and to provide that list to the secretary of state to publish the list on its website.
  • Create the Alabama Voting Rights Act Commission, which would do the following:
    • Demonstrate commitment to the purpose of securing the voting rights of members of a protected class
    • Set forth the requirements for the make up of the committee
    • Set forth the requirements for the organization's certification with the secretary of state
    • Allow the commission to subpoena witnesses, administer oaths, examine individuals under oath, determine material facts, and compel production of records
  • Require the secretary of state to establish a statewide database of information necessary to assist the state and any municipality in evaluating whether any current laws and practices are inconsistent with the Alabama Voting Rights Act, implementing best practices, and investigating any potential infringement upon the right to vote. The bill would set forth additional requirements for the database.
  • Require the secretary of state to designate an employee to serve as manager of the database.
  • Require the secretary of state to publicize their work with local registrars, probate offices, and election administrators to provide semi-annual voter outreach efforts to educate Alabama residents on matters, including, but not limited to, upcoming election dates, voter registration requirements, available methods of voting, and voting locations.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 16, 2025, would expand the early voting period by extending it to the day before Election Day, change rules for siting and staffing vote centers, and make small changes to other sections of the election code. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Expand the early voting period to allow early voting to be offered through the day before Election day, provided that early voting will end earlier if needed to ensure that precinct registers and other election materials are revised for Election Day to indicate which voters requested a mail ballot ("early ballot" in Arizona), which have already voted, and which have inactive registrations. Under existing law, early voting ends at 5 p.m. on the Friday before Election Day, although emergency voting is allowed after that through 5 p.m. on the day before Election Day. The bill would preserve the emergency voting option in any jurisdiction that ends early voting before that time.
  • Limit county recorders' discretion to open early voting sites by requiring the county board of supervisors to specifically authorize the county recorder or other officer in charge of elections to establish additional sites. Under existing law, a specific resolution is not required for the recorder to open additional sites, and only county recorders, not other officers in charge of elections, are allowed to site them. The bill would allow recorders or other officers in charge of elections to make changes to the approved early voting sites, notifying the board and the public as soon as possible.
  • Require the department of administration, beginning in 2026, to coordinate with state agencies and counties to provide available and appropriate state-owned facilities for use as a voting location for any city, county, or state election when requested by the officer in charge of elections.
  • Require the board to make a list of polling places for all precincts publicly available.
  • Create "early voting drop-off centers", defined as a facility in which any voter in the county may return a voted mail ballot (called "early ballot" in Arizona) to a lawful custodian for voted ballots. Under existing law, voters may return their voted mail ballots to early and Election Day voting locations, drop boxes if offered, and by mail. Drop box use is not specifically addressed in existing statute, however, the Elections Procedures Manual, which has the force of law, explicitly authorizes their use.
  • Expand and clarify rules relating to vote centers, by:
    • Allowing any officer in charge of elections, upon a specific authorizing resolution of the county board of supervisors, to use vote centers in lieu of, or in addition to, precinct polling places, both for early voting and on Election Day. Under existing law, only a county recorder may be so empowered.
    • Clarifying that early voting locations may be vote centers, and that Election Day polling places are subject to the laws applicable to polling places. Under existing law, vote centers have been offered for both early and Election Day voting.
    • Providing that a vote center can be used as a ballot replacement location in a mail ballot election.
  • For Arizona's limited universal mail ballot elections, change the rules relating to voters obtaining replacement ballots. The bill would require the county recorder or other officer in charge of elections to set up one or more locations in the appropriate jurisdiction, instead of existing law's requirement that one central location be offered. In addition, the bill would require a voter seeking a replacement ballot to sign an affidavit attesting that they had not cast their original ballot. Under existing law, the voter must attest that the original ballot was lost, spoiled, destroyed, or not received.
  • Authorize a voter to put their completed provisional ballot into the provisional ballot envelope and then the ballot box. Under existing law, only an election official is so authorized.
  • Create a new section of code providing for "voting center election boards" and their qualifications without addressing the existing section of code that provides for such boards. Under the bill and existing law, the county board of supervisors must appoint election boards for each vote center consisting of inspectors, marshals, judges, and clerks of election, but the details of their appointment and who may serve on such boards differ slightly. Specifically, under the bill, a voting center election board would:
    • consist of at least one inspector, one marshal, and as many judges or clerks as deemed necessary. Existing law provides for one inspector, one marshal, two judges and as many clerks as deemed necessary.
    • require different political parties to be represented within each voting center election board generally, and specifically require an equal number of inspectors in the various voting centers in a county to be members of the two largest parties. Under existing law, strict bipartisan balance across offices and within vote centers is required.
    • require vote center election workers to be qualified voters of the county. Under existing law, election workers for precinct polling places must be voters of the precinct in which they serve unless an insufficient number of them are available, and for vote centers, workers must be voters in the state.
    • allow election board workers to be hired for shifts, provided sufficient workers are always present to assist voters. Existing law does not address shift work.

Specifically, the bill would:

  • Permit local election officials to extend general early voting through the Saturday, Sunday, and Monday before Election Day, and eliminate the existing "emergency" early voting process during this period. Under existing law, general early voting ends at 7 p.m. on the Friday before an election, and local officials may offer emergency early voting only to qualified voters through 5 p.m. on the following Monday.
  • Permit on-site tabulation of mail ballots at early voting polling places. Existing law permits this process at Election Day polling places only.
  • Expand the mail ballot verification process to include comparison of the voter's name and address on the ballot envelope and registration record, in addition to the existing comparison of signatures. 
  • Move the deadline earlier for return of mail ballots to drop boxes, and limit return locations on Election Day. Under existing law, through 2025 a mail ballot may be returned to the local elections office or a polling place by 7 p.m. on Election Day; starting in 2026, voters may also return a mail ballot to a polling place on Election Day and present ID, as an alternative to signature matching verification. In addition to these existing provisions, the bill would require that beginning in 2027:
    • For mail ballot return to a drop box at an early voting location, the deadline would be 7 p.m. on the Friday before Election Day.
    • For mail ballot return to the recorder's office, the deadline would remain 7 p.m. on Election Day.  
    • For mail ballot return on Election Day specifically, the ballot must be delivered by hand only, and may only be returned to the office of the county recorder or other official in charge of elections. The bill would also make a conforming change to eliminate the express permission to deposit a completed mail ballot in a drop box at an Election Day polling place with on-site ballot tabulation, for voters who cannot present an accepted form of voter ID. 
  • Increase requirements related to the permanent mail voter list ("active early voting list"). The bill would:
    • Require voters on the list to affirmatively confirm their mailing address once each election cycle. The bill would require local officials to reach out to voters for confirmation by telephone, written notice, or email, or to provide an online portal. Under existing law, which the bill would leave in place, voters are currently removed from the list if they fail to vote in two election cycles and do not respond to notice; if the pre-election notice sent to all list voters is returned as undeliverable and officials are unable to contact them; if their registration is cancelled; or if they request removal in writing. 
    • Expressly prohibit election officials from placing a voter on the permanent mail voter list if the voter's identity and address cannot be verified. Existing law requires officials to verify voters through signature matching of the list request form and original registration form, but does not otherwise specify criteria for rejection. 
  • Eliminate the use of emergency vote centers. 
  • Repeal a provision granting a public school principal authority to deny a request for their school to serve as a voting location based on space not being available or the safety or welfare of the children being at risk.
  • Prohibit the use of foreign money, goods, or services for election administration, create record keeping requirements, and create a civil enforcement action for violations. Existing law prohibits the use of private monies, but is silent as to foreign sources. The bill would:
    • Prohibit any government entity in the state from using money or in-kind goods or services donated by a foreign government or non-governmental source for election administration.
    • Require that all entities that provide services to the government for election administration certify to the secretary of state on an annual basis that they have not accepted such money or services, and require all government entities to provide a quarterly report listing all parties that provide election services..
    • Create a civil right of action for any voter or state officer to enjoin or enforce the new provisions, including specified damages for violations. 

The bill also contains additional provisions related to topics that Voting Rights Lab does not track.


The previous version of the bill contained additional provisions that were amended out of this version. Those provisions would have:

Officials would also have been required to use the number to verify applications for the permanent mail voter list, in addition to the use of signature matching as currently required.
  • Repealed the requirement that the county recorder take necessary steps to contact a voter on the permanent mail voter list before removal and transfer to the inactive voter list, if their pre-election notice is returned as undeliverable.

Specifically, the bill would have:

Under existing law, there is no population size requirement for county recorder offices or city or town clerk offices to be used for voters to cure ballots.

This resolution, as amended on February 12, 2025, proposes statutory changes that would extend the general early voting period; move the deadline earlier for certain methods of mail ballot return; increase requirements for staying on the permanent ballot list; and prohibit use of foreign funds for election administration, among other changes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Extend the general early voting period by moving the end date later, to the Monday before Election Day. Under existing law, general early voting ends on the Friday before an election, with limited emergency voting available through the following Monday. As a conforming change, the resolution would also eliminate this emergency voting period. 
  • Move the deadline earlier for return of a mail ballot to a drop box at a polling place, and require voter ID for return during certain times. Under the bill:
    • For deposit of a mail ballot at a polling place, the bill would move the general deadline from 7pm on Election Day to 7pm on the Friday before the election. 
    • After 7pm on the Friday before an election, in-person return to an early voting location would require an accepted form of voter ID. Existing law permits mail ballot voters to present ID in lieu of signature verification for their ballot, starting in 2026, but does not require ID. 
  • Expressly permit on-site vote tabulation of mail ballots at early voting locations. Existing law provides for on-site tabulation at Election Day voting locations only. 
  • Require election officials to ensure that chain of custody procedures for early ballots are the same as those for in-person Election Day voting.
  • Eliminate the existing requirement that county recorders count the number of early ballots that are returned at voting locations on Election Day and post those totals with the last unofficial results released on election night.
  • Increase requirements related to remaining on the permanent mail voting list ("active early voting list") after enrollment. The bill would:
    • Require voters on the list to make an "affirmative act" to confirm their address. For counties with a population of 500,000+, confirmation would be required for each election cycle; for counties under 500,000, confirmation would be required during the previous four years. Under existing law, officials must issue a notice to each enrolled voter before an election, providing the option to update their residence or request a new mailing address for their ballot, but confirmation is not mandatory.
    • Specify that officials must facilitate affirmative confirmation of a voter's address through at least one of the following: (1) mailed confirmation notices; (2) calling the voter or notifying the voter to call officials; (3) a county website portal.  
    • Provide that if a voter's address confirmation is received after the general deadline for requesting a mail ballot, a ballot will be sent for the following election. Under existing law, failure to respond to an address confirmation notice would generally not prevent a voter from receiving a mail ballot (except that a voter's registration may be inactivated or cancelled due to failure to vote by mail in two consecutive election cycles or if their notice was returned as undeliverable).
    •  Repeal the requirement that the county recorder "take necessary steps" to contact a voter if their pre-election notice letter is returned as undeliverable, prior to placing the voter in inactive status and removing them from the permanent mail voting list. Under the bill, these steps would be taken immediately on return of the notice. 
  • Prohibit the use of foreign money, goods, or services for election administration, create record keeping requirements, and create a civil enforcement action for violations. Existing law prohibits the use of private monies, but is silent as to foreign sources. The bill would:
    • Prohibit any government entity in the state from using money or in-kind goods or services donated by a foreign government or non-governmental source for election administration.
    • Require that all entities that provide services to the government for election administration certify to the secretary of state on an annual basis that they have not accepted such money or services, and require all government entities to provide a quarterly report listing all parties that provide election services.
    • Create a civil right of action for any voter to enjoin or enforce the new provisions, including specified damages for violations. 
  • Eliminate the use of emergency voting centers. 
  • Repeal a provision granting a public school principal authority to deny a request for their school to serve as a voting location based on space not being available or the safety or welfare of the children being at risk.


Final approval of changes proposed by this resolution requires passage by the legislature and approval by a majority of voters at the next general election.

This bill was vetoed by Governor Katie Hobbs on July 1, 2025. As passed by the legislature, it would have extended the general early voting period, created stricter voter ID requirements for certain in-person mail ballot return, made it easier to remove a voter from the permanent mail voting list, shortened the timeframe a voter has to cure their ballot, specified new requirements for polling places, and permitted earlier processing of certain mail ballots. Specifically, the bill would have:

  • Extended the in-person early voting period by setting the general end date at the Monday before an election. Under existing law, general early voting is available through the Friday before an election, and counties may offer "emergency voting" on the following Saturday, Sunday, and Monday. The bill would have eliminated this emergency voting process, and instead required general early voting to be available for these days. 
  • Prohibited election officials from offering in-person early voting after 7 p.m. on the Friday before an election if the county recorder was not able to revise precinct registers and other elections materials in a "timely manner" for use on Election Day. The existing provision for emergency early voting between 7 p.m. on the Friday before an election and 5 p.m. on the Monday before, which the bill would have replaced with general early voting, does not include any prohibition related to readiness of materials for Election Day. 
  • Created a new voter ID requirement for in-person return of a mailed ballot after 7 p.m. on the Friday before Election Day. Under existing law, through 2025 there is no ID requirement or option when returning a mail ballot to a polling place; beginning in 2026, voters will have the option to provide an ID and pollbook signature in lieu of signature verification. The bill would have, as of its effective date, required voter ID for mail ballots returned to polling places by the voter or their agent after 7 p.m. on the Friday before an election. For these ballots, voters would have been required to present an accepted form of ID and sign the signature roster or pollbook. The ballot would have been stamped "ID verified," following specified verification procedures, and would have been tabulated on-site. 
  • Required officials to remove voters from the permanent mail voting list ("active early voting list") if the voter or their agent returned a mail ballot in person after 7 p.m. on the Friday before Election Day without presenting sufficient ID. Existing law has no comparable provision.
  • Moved the deadline earlier for curing mail ballot defects or providing ID for a provisional ballot, to the fifth calendar day after an election. Under existing law, the deadline is the fifth business day after Election Day. 
  • Required public schools that serve grades seven through 12 to provide space for use as a polling place for any city, county, or state election when requested by an election officer, if officials were unable to obtain sufficient voting locations from all of the other locations prescribed under law, and eliminated discretion for school officials to deny requests. Existing law provides that all public schools (without limitation on grade level) must provide space for a polling site, with the exception that a school principal may deny a request if, within two weeks after a request is made, they provide a written statement that either space is not available at the school or the safety or welfare of the children would be jeopardized.
  • Required that all government-owned buildings or facilities that are accessible to the public be made available as voting locations when requested.
  • Required that each polling location include a minimum of at least one "secure ballot box" for voters who present ID when depositing their ballot, as newly provided in other provisions of the bill, and a separate box for voters who do not present ID. Existing statutory and administrative law authorizes the operation of drop boxes at approved "secure locations," such as inside or outside of government buildings, and has no requirements for separate containers.
  • Allowed election officials to remove mail ballots returned by voters who presented ID at voting locations on Election Day from the polling place before the close of polls for counting, provided that all existing chain of custody procedures were followed. Under existing law, no ballots may be removed before the close of polls. The bill would also require the chain of custody log to be available to the public within 48 hours of Election Day.
  • Required election officials in charge of polling places to ensure that only voters who present ID and have their ballot stamped "ID verified" were able to deposit their ballot in the ballot box designated for verified early ballots. 
  • Made conforming changes to various provisions to reflect the new requirements and effective date of the bill, and numerous non-substantive changes.

The bill also contains additional provisions related to topics that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

  • Eliminate emergency voting and instead move up the day on which mail voting can start from 27 days before the election to 29 days before the election. The bill would also allow mail voting to be extended through the Monday before Election Day. Under existing law, mail voting must end on the Friday before Election Day, although emergency voting is available beginning at 7 p.m. on the Friday before Election Day and ends at 5 p.m. on Election Day.   • Require public schools to allow their space to be used as a polling place for any city, county, or state election when requested by an election officer. Under existing law, the principal of the school can deny a request to provide space for use as a polling place if, within two weeks after a request is made, the principal provides a written statement including a reason the election cannot be held in the school.

This bill, as introduced on January 21, 2025, titled the "Arizona State Voting Rights Act" would provide protections from unequal access to voting and political participation based on a voter's race, income level, gender, disability, national origin, language ability, age, sexual orientation, or religion. The bill would:

  • Declare that members of the protected classes mentioned above are entitled to an equal opportunity for voting and political participation as that enjoyed by all other voters. The bill would prohibit the implementation of laws or rules impairing the rights of the protected classes.
  • Give members of the protected classes and organizations composed of such members standing to seek enforcement of the act's provisions in court.
  • Define "covered political subdivisions" as subdivisions in which two percent of the population or 4,000 people of voting age are members of a single language minority and speak English "less than very well." If a political subdivision includes a tribal nation, the two percent analysis is applied to the tribal nation.
  • Require covered political subdivisions to provide voting materials (including registration forms, ballot applications, instructions, and ballots) and notices in each covered language.
  • Require each covered political subdivision to provide at least one election official at each voting location that speaks each covered language.
  • Subject covered political subdivisions to a $5,000 fine for each affected voter for failure to comply with the provisions of the act.
  • Prohibit the state or any political subdivision from implementing any procedure that provides any of the protected classes of equal opportunities for voting and political participation.
  • Create a rebuttable presumption that any regulation that impairs the participation of a protected class within the 90 days before an election is a violation of the act's provisions and allows members of the protected class to seek judicial relief.
  • Authorize courts to provide additional voting hours or days, additional voting locations or methods, voter education, or the restoration of names to the voting rolls when necessary to remedy regulations that unlawfully impair the rights of voters in the protected classes.

This bill, as introduced on February 3, 2025 would make it a crime to harass or interfere with election officials. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create a new class 1 misdemeanor if an individual was convicted of:
    • Threatening, coercing, or intimidating an election official with the intent to impede or interfere with the election official while they are engaged in the performance of election duties or to retaliate against the election official based on the election official's performance of the election official's duties.
    • Knowingly making use of threats of force, coercion, violence, restraint, damage, harm or loss against an election official with the intent to influence the election official in the performance of the election official's duties.
    • Intentionally and physically obstructing an election official from accessing or egressing from a voting location, counting center, elections office, or other elections facility or any other location where an election official performs an official duty
  • Allow an individual to file a civil action to prevent or restrain violations of this section or to recover damages.

HISTORY: {"date":"02/10/2025","summary":"Additionally referred to SENATE Committee on RULES","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 3, 2025, would:

  • Require voters receiving or returning ballots at voting locations with on-site tabulation to provide ID. Those voters' ballots would forgo signature verification. Under existing law, beginning in 2026, voters receiving a a ballot at a voting location with on-site tabulation would be required to provide ID and forgo signature verification. Under the bill, this provision would go into effect on the bill's effective date.
  • Replace emergency voting with three days of early voting. Specifically, the bill would extend the general in-person early voting period to include the Saturday, Sunday, and Monday before an election. Early voting would be available until 7 p.m. on the Saturday and Sunday before Election Day and would be available until at least 3 p.m. and may be open as late as 7 p.m. as determined by the county recorder. Under existing law, standard early voting ends at 7 p.m. on the Friday before an election, and local officials may offer emergency early voting only to qualified voters through 5 p.m. on the following Monday. As a conforming change, the bill would eliminate this emergency voting period.
  • Specify that ballots that are verified in-person do not need to undergo signature verification.
  • Allow ballots returned to voting locations on Election Day after a voter's ID is confirmed to be removed by two authorized election workers, who must each be a member of the two largest political parties. Those individuals would be required to complete a chain of custody log that includes the total count of the early ballots being transported and who delivered the ballots to a designated receiving site. The chain of custody log must be available for inspection by the public, the political parties, committees representing any ballot measures on the ballot, and the candidates on the ballot within 48 hours of Election Day.
  • Change the effective end date for a statute providing that if a voter surrenders their mail ballot to a precinct inspector, the voter is entitled to vote a standard ballot after presenting ID. Under existing law, this statute is in effect through 2025 and under this bill, the statute would be in effect until the effective date of this bill.

HISTORY: {"date":"02/10/2025","summary":"Additionally referred to SENATE Committee on RULES","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 3, 2025, would shift sole and shared election authority from the board of supervisors to the county recorder for election administrative decisions. Specifically, the bill would shift authority:

  • From the board of supervisors to the county recorder for the following scenarios: 
    • When determining the number of election precincts in the county 
    • When designating the number and locations of polling places
    • When authorizing the use and location of voting centers. Under existing law, the county board of supervisors may authorize the use of voting centers upon a specific resolution and the board and the county recorder must work together to determine locations.
    • When authorizing the use of emergency voting centers and when establishing hours or locations. Under existing law, the county board of supervisors may authorize them on a specific resolution of the board and locations must be established in coordination and consultation with the county recorder. The bill would make conforming and non-substantive changes because of this change.
    • When designating sites for voters to deposit marked ballots until 7 p.m. on Election Day for special district mail ballot elections
    • When requesting space for a polling a place from a public school
    • When making available to the public a list of all polling places in which the election is to be held
    • When preparing and providing ballots to be used in elections
    • When designating the central counting place. Under existing law, this location must be designated by the board of supervisors or officer in charge of elections.
    • When directing the proceedings at the counting center. Under existing law, the proceedings are under the direction of the board of supervisors or other officer in charge of elections.
    • When appointing the use of electronic vote adjudication boards to oversee the automatic tabulating equipment's electronic vote adjudication features. Under existing law, the board of supervisors or officer in charge of elections is responsible for appointing the board.
  • From "the county recorder or officer in charge of elections" to the county recorder for the following scenarios: 
    • When determining whether a voter may update their voter registration information when voting at an emergency voting center.
    • When providing for a live video recording of the custody of ballots in a tabulation room in the counting center. 
    • When maintaining records that record the chain of custody for all election equipment and ballots.

HISTORY: {"date":"03/26/2025","summary":"From HOUSE Committee on FEDERALISM, MILITARY AFFAIRS & ELECTIONS:  Do pass with amendment","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as amended on March 26, 2025, would:

  • Create a new voter ID requirement for in-person return of a mailed ballot after 7 p.m. on the Friday before Election Day. Under existing law, through 2025 there is no ID requirement or option when returning a mail ballot to a polling place; beginning in 2026, voters will have the option to provide an ID and pollbook signature in lieu of signature verification. The bill would, as of its effective date, require voter ID for mail ballots returned to polling places by the voter or their agent after 7 p.m. on the Friday before an election. For these ballots, voters would be required to present an accepted form of ID and sign the signature roster or pollbook. The ballot would be stamped "ID verified," following specified verification procedures, and would be tabulated on-site. 
  • Replace emergency voting with three days of early voting. Specifically, the bill would extend the general in-person early voting period to include the Saturday, Sunday, and Monday before an election. Under existing law, standard early voting ends at 7 p.m. on the Friday before an election, and local officials may offer emergency early voting only to qualified voters through 5 p.m. on the following Monday. As a conforming change, the bill would eliminate this emergency voting period.
  • Require voters on the permanent mail voting list and others voting by mail to provide periodic confirmation of their address "through an affirmative act." Under existing law, officials must issue a notice to each listed voter before an election, providing the option to update their residence or request a new mailing address for their ballot. The new confirmation system would additionally:
    • Require all individuals voting by mail who live in a county with a population of 500,000+ to confirm their address each election cycle before receiving a mail ballot. For counties with a population of less than 500,000, the bill would require mail voters to confirm their address during the four year period that constitutes two consecutive election cycles before receiving a mail ballot.
    • Permit voters on the list to confirm their address by mail, telephone, or online portal.
    • For address confirmation received from a voter after the last day for making a mail ballot request, require officials to process the confirmation for the next upcoming election, rather than the immediate election. Under existing law, failure to respond to an address confirmation notice would generally not prevent a voter from receiving a mail ballot (except that a voter's registration may be inactivated or cancelled due to failure to vote by mail in two consecutive election cycles or if their notice was returned as undeliverable).
  • Repeal the requirement that the county recorder take necessary steps to contact a voter if their election notice letter is returned as undeliverable. The bill would instead require the county recorder to move the voter to inactive status and remove the voter from the list. Under existing law, if a notice is returned as undeliverable, the county recorder must "take the necessary steps" to contact the voter at their new address in order to update their address or to move the voter to inactive status. If the county recorder is unable to reach the voter at their new address, they must move the voter to inactive status and remove them from the list.
  • Prohibit any government entity in the state from using money or in-kind goods or services donated by a foreign government or non-governmental source for election administration and would create requirements that all entities that provide services to the government for election administration certify on an annual basis that they have not accepted such money or services, as well as other reporting requirements. Under existing law, there is no similar prohibition.
  • Create a class one misdemeanor for a violation of this bill.
  • Allow the attorney general, any voter, or any state officer to bring a civil action to enjoin or enforce any provision of this bill that prohibits donations from foreign entities and that requires entities providing election administration services to fulfill certification requirements.
  • Eliminate emergency voting
  • Require public schools to allow their space to be used as a voting location for any city, county, or state election when requested by an election officer. Under existing law, the principal of the school can deny a request to provide space for use as a polling place if, within two weeks after a request is made, the principal provides a written statement that space is not available at the school or the safety or welfare of the children would be jeopardized.
  • Repeal the requirement that the county recorder count early ballots returned on Election Day and post unofficial results on its website.

In order to go into effect, this bill would need to be passed by both chambers and approved by a majority of voters at the next general election.


The bill also contains additional provisions related to topics that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

Last Updated April 3, 2025
