HISTORY: {"date":"04/09/2025","summary":"From ASSEMBLY Committee on ELECTIONS without further action pursuant to JR 62(a)","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on February 24, 2025, would:

  • Require individuals registering to vote to provide documentary proof of citizenship beginning January 1, 2026, in addition to certifying under penalty of perjury that the individual is a citizen, as is required under existing law. The bill would make nonsubstantive and conforming changes because of this requirement.
  • Require elections officials to deny the registration of an individual whose citizenship cannot be verified by the elections official based on the documentation provided.
  • Require individuals voting in person to present a valid government-issued form of ID prior to voting. Under existing law, voters are not required to present ID.
  • Require the state auditor to periodically review a random sample of a county's roster to identify individuals who are not qualified electors in that county. If the state auditor determines that fewer than 98 percent of the individuals listed are qualified voters in that county, the state auditor would not send all registered voters mail ballots, as is required under existing law. Instead, the state auditor would be required to only send mail ballots to voters who submit a request. Those voters would be required to submit an application including their name, residence, address where the ballot should be mailed, and their signature. The elections official would be required to begin sending mail ballots no later than 29 days before the election.
  • Require individuals returning mail ballots to include the last four digits of their valid government-issued form of ID. This is not required under existing law. The bill would make nonsubstantive and conforming changes because of this requirement.
  • Require the state auditor to audit county elections officials by reviewing random samples of the signature comparisons conducted by the elections officials to determine whether the signature comparisons comply with the requirements set forth under existing law. The state auditor would be required to report their findings no later than 90 days after each election.
  • Require the state auditor to prepare a remediation plan for an elections official to follow if the state auditor determines that an elections official has a signature comparison error rate of five percent or greater. The state auditor would be required to submit the remediation plan to the secretary of state.
  • Require election officials to count all ballots, except provisional ballots and other ballots that may be cured, by no later than 72 hours after the election. Under existing law, election officials must finalize their results no later than 30 days after the election but there is no deadline by which ballots must be counted. An election official who failed to meet this requirement would be prohibited from sending mail ballots to all registered voters for the next statewide election, as is required under existing law, and instead would be required to send mail ballots only to voters who requested them.

Last Updated April 29, 2025

HISTORY: {"date":"10/03/2025","summary":"Chaptered by Secretary of State.  Chapter No. 2025-279","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on October 3, 2025, does the following:

Regarding curing: 

  • Moves up the deadline by which elections officials must notify a voter that their signatures do not match from "as soon as practicable, but no later than" 22 days after the election to 14 calendar days after a regularly scheduled statewide election. The deadline of 22 days after an election remains the same for a not regularly scheduled statewide election. 
  • Moves up the deadline by which a voter must return their ballot curing statement from 28 calendar days after the election the election to 22 calendar days after the election for a regularly scheduled statewide election. The deadline for a not regularly scheduled statewide election is unchanged at 28 calendar days after the election. 
  • Requires that information about whether a voter has cured their ballot be collected and updated on a daily basis. The daily update must include information about whether a form has been received from the voter to verify their signature and whether a signature has been provided.
  • Allows elections officials to use ballot drop boxes as receptacles to receive a form containing a voter's missing signature if the drop box is clearly and conspicuously labeled that it is used for this purpose. Prior law did not expressly authorize use of ballot drop boxes for that purpose.
  • Allows voters to cure their ballots that are missing a signature by providing their signature electronically. Any form sent to voters alerting them of their missing signature is required to include the appropriate internet website.

Regarding processing and counting ballots:

  • Prohibits election officials from delaying in conducting signature verification on ballots. Prior law did not include an express prohibition.
  • Allows the canvassing of an election to be conducted for less than six hours per day, as is required under existing law, if the only ballots left to count are vote by mail ballots for which a voter has been provided an opportunity to cure their signature and the elections official does not need to conduct the official canvass for at least six hours per day in order to meet the certification deadline.
  • Specifies that if any deadline laid out in this bill falls on a holiday, the deadline will be continued to the next business day.
  • Prohibits an elections official from reviewing or considering a voter's identifying information including gender, name, or address or the amount of time spent reviewing a signature when reviewing a signature.
  • Requires an elections official to update the signature database upon reviewing a voter's signature statement if necessary, even if the ballot is returned untimely.
  • Allows a voter to work with a nongovernmental entity to complete a signature verification statement and envelope statement. Prior law did not include a similar express authorization.
  • Requires the signature verification statement on mail ballots to state that the elections official is required to compare the voter's signature on the the signature verification statement with the signatures appearing in the voter's registration record, including the signature on the voter's driver's license or state ID card.
  • Requires the secretary of state to publish online a single, combined vote by mail signature verification statement and unsigned ballot identification envelope statement. A form developed by an elections official meeting the same requirements can also be accepted and must be available online. Prior law did not specifically apply these requirements to the secretary of state.
  • Requires that if an elections official receives a completed unsigned identification envelope statement with a mail ballot that was not timely submitted, the official is required to compare the voter's signature on the statement and if the official determined that the signatures compare, the official will add the signature from the unsigned identification envelope to the voter's registration record for use in future elections.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended March 25, 2025, would eliminate universal mail voting and vote centers and require voters wishing to vote by mail to apply for a mail ballot. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Repeal the existing law requiring all voters to automatically be sent a mail ballot for every election and instead require that voters apply for a mail ballot between the 29th and seventh day before an election. The voter would be required to sign the application and list their place of residence. Applications received before the 29th day prior to an election would be kept and processed during the application period.
  • Eliminate vote centers. The bill would make nonsubstantive and conforming changes because of this requirement.
  • Create a permanent mail voting list. The bill would allow any voter to apply for permanent mail status if they provide the following information in an application or written request:
    • Their name
    • Their residence
    • The address where the ballot is to be mailed if different from their residence
    • Their signature
  • Require that a voter be removed from the permanent mail voting list if they fail to return a voted mail ballot in four consecutive statewide general elections.
  • Repeal the provision allowing a county elections official to permit any voter to cast a ballot using a certified remote accessible vote by mail system, regardless of whether the voter is a voter with disabilities or a military or overseas voter.
  • Repeal the requirement that any county that does not conduct an all mail election provide at least two vote by mail ballot drop off locations within the jurisdiction where the election is held or at least one vote by mail ballot drop off location for every 30,000 voters within the jurisdiction, as determined on the 88th day before an election, whichever results in more vote by mail drop off locations.
  • Repeal the statute requiring that a jurisdiction with fewer than 30,000 registered voters provide at least one ballot mail ballot drop off location. The location was required to be secure, accessible, and locked and located as near as possible to established public transportation routes.
  • Repeal the requirement that all vote by mail ballot drop off locations be open at least during regular business hours beginning no less than 28 days before the day of the election and on Election Day. The bill would also repeal the requirement that at least one vote by mail drop off location be an exterior drop box that is available a minimum of 12 hours per day.
  • Repeal the requirement that a county that conducts an all mail statewide primary or general election do the following in addition to providing required mail ballot drop off locations:
    • Designate one location on the main campus of each California State University within the official's jurisdiction for an additional vote by mail ballot drop off location 
    • Require the elections official to request that the governing body having jurisdiction over any University of California campus authorize the use of one location on that campus
    • Permit a county to provide a vote by mail ballot drop off location on a campus if the campus is not in session for its fall, winter, or spring term on the day of the election.
  • Require an elections official to process an application to join the permanent mail voting list in the same manner as an application for a vote by mail ballot.
  • Require that the permanent mail voter list be open to public inspection for election and governmental purposes.
  • Require the county elections official to send a copy of the list of all voters who qualify as permanent mail voters to each city elections official by the sixth day before an election.
  • Require that prior to every partisan primary election, county election officials mail every voter on the permanent mail voting list information about how to request a ballot for a particular political party.
  • Repeal the statutes allowing counties to conduct any election as an all mailed ballot election and would repeal all of the corresponding requirements and parameters for conducting an all mailed ballot election. The bill would make nonsubstantive and conforming changes because of this change.

This bill, as enacted on March 26, 2025:

  • Allows candidates nominated by a participating political party in a general election or congressional vacancy election to select their own election watchers at central count facilities. Prior law provided that political parties—not individual candidates—were responsible for appointing watchers at these locations. Voters who believe their ballot was misrecorded could request a correction from the secretary of state before certification. Existing law does not include any public-facing system for ballot-level vote verification.

This bill, as enacted on June 2, 2025:

Under prior law, confidentiality of voter information was limited only to individuals with reason to believe they would face criminal harassment or bodily harm if their address was not kept confidential.

This bill, as enacted on May 13 2025, establishes civil penalties for certain conduct against voters, voter assistants, and election officials. Existing law includes criminal penalties for certain conduct against election officials while executing their official duties, interference with a voter while voting, and intimidation of voters. In addition to these criminal penalties, the bill:

  • Prohibits intimidating, threatening, or coercing individuals for:
    • Voting or attempting to vote
    • Urging or aiding any individual in voting or attempting to vote, including as part of official election administration activity
    • Exercising powers or duties of election administration, including vote counting, canvassing, and certification
    • Status as as part or present participant in election administration
  • Establishes a presumption of intimidation if an individual carries a visible firearm or imitation firearm while engaging in election-related activities, unless proven otherwise by a preponderance of evidence. The bill specifies that this presumption does not apply to law enforcement officers acting within the scope of their duties or uniformed security guards employed by a contract security agency, and requires that a plaintiff must allege that a law enforcement officer or uniformed security guard did more than possess a firearm or holster it to state a claim. 
  • Creates a civil cause of action for aggrieved individuals, election officials, the secretary of state, and the attorney general, for violations of the new prohibitions. Plaintiffs are not required to prove intent, and remedies may include enjoining use or carrying of firearms.

Last Updated June 17, 2025

This bill, as enacted on May 12, 2025, establishes the Colorado Voting Rights Act to prohibit and remedy voter suppression and vote dilution, and increases voter assistance related to disability and language, among other changes. The bill:

  • Establishes the "Colorado Voting Rights Act." The Act:
    • Prohibits political subdivisions from adopting policies that suppress or dilute the votes of protected class voters. Protected classes of voters would include voters who are members of one or more "racial, color, or language minority groups." The bill also expressly prohibits political subdivisions from imposing unnecessary burdens on voters' access to election information, voter registration, or ballots based on their confinement in a local jail.
    • Authorizes aggrieved individuals, organizations, or the attorney general to file lawsuits alleging voter suppression, vote dilution, or unlawful voting prerequisites. Courts must prioritize these cases, and remedies may include preliminary relief before an election.
    • Requires a notification letter to be sent to jurisdictions prior to filing lawsuits (with exceptions), and allows political subdivisions to adopt a resolution with proposed remedies to address alleged violations.
    • Establishes standards for evaluating claims of voter suppression and vote dilution, including what constitutes a prima facie case and the evidence that courts may consider.
    • Permits the attorney general to investigate violations and intervene in litigation. The bill specifies that enforcement by the attorney general is considered as being on behalf of the secretary of state.
    • Requires the secretary of state to collect and publish data on:
      • Population, voting-age population, and citizen voting-age population by demographic groups
      • Precinct-level election results
      • Geocoded locations and hours for all polling and drop box sites
    • Requires political subdivisions to submit precinct-level election results and boundaries to the Department of State following certification.
  • Requires covered facilities serving people with disabilities to post voter information notices 30 days before statewide general and primary elections, including information on voting rights, accessibility, and drop box locations.
  • Expands multilingual ballot access requirements to municipalities (in addition to counties) with over 3,000 residents that are in counties already covered by Colorado’s multilingual ballot access law. Under the bill, beginning, January 1, 2027, municipalities will be required to do one of the following:
    • Create and publish sample ballots in minority languages.
    • Provide at least one in-person location where voters can request a ballot in a minority language.
    • Use qualified translators and notify voters of language access options in mail ballot packets.
  • Expressly specifies that for accepted forms of voter ID, federally recognized tribal IDs and similar documents with a Colorado address are not required to include the individual's photo.

This bill also includes additional provisions related to topics that are not tracked by Voting Rights Lab.

AUTHORNAME: Joint Committee on Government Administration and Elections
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 14, 2025, would:

  • Move up the date on which mail ballots can begin to be processed from the seventh day before the election to the 14th day before the election. 
  • Move up the date by which sorted mail ballots can be transferred by the municipal clerk to the registrars. Under existing law, ballots received by 11 a.m. on the day before the election are delivered by the municipal clerk to the registrars on Election Day for counting. The bill would allow ballots received by 5 p.m. on the fourth day, third day, and second day before the election to be transferred to the municipal clerk on the following day. Ballots received by 11 a.m. on the day before the election would be delivered at 8 a.m. on Election Day. The bill would make nonsubstantive and conforming changes because of this change.
  • Move up the time at which ballots can begin to be counted from no later than 10 a.m. to no later than 8 a.m. The bill would move up the deadline by which ballots received by the municipal clerk prior to the election must be delivered to the registrars to begin counting to between 6 a.m. and 8 a.m. on Election Day. Under existing law, those ballots must be delivered to the registrar between 6 a.m. and 10 a.m. 
  • Require that ballot processing take place at a central location designated by the registrar of voters in writing to the municipal clerk at least 10 days before an election.
  • Require the registrars of voters to use best efforts to notify voters who submitted mail ballots if their ballot was rejected due to a missing signature or missing identification. The registrar would be required to inform the voter that their ballot had been rejected but that they still may be able to vote in person on Election Day. Under existing law, rejected ballots are treated as provisional ballots for federal offices only, but voters are not informed ahead of Election Day that their mail ballot has been rejected. There is no cure process required under existing state law.
  • Require that any voter who has returned a mail ballot but decides instead to vote in person to go to the municipal clerk's office by 5 p.m. on the fourth day before the election to ask that their ballot be withdrawn. Under existing law, the voter must go to the clerk's office before 10 a.m. on Election Day.
  • Require that beginning on January 1, 2026, the registrar of voters display at least one poster at each voting location explaining how voters can look up their proper voting district online.
  • Allow the registrar of voters of a municipality with a population of no more than 35,000 to reduce the number of required polling places and designate those polling places no later than 60 days before a primary. 
  • Require the registrar of voters to notify the secretary of state and candidates seeking nomination to any change in polling places no earlier than 60 days before a primary and no later than 45 days before the primary. The candidate would be permitted to object to a change in the polling places by submitting a signed, written letter to the secretary of state no later than 4 p.m. on the 30th day before the election.
  • Require the registrar of voters to notify voters whose polling location has been changed no later than 21 days before a primary.

The bill also contains additional provisions related to topics that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on April 10, 2025, would create a Municipal Election Accountability Board within the office of the secretary of state for the purpose of reviewing the administration of elections, primaries and referenda, including the conduct of early voting, absentee voting, and same-day registration. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Allow the following individuals or entities to refer matters to the Municipal Election Accountability Board for the following purposes:
    • The secretary of state or the State Elections Enforcement Commission when they are of the opinion that a reasonable likelihood of irregularity or impropriety in the administration of any election, primary, or referendum exists based on any formal or informal complaint received by the secretary of the commission from an individual. The referral must be accompanied by evidence.
    • A judge of the Superior Court when they are of the opinion that a reasonable likelihood of irregularity or impropriety in the administration of any election, primary, or referendum exists based on a matter before the court. The referral must be accompanied by evidence.
    • A municipal clerk, registrar of voters, or moderator if they observe any act or omission that may present an impediment to the timely and orderly administration of any duty required of a municipality. The referral must be accompanied by evidence.
    • The chief executive officer of a municipality when they review a municipality's practices and identify practices that may present an impediment. The referral must be accompanied by evidence. 
    • A citizen when they have a good-faith belief that a reasonable likelihood of irregularity or impropriety in the administration of any election exists. The referral must be accompanied by evidence. 
  • Require the Municipal Election Accountability Board, upon receipt of a referral, to give notice to the municipality. The municipality would be allowed to respond within 10 days. No later than 45 days after receipt of a response or 60 days after receiving a referral if the municipality did not respond, the board would be required to hold a review hearing for the purpose of presenting to that municipality the evidence accompanying the report. The board would vote to determine whether to provide oversight of that municipality at the next scheduled meeting.
  • Provide the appeals procedure for municipalities to appeal decisions made by the board.
  • Require the board, when subjecting a municipality to oversight by the board, to designate that municipality as tier one, tier two, tier three, or tier four depending on how much oversight is needed.
  • Allow the board to require municipalities subject to oversight to:
    • Develop a mitigation plan 
    • Undergo mandatory training of election officials
    • Be subject to an election monitor
    • Undergo inspections, inquiries, and investigations
    • Provide access to records and materials
  • Prescribe the composition of the board, the terms of positions on the board, and the meeting dates.

AUTHORNAME: Joint Committee on Government Administration and Elections
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on April 14, 2025, would:

  • Require curbside voting to be available at each polling place. The registrar of voters would be required to designate an area for curbside voting for voters who are present at the polling place but unable to gain access to the polling place due to an incapacity. 
  • Prohibit an elector voting curbside from having anyone else in the vehicle unless they are also voting or driving the voter. No candidate would be allowed in any vehicle used for curbside voting unless for the purpose of casting their own ballot.
  • Require the secretary of state to adopt regulations to carry out the provisions of this bill that would include, but are not limited to, a model plan that municipalities may implement for curbside voting.
  • Prohibit any individual who has been convicted of a crime from distributing any mail ballot application during their probation or parole period or for a period of 12 years after their release from confinement, probation or parole. The town clerk would be required to reject for filing any mail ballot applications that were distributed in violation of this prohibition. Under existing law, any individual must register with the town clerk before distributing five or more mail ballot applications for an election, not including applications distributed to their own family or to the designee of an applicant. 
  • Create a Translation Advisory Committee within the office of the secretary of state for the purposes of: 1) validating the translations of election-related materials for accuracy and ensuring that such translations meet the needs of the intended audience in a culturally responsive and linguistically appropriate way; and 2) making recommendations to the secretary of state and municipal officials on related matters.

This bill, as introduced on March 4, 2025, would create new requirements for verification of citizenship during voter registration, increase voter ID requirements for certain first-time voters, and increase requirements related to voter registration at the DMV, among other changes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create new citizenship verification requirements for individuals registering to vote. Under existing law, registration applicants must affirmatively confirm their citizenship status on the registration form, subject to the felony offense for false statements (noted on the form), and no documentary verification is required. Under the bill:  
    • For individuals registering with a driver's license or state ID number, election officials would be required to verify that DMV records do not indicate that the ID was originally issued with non-citizen documentation and that the DMV classifies the individual as a citizen. If a DMV-issued ID was obtained using non-United States citizen documentation, the bill would require officials to use "every possible means" to determine if the applicant became a naturalized citizen after obtaining their ID. The bill would also expressly require rejection of an application if verification checks indicate noncitizenship, and require that election officials document the completion of verification procedures. 
    • For applicants registering to vote using only the last four digits of their Social Security number, the bill would require officials to use "all possible means" to verify citizenship. Such voters would be required to present their Social Security card before voting for the first time, and those with work-restricted cards would be required to vote provisionally and provide proof of citizenship for their vote to be counted.
    • For applicants registering without a driver’s license, state ID, or Social Security number, the bill would require officials to verify citizenship status using "all possible means," including the use of data from state agencies such as courts and corrections and family services agencies. If no findings indicate noncitizenship, the application would be considered valid.
    • Regarding verification of a driver's license generally, the bill would direct election officials to "compare information from all available sources" to determine whether the licence is classified as a non-citizen license, surrendered license following a move out of state, or the license of a deceased individual.
  • Require officials to report any determination that an individual has knowingly made a false affirmation on a registration application to the Office of Election Crimes and Security. The existing voter registration application notes the felony offense for false statements, but statutory law does not mandate officials report suspected false statements. 
  • Increase voter ID requirements for certain first-time voters casting ballots in person or by mail. Under existing law, voters who register by mail and have not been issued a driver's license, state ID, or Social Security number, must provide one form of accepted ID (or a copy of such ID when voting by mail ballot). These ID may include, if unexpired and including the voter's name and photo: U.S. passport; debit or bank card; military ID, student ID; retirement center ID; neighborhood association ID; public assistance ID; veteran's health ID; concealed carry license; or government employee ID. Also accepted, if containing the voter's name and residence address: utility bill; bank statement; government check; pay check; or other government document (excluding a voter ID card). The bill would:
    • Apply the special ID rules to individuals who register by any method other than through the DMV, rather than registrations by mail only, and have not been issued a state ID. 
    • Limit the accepted forms of primary voter ID to only a U.S. passport, U.S. birth certificate, U.S. naturalization papers, consular report of birth abroad, or Social Security Card without a work restriction.
    • Require each form of ID, except U.S. passports, to be accompanied by an additional acceptable identification that contains the voter's name and photograph. Under existing law, these ID are accepted on their own as primary ID: 
      • Debit or credit card
      • Military ID
      • Student ID
      • Retirement center ID
      • Public assistance ID
      • Veteran Affairs health ID card
      • Concealed carry license
      • Government employee ID
    • Eliminate from accepted ID, and accept only as proof of residential address, a utility bill, bank statement, government check, paycheck or other government document (excluding voter ID cards), and require that such documents be dated within the last two months. Under existing law, such forms of ID, if current and valid, can be used directly as proof of identification, and there is no two month date limitation.
    • Eliminate neighborhood association IDs as a form of acceptable ID. 
    • Repeal a provision that exempts residents 65 years and older who are otherwise subject to the special voter ID rules from having to provide proof of identification, and require all remaining exempt individuals to provide documentation verifying their reason for exemption. 
    • Allow individuals residing outside of the country but who do not qualify for an exemption to provide alternate forms of ID.  
  • Require driver's licenses or ID cards to include "NC" on the front for individuals who are not U.S. citizens, and require voters who present such a document as voter ID to vote a provisional ballot only. 
  • Increase requirements for voter registration at the DMV regarding applicant signatures and reporting of data from the DMV to the Department of State related to voting eligibility. The bill would:
    • Require applicants who register to vote at the DMV to provide a "wet signature" and an electronic signature affirming the accuracy of the voter registration information presented. Existing law requires an electronic signature only. 
    • Require the DMV to include instructions on updating driver license classifications for individuals marked as non-U.S. citizens when sending renewal applications. Existing law has no comparable requirement. 
    • Require the DMV to provide the Secretary of State with ongoing and periodic notifications related to voting eligibility. Existing law has no comparable requirements. Notifications would include:
      • When a license or ID is obtained with documentation that indicates noncitizenship, specified as: Social Security cards that contain a work restriction, alien registration receipt cards, employment authorization cards issued by the United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS), and proof of nonimmigrant classification provided by DHS.
      • When a driver license has been made invalid due to the issuance of a driver license in another state or due to notification of death. The State Department would be required to notify the relevant local clerk to remove the voter from the statewide registration system.
      • Weekly reports on surrendered licenses and deaths, along with online and written query access to this information for local clerks.
  • Require new routine list maintenance procedures by local election officials, to include at least quarterly review of data from various state agencies to identify voters who are noncitizens, no longer resident, deceased, or otherwise ineligible to vote. The bill would also require at least quarterly review of the voter list for addresses with more registered individuals than permitted by applicable zoning regulations. If any are identified, the election supervisor would be required to use "all available sources" to determine the validity of the registrations. Existing law requires annual list maintenance related to address confirmation only.
  • Expand the data sources regarding voter ineligibility that officials may use to initiate removal from the voter registration list. Under existing law, in addition to certain specified data sources, officials may use information from "any governmental entity" related to voting eligibility. The bill would instead permit use of data from "any credible source," defined as affidavits verified with information from DMV records, county tax records, or other credible sources, from a rental or group living facility manager, a homeowner association manager, or a county resident; or from Social security death index licensees, if the Social Security number is verified by DMV records specifically. 
  • Require third party voter organizations to affirm to state officials that: individuals collecting voter registrations for the organization cannot knowingly solicit noncitizens to register; citizenship status and other eligibility questions must be incorporated into screening questions; and anyone who indicates that they are not a U.S. citizen will be provided with instructions on registering to vote after gaining citizenship. Existing law requires such organizations to register and meet other requirements, but has no provisions concerning citizenship status specifically. 
  • Add an express question regarding citizenship to the voter registration form that all voter registration agencies (except public libraries) must provide to individuals seeking services. 
  • Permits disclosure, as a public record, of a voter's method of registration and type of ID number provided. Existing law provides that the place of registration and ID number provided for registration are confidential, and does not expressly address the method or type for this data.
  • Expressly provide that notice to an election official from the DMV that a voter has received a license in another state will qualify as a written request from the voter for cancellation of their registration. 
  • Require the secretary of state to adopt minimum standards for nonpartisan voter registration that emphasize the importance of updating voter registration information and canceling a voter registration upon moving out of state. 
  • Require any website that instructs voters on how to update their registration to prominently display instructions on how to cancel their voter registration. Existing law has no comparable requirement.  
  • Require the uniform statewide voter registration application to include a space for applicants to provide the last four digits of their Social Security number, in addition to the existing requirement that the form elicit the applicant's driver's license number or state ID number. The voter registration form currently in use prompts applicants with no state ID number to provide the last four digits of their Social Security number, but this field is not required under existing statutory law. 
  • Make numerous conforming changes related to new requirements.

  • Require supervisors to investigate ballots found in mail ballot drop boxes (“secure ballot intake stations”) at the start of the day and notify voters to cure ballots placed outside of authorized hours or without a valid serial number, with referrals to the Office of Election Crimes and Security when necessary. The bill would require supervisors to process ballots placed during authorized hours.
  • Limit the use of mail ballot drop boxes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Establish mail ("absentee") vote processing watchers. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Allow each political party, candidate, political action committee, and political committee to designate one watcher per work area in locations where absentee ballots are processed, including areas for signature verification, ballot duplication, tabulation, and ballot intake station security. 
    • Create a telephone hotline for watchers to report violations of law, including security standards.
    • Expressly authorize candidates and law enforcement officers to be designated as watchers. 
  • Require the Department of State to develop an absentee ballot processing manual, and standards that would:
    • Establish chain of custody procedures for ballots, including monitoring transport, requiring daily validation by the county canvassing board, and implementing corrective actions for broken custody.
    • Prohibit commingling of ballots from different return sources until validated, require separate post office billing permits for ballot-related mail, and assign unique serial numbers to ballots and envelopes.
    • Implement reconciliation and reporting requirements, including daily posting of mail ballot counts, publication of chain of custody validation reports, and pre-certification reconciliation of transported and counted ballots with oversight by the Department of State.
  • Require the Department of State to develop rules for the physical security of election materials and technology, including: 
    • Electronic badge access at mail ballot counting locations
    • Video surveillance of all buildings and parking lots at mail ballot counting locations
    • Ballot transport by at least two people (each from different major parties).
    • Chain of custody of ballots
    • Storage of portable media in a secured area

This bill, as enacted on June 2, 2025, expands various administrative procedures related to citizenship status and expands the involvement of county sheriffs in investigating election crimes, among other changes. Specifically, the bill:

  • Makes minor changes to voter registration procedures and record keeping. The bill:
    • Creates a new type of voter registration status of "unconfirmed," for voters about whom the state registrar or county commissioner has received information from a reliable source indicating that the registered voter is not qualified. This status also expressly includes registration applicants who self-report as non-citizens on the form while still signing the affirmation of citizenship. To make an unconfirmed registration active, the voter must provide evidence that they are qualified to vote.
    • Expressly includes voter registration forms among the "voter registration records" that must be maintained on the statewide electronic voter registration system. 
  • Makes minor changes to polling place procedures. The bill:
    • Authorizes use of an electronic election register or election poll book in lieu of a paper register or poll book if the equipment has been approved by the state commissioner. Prior law was silent as to the use of these systems.
    • Revises the voter's declaration that must be signed before casting a ballot, to include express affirmation of U.S. citizenship. 
  • Makes minor changes to ballot processing. The bill:
    • Specifies that an election board must convene to begin counting mail ballots at no later than 9:00 a.m. on the day of the election. Prior law, which the bill leaves in place, specifies only that the board meet at a time so that the count may be completed by 10:00 p.m. on the day of the election.
    • Expressly provides that mail ballots with defects that are not cured by the deadline must be rejected.
    • Requires ballots, tally lists, and vote abstracts for all elections to be preserved for 22 months. Prior law required preservation of federal materials for this period, and non-federal materials for only six months.
  • Expands mandated and optional sources for voter list maintenance, and express grounds for removal from the list. The bill:
    • Requires the Dept. of Transportation to provide the state registrar with a list of any individual aged 17 or over who has submitted documentation indicating they are not a citizen, and makes conforming changes to require the registrar to use this information when issuing voter ID cards. 
    • Authorizes the state registrar to make administrative rules for the use of federal and state information for voter list maintenance. Prior law had no comparable requirement. 
    • Expressly permits the state registrar to contract with state and federal government agencies and private entities to provide a program for maintaining accurate voter registration rolls. Prior law permitted contracts with "a third party vendor," but did not expressly include these parties. 
    •  Requires cancellation of a voter's registration if they submit documentation of non-citizenship or report to a state or federal agency that they are not a citizen, and notice to the voter of their removal.
  • Increases reporting requirements and changes investigation procedures related to potential election crimes. The bill:
    • Requires local election officials to notify the county sheriff if mailed confirmation for same-day registration is not returned by the voter as required. Prior law required notice only to the state registrar and county attorney.
    • Shifts initial investigation of potential election crimes from the attorney general to county sheriffs or other law enforcement agency with jurisdiction. Under the bill, at the completion of the investigation, the sheriff or agency must submit their results to the attorney general and state commissioner, and the attorney general must explain whether they will pursue charges. Under prior law, the attorney general was required to complete the initial investigation and report a determination on charges to the state commissioner.  
  • Requires county commissioners of elections to notify the state commissioner when the county is subject to a cybersecurity assessment performed by a government agency or other entity.
  • Prohibits ranked choice voting.

The bill also includes additional provisions related to topics that Voting Rights Lab does not track, including affidavits of candidacy.

This bill, as enacted on June 24, 2025, makes minor changes to numerous aspects of election law, including voter list maintenance, reactivation and updates of voter registration, requesting and returning mail ballots, criminal penalties for false statements related to voting, and polling place procedures and equipment requirements, among others. 

  • Regarding voter list maintenance, the bill:
    • Eliminates express authorization for the secretary of state to enter into an agreement with the Electronic Registration Information Center (ERIC) to carry out voter list maintenance, and instead authorizes "written agreements with state and federal governmental agencies and private vendors that provide voter registration eligibility or address data." While membership in ERIC would likely be permitted by the new general authorization, the state is not currently a member, having withdrawn in 2022.
  • Regarding voter registration, the bill:
    • Eliminates the time limit on reactivation of voter registration for individuals who return to their prior jurisdiction after having left and registered in a new parish or out of state. Under prior law, these registrations were reinstated only if the voter returned to their prior jurisdiction within three years. The bill now permits reinstatement of registration upon return with no time limitation. 
    • Expands methods for updating registration due to a name change, and for married individuals: 
      • For general name changes, the bill expands accepted documentation to include a Louisiana driver's license or special ID card, or Social Security number. Prior law limited documentation to only a copy of the court judgment making the name change or a sworn statement.
      • For married individuals, the bill permits registration under either the voter's name or spouse's name or both, as well as a hyphenated form as allowed by existing law, and makes the provision gender-neutral. Prior law addressed "a married woman," and permitted registration under a maiden name, husband's name, or hyphenated name only. The bill also alters registration updates for marriage-related name changes, requiring submission of a new registration application that includes the voter's Social Security number, driver's license or special ID number, and an attestation. Under prior law, marriage-related updates required only a sworn statement to the clerk.  
  • Regarding mail ballot voting, the bill:
    • Expands grounds for removing a voter from the nursing home early voting program (which provides for on-site voting by mail ballot), to include return of an address confirmation notice as undeliverable. Under prior law, voters in the program were removed only by written request or if they no longer reside at the facility listed in their original application. 
    • Permits voters who receive notice that their mail ballot has a defect requiring cure to request a replacement ballot, and permits registrars to hand deliver the replacement to the voter or their immediate family member. Prior law provided for cure of a defective ballot in person only, with no express authorization for receiving a new replacement ballot. 
    • Expands the definition of "immediate family" for the purposes of election provisions, including authorized third party return of a mail ballot, to include a grandparent or grandchild. Prior law limited the definition to the voter's children and siblings, and their spouses; parents; spouse; and in-laws. 
  • Regarding election-related misconduct, the bill:
    • Expressly includes intentionally making a false statement in an attestation under the state's election laws within the existing criminal offense of perjury, punishable by up to $10,000 and five years in prison. The bill also newly defines "affidavit" as a statement signed before a notary or other specified witness, and "attestation" as a signed statement (with no witness requirement), and makes conforming changes throughout the code. Prior law used the terms interchangeably, often for statements signed without a witness.
    • Expands the officials authorized to enforce, or direct enforcement, of specified election-related provisions, to include clerks of court. 
  • Regarding the administration of polling places, the bill:
    • Expands authorization to the secretary of state for relocation of polling places due to an emergency, to include the express authority to consolidate polling places or establish multiple emergency polling places in the same precinct. Prior law authorized "relocation" only.
    • Authorizes consolidating polling places where a single location serves multiple precincts and specifies that such a polling place may serve all its assigned precincts.  Prior law authorized consolidation when "more than one polling place is within the same location," but did not expressly provide that the consolidated polling place serves every precinct. The bill keeps in place the existing authorization to reduce the required number of voting machines for each precinct in such a consolidated location. 
    • Increases the maximum number of voters for each required voting machine at polling locations. 
    • Requires alternate poll workers ("election commissioners") to meet the same qualification requirements as primary poll workers. Under prior law, qualifications for serving as an alternate were slightly different. The bill also eliminates the prior authority for an alternate commissioner who does not serve as a commissioner to have the same powers as a poll watcher.
    • Expands authorization for political parties to appoint Election Day poll watchers, to permit alternate "super watchers," in addition to designated super watchers permitted under existing law. 
    • Expressly authorizes the designation of poll watchers for party primary elections, in addition to primary and general elections as provided by prior law. 
    • Prohibits service as an early voting poll watcher for individuals required to register as a sex offender or child predator. Under prior law this prohibition applied to poll workers and Election Day watchers, but was not expressly applicable to early voting watchers. 
  • Eliminates the authority of political parties to allow unaffiliated voters to participate in the party's presidential primary elections, and makes conforming changes. The bill leaves in place an existing statutory provision that allows unaffiliated voters to vote in the party primary elections for primary offices of a single party, and newly specifies that such voters may not vote in both the first primary of one party and second primary of another. 

The bill also makes extensive additional changes in areas of law not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, including campaign finance, election dates, and ballot form.

  • Repeal the requirement that the registrar prepare a list of the names of voters not entered on the annual register that is available for public inspection and may be posted in the newspaper.

    • The voter requests so in writing
    • The registrars receive notice from the city or town clerk or a death record from the department of public health indicating that the voter has died
  • The registrars receive official written notice that the voter is:

  • The registrars determine that the voter is illegally or incorrectly registered after complaint, notice, and hearing as required under existing law
  • The registrars determine that the voter no longer resides in their city or town.

    • The individual resides at a licensed inn, lodging house, or public lodging house 
  • Repeal the requirement that the registrar send an annual notice on or before the first Monday of June to each voter of the preceding year whose name has not been entered in the annual register of the current year that notifying them that they may be removed from the voting list if they fail to respond to the notice and do not vote in the next two biennial state elections following the mailing of the notice.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 27, 2025, would:

  • Push back the registration deadline from the 10th day before an election to the seventh day. The bill would make nonsubstantive and conforming changes because of this change.
  • Create a permanent mail voting list. The bill would allow voters to sign up for the permanent mail voting list when registering to vote or through an online portal. Under existing law, voters can sign up to receive mail ballots for that calendar year only. Voters would be permitted to remove themselves from the list by filing a form with the secretary of state or by using the online portal. This bill would make nonsubstantive and conforming changes because of this change.
  • Require voters who have been registered through automatic voter registration to receive a form to join the permanent mail voting list with postage prepaid.
  • Require the state secretary to mail all registered voters a form that they could fill out to join the permanent mail voter list no later than June 30, 2026. 
  • Move back the deadline by which mail ballots must be received from 5 p.m. on the third day after Election Day to 5 p.m. on the seventh day after Election Day.
  • Eliminate the process of election officials comparing the signature on a voter's ballot with the signature on their application and would instead require that election officials "examine the completion" of the mail ballot affidavit. The election official would be required to reject the ballot if the ballot was not complete and to notify the voter, as is required under existing law. Under existing law, the election official must reject the ballot if the ballot is improperly executed or if the signatures do not match.
  • Eliminate the requirement that a voter sign an external envelope when submitting a ballot during in-person early voting and would eliminate the requirement that an official examine a voter's ballot envelope prior to submission.
  • Move state primaries from the seventh Tuesday preceding biennial state elections and the fourth Tuesday preceding special state elections to the second Tuesday in June in even-numbered years and the fourth Tuesday preceding special state elections, except that special primaries for senators or representatives in congress would be held on the sixth Tuesday preceding the election.
  • Require the secretary of state to maintain a public facing website for the confirmation of receipt and acceptance of early voting ballots.
  • Require each municipality to maintain at least one secured municipal drop box in a public location that is accessible to voters for no less than 12 hours each day, including business hours. Under existing law, there is no requirement as to how many drop boxes must be available or where they must be located. The bill would require municipalities with more than 25,000 registered voters to maintain at least one drop box for each 25,000 registered voters. A municipality with fewer than 5,000 voters in excess of any 25,000 registered voter increment would be permitted to apply to the state secretary for a waiver of the requirement to maintain additional drop boxes.
  • Require that, to the extent possible, drop box locations be selected by:
    • Proximity to public transportation and availability of parking
    • Equitable distribution across population centers
    • Access for voters with disabilities
    • Use of public buildings
  • Require that drop boxes be maintained from the earliest date that ballots become available through the hour fixed for the closing of polls. 
  • Require that for a biennial state election and any city or town election held on that day, the following municipalities conduct in-person early voting for the following amounts of time:
    • Municipalities with less than 1,000 registered voters must offer no less than eight total hours, including at least two weekend hours. Under existing law, municipalities with less than 5,000 registered voters must offer no less than four hours each weekend with at least one day per weekend, and for no less than two hours on a weekend day in which voting is conducted.
    • Municipalities with at least 1,000 registered voters but no more than 5,000 registered voters must offer no less than 16 total hours, including at least three weekend hours.
    • Municipalities with at least 5,000 registered voters but no more than 25,000 registered voters must offer no less than 24 total hours, including at least four weekend hours. Under existing law, municipalities of this size must offer at least six hours each weekend, with at least one day per weekend, for not less than three hours on a weekend day in which voting is conducted.
    • Municipalities with at least 25,000 registered voters but no more than 40,000 registered voters must offer no less than 40 total hours, including at least eight weekend hours. Under existing law, municipalities of this size must offer no less than four hours each weekend day.
    • Municipalities with at least 40,000 registered voters but no more than 75,000 registered voters must offer no less than 40 total hours, including at least eight weekend hours. Under existing law, municipalities of this size must offer no less than six hours each weekend day.
    • Municipalities with at least 75,000 registered voters must offer at least 48 total hours, including at least 10 weekend hours. Under existing law, municipalities of this size must offer no less than eight hours each weekend day.
  • Require that for any presidential or state primary and any city or town election held on that day, or any primary or election to fill a vacancy for senator or representative in congress and any city or town election held on the same day, in-person early voting be conducted no more than 10 days and no less four days preceding the election as follows:
    • Municipalities with less than 1,000 registered voters must offer no less than four total hours, including at least one weekend hour. 
    • Municipalities with at least 1,000 but no more than 5,000 registered voters offer no less than eight total hours, including at least two weekend hours.
    • Municipalities with at least 5,000 but no more than 25,000 registered voters offer no less than 12 hours, including at least three weekend hours.
    • Municipalities with at least 25,000 but no more than 40,000 registered voters offer no less than 16 total hours, including at least four weekend hours.
    • Municipalities with at least 40,000 or more registered voters offer no less than 20 total hours, including at least five weekend hours. Under existing law, in-person early voting hours do not vary by election type.
  • Require that an early voting ballot cast by a voter who was eligible to vote at the time the ballot was cast must be counted even if that voter moved to a different residence within the commonwealth after.
  • Repeal the requirement that the state secretary deliver early voting ballots to each city and town no later than 30 days before an election and instead require that the secretary prepare early voting materials by that time.
  • Allow, rather than require, town officials to detail police officers to each building that contains a polling place for at least one precinct. Under existing law, this is mandatory.
  • Specify that voted early ballots may be tabulated upon receipt and that city and town clerks would be permitted to remove early voting mail ballots from their envelopes and deposit them into tabulators on any day leading up to the close of the voter registration period.
  • Require the state secretary to conduct comprehensive, culturally competent, and linguistically diverse voter education outreach both digitally, and in paper copy no later than May 1 of every even numbered year.
  • Require the state secretary to approve and implement upgrades to the central registry and voter registration system and to authorize the use of electronic poll books no later than December 31, 2025.
  • Require the creation of a special commission to examine the automatic voter registration processes of the commonwealth, including the processes implemented via the registry of motor vehicles. The commission would be required to issue a report on its findings about automatic voter registration process improvements no later than April 15, 2026.
  • Require the state secretary to create, implement and maintain a centralized digital system into which each city and town clerk must input preliminary results for each presidential or state primary or election. The results would be publicly available on the secretary's website.
  • Make changes to the information contained in the central registry of voters. The bill would require the registry to contain a voter's political party enrollment or designation and any former names and would repeal the requirement that the registry include the voter's occupation, nationality, or veteran status. The bill would also allow the registry to contain the following information about residents age 16 and over:
    • Full name
    • Former name, if any
    • Residential address on January 1 in the current year
    • Residential address on January 1 of the preceding year
    • Date of birth
    • Occupation
    • Veteran status
    • Nationality, if not a citizen of the United States
  • Make the information contained in the central registry available to certain state party committees and political groups at a fair and reasonable cost. The state secretary must also provide this information to election officials at each polling place in digital format. The names and addresses contained in the registry would not be a matter of public record.
  • Require the state secretary to maintain an agreement with the Electronic Registration Information Center, Inc. (ERIC). Massachusetts is already a member of ERIC. 
  • Require the state secretary, rather than the "appropriate local election official" to send mail ballots to voters as soon as they are ready.

The bill also contains additional provisions related to topics that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

Voters with religious objections to being photographed could submit an affidavit when voting that would allow their vote to be counted. Under existing law, an election official may challenge a voter for a variety of reasons but the requirement is permissive, not mandatory. The bill would make nonsubstantive and conforming changes because of this requirement.
    • Allow a voter or an election official to challenge another voter upon personal knowledge or a reasonably supported belief:
      • That the voter submitted a mail ballot with a signature that does not correspond with the voter's registration signature.

This bill, as enacted on June 20, 2025, makes minor changes to timing for standard voter registration, specifies voter registration agencies within state government, and expands access to the voter file, among other changes.  


Concerning voter registration, the bill:

  • Moves the deadline slightly earlier for online voter registration, from midnight on the 21st day before an election to 5 p.m. on that day.
  • Makes minor changes to requirements for transfer of registration information from the secretary of state to local registrars, for applications received from outside agencies:
    • For applications received by the secretary more than 10 days before the "closed period" (beginning 20 days before an election), transfer must be made within ten days of receipt. Prior law required transfer during this period within seven business days.
    • For applications received by the secretary within the closed period (20 days before an election), transfer must be made within 10 business days after the election. Prior law had no express transfer deadline for applications received in this period. 
  • Specifies that if the deadline for changes or withdrawals of party affiliation before a primary election falls on a holiday, changes submitted on the next business day will be processed as received by the deadline. Prior law had no comparable provision.  
  • Specifies and narrows the state offices that must serve as voter registration agencies: 
    • For agencies providing public assistance, prior law required all such entities to serve as voter registration agencies, expressly including offices that administer programs under TANF, WIC, Medicaid, and SNAP. The bill eliminates the requirement that "all state agencies that provide public assistance" serve as registration agencies, and instead specifies offices that administer these additional specific programs:
      • Children's Health Insurance Program
      • Transitional child care services under a program of transitional services 
      • Higher Opportunity for Pathways for Employment program
      • Bridging Rental Assistance program
      • Developmental services advocacy programs administered by a statewide organization for disability rights
      • Mental health advocacy programs
      • Children's advocacy centers
    • For the Department of Labor, Bureau of Rehabilitation Services, prior law required this agency as a whole to serve as a voter registration agency. The bill now specifies this designation for offices within the department that administer:
      • Vocational rehabilitation services
      • Independent living services
      • Deaf, hard of hearing and late deafened ID cards and vehicle placards
      • Deaf, hard of hearing and late deafened telecommunications equipment services
    • For state agencies that provide state funded programs primarily engaged in providing services to individuals with disabilities, the bill repeals the requirement that such agencies serve as voter registration agencies. 
  • Expands grounds for individuals to purchase the voter file. Prior law permitted access to the file by individuals or groups "evaluating the state's compliance with its voter list maintenance obligations." The bill repeals this provision and instead provides:
    • A "person" may purchase a voter file from the secretary of state to "evaluate, monitor, or seek compliance with laws relating to voting rights, election administration and voter registration."
    • The file provided under the provision may contain the same data available to political parties and organizations authorized to access the list for get-out-the-vote activities, and information for cancelled registrations. 
    • Specified "highly sensitive personal information" may not be included in voter data provided under the provision.
  • Expands specified grounds for civil penalties related to unauthorized use of voter list data. Under prior law, civil penalties applied for sale, transfer, or use of voter data outside the specified authorized uses by certain parties, and for use of data to carry out discrimination. The bill clarifies and expands these grounds to include use for:
    • Commercial purposes
    • Unauthorized solicitation
    • Sale or resale
    • Discrimination
    • Any purpose other than specifically permitted uses for data purchased by (1) political parties and organizations for get-out-the-vote campaigns, and (2) individuals for review of compliance with election laws

Concerning polling place procedures and election information, the bill:

  • Authorizes the secretary of state to prepare "other neutral instructional materials and posters" they deem necessary to assist voters at the polling place, in addition to the materials required under existing law.
  • Repeals the requirement that the secretary of state produce and publicly disseminate a guide to election laws, rules, and procedures and conduct a training program for new municipal clerks every two years. The bill leaves in place existing provisions that generally require the secretary to develop guidance materials, on no specifically mandated schedule, for election officials, voters, and mail ballot voting. 
  • Moves the deadline earlier for posting notice of an election, from seven days before Election Day to 21 days before. The bill also repeals the requirement that the notice be posted in every election district within a municipality. 

Concerning mail ballot voting, the bill:

  • Moves the start date later for providing mail ballot applications for a primary election. Under prior law, clerks were prohibited from providing mail ballot applications more than three months before any election. Under the bill, for primary elections only applications may not be provided more than two before. 
  • Expands the types of institutions where on-site mail ballot voting must be made available to residents, to include mental health residential facilities, residential facilities for individuals with intellectual disabilities, and state mental health institutes to vote by mail. Prior law limited this voting procedure to certain nursing homes, residential care facilities, and assisted living facilities.
  • Expressly authorizes officials to "reasonably limit" the inspection of mail ballot applications and envelopes by the public during ballot processing, and give priority to authorized representatives of candidates and political parties. Prior law had no comparable provision. 

The bill also contains additional provisions related to topics that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

Existing law prohibits removal from the list solely for non-voting, and has no confirmation requirement to remain on the list related to non-voting. Under the new removal process:

  • The secretary of state would be required to send notice 180 days after each general November general election to all voters who have not voted in the past eight years or more, requesting confirmation of address and a signature to remain registered.
  • Voters wishing to remain registered would be required to respond to the notice, vote, or engage in "voting-related activity," including requesting a mail ballot or updating their registration, by the first business day after the second general November election following the notice.

  • On receipt of a completed confirmation, clerks would be required to verify the voter's identity by signature matching the form with the voter's signature on file. If the signatures do not match, the clerk must notify the voter that the registration is considered challenged, and provide instructions for verifying their identity. 
  • If a confirmation notice is returned as undeliverable, the secretary must designate the voter's registration as challenged. As with failure to respond for any other reason, registration for these voters would be cancelled if they fail to engage in voting-related activity by the first business day after the second general November election that follows.

VRLANALYSIS:
This resolution, as amended on April 30, 2025, would propose an amendment to the state constitution requiring verification of U.S. citizenship for all registration applicants and currently registered voters, among other changes. Under existing law, registration applicants must sign a statement certifying the truth of their eligibility, including their citizenship status, but further verification is not required. Specifically, the resolution would:

  • Require each new applicant for voter registration, beginning in December 2026, to prove U.S. citizenship by one of two methods:
    • Presentation of documentary proof of United States citizenship at the time of registration or afterwards to the secretary of state or clerk
    • Verification of citizenship by the secretary of state
  • Require the secretary of state to carry out an annual "systematic" process using "all reasonable efforts" to verify whether each registered voter in the current voter file is a citizen. If the secretary's research indicates that a person is not a citizen, they must issue notice to the voter within seven days of the discovery; if the voter fails to respond or provide evidence of citizenship within 60 days, the secretary would be required to cancel their registration. 
  • Authorize the secretary of state to conduct an "individualized review" of a single voter at any time, employing the same efforts to determine whether an individual registered voter is a citizen.
  • Require the statewide voter registration file be updated to reflect whether a voter has presented proof of citizenship.
  • Require the secretary of state to verify a person's citizenship status before automatically registering the person as a voter as a result of conducting business with the secretary. The secretary would not be permitted to automatically register the person if the secretary determines the person is not a citizen.
  • Require voting by provisional ballot only for any registered voter whose citizenship has not been verified prior to voting, and require such voters to provide proof of citizenship by the sixth day after an election for the ballot to be counted.
  • Require the secretary to report annually to the legislature on the removal of registered voters pursuant to the list maintenance program adopted under the resolution.
  • Require voting by provisional ballot for any voter appearing in person who does not have voter ID, and require such voters to provide an accepted form of ID by the sixth day after an election for the ballot to be counted. Under existing law, a voter unable to present photo identification may execute an affidavit to verify their identity and still vote a regular ballot. 
  • Require applicants for a mail ballot to provide their driver's license number, state ID card number, or the last four digits of their Social Security number, in addition to their signature, if applying by any method other than in person, and require verification of both the ID number and signature matching. Under existing law, such mail ballot applications require a signature and signature matching only. 
  • Instruct the legislature to provide a process for individuals to claim financial hardship and obtain a voter ID card at no cost.

Final adoption of the proposed amendment requires passage by two-thirds of the legislature and approval by voters at the next general or special election.

Under existing law, the voter needed to only show the witness proof of residence. This provision would also require the witness to provide their own driver's license number, state ID number, voter ID number, the last four digits of their social security number, or a statement that they do not have any of these numbers. VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 26, 2025, would make various changes to voter registration requirements, including eliminating the requirement that voters provide proof of residency when registering to vote through same-day registration or when submitting a mail ballot. Under existing law, these methods of registration require either documentation or personal vouching of a voter's current residence. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Change same-day voter registration processes by:
    • Eliminating the requirements that a same-day voter registration applicant must make an oath and provide proof of residency or have their residence personally vouched for, and instead require only the standard registration form (which an applicant must certify under penalty of perjury). The bill would also require same-day registrants to vote a newly created "provisional ballot," and set out procedures for casting, verifying, rejecting, and counting these ballots. The provisional ballots of same-day registrants would be counted if the registration application was accepted, and voters whose ballots were rejected would receive notice following the election. Existing law permits voters who meet the requirements for same-day registration to vote a regular ballot, and does not provide for the use of provisional ballots generally.
    • Requiring that any same-day registration applications be entered into the voter registration system within three days after Election Day. Under existing law, they must be entered within 42 days after Election Day.
  • Change requirements for registering to vote by mail by:
    • Eliminating the requirement that applicants who register to vote by mail must include their driver's license number, state ID number, or the last four digits of their social security number.
    • Changing the process for correcting incomplete registration applications submitted by mail. Under existing law, if a mail registration applicant (1) has not provided a form of documentation required for same day registration, (2) has not voted previously in the state in a federal election, and (3) officials are unable to verify their driver's license, state ID, or Social Security number, the applicant must either register in person or meet the requirements for same day registration (including documentation or personal vouching of residency). The bill would simplify the process by requiring, where a mail applicant's eligibility to vote cannot be verified, that the individual submit a general registration application in person, on Election Day, or with a completed mail ballot.
  • Change processes for voters who simultaneously return a mail ballot and apply to vote by:
    • Eliminating the requirement that voters who are simultaneously registering to vote and returning an absentee ballot present proof of residence to the witness for the absentee ballot.
    • Requiring election officials to open ballot envelopes to determine if there is a voter registration application in the envelope. If so, then the application must be removed and the envelope resealed. The auditor would then promptly process the application. Under existing law, the voter registration application is processed by the absentee ballot board during absentee ballot processing.
  • Expressly limit the optional "alternative procedure" for in-person early voting at the county auditor's office in the seven days before an election to only those voters who are already registered to vote. As a result, voters would not be permitted to do same-day registration for this form of voting. Existing law is silent as to whether this procedure may be offered to unregistered voters.
  • Change requirements for challengers by allowing challengers to prove their residency by presenting a student ID or a student fee statement in addition to the other forms of ID already named in statute.
  • Repeal the provision concerning postsecondary institutions submitting enrollment lists to election officials to facilitate proof of residency requirements for students, and the provision requiring election officials to record the number of same-day registration applications that are rejected due to lack of residency proof.
  • Require the secretary of state to conduct a public awareness campaign to encourage people to register to vote before Election Day.
  • The bill also contains provisions that are not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, including changes to the time for canvassing primary and general elections.


Last Updated February 27, 2025
