VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced February 26, 2025, would create new photo ID requirements for in-person voting, same-day registration, provisional ballots, and mail ballot voting, among other changes. Existing law does not require voters to show ID to vote in person, and has less onerous documentation requirements for other voting-related activities than those set out in the bill. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Define accepted forms of "documentary proof of identity and residence" for use as voter ID. Accepted forms of ID would be limited to:
    • an unexpired state driver's license, state ID, or voter ID card, with photo and current residence
    • valid US military ID, with photo and current residence
    • unexpired tribal ID, with photo and current residence
    • receipt for a driver's license, state ID, or voter ID card, with photo and current residence (if receipt lacks photo, this must be accompanied by (1) a license, state ID, or voter ID that is expired or shows prior address, (2) a US passport, (3) a photo ID issued by the state or federal government, (4) a student ID issued by a postsecondary institution that has provided an enrollment list to election authorities, or (5) a tribal ID)
    • a US passport, tribal ID, or US military card that has a photo but does not have the voter's current address, plus one of the following with their address: (1) utility bill or work services order, (2) bank statement, (3) high school transcript, (4) college or university transcript issued by institution in the state, (5) unemployment stub, (6) statement from long-term health care facility, (7) insurance policy, (8) federal or state tax return, (9) property tax statement, (10) vehicle title, (11) property deed or title, (12) SSI statement, (13) mortgage document, (14) lease agreement, (15) unexpired professional license, (16) unexpired Selective Service card, (17) current military orders, (18) cell phone bill, or (19) game or fishing license.
    • for students, a state license, state ID, or voter ID card issued by any state that includes a photograph, and a current fee statement showing state residence
    • for residential facility residents, a license or state ID card, and a certification of residence through the state's official form
  • Require an accepted form of photo ID to vote in person. Under existing law, in-person voters must affirm their identity and residence under penalty of perjury, but are not required to provide documentation.
  • Require in-person voters who lack an accepted form of photo ID to cast a provisional ballot, and set out procedures related to provisional ballot voting and verification. A provisional ballot would only be counted if the voter presents required photo ID within seven days after Election Day, unless they have attempted to procure the documents and were unable to, and attest to that fact. This bill, as introduced on January 8, 2025, would make wide-ranging changes to election administration in the state. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Repeal the existing complaint process for individuals alleging violation of election law, and in its place create the Office of Election Crimes and Security within the office of the Secretary of State. The director of the office would be employed by the Secretary. The bill would grant the office authority to:
    • Review complaints and investigate alleged violations of election law or rules adopted in accordance with election law
    • Initiate independent inquiries into alleged violations of election law
    • Oversee a voter fraud hotline
    • Issue subpoenas as necessary
    • Turn over its findings to the attorney general and to the appropriate local prosecuting attorney if the office determines after an investigation that a violation may have occurred
    • Enter any polling place or office of any election authority as necessary to investigate an allegation
  • Require the office to annually report to the governor and the legislature the details of complaints received and investigations initiated.
  • Require the office to submit potential violations of election law to the attorney general and the prosecuting or circuit attorney with jurisdiction. The bill would grant the attorney general investigative authority and concurrent jurisdiction over any election offense.
  • Require any state agency or agent that receives communication regarding election laws from the Department of Justice or other federal agency to notify the governor and General Assembly within five business days.
  • Require any entity involved in state election administration that intends to implement any federal election guidance on state elections to notify the General Assembly at least 30 days before implementation. All implementation of federal guidance would require approval by the Assembly, which could consist of abstaining from a legislative vote within 30 days of the notification. The Act would impose a fine of $5,000 for violations of these provisions, to be accrued every 30 days until the implementation was withdrawn. 
  • Require any official election administrator who intends to accept or disburse federal election funds to notify the General Assembly of this intent at least 30 days before accepting the funds, or, if the funds have already been accepted, 30 days before the funds are disbursed. Acceptance of funds would be subject to legislative approval, which could consist of abstaining from a vote within 30 days of notification. The Act would impose a fine of the amount of the federal funds plus $1,000 for violation of the provisions.
  • Require an election authority to include any voter who fails to participate in any "voter activity" for two calendar years in a biennial address confirmation process if using a method other than the voter ID card method of registered voters. "Voter activity" would include registering to vote, voting in an election, signing a petition to form a new political party, signing a petition for the nomination of an independent candidate for office, or signing an initiative petition. Under existing law, a voter is included in an address confirmation process if they did not vote or transfer their registration in the preceding four years.
  • Create a duty for election authorities to cancel registration due to a change of address based on the voter's written request or failure to respond to a cancellation notice or engage in "voter activity" in the following two general elections. Existing law does not impart a duty on election authorities to cancel registrations on the occurrence of those conditions. Instead, it prohibits the cancellation of a voter's registration due to a change of address unless the voter requests or the voter fails to respond to the cancellation notice or did not vote for two general election cycles after the notice..
  • Make any "voter activity" within the time period between the issuance of a notice of registration cancellation and the following two general elections sufficient to avoid cancellation of registration. Under existing law, a person must vote to avoid cancellation.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on January 6, 2025, would create online voter registration. Under existing law, an applicant can submit a voter registration application in person or via mail. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the secretary of state to create and maintain an online voter registration system for applicants that would be available until 11:59 p.m. on the 30th day before an election. The system would resume accepting applications on the day following an election.
  • Require voters using the online registration system to: 
    • Consent to the use of the signature on their Montana driver's license or ID card for voter registration purposes
    • Provide the number and date of issuance of their driver's license or state ID card and all other information required by law for voter registration purposes.
  • Require the secretary of state to compare information provided by the applicant using the online system with the information in the applicant's motor vehicle records.
  • Require the secretary of state to reject the application if the information provided by the applicant does not match the motor vehicle records and to provide written notice to the applicant if their application is rejected.
  • Require the secretary of state to add the voter's information to the statewide voter registration system and to send it to the county election administrator for the county in which the applicant resides.

This bill, as introduced on April 1, 2025, would make a variety of minor changes to a wide variety of election laws, including extending the cure deadline, and permitting more time to count mail ballots. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Extend the cure deadline for mail ballots from the third business day after the election to the fourth (the Monday following the election in most cases).
  • Permit all mail ballots to be counted as early as 9 a.m. on election day. Under existing law, mail ballots are counted at 5 p.m. on election day, but UOCAVA ballots may be counted as early as 9 a.m. upon adoption of a resolution. Under the bill, all mail ballots could be counted during that earlier timeframe upon adoption of a resolution. The bill would also remove a requirement that counting continue unabated except for unavoidable necessity by replacing it with a provision under which the county board may not adjourn the meeting until counting is completed.
  • Remove the word "card" from the provisions of law describing acceptable voter ID for the purposes of ensuring that digital versions of ID are considered acceptable.
  • Clarify that a voter may not have their ballot challenged if the voter was qualified to cast the ballot at the time it was received by the county board.
  • Standardize the time for delivery of mail ballots. Under existing law, mail ballots must be delivered to the board no later than 50 days before the election and may be sent to voters immediately thereafter, but in statewide general elections in even-numbered years, this delivery may happen up to 60 days before the election. The bill would standardize this to 50 days for all elections other than second primary elections (which would now have a deadline of 45 days before the election instead of "as quickly as possible" as provided under current law). UOCAVA voters would have their ballots mailed 50 days before each election unless 45 days is specifically authorized by the state board.
  • Change the timing for the counting of early voting ballots. Under existing law, the count of electronic early voting ballots begins when polls close, and paper early voting ballots are counted starting at the same time as mail ballots. Under the bill, all counting of early voting ballots would begin at 5 p.m. on Election Day, and may begin as early as 9:00 a.m. upon adoption of a resolution. The bill would also provide for provisional early voting ballots to be reviewed during the same time period as review of mail ballots, and would require a final decision to be made on provisional ballots by the time of the county canvass.
  • Permit a person deployed by their employer away from the voter's residence to respond to a disaster to the definition of "covered voter."
  • Codify the existing practice of letting persons who are at least 16 years of age but not yet 18 years of age to preregister to vote.
  • Require party leaders to recommend four potential chief judge or judge candidates for each precinct, instead of two as required under current law. The bill would also require only a bipartisan majority vote (instead of unanimous consent as under existing law) of the county board to find additional registered voters to serve as election judges if the parties do not provide sufficient recommendations. Finally, the bill would also repeal a provision of law that limits precincts with fewer than 500 voters to a maximum of two assistants to the election judges.
  • Specify that the list of voters who have requested mail ballots is confidential information. The bill would accordingly clarify that the list of mail ballots applied for, which a county board of elections is required to maintain under current law, should only consist of those applications that were approved.
  • Expand a misdemeanor for prohibited petition activities by adding compensating a person for the number of signatures collected to the list of prohibited actions.
  • Specify that the law which provides for a person to vote in their precinct after residing there for 30 days also applies to a ward or other election district.
  • Provide for an audit of mail ballots and early voting ballots by the state board after each election.
  • Specify that a challenge of a ballot in a municipal primary or election must be made no later than the second business day after the election, instead of the fifth as provided under current law.
  • Require a county board to post notice of its meetings on its website, instead of in a newspaper as required under existing law.

The bill also would make extensive changes in areas of law not tracked by Voting Rights Lab.

      • claims for unemployment benefits

    • Create a presumption that a person wrongfully registered through the automatic voter registration process was registered through no fault of their own.
  • Mandate online voter registration. Online voter registration is currently offered in North Carolina, but it is not required by statute. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Mandate that the state board of elections provide an online application for voter registration, with online assistance available. The site would also be required to accept updates to voter registration.

    • upon release from active punishment to a period of post-release supervision or parole of a person whose sentence was not suspended by the court, or
    • upon the suspension of an active sentence resulting in the imposition of an intermediate or community punishment
  • Fully repeal Senate Bill 747, which passed in 2023. That bill made extensive changes restricting mail voting, expanding access for poll watchers, and prohibiting private funding of elections. Repealing the bill would, among other changes:
    • Extend the deadline for the receipt of mail ballots to the third day after the election, instead of the day of the election.
    • Permit the establishment of drop boxes for mail ballots.
    • Repeal provisions that provided for the cure of mail ballots that did not contain required documentation.
    • Repeal provisions that prohibited private funding of election administration.
    • Repeal provisions expanding the authority of poll watchers.
    • Decriminalize the following misdemeanor offenses:
      • impersonating an election official in the course of duties in registering voters or administering an election
      • affixing or printing an identifier to a mail ballot request form, unless the individual is a state or county board of elections employee
    • Repeal provisions simplifying the process of removing registered voters for non-citizenship.

This bill, as enacted on August 11, 2026, makes numerous changes to North Carolina election law affecting provisional ballots, absentee ballots, ballot counting procedures, early voting, voter identification, and judicial review of State Board of Elections decisions. The bill also establishes new procedures for curing certain deficiencies and changes several deadlines governing when election-related information must be submitted or announced. Specifically the bill:

  • Requires county boards of elections to allow voters who fail to complete a required item on a voter registration form, but provide enough information to be identified and contacted, to correct the omission by 12 p.m. on the fifth business day after the election. 
  • Requires county boards of elections to establish a process for voters to cure a missing signature accompanying a provisional ballot on the affidavit to certify the voter’s identity and eligibility to vote. The county board would be required to notify the voter no later than the close of business on the next business day after reviewing the ballot and provide an opportunity to cure the missing signature. The voter would have until 12 p.m. on the fifth business day after the election to cure the missing signature, after which the county board would count any portion of the provisional ballot for which the voter is otherwise eligible.
  • Allows a voter whose driver’s license number or last four digits of their Social Security number provided on the voter registration form cannot be validated to provide required identification to the county board no later than by 12 p.m. on the fifth business day after the election.
  • Allows voters to bring an acceptable form of identification to the board no later than 12 p.m. on the fifth day after the election when the voter cannot produce acceptable identification when they present to vote in person.
  • Requires county boards to adopt a resolution at least two weeks before Election Day establishing the time and place for the initial counting of official ballots, which must occur between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. on Election Day. Results could not be disclosed before the polls close. The count must be conducted in the presence of, or under the supervision of, county board members of all political parties present. Members of the public would be permitted to observe the count but could not participate or interfere with the process. County boards could also review provisional ballots for approval and take preparatory steps for counting those ballots before Election Day.
  • Requires any resolution adopted to be published once a week for two weeks before the election in a newspaper of general circulation in the county. 
  • Requires county boards to adopt a resolution at least two weeks before voting begins establishing the time for counting absentee ballots, with the count occurring between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. on Election Day. The county board must count all absentee ballots except those challenged before 9:00 a.m. on Election Day and those received after Election Day under the applicable absentee ballot provisions. The county board will also be required to announce the tally of all absentee ballots, except those that are challenged or cast by mail, no later than the fifth business day after the election.
  • Requires county boards of elections to decide whether to count a provisional ballot if they have reason to believe the voter’s affidavit is false. The board must identify and resolve the issue within five business days after the election and before the county canvass.
  • Requires cure documentation for a curable deficiency on an absentee ballot container-return envelope to be received by the county board no later than 12 p.m. on the fifth business day after the election for the ballot to be considered timely. The bill also requires voters to be notified of curable deficiencies no later than the close of business on the next business day following the county board’s review of the ballot.
  • Allows visually impaired voters who requested an accessible absentee ballot to return their completed ballot through an additional secure method.
  • Expands the requirements for in-person return of executed absentee ballots by allowing the voter, the voter’s near relative, or verifiable legal guardian to deliver a ballot to the county board office or an early voting site while it is open for voting. A person other than the voter would be required to complete an affidavit verifying their eligibility to return the ballot.
  • Prohibits any person from knowingly revealing the result of any ballot count before the close of polls on Election Day.
  • Requires county boards, at the conclusion of early voting, to secure voting equipment, paper ballots, and electronic vote records until the initial count of early voting ballots. 
  • Requires a challenged ballot to be excluded from the count when a challenge based on the voter’s death is sustained and the voter died between the time the ballot was cast and 11:59 p.m. on the day before the election.
  • Allows a person seeking judicial review of a State Board of Elections decision to file a petition in either the Superior Court of Wake County or the Superior Court of the county where the person resides, rather than requiring the petition to be filed in Wake County.
  • Allows a qualifying license that has passed its printed expiration date but remains valid under the temporary extension to be used as voter ID. The extension applies to qualifying licenses through December 31, 2027.

A previous version of this bill also contained additional provisions that were amended out, including provisions that would have:

  • Established the Wildlife Resources Commission as a voter registration agency.

  • Require county boards to mail address confirmation notices for voter registration applications received within 100 days of an election within two business days of processing the application and to mail a second notice within one business day if the first is returned as undeliverable. Existing law requires these notices but does not specify mailing deadlines. 
  • Require county boards to process voter registration applications only if the applicant affirmatively indicates they are a United States citizen. Applicants who leave the citizenship question blank must be notified and given 30 days to submit a signed statement under penalty of perjury regarding citizenship before the application is denied.
  • Move the deadline for voters to provide identification when voter registration identification numbers cannot be verified, from 12 p.m. on the third business day after the election to the fifth business day after. 
  • Change the timing for the counting of Election Day and early voting ballots. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Require ballots cast during in-person early voting to be counted between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. on Election Day. Existing law requires such ballots to be counted after the polls close if counted electronically, and at the same time as mail ballots if they are paper ballots counted manually. 
    • Move the deadline later for counting of provisional ballots, from the third business day after the election to the fifth business day after. The bill would also permit preparatory steps for the review of provisional early voting ballots to take place before Election Day, if these steps do not reveal the result of the count before close of polls, and require that officials make a final determination for counting provisional ballots with potentially false affidavits by the date of the county canvass.
  • Slightly increase the cure period for mail ballots, and make other changes to mail ballot processing. The bill would:
    • Move the deadline later for cure of a mail ballot defect, to noon on the fifth business day after the election. Under existing law, the cure deadline is noon on the third business day after the election.
    • Eliminate the existing requirement that the counting of mail ballots be continuous except for "unavoidable necessity," and require instead that the county board not adjourn its meeting until counting is completed.
    • Move the start of mail ballot counting slightly earlier, to 9 a.m. on Election Day. Under existing law, the board convenes at 5 p.m., and by adoption of a resolution before the election may begin the count at 2 p.m. 
    • Expressly provide that a mail ballot can only be counted if transmitted to a county board in accordance with existing law.
    • Move the deadline later for announcing the mail ballot tally, from the third business day after the election to the fifth day after. 
    • Require the State Board of Elections to study and report on the feasibility, costs, and technical considerations of implementing signature verification technology. The study would evaluate other states' use of signature verification software, implementation costs and logistics for North Carolina, and potential challenges related to voter signature retention and accuracy.
  • Modify procedures related to ballot challenges. The bill would:
    • Expressly extend applicability of existing challenge procedures for mail ballots to early voting ballots. Existing law provides for challenges to early voting ballots, but statutory provisions for challenge procedures do not expressly apply to these ballots. The bill would also specify certain record keeping requirements for challenged mail ballots.
    • Revise ballot challenge deadlines by requiring challenges to early voting ballots to be filed by the close of polls on Election Day. Challenges to absentee ballots received by Election Day must be filed by 5:00 p.m. on the fifth business day after the election, while challenges to late-arriving military and overseas absentee ballots must be filed by 5:00 p.m. on the next business day after the receipt deadline.
    • Specify that for ballots challenged due to the death of a voter, the challenge must be sustained if the voter died between casting the ballot and 11:59 p.m. before election day. Existing law has no comparable express provision. 
  • Specify procedures related to the assignment, training, removal, and compensation of election administrators. The bill would:
    • Require each county to appoint a minimum of four emergency election day assistants for each county. Existing law authorizes the State Board to determine the number of such assistants as needed, by certain criteria, but has no minimum. 
    • Specify the content of State Board training for county board election officials. Existing law sets out requirements for frequency of training, but does not include express requirements for its content. 
    • Permit the removal of a precinct official by the county board for incompetency or failure to discharge the duties of office. The bill would also permit an official removed in this matter from being prohibited from serving in any subsequent election. Existing law authorizes the State Board to remove county board members on these grounds, but does not expressly address removal of precinct officials by county officials. 
    • Increase the compensation of county board members from $25 to $100 per meeting.  
  • Authorize the State Board to employ staff counsel or retain private legal counsel to assist in election litigation. Existing law authorizes legal counsel by the attorney general, and permits private counsel only on recommendation of the attorney general and approval from the General Assembly. The bill would also specify the particular circumstances under which the Board may retain private legal counsel.
  • Create and expand criminal offenses related to election activity. The bill would:
    • Create a felony offense for revealing the result of any count of ballots before the close of polls on Election Day.
    • Expand the criminal offense of disorderly conduct at a public building, to include prohibited activity at a location temporarily used for voting during voting hours.
    • Create a misdemeanor offense for a person to steal, deface, vandalize, or unlawfully remove political advertising from the protected area around a polling location.
  • Specify that disclosure of voter registration data received from another state pursuant to a data-sharing agreement is governed by the terms of the agreement, provided the agreement is no more restrictive than the originating state's public records laws.

The bill would also make changes in areas of law not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, including campaign finance and party designations on ballots.

This bill, as introduced on March 25, 2025, would:

  • Establish new crimes and civil penalties meant to protect voters. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Create a Class H felony for threatening or attempting to threaten a person for voting or attempting to vote, voting or attempting to vote for or against a particular candidate, registering to vote, urging or aiding any individuals to vote or attempt to vote as allowed by law, or exercising any lawful powers or duties as an election official or enlisting another person to do the same.
    • Create a Class H felony for knowingly challenging another's right to vote on fraudulent or spurious grounds, engaging in "mass, indiscriminate, and groundless" challenging of voters for the purposes of preventing or delaying their voting or interfering with the orderly administration of an election, or fraudulently advising any person that they are not eligible or registered.
    • Create a Class A1 misdemeanor for intimidating or coercing, or attempting to intimidate or coerce, any person for voting or attempting to vote, voting or attempting to vote for or against a particular candidate, registering to vote, urging or aiding any individuals to vote or attempt to vote as allowed by law, or exercising any lawful powers or duties as an election official or enlisting another person to do the same.
    • Create a Class H felony for various actions employers could take in order to influence the votes of their employees.
    • Establish a private cause of action allowing any victim of the established crimes to seek preventative relief and attorney's fees.
    • Establish a restitution fund which individuals convicted of violations of the above prohibitions could be ordered by a court to pay funds into. The fund would then be used for voter education campaigns.
    • Define "coerce," "intimidate," and "threaten" as used in this section, and establish that a person will be deemed to have committed such acts if they should have known or reasonably should have known that their actions would produce such an effect.
  • Create a felony for intimidating, threatening, or coercing an election worker with intent to interfere with their official duties, punishable by a fine of up to $100,000, imprisonment for up to five years, or both. Violators of this prohibition would also be civilly liable for any injury or loss to the election worker as a result of their intimidation, threats, or coercion. An election worker acting in good faith to prevent election interference or preserve ballot access could not be liable under this section.
  • Establish a class 1 misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of up to $10,000, for an election official who performs or communicates the intention to perform an official act in which that official would refuse to certify results of an election without substantial evidence.
  • Establish standards for post-election audits, including:
    • Being conducted by nonpartisan officials with expertise in elections
    • Being routine and conducted prior to state certification
    • Being transparent and open to the public
    • Preserving integrity of systems and equipment
    • Preserving ballot secrecy and voter privacy
    • Conducted according to statistically sound methodologies
    • Requiring that procedures governing audits be known prior to Election Day
    • Public officials would be prohibited from funding or participating in audits taht do not meet the established standards
  • Direct the state board of elections to conduct a "hand-to-eye" risk-limiting audit of a randomly selected sample of ballots to confirm the machine count. The results of the risk-limiting audit could not change the certified results.
  • Require election observers to complete training established by the state board of elections at least every two years, complete an oath, and wear clear identification. Under existing law, no training is required, an oath is prohibited, and no identification is required.
  • Establish a process by which election workers can apply to the board of elections requesting that their personally identifiable information be withheld from public records.
  • Grant the judiciary the authority to review general assembly determinations regarding contested elections. Existing law prohibits such judicial review.
  • Provide funding for the state board of elections to establish, in coordination with the department of public safety, a new threat-monitoring capability to monitor and analyze threats to election officials and their families by monitoring social media and other websites and maintaining a database of complaints from officials regarding threats.
  • Provide funding for security training for election officials.

This bill, as introduced on January 22, 2025, would eliminate no-excuse mail voting and online voter registration, among other changes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Eliminate no-excuse mail voting. To vote a mail ballot, a voter would have to have one of the following excuses:

    • Caretaker of a person who is hospitalized, ill, or disabled
    • Religious obligation
    • Confined by public order
    • Legal blindness
    • Confidentiality of the voter's residence address
    • Jury duty
    • The voter qualifies to vote a mail ballot under federal law

The bill would also require all voter registration applications to be made in person by the applicant, eliminating the options to register by mail, to register online, or to have another person deliver the application.
  • Delay the sending of mail ballots for statewide elections. Existing law requires mail ballots to be ready for delivery at least 35 days before a statewide general or primary election and 15 days before any other election. Under the bill, they may not be made ready for delivery earlier than 22 days before any election.
  • Standardize the length of the early voting ("in-person absentee") period at 30 days. Under existing law it is 15 days for an election other than a statewide general or primary election.
  • Require ballot drop boxes to have constant video surveillance, be conspicuously marked, and be located in secure, well-lit areas. The bill would also enact other law to ensure the security of drop boxes.
  • Permit an election official to hand count ballots, and require that at least a quarter of ballots are hand counted to verify an electronic tabulation. Voting or counting systems would be required to be re-approved before each statewide primary election.
  • Clarify that an employer or agent of an employer of a voter is generally not permitted to act as an agent to request a mail ballot on the voter's behalf.
  • Require all ballots to be watermarked.
  • Allow candidates to request a recount be done by hand count.

  • Permits a person unable to provide reasonable documentary proof of citizenship to request that an election official contact the secretary of state to attempt to verify the person's citizenship
  • Provides that if the secretary of state is unable to establish the person's citizenship, that a person who claims they are unable to obtain citizenship documentation due to indigence may sign an affidavit to that effect. If an election officer reviews the affidavit and confirms that the person is unable to obtain a citizenship document due to indigence, the person will be provided with a voucher to be used at an appropriate state agency to obtain a copy of the person's birth certificate or other sufficient citizenship documentation.

The bill will be effective July 17, 2026

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on June 9, 2025, would:

  • Automatically enroll all voters on the permanent mail voting list. A voter wishing to be removed from the list could notify the county clerk in writing that they no longer want to receive a mail-in ballot. Under existing law, voters must request to join the permanent mail voting list, allowing them to vote by mail for all future elections although any voter is eligible to join. The bill would leave in place the existing requirement that voters who do not vote by mail for four consecutive years no longer be sent a mail-in ballot for future elections and be notified in writing of this change. The bill would make nonsubstantive and conforming changes because of this new requirement.
  • Allow a voter removed from the permanent mail voting list or a voter wishing to change their mail address to rejoin the list or update their information by filling out a mail ballot application. 
  • Allow a voter who has received a mail ballot but who wishes to vote in person to do so if they surrender their mail ballot.
  • Allow a voter who did not receive their mail ballot to vote a provisional ballot in-person.
  • Allow the county board of elections to begin processing and counting mail ballots 10 days before Election Day rather than 5 days, as is required under existing law.
  • Permit voters to return mail ballots to any polling place. Under existing law, voters can return mail ballots by mail, to ballot drop boxes, or to the county board of elections office.
  • Require that all mail ballot return envelopes contain prepaid postage.

Last Updated June 10, 2025

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on October 27, 2025, would:

  • Create a felony for accessing or attempting to access the area where mail-in ballots are securely stored without the presence of the appropriate election officials representing each of the political parties having membership on the county board of elections. Under existing law, this is not a crime.
  • Increase the penalty for certain election crimes that involve fraudulent voting or interfering with the canvassing of an election from a third degree felony to a second degree felony. 
  • Require the county board of elections to process and canvass mail ballots in the presence of representatives from each political party that have membership on the respective county board. Under existing law, there is no such requirement.
  • Require the county board of elections when deciding to reject a ballot to do so by unanimous vote. Existing law does not specify what the threshold must be for voting.
  • Require that when canvassing mail-in ballots, the county board of elections ensure that mail-in ballots be stored in a secure area that includes at least one of the following security measures: a lock that requires one key from an election official from each political party; video surveillance of the storage area entrance; or a paper or electronic log of individuals who accessed the storage area. Under existing law, there is no such requirement.

Last Updated October 28, 2025

This bill, as enacted on January 20, 2026, expands the notice and cure process. Specifically, the bill:

  • Allows voters to cure mail ballots due to the voter failing to include or seal the mail ballot's inner or outer envelope or failing to complete the certificate of mail-in voter on the inner envelope. Under prior law, ballots with those deficiencies were rejected and those voters were not given the opportunity to cure their ballots.
  • Requires voters whose ballots contain those deficiencies to receive cure notices. Under prior law, election officials were required to send voters who have submitted ballots with curable defects a notice within 24 hours informing them that their ballot has been rejected and informing them how to cure it.
  • Allows voters who receive a cure notice to vote a provisional ballot in-person during the early voting period or on Election Day. Under previous law, voters who received a cure notice for a mail ballot were only permitted to vote by curing their mail ballot.
  • Specifies that the initial decision of whether to accept a mail ballot does not require a vote of the full board, but that the decision may only be made by trained elections employees designated by the county board of elections, subject to supervisory review by the board. The bill also specifies that watchers must be permitted to observe this process.
  • Requires any cure letter, cure form, or replacement ballot sent to a voter to be maintained as part of the voter's registration record.

Last Updated April 16, 2026

This bill, as introduced January 28, 2025, would create new voter ID requirements in New Mexico. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require a voter voting in person to present a current New Mexico driver's license or identification card in order to vote. Under existing law, the voter has the option to present various forms of non-photo ID, including a bank statement, utility bill, paycheck, or a verbal or written statement of their name, address, and year of birth.
  • Require a voter applying for a mail ballot to present a current New Mexico driver's license or identification card, or the voter's social security number, in order to vote. Under existing law, the voter has the option to present various additional forms of non-photo ID, including a bank statement, utility bill, paycheck, or a verbal or written statement of their name, address, and year of birth.
  • Specify that failure to present required ID is grounds for a challenge. 
  • Permit a voter to vote provisionally if the voter's required photo identification is challenged. 
  • Waive the fee for a state identification card if needed for voter identification purposes.
  • Require an online applicant for a ballot to be voted by mail to possess an unexpired New Mexico driver's license or identification card. Under existing law, the license or card could be expired.

Last Updated February 11, 2025

This bill, as introduced on January 29, 2025, would add the Department of Game and Fish as a voter registration agency, allowing qualified electors to register to vote when applying for a hunting or fishing license. Under existing law, voter registration is available only at the DMV and agencies providing public assistance or services for people with disabilities.

Last Updated March 19, 2025

This bill, as introduced on February 20, 2025, would:

  • Require the secretary of state to send the monthly certified list of deceased residents to boards of registration, in addition to county clerks. Current law only requires it to be sent to county clerks.
  • Require county clerks to report voter registration cancellations of deceased residents to boards of registration. Current law only requires county clerks to cancel the registrations without additional reporting.
  • Add a requirement for county clerks to report the cancellation of deceased tribal members' voter registrations to boards of registration. Current law requires county clerks to cancel these registrations based on notarized documentation from tribal authorities but does not require further reporting.
  • Specify powers and duties for Boards of Registration, including ensuring county clerks comply with election laws, maintaining accurate voter lists, and verifying the removal of deceased voters and address changes using motor vehicle records. It would also require Boards of Registration to meet within one month of member nominations, elect a chair and vice chair, independently certify that county clerks' voter list actions are accurate, and mandate county clerks to develop and administer annual training programs to educate Boards of Registration on their responsibilities for maintaining voter list accuracy.


Last Updated March 6, 2025

This bill, as introduced on February 20, 2025, would create a new felony for knowingly soliciting a noncitizen to register to vote or cast a ballot. The bill would specify that including with the solicitation a disclaimer advising noncitizens not to vote does not provide a legal defense.

Last Updated February 24, 2025

This bill, as introduced on March 5, 2025, would direct the Higher Education Department to study ways public institutions can increase youth voter participation and develop strategies to encourage high school and college students to become lifelong voters. The bill would also require the Department to draft a legislative proposal based on its findings to improve youth voter turnout and send its recommendations to the secretary of state, the secretary of public education, and the secretary of higher education.

Last Updated March 6, 2025

This resolution, as introduced on January 29, 2025, proposes an amendment to the New Mexico Constitution ending all disenfranchisement due to criminal convictions, by removing the existing clause that makes residents ineligible on this ground. Under existing statutory law, citizens are disenfranchised while incarcerated for a felony conviction, and have their right to vote automatically restored upon release.


For final adoption to the state constitution, the proposed amendment must be approved by both chambers of the legislature and then approved by a simple majority of the electorate at the next general election.

Last Updated March 5, 2025

This bill, as enacted on April 7, 2025:

  • Permits a voter with no party affiliation on their registration to request a ballot for a major party's primary when voting in person, by requested mail ballot, or in a mail ballot election precinct. Under prior law, only voters affiliated with a political party could vote in that party's primary, and unaffiliated voters were expressly prohibited from participating.
  • Specifies that requesting a party's primary ballot does not change the voter's official party affiliation unless the voter explicitly requests the change.
  • Makes conforming changes consistent with the new provisions.

Last Updated April 16, 2025

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on February 12, 2025, would: 

  • Alter the existing address confidentiality provisions to allow election administrative staff to receive address confidentiality. Under the bill, non-elected and appointed employees of a county clerk or the secretary of state would be allowed to designate a confidential home address that must not be disclosed on voter lists and file maintenance lists. Under existing law, the related confidentiality provisions apply to public officials only.
  • Require the secretary of state to authorize county clerks in disaster-affected areas to develop emergency election plans, including relocating polling places, coordinating with agencies, and addressing mail ballot disruptions. Any changes must be publicly posted and comply with tribal voting laws. The bill expressly prohibits the provision from being interpreted as extending the time period for an election. Existing law does not include similar emergency election procedures. 

The bill also includes provisions not tracked by Voting Rights Lab related to oaths of office, election equipment, vacancies, candidates, and recounts.

Last Updated February 19, 2025

This bill, as introduced on February 19, 2025, would create a new felony for knowingly soliciting a noncitizen to register to vote or cast a ballot. The bill would specify that including with the solicitation a disclaimer advising noncitizens not to vote does not provide a legal defense.

Last Updated February 20, 2025

This bill, as introduced on February 20, 2025, would: 

  • Shorten the early voting period by requiring it to begin the 15th day before an election instead of the 28th day before. 
  • Change required Saturday voting at the clerk's office from the Saturday immediately before the election to the third Saturday before the election. 
  • Shorten the hours of early voting by requiring voting to end at 7PM instead of 9PM. 
  • Require officials to conduct early voting 12 consecutive hours each day instead of eight hours. 
  • Repeal a provision allowing clerks to modify early voting hours or locations with written approval from the secretary of state. 
  • Make conforming changes throughout the Code. 

Last Updated March 5, 2025

This bill, as introduced on February 20, 2025, would:

  • Require county clerks to establish "absentee voter assistance units" in secure congregate facilities such as jails, nursing homes, and hospitals. These units must offer absentee voting, same-day registration, and provisional ballot voting, and must operate for at least two hours, staying open until 7 p.m. if necessary. Existing law allows county clerks to operate mobile polling locations but does not mandate services at secure congregate facilities or specify required services and operating hours.
  • Clarify that absentee voter assistance units are not considered voter convenience centers and may only substitute for them in emergencies. During an emergency, these units could be deployed to temporary congregate settings like shelters or evacuation centers with secretary of state approval.
  • Require that each voter convenience center serve no fewer than ten consolidated precincts on Election Day for general elections and fifteen consolidated precincts on election day for local and primary elections. Existing law requires each voter convenience center to be a consolidated precinct composed of no more than 10 precincts. 
  • Permit same-day registration and provisional voting at absentee voter assistance units, allowing voters to cure their ballot by providing identification or completing an affidavit of identity before statewide election certification.
  • Authorize the designation of mail ballot election precincts for precincts where more than 55% of voters are on the permanent mail voter list. 
  • Require the county clerk to assess and report the supply needs of secure congregate facilities at least 90 days before an election, based on the rolling daily average of eligible voters at each facility. Existing law does not include a similar requirement.


Last Updated April 11, 2025

This resolution, as introduced February 18, 2025, would propose an amendment to the state constitution to permit any voter to request the ballot of any single political party conducting a state-funded primary election, regardless of whether the voter's registration indicates an affiliation with that party. Existing constitutional provisions do not address requirements for voting in primary elections. Under existing statutory law, only voters affiliated with a party are permitted to vote in that party's primary election. 

For final amendment of the constitution, the proposed provision must be passed by both the state legislature and general electorate.

Last Updated February 19, 2025

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on February 3, 2025, would make Nevada's in-person voter ID document requirements more restrictive and impose ID number or document requirements for mail voting. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require voters to show specified proof of identity that includes their name, signature, and photo to receive a ballot in person. The ID would need to be current or expired for less than 4 years or, if the holder is 70 years of age or older, current or expired for any length of time. Currently, no ID is requested or required, except that if a voter's signature does not match their signature of record, the voter may produce a specified ID to provide a matching signature. Under the bill, proof of identity would include the following:
    • Driver’s license or state ID card issued by the DMV
    • ID card issued by this State or another state, the District of Columbia, or any territory of the United States
    • ID card issued by the United States Government
    • ID card issued by a college or university within the Nevada System of Higher Education
    • Identification card issued by a Nevada public technical school 
    • Employee ID card issued by the state or federal government or, an agency or political subdivision thereof
    • U.S. Pass port
    • Military ID card 
    • Tribal ID
    • Concealed carry permit 
  • Require the DMV to issue free ID to registered voters who lack ID to vote and attest that they are experiencing a financial hardship. People seeking free ID would need to prove their registered voter status but not their financial hardship. Existing law does not provide a free ID to such voters.
  • Require voters to put the last four digits of their driver's license or state ID number, or otherwise the last four digits of their Social Security number, on their mail ballot envelope. Voters without such ID numbers would be required to use the ID number issued by the county clerk. Existing law requires voters to sign the oath on the ballot envelope, requires election officials to reject unsigned ballots or ballots signed with a signature that does not match one on record, and provides voters notice of their ballots' rejection and an opportunity to cure the issue.
  • Specify that voters who fail to present proof of identity may cast a provisional ballot. 
  • Make conforming changes to the code, including in the context of challenges to in-person voters and provisional ballots.
  • Clarify that the existing felony prohibiting voting or attempting to vote using another person's name includes voting the mail ballot of another person.

Last Updated February 27, 2025

This bill, enacted on June 3, 2025:

  • Moves the mail ballot delivery timeline earlier by requiring county and city clerks to distribute ballots to voters between the fifth and fourth Mondays before the election (approximately 29 to 22 days before Election Day), instead of no later than 20 days before the election. In Nevada, all eligible voters receive a ballot in the mail for each election. The bill leaves in place the existing requirement that clerks continue mailing ballots to anyone who registers or updates their registration through the 14th day before Election Day, and that out-of-state and UOCAVA voters be mailed their ballots no later than 40 days before the election.
  • Authorizes county and city clerks to allow voters to elect to receive a mail ballot before the fifth Monday prior to an election. Prior law did not permit clerks to issue ballots earlier than the standard distribution period.

The bill also includes provisions not tracked by Voting Rights Lab related to special elections and sample ballots.

Last Updated October 23, 2025

This bill, as introduced on February 10, 2025, would:

  • Direct the secretary of state to compile county reports and submit a summary to the legislature or the legislative commission.

    • Driver’s license or state ID card issued by the DMV
    • ID card issued by this State or another state, the District of Columbia, or any territory of the United States
    • ID card issued by the United States Government
    • ID card issued by a college or university within the Nevada System of Higher Education
    • Identification card issued by a Nevada public technical school 
    • Employee ID card issued by the state or federal government or, an agency or political subdivision thereof
    • U.S. Pass port
    • Military ID card 
    • Tribal ID
    • Concealed carry permit 
  • Require the DMV to issue free ID to registered voters who lack ID to vote and attest that they are experiencing a financial hardship. People seeking free ID would need to prove their registered voter status but not their financial hardship. Existing law does not provide a free ID to such voters.
  • Require voters to put the last four digits of their driver's license or state ID number, or otherwise the last four digits of their Social Security number, on their mail ballot envelope. Voters without such ID numbers would be required to use the ID number issued by the county clerk. Existing law requires voters to sign the oath on the ballot envelope, requires election officials to reject unsigned ballots or ballots signed with a signature that does not match one on record, and provides voters notice of their ballots' rejection and an opportunity to cure the issue.

  • Regulate mail ballot requests and distribution by setting deadlines for third-party distribution, prohibiting mass distribution later than 35 days before an election if the person distributes forms to a total of 500 voters.
  • Mandate public reporting and oversight by requiring mail ballot requests to be publicly available, assigning an inspection board to review ballots, verifying ballot records before Election Day, and enforcing secrecy procedures with penalties for premature disclosure.
  • Create a felony offense for fraudulently requesting a mail ballot in another person's name or coercing them to do so.
  • Clarify that the existing felony prohibiting voting or attempting to vote using another person's name includes voting the mail ballot of another person.

This bill, as introduced on February 19, 2025, would:

  • Require county clerks to affirmatively ask voters who are contacted regarding a mail ballot signature mismatch if the voter wants to update their signature in official records. Under the bill, unless the voter expressly declines, any signature provided to resolve the mismatch would automatically update their voter registration signature. 
  • Specify that county clerks must immediately notify the secretary of state when they determine that a person is eligible to vote after receiving information from automatic voter registration agencies via the database created by the secretary of state.
  • Require the secretary of state, instead of county clerks, to mail a notice to voters who have been automatically registered informing them of their registration.  
  • Repeal a provision that requires county clerks to notify voters in writing within five working days when their name was added to the statewide voter registration list or when their registration information was updated. 
  • Make conforming changes throughout the Code.

Last Updated March 13, 2025

Governor Joe Lombardo vetoed this bill on May 22, 2025. As passed by the legislature, the bill would have expanded the number of required drop boxes and established new security requirements for their operation. Under existing law, ballot drop boxes must be provided at all early and Election Day polling places, and at the clerks' offices, and must be available during hours of business or voting. In addition to these existing requirements, the bill would have:

  • Required counties with a population of 700,000 or more to establish at least 10 mail ballot drop box locations, each open to the public for at least seven hours per day beginning the day after the last day of in-person early voting and ending on the day before election.
  • Required counties with a population between 100,000 and 700,000 to establish at least five mail ballot drop box locations, each open to the public for at least seven hours per day during the designated period.
  • Allowed counties with a population of less than 100,000 to determine the number of mail ballot drop box locations and set their operating hours as needed.
  • Required drop boxes to be monitored at all times and secured when they are not available. Existing law requires only that drop boxes be constructed securely and lockable. 
  • Required the secretary of state to adopt regulations to establish requirements for monitoring and securing drop boxes.


Last Updated May 28, 2025

AUTHORNAME: Assembly Legislative Operations and Elections Committee
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on June 2, 2025:

  • Requires the secretary of state to ensure that voting materials and other election information posted on its website are available in all languages required by federal law and in American Sign Language. If fewer than seven languages are required under federal law, the secretary of state must post materials in the seven most commonly spoken languages in Nevada in addition to American Sign Language. If a language does not have a written form, the information must be provided as an audio recording. Under prior law, there was no requirement to provide voting materials online in a minimum number of languages.
  • Requires the secretary of state to use certified translators for all required translations. If a certified translator is not available, the secretary must make a continuous effort to find one or coordinate with the relevant minority group for assistance. Under prior law, there was no requirement for the use of certified translators.
  • Requires the secretary of state to establish and maintain a toll-free telephone number for voters to receive language interpretation or translation assistance related to elections, including voter registration. The line must provide assistance in the 200 most commonly spoken languages in Nevada and in American Sign Language, and the number must be posted on the Secretary’s website. Prior law did not include a similar provision.
  • Requires the secretary of state to employ a classified state employee to serve as a Language Access Coordinator within the office. Prior law did not include a similar requirement.
  • Requires the secretary of state to ensure that all election-related communications and information are made available in English and Spanish.
  • Permits voters with physical disabilities to use a mobile device to access interpretive services, including American Sign Language, when casting a vote. Under prior law, voters with physical disabilities could receive assistance from a person of their choice but are not expressly permitted to use personal mobile devices for interpretive services.

A previous version of the bill included provisions that were amended out. The provisions would have revised the forms used to register or pre-register to vote to include an instruction to the applicant that they can check a box to receive the sample ballot in a language other than English and a blank space to write in the preferred language. The form would have indicated that not all languages are available, but the information would help the state, county, and city to determine their language access needs. The voter would have only received voting materials in the requested language if the language is one in which the clerk is required to provide translations. The forms would have also been amended to allow applicants to include their state or country of birth. Relatedly, voters' state or country of birth and language preference would have been added to the statewide voter registration list.

Last Updated June 12, 2025

AUTHORNAME: Assembly Legislative Operations and Elections Committee
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on June 6, 2025, requires county and city clerks to provide requested election information or data to the secretary of state no later than the end of the second working day after receiving the request, or provide a written explanation indicating when the information or data will reasonably be available. Prior law did not set a timeframe or require written explanations for delayed responses for such requests.


The bill also includes provisions not tracked by Voting Rights Lab related to candidate requirements.

Last Updated October 23, 2025

Governor Joe Lombardo vetoed this bill on June 5, 2025. As passed by the legislature, this bill would have:

  • Required daily publication of mail and provisional ballot data by county and city clerks beginning the day after in-person early voting started and ending the day after election results were canvassed, no later than 11 a.m. each day. The bill would have created an exception when extenuating circumstances prevented clerks from reporting and required them to post an estimate of when the data would be available. Required data would have included ballots returned, ballots requiring and undergoing signature cures, and provisional ballots counted and uncounted. Existing law has no comparable reporting requirement.
  • Required the secretary of state to post a compilation of the mail and provisional ballot information on the office's website.
  • Mandated monthly online publication of the county’s voter registration list, in alphabetical order, downloadable for free by any person. Voter ID numbers would have been included on this list. Existing law permits, but does not require, publication of the voter list in a county newspaper, but has no express requirements related to online publication. 
  • Revised the existing mail ballot envelope to include space for voters to provide their phone number for contact, if needed, for signature verification.

Last Updated August 8, 2025

Governor Joe Lombardo vetoed this bill on June 12, 2025. As passed by the legislature, this bill would have created a photo ID requirement for in-person voting; required voters whose identity was challenged to show photo ID; created an ID number requirement for mail voting; expanded drop box availability between the early voting period and Election Day; authorized officials to count a mail ballot if either the voter's signature or identifying information on the return envelope was verified; and established an online voter services portal, among other changes.

Regarding ID requirements for in-person voting and voter challenges, the bill would have:

  • Created a photo ID requirement for in-person voting. Voters who did not present a required form of ID at the polling place would have been permitted to cast a provisional ballot, which would only be counted if they presented ID to the county clerk by 5:00 p.m. on the Friday after Election Day. Under existing law, Nevada does not require in-person voters to show photo identification, but their signature must be compared to the signature on record. If the signatures do not match, the voter may provide a specified form of identification to confirm their identity.
  • Prescribed documents that constituted acceptable photo ID. The bill would have required ID to be current or expired within four years (or expired at any time for voters age 70+), and limited to:
    • Nevada driver’s license
    • Photo ID issued by:
      • Any state, D.C., or a U.S. territory
      • U.S. government, including U.S. passport or military ID
    • Photo student ID issued by a public secondary school, Nevada System of Higher Education college or university, or public technical school
    • Employee photo ID issued by the local, state, or federal government
    • Tribal ID
    • Concealed firearm ID
    • Digital identification card issued by the secretary of state
  • Required the DMV to issue free voter photo ID cards for voters without photo ID who attested to financial hardship, and prohibited the agency from requiring proof of hardship.
  • Required the secretary of state to establish a free "digital identification card" available to all registered voters, by Jan. 1, 2028.
  • Required an individual whose voter registration was challenged based on identity to provide, without exception, a photo ID before being issued a ballot. Under existing law, a voter facing a challenge based on identity must either present an official photo ID or have an individual over 18 years old present a photo ID and sign an affirmation confirming the identity of the challenged voter.

Regarding mail ballot voting, the bill would have:

  • Created a new ID number requirement for voting by mail ballot. Under the bill, mail ballot voters would have been required to provide, in addition to their signature, the last four digits of their DMV number; or if without a DMV number, the last four digits of their Social Security number; or if without either, their voter ID number.
  • Authorized officials to count a mail ballot if either the voter's signature or identifying information on the return envelope was verified. Officials would have been required to first do signature matching, and signatures could not be verified, then attempt to verify the ID number. If the clerk verified the ID number, the voter's ballot would be counted; if not, the clerk would have been required to notify the voter to cure their ballot for counting. Existing law requires signature verification on all mail ballot return envelopes and does not permit substitution with other identifying information.
  • Expanded access to cure a rejected mail ballot by requiring clerks to offer phone assistance during evenings and weekends (until at least 7 p.m.), and allowed voters to confirm their signature by electronic mail or text message. Existing law requires clerks to notify voters of signature issues but does not mandate evening and weekend availability or allow text and email as confirmation methods.
  • Expanded drop box availability by requiring county clerks to establish mail ballot drop box locations during the period between the end of early voting and the day before Election Day. Under existing law, county clerks must provide mail ballot drop boxes during early voting and on Election Day, but are not required to provide them in the period between. Specifically, under the bill:
    • In counties with populations of 700,000 or more, at least 10 locations would have been required, each open to the public for at least 7 hours but no more than 12 hours daily.
    • In counties with populations between 100,000 and 700,000, at least five locations would have been required, with the same hours of operation.
    • In counties with fewer than 100,000 residents, clerks would have been authorized to establish any number of drop box locations and set their hours.
    • All drop boxes would have been located at sites used for early voting or Election Day in-person voting.
  • Increased security requirements for drop boxes by requiring that boxes be monitored "at all times" and secured at any time when not in use, and required the secretary of state to establish requirements for doing so. Existing law has no comparable requirements.

Regarding administration of the voter list and voter access to registration and election information, the bill would have:

  • Required the secretary of state to establish and maintain an online "voter services portal," in addition to the existing online voter registration system required under current law. Under the bill, the portal would have allowed voters to:
    • Review and update registration information
    • View sample ballots
    • Find polling and drop box locations
  • Required the DMV to regularly submit specified personal information to the secretary of state for individuals issued a license or state ID. The secretary would have been required to add the information to records for all registered voters, and to note voters who had not been issued a license or ID from the agency. Existing law requires cooperation between the DMV and election officials but does not mandate regular submissions with this level of detail. Transferred personal information would have included each individual's:
    • Name
    • Date of birth and birthplace
    • Last four digits of Social Security number
    • Driver’s license or identification card number
    • Sex
    • Physical and mailing address
    • Citizenship status
    • Telephone number and email address
    • Veteran status
  • Prohibited the secretary of state or local clerks from disclosing voter data received from the DMV for voter registration purposes. This information would have been classified as confidential and not a public record under Nevada law. Under existing law, voters may request that county officials withhold their address and phone number.

AUTHORNAME: Assembly Legislative Operations and Elections Committee
VRLANALYSIS:
Governor Joe Lombardo vetoed this bill on June 12, 2025. As passed by the legislature, this bill would have:

  • Changed voter registration deadlines, and procedures for updates and challenges:
    • Moved the general deadline later for in-person registration, to the day before the start of in-person early voting (currently the third Saturday before Election Day). Under existing law, the general in-person registration deadline is the fourth Tuesday before an election. The bill would also have changed registration deadlines for certain recall and special elections. 
    • Specified that clerks must process registrations of actively registered voters who move to a new county and register to vote, including through transactions at a voter registration agency, as updates, rather than new registrations, and must not require such voters to cast a provisional or conditional ballot based on their new address status.  
    •  Specified requirements for registration challenges made by voters. Existing law requires an affirmation that challenges are based on personal knowledge, but does not define this term. The bill would have defined "personal knowledge" as firsthand knowledge through experience or observation of the facts upon which the challenge is based, and expressly excluded information from third parties such as review of a database or other compilation of information.
  • For mail ballot voting, moved deadlines earlier for qualifying to receive an automatic ballot and the issuance of automatic ballots, and set a new deadline for requesting an automatic ballot after initially declining to receive one: 
    • Moved the deadline earlier for qualifying to receive an automatic mail ballot. Under existing law, mail ballots are sent to all voters registered at least 14 days before an election; the bill would have moved the eligibility date to voter registrations completed at least 18 days before. 
    • Moved the mailing date earlier for mail ballots sent to all active voters residing in-state. Under existing law, clerks must send ballots to these voters no later than 20 days before an election. The bill would have required ballots be sent between the fifth Monday and fourth Monday before.
    • Specified that voters who initially choose not to receive a mail ballot and later wished to receive one must submit a written notice to the county clerk 14 days before the election. Existing law requires voters to send written notice to clerks 60 days before Election Day if they do not want a mail ballot, but does not specify procedures for voters who later wish to receive one.
  • Shifted authority for rules concerning mail ballot processing and created new mandates for timing of the process:
    • Shifted authority for establishing rules related to processing and counting ballots from county clerks to the secretary of state. 
    • Required, instead of allowed, the mail ballot central counting board to begin counting ballots 15 days before the election. The bill would have further required officials to process mail ballots within 24 hours of receipt, unless the secretary of state authorized a waiver.
  • Expanded the data sources permitted for cancelling a voter's registration or pre-registration due to death, by including a sworn affidavit from a relative "within the second degree of sanguinity." Under existing law, clerks may rely only on an authentic death certificate or personal knowledge to cancel registrations on this ground.
  • Permitted county clerks to publish required election notices on their websites, social media, or in any manner they prefer. Existing law requires such notices be published in a newspaper of general circulation.
  • Renamed ballots issued to voters whose registration updates cannot be timely processed before the election, from "provisional ballots" to “conditional ballots," and made conforming changes throughout the Code. Under existing law, ballots issued for both this reason and in other circumstances where the voter's eligibility cannot be verified on different grounds are called provisional ballots.  

This bill also contained provisions not tracked by Voting Rights Lab related to audits, candidates, petitions, and voting systems.


A previous version of the bill included additional provisions that were amended out prior to passage by the legislature. These provisions would have:

  • Required officials to provide eligible incarcerated individuals with access to the state's existing electronic system for registering to vote, and receiving and returning a ballot. Under existing law, this system is available only to UOCAVA voters.
  • Authorized the secretary of state to require any deputy or employee of their office to complete election procedures training. Existing law mandates such training for county and city clerks, and authorizes clerks to require their deputies or employees to attend, but does not expressly grant the secretary authority to require their own subordinates to attend.
