AUTHORNAME: Senate Legislative Operations and Elections Committee
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on June 2, 2025, would require voter registration applications to include an option to opt out of receiving a mail ballot; authorize emergency mail ballot requests from voters who previously opted out; revise registration and confidentiality rules; restrict early release of election results; and repeal certain election provisions, among other changes.

  • Require applications to register and pre-register to vote to include an option for residents to elect not to receive a mail ballot. Under existing law, which would remain in place, officials send all active registered voters a mail ballot unless they opt out; however, there is no requirement that the option be listed on the application.
  • Prohibit residents from registering or pre-registering to vote in more than one state at once and repeal an existing provision prohibiting pre-registering or registering to vote in more than one county.
  • Require voter registration agencies, automatic voter registration agencies, and the DMV to notify voters who register after the last day to register by mail that such voters must complete their registration online in order to vote in the upcoming election. Under prior law, this notice was not required.
  • Expand eligibility for confidential voter registration to include elderly dependents of eligible individuals who meet confidentiality criteria. Under existing law, confidentiality protections include certain election workers and their immediate families but not elderly dependents or non-registrant.
  • Update terminology on voter registration records by changing the designation for voters not affiliated with a political party from "nonpartisan" to "no political party." Under existing law, voters not affiliated with a political party are listed as "nonpartisan."
  • Prohibit the counting of ballots cast on a mechanical voting system before 7:00 a.m. on Election Day, and prohibit posting or releasing election results (or copies of results) before the polls close. Under existing law, when polls are closed, the counting board must prepare to count the ballots voted.
  • Permit registered voters who are unable to access their mail ballot or appear in person at the polls due to an emergency to request a mail ballot from the city clerk between the 46th day before an election and the day before the election, even if they previously opted out of receiving one. The clerk would verify eligibility and ensure the voter has not already voted before issuing the ballot. Existing law does not provide a similar emergency mail ballot request process for voters who previously opted out.
  • Repeal several existing provisions. The repeals would be effective upon passage of the bill while the remainder of the bill generally would take effect on January 1, 2026. The repeals would include provisions that:
    • Prohibit counting boards from counting votes until all ballots are accounted for in the precinct, district or polling place where paper ballots are used.
    • Allow voters who move from one county to another or one precinct to another within the same county after the close of voter registration to retain their residence for purposes of that election.
    • Require the county clerk to send the number of registered voters and their party affiliation to the secretary of state prior to certain elections.

This bill also includes provisions not tracked by the Voting Rights Lab related to audits, candidates, data security, records, and recounts.


A previous version of the bill included provisions that were amended out of the current text. The provisions would have allowed any registered voter who could not access their mail ballot or go to the polls due to illness, confinement, or being called away from home to use the electronic ballot transmission system. Under existing law, only military, overseas, certain disabled, and tribal voters are authorized to use the electronic transmission system.

AUTHORNAME: Senate Legislative Operations and Elections Committee
VRLANALYSIS:
Governor Joe Lombardo vetoed this bill on June 11, 2025. As passed by the legislature, this bill would have specified the registration deadline for automatic voter registration (AVR), expanded acceptable documents for same-day voter registration, and required extended DMV hours around elections in Nevada’s largest counties. Specifically, the bill would have:

  • Specified that the deadline for automatic voter registration through voter registration agencies (such as the DMV) is the 18th day before an election. Existing law expressly provides for a general registration deadline of the fourth Tuesday before an election, and for same-day registration with a provisional ballot, but does not have an express provision concerning the deadline for AVR. 
  • Moved the window for transmitting automatic voter registration information later. Agencies would have had to transmit voter registration data electronically within one working day if collected during the period beginning two weeks before the 18th day before an election and ending on the 18th day before an election. Under existing law, the expedited window begins two weeks before the fifth Sunday before an election and ends on that Sunday.
  • Expanded and clarified voter ID rules for individuals registering same-day during early voting or on Election Day. Specifically the bill would have: 
    • Expanded types of acceptable ID for voters registering early or on Election Day. Under existing law, a voter registering during early voting or on Election Day must present identification to establish both identity and residency. If the voter has a driver’s license or state ID showing their current address, that must be used. If not, the voter may present alternative documents such as a military ID, utility bill, bank statement, paycheck, income tax return, mortgage statement or lease, vehicle registration, property tax statement, or another government-issued document. This bill would have expanded the list of acceptable IDs by allowing voters to register and vote using a Tribal ID card or a current and valid driver’s license or state ID issued not only by Nevada but also by another state, the District of Columbia, or a U.S. territory. 
    • Tightened existing voter ID rules by newly requiring that any paycheck, bank card, or credit union statement used as proof of residency be dated no more than 60 days before the date of registration. Existing law has no date requirement for use of these documents. 
    • Clarified that a DMV-issued ID or a Tribal ID showing the voter’s current residential address also serves as proof of both identity and residency. Under existing law, only a Nevada DMV-issued photo ID with the current address can serve both purposes.
    • Allowed same-day registrants whose DMV-issued ID does not show their current address to establish residency using an original, electronic, or certified copy of specified documents. Existing law does not expressly authorize electronic documents or certified copies, and does not expressly limit the time period the documents must reflect. The documents would have included:
      • Military identification card
      • Utility bill dated no more than 60 days before the day the person is registering to vote
      • Bank statement dated no more than 60 days before the day the person is registering to vote
      • Paycheck dated no more than 60 days before the day the person is registering to vote
      • Income tax return
      • Statement concerning the mortgage, rental, or lease of a residence
      • Motor vehicle registration, property tax statement, or other document issued by a governmental agency
    • Permitted voters who presented out-of-state IDs or Tribal IDs without a current address to vote provisionally by signing a written affirmation and requiring them to submit proof of identity and residency (a Nevada DMV ID, interim document, or Tribal ID showing address) to election officials by 5 p.m. on the Friday after Election Day for their provisional ballot to count. Under existing law, only Nevada IDs are accepted for this process.
    • Permitted voters who have no government-issued ID at all to also vote provisionally by completing a written affirmation and later submitting an appropriate Nevada DMV-issued ID or Tribal ID by 5 p.m. on the Friday after Election Day.
  • Required the DMV in counties with populations over 100,000 (currently Clark and Washoe Counties) to:
    • Remain open on Saturdays and Sundays and offer extended hours beyond 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. during the two weeks before the voter registration mail deadline and the six days following a primary or general election. Under existing law, the DMV in these counties is authorized—but not required—to offer extended hours, and appointments could still be required.
    • Permit applications to obtain or renew a driver’s license or identification card without an appointment during these expanded service periods. 

Last Updated September 18, 2025

VRLANALYSIS:
This joint resolution, as enacted on November 19, 2025, would enshrine existing statutory universal mail-in voting requirements in the Nevada Constitution by establishing constitutional requirements for the distribution, return, and submission of mail ballots. Specifically, the resolution would:

  • Require county clerks to send a mail ballots to all active registered voters who are eligible vote in an election. Mail ballots would need to be sent between the fifth and fourth Mondays before an election for in-state voters, and between the seventh and fifth Mondays for out-of-state voters, unless federal or state law requires earlier mailing. Existing law requires counties to mail ballots to active voters but does not set constitutional mailing windows.
  • Require county clerks to send mail ballots to newly registered or updated voters who make changes at least 14 days before an election.
  • Allow voters to opt out of receiving a mail ballot by submitting written notice to the clerk at least 60 days before an election.
  • Require mail ballot packets to include a ballot, a secrecy sleeve, a return envelope, and instructions, and require the use of non-forwardable envelopes.
  • Require prepaid first-class postage on return envelopes for voters located within the United States, its territories or possessions, or on a military base.
  • Require any polling place used for early voting or Election Day voting to accept mail ballot submissions while in-person voting occurs. Existing law allows drop-off but does not require acceptance at all polling locations.
  • Require county clerks to establish mail ballot return sites during the three days immediately preceding a primary or general election. Counties with 700,000 or more residents must operate at least 10 sites; counties with 100,000–699,999 residents must operate at least 5; counties with fewer than 100,000 residents must operate at least 1.
  • Authorize clerks to establish additional return sites beyond the required minimums and authorize the Legislature to increase those minimums by statute.

Final adoption of the proposed amendment requires passage again during the 2027 Legislative Session before being placed on the 2028 general election ballot for voter approval.

This bill, as introduced on January 8, 2025, would create same-day registration on Election Day, require all voters to be mailed ballots for all elections without changing early voting or Election Voting locations, ostensibly shift control of voter registration lists from the counties and New York City to the state, and change when mail ballots are brought by election officials to nursing homes and similar institutions to be voted in person. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Create same-day registration on Election Day. The bill states that a same-day registrant must complete the ordinary voter registration form and provide the ordinary proofs to support it when registering on Election Day. Existing law does not require an ID document to register or to vote, although it does require a person to provide a driver's license number, a state ID number, or a Social Security number, or affirm that the applicant has none. 
  • Require local boards of election to mail all registered voters ballots at their registration address for all elections for which they are qualified to vote. Existing law requires voters to request mail ballots and to justify their request with an excuse authorized by statute.
  • Allow people who expect to be away from their registration address to request to have their ballot sent to a different address. The bill would require the State Board of Elections to make a standard application but would require local boards to accept any request that substantially complied with the state form. Under existing law, voters requesting mail ballots may request that the ballot be sent to an address different from their registration address. 
  • Eliminate the requirement that 25 people in a residential care facility request absentee ballots before a local board of elections can bring ballots to the facility to assist voters with casting ballots, and require ballots be brought to all such facilities. 
  • Clarify that the use of titles, initials, or customary abbreviations of given names in a voter's or witness's signature on an application to redirect the mail ballot, or on the mail ballot envelope, cannot be the basis for invalidating the application or ballot for a signature mismatch. 
  • Require the State Board of Elections to implement, in a uniform and nondiscriminatory manner, a single, uniform, official, centralized, interactive, computerized statewide voter registration database system. The system would be defined, maintained, and administered at the state level, contain the voter registration lists maintained by each county board of elections, and assign a unique identifier to each legally registered voter. Although counties would be allowed to maintain lists in a parallel system, they would need to facilitate the state's maintenance of the state system. The bill would require the state system to offer various features to assist in election administration, including signature verification. Existing law, not addressed by the bill, requires the State Board of Elections to maintain an interactive, statewide, computerized, voter registration list.

Note: The New York Constitution Art. II, Section 2 authorizes only people who are out of their county or out of New York City, as applicable, and people who are unable to appear to vote in person due to illness or physical disability to choose to vote by mail. Art. 2, Section 5 requires people to register to vote a minimum of 10 days before an election.

This bill, as amended on June 2, 2026, would improve voting rights for incarcerated individuals by providing the eligible residents the ability to register and vote, enforceable in court.

Specifically, the bill would guarantee the right of eligible incarcerated residents to vote by:

  • Declaring that residents who are eligible to register to vote and vote and who are detained, confined, or committed to a correctional facility are "entitled to the free exercise and enjoyment of the elective franchise without discrimination or preference." Under New York statutes, only those convicted of felonies who are also imprisoned lose their voting rights. 
  • Requiring the Department of Corrections to issue regulations directing each facility to ensure the timely delivery, and to facilitate the timely return if applicable, of all official election mail, forms, notices, or communications to any individual detained or confined at such facility and that non-partisan plain language educational materials about the voting rights of individuals currently incarcerated and formerly incarcerated are included in the inmate handbook or similar materials and reentry resources.
  • Requiring the rules and regulations governing correctional facilities recognize the right of qualified detained or incarcerated individuals to register and vote. Such rules would be required to allow access to electronic personal voter registration or voter registration by application, and allow access to mail balloting services ("absentee balloting services") through the electronic mail ballot application transmittal system or by paper application. The rules for both voter registration and mail voting would be required to best effect this spirit and intent while being consistent with the proper discipline and management of the correctional facility.
  • Requiring the superintendent of each correctional facility to cooperate with the board of elections in developing and implementing a plan to facilitate at least one method of voter access for all individuals eligible to vote who are detained or confined at each such facility, including making available space and reasonable accommodations.
  • Authorizing aggrieved individuals to enforce their rights in court.
  • Creating a presumption that if any superintendent, employee, or agent of a correctional facility by commission or omission intentionally frustrates the ability of eligible incarcerated people to register and vote, an election law violation has occurred that may be enforced in court by any aggrieved persons, an organization whose membership includes aggrieved persons or members of a protected class, an organization whose mission, in whole or in part, is to ensure voting access, or the attorney general. That section of code allows multiple remedies including nominal, compensatory, or punitive damages.
  • Regarding mail voting, the bill would:
    • Require counties with at least 100,000 registered voters to provide an absentee balloting program for eligible incarcerated individuals at correctional facilities with at least 75 incarcerated individuals, unless the board establishes a polling place at the facility.
    • Require, for other covered facilities, that boards of elections coordinate with facility officials to provide access to electronic or paper voter registration and, unless a polling place is established, provide absentee ballot applications no later than 21 days before Election Day.
  • Allow local boards of elections generally to open early voting polling places at correctional facilities and local correctional facilities instead of offering a mail balloting program. The polling place would be open for at least three hours beginning on the tenth day before Election Day and ending on and including the ninth day before. The board of elections in New York City would be authorized to open the polling place for at least six hours beginning on the tenth day before Election Day and ending on and including the eighth day before. These early voting sites would be in addition to, not instead of, any others required by law, nor would they impact siting decisions for those required sites. Only voters who are detained, confined, or employed by the facility and eligible to vote in the county in which the facility is located (or in New York City, if the facility is in New York City) would be allowed to vote in the polling place. All other eligible people or voters would be given voter registration forms and mail ballot applications.

The bill:
    • Expands data sources for routine monthly list maintenance, to expressly include the Social Security Administration. 
    • Expands the categories of data expressly included for review, to include dates of birth, license or state ID numbers, and last four digits of Social Security numbers.
    • Specifies requirements for notice to individuals with non-matching data for confirmation of eligibility to vote or an unverified address, and requires voters to cast a provisional ballot if their information is not confirmed prior to voting. 
  • Expands data sources for monthly list maintenance related to deceased individuals. Under prior law, the director of health was required to report all deaths over age 18 to the secretary of state, for transfer to local boards of election. The bill additionally requires the secretary to notify local boards of individuals reported deceased by the Social Security Administration, SAVE database, and State and Territorial Exchange of Vital Events (STEVE) database. 
  • Expands the express grounds for cancellation of a voter's registration, to include, among other grounds, casting a provisional ballot that is not counted due to improper or invalid registration or failure to provide required documentation within the deadline.

Regarding polling place procedures and provisional ballot voting, the bill:

  • Requires election officials to challenge a voter's eligibility if they present a license or state ID that indicates non-citizenship. Prior law had no comparable express provision. The bill also slightly modifies the existing process for citizenship challenges at the polling place, related to standard of proof for citizenship through naturalized parents. Under the bill, challenged individuals may vote a regular ballot if they provide an accepted form of documentation, other than a license or state ID, and declaration of citizenship. If they are unable to provide such documentation, they would be required to vote a provisional ballot, subject the existing requirement to provide documentation within four days of the election for verification of a provisional ballot.
  • For voters required to use a provisional ballot other than due to challenges for a non-citizen license or ID card, permits the use of such ID numbers if the voter has already provided proof of citizenship to the DMV. 
  • Specifies the documents accepted for proof of citizenship. Prior law refers to confirmation of citizenship for voters identified during routine list maintenance processes, and to "official documentation" of citizenship for polling place challenges, but does not specify accepted documents. Under the bill, accepted proof of citizenship includes: 
    • Birth certificate, certification of report of birth, consular report of birth abroad, or a copy of one of the documents
    • Current U.S. passport or passport card, a copy of the ID page of the passport, or a copy of the front and pack of the passport card
    • Certificate of naturalization, a certificate of citizenship, or a copy of one of those documents
    • Ohio driver's license or state ID number, if the board of elections verifies it using previously submitted documentation indicating the applicant is a U.S. citizen
    • Current Ohio driver's license, state ID card, or interim identification form issued on or after April 7, 2023, or a copy of the front and back of that document
    • Driver's license or non-driver ID number from any state, or a copy of the back and front of the document, if the state indicates on the document that the individual is a U.S. citizen
  • Specifies that an applicant's proof of citizenship is not subject to disclosure under the state's public record requirements.

A previous version of the bill contained an additional provision that was amended out of the enacted version. This provision would have moved the return deadline for UOCAVA mail ballots to the same new deadline as general mail ballots (Election Day). Under existing law, UOCAVA ballots are timely if signed by the close of polls on Election Day and received within four days after the election.

This bill, as introduced on March 26, 2025, would:

  • Require residents to provide documentary proof of U.S. citizenship when registering to vote using a state voter registration application. Existing law does not require proof of citizenship. The bill defines documentary proof of citizenship to include the following:
    • Valid U.S. passport
    • Official U.S. military identification card, together with a United States military record of service showing U.S. birth
    • Valid government-issued photo identification card issued by a Federal, state, or tribal government showing U.S. birth
    • A valid government-issued photo identification card issued by a Federal, state or tribal government other than one listed above, if presented together with one or more of the following:
      • A certified birth certificate issued by a state, local government, or tribal government that:
      • Was issued by the state, local government, or tribal government in which the applicant was born
      • Was filed with the office responsible for keeping vital records in the state
      • Includes the applicant’s full name, date of birth, and place of birth
      • Lists the full names of one or both parents
      • Has the signature of an authorized official
      • Includes the date the certificate was filed with the office responsible for vital records
      • Has the official seal of the issuing authority
    • Extract from a United States hospital record of birth created at the time of birth showing the applicant’s place of birth in the United States
    • Final adoption decree showing the applicant’s name and place of birth in the United States
    • Consular report of birth abroad of a citizen of the United States or a certification of the applicant’s report of birth issued by the Secretary of State
    • Naturalization certificate or certificate of citizenship issued by the Secretary of Homeland Security, or any other document or method of proof of United States citizenship issued under specified federal law
    • American Indian Card issued by the Department of Homeland Security with the classification “KIC”

  • Require officials to cancel the voter registration record of an individual who is found to not be a U.S. citizen. Existing law requires removal of the record upon voter request, death, confirmation of the voter moving outside the county, and under a voter removal program.

This resolution, as introduced on April 15, 2025, proposes a constitutional amendment to revise voter qualifications in Pennsylvania. Specifically, the amendment would:

  • Add a requirement that all voters present valid government-issued identification before voting, and provide such ID and a matching signature when voting by mail. Existing law does not impose a constitutional voter ID requirement. Note: A 2012 voter ID law was declared unconstitutional by a Pennsylvania appellate court. The law has not been repealed by the General Assembly, but it is not enforced. Pennsylvania has reverted to the rules that were in place prior to the passage of the voter ID law, which require only those voters who are voting for the first time in an election district to present ID.
  • Require voters to register at least 30 days prior to an election and direct voter registration officials to verify eligibility before allowing registration. Existing law sets the voter registration deadline by statute, not in the constitution.
  • Reduce the state residency requirement for voting from 90 to 30 days before the election and the precinct residency requirement from 60 to 30 days. Existing law requires 30 days of residency in both the state and precinct, but this language would be added to the constitution.

The amendment must pass the legislature in two consecutive sessions before going to voters for approval.

This bill, as introduced on April 15, 2025, would end the permanent mail-in voting list; impose drop box restrictions; create a statewide early voting period; create a voter fraud hotline; prohibit curb-side voting; establish a Voter’s Bill of Rights; and codify online voting, among other changes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • End the permanent mail-in voting list and require voters to apply for mail ballots each election.
  • Place new restrictions on ballot drop-off locations, limiting them to the seven days before an election and requiring bipartisan monitoring, video surveillance, and geographic distribution. Statutes are currently silent on the use of drop boxes, but the secretary of state has issued guidance on their use.
  • Create a statewide early voting period running from the second Friday through the first Wednesday before Election Day, with specific operating rules for early voting centers and satellite offices. Under existing law, a voter may apply for, receive, and return a mail-in ballot in the office of the county board of elections without providing an excuse.
  • Require the secretary of the commonwealth to maintain an election fraud hotline for reporting any known or suspected election fraud or intimidation of election officials and observers. The complaints would be automatically shared with an independent prosecutor and county election integrity officer. Existing law does not require an election fraud hotline.
  • Expressly prohibit several election practices, including: drive-through or curb-side voting, automatic mailing of ballots to voters, ranked choice voting, registering voters without them submitting an application, and participation in the National Popular Vote compact.
  • Create a Voter’s Bill of Rights, along with specific rights for seniors and voters with disabilities, which must be posted at each polling place.
  • Prohibit local and state election officials from accepting private funding for election operations unless distributed by the secretary of state with approval from the Election Law Advisory Board.
  • Require new training for poll watchers.
  • Provide a new election equipment grant program through the Commonwealth Financing Authority and repeal the existing voting apparatus bond program.
  • Establish a new article on voter registration, detailing qualifications, processes for registration (including online voter registration), and revising the SURE system and signature requirements. The bill would authorize an electronic signature for the online application. Online voter registration is currently available but not required by statute. 
  • Require each county to use electronic poll books, provide durable voter ID cards (free of charge) with signature likeness and barcode, and conduct monthly voter roll maintenance, including removing deceased voters and investigating citizenship claims.

The bill includes additional provisions not tracked by Voting Rights Lab related to audits, petitions, judicial intervention, county party coordination, and election equipment.

This bill, as amended on May 12, 2025, would make extensive changes to election law, including expanding voter access by establishing a statewide Election Day-style in-person early voting process; reducing grounds for mail ballot rejection and creating a statewide notice and cure process for mail ballots; requiring the provision of drop boxes for mail ballot return; allowing for an earlier start to ballot processing; and codifying automatic voter registration at the DMV, among other changes. 


Regarding early voting, the bill would:

  • Create a uniform statewide period of Election Day-style in-person early voting, with voting booths and electronic voting systems. Under existing law, the early voting process is limited to casting a mail ballot in person at the county board of elections. The bill's early voting provisions would:
    • Require that in-person early voting be available from the 11th day before Election Day through the Sunday before Election Day, for 8-12 hours a day between the hours of 6:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m., except for certain permitted emergency closures. Under existing law, in-person early voting by mail ballot is available at the county board office from the issuance of mail ballots - generally 50 days before an election - through 5:00 p.m. the Tuesday before Election Day, and is generally available during business hours only on weekdays.
    • Establish requirements for early voting polling places. The bill would:
      • Require counties to provide at least one early voting location, which may be at the office of the county board, and provide an early voting location for every 100,000 registered voters. The bill would require at least one early voting polling place to be located in the same municipality as the county seat, and would permit counties to provide additional polling places at their discretion. 
      • Require early voting be provided in locations eligible to be selected as an Election Day polling place and be accessible to disabled voters. The bill would also specify that counties must consider locations' proximity to public transportation, the availability of parking, travel times, commuter traffic patterns, geographic features affecting access and convenience, population density, existing locations that serve a large number of electors, use of public buildings, cost savings from public buildings, and security considerations. Locations must be published in a newspaper and online no later than 30 days before the election. A list of all locations must also be provided to the secretary of the commonwealth.
      • Permit counties to establish temporary early voting locations with different days and hours of operation than those required for permanent early voting locations. The schedules and locations of such temporary voting locations must be posted on the county board's website.
      • Set out requirements related to early voting place poll workers and poll watchers, and prohibitions related to electioneering and voter privacy.  
  • Permit voters to cast an early ballot at any early voting location in their county. 
  • Require counties to record every voter who votes during early voting and update poll book information to indicate they have cast a ballot. 


Regarding mail ballot voting, the bill would:

  • Create a statewide notice and cure process for missing signatures on mail ballots. While some counties currently provide for notice and cure, existing statutory law has no general requirement or procedure. The bill would:
    • Require election officials to identify mail ballots with missing signatures during pre-processing. 
    • For ballots with missing signatures, require officials to provide notice to the voter within 24 hours by electronic communication or phone if possible, and by letter. The bill would also require counties to publicly post a list of voters whose ballots require cure.
    • Require officials to develop a cure form that can be completed on paper, or by electronic means or telephone. The form must allow the voter to provide a state driver's license number, or last four digits of their Social Security number, or a copy of the following: 
      • Official federal, state, county or municipal document which lists the voter's name
      • Student identification document issued by an institution of higher education in the state
      • Utility bill, telephone bill, bank statement, government check, paycheck or tax or rent receipt which lists the voter's name
    • Set the cure deadline at noon on the sixth day after an election. 
  • Move the deadline earlier for applications for a mail ballot, to 5 p.m. on the 14th day before an election. Under existing law, the application deadline is 5 p.m. on the Tuesday before the election. The bill also modifies the deadline for challenging the validity of a mail ballot application, from 5 p.m. on the Friday before an election, to the earlier of either that time or prior to the pre-canvass of the voter's mail ballot. 
  • Create a permanent mail voter list ("permanent mail-in ballot list"). Under existing law, voters may sign up to automatically receive a mail ballot application each year, which will provide them with a mail ballot for elections in that year. Under the bill, voters on the list would receive mail ballots directly for all future elections, unless they request removal or become ineligible to vote. 
  • Eliminate the date requirement for mail ballot declarations, and reduce grounds for rejecting mail ballots due to markings or damage. The bill would:
    • Eliminate the requirement the mail ballot declarations be dated. Under existing law, declarations must be signed, and following a 2024 court ruling, mail ballots with undated or misdated declarations may not be counted. 
    • Eliminate a ground for mail ballot rejection, by repealing the requirement that a mail ballot must be rejected if it includes any text, mark, or symbol that reveals the voter's identity, political affiliation, or candidate preference. The bill would also provide that ballots that are not sealed in an official envelope must be counted.
    • For mail ballots that are damaged or defective and cannot be counted by tabulation equipment, require officials to create a clearly labeled duplicate ballot to allow for counting.  
  • Require counties to provide drop boxes for mail ballot return, and specify rules for their use. Existing statutory law is silent as to drop boxes, but they have been widely used in past elections by some counties under guidance issued by the secretary of state. The bill would:
    • Require all counties to provide at least two two drop boxes, and require counties with populations over 100,000 to provide additional drop boxes equal to at least one additional drop box for every 50,000 registered voters over 100,000. Counties also may, but are not required to, provide additional drop boxes. Existing guidance has no criteria for numbers of boxes provided.
    • Require drop boxes to be available beginning 30 days before an election, with at least one box available 24 hours a day through the election. Existing guidance has no comparable provisions.  
    • Expressly prohibit counties from prohibiting or inhibiting the use of drop boxes.  
    • Set out requirements for public notice of drop box locations and deadlines for changing locations. Existing guidance has no comparable provisions.
    • Require counties to forward ballots returned to a box outside the voter's county to the proper jurisdiction, and require acceptance of such ballots until 8 p.m. on Election Day. Existing guidance has no comparable provision. 
    • Require video surveillance of drop boxes while they are available, among other security requirements, and require the secretary of state to promulgate additional rules regarding security. Existing guidance requires monitoring of drop boxes, but does not specifically require video surveillance. 
    • Set out requirements related to removal of ballots from drop boxes and chain of custody documentation, generally consistent with existing rules under agency guidance. 
    • Specify the content of signage for drop boxes, including notice of existing restrictions on third party return of mail ballots, criminal penalties for certain prohibited activity with a mail ballot, and notice regarding deposit of a mail ballot outside of a voter's county of residence and potential impact on whether it is counted as timely returned. These requirements expand slightly on existing requirements under agency guidance.
    • Expressly provide that the existing misdemeanor offense for hindering or delaying performance of a duty includes interference with removal of ballots from a drop box or with the deposit of a ballot into a drop box.
  • Provide for paid postage return of mail ballots return and mandate ballot tracking. The bill would:
    • Require prepaid postage for the outer return envelope for mail ballots. Under existing law, counties may, but are not required to, provide prepaid postage. 
    • Require use of USPS Intelligent Mail barcodes on ballots to facilitate ballot tracking.
    • Require the secretary of the commonwealth to develop a mail ballot tracking system. While ballot tracking is currently available, existing statutory law does not require such a system.  


Regarding polling places procedures, the bill would:

  • Eliminate the existing challenge process at polling places, which allows a voter, election officer, overseer, or poll watcher to challenge a voter as to their identity or residency. Under existing law, voters facing such a challenge must present another registered voter to act as witness to affirm their qualification.
  • Allow for the use of digital representation of an accepted form of voter ID, if issued by a system maintained by the state or subdivision, or by an institution of higher education. Existing law requires presentation of ID when voting at a polling place for the first time, and is silent as to the use of digital forms of ID. 
  • Require officials, in the event that a provisional ballot is cast in the wrong election district by a voter registered in the state, to count the ballot as to races for the voter's correct district. Under existing law, a provisional ballot cast in the wrong district is only counted for applicable races if the voter is registered to an address in that county; if the voter is registered elsewhere, the ballot is rejected.
  • Require that county boards of election use electronic poll books that allow real-time tracking of voters by December 31, 2026, at which time they will be used for voter certificates, voting check lists, numbered lists of voters, district registered, and management of voter rolls during elections. The secretary of state would be responsible for creating specifications for electronic poll books and the bill appropriates $7 million to the department of state for counties' procurement of electronic poll books.


Regarding ballot processing, the bill would:

  • Move the start of ballot pre-canvassing earlier, to begin between 9 a.m. on the seventh day before an election, and no later than 7 a.m. on Election Day. Existing law prohibits ballot processing before 7 a.m. on Election Day. The bill would also specify that the pre-canvass meeting may continue until 8 p.m. on Election Day.  
  • Move the start of canvassing earlier, from no later than the third day after an election, to the day after the election.


Regarding voter registration and voter list maintenance, the bill would:

  • Codify the existing availability of automatic voter registration (AVR) at the DMV, and establish new requirements for the process. While existing statutory law provides only for opt-in registration at the DMV, executive action in 2023 established a front-end AVR system at the agency in which applicants are registered unless they affirmatively opt out. For the new statutory AVR process, the bill would:
    • Require all DMV transactions to serve as automatic voter registration for eligible individuals, unless they present documentation or an affirmation demonstrating that they are not a U.S. citizen, or they decline to register. 
    • Require officials to mail notice to all individuals after registration at the DMV, providing the opportunity to choose party affiliation or decline registration. 
    • Make conforming changes related to transmission of data from the DMV to election officials, and modify requirements related to certain address updates. 
  • Simplify procedures for the transfer of voter registration between counties, by eliminating existing requirements for voters to provide notice to election officials and providing for transfer directly between election authorities in certain circumstances. 
  • Designate state institutions of higher education as voter registration agencies, and permit additional offices as designated by the secretary of state. The bill would also amend the registration information form provided by agencies to omit the statement that individuals are not eligible to vote if they have been incarcerated for a felony within the last five years. This eligibility requirement was struck down in 2000. 
  • Expand sources for identification of deceased voters for removal from the voter list. The bill would:
    • Require the Department of Health to provide information to election officials on deaths for residents age 16 and older, and expressly require removal of deceased pre-registered individuals from the voter roll. Existing law requires notice of death for residents age 18 and above and requires removal of registered voters only. 
    • Add ERIC to the additional sources, beyond the Department of Health, that election officials may use to identify deceased voters.  


The bill also includes provisions not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, including changes to requirements for election equipment and election audits.



A previous version of the bill also contained additional provisions that were amended out. They would have:

  • Lowered the age for pre-registration to age 16. Under existing law, otherwise eligible individuals may pre-register if they will be 18 by the next general election.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on June 17, 2025, would impose documentary proof of citizenship requirements for individuals who are automatically registered to vote at the DMV and change the system from front-end to back-end automatic voter registration. Under existing law, individuals are automatically registered to vote during DMV transactions unless they opt out during the transaction, if they provide proof of identity and residence and certify their citizenship through documentation or declaration. Specifically, this bill would:

  • Limit automatic voter registration at the DMV to only those individuals who present documentary proof of U.S. citizenship during an application or renewal of a REAL ID or standard driver's license or personal ID document. DMV officials would be authorized to rely on citizenship documentation submitted in a previous REAL ID application. Submission of such documentation would be considered certification of citizenship for voter registration purposes. Under existing law, the automatic registration requires self-certification of citizenship but does not require documentation. Additionally, existing law does not specify requirements for REAL ID transactions. 
  • Specify that if an applicant does not opt out within 14 days of receiving the notice of their automatic registration, the applicant would be registered to vote. Existing law requires applicants choose whether to opt out during the transaction.
  • End automatic registration for individuals who do not present documentary proof of citizenship and instead provide a two-step, opt-in registration process for these individuals. These applicants would receive a notice and may register by affirmatively certifying their citizenship and returning a signed registration form. Under existing law, applicants may register at the DMV by self-certifying citizenship through declaration without the two-step process.
  • Specify that if the DMV has access to information confirming that an applicant is already registered, the agency would treat the transaction as an address update and transmit that information to election officials, even if the individual did not present citizenship documentation during the current transaction.
  • Exempt from automatic registration individuals using a business address instead of a residential address during their DMV transaction. These individuals would not be offered any registration opportunity under the bill. Under existing law, residency documentation is required, but there is no categorical exclusion for business addresses.
  • Prohibit automatic or streamlined voter registration for individuals who fail to certify, by documentation or declaration, that they are U.S. citizens. The bill would expressly prohibit offering any registration opportunity to individuals who have documented their non-citizenship. Existing law prohibits non-citizens from registering to vote, but does not expressly prohibit offering the registration opportunity in these cases.
  • Expand which additional agencies beyond the DMV may offer automatic voter registration, by permitting agencies to do so if they either collect documentary proof of citizenship or can verify citizenship by database matching or other means deemed reliable by the secretary of state. Existing law limits automatic voter registration to only those non-DMV agencies that verify citizenship through documentation. The bill would also require non-DMV agencies that process transactions for multiple individuals eligible for registration to register each individual according to the procedures applicable to the DMV process.
  • Permit agencies that are not authorized to offer full automatic voter registration to make automatic updates to voter registration address information, if the secretary verifies that the agency collects sufficient information to do so.

Under existing law, a person's right to vote may be challenged only as to whether they are the person they claim to be or on grounds that within 15 days before the election the person has been convicted of a felony or mentally incompetent. The bill would repeal the 15-day provision.
  • Define "resident" as an individual who maintains a "actual fixed, permanent dwelling, establishment, or abode where an individual lives and usually sleeps, for at least 30 consecutive days." Additionally, under the bill, an individual may only have one residence. Existing law defines "residence" as the "place in which a person is domiciled as shown by an actual fixed permanent dwelling, establishment, or any other abode to which the person returns after a period of absence."
  • Make conforming changes to the voter registration form. 
  • Specify that individuals who apply to register to vote using only the address of a commercial mail receiving agency, mail forwarding service, or post office box, without providing a description of the place of their actual habitation will only be registered as a national voter whose eligibility is limited to federal elections.

The bill also includes provisions not tracked by Voting Rights Lab related to candidates.

This bill, as enacted on May 21, 2025:

    • A portal with information related to disenfranchisement due to criminal conviction, using data from the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation. 
  • Requires the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation to share expunged information, upon request, with the coordinator of elections for the purpose of determining an individual's eligibility to register to vote or vote.

Previous versions of the bill contained provisions that were amended out prior to enactment. Those provisions would have:

  • Prohibited a voter from using a temporary driver's license or other temporary state ID as a form of ID when voting. Existing law allows for the use of a "driver's license," with no specified limitations.
  • Prohibited lawful permanent residents of the United States from being able to obtain a permanent Tennessee driver's license, and limited these individuals to temporary forms of ID only.

This bill, as introduced on January 16, 2025 would require individuals registering to vote to provide proof of citizenship, make changes to voter list maintenance procedures, and would make changes to the appeals process for voters flagged as non-citizens. Specifically, the bill would: 

  • Require an applicant to provide an original or a true and correct copy of a birth certificate, a U.S. passport, a U.S. naturalization document, or any document or method of citizenship established by federal law when registering to vote. Under existing law, a voter only needs to check a box stating that they are a citizen.
  • Require an individual registering to vote to attest under penalty of perjury that they meet the requirements for voter eligibility.
  • Require the coordinator of elections to compare the statewide voter registration database with the department of safety database to ensure non-citizens are not registered to vote on a monthly basis. Existing law does not articulate how often this comparison must be done.
  • Require the coordinator of elections to ensure that the citizenship of each registered voter is verified before early voting begins for each election. If the citizenship of an individual who has registered to vote prior to the registration deadline has not been verified, the individual would be allowed to vote a provisional ballot which would not be counted until their citizenship was verified. 
  • Require the coordinator of elections to notify both the state election commission and the county election commission on a monthly basis if sufficient evidence exists that a particular registered voter is not a citizen. Under existing law, the coordinator of elections is only required to notify the county election commission and no timeframe is specified. 
  • Require the county election commission to send notice to any voter flagged as not being a citizen within five business days of receiving notice from the coordinator of elections. The county election commission would be required to send the notice to the address at which the voter is registered by certified mail with return receipt requested. If the county election commission does not receive the return receipt within five business days after the postmark date of the notice, the voter is deemed to have received the notice at such time. Under existing law, the county commission is required to send the notice but no timeframe is specified.
  • Require that if a notice sent by the county election commission is returned as undeliverable, the administrator of elections of the county where the individual is registered would be required to purge the voter from the voter registration database but would be required to maintain the individual's registration and voting history. Under existing law, a voter can be purged from the list for failing to respond to the notice within 30 days of receipt of the notice.
  • Make changes to the appeals process for a voter who wishes to appeal the decision to purge their registration. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Allow a voter who has received notice that they did not provide proper proof of citizenship to appeal to the state election commission no later than 14 days after the county election commission has made their decision. The commission would be prohibited from purging the registration during the appeals process.
    • Require the voter to submit originals or true and correct copies of documentation of citizenship to the state election commission with the voter's notice of appeal.
    • Require the state election commission to conduct a hearing at which the voter must appear in person or by video. The state election commission would be required to enter an order determining whether the individual is a U.S. citizen or not and qualified to vote. If an individual is determined not to be a citizen, that finding would be reported to the district attorney.The determination would be final and subject only to judicial review. Under existing law, an individual who is unable to provide documentation to show proof of citizenship is entitled to appeal to the state election commission and to submit proof of citizenship in person or in writing. The commission is required to conduct a hearing and to forward a copy of its decision to the administrator where the voter lives. 
    • Require that a finding that a person who registered to vote is not a U.S. citizen would be public record. Under existing law, all documentation provided would be confidential and not available for inspection to the public.

This bill would go into effect on July 1, 2025.

This bill, as introduced on January 28, 2025, would make several changes to registration, voter list maintenance, and mail voting. The bill would:

The administrator would be required to maintain a list of suspended voter registrations and a list of restored voter registrations.     • Require the state coordinator of elections to formulate a uniform procedure for automatically verifying the registration eligibility of any individual convicted of an infamous crime and updating the appropriate administrator of elections of any changes to the suspended voter registration list. Upon receiving verification of an individual's eligibility to register, the administrator must allow the individual to become a registered voter or reactivate their registration.

This bill, as enacted on May 2, 2025, modifies the process for restoration of voting rights after disenfranchisement due to a criminal conviction, allowing for restoration of voting separately from other rights of citizenship. Prior statutory law provided for two paths to restoration of voting rights: (1) a "certificate of voting rights restoration," available from incarceration authorities for certain individuals meeting specified criteria, or (2) judicial petition for restoration of "full rights of citizenship," which included voting, gun ownership, and additional civil rights judged together. After a court ruling in 2023 held that restoration of voting rights was permitted only after restoration of full rights of citizenship, the certificate process was effectively moot, as all applicants now had to obtain full citizenship restoration from a court to apply.


This bill eliminates the certificate process from statutory law and modifies the existing court petition process, including authorization for separate consideration of individual rights of citizenship. The bill:

  • Eliminates the certificate of voting rights restoration. Under prior statutory law, this process for restoration of voting rights specifically was available to individuals with convictions after May 1981 (other than for permanently disenfranchising offenses) if they had paid specified costs, or been deemed indigent, and were current with child support obligations. A 2023 court ruling prohibited restoration of voting rights alone, separate from other citizenship rights, making the certificate process substantively moot. The bill eliminates the statutory provisions related to this procedure for restoration, and incorporates most of its substance into the court petition process.
  • Modifies the court petition process to permit a specific determination on restoration of voting rights - separate from restoration of other rights of citizenship - and modifies procedural requirements. The bill:
    • Defines "full rights of citizenship" to include the right to serve on jury, hold public office, hold a fiduciary office, possess a firearm, and vote. Prior statutory law did not include an express definition.
    • Permits petitions for restoration of "rights of citizenship" upon receipt of a pardon, discharge from custody by reason of completed service or expiration of the maximum sentence period, or final discharge by the Board of Parole (or out-of-state/federal equivalent). Under prior law, court petitions were permitted upon a pardon or the end of the maximum sentence period for all convictions, and upon release from incarceration or supervision only for convictions between 1986 and 1996. 
    • Raises the evidentiary standard for restoration petitions, by requiring proof of eligibility by a preponderance of the evidence. Under prior law, for convictions from 1996 onward there was an express presumption in favor of granting a valid petition, and denial was permitted only if a preponderance of the evidence showed ineligibility or good cause. 
    • For convictions after May 1981, requires payment of (1) all court-ordered restitution; (2) beginning in September 2010, all court costs assessed at trial, unless a finding of indigence is made when the petition for restoration is filed; and (3) all child support obligations. Under prior law, these financial requirements applied to certificates of voting rights restoration, but were not generally required for court petitions for full citizenship rights. 
    • Expressly authorizes courts to rule on a petition without a hearing, if prosecutors have raised no objections within 30 days of notice being sent, and to make separate rulings on restoration of various rights of citizenship, such as voting and gun possession. Under prior law, a court could issue a ruling "on the face" of a petition, but there was otherwise no express authorization to forgo a hearing, and courts had no express authority to make separate rulings on voting or other individual civil rights.
    • Expands requirements for notice to prosecutors when a restoration petition is filed, to include notice to the state attorney general and coordinator of elections. Under prior law, notice was required to prosecuting authorities only. 
    • Preserves the other general requirements of the existing court petition process, including permanent disenfranchisement for certain offenses; submission of sworn statements and other documentation of eligibility; procedures for a court to file its final order with state election officials; and procedures for petitioners to file a copy of the order with local election officials to obtain a voter registration card. 
    • For individuals who received restoration by court order prior to the enactment of the bill, sets out procedures for verification of restoration.  
    • Requires state officials to develop forms for the petition for restoration, and for final judicial orders of restoration. 
  • Expressly requires an individual to have voting rights restored for "each felony conviction" to be eligible to register and vote. While the certificate of voting rights restoration application under prior law specified that a separate request must be made for each conviction, prior statutory law did not expressly state this requirement.  
  • Automatically restores voting rights "by operation of law" on the effective date of the act, for convictions prior to January 15, 1973. (NB: Because no crimes were designated for disenfranchisement between 1973 and 1981, convictions in this period do not require restoration.)

This bill, as introduced on February 5, 2025, would modify UOCAVA voting procedures, including creating new requirements for documentary proof of citizenship for first-time registrant voters, creating a UOCAVA ballot witness requirement, and expressly providing for notice of application deficiencies and ballot tracking, among other changes. Specifically, the bill would:

Under the bill, the following documents would be accepted as proof of citizenship:
    • REAL ID document that indicates U.S. citizenship
    • Valid, unexpired U.S. passport
    • U.S. military ID with military record of service showing U.S. as place of birth
    • Valid ID issued by federal, state, or tribal government showing U.S. as place of birth
    • Other form of government-issued ID with additional specified documentation showing U.S. as place of birth
  • Create a new documentary proof of overseas residence requirement for civilian overseas voters and federal-only ballot voters. Existing law has no comparable documentation requirement. The bill specifies that accepted documentation would include:
    • Copy of a current, valid lease or title to a residence not located in the United States, bearing the name and overseas address of the applicant
    • Copy of financial records, such as a bank account, tax return, or other record from a financial agency or institution bearing the name and overseas address of the applicant
    • Document or official record of a foreign government bearing the name and overseas address of the applicant
  • Mandate changes to the state-specific instructions for the federal postcard application, reflecting new documentary proof of citizenship rules.
  • Create a new affidavit and witness requirement for UOCAVA ballots. Existing law has no comparable requirements. The bill would require voters to sign an affidavit attesting to eligibility for UOCAVA voting, witnessed by two individuals aged 18 or older.  
  • Create new procedures related to notice and cure of UOCAVA application deficiencies. Existing law has no express requirements related to cure for UOCAVA applications with missing information. The bill would:
    • Require counties to notify UOCAVA applicants if their ballot application is missing a Tennessee residency address, overseas/current mailing address, voter ID, or documentary proof of citizenship. Officials would be required to contact the individual by email or phone if possible, and record attempts at contact, and the bill would expressly prohibit acceptance of an application lacking necessary documentation of citizenship and/or overseas residence.
    • For applications from individuals who are ineligible or have not provided documentary proof of citizenship, require counties to reject the application and notify the applicant of the grounds, and preserve records of notice for two years. 
    • Specify that a UOCAVA mail ballot application may not be rejected solely due to a mismatch between the identifying information of the voter on the application and the identifying information on file. Instead, the bill would require officials to provide the voter a provisional ballot that would be counted if (1) the ballot is received by the close of polls on Election Day, and (2) the voter provides an affidavit and necessary documentation before the close of the provisional ballot verification period. If the provisional ballot was rejected, the bill would require officials to notify the voter.
  • Require the secretary of state to establish procedures to allow a military or overseas voter or federal-only voter to apply for a mail ballot electronically.
  • Specify requirements for the processing of federal postcard applications, including delivery of a ballot to voters by email.
  • Require the secretary of state, in coordination with the county election commissions, to establish a free ballot tracking system for UOCAVA voters to determine the status of their ballot request and ballot return, any ballot deficiencies, and whether their ballot was counted. The state's existing ballot tracking system includes information on when a UOCAVA ballot is received, but statutory law does not expressly require additional information. 
  • Expressly prohibit electronic UOCAVA ballot return. 
  • Require recording of ballot counts by category of UOCAVA voter, and public reporting and access to data. 
  • Establish specific definitions for UOCAVA voters in the state. Existing statutory law has no express definitions for these categories. The bill would:
    • Define "civilian overseas voter" as U.S. citizen who:
      • Was last domiciled in the state
      • Temporarily lives outside of the U.S. or is outside the U.S. when the polls are open
      • Is not registered to vote in another state
      • Maintains a residence in the state
      • Otherwise satisfies the voter eligibility requirements in the state
    • Define "federal-only voter" as a U.S. citizen who:
      • Was last domiciled in the state
      • Indefinitely or permanently resides outside of the U.S.
      • Before establishing a principal residence outside of the U.S., established a principal place of residence in the state
      • Did not register to vote in another state or establish a principal place of residence in another state 
      • Satisfies the requirements for voter eligibility
    • Define a "military voter" as a U.S. citizen who is:
      • A member of the (1) Active or reserve components of the U.S. military; (b) National guard or the Tennessee National Guard; or (c) Merchant marine of the United States, and their spouse
      • Maintains a residence in the state
      • Otherwise satisfies the voter eligibility requirements in the state

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on June 20, 2025, creates several new misdemeanors in relation to the assistance of voters, among other changes. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires curbside voters to sign a form affirming their need to vote curbside, and specifying that election officers can help curbside voters complete their ballot under only very limited circumstances. A person who knowingly fails to complete the oath would commit a misdemeanor.
  • Changes the requirements for a person who assists seven or more voters by providing transportation to the polling place. Under previous law, a person was required to sign a form describing the nature of their assistance if they provide seven or more voters with simultaneous transportation to the polls. Under the bill, the form is required if the person provides seven or more voters with transportation to the polls across the entire early voting period and Election Day. A person who intentionally failed to complete the form would commit a misdemeanor. The bill also requires each county clerk to report on these assistants to the secretary of state.
  • Modifies the rules for voters voting curbside. Under previous law, a curbside voter was assisted by an election officer. Under the bill, if at least four election officers are present at a polling place, the assistance is required to be provided by two of them. The bill also specifies that an election officer may not assist in marking the bill unless specifically authorized by law.
  • Change the requirements for a voter assistant required to fill out a form describing the nature of their assistance. The bill would remove the exemption for election officers and would also provide that a person who knowingly fails to complete the form commits a misdemeanor.
  • Permits a voter, if the voter is escorting another person who is physically unable to enter the polling place, to vote curbside. Under previous law, only persons who are themselves physically unable to enter a polling place were permitted to vote curbside.
  • Expands the existing prohibition on electioneering near a polling place to provide that electioneering is also prohibited within 20 feet of a parking space that is reserved for curbside voting. The bill also expands the associated misdemeanor offense accordingly.

Specifically, the bill would:

    • U.S. passport or passport card

    • U.S. citizenship papers
    • Identification issued by the agency of the United States responsible for citizenship and immigration
    • Certificate of report of birth or consular report of birth abroad issued by the U.S. Department of State
  • Require registrars to verify the citizenship status of registration applicants who have not submitted proof of citizenship with their application. Under this process:
    • Registrars would be required, within 10 days after the submission of an application that lacks proof of citizenship, to use "all available resources" to verify the applicant's citizenship status, including specified state and federal databases.
    • For applicants whose citizenship is confirmed, registrars would be required to complete the registration.
    • For applicants whose citizenship status cannot be determined, registrars would be required to approve them for a limited federal ballot and provide the voter notice, including instructions for documenting citizenship to receive a full ballot. 
    • For applicants who are confirmed to be non-U.S. citizens, the registrar would be required to reject the application, notify the applicant of the rejection, and forward the application to the attorney general and the county attorney for potential prosecution.

    • For registrants whose citizenship could not be verified, registrars would notify the voter that they are required to vote a limited federal ballot until they have provided accepted proof of citizenship. 
    • For registrants who are confirmed to be non-citizens, registrars would be required to notify the voter, and to cancel their registration if documentation was not received within 30 days.

Under these provisions, voters designated for a limited federal ballot would be required to provide proof of citizenship not later than the sixth day after election day for their ballot to be counted as a full ballot. This bill, as enacted on May 24, 2025, modifies and expands existing grounds for the combination of election precincts. Under prior law, combination of precincts was permitted by recommendation of a county board for counties with a population of 1.2 million or less that do not participate in the countywide polling place program, if (1) the commissioners court could not find a suitable polling location; (2) the needs of all impacted voters were met; (3) changes did not impact groups covered by the Voting Rights Act. Such a combined precinct could contain up to 10,000 voters (standard precincts may contain up to 5,000).  


The bill:

  • Modifies the existing criteria for combining precincts: 
    • Eliminates the population requirement to qualify for this type precinct combination. Under the bill, the only requirement is that the county not participate in the countywide polling place program.
    • Permits combination by recommendation of a party executive committee for primary elections. Prior law allowed for recommendation by a county board only. 
  • Permits precinct combination under a new set of criteria, in addition to the existing grounds. The bill newly authorizes combination by recommendation of the commissioners court, or the county party executive for a primary, if a redistricting plan has resulted in county precincts with fewer than 3,000 registered voters and the consolidation is necessary to avoid unreasonable expenditure. A combined precinct under these new criteria may not exceed the maximum precinct size under existing law, which is 5,000 registered voters.
  • Specifies requirements for allocation of election judges in combined precincts. Existing law had no express provisions concerning allocation.

This bill, as enacted on June 22, 2025, shifts the early voting period later and standardizes requirements for weekend early voting, and modifies requirements for combining voting precincts, among other changes. Specifically, the bill:

  • Moves the early voting period later. Under existing law in effect until 2027, early voting for most elections begins on the 17th day before the election and runs through the 4th day before the election, and for the May election runs from the 12th day and runs through the 4th. Under the bill, beginning in 2027:
    • Early voting for most elections will begin on the 12th day before the election.
    • Early voting for the May election will begin on the 9th day before the election.
    • Early voting for all elections will end on the day before Election Day, and the period must include weekends and holidays. 
  • Standardizes the hours that early voting is offered on weekend days. Under existing law in effect until 2027, early voting on a Saturday or Sunday may be ordered by the authority administering the election, except that in a primary election or the general election for state and county officers there must be at least 12 hours of voting on the last Saturday of the early voting period and at least six hours on the last Sunday. Under the bill, beginning in 2027, early voting will instead be offered as follows:
    • Voting on the first weekend of the early voting period must be conducted for the same amount of time as voting during the week - a minimum of nine hours per day, no earlier than 6 a.m. or later than 10 p.m.
    • Voting on the last four days of the early voting period must be conducted for at least 12 hours on each day, except that voting would be required to be offered for only nine hours on the Sunday before the election.
  • Repeals various provisions to conform with the creation of an uninterrupted early and regular voting period for most elections.
  • Regarding polling places and precinct drawing, the bill:
    • Requires each polling place used during early voting to be used as a polling place on election day. Prior law had no comparable requirement. 
    • Repeals a provision of law that limits the number of counties that may participate in the countywide polling place program.
    • Permits the consolidation of county election precincts with fewer than 3,000 registered voters if the small precinct is the result of changed boundaries after redistricting and the consolidation is necessary to avoid unreasonable expenditure. The bill limits a precinct that is consolidated in this way to the maximum size prescribed by current law, which is 5,000 registered voters.
    • Changes the rules for the combination of precincts. Under existing law, a county with a population of less than 1.2 million that does not participate in the countywide polling place program may combine precincts for a general or special election if no suitable polling place exists within the boundaries of a precinct and the combined polling place will adequately serve the needs of the combined precincts, as long as the combined precinct has 10,000 voters or fewer. Under the bill:
      • A county that does not participate in the countywide polling place program may combine precincts for a general or special election, provided the combined precinct has 10,000 voters or fewer.
      • The county executive committee of a political party conducting the primary election may combine precincts for a primary election, provided the combined precinct has 10,000 voters or fewer.
      • A county that has more than one combined precinct under this provision must ensure that the number of voters residing in the smallest combined precinct is no smaller than 95 percent of the largest combined precinct.
  • Consolidates the processing for ballots voted in person during the early voting period and those voted on the day of the election.
  • Changes the rules for security of voted ballots to conform to the changes made by the changes in the early voting period.

The bill also includes additional provisions related to topics that Voting Rights Lab does not track. 


A previous version of the bill also included additional provisions that were amended out prior to enactment. Those provisions would have removed age as a grounds of eligibility for mail voting and permitted disabled voters to vote in person at the county clerk's office on Election Day during the hours a polling place is open for voting.

Specifically, the bill:
