This bill, as introduced on October 29, 2025, would allow all voters to join the permanent mail voting list. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Allow any voter to join the permanent mail voting list and eliminate the existing permanent mail voting list beginning on January 1, 2029. Under existing law, only voters who are indefinitely confined because of age, physical illness, infirmity, or disability are eligible to join the list. The bill would make nonsubstantive and conforming changes because of this provision.
  • Allow voters to stay on the permanent mail voting list even if they do not return a mail ballot. Under existing law, voters who fail to return a mail ballot are sent a notice informing them that they must renew their application within 30 days or be removed from the list.
  • Require voters to present unexpired proof of identification with their application in order to join the permanent mail voting list. Existing law requires that mail ballots be received no later than the day after Election Day or postmarked on or before Election Day and received by the start of the vote canvass (five days after the election, not counting Sundays).

This bill, as introduced on February 12, 2025, would amend existing statutory language to reflect that voter registration applicants must provide a driver’s license number or state ID number, if issued, and in all other cases must provide the last four digits of their Social Security number. The bill would leave in place the provision that if a person does not have any of the three forms of identification, the secretary of state must assign the applicant a number which will serve to identify them for voter registration purposes.

This bill, as amended on March 6, 2025, would:

  • Move the receipt deadline earlier for ballots returned by mail, to 7:30 p.m. on Election Day. Existing law requires that mail ballots be received no later than the day after Election Day, or postmarked on or before Election Day and received by the start of the vote canvass (five days after the election, not counting Sundays).
  • Prohibit any person, including an election official, from sending a mail ballot application to a voter without a request from the voter, or their family member or caregiver. Existing law is silent as to providing a mail ballot application without a specific request.
  • Create a new misdemeanor offense for:
    • An election official knowingly and intentionally sending a mail ballot application to a voter, their family member or caregiver, without the voter's request
    • Any individual other than an election official knowingly and intentionally sending more than 10 mail ballot applications to a group of voters without their request

The bill would also allow the legislature to intervene as a party in lawsuits concerning the legality or constitutionality of election laws or regulations. This would include cases involving unauthorized changes made through settlement agreements or consent decrees. Existing law does not include a similar provision.

This bill, as introduced on February 12, 2025, would:

This bill, as introduced on February 17, 2025, would:

    • Requiring every county to establish drop boxes for mail ballots. Each county would be required to have at least one drop box per every 10,000 active registered voters. Drop boxes would have to be available at each in-person early voting location and be open from the date that mail ballots are sent to voters until the close of the polls on Election Day.
    • Limiting third-party return of mail ballots so that any person may deliver a maximum of ten ballots in any election.
  • Eliminating the requirement that a disabled voter who wishes to vote by electronic mail ballot must provide written confirmation from a healthcare provider of the voter's disability.
    • Eliminating a lack of secrecy envelope as a basis for rejecting a mail ballot.
    • Eliminating a perceived signature mismatch as a basis for rejecting a mail ballot.
    • Require mail ballot return envelopes to include a list of requirements for voting in plain language with space for the voter to acknowledge and declare adherence to those requirements by signing their name.
    • Allowing counties to pre-canvass mail ballots beginning on the seventh day before Election Day. Pre-canvassing would include inspecting the voter declaration on the envelope, opening envelopes and removing ballots, preparing ballots for counting, and counting, computing, and tallying votes. Pre-canvassing would not include recording or publishing vote totals.
  • Create a cure process between Election Day and the time for canvassing ballots (five days after Election Day) by requiring the county clerk to mail a voter a notice of deficiency describing the problem with any ballot challenged during the processing.   • Change Election Day in-person voting by:
    • Eliminating the requirement that signature verification be conducted on provisional ballots and instead require merely that election authorities can determine that the voter was eligible to cast a ballot.
    • Eliminating the ability of election workers to challenge a ballot because the voter who voted it received third-party assistance but was not entitled to the assistance. The bill would also eliminate the corresponding authorization for such challenged voters to cast a provisional ballot after the challenge.
    • Eliminating signature mismatch between the poll book and the registration record as a basis for challenging a voter and forcing that voter to vote a provisional ballot.
  • Create new misdemeanor offenses covering:
    • A person who uses force or coercion to cause a voter to vote in a manner contrary to the voter's choice or intent or to refrain from voting or to impede a voter's choice when marking a ballot.

This bill, as enacted on March 26, 2025, expands the express terms of the existing qualifications for eligibility to vote. Prior law provided that citizens of the state were permitted to vote, with the exception of prohibitions on those who were: not registered; of minor age (with the exception of voting in a primary election for a general election by which they are age 18); declared mentally incompetent by the court; "under conviction of" treason, felony, or bribery in an election; not a bona fide resident of the state, county, or municipality where they appear to vote. 


The bill revises the qualifications to provide additional detail and scope to requirements, establishing that any citizen of the state may vote, "unless the person" is:

  • Not registered, as under prior law
  • Age 18, with the exception of voting in a primary for a general election by which they will be age 18, as under prior law
  • Determined by a court to be (1) totally mentally incompetent, or (2) partially incompetent without the right to vote. The bill specifies that requalification to vote requires documentation by court order that must include the voter's signature. Prior law did not specify the types of adjudication or specify requalification procedures. 
  • Not convicted of treason, a felony, or bribery in an election, or if convicted, has (1) had their sentence fully discharged including any period of incarceration, parole, supervision, or probation, or (2) been pardoned or otherwise released from disenfranchisement. Prior law noted only being under conviction, without further detail. The bill further specifies:
  • Disenfranchisement begins on the date of adjudication, regardless of pending post-conviction proceedings. 
  • Individuals are not "convicted" of an offense for the purposes of voting eligibility if proceedings are deferred and there is no adjudication of guilt. 
  • A U.S. citizen; prior law required citizenship elsewhere as a qualification to vote, but did not expressly include the requirement in this provision. 
  • Bona fide resident of the jurisdiction where they appear to vote, as under prior law

This bill, as enacted on March 21, 2025, imposes a documentary proof of citizenship requirement on all voter registration applicants, among other changes. Under prior law, all applicants were required to sign a registration oath swearing to their eligibility, including citizenship, before a notary (with a notary exception for individuals subject to UOCAVA). For applicants who do not have an in-state driver's license or Social Security number, required forms of alternative ID include various documents that verify citizenship, but documentary proof is not otherwise generally required. In addition to these existing requirements, the bill:

  • Requires all voter registration applicants to present documentary proof of US citizenship when applying, limited to one of the following:
    • Wyoming driver's license or state ID card that does not indicate the person is a noncitizen, or a REAL ID issued by another state that does not indicate that the person is not a U.S. citizen
    • U.S. passport
    • U.S. birth certificate bearing an official seal, original or certified copy
    • Consular report of birth abroad issued by the U.S. department of state
    • Valid tribal identification card issued by a federally recognized tribe that does not indicate the person is a noncitizen
    • Certificate of U.S. citizenship or naturalization
    • U.S. military draft record or a selective service registration acknowledgment card

HISTORY: {"date":"05/07/2026","summary":"Additionally referred to HOUSE Committee on FINANCE","meta":["[]"],"order":0}
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on May 7, 2026, would layer signature verification on top of existing absentee voting verification requirements, create a cure program for some rejected absentee ballots; make changes to accepted forms of voter ID; require new routine list maintenance procedures and modified the existing annual procedure; create new criminal and civil penalties related to elections; and make various other changes. 


Concerning mail ballot voting, the bill would:

  • Add voter signature verification to existing requirements for absentee ballot verification. Existing law requires absentee voters to have a witness or notary sign their absentee ballot envelope. The bill would maintain that requirement and also require election officials to compare the voter's signature on the absentee ballot envelope to the voter's registration record.
    • The bill would require the use of signature verification software and the signature comparison training for local election officials.
  • Create a cure process for mail ballots that are rejected due to a missing or mismatched voter signature. Under existing law, voters are notified when their mail ballot is rejected, but there is no statewide process for curing defects. Under the new process: 
    • If a ballot is rejected, officials must contact the voter explaining the ballot deficiency, how the deficiency may be cured, and the deadline to cure the ballot. Notice must be sent within 48 hours (and no later than two days after Election Day) by mail, and may be provided by email, text, or telephone if the voter provided that information. The notice must include a printed form for the voter to provide a signature for verification and copy of voter ID for ballot verification.
    • The cure deadline would be 14 days after Election Day, and a rejected ballot would be counted if the voter confirmed that they returned a ballot, and provided a signature and copy of voter ID, and the ballot was otherwise valid. 
    • If the voter indicates on the cure form that they did not return a ballot, the bill would authorize the director of elections to send the signature on the return ballot to the attorney general for investigation.
  • Require officials to provide mail ballot voters with a postage-paid return envelope. Under existing law, voters must pay for postage to return a mail ballot.
  • Move the receipt deadline earlier for all mail ballots returned from outside the U.S. or by UOCAVA voters, to the 10th day after an election. Under existing law, the receipt deadline is the 10th day after a primary or special primary, and the 15th day after a general election or special election. 
  • Move the start of mail ballot processing earlier, from seven days before Election Day to 12 days before. 
  • Require the director of elections to create a procedure for challenging mail ballots, special needs ballots, and questioned ballots during the counting process, that provides a "reasonable amount of time" to submit a challenge. Existing law is silent as to a challenge process. 
  • Require officials to provide an online ballot tracking system that allows voters to know the date a ballot was sent out by officials, delivered, and received back by officials; whether the ballot was counted; and steps required to cure a defective ballot. The bill would specify that any vendor for the system must be a business incorporated in the U.S., and that the system must use multi-factor authentication. Online ballot tracking is not required under existing law, but the state currently provides information online as to delivery and return of ballots, and provides notice to a voter when a ballot is rejected.  
  • Specify that for the existing requirement that completed mail ballots be delivered by local officials to election supervisors for processing "by the most expeditious mail service," such service includes delivery by optical scanning and electronic transmission.

Concerning voter ID, the bill would:

  • Change the list of accepted ID for voter registration and casting a ballot.
    • For registration, the bill would eliminate use of a hunting or fishing license, and add tribal ID to accepted ID. The bill would leave in place the remaining forms of accepted ID: driver's license; state ID card; current and valid photo ID; birth certificate; passport; or waiver of the ID requirement by a registration official who knows the identity of the voter.
    • For voting in person (and certain first-time mail ballot voters), the bill would eliminate use of a hunting or fishing license, and add tribal ID to accepted ID. The bill would leave in place some remaining forms of accepted ID: driver's license; state ID card; current and valid photo ID; birth certificate; passport. The bill would also repeal existing language allowing the use of a utility bill, bank statement, government check, or other government document showing the voter's name and current address, the document must be dated within the previous 60 days. Existing law requires only that these documents be "current."

Concerning voter list maintenance, the bill would:

  • Permit the Division of Elections to use information provided by the Department of Revenue to conduct voter roll maintenance. Existing law has no comparable provision. The bill would also require the Division to submit an annual report to the governor, state secretary, and chief clerk of the House of Representatives annually detailing the number of permanent fund dividend applicant records shared with the division; the effect that shared permanent fund dividend applications had on voter roll maintenance and on election integrity; and security measures taken to protect voter information.
  • Expand the categories of voters who receive an address confirmation notice during annual list maintenance of the voter roll, and shorten the timeframe for inactivating a registration. Under existing law, non-forwardable notice is sent to voters who (1) have had mail returned to election officials as undeliverable in the last two years, or (2) have not contacted the Election Division in the last two years, or (3) have not voted or appeared in vote in the last two general elections. The bill would:
    • Modify the existing categories of voters receiving notice by requiring confirmation from voters who have not contacted the election division in the last two years and also have not voted or appeared in vote in the last 28 months, rather than each category of voters separately, as required under existing law. The bill also expressly provides that registering to vote does not constitute "contact" with the division. Existing law specifies various actions that constitute contact, but is silent as to registration.
    • Expand the categories of voters that receive a confirmation notice to additionally include voters who: 
      • During the last 28 months, (1) registered to vote in another state, (2) received a driver's license in another state, (3) registered a vehicle in another state, (4) received public assistance from another state, (5) served on a jury in another state, (6) received a homestead or residential property tax exemption in another state, or (7) received a benefit available only to residents of another state.
    • Require that confirmation notices be sent by forwardable mail and to the voter's email address, if available. Under existing law, initial confirmation notice must be sent by non-forwardable mail only. 
    • Require officials to inactivate a voter's registration if the voter fails to respond to the confirmation notice or provides an incomplete or ambiguous response within 45 days, and require notice to state the response deadline. Under existing law, officials may only inactivate a voter's registration if (1) an initial confirmation notice is returned as undeliverable, and the voter has not contacted the election division or voted or appeared to vote in the last four years; and (2) the voter fails to respond to a second confirmation notice, sent by forwardable mail, within 45 days.
  • Require new routine list maintenance procedures, in addition to the existing annual address confirmation process. The bill would require the adoption of regulations to review voter registrations and update the master register, and direct the Division of Elections to:
    • Review the list for deceased voters, voters convicted of a felony involving moral turpitude, voters not qualified to vote, voters registered to vote in another state, whether the number of registered voters on the master list exceeds the number of eligible voters in the state, and voter registration information data breaches. 
    • Gather and examine available data from other states and information from the USPS forwarding databases, motor vehicle records, Department of Corrections records, property and sales tax records, U.S. Social Security Administration databases, jury duty records, national change of address records, and similar records. 
    • Annually audit the master register in consultation with an external, nationally recognized subject-matter expert. The division would be required to publish a report describing the audit by April 1 of each year.
    • Specify requirements for notice to voters under the removal provisions, and authorize the division to contact a voter and request information from the voter to determine their residence, in addition to issuing a required notice. 

Concerning voter registration, the bill would:

  • Expand grounds for challenges to a voter based on their residence. Under existing law, the address of a voter on their registration record is presumptive evidence of their voting residence, and may only be negated by the voter changing their residence in writing. Under the bill, the presumption may also be rebutted by providing evidence to the division that the voter has established residence in another country, state, or place in Alaska.
  • Require officials to post data about any breach of confidential voter information, and specify the scope and timing for such reports. 
  • Repeal a provision allowing an elections official to substitute a mailing address provided by a voter for the Permanent Fund Dividend program as the mailing address for the voter's registration record. 


Concerning criminal and civil penalties related to elections, the bill would:

  • Create a new class C felony for intentionally opening or tampering with a submitted mail ballot or package of ballots without express authorization from the director or intentionally breaching, hacking, altering, or tampering with election machinery. 
  • Create a new class C felony for knowingly disclosing, sharing, or reporting official election results, returns, or any confidential election data to an individual who is not an election official before the close of polls on Election Day.
  • Prohibit the use of "synthetic media" in electioneering activity with the intent to influence an election, and create a private right of action for individuals harmed by its use. The bill would set out definitions for prohibited and exempt conduct, defenses, and forms of relief. 

Concerning election outreach, data security, and observation of counting processes, the bill would:

  • Require the elections director to employ a rural community liaison responsible for collaborating with tribes, municipalities, corporations, regional nonprofit corporations, and other community organizations to facilitate access to early and mail voting in rural areas of the state and ensuring that rural areas of the state are fully staffed.
  • Require the Division of Elections to provide a report to the legislature by the first day of the 35th Legislature recommending options for expanding early voting in rural communities and low-income neighborhoods.

The bill also contains additional provisions related to topics that Voting Rights Lab does not track.


The new signature comparison and cure provisions for absentee ballots would be effective on June 1, 2027.

The resolution would also commit the legislature to monitoring the implementation of any federal voter registration requirements to ensure that no eligible Alaska citizen is denied the right to vote by citizenship documentation barriers.

This constitutional amendment, as enacted on June 12, 2026, would, if approved by voters, make the following changes:

  • Require all voters to provide government-issued identification before voting in person or by mail. Under existing law, Arizona requires in-person voters to provide ID before receiving a ballot, and mail voters ("early voters") prove identity through signature verification. This bill would also limit the forms of identification currently allowed in statute by prohibiting the use of non-government-issued identification, such as a bank statement, to verify a voter's identity.
  • Require all voting locations to provide on-site tabulation – including during early in-person voting. Under current law, counties may provide on-site tabulation, but are not required to do so.
  • Provide that only citizens of the United States are eligible to vote for any office or ballot measure in any election in Arizona. This is the same as existing law.
  • Require elections to be decided solely by citizens. Under current law, only citizens are eligible to vote.
  • Stipulate that any laws enacted by the people or the legislature must be reasonably connected to legitimate state interests, including timely and accurate election results, efficient election administration, election security, and public confidence in elections. Current law is silent on this issue.

In order to go into effect, this bill needs to be approved by a majority of voters at the November 2026 general election.

Under existing law, voters may return their mail ("early") ballots in person and by mail through the close of polls on Election Day; voters may also cast early ballots in person through 7 p.m. on the Friday before Election Day, but counties may offer emergency in-person voting on the Saturday, Sunday, and Monday before Election Day.

  • Required all voters to provide government-issued identification "concurrent" with casting a ballot. Under existing law, Arizona requires in-person voters to provide ID before receiving a ballot, but mail voters ("early voters") are not required to provide ID and are instead subject to signature verification.

  • Extend the early in-person voting period by moving the end date later, to the Monday before Election Day. Under existing law, early in-person voting ends on the Friday before an election, with limited emergency voting available through the following Monday. As a conforming change, the resolution would also eliminate this emergency voting period. 
  • Move the deadline earlier for return of a mail ballot to a drop box or a voting location, and require voter ID for return during certain times.
    • For return of a mail ballot at a drop box or voting location, the bill would move the deadline from 7pm on Election Day to 7pm on the Friday before the election. 
    • After 7pm on the Friday before an election, in-person ballot return to a voting location would require voters to present an accepted form of voter ID. Existing law permits these voters to present ID in lieu of signature verification but does not require voters to do so. 
  • Expressly permit on-site vote tabulation of mail ballots at early voting locations. Existing law provides for on-site tabulation at Election Day voting locations only. 
  • Require election officials to ensure that chain of custody procedures for early ballots are the same as those for in-person Election Day voting.
  • Eliminate the existing requirement that county recorders count the number of early ballots that are returned at voting locations on Election Day and post those totals with the last unofficial results released on election night.
  • Repeal the requirement that the county recorder "take necessary steps" to contact a voter if their pre-election notice letter is returned as undeliverable, prior to placing the voter in inactive status and removing them from the permanent mail voting list.
  • Prohibit the use of foreign money, goods, or services for election administration, create record keeping requirements, and create a civil enforcement action for violations. Existing law prohibits the use of private monies, but is silent as to foreign sources. The bill would:
    • Prohibit any government entity in the state from using money or in-kind goods or services donated by a foreign government or non-governmental source for election administration.
    • Require that all entities that provide services to the government for election administration certify to the secretary of state on an annual basis that they have not accepted such money or services, and require all government entities to provide a quarterly report listing all parties that provide election services.
    • Create a class 1 misdemeanor for knowingly failing to provide accurate or updated certification to the secretary of state.
    • Create a civil right of action for any voter to enjoin or enforce the new provisions, including specified damages for violations. 
  • Eliminate the use of emergency voting centers. 
  • Repeal a provision granting a public school principal authority to deny a request for their school to serve as a voting location based on space not being available or the safety or welfare of the children being at risk.

This bill also includes provisions relating to foreign contributions to ballot measure campaigns that Voting Rights Lab does not track.


Final approval of changes proposed by this resolution requires passage by the legislature and approval by a majority of voters at the November 2026 general election.

The bill would take effect following the standard period following adjournment of the general assembly, unless referred to voters by a referendum petition. In that case, the bill or provisions would not take effect until approved by the voters at the November 2026 general election.

AUTHORNAME: Joint Committee on Government Administration and Elections
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as enacted on May 15, 2026, establishes no-excuse mail ballot voting; creates a permanent mail ballot application list; establishes a cure process for missing signatures on mail ballot envelopes; establishes risk-limiting audits; and creates new election interference offenses, among other changes. Specifically, the bill:

  • Expands access to mail ("absentee") voting and modifies mail voting procedures:
    • Establishes no-excuse mail ballot voting. Prior law required voters to provide a qualifying excuse, such as physical disability, sickness, or out-of-town absence, to vote by mail.
    • Establishes a permanent mail voting application list available to all voters. Under the bill, any voter can request permanent mail status to automatically be issued a mail ballot application prior to all future elections. Under prior law, permanent mail voting status was restricted to voters with a permanent physical disability or long-term illness certified by a medical provider. The bill requires the removal of a voter from the permanent application list if their ballot application is returned as undeliverable, they submit a National Change of Address form indicating a move out of state, registrars receive official data they moved or registered in another state, or they are placed on the inactive registry list. A previous version of the bill would have created a true permanent mail voter list, where opted-in voters would have been mailed a ballot for all future elections without needing to submit an application for each election.
    • Allows voters to apply for an absentee ballot through an online system maintained by the secretary of the state by importing the applicant's signature from the Department of Motor Vehicles.
    • Establishes a cure process for missing signatures on mail ballot return envelopes. The bill requires the municipal clerk to use "best efforts" (including phone and email) to contact the voter within 24 hours. The voter is permitted to cure the ballot by appearing in person at the clerk's office until the close of polls on Election Day. Under prior law, unsigned ballots were simply marked "rejected" with no explicit cure process.
    • Eliminates the "inner envelope" for mail ballots and simplifies instructions. The bill requires voters to place their marked ballot directly into a single return envelope accompanied by a privacy sleeve. Municipal clerks are also required to include a new simplified instruction sheet. Prior law required a separate inner envelope and lacked the simplified instruction mandate.
    • Establishes procedures for municipal clerks to mail applications directly to voters with their name and barcode pre-printed, centralizing the process. Prior law had no comparable provisions.
    • Requires the secretary of the state to develop and install integrated statewide ballot-tracking software. The software allows voters to track the status of their application and ballot. Prior law had no comparable statutory requirement.
    • Requires registration for mail ballot application distributors. Individuals who distribute five or more mail ballot applications are required to register with the municipal clerk, subject to certain exemptions. Prior law did not require distributors to register.
    • Establishes specific application forms for incarcerated voters. The bill mandates the creation of a specifically designated, consecutively numbered mail ballot application form exclusively for voters incarcerated in a Department of Correction facility, containing a dedicated space for the applicant's facility mailing address. Prior law had no comparable requirement.
    • Requires disclosures on unsolicited mail ballot applications. Candidates, parties, or committees mailing unsolicited applications are required to include a disclaimer stating who paid for and approved the mailing. Prior law required only a warning about eligibility requirements and penalties.
    • Mandates video surveillance of drop boxes. Municipalities are required to provide a video recording device for each secure drop box by July 1, 2025, capturing the location, date, and time. Prior law did not expressly mandate video surveillance for drop boxes.
    • Requires the State Elections Enforcement Commission to prepare a summary of mail voting laws for public dissemination. Prior law had no comparable requirement.
    • Establishes a task force to study mail ballot access and delivery methods in unconsolidated cities and boroughs.
  • Modifies audits and other post-election procedures:
    • Replaces the standard manual audit for state elections with risk-limiting audits (RLAs). Beginning in 2027, RLAs featuring a maximum 5% risk limit are required to be used. The bill requires the secretary of the state to order a full manual recount of all ballots for an office if an RLA produces an "INCONCLUSIVE" outcome. Prior law relied on manual or electronic audits of a random 5% of voting districts.
    • Creates an RLA pilot program for the 2026 state election. The secretary of the state is required to randomly select three municipalities of varying population sizes to participate. Prior law had no comparable provision.
    • Requires the results of municipal manual or electronic audits to be sent to The University of Connecticut for analysis. The university must submit a written report identifying any discrepancies to the secretary of the state and State Elections Enforcement Commission. Prior law had no comparable requirement.
    • Authorizes the use of high-speed tabulators for recanvasses. A recanvass is permitted to be conducted using a different voting tabulator or a high-speed tabulator borrowed from the state. Prior law required the recanvass to be performed using the original tabulator from the election.
  • Establishes protections against election interference:
    • Authorizes the attorney general to seek equitable relief for federal election interference. The attorney general is authorized to seek preliminary or permanent injunctive, declaratory, or equitable relief from the state Supreme Court to prevent or redress interference. Prior law had no comparable provision granting this specific equitable relief channel to the attorney general.
    • Requires the reporting of election subpoenas. Municipal officials or election workers who receive a subpoena or warrant for election records or equipment are required to provide a copy to the attorney general and secretary of the state within 36 hours. Prior law had no comparable requirement.
    • Prohibits election offenders from serving in election administration. Individuals convicted of violating Connecticut election laws are explicitly barred from serving in positions of trust within the election administration process, such as serving as election officials. Prior law had no comparable prohibition.
    • Modifies the 250-foot polling place buffer zone. The bill explicitly exempts off-duty officers (allowing them to vote and engage in protected political expression), individuals residing within 250 feet of the polling place, and individuals merely passing through the zone to reach a different destination. Prior law did not specify these exemptions.
  • Permits eligible 17-year-olds to vote early and by mail in primaries. Citizens who are 17 years old, but will be 18 by the day of the general election, are explicitly authorized to cast a ballot in a primary election during the early voting period or by mail ballot. Under prior law, these 17-year-olds were permitted to vote in the primary, but the statute was silent regarding their use of early and mail voting.
  • Establishes a task force to study efforts to achieve 100% voter participation in the state by 2030, and authorizes municipalities to establish their own pilot programs to promote this goal via voter outreach and education campaigns.

Some provisions from previous versions of the bill were amended out of the current text. These provisions would have:

  • Authorized the secretary of the state to establish a secure electronic ballot transmission system for the return of mail ballots by military/overseas voters, voters with a disability, federal-only voters, and all voters with permanent mail voting status. This provision effectively would have authorized electronic ballot return for any voter in the state.
  • Required election officials to conduct nationwide criminal background checks on petition circulators and individuals distributing mail ballot applications.
  • Required the secretary of the state to conduct a statewide public awareness mailing campaign regarding the new voting laws.
  • Broadened the authority of the State Elections Enforcement Commission by allowing it to investigate and hold hearings regarding alleged violations of regulations related to elections, primaries, and referendums (prior law limited this authority to violations of statutes).
  • Required the secretary of the state to review current procedures regarding in-person, off-site voter registration applications to assess accessibility for persons with disabilities, and submit a report with legislative recommendations.
  • Modified the reasons and process for removing municipal clerks from office, allowing the secretary of the state or the State Elections Enforcement Commission to refer misconduct or incompetence directly to the attorney general.

AUTHORNAME: Joint Committee on Government Administration and Elections
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on April 9, 2026, would prohibit firearms and unauthorized law enforcement near election sites; establish new felony offenses for tampering with drop boxes or sharing voting equipment with unauthorized parties; and increase penalties for harassing election workers, among other changes. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Prohibit firearms and deadly weapons near elections sites, and create a new felony offense for possessing them within 250 feet of such locations. Elections sites include polling places, early voting and same-day registration locations, absentee drop boxes, and central counting locations. The bill provides limited exceptions for peace officers on duty, firearms secured in locked containers in vehicles, and individuals briefly passing through the area. Existing law has no comparable prohibition.
  • Prohibit unauthorized law enforcement presence near elections sites, and create a new felony offense for violations. The bill would prohibit law enforcement officers or federal agents from coming within 250 feet of an elections site, including for the purpose of attempting to examine voter qualifications or loitering. It provides narrow exceptions for exigent threats, repelling armed enemies, acting under a judicial warrant with 24 hours’ notice to the secretary of the state and attorney general, responding to a request from an election moderator to suppress disorder, or briefly passing through the 250-foot radius while en route to another location. Existing law is silent as to the presence of law enforcement at elections sites.
  • Prohibit face-obscuring masks and unauthorized identification checks within 250 feet of an elections site. The bill would prohibit anyone from wearing a mask that obscures their identity, unless medically or religiously necessary, or reasonable given weather conditions provided the individual complies with a moderator's request to remove it. It would also prohibit anyone from requiring another person to present identification within the 250-foot radius. The bill expressly exempts election officials performing their lawful duties from the identification restriction. Existing law has no comparable provisions.
  • Create a new felony offense for tampering with absentee ballot drop boxes. The bill would make it a class D felony to unlawfully tamper with, alter, destroy, or carry away a drop box, or to fraudulently deposit ballots into a drop box. Existing law penalizes fraudulent voting and ballot tampering generally, but does not have a specific provision addressing drop boxes.
  • Create a new felony offense for unauthorized sharing of voting equipment. The bill would make it a class D felony for any election official to provide a voting tabulator, or its parts, to any third party not authorized by the secretary of the state. While existing law penalizes election officials who tamper with tabulators to defraud or deceive, it does not expressly prohibit providing them to unauthorized third parties.
  • Increase the penalty for harassing election workers. The bill would elevate the penalty for publicly disclosing an election worker's personal identifying information with the intent to harass, terrorize, or improperly influence them. Under the bill, a subsequent offense would become a class C felony. Under existing law, the offense is a class A misdemeanor. The bill would also expand the definition of "election worker" to explicitly include assistant municipal clerks.
  • Expand the attorney general's authority to protect elections and voting rights. The bill would:
    • Establish a mandatory reporting process for election-related subpoenas. The bill would require municipal officials and election workers to provide a copy of any subpoena, warrant, or request for election records, tabulators, or ballot boxes to the attorney general and secretary of the state within 36 hours of receipt. Existing law has no comparable requirement.
    • Authorize the attorney general to seek expedited injunctive or declaratory relief directly from the state Supreme Court to prevent or redress interference in federal elections. Existing law has no comparable provision.
    • Expand the attorney general's existing authority to bring civil actions against individuals who interfere with constitutional rights, to include interference by "physical obstruction" and the establishment of a "policy" that causes the deprivation of rights.

This bill, as enacted on March 3, 2026, modifies early voting and same-day registration procedures, limits the public disclosure of voter data, and expands municipal recanvass requirements, among other changes. Specifically, the bill:

  • Makes changes to early voting:
    • Changes early voting tabulation procedures. The bill eliminates the requirement that voters place their marked early voting ballot into an early voting envelope. Instead, voters must complete a printed affirmation in a log book and deposit their ballot directly into a voting tabulator. Prior law required voters to place their early voting ballot in an envelope, sign an affirmation on the outside, and deposit it in a secure receptacle.
    • Establishes an annual certification process for early voting locations. The bill requires registrars of voters to certify these locations to the Secretary of the State annually by February 15. Prior law required certification 60 days before an election.
    • Provides a backup process for early voting location designation. The bill authorizes the municipal legislative body or board of selectmen to designate the early voting location if the local registrars of voters cannot agree. Prior law granted designation authority exclusively to the registrars, but was silent on resolving disagreements.
    • Increases reporting requirements for moderators. The bill requires registrars to submit the names and mobile phone numbers of early voting moderators to the Secretary of the State 14 days before early voting begins. Prior law had no comparable requirement.
    • Prohibits partisan activity by early voting officials. The bill prohibits early voting officials from performing services for any political party or candidate on the days they serve. Prior law had no comparable provision.
  • Changes voter registration and same-day registration:
    • Moves the deadline for an unaffiliated voter to enroll with a party prior to a primary by mail or other non-in-person methods earlier, from five days before a primary to 18 days before. The deadline for an unaffiliated voter to enroll with a party in person remains noon on the last business day before the primary election.
    • Shifts same-day registration location certification to an annual February 15 deadline, from 45 days before each election.
    • Applies the new reporting requirements for moderator contact information and the prohibition on partisan activity to same-day registration officials. Prior law lacked these requirements.
  • Limits disclosure and use of voters' personal information and ballots:
    • Exempts all cast ballots, including write-in ballots, from public disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act. Prior law had no comparable exemption for cast ballots.
    • Limits the public disclosure of voter registration information to only the year of birth, unless requested for a state governmental purpose. Prior law permitted the disclosure of both the month and the year of birth.
    • Prohibits commercial and personal use of voter data. The bill expressly prohibits the use of voter registration information for personal, private, or commercial purposes, including harassment or marketing, subject to civil penalties. Prior law had no comparable provision explicitly banning these uses for the general voter list.
  • Expands post-election recanvass requirements. The bill requires that when a discrepancy triggers a recanvass, officials must recanvass the returns of every voting tabulator and all absentee and write-in ballots used in the entire municipality. Prior law required a recanvass only for the specific voting district where the discrepancy was found
  • Requires absentee ballot counters to maintain a log of each rejected absentee ballot and the specific reason for its rejection, which must be transmitted to the secretary of the state. Prior law required counters to endorse the reason for rejection on the ballot envelope, but did not require a separate log.
  • Prohibits registrars of voters from appointing as an election moderator any person convicted of a felony involving fraud, forgery, larceny, embezzlement, or bribery, or any election-related criminal offense. Prior law had no comparable restriction.
  • Authorizes the secretary of the state to commence a declaratory judgment action in Superior Court during the 90 days preceding an election if an elector alleges their voting rights are aggrieved. Prior law did not grant the Secretary this specific declaratory judgment authority.

The bill also contains additional non-substantive changes and provisions related to topics that Voting Rights Lab does not track, such as public education, intermediate care facilities, and municipal pensions.

AUTHORNAME: Joint Committee on Government Administration and Elections
VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as amended on April 9, 2026, would establish new security requirements for election sites, restrict access to voting equipment, and expand the authority of the attorney general to intervene in election interference. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Establish new criminal offenses and elevate penalties for election-related misconduct. Specifically, the bill would:
    • Create a Class D felony for a first offense and a Class B felony for subsequent offenses for the possession of a firearm or deadly weapon within 250 feet of any elections site, including polling places, early voting locations, same-day registration locations, absentee drop boxes, and counting or recanvass locations. Exceptions would be made for unloaded and locked weapons in vehicles, peace officers on duty, and individuals briefly passing through the radius. Existing law has no comparable blanket prohibition for all election sites.
    • Create a Class C felony, punishable by disenfranchisement, for officers or agents authorized to use force or make arrests by the state or federal government who knowingly enter, loiter, or attempt to examine voter qualifications within 250 feet of an elections site. This prohibition would not apply to officers acting under a judicial warrant with 24 hours' prior notice to the state, operating under exigent circumstances to protect life or property, or responding to a request by the secretary of the state or moderator to suppress disorder. Existing law has no comparable provision.
    • Create a Class C felony, punishable by disenfranchisement, for wearing a mask or face covering that obscures a person's identity within 250 feet of an elections site, unless the covering is medically necessary, of religious significance, or is reasonable given the weather conditions (provided the individual complies with a moderator's request to remove it).
    • Create a Class C felony, punishable by disenfranchisement, for requiring any person to present any form of identification within 250 feet of an elections site, except to the extent required by election officials performing their lawful duties. Existing law has no comparable provision.
    • Create a new Class D felony for knowingly tampering with, altering, destroying, or carrying away a ballot drop box, or fraudulently depositing or introducing ballots into or from a drop box. Existing law criminalizes destroying ballots, but does not have a specific felony targeting drop box tampering.
    • Create a new Class D felony for any election official who provides a voting tabulator, or any part or appliance thereof, to an unauthorized third party. Existing law criminalizes tabulator tampering, but does not explicitly criminalize handing over equipment to unauthorized parties.
    • Expand an existing Class A misdemeanor prohibiting the public disclosure of an election worker’s personal identifying information with the intent to harass or improperly influence them, making any subsequent offense a Class C felony. The bill would also expand the definition of “election worker” to include assistant municipal clerks.
  • Authorize the attorney general to seek injunctive, declaratory, or equitable relief to prevent or redress interference in federal elections. The bill would establish an expedited judicial process wherein a judge may issue ex parte orders to preserve the status quo, including ordering election workers to retain custody of voting tabulators and records. Existing law has no comparable provision.
  • Expand the attorney general’s existing authority to bring civil actions against those who interfere with civil rights by threats, intimidation, or coercion to also include interference by "physical obstruction" and to apply to the establishment of a "policy" that deprives individuals of their rights.
  • Require municipal officials or election workers who receive a subpoena, warrant, or request to inspect election records or equipment to provide a copy to the attorney general and the secretary of the state within 36 hours. Existing law has no comparable provision.

Last Updated May 20, 2026

This bill, as enacted following a congressional review period on April 3, 2026, establishes new rules and associated crimes for candidate, initiative, referendum, and recall petitions. Specifically, the bill:

This bill, as enacted on August 6, 2026, establishes a "Delaware John Lewis Voting Rights Act" to provide equal opportunity to engage in the electoral process. Specifically, this bill:

  • Defines relevant terms, such as "polarized voting," "political subdivision," and "protected class," necessary for interpreting the Act.
  • Creates a "democracy canon" that directs a liberal interpretation of all laws and regulations related to voting and prescribes that, to the extent any discretion is required, interpretation be weighted in favor of making the right and ability to vote more accessible, safeguarding the voting rights of all members of protected classes, and ensuring that members of protected classes are protected from discrimination in voting.
  • Establishes grounds and mechanisms for challenging voting discrimination and specifies that enacted legislation can be invalidated if they violate the state constitution.
  • Prohibits voter suppression when policies or practices are likely to result in "a material disparity in voter participation, access to voting opportunities, or the opportunity or ability to participate in any stage of the political process between protected class members and other members of the electorate" or "based on the totality of the circumstance, an impairment of the equal opportunity or ability of protected class members to participate in any stage of the political process."
  • Prohibits vote dilution.
  • Provides for legal standing broadly, including for individuals, organizations, and the Attorney General, for all portions of the Act.
  • Authorizes remedies upon the findings of illegal voter suppression or vote dilution.
  • Requires the Department of Elections to one or more languages, other than English, that will be available in elections for local offices if the Department finds that a significant and substantial need exists for such assistance. The bill mandates such assistance if more than 2%, but no fewer than 100, eligible voters speak a language other than English and are not English proficient.
  • Prevents intimidation, deception, or obstruction of the right to vote. 
  • Authorizes damages upon findings of voter intimidation, deception, or obstruction of the right to vote.

Last Updated August 11, 2026

This bill, as enacted on June 18, 2026, would make technical changes to conform statute with current practices regarding residency, electronic voting equipment, post-election audits, and curing ballots. Specifically, this bill:

  • Adds definitions for terms already in use in the elections code, such as "absentee ballot" and "provisional ballot."
  • Creates a new section to codify how residency is determined for the purpose of registering to vote. Stipulates that a place of residence is fixed, physically inhabited by the resident, and broadly defined to include non-traditional places of residence. Provides that an individual does not lose residency if they intend to return to their place of residence after an absence or if they maintain multiple paces of residence. Provides that if an individual relocates to a new residence with the intent to remain there indefinitely, then they must register to vote at that new location. Current law is silent on this issue.
  • Updates requirements for electronic voting systems to provide for the designation of software to be installed on voting equipment, expands the criteria that must be considered when designating such software, establishes a deadline for the State Election Commissioner to designate such software, and allows the Commissioner to change the designated version of software for security purposes.
  • Repeals language about party designees at voting equipment testing. Under current law, testing is open to the public.
  • Revises current post-election audit laws into four sections to improve clarity about the audit process and audits applicable only to specific offices.
  • Clarifies that only absentee ballots are hand-marked.
  • Clarifies who can determine voter intent when a scanning device cannot accurately read an absentee ballot. Current law references "election officers," and the bill specifies that a team of election judges, the county elections director, and county elections deputy director can do so.
  • Codifies the current procedure to cure absentee ballots, which requires election officials to contact voters and allow them to fix a deficiency by the close of polls on Election Day. Current law is silent on this issue.
  • Repeals the requirement for provisional ballots to be used if a court orders a polling place to be kept open beyond the normal time and allows voters to cast regular ballots.


This bill also addresses candidate residency, which is not tracked by Voting Rights Lab.

Last Updated June 30, 2026

This bill, as enacted on August 17, 2026, makes several technical and clarifying updates to post-election processes. Specifically, the bill

  • Clarifies terms and adds definitions to align with current practices regarding tabulation, certification, and County Superior Courts.
  • Specifies that the Superior Court certifies election results by tabulating all ballots cast.
  • Stipulates that the Department of Elections must provide early voting ballots and provisional ballots to the Superior Court. Statute is silent on whether these materials should be provided to the Court along with voting machine and absentee ballot reports.
  • Clarifies the requirements for the contents of election certificates and their delivery.

Last Updated August 20, 2026

This bill, as introduced on January 13, 2026, would require the Florida Commission on Offender Review to develop and maintain a database to help individuals with felony convictions determine if their voting rights have been restored. This bill, as enacted on May 5, 2026, narrows exceptions to voter ID requirements, creates new voter list maintenance practices, and clarifies the conduct constituting an election offense. Specifically, the bill:

  • Eliminates the attestation of another registered voter as an option for persons lacking required voter identification.
  • Requires the cancellation of voter registration for anyone whose voter registration has been designated as incomplete, pending, or unconfirmed for ninety days if the commissioner has been unable to contact them or the voter has failed to supply or correct any missing or inaccurate information.
  • Specifies that conduct constituting the offense of election misconduct is an offense if committed on any day in which voting takes place in person. Under existing law, election misconduct is defined as certain acts taking place on election day.

The bill contains additional provisions not tracked by Voting Rights Lab, including provisions concerning certain local election filings.

Provisions from a previous version of the bill were amended out of the current text. They would have:

  • Specified that the online application voters may use to track the status of their mail ballot request form or mail ballot must allow a voter to choose to receive notification of changes in the status of the voter’s absentee ballot request form or absentee ballot by electronic mail, text message, or other electronic means.
  • Required the implementation of a postal service barcode for mail ballots.

This bill, as amended on February 25, 2026, would create a requirement that the state registrar of voters attempt to verify the citizenship of all registered voters. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the registrar of voters to attempt to verify the citizenship of all registered voters using the federal systematic alien verification for entitlements system, and provide notice to county commissioners of the results. This check would include a monthly check of all newly registered voters.
  • Require that, when a county commissioner receives notice that the registrar was unable to verify a voter as a citizen, the commissioner designate the voter as "unconfirmed" and send notice that the voter must provide proof of citizenship to remain registered. Notice to an affected voter would include information on how to verify the voter's citizenship, how to contact the proper federal agencies to correct their information, and how to cancel their registration.
  • Require a voter's registration to be canceled if the voter receives notice as provided under the bill and does not provide proof of citizenship within 90 days of receipt.
  • Instruct the state registrar to adopt rules as needed to implement the legislation, which would presumably include establishing what constitutes proof of citizenship.

Last Updated February 26, 2026

This bill, as introduced on January 5, 2026, would impose numerous substantial changes on Indiana elections that would limit voter access and threaten voter privacy. The bill would:

  • Prohibit in-person early voting. Existing law allows up to 28 days of early voting (in-person absentee voting).
  • Limit the availability of absentee voting to members of the military, voters with disabilities, voters working the polls on Election Day, UOCAVA voters, and voters age 65 or older. Existing law provides several other reasons for absentee voting, including absence from the precinct on Election Day, confinement due to illness or injury, work schedule, religious observance, and unavailability of transportation to the polls.
  • Require absentee voters to include a copy of their photo ID and the last four digits of their Social Security number with their returned ballot for verification purposes. Existing law requires election officials to compare the ballot signature with the voter's signature on file for verification.
  • Move the absentee ballot return deadline to noon on Election Day. Existing law allows voters to return ballots until 6 P.M. on Election Day.
  • Require all elections to be conducted on paper ballots designed and printed in Indiana. The ballots must include a watermark and a unique serial number. Polling locations must have one accessible voting system to comply with the requirements of HAVA.
  • Require election officials to count the paper ballots by hand beginning at 7 A.M. on Election Day.
  • Require election officials to open and count mail-in ballots at precinct locations beginning at noon on Election Day. Under existing law, mail-in ballots may be verified by county officials on receipt.
  • Require ballot counting at precinct locations to be recorded and live streamed. Voters at polling locations must place completed ballots in a transparent ballot box.
  • Require each precinct worker to affirm the final vote totals, be present for the calling in of results to the county board, and receive a copy of the final vote totals. The county board must announce election results on the night of the election.
  • Require the use of paper pollbooks
  • Deem voted ballots as not confidential records. Election officials must maintain election records at secure county-owned facilities. Only the county clerk and a member of the opposing political party may have access to the stored records.
  • Allow all Indiana citizens to inspect and copy voter lists, pollbook signatures, voter histories, absentee voting applications and signatures, chain of custody records, and ballots (except those belonging to individuals in the address confidentiality program).
  • Require the Secretary of State to select randomly 10 counties for a post-election hand recount following each election.
  • Require the Secretary of State to maintain a statewide public voter database. The Secretary must reconcile the list monthly with various named databases and any other database the Secretary "deems useful."
  • Prohibit vote centers and internet voting.
  • Limit absentee ballot return to the voter or an immediate family member. Existing law also allows a voter to name an attorney-in-fact for ballot return.
  • Require voter registration applications to include an undefined "proof of citizenship" and the voter's signature.
  • Prohibit third party organizations from conduction voter registration activities.
  • Prohibit staffed and unstaffed drop boxes. Existing law allows staffed drop boxes.
  • Prohibit the use of digital ID for voter ID purposes.
  • Prohibit anyone from sending a voter an absentee ballot application unless the voter requests one.
  • Create a Class A misdemeanor for any violation of the provisions of the bill. Additionally, any person convicted of a violation would be ineligible to register or vote for 10 years following conviction.
  • Require the Attorney General to create an "Elections Crime Unit" to investigate allegations of election law violations. The Unit would have jurisdiction throughout Indiana, but would not limit the jurisdiction of local officials to investigate and prosecute election law violations. The Unit would administer an election fraud hotline and would submit an annual report to the legislature.

This bill, as enacted on April 9, 2026, makes various changes to voter list maintenance and removal practices and restricts online voter registration by third parties. The bill:

  • Adds new data sources and processes for removing noncitizens:
    • Requires the secretary of state to compare the voter registration system against the systematic alien verification for entitlements (SAVE) database twice a year. One check must occur at least 180 days before a regularly scheduled federal election. 
      • The secretary of state must report potential noncitizen registrations identified to county election officials for immediate review.
      • County election officials must notify the voter, place them in a challenged or pending verification status until they confirm their citizenship, and remove any voters confirmed ineligible.
    • Requires the secretary of state to submit an annual report to the legislature of the number of records checked against the SAVE database, the number of voters flagged as potential non-citizens, the number of voters flagged as potentially deceased, and the number of voters ultimately removed from the registration database that were first identified as potentially ineligible in the SAVE system.
    • Requires state agencies that provide public assistance benefits and are designated as voter registration agencies under the National Voter Registration Act to prepare a quarterly report for the secretary of state of the names and personal information of noncitizens receiving public assistance.
  • Adds new data sources and processes for removing voters who have changed their address to another jurisdiction:
    • Requires the division of motor vehicles to provide the secretary of state with a quarterly list of residents who have received a licenses from another jurisdiction.
      • The secretary must compare these lists to the statewide voter registration system and, on finding a matching registration, direct the county election official to remove them within five business days.
      • The county election official must notify removed persons they may have their registration reinstated by providing proof of residency in Kansas.
    • Adds the division of motor vehicles as a source of change of address data triggering a confirmation notice from a county election official.
    • Authorizes the secretary of state to obtain change of address information from federal agencies and provide it to local election officials.
  • Adds new data sources and processes for removing deceased voters:
    • Requires the secretary of state to request a list of deceased residents from the Social Security Administration at least once a year.
    • Adds family notarized attestations of the death as a valid reason for removal.
    • Specifies that voters appearing in a list of deceased persons provided by the Social Security Administration must have their death verified by other reliable means before removal.
  • Change processes for removing convicted felons:
    • Extends the secretary of state's deadline for notifying county election officials of a felony conviction in a US District Court from five days after notice to five business days.
    • Creates a deadline of five business days after notice for local election officials to remove convicted felons from registration records. Under prior law, removal is required but no deadline is specified.
  • Requires the secretary of state to provide appropriate county election officials with the results of any duplicate voter registration checks twice a year.
  • Allows the secretary of state to obtain comparisons of voter registration records from other jurisdiction and provide them to county election officials.
  • Prohibits individuals or non-goverment third-party groups from operating websites that accept and transmit voter registration applications unless approved by the secretary of state. To qualify for approval, websites must meet specified technological, security, and privacy requirements. A violation of this prohibition is a misdemeanor offense.

Last Updated April 13, 2026

This bill, as amended on February 17, 2026, would change multiple aspects of the voting process, including mail voting, early voting, and voter registration. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Modify the mail voting (“advance voting”) process. The bill would:
    • Move the deadline for submitting an application for a mail ballot earlier, from seven days before Election Day to 14 days before.
    • Move the start date for officials to issue mail ballots earlier, from 20 days before Election Day to 22 days before.
    • Move the deadline for mail ballots to be received, from 7 p.m. on Election Day to the close of polls on Election Day. Under existing law, polls must close by 7 p.m. but may remain open until 8 p.m. under certain conditions. The bill would also delete the provision allowing the secretary of state to adopt rules and regulations to implement this section.
  • Restrict the in-person early voting period. The bill would:
    • Move the last day of early voting earlier, from noon on the day before Election Day to the Friday before. The bill would provide an exception for counties that opt in to holding weekend early voting.
    • Expand optional weekend early voting hours to no later than noon on the Sunday before the election. Under existing law, counties can hold optional early voting only on the Saturday preceding the election. The bill would also require county election offices holding weekend early voting to publish notice of voting times on the county website beginning at least three weeks prior to the election.
    • Move the deadline for new voter registrations earlier, from the 21st day before Election Day to the 25th day.

A provision from a previous version of the bill was amended out of the current text. It would have moved the deadline for new voter registrations earlier, from the 21st day before Election Day to the 23rd day.

This bill, as vetoed on April 8, 2026, modifies mail ballot signature verification requirements, establishes a trigger law to restrict mail and early voting access if those requirements are enjoined by a court, and creates a new venue requirement for election litigation. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Permit a third party to sign a mail ballot envelope if the voter cannot provide a signature consistent with their signature on record in the voter registration database. Under existing law, this is only permitted for voters who cannot physically sign their envelope.
  • Trigger restrictions on mail and early voting eligibility if the state's mail ballot signature verification requirement is enjoined by a court order or judgment.
    • Require the secretary of state to monitor relevant litigation and publish a notice in the state register in the event of such an order or judgment to implement new restrictions. The notice must be published in the next scheduled publication of the register or, if the judgement is issued on or after 45 days before an election, the first register following the certification of results.
  • Limit eligibility for mail and early voting ("advance voting") to voters who cannot vote in person on election day due to:
      • Absence from their county of residence
      • Illness, disability, or religious belief or practice
      • Service as an election judge or clerk
    • Absence as a uniformed or overseas voter

Under existing law, no excuse is required to apply for a mail ballot or vote in person during early voting.

  • Require any legal challenges to state election statutes, regulations, or rules to be brought in the Shawnee County District Court, and require that any action brought in another court be transferred there. Existing law has no comparable provision.

Last Updated April 14, 2026

This bill, as signed by Governor Jeff Landry on May 14, 2026, makes several changes to voter registration, mail voting, and election administration more generally. Specifically, this bill makes the following changes:

  • Regarding voter registration, the bill:
    • Allows a registered voter who is no longer capable of signing their name or making a mark due to a physical disability, to authorize another person to sign documents on that voter's behalf.
    • Removes the requirement for a voter who was previously registered in a different parish to surrender that notice of registration (if available) when registering in a new parish. Requires the previous parish registrar to cancel the voter's previous registration.
    • Requires that a change of registration based on a change of residence within a parish that is received after the closing of registration for a closed primary election goes into effect the day after the second party primary. Current law is silent on this specific situation.
    • Requires that a change of registration based on a change of residence within a parish -- and when the change of residence does not change any issues or offices upon which the voter can vote -- can go into effect for a special primary election or general election only if the change was made before the close of registration for the general election. Under existing law, the registration change does not need to be made before the closing of the registration period.
    • Allows a law enforcement officer whose address is confidential to submit written notice to the registrar of voters that their name no longer needs to be kept confidential. Current law is silent on this process.
    • Provides that the Department of State does not need to conduct a canvass of registered voters in a calendar year when there is less than sixty days between an election and the opening of qualifying for a regularly scheduled election. Under existing law, the Department of State is required to canvass the registered voters twice a year.
    • Removes the requirement that address information used to prevent a person from being placed on the inactive voter list must come from the United States Postal Service.
    • Changes the address confirmation notice to an address confirmation form and make conforming changes throughout.
    • Provides that if a voter on the inactive list applies to vote by mail, that the registrar must transfer the voter's name to the official list and update their registration record. Existing law makes the same provision for voters on the inactive list who vote by mail or during early voting.
    • Changes the limitation on canceling voter registrations between any primary and the subsequent general election to between any open primary and subsequent general election. The bill would also add voter ineligibility (except for change of residence) to the list of exceptions to this prohibition.
    • Allows the voter information of a person who is 17 years old to appear on a precinct register when that person will be 18 years old within seven days before an election. Under existing law, voter information of a person who is 16 or 17 years old is prohibited from disclosure, including on a precinct registrar.
  • Regarding election administration, the bill:
    • Removes the requirement that the parish board of election supervisors must meet at 10 a.m. on the fifth day after an election to count absentee and early ballots. The bill would allow the board to meet anytime on those days.
    • Changes voter assistance procedures so that only the person assisting the voter -- and not the voter -- must complete the voter assistance form.
    • Changes the number of compiled statements of election returns that the parish board of supervisors must prepare from two to one and require that an electronic copy be transmitted to the secretary of state.
    • Requires the parish clerk and registrar to confirm the feasibility of precinct boundary changes in writing and for the parish governing authority to submit that confirmation to the secretary of state.
    • Requires an early voting commissioner to be a qualified voter and to meet the same qualifications as an Election Day commissioner. Under existing law, early voting commissioners are not explicitly required to be qualified voters.
    • Changes the deadline by which a list of early voting watchers must be filed with the registrar from the fourteenth business day before the first day of early voting to the tenth business day before the first day of early voting.
    • Allows the secretary of state to contract for the delivery of voting machines and equipment without reference to a specific method of procurement. Existing law stipulates a specific method of procurement.
    • Changes the end of the time interval in the Election Code that ends on a Sunday or other legal holiday from noon of the next legal day to 4:30 p.m. of the next legal day.
  • Regarding mail and early voting, the bill:
    • Expands eligibility for mail (absentee) voting to employees of the Department of State; current law allows employees of the secretary of state to do so.
    • Requires mail voters to completely fill in the oval of each selection on their ballot and provide that selecting more than the number of candidates for an office or making selections for and against the same candidate will render the selections for that office void. Existing law is silent on this issue.
    • Provides that if the time selected by the parish board of election supervisors to count mail and early ballots is after 4 p.m. on Election Day, that the start time must be submitted to the commissioner of elections for approval by the fourth day before Election Day. Existing law does not require the board to get approval.
    • Changes ballot change procedures. Under existing law, challenges to mail or early ballots may be filed no later than the fourth day before Election Day. The bill limits that to only mail ballots and instead provides that early ballots may be challenged prior to the voter casting a ballot, in which case the voter must vote on a paper ballot rather than a voting machine.
    • Requires the secretary of state to promulgate rules regarding the rejection of mail or early ballots with distinguishing marks. Existing law provides for which ballots with distinguishing marks should be rejected, but does not explicitly direct the secretary of state to adopt rules for implementation.
    • Alters the ballot curing process to stipulate that the failure of a witness to provide their printed name or address on the ballot certificate is not a deficiency requiring cure.
    • Extends the nursing home early voting program by moving back the end date from seven days before the election to four days before the election.
  • Regarding election contests, the bill:
    • Authorizes a qualified elector to challenge the placement of a constitutional amendment on the ballot. Existing law allows challenges to candidacy, election results, recall petitions, and the calling of special elections to fill vacancies. Clarifies that the secretary of state is a proper party in an objection to the placement of a constitutional amendment on the ballot.
    • Provides the first day that actions contesting an election, candidacy, recall petition and more can be filed. Existing law provides deadlines by which actions must be filed, but is silent as to when actions may begin to be filed. Specifically, actions contesting an election can begin no earlier than the day after the election; actions contesting the calling of a special election can begin no earlier than the date the election is called, and actions objecting to the placement of a constitutional amendment on the ballot can begin no earlier than the date of the final passage of the join resolution calling the election and no later than 4:30 p.m. of the 30th day after the final passage.

This bill also contains provisions related to local election officials, candidates, and party primaries that Voting Rights Lab does not track.
