This bill, as introduced on July 20, 2026, would make various changes to Massachusetts law governing presidential electors and the certification and transmission of presidential election results. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Conform Massachusetts law governing presidential electors and the certification of presidential election results to the federal Electoral Count Reform Act of 2022, including:
    • Revise the deadline for presidential electors to be deemed elected following the governor's proclamation to provide that the electors are deemed elected at the expiration of 14 days from the proclamation or six days before the meeting of presidential electors, whichever is sooner.
    • Require the governor's certificates of election to presidential electors to take the form of duplicate originals of a certificate of ascertainment of appointment of electors and require the governor to transmit the certificate to the Archivist of the United States by the most expeditious method available.
    • Require a copy of the certificate of ascertainment to be publicly posted on the state secretary's website on the same day it is transmitted.
    • Require certificates of ascertainment to bear the state seal, contain at least one security feature established by the state secretary for authentication purposes, and identify the presidential electors appointed and the vote received by elector nominees who received at least one-fifth of the votes cast for electors.
    • Require the governor, when submitting the Commonwealth's certificate of ascertainment under federal law, to certify that the appointed electors will serve unless a vacancy occurs before the conclusion of the meeting at which electoral votes are cast and that any substitute elector will be reflected in an amended certificate of ascertainment.
    • Establish procedures for preparing, signing, transmitting, preserving, and publicly posting certificates of vote following the meeting of presidential electors.
    • Require six sets of certificates of vote and accompanying certificates of ascertainment to be transmitted to specified federal and state recipients, including the President of the United States Senate, the Archivist of the United States, the state secretary, and the chief judge of the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts.
  • Establish procedures for judicial review of the appointment of presidential electors, including:
    • Provide that the Supreme Judicial Court for Suffolk County has original and exclusive jurisdiction over petitions concerning the determination of presidential electors.
    • Require a final order in such a proceeding to be issued no later than the day before the date on which presidential electors convene in order for the determination to have conclusive effect.
  • Establish alternate presidential electors and require elector pledges, including:
    • Require each presidential elector nominated by a political party's state committee to have an alternate elector nominee.
    • Require the state committee to submit the names of both the elector nominee and alternate elector nominee to the state secretary.
    • Replace the existing elector pledge with a pledge under which an elector agrees to serve and to cast ballots for President and Vice President for the nominees of the political party that nominated the elector.
    • Provide that the pledge would apply to a successor presidential or vice-presidential candidate nominated by the political party if the original nominee dies or withdraws before the meeting of presidential electors.
  • Establish procedures for filling vacancies among presidential electors, including:
    • Provide that an elector who is not present when elector voting is required is deemed to have vacated the position.

This bill, as introduced on June 23, 2026, would eliminate no-excuse mail voting and require voters to qualify under specified statutory grounds to cast a mail ballot. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Eliminate no-excuse mail voting and impose an excused requirement for mail voting. The bill would narrow the definition of a qualifying "absent voter" to include only a registered elector who cannot attend the polls for one of several specified excuses. Existing law allows any registered voter to vote absentee without providing a reason.
  • Require one of the following qualifying excuses for mail voters: 
    • Physical disability
    • Religious tenets
    • Service as an election inspector in another precinct
    • Be 60 years of age or older
    • Absence from the city or township during the entire time polls are open
    • Confinement in jail while awaiting arraignment or trial 
  • Expressly exclude certain former residents from absentee voting. The bill would provide that the absent voter definition does not apply to an individual who has moved out of state and no longer maintains an actual residence in the state, regardless of the length of the individual’s residence outside the state. The bill would specify that storing personal effects, owning property rented or leased to others, or making occasional brief visits to a former domicile does not constitute a voting residence in Michigan, subject to exceptions for certain military and overseas voters. Existing law does not include this limitation in the absent voter definition.
  • Repeal the permanent mail voting list. Existing law gives all registered voters the right to submit a single signed application to receive absentee ballots for all future elections.
  • Remove a provision that allows a military or overseas ballot received within six days after Election Day to be considered timely when the postmark is missing or unclear, if the ballot return envelope or voter certificate is dated on or before Election Day. Under the bill, the post-election receipt period would still apply only when the ballot return envelope is postmarked on or before Election Day and received within six days after the election. 
  • Make conforming changes to the state's physical and online mail ballot application. Existing law provides an online absentee ballot application process for registered voters generally.

This bill, as introduced on June 30, 2026, would create a constitutional amendment that would grant voters the right to early voting in all primary and general elections in even-numbered years. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require county boards to designate a minimum of 14 days prior to the election for early voting, select early voting site locations, and determine staffing needs and hours for each site, subject to the following:
    • Require all early voting sites to operate uniformly on weekdays and remain open continuously from at least 8 a.m. to 7:30 p.m., unless the county board determines that voter demand allows for closure at 6 p.m.
    • Require all early voting sites operating on a Sunday to have uniform opening and closing times.
    • Require all early voting sites to be open on the last Saturday prior to Election Day from at least 8 a.m. to 3 p.m.
  • Authorize the General Assembly to appropriate funds to county boards of elections to support the administration of early voting.
  • Require the county boards to increase the staffing, hours, number, and locations for early voting sites to match the needs of voters during designated early voting days.
  • Provide for same-day voter registration during the early voting period by requiring county boards of elections to allow eligible individuals to register and vote at any early voting site.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on August 4, 2026, would make various changes to laws pertaining to elections.. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Prohibit the presence of state or federal troops or armed military personnel at voting places during the 17 days before an election through the close of voting on Election Day, subject to certain exceptions, and establish enforcement mechanisms, including:
    • Prohibit a person acting under color of law from ordering or authorizing the presence of state or federal troops or armed military personnel at a voting place, including parking areas used for voting, unless the force is necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States.
    • Clarify that the prohibition would not prevent members of the armed forces from exercising their right to vote.
    • Exempt law enforcement personnel whose presence is otherwise required by law, who are responding to a specific emergency or disturbance, or whose assistance is requested by an election officer with jurisdiction over the election.
    • Authorize a person aggrieved by a violation to seek preventive relief in district court, including a temporary or permanent injunction, restraining order, or other court order, and allow courts to award reasonable attorneys' fees to a prevailing party.
    • Authorize courts to impose a civil penalty commensurate with the seriousness of the violation, in addition to any other applicable fines or penalties.
    • Provide that the new provisions would be enforced in addition to existing civil and criminal penalties under North Carolina election law.
  • Establish new prohibitions and penalties for voter intimidation, threats, and coercion, applicable to in-person voting, early voting, absentee voting, and ballot-return activities, including:
    • Define “coerce,” “intimidate,” and “threaten” for purposes of the new provisions.
    • Make it a Class H felony to:
      • Threaten or attempt to threaten a person for voting, attempting to vote, voting for or against a particular candidate, registering to vote, assisting or encouraging another person to vote, or exercising lawful duties as an election official.
      • Knowingly challenge a person's right to vote on fraudulent or spurious grounds.
      • Engage in mass, indiscriminate, and groundless challenges intended to prevent voters from voting, delay voting, or interfere with the orderly administration of an election.
      • Fraudulently advise an eligible or registered voter that the person is ineligible to vote or is not registered.
  • Make it a Class H felony for an employer to use an employee's pay or employment to influence voting, including by placing political threats or messages on pay envelopes or communicating that an employee's pay or continued employment is conditioned on voting, not voting, or voting for or against a particular candidate.
  • Make it a Class A1 misdemeanor to intimidate, coerce, or attempt to intimidate or coerce a person for voting, attempting to vote, voting for or against a particular candidate, assisting or encouraging another person to vote, or exercising lawful duties as an election official.
  • Authorize persons aggrieved by a violation to seek preventive relief in district court, including temporary or permanent injunctions, restraining orders, or other court orders, and allow courts to award reasonable attorneys' fees to prevailing parties.
  • Establish a Voter Intimidation Restitution Fund and authorize courts to impose restitution fines commensurate with the seriousness of the offense. Upon appropriation, funds would be provided to the State Board of Elections for voter education campaigns addressing the specific violations and for associated administrative costs.
  • Amend existing election law to make it a Class 2 misdemeanor to demand citizenship documentation from a voter beyond what is required by State law at any point during the voting process.
  • Establish protections and penalties for intimidation, threats, or coercion of election workers, including:
    • Create a civil cause of action allowing an election worker to recover damages for injury or loss resulting from intimidation, threats, or coercion intended to impede, intimidate, or interfere with the worker's official duties. The provision would define an election worker to include election officials, poll workers, and election volunteers performing election-related duties.
    • Establish criminal penalties of a fine of up to $100,000, imprisonment for up to five years, or both for violations.
    • Provide immunity for election workers acting in good faith to prevent election interference or preserve ballot access in accordance with the new provisions.
  • Establish uniform early voting hours across all early voting sites and extend required weekend hours, effective January 1, 2027, for elections held on or after that date, including:
    • Require all early voting sites to be open from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. on each Saturday during the early voting period.
    • Require all early voting sites to be open from 12 p.m. to 5 p.m. on each Sunday during the early voting period.
    • Require all early voting sites to be open on the same days and for the same hours throughout the county.
    • Extend the deadline for in-person early voting on the last Saturday before the election from 3 p.m. to 5 p.m.
  • Establish the “Safeguard Fair Elections Act” and prohibit public officials from refusing to certify the actual results or count of an election without clear and convincing evidence, and establish penalties for violations, including:
    • Establish legislative findings that efforts to subvert vote counting and the recognition of election winners undermine democracy and the rule of law, and state that public officials have a responsibility to place loyalty to the Constitution, laws, and ethical principles above partisan politics.
    • Define “clear and convincing evidence,” “official act,” and “public official” for purposes of the new Article, with “public official” including elected and appointed officials, government employees, election judges, and poll workers.
    • Prohibit a public official from performing, or communicating an intention to perform, an official act in which the official refuses to certify the actual results or count of an election without clear and convincing evidence.
    • Provide that a public official who performs or communicates an intention to perform an act in violation of the prohibition would automatically resign from office, and that the official act would be null and void.
    • Establish a Class 1 misdemeanor for a willful violation, punishable by a fine of up to $10,000.
    • Provide that the new provisions would be enforced in addition to any other existing civil and criminal penalties under North Carolina election law.
  • Establish requirements governing post-election audits, including prohibiting public officials from funding or participating in audits or reviews that fail to meet specified best practices, including:
    • Require the State Board, when conducting post-election audits, to ensure each audit is conducted by nonpartisan election officials with relevant expertise.
    • Require post-election audits to be routine and completed before State certification.
    • Require audits to be transparent and open to public observation.
    • Require audits to preserve the integrity of election systems and voting equipment, as well as ballot secrecy and voter privacy.
    • Require audits to use statistically sound methodologies.
    • Require State or county procedures governing audits to be established before Election Day and before election results are known.
    • Prohibit public officials from providing funding for or participating in a post-election audit or review that does not comply with these requirements.
  • Require the State Board to conduct a risk-limiting audit after each general election in every county, in addition to any other audits required by State or federal law, and establish requirements for those audits, including:
    • Define a “risk-limiting audit” as a hand-to-eye recount of a randomly selected sample of ballots in a contest that provides strong statistical evidence that the machine-counted results are correct, based on a specified risk limit.
    • Require the State Board to establish the requirements for conducting risk-limiting audits.
    • Provide that a risk-limiting audit conducted under this section would not change the results of an election.
  • Require election observers to complete training before serving as an observer and additional training at least once every two years, as applicable, with the State Board responsible for establishing training standards and requirements.
    • Observer name tags must include the observer’s name, role, and partisan affiliation.
  • Establish the “Voter Protection and Reliance Act” to protect voters’ reliance on election laws and procedures in effect when they cast their ballots and expedite litigation challenging election procedures or election outcomes, including:
    • Provide that voters have the right to have their ballots counted based on the laws and established election procedures in place on Election Day, and prohibit later-enacted laws, judicial rulings, legal interpretations, or subsequently established procedures from being used to deny or abridge that right.
    • Prohibit administrative bodies, courts, and election officials from excluding votes from canvass, failing to certify an election, withholding a certificate of election, or failing to seat a prevailing candidate based on a law, judicial ruling, legal interpretation, or election procedure that was not in effect or established by Election Day.
    • Establish when a law or election procedure is considered effective or established, including constitutional provisions, statutes, regulations, directives, administrative memoranda, procedures, and established patterns or practices in effect on Election Day.
    • Require adjudicators to construe facts and draw inferences in favor of finding that an election procedure was established, based on voter reliance and the availability of legislative or judicial recourse before Election Day, and to construe conflicting procedures in favor of the voter.
    • Require that, if an election procedure changes during absentee or early voting or on Election Day, the procedure in effect when the voter cast a ballot, applied for a provisional ballot, or submitted an absentee ballot would govern.
    • Clarify that the provisions would not prevent an eligible voter from challenging the unlawful denial of the right to register to vote, cast a ballot, or have a ballot counted.
    • Establish expedited procedures for litigation filed within 90 days before the earliest date absentee ballots may be mailed for an election or after an election when the action challenges the election outcome.
    • Define a “covered action” to include civil actions in State court and protests before the State Board or a county board of elections challenging the general applicability, meaning, interpretation, validity, or understanding of an established election procedure.
    • Generally require covered actions to be filed in the Superior Court of Wake County, except for actions concerning an established election procedure solely of a single county board of elections.
    • Require a superior court judge who determines that a covered action falls under Rule 42 of the Rules of Civil Procedure to immediately order a transfer under that rule, with the Chief Justice required to appoint a three-judge panel within five days.
    • Require plaintiffs to serve the State Board or other appropriate election authority within 24 hours of filing and require the court to hold an initial scheduling conference within five days, with authority to shorten response deadlines and expedite the case.
    • Require any appeals in covered actions to be heard on an expedited schedule.
  • Require the State Board to establish a standing, community-led advisory committee to monitor risks of voter intimidation and recommend mitigation strategies by establishing the process and criteria for selecting committee members. The committee must include representatives of community organizations, election administrators, disability access advocates, and language-access partners.
  • Extend the deadline for a registered voter to challenge another person’s right to register, remain registered, or vote in the county from the 25th day before an election to 90 days before a primary, general, or special election, unless otherwise required by federal law.
    • Require notices of preliminary hearings on voter challenges to be provided in the challenged voter’s language of record, when available.
  • Require the chair, before the board hears a challenge to an absentee ballot, to provide the challenged voter with written notice identifying the basis for the challenge, required response steps, and deadlines for resolution.
    • Require the board to proceed with a hearing on the absentee ballot challenge after the applicable notice and response deadlines have been met.
  • Prohibit the State Board or a county board of elections from disclosing information covered by this subsection in response to a request from the federal government or a federal agency or department without a court order or an arrest warrant signed by a judge.
  • Extend the canvassing period during which county boards of elections or the State Board may verify voter eligibility and count provisional ballots through the canvass meeting at 11:00 A.M. on the tenth day after the election, and allow voters who cast provisional or absentee ballots to correct identified deficiencies until 5:00 P.M. on the day before the tenth day after the election.

This bill, as enacted on April 15, makes several changes to elections and voting in Nebraska. The bill:

  • Changes requirements regarding limitations on the number of registered voters per precinct;

  • increased requirements related to election worker training.

The bill requires the secretary to send certain absentee ballot requests to the department of justice, election law unit for review; including, requests made by multiple voters at a common address. The bill requires the secretary to submit a report regarding absentee ballot requests and requests sent to the election law unit.

If an audit reveals non-citizenship activity, the Secretary of State is required to send the information to the attorney general for review.

The bill requires the secretary of state to develop and distribute election administration forms detailing required counting of absentee ballots. The bill changes the pre-election certificate to require the moderator and clerk to verify the number of official and absentee ballots received.

Under prior law, correction or revision of the checklist for a town meeting or election could only be conducted on a Saturday, 6-13 days before the election.

This bill, as amended on May 14, 2026, would expand the felony offense of improper influence to include the immediate family members of a public servant, party official, or voter. The bill would provide for mandatory minimum civil penalties for certain violations of the offense. This section of the bill would be effective January 1, 2027.


This bill makes changes not tracked by Voting Rights Lab.

The bill would permit ballot counting to be paused by the moderator if counting will extend beyond 12:00 am on Election night. Counting would resume the next day at time determined by the moderator. The bill would require the scene to be recorded, and if possible, live broadcast of the scene would be available on the governing entity's website and local cable channel. This bill would permit up to 5 members of the public present in the room while counting is being conducting.

Last Updated March 27, 2026

This bill, as introduced on January 7, 2026, would establish new voter registration requirements by requiring applicants to provide evidence of New Hampshire citizenship or a card attesting to their New Hampshire citizenship. The bill would define New Hampshire citizenship as individuals who were born in New Hampshire or individuals who have pledged an oath of allegiance to New Hampshire and received a New Hampshire citizenship card. Under existing law, voter registration applicants must provide evidence of US citizenship, identity, age, and domicile.

Last Updated January 9, 2026

This bill, as amended on March 26, 2026, would require the Secretary of State and localities to provide election clerks access to data from the centralized voter database, records from the Department of Safety, and New Hampshire vital records for voter registration purposes on Election Day during polling hours. The bill would require a secure electronic transmission of voter registration related data between the Department of Safety and the Secretary of State. The bill would require the SOS to send a report to multiple entities including the minority and majority leaders of the House of Representatives and Senate regarding any investigation into duplicate matches of voters from out of state. 


Under existing law, Department of Safety and the Secretary of State may share some voter related data however this data may not be explicitly used for voter registration purposes.

Last Updated April 2, 2026

This bill would permit voters of any registered political affiliation to vote in any political party's primary. Currently only politically unaffiliated voters may vote in any political party's primary.

Last Updated January 15, 2026

The bill, as introduced on January 7, 2026, would require the Secretary of State to establish an online voter registration process in which applicants may submit a voter registration application and required documentation. The Secretary of State would be required to send the application and documentation to the appropriate clerk for processing.

Last Updated January 7, 2026

This bill would require the election return form to provide the number of individuals who attempted to register to vote but were denied due to lack of required documentation. Currently, there is no requirement to record this information.

Last Updated January 7, 2026

This bill, as enacted on July 2, 2026, would require:

  • The secretary of state and localities to provide election clerks access to data from the centralized voter database on Election Day during polling hours.
  • A secure electronic transmission of voter registration related data between the department of safety and the secretary of state and permits that data to be shared with clerks for voter registration purposes.
  • The SOS to send a report to multiple entities including the minority and majority leaders of the House of Representatives and Senate regarding any investigation into duplicate matches of voters from out of state. 


Under existing law, department of safety and the secretary of state may share some voter related data however this data may not be explicitly used for voter registration purposes.


This bill would be effective July 30, 2026.

Last Updated July 10, 2026

This bill, as enacted on June 19, 2026, amends the process and requirements by which a person may receive a voucher exempting them from paying for a photo ID card to be used for voter purposes only. The bill provides that the city clerk is the only entity with access to the voucher form. Previously, a person could receive the voucher from the secretary of state. The bill requires an applicant of the form to provide proof of domicile Previously, the person's name would only need to be on the checklist.

Summary pending as of 4/21/2026

This bill, as enacted on July 2 2026, creates the "John R. Lewis Voter Empowerment Act of New Jersey," establishing comprehensive voting rights protections and a pre-clearance system for certain election policies. Specifically, the bill:

  • Prohibits vote dilution and suppression. Specifically, the bill:
    • Prohibits state agencies, local election offices, or political subdivisions from enacting or implementing any voting qualification, prerequisite, or policy that results in a denial or abridgement of the right to vote for members of a protected class.
    • Prohibits the use of any election method that impairs the equal opportunity or ability of protected class members to participate in the political process, elect candidates of their choice, or influence election outcomes.
    • Prohibits any policy or practice that places a material burden on the right to vote on the basis of a voter's disability, unless the policy is narrowly tailored to promote a substantial state interest.
    • Broadens the existing prohibition on interfering with the right to vote to include deceiving or attempting to deceive an individual with the intent to interfere with the right to vote.
    • Establishes specific factors for courts to consider when determining if a violation has occurred, including the history of discrimination in the political subdivision, the extent to which protected class members have been elected to office, and the use of overt or subtle racial appeals in political campaigns.
  • Create sa new pre-clearance system for covered voting policies. The bill would:
    • Requires "covered entities" to obtain pre-clearance from the newly established Division of Voting Rights before enacting or implementing any "covered policy".
    • Defines "covered entities" to include political subdivisions that have a history of voting rights or civil rights violations within the past 15 years, or that meet certain demographic thresholds combined with high arrest rates or low voter turnout among protected classes.
    • Defines "covered policies" to include changes to methods of election, annexation, consolidation, list maintenance methodology, polling or drop box locations and hours, election dates, voter registration, language assistance, districting or redistricting, and any additional topics designated by the Division of Voting Rights.
    • Establishes a process for the Division of Voting Rights to review pre-clearance submissions, including periods for public comment and specific timelines for the Division to grant or deny pre-clearance.
    • Permits a covered entity to enact or implement a covered policy immediately if pre-clearance is granted. If pre-clearance is denied, the covered policy may not be enacted or implemented.
    • Allows affected political subdivisions to appeal a denial of pre-clearance to the Law Division of the Superior Court of New Jersey.
  • Establishes a "notification letter" process prior to litigation. The bill requires prospective plaintiffs to send a written notice to a political subdivision at least 50 days before commencing a judicial action under the vote suppression or vote dilution provisions. The political subdivision may then pass a resolution affirming its intent to enact a remedy, which grants the political subdivision 140 days to implement the remedy before the plaintiff can file suit.
  • Expands language assistance requirements. The bill:
    • Requires local election offices and political subdivisions to provide voting assistance and materials in languages other than English if more than two percent (but not fewer than 100 individuals) or more than 4,000 eligible voters in the jurisdiction are limited English proficient and speak a shared language.
    • Requires translations to be provided in a manner that conveys the intent and essential meaning of the original text, and prohibit the sole reliance on automatic electronic translation services.
    • Requires the Division of Voting Rights to conduct a study every two years to identify political subdivisions that may require changes in language access coverage.
    • Specifies that no newly designated language assistance requirement may apply to any election occurring fewer than 120 days after formal designation by the Division.
    • Requires the Division to establish and administer a centralized translation and ballot terminology clearing house to assist political subdivisions in complying with language assistance requirements.
  • Creates a new Division of Voting Rights within the Department of the Treasury, which would be responsible for enforcing these provisions. The Division's duties includes conducting investigations, promulgating rules, litigating cases, and issuing advisory opinions.
  • Requires extensive public hearings for municipal and county redistricting. The bill requires political subdivisions proposing redistricting plans to hold a specified number of public hearings, varying from two to four depending on the population of the political subdivision, both before and after drafting the plans.
  • Establishes a central "Voting and Elections Database." The bill requires the Division of Elections to maintain a publicly accessible database containing elections and voting data from all local election offices and political subdivisions. Political subdivisions are required to transmit specific election results and district configuration data to the division within 120 days after each election.
  • Creates a civil cause of action and penalties. The bill:
    • Allows aggrieved persons or organizations to file civil actions in Superior Court for violations of the Act.
    • Holds any party that violates the Act liable for damages, including nominal, compensatory, and punitive damages.
    • Requires the court to award reasonable attorneys' fees and litigation expenses to the prevailing plaintiff.

Last Updated August 19, 2026

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on May 7, 2026, would enable incarcerated voters to apply for and receive mail ballots. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the secretary of state to coordinate with the commissioner of the department of corrections in providing mail ballot applications to qualified voters who are detained or incarcerated reasons other than a conviction for an indictable offense. Existing law does not require coordination between departments in providing mail ballot applications to voters.
  • Authorize detained voters to list the location where they are detained or incarcerated as a secondary address to which the ballot can be sent.
  • Require the department of corrections to ensure delivery of the mail ballot to a voter in the event that a voter who requested a mail ballot is subsequently transferred to another location. Existing law does not include a similar provision.

Last Updated May 11, 2026

This bill, as introduced on June 1, 2026, would modify the voter information notice, or “voter’s bill of rights,” that county boards of elections are required to post in each polling place and specially designated early voting location. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the voter information notice to include a statement that “VOTER FRAUD IS A CRIME” and general information about federal and State laws prohibiting fraud or misrepresentation and the penalties for those offenses.
  • Require the notice to explain that only U.S. citizens may vote and that a noncitizen convicted of unlawful voting may be subject to removal from the United States and may jeopardize eligibility for U.S. citizenship in the future.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on September 14, 2026, would eliminate automatic voter registration, restore the “opt-in” voter registration process, and require proof of citizenship for voter registration at the Motor Vehicle Commission. Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require the Motor Vehicle Commission to give a person the option to register to vote while simultaneously applying for a driver’s license, examination permit, probationary driver’s license, or non-driver identification card.
  • Require documentary proof of United States citizenship when applying to register to vote at the Motor Vehicle Commission. The Chief Administrator, in consultation with the Secretary of State, will be required to prescribe acceptable forms of documentary proof of citizenship. The forms must include at a minimum:
    • A certified copy of a birth certificate issued by a state of the District of Columbia OR
    • Documentation of naturalization or derivative citizenship issued by the United States Department of State or the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services
  • Require the Motor Vehicle Commission to stamp completed voter registration applications with the date it was received and forward to the Secretary of State no later than the 10th day following acceptance.
  • Require each voter registration application received by the Motor Vehicle Commission to be considered and processed as the replacement for any pre-existing voter registration.
  • Require the Motor Vehicle Commission to report change-of-address notifications to the Secretary of State within 10 days of receipt and use the notifications to update voter registrations unless the individual indicates the change is not for voter registration purposes.

Last Updated September 15, 2026

VRLANALYSIS: Summary pending as of 4/21/2026

This bill, as amended on June 6, 2006, would create the "John R. Lewis Voter Empowerment Act of New Jersey." Specifically the bill would:

  • Prohibit any state agency, local election office, or political subdivision from enacting or implementing any voting qualification, prerequisite to voting, law, ordinance, standard, or policy that results in a denial or abridgement of the right of members of a protected class to vote. It would specifically prohibit policies that burden the right to vote for any individual on the basis of age, disability, sexual orientation, including gender identity and gender presentation, or criminal history.
  • Prohibit any local election office or political subdivision from using any method of election that would impair the equal opportunity of protected class members in the political process.
  • Create a set of factors to be analyzed to determine if violations of the bill have occurred.
  • Authorize courts to implement appropriate remedies for abridgment of the rights of protected classes, including transitioning to an alternative method of election, changes to the days, locations, and methods of elections, additional voter education, expanded voter registration, and adding voters back to voter rolls. Courts would be permitted to retain jurisdiction as necessary to ensure the remedies are implemented.
  • Require localities to give members of the public opportunities to participate in the redistricting process. Localities would also be required to conduct additional outreach to limited English proficient communities so that they may participate in the process.
  • Give members of protected classes and organizations composed of members of protected classes standing to sue for enforcement of the act's provisions.
  • Require potential plaintiffs to send a locality a letter at least 50 days prior to filing suit, during which time the locality may take steps to remedy the alleged violation.
  • Require localities to provide voting materials in languages other than English if more than two percent of the voting age population, but no fewer than 100 individuals, speak a language other than English and have limited proficiency in English or more than 4,000 individuals speak a language other than English and have limited proficiency in English.
  • Require "covered entities" to preclear regulations regarding many election-related practices with the attorney general or a court. The bill defines covered entities as any political subdivision that has been subject to court orders related to civil rights violations in the last 25 years, localities with certain arrest rate data, localities with certain dissimilarity indexes, localities with certain poverty rates, localities with certain voter participation rates, localities that failed to provide voter data to the New Jersey Voting and Elections Institute in the last three years, and localities that enacted a policy without obtaining preclearance in the past 25 years.
  • Create a process for a covered entity to obtain preclearance from the attorney general.
  • Designates the Division on Civil Rights within the Office of the Attorney General to have general jurisdiction and authority to enforce the provisions of the act.
  • Require the Attorney General to maintain a firewall and establish any additional safeguards necessary to avoid actual or perceived conflicts of interest and preserve the independence of voting rights enforcement functions.
  • Require the attorney general and secretary of state to engage in public education efforts to inform the voting eligible population about their voting rights, including which populations are protected classes, which languages access materials are available, and any causes of action and avenues of redress available under the bill.
  • Prohibit any person from intimidating, deceiving, or obstructing the rights of voters. Any individual or organization impacted by a violation of this bill can bring an action in court.
  • Establish the New Jersey Voting and Elections Institute at a public university to maintain and administer a database of elections and voting data that is available to the public.
  • Specify that the provisions of the bill would take effect on August 15, 2026, except for provisions establishing language assistance requirements, election-policy preclearance requirements and procedures, and a centralized public database of election information and data, which would take effect on October 1, 2027.

The bill also contains additional provisions related to topics that Voting Rights Lab does not track.

Last Updated August 26, 2026

This bill, as introduced on June 26, 2026, would amend New Jersey election law to require municipalities that hold nonpartisan regular municipal elections in May, pursuant to the 'Uniform Nonpartisan Elections Law,' to conduct early voting for those elections. 

Under current law, such municipalities were permitted, but not required, to conduct early voting by adopting an ordinance. Municipalities holding municipal elections in November on the day of the general election were already required to conduct early voting.

Specifically, the bill would:

  • Require early voting to begin on the 4th calendar day before a regular municipal election held in May and end on the 2nd calendar day before that election unless the municipal governing body adopts an ordinance to extend the early voting period to begin on the 8th calendar day before the election.

This bill, as introduced on March 27, 2026, would:

  • Prohibit a municipal officer or employee who is a candidate for nomination or election to any elective office from using, causing another person to use, or participating in the use of government funds or resources for a mass mailing sent out less than 90 days before the primary or general election for that office. For a special election, the prohibition would apply from the day the special election is declared through Election Day. Existing law does not include this specific restriction.
  • Create a civil penalty for violation of the prohibition of at least $1,000 and not more than $5,000.
  • Define a mass mailing as more than 100 identical or nearly identical pieces of literature or other mass communication mailed or delivered to residents, voters, or a group or classification of them, unless the communication is in response to a specific public inquiry or request. Covered communications would include newsletters, pamphlets, informational materials, robocalls, emails, text messages, websites, social media accounts, and other telecommunications.
  • Specify exceptions for certain official communications, including those required by law, communications necessary to safeguard public health and safety, standard responses to inquiries or requests, ordinary communications between municipal officers and their constituents, or press releases sent to the media. The bill would also preserve existing ethics rules and the authority of county and local boards of ethics.

This bill, as introduced on May 27, 2026, would:

  • Clarify that an absentee or early mail ballot is deemed time received before the close of polls on Election Day if it is returned in an envelope with a U.S. Postal Service or foreign postal service postmark dated no later than Election Day. However, ballots that otherwise would not be counted under federal timing rules would only be eligible to be counted for nonfederal elections. Existing law allows absentee and early mail ballots postmarked by Election Day to be counted if received within seven days after the election.
  • Apply the same rule to military ballots by deeming them timely received before the close of polls on Election Day if it is returned in an envelope with a qualifying postmark dated no later than Election Day, but ballots otherwise barred from counting under federal-election timing rules would only be eligible to be counted for nonfederal elections. Existing law counts military ballots postmarked or signed and dated by Election Day if received within seven days after a primary election or 13 days after a general or special election.
  • Create a fallback rule if a court limits federal ballot counting by specifying that if a court determines that only ballots received by Election Day may be counted for federal elections, otherwise timely ballots may still be counted for nonfederal elections.

This bill, as introduced on May 27, 2026, would:

  • Require every early mail, absentee, special, or other ballot that may be returned by mail to include a written notice explaining all lawful return methods (including mail, express delivery, delivery to a board of elections, early voting site, Election Day poll site, or ballot drop box). Existing law allows these return methods but does not require this standardized notice.
  • Require the notice to advise voters to return ballots as soon as possible, consider alternatives to domestic mail if returning a ballot close to Election Day, and seek a hand cancellation date when mailing. Existing law does not require this specific timing guidance.
  • Require the state board of elections, county boards, and New York City Board of Elections to post the notice on their websites, send it to available email addresses or phone numbers for voters who requested early mail ballots, and post it on official social media accounts.
  • Authorize the state board of elections to issue rules and regulations necessary to implement the notice requirement.

This bill, as introduced on May 29, 2026, would:

  • Create criminal offense for troops or armed government presence at polling places. Under the bill, it is punishable by a fine, imprisonment for up to five years, or both, for an officer of the army or navy, or another person in the civil, military, or naval service of New York or the United States, to order, bring, keep, or control troops or armed persons at a place where an election is held, unless necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States and where the person acts in violation of federal law. Existing law does not include a similar offense.
  • Specify that the prohibition does not prevent members of the armed forces from voting and does not apply to law enforcement responding to a specific emergency or disturbance at the request or authorization of the presiding election officer, law enforcement presence otherwise required by law, or state or national guard members activated by the governor to perform election-related duties under election officer supervision.
  • Create criminal offense punishable by up to five years in prison for election interference by armed forces. The prohibited behavior includes: interfering with elections by prescribing voter qualifications, preventing qualified voters from voting, compelling election officials to accept votes from unqualified voters, imposing different election regulations, or interfering with election officials’ duties. Existing law does not create this state-level offense.
  • Create criminal penalties for election interference by certain government employees. The bill would make it punishable imprisonment for up to one year, or both, for a federal, state, or local administrative employee connected to an activity financed in whole or in part by federal or state loans or grants to use official authority to interfere with the nomination or election of a candidate for federal, state, or local office, where the person acts in violation of federal law. Existing law does not create this state-level offense.
  • Allow a person impacted by a violation to seek civil relief and recover reasonable attorney’s fees, expert fees, litigation expenses, and costs if successful. The bill would also authorize election officers and the attorney general to bring actions for equitable relief, including temporary or permanent injunctions, restraining orders, or other orders. Existing law does not provide this specific civil enforcement framework.
  • Authorize the attorney general jurisdiction to prosecute offenses created by the bill and require civil actions brought under the bill to receive expedited pretrial and trial proceedings and an automatic calendar preference. Existing law does not provide these specific enforcement procedures.

Last Updated June 9, 2026

This bill, as introduced on June 1, 2026, would:

  • Authorize the legislature to decide the wording that appears on the ballot for a proposed constitutional amendment and the abstract, or summary, that explains the amendment to voters. Under the bill, the legislature could do this in the same concurrent resolution that sends the amendment to voters or in a separate concurrent resolution adopted by both houses at least 120 days before the general election. Existing law does not include this specific process for the legislature to set the ballot language and abstract.

The bill would not require the language to meet a specific readability score.

This bill, as amended on January 9, 2026, would:

  • Create a misdemeanor offense for knowingly disseminating restricted personal information of an election officer with the intent or knowledge that it will be used to threaten, intimidate, or facilitate violence against the election officer. Existing law does not specifically criminalize the targeted dissemination of election officers’ personal information.
  • Expand eligibility for the state's address confidentiality program to include election officers, allowing them to use designated substitute addresses to protect against threats of violence. Existing law limits eligibility primarily to victims of domestic violence, stalking, and related offenses, and certain other protected groups.
  • Prohibit any person from intimidating or attempting to intimidate an election officer based on the officer’s performance of election duties, assistance to voters, or status as a past or present election officer, including through the use or threat of force, violence, restraint, duress, or other conduct that reasonably interferes with the execution of election duties. Existing law does not contain a standalone prohibition specifically addressing intimidation or obstruction of election officers in the election law.
  • Prohibit obstruction or interference with access to polling places, election offices, or voting equipment when such conduct reasonably prevents election officers from carrying out their duties. Existing law addresses certain forms of election interference but does not expressly frame obstruction as a civil violation tied to election officer protection.
  • Create a rebuttable presumption of intent to intimidate or interfere with election administration when a person visibly possesses a firearm, rifle, or shotgun at a polling place in violation of existing weapons restrictions, with exceptions for law enforcement and peace officers acting within the scope of their duties. Existing law regulates weapons at polling places but does not create a presumption related to election officer intimidation.
  • Authorize election officers, boards of elections, the state board of elections, the attorney general, and certain organizations to bring civil actions for violations, and authorize courts to impose tailored remedies. Existing law does not provide a dedicated civil enforcement mechanism for election officer intimidation claims.

This bill, as enacted on May 27, 2026:

  • Prohibits state and municipal government employees from granting or facilitating access to a polling location by an immigration authority engaging in immigration enforcement when doing so would violate specified federal voting rights protections, unless an exception applies.

  • Allows sensitive locations, including polling places, to deny certain immigration enforcement access, unless the individual presents a qualifying court order or judicial warrant. Prior law did not include a similar provision.

This bill also includes provisions not tracked by Voting Rights Lab related to public safety, firearms, drones, alcohol regulation, ethics and lobbying, workers’ compensation, procurement, insurance, immigration enforcement, education, law enforcement identification, industrial development agencies, local finance, and city charter commissions.

This bill, as introduced on April 21, 2026, would lower the voting age to 16 years and create a voter registration and civics education program for high school students. The bill would make conforming changes to voter registration forms and other parts of the election code. Under existing law, people may preregister to vote at 16, but cannot vote until they turn 18. The New York Constitution Art II, section 1 requires voters to be 18 years old, however, the bill references a proposed an amendment to change that requirement. The bill expressly delays implementation of the voting age provision until the amendment is adopted, but the registration and civics education program would take effect upon enactment.

The voter registration and civics program the bill would create would:

  • Require high schools to annually:
    • Distribute a pre-filled voter registration form and a voter registration opt-out form to each student who will be 16 years old on or before December 31 of the year. School administrators would be required to complete all information on the voter registration forms for each student, except for their citizenship status, party affiliation, signature, and date the form is signed. Students would be directed to correct any errors on the form.
    • Give students classroom time to complete whichever form they wish and then turn in both. Schools would be required to dispose of the voter registration forms for students who opted out of registration.
  • Require schools to teach high school students civics education for at least eight full class periods each year, in accordance with the New York Department of Education's social studies framework for those grades.

This bill, as enrolled on June 11, 2026, would have required photo identification to cast mail ballots, created a secure online portal for mail ballot applications, and waived certain identification card and vital records fees for individuals experiencing homelessness. Specifically, the bill would have:

  • Required photo ID for mail ballot applications and returned ballots. Beginning with the November 2, 2027 general election, the bill would have required mail voters to provide photo ID when applying for mail voter’s ballots or, if they did not provide photo ID at application, their driver's license or state ID number or the last four digits of their Social Security number. Such voters would still have needed to provide photo ID when returning their voted ballot. Existing law allows voters to use an Ohio driver’s license or state ID number, the last four digits of a Social Security number, or a copy of photo ID for mail ballot identification.
  • Created exceptions and alternative identification procedures. The bill would have allowed certain voters to use alternative ID instead of a copy of photo identification, including uniformed services and overseas voters, voters with religious objections to being photographed, voters with severe medical conditions, physical disabilities or infirmities, voters confined in jail or workhouse, voters who lacked mobility to obtain photo ID, and voters with another material obstacle. Existing law does not require this alternative-identification process because photo identification is not generally required for mail ballots.
  • Required the secretary of state to establish a secure online portal beginning September 3, 2027, for the November 2, 2027 general election. The portal would have allowed electors, including uniformed services and overseas voters, to apply for absent voter’s ballots electronically and would have required applicants to submit identifying information and verification through photo identification, live capture or upload, or permitted alternative identification. Existing law generally requires absentee ballot applications to be submitted in writing by mail or in person, with separate electronic procedures for uniformed services and overseas voters.
  • Made conforming changes to the absentee ballot application, identification envelope, curing, processing, and counting procedures to reflect the new photo identification requirements.
  • Required public libraries, the secretary of state, boards of elections, and the registrar of motor vehicles to provide electors with a free copy of their photo ID upon in-person request for purposes of casting mail ballots by mail. Existing law does not include this free-copy requirement for mail voting.

The bill also includes provisions not tracked by Voting Rights Lab related to individuals experiencing homelessness.

This bill, as introduced on February 27, 2026, would impose documentary proof of citizenship requirements for individuals who are automatically registered to vote at the DMV and change the system from front-end to back-end automatic voter registration. Under existing law, individuals are automatically registered to vote during DMV transactions unless they opt out during the transaction, if they provide proof of identity and residence and certify their citizenship through documentation or declaration. Specifically, this bill would:

  • Limit automatic voter registration at the DMV to only those individuals who present documentary proof of U.S. citizenship during an application or renewal of a REAL ID or standard driver's license or personal ID document. DMV officials would be authorized to rely on citizenship documentation submitted in a previous REAL ID application. Submission of such documentation would be considered certification of citizenship for voter registration purposes. Under existing law, the automatic registration requires self-certification of citizenship but does not require documentation. Additionally, existing law does not specify requirements for REAL ID transactions. 
  • Specify that if an applicant does not opt out within 14 days of receiving the notice of their automatic registration, the applicant would be registered to vote. Existing law requires applicants choose whether to opt out during the transaction.
  • End automatic registration for individuals who do not present documentary proof of citizenship and instead provide a two-step, opt-in registration process for these individuals. These applicants would receive a notice and may register by affirmatively certifying their citizenship and returning a signed registration form. Under existing law, applicants may register at the DMV by self-certifying citizenship through declaration without the two-step process.
  • Specify that if the DMV has access to information confirming that an applicant is already registered, the agency would treat the transaction as an address update and transmit that information to election officials, even if the individual did not present citizenship documentation during the current transaction.
  • Exempt from automatic registration individuals using a business address instead of a residential address during their DMV transaction. These individuals would not be offered any registration opportunity under the bill. Under existing law, residency documentation is required, but there is no categorical exclusion for business addresses.
  • Prohibit automatic or streamlined voter registration for individuals who fail to certify, by documentation or declaration, that they are U.S. citizens. The bill would expressly prohibit offering any registration opportunity to individuals who have documented their non-citizenship. Existing law prohibits non-citizens from registering to vote, but does not expressly prohibit offering the registration opportunity in these cases.
  • Expand which additional agencies beyond the DMV may offer automatic voter registration, by permitting agencies to do so if they either collect documentary proof of citizenship or can verify citizenship by database matching or other means deemed reliable by the secretary of state. Existing law limits automatic voter registration to only those non-DMV agencies that verify citizenship through documentation. The bill would also require non-DMV agencies that process transactions for multiple individuals eligible for registration to register each individual according to the procedures applicable to the DMV process.
  • Permit agencies that are not authorized to offer full automatic voter registration to make automatic updates to voter registration address information, if the secretary verifies that the agency collects sufficient information to do so.

VRLANALYSIS:
This bill, as introduced on March 5, 2026, would impose documentary proof of citizenship requirements for individuals who are automatically registered to vote at the DMV and change the system from front-end to back-end automatic voter registration. Under existing law, individuals are automatically registered to vote during DMV transactions unless they opt out during the transaction, if they provide proof of identity and residence and certify their citizenship through documentation or declaration. Specifically, this bill would:

  • Limit automatic voter registration at the DMV to only those individuals who present documentary proof of U.S. citizenship during an application or renewal of a REAL ID or standard driver's license or personal ID document. DMV officials would be authorized to rely on citizenship documentation submitted in a previous REAL ID application. Submission of such documentation would be considered certification of citizenship for voter registration purposes. Under existing law, the automatic registration requires self-certification of citizenship but does not require documentation. Additionally, existing law does not specify requirements for REAL ID transactions. 
  • Specify that if an applicant does not opt out within 14 days of receiving the notice of their automatic registration, the applicant would be registered to vote. Existing law requires applicants choose whether to opt out during the transaction.
  • End automatic registration for individuals who do not present documentary proof of citizenship and instead provide a two-step, opt-in registration process for these individuals. These applicants would receive a notice and may register by affirmatively certifying their citizenship and returning a signed registration form. Under existing law, applicants may register at the DMV by self-certifying citizenship through declaration without the two-step process.
  • Specify that if the DMV has access to information confirming that an applicant is already registered, the agency would treat the transaction as an address update and transmit that information to election officials, even if the individual did not present citizenship documentation during the current transaction.
  • Exempt from automatic registration individuals using a business address instead of a residential address during their DMV transaction. These individuals would not be offered any registration opportunity under the bill. Under existing law, residency documentation is required, but there is no categorical exclusion for business addresses.
  • Prohibit automatic or streamlined voter registration for individuals who fail to certify, by documentation or declaration, that they are U.S. citizens. The bill would expressly prohibit offering any registration opportunity to individuals who have documented their non-citizenship. Existing law prohibits non-citizens from registering to vote, but does not expressly prohibit offering the registration opportunity in these cases.
  • Expand which additional agencies beyond the DMV may offer automatic voter registration, by permitting agencies to do so if they either collect documentary proof of citizenship or can verify citizenship by database matching or other means deemed reliable by the secretary of state. Existing law limits automatic voter registration to only those non-DMV agencies that verify citizenship through documentation. The bill would also require non-DMV agencies that process transactions for multiple individuals eligible for registration to register each individual according to the procedures applicable to the DMV process.
  • Permit agencies that are not authorized to offer full automatic voter registration to make automatic updates to voter registration address information, if the secretary verifies that the agency collects sufficient information to do so.

This bill, as enacted on June 23, 2026, changes the state's mail in absentee, and emergency absentee applications and third party observation process. The bill changes the mail in absentee and emergency absentee ballot applications and requires the applicant to provide the last four digits of their social security number or entire driver's license or state ID number. The bill amends the observer process regarding processing mail in absentee ballots by requiring a secure place for observers to oversee the process. The bill changes the signature matching process to permit officials to use other information such as driver's license and last four digits of social security number. The bill eliminates the requirement for election officials to match the signature on the certification envelope with the voter's ballot application.

    • Tribal IDs

This bill, as enacted on March 25, 2026, creates a documentary proof of citizenship requirement for Utah voters. Specifically, the bill:

  • Requires voters to present documentary proof of citizenship, either at the time of registration to vote or before voting, to be eligible to vote for any office or proposition other than federal offices. Specifically, the bill:
    • Bifurcates elections by creating a "standard ballot," on which all offices and propositions would appear, and a "federal ballot" on which only federal offices would appear.
    • Requires voters who have not presented documentary proof of citizenship to vote a federal ballot. Specifically, the bill:
      • Requires both new registrants and existing registrants who have not been proven to be citizens to vote only a federal ballot until their citizenship is proven.
      • Requires clerks to inform registered voters who have not provided such proof that they will only be eligible to vote a federal ballot until they do so.
      • Permits a voter to view their status on the electronic election information system maintained by the state.
    • Defines documentary proof of citizenship as one of the following:
      • a Utah driver license number or state ID card number that verifies United States citizenship
      • a birth certificate that verifies U.S. citizenship
      • a U.S. passport
      • an alien registration number that verifies U.S. citizenship
      • naturalization documents
      • a Bureau of Indian Affairs card number, tribal treaty card number, or tribal enrollment number
      • a certificate of degree of Indian blood or a Bureau of Indian Affairs affidavit of birth
      • verification of citizenship through the federal SAVE database
      • any other document or method of proving citizenship that is established in accordance with federal law
    • Modifies voter registration forms to require applicants to specify whether they are intending to register to vote only on federal races. If so, the applicant is not required to provide documentary proof of citizenship.
    • Treats any proof of citizenship submitted by a voter as private.
  • Requires election officers, including the lieutenant governor, to review voter registration records independently to determine whether any noncitizens are registered to vote. Specifically, the bill:
    • Permits the officer to use any lawful tools at their disposal to make the determination.
    • Prohibits an officer from requiring an individual who registered to vote only on federal races to provide proof of citizenship.
    • Provides for a registered voter identified as a noncitizen under this process to be notified and given an opportunity to dispute the determination.
    • Requires a person identified as a noncitizen under this process to be removed from the rolls unless the person refutes the determination within 30 days.
    • Requires a person identified as a noncitizen to vote provisionally until the question of their citizenship is resolved.
  • Makes conforming changes throughout statute.

Last Updated March 30, 2026

This bill, as enacted on March 24, 2026:

Under previous law, if the lieutenant governor provides data on deceased voters from the U.S. Social Security Administration, the county clerk was required to remove the voter from the rolls within ten business days.   • Changes the notice requirement for early voting polling locations. Under the bill, such notice must be given in compliance with existing Utah law for "Class A" notice, which requires public notice on the Utah Public Notice website, the election authority's website, and at a public location reasonably likely to be seen by residents of the affected area.

The bill also contains numerous provisions not tracked by Voting Rights Lab.

This bill, as amended on February 27, 2026, would:

  • Change the acceptable methods for returning a ballot that is mailed to the voter. Under existing law, a voter who receives a mail ballot may return the ballot by mail, by returning it to an Election Day voting center, or placing it in a drop box. Under the bill, a voter would only be permitted to return their ballot by mail if the ballot is sealed in a "mail-in return envelope." All voters would receive such envelopes with their mail ballots until 2029, but beginning in that year would have to specifically request one. UOCAVA voters would be an exception to the rule that a mail ballot must be returned in a mail-in return envelope.

This bill as amended on February 27, 2026, would make various changes to election law relating to the Secretary of State's powers regarding election administration and establish a mandatory process for investigating and prosecuting alleged violations of election laws, frauds, or irregularities. The bill would also require the appointment of special prosecuting attorneys through the West Virginia Prosecuting Attorneys Institute when election law violations are reported by the Secretary of State.

Specifically the bill would:

  • Change the Secretary of State’s authority to issue orders and promulgate legislative rules governing election procedures from “shall have the authority” to “may,” making the authority permissive rather than mandatory and requiring consultation with the State Election Commission.
  • Change the Secretary of State’s authority to require statistical and other election-related reports from county commissions and court clerks from mandatory authority (“shall have authority to”) to permissive authority (“may”).
  • Require the Secretary of State to investigate election fraud and irregularities, provide written reports of violations to appropriate prosecuting officials, and toll applicable statutes of limitations while investigations and prosecution referrals are pending.
  • Establish a special-prosecutor referral process for reported election-law violations, requiring the county prosecutor to refer the matter to the West Virginia Prosecuting Attorneys Institute, which must appoint a special prosecuting attorney. The special prosecutor must report within 60 days whether criminal proceedings will be initiated or provide status reports every 60 days until a final determination is made.
  • Change the Secretary of State’s authority to administer oaths, issue subpoenas and subpoena duces tecum, and conduct hearings concerning election-law administration and enforcement from “shall also have the power” to “may,” making these authorities permissive rather than mandatory.
  • Change the Secretary of State’s authority to implement emergency election procedures and rules during a natural disaster, terrorist attack, war, or general emergency from “shall also have the power” to “may,” making the authority permissive rather than mandatory.
  • Require each county prosecuting attorney to be available for appointment as a special prosecuting attorney to handle referred violations of state election laws, election fraud, or registration and election irregularities, with the appointed prosecutor receiving reimbursement for legitimate travel and related expenses and the county responsible for prosecution costs.

This bill, as enacted on April 1, 2026, establishes detailed criteria for determining voter residency and creates a formal process for election officials to challenge the residency of registration applicants. Specifically, the bill:

  • Replaces the existing requirement that a voter be a "bona fide resident" with a requirement that they be a "legal resident," defined as requiring both physical presence in the jurisdiction and an intent to remain indefinitely.
  • Establishes specific factors for determining a person's legal residency, including the physical character of the residence, place of employment, location of vehicle registration, and the address on file for government benefits and tax filings. Prior law did not provide statutory factors for determining residency.
  • Creates a formal process for the secretary of state or county clerks to challenge the residency of any person offering to register to vote. The bill requires clerks to notify the applicant by certified mail; if the applicant fails to appear in person at the clerk's office within 30 days with evidence of residency, or if the notice is returned as undeliverable, their registration application must be declined. Prior law had no comparable provision for registration application challenges by election officials.
  • Codifies specific rules for determining residency for certain groups, expressly permitting spouses to establish separate domiciles and allowing college students to claim residency where they attend school, regardless of their intent to remain after graduation. The bill also protects the residency status of individuals who relocate temporarily for teaching or government service. Prior law was silent as to these specific residency rules.
  • Clarifies that individuals convicted of a felony, treason, or election bribery may not register or remain registered to vote while serving their sentence, expressly including any period of incarceration, probation, or parole. Prior law provided that such individuals could not vote until their sentence was fully discharged, but did not explicitly address their ongoing registration status.

This bill as amended on January 28, 2026, would make various changes to election law relating to the acceptance and counting of ballots cast in an incorrect precinct. The bill would address provisional ballot procedures, prohibit counting ballots cast in incorrect precincts with limited exceptions, and remove county commission discretion regarding certain technical errors. The bill also proposes criminal penalties for election officials who fail to reject certain ballots or count ballots in prohibited circumstances. 

Specifically the bill would:

  • Prohibit counting any ballot cast in an incorrect precinct, except for handicapped voters whose polling location is not accessible.
  • Change provisional ballot counting from discretionary ("may") to mandatory ("shall") prohibition on election day.
  • Remove county commission discretion to disregard certain procedural violations, requiring rejection of non-compliant ballots without discretion.
  • Require provisional ballots that fail to comply with statutory or election-procedure requirements, including following absentee-voting procedures, to be rejected without discretion, and establishes a misdemeanor penalty for intentional violations committed with fraudulent intent, punishable by a fine of $1,000 to $10,000, up to one year in prison, or both. 
  • Make it a felony to knowingly and intentionally count an absentee ballot that does not comply with statutory absentee-voting requirements, when done with intent to commit fraud, including ballots submitted after the deadline or without the absentee voter’s signature. The penalty is a fine of $10,000 to $20,000, imprisonment for 1 to 5 years, or both.

This bill, as introduced on January 14, 2026, would modify an existing section of the election code by specifying five distinct misdemeanor offenses related to preventing or obstructing election activities. Existing law makes it a misdemeanor to obstruct an election or prevent any “officer” by force, menace, fraud or intimidation from performing their election duties, this includes by violence, threatening gestures, and speeches. The bill would specifically prohibit conduct that by force, physical acts, or intimidating language:

  • prevents, or attempts to prevent, any election officer, election worker, or other person whose job it is to assist in holding an election (including counting ballots and certifying election results) from discharging their duties.
  • prevents, or attempts to prevent, an election being held;
  • obstructs, or attempts to obstruct, the holding of an election;
  • prevents, or attempts to prevent, a voter from attending an election or freely exercising their right to vote; or
  • prevents, or attempts to prevent, an election officer or election worker from entering or exiting a polling place.

The accused party would then be required to submit a written response within 10 business days of receiving the notice. Under existing law, the State Election Commission is authorized to investigate alleged violations, but there is no specified notice procedure or timeline.

This bill, as amended on February 11, 2026, would modify procedures for a post-election ballot audit. Under existing law, each county clerk is required to conduct an audit of election results not later than the first Thursday following a primary, general, or special election. Under the bill:

  • The clerk would be responsible for ensuring minutes of the audit are taken.
  • The clerk would be required to notify party leaders and independent candidates of the time and place of the audit. The audit would be observed by at least two voters in the county who are members of different parties, and other party representatives and candidates would be permitted to be present. If insufficient observers are available, the clerk would appoint persons to serve as observers.

This bill, as enacted on February 27, 2026, makes a change to preregistration for persons less than 18 years old. Under previous Wyoming law, a person who is not yet 18 years of age could preregister to vote if the person would be 18 years old by the date of the next general election. Under the bill, the word "general" is struck from the statute, meaning that a person may preregister only if they will be 18 by the date of the next election (whether that election is a general election or not).
